# Concerning Galatino — Doctor Salomon Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and biblical critic known for his work on "Sacred Philology."</note> in *Sacred Philology*, book 2, part 2, judges thus:

Regarding the Jews (especially the more ancient ones), just as we consider the audacity of Pietro Galatino <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540) was an Italian Franciscan who used Jewish texts to defend Christian doctrines, notably in his work *De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis*.</note> to be hardly worthy of approval—since he attributes far too much to the Talmud and other Jewish writings, both in explaining the Scriptures and in correcting them and purging them of errors he only imagines—so too we must not condemn the hasty judgment (to speak most mildly) of those who completely forbid Christians from reading them (as if there were <term>no benefit</term> <note>original Greek: *ουδεν οφελος* (ouden ophelos)</note> in them), and who do not value their writings and interpretations even as much as a hollow nut.

The opinion of Mr. Schickard <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635) was a German polymath and professor of Hebrew.</note> is pleasing; he says: "There is some distinction among the Jews. Those ancients hid many things in their own way through parables, which our local little Jews—truly <term>vinegar the offspring of wine</term> <note>original Hebrew: חמץ בין יין (*chametz ben yayin*); a proverbial expression referring to a degenerate son of a noble father.</note>, unlike their ancestors and degenerate sons—judge crudely." Therefore, one should not act out of blind zeal, nor attend so much to *who* says a thing, as to *what* is said.

Isaac Casaubon <note>A renowned classical scholar and philologist (1559–1614).</note>, a most sharp-witted man, in *Exercise 15 against Baronius*, chapter 5, judges thus: "The Rabbis, when the Hebrew language is being discussed, or the property of some word, or some Talmudic institution, are of no small [use] to Christians, provided they are not <unclear>biased</unclear>. But when one moves from words to things, or to history, and to the meaning of Holy Scripture (especially in those places where the Messiah is discussed), unless we wish to be deceived and misled, no faith at all should be placed in them."

### Concerning Galatinus, Dr. Salomon Glassius in *Philologia Sacra*, book 2, part 2, judges thus:

Regarding the Jews (especially the ancient ones, where you think the boldness of Petrus Galatinus is less to be approved, because he attributes far too much to the Talmud and other writings of the Jews—both in explaining the Scriptures and in correcting them, and in purging them of errors he imagines): so too, one must not condemn the hasty judgment, to speak mildly, of those who strictly forbid Christians from reading them (as if they were <unclear>apparitions</unclear> <note>original Greek: ὄψεις</note>) and who deem their writings and commentaries not worth a hollow nut. 

The mind of Mr. Schickard <note>Wilhelm Schickard, a 17th-century polymath and Hebrew scholar</note> is pleasing, who says: "There is some distinction among the Jews. Those ancients hid many things in their own way through parables, which our modern petty-Jews—truly <gloss>a son of vinegar from a son of wine <note>original Hebrew: בן חֹמץ בן יין; a common Rabbinic idiom for a wicked son of a righteous father</note></gloss>, the degenerate and most unlike children of their ancestors—judge crudely." 

Therefore <term>igitur <note>Latin: therefore</note></term>, one must not, out of blind zeal, "throw the baby out with the bathwater" (as they say), but one must cautiously distinguish <gloss>between the sacred and the profane <note>original Hebrew: בין קֹדשׁ ובין חֹל</note></gloss>; nor should one look so much at *who* says it as at *what* is being said. 

Casaubon, a most sharp-witted man, in *Exercitationes 16 against Baronius*, chapter 4, judges thus: "When it comes to the Hebrew language, the property of some word, or some institution of the Talmudists, Christians rightly attribute no small value to the Rabbis. Where, <term>however <note>abbreviation for 'vero'</note></term>, one moves from words to things or to the expository sense of <term>Holy Scripture <note>original Latin abbreviation: Srae S., for Sacrae Scripturae</note></term> (especially in those places where it concerns the Messiah), unless we wish to be deceived and misled, no faith at all should be placed in them."

Dr. Frantz commends Galatinus in Disputation 1 <unclear>against</unclear> Smaltz, page 83 and following. (Thus therefore in the theological collection).

## TO THE READER.

<image-desc>Historiated ornamental initial 'N' depicting two figures in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>In our age—which is as unjust as it is polluted by unspeakable crimes—it is no wonder that all those heresies, which were long ago laid to rest and condemned by the Catholic Church (in which alone the writings of the New and Old Testaments are held in high esteem), are now rightfully springing up again. For almost everyone is now permitted to propose to others whatever they have dreamed of by night or pondered by day, led by Satanic suggestions. And what is amazing is that these heresies always find followers and supporters who are so bold, so frivolous, and so shameless that they dare to thrust whatever comes to their lips as if it were a Divine oracle upon the simple-minded, who are easily led astray.

The cautious are deceived and beautifully persuaded by the charm of words, so that they think everything these men babble was brought forth as if from the <term>tripod of Apollo<gloss>An ancient Greek reference to the Pythia, the priestess at Delphi who sat on a tripod to deliver oracles; here used to mean a supposedly infallible pronouncement.</gloss></term>, or spoken by **CHRIST** himself, the Son of God. Therefore, we are not warned in vain by **CHRIST** himself not to believe all those who say: "Behold, here is **CHRIST**, or behold, there he is." They are seduced, and they seduce others, so that they do not seem to wander in error alone. 

Yet this is the consolation of the Church: that God always raises up some from among the elect who may oppose themselves to these impious seducers, refute the false dogmas being scattered about, and bring forth the Truth from the <note>original: "panoplia"</note> full armor of the divine Scriptures, so that no escape remains for the false prophets to either respond or defend their own views. Professors of Theology ought to diligently drag this troop of impious men out of their hiding places through sound doctrine. 

Did not the Satanic offspring of <note>Arius (c. 256–336) was a priest whose teachings—denying that Jesus was of the same substance as God the Father—led to the first major Christian council at Nicaea.</note> **Arius** cause much trouble for the godly, only to be finally destroyed by the word of **CHRIST**? Did not <note>Paul of Samosata was a 3rd-century bishop condemned for his views on the nature of Christ.</note> **Samosatenus** perish by his own knife? And were not also the <term>Anabaptists<gloss>A radical wing of the Reformation; the author groups them here with ancient heretics.</gloss></term>, **Storch**, <note>Niklaus Storch (d. 1525), a leader of the "Zwickau Prophets."</note> **Servetus**, <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish scholar executed for his anti-Trinitarian views.</note> and countless others exposed to the mockery of the whole world because of the rages they devised without the authority of God’s word? The same fate befalls all heretics. 

However, when **PIETRO GALATINO** noticed the arrogance, pride, and insolence of the Jews toward the Christian religion, he considered it his duty—having made no small progress in <term>Hebrew literature<gloss>The original Latin "Hebraicis literis" refers generally to the study of the Hebrew language and Jewish texts.</gloss></term>—to finally bring something forward into the public (and indeed he set his hand to it successfully). He wrote these **Twelve Books**, filled with every kind of erudition and learning, for the benefit of the Church of **CHRIST** as it wavered amid various opinions. He wrote against that treacherous crowd which not only denies both the divinity and humanity of **CHRIST** (even though they are convicted by the Scriptures), but also overturns all the Scriptures, especially those of **Moses** and the **Prophets**. They devise false interpretations against the genuine sense of Scripture and even against the **Rabbis**, whom they hold in the highest esteem. For those ancient Rabbis described the times of **CHRIST** so clearly that, among men of sound mind, the testimonies which the **Talmudists** recorded regarding the kingdom of **CHRIST**, his passion, and Re— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Resurrection" (Resurrectione).</note>

<summary>This preface introduces Pietro Galatino’s 12-book defense of Christianity, framing it as a necessary response to both Protestant "heresies" and Jewish rejection of Christ by using Jewish texts (Talmud/Rabbis) to prove Christian doctrine.</summary>
<keywords>Pietro Galatino, anti-heresy, Arianism, Anabaptists, Michael Servetus, Christian Hebraism, Talmudists, polemic, Counter-Reformation</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader." It concludes a sentence regarding the emergence of heresies and introduces the merits of the author, Pietro Galatino, and his use of Hebrew sources to prove Christian truths. It also credits the editor, Francesco Stancaro, and mentions the inclusion of Johann Reuchlin's work on the Kabbalah.</meta>

[re]surrection. **GALATINUS**, certainly a wise man, perfectly learned in Hebrew, <term>Chaldaic<gloss>An older term for Aramaic, the language of the Babylonian Talmud and various biblical passages.</gloss></term>, Greek, and Latin letters, directs his writings toward a single goal (leaving the life of the Jews—devoted to greed, deceitful, and contaminated by various crimes—to God the judge). Nor could anyone more clearly deliver the promises made to the Fathers concerning **CHRIST**, namely to Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses, the Prophets, David, and countless other faithful servants of God. 

In addition, he describes the times in which the scepter was taken away from the Jews, their Judges were either overthrown or killed (whom they called the <term>Sanhedrin<gloss>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews in ancient Israel.</gloss></term>), and they lost the use of Sacrifices. They are now without a Priesthood, without the multitude of Levites, and without a King, after the Temple was destroyed and all things were reduced to desolation. The miracles that once happened both inside the Temple and outside have vanished; and the wretched people have been cast out into every corner of the earth. These are certain signs that **CHRIST**, whom the holy Fathers expected, has come and has purged the world of sins. 

Furthermore, their own Rabbis—whom they dare not deny—described those final times with beautiful words; so that they could easily grasp the Truth, if they were not insane in their opposition to the religion of **CHRIST**. Yet this blinded nation continues with an obstinate spirit to defend things against their own conscience, to devise false interpretations, and to imagine an outward Kingdom of **CHRIST** and a most splendid procession in which their own Messiah is to enter. 

I tell you, honest reader, our Author handles all these things so skillfully in a <term>dialogue style<gloss>A literary format where information is presented through a conversation between characters; Galatino's work is written as a debate between himself, Reuchlin, and a Jewish interlocutor.</gloss></term> that you can desire nothing more in this matter. And whoever reads this book with an attentive mind will feel that great benefit has accrued to them when they wish to study the Bible; especially in obscure and little-known passages, the Author has focused all his effort so that the reader can go through the **Old Testament** without hesitation. 

Everything is divided into Chapters. Scriptural passages are noted throughout, so that the reader's mind does not waver while searching for the quoted locations. Furthermore, he brings forward whatever has been said anywhere about **CHRIST**, with interpretations not gathered from <term>the crossroads<gloss>original: "ex trivio"; meaning common or vulgar sources.</gloss></term>, but from the Jewish Rabbis who wrote about the Messiah's kingdom before **CHRIST** was born, as well as from Christian Doctors. You have here (to summarize much in a few words) a Commentary on all the difficult passages of the entire **Old Testament**. Does this not offer itself as a great treasure, which a student of Theology cannot do without except to his own greatest loss? 

Moreover, the honest reader will easily perceive, if he compares the old edition with this new one, how much diligence Master **Francis Stancarus**, most highly skilled in Hebrew literature, applied in correcting these books. <note>Francesco Stancaro (1501–1574) was an Italian theologian and Hebraist who edited this version of Galatino's work.</note> No one believes how easily even well-written copies can become corrupted. 

There has also been added the <term>Cabalistic works of Capnio<gloss>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), whose Greek-style pen name was "Capnio," was a pioneer of Christian Kabbalah. His "De Arte Cabalistica" is included in this volume.</gloss></term>, a fitting subject for this work, in which much mention is made of the ancient Fathers who awaited **CHRIST** the redeemer with the greatest longing, and knew best that the lost salvation was to be recovered upon the <term>wood<gloss>A traditional reference to the wood of the Cross.</gloss></term>. 

Truly, <note>original: "vino vendibili non opus est suspensa hedera"</note> "good wine needs no ivy-bush." <note>A Latin proverb meaning that a good product does not need an advertisement; an "ivy-bush" was a traditional sign for a tavern.</note> All things, however, look toward this goal: that the Church founded by the Apostles may be rebuilt, setting aside the sects and opinions which have never failed to bring in a sea of evils, and have either changed or utterly overthrown all well-established Republics. The Jews are a daily example to us, that we should not fall into the wrath of God through impenitence after the Truth has been recognized.

->Farewell.<-

->TO THE MOST INVINCIBLE<-

# MAXIMILIAN CAESAR,
### EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS,
->ALWAYS AUGUST; AN EPISTLE OF PIETRO GALATINO<-
->of the Order of Friars Minor.<-

<margin>Galatino defends Capnion.</margin> <note>Capnion is the Greek-derived pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish mysticism.</note>
For a long time now, I have been distressed with no small anxiety of mind, *August Caesar Maximilian*, as I saw the multifaceted and exceptional learning of *Capnion* being so unworthily torn apart by the pestilential and poisonous bites of the envious; to the point that some have even dared to falsely slander many of his sayings—which are in greatest harmony with the Orthodox faith—with the mark of heresy. And although I realized that this was being done as an evil—or rather a most wicked—example to all learned men, if such a bad reward were paid for so many exhausted labors and sleepless nights, nevertheless, I did not dare to write anything, nor even to open my mouth to attempt to defend a man so learned and outstanding in every kind of virtue against the reckless ignorance of the wicked. I feared lest I be accused of the vice of rashness and arrogance if I—endowed with barely mediocre talent and not sufficiently equipped with much erudition—should wish to act as a patron, voluntarily and uncalled, for a man so skilled and excellent in the <term>threefold learning of languages<gloss>Proficiency in the three "sacred" languages: Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</gloss></term>, and therefore more than sufficiently capable of defending himself along with the truth itself.

But indeed, since my most Reverend Lord, Lord *Lorenzo Pucci, Cardinal of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs*, a most sharp investigator of the Christian faith and most observant of Your Majesty (as he ought to be), had exhorted me all the more keenly to undertake a defense of this kind with a spirited mind, he compelled me to necessarily undergo the heavy burden of this task, which is unequal to my shoulders. He did so because he thought that even Your Majesty's honor was at stake if even the mere suspicion of a charged crime should touch your counselor <note>Reuchlin served as a legal counselor to the Emperor and other German princes.</note>. In addition, there was the will of the most Holy *Pope Leo X*, which urged me toward this most of all. Since I was not unaware that the Pope himself, as a unique cultivator of truth and wisdom, greatly desired both that *Capnion* be freed from such slanders, and that Your Majesty be complied with in this matter all the more because he wished his prayers to be satisfied most vehemently. While I was uniquely intent on this matter, and in unearthing the secrets found in the <term>Talmud<gloss>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</gloss></term>, both for the Catholic faith...

...[not sufficient] strength to provide the confirmation that I was sweating over to protect the cause of Capnion <note>original: "Capnionis"; referring to Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522)</note>. Then, your Majesty's letters repeatedly arrived, most humanely urging me to finish this work as quickly as possible. These came along with many other letters most kindly written in my recommendation to the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Leo X</note>, the Catholic King <note>Charles V, then King of Spain and future Emperor</note>, and several Cardinal Fathers of the Christian Commonwealth. Moved by this extraordinary and almost incredible kindness, I began not only to press on more urgently and ardently with these "night-watches" <note>original: "vigilias"; a metaphor for scholarly labor performed late at night</note> I had begun so they might hasten toward their end, but I also decided to consecrate whatever the results might be to your divine power <note>original: "numini"</note>. I do this so they may come forth into the light under better omens and, having shaken off the darkness of errors, might reveal the light of Truth with much greater confidence. 

For indeed, it was not fitting that a <margin><unclear>Spiritual</unclear></margin> work titled **ON THE SECRETS OF CATHOLIC TRUTH** <note>original: "DE ARCANIS CATHOLICÆ VERITATIS"</note>, composed for the benefit of the Christian Commonwealth, should be dedicated to anyone other than the best preserver, defender, and promoter of both Catholic Truth itself and the entire Christian Commonwealth. If this dedication of mine does not at all measure up to your Majesty’s highness, nevertheless, because you will be able to understand that it proceeded from a most devoted mind, you will deign to consider it well and receive it with a calm countenance (as is your custom). Receive it now, therefore, Most Sacred Emperor: and in your mercy, support, protect, and cherish me as I labor tirelessly in the vineyard of the Lord, as one among the lowest (though unworthy) servants of your Majesty.

->G A L A T I N U S.<-

<margin>Galatinus, Capnio, Hogostrat.</margin>
<margin>Judgment on the Talmud</margin>
**A**S far as I am able to perceive from those things which have so far been said back and forth between you in my presence: a no small dispute is being waged between you concerning the Talmud <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara</note>, from which your entire controversy takes its origin. For one of you indeed attempts to condemn the Talmud as entirely evil and utterly repugnant to the Christian religion; and he contends to prove this by many articles formed against the other's little book, titled **THE EYE-GLASS** <note>original: "OCVLARESPECVLVM"; referring to Johannes Reuchlin's 1511 work *Augenspiegel*, written to defend Jewish books from being burned</note>. The other, however, strives with the greatest zeal to protect the Talmud itself, as being good in many respects, and most profitable, convenient, and necessary for the Catholic truth to crush the very hard neck of the Jews <note>A common biblical metaphor for stubbornness or "stiff-necked" resistance to conversion</note>. Since, therefore, each of you seems to seek nothing other than the truth—for (as I myself believe) you have both met with me for no other reason than for the sake of searching out Truth itself—and since I too shall say nothing except what savors of Christian truth for the definition of the articles to be discussed, for that reason I think I shall perform a worthwhile service for the Christian Commonwealth if, before we come to the articles themselves, I do not neglect to unlock the secrets of the Catholic faith lying hidden in the Talmud itself. These shall serve both as the foundation of your dispute and for the understanding of the Truth to be tracked down, by which the perfidy of the Jews of our time is most greatly convicted. For through the Talmudic writings of the ancient Jews, not only are all the cavillations <note>trivial or annoying objections</note> of the more recent Jews—who strive with every effort to pervert the prophecies of the Prophets—utterly refuted, but the Truth of the Orthodox dogma also shines forth most clearly.

**CAPNIO.** <note>Capnio is the Greek pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and Hebraist.</note> You will do very well indeed, my Galatinus. For in this way, the errors of the Jews of our century will be especially refuted, and most powerful testimonies against them will be brought forward from their own writings for the Christian truth, which they never cease to impugn. But so that they may be less able to resist such great truth, it is necessary that you report the very oracles of the holy seers, or the sayings of the ancient Talmudists, which you are going to bring against the Jews themselves, exactly as they are written—namely, in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> and in Hebrew.

**GALATINUS.** I shall indeed do most gladly, my Capnio, what you urge: both on account of those things which you have said, and especially so that while the Jews see themselves conquered by their own weapons, they may be forced to acknowledge the truth which they never cease to deny. Once acknowledged, they may not neglect to both confess and guard it, if they wish to look out for themselves; lest at last, cast out from the Heavenly kingdom into the outer darkness, they suffer eternal evils. But since to observe this in all cases would be both very difficult and unpleasant, I shall take care to recount in Hebrew or Chaldean, as they have them, only those things which, above the rest, both express and attest to the truth against them. Everything, however, which it will be necessary for me to bring forward from their Scriptures—

<margin>Faithfully translated writings of the Jews.</margin>
—I shall attempt to translate into our language as faithfully as the Latin tongue allows...

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

...speech, so that they can neither deny the truth, nor dare to say that it is not so among them. Therefore, in translating the words of the sacred page itself, wherever I find a deviation from the Hebrew in our codices, I shall follow neither the Septuagint <note>The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> nor any other interpreter; instead, I shall translate them into our language exactly as the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraica veritas"; a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the authentic Hebrew text of the Bible</note> holds them. For by this means, every path of escape will be blocked for the false-speaking Jews; and very many, nearly infinite passages of Holy Scripture—which are found to be vitiated and corrupted among both the Latins and the Greeks, partly through the length of time and partly through the fault of scribes—will be corrected truly and most handsomely for the sake of our faith. In these passages, the Christian truth shines far more clearly and more perfectly among the Hebrews than in our Latin or Greek editions. On account of this, I have no doubt that I will be criticized by many, and especially by those who are accustomed to find fault with whatever they have not done themselves, and who disparage everything they do not understand. Indeed, Truth has many enemies, and rivals have never been lacking to those who constantly profess it. For even Athanasius and Chrysostom suffered such things among the Greeks, as did Augustine and Jerome among the Latins, and finally all who have uniquely embraced Truth itself. Against them, I invoke nothing other than Truth itself, which I hope (with Divine help favoring me) will be a shield for me on all sides. Furthermore, I subject and submit myself and all my assertions, both in these matters and in all others, to the determination of Pope Leo X <note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521) was a patron of the arts and oversaw the beginning of the Reformation</note>, the finest cultivator of Truth itself, and of the Most Holy Roman Church.

**Hogostratus.** Since I see that you are going to say marvelous and unheard-of things to reveal the Truth, I would wish that, so we might more quickly and easily obtain that Truth we seek so earnestly (with you unlocking it), you would satisfy my inquiry if any doubt should enter my mind, provided it is not a burden to you.

**Galatinus.** That will indeed be very pleasant to me, and not at all unwelcome. For that reason, I would first ask this of you—who are mighty with no small skill in Divine and human Philosophy—and of Capnio <note>Johannes Reuchlin, known by his Greek name "Capnio," was a pioneering German humanist and Hebraist</note> himself—who is not only excellently endowed with every kind of literature but is also a most eloquent interpreter of the three languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note> through which Divine secrets are opened: that whatever doubts occur, they should by no means pass by undiscussed. Rather, let them be brought forward to be examined by us in turn. For I also will not remain silent regarding whatever my opinion may bring to those same doubts, according to the capacity of my modest talent. But because it is very difficult, and almost impossible, for a weak man (such as I know myself to be) to walk confidently along that path where even some of the strongest have had to stumble (for I confess that I must necessarily undertake many things unequal to my strength, and far greater, in order to track down Truth of this kind), I have therefore decided that Divine help must first be implored. Thus, while prayer itself to God shall be as a staff for me, and His word a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths, I may walk secure and safe among the ranks of enemies. By defeating them with their own weapons, I may be able to take away from them—as if from unjust possessors—the truth which they have among them but do not know, neglect, and attack. Thus, at last, when the truth itself is found in the Talmudic books, it may be clearer than light what ought to be rightly thought concerning the Talmud itself, about which there is a war between you. So that this may be done more rightly and better, it will be necessary for our entire discourse to revolve chiefly around twelve points. Concerning these, twelve specific Books ought to be composed, in each of which very many mysteries of our faith may be unlocked.

### CHAPTERS OF THE FIFTH BOOK.

The objections of the more recent Jews, claiming that Jesus of Nazareth was not the Messiah because the Messiah himself has not yet come. Chapter I

Regarding the first objection of the Jews: that the Messiah was supposed to come at the end of days. II

Regarding the second objection of the Jews: that the Messiah has not yet come because the mountain of the house of the Lord has not yet been elevated above the mountains and hills. # ON THE TALMUD.
### CHAPTER ONE.
#### *Concerning the ancient and authentic scriptures of the Jews.*
-> G A L A T I N V S. <-

<margin>A</margin> To refute the unbelief <note>Latin: *perfidiam*. In this historical context, the author refers to the Jewish rejection of Christian doctrine.</note> of the Jews through their own Talmudic writings, it is first necessary to know that there are two types of teachings among them, upon which their Synagogue has never ceased to lean, both now and in the past. One of these they call תורה שבכתב *Torah she-bi-khtav* <note>original: "תורה שבכתב"</note>, that is, the Law which is in writing, or which was handed down in writing. The other <margin>B</margin> they call תורה שבעל פה *Torah she-be-al peh* <note>original: "תורה שבעל פה"</note>, that is, the Law which is in the mouth, or which was handed down by word of mouth. They say this is nothing other than an explanation of the Law itself, which they assert was delivered to Moses along with the written Law. For as the ancient Talmudists testify in the first chapter of the book called ברכות *Berakhot* <note>original: "ברכות", meaning 'Blessings'—the first volume of the Talmud</note>, Moses received both the Law and the exposition of that Law on Mount Sinai by the same spirit. This explanation of the Law tends toward a twofold sense: namely, the literal and the spiritual or mystical. They affirm that Moses wrote down neither of these, but <margin>C</margin> delivered both orally. And they say this is the Law of which it is read in בפרקי אבות *Pirkei Avot* <note>original: "בפרקי אבות", meaning 'Chapters of the Fathers'</note>: "Moses received the Law from Sinai and delivered it to Joshua; and Joshua to the elders; and the elders to the prophets; and the prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Assembly." This kind of tradition (as gathered from various <margin>D</margin> volumes of the Talmudists, and as reported by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> at the beginning of his *Deuteronomy* <note>Referring to the Mishneh Torah, also called Mishneh Deuteronomy.</note>) happened to be carried out in this order: For when Joshua had received this exposition of the Law from Moses, he delivered it to Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, who was the grandson of Aaron; he is called Phinees by us, though the name is corrupted. Phinehas delivered it to Eli the priest. Eli to Samuel the prophet and priest. Samuel to King David. David to Ahijah the prophet. Ahijah to Elijah the <margin>E</margin> prophet. Elijah to Elisha the prophet. Elisha to Jehoiada the High Priest. Jehoiada to Zechariah the prophet. Zechariah to Hosea the

<column-break/>

prophet. Hosea to Amos the prophet. Amos to Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah to Micah the prophet. Micah to Joel the prophet. Joel to Nahum the prophet. Nahum to Habakkuk the prophet. Habakkuk to Zephaniah the prophet. Zephaniah to Jeremiah the prophet. Jeremiah to Baruch the scribe. Baruch to Ezra the priest and scribe. Up to this point, we do not read that the Jews had any other scripture besides the Bible, which they call מקדשיא *Mikdash-ya* <note>original: "מקדשיא", meaning 'The Sanctuary of God' or 'Holy Thing of God'</note>; for until those times, no one is found to have committed anything regarding the explanation of the Law to writing.

CAP. <note>Capnio, the persona of the Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note> So that none of our people remain ignorant of which books the Jews receive as sacred and divine, tell me, I pray, in what way is the מקדשיא *Mikdash-ya*, that is, the Bible itself, distinguished among them?

GAL. <margin>The division of the Bible according to the Hebrews.</margin> The Jews (as you yourself know) call the Bible ארבעה ועשרים *Arba'ah ve-Esrim* <note>original: "ארבעה ועשרים", meaning 'Twenty-four'</note>, because it contains that many books. For they divide it into four parts. The first of these, which they call תורה *Torah*, that is, the Law, or חומש <margin>The Five.</margin> *Humash* <note>The Hebrew term for the Pentateuch, derived from 'five'.</note>, that is, the fivefold book, which the Greeks call the Pentateuch, contains five books named after their opening words. For the book of Genesis they call בראשית *Bereshith*, <margin>Bereshith.</margin> which is the same as "In the beginning." Exodus they call ואלה שמות *Ve-elleh shemot*, that is, "And these are the names." Leviticus, ויקרא *Va-yikra*, that is, "And he called." Numbers, במדבר סיני *Be-midbar Sinai*, that is, "In the desert of Sinai." Deuteronomy, אלה הדברים *Elleh ha-devarim*, that is, "These are the words." The second part comprises four books, which they call נביאים ראשונים *Ne- <margin>Second part.</margin> vi'im Rishonim*, that is, the Former Prophets. These are יהושע *Yehoshua*, who is called Joshua among us; שופטים *Shofetim*, that is, Judges; שמואל *Samuel*, which among us contains the first and second books of Kings <note>Known as 1 and 2 Samuel in modern English Bibles.</note>; and מלכים *Melakhim*, that is, Kings, which among us includes the third and fourth books of Kings <note>Known as 1 and 2 Kings in modern English Bibles.</note>. The third <margin>Third part.</margin> part also contains four books. These they call נביאים אחרונים *Nevi'im Aharonim*, that is, the Latter Prophets. These are Isaiah, Jeremiah, and *Ichezkel*, who is called Ezekiel by us...

<summary>This page introduces the concept of the "Twofold Law"—the written Torah and the oral tradition—detailing the historical chain of transmission from Moses to Ezra. It also begins a systematic classification of the Hebrew Bible into its traditional divisions.</summary>
<keywords>Torah, Oral Law, Talmud, Pentateuch, Chain of Tradition, Maimonides, Hebrew Bible, Prophets, Jewish Scripture</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of the books of the Hebrew Bible and begins Chapter II, which transitions into a dialogue between Capnio (the scholar Johannes Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding the history of Jewish sages and their meeting with Alexander the Great.</meta>

[It is] called; and the book of the twelve Prophets, whom we call the Minor Prophets. Finally, the fourth part, which they themselves call <term>כתובים *Ketuvim* <note>original: "Chetuuim"</note></term>, that is, the "Hagiographa" or "Holy Writings," contains eleven books. The first of these is titled <term>דברי הימים *Divrei Ha-yamim* <note>original: "Dibre haiamim"</note></term>, that is, the "Words of the Days," which we call by the Greek name *Paralipomenon* <note>Known in English as the Books of Chronicles. The Greek name means "things omitted," implying it contains history left out of the Books of Kings.</note>. The second is <term>תהלות *Tehillot*</term>, or <term>תהילים *Tehillim*</term>, or by shortened form <term>תלים *Tillim*</term>, that is, "Hymns" <note>The Book of Psalms</note>; although *tillim* also signifies "heaps," the singular of which is <term>תל *tel*</term>, meaning a mound or heap. This is not irrelevant to the subject, since the Psalms are, as it were, certain "heaps" of wise sayings. This book we call by the Greek name *Psalterium* (Psalter). The third is <term>משלי שלמה *Mishlei Shelomoh*</term>, that is, the "Proverbs," or rather the "Parables of Solomon." The fourth is <term>איוב *Iyov*</term>, whom we call by the corrupted name "Job." The fifth is **Ruth**. The sixth is <term>קהלת *Koheleth*</term>, that is, the "Assembler" or "Preacher," whom we call **Ecclesiastes**. The seventh is <term>איכה *Eikhah*</term>, that is, "How" <note>The book is named after its opening word</note>, which is titled by us as the book of **Lamentations** or "Threnodies." The eighth is <term>שיר השירים *Shir Ha-shirim*</term>, that is, the **Song of Songs**. The ninth is **Esther**. The tenth is **Daniel**. Finally, the eleventh is **Ezra**, which they count as one book along with Nehemiah.

These twenty-four books alone, which we have enumerated, the Jews hold as sacred and divine. For although they possess the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the first book of Maccabees, they do not count them among the twenty-four. As for the third and fourth books of Ezra, I myself have not yet seen them in Hebrew; however, some of them say that they have been recently found in Constantinople. But the second book of Maccabees, and the book of Philo the Hebrew, which is called the **Wisdom of Solomon**, I have found nowhere among the Hebrews, but have seen them only in Greek. Furthermore, the **Hymn of the Three Youths**, and the histories of **Susanna**, **Bel and the Dragon**, which we have in our version of Daniel, they do not have at all. I have said these things so that we might know which books the Jews approve as authentic. It is certain, therefore, that besides the aforementioned twenty-four books, no scripture existed among the Jews until the time of Ezra.

For the commentaries on the Law themselves, both literal and spiritual or mystical, were spread from the time of Moses the Lawgiver himself down to the Babylonian captivity only through a certain order of succession (as has been said) among the prophets and wise men. But after the Babylonian captivity, when Ezra himself rewrote the Law—which had been burned during the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple—the rest of the wise men began to write down the explanation of that Law. This was done lest, if another destruction of the city should happen to occur in which all the wise men might perish, the explanation of the Law itself should perish along with them. From this it truly happened that all those wise men who lived from the Babylonian exile until the first writing of the Talmudic codex (who are called "the Men of the Great Synagogue" in the <term>פרקי אבות *Pirkei Avot* <note>original: "pirke auoth", meaning 'Chapters of the Fathers,' a famous tractate of the Mishnah</note></term>, or "Chapters of the Fathers") and who are known to have taught the Law, handed down the exposition of that Law to their students by both word and writing. Their authority among the Jews is so great that their writings, from which the Talmud was later compiled, hold the first place after the Prophets. Nor is this without merit, since their doctrine was handed down to them immediately by the Prophets themselves, whose disciples and successors they were. Therefore, it is no wonder if those who preceded the coming of Christ, in explaining the Law and the Prophets, handed down in writing almost infinite and quite wonderful things concerning Christ and the truths of the Christian faith, all of which are inserted here and there within the Talmudic books.

<margin>The fourth part.</margin>

### CHAPTER II.
->*Concerning the ancient Jewish sages, called the Men of the Great Synagogue.*<-

### CAPNIO <note>The scholar Johannes Reuchlin, using his Greek-derived pen name.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a landscape with a building and foliage.</image-desc>

I WOULD wish that you would also reveal the order of these men, and how one succeeded another in teaching the Law.

**GALATINVS.** Just as it is clearly evident in many places in the Talmud itself, and as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous philosopher and jurist Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> records in the beginning of his *Deuteronomy* <note>Referring to the preface of Maimonides's code, the *Mishneh Torah*.</note>, Ezra himself, the teacher of the Law, handed down the exposition of the Law to Simon the Priest, who was also called Jaddus <note>Identified as Jaddua, the High Priest mentioned in Nehemiah and Josephus.</note>. This is that Jaddus who, when he heard that Alexander the Macedonian had set out toward Jerusalem after capturing Gaza, began to be seized by no small dread and fear. For because of previous defiance, he was terrified of the King’s indignation. Wherefore, he was warned in a night vision by a divine oracle that others should go out in white garments, while he himself and the rest of the priests, dressed in their lawful robes, should meet the angry Emperor when he was not far from the city.

When they had done this, and Alexander saw the High Priest himself adorned in a hyacinth-blue and gold robe, and wearing upon his head both the miter and the golden plate on which the <term>τετραγράμματον *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note></term> was written: he immediately approached him alone, worshipped the Name of God, and first venerated the Priest himself. When the kings of Syria and all the others who were with him saw this, they were vehemently struck with amazement. No one, however, except Parmenio <note>Alexander's second-in-command</note> dared to ask him why, when all others worshipped him, he himself had worshipped the High Priest.

Answering him, Alexander said: "I worshipped not this man, but the God whose high priesthood he exercises. For I saw him in this very habit in a dream when I was still in Macedonia, and was thinking to myself how I might be able to conquer Asia. He warned me that I should by no means delay, but should cross over confidently; and he promised that he would lead the army and deliver the power of the Persians to me. Therefore I fell prostrate and worshipped him. For I believe that from that time I have been directed by divine light to conquer Darius and dissolve the power of the Persians. Therefore, I trust that all things which turn in my heart and which are hoped for by me will come to pass." Now that Jaddus, or Simon (to return to where I turned aside)...

# BOOK ONE.
## A ii
<meta>catchword: ctos</meta>

->(I have returned [to the point])<- the explanation of the law itself was handed down by Antigonus of the town of Socho. Antigonus then handed it to Joseph, son of John, and Joseph, son of Joezer. These, in turn, passed it to Nittai of Arbela and Joshua ben Perahiah. The later Jews falsely claim that our Redeemer, Jesus, was a student of this Joshua. However, it is clearly shown that they are lying (as we shall discuss more extensively elsewhere) by the fact that from the time of Hyrcanus I—during whose days this Joshua flourished—until Pilate, under whom Christ suffered, 110 years passed.

These men, Nittai and Joshua, again passed the exposition of the law to Judah ben Tabbai and Simeon ben Shetah. These passed it to Shemaiah and Abtalion. These, in turn, passed it to Hillel and Shammai, about whom Josephus records many excellent things in his book *Antiquities*. <margin>Hillel.</margin> Hillel flourished, as it is stated at the beginning of the book **Sabbath** <note>The Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*.</note>, one hundred years before the destruction of the second Temple; and as one reads in **Bava Batra**, he had eighty disciples, all endowed with excellent wit and learning. By reason of their discipline, they were all called his "sons." They were so outstanding that (as is read in the same place) thirty of them were worthy for the Divine Presence <note>original: *divinitas*, likely referring to the *Shekhinah*.</note> to descend upon them, just as it had upon Moses himself. Thirty were worthy for the sun to stand still for them, as it did for Joshua. The remaining twenty were called "mediocre." The greatest among them was Jonathan ben Uzziel. The smallest of them all was Johanan ben Zakkai, whom the Jews call Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai. Yet even he (as the ancient Talmudists said) did not fail to know the Scripture, the Talmud, or anything else, down to the fables of foxes and the narrations of demons. If he, who is recorded as the smallest of all Hillel’s disciples, turned out to be such a great wise man, what must be thought of the others?

Hillel and Shammai handed the exposition of the law to the same Johanan ben Zakkai and to Simeon the Just <note>The author here conflates Simeon the Just with the Simeon who held the infant Jesus in the Gospel of Luke.</note>, the son of Hillel himself. This order, brought down thus far, is drawn out from the chapters of the fathers called <term>**Pirkei Avot** <note>original: *Pirke auoth*. Often translated as "Ethics of the Fathers," a tractate of the Mishnah detailing the lineage of tradition.</note></term>, <margin>Simeon the Just.</margin> where the last of all is placed Simeon the Just, who took Christ in his arms. From this, it is indeed openly shown that the scepter of the Jewish Academy utterly failed at that point.

Nevertheless, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides.</note>, following this order of teaching further, says that this same Simeon the Just had a student named Gamaliel, surnamed "the Elder," <margin>Gamaliel, surnamed the Elder.</margin> at whose feet the Apostle Paul learned the Law. Therefore, this Gamaliel was that teacher of the Law, most respected by the entire Jewish people, who—when the High Priest and the whole council wanted to kill Peter and the other Apostles—strived with every effort to plead for them and deliver them from death. While delivering a speech on their behalf in the council, he said these things among others:

<margin>Gamaliel’s speech for the liberation of the Apostles.</margin>

> Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do to these men. For before these days, Theudas appeared, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him; he was killed, and all who believed him were lost and reduced to nothing. After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and led the people away after him; he also perished, and all who followed him were scattered. And now, therefore, I say to you: Withdraw from these men and leave them alone; for if this counsel or this work is from men, it will be destroyed. But if it is from God, you will not be able to destroy it, lest perhaps you be seen as those who fight against God. <note>This is a Hebrew translation of Acts 5:34-39, which Galatinus provides in the text as an excerpt from a Hebrew version of the New Testament or a reconstructed text.</note>

This was that Gamaliel. Afterward, Rabban Simeon his son, who was later killed by Hadrian Caesar, was his student. Finally, he had his son, named Judah, as a student. The Jews, because of the excellence of his teaching and integrity, surname him **Rabbenu Hakkadosh**, which means "Our Holy Teacher." <margin>Rabbi Judah, who is also called Rabbenu Hakkadosh.</margin> However, there was also another "Holy Teacher" who flourished in the time of the Roman consuls, distinguished both in learning and the spirit of prophecy, and who wrote many and indeed wonderful things about Christ. For this reason, more recent Jews, deceived by the similarity of the name, think that this man was that one. Thus it happens that, using this caution, they strive to deny whatever things he predicted would come regarding Christ.

Almost all these men whom we have mentioned as presiding over the Jewish Academy after Ezra, as well as others from their almost innumerable students, left behind many writings concerning the explanation of the Law. From these, the Talmud was later composed.

**CHAPTER [III]**
**CAPNIO.** Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note>, in the beginning of his *Deuteronomy* <note>Referring to the *Mishneh Torah*.</note>, reports that until Rabbi Judah, the son of Simeon—who lived 120 years after the burning of the second Temple—no one had handed down anything in writing regarding the explanation of the Law; rather, among the wise men succeeding one another, it was revealed by word of mouth only.

**GALATINUS.** It is indeed true that Rabbi Moses the Egyptian asserts that. It must be thought that he did this for two primary reasons. First, so that the secrets of the Messiah, which had been detected in the expositions of the Law and the Prophets before the birth of Christ, would remain hidden from Christians. Second, so that the writings of later men might be rendered more "authentic" because of this. But it can be clearly seen that he spoke falsely from the fact that many writings concerning the exposition of both the Law and the Prophets are found written before the birth of Christ, as appears brilliantly in many places in the Talmud itself.

Joshua <margin>Joshua ben Sirach.</margin> ben Sirach also, who flourished in the times of Ptolemy Euergetes I, clearly testifies to this when, in the preface of his book (which among us is called *Ecclesiasticus*, but among the Hebrews is titled **Mishlei**, that is, "Proverbs"), he says among other things: "The wisdom of many and great things has been demonstrated to us through the Law and the Prophets and others who followed them, in which things Israel ought to be praised for the sake of doctrine and wisdom. Since it is necessary not only for those speaking to be skilled, but even for outsiders to be able, both by learning and by writing, to become most learned." And after a few words: "But," he says, "the Law itself and the Prophets and the rest of the other books have no small difference when they are spoken among themselves. For in the thirty-eighth year, in the times of King Ptolemy Euergetes, after I came into Egypt and had been there for a long time, I found books left there of no small or contemptible learning."

<vocab>
**Antigonus of Socho**: A Jewish sage of the 3rd century BCE, known for the maxim "Be not like servants who serve the master for the sake of receiving a reward."
**Nittai of Arbela**: A leader of the Sanhedrin during the Maccabean period.
**Joshua ben Perahiah**: A contemporary of Nittai of Arbela; medieval polemics often incorrectly tried to link him chronologically to Jesus.
**Hillel**: One of the most important figures in Jewish history, founder of the House of Hillel and a primary authority of the Mishnah.
**Shammai**: The contemporary and frequent legal opponent of Hillel.
**Simeon the Just**: A high priest, though the author here identifies him with the Simeon of the New Testament.
**Gamaliel the Elder**: A leading authority in the Sanhedrin and teacher of the Apostle Paul.
**Rabbenu Hakkadosh**: Judah the Prince (Judah Ha-Nasi), the redactor of the Mishnah (c. 200 CE).
**Joshua ben Sirach**: The author of the wisdom book Ecclesiasticus (2nd century BCE).
**Talmud**: The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing the Mishnah and Gemara.
**Pirkei Avot**: "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings and the lineage of the oral tradition.
</vocab>

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the authentic Jewish writers who preceded the coming of Christ, from whose writings the Talmud was chiefly compiled.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>The Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint.</note></margin>
From those, therefore, who preceded the coming of Christ, who among them especially explained the Law and the Prophets and committed the secrets of the Messiah to writing? GALATINUS: Although very many wise men of this kind existed, lest I be tedious, I will bring forward a certain few. And first, indeed (omitting those who came before them), I will bring forward those seventy-two translators <note>The Septuagint, the famous group of Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> who were distinguished among the rest not only in the Hebrew, Chaldean <note>Aramaic.</note>, and Greek languages, and in every kind of discipline, but also by the Holy Spirit. For when, around the 250th year before the birth of Christ, at the request of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the King of Egypt who commissioned the Septuagint.</note>, they had been sent to Alexandria by the High Priest Eleazar to translate the entire Bible into the Greek tongue, Ptolemy himself, wishing to make a test of the purity of their edition, separated them (as not only the Talmudists and Philo, the most eloquent of the Hebrews, but also Augustine and certain others of our own testify) into seventy-two small cells. Yet they were so harmonious in their writing that they did not differ by even a single word, but in one sequence of writing, in one context of words and letters, and at the same moment of time, they transformed that entire divine volume into the Greek speech. This must surely be ascribed not to human but to divine power. Therefore, there is no doubt that they also committed other things to writing by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit for the explanation of the Law and the Prophets, in which they happened to say much concerning Christ. That many others were able to do so at that time is clear from this: if those seventy were chosen as the elders from each tribe, it is certainly consistent with reason that there were many other men of the same kind then among the Hebrews who could have handed down expositions of the Law and the Prophets in writing. Joshua ben Sirach <note>original: "Iehofuas Syrach."</note> reports (as has been said) that he found their books in Egypt. Of these, Joshua his grandfather was one. He, flourishing at that time—or rather (as some think) being one of the seventy-two translators—wrote many things most worthy of memory, just as Joshua ben Sirach his grandson himself attests, saying: "My grandfather Joshua, after he had given himself more fully to the diligence of reading the Law and the Prophets, and the other books which were handed down to us by our fathers, wished himself also to write something of those things

<column-break/>

which pertain to doctrine and wisdom, so that those desiring to learn and to become skilled in them might attend more and more in mind and be strengthened for a lawful life." Imitating him afterward, Joshua ben Sirach himself published, among other things, that illustrious book which we call *Ecclesiasticus*; the Hebrews, however, name it משלי <note>original: "Misle."</note> *Mishlei*, that is, *Parables*. Although it is not among the twenty-four books of Sacred Scripture <note>The Hebrew Bible canon.</note>, it nonetheless holds great authority among them. In this book, although it deals chiefly with the obedience of subjects, the institution of good morals, and the praises of the holy Fathers, mention is nevertheless frequently made in it of the divinity of the Messiah and the incarnation of the Divine Word. Afterward, in the 160th year before the birth of Christ, that Aristobulus, a distinguished philosopher of the Peripatetic sect <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, being a Jew by nation, wrote commentaries on Moses at the encouragement of Ptolemy Philometor, where he discussed many things beautifully concerning the Messiah. Moreover, Rabbi Iodam and Rabbi Ibba, not long after, handed down many things in writing concerning the Messiah. After them, Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai <note>original: "Simeon filius Iohai," the traditional author of the Zohar.</note> also wrote many outstanding things concerning the Messiah and his divinity. His sayings occur frequently to those turning the volumes of the Talmud. He also composed a book which he titled מחקר הסודות <note>original: "Mechkar hassodoth."</note> *The Investigation of Secrets*, in which he revealed many mysteries concerning the Messiah (as will be clear in what follows). He, moreover, is believed to have been the author of the books of Commentaries on Genesis, which are read as being written in the more secret language of Jerusalem <note>Likely referring to the Aramaic of the Zohar or related mystical texts.</note>: where very many mysteries of the Christian faith are lucidly opened. Furthermore, in those things which he published in writing in the <term>Cabalistic faculty</term> <note>Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, in which he earned the leadership above all others: among other secrets of the divinity, he suggests the mystery of the divine Trinity distinctly and most clearly, oftentimes expressly naming Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. After him, Rabbenu HaKadosh <note>original: "Rabbenu Haccados," meaning "Our Holy Teacher," the title for Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note>, which is translated into Latin as "Our Holy Doctor," wrote a book which he called גלי רזיא <note>original: "Gale razeya."</note> *The Revealer of Secrets*; he was certainly not called a holy doctor without reason, since, inspired by the Holy Spirit, he so plainly opened all the mysteries of our Lord Jesus Christ in that book that he seems not to have predicted future things, but to have narrated events like an Evangelist. Shortly after him, Rabbi Nehumia ben HaKana <note>original: "Nehumias Haccanæ filius."</note> followed; he not only most clearly disclosed those things which had been secretly handed down by the Prophets concerning the Messiah, but even asserted that he himself was only fifty years away from His advent. Whence, hoping and rejoicing that he would see Him, he wrote a letter to make Him more certain of the mysteries of the Messiah, which he wished to be called אגרת הסודות <note>original: "Iggereth hassodoth."</note> *The Epistle of Secrets*. At almost the same time (namely, in the forty-second year before the birth of Christ), Jonathan ben Uzziel <note>original: "Ionathas Vzielis filius."</note>, a pupil of Hillel and a fellow-disciple of Simeon the Just <note>The Simeon who, according to the Gospel of Luke, held the infant Jesus in the Temple.</note> who took the infant Christ in his arms, translated the entire Old Testament into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic.</note> language and explained it, thus translating sense from sense and so explaining every most obscure word: so that whatever things concerning the Messiah were written doubtfully and hiddenly...

<margin>What a Targum is.</margin>
...he rendered it certain and most clear: so much so that his edition seems not so much a translation as a gloss and exposition, which the Hebrews call <term>Targum <note>original: "תרגום", a term for an Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>, that is, a translation. And it is of such great authority among them that not only does no one dare to contradict it, but all everywhere grant it no less faith than the text itself: both because of the holiness and skill of the man, and especially because of the truth of the interpretation and exposition itself. Therefore, whenever they find anything ambiguous or difficult to understand in the text of the sacred books, they always recur to that same translation and clarification. For this reason, regarding this same Jonathan (as is read in the <term>Bava Batra <note>original: "בבא בתרא", one of the tractates of the Babylonian Talmud dealing with civil law and property.</note></term>), the Masters have said that in the hour when he was occupied with that edition and exposition, if a fly or any flying thing flew over him or over the paper, it was immediately burnt up from heaven without any harm to him or the paper.

<margin>Onkelos.</margin>
CAPNIO: Many also say that Jonathan did not translate the <term>Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible (Genesis to Deuteronomy).</note></term> into Chaldean <note>Aramaic.</note>: for they say it was translated by <term>Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism.</note></term> the convert, whom the Hebrews assert was the son of Emperor Titus’s sister: as is held in the <term>Tractate Gittin <note>original: "מסכת גיטין", the Talmudic tractate regarding divorce.</note></term>, that is, in the treatise on bills of divorce, in the <term>Perek <note>original: "פרק", meaning "chapter".</note></term> (that is, in the chapter) which begins <term>Ha-Nizakin <note>original: "הניזקין", meaning "those who have been damaged".</note></term>. From this they infer that Jonathan did not produce the entire Chaldean Bible. GALATINUS: Without a doubt, Jonathan translated the entire Bible into Chaldean (as I said before, and I think you are not unaware). But his translation of the Pentateuch is very rare; therefore, it is denied by those who have not seen it. I, however, saw it once. It begins thus:
-> From the beginning the LORD created the heavens and the earth <note>original Aramaic: "מן אוולא ברא יי ית שמיא וית ארעא".</note> <-
But that which is by Onkelos begins thus:
-> In the beginning the LORD created the heavens and the earth <note>original Aramaic: "בקדמין ברא יי ית שמיא וית ארעא".</note> <-
This Onkelos also turned and explained the entire Bible in Chaldean. His edition and exposition, although now (except for the Pentateuch) it is hardly found anywhere, is nevertheless of no less value among the Jews than that of Jonathan, which we just mentioned. This they also call a Targum, because it too is in Chaldean, just like the other: and both happen to be written in Hebrew characters. Jonathan's edition of the Psalter is also in the possession of very few. Those who have it hide it as much as they can, because of the mysteries of the Christian faith which it contains.

His excellent sayings are found scattered in the Talmudic books. From

### CHAPTER IV.
*Concerning the Jewish writers who happened to live shortly after the suffering of Christ, and what they thought of him.*

-> HOGOSTRATUS. <-

Since all these whom you have enumerated preceded the coming of Christ, and many of them were inspired by the Holy Spirit, no one would think it should be denied at all that by explaining the Law and the Prophets, they wrote correctly about the Messiah. But regarding those who happened to write after the suffering of Christ, and who remained in Judaism with stubborn minds, it is certainly clear that no one ever correctly explained either the Law or the Prophets speaking of the Messiah, but rather twisted them to a false sense according to their own perfidy. GALATINUS: Although that may be correctly said of the Jews of our time, who are the most foul dregs of all their race, it does not hold true universally for the ancients. Among them, some indeed seem to correctly clarify the prophecies speaking of Christ according to the true sense: some truly thought well of the Lord Jesus himself and of Christians, as is clearly evident in the writings of both. And to say nothing of the others for now, I will bring forward for example's sake only two whose authority is most powerful among the Jews: namely Philo, born of priestly lineage, and Josephus the son of Matthias. These men, in their own books, not only confess our Lord Jesus Christ, but also adorn him with wonderful and divine praises, and they follow his followers with the greatest praise.

He published, moreover, that excellent and certainly divine volume which he called the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon.

Although he does not for the most part remain in universality (as Solomon does), but approaches that very particularity which he intends, being (as I think) unable to restrain himself from revealing the truth which he pursues. <meta>This page continues the dialogue regarding the authority of Jewish texts and their relationship to Christian truth. # BOOK THE FIRST.

->A<-

Solomon <note>original: "Selomo"</note> warns against falling, when he says: "My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them." Then follows: "If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood,'" with the rest that follows. What else is this entire passage than what Philo reports happened in his own time, saying: "The impious said among themselves, thinking not rightly," with the rest that follows? And descending even further into specifics: "Let us put," he says, "wood into his bread." In this, by "wood" he designated the cross; and by "bread," he meant Jesus our Lord himself—taking the parable of bread from the parable then made common (as I believe) from the mouth of the Lord himself, who said: "The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world." From this, through the words of the same Lord, he teaches that what Solomon had said would one day happen regarding the same Lord was fulfilled in him. Therefore, since both the subject matter and the art of obscurity and concealment are the same, and no other difference occurs than that of future and past time, for these reasons that book of Philo is rightly called the **Wisdom of Solomon**: since in it he most excellently suggests the divinity, innocence, and passion of Christ himself, who is both the Wisdom of the Father and is called the Prince of Peace. Whence, to rebuke the ingratitude and impiety of the Jews, he says these things in the person of those whom he calls impious, writing in Greek: <note>original: "ἐνεδρεύσωμεν τὸν δίκαιον... ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάζει." — This is Wisdom of Solomon 2:12-13.</note> "Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is useless to us, and he opposes our works, and reproaches us for sins against the law, and publishes abroad the sins of our discipline. He promises that he has knowledge of God, and calls himself the son of the Lord." And a little later he adds: <note>original: "Εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ὁ δίκαιος υἱὸς Θεοῦ... ἀνθεστηκότων." — Wisdom 2:18.</note> "For if the righteous man is the Son of God, He will uphold him, and deliver him from the hand of those who oppose him." And finally concluding, he says: <note>original: "θανάτῳ ἀσχήμονι καταδικάσωμεν αὐτόν" — Wisdom 2:20.</note> "Let us condemn him to a shameful death." These things, and others which the Jews had done against Christ, he records in the second chapter of this book. Indeed, in the following chapters of the same book, he predicts much concerning the victory of the martyrs, the immortality of souls, heavenly glory, the state of the Church of Christ, and the universal judgment. For this reason, the holy Council of Nicaea deservedly received this book as written by the dictation of the Holy Spirit, and placed it among the sacred and divine volumes. Furthermore, Josephus (to omit those things which he narrates with great praise concerning John the Baptist and James the Apostle, surnamed the Just) in the eighteenth book of his *Antiquities*, describing the times of Tiberius Caesar under whom Christ suffered, records these things concerning Christ himself in Greek: <note>original: "Τοῦτον τὸν χρόνον ἰησοῦς σοφὸς ἀνὴρ... οὐκ ἐπαύσαντο οἱ τὸ πρῶτον ἀγαπήσαντες." — This is the famous 'Testimonium Flavianum' from Josephus.</note> "At this time was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is right to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure, and he drew to himself many Jews and many also from the Gentile world. This was the Christ, and when Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men among us, had condemned him to the cross, those who had loved him at the first did not cease to do so."

<margin>Josephus.</margin>

<column-break/>

"For he appeared to them on the third day, living again, for the divine prophets had spoken these and ten thousand other wonderful things about him." <note>original: "ἐφάνη γὰρ αὐτοῖς τρίτην ἡμέραν... εἰρηκότων." — Conclusion of the passage from Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.3.</note> These are the words of that Josephus, whom the Jews consider perhaps the greatest. These most excellent men, therefore, Philo and Josephus—who although they wrote in Greek, were both Jews and most sharp rivals for their ancestral traditions—would never have held such a good opinion of Christ, nor reported what they said of him so truthfully, unless they had correctly understood those things which had been foretold by the Prophets concerning the Messiah. Therefore, there is no doubt that if they wrote these things about him in Greek, they also wrote many other things in Hebrew, explaining the Law and the Prophets. For both were most skilled in both languages and were initiated into the sacred letters from their very cradles. Whence it is also fair to believe that many others existed besides them in those same times who both felt rightly concerning the Lord Jesus Christ and, explaining the prophecies of the prophets, wrote the truth about him. If, then, these men recognized the truth, why did they neglect to embrace it? For it is well known (to pass over others) that both Philo and Josephus, whom you brought forward as examples, by no means adhered to Christ, but remained in Judaism until their deaths. **GALATINUS.** <term>GAL. <note>The speaker Pietro Galatino.</note></term> That is indeed true, especially of Josephus; not to mention Philo, who when he came to Rome as an ambassador of his nation to Gaius Caligula, maintained a very familiar acquaintance with Peter, the prince of the Apostles. However, I would not wish you to be ignorant of the fact that after the Lord’s resurrection, the Jews were divided into a threefold kind. For some, seeing the sayings of the prophets fulfilled in him, adhered to him in both faith and work, as did that elder **Gamaliel**, whose sayings are of the greatest authority among the <term>Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note></term>. And almost infinite others did the same—not only from the common people or the ignorant, but from the more noble and wise. For as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "A great part of the priests were obedient to the faith." And some of these wrote many wonderful things about Christ. Certain of their small works still exist among the Jews, although they strive with all their might to hide them so they do not come into our hands. And among the rest are those things which **Rabbi Haccanas**, son of Nehumia, committed to writing; who, when he had written all the deeds and miracles of our Redeemer just as he had seen them with his eyes, finally said this: <note>original: "אני הקנה אחד מן המאמינים בו וטבלתי במים הקדושים ובדרכיו הישרים אני הולך"</note> "I am Haccanas, one of those who believe in him, and I have washed myself in holy waters, and I walk in his upright ways." Indeed, some of them believed that the Lord Jesus himself was that Messiah of whom the Prophets had spoken, yet they were reluctant to abandon the Mosaic observances—

<margin>A threefold kind of Jews. Gamaliel the elder.</margin>

<margin>Rabbi Haccanas.</margin>

...they were unwilling to seek. These adhered to Christ by faith alone and not by works. For while they indeed confessed Christ, they nevertheless persevered in Judaism. Such a person (as I believe) was Josephus, and almost countless others. The book of the Acts of the Apostles mentions these in chapters 15 and 21, where it is said: "You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealots for the law?" <note>Acts 21:20. The text argues that early Jewish believers in Jesus continued to follow Mosaic Law.</note> In this, however, they erred greatly. For it is clear that all the ceremonies of the Old Law, since they stood as figures of Christ and his deeds, reached their absolute end in him. Very many of these men also wrote some true things about Christ and correctly explained the prophecies in many respects. Finally, other Jews, wishing to adhere to Christ neither by faith nor by work, chose like blind men to remain stubbornly in their perfidy. Yet even they (see how great is the power of truth!) were not able to deny the truth entirely. For in explaining the Law and the prophets, compelled by truth alone, they were unable to remain completely silent about it in many passages. This must be thought to have happened by divine arrangement, so that we might have testimonies of the truth from its very enemies and those who deny it. Nor does this prejudice the truth because they themselves did not believe; rather, it adds more to the testimony, because even as unbelievers, they could not lean against it and deny it. From the sayings and writings of these men, and of all others who handed down anything in writing after the Babylonian captivity, the volume of the **Talmud** was gathered and put together.

### CHAPTER V.

->*Who was the author of the Talmud itself, when it was published, into how many parts it is divided, and which matters it chiefly treats.*<-

->CAPNIO<-

<margin>Mishna.</margin>
Since I have found various opinions regarding the author of the Talmud itself and the time when it was published—for some write that it was completed around the year 300 after the birth of Christ; while Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, in his *Apology*, says it was not compiled until the year 150 of the Virgin’s delivery—I have indeed found in Hebrew writings that the Talmud itself was collected by several Doctors and reduced into one body, like a Decree, by Rabbi Assé. Therefore, I would also like to hear your opinion on this. GALATINUS: In the 120th year after the burning of the second Temple <note>c. 189–190 AD</note>, Rabbi Judah, son of Simon—whom they call "The Holy" because of his excellence in doctrine and uprightness—by a decree of the entire Synod of Jewish wise men, gathered into one volume the explanations of the Law and the prophets and all the writings which other Doctors had written up to that point, both before and after the coming of Christ. This volume he called **משנה** *Mishna*, which means a "repeated reading" <note>or "instruction"</note>. But about 300 years after the destruction of the same Temple, Rabbi Jochanan, taking as colleagues Rab and Samuel, collected the *Mishna* itself and whatever other writings he could obtain, and composed the Jerusalem Talmud. Finally, in the year 436 AD, Rabbi Assé, together with Rabina, reduced all the writings of his predecessors into one,

<column-break/>

and wove together the Babylonian Talmud, by which the entire Synagogue of the Jews is now governed. However, prevented by death, he was unable to finish it. Soon after, his son, together with Maremar, gave the completion to the work. Moreover, "Talmud" is the same as "Doctrine" or "Discipline," embracing all the earlier commentaries and statutes, as well as certain histories of those times—a work truly full on all sides of divine and natural, as well as political and legal wisdom. CAPNIO: For a clearer understanding of the Talmud itself, I also desire to know which matters are chiefly dealt with in it. For some say it is divided into four parts: in the first, holy matters, feasts, and ceremonies; in the second, plants and seeds; in the third, marriage and wives; and in the fourth, judgments and laws are treated abundantly. Petrus Niger, however, divides it into six parts. GALATINUS: Without doubt (as you yourself know), the Talmud is distinguished into six primary parts, which they call **סדרים** *sedarim*, that is, "orders," or "ordinances," or "directions," because the *Mishna* had previously been divided into that many and the same parts; for the Talmud is almost nothing else than a certain commentary on the *Mishna* itself.

The first of these parts is called **סדר זרעים** *Seder Zeraim*, that is, the "Order of Seeds." The second, **סדר מועד** *Seder Moed*, the "Order of Festivals." The third, **סדר נשים** *Seder Nashim*, the "Order of Women." The fourth, **סדר נזיקין** *Seder Nezikin*, the "Order of Damages" or "Injuries." The fifth, **סדר קדשים** *Seder Kodashim*, the "Order of Holy Things." The sixth, **סדר טהרות** *Seder Teharoth*, the "Order of Purifications." Each of these parts is divided into several **מסכתות** *massachoth*, that is, "tractates" or "books," and any **מסכת** *massacheth*, that is, any book, into several **פרקים** *perakim*, which are "distinctions" or "chapters."

For the first part is distinguished into eleven books. The first of these, which is called **מסכת ברכות** *Massecheth Berachoth*, that is, the "Tractate of Blessings," has nine chapters, in which it treats chiefly of blessings, of giving thanks to God, of prayers, and divine praises. The second, called **מסכת פאה** *Massecheth Peah*, that is, the "Tractate of the Corner" or the "Angular Part," contains ten chapters, in which it treats of the corner portion of the harvest or crops which had to be left for the poor <note>Based on the biblical command in Leviticus 19:9</note>. The third is named **מסכת דמאי** *Massecheth Demai*, that is, the "Tractate of Doubt," and is distinguished into ten chapters, dealing with the giving of tithes on doubtful things. The fourth, which is called **מסכת תרומות** *Massecheth Terumoth*, that is, the "Tractate of the Two out of a Hundred," is divided into eleven chapters, treating of the separation of two out of every hundred fruits, which were to be given to the priests. The fifth, called **מסכת שביעית** *Massecheth Sheviit*, that is, the "Tractate of the Seventh," is divided into ten chapters, dealing with the seventh year, in which nothing at all was to be sown, nor was the earth to be cultivated. At that time, both the fruits of the trees and whatever the earth brought forth of its own accord were common to all. The sixth, named **מסכת כלאים** *Massecheth Kilayim*, that is, the "Tractate of Mixtures," has nine chapters, treating of all kinds of things that...
