The seventh, which is called the <term>tractate of the first tithe</term> <note>original: "massecheth maaser rishon"</note>, contains nine chapters, in which he discusses the first tithes that were owed to the Levites, from which the Levites themselves were bound to grant tithes to the Priests. The eighth, which is named the <term>tractate of the second tithe</term> <note>original: "massecheth maaser sheni"</note>, is distinguished into five chapters, in which he treats the second tithes; these were to be set aside after the tithes had been presented to the Levites, and were to be eaten and consumed in Jerusalem. The ninth, which is called the <term>tractate of the dough-offering</term> <note>original: "massecheth challah"</note>, is distinguished into four chapters, in which he discusses the cake of bread, whether a loaf or a roll, which always had to be taken from the dough and given to the Priests. The tenth, which is termed the <term>tractate of the closure</term> <note>original: "massecheth orlah," referring to the "uncircumcision" or prohibition of young trees</note>, is divided into three chapters, in which he treats the "closure" of trees that occurred when they were planted, as a sign that for three years no one was permitted to eat of their fruit. The eleventh, which is called the <term>tractate of first-fruits</term> <note>original: "massecheth bikkurim"</note>, has four chapters, in which he discusses the first-fruits to be offered in the Temple, which they were bound to offer from only seven things: namely, wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates.

<margin>The second part of the Talmud, called the Order of Festivals.</margin>
The second part encompasses twelve books. The first of these, which is named the <term>tractate of the Sabbath</term> <note>original: "massecheth Shabbat"</note>, contains twenty-four chapters, in which he treats the Sabbath and those things which were permitted or prohibited on the Sabbath day. The second, which is called the <term>tractate of mixtures</term> <note>original: "massecheth eruvin," referring to the legal "joining" of domains to allow carrying</note>, is divided into ten chapters, in which he discusses the communal associations which were permitted among the Jews on the Sabbath. The third, which is called the <term>tractate of Passovers</term> <note>original: "massecheth pesachim"</note>, is divided into two parts: in the first, he specifically discusses unleavened bread and those things which were to be prepared for the solemnity of the Passover; in the second, however, he treats the Passover lamb. The entire book is distinguished into ten chapters. The fourth, which is named the <term>tractate of shekels</term> <note>original: "massecheth shekalim"</note>, is divided into eight chapters: in which he treats the collection of shekels, which had to be done for the purchase of the two lambs that were offered daily in sacrifice—one in the morning, the other in the evening.

<margin>What a shekel is.</margin>
Now, although a <term>shekel</term> <note>original: "siclus"</note> is properly a certain measure of weight—according to that passage in Leviticus 27: *a shekel has twenty gerahs* <note>original: "obolos"</note>—since it is derived from the Hebrew verb *shakal*, which means "to weigh," in this context it is a type of coin weighing twenty gerahs. For every man, after he had passed his twentieth year, was bound to pay half a shekel each year according to the weight-measure of the Temple, for the purchase of the two aforementioned lambs to be offered in the continual sacrifice for the redemption of souls. The fifth, which is called the <term>tractate of the days</term> <note>original: "massecheth yoma," referring to "The Day" of Atonement</note>, contains eight chapters, in which he discusses the Day of Atone-

<column-break/>

-ment, and those things which were to be done on such a day. The sixth, which is termed the <term>tractate of the booth</term> or tabernacle <note>original: "massecheth sukkah"</note>, has five chapters, in which he discusses the Feast of Booths or Tabernacles. The seventh, which is named the <term>tractate of the good day</term> <note>original: "massecheth yom tov," often called Beitzah</note>, is distinguished into five chapters, in which he treats all things that were permitted or prohibited on any feast day, except for the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement. The eighth, which is called the <term>tractate of the head of the year</term> <note>original: "massecheth rosh hashanah"</note>, is divided into five chapters, in which he discusses everything pertaining to the solemnity of the New Year. The ninth, which is named the <term>tractate of fasting</term> <note>original: "massecheth taanit"</note>, is divided into four chapters, in which he treats the fast that was to occur four times in the year, as well as other fasts. The tenth, which is called the <term>tractate of the scroll</term> <note>original: "massecheth megillah," literally "the history"</note>, contains four chapters, in which he discusses the story of Esther, which was to be read during that solemnity, and things pertaining to that feast. The eleventh, which is termed the <term>tractate of the minor festival</term> <note>original: "massecheth moed katan"</note>, has three chapters, in which he treats the minor feast days that fell between the first and last days of Passover and Tabernacles. For the first and last days of those solemnities were more solemn than the others in between. The twelfth, which is named the <term>tractate of the festival offering</term> <note>original: "massecheth chagigah"</note>, is distinguished into three chapters, in which he discusses the commandment by which all males were bound to go to Jerusalem three times a year: namely, at the feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles.

<margin>The third part of the Talmud, called the Order of Women.</margin>
The third part contains seven books. The first of these, which is called the <term>tractate of sisters-in-law</term> <note>original: "massecheth yevamot"</note>, is distinguished into sixteen chapters, in which he discusses the commandment regarding taking the wife of a brother who died without children, in order to raise up his seed. The second, which is termed the <term>tractate of contracts</term> <note>original: "massecheth ketubot"</note>, is divided into thirteen chapters, in which he discusses the contracts of dowries and the obligations which both the husband toward the wife, and the wife toward the husband, were bound to keep. The third, which is named the <term>tractate of vows</term> <note>original: "massecheth nedarim"</note>, is divided into eleven chapters, in which he treats the vows of women. The fourth, which is called the <term>tractate of the Nazirite</term> <note>original: "massecheth nazir"</note>, contains nine chapters, in which he treats the vow of the Nazirites—that is, those separated from the vanities of the world—who, during the duration of their vow, were not permitted (among other things) to drink wine, nor to taste anything produced from the vine, nor to cut their hair, nor to touch any corpse. The fifth, which is named the <term>tractate of the wayward woman</term> <note>original: "massecheth sotah," literally "diversion"</note>, has nine chapters, in which he discusses the diversion a wife makes from her husband by adhering to another. The sixth, which is called the <term>tractate of the bills of divorce</term> <note>original: "massecheth gittin"</note>, is distinguished into nine chapters, in which he treats bills of divorce and the dissolution of marriage. The seventh, which is called the tractate of betrothals... <note>The text cuts off here.</note>

The fourth part of the Talmud, called the Order of Damages.

...is called the [Order] of Matrimony. It is divided into four chapters <note>The author uses "capita" (chapters) here likely referring to tractates or sub-sections</note>, which deal with betrothals, weddings, and matters pertaining to them. The fourth part is likewise divided into seven books. The first of these is called <term>the tractate of damages</term> <note>original: "massecheth nezikin"</note>, or injuries (matching the name of the Order itself), and is distinguished into three "gates" <note>original: "bauoth," from the Hebrew 'Bava'</note>, or positions. The first of these is called the <term>First Gate</term> <note>original: "baua kama"</note>; it is divided into ten chapters which treat all forms of damages and injuries usually caused by both men and beasts. The second is called the <term>Middle Gate</term> <note>original: "baua mazya"</note>; it is also divided into ten chapters dealing with lawsuits, rights, usury, and leases. The third is called the <term>Last Gate</term> <note>original: "baua bathra"</note>; it is similarly divided into ten chapters treating sales and purchases, partnerships, and heirs and inheritances. The second book, which is called the <term>tractate of the Ordinary Judges</term> <note>original: "massecheth sanhedrin"</note>, has fourteen chapters; it deals abundantly with the presiding judges, the trials, and everything pertaining to legal judgment. It also discusses those who have a portion in the world to come and the Messiah, particularly in the chapter <term>"Helek"</term> <note>original: "perek helec"</note>, named for its opening word, "Part." The third, called the <term>tractate of oaths</term> <note>original: "massecheth sceuuoth"</note>, contains eight chapters chiefly treating oaths and the guardians of property. The fourth, called the <term>tractate of testimonies</term> <note>original: "massecheth edujoth"</note>, is distinguished into eight chapters: it deals with the legal determinations made based on the testimonies of predecessors who were men of great authority. The fifth, called the <term>tractate of strange service</term> <note>original: "massecheth auoda zara"</note>, is divided into five chapters treating idolatry and those matters in which Jews must not communicate with other nations, regarding both social conversion and food or drink. The sixth, called the <term>tractate of the fathers</term> <note>original: "massecheth auoth"</note>, is partitioned into five chapters—commonly called the <term>Chapters of the Fathers</term> <note>original: "pirke auoth"</note>—which deal with the ancient fathers who flourished from the time of Moses down to Simeon the Just, renowned for both their teaching and sanctity. The seventh, named the <term>tractate of sentences</term> <note>original: "massecheth horaioth"</note>, has three chapters specifically treating the rulings determined by the Sanhedrin (the ordinary judges) and the penalties for those who violate them. Some add another book to this part, which they call the <term>tractate of lashings</term> <note>original: "massecheth maccoth"</note>, placing it in the third position; it deals with the lashings with which criminals were to be punished according to the judges' sentence. However, those who assign only seven books to this part do not distinguish this from the second book, but make one out of both. The fifth part contains eleven books. The first, called the <term>tractate of sacrifices</term> <note>original: "massecheth zeuahim"</note>, has fourteen chapters in which the immolation of sacrifices and the manner and place of sacrificing are copiously discussed. The second, called the <term>tractate of common slaughter</term> <note>original: "massecheth holin"</note>, is divided into twelve chapters treating the slaughter of clean animals, not for sacrifice, but for the common use of men. The third, called the <term>tractate of meal offerings</term> <note>original: "massecheth menahoth"</note>, is distinguished into thirteen chapters dealing with the flour of the grain which was to be offered to the Priests in the temple. The fourth, called the <term>tractate of the firstborn</term> <note>original: "massecheth bechoroth"</note>, is partitioned into nine chapters treating firstborn animals, both those to be offered and those to be redeemed. The fifth, named the <term>tractate of valuations</term> <note>original: "massecheth erachin"</note>, has nine chapters dealing with the prices or values of things that a person promised to give to God. The sixth, called the <term>tractate of exchange</term> <note>original: "massecheth temura"</note>, is distinguished into seven chapters treating how an exchange of sacrifices is by no means to be made. The seventh, called the <term>tractate of transgression</term> <note>original: "massecheth meila"</note>, is divided into sex chapters dealing with the sacrilege of those who used sacrificed things that were not permitted to them. The eighth, called the <term>tractate of destructions</term> <note>original: "massecheth carethoth," referring to the 'cutting off' or spiritual extirpation of the soul</note>, is partitioned into six chapters treating the destruction of souls in the future age or after this life due to their sins, and the specific sins for which souls are lost. The ninth, called the <term>tractate of the continual [sacrifice]</term> <note>original: "massecheth tamid"</note>, has six chapters dealing with the continual sacrifice of the two lambs which took place daily in the temple. The tenth, called the <term>tractate of dimensions</term> <note>original: "massecheth middoth"</note>, contains five chapters treating the dimensions and measurements of the temple. The eleventh, called the <term>tractate of nests</term> <note>original: "massecheth kinnin"</note>, is distinguished into five chapters dealing with the offerings of young pigeons and turtledoves which the poor were bound to offer in the temple. The sixth part embraces twelve books; the first, called the <term>tractate of vessels</term> <note>original: "massecheth chelim"</note>, is divided into thirty chapters treating the purification of vessels of every kind and material, as well as cloths and garments which might have been polluted by some contamination. The second, named the <term>tractate of habitations</term> <note>original: "massecheth ahaloth," literally 'tents'</note>, is partitioned into eighteen chapters dealing with the purification of houses and other things from the uncleanness contracted by reason of a dead human body. The third, called the <term>tractate of plagues</term> <note>original: "massecheth negaiim"</note> or afflictions, has fourteen chapters treating the purification of human bodies from uncleanness contracted by reason of leprosy and other plagues, as well as the purification of other...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Sixth Order of the Talmud, "Tohorot" (Purities), which deals with ritual cleanliness and the methods of purification. BOOK ONE.

...of things designated for human use, arising from strikes or contact. The fourth, which is called <term>the tractate of the heifer</term> <note>original: "massecheth para," referring to the Red Heifer</note>, or the cow, contains twelve chapters, which deal with the ashes of the red cow or heifer, so that by their sprinkling both men and other things that had been polluted by a human corpse could be purified. The fifth, which is named <term>the tractate of purifications</term> <note>original: "massecheth taharoth"</note>, is distinguished into ten chapters, in which the purification from uncleanness contracted from sources other than a dead human body is treated. The sixth, which is denominated <term>the tractate of gatherings</term> <note>original: "massecheth mikvaoth"</note>, or collections of waters, is divided into ten chapters, which deal with the spring and the waters in which people of both sexes were baptized <note>The author uses "baptizabantur" to describe ritual immersion (mikvah) to make it more familiar to a Christian audience.</note>, so that they might be purified from spiritual uncleanness. The seventh, which is called <term>the tractate of the menstruant</term> <note>original: "massecheth nidda"</note>, is partitioned into ten chapters: in which the purification of women is treated, concerning uncleanness contracted both by reason of menstruation and by reason of childbirth. The eighth, which is called <term>the tractate of emissions</term> <note>original: "massecheth zauin"</note>, has ten chapters, which deal with the purification of men from the uncleanness arising from the discharge of seed through the male member. The ninth, which is called <term>the tractate of irrigated things</term> <note>original: "massecheth maskin," likely referring to Machshirin</note>, is distinguished into six chapters, in which the purification of irrigated things from uncleanness contracted through contamination is treated. The tenth, which is named <term>the tractate of the one baptized for the day</term> <note>original: "massecheth tebul iom"</note>, is divided into four chapters: in which it deals with one who has immersed on that same day, who, although he was purified from spiritual uncleanness by the washing of that water, was nevertheless not perfectly so until he made an offering in the temple on the following day for the uncleanness from which he had been purified by water. The eleventh, which is denominated <term>the tractate of hands</term> <note>original: "massecheth iadaim"</note>, is partitioned into four chapters: in which the washing of hands for those wishing to touch sacred things or eat of consecrated foods is treated, as well as the vessel and the waters with which their hands were to be washed. The twelfth, which is called <term>the tractate of the stalks of fruits</term> <note>original: "massecheth okazin"</note>, has three chapters: in which it is declared when the stalks to which apples and other fruits are attached were said to be contaminated by contact with unclean fruits. Therefore, of the whole Talmud (as is evident from what has been said) there are six primordial parts, sixty books, and five hundred and thirty-two chapters. In these are found many, and almost infinite, <term>traditions</term> <note>original: "ghemaroth"</note> scattered about—that is, concluded traditions or determined conclusions—containing almost innumerable secrets concerning the Messiah and very much in agreement with our faith, which were handed down and written by the ancient Jews many years before the Talmud was completed. For it hardly ever happens in the Talmud itself that any <term>tradition</term> <note>original: "ghemara"</note> is found—that is, a tradition or conclusion handed down, concluded, and determined by those ancient fathers—

<column-break/>

which does not express some secret of Catholic truth, either explicitly and openly, or implicitly and through figures. As will be most widely evident in the following pages.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### That the Talmudists, in order to search out the secrets of the Law, followed the allegorical sense most of all. The Cabalists, however, followed the anagogical sense; and what the Cabala is, and why our ancient [Christian] writers did not mention the Cabala.

-> HOGOSTRATVS. <-

<image-desc>A decorative letter 'S' featuring a coiled dragon or serpent.</image-desc>

**S**ince the Jews understand everything only literally—for they do not (as is commonly said) consider anything but the husk of scripture—how is it true that the Talmudists followed a spiritual and mystical sense? **GALATINVS.** That can indeed be rightly said of the Jews of our time, who, in order to escape the truth, occupy themselves only with the literal husk of the law, utterly rejecting all allegories and figures. For the whole assembly of more recent masters and younger Talmudists, as if blinded in mind and completely neglecting the light of the soul, embrace only the historical and literal sense of the divine words. But the ancients were accustomed to seek out the secrets of the law only through the spiritual and mystical sense. How much the spiritual sense exceeds the literal for investigating the secrets of the law, the Talmudists show very frequently, for they say the literal sense <margin>*The spiritual and literal sense.*</margin> is a <term>small matter</term> <note>original: "Dauar catan"</note>, but the spiritual or mystical sense is a <term>great matter</term> <note>original: "Dauar gadol"</note>. And they call the literal sense a <term>parable</term> <note>original: "Massal"</note>, that is, an example, as Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> relates in the first tractate of the book *Moreh* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed</note>. Furthermore, they compare the literal sense itself to a candle, which is bought for a tiny farthing; but the allegorical or figurative sense, which they call <term>the clarity of the law</term> <note>original: "Buria shel torah"</note>, is eventually found by those seeking it through such a candle—that is, through the literal sense or example. The same Rabbi Moses declares this very well and most beautifully near the beginning of the same book, saying: "Know that the key to the understanding of all things that the Prophets said is to understand parables, metaphors, similitudes, and enigmas." For you know it was said in Hosea, chapter 12: <note>original: "וביד הנביאים אדמה"</note> *And in the hand of the prophets I will use likenesses.* And again in Ezekiel, chapter 17: <note>original: "בן אדם חוד חידה ומשול משל אל בית ישראל"</note> *Son of man, pose a riddle, and speak a parable to the house of Israel. A great eagle with wings.* And a little later: *And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say now to the rebellious house: Do you not know what these things mean? Tell them: Behold, the king of Babylon has come to Jerusalem, and has taken its king.*

This means: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say now to the rebellious house, do you not know what these things mean? Say, behold, the King of Babylon is coming to Jerusalem, and he will take its King." <note>A reference to Ezekiel 17:11-12</note> And so forth. You know again what the wise man said in the twenty-fifth chapter of Proverbs: <term>Apples of gold in carvings of silver is a word spoken according to its two faces.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "תפוחי זהב במשכיות כסף דבר דבור על אפניו" (Proverbs 25:11). The author interprets the Hebrew word "ofnav" (circumstances/wheels) as "faces" or "aspects."</note> Hear, I pray, the exposition of this sentence. The silver carvings are silver meshes, in which the holes are very tiny, yet they can be penetrated by sight. Therefore, the sense is: A word spoken according to its two faces—that is, according to its interior and exterior sense—is like an apple in a silver mesh. It is as if he were saying it is necessary for the exterior sense to be precious and good, like silver. But the interior sense is much better, like gold, so that the exterior is to the interior as silver is compared to gold. It is also necessary that there be something in the exterior sense that leads and draws the observer toward the interior. Just as a golden apple clothed in a silver mesh, when viewed from a distance or without much scrutiny, appears entirely silver. But when one who has sharp sight, provoked by the value and beauty of the silver, approaches, he will surely see a golden apple hidden within. Thus, then, are the words of the prophets. For frequently those things that are on the outside are wisdom useful for many things: such as for the regulation of morals and the state of the human congregation. This is evident on the surface of the Proverbs of Solomon. However, those things that are within are wisdom extremely useful in matters of faith according to the truth. These are the words of that Egyptian, Rabbi Moses. <note>Referring to Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and jurist often called "Rambam."</note> From these things, therefore, it is clear that the Talmudists considered the secrets of the law only through the spiritual and mystical sense. But this will become far more evident in what follows. I omit, however, the Kabbalists and those versed in Kabbalah itself, who consider the secrets of the law only through anagogical <note>A term for the highest level of spiritual or mystical interpretation.</note> understanding. **Hog.** <note>Hogostratus (Jacob van Hoogstraten), a Dominican inquisitor and critic of Jewish literature.</note> This name "Kabbalah" is found nowhere among the holy fathers, nor among the Doctors of the Church, nor among our masters. Because of this, such a name is rendered highly suspect. **Gal.** <note>Galatinus (Pietro Galatino), the defender of the mystical tradition in this dialogue.</note> In ancient times, it was forbidden for this faculty which they call Kabbalah to be handed down to anyone unless they were most learned and advanced in age. For this reason, it was not permitted for even a small part of it to be committed to writing. Hence, besides those things brought forward as handed down by Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai, few or no other things written by the ancients are found. For as it is said in the book <term>The Festival Offering</term> <note>original: "חגיגה" (*Hagigah*), a tractate of the Talmud.</note>, in the chapter <term>They do not expound</term> <note>original: "אין דורשין" (*En dorsin*), referring to a section of the Talmud that limits the teaching of mystical subjects.</note>, no one was allowed to write anything about Kabbalah, but they handed it down by mouth only. From this, they not ineptly called it <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "קבלה"</note>, which in Latin is interpreted as "reception." However, the teachers of the more recent Jews, lest that ancestral dogma should vanish, published something about this faculty in writing; yet they did so sparingly and obscured by several veils. By this, it indeed happens that very few are able to grasp its correct understanding. If, however, any believe they have attained something from it, they soon store it in their heart as a secret to be

<column-break/>

revealed to no one, lest—on account of the holy Trinity of divine persons and other mysteries of Catholic truth shining forth there—it might happen that some of the Jews would be affected by scandal. Therefore, it is no wonder if this name "Kabbalah," or the faculty designated by that name, has rarely been on the lips of the saints and other wise men until now, and if our ancient authors did not mention it. Yet some among the younger men, being skilled in the Hebrew language, and excelling others in diligent wit and divine philosophy, attending to the utility, excellence, and sublimity of this science, have not only mentioned it but have even written much. For Giovanni Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance humanist who sought to harmonize Kabbalah with Christianity.</note> was the first to begin to suspect some things about it as if from a distance. Afterward, Agostino Giustiniani, Bishop of Nebbio, disclosed some things more broadly in his commentaries on the Psalter. Our Capnio <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a key German humanist and Hebraist; "Capnio" is his Greek-derived pen name.</note> also, in the three books which he most elegantly inscribed to the current Supreme Pontiff Leo <note>Pope Leo X.</note> concerning the Kabbalistic art, brought very many outstanding things to light. He did this to show openly that far more and far higher things than all others have written on this matter so far were soon to be produced by him, which would bring the clearest light to so obscure a subject. Last of all, I, as if gathering clusters after the vintage, have decided to intersperse into these things I am about to say—only where necessary—those parts of this Kabbalistic wisdom that seem necessary for relating the secrets of Catholic truth.

# BOOK ONE.

...then handed down to their ancestors by Moses himself in a succeeding order, as the Jews relate. Wherefore, it is a shameful thing for Christians even to name the Talmud itself. GALATINUS: You have touched upon three points briefly, Hoogstraten.

<margin>Galatinus's response.</margin>
But you are certainly very much mistaken (if I may say so with your permission). Since it is quite useful to our faith to uncover the truth in this place as I perceive it, I will respond to the things you have said for the sake of manifesting that very truth. And as to the first point, I confess many absurdities are placed there; however, not everything that seems absurd is truly absurd. For those ancient Talmudists handed down nearly infinite secrets through figures and enigmas, which seem like foolishness and absurdities to those who do not understand them. Yet, in truth, innumerable secrets regarding the Messiah and Catholic truth lie hidden within them. From this arose the error of the younger Jews, who, while ignorant of the ancient manner of theologizing and philosophizing, turn many secrets of the Talmudic work into mockeries and blasphemies. From this also, many of our own people, while they are unable to understand mysteries of this kind, presume to revile and condemn them. 

<margin>Regarding the first point.</margin>
<margin>The ancient Talmudists handed down the secrets of the law under figures and enigmas.</margin>

To say nothing of others, a certain man endowed with no small skill in divine and human letters, writing against the Jews, recounts many things of this same kind; not understanding them well himself, he calls them follies and inconsistencies. And among other things which he says are found written in the Talmud against divine perfection, he especially relates this: That when God established the firmament, not being strong enough to finish it, He left a certain hole in it on the northern side. The Jews assert (as that Doctor says) that He did this so that if anyone should ever arise wishing to make himself equal to God, God—opposing him with the completion of the hole—might say to him: "If you are God, just as I am, close that place which I have left open, if you can." 

Indeed, it escapes no one how blatant a lie this is. For we always see the highest axis of the northern pole above us, never hidden, and we see it as entirely whole and perfect. From this, the foolishness of this error is clearly evident. All these things are according to the opinion of that Doctor. Although he said these and all other things with a good intention and zeal for the Christian faith, he was nevertheless (to tell the truth) not a little deceived. Nor does God, who is the supreme truth, need our lie for the exaltation of His faith. This is especially true since many of those things which he rejects as entirely erroneous, if they are understood rightly (as is proper), are more profitable to us for the truth of the Catholic faith against the Jews than if they were thought (as he says) to be words utterly foreign to truth and reason. For to let other things pass, this example concerning the hole of the firmament left in the part of the north, which he introduces as a greatest inconsistency—if it is understood rightly—will be seen not only to be no inconsistency, but also most consistent with our faith. Wherefore, so that the truth of the Catholic faith might appear more clearly to the confusion of the Jews' perfidy, I will first relate the words of that same example in Hebrew exactly as they are written in the Talmud. Then I will unlock the mystery which

<column-break/>

lies hidden in that same example for the truth of our faith against the Jews of our age. Therefore, Rabbi Eleazar, not the least of the ancient Talmudists, places that same example in his chapters in the book *Zohar*: <note>original Hebrew: רוח פנת צפון ברא הקדוש ברוך הוא ולא גמרה לפי שאמר הקדוש ברוך הוא כל מי שיאמר שהוא אלוה יבא ויגמור את הפנה הזאת שהנחתי ידועה לכל שהוא אלוה</note> That is: "The Holy One, blessed be He, created the side of the northern part and did not complete it, because God said: 'Whoever says he is God, let him come and perfect this part which I have left, and all shall know that he is God.'"

Certainly, great mysteries are hidden in these words. For first, it is shown that it is possible for some man to be God. Next, that the sign of his divinity is that he is able to perfect the northern part. For a right understanding of these things, it must be known that the ancients were accustomed to call the malice of men and the depravity of demons "the left side" or "the north" allegorically, according to that saying in the first chapter of Jeremiah: "From the North shall all evil be opened upon all the inhabitants of the earth" <note>Jeremiah 1:14</note>; and in the tenth chapter of Ecclesiastes: "The heart of a fool is in his left hand." <note>Ecclesiastes 10:2</note> Moreover, no malice of men or temptation of demons is greater than that which leads to the worship of idols. Therefore, the cult of idols is attributed chiefly to the North, as is easily evident in the eighth chapter of Ezekiel. 

What else, therefore, is designated by this "hole" than the temptation or power of demons, which primarily regards the worship of idolatry? Why also is that hole said to be left by God, except because, by His permission, the cult of idolatry itself proceeded from free will (which God Himself had given to man) through an evil choice? Therefore, according to the doctrine of the ancient Talmudists in this example, the sign of divinity is the ability to entirely overcome the power of demons and to explode <note>The word "explodere" here carries the sense of driving out or rejecting with contempt, like hissing a bad actor off a stage.</note> idolatry. This is also clearly proved by that which is written in the book **זוהר** (*Zohar*). Where Rabbi Rasanad, upon the fourth chapter of Genesis, says: <note>original Hebrew: שכינה הנקראת אתה המשול במלאך המות</note> That is: "The Presence of God <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>The divine presence or indwelling of God.</note> called **אתה** *Atta* <note>Hebrew for "You."</note>, shall rule over the angel of death"—that is, the devil. And in the same place: <note>original Hebrew: מלת אתה רומז חכמת אלהים</note> That is: "The word *Atta* hints at the Wisdom of God." 

From this, it is clearly held that through the Wisdom of God (which in divine matters is attributed to the Son) united to human nature, the diabolical power was to be conquered. In this example, therefore, the ancient Talmudists mystically handed down the divinity of the Messiah, which was to be recognized chiefly by this sign: That the Messiah would complete the northern part itself; that is, he would conquer the devil by liberating the human race from his power, and by exploding his worship—that is, idolatry—from the world. No one could rightly deny that Christ did this, chiefly because through His Apostles, idolatry was utterly exploded. From this it is clear that through this Talmudic example, which our Doctor introduces as a greatest inconsistency against the perfection of God, not only is the depravity of the Jews confounded (who believe the Messiah will be a pure man and not God), but also it is excellently proved that our Lord Jesus himself was the true Messiah.

# BOOK ONE.

<meta>catchword: was</meta>

<margin>He speaks of a certain trifling Jesus, not of Christ, as is read in the *Seder Olam* <note>The *Seder Olam Rabbah* is a 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology detailing the history of the world from creation to the revolt of Bar Kokhba.</note>.</margin>...to be that many evil and shameful things are said in the Talmud concerning Jesus the Nazarene. However, these things are not related to our Savior Jesus, but to a certain other person. For as the Talmudic histories narrate in the chapter <term>Helec</term> <note>Referring to the chapter "Helek" in the tractate Sanhedrin of the Babylonian Talmud.</note>, while the Second Temple was standing and Hyrcanus the Maccabee (the son of Simon the Maccabee) was reigning, a certain Rabbi Joshua, son of Perachiah, was returning from Alexandria to Jerusalem. He entered an inn along with his disciples and, looking at the house, said: "How beautiful it is!" But one of his disciples, Jesus by name, who was also called a Nazarene, believing that his teacher had spoken those words about the innkeeper's wife, replied and said: "Truly she is beautiful, if only she did not have deep-set eyes." The Rabbi was then kindled with a sudden anger against him and said: "Wretch! Do you think of such a nefarious deed?" With this said, he immediately cast him out from his company and that of his fellows with a curse of excommunication. Wherefore this Jesus, seeing himself affected by such contempt and reproach, set up a stone and bowed down to worship it, leading many Jews to the worship of that same idol. He was also a sorcerer, and was eventually hanged for his crimes. From this, it is read concerning him in the chapter *Sotah*: <note>original: "ולא כרבי יהושע בן פרחיה שהיה דוחה ישו הנצרי בשתי ידים"</note> This is: **Not like Rabbi Joshua, who repulsed Jesus the Nazarene with both hands.** Since, therefore, in various places of the Talmud itself, this Jesus the Nazarene is mentioned—born of an adulteress and a polluted woman, an idolater, a sorcerer, a subverter of the law, and finally hanged with great dishonor—very many people, nearly innumerable due to ignorance of history and perhaps deceived by the wickedness of more recent Rabbis, think all those shameful things are said about our most glorious Savior Jesus. But the falsehood of this error can be most clearly proven by this: that as is also evident in the Talmudic histories, that Hyrcanus the Maccabee under whom this Jesus the Nazarene lived (to whom all those shameful things are referred) reigned approximately 110 years before Pontius Pilate, under whom Jesus Christ suffered.

<margin>Regarding the third point</margin>Lastly, to that point that the Jews assert the Talmudic traditions were handed down by God to Moses along with the law on Mount Sinai, then revealed by Moses to the ancient fathers in a succeeding order, and finally written down in the Talmud by their ancient Doctors: I say that to believe this of everything in the Talmud is nothing other than the madness of a headlong mind. But regarding those things which taste and smell of Catholic truth, and which put forward the sayings of the prophets and holy fathers, and express the Christian faith in a certain wonderful and incredible way (as we shall say most extensively in the following sections, God willing), and which both confound and destroy the perfidy of the more recent Jews—I do not think this should be denied at all. For traditions of this kind are entirely contrary to those things which the Jews of our time think, erring about the Messiah and very many other things. From this it follows that such things are by no means to be rejected, even if they are found among such perfidious people; just as no one, unless entirely deprived of his mind, would despise the Law and the Prophets simply because he found them among them. Nor would anyone, unless 

<column-break/>

lacking reason, despise a precious gemstone because it was found in the head of a dragon or a toad. Nor would anyone, unless foolish and insane, think honey should be rejected because it is the spit of bees, or reject something else perhaps less worthy because it is found among those animals which have a sting with poison—provided he knew how to convert it to his own useful purposes or those of his people, and did not ignore how to avoid the harm of the sting. Therefore, traditions of this kind are by no means to be rejected: both because they could have reached those who wrote them from Moses and the Prophets and the rest of the fathers in a succeeding order—indeed, we can think they came from nowhere else than from the prophets and those holy fathers—and especially because nothing so powerful can be found to refute the impudence of the Jews, and nothing so effective to convict their wickedness. Finally, what is more pleasant to a Christian than to snatch the sword from the hands of the enemies and, following the example of David, cut off the head of the infidels with their own blade, or like Judith, sever it with their own dagger?

<margin>The decree of Clement V.</margin>For this reason, it was not done without divine providence that Pope Clement V, with the approval of the holy council, established that the Talmudic books of the Jews should be translated into the Latin language by faithful men skilled in the Hebrew tongue, and should be publicly read by Christians. This is found in the *Clementines*, under the heading "Regarding Teachers" [*De Magistris*], where it is said among other things: **With the approval of this holy council, we have provided for the erection of schools for the types of languages listed below wherever the Roman Curia happens to reside, as well as in the studies of Paris, Oxford, Bologna, and Salamanca; decreeing that in each of those places there shall be maintained Catholic men having sufficient knowledge of the Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, and Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> languages—namely, two experts in each language—who shall direct the schools there and, faithfully translating books from those languages into Latin, shall successfully teach others those languages and transfer their skill through diligent instruction to them, so that being sufficiently instructed and taught in such languages, they may, with God as the author, produce the hoped-for fruit, being about to propagate the faith healthfully among those infidel peoples.** Thus it is said there. Where it is spoken regarding the translating and public reading of the Jews' books, it is not to be understood regarding the Bible, since it has been translated so many times; nor does it belong to the Jews, but rather to us, or at least it is common to both. Instead, it must be understood regarding other books of the Jews, and especially the Talmudic ones, in which so many Catholic truths are contained, as will be most extensively clear in what follows. Therefore, from all these things that have been said, it is clearer than the midday light that the Talmud itself is to be received by Christians—though not in everything, but only in those things which are good. The ancient Talmudists themselves confess this, as is clearly evident in the book <term>Hagbiga</term> <note>The tractate Hagigah in the Talmud.</note>, where it is read among other things: **What is it that is written in Malachi 2: "Because the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, since he is the Angel of the Lord of hosts"? ### CHAPTER VIII.

->*That through Talmudic traditions, corruptions of the Holy Scriptures are best corrected, which are found everywhere both in our edition—whether Greek or Latin—and in the Hebrew text.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

Who, then, was the author of these corruptions which you assert are corrected through Talmudic traditions? And when did they happen? Specifically, was it before Christ’s passion, or after? GALATINUS. The impudence of certain younger Jews is so great that they do not blush to blame them on Saint Ezra <note>The biblical priest and scribe who led the return from Babylon</note>. But we easily prove they lie impiously from this: if Ezra (as they falsely say) had done it, certainly such depravations and corruptions would not be called <term>תקון סופרים</term> *Tikkun Soferim* <note>original: "Ticcun sophrim"</note>, that is, "Aptations or corrections of the scribes or sages," but <term>תקון עזרא</term> *Tikkun Ezra*, that is, "Aptations or corrections of Ezra." From this it is clearly evident that the author of them was not Ezra, but the scribes themselves who lived after Ezra. However, it can be gathered that these occurred long before the birth of Christ from the fact that Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel, the Aramaic translator <note>Chaldaicus interpres</note> of the divine scripture, and a student of Rabbi Hillel, followed these *Tikkun Soferim*—that is, the scribes' corrections—in many places in his translation. CAPNIO. If, therefore, those who made these types of corruptions in the sacred writings preceded the coming of Christ, it must undoubtedly be said that they did not do so motivated by hatred [for Him]. consistent with the Christian faith, which the ancient Jews strove with all their might to hide from the Gentiles. For this reason also, the <term>סופרים</term> *Soferim* <note>original: "sophrim"</note>, that is, the scribes or sages, erased many things from the divine scriptures as if they were absurd, or as if they were things that the nations of the Gentiles should not even dream of—as men who did not yet fully weigh the loftiness of the divine counsel regarding the salvation of the human race. ...what a weariness <note>Latin: "vilitas"; usually translated as "weariness" in Malachi 1:13</note>, and you have made it expire, or you have afflicted it, says the Lord of hosts. Just as it is in Job chapter 11: **ותקותם מפח נפש**, that is, "And their hope is the affliction of the soul." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Moreover, that this word **והפחתם** *vehippachtem* signifies expiration, or affliction, or vexation, is excellently shown by Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and commentator</note> when he says: "That which is read in Job chapter 31, 'And the soul of its lords **הפחתי** *hippachti*,' that is, 'I have afflicted'; likewise in Malachi chapter 1, **והפחתם** *vehippachtem* signifies labor and vexation, or the affliction and vexation of the soul. For he who has affliction or vexation of soul is just as if his soul were expiring and departing from him." Thus he says. From this it is clear that in Malachi chapter 1, where our edition <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has, "Behold, of labor, and you have puffed it away, says the Lord of hosts," it is entirely corrupted. Thus he says. And first, that passage in **Genesis 18** which is held among us as, "Abraham truly still stood before the Lord," ought to be corrected to, "But God still stood before Abraham." <note>The Scribes felt it was disrespectful to say God stood waiting for a human, so they flipped the subjects.</note> Next, that which in **Psalm 17** <note>Psalm 18 in modern Bibles</note> our edition has as, "And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself shall teach me," should also be corrected to, "And you shall give me your shield of salvation, and your right hand shall strengthen me, and your humility, or your poverty, or your gentleness, shall multiply me, or nourish me." 

Also, that which is read among us in **Numbers 11**, "And let them find grace in your eyes, lest I be afflicted by such great evils," should be corrected to, "If I have found grace before your eyes, and let me not see your evil." <note>The original sense implied Moses seeing God's "evil" (punishment), which scribes changed to "my wretchedness."</note> Also, that which we have in **Job 7**, "What shall I do to you, O guardian of men? Why have you set me against you, and I have become heavy to myself?" should be corrected to, "What shall I do to you, O guardian of man? Why have you set me as a target against you, and I shall be a burden upon you?" 

Likewise, that which is read in our version of **Job 32**, "But they had only condemned Job," is correctly to be read as, "And they shall condemn God, or act impiously toward God." Furthermore, that which is held among us in **Ezekiel 8**, "Is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they should do these abominations which they have done here? For filling the land with iniquity, they have turned to provoke me: and behold, they apply the branch to my nostrils," is to be corrected to: "Is it a light thing for the house of Judah to have done the abominations they have done here? For they have filled the land with iniquity, and they shall repeat to provoke me, and they themselves shall be sending a stench to my nose." 

Moreover, that which is in our version of **Hosea 4**, "According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame," should be corrected to, "As is their multitude, so they sinned against me; I will change My glory into shame." Finally, that which our edition has in **Jeremiah 2**, "But my people have changed their glory into an idol," must be corrected thus: "But my people have changed My glory for that which will not profit."

Then there is the second mode of **תקון סופרים** *Ticcun Sophrim* <term>Correction of the Scribes</term>, which is found in certain places of Holy Scripture where, leaving aside what the Prophets had written, they did not change the letters themselves, but presumed to add points <note>vowel marks</note> differently than the text naturally required. For the Hebrews do not have vowels, but use certain points in place of vowels. Therefore, from that variation of points, it is read far differently than what was written, and a far different sense is rendered.

<margin>The second mode of the corruption of Holy Scripture.</margin>

->**CAPNIO:** Who pointed the Bible?<-

**GAL.:** Moses (as you yourself well know) did not point the Law; hence that which the Jews keep with veneration in their Synagogues they have written without points. Nor did any of the prophets point his own book. But later men pointed the Law, the Prophets, and the **Hagiographa** <term>the "Holy Writings" or Ketuvim, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</term>. Some therefore say that Ezra first pointed the sacred volumes. Others, however, affirm that it was not Ezra, but two others who lived after Ezra, one of whom was called **Ben-Naphtali** and the other **Ben-Asher**, who first applied points to the sacred letters. Their opinion is the more common one. Now, you might relate some examples of those things which the Sophrim—that is, the scribes—corrupted by this kind of change of points in the sacred letters.

**GAL.:** One of these is that which is read in the **second book of Kings, chapter 16** <note>2 Samuel 16 in modern Bibles</note>. For there it was written among them: "Perhaps the Lord will look upon his humility, or affliction, or poverty, or gentleness, and the Lord will return good to me for his cursing." But the Scribes, wishing to "correct" this, took the word **בעוני** *beonjo*, which naturally ought to have been pointed to mean "his humility" or "his affliction," and instead pointed it as **בעיי** *beeni*, which means "in my eye." Because of this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explains this word **בעיי** *beeni*—that is, "in my eye"—as "into the tears of my eye." 

Something very similar to this is in **Micah 1**: "I will lay all her idols in desolation, or destruction." And a little later: "Over this I will wail and lament; I will go stripped and naked." And shortly after: "For her wound is painful and desperate. For it has come even to Judah, it has reached even to the gates of my people, even to Jerusalem. In Gath, do not announce it; weeping, do not weep. In the house of dust, I have been rolled in the dust," **התפלשתי** *hithpallashti*, that is, "I am rolled or surrounded," or "I rolled or surrounded myself." This is how it is and was written. But the Scribes, wishing to correct it, pointed it as **התפלשי** *hithpallashi*, which means "roll yourself" (in the feminine gender). From these words of Micah, it is clearly held that God was to be rolled in the ground or dust—notwithstanding that the Prophet used **התפלשתי** *hithpallashti*, that is, "I rolled myself" (in the past tense), following the manner of the prophets, who very often use the past for the future to suggest the absolute certainty of a future event. Hence, regarding **Isaiah 42**, "I have done these things for them," Rabbi Solomon says in his gloss: "'I have done for them' means 'I will do for them'; for every prophetic tongue speaks of the future as if it were already done." Thus says Rabbi Solomon. 

It should not be ignored here that this word **עפר** *aphar*, which is ground or moistened dust, was also used by Abraham when, speaking with the Lord and wishing to express the lowliness and condition of the human body, he said in **Genesis 18**: "Behold, I pray, I have taken upon me to speak to the Lord, I who am **עפר** *aphar*, that is, ground or moistened dust, **ואפר** *veepher*...

of dust I was wrapped," or "I surrounded myself." Finally, the third mode of the <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> by which the Holy Scripture happened to be altered, is when Moses and the Prophets left what they wrote in the text itself, but placed something else outside in the margin. They call what is in the margin the <term>Keri</term> <note>Hebrew: "read"</note>, meaning it is to be read aloud, and what is inside the text they call the <term>Ketiv</term> <note>Hebrew: "written"</note>, meaning it is to be written. And the <term>Targum</term> <note>the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note>, for the sake of courtesy, placed in its stead *Iscauenna* <note>original Hebrew: ישכבנה</note>, which means "he shall lie with her." And this is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, a correction of the scribes. Thus says Rabbi Selomo. Likewise, the same Rabbi says regarding **Isaiah 36**: "And Rabshakeh said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?" The gloss of Rabbi Selomo there says: *Horehem* <note>original Hebrew: חוריהם</note> means their dung, which is the waste exiting from the lower opening; but the Scribes corrected this into a beautiful and courteous language, wishing that *tsoatham* <note>original Hebrew: צואתם</note>, meaning "their excrement," should be read. For the teachers decreed that scriptures written discourteously for the purpose of reproach should be read courteously and politely. Just as in **Deuteronomy chapter 28**, where it is written *baapholim* <note>original Hebrew: בעפולים</note>, meaning "with tumors," they placed in the margin to be read *battehorim* <note>original Hebrew: בטחורים</note>, meaning "with hemorrhoids" or "dysentery." Likewise, where Moses wrote *Isgalenna*, that is "he shall ravish her," they placed on the outside *Iscauenna*, that is "he shall lie" or "sleep with her." Furthermore, in **Isaiah chapter 36**, where "their dung" is written, they placed on the outside "their excrement."

<column-break/>

A Likewise, where the Prophet put *sethnehem* <note>original Hebrew: שיניהם</note>, meaning "their urine," the scribes put *meme raglehem* <note>original Hebrew: מימי רגליהם</note>, meaning "the waters of their feet." And many other similar things. All this is from Rabbi Selomo. Also in the prophet **Hosea chapter 9**, it is thus: and it was written *ci gam oi lahem besari* <note>original Hebrew: כי גם אוי להם בשרי</note>, "for even woe to them, my incarnation is from them." But the Scribes, contrary to the nature of the word itself, pointed the word *besari* <note>meaning "my incarnation" or "my flesh"</note> as *besuri* <note>original Hebrew: בשורי</note>, which B signifies "in my departing." I say "contrary to the nature of the word" because *besuri*, which is inside the text, is written with the letter *shin* <note>ש</note>, exactly as the Prophet Hosea had written it. Therefore *besari*, meaning "my incarnation" or "my flesh," ought to have been pointed with an *aleph* <note>א</note>, as if saying *basar*, "let flesh come." But *besuri*, which they placed on the outside and which signifies "in my departing," is written with the letter *samech* <note>ס</note>. Whence Rabbi Selomo, explaining this place, says: "For even woe to them," namely the fathers, *besuri* as if it were *besuri* <note>with a samech</note>, that is, "in C my departing from them." And it is one of those words in which a *shin* is written and a *samech* is read. Also <term>Rabbi Chimhi</term> <note>David Kimhi, or Radak, a medieval grammarian and commentator</note> in the *Book of Roots* <note>Sefer HaShorashim</note> says that "For even woe to them, *besuri*" is written with the letter *shin* and read with *samech*. All this from Rabbi Selomo. From these things which we have said here concerning the third mode of the <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, three texts among others are corrected. The first of these is in **Deuteronomy chapter 28**, which D is held among us as: "You shall take a wife, and another shall sleep with her." This text, according to the Hebrew truth, is to be corrected thus: "You shall betroth a wife, and another man shall ravish her." The second text is in **Isaiah chapter 36**, which reads among us: "And Rabshakeh said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak all these words? And not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you?" This text should be corrected thus: E "And Rabshakeh said, Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?" Finally, the third text is **Hosea 9**, which the author of our edition, following the error of the <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, translated thus: "But also woe to them when I shall depart from them." This text, however, must be thoroughly corrected to: "Because also woe to them, my incarnation," or F "my flesh is from them." **CAPNIO** <note>Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist</note>: Tell me, I pray, any others of these types among them, if there are any. **GAL** <note>Pietro Galatino, the author of the work</note>: Truly, they are so many that it is almost impossible to tell them all. I will, therefore, tell some others from the many. However, I would wish that if any of these things already said happen to be repeated, it should not be attributed to rambling. For it is hardly possible to report the words of those who happened to say the same things separately and precisely (as we G must do when acting against the Jews, lest they deny what we say) without repeating the same thing several times. Thus, in the book *Siphre* <note>an ancient halakhic midrash on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>, which is highly authentic among them, it is held among other things regarding **Numbers chapter 10**: "Arise, Lord, and let [your enemies] be scattered..."

### BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> ...your enemies, and let those who hate you flee. <note>Referencing Numbers 10:35, the prayer said when the Ark of the Covenant moved.</note> Does He who spoke and the world was made have those who hate Him? Scripture announces and teaches that everyone who hates Israel is regarded as if he hated Him who founded the world by His word. And so He Himself says in **Zechariah chapter 2**: "For he who touches you, touches the apple of His eye." <note>Zechariah 2:8</note> Regarding this, Rabbi Judas says: It was not originally said "the apple of *his* eye," but "the apple of *my* eye" <note>original: "pupillam oculi mei"</note>. From what is written in the law, it can be said: Scripture was speaking against the One above—that is, against God—but the later version of scripture <note>Galatinus uses "scriptura recens" to refer to the text as edited by the Scribes</note> renamed it; <margin>B</margin> that is, it said one thing in place of what had been written. It is the same case in **Job chapter 7**: "Why hast thou set me as a mark against thee? And I shall be a burden to thee?" <note>Job 7:20. The current Hebrew text reads "a burden to myself," which Galatinus argues was changed from "a burden to thee [God]."</note> From what is written in the law, it can be said: Scripture was speaking against the One above, that is against God, but the later scripture renamed it; that is, it named something else in place of what had been written. Similar to this is that passage in **Ezekiel chapter 8**: "And they are putting a branch to my nose." <note>Ezekiel 8:17. Galatinus suggests the Scribes changed "my nose" to "their nose" to avoid the image of God having a nose that could be offended by a stench.</note> From what is written in the law, it can be said: something similar is held in **Habakkuk chapter 1**: "Art thou not from everlasting, O Lord my God, my Holy One? Thou shalt not die." <note>Habakkuk 1:12. Galatinus argues the original was "Thou [God] shalt not die," but scribes feared this implied God *could* die, so they changed it to "We shall not die."</note> From what is written in the law, it can be said: Scripture speaks against God, but in its place the later scripture said: "we shall not die." Similar to this is that in **Psalm 106**: "And they changed my glory." For that, however, the later scripture said: "their glory." <note>Psalm 106:20</note> Still similar is that in **Numbers chapter 11**: "And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favor in thy sight; and let me not see thy wretchedness." <note>Numbers 11:15. The standard text reads "my wretchedness."</note> From what is written in the law, it can be said: Scripture spoke against the One above, but in its place the later scripture said something else. Similar moreover to this is that in **Numbers chapter 12**: "As one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of our mother's womb, and half of our flesh is consumed." <note>Numbers 12:12</note> From what is written in the law, it can be said: Scripture was speaking against the One above, but the later scripture renamed it—which the scribes corrected—by putting "his mother" and "his flesh." All these things are from the book <term>Siphre</term> <note>Sifrei, an ancient Jewish legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>. In many other books, many things of this kind are found, <margin>E</margin> and especially in the commentaries of **Rabbi Moses the Preacher** <note>Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan of Narbonne (11th century)</note> on **Genesis**, upon that passage in **Genesis chapter 18**: "And Abraham still stood before God." <note>Genesis 18:22. Traditional Jewish commentary notes that the original text said "The Lord still stood before Abraham," but was changed for piety.</note> And in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>The Midrash on the Psalms</note>, that is in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that verse of **Psalm 18**: "And thou hast given me the shield of thy salvation." And at the end of the book of **Ben-Asher**, which is called <term>Dikduk</term> <note>A work on Hebrew grammar and Masoretic notes</note>, and in very many other places, in which both those things we have related and not a few others of this kind are placed—differently, however, according as they occur to be explained by the Doctors of the Jews themselves. <margin>F</margin> But omitting the others, I will bring forward a few of these which are placed in the aforementioned commentaries of the same Rabbi Moses the Preacher in the place cited above, besides those which have been brought from there. For there, among other things, is placed that verse of **Psalm 22**: "Dogs have compassed me, the synagogue or council of the malignant have besieged me, <term>כרו</term> *caru*, that is, they pierced my hands and my feet." They removed from there <term>כרו</term> *caru*, which signifies "they pierced," and they wrote <term>כארי</term> *caari*, which is the same as <margin>G</margin> "like a lion." <note>This is a famous point of contention: the Christian reading "they pierced" vs. the Masoretic Jewish reading "like a lion."</note> Likewise in that which is written in the book of **1 Kings chapter 12**: "We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse; return <term>לאלהיך</term> *le-elohecha*, that is, to your gods, O Israel." They removed from there

<page-num>36</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> <term>לאלהיך</term> *le-elohecha*, that is "to your gods," and they placed <term>לאהליך</term> *le-ohalecha*, which signifies "to your tents." <note>1 Kings 12:16. Galatinus argues the rebels originally called Israel back to their idols, but scribes softened it to "tents."</note> And with certain other things of this sort interspersed, the same Rabbi proceeds: "From this, however, it is clear why the men of the Great Synagogue were called <term>Sophrim</term>, that is, counters, because they themselves counted all the letters which are in the law, and they investigated and explained them." All these things are in the exposition on Genesis by **Rabbi Moses the Preacher**: where also very many other things of this kind are placed, which I have thought should be omitted lest I become longer than is right. By those things, however, which we have now brought forward in the two above-mentioned traditions, three texts are corrected beyond the others, which are read as vitiated and corrupt both among us and among the Hebrews. And the first text is that which is held among us in **Numbers chapter 12** thus: "What is cast forth from his mother's womb, behold now half of his flesh is devoured." This text, however, is to be chastened thus: "What is in its exit from the matrix of **our** mother, and half of **our** flesh is eaten." The second text is that which is read among us in **2 Kings chapter 12** <note>Actually 1 Kings 12:16</note> thus: <margin>C</margin> "We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse; return to thy tents, O Israel." This text also ought to be corrected thus: "We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse; return to **your gods**, O Israel." Finally, the third text is that which our edition has in **Habakkuk chapter 1**: "Art thou not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One, and we shall not die?" This also <margin>D</margin> ought to be chastened thus: "Art thou not from of old, O Lord my God, my Holy One; **thou shalt not die**?" From all these things, therefore (as has been plainly seen), not only is the sacrilegious audacity of the scribes detected, but the text of the Holy Scripture itself is most excellently chastened: not only among them, but also among us, who in our editions, both Greek and Latin, have followed the depravations of those same scribes until now.

**CAPNIO.** <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note> I wonder that Saint Jerome (to say nothing of other interpreters of the divine page), who stood out among our people, both Greek and Latin, as a student of Hebrew letters above the rest, did not detect these depravations.

**GALATINUS.** That ought by no means to seem a wonder to you, since these depravations cannot be detected except through the traditions of the Talmudists, contained in the **Talmud** and the aforementioned books, which never came to the notice of Jerome, as can easily be gathered from his words. For he himself, writing to Oceanus, says: "By labor and price, I had Bar-Anina the Jew as a nightly teacher; for he feared the Jews, and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus." <note>Jerome had to study Hebrew with a Jewish teacher in secret at night.</note> Just as he had a penury of Jewish masters, so perhaps he also had a penury of books, and especially of the Talmud itself, which the Jews strove to hide with all their might on account of the secrets of the Messiah contained in it which are consistent with our faith. Wherefore it is not at all to be wondered at if he did not find those things. For if he had found them, he would surely have judged it a crime to pass over such great mysteries of our faith in silence, and he would have correctly translated the truth which Moses and the other Prophets had placed in the aforementioned locations.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>How one should proceed against the Jews through their own scriptures.</margin>

->CAPNIO.<-

Now that we have been worthy to approach you—you who, inspired by divine power, are able to reveal these secrets so wonderful and divine lying hidden in the Talmudic books of the Jews—we ask you with all earnestness that you think none of these things should be hidden from us. Rather, for the honor of Almighty God himself, for the glory of the most holy Christian Church, for the confirmation of the Orthodox faith, for the salvation of souls, and for the manifestation of Catholic truth, do not neglect to unlock each of them for us as we shall ask. GAL. I indeed, as much as I am able, shall strive to satisfy your wishes. But if I say anything good, attribute it not to me but to God, from whom (as the *Polycraticus* <note>A work by John of Salisbury</note> says) *all good things proceed* <note>original Greek: "πάντα τὰ ἀγαθὰ προέρχονται"</note>; and rightly so. For as Plato bears witness, *from the one Good come all good things* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀγαθοῦ πάντα τὰ ἀγαθὰ"</note>. But whatever evils there be, ascribe them to my ignorance. First, therefore, one must know that the sacred Old Scripture contained all the articles of the Catholic faith wrapped in various figures and enigmas, and as if covered with veils and sealed with certain seals. This was so that when Christ came, the veils and seals being removed by Him, they might be clearly revealed and become public; so that when the Truth was present, the figures might cease; when the Light appeared, darkness might be driven away; and with the sun now risen, whatever was obscure might be rendered clear and bright. For Christ Himself is the Truth, the Light, and the Sun of Justice, who (according to John the Evangelist) "illuminates every man coming into this world." Wherefore He Himself said in John chapter 8: *I am the light of the world; he who follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life* <note>original Greek: "ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου· ὁ ἀκολουθῶν ἐμοὶ οὐ μὴ περιπατήσῃ ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ, ἀλλ’ ἕξει τὸ φῶς τῆς ζωῆς"</note>. But the younger Jews, since they are utterly blinded by the impiety of their treachery, twist the correct sense of Divine Scripture against us and wage war upon us. But we, through the traditions of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Sages of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>—who, explaining the sayings of the Law and the Prophets, speak more clearly about these very articles—easily convict them. Therefore, so that their falsehood may be better detected and the Catholic truth itself may shine forth more brightly, I will do two things in each of these secrets. First, I will bring forward the very sayings of the Law and the Prophets which they strive to pervert with false expositions and twist against us, and I will explain them correctly for our purpose through their own scriptures, refuting their false expositions by <term>Talmudic</term> authorities. Then, I will

<column-break/>

prove the very secret of Catholic truth against them by the testimonies of the <term>Talmudists</term>. For thus are Talmudists easily convicted by Talmudists. HOC. <note>Jakob van Hoogstraten, the Inquisitor</note> If Talmudists could be convicted by Talmudists regarding the error of their treachery, they would surely be divided among themselves and opposed to each other. But since they have all always been and persist in being obstinate in the same error of treachery, it follows indeed that they are neither divided among themselves nor opposed to each other regarding this kind of error. Therefore, it is clear that <term>Talmudists</term> can by no means be convicted by <term>Talmudists</term>. GAL. Although the Babylonian <term>Talmud</term> (to speak of that which was published last) was compiled in the year 477 after the birth of Christ, nevertheless, there are three kinds of Talmudists. For some preceded the advent of Christ, and some followed after, up until that time when the same Talmud was finished. Both of these are called Talmudists because the Talmud itself was compiled from their writings (as we have said elsewhere). Whence both are not without reason called the "ancient Talmudists." But those are called the "more recent" or "younger Talmudists" who, following long after, have attempted to pervert the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets concerning the <term>Messiah</term> against Christian dogma, in opposition to the opinions of the ancient Talmudists. That these [modern] Talmudists, therefore, can be convicted by those ancients who preceded the birth of Christ, no one doubts, as will be shown most extensively in the following pages. Furthermore, no one should think to doubt that they can also be convicted by those who happened to live after Christ until the edition of the Talmud itself, since, moreover, the greatest part of them accepted the faith of Christ, even if they remained zealots for the Mosaic Law <note>original: "legalium æmulatores"</note>, as we have shown above. But since these [modern Jews] have never received the faith of Christ, but rather do not cease to attack it with every effort, it is plainly established that those [ancients] and these [moderns] do not dwell in the same error of faith. For although those [ancients] erred in keeping the legal rites, they nevertheless adhered to Christ and confessed Him. But these [moderns] both keep the legal rites and stubbornly deny and persecute Christ. These [moderns], moreover, since they are utterly ignorant of their [the ancients'] way and art of philosophizing and theologizing, turn many mysteries and secrets, which the ancients handed down enigmatically and parabolically, into mockery and blasphemies. For which reasons, when we shall disprove the errors of these [moderns] through the sayings of those [ancients], we shall most excellently overcome these by those. And so (as I said) <term>Talmudists</term> will be convicted by <term>Talmudists</term>. Wherefore let us now proceed to the secrets of Catholic truth.

# ON THE DIVINE TRINITY
### AND ON THE DIVINE NAMES THROUGH
#### WHICH THE TRINITY OF GOD ITSELF, WITH THE 
#### undivided unity of essence, and His perfections 
#### are most excellently introduced.

->CHAPTER ONE.<-

->*That God is Three and One.*<-

<margin>CAPNIO.</margin>
Among other things, the more recent Jews <note>Galatinus distinguishes between "ancient" Jews (the Talmudists/prophets) and "recent" Jews of his own era, whom he views as having lost the true interpretation of their own scriptures.</note> especially object to us that when they hear us confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they say we worship three gods and that we propose a plurality of Gods. This is something that we, in fact, abhor far more than they do. For that reason, you must first prove from the sayings of the Prophets and the testimonies of the ancient Talmudists that God is both Three and One. <margin>GAL.</margin> The Christian religion does indeed believe that God is one in the simplicity of substance and nature. But it confesses three persons, which are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whose properties are fatherhood, generation, and procession: these are not three in essence nor in nature, but are purely one. Therefore, God is indeed three in persons, but one in essence. Moreover, there is no need to prove with many words that God is one, nor to dwell longer on proving it; for the unity of God itself is so firm and so fixed a conception of the mind that, naturally, there cannot be anything but one God. Both the Jews and all who believe the Law confess and proclaim this. <margin>CAPNIO.</margin> It is enough here, then, if concerning the sacrament of the divine Trinity, the error of the younger Jews is refuted through the opinions of the ancients. <margin>GAL.</margin> In a matter so arduous and difficult, their foundation must first be utterly demolished; then, the falsehood of the expositions by which they pervert the sacred letters must be rejected. Wishing to avoid prolixity, we shall do both at once in this matter as in many others. Therefore, the reason upon which they lay the foundation of this error is primarily that they poorly understand and falsely explain that which is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 6:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one" <note>original Hebrew: שמע ישראל יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד (*Shema Yisrael Adonai Eloheinu Adonai Echad*). This is the central prayer of Judaism.</note>. Although these words are clear in themselves, nevertheless, because of the word "one" which is placed there, the Jews of our age, struck by blindness of mind, take the cause of their error from the very place where they ought most to gain a notion of the Trinity itself. For from this, they think God is "one" in such a way that they entirely exclude a plurality of persons from Him. <margin>B</margin> <note>CAPNIO speaking</note> Our text contains these words differently than you have translated them. For it says: "Hear, Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one." <margin>GAL.</margin> I admit it is so. For thus the Greek text has it, which our version follows in almost everything. For it says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one" <note>original Greek: "ἄκουε Ἰσραὴλ, κύριος ὁ θεός σου κύριος εἷς ἐστιν"</note>. But it is certainly clear that the Hebrew text expresses the truth against the Jews themselves far better than our version, whether Greek or Latin. The reason why our edition, both Greek and Latin, has "Lord" in this place (where I translated "God") <margin>C</margin> is because the Hebrew text there has <term>יהוה</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, often transliterated as YHWH.</note>, which is the name of God, that "four-lettered" name which designates God not through an effect, but through His essence. But since the divine essence, according to its own proper being, can in no way be grasped by the mind, it is therefore considered a sacrilege among the Jews for the name itself to be pronounced by the mouth as the letters themselves sound from which it is composed. Therefore, wherever they encounter this name, they do not dare to utter it at all, but in its place they utter this name <term>Adonai</term> (אדני), which is the same as "Lord"; yet the letters of the name itself signify not "Lord," but "God" through essence. The author of both the Greek and Latin editions, therefore, translated the name according to the significance of its pronunciation, but omitted the significance of the writing, which is more important. But I, to whom the truth is especially dear—
