<header>BOOK TWO.</header>

...is to reveal the truth that the Jews deny through their own scriptures. I have translated this according to its proper meaning, so that I might show more clearly that the Triune and one God is designated in the aforementioned words. For that great Moses did not place the name of God there three times for any other reason than to distinctly suggest the Trinity of divine persons. However, in the word "one," which he added immediately after, he hinted that the three divine persons are not three Gods, but one God. This is (as Damascene says) <note>original Greek: "μία οὐσία, μία φύσις, μία θεότης"</note> **one essence, one nature, one deity.** Therefore, the Trinity of persons in no way detracts from the unity of the divine nature. 

Furthermore, the Jews can by no means deny that through the tripled name of God in those same words, three divine persons are designated—namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—since Rabbi Simeon, son of Yohai, in the book called the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The Zohar is the foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), attributed by tradition to the 2nd-century sage Simeon bar Yochai.</note>, says the following regarding this text: <margin>Zohar</margin> <margin>Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai.</margin> <margin>Exposition of Rabbi Ibba.</margin> "Hear, O Israel: Rabbi Ibba says, this is the ancient Israel, **Lord** <note>original: "יהוה" (the Tetragrammaton)</note>, that is God, who is the principle of all things, the ancient of ancients, the garden of roots, and the perfection of all things. And He is called the Father, **Our God** <note>original: "אלהינו Elohenu"</note>, that is our God, the depth of rivers, and the fountain of sciences, which proceed from that Father. And the Son is called **Lord** <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, that is God: this is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the two, and is called the 'measure of the voice.' He is one, so that He may conclude and bind one with the other. For one cannot be divided from the other. And for this reason it says **Hear** <note>original: "שמע Scema"</note>, that is, gather together, O Israel, this Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and make Him one essence, and one substance, because whatever is in one, is in the other. He was the whole, He is the whole, and He shall be the whole." So says he. 

The same Rabbi Simeon also says there: "This secret of the Son shall not be revealed to everyone until the Messiah comes. Because then (as Isaiah says) the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of God, just as the waters cover the sea." So says he. Many others also wished that the Trinity of divine persons be signified by the name of God being placed three times in the same text, but because such a great mystery was to be revealed by the Messiah alone, they said it was not permitted for them to explain it; as is clearly evident through Rabbi Menahem Recanati in the book of the Zohar regarding the same text of Deuteronomy. For this reason, the Talmudists <note>The scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> did not speak as expressly about the mystery of the Trinity as the Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism.</note>, who explicitly bring forth the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, not only regarding this text, but also in many other places. <margin>Zohar</margin>

<margin>Why the mystery of the Trinity was not explicitly handed down under the Old Law.</margin> <margin>The mystery of the Trinity was to be explicitly revealed through the Messiah.</margin> **CAPNIO.** Why did God not wish the mystery of the Trinity to be handed down so explicitly in the Old Testament, but instead reserved it to be revealed in the future through the Messiah? **GALATINUS.** The Jewish people (as I do not doubt you know) were extremely prone to idolatry, and the entire Old Law was established to avoid this. Therefore, lest they fall into the error of those who worshiped many gods, it was cautiously arranged by divine providence that the secret of the divine Trinity itself should be handed down to them not explicitly, but implicitly. But since idolatry was to be utterly exploded by the Messiah, and the entire world was to be brought back to the worship of the one God, for that reason, the Sacrament of the Trinity was reserved for the days of the Messiah to be explicitly and openly revealed. This is also what every 

<column-break/>

school of the Cabalists plainly testifies, asserting that the secrets of the divine Trinity itself ought to remain hidden only until the time of the Messiah. At that time, however, when all suspicion of idolatrous error was to be removed, even the secrets of the divine Trinity itself were to be openly uncovered. 

**CAPNIO.** Since in the aforementioned words—"Hear, O Israel, God, our God, God is one"—the name of God is placed three times, why is it that "Our" is added only to the second name, and not to the first or the third? <margin>Why "Our" is added to the second name of God, and not the first or third.</margin> **GALATINUS.** That was certainly not done without reason. For from this it is clearly suggested that neither the Father, who is the first person in the Trinity, nor the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the same Trinity, but only the Son, who is the second person of the same Trinity, was to be ours through the participation in our humanity. To this, that which is written in Psalm 67 is also similar: "May God bless us, our God, may God bless us, and let all the ends of the earth fear him." Where, in the fact that "God" is placed three times, the distinction of the three divine persons is designated. In the fact that "Our" is joined only in the second place, it is hinted that only the Son would be ours through the assumption of our nature. In the fact that at the end it is said, "let them fear **him**," and not "them," the unity of the persons regarding nature and identity is shown. This is to openly demonstrate that the three divine persons are not three Gods, but only one God. 

Isaiah also showed this openly when he said in chapter 6, <note>original Hebrew: "קדוש קדוש קדוש יהוה צבאות מלא כל הארץ כבודו"</note> **Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory.** For in the fact that he says "Holy" three times, he expressly designates the three divine persons. This is openly proven by Rabbi Simeon, son of Yohai, and by Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, regarding this text. For Rabbi Simeon says thus in Hebrew: <note>original Hebrew: "קדוש זה אב קדוש זה בן קדוש זה רוח הקדש"</note> **Holy, this is the Father; Holy, this is the Son; Holy, this is the Holy Spirit.** And Rabbi Jonathan says thus in Aramaic: <note>original Aramaic: "קדוש אבא קדוש ברא קדוש רוחא קדישא"</note> **Holy Father, Holy Son, Holy Holy Spirit.** 

**CAPNIO.** Younger Jews would say here that this is by no means found in Jonathan. **GALATINUS.** It is indeed true that it is not found in those books of Jonathan which they now more frequently have at hand (as you yourself know), since their ancestors erased it from there, and wrote in that place as the books which happened to be written afterward contain. However, in the oldest books, which are very rare, it is found exactly as I have related. I myself saw one of these when I was in Lecce, at the time when the Jews were being expelled from the entire Kingdom of Naples by the order of the Catholic King. And that book in this place held exactly as I have related. Moreover (to return to the words of Isaiah), in the fact that after those three names—holy, holy, holy—immediately the name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God (YHWH), considered too sacred to pronounce in Jewish tradition.</note>, which is **Lord** <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, is placed only once, through which the divine essence is signified, it is clearly hinted that those three persons are not three Gods, but one God. Isaiah's words, just like those of Deuteronomy—"Hear, O Israel: the Lord, our God, the Lord is one"—are spoken by every Jew at least twice a day, namely in the morning and the evening. This custom is preserved among them to this day: so that while the Jews themselves pronounce these very words with their mouths, they might also testify in their hearts that they believe both in the trinity of divine persons and the unity of the divine essence, just as those words designate.

### CHAPTER II.

->*That the trinity of persons does not detract from the unity of the divine essence, through a reasoning founded upon the scriptures of the Jews.*<-

### CAPNIO.

Even if we should not fight with the Jews of our time using pure reason—since they have the eyes of their minds clouded by the error of faithlessness <note>original: "perfidiæ," a common historical term in Christian-Jewish polemics to describe the rejection of the Christian Gospel</note> and completely lack the light of reason by which they might perceive the truth—nevertheless, because they can by no means deny the reasoning that is founded upon their own scriptures, you would do well, my Galatinus, for the greater refutation of their error and the clearer expression of Catholic truth, if you would prove that the trinity of persons can exist with the unity of the divine essence, without any loss to that same unity, using reasoning strengthened by Hebrew testimonies. 

GALATINUS: I shall certainly do so, and indeed as briefly as possible. Would they not, therefore, consider it granted that God is in different places? 

CAPNIO: Entirely so. For the Talmudists affirm this everywhere, and the Holy Scripture asserts it; which especially in Psalm 139 among them <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 139:8-10. The author notes it is numbered the same in the Jewish tradition.</note> says: "If I ascend to the heavens, you are there; and if I lie down in hell, you are present. If I take the wings of the morning, if I dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me." <note>original Hebrew: אם אסק שמים שם אתה ואציעה שאול הנך אשא כנפי שחר אשכנה באחרית ים : גם שם ידך תנחני ותאחזני ימינך</note> From these words, it is clearly evident that God is everywhere. 

GALATINUS: Now, this cannot be true according to different parts. For since God is a spirit and supremely simple—as they themselves also say—He is entirely lacking in any diversity or composition of parts. For in the "Book of Formation," <margin>Sefer Yetzirah</margin> which they call <term>Sefer Yetzirah</term> <note>The Sefer Yetzirah is one of the oldest books of Jewish mysticism, detailing the creation of the world through numbers (Sefirot) and letters.</note>, in the section where the ten <term>Sefirot</term> <note>Sefirot are the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals Himself.</note> are placed—that is, the ten incorporeal and abstract numbers, or rather ten incorporeal and secret unities, the first of which is placed as God Himself, the most abstract of all—it is written as follows: "The Spirit of the living God <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים חי</note>, blessed and more blessed is the name of Him who is the life of the ages, voice, spirit, and word: this is the Holy Spirit," <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים חי ברוך ומבורך שמו של חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבר זה רוח הקדש</note> whose beginning (as other books have it) cannot be searched out, and whose end has no limit. Thus it is said there. Nor would they say that He is in different places successively. For then He would be changeable according to location, which they entirely deny, since it can in no way befit God. For since He is eternal, im-

<column-break/>

<page-num>44</page-num>
<margin>A</margin> measurable, and supremely simple, He cannot be changed according to time, nor according to place, nor according to form. Therefore, they also, just like us, assert that He is altogether immutable: since God says of Himself in Malachi, chapter 3: "I am the Lord, I change not." <note>original Hebrew: אני יהוה לא שניתי</note> For that reason, they must confess that God (though He is one) is, in the truth of His unity, wholly in different places at one and the same time. Therefore, it is also necessary for them to grant that the Divinity itself (even if it exists as only one in number) can be 
<margin>B</margin> wholly and simultaneously in several persons. If they grant that first point, why do they deny this second one, when one must be granted no more than the other? But they certainly cannot deny this, since not only the ancient Talmudists and Kabbalists (as has already been shown) confess it everywhere, but the divine utterances also bear witness to it. For wherever in the sacred letters of the Old Testament the essence of the one God is suggested, 
<margin>C</margin> almost always in the same place a plurality of three persons is also hinted at. And conversely, in whatever place the trinity of persons is expressed, almost always in that same place the unity of the divine substance is also explained, lest either the trinity of persons be excluded from the divine nature because of the unity of the singular God, or several Gods be believed in because of the trinity of persons: but rather, so that in the one case, the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>Hypostasis is a theological term for a distinct person of the Trinity who shares the same essence.</note> themselves may be believed to be distinct from one another without confusion, while in the other case the 
<margin>D</margin> unity of God himself is entirely preserved. <margin>E</margin> interpreted among us as "I, I, He." What, therefore, is designated there by these three divine names, if not the plurality and distinction of the three divine persons? And what is suggested by that which is immediately added in the same place, "And there are no gods with me," if not that those three divine hypostases, designated by those three divine names, are not three Gods, but one God? For although the entire divine essence is in the Father, entirely in the Son, and entirely in the Holy Spirit: since the Father is true and perfect God, from whom are all things; and the Son is true and perfect God, through whom are all things; 
<margin>F</margin> and the Holy Spirit is true and perfect God, in whom are all things: yet because the divine nature itself is altogether one in the three, therefore the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God, who made all things, and from whom, through whom, and in whom all things proceed, subsist, and are given life, and to whom at last all things are led back. For as that Gregory Nazianzen, easily the prince of Greek theologians, says: "One is God, the Father, from whom all things; and the Son, through whom all things; and the Holy Spirit, 
<margin>G</margin> in whom all things. These prepositions—'from whom', 'through whom', and 'in whom'—do not divide the natures, but characterize the properties of the one and unconfused nature." <note>original Greek: Εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς, ὁ πατὴρ, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ ὁ υἱὸς δι’ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐν ᾧ τὰ πάντα. αὗται δὲ αἱ προθέσεις, τὸ ἐξ οὗ, καὶ δι’ οὗ, καὶ ἐν ᾧ, οὐ μὴν τὰς φύσεις τέμνουσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰς τῆς μιᾶς καὶ ἀσυγχύτου φύσεως ἰδιότητας χαρακτηρίζουσιν.</note> That is: One God is the Father from whom all things, and the Son through whom all things, and the Spirit...

...the Holy Spirit in whom all things [exist]. For these prepositions—"from whom," "through whom," and "in whom"—do not indeed divide the nature, but characterize the properties of the one and unconfused nature. How these things come to be is shown by John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century monk and theologian, famous for his "Exposition of the Orthodox Faith."</note>, who attempted to explain this mystery no less elegantly than subtly in the book he titled *On Divine Tradition*, saying thus in chapter 49, among other things: "In the Godhead we confess one nature, but we say there are three hypostases <note>original Greek: ὑποστάσεις; a theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity</note> in truth. And all natural and essential things we call simple. But the difference of the hypostases we recognize only in the three properties: the uncaused and paternal, the caused and filial, and the caused and proceeding. We understand them to be inseparable and without distance from one another, united and interpenetrating one another without confusion. They are united without confusion (for they are three, even if they are united) and divided without distance; for although each exists by itself—that is, is a perfect hypostasis, and possesses its own property, which is a different mode of existence—yet they are united in essence and in natural properties, and in that they are not at all distant from the paternal hypostasis, and they are and are called one God." <note>This long quote is provided first in the original Greek and then in the author's Latin translation; both are rendered here into English.</note> That is to say, in the divinity we confess one nature, but three hypostases, which we say exist according to truth. And all things natural and essential, we call simple. But the difference of the hypostases we know in only three properties: namely, in the unproduced and paternal, the produced and filial, and the produced and proceeding. Moreover, we know them to be inseparable, and not distant from one another, and united and falling into one another without confusion. And they are indeed united without confusion (for they are three, even though they are united); but distinct without distance. For although each one subsists by itself—that is, is a perfect hypostasis, and possesses its own property, that is, a different mode of subsistence—nevertheless they are united in essence, and in natural properties, and by the fact that they are in no way distant from the paternal hypostasis, and they both are, and are called, one God.

### CHAPTER III.
*On the distinction of the divine persons. And on God the Sender, and God the Sent.*

### CAPNIO.

Since we are at war <note>referring to a theological debate or polemic</note> with the Jews of our age, who do not receive our scriptures <note>the New Testament</note>, I would therefore wish that you would show the mysteries of our faith through their own scriptures alone. Therefore, omitting the sayings of our doctors, both Greek and Latin, prove the distinction of the divine persons from the Hebrew scriptures. GALATINUS: I will do so with a willing heart, and indeed in all other matters, not just this one. For a testimony is more powerful when it is taken from the adversaries. First, therefore, hear the prophet Zechariah <note>Zechariah 2:10–11</note> concerning the distinction of the divine persons, and concerning God the Sender and God the Sent, saying thus in the second chapter: "Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord <note>the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter holy name of God: יהוה</note>. That the Father is God the sender, and His Word or the Son of God is God the sent, is clearly gathered from the words of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai <note>A 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with the authorship of the Zohar</note> when, in the beginning of the book *Tahanith* <gloss>On Fasting</gloss> of the Jerusalem [Talmud], he says: "Israel migrated to Babylon, and the *Shekhinah* <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> migrated with them." That passage of Daniel is also by no means foreign to the purpose, when in chapter 9 he says: <note>original: שמע אלהינו אל תפלת עבדך ואל תחנוניו ואחר פניך על מקדשך השמם למען יהוח</note> "And now, hear O our God the prayer of your servant, and show your face upon your sanctuary which is desolate, for the sake of the Lord." Here one finds an argument that the Messiah is *Adonai* <gloss>the Lord</gloss>.

CAPNIO: Rabbi Solomon, in order to extinguish the mystery of the Trinity, says that Isaiah spoke these words about himself, who at the time of the giving of the Law was on Mount Sinai together with the other Prophets. Hence, in his commentary on this place, he says: "Rabbi Tanhuma says that it is held from this place that all the Prophets stood on Mount Sinai. And from this it follows that the Prophet speaks of himself when he says: 'From the time it came to be,' namely of that speech which was spoken openly and not in secret, [by Him] who is the giver of the Law, 'there I was.'" Rabbi Solomon also affirms the same thing regarding that passage in Malachi chapter 1: "The burden of the word of the Lord in the hand of Malachi," saying: "Long ago, many days before, this had been delivered into his hands." Hence our masters declared in the extra-canonical *Mechilta* <note>An ancient commentary (midrash) on the book of Exodus</note> that all the Prophets stood on Mount Sinai when the law was given to Moses, and that the prophecies were delivered to them there. For that reason, Isaiah says: "From the time it came to be, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and His Spirit." Therefore, so that the wickedness of this Rabbi and the others of the younger generation following him may be confounded, it is necessary that you refute this childish fiction through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists. 

GALATINUS: Among other things, let Rabbi Solomon and his followers hear what is written in the book *Mechilta*, which it is a sin for them to contradict. When commenting on Exodus chapter 19—"And they came into the desert of Sinai, and rested, and pitched their tents in the desert"—it is said in this way: "The law was given publicly, in an open place. For if the law had been given in the land of Israel, the Jews would have said to the nations of the world, 'You have no part in it.' But it was given in a sprawling desert, publicly and in an open place, so that whoever wished to receive it might come and receive it." Can it be said that it was given in the night? That which is said in Exodus 19 teaches otherwise: "And it came to pass on the third day, when morning came." Can it also be said that it was given in silence? That which was said in the same place teaches otherwise: "And there were voices and lightning," along with the rest. Can it still be said that they did not hear the voice? What should be said to this, that passage of the Psalm suggests: "The voice of the Lord is in strength, the voice of the Lord is in magnificence, the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars of Lebanon," with the rest. Rabbi Joses said: "And behold, God himself, holy and blessed, says to Isaiah [in chapter] 48: 'I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time it came to be, there I was.'" Likewise, in the same book, on that passage of Exodus 20, "I am the Lord your God," Rabbi Nathan said: "If you say the word of God was in secret, does He not say Himself in Isaiah, 'I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time it came to be, there I was'?" 

Behold how clearly these two of the ancient Doctors of the Jews assert that God spoke those aforementioned words: "From the time it came to be, there I was." Therefore, Isaiah did not speak those things about himself, as Rabbi Solomon falsely asserted. From these traditions it also clearly appears that it is absurd...

The absurdity and falsehood of this fiction is most evident from the fact that neither Moses nor any of the prophets can be found to have ever openly mentioned this. Nor can they cloak their madness by saying that the souls of the prophets were present at the giving of the law without their bodies (which seems to smack of the error of those who say all souls were produced at the same time). This clearly contradicts both the Holy Scriptures and the judgment of the ancient Doctors. Indeed, in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>Genesis Rabbah, a collection of ancient Jewish explanations of the book of Genesis</note> on that passage in Genesis 5 where it says, "This is the book of the generations of Adam," it is read as follows: It is written in Isaiah 57: "For I will not contend forever with the first Adam, nor will I be angry to the end with his generations; for the spirit shall be clothed, or put on, from my face." Rabbi Tanhum said: "The King Messiah will not come (that is, in his second coming) until all the souls are created that rose in the thought of God to be created." Where is the proof? From what was said in Isaiah 57: "And the souls I have made"—that is, for the sake of the souls I made (you may supply) the world. From these words it is clearly shown that souls are created daily until the end of the world. This is held far more expressly by what Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, also known as Radak (c. 1160–1235), a grammarian and biblical commentator</note> says in the *Book of Roots*, when explaining that passage in Zechariah chapter 12, "And forming the spirit of man in the midst of him," he says: "Our Master Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> explained this; that is, from what he says, 'In the midst of him,' he means that the Creator creates the soul upon the perfection of the human body." And this is what he says: "In the midst of him." These are the words of that Rabbi Kimhi. From these things, therefore, it is clearly evident that those who say the souls of the prophets (which happened to be created much later) were present on Mount Sinai when the law of Moses was handed down, are far removed from the truth.

That Rabbi, as if he were a junior student, being unable to deny that the Messiah, according to his divinity, was always in God and existed before the creation of the world, always puts a lie in place of the truth. He seeks with every effort to subvert our faith, lest the mystery of the divine Trinity and the divinity of the Messiah—revealed in the sayings of the Prophets and the traditions of the ancient Doctors—should appear. Therefore, like a most cunning little fox who does not walk in straight paths but always in twisted windings, he strives to pervert this writing of Isaiah (where both the distinction of persons and God sending and God being sent are clearly expressed) against the explanations of the ancient Talmudists. He wants those words, "And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit," to refer to Isaiah. It follows: "From the time it came to be, there was I." That is, when Adam was made in time, I was there. "There," that is, in Adam himself, according to the substance of human flesh.

### HOGSTRATUS
Our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has it this way in this place: "From the time before they were made, I was there."

### GALATINUS
The author of our edition took the whole speech to be about the divinity of Christ; for that reason, he referred the whole thing to his divinity. We, however, following the Hebrew truth, take it partly for the divinity and partly for the humanity of which Christ consists. This more closely agrees with the truth, both because the Hebrew letter does not say "before," but **from the time it was** <note>original Hebrew: "me-hiyotah"; literally "from her/its being"</note>, using a feminine demonstration, as is clear to those who know Hebrew letters. Therefore, the text should be explained thus: "From the hour it came to be," that is, from the hour of the creation of the flesh of my mother in the formation of the body of Adam. Therefore, the text there speaks not of the divinity, but of the humanity of the Messiah. For if it were speaking of the divinity, it would have said "before it was made." Furthermore, because according to the Cabalists <note>Mystics who study the hidden meanings of the Torah</note>, the four-letter name of God (**YHWH**) <note>The Tetragrammaton, the most holy name of God</note>—in place of which they pronounce **Adonai**—which we translate as "Lord," properly signifies the Father (because that name properly implies the divine essence, and the Father is the principle and origin of the whole divinity), and **Elohim**, which is translated as "God," properly designates the Son; and since the text says, "And now **the Lord God** <note>original Hebrew: "YHWH Elohim"</note>—that is, the Lord God—has sent me, and his spirit," who is the Holy Spirit, it is indeed most evidently shown that the speech here is not about the divinity of the Messiah, but about his humanity. For if, according to the doctrine of the theologians—and especially of the "Subtle Doctor" <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Scholastic theologian</note> in Distinction 15 of the First Book, and Bonaventure <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan theologian</note> in the same distinction, question three—"to be sent" in divine matters is nothing other than to be manifested, to proceed, and to be known as being from another, and implies a certain sub-authority, it follows that the Son, according to his divinity, is sent neither by himself nor by the Holy Spirit...

...to be possible, but only from the Father: since he does not have existence from himself, nor from the Holy Spirit, but only from the Father. Therefore it is necessary to say—according to both the Hebrew Kabbalists and our own theologians—that the saying, "To exist from his own time" (that is, when he was made in time), must be understood not regarding the Messiah's divinity, but regarding his humanity. Therefore, when it says: "And now the Lord God, or God God, has sent me, and his Spirit," <note>Isaiah 48:16</note> the words are to be explained according to the Kabbalists in this way: "The Lord" or "God" <note>original: "tetragrammaton," the four-letter name of God, YHVH</note>—that is, the Father; "God"—that is, the Son; and "His Spirit"—that is, the Holy Spirit, has sent me, so that I might be the Redeemer of Israel. In this, three things must be noted. First, indeed, that the Kabbalists hold that the name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>original: יהוה (YHVH)</note>, represents God's mercy; but *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note>, which is the same as "God," represents God’s justice. For this reason, when it says here, "The Lord God," or "God (the Tetragrammaton) God," no conjunction is used: this is to designate that in the mission of the Messiah's humanity, the mercy and justice of God were to be united for the redemption of the human race. This is according to that passage in Psalm 85: "Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed." The second point is that it does not say "their Spirit"—namely, of the Father and the Son—but "his Spirit": to denote that the Father and the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, are not two breathers, but both are only one breather and one principle of the Holy Spirit himself. The third and final point is that it does not say, "they sent me," but "he sent me": in order to suggest the unity of the divine essence, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*On the distinction and number of the divine persons through their properties.*<-

### CAPNIO.

I think it would be of no small benefit, both for a clearer manifestation of the truth and for the greater confusion of the modern Jews, if you were to show that the distinction and number of the divine persons through their properties is also held among them. GAL. I will do that gladly. That they themselves clearly demonstrate both the number and distinction of the divine persons through their properties is first easily apparent from what is contained in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: מדרש תלים; an ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note>, in that place where Psalm 50 says: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth." <note>original: אל אלהים יהוה דבר ויקרא ארץ (El Elohim YHVH dibber va-yikra aretz)</note> For there it is read as follows: "Why is the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, mentioned three times? To teach that with these three names the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, corresponding to the three <term>Middoth: attributes or properties</term> by which the world was created: and these are Wisdom, Knowledge, and Understanding. From where is Wisdom proven? From what was said in Proverbs 3: 'The Lord by wisdom founded the earth.' From where is Knowledge? From what was said in the same place: 'By his knowledge the depths erupted.' From where is Understanding? From what was said: 'He prepared or adorned the heavens with understanding.' And because of this He himself says in Exodus 20: 'For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God.' <note>original: כי אנכי יהוה אלהיך אל קנא (Ki anochi YHVH Elohecha El kanna)</note> Behold, three properties in place of the three by which the world was created. So also the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben said in Joshua 22: 'The God of gods, the Lord; the God of gods, the Lord, he knows.' <note>original: אל אלהים יהוה אל אלהים יהוה הוא יודע (El Elohim YHVH, El Elohim YHVH, hu yodea)</note> What did they see that made them repeat this same thing twice? They said it first, 'God, God, Lord,' because by these the world was created: and then they said, 'God, God, Lord,' because in these three also the Law was given."

<page-num>52</page-num>

"But could one of them, by himself and separately, have created the world? Not at all: but the two others united with him necessarily created it." These things are in the Talmud <note>Galatinus often uses "Talmud" broadly to refer to various rabbinic writings</note>. These are placed in almost the same words in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>original: Rabbi Mosis hadarfan (11th century French rabbi)</note> upon that passage of Genesis 1: "In the beginning *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note> created the heaven and the earth." All of these things agree sufficiently with the Christian faith, except for this: that these three divine <term>Middoth: attributes</term> by which they assert the world was created are called Wisdom, Knowledge, and Understanding. For although these seem to be several properties in name, in reality they are but one. Nevertheless, elsewhere among them, three properties are found which, according to the orthodox faith, are one God. Indeed, in the exposition of Rabbi Moses the Preacher on the book of Genesis, upon that 42nd chapter, "Joseph himself was powerful over the land," it is read that Rabbi Elazar said: "The world was not created except by the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said in Psalm 33: 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were made.'" <note>original: בדבר יהוה שמים נעשו (Bidevar YHVH shamayim na'asu)</note> Where also Rabbi Simeon says: "God breathed the breath of his mouth, and the world was created, as it is said in Psalm 33: 'And by the breath of his mouth all their host.'" <note>original: וברוח פיו כל צבאם (U-veruach piv kol tzeva'am)</note> This is the tradition. In these, these three—God, His Word, and the Spirit—are set down as having converged distinctly and openly in the production of the world. Now, what else are these three but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? For the Word is really distinguished from the speaker, and the spirit from the breather. Therefore, between God the creator of the world, and His Word through which the world was created, and God breathing, and His spirit in which He produced the world, there must be a real distinction. It is read regarding that passage in Psalm 21: <margin>A</margin> *For the leader, a Psalm of David. O Lord, in Your strength the king shall rejoice, and in Your salvation how greatly shall he exult!* <note>original Hebrew: למנצח מזמור לדוד יהוה בעזך ישמח מלך ובישועתך מה יגל מאד</note> That is: To the Victor, or For the victory, a Psalm of David. God, in your strength the king shall be glad, and in your salvation how vehemently shall he exult? For there it is said word-for-word that this is as if the scripture says in Isaiah 11: *And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, who shall stand as a sign to the people.* And it is added: *And he will give power or strength to his King, and will exalt the horn of his Messiah.* It follows in the same Psalm: <margin>B</margin> *You have given him his heart’s desire, and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah.* <note>original Hebrew: תאות לבו נתתה לו וארשת שפתי בל מנעת סלה</note> That is: You have granted him the desire of his heart, and the declaration or sentence of his lips you have not prohibited forever. What is this "sentence of his lips" if not the faculty or knowledge that will be in his lips? Because when he himself has decreed it, his words shall remain. It follows: *For you meet him with the blessings of goodness.* <note>original Latin: Quoniam præfacient vel præuenient eum benedictiones boni, vel bonitatis</note> Rabbi Judah said: <margin>C</margin> *For you meet him with the blessings of goodness. Rabbi said: The blessings of Moses, who was called "good," as it is said in Exodus 2: "And she saw him, that he was good." The Masters said: the blessings of the Torah, as it is said in Proverbs 4: "For I have given you good doctrine; do not forsake my law, for I was my father's son, tender and the only one in the sight of my mother."* <note>original Hebrew: כי תקדמנו ברכות טוב רבי אומר ברכות משה שנקרא טוב שנ' ותרא אותו כי טוב הוא רבנן אמרי ברכותיה של תורה שנאמר כי לקח טוב נתתי לכם תורתי אל תעזובו כי בן הייתי לאבי רך ויחיד לפני אמי</note> That is: For the blessings of the good one shall go before him. Rabbi said: The blessings of Moses, who was called good. Just as it is said in Exodus 2: *And she saw him, that he was good.* The Masters said: because the blessings of the law—namely, they shall go before the King Messiah. As it is said in Proverbs 4: <margin>D</margin> *Because I have given you good instruction: do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender and the only child of my mother.* All this is tradition. From which it clearly appears that all these words of Solomon are to be understood not concerning Solomon himself, but concerning the Son of the holy and blessed God.

<term>CHAPTER.</term> <margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin> The Jews of our time, although they are unable to contradict this tradition—which clearly explains these words as referring to the Son of the holy and blessed God and not to Solomon—nevertheless say that these words which are connected to the same <margin>E</margin> clause, *Alone or only child of my mother,* can in no way fit God. Therefore, attributing those words to Solomon, they consequently explain the whole text as being about Solomon himself.

<term>GALATINUS.</term> These words can in no way be correctly verified concerning Solomon, who was not the *only* son to his father, since David himself had many other sons, as is held in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 4. Nor was he the *only* son of his mother, since Bathsheba his mother had another son besides him. <margin>F</margin> For even if she had another before him, that one had died as a small infant before Solomon himself was born, as is clear in the second book of Kings, chapter 12. Therefore, since these words—*Alone or only child of my mother*—cannot be understood concerning Solomon, they must be understood concerning the only Son of God according to the aforementioned tradition. He was not only the Son of God according to his divinity, begotten from eternity, but also according to his humanity, he was the *alone* or *only* son of his mother—that is, out of all the children of the Synagogue <margin>G</margin> (which, on account of the divine incarnation, ought to be called the "Mother of God")—he alone was to be the Son to God the Father through the union of the divine nature. For according to the opinion of John

<column-break/>

Damascene, the Son of God was to assume human nature in an <term>atom</term> <note>original Greek: ἀτόמῳ; meaning in an individual or indivisible instance</note>—that is, in an individual person. He alone, as a man out of all the individuals of the human race, was predestined to be the Son of God because of the hypostatic union <term>hypostatic union: the union of Christ's humanity and divinity in one individual person</term> of the Godhead. This is according to what was said by Paul in Romans, chapter 1: *Who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined the Son of God.* For this reason, he most aptly says here through Solomon: *I was a son to my father,* regarding his divinity; and *the alone or only child of my mother,* that is, the Synagogue, regarding his humanity. Moreover, that the Synagogue <margin>The Synagogue was called the Mother of God.</margin> should be called the "Mother of God" by reason of the divine incarnation that was to come from her, is proven by the sayings of the ancient Talmudists in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim*—that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs—concerning that which is said in the 3rd chapter of the same book: *Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him.* We shall see this abundantly in the 25th chapter of the third book.

<term>CAPNIO.</term> Although what you have said is so true and <margin>Another objection of the Jews.</margin> so clear that the Jews of our century cannot deny it by any false argument, they nevertheless—as if most obstinate in the error of their faithlessness—flee to another falsehood so that they may escape the truth. They say that after these words, *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender and the only child of my mother,* these other words are immediately added: *And he taught me and said to me, let your heart hold fast my words, keep my commandments and live.* <note>original Hebrew: ויורני ויאמר לי יתמך דברי לבך שמר מצותי וחיה</note> That is: *And he taught me, and said <margin>H</margin> to me: Let your heart receive my words, keep my precepts, and live.* They argue that these things, along with the rest that follow there, can least of all be appropriate for God; therefore, those preceding words should not be referred to God either, but to Solomon, just as those following things are referred to him.

<term>GALATINUS.</term> It is easy to answer <margin>The Response.</margin> these points, seeing as the Son of God was to have a dual nature in the Messiah: namely, the divine nature, by which he was the Son to God his Father from eternity, begotten before the ages without a mother; and the human nature, according to which he is called the Son of Man, born in time from a mother without a father. Just as there had to be a dual nature in the Messiah, so also there was to be a twofold wisdom in him, both having their origin from God the Father. For although the wisdom of the Son in divine matters is one and entirely the same as the wisdom of the Father, yet because the Son is begotten by the Father, just as he has his being eternally from the Father, so also he received from the Father from eternity both wisdom itself and all things which he has according to his divinity. Even the wisdom which he was to have according to his humanity had to have its origin from God himself, who was to imbue his soul from the instant of its creation with the highest grace and all habits above all others. Since, therefore, Solomon speaks in this book parabolically and enigmatically concerning the Son of God—who was to become a man just like each of us—he did so in order to suggest through parables and enigmas not only that the wisdom which the Son himself was to receive according to his human nature would emanate from God the Father, but also that the wisdom which he had eternally according to his divinity proceeded from the eternal Father through...

Galatinus refutes Jewish objections by explaining how the Synagogue can be considered the "Mother of God" in the context of the Incarnation.</summary>

# BOOK TWO.

C iij

...instructions, warnings, and corrections by which a human father strives to make his son wise and prudent, he compares the Son of God himself to the Father, adapting these sorts of instructions and corrections to His wisdom as far as possible. Therefore, regarding the words spoken just a moment ago, some refer to the divine nature of the Son of God, and others to the human nature he was to assume. The words themselves clearly indicate both of these things. For when he says: *Hear, children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know prudence: for I have given you a good doctrine or document, that is, a good law,* <note>proverbs 4:1–2</note> this cannot possibly be understood as referring to Solomon. For if Solomon had been speaking here of his own wisdom, he would have said "I will give," not "I have given," especially since he said, *Hear, children, the instruction of a father.* It is necessary, therefore, that this speech be made in the name of Him who had previously given the law to the Hebrews; and this is God alone. Therefore, that speech should not be referred to Solomon, but to God.

This also applies to what follows immediately, namely: *Do not forsake my law, for I was a son to my father, tender, and the only one (or unique) among the sons of my mother.* <note>Proverbs 4:2–3</note> Since the word "for" indicates a cause, it must provide the reason for the preceding clause; it is as if he were saying openly: "This is the reason why you should not forsake my law: because I was a son to my father." But if the speech were about Solomon, no reason would be given for not forsaking his law. For men would not be obliged to keep his law simply because he was the son of David. If he had said, "do not forsake my law because I received it from my father David," then he would indeed have given a reason for not forsaking it—though even then it would have to be known that everything handed down by David was right and to be observed, which was not always evident.

It is clear, then, that Solomon spoke here not of himself, but in the person of the Son of God. His law had to be observed <margin>Why the Son of God is called "tender."</margin> because he was the Son of God. He calls himself "tender" <note>original Latin: "tener"</note> not only to suggest the tenderness of his immense piety, but also to hint at the capacity of his infinite wisdom. For according to the Aristotelian saying in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, De Anima, II, 9, 421a; a medieval physiological theory suggested that people with "soft" or "tender" skin/flesh possessed superior intelligence and sensitivity.</note>, those who are hard of flesh are unfit in intellect, but the soft—that is, the tender—are well-suited. Therefore, to show this excellent disposition of his for receiving his father’s instructions, he said he was "tender," meaning he was well-teachable and most capable of right and infinite wisdom. 

But to whom was he tender? *To my father,* he says. He must therefore be speaking of such a father who can teach nothing but what is right; and this is God alone. Thus the words are to be explained: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my Father, tender.* This means: because I received those things from my father, who cannot err in teaching, nor could I err in learning, because I was "tender"—that is, of the best and infinite capacity to receive it. And he is the *only one or unique of the sons of my mother,* that is, of the Synagogue, as we explained above. 

**Galatinus:** Where you translated "son" or "of the sons of my mother," our text has "before my mother" <note>original Latin: "coram matre mea"</note>; others have translated it as "in the presence of my mother."

**Galatinus:** The word *libne* <note>Hebrew: לבני</note> which is placed here, and is written with the letter *beth* (ב), signifies neither "before" nor "in the presence of," but properly means "to the sons" or "of the sons." For "before" and "in the presence of" are signified by the word *liphne* <note>Hebrew: לפני</note>, written with the letter *pe* (פ). From this it is clearly evident that those who translated this passage as "before my mother" or "in the presence of my mother" were deceived by the similarity of the words and read *liphne* instead of *libne*.

<column-break/>

As for what follows—*And he taught me*—along with the rest, Christ mentioned this about himself when he says in the 8th chapter of John: *As the Father taught me, these things I speak.* And again: *I always do those things that are pleasing to him.* He says other things in the same place that agree with almost the same sentiment. In these, he openly shows both that he was taught by the Father and that he received from him the commands for those things he was to do in the world. Regarding what is said here—*Keep my precepts*—he reported that he himself fulfilled this, saying in John 15: *I have kept my Father's commandments and I remain in his love.* Finally, that which is added at the end—*And live*—he explained about himself when he says: *Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.* Therefore, he says, *Live*—that is, have life in your power. Hence he himself says: *I have the power to lay down my soul, and I have the power to take it up again.*

#### Regarding the Holy Spirit.
### CAPNIO.

V Since you have spoken sufficiently in the preceding sections about the Father and the Son, clearly proving that God is called "Father" in Holy Scripture and that his begotten wisdom is called the "Son," it remains now for you to discuss something regarding the Holy Spirit in detail. 

**Galatinus:** I often find the Holy Spirit called "Goodness," or "Good Will," and "Charity" or "Affection" <margin>How the Holy Spirit is named by the Hebrews.</margin> or "Love" by the ancient Jews. I find that he proceeds from the Father and the Son as from a single principle, and that together with the Father and the Son he produced the world, spoke through the Prophets, and was to come upon the Messiah and remain perfectly. For regarding God's goodness or his good will, it is found in Psalm 143, where David, pouring out prayers to the Lord, says: *Teach me to do your will, for you are my God; your good Spirit (or the Spirit of your goodness) shall lead me into the right land.* <note>original Hebrew: למדני לעשות רצונך כי אתה אלהי רוחך טובה תנחני בארץ מישור</note> That this "Good Spirit" or "Goodness" is called the Holy Spirit is shown by the same Prophet in Psalm 50, saying: *Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold, sustain, or confirm me with a liberal Spirit (or the Spirit of liberality).* <note>original Hebrew: השיבה לי ששון ישעך, ורוח נדיבה תסמכני</note> This Holy Spirit is equal with the Father and...

# BOOK TWO.

We are taught that the Son was the author of the world and the maker of men from what was said by Elihu in the 33rd chapter of Job: <note>Job 33:4</note> <note>original: "Ruach El asatani ve-nishmat Shaddai techayeni"</note> "The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life." And in the Psalm-writer, Psalm 103: <note>Psalm 104:30 in modern numbering</note> <note>original: "Tishlach ruchacha yibare’un ve-techadesh penei adamah"</note> "Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth." And again, Psalm 33: <note>Psalm 33:6</note> <note>original: "Bi-dvar Yahweh shamayim na’asu u-ve-ruach piv kol tzeva’am"</note> "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made; and all the host of them by the spirit of his mouth." Among the Hebrews, the "host of heaven" refers to the Sun, Moon, Stars, and all the powers and angels therein. Therefore, it was not without reason that Saint Job said in chapter 26: <note>Job 26:13</note> <note>original: "Be-rucho shamayim shifrah"</note> "By his spirit he hath adorned the heavens." Furthermore, Isaiah excellently shows that this Holy Spirit was to come upon the Messiah and find perfect rest there, when he says in chapter 11: <note>Isaiah 11:1–2</note> <note>original: "Ve-yatzah choter mi-geza Yishai ve-netzer mi-shorashav yifreh ve-nachah alav ruach Yahweh"</note> "There shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots: and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him," or the Spirit God, that is, the Spirit who is God.

Indeed, these words are interpreted by the Hebrews themselves, according to the literal sense, as referring to nothing but the Messiah. This is clearly evident in countless places in the Talmud itself, and especially in the *Bereshit Rabbah* and *Zuta* <note>original: "bereschit rabba vezehira"</note>—that is, in the Great and Lesser expositions of Genesis. There, concerning that verse in Genesis chapter 1, "And the earth was void and empty," the literal reading is as follows: "Rabbi Simeon explained this scripture as referring to the four kingdoms, saying: 'The earth was void'—this is the Kingdom of Babylon, of which it was said in Jeremiah chapter 4, 'I beheld the earth, and lo, it was void.' 'And empty'—this is the Kingdom of the Medes, as it is said in Esther chapter 6, 'They hasted to bring Haman.' <note>The connection here relies on a Hebrew wordplay common in Midrashic interpretation.</note> 'And darkness was'—this is the Kingdom of the Greeks, which darkened the eyes of the Jews with its decrees. 'Upon the face of the abyss'—this is the wicked kingdom, that is, the Roman Empire. For just as the abyss is inscrutable and lacks a bottom, so too this wicked kingdom is unsearchable and has no bottom. 'And the Spirit of <term>Elohim</term> <note>Elohim is a plural noun for God; the author uses this to argue for the plurality of persons in the Trinity.</note>—that is, of the Gods—was hovering over the waters'—this is the Spirit of the Messiah, of whom it was said in Isaiah chapter 11, 'And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.'" Through whose merit will the Spirit serve and come hovering over the face of the waters? Through the merit of repentance, which is likened to water, as it is said in Lamentations chapter 2: "Pour out thy heart like water before the face of the Lord." All of this is from the tradition.

To these things, it seems necessary to add what Rabbi Solomon <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> said in explaining that passage in Exodus chapter 15: <note>Exodus 15:8</note> <note>original: "U-ve-ruach apecha ne’armu mayim"</note> "And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together." Where he says: "By the spirit of thy nostrils—that is, by the spirit proceeding from the nostrils of thy nose." And the scripture speaks of the <term>Shekhinah</term>, <note>The Divine Presence or indwelling of God.</note> that is, of the divinity. So also Job says in chapter 4: "By the blast of his nostrils are they consumed." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. It also seems to fit aptly with the preceding points what is said in the *Midrash Tehillim* (that is, in the gloss on the Psalms) concerning that verse in Psalm 18: <note>Psalm 18:15–16</note> "Then the springs of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the

<column-break/>

breath of thy nostrils." For there it is read that Rabbi Hannina said: "'At thy rebuke' is not to be taken literally, but 'at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils,' as it is said in Exodus chapter 15: 'Thou didst blow with thy spirit, and the sea covered them.'"

Therefore, for the understanding of these things, it must be noted that from what was brought forward shortly before—"And the Spirit of <term>Elohim</term> (Gods)" (a manner of speaking about God which Catholic caution does not usually admit)—it is quite clearly hinted that the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son. This is most especially true because in that same tradition it is said that the Spirit of *Elohim* (of the Gods, or of God, if we take the plural for the singular) is the Spirit of the Messiah. From the truth of this matter, it necessarily follows that the Messiah already existed then according to his divinity.

Furthermore, that the "two nostrils" of the divinity—that is, the two <term>middot</term> <note>Attributes or properties, here used to refer to the Persons of the Trinity.</note> or two persons, namely the Father and the Son—are "one nose," that is, only one principle breathing forth the Holy Spirit, is clearly evident from what is added consequently to the aforementioned tradition. That this procession of the Holy Spirit from the divine nostrils is to be understood literally as being about the Spirit of God, and not about anything else, is manifestly shown by what was last brought forward from the Psalm and its gloss.

Moreover, that this Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, is the true and perfect God, is demonstrated chiefly by the fact that the Psalm-writer affirms everywhere that he is present—not merely locally, but "replenishingly" (which belongs to God alone)—when he says in Psalm 139: <note>Psalm 139:7–10</note> <note>original: "Anah elech me-ruchacha..."</note> "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? Or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: and if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." When he says, "If I take the wings of the morning," his meaning is: "If I were to take on the manner of the dawn, which appears from the east in a moment."

That there is in God a certain <term>midda</term> (that is, a property) which is called delight or charity, is chiefly hinted at by what is read in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* (that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs) concerning those words in chapter 3: <note>Song of Songs 3:9–10</note> <note>original: "Apiryon asah lo ha-melech Shelomoh..."</note> "King Solomon made himself a portable pavilion <note>Often translated as a litter, palanquin, or chariot.</note> of the wood of Lebanon. He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love." These words are explained there as follows: "The portable pavilion"—this is the Throne of Glory. "King Solomon made for himself"—the King who is His Peace <note>A wordplay on "Shelomoh" (Solomon) and "Shalom" (Peace).</note>, namely God. "Of the wood of Lebanon"—this is the House of the Holy of Holies. "He made the pillars thereof of silver"—behold those of whom it was said in Job chapter 26: "The pillars of heaven shall be broken or moved." The bottom—

The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit is God.

# BOOK TWO.

<sig>iiij</sig>

<margin>
*What the Holy Spirit is according to the ancient Hebrews.*
</margin>

...its base or golden support: <note>Referring to the description of the palanquin in Song of Solomon 3:9–10.</note> these are the words of the Law, of which it is said in Psalm 19, "More to be desired than gold, or even much fine gold." <note>Psalm 19:10; original Latin: Psalm 18. Desiderabilia super aurum.</note> Its seat is purple: behold what is said in Psalm 68, "To him who rides upon the heaven of heavens *Kedem*" <note>Psalm 68:33; original: קדם</note>, that is, of antiquity or of the east. Its interior is inlaid or kindled with love or charity: Rabbi Azariah said this love or charity is the *Shekhinah* <note>original: שכינה</note>, that is, the Divine Presence itself, or the glory of God. These things are found in the Midrash mentioned above. From these it is clearly shown that no one is better understood by "Solomon" in this passage than the Messiah. Therefore this Solomon, that is the Messiah, made for himself an *appirion* <note>original: אפריון</note>, that is, a bridal chamber or a portable pavilion, namely his own body: which is the throne of glory, as was said at the beginning of this Midrash. He made it indeed from the "woods of Lebanon," which are the house of the Holy of Holies, according to the rabbis' interpretation: which fits perfectly with those parts of his mother from which he himself formed his body by the power of his divinity. Its columns are silver because of their purity, namely the four humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient and medieval medicine believed determined a person's health and temperament.</note>, of which both his and every human body consists; these were shaken and broken when, as he hung on the cross, all his blood—in which all the humors exist together—was poured out. The golden support was his precious soul. The purple seat or throne was his flesh, all reddened by that precious blood. Its interior was indeed the heart, *ratzuph* <note>original: רצוף</note>, that is, paved; or according to another meaning, kindled as if with burning coals of love or charity. Since this is the *Shekhinah*, that is divinity, as has been shown through Jewish tradition, it follows that the Messiah according to his humanity was to be filled with the Holy Spirit. Isaiah suggests this excellently when he says in the 61st chapter in the persona of the Messiah: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me." <note>Isaiah 61:1; original: רוח אדני יהוה עלי יען משח יהוה אותי</note> Here the Prophet (as Rabbi David Kimhi says in the book *Serafeim* <note>Likely referring to Kimhi's *Sefer Hashorashim* or "Book of Roots."</note>) spoke in the person of the Messiah. It is as if the Messiah said: "Because God anointed me, he sent me to preach to the poor or the humble." From this it is clear that the Holy Spirit is called love or charity, not only because he proceeds from the Father and the Son by way of the will, but also because he is the love by which the Father and the Son mutually love each other. Therefore, as gathered from what has been said, those ancient and old fathers of the Jews understood nothing else by the Holy Spirit than the third person in the Godhead, produced from eternity by the Father and the Son in a single breathing by way of the will, really distinct from them, but essentially the same as them. For as has been said, although the three divine persons are really distinguished from one another, yet essentially they are entirely one and the same.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*That the three divine persons are one essence, and that each of them is in the other by circumincession.*<-
<note>Circumincession (or perichoresis) is a theological term describing the mutual indwelling of the three Persons of the Trinity, where each person remains distinct but contains and is contained by the others.</note>

<column-break/>

**CAPNIO.**
<note>Capnio is the Hellenized name of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian scholar of Hebrew who acts as a student in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring floral motifs and a central shield-like shape.</image-desc>

**I WISH**, for a clearer expression of this Catholic truth and for the greater confusion of the younger Jews, that you would prove through some of their own doctors that the three divine persons are one essence, one nature, and that one is in the other by circumincession. **GALATINUS:** Although I could produce many witnesses from among them to prove it, yet lest I be tedious, let it suffice to bring forward one from all of them, whom the more recent Jews can least contradict, namely Rabbi Isaac ben Shola, a man of great authority among them. In his commentaries on the Psalter, he often asserts this very thing, and especially upon that verse of Psalm 111: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever." <note>Psalm 111:10; original: ראשית חכמה יראת יהוה שכל טוב לכל עושיהם תהלתו עומדת לעד</note> He speaks thus: 

"The Wisdom which is hinted at in this verse is the divine Wisdom. For 'Wisdom' is that which is 'found from nothingness' <note>A common Kabbalistic play on Job 28:12, where Wisdom/Chokhmah emerges from the Nothingness/Ayin of the Divine.</note>, and it is hinted at in the word *Bereshit* [In-the-beginning], specifically in the letter *Bet*. The Sages said: do not read it as the letter *Bet* but as *Bayit* [House], as it is said, 'Through wisdom a house is built.' And this attribute is hidden and concealed, sealed with the 'Seal of Mysteries,' in the sense that it is said, 'it is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the heaven,' and it says, 'God understands its way and He knows its place' <note>Job 28:21–23</note>—meaning that no other besides Him knows the paths engraved in it. Wherever the Sages hid the attributes, they counted Wisdom as if it were the first, because it is drawn from the Fountain of Life and is the beginning of the counting. They counted the inner attribute which is the source and the spring... The masters of Wisdom call this inner attribute by many names: some call it 'Crown' [*Keter*] because all the attributes are crowned by it and it is within them; and some call it 'Nothing' [*Ayin*] because thought cannot grasp it... if you merit to understand this, you will know the secret of the high mountains. As for the other names... they all point to this way: 'He causes light to dwell.' In this verse, he hinted at this attribute with the word 'beginning' [*reshit*] and Wisdom was included. Our Rabbis of blessed memory said: all the prophets prophesied through a mirror that does not shine, but Moses our teacher looked through a single mirror that shines... furthermore, in this verse, 'the fear of the Lord' is the light of the 'beginning.' In the existence of the three attributes we mentioned, they are called 'Faces' [*Panim*], included one within the other. Thus it says, 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,' and the Sage said, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom,' and he said, 'Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding.' You have learned that these three are chosen as crowns for a single, perfect, and unique Crown. They are the 'Three Mothers' who are twins to the world. They are the 'sayings of the Lord, pure sayings'—seven counts filled and good in a single branch. Because they are a strong bond and a law, he included them all together in the word 'truth': 'a good understanding have all they that do them.' And it says, 'his praise stands forever' regarding that inner attribute we mentioned... and it says, 'He is your praise and He is your God.' Understand this."

<margin>
*Wisdom in divine things.*
</margin>

This means that Wisdom, of which we understand in this text, is manifest in divine things.

### BOOK TWO.

...Wisdom which goes forth from *Meain* <note>Hebrew: מאין, literally "from whence," but here interpreted as "from Nothingness" or the "Hidden Source"</note>, that is, from the supreme and most abstract intellect of God, and is found in the word *Bereshit* <note>Hebrew: בראשית, "In the beginning"</note>, that is, in the beginning, specifically in the letter *Beth* <note>The first letter of the Torah</note>. And for this reason they said: Do not call it *Beth*, but *Baith*, which means "a house." Just as it is written: "By wisdom a house is built." <note>Proverbs 24:3</note> And this property is covered, hidden, and sealed—sealed, that is, with the seal of secrets. As it is written: it is covered and hidden from the eyes of all living things, and concealed from the birds of the heavens. And it says: "God understands its ways, and He knows its place." It is as if to say: no one besides Him knows the paths that are carved into it. And whenever the sages enumerated the properties <term>Properties: In this context, these are the 'Sefirot' or divine attributes through which God acts in the world.</term> of God, they placed Wisdom as the beginning, since it is drawn from the fountain of life and is the principle of every number. And they called that intrinsic property the most overflowing vein of copper <note>original: *aeris*</note>, which the common people call an ore-mine; and a fountain or emanation is discovered within it, just as there are flowing veins of silver. And it is said that as is the shadow of wisdom, so is the shadow of silver.

The authors of wisdom have named this intrinsic property by many names: for some called it the "Crown" <note>Hebrew: *Keter*</note>, because the individual properties are crowned by it, and it by the individuals. Others, however, named it *Ain* <note>Hebrew: אין, "Nothingness"</note> because there is no one who can comprehend it through imagination (for it is attainable by the intellect alone). And to this alludes what was said: *Meain*, that is, "from whence shall my help come?" <note>Psalm 121:1</note> (For *Meain* indeed seems to signify the incorporeal, abstract, secret, and intellectual.) And if you are fortunate in understanding my words, you will know the secrets of the highest mountains, since this property is like a light by which all other properties are crowned in the "Way of Light." Therefore, in this text, observe this property in the word "Beginning," in which Wisdom is contained. The teachers therefore said that all the prophets prophesied in a vision that was not clear; but Moses prophesied in a clear and bright vision <note>Refers to the Rabbinic concept of the *Aspaklaria Me’ira*, or "shining mirror" of prophecy</note>: as it is written, "And the Beginning appeared to him."

Next follows "The Fear of the Lord." And this is further explanatory of the "Beginning." As it is written: "God has acted so that men should fear before Him." And these are those three properties called "Faces" <note>original: *Facies*; likely referring to the three highest Sefirot</note>, and they are contained within one another. And therefore it is said: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." And the wise man says: "Indeed, the fear of the Lord is wisdom." It is also said: "Acquire wisdom, acquire prudence." Behold, you have learned that these three crowns are one crown, in a most perfect unity. And they are a most choice thing, three foundations of the world which are equal (that is, by which the world is established). And they are the ascending lights, pre-eminent over all else, to the extent that everything is illuminated by their light. And the words of God are pure and precious words, the meaning of the seven ears of grain on one stalk, which are full and good. And because they are one strong and inseparable bond, all are gathered into one. As it is written: "A good understanding to all who do them," that is, to those who focus upon them. As it is also said elsewhere: "Truly God has made this day." But he said: "His praise endures forever," because of that intrinsic property which we have

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> mentioned. And he also says: "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever." And he said: "He is your praise, and He is your God." And understand this. All these things were said by the aforementioned Rabbi. From which many excellent things, very much in agreement with our faith against the Jews of our time, are held, and especially seven points.

First: that the three properties by which the three Divine Persons are distinguished—which he says, from the words of the Psalmist, are the Beginning, Wisdom, and the Fear of God. And this is indeed correct. For by "Beginning" he understands the Father, both because the Father is the first person in the Trinity, and <margin>B</margin> also because He is the beginning and origin of the whole divinity. By "Wisdom" he suggests the Son, who is the Wisdom of the Father. By "the Fear of God" he hints at the Holy Spirit, who is not incongruously called the "Fear of God" by His effect: since He instills the fear of God into the hearts of the faithful into whom He enters, lest through sin they be separated from Him to whom they are joined by grace, and lest through sin they lose God Himself, whom they possess dwelling within them by grace. <margin>C</margin> He proves this also by that saying: "God has acted so that I might fear before His face."

Second: that he says this Wisdom proceeds *meain* <note>original: מאין</note>, that is, from the supreme and most abstract intellect, which is God. For this Hebrew word *meain* carries all these meanings: wishing by this to show that the Son in divine matters is produced from the Divine Intellect. For a fertile memory—which is nothing other than the intellect having its object present, namely the Divine Essence—produces the Word, that is, the Son, who is the begotten knowledge <margin>D</margin> and Wisdom of the Father.

Third: that he says this Wisdom is a most abundant vein of copper, in which a fountain or emanation is discovered: by this openly wishing to suggest that the Son of God is the "Art of the Father" and the Word through through which all things were made.

Fourth: that he says this Wisdom is like a light by which all other properties are crowned in the Way of Light. By this he clearly implies that the Son is Light from Light, or the Light of the World, as the <margin>E</margin> Son Himself says in John 8, which illuminates every man coming into this world (John 1).

Fifth: that he says these three properties are called "Faces," that is, Persons, in the manner of the Greeks, who call persons *prosopa* <note>original: πρόσωπα</note>, that is, "faces."

Sixth: that he says these three Persons are contained within one another: demonstrating that the Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Son in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit in the Father and the Son by "circumincession" <term>Circumincession: Also known as 'perichoresis' (Greek: περιχώρησιν), the theological concept of the mutual indwelling or interpenetration of the three persons of the Trinity.</term>.

Seventh: that he says these three crowns are one <margin>F</margin> crown in a most perfect unity. By this he clearly shows that the three Divine Persons are entirely one essence and one nature. He also expressly affirms this in the exposition of the following Psalm, where, regarding Psalm 112: "The wicked shall see and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth and melt away; the desire of the wicked shall perish," <note>Psalm 112:10</note> he says among other things: <margin>G</margin> <note>original Hebrew: הפסוק הזה רומז למדת הדין שלמטה כי הרשע בועט ביסורין וחורק שניו כלפי שכינה ומפני זה תאות רשעים תאבד ועל כיוצא בזה נאמר כי ה' אלהיך אש אוכלת הוא ואומר אש לפניו תאכל וסביביו נסערה מאד הרי חתם בדמיון מה שפתח במזמור הראשון להודיע כי הכל אחד וחמדות</note> "This verse hints at the Attribute of Judgment below, for the wicked person kicks against sufferings and gnashes his teeth toward the Divine Presence <note>Shekhinah</note>, and because of this 'the desire of the wicked shall perish.' And concerning such a matter it is said, 'For the Lord your God is a consuming fire,' and it says 'a fire shall devour before Him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about Him.' Thus he concluded with the same likeness with which he opened in the first Psalm, to make known that all is one and desirable..."

<margin>A</margin>
<note>This Hebrew text is the source for the Latin translation in Margin B.</note>
And these attributes that were mentioned are the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His name is He, may He be blessed. For this reason, He acts through the living beings in a carved-out measure according to their strength, included within the attributes and numbered among them. But from the side of His own essence, everything returns to one place, and everything is a complete unity. These attributes are neither limited nor separate from Him. Anyone who defines or separates one of them, or adds to them, or subtracts from them, is called "one who cuts the shoots" <note>Hebrew: *kotzetz ba-netiot*, a Talmudic idiom for heresy, specifically dualism or misinterpreting the divine unity</note>, and his punishment is great, like that of Elisha Acher <note>A famous rabbi who became an apostate</note>. However, from these attributes downward is the world of separate things, although we have no proof for this matter except for this: "And a river went out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided." And if you contemplate what I have hinted to you, you will merit the secret of this verse.

<margin>B</margin>
That is, this text signifies the attribute of infernal judgment. Since the impious man will kick with his feet and grind his teeth against the divinity. And because of this, the desire of the impious shall perish. Hence it is said: "For the Lord your God is a consuming fire." And furthermore: "A fire shall burn before Him, and it shall utterly consume those things that are round about Him." Behold, he has expressed the meaning of what is contained in the preceding Psalm, to teach that all are one. And these properties <term>Properties: In this context, the Sefirot or divine attributes.</term> which we have commemorated are the name of God, and His name is exalted. And since they operate around His creatures, according to the property suitable to them and according to their power, therefore He Himself is contained in those properties and is numbered with them. But if you consider Him in His substance, all things tend toward one place, and all are one unity, perfect on every side. And these properties are not defined nor separated. For if anyone should define, separate, add to, or diminish one of the said properties, he would rightly be called "a cutter of the plants," and his punishment would be great, like that of the latter Elisha. From these properties downward, however, consists the world of things that are defined and separated; although we have no authority for this matter, except only that which says: "And a river goes out from paradise to water the garden, and from there it is divided." And if you observe those things about which I have warned you, you will be fortunate in understanding the mystery <note>original: *sacramentum*</note> of this text. Thus far speaks the same Rabbi Isaac ben Shula. From whose two aforementioned expositions, it is clearly shown that the three divine persons are one essence and one nature, and that each of them is in the remaining two through circumincession <term>Circumincession: Also known as perichoresis; the theological concept that the three persons of the Trinity exist within one another.</term>—which was to be proven.
