### CHAPTER VIII.

*That the mystery of the divine trinity is most excellently and distinctly hinted at through the image of God, in which man was made.*

### CAPNIO <note>The scholar-persona of Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a landscape with a building and foliage.</image-desc>
**A**las, the Jews of our time are carried away by such a great desire for contradicting us that they affirm that man—whom Holy Scripture clearly asserts was made in the image of God—was *not* created in the image of God. They attempt to twist the Scripture itself to mean something else, so that they may escape the mystery of the divine trinity revealed in the creation of man. Therefore, it is now necessary for you to prove, through the writings of their own ancient [sages], both that man was made in the image of God, and that through this very image of God reflecting in him, the secret of the divine trinity is suggested. <margin>GAL.</margin> <note>Galatinus, the other interlocutor in the dialogue.</note> They certainly cannot deny that the holy Trinity of God, and His individual unity, made man in His own image and likeness, since the text itself is clear in the first part of Genesis, which says: *Vayomeru Elohim* <margin>B</margin> *na'aseh adam be-tsalmenu ki-demutenu.* *This is: And Elohim [Gods] said, let us make man in our image, according to our likeness.* <note>The author uses the plural "Gods" for "Elohim" to argue for the Trinity.</note> And after a few [verses]: *Vayivra Elohim et ha-adam be-tsalmo, be-tsalem Elohim bara oto.* *That is: And Elohim [Gods] created man in his image; in the image of Elohim [Gods] he created him; male and female he created them.* <margin>C</margin> <margin>CAP.</margin> Why did he first place the word that signifies "to make," saying, "Let us make man," and then use the word signifying "creation," saying, "And Elohim created man," along with the other things that follow? <margin>GAL.</margin> Because the bodies of Adam and Eve were compacted from matter, but their souls were created from nothing. Therefore, he first placed the word that signifies "to make" [fashioning matter]; then he used the word for "creation" [bringing from nothing]. Thus, the perfidy of the Jews of our century can by no means deny that man was made in the image of God, since their ancient [sages] confess it everywhere. For to bring forward the first testimony of Abraham himself, it is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A commentary on the Psalms</note> upon that verse of Psalm 37: *Al titchar ba-mere'im al tekane be-osei avlah.* *This is: Fret not yourself because of evildoers, nor be envious of those who work iniquity.* Our father Abraham said to Melchizedek—who was Shem the son of Noah, and who because he offered sacrifice was called the priest of the most high God—"By what manner, or for what reason, did you come out of the ark?" He answered, "Because of *tsedaka* [righteousness/charity], that is, the alms which we performed there." Abraham said to him, "And what kind of alms could you do there, when there was no one there except Noah and his sons? To whom then did you do alms?" He answered him, "To the wild beasts, the cattle, and the birds. For we did not sleep the whole night, but gave now to this one, now to that one." Abraham therefore said, "If these men who did charity to wild beasts, cattle, and birds received a reward, how much more if I do charity to the sons of Adam, who are in the image of the holy and blessed God, shall I receive a reward and be delivered from those who oppose me?" And immediately in that hour he performed—let it be added—charity: just as it is written in Genesis chapter 18. And he planted an *eshel* <note>A tamarisk tree, often interpreted as an inn or orchard for hospitality</note>, that is, an orchard or a lodging-place, for receiving guests. Next, I will bring forward that which is written in the *Bereshit Ketanna*, that is, in the lesser exposition of Genesis. For there it is read thus word for word: In the day that He created...

# BOOK TWO

->**God** <note>original: "Elohim"</note>, that is, Gods; **Adam**, in the likeness of **God** <note>original: "Elohim"</note>, that is, of the Gods, He made him.<-

Rabbi Akiva said: It is written in the 19th chapter of Leviticus: *And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.* A great part of this matter is that you should not say, "Since I have been disgraced, let my neighbor also be disgraced." Rabbi Tanhuma <note>A 4th-century Palestinian rabbi famous for his homiletic midrashim</note> said: If you do this, know whom you are disgracing: for you despise him of whom it is written, *In the likeness of God He made him.* Thus far the tradition.

Let the more recent Jews also hear what is read in the book *Mechilta* <note>A legal commentary (midrash) on the Book of Exodus</note> regarding that passage in Exodus 20: *Neither shall you go up by steps unto my altar, that your nakedness be not discovered thereon.* For it is said there: "Behold here an argument of <term>kal vahomer</term> <note>A logical principle in Jewish hermeneutics: an inference from a minor premise to a major one</note>, that is, from the lesser to the greater. For if concerning stones, in which there is no knowledge of good and evil, the <term>Place</term> <note>Hebrew: "Makom," a common rabbinic title for God, implying His omnipresence</note> Himself (for the Jews are accustomed to call God 'the Place' because He is present everywhere and in every place) said that you should not walk upon them contemptuously or dishonorably, how much more does reason require that you should not walk contemptuously and insultingly with your neighbor, who is made in the likeness of Him who spoke and the world was made." This is the tradition.

Nor should we omit here what is read in *Bereshit Rabba* <note>The Great Midrash on Genesis</note> regarding that first chapter of Genesis: *And God created man in His own image.* It is read in this way: "The heretics asked Rabbi Semlai: 'What is this that is written: *And God said, Let us make man in our image after our likeness?*' He said to them: 'Read what follows: *And God created man.* It is not written "and they created," but *He created*.'"

Rabbi Hoshahaja said: "At the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, first created man in His own image, the ministering angels were mistaken in him and wanted to say before him, 'Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God of hosts.' <note>The angels mistook the first man, Adam, for God because of the brilliance of his divine image</note> But what did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, and they immediately knew that he was but a man. And this is what is written: *Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?* <note>Isaiah 2:22</note> That is, he was accounted as God because of the likeness of God which he bears." Thus far the tradition: which, whether it be true or not, nevertheless proves excellently that the ancient teachers of the Jews held that man was created in the image of God and most like Him.

**Chapter: How did the ancient Jews hold that man was made in the image of God and most like God?**

Galatinus: <note>The speaker or authorial voice</note> According to the soul, certainly, in which the image of the divine Trinity shines forth most excellently and expressly. Therefore, one should note what Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> asserts on this matter in the book called *The Guide for the Perplexed*: "From this," he says, "that God said, *Let us make man in our image,* men are led to believe that God is corporeal, possessing all lineaments and members, as well as a spirit." Which

<column-break/>

having been finally rejected, he says (and rightly indeed) that man was created in the image of his Creator not as to the body, but as to the intellect. And he affirms that it is of this image that Psalm 39 speaks: *O Lord, in the city you shall bring their image to nothing* <note>or "despise their image"</note>. Indeed, the image of sinners is despised, but by no means is it reduced to nothing; as it is said in the same Psalm 39: *Surely man walks in an image* <note>or "as a shadow"</note>; that is, everyone existing in this world. From this it clearly appears that the author of our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> did not correctly translate the aforementioned words when he said, "Lord, in your city you shall reduce their image to nothing."

<margin>
What the image of God in man is.
</margin>

Therefore, when it is said in Genesis 1: *God* <note>original: "Elohim"</note> *said, let us make man in our image, after our likeness,* just as by "God" <note>Elohim</note>, according to the exposition of the ancient Jews, are understood the three <term>Middoth</term> <note>Attributes or measures</note> through which they said the world was created—that is, the three divine persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so by the "image of God" <note>Elohim</note> must be understood the three powers of the soul: namely, memory, intelligence, and will, in which the image of the divine Trinity consists.

For from memory, intelligence is formed. For there is nothing from which intelligence itself may be formed except from memory, insofar as memory is the holding of the knowledge of a thing within oneself. Unless, therefore, knowledge is present in the soul, there is nothing by which intelligence may be formed. Furthermore, when intelligence extends itself and its knowledge, and accepts that which is true in the manner of the good and the fitting, immediately from memory and intelligence is formed the appetite, which is the will.

Just as, therefore, intelligence is formed from memory, so in divine matters the Son is generated from the Father. And just as from memory and intelligence extended, and as it were "breathing" the good, the will is formed, so from the Father and the Son, as if from one principle of breathing, the Good is breathed, which is the Holy Spirit. And just as these three powers—memory, intelligence, and will—are one soul, so the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. And this is the image of God in which man was created, according to the opinion of the ancient Hebrews; although they did not remain silent about other likenesses of God in the soul.

<margin>
Likenesses of God in the soul.
</margin>

For in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>Commentary on the Psalms</note> regarding Psalm 103: *Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless His holy name.* And in *Vayikra Rabba* <note>The Great Midrash on Leviticus</note> on the 4th chapter of Leviticus: *The soul that sins, it shall die,* it is read thus literally:

"The Rabbis said: Just as the soul fills the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, fills His world. Just as the soul bears the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, bears the world. Just as the soul is unique in the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, is unique in His world. Just as the soul does not eat and does not drink, so the Holy One, blessed be He, does not eat and does not drink. Just as the soul is pure in the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, is pure in His world. Just as the soul sees and is not seen, so the Holy One, blessed be He, sees and is not seen. David said: 'Let the soul, which possesses all these qualities, come and praise the Holy One, blessed be He, who possesses all these qualities.'"

It concludes with a list of parallels between the properties of the soul and the properties of God, such as invisibility and omnipresence within their respective domains.</summary>

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "הללו ותהללו להקדוש ברוך הוא שיש בו כל המדות הללו"</note> Praise and give praise to the Holy One, blessed be He, for in Him are all these qualities: that is, the Masters said, as the soul fills the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, fills His world. As the soul rules the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, rules the world. As the soul is one in the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, is one in His world. As the soul does not eat, nor does it drink, so the Holy One, blessed be He, neither eats nor drinks. As the soul dwells in the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells in the higher world. As the soul sees and is not seen, so the Holy One, blessed be He, sees and is not seen.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore David said: Let the soul, in which all these properties exist, come and praise the Holy One, blessed be He, in whom all these properties also exist. All these are the preceding traditions. However, in these things, although the soul is considered somewhat similar to God, this similarity—because it is accidental, consisting only of the soul’s accidental qualities—cannot be the very "Image of God" <note>original: "Imago Dei"</note> in which the soul itself was created. For it is necessary that this image consist of those natural properties and powers of the soul by which the soul itself is made capable of knowing and loving God Himself.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Where the Image of God in the soul consists.</margin> These powers are none other than memory, intellect, and will. It is necessary, therefore, that the image of God itself, in which man was made, consists of these. For just as there are three persons in God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so there are three powers in the soul: memory, intellect, and will. In memory, indeed, the image of the Father shines forth, because a fertile memory produces the word through the act of speaking. In the intellect, truly, the image of the Son is expressed, because the Son is begotten by way of intellect and nature. Hence, in divine matters, the Son is the "begotten knowledge" <note>original: "noticia genita"</note> through which the Father knows Himself. In the will, however, the image of the Holy Spirit is suggested, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son by way of the will, as from one principle and one breather <term>spiratore</term> <note>A technical term in Trinitarian theology referring to the joint action of the Father and Son in the "breathing forth" or procession of the Holy Spirit</note>. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the love with which the Father and the Son mutually love one another. And just as the Son is begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, so the intellect arises from memory (taking intellect for both the faculty and its act) and the will has its origin from both, that is, from memory and intellect (taking will for both the faculty and its act). Indeed, the image of the divine Trinity itself (as it pleases our theologians, and especially <note>Duns Scotus, a hugely influential medieval philosopher and theologian</note> Scotus in Book 1, distinction 3, final question) consists not in the first acts of the soul alone, but in the first and second acts taken together <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "first act" is the existence of a power, like the ability to think; a "second act" is the exercise of that power, like an actual thought</note>. For in those, not only do the distinction, origin, and production of the divine persons shine forth most clearly (as has been said), but also their identity and the unity of the divine essence are expressly represented. For just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God, so memory, intellect, and will are not three souls, but only one soul, since there is but one substance of it.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Concerning the name of God **Elohim** <note>original: "אלהים"</note>, and how the divine Trinity is suggested through it.<-

<column-break/>

<header>CAPNIO <note>The Latinized name for Johann Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist</note></header>

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc> SINCE nothing is more suitable or more powerful for proving the mystery of the divine Trinity against the younger Jews than the explanation of divine names, it is therefore necessary for you to prove that same mystery now by explaining the names of God themselves. And first, you must do this through **Elohim** <note>original: "אלהים"</note>, which is more common than the others. GALATINUS: **Elohim** (as you yourself know) is a plural noun, and it signifies what "Gods" does among us. Its singular is **El**, that is God, or rather **Eloah**, which is also the same as God. Therefore, although this name **Elohim** designates plurality, it is nevertheless usually joined with a singular verb whenever it is taken for the true God in Holy Scripture. For instance, in the beginning of the book of Genesis: <note>original Hebrew: "בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ"</note> *In the beginning, Elohim created the heaven and the earth.* This means: *In the beginning, the Gods created heaven and earth.* Where our Greek and Latin editions have "God" <note>singular</note>, the "Hebrew truth" <note>original: "Hebraica veritas," a phrase often used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note> says "Gods" <note>plural</note>. This was certainly not done without a great mystery. For because, according to the opinion of Saint Augustine, the works of the Trinity are inseparable in their outward action, for that reason the great Moses—in order to suggest that all three divine persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, concurred at once in the creation of the world—said **Elohim**, that is "Gods" in the plural, and not **Eloah** or **El**, that is "God" in the singular. To show, however, that those three persons are not essentially distinguished but are entirely the same—that is, that they are one God and not three Gods—he said **bara** <note>original: "ברא"</note>, that is "He created" in the singular, and not **bareu** <note>original: "בראו"</note>, that is "they created" in the plural. It is established, therefore, that through the name **Elohim** joined with a singular verb, both the Trinity of persons and the unity of the divine essence are most excellently designated.

The more recent Jews, however, since they can by no means deny this text, attempt to pervert it with a certain false exposition. For they say that although the name **Elohim** is plural, it is nevertheless used indifferently in both singular and plural senses, and when it is used for the true God, it is always held to be singular and not plural. And so they say it is held here, when it is said, "In the beginning **Elohim** created." From this they conclude that since **Elohim** is not held plurally in this place but singularly, we can by no means infer from it that the Trinity of persons is suggested. But perhaps they could say these things to those ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are not entirely lacking in knowledge of them. We, therefore, who are not altogether inexperienced in them, will prove that they explain this text falsely, both through the Hebrew texts of Holy Scripture and through their own Doctors. For in the *Bereshith Ketanna* <note>The "Little Genesis," likely referring to a specific midrashic compilation</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of Genesis upon this text, it is read that Rabbi Huna said: "Unless this word had been written, it would not have been permitted to say: 'And **Elohim** [Gods] created the heaven and the earth.'" Also, upon that passage of Genesis 1: <note>original Hebrew: "ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו בצלם אלהים ברא אותו"</note> *And Elohim created Adam in His image, in the image of the Gods He created him,* it is read thus: The heretics <note>original: "hæretici," translating the Hebrew 'minim,' often used by rabbis to refer to early Christians or dualists</note> asked Rabbi Semlai...

### BOOK TWO

"How many Gods created the world?" He said to them, "Let me and you search from the days of old." In the commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>A 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> on the book of Genesis, it is held that he responded to them in this way: "Let me and you search from the Law <note>original: "à lege," referring to the Torah.</note>." For it is not written, "The Gods created Adam," but "God created Adam" <note>The author is pointing out that while the noun is plural, the verb is singular.</note>. Again they questioned him; "What of that which is written: 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth'? For it is not written, 'In the beginning the Gods created,' but 'In the beginning God created.'" Rabbi Semlai said, "In every place where you find an objection used by the heretics, you also find the medicine for it right by its side." Similar to this is what is held in the book of the **Sanhedrin** <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with legal and religious councils.</note>, in the chapter that begins **One of the money judgments**, near the end, where it is said that Rabbi Yohanan spoke thus: "Every place from which the Epicureans <note>original: "Epicurei," a term used in Jewish tradition to refer to heretics or those who deny divine providence.</note> became heretics has its response right by its side." For where it is said, "Let us make man in our image," it is also added there, "And **Elohim** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note> (that is, God) created man in his own image." And when it is said in Genesis 11, "Let us go down and confuse their lips," it is also said in the same place, "And the Lord descended to see the city and the tower." And where it is written in Genesis 35, "Because there the Gods appeared to him," it is also read in the same place, "And make there an altar to the God who appeared to you." Likewise in the same place: "And let us arise and go up to the house of God, and I will make there an altar to the God who heard me in the day of my tribulation." Thus far the tradition.

Many other places besides these are found in the sacred writings, in which both the name **Elohim** and certain other names spoken of God are placed in the plural; indeed, no interpreter has translated this way of speaking about God literally, as it would seem very incongruous. Therefore, however (as I judge), the scripture of the ancients allowed this so that the impiety of the more recent Jews, who deny the plurality of the divine persons, might be more strongly refuted. Some of these points are brought into the exposition of Genesis ascribed to Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, where, upon that verse, "In the beginning **Elohim** (that is, God) created the heavens and the earth," it is said word for word: The heretics asked Rabbi **Semlai**, saying, "How many Gods created the world?" He replied, "Let me and you seek this from the Law." They said to him, "Behold, it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 4: 'What great nation is there that has Gods approaching it?' Behold, there are two **principles** <note>original: "ressuioth," meaning domains or powers.</note>." He said to them, "Read the end of the verse: 'As the Lord our God in all our calling upon him.' For it is not written 'upon them,' but 'upon him.'" They said to him, "Behold, it is still written in the last chapter of Joshua: **You will not be able to serve the Lord, because he is Holy Gods** <note>original: "Non poteritis seruire Deo, quia Dii sancti ipse." The Hebrew text uses the plural adjective "Kedoshim" (Holy) with the plural noun Elohim, but a singular pronoun.</note>." He said to them, "Read the end of the text: for it does not say, 'Because they are Holy Gods,' but 'Because he is Holy Gods.'" They said to him again: "Behold, it is written in 2 Samuel chapter 7: **And who is like your people Israel, a unique nation on earth, for whom the Gods went to redeem** <note>original: "iuerunt Dii ad redimendum."</note>." He said to them, "Read what is written following it: for it is not written **to them** <note>original: "lahem"</note>, that is

<margin>A</margin> for themselves in the plural, but **to redeem for himself** <note>original: "lo"</note>, that is, for himself in the singular. Again they said to him, "Behold, it is written in Jeremiah chapter 23: **And you have perverted the words of the Living Gods** <note>original: "Deorum viuentium"</note>." He said to them, "Read the end of the text: for it is not written 'of the Lords of hosts,' but **of the Lord of hosts our God** <note>original: "יהוה צבאות אלהינו"</note>." This is the tradition: where this name **Elohim** is taken for the true God, and yet it is joined with an adjective of plural number; which would by no means happen if it (as they say) were always held in the singular when referring to the true God.

Furthermore, similar to this way of speaking about God is what we read written in Hosea chapter 11: **Ephraim has surrounded me with denial or lies, and the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah will still be ruling with God, and with the faithful Holy Ones** <note>original: "cum sanctis fideli."</note>. Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says, "With the faithful Holy Ones, that is, with the holy and blessed God." Nor do I think we should overlook what is read in the **Midrash Kohelet** <note>An ancient commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, the exposition of Ecclesiastes, upon that 5th chapter: **If you see the oppression of the poor, and the taking away of judgment and justice in the city, do not wonder at such a will: for the high one watches over the high one, and there are High Ones over them.** For there it is said, "If you see the oppressors of the poor and needy, and justice—that is, the just man living—forever multiplying goodness and peace for himself, you should fear the judgment of Gehenna. Because the high one watches over the high one: these are the Angels; and there are High Ones over them: This is the holy and blessed God."

Furthermore, in many places we find this name **Elohim**, when it is taken for the true God, coupled with a verb of plural number, which would in no way happen if it were always held in the singular when referring to the true God. And to pass over almost infinite other examples of that kind, I will bring forward one which most especially serves the purpose. For thus it is written in the 1st chapter of Genesis: **And Elohim said, Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness.** If therefore in this place **Elohim** were held singularly, he would not have said "Let us make," but "I will make." Nor would he have brought forth "in our image, according to our likeness," but "in my image, according to my likeness." However, he said "in our image, according to our likeness," and not "in our images, according to our likenesses," so that he might indicate the identity of the persons and the unity of the divine essence. For even if the three divine **hypostases** <note>A technical term for the individual "Persons" of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).</note> are personally distinguished from one another—since the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another—nevertheless, they are not distinguished essentially, but are altogether the same. Since therefore this name **Elohim** is taken here for the true God, and is uttered with the verb "let us make," which is plural...

However, the later Jewish scholars try to pervert the truth of this text with certain irrational, not to mention false, expositions. For some say that God spoke in the plural when he was about to create man because he consulted his "celestial family" <note>Referring to the assembly of angels.</note>. Their statement is surely empty and void, as is most evident from the fact that all celestial beings serve God, and he does not need their counsel. 

<margin>
Refutations.
</margin>

But others, such as Rabbi David <note>David Kimhi (Radak), a medieval grammarian.</note> and Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides (Ramban), a major 13th-century commentator.</note>, say in this place that God used this mode of speaking because he was then speaking with the Earth, because the man he was about to make had to consist of both divine and earthly matter. But this statement is surely so foolish and ridiculous that it needs no refutation. It is indeed a ridiculous folly to say that God called upon the earth to be his helper in the creation of man. 

Finally, some say that, speaking grammatically, the name **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים</note> is not joined in this place with the plural verb "Let us make," but with the verb "He said," which is singular. For the text says, "And **Elohim** said." And afterwards follows, "Let us make man." This also is nothing. For even if **Elohim** is not immediately connected to the verb "Let us make," it is nonetheless connected indirectly, which is exactly the same thing. For no one other than **Elohim** said, "Let us make man." Moreover, although the name **Elohim** used here for the true God is coupled indirectly rather than directly with a plural verb, it is directly coupled in many other places, as is easily apparent to those who read the Bible written in Hebrew characters. 

Yet these men, and all others who strive to distort the meaning of this text, are easily convicted by what is found in the **Midrash Koheleth** <note>A rabbinic commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, regarding what is held in the second chapter: "For who is the man who shall come or enter after the King, whom they have already made him?" <note>original Hebrew: כי מה האדם שיבוא אחרי המלך את אשר כבר עשוהו — Ecclesiastes 2:12. The Latin notes the plural "made" (fecerunt/עשוהו).</note> For it is said there: "After the King—namely, the King of other kings, the holy and blessed God—will you then be able to stand?" It teaches through this that it must be noted that it is not written "he who made him," but "those who made him." Because this is written in the Law <note>The Torah.</note>, it can be said: for the holy and blessed God, and his House of Judgment, made him. 

But if you say from this, "Therefore there are two principles," it does not follow. For was it not already said in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: "He himself made you, and adjusted, or prepared, or adorned you"? Thus far the tradition. In which three things are put forward that are very worthy of note and most fit for the matter at hand. The first is that the plural verb, "They made," is joined with the singular name, "King," in the creation of man, because when God founded man, he spoke in the plural, saying, "Let us make man in our image." Hence the Psalmist said in Psalm 149: "Let Israel rejoice in his makers; let the children of Zion exult in

<column-break/>

their king." <note>original: ישמח ישראל בעשיו בני ציון יגילו במלכם — Psalm 149:2. The Hebrew word for "maker" here is plural.</note> From this also Isaiah says in chapter 54: "Because your masters are your makers, the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) of hosts is his name." <note>original: כי בעליך עשיך יהוה צבאות שמו — Isaiah 54:5. Both "husband/master" and "maker" are plural in the Hebrew text.</note> 

The second point is when it is said in this tradition: "That the holy and blessed God, and his House of Judgment, made man." Where, by "the holy and blessed God," the unity of the divine nature is shown; but by the "House of Judgment," the trinity of persons is suggested. For among the Jews, a "House of Judgment" <note>term: Beth Din; a rabbinical court.</note> was named when at least three men together delivered a sentence; although there could be more, there could not be fewer, provided they were always an odd number. Therefore, the House of the Judgment of God is nothing other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 

For this reason, in the **Bereshit Rabbah** <note>A midrashic commentary on Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding that in the 19th chapter: "And the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur and fire," <note>original Hebrew: ויהוה המטיר על סדום ועל עמרה גפרית ואש — Genesis 19:24.</note> Rabbi Elazar said: "In every place where the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) is placed in scripture, it is always understood as Himself and his House of Judgment." This same Rabbi affirms the same in the **Midrash Shir HaShirim** <note>Commentary on the Song of Songs.</note>, on that in the 1st chapter: "I have compared you, my love, to my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots, or among his riders." 

The third point is when it is added in the same tradition that God and his House of Judgment are not two principles of all created things, but only one single principle. From which it is clear that the ancient Jewish Doctors did not deny the mystery of the divine trinity, but only multiple principles, or multiple Gods—which the Christian religion detests no less. Since these things are so, it is clearer than light that by the name **Elohim**, the three divine persons ought to be understood, who concurred together as a single principle for the production of all things.

# BOOK SECOND

...named. When he was questioned by Antoninus, Consul of the City of Rome, regarding the meaning of this name, he revealed many complex matters. His words are recorded by Rabbi Nehumias, son of Haccana, in the *Epistle of Secrets* written to his son Haccana, which the Hebrews call the *Igghereth Hassodoth* <note>original: אגרת הסודות; a mystical work attributed to the 1st-century sage Nehunyah ben HaKanah.</note>. He speaks thus:

> The Roman Consul asked our Holy Teacher <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century compiler of the Mishnah, who according to legend was a friend of a Roman emperor named "Antoninus."</note> to teach him the truths of the Four-Letter Name, the Twelve-Letter Name, and the Forty-Two-Letter Name. He replied: Because you ask to be taught the truth—that is, the meaning of the Four-Letter Name, the Twelve-Letter Name, and the Forty-Letter Name—I inform you that these are divine secrets which ought to be hidden from every man. However, because I recognize you as one of the most blessed students, and it is reasonable to reveal these things to such men (since the people of that nation <note>referring to Rome</note> should not have such things hidden from them), I inform you that God has no name which we can truly comprehend. This is because His essence is His name, and His name is His essence. Just as we can have no comprehension of His essence (for with such knowledge, we would be equal to Him), so we cannot comprehend His name. Nevertheless, all His names have a meaning. The Four-Letter Name is the most essential to His actions and shows a more perfect and essential knowledge, as far as we are capable of receiving it. From this name, all His other names are joined and proceed. For this reason, this name is called the *Explicit Name* <note>original: שם המפורש; *Shem HaMephoras*, the distinct or "unutterable" name of God.</note>, not because it is His essential name in itself, but because we call it so since it is the highest thing our faculty can comprehend, and we cannot ascend any higher. You should also know that the Twelve-Letter and Forty-Two-Letter names are not single words made of twelve or forty-two letters, but in whichever name it may be, there are various different words that point to one meaning.

This means: Antoninus, Consul of the City of Rome, once asked the Holy Rabbi to instruct him in the truth—specifically regarding what is signified by the four-letter name, the twelve-letter name, and the forty-two-letter name. He replied: Since you ask to be informed of the truth—namely what the four, twelve, and forty-two-letter names demonstrate—I make it known to you that these are divine secrets that must remain hidden from all men. However, because I know you to be a well-deserving scholar, and it is consistent with reason to reveal such things to men of this kind, for such things should by no means be hidden from them, I therefore inform you that God has no name of which we can have knowledge; for His substance is His name, and vice versa. And just as we can have no knowledge of His substance (since if it were known, we would be made equal to Him), so we cannot have knowledge of His name. Nevertheless, all His names are attributes. And because the four-letter name is more peculiar to His operations, and shows a more perfect knowledge of Him, and is more suited to Him as far as our understanding allows, and because all His other names proceed from this name, therefore this name is called the **Shem HaMephoras** <note>original: שם המפורש; the Explicit Name</note>. This is not because it is His substantial name in itself, but because we say it is so because it is as much as our capacity can comprehend, and we cannot ascend higher. You should note, however, that the twelve-letter name and the forty-two-letter name are not names

<column-break/>

in which each single word consists of twelve or forty-two letters, but each of them consists of various words that demonstrate one thing. Thus far his words. Furthermore, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), the most influential medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> in the book *The Guide* <note>original: *More Nevuchim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*</note>, in the sixty-first chapter of the first part, says word-for-word: All the names of the Creator found in all books are derived from His effects, except for one name, which is **YHWH** <note>The Tetragrammaton.</note>. This is the name specifically appropriated to the Most High Creator. Because of this, it is called the **Shem HaMephoras**, that is, the "Explicit Name." He means to say that this name signifies and demonstrates the Creator's substance and His "whatness" with perfect and manifest demonstration and meaning, in which there is no ambiguity or mixture. That is to say: there is nothing in this name that is common to both God and the creature. His other glorious names, however, signify ambiguously and with mixture, because they are derived from actions similar to those found in us. For instance, even the name **Adonai** <note>original: אדני; meaning "Lord" or "My Lord."</note>, which is used in place of **YHWH** (the four-letter name), is derived from the word **Adon** <note>original: אדן</note>, which means "Master" or "Lord." From this it follows that an Angel is also called **Adonai**, as is said in *Genesis chapter 18*: *Adonai, I pray thee, if I have found favor in thy eyes.* <note>Standard Bibles usually translate this as "My Lord" or "Lord." The author notes that the title "Lord" can apply to both God and respected beings like angels.</note> I have shown you this regarding the word **Adonai**, by which the name of the Creator is pronounced, because it is more specifically appropriated to the Most High God than all other names that identify the Creator. But the others, such as **Daiian** <note>original: דיין</note> meaning "Judge," and **Tsadik** <note>original: צדיק</note> meaning "Just," and **Hannun** <note>original: חנון</note> meaning "Gracious," or "Pious" and "Merciful"—it is manifest that these are common and derived terms. But for the name written with four letters, **YHWH**, no known derivation is found, nor does it share a meaning with anything else. There is no doubt that this glorious name—which is not uttered, nor pronounced, nor spoken except in the sanctuary by the sanctified priests of the Lord, and only in the priestly blessing, and then only by the High Priest on the day of the fast of glorious sanctification <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.</note>—is that name in which there is no shared quality between the Creator and anything else. Briefly, I say that the highness and excellence of this name is considered so great, and such great and terrible caution is taken so that no one speaks it, because it signifies the Creator's substance; thus, no creature communicates with Him in 그 meaning. Just as our masters asserted, speaking in the person of God: "My name is unique, or appropriated to me alone." All other names of God signify qualities and other attributes. And when these names of the Creator, derived from His works, were multiplied, they caused it to pass over the hearts of some of the sons of Adam that He Himself might have many qualities, according to the multitude of works from which those names are derived. For that reason, He promised to give men understanding which would remove such error from them. For it is said in *Zechariah chapter 14*: *In that day the Lord shall be one, and his name one.* He means to say that just as the Lord Himself is one, so then...

...He shall be called by only one name, which signifies His substance or essence without being derived from any action. It is said in the <term>Pirke</term> <note>original: פרקי; "Chapters," referring to the *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a famous 8th-century collection of Jewish traditions and lore.</note> of Rabbi Eliezer, that when the world had not yet been created, there was only the Holy and Blessed God and His Name. Observe how clearly this shows that all these other names of God were newly found and derived after the creation of the world. It is indeed certain that they are all named from various works found in the world. But when you consider God’s essence stripped of every operation, there will be no derived name for Him at all, but only one to designate His essence. Among us, there is no name that is not derived, except for the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>Greek for "four letters."</note>, <term>YHWH</term> <note>original: יהוה; the four-letter name of God, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, which is the <term>Shem Ha-Mephoras</term> <note>original: שם המפורש; the "Explicit Name" or "Distinct Name."</note>, that is, the name set forth absolutely. You should not believe it to be anything other than this. Nor should the vanities of those who write short charms pass through your heart, nor those things you have perhaps heard from them or found in their most vain books—certain names of deluded men, composed by them and signifying nothing at all, which they call divine names. They say that great holiness and purity are necessary to achieve an effect, and that it is possible for a man to perform miracles with names of this kind. It does not befit a prudent man to listen to such vanities and insanities, let alone believe them. Nor is there any other name called the <term>Shem Ha-Mephoras</term> (the Explicit Name) except this glorious four-letter name, which is by no means read according to its letters. They spoke clearly with an explanation in the book called <term>Sifre</term> <note>original: ספרי; an ancient legal commentary on the biblical books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, regarding that passage in Numbers chapter 6: *Thus you shall bless the children of Israel.* "Thus," that is, in this language. "Thus," that is, with the <term>Shem Ha-Mephoras</term>. It was spoken in the Sanctuary exactly as it is written; but in the city, it was spoken according to its common pronunciation—that is, <term>Adonai</term> <note>original: אדני; "My Lord."</note> was said in its place. It is also said in the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> regarding that same passage of Numbers chapter 6: "Thus," that is, with the <term>Shem Ha-Mephoras</term>, or with its proper pronunciation. He teaches what is to be said when He says: *And place, or name, my unique name,* specifically for Me. Behold, it is explained there that the <term>Shem Ha-Mephoras</term> is the name of four letters, and that it alone signifies and shows the Creator’s substance without any other mixture or meaning. Therefore, the masters said in the person of God: *My name is unique to Me.* All these things were said by Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Commonly known as Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>. 

**CAPITO:** I beg you, tell me how this four-letter name is pronounced, as it is written, or as the letters themselves sound. 

**GALATINUS:** Some of our people say this name sounds like **Jova** in our letters. From this, they say that perhaps the name of **Jove** <note>The Roman name for Jupiter.</note> crept in among the ancients. But they are surely most mistaken, bringing such a pagan blasphemy out of so holy a name. For these four letters <term>YHWH</term>, if they are read as they are pointed with vowels, do not yield **Jova**; but (as you yourself know best) they produce **Jehovah**: although the Jews do not dare

<column-break/>

to pronounce it as it is written, but in its place they utter <term>Adonai</term>, which is the same as "Lord." Those who contend that it sounds like **Jova** in our letters try to prove it primarily from what the Hebrew Grammarians say: that when a <term>Sheva</term> <note>original: שוא; a Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very brief "e" sound or no vowel at all.</note> follows one of the guttural letters, often both the *Sheva* itself and the guttural letter are removed together by a shortening of the word. For example, <term>Yehuda</term> <note>Judah</note> is sometimes both written and pronounced as <term>Yuda</term>; and <term>Yehoshua</term> <note>Joshua</note> as <term>Yoshua</term>; and <term>Yehoiachin</term> as <term>Yoiachin</term>; and <term>Tehillim</term> <note>Psalms</note> as <term>Tillim</term>; and many other things of that kind. They wish for the same thing to happen similarly in this great name of God. From this, they infer that it sounds like **Jova** among us, since in it the *Sheva* precedes the letter *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה, a guttural breath.</note>. But if this were true, the name itself would not be written as <term>YHWH</term> but as <term>YWH</term> without the *Sheva* and the letter *He*. And thus it would not be a *Tetragrammaton*, or of four letters, but of only three, which is not even permitted to be thought. For it is a sin for anything to be added or taken away in that name. Rather, it ought to be both written and pronounced (if it is to be pronounced at all) exactly as God Himself commanded Moses it should be written. Therefore, the rule of the Hebrew Grammarians which they bring forward has no place in this matter, even though in the remaining twenty-four sacred books it is found to be kept nowhere or only very rarely, appearing instead only in other books, and especially among the Talmudists. Therefore, it is necessary that the Tetragrammaton name of God itself be both written and pronounced with the *Sheva* and the letter *He*, which has a soft aspiration. Therefore, let those who affirm that it sounds like **Jova** among us beware. For it is not to be pronounced **Jova**, nor **Jeoua**, but **Jehovah** with a soft aspiration, just as it is written. 

**CAPITO:** How do the Hebrews interpret this name? 

**GALATINUS:** Some among them interpret it as "The Generator"; others as "He who brings into being," or "He who gives being to all"; and others as "The One and all things," or "All things united as a cause," or "The One containing all things preeminently." 

**CAPITO:** Why do the Jews not dare to pronounce this name? 

**GALATINUS:** Because of those things contained in the book <term>Chiddushim</term> <note>original: חדושים; "Novellae" or new interpretations, here likely referring to the Talmudic tractate Kiddushin.</note>, that is, of sanctifications, in the chapter <term>Asarah</term> <note>original: עשרה; referring to the chapter *Asarah Yohasin* (Ten Lineages) in the Talmud.</note> regarding that passage of Exodus chapter 3: *This is my name forever.* For it is read there that a certain elder said it is not written <term>le-olam</term> <note>original: לעולם; "forever"</note>, but <term>le-alam</term> <note>original: לעלם; "to be hidden," a wordplay based on the same spelling without vowel points.</note>, that is, that it should be concealed. Rabbi Abina objected, saying: "It is written, *This is my name.* and it is also written in the same place, *This is my memorial.*" The Holy and Blessed God said: "I am not read as I am written: for I am written with *Yod*, *He*, *Vav*, *He*—namely <term>YHWH</term>, which is the Tetragrammaton name—and I am read with *Aleph*, *Daleth*, *Nun*, *Yod*, which letters make <term>Adonai</term>, which is the same as 'Lord'." Therefore, the masters commanded that *Adonai* ought to be read in its place. These things are found there. Wherefore, as is read in the book *Sanhedrin* in the chapter *Helek*, Abba Saul said: "He who pronounces the four-letter name itself according to how its letters sound, has no

...will have a portion in the world to come. For that reason, wherever they found that name, they did not dare to pronounce it at all, but instead spoke the name *Adonai* <note>original: אדני; "My Lord."</note> in its place. However, the priests would pronounce it as it is written while they were blessing the people in the sanctuary. For it was not permitted to speak the ineffable name outside of the sanctuary (as you yourself write in that most beautiful letter which I received from you a second time). Rabbi Moses, the son of Maimon <note>Better known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, affirms this in the sixty-first chapter of the first part of his book, *The Guide* <note>original: *More* (Moreh Nevukhim); *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>, saying: "We are commanded to be blessed by the priests, and there is the name of the Lord according to its proper writing; and that is the <term>שם המפורש</term> *sem hammephoras* <note>The "Explicit Name" or "Distinct Name."</note>, that is, the name of God set forth." These are his words. 

Moreover, this blessing with the four-letter name of God—which was performed with three fingers of both palms raised and two pressed down to signify the trinity of divine persons meant by the name itself—ceased entirely with Simeon the Just <note>A High Priest in the Second Temple period, often identified with the Simeon who met the infant Jesus in the Temple.</note>, who took the infant Christ in his arms. As the same Rabbi Moses testifies in the same place with these words: "From the time that Simeon the Just died, his brother priests ceased to bless the people with the four-letter name of God; instead, after him, they blessed with a name of twelve letters." These are his words. He also says there: "When this name was pronounced in the sanctuary and in the blessing of the people, it was not known to every man in what manner it was pronounced, or with which vowel each of its letters should sound, and whether some of them should be doubled or spoken simply or softly. There were, however, wise men who received the meaning of the name and the manner of its pronunciation from one another; they taught no one except a disciple worthy of them, and only once a week." 

I am of the opinion that when the wise men taught their sons the four-letter name only once a week, this was not solely to teach how it was pronounced, but also its meaning, for which a name of this kind was devised and assigned. For in it, surely, is a divine mystery. Thus far the Rabbi. 

<margin>CHAPTER</margin> If this name was sometimes pronounced among them (as you have excellently proven), why then was it called "ineffable"? 

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> This cannot be without a great mystery. For this name is not called ineffable regarding the actual sound of the name, since they themselves (as has been said) sometimes pronounced it, and it can easily be spoken just as it is written if the letters are read with their marks and points—for from these (as said) the word *Jehovah* is produced. Rather, it is entirely ineffable regarding the meaning of the mystery. For it signifies the divine essence so distinctly that it openly suggests the trinity of divine persons and their eternal distinction, origin, and production along with His most simple unity. 

Because, therefore, the Triune and One God, who is entirely ineffable and incomprehensible, is signified by this name, the name itself is called ineffable. For that reason, the ancient Jews, taught by that great Moses, established that this name should not be spoken at all to designate this ineffability of the divine trinity and unity. Instead, wherever it was found, this name <term>אדני</term> *Adonai*, which is interpreted as "Lord," ought to be pronounced in its place. Therefore, wherever we encounter this name to be interpreted, we are accustomed to translate it into Latin sometimes as "God," according to its meaning, and sometimes as "Lord," according to its pronunciation, as seems most fitting. 

On account of this ineffability of God, Rabbenu Haccados <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah.</note> said (as we mentioned a little earlier) that God Himself has no name of which we can have knowledge. Even that Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic.</note> seems to feel this when he says: <term>ὁ γὰר θεὸς ὢן ἀνώνυמוς</term> <note>original Greek: "ho gar theos on anonymos."</note>: that is, "For he is God who is without a name." And again, regarding the ineffability of this name, he says: <term>ἐκ τὸ ὄνομα ἐδύנאται ἀνθρωπίνῳ στόματι λαληθῆναι</term> <note>original Greek: "ek to onoma edynatai anthropino stomati lalethēnai."</note>: that is, "Whose name cannot be spoken by a human mouth." Even a demon could not keep silent about this. For the Delphic Apollo, when someone asked what God was, replied among other things: <term>ᾧ τὸ ὄνομα μηδὲ λόגῳ χωρούμενον</term> <note>original Greek: "hō to onoma mēde logō chōroumenon."</note>: that is, "Whose name is not to be captured even by a word."

### CHAPTER X.

->*How the mystery of the divine trinity is distinctly expressed through the four-letter name of God.*<-

### CAPNIO.

I ask you now to reveal in what manner this four-letter name of God distinctly suggests the secret of the divine trinity and unity. 

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> If you look more diligently at this name of four letters (which is nevertheless only made of three, for it is written with only three distinct letters; yet because one of them is doubled, it is called "of four letters" or the <term>tetragrammaton</term>), you will see that the same name is both one and three. In that it is one, it regards the unity of essence; in that it is three, it regards the trinity of persons. 

<margin>CAPNIO</margin> I pray you explain these things more clearly. 

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> Hear Rabbenu Haccados speaking most excellently and clearly on this matter in the first petition of his book titled <term>גלי רזיא</term> *Gale razeia* <note>The *Revealer of Secrets* (Gali Razaya), a kabbalistic work.</note>. His words are these: "And after we have opened this to you, look: that the name of four letters, according to the form of its writing in our Hebrew language, is this: יהוה [YHWH]. He is God the Begetter, and because there cannot be a Begetter without a Begotten, it is fitting to share the love from the Begetter to the Begotten and conversely from the Begotten to the Begetter. For if this were not so, He would not be a Begetter; and if He did not share love from Begetter to Begotten, the Begetter would be separate from the Begotten and they would be two essences. But we desire the Begetter and the Begotten to be one essence, and therefore it is necessary for love to be extended from one to the other. And therefore, from this Explicit Name is derived the name of twelve letters, for he is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which in our Hebrew language are twelve letters written thus above. And because nothing is found in God which is not God from the name of twelve..."

Ten letters are used for the name of forty-two letters <margin>A</margin> which is Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God, three in one, one in three, which in Hebrew are the forty-two letters of the appearance of the aforementioned name; and know these names to be among the divine secrets which ought to be hidden from everyone until our righteous Messiah comes, and I have revealed them to you, so you must stand firm in the secret: <note>original: "עשר אותיות משתמש שם ארבעים ושתים אותיות..." This Hebrew passage provides a mystical Trinitarian reading of a traditional Kabbalistic name of God.</note> That is, after I have opened this to you, observe the name of four letters, according to its writing (for so it is written in our Hebrew language, יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH.</note>), that it signifies God the begetter himself. And because there cannot be <margin>B</margin> a begetter without a begotten, necessarily love must proceed from the begetter into the begotten, and vice versa: for if this were not so, He would not beget. And if love did not proceed from the begotten into the begetter, the begotten would be divided from the begetter, and there would be two substances. Therefore, we maintain that the begetter and the begotten are one substance. For that reason, it is necessary for love to proceed from the one into the other. Consequently, from this <margin>The name of twelve letters.</margin> <term>Sem hammephoras</term> <note>The "Explicit Name."</note>, the name of twelve letters is derived. And it is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These are written in our Hebrew language with twelve letters. Furthermore, because nothing is found in God which is not God, from the name of twelve letters emanates the name of forty-two letters, <margin>The name of forty-two letters.</margin> which is Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God, Trinity in Unity, and Unity in Trinity. These in Hebrew are forty-two letters. You ought to note, however, that these names <margin>D</margin> are from the divine secrets, which must be hidden from anyone until our righteous Messiah comes. I have revealed those things to you; you, however, must hide them strictly. Thus says that <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah, whom Galatinus claims held secret Christian views.</note>.

**Cap.** Although this Rabbi—whom they deservedly call <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term>, that is, our holy master—has most excellently proved through the four-letter name of God, the Trinity of divine persons, the unity of the divine essence, that the Son is begotten by the Father, and that the Holy Spirit (whom he rightly calls Love) proceeds from both, and that each one is true God, and the three are one essence and one God: yet, because his book <term>Gale razeia</term> <note>The "Revealer of Secrets."</note> is very rare, and those who possess it hide it completely because of the mysteries of the Christian faith contained within it (to the point that some of them dare to say it was forged by us), it would be best if you would reveal the secrets of the divine Trinity through this most holy name according to the opinions of other ancient writers, both Talmudists and Kabbalists, as I shall question you, so that the truth itself may become more clearly known and the blindness of the younger Jews more apparent. First, therefore, relate what the letters of this name mean.

**Gal.** The letters of this name, although (as I said) they are four in number—whence in Greek it is not inaptly called <term>tetragrammaton</term> <note>A "four-lettered" word.</note>—in truth there are only three: namely, <term>iod</term>, <term>he</term>, and <term>vau</term>. <margin>What the letters of this name signify.</margin> And because the second is placed twice, namely in the second and fourth place, they are reckoned to be four. Therefore, the three letters of this name designate the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>The individual "persons" or "subsistences" of the Trinity.</note>. For the first, <term>iod</term> <note>The letter Y.</note>, which is interpreted as "principle" or "beginning"—because it is the beginning of all other letters, since every one takes the origin of its writing from it, while it takes its origin from none—most rightly suggests the Father in the Godhead. For He, being from no one, while the other persons emanate from Him, is called the "principle without a principle." The second, namely ה <term>he</term> <note>The letter H.</note>, which signifies "to be" or "to live," most aptly hints at the Son in the Godhead, through whom all things that were made began to be, and whatever was made, in Him was life. The third, namely ו <term>vau</term> <note>The letter V or W.</note>, which denotes the connecting word "And," excellently expresses the Holy Spirit, who, since He is the love of the Father and the Son by which they love each other in turn, is rightly called the "copula"—that is, the bond of both.

**Cap.** Why is only the second of these letters doubled?

**Gal.** To suggest that only the Son, who is the second person in the Trinity, has a double respect. For the Father, who is the first person, since He is only producing and not produced, has only one respect in this regard. The Holy Spirit also, who is the third person, since He is only produced and not producing, likewise has only one respect. But the Son himself, who is the second person, since He is both produced and producing, has two respects: for He is both produced by the Father, and together with the Father He produces the Holy Spirit.

**Cap.** For what reason, in the ancient books of the Hebrews, is this four-letter name found written as three <term>iod</term> letters, which are also enclosed in a circle, and have the <term>camez</term> <note>Qamets: a Hebrew vowel mark representing a long 'a' sound.</note> point placed under them, in this way:
<image-desc>Three Hebrew 'yod' letters arranged in a triangle within a circle, with a 'qamets' vowel mark underneath.</image-desc>

**Gal.** Two secrets are suggested in this: one of which is that (as we said) <term>iod</term> is the same as "principle." Therefore, although "principle" in the internal works of the Trinity belongs to the Father alone, in the external operations it is common to the three persons. The three <term>iods</term>, therefore, are the three divine <term>hypostases</term>. The single <term>camez</term> placed under the three <term>iods</term> is the divine nature, which is communicated to each <term>hypostasis</term> as a whole and indivisibly. The circle by which the three <term>iods</term> are enclosed is the identity of the divine essence itself, by which the divine <term>hypostases</term> themselves concur together as a single principle and a single first cause in the actions of all things. The other secret is that the three equal <term>iods</term> signify the equality of the three persons; the <term>camez</term> designates the one divine essence existing in those three divine persons. The circle of the essence itself denotes identity, by which each person is said to be in the others through <term>circumincesio</term> <note>Circumincession or Perichoresis: the theological concept of the mutual indwelling of the three Persons of the Trinity.</note>.

**Cap.** What do the three syllables of this name signify?

**Gal.** They signify the three divine persons to each other. For just as each syllable of this name (as the Kabbalists say) signifies that whole which the name itself imports, so any divine person, since He is perfect God, contains the whole divinity in himself: nor is the divinity itself more in the three persons together than it is in each one, but it is whole in each one, and whole in the three. Therefore, the three syllables of this name designate the three divine persons, each of whom is true and perfect God. For the Father is true and perfect God, and the Son is true...

<margin>Three divine names composed from the letters of this name.</margin>
**Capnio.** What are those three divine names which the ancient Hebrews asserted were composed from the four letters of this name? **Galatinus.** These are: יה *Yah*, הו *Hu*, and ויהו *Vehu*. The first is composed of the first and second letters, namely *iod* and *he*, as יה *Yah*, which is the same as God and designates the Father, who is the source of all divinity. The second name consists of the second and third letters, הו *Hu*, which is interpreted as "He Himself" and signifies the Son; for He is truly the one whom the Prophets foretold would come to save the human race, and whom they sometimes pointed to with a finger, according to Isaiah chapter 35: אלהיכם הוא יבא ויושעכם <note>original: "Eloheichem hu yavo v’yoshachem."</note> *that is, God himself will come and save you*. Finally, the third name is formed from the third and fourth letters, namely *vau* and *he*, as ויהו *Vehu*, which sounds the same as "And He Himself," and denotes the Holy Spirit. This is because He too was to be sent visibly after the Son, though not in the same manner. For the Son was to be sent in a human nature <term>hypostatically</term> <note>meaning the union of divine and human natures in one person</note> united to Him. The Holy Spirit, however, appeared in the form of a dove and in tongues of fire, not hypostatically united, but as if under a sign. Furthermore, because the second name descends from the first, and the third from the second (for the letter ה *he* is common to the first and second names, and ו *vau* is common to the second and third), it is clearly shown that the Son is <term>consubstantial</term> <note>of the same substance or essence</note> with the Father, by whom He was begotten, and the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Son, who is consubstantial with the Father. Thus it is openly clear that the Son is in the Father, the Father is in the Son, and the Holy Spirit is in both. **Capnio.** I also believe it was not done without a great mystery that all the letters of this name are the same as those from which the three tenses—past, present, and future—of the substantive verb <note>The verb "to be."</note> in the indicative mood are formed among the Hebrews. **Galatinus.** It is exactly as you say. In this, two secrets are revealed. The first is that, just as only the substantive verb signifies substance (which is why it is called substantive), while others signify accidents (which is why they are called adjectives), so only the substantive verb in the indicative mood designates stability, while others designate flux. Therefore, because all the letters of this name are taken from the substantive verb in the indicative mood, the absolute and eternal stability of the divine persons is denoted. The other secret is that this name consists of the same letters from which the three tenses of that verb are composed—past, present, and future. In Hebrew they sound like היה *haiah* (He was), הוה *houe* (He is), and יהיה *ihie* (He will be). From this, the eternity of these persons is most clearly evident: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit always have been, are, and shall be. **Capnio.** Why is this name called among the Hebrews שם המפורש *Shem ha-Mephorash*, which for us means the "Exposed" or "Declared" name? **Galatinus.** Although the four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note> distinctly suggested the mystery of the divine Trinity within the unity of essence, the declaration of this mystery was reserved for the Messiah. It was not explicitly explained in the Old Testament, lest that unrefined and worldly people fall into the error of worshipping a plurality of gods. This is why Moses spoke to them with a veiled face: to imply that such secrets ought to be handed down only through figures and riddles. Those who were inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit and understood the meaning of this name passed it on only to a very few worthy people. They explained the name first through a name of twelve letters, and finally through a name of forty-two letters. However, as Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Also known as Maimonides, the famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> says in the book *Moreh* <note>The "Guide for the Perplexed."</note>, in chapter 40 of the first part: they did not claim that either the twelve-letter name or the forty-two-letter name was the *Shem ha-Mephorash*, that is, the "Exposed Name." For the *Shem ha-Mephorash* is only the unique name of the holy and blessed God, which is the name of four letters, as we showed just above. These other two names necessarily provided a man with knowledge and notice of God, because through them the four-letter name itself was explained. They called this Tetragrammaton the *Shem ha-Mephorash* because the ancient Hebrews explained it through names of twelve and forty-two letters, and it was to be explained even better, more distinctly, and more clearly by the Messiah.

### CHAPTER XI.

->*Regarding the twelve-letter name of God: And how the ancient Jews used it to explain the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' with floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

IN order to have an even clearer and more perfect knowledge of the four-letter name, we must now speak of the names through which you asserted it was explained by the ancient Jewish sages. Once these are understood, its explanation and significance can be easily known. Therefore, first discourse upon the name of twelve letters: what it was, and how the Tetragrammaton came to be explained by those fathers through it. **Galatinus.** For a better understanding of what I am about to say regarding both this twelve-letter name and the other name of forty-two letters, the words of Rabbeni Haccados <note>The "Holy Rabbi," usually referring to Judah ha-Nasi, though here attributed to a mystical source.</note> should be noted. In the first petition of that book which he called גלי רזיא *Gale Razia*, that is, the "Revealer of Secrets," he says (as we have already seen above): The name of twelve letters and the name of forty-two letters are not truly names where one consists of twelve and the other of forty-two letters, but each of them contains various words which...

SECOND BOOK.
D iiij
<meta>Catchword: they showed</meta>

...they show. Therefore, so that I might say nothing myself regarding the Name of Twelve Letters, I shall bring forward only those things which Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> says about it in the sixty-first chapter of the first part of the book *More* <note>The *Moreh Nevuchim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>. For there he says, word for word: "There was still a name among them, which they called the 'son of twelve letters'; which certainly was held in holiness and reverence, though less so than the Name of Four Letters. However, as far as I am concerned, what I strongly suspect is readily apparent: that it was not a single name, but two or three names joined together, the letters of which totaled twelve. And those ancient holy fathers, whenever the Name of Four Letters occurred in Holy Scripture—namely יהוה <note>original: "YHWH"</note>—they would pronounce and explain it using those twelve letters; just as today we pronounce it with these four: *aleph, daleth, nun, iod*, that is, as אדני *Adonai* <note>meaning "My Lord."</note>. Nevertheless, that Name of Twelve Letters undoubtedly carried a significance of greater unity than what this name אדני *Adonai* signifies. Nor did they forbid anyone from knowing it; rather, they taught it to anyone who wished to learn it. They did not do so, however, with the Name of Four Letters; for those who knew it taught it to no one except their own sons and disciples, and only to those who were worthy of knowing it, and this only once a week. But when schismatic and insolent men increased in the world and learned the Name of Twelve Letters, they corrupted the faith with it—as happens to one who is imperfect when he perceives that a matter is not exactly as it seemed to him at the beginning. For this reason, those fathers hid that Name of Twelve Letters and taught it to no one further, except to the honorable and modest who were in the priesthood, so that they might bless the people with it in the sanctuary. This was after they forbade the remembrance of the 'Expounded Name' <note>The *Shem HaMephorash*, the specifically articulated name of God.</note> in the sanctuary because of the malice of the children of Adam." Which, as this same Rabbi asserts, happened immediately after the death of Simeon the Just <note>A High Priest in the Second Temple period, often identified with the era of Alexander the Great.</note>, who was the last of all to bless the people with the Name of Four Letters. All these things are from Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, son of Maimon. Since, therefore, this Rabbi says that the Name of Twelve Letters was not one name, but two or three names consisting of twelve letters, through which those ancient fathers pronounced and explained the Tetragrammaton—which distinctly suggests the mystery of the divine Trinity—it is certain beyond doubt that this Name of Twelve Letters was none other than these three names: אב בן ורוח הקדש <note>original: "Ab, Ben, ve-Ruah ha-Kadosh"</note>. That is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Jews’ own writings provide evidence for this wonderful explanation. For if these names are written in Hebrew letters, thus: אב, *ab*, that is, Father; בן, *ben*, that is, Son; ורוח הקדש *ve-ruah haccados*, that is, and the Holy Spirit—or even if we call Him the Holy Spirit as they more frequently do, רוח הקדש *Ruah haccodes*, that is, the Spirit of Holiness, or of the Sanctuary—and we say it like this: אב בן רוח הקדש, that is, Father, Son, and Spirit of Holiness or the Sanctuary: in both ways these names consist of twelve letters. For the first, namely אב *ab*, which is Father, is composed of two letters. The second, namely בן *ben*, which is the same as Son, is also written with two letters. The third, with the conjunction *vau* and the name ורוח הקדש *ve-ruah haccados*, which is Holy Spirit, or as they say, רוח הקדש *ruah haccodes*, that is, the Spirit of Holiness or the Sanctuary: in both ways among them it is written with no more than eight letters, which, together with the aforementioned four, complete the number twelve. It is clear, therefore, that the Name of God of twelve letters, through which the Tetragrammaton was explained, was nothing else but these three names: אב בן ורוח הקדש <note>original: "Ab, Ben, ve-Ruah ha-Kadosh"</note>, which is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which are written with twelve letters among the Hebrews. Which Rabbenus Haccados <note>Literally "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> affirms in the aforementioned book and place (as seen above), saying: "From this 'Expounded Name' is derived the Name of Twelve Letters, which is: Father, Son, and Spirit of Holiness." Now, these three names were called "one name" to imply that the three divine persons expressed by those three names are one according to nature, that is, one God.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Concerning the Name of Forty-Two Letters, by which the ancient Jews most clearly explained the secret of the divine Trinity and Unity.*<-

The Name of Twelve Letters.

NOW it remains for you to say what the Name of God of forty-two letters is, and how the Name of God, the Tetragrammaton, was explained by the ancient Jews through it. GALATINUS: Through the Name of God of forty-two letters, the ancient Hebrews explained the Name of God of twelve letters. Just as they asserted that the Name of Twelve Letters was derived from the Name of Four Letters, so they said the Name of Forty-Two emanated from the Name of Twelve Letters. Therefore, so that I may say nothing of my own regarding this name (just as I have done with the others, but only report what they themselves asserted), first hear what Rabbi Moses son of Maimon says in the sixty-second chapter of the first part of the book *More*: for he says thus: "Rabbi Tarfon said: Once I went up to the platform <note>The *duchan*, where priests delivered the blessing.</note> after my mother's brother, and I inclined my ear toward the priest, and I heard him muffling [swallowing] the name while his brothers the priests were singing. And they also had a name of forty-two letters. And it is known to every person of understanding that it is impossible in any way for forty-two letters to be a single word; rather, these were many words whose total letters were forty-two. There is no doubt that all of them point to matters by which the knowledge of those matters brings one closer to the truth of His essence, blessed be He, in the manner we have said. Truly these many words were called a 'name' because they point to a single matter alone, like other specific names. And indeed, those words were many for the explanation of the matter, because a single matter cannot be understood except by many words." <note>This Hebrew passage is Maimonides' discussion of the mystical names used by the priests in the Temple, emphasizing that these names are not magical spells but complex descriptions of God's essence.</note>

<margin>A</margin> Understand and know that this matter which is learned was from the subjects indicated by those names alone, using the first letters of every concept. That is to say: Rabbi Tarphon said, "I once followed my mother's father into the Temple, and I inclined my ear toward the priest, and I perceived that his brothers, the priests, were asking him questions. For it was never said that the Name of Twelve or the Name of Forty-Two Letters was the <term>Sem hammephoras</term> <note>original: "Shem HaMephorash" — the Explicit or Distinct Name of God.</note>, that is, the "Exposed Name." Whoever possesses the knowledge of that name, and is cautious regarding it, and guards it with purity, is loved by those above and desired by those below; he is feared by all creatures, his discipline is perpetual in his hand, and he shall obtain two worlds: the present

and the future. And this is what is written in the Talmud. Oh, how great is the distance between what men understand from these words and what was in the mind of the speaker! For many judge that they are merely letters to be spoken, and also that there is no underlying reason in them by which those aforementioned sublime ranks are acquired, and that they are necessary for composing those formulas mentioned by the sage we named above. After this, those lies were written down, which those wicked men invented from their own hearts, and those writings reached the hands of the foolish, who utterly lacked the reason by which they could discern true from false. They put their faith in those scriptures, trusting that they were true." Now, these words consisting of forty-two letters, through which a distinct and perfect explanation of the Name of Four Letters was held among the most ancient Hebrews, were these: <gloss>Father God, Son God, and the Holy Spirit God: yet not three Gods, but one God.</gloss> <note>original: אב אל בן אל ורוח הקדש אל אבל לא שלשה אלהים כי אם אלוה אחד</note> The letters of these words in Hebrew are forty-two, whether <gloss>Holy Spirit</gloss> <note>original: "Ruach Ha-Kodesh"</note>, as we say, is placed there, or <gloss>Spirit of Holiness</gloss> <note>original: "Ruach Ha-Kodash"</note>, as they say; since the letters are the same in either case, even if the pointing is different.
