it is found, so that when many words or names occur in the same clause, the letter ו <note>vau, equivalent to 'and'</note>—which makes a word conjunctive—is always found placed with the last one. To pass over other examples of this kind, I will bring forward as an example that passage from Exodus, chapter 3: <note>original: יהוה אלהי אבותיכם אלהי אברהם אלהי יצחק ואלהי יעקב שלחני אליכם</note> *The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, **and** the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.* Do you see how the letter ו <note>vau</note>, which creates the conjunction, is placed only with the last name? You will find it so in similar cases as well. Furthermore, we say that a certain one of their ancient leaders—whom they call *Rabbenū Haccados* <term>Our Holy Master; traditionally referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the redactor of the Mishnah</term>, whom it is considered a sin among them to contradict—explained the four-letter Name of God <term>the Tetragrammaton, YHWH</term> through forty-two letters in another way in the first petition of the book *Gale razeia* <term>Revealer of Secrets</term>. In this explanation, he places the letter ו <note>vau</note> nowhere. For he says (as we have mentioned above): "Because nothing is found in God which is not God, from the Name of Twelve Letters emanates the Name of Forty-Two Letters, which is: <note>original: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקדש אלהים, שלשה באחד אחד בשלשה</note> **Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God: Three in one, and one in three**; or, Trinity in Unity, and Unity in Trinity." Here there are forty-two letters. Although the specific phrasing of the explanation may vary, the meaning of the explanation does not vary at all; it is exactly the same in both cases. For those ancient fathers, who were disciples and successors of the prophets, when they explained the four-letter name of God—either through the Name of Twelve Letters or the Name of Forty-Two Letters—all converged on one and the same meaning, even if they explained it in different ways. They expressed the three divine persons—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—using the very same names by which we express them. They asserted each of these to be God, yet they said they were not three Gods, but one God. Thus, they expressly explained the Trinity of the divine persons along with the Unity of the divine essence through forty-two letters. This was the true and perfect explanation of the four-letter Name of God, which the ancient Hebrews achieved through the Name of Forty-Two Letters. However, the more recent Jews are entirely ignorant of this; therefore, their prayers are not heard at all, as it is said in the *Midras tehilim* <term>Midrash on the Psalms</term>, regarding the verse in Psalm 91: <note>original: אשגבהו כי ידע שמי יקראני ואענהו</note> *I will exalt him because he has known my name; he shall call upon me, and I will answer him.* For there it is read: <note>original: אמר רבי יהושע בן לוי בשם רבי פנחס בן יאיר מפני מה מתפללין ישראל בעולם הזה ואינן נענין על ידי שאינן יודעים בשם המפורש אבל לעתיד לבא הקדוש ברוך הוא מודיען שני כי ידע שמי באותה שעה הן מתפללין ומיד נענין שני יקראני ואענהו</note> *Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said in the name of Rabbi Phineas son of Jair: Why do the Israelites pour out prayer in this world and are not heard? Surely because they do not know the "explicit name" <term>Shem HaMephorash</term>, the four-letter name. But in the future to come, the Holy God,*

<column-break/>

### 90

and blessed, will teach it to them, as it is said in Isaiah 52: *My people shall know my name.* Then they shall truly pray and be heard. As it is said: *He shall call upon me, and I will answer him.* This is the tradition. Therefore, since according to this tradition God Himself was to teach men this blessed name by clearly relating the mystery of the divine Trinity through its true explanation—which was to happen in the time of the Messiah, as *Rabbenū Haccados* testified in the preceding sections—the Lord Jesus, the true Messiah and the true Son of God, most perfectly taught his disciples (who were Israelites) by most openly revealing the mystery of the divine Trinity. As he said in Matthew, chapter 28: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.* In this formula, therefore, in which he commanded those who had been instructed to be baptized—when he set forth the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—he clearly signaled that he had already thoroughly taught his disciples the secret of the Trinity and the divine Unity. Indeed, these three names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—express the Trinity of the divine persons. Furthermore, in saying "in the name" and not "in the names," he evidently showed that there is one essence and nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And this is undoubtedly the truest and most distinct explanation of the four-letter Name of God, which was explicitly contained in both the Name of Twelve Letters and the Name of Forty-Two Letters. With these names, therefore—namely of twelve and forty-two letters—our Lord Jesus Christ most perfectly explained the four-letter Name of God to his disciples. For this reason, addressing the Father (as held in John, chapter 17), he said: *Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me.* And again he said: *These have known that you sent me, and I have made your name known to them.* Following the teaching of the disciples of Christ, Athanasius <note>Author of the Athanasian Creed</note> excellently and perfectly explained the four-letter Name of God: first through the Name of Twelve Letters—which is (as was clear a little above) Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and then through the Name of Forty-Two Letters, saying: *God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; and yet they are not three Gods, but there is one God.* From these things it is clearly evident that the faith of the ancient Hebrews and our own faith was one and the same.

He concludes that ancient Jewish faith was identical to Christianity, though modern Jews have lost this knowledge.</summary>

### SECOND BOOK.

but why is this name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>, which we mentioned a little while ago, called ארבע אותיות <note>original: *Arbah othioth*</note>, that is, "of four letters," or the Tetragrammaton? GALATINVS. Because the letters of no other name so distinctly indicate the inner secrets of the divinity. For this name יהוה <note>YHWH</note>, which we said a little earlier is proper to God alone and signifies the divine nature more distinctly than others, there is no doubt that it also designates the secrets of the divine Trinity and Unity above all others. Other names of God, however, since they are not proper to God but <margin>B</margin> are derived from works similar to those found in us <note>i.e., names based on divine attributes like "Judge" or "Mighty"</note>, do not so distinctly suggest the mysteries of the divine Trinity and Unity as that one does. For this reason, it alone among the others is called the Tetragrammaton by way of excellence, even if certain other names of God are found written with four letters among them. CAPITO. Therefore, for a greater expression of Catholic truth, I would like you to say something about each of those names I brought forward as examples. And first, indeed, in what way is the trinity of divine persons suggested by <margin>C</margin> the name אדני <note>original: *Adonai*</note>, which they pronounce in place of the Name of Four Letters? GALATINVS. Certainly, the trinity of divine persons is designated through this name אדני <note>original: *Adonai*</note>, which is interpreted as "Lord," though in a somewhat blended way. For just as the name אלהים <note>original: *Elohim*</note> implies plurality (as we showed above), so also אדני <note>original: *Adonai*</note> is a plural name. For from this name אדון <note>original: *Adon*</note>, which is singular and signifies that which is "Lord," comes this plural אדונים <note>original: *Adonim*</note>, <margin>D</margin> which is the same as "Lords." From the singular name אדון <note>original: *Adon*</note>, comes אדוני <note>original: *Adoni*</note>, which is interpreted as "my Lord"; but from the plural אדונים <note>original: *Adonim*</note> comes אדני <note>original: *Adonai*</note>, which is a divine name and properly signifies the same as "my Lords." Therefore, those ancient fathers, taught by Moses, ordained that God be called "Lords" in the plural number, so that from this it might be openly shown that the universal lordship of all things is common to the three divine persons. For the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord. However, to imply that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Lords, but one Lord, it was decreed that the name אדני <note>original: *Adonai*</note> itself, although it is plural, should only be joined with a verb in the singular number, or with an adjective likewise in the singular.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*Regarding the name of God אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note>, through which the eternal stability of the divine Trinity is best suggested.*

->GALATINVS.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C featuring a floral or foliate pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>
WHEN Moses had said to God—by whom <margin>G</margin> he was to be sent to liberate the children of Israel from the shameful servitude of Pharaoh—"Behold, I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them,

<column-break/>

'The God of your fathers has sent me to you.' If they say to me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?" God, therefore, wishing to reveal His name to him, answered (as it is held in the 3rd chapter of Exodus): כה תאמר לבני ישראל אהיה שלחני אליכם <note>original: *Affer Ehie...* - "Thus shall you say to the sons of Israel: 'I Will Be' has sent me to you."</note> that is: "I was, I am, and I will be," אהיה אשר אהיה <note>original: *Ehie, aser ehie* - "I am that I am" or "I will be what I will be."</note>. That is, אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note>, which is: "He who was, is, and will be." And He said: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note>—that is, He who was, is, and will be—has sent me to you." Here, therefore, is placed the name of God אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note>, which encompasses the differences of the three tenses of the indicative mood of the substantive verb: namely, the past, the present, and the future, which are "I was," "I am," and "I will be." Therefore the name itself, אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note>, is interpreted as "I was, I am, and I will be." For the second and third letters of the name itself, namely *he* and *yod*, designate the first person, which is the third word of the past tense of the same verb among them, which is היה <note>original: *haithi* - "I was"</note>; the fourth letter of that name, namely *he*, indicates the first person of the present tense, which is הוה <note>original: *houe* - "I am"</note>; but the first letter, namely *aleph*, which is usually placed at the beginning of the first person of the future tense of any verb, denotes the first person of the future tense of the same verb. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that this name אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note> contains within itself the differences of the three tenses of the indicative mood of the substantive verb. Wherefore, "I was, I am, and I will be" is most aptly interpreted to suggest the supreme, all-encompassing, and everlasting stability of God, who always was, is, and will be. Then, to show the Trinity of persons and the unity of essence, God Himself, addressing Moses, added in the third chapter of Exodus: כה תאמר אל בני ישראל יהוה אלהי אבתיכם אלהי אברהם אלהי יצחק ואלהי יעקב שלחני אליכם <note>original: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you."</note> In that He said "God" three times, He expressly suggested the Trinity of persons; but in that He said "Lord" once, and did not say "they sent," but "sent" <note>in the singular</note>, He demonstrated the unity of the divine nature. Finally, to imply that this name אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note> was His own—through which the eternal and all-encompassing stability of the divine Trinity and Unity is imported—He immediately added: זה שמי לעולם <note>original: *Ze shemi l'olam*</note>, that is, "This is my name forever." CAPITO. Since these things are as you say, I wonder greatly why the author of our edition <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> did not translate this passage in the way you have. For he says that God spoke to Moses thus: "I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: 'He who is' has sent me to you." GALATINVS. That should not seem strange to you, since this name אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*</note> can hardly be translated as it sounds, except through a certain circumlocution. For there are many things in the secrets of the Law and the Prophets which the Hebrew manner of writing and reading suggests, which nevertheless cannot be transferred into another language; this appears most especially in the divine names themselves, in which the Greek as well as the Latin editions often fail. Origen beautifully testifies to this when, in his work *Against Celsus*, he says that in certain...

...that a wonderful power lies hidden in certain sacred names, and for this reason, these very names cannot be translated from Hebrew into another language. **CAPITO.** Although the things you have said regarding the name אהיה <note>original: *Ehie*; usually translated as "I AM"</note> are so true that they cannot be denied in any way, there is still one thing that I wonder at greatly. For when God spoke of this name, He said: זה שמי לעלם <note>Exodus 3:15: "This is my name forever."</note> which all our interpreters (as you have also interpreted it) translate as, "This is my name forever." Indeed, this interpretation would be true if the word לעלם <note>original: *Leolam*; meaning "forever"</note> were written with the letter *vav* <note>The letter 'ו'</note>. But since it is written without the *vav*, it should not be pointed <note>referring to vowel markers</note> as לעולם <term>leolam</term>, but as לעלם <term>leallem</term>. Since this word derives from the verb עלם <note>original: *alam*</note>, which means "to conceal" or "to hide," it should be understood not as "forever," but as "for concealing." Therefore, that saying of God ought to be rightly translated as: "This is my name to be hidden," or "to be kept secret." By this, it is clearly given to be understood that secrets other than those you have mentioned lie hidden in the name אהיה <note>Ehyeh</note>, which are left for the Kabbalists to discuss. I would therefore like to know from you what those secrets are, lying hidden in this divine name. <term>GALATINVS.</term> I would prefer to learn these things from you, who not only have an excellent knowledge of Hebrew letters, but also excel others in the skill of Kabbalistic wisdom. Nevertheless, to satisfy your request, I will bring forward the words of Rabbi Abraham Pici, who, in the booklet he published concerning the meaning of the <term>taghin</term>—that is, the "crowns" or "tips" which are written above the letters of the Law—says the following:

> Behold, I awaken you to the matter of the secret of this sign, which is greater than seven letters. Look into them and you will find upon them twenty-one crowns, and this is the secret of *Ehyeh* <note>The name "I AM," which has a numerical value of 21</note>. This sign is included with the Great Name <note>the Tetragrammaton</note>. Regarding this, it was hinted when God said to Moses, "I AM THAT I AM," and the verse ends with "I AM has sent me to you." This means the word *Ehyeh* is said three times, corresponding to the three crowns on each and every letter, so that the secret of its calculation is joined in the whole sign. Another thing: the three crowns on each letter correspond to the three Patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who are mentioned immediately after when it says, "God said to Moses: I AM THAT I AM... thus shall you say to the House of Jacob: The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name forever <note>written here as *leallem*, "to be hidden"</note>, and this is my memorial for all generations." Examine the letters of the names of the Patriarchs and you will understand the secret of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, as we have explained. Also, when you examine closely, you will understand the secret of *Yah* <note>The short form of God's name, YH</note>, for you will find fifteen crowns above the names of the Patriarchs. Here you have the mystery of the Thirteen Attributes, the mystery of *Ehyeh*, and the mystery of the Great Explicit Name <note>The *Shem HaMephorash*</note>. Indeed, regarding each name of the Patriarchs, the Divinity is mentioned, for it says: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. When you look closely at the name *Elohe* <note>"God of..."</note>, you will find the Name hinted in it twice, and let him who understands, understand. This is what He meant by "This is my name *leallem*"—it is written so to mean this is my name "to be hidden," for it is not to be revealed except to a person who is humble and understands the Kabbalah. Furthermore, this is hinted at in the Prophets: "The Lord is in His holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before Him." Thus he hinted at the secret of *YHWH* and the secret of *Adonai*, which are included in that name. You will also find the Great Name hinted at in this verse: "And they shall say to me, what is his name? What?" <note>Exodus 3:13</note>. For through the way of these texts regarding the name *Ehyeh*, it is said: "This is my name to be hidden" (as if to say, that which must be hidden), just as it is written, "*Ehyeh* has sent me to you."

These are all his words. From these, not only are the secrets lying hidden in this name אהיה <note>Ehyeh</note> made plain to those who are not ignorant of Hebrew letters, but it is also clearly shown that there is a plurality of persons within the unity of essence in God. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Galatinus and Capnio (the scholar Johannes Reuchlin) regarding the mystical properties of Hebrew names. Having discussed the names of God related to existence (Ehyeh) and Lordship (Adonai), they now turn to the protective name AGLA and the name of self-sufficiency, Shaddai, before beginning an explanation of the "72-Letter Name" derived from the Book of Exodus.</meta>

### CHAPTER XV.

->*Concerning the name of God אגלא Agla, through which the infinite power of the divine trinity is expressed.*<-

->GALATINVS.<-

So that I may say at least a few things regarding the name of God אגלא <note>original: *Agla*</note> to satisfy your request, I would have you know that the name of God *Agla* itself (as its letters indicate) denotes nothing other than the eternal and infinite power of God, which He possesses in respect to creation, whether yet to be produced or already produced. For its first letter, namely א <note>Aleph</note>, stands for אתה <note>original: *atta*; "You"</note>. The second, namely ג <note>Ghimel</note>, stands for גבור <note>original: *ghibbor*; "Mighty"</note>. The third, namely ל <note>Lamed</note>, stands for לעולם <note>original: *leholam*; "Forever"</note>. Finally the fourth, namely א <note>Aleph</note>, stands for אדני <note>original: *Adonai*; "Lord"</note>. From this it is clearly evident that the name *Agla* itself signifies nothing else than this whole phrase: *Atta Ghibbor Leholam Adonai*. That is, "You are mighty forever, O Lord." From these things, therefore, it is plain that this same name *Agla* openly expresses the very omnipotence of the divine trinity.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*Concerning the name of God שדי Saddai, through which the all-encompassing sufficiency of the divine trinity, by which God alone is sufficient unto Himself, is best designated.*<-

->CAPNIO.<-

There is also another name of God which frequently occurs in the sacred scriptures, called שדי <note>original: *Saddai*; usually written as Shaddai</note>. I ask that you say something about it as well. GALATINUS: One must note, therefore, what Rabbi Moses, son of Maimon <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, says about this name in that book which is titled among the Jews מורה הנבוכים <note>original: *More hannebochim*; "The Guide for the Perplexed"</note>. There, at the end of the forty-second chapter of the first part, he says among other things: "The name *Shaddai* is composed of the word די <note>original: *dai*; "enough" or "sufficient"</note> and from the letter ש <note>Shin</note>." Now the word *dai* signifies sufficiency, as is clear from what is said in Obadiah: *If thieves came to you, or if robbers by night, how would you have been silenced? Would they not have stolen their sufficiency?* <note>original Latin/Hebrew quote of Obadiah 1:5; *daiam* refers to "their fill" or "as much as they wanted"</note>. Furthermore, the letter *Shin* which is placed before this name *Shaddai* is the same as אשר <note>original: *aser*; "who" or "which"</note>. Therefore, *Shaddai* is the same as *Asher-dai*, that is, "He who is sufficient," or "He who is the sufficiency." For this reason, this name is never found among the Hebrews except when spoken of God alone. And this is not surprising, since its meaning is (as

<column-break/>

has been said) "He who suffices," or "He who is sufficient": which is clearly appropriate to God alone. For, as the philosopher Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian theologian and jurist</note> says in the book written concerning the names of God, God alone is simply and absolutely rich and the maker of wealth. For He depends on no other, neither in substance nor in qualities, but with all things pertaining to Him, He is entirely immune from all dependence. Then he adds: "The one who is rich and sufficient unto himself, absolutely and in truth, is he who needs no other: and this is God alone." Regarding all others, however, this is said figuratively or in a limited sense. Thus far Algazel. Since, therefore, God alone is three and one and sufficient unto Himself, for that reason the name שדי <note>Shaddai</note> rightly carries and signifies the sufficiency of the divine trinity, by which God is self-sufficient.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->*Concerning the seventy-two names of God, through which the perfections of the divine trinity and unity are most aptly hinted at.*<-

->CAPNIO.<-

Since many have said many things about the seventy-two names of God, and some indeed have said things that are empty and worthy of laughter, I would finally like to hear your opinion on them, for the sake of a greater knowledge of the divine names. GALATINUS: So that I may speak of these things using only what I have received from the Kabbalistic books: first, I will bring forward the texts from which the names themselves are formed from the fourteenth chapter of Exodus, where it is said in Hebrew: <note>Exodus 14:19-21: The account of the Angel of God and the pillar of cloud moving behind the Israelites at the Red Sea, and Moses stretching out his hand to divide the waters.</note> *And the Angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved himself and walked behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from their face and stood behind them. And it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel; and it was a cloud and darkness, and it lit up the night, and one did not approach the other all night. And Moses extended his hand over the sea, and God took away the sea with a strong South wind all night, and turned the sea into dry land, and the waters were divided.* This series of words is distinguished among the Hebrews into three פסוקים <note>original: *pesukim*; "verses"</note>. Each of these consists of seventy-two letters. From these, the Kabbalists have extracted the seventy-two names of God in a certain wonderful way. And they have done this in ten modes.

The first of these is that first, the first letter of the first verse is taken, which is ו <note>Vav</note>. Next, the last letter of the second verse, which is ה <note>He</note>. Finally, the first letter of the third verse, which is ו <note>Vav</note>. From these three letters the first name of the first mode results, which is והו <note>VHV</note>. <meta>The previous page concluded Chapter XVI, discussing the name Shaddai. This page continues the technical explanation of how the 72 divine names (the Shem HaMephorash) are derived from the three verses of Exodus 14:19-21, moving from the theory of their construction to the presentation of the names in various "modes" or permutations.</meta>

SECOND BOOK. 98

the verses take the letter which is י <note>Yod</note>: then the penultimate of the second verse, which is ל <note>Lamed</note>: finally the second of the last verse, which is י <note>Yod</note>. And thus they constitute the second name, which is ילי. And so, keeping this order, they proceed continually until the total number of letters is exhausted. This is easily apparent to anyone looking at the names of the first mode themselves.

<margin>Rule for the names of the second mode.</margin> But the names of the second mode are formed by them from the same letters in this way. First, therefore, take the first letter of the first verse (or text), which is ו <note>Vav</note>: and the first of the third, which is likewise ו <note>Vav</note>. And thus you will form the first name of the second mode, which is וו. Next, if you take the second letter of the first text, which is י <note>Yod</note>: and the second of the second text, which is likewise י <note>Yod</note>: and the second of the third text, which is also י <note>Yod</note>, you will constitute the second name of the second mode, which is ייי. Likewise, from the third letter of the first text, which is ס <note>Samech</note>: and from the third of the second, which is ב <note>Beth</note>: and from the third of the third, which is ט <note>Tet</note>, the third name of the second mode is composed, which is סבט. And so, proceeding in this order until all the letters of the same texts are exhausted, seventy-two names of the second mode are produced: as can be seen by looking at those same names of the second mode. However, as to the rules of how the names of the remaining eight modes are composed from those same letters, I do not provide them now for the sake of avoiding prolixity <note>meaning: "wordiness" or "tedious detail"</note>, but I leave them for studious men to investigate. For everyone will think (as I believe) that I have done enough, when he sees that I have recorded all the names of the ten modes themselves (just as I found them in the books of the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Christian and Jewish practitioners of Kabbalah, a form of Jewish mysticism</note>), while only explaining the construction of the first and second modes. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio (the Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin) and Galatinus, moving from the singular names of God to the complex derivation of the seventy-two names. It maintains the theme of finding Christian theological truths, such as the Trinity, within Hebrew nomenclature and Kabbalistic methodology.</meta>

SECOND BOOK.

### CHAPTER XV.

->Concerning the name of God *Agla*, through which the infinite power of the divine trinity is expressed.<-

->GALATINUS.<-

So that I may say even a very few things concerning the name of God *Agla* <note>original: אגלא</note> to satisfy your request, I would have you know that the name of God *Agla* itself (as its letters indicate) denotes nothing other than the eternal and infinite power of God, which He possesses in respect to creation, whether yet to be produced or already produced. For its first letter, namely *Aleph* <note>א</note>, stands for *Atah* <note>אתה</note>, which is "Thou." The second, namely *Gimel* <note>ג</note>, stands for *Gibbor* <note>גבור</note>, which is interpreted as "Mighty." The third, namely *Lamed* <note>ל</note>, stands for *Le-olam* <note>לעולם</note>, which is the same as "forever." Finally the fourth, namely *Aleph* <note>א</note>, stands for *Adonai* <note>אדני</note>, which is translated into our language as "Lord." From this it is clearly evident that the name *Agla* itself signifies nothing other than this whole phrase: "Thou art Mighty forever, O Lord" <note>original: *Atah Gibbor Le-olam Adonai* / אתה גבור לעולם אדני</note>. From these things, therefore, it is plain that the same name *Agla* openly expresses the very omnipotence of the divine trinity.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->Concerning the name of God *Shaddai*, through which the all-encompassing sufficiency of the divine trinity, by which God alone is sufficient unto Himself, is best designated.<-

->CAPNIO.<-

There is also another name of God which frequently occurs in the sacred scriptures, called *Shaddai* <note>original: שדי</note>. I ask that you say something concerning it as well. GALATINUS: One must note, therefore, what Rabbi Moses, son of Maimon <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides, 1138–1204</note>, says about this name in that book which is entitled among the Jews *Moreh Nevukhim* <note>original: מורה הנבוכים / "The Guide for the Perplexed"</note>. For there, at the end of the forty-second chapter of the first part, he says among other things: The name *Shaddai* is composed of the word *Dai* <note>די</note>, which is "it suffices," and from the letter called *Shin* <note>ש</note>. Now the word *Dai* signifies "sufficiency," as is evident from what is said in Obadiah: "If thieves had come to you, or robbers by night, how you would have been destroyed! Would they not have stolen their sufficiency?" <note>original: *daiam* / דים. Reference to Obadiah 1:5</note> Furthermore, the letter *Shin* which is placed before this name *Shaddai* is the same as *Asher* <note>אשר</note>, that is, "who" or "which." For this reason *Shaddai* is the same as *Asher Dai*, that is, "He who suffices," or "He who is sufficient," or "He who is sufficiency." Therefore, this name is never found among the Hebrews except when spoken of God alone. And it is no wonder, since its meaning is (as has been said) "He who suffices"; it is manifest that this fits God alone. For, as the philosopher Algazel <note>The Persian theologian Al-Ghazali, 1058–1111</note> says in the book inscribed *On the Names of God*, God alone is simply and absolutely rich and enriching. For He depends on no other, neither in substance nor in qualities, but with all things pertaining to Himself, He is entirely immune from all dependency. Then he adds: Therefore, he who is absolutely and in truth rich and sufficient unto himself is he who needs no other: and this is God alone. Concerning all others, however, this is said figuratively or in a limited sense. Thus far Algazel. Since, therefore, God alone, three and one, is sufficient unto Himself, for that reason the name *Shaddai* rightly conveys and signifies the sufficiency of the divine trinity, by which God is sufficient unto Himself.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XVII.

->Concerning the seventy-two names of God, through which the perfections of the divine trinity and unity are most aptly suggested.<-

->CAPNIO.<-

Since many people have said many things concerning the seventy-two names of God, and some indeed have said things that are empty and worthy of laughter, I would wish finally to hear your opinion on them, for the sake of a greater knowledge of the divine names. GALATINUS: So that I may say regarding these only those things which I have received from the Kabbalistic books, I will first bring forward the texts from which the names themselves are formed, from the fourteenth chapter of Exodus, where it is said thus in Hebrew:

"And the Angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, removed and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud removed from before them and stood behind them. And it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel; and it was a cloud and darkness, but it gave light by night, so that the one came not near the other all the night. And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the Lord caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided." <note>Exodus 14:19-21. In Hebrew tradition, these three verses each contain exactly 72 letters.</note>

This series of words is distinguished among the Hebrews into three *Pesukim* <note>פסוקים</note>, that is, texts or verses. Each of these consists of seventy-two letters. From these, the Kabbalists have extracted seventy-two names of God in a certain miraculous way. And they have indeed performed this in ten modes.

<margin>Rule of the names of the first mode.</margin>
The first of these is that the first letter of the first verse is taken first, which is *Vav* <note>ו</note>. Immediately after, the last letter of the second verse, which is *He* <note>ה</note>; finally, the first letter of the third verse, which is *Vav* <note>ו</note>. From these three letters results the first name of the first mode, which is *VHV* <note>והו</note>. Next, the second of the first verse...

BOOK TWO.
E
<meta>catchword: Which</meta>

verses take the letter which is *yod* <note>י</note>: then the second-to-last letter of the second [verse], which is *lamed* <note>ל</note>: and finally the second letter of the last [verse], which is *yod* <note>י</note>. And in this way they establish the second name, which is *Yeli* <note>ילי</note>. Keeping to this order, they proceed continuously until the entire number of letters is exhausted. This is easily apparent to anyone looking at the names of the first mode.

<margin>Rule for the names of the second mode.</margin>
But the names of the second mode are formed from the same letters according to them in this way. First, take the first letter of the first verse or text, which is *vav* <note>ו</note>: and the first of the second, which is also *vav* <note>ו</note>: and the first of the third, which is likewise *vav* <note>ו</note>. Thus you will form the first name of the second mode, which is *Vav-Vav-Vav* <note>ווו</note>. Then, if you take the second letter of the first text, which is *yod* <note>י</note>: and the second of the second, which is similarly *yod* <note>י</note>: and the second of the third, which is also *yod* <note>י</note>, you will establish the second name of the second mode, which is *Yod-Yod-Yod* <note>ייי</note>. Likewise, from the third letter of the first text, which is *he* <note>ה</note>: and from the third of the second, which is *bet* <note>ב</note>: and from the third of the third, which is *tet* <note>ט</note>, the third name of the second mode is constructed, which is *He-Bet-Vav* <note>original: הבו; the text describes the letters He, Bet, and Tet (הבט), but the transcription shows a Vav at the end</note>. By proceeding in this order until all the letters of these same texts are exhausted, seventy-two names of the second mode are produced, as can be seen by examining these very names of the second mode. 

As for the names of the remaining eight modes—how they are composed from these same letters—I do not hand down the rules now for the sake of avoiding lengthiness, but I leave them to be investigated by diligent students. For everyone will think (I believe) that I have done enough when they see that I have recorded all the names themselves of the ten modes (just as I found them in the books of the Kabbalists <note>The author refers to the Jewish mystical tradition which Christian scholars of this period were attempting to harmonize with Christian theology</note>), after having explained the construction of the names of the first and second modes. These are as follows:

<margin>A</margin>
**Capnio.** Some of our people say that the names of the first and second mode, punctuated as you have set them down, are not Hebrew, because they are punctuated contrary to the custom of Hebrew writing. <note>Capnio is the character representing Johann Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note> **Galatinus.** Perhaps those who say this are of that class of men who, failing to measure themselves or their own abilities correctly, believe they know everything to such an extent that whatever they themselves do not know, they imagine no one knows. You, however, would by no means say such a thing, both because you have always loathed the character of such men, and also because you have (I believe) frequently read these same names punctuated in this way in Kabbalistic books, and especially those of the first mode. I too have found them punctuated exactly so in many places: and particularly in Rome, in the library of the Supreme Pontiff, in that place where the books of Flamineus are kept, a man once most skilled in the three languages <note>The "three languages" refers to Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, the core of Renaissance humanism. "Flamineus" refers to Agostino Giustiniani, a bishop and scholar of these tongues.</note>. Therefore, let those who deny that these names are Hebrew when so punctuated seek them there among the Hebrew codices, and they will find the names of the first mode punctuated in this very way. And even if they have been somewhat corrupted there by the fault of the scribes, I have nevertheless taken care to restore them more correctly according to the rules of the Kabbalists. **Capnio.** It is not without reason, then, that some desire to know why these names are punctuated with such marks. **Galatinus.** Although this is a greatest secret among the Kabbalists—so much so, indeed, that they command it should by no means be written down, but revealed only by word of mouth, and only to a very few who are worthy, lest by casting pearls before swine <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6, warning against sharing sacred knowledge with those who would disrespect or misuse it.</note> the divine names should become known to the unworthy and the vile—nevertheless, I, whose heart is set above all on hiding the truth from no one, but rather on making it open to all, say this:

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
The reason these names are punctuated in this way is that the letters from which they are composed are found punctuated thus in the aforementioned texts <note>Refers to the verses in Exodus 14:19-21.</note>. For indeed, the letters found punctuated in those texts, together with the points themselves, concur in the formation of these names. However, those letters which are not punctuated in the same texts—such as those placed at the end of words, which for the most part do not happen to be marked—are punctuated in these names with the points that their natural pronunciation requires. This is clear to anyone looking at the names themselves. Nor did the Kabbalists wish them to be punctuated thus without a great mystery, since from this kind of punctuation, there results in each of these names a trinity of syllables, which distinctly designates the Trinity of Divine Persons in one divine essence. <note>Galatinus is arguing that the three-vowel structure of each name is a hidden proof of the Christian Trinity within Jewish mysticism.</note> **Capnio.** How are these names interpreted? **Galatinus.** Some of our people have interpreted the names of the first mode in this way:

<margin>C</margin>
Exalter, Helper, Hope, Salvation, Sought-after, Proclaimed, Patient, Adorable, Memorable, You, To be exalted, Timely; Celebrated, Uplifter, Being, Advocate, Ruler, Justice, Listener, Rescuer, Strong, Right Hand, Guardian, Awaited; Wonderful, To be invoked, Savior, Swift, Healer, From youth, Alone, Upright, Thoughtful, Expectation, Prayer, Glory; Face, Refuge, Helper, Repeller, Deliverer, Guardian, Of the morning, Teacher, Compassionate, Worker, Magnificent, Revealer; Greatest, Merciful, Joyful, Most High, True,

<header>THIRD BOOK.</header>

<margin>A</margin>To these seventy-two verses mentioned before, which are taken from various Psalms, they apply the seventy-two interpretations placed earlier; they claim these belong to those seventy-two names of God which are formed from the letters of the three previously mentioned texts in the first method. But they are certainly very much mistaken. For these interpretations are clearly recognized as belonging not to the names themselves, but rather to the verses to which they are applied. For the Jews, according to the sense of these seventy-two <margin>B</margin> verses, devised these seventy-two interpretations to match the seventy-two names of God, so that they might serve as a kind of index for those same verses. This is clearly evident from the fact that these interpretations correspond not to the names of God themselves, but to the verses to which they are applied. For this name **Exalter** <note>original: *Exaltator*</note> has no correspondence with the name **YHV** <note>Hebrew: יהו</note>, but only fits the verse to which it is applied: namely, *And You, O God, are a shield around me, my glory, and the exalter of my head.* <note>Psalm 3:3</note> Similarly, **Helper** <note>original: *Auxiliator*</note> in no way <margin>C</margin> agrees with the name **LLY** <note>Hebrew: ללי</note>, but only with this verse to which it is applied: *And You, O God, be not far off; my strength, hasten to my help.* <note>Psalm 22:19</note> You will find the same thing in all the others if you look closely. **Capnio.** How then are these names of God to be correctly interpreted? **Galatinus.** I have not yet found any interpretation of these names among the Hebrews. For even if some of the Kabbalists <note>term: Cabalistarum; practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) whose methods were being adapted by Christian scholars</note> occasionally make mention of these seventy-two names of God, and say that divine perfections are designated through them, none of them whose books I have been able to see has yet dared to interpret the names themselves. However, one thing must be especially noted in them (which serves our purpose greatly against the Jews of our time): that each of these names is composed of three letters and consists of three syllables to designate the Trinity of the divine persons and the unity of the divine essence, as appears especially in those which we placed above in the first and second method.

# THIRD BOOK
## ON THE DIVINITY OF THE MESSIAH
### AND CONCERNING HIS DIVINE NAMES
-> DESIGNATING HIS OWN <-
-> NATURE. <-

### CHAPTER ONE.
#### That the Son of God was to be incarnated, taking a body from a woman.

<margin>D</margin> **CAPNIO.** Since you have sufficiently proved through the Jewish scriptures that God is three and one, it is now fitting for you to say something about what is contained in their books regarding the incarnation of the Son of God. **GALATINUS.** It is certainly necessary, not merely fitting, since we must speak most especially against their lack of faith <note>original: *perfidiam*. In this historical context, "perfidy" was a standard theological term for the Jewish refusal to accept Christian interpretations of scripture</note> concerning matters that pertain to the Messiah. While they deny that He was to be both God and man, they are completely unwilling to believe in the work of the divine incarnation. The Prophet Habakkuk prophesied well of their disbelief in the first chapter, saying: *Because a work is being done in your days which you will not believe when it is told.* <note>Habakkuk 1:5. Reuchlin provides the Hebrew: כי פועל פועל בימיכם לא תאמינו כי יסופר</note>. It is certain that the Prophet spoke here concerning the work of the divine incarnation, which the greatest part of the Jews, in their obstinacy, <margin>E</margin> would by no means believe. **HOGSTRATUS.** Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate bible</note> has it differently in this place. For it says: *Because a work has been done in your days, which no one will believe when it is told.* **GALATINUS.** The Hebrew Truth <note>term: Hebraica veritas; a scholar's term for the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament, often contrasted with the Latin Vulgate</note> which I have translated here is far better than what the author of our edition translated. For whether this work is to be understood literally regarding Nebuchadnezzar, or mystically regarding the incarnation of the Messiah, however it may be, if we wish to look at the force of the words, neither our edition nor the Greek edition (when it says, *No one will believe the truth*) seems consistent. For first, if it is understood to be about Nebuchadnezzar, all the Jews believe it. But second, if it must be explained as being about the incarnation of Christ, both countless Gentiles and very many Jews have believed it. Therefore, our translation, by not following the sense of the Hebrew Truth in this, and by receiving a misinterpretation of this kind, forces us to explain *No one* as *rarely* or *few will believe.* But the Hebrew letter admits no such thing...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio and Galatinus. # THIRD BOOK.

### E iij

...brings a false accusation; indeed (which ought to be very pleasant to us), it implies an evident necessity for understanding the marvelous and stupendous work of the divine incarnation. This work was performed in the days of the Jews—that is, while they still held the land of promise. For truly, no works were done in the days of the Jews which, when told to them, they would not believe, except for the work of the incarnation alone, and those things which follow from it. Therefore, when Paul (as witnessed by Luke in the thirteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles) wished to affirm to them that our Redeemer Jesus is the Messiah, he followed not our version, but the Hebrew text, saying: *Because I work a work* <note>original: "Quia opus operor"</note> (that is, the incarnation of Christ, says the gloss) *which you will not believe, even if someone tells it to you.* <margin>B</margin> **CAPNIO.** In order, therefore, that their obstinate perfidy may be convinced that the only-begotten Son of God had to be incarnated, I beseech you to prove it through one of their own teachers, whom they themselves cannot contradict. **GALATINUS.** Out of the many whom I could now bring forward to prove this, it should be enough to cite that Rabbi Simeon, son of Jochai, a man of the greatest authority among them. He, in his commentaries on the book of Genesis—written in the more secret language of Jerusalem <note>Referring to Aramaic/the language of the Zohar</note>, of which he is believed to be the author—most frequently and openly mentions the mystery of the divine incarnation itself. For upon that saying in Genesis 17: *Walk before me, and be perfect*, he says: <margin>D</margin> <note>Original Aramaic text omitted in translation but its content follows in English.</note> <margin>E</margin> *This is to say: And because it was declared what that fear was, it was declared by reason of strength—namely, those strengths which came into the left side of the female, and he was joined to the female in one place. Moreover, he marked, or rather first settled, in that hidden member which is in all the bodies of females. That place, indeed, is called the matrix <term>matrix: the womb</term>, and is hidden among all. Furthermore, this womb was crafted so that this fear might be incorporated into it—which fear is also called mercy—and might be joined to that strength which encompasses five strengths. But this mercy also embraces five mercies. Mercy from the right, strength from the left. This shall come into that, and he shall be called Man <note>original: "homo" / Hebrew: "Adam"</note>, who embraces every part, that is, all attributes. Therefore, he shall be crowned by all forever, until the Ancient of Ancients remains King. He shall build the worlds and prepare the adornments, so that the female may reside for the sake of incorporation. Nor shall they be perfect until the highest mercy rests in her. Truly, he shall be firm, and this fear—which is also called mercy—shall be incorporated fittingly in the female.* Thus he spoke. Here, by "fear," he understands God; since God <margin>God is not called "fear" without reason.</margin> Himself, among His other names, is not incongruously called "Fear," because it is fitting that He be feared by all. God, therefore, is that "fear" who (as this Rabbi says in the preceding words) did not abhor the body of a woman for the sake of the salvation of those who fear Him. From this, the mystery of the divine incarnation is clearly evident. **CAPNIO.** I would wish you to show this same mystery of the divine incarnation even more clearly through this same Rabbi. **GALATINUS.** I will do so most gladly. Listen, therefore, to what he says in the same commentaries on the book of Genesis regarding that verse: *Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.* <margin>B</margin> For there he says: <note>Original Aramaic text omitted; English translation follows.</note> <margin>C</margin> <margin>E</margin> *That is: It is handed down in the book "Seniothade Fitra" <note>likely referring to the Sifra Detzniuta, or "Book of Concealment," a section of the Zohar</note>, that is, of Shame and Concealment: After it was determined in the heavens concerning the formation of man in general, the holy body and the female were incorporated. But in the third time (which follows the first time of the holy fathers and the second time of the prophets), this greatest union was completed, and the upper worlds and lower worlds were joined and incorporated. From that point on, the upper world was incorporated into the lower world, by means of the <margin>F</margin> holy body. In a certain way, they laughed and rejoiced together, and were made into one body: because that which was above was also below. The holy and blessed God above, and the holy and blessed God below. And the spirit, leaping forth from the sheath <note>original: "vagina" - here meaning a covering or the womb</note>, came into one body, and in all these things only one was seen—He, naturally, to whom it is said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of His glory. And all this is one body. It is likewise handed down: Afterward they joined themselves like two bodies, <margin>G</margin> when one penetrates the other. As it is written: "We will make you a golden chain with studs of silver." Justice and mercy were bound together, and were united by the Word; nor did one depart without the other...*

# THIRD BOOK.

...[it is said.] Therefore, it has been handed down to us in this way: When the body is divided from this world—that is, when men die to the universe—everything that belongs to the man by no means ascends to the heights in the same way as that which we call the **holy body** ascends. This body is of such great dignity that it is not called "Adam," that is, "earthly man," and in this it certainly differs from all other bodies. We also read: *A golden collar and silver studs* <note>original: "Torquem aureum & notas argenteas," a reference to Song of Solomon 1:11</note>. Since justice and mercy are one, for there is no justice without mercy. And therefore it follows: *Your cheek is made beautiful because of the collar, and your neck is made beautiful because of the pearls.* **The collar.** Just as it was said, "A golden collar with pearls"; it is also written, "silver studs on your neck." For among all women, holiness—indeed, divinity—is found in this Matron <note>In the Zohar, the "Matron" or *Matronita* refers to the Shekhinah (Divine Presence). Christian Kabbalists like Galatinus identified her with the Virgin Mary</note>, who was accustomed to descend upon Jerusalem and upon the sanctuary. And all these things occurred after the Word assumed a body in her, and was made from the whole of humanity—that is, a man full of faith. And what is "full of faith"? It means that in him, the whole of faith is found. These are all the words of the same Rabbi, in which, among other marvelous things he says, he openly shows that the Word of God himself, or the Son of God, is true God and true man, because he descended from the heavens and took a body from a woman whose holiness admits no comparison. What, therefore, could be clearer, what more lucid, what more manifest than what this Rabbi—who preceded the birth of Christ by many years—could have said to indicate the mystery of the divine incarnation? Do you wish, my Capnio <note>Capnio is the Greek-based pseudonym of the scholar Johannes Reuchlin</note>, to hear him still uncovering the same incarnation of the Messiah in clear words? Listen, I pray, to what he brings forth in the aforementioned commentaries concerning the same mystery upon that passage of Genesis, *These are the generations of Noah.* For there, explaining that saying in the nineteenth chapter of Job, <term>And from my flesh I shall see God</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ומבשרי אחזה אלוה"</note>, he says thus: <term>What is meant by "And from my flesh"? It should have said "From my own self"; rather, "from my flesh" is meant literally. And what is this? It is that which is written: "And holy flesh shall pass from you" and it is written "And my covenant shall be in your flesh." And it is taught: every time a man is marked with this sign, through this woman he truly sees the Holy One, blessed be He, and the holy soul is united in him, etc. For he who does not keep this sign, of him it is written "By the breath of God they shall perish," because this sign of the Holy One, blessed be He, was not indicated, etc. If he keeps it, the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) does not depart from him. When is the holiness within him? When he is joined [in marriage], and this one enters into his place... and the male and female are joined as one and are called by one name. Then the supreme Mercy rests upon them. From what place does it rest? On the side of the male. And what is Mercy, but that which comes and goes out from the supreme Wisdom and is crowned by the Word? And for this reason the female is protected... God (Eloah), behold He is the strong light; where male and female are joined as one, He is called "Eloah" (God), and the holy soul is united from this place, though not bound by it. And regarding this it is written: "And from my flesh I shall see God," for this is the perfection of everything, literally from my flesh. And because of this, the holy ones of Israel are blessed, who say that the Holy One, blessed be He, is blessed in this world and in the world to come; concerning them it is written: "He shall guard him..."</term>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <term>We have learned that whoever guards this [covenant], the kingdom is established and guarded for him. From where do we know this? From Boaz, of whom it is written: "As the Lord lives, lie down until morning," for he wrestled with his inclination until this oath, and he guarded this covenant. Because of this, he merited that from him should come forth kings ruling over all other kings, and the King Messiah, who is called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He.</term> That is: What does "From my flesh" mean? For it would have been more fitting to say, "From my substance." Nevertheless, he said, "From my own flesh." This, moreover, is what is written: *And holy flesh shall pass over you.* And furthermore it is written: *And my covenant shall be in your flesh.* <margin>B</margin> This signifies the sign that was given to us. For as often as a man shall be marked by this sign which proceeds from Him, he shall see God Himself, and his holy soul shall become one with Him. But as often as he shall not keep this covenant, it is written of him: *By the breath of God they shall perish.* For indeed that sign is of God, and they do not observe it. But if you have been worthy of that sign and have guarded it, divinity shall by no means depart from you, and in <margin>C</margin> time you shall be bound to holiness, and you shall ascend into the prepared place. But what is the reason for what we read above concerning the union of the holy soul—that is, of God—to man? Surely no other than that one male and one female shall be joined into one, which shall be called by one name: just as justice proceeding from the heavenly mercy, which shall rest upon them. In this word is the rest of the clarity or splendor of the male. And what is mercy? Mercy, I say, which shall come <margin>D</margin> from the highest wisdom, and shall be crowned by the Word, and therefore shall be incorporated into the woman. But it has also been handed down to us thus: God, behold God the strong illuminator. The letter <term>daleth</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ד</note> being masculine, and the letter <term>he</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> being feminine, are joined into one, which is called *Eloah* (God). And His most holy soul is placed in this place, yet not bound in it. And therefore it is written: *And from my flesh I shall see God.* Since this happiness is considered universal. It follows: *And from my flesh*—as if he were to say, "From this very <margin>E</margin> flesh of my own." On account of this, those of the people of Israel shall be meritorious—the holy ones at least—who shall say that this is God; they shall be meritorious both in this world and in the world to come. And for the sake of this thing it is written: *He who shall guard this covenant.* And from this we have learned that he who shall guard this pact, God shall guard him. But what is the proof of this matter? This is clear in Boaz, who said to the Moabitess woman <note>Ruth</note>, *As God lives, may you lie until morning.* And although he was enticed by concupiscentia <note>physical desire</note>, <margin>F</margin> yet he guarded this covenant. Wherefore he merited that from him should go forth the most powerful Kings of all other Kings, and moreover the King Messiah, who is called by the name of the holy and blessed God. Thus far the words of Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai. From whose sayings, it is established clearer than the midday sun that God Himself was to be incarnated from a woman, and that the Messiah himself was to be true God and true man.

# BOOK THREE.

### CHAPTER II.

->What is implied by the name, Messiah, and concerning the two<-
->natures and the one person of the Messiah.<-

->CAPNIO.<-

<margin>A</margin> This is one thing among others that you must strive most of all to prove against the modern Jews through their ancient scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was to be true God, and not merely true man. <margin>GAL.</margin> I shall endeavor to do that with all my strength, and all the more effectively because they deny it so obstinately. <margin>HOG.</margin> So that what you are about to say concerning the divinity of the Messiah may be better understood, it is necessary that you first explain what is implied by the name "Messiah." <margin>GAL.</margin> Just as there are (as has been said) three persons in the divinity, which, although they are distinguished from one another without separation, are nevertheless united to one another without confusion through mutual indwelling—which the Greeks call <term>perichoresis</term> <note>original: "περιχώρησιν"; a theological term describing the relationship between the three persons of the Trinity</note>—so in the one Christ we confess there to be three substances: namely, the divinity, the rational soul, and the human body. These are united without confusion in such a way that they are distinguished inseparably. And just as the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>distinct persons or individual realities</note> are one God, so these three—divinity, soul, and body—constitute the one Messiah promised in the Law, who is nothing other than these three things. <margin>D</margin> For he is both perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and human flesh. However, we do not say that he is "composed" of these as a man is composed of soul and body, or as a body is composed of the four elements. For that which is composed is indeed something different from the parts of which it is made. But Christ, or the Messiah, is neither something else from those things of which he consists, nor anything other than those very things which are united in him. For as <term>Damascene</term> <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and scholar</note> says in his book *On the Tradition of the Orthodox Faith*, chapter forty-seven: <note>original: "ἐκ θεότητος καὶ ἀνθρωπότητος θεὸν τέλειον, καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν λέגεσθαι ἐκ δύο τε καὶ ἐν δυσὶ φύσεσι ὁμολογούμενον"</note> *From divinity and humanity, we confess the same one to be and to be called perfect God and perfect man, recognized out of two and in two natures.* Therefore, he who is both perfect God and perfect man is called in Hebrew <term>Massiah</term> <note>original: "משיח"</note>, in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> <term>Mesicha</term> <note>original: "משיחא"</note>, in Greek <term>Christos</term> <note>original: "χριστὸς"</note>, and in Latin he can be called <term>Unctus</term> [Anointed]. The same John Damascene proves this most beautifully in the same place, saying: <note>original: "τὸ χριστὸς ὄνομα τῆς ὑποστάσεως λέγομεν, οὐ μονοτρόπως μὲν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δύο φύσεων ὑπάρχον σημαντικόν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἔχρισεν. χρίων μὲν ὡς θεὸς, ὃς ἔχρισε τὸ σῶμα τῇ θεότητι αὐτοῦ, χριόμενος δὲ ὡς ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐστι τοῦτο κἀκεῖνο, χρίσις δὲ ἡ θεότης τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος"</note> *We say the name "Christ" refers to the person [hypostasis], not in a simple way, but as being significant of two natures: for he anointed himself. He was the anointer as God, who anointed the body with his divinity; and he was the anointed one as man, for he himself is both this and that. Moreover, the anointing of the human*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *ity is the divinity.* <margin>CAP.</margin> These things are indeed beautiful; but since the Jews of our age, who think the Messiah will be a mere man, would deny them, it is necessary for you to demonstrate them through their authentic scriptures. <margin>GAL.</margin> Let them hear David first, speaking thus of the Messiah in the forty-fifth Psalm (according to the Hebrew truth): <margin>Ps. 45</margin> <margin>B</margin> **Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of equity. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.** <note>original: "כסאך אלהים עולם ועד שבט מישר שבט מלכותך אהבת צדק ותשנא רשע על כן משחך אלהים אלהיך שמן ששון מחבריך"</note> Indeed, the Chaldean translator <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>, whom the Jews now more frequently have at hand, translated these words into Chaldean as: *Your throne, O God, is in the heavens forever and ever; a mighty kingdom is the scepter of your kingdom. And you, King Messiah, because you have loved righteousness and hated malice, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil or ointment of joy more than* <margin>C</margin> *your associates or friends.* From this Chaldean translation, therefore, it is clearly evident that the Prophet was speaking here of the Messiah. In his words, not only is this name, Messiah—which is the same as "Anointed"—clearly expressed (since he is called Messiah or Christ from the anointing), but also the two natures are most clearly suggested. Regarding his humanity, he was to be anointed—both as King and as Priest—with the oil of gladness (that is, the anointing of divinity) above his "participants" or "companions," that is, above <margin>D</margin> other men who share with him the condition of one and the same human nature. Furthermore, the two natures, divine and human, which were to be united <term>hypostatically</term> <note>united in one person</note> in him, are most clearly implied. For when he says, *Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your Kingdom,* he clearly indicates that the one he addresses is God; wherefore he also openly confesses his divinity. <margin>E</margin> But when he immediately says to the same person, *You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your participants or companions,* he undoubtedly confesses the same person to be man also, openly manifesting his humanity. For since there is only one God, it would certainly be a wicked thing to say that he has either a "God" or a "companion." If the modern Jews do not believe that the Prophet said these things regarding this name, Messiah, and concerning the dual nature (divine and human) implied by it, <margin>F</margin> let them hear the sayings of their ancient Teachers, who spoke more clearly about the two natures and the single person of the Messiah. And first, those things which are read in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>The "Little Genesis," a Midrashic commentary</note>—that is, in the exposition of Genesis—where it is said: *And he took of the stones of that place.* And in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>Exposition of the Psalms</note> upon that verse of the ninetieth Psalm: *For he has given his angels charge over you.* Where it is read literally as follows: <margin>G</margin> **Rabbi Nehemiah says: There were three stones; and [Jacob] said, "If God unites his name upon me as he united it upon my fathers, let them all become one." He arose and found them all [to be one], as it is said: "And he took the stone," which teaches that they all became one. But the Rabbis say: No fewer than two stones.** <note>original: "רבי נחמיה אומר שלשה אבנים היו ואמר אם אלהים מיחד שמו עלי כשם שייחד על אבותי יעשו כולם אחד עמד ומצאם כולם דהא שנאמר ויקח את האבן מלמד שנעשו כולם אחד ורבנן אמרו פחות משני אבנים"</note> That is, Rabbi Nehemiah says:

# BOOK THREE.

<header>BOOK THREE.</header>

Jacob took three stones—that is, Jacob—and said, "If God unites His name over me, just as He united it over my fathers, let them all become one." He stood, and found them all made into one, as it is said in Genesis chapter twenty-eight: *And he took the stone.* <note>Genesis 28:11; the text uses the singular "stone" to imply the many became one.</note> Indeed, by this word he teaches that all were made one. The Masters, however, said less, because they spoke of two stones. This is from the <term>Midrash</term> <note>original: "Midras"; a Jewish mode of biblical exegesis and commentary</note>. Therefore, whether he took three stones or two, or perhaps first three and then two, in both cases the union of the Messiah is most excellently signified. For the union of two stones signified the union of two natures in Christ: namely, divinity and humanity. But the union of three stones designated the union of three substances in the one person of Christ: namely, the Word, the soul, and the body. 

This union is also excellently attested by what is said in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, regarding that which is spoken in Isaiah chapter 23: *And it shall come to pass in that day, and Tyre <note>original: "צור Tsor"</note> shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days (or like the days of the King) who are united.* Who is this "united King"? I say that this is the King Messiah. But the <term>Rabbi</term> <note>referring to Judah the Prince, the primary editor of the Mishnah</note> said: "This is two (namely, natures) and three generations (that is, substances)." As it is said in Psalm seventy-one: *They shall fear thee with the sun and before the moon, throughout generation and generations.* <note>Psalm 72:5 in modern numbering</note> The <term>Gloss of Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>The famous commentator Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki)</note> says: It is as if he says, the Messiah—of whom it is written, *Before the sun his name is Innon* <note>original: "ינון innon"; a traditional name for the Messiah derived from Psalm 72:17</note>, that is, the Son or the Begotten—the Israelites shall fear thee; and *before the moon*, that is, before the Kingdom of the house of David, which is likened to the moon, as it is written in Psalm 88: *It shall be established forever like the moon.* 

Likewise, another gloss of the same man on that passage of Isaiah: *Like the days of the united King.* He says: "The days of David were seventy years, and I do not know what this sign given here means." Since these things are so, it must be carefully noted how the Talmud in this aforementioned tradition says the Messiah is the "united King." Then, what is more wonderful is how this Rabbi (who is called "the Rabbi" by way of excellence and is considered holy) suggests what he had received from the Fathers: the matter and form of the Messiah's union. He says that *this* <note>original: "זה Ze"</note>—that is, the Messiah of whom prior mention was made, or "this" which refers to the union of the King Messiah—is "two," namely God and man, or two natures united in the Messiah, the divine and the human; and "three generations" of the substances of these three natures: namely, the Word of God, the rational soul, and the human body. He proves this through the Prophet, who, addressing the Messiah in the Spirit, says in Psalm seventy-one: *They shall fear thee*—namely the Israelites, as they themselves explain, or whoever else—*with the sun*, namely that sun of which it is said in Psalm eighty-three: *The Lord God is a sun and a shield, he will give grace and glory.* <note>Psalm 84:11</note> In saying, *They shall fear thee with the sun*, he suggests the conjunction of the divinity and humanity of the Messiah. But in what follows, *And before the moon*, he means before the Kingdom of David (as Rabbi Solomon explains) or before the Church, which is compared to the moon, according to 

<column-break/>

that which is written in the sixth chapter of the Song of Songs: *Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun?* Next, let them see <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>Our Holy Teacher, Judah the Prince</note> speaking openly about this matter; who, in the book he named *Gale Razaia* <note>original: "גלי רזיא"; meaning "Revealer of Secrets"</note>, commenting on that passage of Isaiah chapter nine, *Of the increase of his government*, says among other things: "Just as the letter *He* <note>ה</note> is composed of *Daleth* <note>ד</note> and *Vau* <note>ו</note>, so the King Messiah is composed of divinity and humanity. And just as these two *He*'s are two *Daleth*'s, and from these proceed two *Vau*'s, like two sons arising from them, so in the substance of the King Messiah are found two sonships, one of which is of divinity, by which he is the Son of God; the other shall be of humanity, by which he will be the son of prophecy, of whom Isaiah said in the eighth chapter, *And I went unto the prophetess, and she conceived and bare a son.* And just as each of these letters *Daleth* and *Vau*, which make up the *He*, is distinct from the other, although both are one letter, so in the Messiah, the substance of divinity will be distinct from the substance of humanity, and vice-versa. Which two, joined together, are the Messiah." 

These are the words of him whom the Jews call "our holy master." From these things, therefore, which have been said, it is manifest that this name "Messiah" imports two natures, namely divine and human, and embraces three things in one person: namely, the human body, the rational soul, and the Word of God.

### CHAPTER III.

->*What the Word of God is according to the Hebrews, and that the Word of God is <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "ὁמוούσιον"; meaning of the same substance or essence</note> with God.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>
*Vitri*
</margin>

To prove the divinity of the Messiah, it is necessary above all to say what the ancient Jews thought concerning this "Word of God." GAL. Therefore, it must necessarily be noted that just as man has a triple word—namely, that which is written on paper, that which is uttered by the mouth, and that which lies hidden in the mind (and to this last the name "word" more properly applies, since it is the cause and principle of the others: for no actions of men would exist unless they were first spoken in the mind; wherefore that saying of a certain Arabic poet is not to be entirely despised when he says, "The word is indeed in the heart, but the tongue was made to be the heart's interpreter")—so also according to the Hebrews, God Himself, in whose image man was made, is said to have a triple Word. For He has the Word written in the books of the Prophets; He has also the Word which is uttered by the mouths of the saints and teachers, of which He Himself says in Jeremiah chapter 1: *Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.* <note>Jeremiah 1:9</note> He also has the Word in Himself, from Himself, and not from anoth— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "aliun-" for the page turn.</note>

<summary>This page uses Jewish mystical and legal texts, such as the Midrash and the Gale Razaia, to argue that the Messiah possesses both a divine and human nature within one person, using the Hebrew letter He as a symbolic illustration. It also begins a discussion on the "Word of God" as having a triple existence: written, spoken, and mental.</summary>
