<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section regarding the divine nature of the Messiah. It specifically identifies the "Word of God" (the Logos) as being the same as the "Beginning" mentioned in Genesis and the "Wisdom" described in Proverbs, using Aramaic translations (Targums) to prove this was an established tradition.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

...from elsewhere. Concerning this, the Psalmist in Psalm 33 says: <margin>A</margin> *For the word of the LORD is right; and all his works are done in truth. He loveth righteousness and judgment: the earth is full of the goodness of the LORD. By the word of the LORD were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.* <note>original: "כי ישר דבר יהוה..." etc. This is Psalm 33:4–6.</note> This "Word of the LORD," through which not only the four elements but the heavens themselves were made, is nothing other than that "Beginning" <note>original: "ראשית Re-shith"</note> of which it is written in the first chapter of Genesis: <margin>B</margin> *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* <note>original: "בראשית ברא אלהים..." etc. Genesis 1:1.</note> For it is clear that this "Beginning" is nothing but the begotten Wisdom of God, as is said in the person of Divine Wisdom itself in the eighth chapter of Proverbs: *The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.* <note>original: "יהוה קנני ראשית דרכו..." etc. Proverbs 8:22.</note> From this it is evident that the "Beginning" by which the world was created and the "Wisdom" which God possessed are entirely the same thing in reality, even if they differ in <margin>C</margin> name. Furthermore, that which is called here the "beginning of his way"—that is, of his creation—is that very Word of God by which (as has been said) the heavens were made. Concerning this, the Holy Scripture embraces all the works of God under one name of power, though it divides them into various names in different places, saying in Psalm 104: <margin>D</margin> *O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all.* <note>original: "מה רבו מעשיך יהוה כלם בחכמה עשית" etc. Psalm 104:24.</note> You see, therefore, that whether you say "the Beginning," or "the Word," or "the hand," or "the arm of God," or anything else of this kind, you do not indicate a diversity of things, but only the one power and wisdom of God by which He made all things.

It should also be carefully noted that when it was said just before, *For the word of the LORD is right; and all his works are done in truth,* it immediately adds <margin>E</margin> regarding that same Word: *He loveth righteousness and judgment.* This clearly implies that the Word we are discussing is a rational substance and <term>ὁμοούσιον</term> <note>original: "homoousion"; a Greek theological term meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial." It defines the relationship between God the Father and God the Son.</note>, or consubstantial, with God. Indeed, to love righteousness and judgment is a property of a rational and intellectual substance. For this reason, the Word of God itself is frequently called the "eye" or "eyes of God." For instance, where the Lord says concerning the Jews in the seventh chapter of Ezekiel: *And mine eye shall not spare thee,* <margin>F</margin> <note>original: "ולא תחוס עיני עליך" etc. Ezekiel 7:9.</note> Jonathan, in the Aramaic translation <note>original: "translatione Chaldaica"; refers to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues.</note>, says: *And my Word shall not have mercy upon you.* <note>original: "ולא ארחמא מימרי עלוהי" etc.</note> See here: where the Prophet, speaking in the person of God, placed "my eye," the Aramaic translator said "my Word" <note>original: "Memri," a common Aramaic term for the divine Word in the Targums.</note>. Moreover, in saying that "my Word had mercy upon them," he clearly shows that the Word of God has life, since having mercy is a property of a living being. And this is what is <margin>G</margin> said in the first chapter of John: *In him was life.* That which is also written in the twenty-fourth chapter of Jeremiah: *And I will set mine eyes upon them for good,*

<column-break/>

the same Jonathan translated into Aramaic as: *And I will set my Word upon them for good.* <note>original: "ואשוי מימרי עליהון לטבא"</note> Similarly, where the Lord says the opposite against them in the ninth chapter of Amos: *And I will set mine eyes upon them for evil, and not for good,* Jonathan himself explained it in Aramaic as: *And I will set my Word upon them for evil, and not for good.* To also suggest the consubstantiality of this Word with God, the Word of God is sometimes called in the Sacred Scriptures the "Face of God," sometimes the "Mouth of God," and sometimes the "Hand of God." It is called the "Face of God" in the fifth chapter of Jeremiah, where it is said: *Fear ye not me? saith the LORD: will ye not tremble at my face, which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it?* Jonathan himself translated this into Aramaic as: *Will you not fear before my Word, you who have placed the sand as a limit to the sea?* That it is called the "Mouth of God" is held from what Isaiah uttered in the forty-eighth chapter in the voice of God, saying: *I have declared the former things from the beginning; and they went forth out of my mouth.* This, Jonathan turns into Aramaic: *The ancient things I saw from the beginning, and from my Word they proceeded.* Similar to this is what is read in the fifteenth chapter of Jeremiah: *Therefore thus saith the LORD, If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before my face: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth.* This, too, the same Jonathan translated into Aramaic: *Therefore thus says the LORD, if you return, I will bring you back, you shall serve before me. And if you turn the wicked to become righteous, you shall fulfill the pleasure of my Word.* Where the Prophet used "precious and vile," this man explained it as "righteous and wicked." And where the former said "the mouth of God," the latter translated it as "his Word." Finally, that the Word of God is called the "Hand of God" is most evident from what is read in the forty-eighth chapter of Isaiah: *Mine hand also hath laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand hath spanned the heavens.* For Jonathan explains this in the Targum thus: *By my Word also I founded the earth, and by my power I suspended the heavens.* Again, what is said in the forty-fifth chapter of the same Prophet: *I have made the earth, and created man upon it: I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I commanded.* The same translator explained this in Aramaic: *I by my Word have made the earth, and man upon it I created; I by my power...*

It uses Aramaic Targums to show that biblical metaphors like the "Eye," "Face," and "Hand" of God were traditionally understood as references to this divine Word (Memra).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio and Galatinus regarding the identity of the "Word of God" (Logos) and "Wisdom." The previous page established that the "Beginning" in Genesis and "Wisdom" in Proverbs refer to the same divine entity. This page focuses on refuting contemporary Jewish interpretations that identify this "Wisdom" as the Mosaic Law, arguing instead for its identity as the Divine Word and God Himself.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

...I suspended the heavens and all their host I perfected. <note>original: "תליה שמיא וכל חילהון שכללית"</note> That is, "I by my word, or through my word, made the earth; and I created humans upon it. I in my power stretched out the heavens, and all their virtues I confirmed." From all these things which have now been said, it is clearly manifest that the Word of God—which is the same as the Wisdom of God, by which He created the world from nothing and perfected it—is of the very same substance as God Himself.

<margin>The heretical interpretation of the younger Jews.</margin>
**CAPNIO.** The more recent Jews, regarding that passage in the 8th chapter of Proverbs, *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way,* which you have interpreted as the uncreated Wisdom of God (which is the Word through which God made all things), assert instead that this Wisdom is the Mosaic Law. They say that the Law speaks of itself in that same place, saying, *I love those who love me.* Since this is entirely contrary to the Catholic truth and indeed heretical, it is necessary for you to refute it using their own authentic scriptures.

**GALATINUS.** That is truly so absurd that it hardly needs a refutation. For if the Law of Moses is capable of neither love nor hate—except perhaps as other such inanimate things written on parchment—how can they say that it speaks of itself, *I love those who love me*? For to love is a property of a rational nature. Furthermore, if the Law of Moses itself came into being at that time when it took its beginning on Mount Sinai, how could it have been with God before the start of all things? How could it say of itself, *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before he made anything,* along with the rest that follows? Likewise, they say in this place that this word *Kana* <note>original: קנה</note> is equivocal, and sometimes means "to buy" and sometimes "to possess." They say it means "to possess" in the passage where Melchizedek, blessing Abraham in Genesis 14, said: *Blessed be Abram by the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth.* <note>original: "ברוך אברם לאל עליון קונה שמים וארץ"</note> But here, they claim the word *Kana* means "to buy." Therefore, one must ask them: if God "bought" the heaven, the earth, and the Law itself, who was the seller of these things? Certainly, they can name no one. Therefore, it is shameful even to dream of such things, let alone speak them. Let them cease even thinking such things and, according to the ancient traditions of their own Teachers, believe that Solomon in this place was mindful not of the Mosaic Law, but of the very Wisdom of God through which God fashioned the world. Let them also read what is written in the book of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The primary body of Jewish law and the high court in ancient Israel.</note> in the chapter entitled *Dine Mamonoth* <note>original: דיני ממונות; literally "Monetary Laws" or "Judgments of Wealth."</note> regarding that passage in Proverbs 9: *Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven columns; she has slaughtered her victims, she has mixed her wine, she has also furnished her table; she has sent out her maidens to call from the highest points of the city.* <note>Proverbs 9:1–3.</note> For there, these things are explained thus: *Wisdom has built her house.* This is the *Middatho* <note>original: מדתו; "his attribute" or "his property."</note>—that is, the property of the Holy and Blessed God Himself, who created the entire world in wisdom, or through wisdom. Just as it is said in Psalm 104: *How manifold are your works, O God, in wisdom you have made them all.* *She has hewn out her seven columns*—that is, the seven days of *Berethith* <note>original: בראשית; meaning "In the beginning" or the days of Creation in the book of Genesis.</note>—that is, the creation in the book of Genesis. *She has slaughtered her victims,* or cooked her victims. By this are understood the seas, rivers, and all the necessities of the world. *She has sent out her maidens to call.* These are the first Adam and Eve. All this is from tradition. From these things it is most evidently clear that the Wisdom which constructed her house (that is, the world) is one of the three *Middoth* <note>original: מדות; "Attributes" or "measures" of the divine.</note>—that is, properties of the Holy and Blessed God, through which they say (as we showed above) the world was established, although they use the term "property" far more broadly than we do. Moreover, we have already proved that this property of God—namely Wisdom, through which God created the world—is exactly the same thing as the Word of God.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER IV.

#### That God is the Word, and the Word of God is Himself God.

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a seated figure in a landscape.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH you have already proven quite abundantly in the preceding arguments that the Word of God is of the same substance as God—from which it necessarily follows both that God is the Word and the Word of God is Himself God—nevertheless, so that the very stiff necks of the younger Jews may be further crushed, I pray you might now show more openly that God is the Word, and the Word of God is God.

**GALATINUS.** That God is indeed the Word is primarily evident from the fact that where Isaiah in chapter 45 says, *Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation,* <note>original: "ישראל נושע ביהוה תשועת עולמים"</note> the Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase/translation of the Prophets.</note> says: *Israel shall be saved in the Word or through the Word of God with an eternal salvation.* <note>original: "ישראל במימרא דיי יתפריק פורקן עלמיא"</note> Where Isaiah said "in God" (using the Tetragrammaton, <note>The four-letter divine name YHWH, which the text notes is attributed to no one but God.</note> a name attributed to no one but God), the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> interpreter translated it as "in the Word of God." By this, he openly shows that God is the Word. Likewise, where it is said in Hosea chapter 1, *And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the LORD their God,* <note>original: "ואת בית יהודה ארחם והושעתים ביהוה אלהיהם"</note> the same interpreter translates into Chaldean: *And upon the house of Judah I will have mercy, and I will save them in the Word of the LORD their God.* <note>original: "ועל דבית יהודה ארחם ואפחקינון במימרא דיי אלוההון"</note> Also, that which Isaiah says in chapter 8, *And the LORD added to speak to me yet again,* <note>original: "ויספ יהוה דבר אלי עוד"</note> Jonathan himself translated in Chaldean as: *And the Word of the LORD added to speak to me yet again.* <note>original: "ואוסיפ מימרא דיי למלל לי עוד"</note> Likewise, what the same Prophet said in chapter 41, *Fear not, for I am with you,* <note>original: "אל תירא כי עמך אני"</note> he translated as, *Fear not, for my Word is in your help.* Likewise, what is said in the same place: *Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel; I am your help, says God, and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.* <note>original: "אל תיראי תולעת יעקב מתי ישראל אני עזרתך נאם יהוה וגואלך קדוש ישראל"</note> This he rendered in Chaldean...

# BOOK THREE.

...expounded: "Fear not, tribe of the house of Jacob, seed of the house of Israel; my word shall be for your help, says God and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel." Furthermore, consider what that same Prophet says in chapter 44: "Thus says the Lord your redeemer from the womb, I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens *leuaddi* <term>leuaddi: by myself alone</term>, and establishing the earth *meitti* <term>meitti: by him who is with me</term>." This is how the Targum <note>The Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> explains it: "Thus says the Lord who redeemed you, and who formed you from the womb: I am the Lord, the author of all things; I stretched out the heavens by my word <note>original: "verbo meo"</note>, or through my word. I founded the earth by my power or strength." This resonates strongly with the statement of the Evangelist: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was nothing made." <note>A reference to the opening of the Gospel of John</note> Consider also what is said in the ninth chapter of Hosea: "My God will reject or cast them away, because they did not hear him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations." Jonathan explains this in the Targum as: "My God will cast them away, because they did not receive his word, and they shall be wanderers among the nations." Since, therefore, in all these instances—and many others where the Prophets placed "Lord" or "God" (<term>tetragrammaton: the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</term>)—the aforementioned Rabbi Jonathan, a man of the greatest authority among them, translated and explained it in the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note> as "the Word of God," it follows logically that God himself is the Word, and the Word of God is God, which was the point to be proven.

### CHAPTER V.

*That the Messiah is the Word of God, whom God was to send to heal the whole human race.*

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> Now it remains, for a fuller understanding of this matter, that you show the Messiah to be the Word of God, whom God was to send to heal the whole world. **GALATINUS.** That the Messiah is the Word of God is most clearly evident from the fact that where David, in the one hundred and tenth Psalm, calls the Messiah his Lord, saying, *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand* <note>original Hebrew: "נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני"</note>, there Rabbi Jonathan, in the Chaldean translation, says: "The Lord said to his word, sit at my right hand" <note>original Aramaic: "אמר יהוה למימריה תב לימיני"</note>. Some people object to me here, saying that it is not written this way in the Chaldean translation, and they even deny that the translation belongs to Jonathan. To them I respond: it is indeed true that it is not found that way in the Chaldean translation which they have seen, and that one is not by Jonathan; for it is (as most agree) by Rabbi Joseph the Blind, or (as others will have it) by Rabbi Aquila. That version says: "The Lord said in his word that he would give me dominion, because I sat down to learn the law; wait at my right hand" <note>original Aramaic: "אמר יהוה בממריה למיתן לי רבנותא..."</note>. However, the translation of Jonathan, which they have not yet seen, is exactly as I reported it. This <margin>B</margin> is clearly evident in the *beſepher kibutſim* <term>beſepher kibutſim: In the Book of Collections</term>, which is a collection of the opinions of the wise. In that place, where it is proved that the Messiah is the one whom David said would sit at the right hand of God, it says: "This is explained from what they said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note> regarding the verse: *And you gave me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me.* Rabbi Iodan said, in the name of Rabbi Hama: In <margin>C</margin> the time to come, the Holy and Blessed God will cause the King Messiah to sit at His right hand, as it is said in Psalm 110: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* The Targum—that is, the Chaldean translation of Jonathan ben Uzziel—explains it thus: 'The Lord said to his word, sit at my right hand.'" Thus far the tradition. The same is also confirmed in that same *Midrash Tehillim* regarding the verse in Psalm 2: *I will tell of the decree: the Lord said to me, You are my son, today I have begotten you.* <margin>D</margin> For it is said there: "They tell of the mysteries <note>Galatinus translates 'hukkah' (decree) as 'mysteria' (mysteries)</note> of him, namely the King Messiah, in the scripture of the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa <note>The 'Holy Writings' or 'Kethuvim', the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>. In the scripture of the Law, Exodus 4: *Israel is my firstborn son.* In the scripture of the Prophets, Isaiah <margin>E</margin> 52: *Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up.* In the scripture of the Hagiographa, Psalm 110: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.*" From these traditions, it is openly shown that he is undoubtedly the Messiah whom David predicted would sit at the right hand of God. From this, through Jonathan’s Targum, it is clearly concluded that the Messiah is the Word of God. Therefore, it is no wonder if David called the Messiah himself his "Lord." **CAPNIO.** Now, therefore, <margin>F</margin> it remains to prove that God would send this Word of His to heal the whole world. **GALATINUS.** This can be seen especially from what is read in the commentaries of Rabbi Isaac Arama on the book of Genesis, in the exposition of the forty-seventh chapter, or thereabouts, where it deals with the place given to Jacob in which he could dwell comfortably. It reads as follows: "He shall send his word and heal them, and deliver them from their destructions." Rabbi Samuel the Levite <margin>G</margin> said: "The word of the Lord is His messenger, as it is written: Is not my word like this..."

# BOOK THREE.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*That Jesus of Nazareth, the true Messiah, is the Word of God, sent by the eternal Father for the salvation of mankind.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "כאשר נאם יהוה..."</note> Just as the Lord spoke, and this is what he said: "Your word shall come and we will honor you." When the Word of God comes, who is his messenger, I will honor him. Rabbi Saul said: "But did the prophets not come, and we killed them and shed their blood? How shall we now receive his word, or why should we believe?" He said to him: "Because he will heal them and rescue them from their destructions, and through these miracles we shall believe him and honor him." He said to him: "Why did it not say 'he will send his word and heal *us*,' but rather 'heal *them*?'" Because it appears he was speaking of a specific group. He answered him: "You have spoken the truth; for the Word came to heal everyone, but none received him except for those individuals who were considered of coarser intellect among the common folk—fishermen and servants of the sea." And this is what is meant by: "They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; these see the works of the Lord." These truly received it; and though they seemed unable to receive anything intellectual because of their rusticity, they received the truth of prophecy and vision because they believed his word. And this is what is written: "And he believed in the Lord, and it was counted to him as righteousness." <margin>B</margin> This is what is meant by: "He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions." <note>Psalm 107:20</note> Rabbi Samuel the Levite says: "The Word of God is his messenger, of whom it is written: 'Truly my word is like fire,' says God." And this is what was said: "Your word shall come, and we will honor you." Surely when the Word of God comes, who is his messenger, then we will honor him. Rabbi Saul said: "Did not the Prophets come, and we killed them and poured out their blood? How then shall we now receive his word? Or for what reason shall we believe him?" Rabbi Samuel answered him: "Because he will heal them and rescue them from their plagues; because of these signs, I say, we will believe him and hold him in honor." Then he said to him: "Why did he not say: 'He will send his word and heal *us*,' but instead said, 'and heal *them*'?" He replied: <margin>D</margin> "This is so (as I perceive it) because he was speaking of a part, and of some only, but not of all." (This is indicated according to the property of the Hebrew language in the word *Eos* <note>original: "them"</note>). He said to him: "You certainly speak the truth. For his word came to heal all universally, not just the ancients or in part; but it was not received except by some particular individuals, who were considered among all to be of a coarser wit: fishermen, and those who occupy themselves at sea." And this is what was said: "Those <margin>E</margin> going down to the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, these have seen the work of God." <note>Psalm 107:23-24</note> These men, if you consider it rightly, did not seem fit to be able to admit anything intellectual, or pertaining to the intellect, because of the rudeness of their senses. They, I say, received the truth of prophecy and vision, because they believed his word. And this is what is written: "He believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." From these things it is clear that God would <margin>F</margin> send his Word—that is, his Son, the true Messiah—to heal the whole human race. Yet not all were to be healed, but only those who would receive him and believe in him, and especially unlearned men and fishermen, as were the Apostles. From which it is clearly concluded that Jesus our Lord was the true Word of God, and the true Messiah sent from the eternal Father for the salvation of mankind.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a floral pattern.</image-desc> I would wish for you to prove this conclusion: namely, that our Lord Jesus of Nazareth was the true Word of God, and consequently the true Messiah, sent into the world by the eternal Father for the salvation of mankind. GALATINUS: So that I may say nothing of myself in this place, hear the words of Libertatus Cominetus, a Spaniard (for such is the man's name), who recently converted from Judaism to the faith—a man not only exceptionally learned in the divine scriptures, but also skilled in fourteen languages. For he, explaining that passage of the 147th Psalm: *He sends his word and melts them; he causes his wind to blow and the waters flow,* <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "ישלח דברו וימסם..."</note> says thus: "He sends his word and melts them." It seems it should have been said, "He *speaks* his word," and not "He *sends* his word." For it is more fitting for a word to be pronounced and uttered than to be *sent*, which seems to belong to a messenger. And the scripture agrees with this, saying: "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light." It did not say: "And God *sent* his word to make or create the light," because the language of 'sending' does not apply unless there is a messenger, as when he said: "Behold, I send to you Elijah the prophet." This means that God used to send the Prophets to tell his word and show his wonders. We also see this in the case of the bronze serpent, which God commanded to be made by the hand of Moses his prophet, in order to heal Israel when they looked upon it. For it would have been more fitting in those times for him to heal them by a word alone, so that the people might see his wonders and believe him, rather than with that serpent, which put a fear in the hearts of the people that it was a work of sorcery—what today is called Magic. Truly, if he had healed them by a word alone, he would have removed all fears from their hearts. But what appears to me from this verse is that David prophesied the coming of Jesus, the Messiah of our righteousness, by saying "his Word." For the truth is that he would be his Word, and who could vow his words? And just as speech is not a thing separate from itself, so he is not separate from God. And this is what was said: "Your word shall come and we will honor you." He did not say "we will honor *it*," but rather shows that he, the Exalted One, and his Word are one thing. For those who honor the Speech, honor Him; and those who honor Him, honor the Speech; and they are inseparable in their essence. And this is the Word which was prophesied to come to heal the sick and revive the dead by a word—and he himself was the Word. This was seen in Jesus, the Messiah of our righteousness, who healed so very many sick people and revived Lazarus who had been dead for four days. And these things are not fitting for anyone but God. And close to this it says: "He causes his wind to blow and the waters flow." It seems there is no connection between the healing of bodies and the flowing of waters at all. But you will understand how the prophet David [spoke] the truths by saying *yashev* <term>yashev: he returns/dwells</term> and he did not say *yashiv* <term>yashiv: he will cause to return</term>, which means that God will cause his Holy Spirit to dwell with him and at his right hand. After this "the waters flow," which means that the holy waters shall remain to save his people, and they are the cause of our salvation, as it is said: "And you shall draw water with joy from the wells of salvation," through which God is joined to us, as he said: "When you pass through the waters, I am with you." He did not say "in the waters," but "with the waters," meaning <margin>G</margin> the holy waters. This is: "He sends his word and melts them." It seems it should have been said, "He will speak his word," not "He will send his word." For it is more appropriate for a word to be pronounced and brought forth than to be sent, which is the role of a messenger. And the scripture which says:

<meta>This page continues the discourse between Capnio (the scholar Johann Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding the divinity of the Messiah. The previous page discussed the Messiah as the "Word" (Memra) who heals; this page extends that argument to show that the Messiah is not only the Word but also the "Son of God," using Jewish commentaries and the Hebrew language to prove the point to a skeptical audience.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

<sig>F</sig>
<meta>Catchword: hendit</meta>

<margin>A</margin> God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. However, He did not say, "God sent His word to create the light," because a "sending" cannot be fulfilled without a messenger being sent. For this reason, it was said: "Behold, I send to you Elijah the Prophet," <note>Malachi 4:5</note> which implies that God sends Prophets to announce His word and to manifest His wonders. Therefore, the bronze serpent <note>The *Nehushtan*, a pole with a copper serpent made by Moses to heal Israelites from snakebites; see Numbers 21:9.</note> increases the question—the serpent which God commanded to be made by the hand of His prophet Moses, so that the people of Israel might be healed when they looked upon it. For it appears more rational and fitting, especially in those times, that God <margin>B</margin> should have healed the people by a word rather than by the sight of a serpent, a thing which could have led to a suspicion of magical incantations. And yet, He did not heal by a word then. How, therefore, does it fit what the Prophet says: "He shall send His word, and He shall heal them"? <note>Psalm 107:20</note> This is resolved thus: as far as I can perceive, David in that place prophesied the coming of Jesus the Messiah our Just One, who is rightly called His "Word." But the truth is that Jesus is the Word <margin>C</margin> of God, and is the messenger of God’s words. And just as God's Word is not something distinct from the essence of God, so also the Messiah is not entirely distinct from the divine substance. And this is what is written: "Your word shall come, and we will honor You." <note>A phrase often cited in these polemics as a variant or interpretation of prophetic texts.</note> For if the Word were entirely divided from Him, he would have said, "And we will honor *it*." By these words, it is clearly shown that God and the Word of God are one and the same, since it is considered the same thing to honor God and the Word of God, as they are by no means distinct in essence. And this is the Word about whom it was prophesied that he would come <margin>D</margin> to heal the sick and to raise the dead by a word; and the very Word by which they were healed was the same Word that performed the healing. All these things were fulfilled in Jesus the Messiah, our Just One: by whose works almost innumerable sick people were healed, and Lazarus was raised from the dead, even after the fourth day of his death. And these things belong to God alone. It agrees with our exposition what immediately follows: "His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow." <note>Psalm 147:18</note> For although they might seem to have no connection—that is, healing the sick and the flowing of waters—it is nevertheless the truest sense of the Prophet, who also said, not without mystery, "His spirit shall blow," and <margin>E</margin> did not say, "His spirit shall return"; demonstrating that God would cause His Holy Spirit to blow from Himself. And he added: "And the waters shall flow," signifying that holy waters were to remain for the salvation of His people. These waters are indeed the causes of our salvation, just as it is written: "You shall draw waters from the fountain of salvation with joy." <note>Isaiah 12:3</note> For through the intervention of holy waters, God is joined with us, as it is written: "When you pass through those waters, I am with you." <note>Isaiah 43:2</note> And he did not say merely "through waters," but "through *those* waters," demonstrating that he spoke not of just any waters, but of the holy waters, which are the waters of baptism. All these things were stated by the aforementioned Doctor, a most learned man of the Hebrews recently converted to the truth of the Christian <margin>G</margin> faith, by which he most excellently proves that Jesus of Nazareth our Lord was the true Word of God, and consequently, the true Messiah, sent by the eternal Father for the salvation of men—which certainly was the point to be proved.

---

### CHAPTER VI.

#### That the Messiah is the Son of God, as well as concerning the word <term>בר</term> (*bar*: "son"): and what the "Firstborn" is, according to the Hebrews themselves.

-> CAPNIO. <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a classical figure or deity within a circular frame, surrounded by floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc> ALTHOUGH it follows from what you have said that the Messiah is the Son of God—for if the Messiah himself is the Word of God, it is necessary beyond doubt that he is also the Son of God—nevertheless, so that the perfidy of the Jews of our age may be more and more defeated by their own weapons, you ought to demonstrate more expressly through their own scriptures that the Messiah himself is the Son of God. GALATINUS: First, let that Psalm which begins "Why have the nations raged" <note>Psalm 2</note> be brought against them, which is explained by the ancient Jews as being about the Messiah, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> bears witness, saying of it: "Our teachers have explained this Psalm concerning the Messiah." In the conclusion of that same Psalm, it is read: <term>נשקו בר פן יאנף ותאבדו דרך כי יבער כמעט אפו אשרי כל חוסי בו</term> <note>original: "Nasseku bar pen ye’enaf..."</note> That is: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way: For his wrath will be kindled in a short time: Blessed are all those who hope in him." David was therefore urging the judges of the earth to receive this kiss of the Son of God, as is shown by Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar.</note>, who, explaining this, says: <term>נשקו בר</term> *Nassecu bar*, that is, "Kiss the Son"; behold, serve the Lord, in contrast to what he had said above, namely, "against his Messiah." The explanation of this word <term>בר</term> (*bar*) is the same as that which is in Proverbs, the thirty-first chapter: <term>מה ברי ומה בר בטני ומה בר נדרי</term> <note>Proverbs 31:2</note> That is: "What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?" And thus it is written in this same Psalm: <term>בני אתה</term> (*beni attah*), that is, "You are my son." <note>Psalm 2:7</note> Thus says the same Rabbi Abraham. Also in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient homiletic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Psalms.</note>, that is, in the explanation of the Psalms, it is said upon these same words: <term>נשקו בר הוא מר, דכתיב חסד ואמת נפגשו צדק ושלום נשקו. אמר רב משל למלך שכעס על בני המדינה והלכו בני המדינה ופייסו את בן המלך שיפייס את המלך והלך את הבן ופייס את אביו כיון שנתפייס לבנו הלכו בני המדינה לומר המנון למלך אמר להם לי אתם חומנין לכו ואמרוהו לבני שבלא הוא כבר אבדתי את המדינה וזהו נשקו בר</term> That is: This is what is written in Psalm 85: "Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed." <note>Psalm 85:10</note> Rab said: This is like a King who was angry with the citizens of a city. The citizens went and pleaded with the King's son to appease the King. The son went and appeased his father. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between the scholar Capnio (Johann Reuchlin) and the converted friar Galatinus. In the previous section, they discussed the "Word of God" as a healing force. ...show discipline, he has here. **GAL.** The author of our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translated by St. Jerome.</note>, having been deceived by the ambiguity of terms, translated many things quite differently than the Hebrew truth holds. For although this word בר (*Bar*) <note>original: "Bar"</note> sometimes signifies "son," sometimes "discipline" or "doctrine," sometimes "grain," sometimes "pure" or "clean," and sometimes "chosen"—as Saint Jerome also seems to feel when he writes to Pammachius in his apology against Rufinus—*Bar* among the Hebrews signifies diverse things. For *Bar* is said for "son," as in that phrase *Bar-jona*, that is, "son of a dove"; and *Bartholomew*, that is, "son of Ptolemy"; and *Barnabas*, that is, "son of a Prophet"; and *Barchineus*, and *Barchisæus*, and *Barabbas*. It also means wheat, and a bundle of thorns, and "chosen," and "pure" (these are the words of Jerome). 

Nevertheless, in this place <note>Psalm 2:12</note>, *Bar* is not understood except as "son," just as the aforementioned Rabbi Abraham <note>likely Abraham Ibn Ezra, a medieval Jewish commentator</note> understands it in his exposition of this text. And although the Chaldean interpreter <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>—whom the Jews now more frequently have at hand (whether it be the blind Rabbi Joseph, as some prefer, or Rabbi Aquila, as others will have it)—took *Bar* in this place for "doctrine," saying: קבילו אולפנא (*Kabbilo ulphana*), that is, "Receive doctrine"; yet it is more rightly and appropriately understood as "son," as we have said. For in this way it both favors our faith more (as it seems) and agrees more with the exposition of the ancients (as was evident in the traditions mentioned above), and fits better with the literal truth. 

For that which follows—"Lest he be angry"—along with the rest, cannot apply to anyone except the Son of God. From this it is also clear that their interpretation is not true who, in order to escape the truth and deny the divinity of the Messiah, interpret these same words נשקו בר (*nassecu bar*) as "worship purely." However, that kiss with which the Church of the ancients, by kissing the Son of God, sought to be kissed by him, was nothing other than the instruction and doctrine to be brought forth from the very mouth of God, who had given them the law through the hand of Moses. For this reason (as the ancient Talmudists explained), that which is said in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: ישקני מנשיקות פיהו (*Yishakeni mi-neshikot pihu*), that is, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth," signifies: "Let the Messiah, the Son of God, kiss me with the kisses of his mouth," which is to say: "Let him personally instruct and teach me with his own mouth, and let him not despise the touch of my mouth when I ask him about the way of salvation." 

Let him no longer send Moses, who had a heavy tongue; nor Isaiah, who said he was of polluted lips; nor Jeremiah, who said he knew not how to speak because he was a child; but let the Son of God himself, who is the Wisdom and Power of the Father, come and teach me with his own mouth. By this it is also proved that the Messiah is the Son of God, because God himself says this of him in Psalm 89: הוא יקראני אבי אתה אלי וצור ישועתי אף אני בכור אתנהו עליון למלכי ארץ (*Hu yikra’eni avi attah eli ve-tsur yeshuati af ani bechor etnehu elyon le-malkhei arets*). That is: "He shall call me, Thou art my Father, my God, and the strength of my salvation. I also will make him my firstborn, highest above the Kings," or "of the kings of the earth." That this must be understood regarding the Messiah, Jewish perversity can least of all deny; since in the gloss upon that passage of Exodus chapter 13, "Sanctify to me every firstborn," it is written that Rabbi Nathan said: "The Holy and Blessed God said: Just as I made Jacob a בכור (*Bechor*), that is, a firstborn, as

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> it is said in Exodus 3: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn,' so I will make the King Messiah a firstborn; as it is said in Psalm 89: 'I will make him my firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth.'" This is from the aforementioned gloss. From the end of which it clearly appears that the saying of the Psalmist which we just presented—"He shall call me, Thou art my Father"—along with the rest that was said, ought to be understood as referring to the Messiah. 

For the understanding of this, it should be noted that this word בכור (*Bechor*), which is interpreted as "firstborn," has no relation among the Hebrews to another <note>Meaning it does not necessarily imply subsequent siblings in this context.</note>, but is a name imposed upon him before whom none was born of the same father and the same mother. Thus the Messiah was to be a firstborn in some sense, as Jacob had already been, according to the flesh—that is, before whom no one else was born first—given to men according to his divinity, which must necessarily be in him, and he himself must be God. Therefore he says well, "I will make him a firstborn." In that *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A Rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note> also, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that verse of the second Psalm: יהוה אמר אלי בני אתה אני היום ילדתיך (*Adonai amar elai beni attah ani ha-yom yeladtikha*), that is, "The Lord said to me, Thou art my son, today I have begotten thee," this same point is proved.

### CHAPTER VI.
#### That Messiah is a name of God, and that the name of God is God himself.
### CAPNIO.

<margin>D</margin> SINCE the divinity of the Messiah is most clearly evident through his names, which are found assigned to him in the sacred scriptures, he must therefore be proved to be the true God primarily through those same names. **GAL.** Before all things, therefore, it must be known that the Messiah is himself the "Name of God," and the name of God is God. Moreover, that the name of God is God is clearly held in the *Midrash Tehillim* upon that passage of Psalm 24, which begins: ליהוה הארץ ומלואה (*La-Adonai ha-arets u-melo’ah*), that is, "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." For there it is said literally: "It is written, 'I am God who makes all things, stretching out the heavens by myself, establishing' or 'laying out the earth by him who is with me.'" For מאתי (*me-itti*) <note>Literally "from me," but the author argues for a reading of "with me."</note> is written there, that is, "through him who is with me," or "beside me." 

It is also written in Isaiah chapter 44: "Who then was אתי (*itti*), that is, 'with me'?" My name was mixed together with me in the creation of the world. Therefore David said before the Holy and Blessed God: "Because you created the heavens and the earth with your name, I shall attribute those things to your name," saying, "The earth is the Lord's (the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH.</note>) and the fullness thereof." Thus far the tradition. Wherein, among other things, that which is said about the name itself is very much in agreement with our faith: namely, that it was with God in the creation of the world. For the name of God itself is one of the properties of God, with which God himself created the world. Nor is this name anything other than the Son of God, or the Word, by which, or through which, God himself founded the world out of nothing. This is expressed more clearly in the Chaldean translation of Rabbi Jonathan...

Then it follows: "And there shall come to Zion a **Redeemer** (*Goel*), and to those who turn from iniquity in Jacob, said the Lord." All these are the tradition. ### CHAPTER IX.

->*That the Messiah was to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton).*<-

<column-break/>

### CAPNIO.

I would like you to prove here that the Messiah was to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton), by which the divine essence itself is designated. **GALATINUS.** To prove this, I will first bring forward the words of Jeremiah, speaking thus in the twenty-third chapter: **"Behold, the days are coming, says God, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch; and a King shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence. And this is his name by which they shall call him: The Lord (the Tetragrammaton) our Righteousness."** The Jews cannot deny that this prophecy is understood to be about the Messiah: both because the Talmudists explain it as being about the Messiah, and also because of the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum</note>, which speaks openly of the Messiah. In this prophecy, not only is a twofold nature of the Messiah expressed—divine and human—but it is also clearly shown that the Messiah himself was to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton), when it is said: "And this is his name by which they shall call him, The Lord (the Tetragrammaton) our Righteousness."

**CAPNIO.** The Jews of our time say that Jeremiah did not say "they shall call" here, as we have it, but "he shall call." For this reason, they assert the sense of these words is: "This is the name of him who shall call him (namely, the Messiah): God our Righteousness."

**GALATINUS.** They are plainly lying, and by falsely marking the vowels, they strive to corrupt the text. For from **they shall call** (*yikreu*), they want to make **he shall call** (*yikra*). But that they are manifest forgers is most evidently clear through nearly all the writings of their ancients. First, through the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, who translated this passage exactly as our edition has it. Next, through the Targum of Rabbi Jonathan, who thus turns these same words into Chaldean: **"Behold, the days are coming, says God, and I will establish for David the Messiah of righteousness."** And afterwards he adds: **"And this is the name by which they themselves shall call him,"** etc. The same Prophet also refutes their falsehood in no small measure when he says again in the thirty-third chapter: **"Behold, the days are coming, says God, and I will perform the good word which I have spoken to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah. In those days and at that time, I will cause the branch of righteousness to grow for David; and a King shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Jerusalem shall dwell in confidence. And..."**

Similarly, He called Israel by His name, as it is said in Psalm 82: "I said, you are gods." And they shall be called holy, as it is said: "You shall be holy, for I, your God, am holy." It is also written: "For the people is holy." Furthermore, He called the King Messiah by His own name. And what is His name? "The Lord <note>original: "Deus (tetragrammaton)" — the four-letter sacred name of God, YHWH</note> is a man of war." And concerning the King Messiah, it is written in Jeremiah 23: "And this is His name by which they shall call Him: The Lord <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note> our Righteousness." Even Jerusalem was called by His name, as is said in the final chapter of Ezekiel: "And the name of the city from 그날 (that day) shall be, The Lord <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note> is there."

Thus far the tradition. From this, it is not only abundantly and clearly held that the Messiah was to be called by the name of God, but many very beautiful points are gathered. Since no one except God can be called by the name of God, and the Messiah Himself has been called by this name by God Himself (as has been shown here), it follows that the Messiah is God Himself. Otherwise, God would have falsely called Him by this name or commanded Him to be so called, which is a wicked thing even to think.

**CHAPTER:** The Jews of our age attempt to render this conclusion void, saying that not only the Messiah, but also Moses, Israel, and the city of Jerusalem are found to be called by the name of God, as the very traditions you have just brought forward clearly show. From this they infer that the Messiah cannot be proven to be God simply because He is found addressed by the name of God; for no one would say Moses, Israel, or Jerusalem are gods just because they are found named with the name of God.

**GALATINUS:** They refuse to pay proper attention (for they only desire to deceive) to the fact that, as is clear in those same traditions, neither Moses nor Israel were called by this name of God—the Tetragrammaton—by which only God and the Messiah alone are called. Nor is anyone found anywhere called by this name in the same form that God Himself and the Messiah are called. Rather, they are called by another name, <term>Elohim</term> <note>A Hebrew word for God that can also be used for judges, angels, or even false gods depending on context</note>, which is found extended not only to Moses and the other Israelites, but also to angels, and indeed even to demons and idols many times. As in Psalm 96: "All the gods of the peoples are demons," or idols. One also reads in Genesis chapter 35 that Jacob said to his household and all who were with him: "Take away the <term>Elohim</term> <note>foreign gods</note> who are in your midst." Almost innumerable other examples of this kind are found in the Old Testament.

Regarding Jerusalem, however—which the younger Rabbi Judah asserts is called by the name of the Lord just as the Messiah her King is—I say that this refers to the heavenly Jerusalem, not the earthly one; and it is named with this name in a far different way than the Messiah. For when this name is spoken of the Messiah, it is spoken with a <term>toar</term> <note>original: "תואר" — an adjective</note>, that is, with the adjective "Righteous," and in that way and form in which it is most frequently spoken of God. As in that saying in Psalm 129: "The Lord <note>Tetragrammaton</note>, the Righteous one, will cut the cords of the wicked." Likewise in the first chapter of Lamentations: "The Lord is Righteous..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "...for I have provoked His mouth to bitterness." And this manner of speaking properly belongs to one who wishes the essence, quality, and truth of any thing to be understood, since names ought to be in harmony with the things they describe.

However, when it is spoken concerning the Jerusalem above, it is not with a <term>toar</term> (adjective), but with a local adverb <term>samma</term> <note>original: "שמה" — meaning "there"</note>, that is, "there." By this it is clearly demonstrated that the city itself is not God, but that God Himself exists in it through His glory. Thus it is clear then that the name is in harmony with the reality. This manner of speaking is customary among those who name their sons "God has given," "God save," and others of this kind; yet no one would be so insane as to call his son "God" with an adjective, such as "Righteous God," or "Holy God," or "his God," and such like. For by this method he would clearly pretend the son was God Himself, which no one doubts is very impious. 

Therefore, since God called the Messiah by His own name in this way, and decreed that He should be so named (as has already been proven), it necessarily follows that the Messiah is undoubtedly God. Otherwise, since names must be in harmony with the things they name, He would have falsely ordered Him to be called by a name proper to Himself—which is a most foul thing to think of God, let alone to say.

**CHAPTER:** In the book <term>Bava Batra</term> <note>A volume of the Babylonian Talmud dealing with civil law and property</note>, in the chapter beginning "He who sells a ship," I remember reading this: Rabbi Jonathan said, "Three are called by the name of God, holy and blessed. These are: the Righteous, the Messiah, and Jerusalem." And the Righteous indeed, as it is said: just as God is called righteous, so also they themselves are called righteous, and thus are called by the name of God. But the Messiah is called by the name of God as it is said in Jeremiah chapter 23: "And this is His name by which they shall call Him: The Lord our Righteousness." Jerusalem is also called by the name of God, as it is written in the last chapter of Ezekiel: "And the name of the city from that day, The Lord [is] <term>samma</term>." And do not read it as <term>samma</term> (there), but as <term>sema</term>, which signifies "His name."

**GALATINUS:** This Rabbi, in order to extinguish the light of the Messiah's divinity, did not shrink from falsifying the text of Holy Scripture. But the impudence of his falsehood is so great that even the Jews utterly refuse to comply with him in this; for absolutely no one reads <term>sema</term> (His name) in that place, as he says it should be read, but almost everyone reads <term>samma</term> (there), as it is written. For thus in the last chapter of Ezekiel the scripture is found to this day: "And the name of the city from that day, the Lord is there." From which it is clear that <term>samma</term> (there) is written there, and not <term>sema</term> (His name). This is clearly shown in the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum of the Prophets</note>, which says: "And the name of the city they shall explain from the day in which the Lord placed His divinity there." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note> says: "It is as if to say, it shall not be called, or it shall not be said of it a name, except the first name, which..."

<summary>This page argues that the Messiah is divine because he is uniquely called by God's holy four-letter name (the Tetragrammaton) combined with the adjective "Righteous." It refutes Jewish objections by distinguishing this specific naming from the more general titles given to Moses, Israel, or Jerusalem.</summary>

### BOOK THREE

...it was his from the day on which Abraham bound his son Isaac. For the name by which he called it was <note>original Hebrew: יראה, *yireeh*</note> "He will see," and the city itself was called <note>original Hebrew: שלם, *salem*</note> "Peace": Behold, Jerusalem <note>A combination of *Yireh* and *Salem*</note>. This is according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to the famous medieval commentator Rashi</note>. From this, it is clearly evident that Jerusalem was never called, nor will ever be called, by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton). To confirm this, I will bring forward what is written in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note> regarding Psalm 76. There, it is read word-for-word regarding the verse, "And his tabernacle was in Salem": You find that the house of the sanctuary was called Salem, just as it is written in *Genesis chapter 14*: "Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine; and he was the priest of the most high God." And he is Shem, the son of Noah. And again in *Genesis 9*: "May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem." For God dwelt in his tent, in which he ministered to Him. Behold, this is Shem. 

But Abraham called the house of the sanctuary <note>original Hebrew: יראה, *yireeh*</note> "He sees" or "He will see," as is said in *Genesis chapter 22*. What does "The Lord will see" mean? Abraham said, "Lord of the world, let this day be memorable before You; for I have an answer I could give You. For yesterday, or recently, You said to me: 'In Isaac shall your seed be called' (*Genesis 21*). And now You say: 'Take your son' (*Genesis 22*)? When, therefore, my children come to this judgment, I pray You, remember this day for them, and shine Your face upon them." 

The Holy and Blessed God said: "How then shall I call this place? For if I call it 'Salem,' as the one who said it [Melchizedek], I shall erase the words of my friend Abraham, who called it 'He will see.' But if I call it 'He will see,' I will void the name of the righteous man [Shem]." What then did the Holy and Blessed God do? He mixed the names by which both had called the place, and called it Jerusalem. Thus far the tradition: from which our purpose is clear.

<margin>CHAPTER 22</margin>The more recent Jews, not content with these things (for they still persist more obstinately than usual in their faithlessness), say that many other things besides the Messiah are found in the sacred scriptures to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton). One of these, they say, is found in the *Book of Genesis 22*: <note>original Hebrew: ויקרא אברהם שם המקום ההוא יהוה יראה</note> "And Abraham called the name of that place, The Lord <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note> will see/provide." Another is the altar, of which it is read in *Exodus chapter 17*: <note>original Hebrew: ויבן משה מזבח ויקרא שמו יהוה נסי</note> "And Moses built an altar, and called its name, The Lord <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note> is my banner." Furthermore, the altar that Gideon built, he called "The Lord <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note> is peace," as is held in *Judges chapter 6*. From all these, the younger Jews try to argue that not only the Messiah, but even altars—which are inanimate things—are called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton). 

GALATINUS: If they were willing to carefully consider those things we said a little earlier, they would certainly not say such trifles; for they would have a sufficient answer to all these, and to others of this kind, from their own sources. But since they no longer have any place to break out, they flee again like foxes to the hole from which they were driven. Therefore, so that a more glorious triumph may be had over them—using their own scriptures as a sword violently snatched from their own hands—and

<column-break/>

cutting the throat of their wickedness, we shall respond to each of these points individually. 

Regarding the first point, although it can be answered sufficiently through what was said just above about Jerusalem, I will bring forward the Aramaic explanation of Rabbi Onkelos <note>The *Targum Onkelos*, a highly respected 2nd-century translation of the Torah into Aramaic</note> to provide a specific response. Concerning that verse in *Genesis chapter 22*, "And Abraham called the name of that place, the Lord will see," he says: <margin>A</margin> <note>original Aramaic: ופלח וצלי אברהם תמן באתרא ההוא אמר קדם יהוה הכא יהון פלחין דריא</note> That is: "And Abraham worshipped and prayed there in that place, and said before the Lord: Here the generations shall be worshippers of You, or servants to You." <margin>B</margin> From this *Targum*, therefore, it clearly appears that Abraham did not at all call that place by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton). 

To the second point, a response is likewise first given through the *Targum*. For those words in *Exodus chapter 17*, "And Moses built an altar, and called its name, The Lord is my banner," the same Rabbi Onkelos explains thus: <note>original Aramaic: ובנא משה מדבחא ופלח עלוהי קדם יהוה על דעבד ליה ניסין</note> That is: "And Moses built, and worshipped or served—that is, sacrificed—upon it before the Lord, who performed signs for him." <margin>C</margin> From this Aramaic explanation, it is transparently clear that the altar was not called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) by Moses. 

Next, this same point is openly proved by a gloss placed in the book *Mechilta* <note>An ancient Jewish legal commentary on Exodus</note> regarding the same words. For it says: "And Moses built an altar, and called its name, the Lord is my banner." Rabbi Elai the Place <note>original: Hammakom — likely a title or place name</note> said: These words <margin>D</margin> signify that God called it—namely, the altar—<note>original Hebrew: נסי, *Nisi*</note> "My banner" or "My sign." By the explanation of this Rabbi, nothing is found among them more effective for refuting the words of those who wish to involve the aforementioned altars and other places in the name of God along with the Messiah. And for anyone who understands, the way this Rabbi vocalizes the words themselves can be an evident response to all their other objections. 

Finally, regarding the third point, <margin>E</margin> an answer can also be given through the *Targum*, which translates and explains those words of *Judges 6*, "And Gideon built an altar there to the Lord, and called it, The Lord of Peace," in Aramaic as: "And Gideon built an altar there to the Lord, and served—that is, sacrificed—upon it before the Lord (the Tetragrammaton), who made peace for him." This *Targum*, therefore, openly shows that the altar was not called by the name of God. 

This appears no less clearly from what is found in the introduction to the explanation of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, <margin>F</margin> which is called *Echa Rabbeti* <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a collection of midrashic homilies on the Book of Lamentations</note>. For there it is read that Rabbi Huna said: "It is unlawful for a man to question his neighbor or his friend in an unclean place—specifically, when he is performing what nature requires [using the latrine]. For he is not to be greeted then, nor is he to be asked how he is, or whether he has peace." And from where is the proof? From what is written in *Judges chapter 6*: "And Gideon built an altar there to the Lord, and called it, God is peace." If, therefore, an altar—which neither eats, nor drinks, nor smells, nor speaks, nor was built except to appease for Israel—was called "Peace," how much more so should he who loves peace be honored? <margin>G</margin>

### BOOK THREE

...loves, and sends peace between Israel and their Father who is in heaven. Thus far the quote. Furthermore, that the Messiah—who was to establish peace between God and men—should be called "Peace" is held in that same introduction to the Lamentations of Jeremiah, based on the words of Rabbi Jose the Galilean, who said: "Even the name of the Messiah is called <note>original Hebrew: שלום, *salom*</note> Peace, just as it was said in the ninth chapter of Isaiah: 'Eternal Father,' or Father of Eternity, 'Prince, Peace.'" <note>This refers to Isaiah 9:6, a verse traditionally used by Christians to argue for the divinity of the Messiah.</note> Therefore, the aforementioned text from the Book of Judges, as shown previously, is not to be interpreted as the Jewish objection suggested, but in one of two ways: either that Gideon built an altar there to the Lord and "God called it Peace," as appeared in the aforementioned tradition; or, "He called it the Peace of the Lord," as our edition has it. Both ways are more consistent with the truth according to the earlier expositions of the ancient Talmudists. From these sayings, it is most clearly established that, despite the false claims of more recent Jewish scholars, nothing is found called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) except God Himself and the Messiah. From this, it is manifest that the Messiah is God Himself, since a name of this kind belongs to God alone. Hence, it is not surprising if the sacred scriptures sometimes announce that the Messiah himself is the name of God (the Tetragrammaton).

### CHAPTER X

->*That the Messiah is the name of God, the Tetragrammaton.*<-

### CAPNIO
<note>Capnio is the scholar-persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Renaissance Hebraist.</note>

<margin>GAL.</margin> What you said last—that the Messiah is the name of God (the Tetragrammaton), or the name of four letters—I would like you to prove now by the authority of Divine Scripture, according to the expositions of the ancient Talmudists. That the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, is the Messiah himself is most evidently shown by what is said in the twenty-eighth chapter of Isaiah: <note>original Hebrew: ביום ההוא יהיה יהוה צבאות לעטרת צבי ולצפירת תפארה לשאר עמו</note> "In that day shall the Lord (Tetragrammaton) of hosts be for a crown of joy," or honor, or beauty, "and for a garland of ornament," or exultation, "for the remnant of his people." For Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, translating these words into the Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldæum"</note>, explained them thus: <note>original Aramaic: בעדנא ההיא יהי משיחא דיי צבאות לכלול דחדוה ולכתרא דתושבחתא לשארה דעמיה</note> "In that time the Messiah of the Lord (Tetragrammaton) of hosts shall be for a crown of joy, and for a garland of exultation," or praise, "for the remnant of his people." Where Isaiah placed the name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, there Rabbi Jonathan translated "Messiah" <note>original Aramaic: משיחא, *messiha*</note>. Therefore, it is clear that the Messiah is the name of God, the Tetragrammaton. Also in the *Bereshit Rabbati*—that is, in the abbreviated exposition on Genesis—concerning that verse in Genesis chapter 49: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah..."

<column-break/>

"...and a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes" <note>original Hebrew: עד כי יבא שילה</note>—that is, the Messiah; so it is said: These are those sitting <note>original Hebrew: יושבי, *yoshevei*</note> in Jabez, teaching the <term>halachoth<gloss>Jewish religious laws or legal rulings</gloss></term>—that is, the judicial sentences—in the Great Sanhedrin, which sits in the <term>Lishkat HaGazit<gloss>The 'Chamber of Hewn Stone' in the Temple where the high court met</gloss></term>—that is, in the carved consistory in the portion of Judah. Regarding them it was said in the first book of Chronicles, chapter two: "And the families of the scribes sitting in Jabez": until Shiloh comes, that is, the Messiah. For it shall come to pass that the nations of the world shall bring a gift to the Messiah, the son of David, just as it was said in the eighteenth chapter of Isaiah: "In 그 time a gift shall be brought to the Lord (Tetragrammaton) of hosts." Thus far the aforementioned *Bereshit*. Since, therefore, the gift which Isaiah predicted was to be brought to God by the written name of the Tetragrammaton, and this tradition explained that it would be offered to the Messiah, the son of David, it follows plainly from this that the Messiah himself is the name of God, the Tetragrammaton: which was to be proved.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, this same point is best proven by that passage in the eighth chapter of Isaiah, saying: "Sanctify the Lord (Tetragrammaton) of hosts himself. And let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctification," or preparation, "and for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of ruin to both houses of Israel, for a snare and a trap to the inhabitant of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken. Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples. And I will wait for God, who hides his face from the house," or family, "of Jacob: and I will hope in him." Regarding these very words, the sons of Rabbi Hiyya said thus (as read in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter beginning "One of the civil judgments"): "The son of David," that is, the Messiah, "shall not come until the two houses of the fathers in Israel are finished," or destroyed, "which are the Head of the Captivity in Babylon, and the <term>Nasi<gloss>Prince or President of the Sanhedrin</term></term>—that is, the prince who is in the land of Israel: as it is said in Isaiah chapter 8, 'And he shall be for a sanctification, and for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of ruin to both houses of Israel.'" If, therefore, this tradition asserts that those words of Isaiah—"Sanctify the Lord (Tetragrammaton) of hosts himself"—along with the rest, are to be understood as referring to the Messiah, whom the Jews call the son of David, and where Rabbi Solomon also places the Savior of Israel, it is certainly a consequence that the Messiah himself is the name of God (the Tetragrammaton), and the true God and Savior of Israel, since this name Tetragrammaton can belong to no pure creature. Indeed, regarding that name, we read in Exodus chapter 6 that God spoke thus to Moses: "And God spoke to Moses, and said to him: I am the Lord (Tetragrammaton). And I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God <note>original Hebrew: שדי, *Shaddai*</note>—that is, Almighty—but by my name the Lord (Tetragrammaton) I was not known to them."

[made known] to them. <note>This completes a sentence from the previous page regarding God's revelation to the patriarchs.</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "I did not make myself known to them," it refers specifically to the true essence which is in me. ### CHAPTER XI

->That the four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton, belongs to the Messiah according to his whole being.<-

### CAPNIO

You have most excellently proved that the Messiah was to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton), that he is that very name, and that the same name belongs to him according to his divinity. However, because the Messiah is nothing other than a composite of the person of the Son of God and both natures joined together, I would now like to know from you whether this name, the Tetragrammaton, belongs to the Messiah according to his whole being. That is, does it apply to both natures—I mean the divine and the human—which are sustained by the one person of the Messiah himself, as well as to the three substances which the one and same Messiah contains within himself united without confusion: namely, the Word of God, the rational soul, and the human body? GALATINUS: Precisely so. For just as <margin>What the letters of the four-letter name of God signify.</margin> the three letters of this name—the first ones, namely *yod*, *he*, and *vav* <note>original: י , ה , ו</note>—designate by their diversity (which they have both in shape and in name) that there are three *middoth* <note>A Hebrew term meaning "measures" or "attributes," here used to refer to the Persons of the Trinity.</note> in God, that is, properties or persons distinct from one another; and yet one of them, namely *he*, which is at the end of the name and also at the beginning and end of the name *Havayah* <note>original: הויה, meaning "Being" or "Essence."</note> (which is the same as essence), indicates that the three divine persons are one essence—wherefore there are not three Gods, but one God, as was shown most extensively above—so too it can be said, not inappropriately, that because there are three letters in this name that differ from one another in sound and shape (namely *yod*, *he*, and *vav*), and then one of them (the *he*) is placed again at the end of the name to complete and perfect it, it is clearly implied that when the name is spoken of the Messiah, the three distinct substances in him—the human body, the rational soul, and the divinity itself—are so joined and united to one another that although the first two are united to the third, there are not two persons in the Messiah (God and man), but only one; nor are there two Messiahs, but only one. For just as the three different letters mentioned above produce one glorious name of God, so these three—body, soul, and the Word of God—make one Messiah or Christ. For although there are two natures in Christ—one of which is divine, by which he is of the same substance as the Father, co-eternal, and equal in all things except for his being begotten; and the other human, by which he is of the same substance as his mother and entirely similar in nature—nonetheless, the person in him is only one, which is divine

<column-break/>

and sustains both natures. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and philosopher.</note> most excellently testifies to and explains this in his book *On Different Questions*, saying in the third chapter: <note>original Greek: ἡ ἁγία καθολικὴ καὶ ἀποστολικὴ ἐκκλησία ὅτι ἢ κύριον ἡμῶν ἰησοῦν χριστὸν, μίαν ὑπόστασιν δογματίζει, καὶ δύο φύσεις, ὑπόστασιν, τὸν σαρκωθέντα υἱὸν, φύσεις δὲ, θεότητά καὶ ἀνθρωπότητα...</note> "The holy Catholic and Apostolic Church teaches that in our Lord Jesus Christ there is one *hypostasis* and two natures: the *hypostasis* <note>A theological term for "person" or "individual underlying reality."</note> is the incarnate Son; the natures are the divinity and the humanity. The body, animate and intellectual, which he assumed, it does not call a *hypostasis*, lest there be found, I say, two *hypostases* (which the heretic Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop whose views led to the belief that Christ was two separate persons, one divine and one human.</note> falsely claimed); but it calls it *enypostaton* <note>A term meaning "subsisting in," used to describe how the human nature of Christ exists within the person of the Divine Word rather than as its own separate person.</note> as receiving its being in the *hypostasis* of the Son. For the Son of God himself, being one *hypostasis* of the holy Trinity, became the *hypostasis* for the body he assumed. Therefore, the body of the Lord is indeed *enypostaton*, but not a separate *hypostasis*." And just as the four-letter name of God, when spoken of God, is explained by the twelve-letter name of God, which is <note>original Hebrew: אב בן ורוח הקדש</note> Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so the same name, when spoken of the Messiah, is also explained by a name of twelve letters, which is <note>original Hebrew: גוף נפש ובן אל</note> Body, Soul, and Son of God. For "Body" (*Guph*) is written by them with three letters; "Soul" (*Neshamah*) with four; and "and Son of God" (*v'Ben El*) with five. All these together are twelve in number. And just as the name of twelve letters, when spoken of God, is explained by a name of forty-two letters—which according to *Rabbenu Haccados* <note>Judah the Prince (c. 135–217 AD), the chief redactor of the Mishnah.</note> is <note>original Hebrew: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקודש אלהים שלשה באחד אחד בשלשה</note> Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God, three in one, and one in three (or three in unity and unity in trinity); or according to others <note>original Hebrew: אב אל בן אל ורוח הקדש אל אבל לא אלוה אלא אלהים כי אם אלוה אחד</note> Father God, Son God, and Holy Spirit God, yet not three Gods, but one God (the letters of which in Hebrew are forty-two in number in both versions)—so when it is spoken of the Messiah, it is likewise explained by a name of forty-two letters, which is: <note>original Hebrew: כאשר הנפש המשכלת והבשר אדם אחד כך האל והאדם משיח אחד</note> Just as the rational soul and the flesh are one man, so God and man are one Messiah. These letters in Hebrew are indeed forty-two. For *Caa-asher* (just as) is written with four letters; *Hanne-phes* (the soul) likewise with four; *Hammaschleth* (rational) with six; *Vehabafar* (and the flesh) with five; *Adam* (man) with three; *Ehad* (one) likewise with three; *Cach* (so) with two; *Hael* (God) with three; and *Veha-adam* (and man)...
