### CHAPTER XII

->*That the Messiah is the Face of God.*<-

#### CAPNIO

Now you must speak regarding the remaining names of the Messiah that suggest his divinity. GALATINUS: First, therefore, I shall show that the Messiah is called the "Face of God." This is most clearly evident through that passage of Malachi, where he says in the third chapter: <note>original Hebrew: "הנני שולח מלאכי..."</note> "Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom you delight in. Behold, he shall come, says the Lord of hosts. But who may abide the day of his coming? And who shall stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap." <note>Malachi 3:1–2.</note> Fullers' soap is that which laundrymen use to wash cloths, which in Arabic is called *gazul*.

That this prophecy speaks of the Messiah is clearly shown by Rabbi Moses, the son of Maimon, <note>Known as Maimonides or Rambam (1138–1204).</note> in the *Hilchoth Melachim* [Laws of Kings], that is, in the "Decisions of the Kings," where he says: "In the days of the King Messiah, through the Holy Spirit which shall rest upon him, the genealogy of Israel shall be declared through his mouth, as it is said in Malachi chapter 3: 'Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face.'" Therefore, the younger Jews cannot possibly deny that the aforementioned words of Malachi were spoken concerning the Messiah. This "messenger" of whom the Prophet first speaks was John the Baptist, who was sent by God so that he might prepare the way for the Face of God—that is, the Messiah. 

Furthermore, that the Messiah is the "Face of God" is held by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher and commentator from Narbonne.</note> upon that passage in Genesis chapter 22: "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes," where he says: "This is what is written in Hosea chapter 6: 'After two days he will revive us, and on the third day he will raise us up (or lift us up), and we shall live before his face. And we shall know, if we follow on to know the Lord.'" Afterwards he adds: "'He will revive us after two days, and we shall live before his face,' which is the King Messiah, as it is said in Psalm 80: 'O Lord God of hosts, convert us, and show us your face'—that is, your Messiah—'and we shall be saved.'" And this is: "On the 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> third day he will revive us." This is the tradition. Moreover, concerning this Face of God, it is said in the *Bereßith ketanna* [Little Genesis], that is, in the small exposition of Genesis: where, regarding that passage in Genesis chapter 3, "And the Lord God sent him out of the garden (or paradise) of pleasure," Rabbi Nahmija says: "Adam was sent out of paradise in this world, but in the world to come he shall not be sent out." Such a saying is supported by what is written in Psalm 17: "I will behold your face in righteousness (or through justice); I shall be satisfied when your *Temunathecha* [form] shall arise"—that is, your form, or your figure, or your image, or your likeness. The Holy and Blessed God said: "In 그 hour I will justify him"—namely Adam—"from that sentence." David said to the Holy and Blessed God: "And in that hour in which he shall awaken, he who is in your likeness shall rise again; I shall be satisfied, and in righteousness I will behold your face, that is, your Messiah." 

In the Glosses of Rabbi Solomon [Rashi], on "I will behold your face," it says: "As it is said in Isaiah chapter 52: 'For they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall dwell in Zion.'" This, Jonathan translated into Aramaic as: <note>original: "ארי בעיניהון יחזון..."</note> "For with their eyes they shall see the power (or strength) which God shall work when his Divinity [Shekhinah] shall sit or dwell in Zion." From these things, therefore, it is manifest that the Messiah is both said to be and is the Face of God. And this is only because of his divinity, on account of which all names that are spoken of God fit him most appropriately.

### CHAPTER XIII

->*That the Messiah is the Light which is God.*<-

#### CAPNIO

If all names attributed to God are most rightly spoken of the Messiah (as you say) because of his divinity, it certainly follows that just as God is called "Light" by essence, so also the Messiah himself should be called "Light" by essence. Therefore, I pray you, would you also be willing to prove that? 

GALATINUS: That God is therefore illumination, or light, and the Messiah is light with God before the constitution of the world, is best proved by what is written in the *Midras tillim* [Midrash on the Psalms]. For there, upon that passage of Psalm 36: <note>original: "כי עמך מקור חיים..."</note> "For with you is the fountain of life: in your light shall we see light. Continue your lovingkindness to those who know you," Rabbi Yohanan said: "An event happened to a certain man, that when he lit a lamp in the night, it was extinguished; and when he had lit it again and again, he said: 'How long shall I labor in my walking? I will wait until the sun rises.' So Israel, when they had been made slaves in Egypt, Moses and Aaron stood up and redeemed them. Again they were reduced to slavery in the days of Sisera, and Barak and Deborah redeemed them. Then from the Midianites, Gideon [redeemed them]. And so by the hand of Shamgar. Thus also by the hand of each of the Judges they were redeemed from slavery...

### BOOK THREE

They were made servants again in Babylonia, and were redeemed through the hands of Ananias, Misael, and Azarias. <note>These are the Hebrew names of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel.</note> And finally, they were led back into servitude through Edom. <note>In medieval Jewish-Christian polemics, "Edom" was frequently used as a coded term for Rome or the Christian Church.</note> Therefore, Israel said: "Behold, we are exhausted by subjections and redemptions; now subjugated, now redeemed. We no longer seek for flesh and blood to shine upon us, but for the Holy and Blessed God Himself in His very substance." This is as it is said in the hundred and eighth Psalm: "God is the Lord, and he has shone (or will shine) upon us." <note>Psalm 118:27; the author cites it as Psalm 108 following the Vulgate numbering.</note> And again, Isaiah says in the forty-fifth chapter: "Israel shall be saved in God (or by God, the Tetragrammaton) with an eternal salvation." Thus far the tradition. The Commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "Israel shall be saved with an eternal salvation through the King Messiah." In the *Great Lamentations* <note>original: "Echa rabbethi," a Midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition upon the lament of Jeremiah, concerning that passage in the first chapter of Lamentations, "The comforter who should restore my soul is far from me," it is asked: "What is the name of the Messiah?" Those of the house of Rabbi Hanina said, "Mercy <note>original: "חנינא Hanina"</note>—that is, piety or mercy—is his name," as it is said in Jeremiah, chapter 16: "Therefore I will show you no mercy <note>original: "חנינא Hanina"</note>." But those of the house of Rabbi Jannai said, "Yinnon <note>original: "ינון Iinnon"</note>—that is, son, or begotten, or born—is his name," as it is said in the seventy-second Psalm: "His name shall be Yinnon <note>original: "ינון Iinnon"</note> before the sun." However, Rabbi Bibba said, "Light <note>original: "נהירא Nehira"</note>—that is, illumination—is his name," as it is said in the second chapter of Daniel: "And the light is with him." Moreover, it is written in the *Lesser Great Genesis* <note>original: "Bereshith rabbat ketanna," likely referring to a specific Midrashic compilation.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of Genesis regarding that passage in the first chapter of Genesis, "Let there be light," in this way: "This is what was said in Psalm 97: 'Light is sown (or has arisen) for the righteous.'" Furthermore, Rabbi Abba said: "This light is the light of the King Messiah," according to that passage of Psalm 36: "For with thee is the fountain of life, and in thy light we shall see light." This is the light of the Messiah, which he mentions because the Holy and Blessed God saw the Messiah and his generation, and preserved him under the throne of His glory. This is the tradition. From which it is greatly to be noted that before the Messiah existed according to his humanity, he already existed according to his divinity as light and illumination with God, and as the principle by which God created the world. With these things the saying of our Lord is most in harmony: "Before Abraham was, I am." And: "I have come as a light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in darkness," John 13. <note>The author likely intended John 12:46.</note> See how worthy these things are against the Jews of our time, who, denying the divinity of the Messiah, assert that he must be born only from the seed of man. To them it must be said: That light placed under the throne of God is the Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of the Father, and His throne and power.

### CHAPTER XV

->That the name of God *Shaddai* <note>original: "שדי Saddai"</note> properly belongs to the Messiah.<-

### CAPNIO

<margin>A</margin> I remember hearing, when you were discussing the divine names earlier, that the name *Shaddai* <note>original: "שדי Saddai"</note> belongs to God alone. For because this name is interpreted as "Almighty," or "He who is sufficient," and God alone is almighty and alone sufficient unto Himself—needing no other—therefore this name *Shaddai* belongs to Him alone. Even if I do not doubt in the least that all names said of God are likewise most aptly said of the Messiah according to his divinity, I would nevertheless wish, for a greater manifestation of the Messiah's divinity, that you would give the reason why this name *Shaddai* properly fits the Messiah himself, and prove through Hebrew testimonies that it properly belongs to him. GALATINUS: If, therefore, you wish to hear why this divine name *Shaddai*—which (as we have said elsewhere) is the same as "He who is sufficient" <note>original: "אשר די asser dai"</note>, that is, He who suffices, or He who is sufficient, or He who is sufficiency—is properly fitting to the Messiah alone, hear holy Job speaking thus in the 33rd chapter: "The Spirit of God made me, and the soul of the Sufficient One [*Shaddai*] gave me life." <note>original: "שדי תחיני רוח אל עשני ונשמת," Job 33:4.</note> He says, "The soul of *Shaddai*," that is, of Him who suffices or who is sufficiency. Since, therefore, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit has a soul, but only the Son of God—who is the power and wisdom of the Father, and who has that soul which He united to Himself in the Messiah—it clearly follows that Job was speaking of the Son of God alone when he said: "And the soul of *Shaddai* shall give life" (for "has given me life"); namely, the soul of him who alone is enough to redeem and save the human race. For he alone, being in the form of God, was the one who, by assuming human nature, was to come not to be served, but to serve, and to give his soul as a redemption for many, as he himself said in Matthew 20, according to that passage of Isaiah 53: "He exposed (or poured out) his soul unto death." <note>original: "הערה למות נפשו"</note> Also, that saying in the first chapter of the Song of Songs properly fits the Messiah as God and the Son of God, and not God the Father nor the Holy Spirit: "Tell me, you whom my soul loves," meaning the people or the nation (as the ancient Talmudists explain) for whom "I gave my soul" <note>original: "נפשי naphsci"</note>. For it was fitting that what is read in the book *Yoma* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement.</note> should happen, in the chapter that begins *Tereph*, where it is said word for word: "It is a tradition from the house of Rabbi Ishmael that thus is the measure of judgment walking: for it is expedient that the innocent come and satisfy for the guilty, and not that the guilty come to satisfy for the guilty." This is the tradition. and a most excellent one. For hands that hold mud cannot wipe away filth, and when he who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry one is provoked to worse. From these things that have been said, it is (as I think) sufficiently manifest that the name *Shaddai* properly belongs to the Messiah alone, who alone was sufficient to redeem the human race. Concerning whom it is written in Psalm 91: "He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide (or lodge) in the shadow of *Shaddai*." <note>original: "יושב בסתר עליון בצל שדי יתלונן"</note> These words can indeed be most aptly explained: "He who is dwelling shall be in a secret place" (that is, in his most sacred body), the "Most High" (that is, the Son of God); "In the shadow" (that is, in the womb of the most blessed and purest Virgin), "*Shaddai*" (that is, he who alone suffices to satisfy for the human race) "shall lodge" (that is, he shall stay for only nine months).

### CHAPTER XV.

#### That the name of the Messiah, *Yinnon*, fits him according to his divinity.

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>Psalm 72</margin>
Since one of the specific names of the Messiah is *Yinnon* <note>original: "ינון iinnon"</note> according to that verse: *Before the sun, his name shall be Yinnon* <note>original: "לפני שמש ינון שמו lipne schemesch iinnon schemo"</note>—that is, "His name shall endure forever; his name was *Yinnon* before the sun"—I would like to know from you in what way or by what reasoning this name fits the Messiah. GALATINUS. This name *Yinnon* is derived from the Hebrew word *nin* <note>original: "נין nin"</note>, which is the same as "son," or "one born," or "one begotten." For that reason, this name specifically belongs to the Messiah alone, who, according to his divinity, was alone born or begotten by the eternal Father "before the sun"—that is, before the condition of the world, or from eternity. For since *Yinnon* (as we have said) is interpreted as "son" or "one born" or "one begotten," it cannot fit the Father in divine matters, nor the Holy Spirit. For the Father was made by no one, nor created, nor begotten, nor proceeding; and the Holy Spirit is neither born nor begotten, but is breathed and proceeds from the Father and the Son as from a single principle. Nor can this name fit any creature. For no creature was born or produced "before the sun," that is, before the ages. Therefore it is clearly evident that the saying of the Psalmist brought forward by you—"before the sun his name was *Yinnon*"—cannot be said of any created thing, but only of the Son of God, who was eternally born of the eternal Father; thus it happens that this name *Yinnon* can apply to no one but the Messiah alone. Furthermore, this name *Yinnon* is translated into our language as "he will act as a son" or "he will cause to be born," which is not without its own mystery regarding the Messiah. For he himself, as if making them sons again, will cause all the dead to be born when he raises them from the dust of the earth. This fits him specifically according to his divinity. For how could he raise all the dead from the dust of the earth if he were not the true Son of God? Moreover, that the Messiah was called *Yinnon* "before the sun" for this reason is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrash (rabbinic commentary) on the Psalms.</note> upon that verse of Psalm 93: *Your throne is prepared from of old; you are from everlasting.* <note>original: "נכון כסאך מאז מעולם אתה"</note> Where it is said: "The King Messiah is one of the seven things that ascended into [God’s] thought before the creation of the age, as it is said in Psalm 72: 'Before <margin>Opposition.</margin> the sun, his name was *Yinnon*.'" Because it is destined that he himself *yannin* <note>original: "ינין iannin"</note>—that is, will cause all those sleeping in the dust to be born again. This is the tradition. CAPNIO. The Jews of our age, being the worst of all, and desiring to entirely suppress the divinity of the Messiah, say that we cannot call the Messiah the Son of God begotten from eternity just because his name was *Yinnon* before the sun, since seven things (as they say) were created two thousand years before the constitution of the world. They gather the folly of this fiction from what is held in the book *Pesah Sheni* <note>original: "פסח שני"; referring to a section of the Talmudic tractate Pesachim, meaning "The Second Passover."</note>, that is, the "Second Passover," in the *Perek* <note>chapter</note> in which it is read: "It is handed down that seven things were created before the wor-

<column-break/>

ld was created: These are the Law, repentance, Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, the house of the sanctuary [the Temple], the throne of glory, the garden of pleasure [Eden], and the name of the Messiah." The same thing is also held in the *Midrash Bemidbar Sinai*, that is, in the Gloss on the book of Numbers, chapter 7. GALATINUS. It is no wonder if, having been deservedly struck by God with <margin>Refutations.</margin> insanity and blindness, they speak such foolish and absurd things. For who would consider this fiction to be anything but the speech of those utterly lacking in reason? For although any number, or any multitude of parts of motion according to "before" and "after," constitutes time, regardless of what the motion is: nevertheless, the hour, day, month, and year—and even spring, summer, autumn, and winter, which are parts of the year—it is impossible that these are not parts of the motion of the heavens. How then did such a great multitude of years, specifically two thousand, precede the world? And in what way were there parts of a year, when there was neither motion of the heaven, nor the heaven itself at all? How also can they believe that the Law—which commands that a tooth be punished for a tooth, an eye for an eye, a hand for a hand—was created before the condition of the world, when there was as yet no tooth, nor eye, nor hand? This can also be said of all judicial matters. The Law also mandates the keeping of the Sabbath, and the performance of sacrifices and circumcision: things which neither existed before the constitution of the world, nor was there anyone existing upon whom such things could be enjoined. A similar response can be given concerning the rest of the ceremonial laws. Furthermore, the Law commands not to kill, not to steal, not to commit adultery: how then can it be maintained that this Law was established before the creation of men and the world, when there was neither anyone to act nor anyone to suffer these things? This can also be said of the rest of the moral laws. How, moreover, can they say that repentance, which naturally follows sin, preceded sin itself and sinners? And by what reasoning do they assert Gehenna was created before the world, when they have their own Talmud openly against them, even in that very book which they allege for themselves? Let them read, therefore, the same book *Pesah*, the chapter that begins *Macom* <note>Referring to the chapter "Makom she-nahagu" in the tractate Pesachim.</note>. For there Rabbi Jose is said to have spoken thus: "The fire which the Holy and Blessed God created on the second of the Sabbath <note>Monday</note> shall not be extinguished forever: as it is said in the last of Isaiah, 'And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who rebelled against me: for their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished. And they shall be an object of loathing to all flesh.'" There is also a tradition that Rabbi Babas <note>original: "בבא Baua"; likely referring to a Sage in the Talmud.</note> said: "Why was it not said on the second of the Sabbath, 'And God saw that it was good'? For this reason: because on that day the fire of Gehenna was created." All these things are there. Where we have two witnesses of the greatest authority among them, that the fire of Gehenna was created on the second day of the creation of the world. Since, therefore, it is written in the nineteenth chapter of Deuteronomy: *By the mouth of two witnesses, or by the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established* <note>original: "על פי שני עדים או על פי שלשה עדים יקום דבר"</note>, they must concede that these masters spoke the truth. From the truth of this matter, it clearly follows that it is entirely false that the fire of Gehenna was produced before the creation of the world. Furthermore, the Temple, which was made by hand and from created things...

Galatinus refutes the literal Jewish interpretation of 'seven things created before the world,' using logic to show that time, law, and punishment cannot exist without a physical universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section regarding the pre-existence of the Messiah's name. It refutes a literal physical existence before Adam, clarifying that the Messiah's "pre-existence" refers to his eternal divine nature as the Son of God.</meta>

...constructed, how could it exist before the very things of which it consisted? Finally, he who was born from the seed of Adam, how could he have been created before Adam? What greater madness can there be, then, than to believe such things, let alone to say them? They grope, therefore, like the blind for a wall, according to that passage in Isaiah, the fifty-ninth chapter, speaking in their person: <note>original: "נגששה כעורים קיר וכאין עינים נגששה nagshshah cha-ivrim qir u-che-ein einayim nagshshah"</note> This means: *We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes.* <note>Isaiah 59:10</note> Therefore, the name of the Messiah is not said to exist before the ages in order to suggest that he was created then—since before the ages nothing at all was created—but so that the Messiah himself might be shown to be begotten by the Father from eternity according to his divinity. And for this reason the Prophet said, *Before the sun, Yinnon was his name* <note>original: "ינון innon"</note>; for *Yinnon* (as we said before) signifies both "one who is born" and "one who causes to be born." Thus, two things are hinted at in this one word: namely, the eternal birth of the Messiah, by which he was eternally born of the Father, and the resurrection of the dead, whom he himself will raise at the end of the world, making them, as it were, to be born anew.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*That the Messiah in Holy Scripture is frequently called the "Sprout," to signify that it was more fitting for the Son to be incarnated than the Father or the Holy Spirit.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

Among the other names of the Messiah, I find him very often called the "Sprout" <note>Latin: *Germen*; Hebrew: *Tsemach*</note>, especially in Zechariah, when he says in the sixth chapter: <note>original: "הנה איש צמח שמו Hineh ish Tsemach shemo"</note> That is, *Behold the man, the Sprout is his name.* <note>Zechariah 6:12</note> I would therefore like to hear the reason why the Prophets thought he should be called by this name. GALATINUS. Truly, the Messiah is called the "Sprout" for good reason. In this, it is openly shown that the divine incarnation and the assumption of human nature were fitting for the person of the Son of God, and not for the person of the Father or the Holy Spirit. Thus, he would not be the "Son" of Adam, Abraham, and David in his humanity unless that <term>midda<gloss>attribute or property</gloss></term>—that is, the person or property—which was the "Son" in the divinity, was the same. Otherwise, there would be one Son in humanity and another in divinity. Isaiah and Jeremiah, according to the *Targum* <note>The Aramaic paraphrase/translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>—that is, according to the Chaldean translation—most evidently suggest that this was to be fulfilled in the single person of the Messiah. For Isaiah says in the fourth chapter: <note>original: "ביום ההוא יהיה צמח יהוה לצבי ולכבוד ופרי הארץ לגאון ולתפארת לפליטת ישראל"</note> That is, *In that day the Sprout of God shall be for beauty (or joy) and for glory (or honor); and the fruit of the earth for loftiness (or nobility) and for ornament to the remnants of Israel.* <note>Isaiah 4:2</note> Where the Targum says: <note>original: "בעירנא ההיא יהי משיחא דיי לחדוא וליקר"</note> This means: *In that time the Messiah of God shall be for joy and honor.* Jeremiah likewise says: <note>original: "והקמתי לדוד צמח צדקה"</note> That is, *In those days and at that time, I will cause a Sprout of righteousness to bud for David.* <note>Jeremiah 33:15</note> Where the Targum also says: *In those days and at that time, I will raise up for David a Messiah*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *of righteousness.* Since, therefore, wherever each Prophet says "Sprout," the Targum places "Messiah," it is openly given to all to understand (provided they do not have the eyes of their heart blinded by the fog of error) that just as the Messiah was truly the "Sprout of God"—that is, the Son of God according to his divinity, as Isaiah says—so he was to be the "Sprout of David"—that is, the Son of David according to his humanity, as Jeremiah says. From these two, it <margin>B</margin> clearly results that the Messiah is, in the unity of his person, both the Son of God and the Son of David at the same time, though in different ways. For he is the Son of God before all time, but in time he is the Son of David. He is also the Son of God immediately and without a mother; but the Son of David after many intermediaries of both the just and the unjust, from a mother alone without a father. Indeed, Jeremiah indicates this clearly enough through the name "Sprout" and the verb "to sprout." Isaiah also shows the same in the aforementioned words, when he first says "Sprout of God" and soon after <margin>C</margin> adds "fruit of the earth." For who is this fruit of the earth, if not the Messiah born of the Virgin? Regarding whom it is written in the sixty-seventh Psalm: <note>original: "יודוך עמים אלהים יודוך עמים כלם ארץ נתנה יבולה"</note> That is, *Let the peoples praise you, O God, let all the peoples praise you; the earth has given its fruit.* <note>Psalm 67:6, or 66:7 in some numbering</note> Concerning this most blessed incarnation of the Son of God, it is also said in the eighty-fifth Psalm: *Truth shall sprout from the earth, and righteousness shall look down (or be extended) from heaven.* <note>Psalm 85:11</note> For when it is said, "Truth shall sprout from the earth," "Truth" is taken to mean the Son of God, who, like a sprout from the earth—that is, from the most pure Virgin—was to be born through the assumption of flesh. Furthermore, that the Messiah is the "Sprout" is held by what is read in the *Echarabbethi* <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a traditional Jewish commentary</note>—that is, in the exposition upon the Lamentations of Jeremiah—regarding what is said in the first chapter of Lamentations: *Because the comforter, who should restore my soul, is far from me.* For it is said there: *What is the name of the Messiah?* <margin>E</margin> Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: <note>original: "צמח tsemach"</note> *Tsemach*—that is, "Sprout"—is his name; as it was said in the sixth chapter of Zechariah, *Behold the man, the Sprout is his name.* Also, in the book which they call *Tanhuma* <note>A collection of homiletic midrashim</note>—which is for the most part an exposition of the book of Numbers—regarding what is said in the first chapter of Numbers, *And the Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai,* it is said: *What did he say to him?* That which is written in the first chapter of Numbers: <margin>F</margin> *Take a census (lift the head) of all the congregation of the children of Israel.* The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: *Because of this I have given you the lifting of the head (or suspension).* For just as I am suspended over the whole world—as it is said in the last chapter of the first book of Chronicles: *Yours, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory (or eternity), and yours is the praise (or confession); for all that is in heaven and in earth is yours, O Lord, the Kingdom is yours, and you lift yourself up as Head over all*—so also have I given to you the lifting of the head, as it is <margin>G</margin> said in the first chapter of Numbers: *Lift the head.* This is so that what was said in the 147th Psalm might be fulfilled: *And he has exalted the horn of his people.* And thus he himself says in the first chapter of Numbers: *A man who is the head of the house of his fathers*—namely, God himself.

<summary>This page discusses why the Messiah is referred to as the "Sprout" (Tsemach) in prophecy, arguing that this title perfectly encapsulates his dual nature as the eternal Son of God and the human Son of David. It draws on Aramaic Targums and Rabbinic midrashim like Lamentations Rabbah to support the claim that the Son, rather than the Father, was the person of the Trinity destined for incarnation.</summary>

Rabbi Rahmon said: "The 'Man of God' in this place is none other than the Messiah, the son of David, of whom it was said in the sixth chapter of Zechariah: *Behold the man whose name is the Sprout.* <note>Zechariah 6:12; original Latin: "Ecce vir Germen nomen eius."</note> Jonathan translated this as: *Behold the man whose name is the Messiah.* Of him, Isaiah also says in the fifty-third chapter: *A man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity,* or *known by infirmity.*" <note>Isaiah 53:3; original Latin: "Vir dolorum & sciens infirmitatem."</note> Thus ends the tradition. From this, our proposition is clear.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->*That the Messiah is called "Dew," to signify the descent of the Son of God into the womb of the virgin.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> Since you have already begun to speak of the incarnation of the Son of God, you should now speak of the names of the Messiah that suggest this divine incarnation.

GALATINUS. I will gladly do as you urge. First, I will prove that it is quite fitting for the Messiah himself to be called "Dew" <note>Latin: *Ros*</note> to designate his descent into the virgin's womb according to his divinity. We find that the Messiah is called Dew in many places, and especially in Hosea, where God Himself speaks through his mouth in the 14th chapter: <note>original Hebrew: "אהיה כטל לישראל יפרח כשושנה ehyeh ka-tal le-yisra'el yifrach ka-shoshannah"</note> This means: *I will be as the dew to Israel, and he shall sprout (or blossom) like the lily.* <note>Hosea 14:5</note> Jonathan, <term>son of Uzziel</term> <note>The traditional author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets.</note>, translating this into Aramaic, explained it thus: <note>original Aramaic: "אהי ממרי כטלא לישראל יזהרון כשושניא ehi memri ke-tala le-yisra'el yizharun ke-shoshanya"</note> That is: *My Word shall be like the dew to Israel, and they shall be beautiful as the lily.* That the "Dew" in this passage refers to the Messiah is clearly shown in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note> when discussing the title of Psalm 45, which is: <note>original Hebrew: "למנצח על שושנים la-menatzeach al shoshannim"</note> This means: *To the Victor (or To the victory) upon the lilies.* It is said there: "The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: Everything depends on you. For just as this lily sprouts or blossoms and yet its heart is turned upward, so you too should perform <term>teshuva</term> <note>Hebrew: "תשובה," meaning repentance or return to God.</note> before me, and let your heart be right, or directed upward, like the heart of such a lily. And then I will bring the <term>Goel</term> <note>Hebrew: "גואל," meaning the Redeemer.</note>, that is, the redeemer; as it was said in the 14th chapter of Hosea: *I will be as the dew to Israel.* And when? *When he shall sprout or blossom like the lily.* And for this reason it is said: *To the Victor upon the lilies.*" Thus far the tradition. From this, it is clearly evident that the "dew" in the aforementioned words of Hosea is the Messiah, and that the Messiah is the Word of God, as Rabbi Jonathan explains in the Targum; and also that he is God, as the speech of the Prophet himself suggests, speaking in the person of God concerning the same dew: *I will be as the dew to Israel.* Regarding this dew, we also read in the book <term>Taanith</term> <note>Hebrew: "תענית," a Talmudic tractate regarding fasts.</note>: "Rabbi Berachiah said: The Assembly of Israel asked indiscreetly when it said in the 6th chapter of Hosea: *And let him come to us like the rain, like the early and late rain to the earth.* The Holy and Blessed God said to her: My daughter, you ask for a thing that is sometimes sought and sometimes not sought; but I will be for you a thing that is always sought, as it is written in the fourteenth chapter of Hosea: *I will be as the dew to Israel, and he shall sprout or blossom as the lily.*"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the same dew, David says in the 110th Psalm (according to the Hebrew): <note>original Hebrew: "מרחם משחר לך טל ילדותך mirrechem mishchar lach tal yaldutcha"</note> That is: *From the womb of the dawn (or from the aurora), you have the dew of your birth.* That "dawn" here is most fittingly understood as the mother of the Messiah, we shall discuss elsewhere when we deal with the Messiah’s new manner of being born. For now, it suffices to prove this through what Rabbi Isaac Arama says in his commentaries on the book of Genesis, when in the exposition of chapter 47 (or thereabouts), where mention is made of the place given to Jacob in which he could comfortably dwell, he says: <note>Isaac Arama quotes Psalm 110 and Psalm 72 in Hebrew.</note> That is: *Help from the dawn is the dew of your birth for you.* We do not find any man, even a prophet, whose birth was prophesied before the birth of his father and mother, except only for our righteous Messiah. And for this reason he says: *Help from the dawn is the dew of your birth for you.* That is: before the womb of your mother was created, your birth was prophesied. And with this agrees that passage: *Before the sun, his name was Yinnon (the son or the begotten).* <note>Psalm 72:17</note> The meaning of which is: that before the sun was created, the name of our Messiah was subsisting and firm, and he sat at the right hand of God. And this is what he says: *Sit at my right hand.* And elsewhere: *He shall prepare the throne in mercy, and he shall sit upon it in truth.* Thus says Arama.

<margin>D</margin> That the "Dew" in this place, proceeding from the womb of the dawn, is the Messiah, we shall prove through what is written in the commentaries of Moses Hadarsan on the book of Genesis. For there, regarding that passage of Genesis, "And Reuben said to them," it is said: "The Redeemer whom I am about to raise up from us shall be without a father." and shortly after it is added: "Of him David also says in Psalm 110: *From the womb of the dawn, you have the dew of your birth.*"

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, the Messiah is not unfittingly called "Dew." First, because of the similarity of his descent. For dew descends from on high, and its descent is hidden from our sight. For it descends by night, and especially in the springtime, and it refreshes and fertilizes the earth. In the same way, the divine power fertilized the most blessed virgin during the night. For just as the oyster, receiving the dew at night and in the springtime, generates within its inner parts the pearl <note>Latin: *margarita*</note>, a most precious gem, so the glorious virgin, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and she conceived the Son of God, generated the Messiah, the precious pearl. Just as the dew, gently spreading itself over the surface of the grass, grants greenness and vigor to the herbs and plants, and that which had withered and been consumed by the daytime heat, the night dew moistens, cherishes, and raises up; so our true Messiah grants greenness and vigor to those who believe in him and persevere in good, and he rules them and raises them up to eternal life. Furthermore, just as the dew collects itself at the tips of the grass and returns to its origin, so the Messiah our redeemer raised himself to the height of the cross, and from there returned to his glory. For these reasons, the Messiah was not incorrectly called "Dew" by the ancient fathers: so that from this, his hidden [nature]... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "occulta" (hidden/secret).</note>

BOOK THREE

<meta>Catchword: says,</meta>

and the incomprehensible incarnation and birth of the Son of God would be designated. For this reason, it is not without cause that in the 45th chapter of Isaiah it is said: <note>Isaiah 45:8; original Hebrew: "הריעו שמים ממעל ושחקים יזלו צדק תפתח ארץ ויפרו ישע וצדקה תצמיח יחד אני יהוה בראתיו hary'u shamayim mi-ma'al ve-shachakim yizlu tzedek tiftach eretz ve-yifru yesha ve-tzedakah tatzmiach yachad ani Adonai berativ"</note> This is: *Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the skies rain down justice; let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let justice spring up likewise. I, the Lord, have created it.* Here, by "heavens," the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are understood. Concerning these, Lucifer, when he was in the empyrean heaven, spoke thus as read in the 14th chapter of Isaiah: <note>Isaiah 14:13; original Hebrew: "אל כוכבי אל ארים כסאי ממעל el kochvei el arim kis'i mi-ma'al"</note> This is: *I will ascend to the heavens, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God:* along with the rest until those words, *And I will be like the Most High.* The "clouds," however, were the prophets; the "Earth" is the blessed Virgin opening her consent; and thus the Holy Spirit and she herself brought forth "salvation," that is, Jesus, whose name is the same as salvation. And she herself sprouted "Justice," that is, the Messiah, who is equally God and man.

### CHAPTER XVIII.
### That the Messiah should be called Emmanuel: and that this name belongs to the Messiah alone.
### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>
Since Isaiah said the Messiah should be called Emmanuel (for so he says in the seventh chapter: <note>Isaiah 7:14; original Hebrew: "הנה העלמה הרה ויולדת בן וקראת שמו עמנו-אל hinneh ha-almah harah ve-yoledet ben ve-karat shemo immanu-el"</note> This is: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she herself shall call his name Emmanuel.*), tell me, I pray, by what reasoning this name fits the Messiah himself. GALATINUS. "Emmanuel" (as you well know) is interpreted in English as "God with us." Therefore, the most blessed Virgin herself, having been forewarned and instructed by the Angel Gabriel, was to call the Messiah himself "Emmanuel," so that from this, the conjunction and union of the divine and human natures in the one person of the Messiah might be clearly demonstrated. For the Messiah was to be both God and man. Therefore, to him alone does this name Emmanuel—which sounds like "God with us" in English—rightly belong. CAPNIO. Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> has: *And his name shall be called Emmanuel.* GALATINUS. That is certainly so. But the Hebrew text says exactly this (as I have translated it): *She herself shall call.* This agrees far better with the truth of our faith. For from the fact that the Prophet said, *She herself shall call his name Emmanuel,* he shows that the Messiah would not have a human father to impose a name upon him. For among the Hebrews, fathers almost always, and not mothers, were accustomed to give names to their sons; as appears in many places in the Old Testament, and is clearly gathered from the birth of John the Baptist. Therefore, from the fact that the Prophet attributed the giving of the name—which pertained to the father—to the mother alone, he clearly wished to intimate that the Messiah would not have a father on earth who could give him a name. This the Angel also seems to have suggested in what he said to Mary: *You shall call his name Jesus.* "You shall call," he said, and not "He shall be called," so that he might openly show himself to be in agreement with the Prophet. Or it can be said another way, and not ineptly indeed, that when the Prophet said, *And she herself shall call his name Emmanuel,* which is "God with us," he clearly suggested through this that

<margin>
This view is refuted in Ravanellus under the word "Name" and in Glassius's *Philologia Sacra*, book 1, tract 3, observation 9.
</margin>

<column-break/>

she alone was meant to know with certainty that the Messiah, her son, was both God and man, since she alone was to call him Emmanuel. For although he was to be called by another name <note>Referring to the name Jesus.</note>, she alone could say of him with certainty, "Emmanuel," that is, "God with us." Therefore, not without reason did he say: *And she herself shall call his name Emmanuel.* It is as if he said openly: *And she shall call him within herself "God with us,"* because she alone could say this with certainty. Luke also seems to suggest this when he says: *But Mary kept all these words, conferring them in her heart.* Therefore, also in her heart, that is, within herself, she was to call him Emmanuel. This is also confirmed by what she said to the servants at the wedding: *Whatever he says to you, do;* as if she were keeping within herself the knowledge that her son was God, who could produce wine from anywhere. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the Hebrew text is more correct for our faith than our own version. CAPNIO. These things are indeed excellently said. For from these, one can easily respond to the perversity of the Jews of our time, who say that the Messiah, the Son of God, was by no means called Emmanuel by his mother, but *Iesuah*, that is, Jesus; from which it happened that he was afterwards called "Jesus" by all Christians (as they assert). Therefore, I would like you to use their own scriptures to convict them of their treachery—those who, attributing these words, *Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel,* to the wife of Isaiah and his son, say that he was called Emmanuel by his mother or by the Holy Spirit. They prove this by the testimony of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, who explains this passage thus: "*Behold the 'almah', that is, my wife, shall conceive this year, which is the fourth of King Ahaz; and she shall bear a son, and she herself—namely the 'almah' or the Holy Spirit (for 'spirit' is of the feminine gender among the Hebrews)—who will be or will descend upon her, shall call his name Emmanuel; as if to say, that our Creator will be with us.*" These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. GALATINUS. Let us grant them that this exposition is true and good, with this one exception: that he says Isaiah here used *almah* for his own wife, and consequently that Isaiah's own son was to be called Emmanuel. That *almah* here must be understood not as Isaiah's wife, but as the mother of the Messiah, we shall prove most extensively in the following sections when it comes time to speak of the virginity of the Messiah's mother. For now, let it be enough for us to show that this Emmanuel was not, nor could have been, the son of Isaiah and his wife. This is first evident from the fact that in the 8th chapter of the same Prophet it is said: <note>Isaiah 8:7-8; original Hebrew: "ולכן הנה אדני מעלה עליכם את מי הנהר העצומים והרבים את מלך אשור ואת כל כבודו... והיה מטות כנפיו מלא רחב ארצך עמנו-אל u-le-chen hinneh Adonai ma'aleh aleichem et mei ha-nahar ha-atzumim ve-ha-rabbim et melech ashur... ve-hayah muttot kenafav melo rochav artzecha immanu-el"</note> *And because of this, behold, the Lord will cause the waters of the river, strong and many, the King of Assyria and his weight (or glory), to rise up over you.* And the rest until: *And the extension of his wings shall be the filling of the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel.* This, however, can by no means apply to the son of Isaiah, because he was a private person and never had any land subject to his own dominion. For this reason, certain others, explaining this prophecy as referring to Hezekiah, the son of King Ahaz, say that he was called Emmanuel. Their opinion is first refuted by Rabbi Solomon himself, who, explaining this passage, speaks thus:

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the prophecy in Isaiah 7:14. It moves from the identification of the Virgin to the specific name and nature of the child, Emmanuel.</meta>

BOOK THREE

<sig>G ii</sig>
<meta>catchword: state</meta>

it says, *And she shall call his name Emmanuel.* There are some who explain this as being said of Hezekiah. But this is not possible. For if you number his years, you will find that he was born nine years before his father's reign. This is what Rabbi Solomon <note>R. Selomo refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> says, whose assertion can be proved in this way: Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, reigned for sixteen years, as is held in 1 Kings, chapter 16. <note>The text cites "3 Regum," which in the Vulgate numbering refers to what modern Bibles call 1 Kings.</note> Hezekiah his son succeeded him in the kingdom when he was twenty-five years of age, as is gathered from 2 Kings, chapter 18. <note>The text cites "4 Reg." which refers to modern 2 Kings.</note> From this it is clear that in the first year of the reign of Ahaz, Hezekiah himself was nine years old. Since, therefore, this prophecy (as Rabbi Solomon says) was made in the fourth year of the reign of Ahaz, it is clear that Hezekiah was thirteen years old at that time. From these facts, therefore, it is manifestly evident that this prophecy can only be explained as referring to the Messiah, since he alone is truly Emmanuel.

**CAPNIO.** <note>The character "Capnio" represents the Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note> Your Christ (the Jews say) was called Jesus, and not Emmanuel. Therefore, you cannot say that he was that Emmanuel of whom the Prophet speaks.

**GALATINUS.** <note>The character "Galatinus" represents the author, Pietro Galatino.</note> A name of nature is one thing; a name of imposition <note>A given or bestowed name.</note> is another. For it is established that the nature itself, which gives form to a thing, also gives the same name to the thing: just as it gives both humanity and the name "man" to a person. For no one is named "man" except because of the nature of man in which he participates. In the same way, our Messiah is called *Emmanuel*, which is interpreted as *God with us*—that is, God and man—both by the Holy Spirit and by his mother. He is both believed to be and is called such by all Christians, since he participates in two natures: namely, the divine and the human. In this manner, he was called by many and diverse names by the Holy Spirit through the Prophets, signifying his divine or human nature, or both at once. Emmanuel, therefore, is a name of nature, designating the union of both natures which was to occur in the womb of the Virgin. *Jesus*, however, is a name of imposition, which is interpreted as Savior, or Health, or Salvation.

**CAPNIO.** The Jews still insist on this, because concerning this Emmanuel the Prophet immediately added: <note>Isaiah 7:15; original Hebrew: "חמאה ודבש יאכל לדעתו מאוס ברע ובחור בטוב chemah u-devash yokhal le-da’ato ma’os ba-ra u-vachor ba-tov"</note> This is: *Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good.* This (they say) hardly fits your Christ, whom you say had the fullness of knowledge from the very instant of his conception. From this they infer that he is not this Emmanuel whom the Prophet mentions.

**GALATINUS.** They cannot possibly deny that frequently in Holy Scripture, spiritual things are signified through bodily things. Therefore, the Prophet predicted that our Emmanuel would eat butter and honey to hint that he would possess within himself the nature and truth not only of humanity, but also of divinity. For butter, which is made from the milk of animals, suitably designates humanity. Honey, however—because of its supreme sweetness and because it often comes invisibly from the airy heavens like dew—sufficiently and appropriately signifies divinity. Concerning both of these, Isaac said to Esau, when Esau was urgently asking to be blessed by him in Genesis 27: <note>Genesis 27:39; original Hebrew: "הנה משמני הארץ יהיה מושבך ומטל השמים מעל hinneh mi-shmannei ha-aretz yihyeh moshavekha u-mi-tal ha-shamayim me-al"</note> That is, *Behold, from the

<column-break/>

fatness of the earth shall be your dwelling* (or rest, or habitation), *and from the dew of heaven from above.* It is as if he were saying: from the humanity and divinity of the coming Messiah.

**CAPNIO.** The Jews again object to that which follows concerning Emmanuel himself in Isaiah in this manner: <note>Isaiah 7:16; original Hebrew: "כי בטרם ידע הנער מאוס ברע ובחור בטוב תשב האדמה ki be-terem yeda ha-na'ar ma'os ba-ra u-vachor ba-tov te'azev ha-adamah"</note> That is: *For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land shall be forsaken,* along with the rest that follows. They say, therefore: If your Christ was this Emmanuel, you cannot excuse him from ignorance. Since you assert that there was no ignorance in him, you can by no means say that he was this Emmanuel.

**GALATINUS.** This saying of Isaiah ought to be understood regarding the human knowledge of Christ. Therefore, although there was no ignorance in him, because he was made man in time, he also possessed human knowledge in time; and before he possessed that [human] knowledge, the liberation of that land and people foretold by Isaiah was completed. Thus, the Prophet’s saying is to be explained: *Before the child shall know to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land shall be forsaken,* and so on. This means: *Before he becomes man*, or, *Before he is conceived and born of the aforementioned Virgin, the land shall be forsaken,* etc. In the same way, one must respond to what is said of the same child in the following chapter: <note>Isaiah 8:4; original Hebrew: "כי בטרם ידע הנער קרא אבי ואמי ki be-terem yeda ha-na'ar kera avi ve-immi"</note> That is: *For before the child shall have knowledge to cry* (or to say) *My father, and my mother*—which is to say: *Before he becomes man*, or *before he arises as a man.* Furthermore, that this child of whom Isaiah speaks is God and man, and consequently truly to be called Emmanuel, appears most clearly from what Isaiah sets down in the same place, saying: <note>Isaiah 8:1; original Hebrew: "ויאמר יהוה אלי קח לך גליון גדול וכתוב עליו בחרט אנוש למהר שלל חש בז va-yomer Adonai elai kach lekha gilyon gadol u-khetov alav be-cheret enosh le-maher shalal chash baz"</note> That is: *And God said to me, Take a great volume, and write in it with the pen of a man: To the quick spoiler, to the swift plunderer.* <note>The names Maher-shalal-hash-baz.</note> These things are explained by Rabbi Solomon thus: *Take a great volume*, that is, a roll of paper or a writing tablet. *And write in it with the pen of a man*, that is, in such a script and in such a manner that every man may be able to run through it, whoever reads it, even if he is not wise. Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> translated it this way: write <gloss>explicitly</gloss> <note>original: "mephoras"</note>, that is, clearly. And why did he say "Great," when he commanded only these four names to be written in it? There are some who explain that the substance of the writing consists of those four, but that many more things were written in that volume. Thus says Rabbi Solomon. But Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (Radak, 1160–1235), a famous medieval biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> says the same thing with a greater explanation regarding the word <gloss>stylus</gloss> <note>original: "Heret"</note>. Therefore, many more things than these four words were written in that volume concerning this child to be called Emmanuel, as Rabbi Solomon says. These four words, however, are like the titles of what follows—namely: *Quick, Spoiler, Swift, Plunderer*—which suit the Messiah perfectly. For he was to be the quick spoiler of hell and a swift plunderer. Many other things which Isaiah wrote in the same volume about him look partly toward his divinity, and partly toward his humanity and divinity together. As is clearly hinted by these things.

he deservedly should have been called Emmanuel. From this it follows most evidently both that the Messiah is God and that this child is the Messiah. He also wrote in the aforementioned great volume that which follows immediately after: **For a child is born to us, a son is given to us** <note>original: "כי ילד ילד לנו בן נתן לנו" — Isaiah 9:6.</note>, along with the rest; which we shall show more extensively elsewhere through their own scriptures was similarly spoken of the Messiah as both God and man. ### CHAPTER XIX.

->*Concerning certain names of the Messiah imposed upon him by effect, from which his divinity is clearly shown.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

Since many other names of the Messiah besides Emmanuel are found in Isaiah in the same passages you have now introduced, through which his divinity is manifestly shown, it is therefore right that if you have said so much about "Emmanuel," you should also say something about these names. GALATINUS: So that I do not pass them over, I will first introduce Isaiah himself speaking in chapter 9: **For a child is born to us, a son is given to us. And the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Everlasting Father (or Father of Eternity), Prince, Peace, for the increase of the government and of peace there shall be no end.** <note>Isaiah 9:6-7. The Hebrew text is provided in the source.</note> Since these names can apply to no one but God, it necessarily follows from them that the Messiah is God. CAPNIO: Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explains these names not of the Messiah, but of King Hezekiah. For he says: "And he—that is, the Holy and Blessed God, who is wonderful, a counselor, the mighty God, and the everlasting father—called his [Hezekiah's] name: Prince of Peace." GALATINUS: Among the Jews, Chaldeans, and Arabs, there is (as you yourself know) no diversity of cases, since among them all nouns are indeclinable, though they have singular and plural forms. Therefore, Rabbi Solomon himself (whom almost all the younger Jews follow), in order to withdraw the testimony of this prophecy from our faith, attempted to explain these names concerning King Hezekiah against the expositions of all the ancients. He made the first six of these names the nomina-

<margin>
False exposition.
Refutation.
</margin>

<column-break/>

-tive case, which he attributes to God; but the last two he made the accusative, which he imposes upon Hezekiah. We, however, adding nothing to the words of the Prophet and changing nothing there—as he does, who adds and changes much to pervert the meaning of the prophecy—say that this child born to us and given to us is the Messiah, according to the <gloss>marginal or interlinear explanations</gloss> of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. According to his humanity, he was born to us of the Virgin Mary, and according to his divinity, he was to be given to us by the Eternal Father. His name was called by the Holy Spirit—of whom David says in 2 Samuel chapter 23, "The Spirit of God spoke in me"—through Isaiah: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Everlasting Father, Prince, Peace. Moreover, this is excellently supported by the authority of the ancient Talmudists, by whom the fraud of Rabbi Solomon is vehemently exploded. For in **Echarabbethi** <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, it is said that one of the names of the Messiah is Peace. For so Rabbi Jose the Galilean says there: "The name of the Messiah is also called **Salom** <note>Shalom</note>, that is, Peace, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 9: Everlasting Father, Prince, Peace." This is the tradition. From which it is clearly held that not only the last two names placed in the predicted prophecy—namely, Prince and Peace, which Rabbi Solomon attributed to Hezekiah—but also Everlasting Father and all the others which he attributes to God, are understood to be spoken of the Messiah. Also in **Beresith Rabba** <note>Genesis Rabbah, a midrashic text on Genesis.</note>, regarding that verse in Genesis "And Pharaoh said to Joseph," it is said: "It is written in Zephaniah chapter 3: 'For then I will turn to the people a chosen (or purified) lip, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder.' Now 'the name of the Lord' here is nothing but the King Messiah, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 30: 'Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar.' And why is it said, 'And they shall serve him with one shoulder'? Certainly because the government shall be upon his shoulder." Thus far the tradition. From which it is manifestly shown that the aforesaid words of Isaiah were spoken of the Messiah and not of Hezekiah. This same thing is also clearly evident through the Chaldaic exposition <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. For Rabbi Jonathan son of Uzziel translated and explained these same words in Chaldaic thus: **The prophet said to the house of David: For a child is born to us, a son is given to us, and he shall receive the law upon himself to keep it; and his name shall be called from before (the Lord), who is wonderful in counsel, the mighty God, he who endures forever, the Messiah, in whose days peace shall be multiplied upon us.** <note>The Hebrew/Aramaic text of the Targum is provided in the source.</note> Thus far the <term>Targum</term>. CAPNIO: When the Targum says, "And his name shall be called from before," or "from the presence of," from whose presence, or before what, was the name of the Messiah to be called? GALATINUS: We have already said that from the part of the Holy Spirit, who spoke through this Prophet as through others, the name of the Messiah was called, and that it was even called before he was born; according to that of the Psalm: "Before the sun, **Innon** <note>original: "ינון" — a messianic name derived from Psalm 72:17, often interpreted in Jewish tradition as one of the names of the Messiah existing before creation.</note> was his name." From these things, therefore, it is clear that the names themselves which are placed in the aforementioned prophecy of Isaiah can only be understood of the Messiah.

### CHAPTER XX.

->*That the proper name of the Messiah ought to be Jesus. And concerning the excellence of this name.*<-

### CAPNIO.

Among the other things I most desire to hear from you is the excellence of this most holy name, Jesus. For when I pronounce it, my whole mouth is filled with a certain wonderful sweetness. Therefore, for the greater confusion of the Jews of our age, who do not shudder to blaspheme Jesus himself, I pray you reveal something of the loftiness of this most glorious name: and especially whether this name is, among all other names of the Messiah, more proper to him and more fitting for him. GALATINUS: Since the Messiah was to be both perfect God and perfect man, therefore the Prophets—to suggest the truth of both his natures—sometimes call him God, using the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), held to be so sacred it is not spoken aloud by Jews.</term> or another divine name; and sometimes they call him man, or by other names designating human nature. But because the salvation of the human race could only be achieved through God hypostatically <term>hypostatically: refers to the "Hypostatic Union," the Christian doctrine that Jesus is one person with two distinct natures, divine and human.</term> united to humanity,

<column-break/>

therefore this name JESUS, which is interpreted as Savior, is more proper and fitting to the Messiah himself among the other names attributed to him. For it not only implies both natures—namely the divine and human—which were to be hypostatically united in the Messiah himself, but it also most clearly suggests the salvation of the human race which he himself was to work. Indeed, this name was imposed upon him from eternity through eternal predestination by the Eternal Father, and was later revealed to the Prophets by the same. Wherefore Habakkuk, as if giving thanks to God, said in chapter 3: *But I will rejoice in the LORD; I will exult in God my Jesus.* <note>original Hebrew: "ואני ביהוה אעלוזה אגילה באלהי ישעי" — Habakkuk 3:18. The Hebrew word "ישעי" (yishi) means "my salvation," but Galatinus interprets it here as a direct reference to the name Jesus.</note> And Ezra, speaking in the person of God the Father in the 3rd chapter of the third book, said thus: *My son Jesus shall be revealed, with those who shall rejoice with him.* <note>original Hebrew: "יגלה בני ישוע עם אותם שישמחו" — This is a Hebrew translation of a passage from the apocryphal book 4 Ezra (or 2 Esdras) 7:28.</note> And again in the same place he says: *My son Jesus shall die, and the world shall be turned to me.* <note>original Hebrew: "ימות בני ישוע ומשיח אלי העולם" — 4 Ezra 7:29. These verses were often cited by Renaissance theologians as pre-Christian evidence of Jesus' divinity.</note> Rabbenu Haccados also, in the book *Gale Razeya*, addressing the Consul Antoninus, says these things among others concerning the name itself: "Because the Messiah shall save men, he shall be called *Jeshuah* <note>Hebrew: ישוע (*Jeshuah*), meaning "he will save" or "salvation."</note>. However, the Gentiles of another nation who follow his faith shall call him Jesus." And therefore you will find this name, Jesus, designated in the text of Genesis, chapter 49: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," in the first letters of these words: *Yavo Shilo Velo*. <note>original Hebrew: "יבא שילה ולו" — Genesis 49:10. Galatinus is using "Notarikon," a kabbalistic method where the first letters of words form a new word. The letters Yod, Shin, and Vav (י-ש-ו) form the name "Jesu."</note> For if you take the first letters of these words, the same letters will form *Jesu*. So says that Rabbenu, whom the Jews call our holy Master. Because, therefore, the Gentiles who were to believe in him also had to be saved through him, this name was revealed not only to the Prophets and the ancient Jews, but also—for a clearer expression of the truth—to some among the Gentiles. For the Erythraean Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses in Greek tradition; Christian scholars believed they had foretold the coming of Christ to the pagan world.</note> (to keep silent about others) composed certain verses about the end of the world, from whose first letters, if read correctly, these words result: *Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, Cross.* <note>original Greek: "Ιησούς χριστός θεού υιός, σωτήρ, σταυρός." This refers to a famous acrostic found in the Sibylline Oracles.</note> CAPNIO: Since the Prophets also predicted that the Messiah should be called by other names, the more recent Jews utterly deny that the proper name of the Messiah ought to have been Jesus. GALATINUS: They certainly cannot deny it: both because (as we have shown) not only the Prophets but also their own ancient teachers assert this; and also because it is proven by reason. For if the human race was only to be saved through the Messiah, and the name Jesus is interpreted as Savior, it follows plainly that this name can properly suit no one else but the Messiah. Therefore, it is necessary for them to concede that this alone must have been the proper name of the Messiah himself. Other names by which he was called even by the Prophets themselves are taken (as we said) from the effect of salvation itself, since they concern only either the beginning, or the middle, or the end of our salvation. But this name Jesus sufficiently contains the whole process of our salvation: namely, the beginning, middle, and end.

# THIRD BOOK

Wherefore he includes all other names within himself. Therefore, he ought to have been named by this name more than any other. **CAPNIO:** This, then, seems to me to be that name of which Isaiah speaks in chapter 62, saying: <margin>XII. 2</margin> <note>original Hebrew: וקרא לך שם חדש אשר פי יהוה יקבנו</note> That is: "And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of God shall name." Why, then, did he say it would be a "new" name? **GALATINUS:** Because it was to be bestowed upon no one before the Messiah. For one reads in the Holy Scriptures of no one ever having existed who was called by this name. This was done for this reason above all: so that it might be openly shown from this that the name could rightly and properly belong to no one except the Messiah, the true Savior. **HOGSTRATUS:** On the contrary, we read in the Holy Scripture that three others were called by this name. **GALATINUS:** Who are they, I pray? **HOGSTRATUS:** Joshua son of Nun <note>original Latin: Iesus Naue</note>, Jesus son of Sirach, and Joshua son of Jozadak <note>original Latin: Iesus Iosedec</note>; whom our Doctors say were a "figure" <term>figure: a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality in Christian theology</term> of the true Jesus. For just as Joshua son of Nun, a most brave man, introduced the children of Israel into the land of promise after their enemies were conquered; and Jesus son of Sirach, a most wise teacher, renewed wisdom in his own times (as is read); and Joshua son of Jozadak, a most holy priest, built a temple for the Lord; so Christ, the true Jesus, having overcome the enemies of the human race by his own strength, introduced his faithful ones to the heavenly homeland. By his wisdom and truthful doctrine, he illuminated the world, purging it of errors. By his own holiness, being himself a priest forever, he constructed a spiritual temple—that is, the Church of the faithful—out of living and chosen stones. **GALATINUS:** I grant that they bore the "figures" of the true Jesus, but I entirely deny that they were called by the name "Jesus." For in this (to speak the truth), very many of our people are greatly mistaken, thinking they were called by this name. It is certain that this has arisen from ignorance of the Hebrew letters. For every one of those whom they claim are called by this name "Jesus" was not called <note>original Hebrew: ישוע</note> *Yeshua* (that is, Jesus), but <note>original Hebrew: יהושוע</note> *Yehoshua*. This is not the same name as *Yeshua* (Jesus), but is far different from it and signifies something else. For *Yeshua*, or Jesus, is the same as "Savior," or "health," or "salvation." *Yehoshua*, however, is interpreted as "God will save." As is clearly evident from the name itself, saving belongs to none of them, but to God alone; who, being hypostatically <term>hypostatically: the union of divine and human natures in one person</term> united to human nature, would be the true *Yeshua* or Jesus—that is, the Savior—of the human race. Therefore, they themselves were not called <note>original Hebrew: ישועות</note> *Yeshuoth* or Jesus (that is, Saviors or Salvations), but *Yehoshua* (God will save). This was to openly imply that only one Savior was to come, who would be both God and man. God, indeed, so that he might be able to save; but Man, so that by undergoing death for the salvation of the human race, he might satisfy divine justice, which required that the one making satisfaction be of the same race as the transgressor. **HOGSTRATUS:** For this reason, some of our people say—and not without cause—that this name "Jesus" is nothing other than the very name of God, the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</term>. For it is well known that the principal letters of that name are three: namely, *yod*, *he*, and *vau* <note>the Hebrew letters Y, H, and W/V</note>, since the fourth letter is only the second one placed twice in the same name—specifically in the second

<column-break/>

and fourth place. These three letters indeed seem to correspond to our letters: I, H, V. When these are joined together in this way, *Ihu*, they form this blessed name. A title <note>the "title" refers to a scribal abbreviation mark or "tittle" placed over the name</note> is placed above it, so that the cross through which we are saved may be designated. From this it is manifest that this name Jesus is nothing other than the Tetragrammaton name of God. **GALATINUS:** That would certainly be beautiful if it could be verified in every language. For those three letters of the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) only seem to have this conformity with the name "Jesus" when it is written in Latin letters. For in Hebrew letters it is written <note>original Hebrew: ישוע</note> *Yeshua*, and in Greek <note>original Greek: Ιησους</note> *Iesous*. In all of these, besides the first, no other letter is placed among those from which the Tetragrammaton name of God is composed. Therefore, since this similarity of letters is not preserved in the Hebrew language (to say nothing of others)—the language in which it ought to be preserved above all, since both names are Hebrew—it seems it should by no means be said that the name "Jesus" is entirely the Tetragrammaton name of God. For although Christ is properly and directly to be called by the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) as true God (as we showed above), nevertheless, since that name belongs to him only according to his divine nature, while this name "Jesus" belongs to him according to both natures, divine and human, it follows without doubt that this is not that, nor is the meaning of both the same, as has been made clear enough (I believe) in the preceding sections. Furthermore, many secrets of this most holy name "Jesus" remain to be related, which are saved to be told more opportunely in another place. But for now, let it suffice that we say something of those names of the Messiah which are spoken of him in the Sacred Page metaphorically or antonomastically <term>antonomastic: using an epithet or title instead of a proper name</term>, as far as concerns our purpose.

### CHAPTER XXI.

#### That the Messiah is called "Rock," or "Stone," for multiple reasons.

### CAPNIO.

WHY then was the Messiah called a Stone? **GALATINUS:** Not without cause. And this is what is written in Daniel, chapter 2: "The stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." Moreover, that the Messiah is the cornerstone rejected by the Jews is found in Isaiah, chapter 28, saying thus: <note>original Hebrew: לכן כה אמר אדני יהוה הנני יסד בציון אבן אבן בחן פנת יקרת מוסד מוסד המאמין לא יחיש ושמתי משפט לקו וצדקה למשקלת</note> That is: "Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I have founded in Zion a stone, a tried stone (or a strong one), a cornerstone, a precious one, a foundation of foundations. ### THIRD BOOK.

<margin>A</margin> ...to the line, or to the measure, and justice to the weight. Where the commentary <note>original: glossa</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar</note> says this: "'I have founded' is a past-tense verb; wherefore it should be explained from the past like this: 'Behold, it is I who have already founded a stone in Zion,' that is, it has already been determined and decreed before me, and I have established the King Messiah, who is the stone *bohan* <term>bohan: a Hebrew word meaning strength or fortress</term>, which signifies strength or fortification. However, as for what is called 'the foundation of the foundation'—that is, the foundation of foundations—it should be understood as if one were saying 'the most perfect foundation.'" These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note>, however, translated the Hebrew into Aramaic as: <margin>B</margin> <note>original: הא אנא ממני בציון מלכא משיחא מלכא תקיף גיבר ואימתן</note> "Behold, I am appointing in Zion the King Messiah, a king powerful, mighty, and awesome." That is: "The Lord God said, 'Behold, I establish in Zion the King Messiah, a powerful, robust, and strong King.'" Regarding this stone, the Psalmist also says in Psalm 118: <note>original: אודך כי עניתני ותהי לי לישועה : אבן מאסו הבונים היתה לראש פנה : מאת יהוה היתה זאת היא נפלאת בעינינו : זה היום עשה יהוה נגילה ונשמחה בו</note> "I will confess to you, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation. The stone which the builders rejected <margin>C</margin> has become the head of the corner. This thing was from God, and it is wonderful in our eyes. This is the very day which the Lord has made; we will exult and rejoice in it." That these words are understood to be about the Messiah is clear through the commentary of Rabbi Solomon on that passage in Micah, chapter 5: <note>original: ממך לי יצא להיות מושל בישראל</note> "Out of you shall he come forth to me, who is to be the Ruler in Israel." For he says there: <note>original: זה משיח בן דוד וכן נאמר אבן מאסו הבונים וגו'</note> "This is the Messiah, son of David, just as it was said in Psalm 118: 'The stone the builders rejected,' etc." Concerning this stone, one also reads in Zechariah, chapter 3: <margin>D</margin> <note>original: הנני מביא את עבדי צמח כי הנה האבן אשר נתתי לפני יהושע על אבן אחת שבעה עינים הנני מפתח פתחה נאם יהוה צבאות ומשתי את עון הארץ ההיא ביום אחד</note> "Behold, I bring my servant the Branch. For behold the stone which I have set before Joshua. Upon one stone are seven eyes. Behold, I will open its opening, says the Lord of hosts, and I will take away the iniquity of that land in a single day." These words <margin>E</margin> Rabbi Jonathan translated into Aramaic in this way: <note>original: אנא מייתי ית עבדי משיחא ויתגלי ארי הא אבנא די הבית קדם יהושע על אבנא חדא שבעא חזואן לה הא אנא גלי חזיתהא אמר יהוה צבאות ואעדי ית חוב ארעא ההיא ביומא חד</note> "Behold, I will bring my servant the Messiah, and he shall be revealed. Behold the stone which I have set before Joshua; upon the one stone are seven visions. Behold, I will reveal its visions, said the Lord of hosts, and I will take away the guilt of that land in one day." Also, regarding this stone in <margin>F</margin> *Beresith Rabba* <term>Beresith Rabba: Genesis Rabbah, an ancient collection of Jewish interpretations of the book of Genesis</term>—that is, in the commentaries on the book of Genesis—regarding the statement in the twenty-eighth chapter of that book, "And Jacob went out from Beersheba," Rabbi Moses Hadarsan says: "This is what is written in Psalm 121: 'I will lift up my eyes to the mountains, from whence comes my helper,' or 'my help.' And so Zechariah says in chapter 4: 'Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel?' This is <margin>G</margin> the stone of Jacob, as was said in Genesis chapter 28: 'And he took the stone which he had placed at his head,' or 'for his head-rests.'" From all these things which have been said, it...

<column-break/>

...clearly appears that the Messiah is not without reason called a stone, cutting itself from the mountain without hands, as is held in Daniel chapter 2. And a stone for the offense and stumbling of the wandering Jews, and for the sanctification of the elect, as is said in Isaiah chapter 8. And also the cornerstone and headstone rejected by the Jews, as we have now proved. Wherefore Peter, that prince of the Apostles, not without merit says these things about this stone in the second chapter of his first epistle: "Coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves as living stones are built up into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For which reason the scripture contains: 'Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, tested, chosen, precious, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.'"

### CHAPTER XXII.

->*That the Messiah is called Tender, to suggest his immense piety.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>R</margin> I find the Messiah is sometimes called **רך** *Rach*, that is, "Tender" in the sacred writings, as in that saying of Solomon in Proverbs chapter 4: <note>original: בן הייתי לאבי רך ויחיד לפני אמי</note> "I was a son to my father, tender and the only one," or "the unique one among the sons," or "of my mother’s sons." You have already discussed how these things should be understood in the fifth chapter of the previous book. Now, therefore, tell me why he is called "tender." **GALATINUS:** Chiefly because of the immense tenderness of his piety <note>The Latin 'pietas' implies both mercy and dutiful love</note>. This is most clear from what is said in Ezekiel chapter 17: <note>original: כה אמר אדני יהוה ולקחתי אני מצמרת הארז הרמה ונתתי מראש יונקותיו רך אקטוף ושתלתי אני על הר גבוה ותלול</note> "Thus says the Lord God: And I myself will take from the top of the high cedar, and will give from the head of its shoots. I will pluck a tender one, and I will plant it upon a high and prominent mountain." Where the commentary of Rabbi Solomon says: "'And I will take the top of the cedar': the King Messiah. 'I will pluck a tender one.' For there is no way to have mercy except through the tender one, who is growing and binding together and held tight." Thus says Rabbi Solomon. In these words, the tenderness of divine piety is most evidently touched upon, as well as the grafting and fruitful planting of the most merciful divinity into the trunk of humanity. For which reasons Jonathan himself translated those words into Aramaic as: <note>original: ואקריב אנא ממלכותא דבית דוד דמתיל בארזא רמא ואקימינה</note> "And I will bring near from the Kingdom of the house of David, which is likened to a tall cedar, and I will raise it up." Finally, it follows in the same prophecy: <note>original: והיה לארז אדיר ושכנו תחתיו כל צפור</note> "And it shall be a noble cedar, and every bird shall dwell under it, and every winged creature shall dwell in the shadow of its branches." Jonathan himself translated and explained this in Aramaic as: "And he shall be a robust King, and all the righteous shall rest upon him, and all the humble..."
