### THE THIRD BOOK.

Therefore, [the name Jesus] includes all other names within itself. For this reason, the Messiah ought to have been named by this name more than any other. **CAPNIO.** This, then, seems to me to be that name of which Isaiah speaks in chapter 62, saying: <margin>12:2</margin> "And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name." <note>original Hebrew: וקרא לך שם חדש אשר פי יהוה יקבנו</note> Why, then, did he say it would be "new"? **GALATINUS.** Because it was to be given to no one before the Messiah. For we read of no one in the sacred scriptures who was ever called by this name. This was done primarily so that it might be clearly shown that the name could correctly and properly belong to no one except the Messiah, the true Savior. **HOGSTRATEN.** On the contrary, we read of three others in the sacred scripture who were called by this name. **GALATINUS.** Who are they, I pray? **HOGSTRATEN.** Joshua son of Nun <note>original: Iesus Naue; in Latin, Joshua is often written as 'Iesus'</note>, Jesus son of Sirach <note>The author of the Wisdom of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus</note>, and Jeshua son of Jozadak <note>original: Iesus Iosedec; the High Priest during the return from the Babylonian exile</note>. Our Doctors say these figures were types <note>symbolic precursors</note> of the true Jesus. For just as Joshua son of Nun, a most brave man, introduced the children of Israel into the land of promise after their enemies were defeated; and Jesus son of Sirach, a most wise teacher, renewed wisdom in his own times (as we read); and Jeshua son of Jozadak, a most holy priest, built a temple for the Lord; so too Christ, the true Jesus, having overcome the enemies of the human race by his own strength, introduced his faithful to the heavenly homeland. By his wisdom and truthful doctrine, he illuminated the world, purging it of errors. And by his holiness, being himself a priest forever, he constructed a spiritual temple—that is, the Church of the faithful—out of living and chosen stones. **GALATINUS.** I grant that they acted as types of the true Jesus, but I entirely deny that they were called by the name of Jesus. In this (to tell the truth), very many of our people are greatly mistaken, thinking they were called by this name. This certainly arises from an ignorance of Hebrew letters. For every one of those whom they claim were called by the name "Jesus" was not called *Yeshua* <note>original: ישוע</note>—that is, Jesus—but *Yehoshua* <note>original: יהושוע</note>. This is not the same name as *Yeshua* (Jesus), but is quite different from it and signifies something else. For *Yeshua*, or Jesus, is the same as "Savior," "Health," or "Salvation." *Yehoshua*, however, is interpreted as "God will save." As is clearly evident from the name itself, to save was not the role of any of those men, but of God alone. He, being hypostatically united to human nature, would be the true *Yeshua* or Jesus—that is, the Savior—of the human race. Therefore, they themselves were not called *Yeshuoth* <note>plural: Saviors</note> or Jesus, but *Yehoshua* (God will save), so that it might be openly hinted that only one Savior was to come, who would be both God and man. God, indeed, so that he might be able to save; but Man, so that by undergoing death for the salvation of the human race, he might satisfy divine justice, which required that the one making satisfaction be of the same race as the transgressor. **HOGSTRATEN.** For this reason, some of our people say, not without cause, that this name "Jesus" is nothing other than the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name of God: YHWH</note> itself. For it is established (as you have excellently declared) that the principal letters of that name are three: namely, *Yod*, *He*, and *Vav* <note>original: iod, he, vau</note>, since the fourth is only the second letter repeated in the second and fourth positions. These three letters seem to correspond to our letters I, H, and V. When these are joined together in this way—*Ihu*—they form this blessed name. A title [a line or mark] is placed above it so that the cross through which we are saved might be designated. From this, it is manifest that the name "Jesus" is nothing other than the name of God, the Tetragrammaton. **GALATINUS.** That would indeed be beautiful if it could be verified in every language. But those three letters of the name of God seem to have this conformity only with the name "Jesus" when written in Latin letters. For in Hebrew letters it is written *Yeshua* <note>original: ישוע</note>, and in Greek *Iesous* <note>original: Ιησους</note>. In all of these, except for the first, no other letter is used from those which compose the Tetragrammaton. Therefore, since this similarity of letters is not preserved in the Hebrew language (to say nothing of others)—where it ought most especially to be preserved, since both names are Hebrew—it seems it should not be said at all that the name "Jesus" is the Tetragrammaton. For although Christ is properly and directly called by the name of God (Tetragrammaton) as the true God (as we showed above), nevertheless, since that name belongs to him only according to his divine nature, while this name "Jesus" belongs to him according to both natures, divine and human, it follows without doubt that this name is not that one, nor is the meaning of both the same, as has been sufficiently and abundantly shown in the preceding sections. Furthermore, many secrets of this most holy name of Jesus would have to be reported, but they are reserved to be spoken of more opportunely in another place. For now, it is enough that, as far as our purpose is concerned, we say something about those names of the Messiah which are said of him metaphorically or by way of antonomasia <note>using a title or epithet instead of a proper name</note> in the sacred pages.

### CHAPTER XXI.

->*That the Messiah is called a Rock, or a Stone, for manifold reasons.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

Why, then, is the Messiah called a Stone? **GALATINUS.** Not without reason. For there it is read word-for-word: "After the King Messiah has taken vengeance on Esau, he himself shall become a great King." And this is what is written in Daniel chapter 2: "The stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." He who believes shall not be in haste. And I will set judgment..."

### CHAPTER XXIII.
#### That the Messiah is called "The Just One" by way of a title and by way of excellence.

-> CAPNIO <-

I have also frequently read among the Prophets, as well as among the Talmudists, that the Messiah is called "The Just One." And although I am not unaware that he is so named <term>antonomastically</term><note>Antonomastic refers to a figure of speech where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name, such as calling the Messiah "The Just One."</note> and by way of excellence, I would nevertheless like to hear something from you on this matter for a greater expression of this truth. GALATINUS: There is no need for many words to prove that the Messiah is called <term>Tsadic</term><note>original Hebrew: צדיק</note>—that is, "The Just One"—by way of title and excellence, since this is evident in countless places in both the Holy Scriptures and the Talmud itself. However, to satisfy your request, as you urge me to say something about this, and so that we do not seem to have passed it over in complete silence, I shall say just a few things on the subject. First, I will bring forward Zechariah, who says in chapter 9: <note>original Hebrew: גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירו שלם הנה מלכך יבו לך צדיק ונושע הוא עני ורכב על חמור ועל עיר בן אתונות</note> "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you, the Just One and the Savior Himself; poor, and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey." By this prophecy, not only is the Messiah named "The Just One" by way of excellence, but also his divinity and humanity are clearly expressed. Indeed, his divinity is expressed in that part which says, "the Just One and the Savior Himself." For this Hebrew word <term>Hu</term><note>original Hebrew: הוא</note>, which in Latin is the same as "Himself" [Ipse], is a divine name among the Hebrews and properly signifies God. This is clearly evident in Isaiah, chapter 42, where God himself says: <note>original Hebrew: אני יהוה הוא שמי</note> "I am the Lord, *Hu* (He/Himself) is my name." Therefore, when Zechariah said, "The Just One and the Savior *Himself* shall come to you," what else did he wish to express than that which Isaiah clearly stated in chapter 35, saying: <note>original Hebrew: אלהים הוא יבא ויושעכם</note> "God Himself will come and save you." For to save belongs properly to God alone. However, the other things which are added in the same prophecy of Zechariah explain the humanity of the Messiah, according to which he was to be poor, and finally, as his passion drew near, he was to enter Jerusalem riding upon a donkey and its colt for the sake of saving the human race. From this, the false opinion of the Jews—who think the Messiah will reign temporally over the whole world—is mostly refuted. For since a temporal worldly kingdom and poverty do not agree at all, nor can they exist together, it must necessarily be granted that the Kingdom of the Messiah, according to the prophecy of this Prophet, was to be not temporal, but spiritual. Therefore, he said, "My kingdom is not of this world." CAPNIO: Since the more recent Jews are most obstinate, in order to be able to deny the divinity of the Messiah expressed by this Prophet,

they say that in the Hebrew text it is written <term>noscha</term><note>original Hebrew: נושע</note>, which is interpreted as "saved," and not "savior"; which can in no way be applied to God. For even if it is proper to God to save, it can by no means be fitting for Him to be saved. From this they conclude that since the Messiah in this prophecy is called "saved" and not "savior," he is not God himself, but the Messiah must be saved from the sword of Gog and Magog on account of his own justice. GALATINUS: We shall respond to them in this place with nothing other than what the ancient Talmudists say. Therefore, I will cite the words of Rabbi Berachiah, which Rabbi Menahem Rekanati relates regarding Genesis chapter 3, saying: "The salvation of Israel is the salvation of the Holy and Blessed God; as Rabbi Berachiah the priest said, because it is written in Zechariah chapter 9, 'Just and Saved,' and not 'Just Savior Himself'." Wherein that ancient priest tries to show that God, by saving Israel—that is, the faithful—is said to be "saved," because this Prophet says, "Just and Saved." For by "The Just One" (as his words plainly sound) he understands God. And the reasoning upon which his saying seems to be founded is this: because just as the perfection of a work is accustomed to redound upon the worker, so the salvation of the human race in a certain way reflects back upon God. Therefore, according to the exposition of this Talmudist, the Prophet called the Messiah "saved" because, since he himself as God was to save the human race, the salvation of the human race itself was to redound upon him as the author of salvation. For this reason, the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in this place, following the sense rather than the words, not ineptly translated it as <term>just and savior</term><note>original Greek: δικαιος καὶ σωτηρ</note>; whom the author of our edition imitated, correctly translating it "Just and Savior." It is also proved by this that the Messiah is called "The Just One" by way of title and excellence, because in the book *Yoma*, in the chapter *Amar lahem* (He said to them), it is read in this way: "Rabbi Eliezer said, the world was created even for the sake of one Just One. As it is said in Genesis chapter 1, 'And God saw the light, that it was good.' But there is no 'good' except <term>Tsadic</term>, that is, the Just One, which is the Messiah. As it is said in Isaiah chapter 3, 'Say to the Just One, for he is good'." That the world was created for the sake of the Messiah is also found in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, where it is read that Rabbi Johanan spoke thus: "The world was not created except for the sake of the Messiah." Nor should we omit in this place what is said in the book *Chagigah*, in the chapter *En dorsin* (They do not seek). For there it is read literally: "There is a tradition that Rabbi Yose said: Woe to the creatures who see, and know not what they see; who stand, and know not upon what they stand. For upon what does the Earth stand? Upon columns; as it is said in Job chapter 9: 'Who shakes the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble.' The wise men said that the Earth stands upon twelve columns. As it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 32: 'When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people (that is, the nations) according to the number of the children of Israel.' But Rabbi Eliezer said that the Earth stands upon one column, and <term>Tsadic</term> (the Just One) is its name." Thus far the tradition. In which the opinion of the ancient Jewish sages is greatly to be noted,

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->*That the Messiah is called "The Man of War" (just as God is called by that name) because of the victory he was to obtain against the devil.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>Exodus 15</margin>
AMONG the other names that are spoken of the Messiah either by title or metaphor, none so expressly suggests his divinity as this name "Man of War," which properly belongs to God alone. Therefore, it is necessary for you to say something about this as well. GALATINUS: First, therefore, it must be proven that this name "Man of War" properly suits God alone. Then, however, it must be shown that the Messiah is properly called "Man of War," and consequently that he himself is God. For the first point, I bring forward what is written in the book called <term>Mechilta</term><note>original: מכילתא; an early Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus.</note>. For there, concerning that passage in Exodus 15: <note>original Hebrew: יהוה איש מלחמה יהוה שמו</note> "The Lord is a man of war, the Lord [the Tetragrammaton] is His name," it is read among other things: "How can this be said? For is it not written in Jeremiah 23, 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.' What then does he teach should be said when he says, 'The Lord is a Man of War'?" But this was said because the Holy and Blessed God said, "On account of your guilt, and on account of your sanctification, I will sanctify or prepare my name among you." There follows: "The Lord [the Tetragrammaton] is His name." For in His own name He Himself fights, and this is not suitable to any other of <term>His attributes</term><note>original Hebrew: ממדותיו, mimmiddothau</note>. And for this reason David said in 1 Samuel 17: "You come to me with a spear, and a sword, and a shield; but I come to you in the name of the Lord, or with the name of the Lord of Hosts." All this is tradition. From these things, three most worthy points are gathered. First, that God was going to so sanctify or prepare His name among the Jews that He Himself would be not only a man, but also a man of war. Second, that God was going to do this so that He might sanctify or cleanse them from their guilt or sin. Third, that for God to become a man of war suits none of the attributes of God, but only the property of His name. Fourth and final...

<column-break/>

<page-num>162</page-num>
<margin>From now on</margin>
...ly, it can be added to the aforementioned things that it is very difficult for faithless Jews to believe such things: since God fills heaven and earth, as proven here by Jeremiah—indeed, what is greater, since, as Solomon witnesses, the heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him, as is said in 2 Chronicles 2—how could it be credible, unless God had said it, that God Himself could become a Man? But he is surely too foolish and impious who suspects that those things which God Himself asserts are impossible, or seeks another author in them. From these things, therefore, which have been said in this tradition, it is concluded that this name "Man of War" suits God alone by reason of the property of His name (the Tetragrammaton). It remains now for us to show that the Messiah is the "Man of War." Therefore, those things which Rabbi Yochanan said in the chapter *Helec*<note>A famous chapter in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin (Chapter 11) concerning the afterlife and the Messiah.</note> are greatly to be noted concerning that which is said in Zechariah chapter 1: <note>original Hebrew: ראיתי הלילה והנה איש רכב על סוס אדם והוא עומד בין ההדסים אשר במצלה ואחריו סוסים אדמים שרקים ולבנים</note> "I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red or blood-colored horse: and he was standing among the myrtle trees that were in the valley: and behind him were red, dappled, and white horses." There, the same Rabbi says: "I saw," he said, "by night: for the Holy and Blessed God wished to turn the whole world into night: And behold, a man riding upon a red horse: this man is none other than the Holy and Blessed God: and he was standing among the myrtle trees: the myrtles are none other than the righteous: just as it is said in Esther chapter 2: And he was the foster-father of <term>Hadassah</term><note>original: הדסה; the Hebrew name for Queen Esther, derived from the word for myrtle.</note>, that is Esther, for *Hadas* in Hebrew is called *myrtus* in Latin." Thus far the tradition. For the understanding of this, it must be noted that in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term><note>The traditional Jewish commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note> on Psalm 20, it is read in this manner: "The Holy and Blessed God calls the Messiah by His own name." And what is His name? The Lord (the Tetragrammaton) is His name. Since, therefore, in the aforementioned tradition found in the chapter *Helec* of the book *Sanhedrin*, it is said that God the Man of War (as said in Exodus 15) is the Holy and Blessed God riding upon a red horse; and in the other preceding tradition which is found in *Midrash Tehillim* it is said that God calls the Messiah by His own name (the Tetragrammaton), and that God the Man of War is the Messiah himself, whose name is the Lord (the Tetragrammaton); it is necessarily consequent that the Messiah is God himself. For no one shares in this most glorious name with God (as was demonstrated in the preceding parts). Furthermore, the red horse upon which the Prophet saw the Holy and Blessed God riding is nothing other than the body of the Messiah, made red by his most precious blood in the battle of his passion, by which he was to conquer the devil. Therefore, he is not inaptly called "Man of War" in this place. Furthermore, the ancient Talmudists did not incongruously wish the righteous men and women to be figured here by the myrtles: since the Prophet said that God Himself, riding upon a red horse, stood among the myrtles that were in the valley, by which humility is designated. This was surely fulfilled then when (as is said in John chapter 19) there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene, and also John the Apostle: to whom he himself, standing and stretched out on the cross, commended his virgin mother as a virgin. Finally, the red horses that went out after him, none...

...are better than the Apostles and the other martyrs, who were made red by the blood of their martyrdom. But what of the dappled horses? Who are they more rightly called than the teachers and preachers, who are endowed with various lessons of doctrine and virtue? Like horses, they run to and fro, now here, now there, by writing and teaching. Furthermore, the white horses are none other than the virgins, both men and women, who are adorned with the brightness of snow-white virginity. All these are not without reason designated by horses, since horses are more fit for battle than other animals. Indeed, the Martyrs conquer the world; the Teachers or Preachers conquer the devil; and the Virgins conquer their own flesh by fighting. Thus it happens that these groups, above all other kinds of men, are granted the <term>aureola</term><note>A "golden crown" or celestial halo believed in medieval theology to be a special reward for martyrs, virgins, and teachers.</note> as a prize for victory in their heavenly fatherland.

### CHAP. XXII.

->*That the Messiah is not without reason often called David in the sacred page.*<-

->CAPNIO<-

<margin>A</margin> I find that the Messiah is many times called David and Solomon, which is highly relevant to our purpose against the <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> unbelief of the Jews of our age. Therefore, first prove that the Messiah himself was rightly called David, and then Solomon, by the Prophets and by the <term>Talmudists</term><note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>. GALATINUS: First, then, hear what is read word-for-word in the book *Sanhedrin* in the chapter *Helec*: "Rabbi Yehuda said: It shall come to pass that the Holy One, blessed be He, will himself raise up or establish for Israel another David, as it is said in Jeremiah chapter 30: <margin>chapter</margin> <note>original Hebrew: ועבדו את יהוה אלהיהם ואת דוד מלכם אשר אקים להם</note> 'And they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will raise up, or establish, for them.'" For he does not say "I have established," but "I will raise up." This is the tradition. Likewise, in the Jerusalem book *Berachoth* <note>The "Blessings" tractate of the Talmud.</note> in the chapter *Haia kore* (that is, "He was reading"), it is said: It is written in Hosea chapter 3: <note>original Hebrew: אחר ישבו בני ישראל ובקשו את יהוה אלהיהם ואת דוד מלכם ופחדו אל יהוה ואל טובו באחרית הימים</note> "Afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek the Lord their God, and David their King; and they shall fear the Lord, and his goodness in the end of days." The <term>Rabbanan</term><note>Aramaic for "The Masters" or "The Rabbis."</note> (that is, the Masters) said: "That King Messiah—if he is among the living, David is his name; if indeed he is among the dead, David is his name." This is the tradition, from which the point is made quite clearly. Furthermore, Rabbi Jonathan interpreted the aforementioned words of Hosea in this way in <term>Chaldean</term><note>The author refers to Aramaic, specifically the Targum or translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>: <note>original Aramaic: בתר כן יתובון בני ישראל ויתבעון ית פולחנא דיהוה אלההון וישתמעון למשיחא בר דוד מלכהון</note> "And after these things the children of Israel shall return, and seek the worship of the Lord their God, and shall obey the Messiah, the son of David their King." Finally, in the book *Sanhedrin* in the chapter *Helec*, it is read thus: "Rabbi Yehuda of the house of Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Samuel: That King Messiah—if he is among the living, David is his name; if indeed he is among the dead, David is his name." From these premises it is shown clearly enough—

<column-break/>

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>THIRD BOOK.</header>

—that Psalm 89 speaks of the Messiah. But if it speaks of the Messiah, why then must that saying of the same Psalm also be understood concerning the Messiah, when it says: <margin>A</margin> <note>original Hebrew: כרתי ברית לבחירי נשבעתי לדוד עבדי עד עולם אכין זרעך ובניתי לדור ודור כסאך : ויהו סלה</note> "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn to David my servant: Your seed I will establish forever, and I will build up your throne to generation and generation." And the heavens shall confess (or praise) your wonder, O God <note>original: "tetragrammaton" (the four-letter name of God, YHWH)</note>, and also <margin>B</margin> your faithfulness in the assembly of the saints. From the meeting of these words it is manifest that the Messiah is God. For God in this place addresses David, who, through what has been said, is established to be the Messiah. Since, therefore, He calls him by the name of four letters, which is <note>original Hebrew: יהוה (YHWH)</note>, and which can suit no one but God, it is shown openly and without doubt that the Messiah is God himself, not only man. This can be most especially <margin>C</margin> clear from the fact that those things said there suit the Messiah more than David himself. For in the person of God the Father, that which was stated is most fittingly said: namely, "I have made a covenant with my chosen"—which is to be understood of the Messiah according to his humanity, according to that which is said in Isaiah the forty-second chapter: <note>original Hebrew: הן עבדי אתמך בו בחירי רצתה נפשי</note> "Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen, in whom my soul (or my person) is well pleased." <margin>D</margin> That this is to be understood of the Messiah is clear through Rabbi Jonathan in the <term>Targum</term><note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> saying: <note>original Aramaic: הא עבדי משיחא מקר ביניה</note> "Behold my servant the Messiah, I will bring him near." Then it follows in the same Psalm, "I have sworn to David my servant," that is, to the Messiah, who will serve me by leading the lost sheep to the folds of paradise. Furthermore, that the Messiah is called David is held in the *Echa Rabbethi* (that is, in the exposition on the Lamentations of Jeremiah) regarding that which is said in the first <margin>E</margin> chapter of Lamentations: "Because the comforter is far from me." For there it is said: "Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Samuel: That King Messiah—if he is among the living, David is his name; if among the dead, David is his name." Rabbi Tanhuma said: "I say, as proof of this, that which is written in Psalm 18: <note>original Hebrew: מגדיל ישועות מלכו ועושה חסד למשיחו לדוד ולזרעו עד עולם</note> 'Magnifying the salvations of his King, and showing mercy to his Messiah, to David and to his seed forever.'" This is the tradition. Furthermore, Rabbi Jonathan teaches that this "David" is also to be understood as the Messiah in Jeremiah chapter 30: "And they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will establish for them." For Jonathan himself translated this <margin>F</margin> into Chaldean: <note>original Aramaic: ויפלחון קדם יהוה אלההון וישתמעון למשיחא בר דוד מלכהון דאקים להון</note> "And they shall worship before the Lord their God, and shall obey the Messiah, the son of David their King, whom I will establish for them." From which it is clear that Ezekiel chapter 34 should also be taken as referring to the Messiah: <note>original Hebrew: והושעתי לצאני ולא תהיינה עוד לבז ושפטתי בין שה לשה</note> <margin>G</margin> "And I will save my sheep, and they shall no longer be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle." Which Jonathan thus explained in Chaldean: "And I will deliver my people..."

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin>
"For my people, and they shall no longer be a prey; and I will judge between man and man. And I will set up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd." <note>original Hebrew: "לעמי ולא יחסרון עוד לביזוא ואירון בין גבר לגבר ואקים עליהון פרנסא חד ויפרנס יתהון ית עבדי דוד דהוא יהא יפרנס יתהון והוא יהי להון לפרנס" — This is a Targum (Aramaic translation/paraphrase) of Ezekiel 34:22-23.</note> That is: "And I will save my people, and they shall no more be a prey. And I will judge between man and man. And I will set over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David. He himself shall feed them, and he himself shall be a shepherd to them." Rightly, therefore, is it said in the aforementioned Psalm: "I have sworn to David my servant," that is, to the Messiah. What He swore to him, however, is shown when it immediately adds: <margin>B</margin> "I will establish or prepare your seed forever": that is, your disciples, and others believing in you. For disciples and others instructed by someone are rightly called both "children" and "seed" of the one by whom they were taught (as we shall show elsewhere). It follows: "And I will build up your throne to generation and generation" (namely, the Jewish and the Gentile generations) *sela* <note>original: "סלה"</note>, that is, perpetually or always.

<margin>C</margin> Since the Hebrew word *Sela* <note>A term often found in the Psalms, likely a musical or liturgical direction, but interpreted here by the author as a temporal marker of eternity.</note> which is placed there, has neither interruption nor end, and therefore can be translated as "into eternity," or "into the ages of ages," or "always," or "perpetually," it is indeed clear that the saying, "And I will build your throne unto generation and generation *sela*," that is, perpetually, can fit neither David the former King, nor any of his sons, but only the Lord Jesus, the true Messiah. His throne is the Christian people, established by divine power from two generations, namely the Jews and the Gentiles. <margin>D</margin> For more than one thousand four hundred years have now passed since the throne of David himself, or rather the kingdom of the Jews, was utterly destroyed and wiped out. Nor is Jewish <note>original: "prauitas" — a common but harsh medieval polemical term for "obstinacy" or "error."</note> stubbornness able to deny this, since in the book *Sota* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the "suspected adulteress" ritual.</note> in the chapter "The Beheaded Heifer" <note>original: "עגלה ערופה" (Egla Arupha). See Deuteronomy 21.</note>, it is written in this manner: "From the time the first house [the Temple] was destroyed, the cities of refuge ceased, and the *Urim and Thummim* departed" <note>original: "אורים ותומים" — sacred lots used by the High Priest to consult God; the author glosses them as "lights and simplicities."</note>, that is, the lights and perfections, and those things by which they consulted God; and the King was taken away from the house of David.

**P.** I would like you to prove through their writings as well that the other things connected to the Messiah in that same Psalm apply more to our Lord Jesus Christ than to David himself.

**GAL.** That will certainly be more clearly evident if we first bring forward the words of the Psalmist himself and translate them according to the Hebrew truth. <margin>E</margin> Thus, after some intervening verses, it is added in the same Psalm:

> ->Then you spoke in a vision to your saints and said: "I have placed help upon a mighty one; I have exalted one chosen from the people. That is: Then you spoke in a visio-

<margin>D</margin> That part, therefore, "Then you spoke in a vision to your saints," fits the Messiah most excellently, and consequently our Lord Jesus Christ. For it is written in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with the high court and legal procedures.</note> in the chapter *Helec*: "Rabbi Yohanan said thus: 'All the Prophets prophesied only until the days of the Messiah; but regarding the days of the world to come, eye has not seen [them].'" ### Chapter XXVI.

->*That the Messiah is many times called Solomon in the sacred scriptures, to suggest the incarnation of the Son of God, which was to come from the seed of David.*<-

#### CAPNIO <note>Capnio is the Latinized name of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist who acts as an interlocutor in this dialogue.</note>.

It remains for you to explain why the Messiah is called "Solomon" in the Jewish writings, and not without reason. 

**GALATINUS.** In many places where the divinity, incarnation, and redemption of the Messiah are expressed, it happens that He is called "Solomon." First, then, listen to what is said in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the Song of Solomon (Canticles).</note>, on that verse in the third chapter of the same book: "Go out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him" <note>Hebrew: צאנה וראנה בנות ציון במלך שלמה בעטרה שעטרה לו אמו</note>. There it is said literally: "Go out and see, daughters of Zion," that is, sons marked for me by tonsure, circumcision, and fringes, "King Solomon," that is, the most perfect King, who created all his creatures *Shelemoth* <note>original Hebrew: שלמה — a wordplay on "Solomon" and "perfection" or "completeness."</note>, that is, perfect. For He created the sun and the moon in their fullness. Adam and Eve were also created like youths of twenty years. Likewise, in another interpretation: "King Solomon," that is, the King whose

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> peace is peace. In another way: "King Solomon," that is, the peaceful King, who brought peace to His creatures through His works. Just as He brought peace to the fire for our father Abraham, and for the three youths Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He also brought peace to the sword of Isaac. Again, He also brought peace to the Angel of Jacob. In yet another way: "King Solomon," that is, the King who made peace among His creatures. Hence Rabbi Iohanan said: It is written in Job 25, "He makes peace in His high places." For the firmament is made of water, and the stars of fire, yet they do not destroy one another.

<margin>B</margin> It follows in the Song of Songs: "With the crown with which his mother crowned him." Rabbi Iohanan said that Rabbi Simon asked Rabbi Eleazar, the son of Rabbi Jose, and said to him: "Is it possible that you have heard from your father what is meant by 'the crown with which his mother crowned him'?" He answered him, "Yes." He said to him, "How so?" He told him, "In the beginning, the Holy and Blessed God loved Israel, and He called them 'my daughter' <note>Hebrew: בתי / Butti</note>. And this is what is written in Psalm 45: 'Hear, daughter, and see.'"

<margin>C</margin> "But He did not cease to love them until He called them 'my sister' <note>Hebrew: אחותי / Ahothi</note>: as it is said in Song of Songs 5: 'Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one.' Again, He still did not cease to love them until He called them 'my mother' <note>Hebrew: אמי / Immi</note>: as it is said in Isaiah 51: 'Attend to me, my people, and my mother, listen to me' <note>Hebrew: הקשיבו אלי עמי ולאומי אלי האזינו — The Latin text notes that while the standard text says 'my nation' (le'ummi), the interpretation reads it as 'my mother' (immi).</note>. For 'my nation' <note>Hebrew: לאומי / Lummi</note> was not written there, but 'my mother' <note>Hebrew: אמי / Immi</note>."

<margin>D</margin> Rabbi Simon rose and kissed him on the head, and said, "If I had come for no other reason than to hear this word from your mouth, it would have been enough for me" <note>Hebrew: דיי / Dai — 'enough'. This is a reference to the 'Dayenu' sentiment of gratitude.</note>. Rabbi Hanina said: "We have searched through all the scriptures, and we have not found that Bathsheba <note>Hebrew: בת-שבע</note> ever made a crown for her son Solomon." All this is found there. From these things it is held that the Synagogue <note>meaning the congregation or the Jewish people as a whole</note>, or the Jewish people, is called the mother of Solomon, that is, of God. This was also said through Hosea, although it was later changed by the Jewish scribes: so that from this it might be openly shown that the incarnation of God was to come from the Jews. They cannot deny this, since at the beginning of this aforementioned *Midrash* (exposition), Solomon is described as the Creator of things—which can apply neither to Solomon the son of David, nor to any mere man. The incarnation of this Solomon, that is, of the Son of God, is also openly hinted at in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>. For upon that verse of Psalm 4: "When I call, answer me, O God of my justice; in distress you have enlarged me" <note>Hebrew: בקראי ענני אלהי צדקי בצר הרחבת לי</note>, it is said word for word: "David was troubled and distressed concerning the wife of Uriah. For the Israelites were disparaging him and speaking behind his back, saying, 'Can there be salvation for one who stole a sheep and killed the shepherd?' But the Holy and Blessed God enlarged him, as it is said in 2 Samuel 12: 'And Nathan said to David, The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die.' And again it says in 1 Chronicles 22: 'Behold, a son is born to you; he shall be a man of rest, and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about: for Solomon shall be his name.' And what then? Were not all the other sons of David born to him? And what is meant by 'born to you' <note>Hebrew: נולד לך / Nolad lach</note>, that is,"

that is, "Is he born to you?" <note>original Latin: "Natus est tibi?"</note> To you, meaning for your care or for your healing—specifically for the healing of your sins that are within you. And by whose hand? By the hand of Nathan, as it is said in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 12 <note>This refers to 2 Samuel 12:25 in modern Bibles.</note>: "And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and called his name *Jedidiah* <note>Hebrew: ידיד-יה, meaning 'Beloved of the Lord'</note>, on account of <note>Hebrew: בעבור, *ba'avur*</note> the four-letter name of the Lord." All of this is part of the tradition. From this, it clearly appears that when the scripture says, "A son is born to you," along with what follows, all these things are to be understood as referring to the Messiah under the veil of Solomon's name, even though on the surface they seem to be said of Solomon.

For the things set forth in this exposition—namely, that a son was to be born to David to provide medicine for him and to heal him of his sins—cannot in any way apply to David’s son Solomon. Solomon himself was quite unfit to provide medicine for his own sins or to heal his own crimes, if one considers his works even briefly. For thus it is written of him in the Third Book of Kings, chapter 9 <note>1 Kings 11 in modern Bibles.</note>, among other things: "But King Solomon loved many foreign women, as well as the daughter of Pharaoh: women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and others from the nations concerning which the Lord had said to the children of Israel, 'You shall not go in to them, and they shall not come in to you, for they will surely turn your heart after their gods.' Solomon clung to these in love. And he had seven hundred wives who were princesses, and three hundred concubines. And his wives turned away his heart. And it came to pass in the time of Solomon's old age, when his wives turned his heart after strange gods, that his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father. And Solomon walked after *Ashtaroth* <note>Hebrew: עשתרות, a Sidonian goddess</note>, the goddess of the Sidonians, and after *Milcom* <note>Hebrew: מלכום</note>, the idol of the Ammonites. And Solomon did evil in the sight of the Lord, and did not fully follow the Lord like his father David. Then Solomon built an altar to *Chemos* <note>Hebrew: כמוש</note>, the idol of Moab, on the mountain facing Jerusalem, and to *Molech* <note>Hebrew: למלך</note>, the idol of the children of Ammon. And he did likewise for all his foreign wives who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods."

All of this is found there; I have not bothered to provide the Hebrew text here lest the length cause boredom, but I have striven to translate it word-for-word according to the Hebrew truth. If, therefore, hands that hold mud are unable to wipe away their own filth, much less the filth of another, it is certainly a great folly to believe that Solomon himself—so foully described here and so infected by his own faults—was sufficient to cure the faults of his father, or that one so defiled by his own uncleanness was fit to wash away his father's crimes.

Therefore, when it is said in the aforementioned tradition that David was to be healed of his sins through a son born to him whose name would be Solomon, this can by no means be understood of the shameful Solomon, but rather of the one under the veil of this name who is not only Solomon (meaning "the Perfecter" and "the Peaceful," as was said a little earlier in another tradition), but is also *Shalom* <note>Hebrew: שלום</note>, which means "Peace." This is just as it is said in the *Pethihath Rabbethi* <note>The "Great Prologue" to the Midrash on Lamentations.</note>, where we read: "Rabbi Jose the Galilean said: The name of the Messiah is also called *Shalom* (Peace), as it is said in the ninth chapter of Isaiah: 'Eternal Father, Prince of Peace' <note>Hebrew: שלום, *Shalom*</note>." To this Solomon, the son of David—that is, to the Messiah himself—it belongs to heal not only David his father, but also all who are to be saved, and to heal them from all their sins by the merit of his passion. This is according to Isaiah, chapter 53: "The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his wound we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, each of us has turned to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the sin or iniquity of us all" <note>Galatinus provides the Hebrew text for Isaiah 53:5-6 and then a literal Latin translation, here rendered into English.</note>.

Furthermore, the conclusion of the words written in the twenty-second chapter of the First Book of Chronicles clearly demonstrates that those words must be understood of the Messiah, the true Solomon, when it is said by the voice of God: "And he shall be to me as a son, and I will be to him as a father. And I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever" <note>Hebrew: והוא יהיה לי לבן ואני לו לאב והכנותי את כסא מלכותו על ישראל עד עולם</note>. This can in no way apply to Solomon, the son of Bathsheba, whose throne over Israel failed in the time of his son Rehoboam when Jeroboam began to reign over Israel. For thus it is written in the twelfth chapter of the First Book of Kings: "And Israel rebelled against the house of David until this day. And it happened when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the whole assembly and made him king over all Israel. And there was none following the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone." Moreover, the house of David (and consequently the house of Solomon) lost even this tribe of Judah during the time of the Greeks, when the Maccabees—whom the Jews call the *Hasmonai* <note>Hebrew: חשמונאו, the Hasmoneans</note>—obtained it.

<margin>Objection of the more recent Jews.</margin>
**CAPNIO:** Since it is first said in that passage, "He shall build a house for my name," and afterward it is added, "And he shall be to me as a son," with the other things you have brought forward, the Jews object to us that these words must be understood literally of Solomon, who built the temple to God, and not of the Messiah. And even if they were to be understood of the Messiah, they say they cannot be understood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who erected no material temple to God.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
**GALATINUS:** Just as "the house of Israel" and "the house of David" and such phrases in many places in Holy Scripture do not refer to a pile of stones and wood, but to the congregation of people itself; so also here, the "house of God" to be built by the spiritual Solomon (the Messiah) should be understood not as a material structure, but as a spiritual one, which in Greek is called the *Ecclesia* <note>meaning 'assembly' or 'church'</note>. Therefore, although the material Solomon built a material house for God, the spiritual Solomon (the Messiah) was to build a spiritual house for Him—one far more excellent and far more perfect—made of "living and chosen stones," which are the Jews and Gentiles who were to believe in him. Just as the ancient Talmudists interpreted Solomon here mystically as the Messiah...

So too here, through the material house of God which was to be built by the physical Solomon, we must understand the Church of the faithful which was to be gathered together by the Messiah. All of these things will become more manifest if those preceding words are correctly examined. For when David was thinking of building a house for the Lord, the Prophet Nathan spoke to him in the person of the Lord, as is held in the seventeenth chapter of the first book of Chronicles <note>original Latin: "primi libri Paralipomenon," the Greek-derived name for the Book of Chronicles</note>: <margin>A</margin> **And it shall come to pass, when your days are fulfilled to go be with your fathers, that I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall be of your sons; and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son; and I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it from him that was before you. But I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever; and his throne shall be established for evermore.** <note>The Hebrew text provided in the manuscript corresponds to 1 Chronicles 17:11-14</note>. This means: "When you have completed your days to go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who will be from your sons. And I will establish his Kingdom. He himself will build a house for me, and I will strengthen his throne into eternity. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. And I will not take my mercy from him, as I took it from him who was before you. And I will station him in my house and in my Kingdom even into eternity. And his throne shall be most firm for evermore." So it says there: things which can in no way be understood as referring to Solomon. This is easily and clearly evident if the words themselves are correctly considered (as is proper). For when he says, "When you have completed your days to go to your fathers"—that is, "when you are dead, I will raise up your seed after you"—it is clear that this was not said of Solomon, since Solomon himself was created King while his father was still living. Furthermore, if he had wished to speak of Solomon, he certainly would not have said "who shall be of your sons," but "who shall be of you." Also, what follows—"And I will station him in my house and in my Kingdom even into eternity, and his throne shall be most firm for evermore"—is openly recognized as not being said of Solomon. For Solomon was neither stationed in God's house or Kingdom, nor was his throne "most firm." And since such stability belongs to God alone, it follows plainly that the one being discussed was to be both God and man. Therefore, by that "house" which he was to build, we understand the Holy Church, which was to be built upon the most solid and firm rock. Concerning this, it is written in the ninety-third Psalm <margin>B</margin> <note>Psalm 93:5</note> **Holiness is beautiful for your house, O LORD, for length of days.** <note>original Hebrew: לביתך נאוה קדש יהוה לאורך ימים</note>. From the aforesaid, therefore, it is clearly evident that according to the divine scriptures and the Talmudic traditions, the Messiah was called "Solomon" to hint at his incarnation, which was to come from the seed of David. For this reason, he was also called "David," as was seen more extensively in the preceding chapter.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

->*On the fellowship of divinity and humanity. And on God’s equality and participation with man.*<-

->CAPNIO.<- <note>"Capnio" was the Greek pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist of the Renaissance.</note>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "A" featuring a classical figure seated in a landscape with architectural elements in the background.</image-desc>You have spoken enough and in great detail in the preceding sections about the names of the Messiah, by which both the incarnation of the Son of God and the dual nature of the Messiah himself—namely, the divine and the human—are excellently suggested. Therefore, you ought now to say something also about those things which express that same incarnation of the Son of God. Thus, when you have proved that the Messiah—whom the younger generation of Jews assert will be a mere man—was to be simultaneously God and man, mixed from both natures, their lack of faith may be more evidently refuted. Wherefore, first show the fellowship of divinity and humanity, and the future equality and participation of God with man. <margin>B</margin> GALATINUS: Concerning the fellowship, participation, and equalization of God with man—through which the firmness of our faith is greatly strengthened and the wickedness of the Jews of our time, who deny the incarnation of the Son of God, is countered in many ways—certainly many things are found said by their own ancient scholars in their books. First, therefore, we must hear what Isaiah says in chapter 35 in these words: <margin>C</margin> **God himself, the retribution, will come and save you.** <note>original Hebrew: גמול אלהים הוא יבא ויושעכם</note>. This means: "The retribution of God, or the retribution, or the reward, or the prize—God himself will come and save you." Rabbi Jonathan, in the Targum <note>The Targum is an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>, explained it thus: **The Lord God himself will be revealed.** <margin>D</margin> **He will be revealed and will save them.** <note>original Aramaic: יתגלי ויפרוק להון</note>. Here, because Rabbi Jonathan explained it as "God himself will reveal himself," where the Prophet said "God himself will come," it is openly shown that the "coming" of God is nothing other than his "revealing" himself, according to the exposition of the ancient Jews. For since God, through his immensity, is present everywhere and is contained in no place, it is quite clear that the Son of God was not going to come according to his nature as God, but according to this: that having assumed human flesh and been made visible, he ought to appear as a man. For if he were to come only as God, he would not have "come" to those who were unable to see him. Such a God, therefore, was to come to us as we are able to see. Unless, therefore, he had been going to assume the form of a visible nature, he would least of all have been said to "come" to us. The ancient fathers understood this perfectly, as noted in that saying from Isaiah chapter 25: <margin>E</margin> **And they shall say in that day, behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him, and we will rejoice and be glad in his salvation.** <note>original Hebrew: ואמר ביום ההוא הנה אלהינו זה קוינו לו ויושיענו זה יהוה קוינו לו נגילה ונשמחה בישועתו</note>. These words are to be explained in no other way than how the ancient Talmudists themselves explained them. They taught through these words that there would eventually be a time when the world would see God with its eyes, and people would point him out to one another with a finger. For in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A traditional Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note> regarding that verse from Psalm 40, <margin>F</margin> **Waiting, I have waited,** <note>original Hebrew: קוה קויתי</note> it is said: "This is what is written in Isaiah chapter 25: 'And it shall be said in that day, Behold, this is our God; we have expected him, and he will save us.'" And it is also said in Lamentations chapter 3: "God is good to those who wait for him." For because the nations of the world do not cease saying, "Where is their God?", it is destined that the Holy and Blessed God will sit in the midst of the righteous, and they will point him out with a finger; as it is said in Psalm 48: <margin>G</margin> **For this is God, our God forever and ever: he will lead us even unto death.** <note>original Hebrew: כי זה אלהים אלהינו עולם ועד הוא ינהגנו על מות</note>. Especially if we attend to the words of Job himself, which immediately precede this text: <note>original Hebrew: ואני ידעתי גאלי חי ואחרון על עפר יקום: ואחר עורי נקפו זאת ומבשרי אחזה אלוה</note> That is: **And I know that my redeemer lives. And at the last he shall rise upon the earth; and afterward these things shall be wrapped in my skin. And from my flesh I shall see God.** <note>Job 19:25-26</note> In what sense this God is called the "last" in the flesh, and who or of what sort he may be, Isaiah clearly shows in chapter 44, saying: <note>original Hebrew: כה אמר יהוה מלך ישראל וגאלו יהוה צבאות אני ראשון ואני אחרון</note> That is: **Thus says the Lord** <note>represented by the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note> **the King of Israel and his redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first and I am the last.** <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> Also in the book called *Siphre* <note>Sifra, a legalistic commentary on Leviticus</note>, regarding that saying in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus: <note>original Hebrew: והתהלכתי בתוככם והייתי לכם לאלהים ואתם תהיו לי לעם</note> That is: **And I will walk in the midst of you, and will be your God, and you shall be my people.** It is read in this manner: They illustrated this by an example, saying that this matter is like a King who went out to walk with his gardener in an orchard, and that gardener shrank back from the presence of the King. The King then said to him: "Why do you shrink back from my presence? Behold, I am just like you." So it shall be in the time to come, when the Holy and Blessed God walks with the righteous in the paradise of pleasure. But the righteous, seeing him, will tremble at his presence. Then the Holy and Blessed God will say to them: "Why do you tremble at my presence? Behold, I am conformed to you; I am even as you are, and I am similar to you." But because I said to you, "Behold, I am as you are," will it be possible that you should not have reverence for me? He teaches what must be said to this in what follows in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus: **And I will be your God, and you shall be my people.** If you do not believe me from all these words, believe because I am your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt. This is from the Talmud. Nearly the same thing is written in the book *Taanith* <note>A volume of the Talmud concerning fast days</note>, at the end of the chapter which begins *Bislosa perakim*: where it is said: Rabbi Eleazar said that Rabbi Halabu said: In the future, the Holy and Blessed God will make a circular dance for the righteous in the garden of pleasure. And he himself will stand in their midst, and each one of them will point him out with his finger; as it is said in Isaiah 25: **And they shall say in that day: Behold, this is our God, we have waited**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **for him, and he will save us. This is the Lord for whom we have waited; we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.** <note>Isaiah 25:9</note> This is the tradition. If, therefore (as they themselves say), traditions and explanations of this kind were handed down from God to Moses on Mount Sinai, they must necessarily concede—unless they have an entirely blinded intellect—that through the texts introduced in these traditions, as well as by what their ancient masters said regarding those same texts, God was to become human, while always preserving the glory of his divinity in all things.

<margin>B</margin> This "walking" can in no way be appropriate for God [simply as God], since walking means to be moved from place to place. This is impossible for God the Creator according to the nature of divinity, as is agreed by all wise men; it is entirely unsuitable, just as it is for him to be capable of corruption. For "walking" is said to be the property of a creature that possesses a body and feet. Furthermore, God is in every place, though not locally <note>i.e., not confined to a specific physical spot</note>, and he fills the whole world: as is gathered from Jeremiah, who says: **Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.**

<margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, God is everywhere and is essentially absent from nowhere, it follows that he cannot desert one place and go to another, which is what "walking" is. For that is entirely contrary to the nature of divinity.

<margin>D</margin> **GALATINUS:** <note>GAL. likely refers to the author, Galatinus, speaking in his own voice</note> Therefore, for the fulfillment of God's promise (who said in Leviticus 26, "I will walk in your midst," as we have just related), and for the truth of Holy Scripture (which asserts many things of this kind about God), and also for the confirmation of the aforementioned traditions (which seem to explain scriptures of that sort in favor of the truth of our faith), we say most briefly: God spoke through the Prophets in such a way as to openly suggest that he would one day unite a human being to himself in such a true and such a powerful union, that when the man united to him was seen, God himself would be said to be seen. And when that man walked among other men, God himself could truly be said to walk. And we, pointing at that same man with our finger, could truly say: "This is our God."

<margin>E</margin> Baruch also confirms this excellently, when in chapter 3 he says: <note>original Hebrew provided in text</note> That is: **This is our God, and no other shall be esteemed in comparison with him. He found out all the way of wisdom, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men.** <note>Baruch 3:35-37</note>

<margin>F</margin> What could be said clearer than these words? What plainer? What more evident? What more manifest? For if it is certain that God, according to his divinity, can neither be seen by eyes nor converse with men—since only colors are seen, and conversation properly occurs between those of the same essence <note>original Greek: ὁμοουσίους (homoousious), meaning "of one substance"</note>—the Jews must necessarily concede that it was surely to be that God would one day become human, so that according to his humanity he could both be seen with eyes and converse with men. For this reason, he is frequently called "brother of Israel" and "his kinsman" in the sacred writings.

<summary>This page argues that ancient Jewish oral traditions and scriptures like Isaiah and Leviticus predict the Incarnation, explaining that God "walking" among men refers to Him taking a physical human form. The author uses Rabbinic parables and the Book of Baruch to bridge the gap between God's invisible, omnipresent nature and His visible presence as the Messiah.</summary>

### BOOK THREE

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

->*That God was called the brother of Israel, and that the Messiah is the one intended to show that God, by assuming our nature, was to become our brother.*<-

### CAPNIO.

This is the point you must most clearly reveal here: that to signify the future incarnation of the Son of God, God himself was called the "brother of Israel" by the ancient Jews. This is easily seen first in the book *Mechilta* <note>An early Rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus</note>, that is, in the exposition of Exodus. There, commenting on the verse in Exodus chapter 14, "Why do you cry out to me?", it is read: Rabbi Halcusi said, and does not the Scripture already say in Proverbs chapter 17: **At all times a friend loves, and a brother is born for adversity?** <note>original Hebrew: בכל עת אהב הרע ואח לצרה יולד</note> This refers to God, holy and blessed, who said: "I will be a brother to Israel in the hour of their trouble or distress." Just as it is said in Psalm 122: **For the sake of my brothers and my friends (or neighbors, or companions), I will now speak peace within you.** <note>original Hebrew: למען אחי ורעי אדברה נא שלום בך</note> Thus far the tradition. From this it is clearly held that God is called the friend and brother of Israel, who according to his humanity was to be born for adversity.

Regarding the truth of the aforementioned tradition, it is strongly supported by what is written in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the verse in Psalm 4: "Hear me when I call, O God of my righteousness." For there it is read literally: Rabbi Jodan said, "One who turns to or runs after flesh and blood <note>a Hebrew idiom for a mortal human being</note> has a patron. But when the time of trouble or distress arrives, he does not immediately enter into the patron's presence. Instead, he comes and stands before the patron’s gate and calls his servant, and the servant says, 'Look, he is waiting before the gate.' God, holy and blessed, does not act this way. For when the time of trouble or distress comes to Israel, he will not call Michael or Gabriel, but will call upon God himself, and He himself will hear him." And this is what is written in Joel chapter 2 <note>Joel 3 in some older Latin numbering</note>: **And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) shall be delivered.** <note>original Hebrew: והיה כל אשר יקרא בשם יהוה ימלט</note>

And further down: Rabbi Simeon said: "Flesh and blood has a *karob* <note>original Hebrew: קרוב</note>, that is, a kinsman or relative, and if that kinsman is wealthy, he will acknowledge him. But God, holy and blessed, does not act this way. For when Israel is in a state of humility, then He calls them brothers and relatives, just as it is said in Psalm 122: 'For the sake of my brothers and my relatives, I will now speak peace within you.'" Likewise, further down: Rabbi Aben, in the name of Rabbi Aha, said: "Flesh and blood having a *karob* (that is, a relative) who is a captive or plundered, is ashamed to acknowledge that he is his relative. But God, holy and blessed, caused the captive and plundered Israel to be led out, and yet he expressly calls them *kerouim* <note>plural of karob</note>, that is, relatives or kinsmen; as it is said in Psalm 148: **For the children of Israel, a people near (or related) to him, Hallelujah.**" <note>original Hebrew: לבני ישראל עם קרובו הללויה</note> And again further down, God, holy and blessed, said in

<column-break/>

Isaiah 65: **And it shall be, that before they call, I will answer; and I will hear.** Although this is so, it is nevertheless necessary that their calling be done in truth; as it is said in Psalm 145: **The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.** <note>original Hebrew: קרוב יהוה לכל קראיו לכל אשר יקראוהו באמת</note> Is it possible for him to be near to everyone who calls on him? What follows teaches us what should be said to this: "To all who call upon him in truth." Thus far the tradition.

From this it clearly appears that God is the brother, the relative, and the patron of Israel, and all who call upon him in truth shall be delivered by him from their adversities. Now, therefore, it remains to be proved that this God, holy and blessed, who is so often called the brother, kinsman, and relative of Israel, is the Messiah. This is openly shown by both the *Midrash* and the *Targum* <note>The Aramaic translation or paraphrase</note> of *Shir HaShirim*, that is, the exposition or gloss and the Chaldean translation of the Song of Songs, regarding the verse in Song of Songs chapter 8: **Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother? If I found you outside, I would kiss you; and yet they would not despise me. I would lead you and bring you into my mother's house; you would teach me.** <note>original Hebrew: מי יתנך כאח לי יונק שדי אמי אמצאך בחוץ אשקך גם לא יבוזו לי אנהגך אביאך אל בית אמי תלמדני</note>

For the *Midrash* (the gloss) says there: "The Assembly of Israel spoke these words to God, holy and blessed. And He said to her, 'What kind of brother shall I be to you? Shall I be like Cain was to Abel?' For Cain killed Abel, as it is said in Genesis chapter 4: 'And Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him.' 'Or like Ishmael was to Isaac? Or like Esau to Jacob? Or like the brothers of Joseph to Joseph, who hated him?' As it is said in Genesis 37: 'And they hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him.' And again, 'And his brothers envied him.' 'What kind of brother, then, shall I be to you?' Behold, it must be said: 'Like Joseph was to Benjamin, who loved him as his own heart'; as it is said in Genesis chapter 43: 'And Joseph saw Benjamin his brother, the son of his mother, and Joseph made haste, for his compassion was moved toward his brother, and he wanted to weep.'"

It follows: "I will lead you, and bring you in." This means: "I will lead you down from the higher things to the lower things" <note>Interpretation: from heaven to earth, implying the Incarnation</note>. "I will bring you into my mother's house"—this refers to Sinai. Rabbi Berechiah said: "Why is Sinai called my mother's house? Because from there Israel was made like a suckling, or an infant son of one day." This is the tradition.

Furthermore, the *Targum* (the Aramaic edition of Rabbi Jonathan) explains those words of the Song of Songs, "Who will give you to me as my brother?", along with the rest, in Aramaic as follows: "When the King Messiah reveals himself to the Assembly of Israel, the children of Israel will say to him, 'You shall be a brother to us.'" Likewise, the Jerusalem *Targum* (otherwise called the Vulgate Edition) translates and explains the same words in Aramaic thus: "In that time the King Messiah shall be revealed to the Assembly of Israel, and the children of Israel shall say to him: 'Come, you shall be to us as a brother, and we shall go up to Jerusalem, and we shall suck with you the meanings of the Law, just as an infant sucks from its mother's breasts.'" There follows in the text: "I will lead you and bring you into my mother's house; you shall teach me." The *Targum* of Rabbi Jonathan explains this as: "I will lead you, the King Messiah; I will bring you into the house of my sanctuary. And you shall teach me."

You will teach me to fear before the face of God and to walk in his ways, and there we will dine upon the feast of *Leviathan*." <note>A traditional Jewish metaphor for the banquet at the end of time</note> Therefore, from these Targums—that is, from these ancient Aramaic expositions—it is most clearly evident that the King Messiah is that "brother of the Church" whom the preceding Midrash <note>A Rabbinic commentary</note> asserted was the holy and blessed God, brought down from the highest realms to the lowest. This same point is also excellently shown in *Beresith Rabba*, that is, in the Great Exposition on Genesis. Although many of the things previously mentioned are repeated there, it is not useless to report them two or three times as they are read in various books, if only to further confound more recent Jewish interpretations. Thus, the aforementioned *Beresith Rabba*, commenting on that saying in Genesis chapter 28, "And Jacob went out," says exactly this: "It is written in Zechariah chapter 4: **Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel?** This 'great mountain' is the Messiah." In it, many things are set down that are most worthy of reporting for our faith. Namely: that the Messiah is called a "great mountain," meaning greater than the Patriarchs and the ministering angels of God, who are more excellent than all others according to the traditions of the ancient Talmudists. Also, that he himself is the helper coming from God. And that the God of Jacob is in him. And that God is a citizen, a neighbor, or a kinsman, and a brother of Israel. To prove this, the previously mentioned authority of the Song of Songs is brought in, namely: **Who will give you to me as my brother?** which the Targum (as has been seen) explains as referring to the Messiah. Consistent with these things, and truly wonderful, is what is written in the book *Tanhuma* <note>An early collection of homiletic Midrashim</note> regarding that verse in Leviticus chapter 25: **If your brother becomes poor and sells some of his possession, and his redeemer, a relative or kinsman near to him, comes and redeems it.** <note>original Hebrew: כי ימוך אחיך ומכר מאחוזתו ובא גאלו הקרב אליו וגאל</note> For it is said there: **And his redeemer shall come**—this is the holy and blessed God; as it is said in Jeremiah chapter 50: **Their redeemer is strong, the Lord of hosts is his name; he will surely plead their cause** <note>original: גאלם חזק יהוה צבאות שמו ריב יריב את ריבם</note> (or "fighting, he will fight their war"): **a relative or kinsman to him.** This is the holy and blessed God; as it is said in Psalm 148: **And he shall exalt the horn of his people, the praise or joy for all his saints (or his kind ones), for the children of Israel, a people near or related to him, Hallelujah** <note>original Hebrew: הללו יה</note>, that is, "Praise the Lord." This is the tradition. Concerning this, I wish to ask three things of the Jews: Namely, how has the holy and blessed God become kin or near to Israel? From what prison or captivity was he to redeem man? And what was their "cause" which he was to plead, or what was their "war" which he was to fight?

### CAPNIO.
Because I know the Jews can in no way respond to these things rationally and correctly (for they are struck by God with insanity, blindness, and stupor), you yourself should answer them according to the Christian truth.

### GALATINUS.
Thus, the holy and blessed God then became kin and near to Israel when the soul and body of the Messiah were assumed by the "Soul of God," which is the Word and Wisdom and the Son of God (as will be proven a little further below). ### BOOK THREE. 180

...my spirit upon him: He will bring forth judgment to the nations. Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets</note>, translating this into Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaicè"</note>, explained these words as: "Behold my servant the Messiah, I will bring him near; my chosen one, in whom my Word <note>original: "Memra"</note> has taken delight. I will put my Holy Spirit upon him, or through him. He will reveal judgment to the nations." And a little later in Isaiah it is added: "He will set judgment in the earth. And the islands will wait for his law." Jonathan likewise explained these words by turning them into Aramaic as: "He will establish judgment on the earth, and the nations will hope in his law." This is sufficient for the first question. Regarding the remaining two, the answer will be clear in the following sections. 

**CHAPTER:** Since the Prophet, speaking in the person of God, said: "My chosen one in whom my soul is well pleased," what is understood there by the "soul" of God? 

**GALATINUS:** Where the Prophet speaks in the person of God and says "My soul," Jonathan there translated it as "My Word." For as you have heard, he says with the voice of God: "My chosen one, in whom my Word has taken delight." Therefore, I dare to say that the "soul of God" there is nothing other than the Son of God, who is also called the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, and the Power of God. From all the preceding points, it is abundantly clear that to hint at the future incarnation of the Son of God—and the kinship between the divine and human natures in Christ—God was many times called a relative or kinsman, and the brother of Israel, by the ancient Jews.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

->*That God himself would teach men with his own mouth, and that this is the Messiah.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

I remember reading in many books of the Jews that at some point it was destined for God himself to take up a familiar association with men and teach them with his own mouth. From this, the divine incarnation itself is most strongly hinted at. 

**GALATINUS:** It is exactly as you say. For we read this in the *Midrash Midbar Sinai* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the book of Numbers</note>, on the 23rd chapter, at the place where it is written: "As in time it will be said to Jacob and to Israel: What has God done?" <note>Numbers 23:23</note>. The eye of Balaam saw that the people of Israel would sit before the Lord in the future, just as a disciple sits before a master, asking him about every <term>parashah</term> <note>a section or chapter of the Torah</note> why it was written. As it is said in Isaiah chapter 23: "For those who sit before the Lord shall have merchandise, to eat until they are satisfied, and to be clothed in precious, or strong garments." And again in chapter 30 it says: "And your teacher shall no longer fly away [be hidden]. And your eyes shall see 

<column-break/>

your teacher." And the ministering angels will ask them, saying: "What has the holy and blessed God taught you?" They will say this because they will not have the power to enter into the midst of the people; as it is said in Numbers chapter 23: "As in time it will be said to Jacob and to Israel: What has God done?" So far the tradition. 

Rabbi Shelomo <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> showed that this was to be fulfilled in the days of the Messiah when he explains the words of Isaiah first brought up in that tradition, along with some preceding verses. For where Isaiah chapter 23 says: "And her merchandise and her hire shall be a sanctuary, or holiness to the Lord," his gloss says: "It will come to pass that the righteous will disregard those things when the King Messiah comes." And this is what is written consequently in the same Prophet: "It shall not be stored in a granary, nor shall it be treasured up; for to those who sit, or dwell, before God, there will be merchandise, that they may eat to satiety and be clothed in precious or strong garments." Rabbi Jonathan translated these things into Aramaic thus: "And her merchandise shall be holy before God. It shall not be gathered into a granary, nor shall it be treasured, because for those who minister before God there shall be a reward, that they may eat to satiety and be clothed in precious things." 

What is read in the book *Siphre* <note>An ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> also fits this purpose perfectly. When commenting on that saying in Deuteronomy chapter 32: "Remember the days of old, consider the years of generation after generation," it says: Moses said to them: "In the time when the Place itself—that is, God—brings tribulations upon you in this world, remember how many good things and how many consolations He is going to give you in the world to come." It follows: "Consider the years of generation after generation." This is the generation of the Messiah, in which there are three generations, as it is said in Psalm 72: "They shall fear you with the sun and before the moon, for a generation of generations." It follows in Deuteronomy chapter 32: "Ask your father, and he will declare it to you." For it will come to pass that Israel shall be seeing and hearing, as those who hear from the mouth of the holy and blessed God, according to the sense in which it was said in Isaiah chapter 30: "This is the way, walk in it, whether to the right or to the left." And again it is said in the same Prophet in the same place: "And God shall give you the bread of narrowness and the water of affliction; but your teacher shall no longer fly away [be hidden], or, your teacher shall no longer cover himself with a wing. And your eyes shall see your teacher." 

All this is the tradition. But Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, translated these last words of Isaiah into Aramaic as: "And his Divinity <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> shall no longer depart from the house of the sanctuary, and your eyes shall be seeing his Divinity." Where the Prophet first said "your teacher" and then "your teacher" again, Jonathan in the Targum (as now seen) placed "His Divinity." From this it is surely clear that it was destined for men to have God as their teacher, whom they would see with their eyes, and from whom the way of truth would be learned. This certainly could not have happened unless it were destined for God to become man from both natures—divine...
