### BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> although it is also mixed with the human. Regarding that word, "The bread of adversity and the water of affliction," <note>Isaiah 30:20</note> the commentary <note>original: "glossa"</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says this: "You will not have the opportunity to pursue pleasures as you have done until now." As it is said in Amos, chapter 6: <term>השותים במזרקי יין</term> <note>original: "Ha-shotim be-mizreke yayin"</note> which means, **Those who drink wine in bowls.** For when you were pursuing pleasures, you were unable to see God, the Holy and Blessed One. Just as it is said in Isaiah 6: <term>השמן לב העם הזה ואזניו הכבד</term> <note>original: "Hashemen lev ha-am ha-zeh ve-oznav hakbed"</note> <margin>B</margin> **and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes.** But when you have eaten little, your eyes will see your teacher, <term>ולא יכנף</term> ***Velo iuccaneph***, that is, **And he shall not be veiled from you by the wing of his cloak.** It is as if he were saying: your teacher will not hide his face from you. <term>מוריך</term> ***Morecha***, that is, **your teacher**—which is God, the Holy and Blessed One—who will teach you <term>להועיל</term> ***Lehoil***, that is, **to benefit**, or **to ascend.** These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

From these things, the significant error of some of our people is evident. For where the Jewish tradition <note>original: "Iudaica prauitas," literally "Jewish depravity," a common polemical term for Jewish interpretation that the author here surprisingly uses to support his own point</note> asserts that this teacher is God, audible and visible according to the literal sense—which fits perfectly with the Messiah as God and man—those others affirm that this same teacher was Ezra, according to the letter. This is easily seen to be entirely false, because that saying of Isaiah—"And your teacher will not fly away from you"—cannot apply to Ezra, nor to any mere human being, but only to him who finally said to those who believed in him and those who would believe, in the last chapter of Matthew: **Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.** For although he went to the Father in his humanity, nevertheless, in the form by which he is equal to the Father, he never departs from his faithful ones.

It is also highly noteworthy that the aforementioned tradition, explaining that passage in Deuteronomy 32, "Consider the years of generation and generation," <note>Deuteronomy 32:7</note> speaks in this way: "This is the generation of the Messiah, in whom there are three generations." Here, it should be understood that nothing else is being said—that the generation of the Messiah is "generation and generation," and yet in him there are three generations—except that the Messiah’s generation is twofold: the divine, by which he was begotten by the Father before all ages, and the human, by which he was born of a mother in time. Consequently, it follows that there are "generations"—namely three substances: the body, the soul, and the divinity. And again, these two and three are the one Messiah.

To the things already said, we may fittingly connect what is read in the preface of the *Midrash* <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary</note>, that is, the exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, in these words: "In the future, God, the Holy and Blessed One, will sit and explain the meaning of the law before the righteous, revealing it to them through the hands of the Messiah." As it is said in Proverbs 2: <term>יצפן לישרים תושיה מגן להולכים</term> <note>original: "Yitzpon la-yesharim tushiyah magen la-holechim"</note> This means: **He reserves, or hides, wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk simply, or perfectly.** Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra said: "He conceals the King’s law, because he hides from them the word of wisdom until its time comes, and he shall explain it with his own mouth before the masters." And regarding this, it is said in Proverbs 15: <term>ודבר בעתו מה טוב</term> <note>original: "Ve-davar be-ito mah tov"</note> That is: **And a word in its season, how good it is!** Thus far the tradition.

From all these things that have been said, it is clearly evident that God, with his own mouth, was to be the teacher of men, having been made visible and audible. This was undoubtedly fulfilled when the Son of God, having assumed human flesh, was made visible and audible; being found in appearance as a man, he taught his disciples and the crowds of people, and when questioned by the Scribes and Pharisees, he answered their questions.

### CHAPTER XXX.

->*That God should be made equal to the Church, and that the Messiah was to be the head of the Church.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> To suggest this incarnation of the Son of God (as I judge), God himself called the Church his sister and companion, saying in the 5th chapter of the Song of Songs: <term>פתחי לי אחותי רעיתי יונתי תמתי</term> <note>original: "Pitchi li achoti rayati yonati tamati"</note> That is: **Open to me, my sister,** <margin>C</margin> **my companion, my dove, my perfect one.**

**GALATINUS:** It is certainly as you say. But another, greater mystery lies hidden in those words, which is most relevant to our purpose. For where it is now written <term>תמתי</term> ***tammathi***, meaning **my perfect one**, Solomon actually wrote <term>תאומתי</term> ***teummathi***, which means **my twin**. For the ancient Talmudists testify that it was written this way. We read in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>The Midrash on the Song of Songs</note>, in the exposition of this text, that Rabbi Immai said that <term>תאומתי</term> ***teummathi***, meaning **my twin**, <margin>D</margin> was what was written. From what is written in the law, this can be stated. Rabbi Judah said there in the name of Rabbi Levi: "My twin" was said by God because, just as it happens with twins of this kind—that if the body of one feels something, the other is immediately troubled and stirred—so it can be said from what is in the law, because God said in Psalm 91: **I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him, and honor him, and I will show him my salvation.**

This is the tradition. From which it is clearly shown that God and the Church were to be like two twins. And then God, existing alongside man and preserving him, would be honored and would deliver him from tribulation. This cannot be understood except as the Incarnation. From this, it is plainly inferred that the Messiah was to have a dual nature: divine and human. Thus, in the one, he would be true and perfect God; in the other, true and perfect man.

<margin>CAPNIO.</margin> According to which nature was the Messiah to be the head of the Church? Was it according to <margin>I</margin> the divine nature, or the human nature, or both together?

**GALATINUS:** I say according to both together, although far more according to the human than according to the divine. For he ought to be the head of the Church more properly according to that nature which made it more fitting for the Church to be his mystical body. But according to his human nature, it is much more fitting for the universal Church of Christ to be his mystical body than according to his <margin>G</margin> divine nature, since he properly has members <note>limbs or body parts</note> according to his human nature, and not according to his divine nature. Therefore, although the Messiah was to be the head of the Church according to both natures, he is so far more properly according to the human. <margin>CAPNIO.</margin>

### BOOK THREE.

<margin>The Messiah to be the head of the Church.</margin>In order to more fully expose the faithlessness of the Jews, it must be proven in this place that the Messiah was to be the head of the entire Church, which was to be gathered from both Jews and Gentiles. **GALATINUS:** First, therefore, I will bring forward Hosea, who speaks openly about this "head" and "body" in his first chapter: <term>ונקבצו בני יהודה ובני ישראל יחדו ושמו להם ראש אחד ועלו מן הארץ כי גדול יום יזרעאל</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-nikbetzu benei Yehudah u-venei Yisrael yachdu ve-shamu lahem rosh echad ve-alu min ha-aretz ki gadol yom Yizre’el"</note> These words are interpreted thus: **And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head. And they shall go up from the land: for great is the day of Jezreel.** <note>Hosea 1:11</note> Regarding this, the commentary <note>original: "glossa"</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> says: **And they shall appoint for themselves one head**, namely, David their King. **For great shall be the day of Jezreel**, that is, the day of the gathering of their seed. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. 

Moreover, all of this was fulfilled when the Apostles and the other disciples of Christ (some of whom were from the tribe of Judah, such as James, John, the other James, and his brothers, and some from each of the other tribes) were gathered together into the one faith of Christ along with converts from the Gentiles; and they appointed for themselves one head, David their King, which is to say, the Messiah. That "David" is understood to mean the Messiah has been made widely clear in the preceding sections, where among other things it was said that whether the Messiah be among the living or the dead, his name is David. 

The prophecy continues: **And they shall go up from the land**, meaning, from earthly perception and way of life, and from the humility of the literal letter, to the height of spiritual understanding. **For great is the day of Jezreel**, which in Latin sounds like "what God will sow" <note>the name Jezreel translates to "God sows"</note>. For that day was great, not only in duration but also in miracles and many other things, which God sowed throughout the world through the Apostles and the other disciples of Christ and their successors, so that they might bring forth the fruit of preaching. He has not ceased to sow this even until now, nor will He ever cease to sow it until the end of the world. 

Therefore, it came to pass that the Gentiles, who were not the people of God, became the people of God. Hosea himself well predicted this through the voice of God in the second chapter, saying: <term>וזרעתיה לי בארץ ורחמתי את לא רחמה ואמרתי ללא עמי עמי אתה והוא יאמר אלהי</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-zara'tiha li ba-aretz ve-richamti et Lo-ruchama ve-amarti le-Lo-ammi ammi attah ve-hu yomar Elohai"</note> which is: **And I will sow her for myself in the land: and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy: and I will say to those who were not my people, "You are my people." And he shall say, "You are my God."** <note>Hosea 2:23</note> 

Next, hear Micah, saying in his second chapter: <term>ויעבר מלכם לפניהם ויהוה בראשם</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Va-ya'avor malkam lifnehem va-Adonai be-rosham"</note> That is: **And their King shall pass before them. And God shall be at their head.** <note>Micah 2:13</note> Furthermore, that the Messiah was to be the head of the Church of Israel is found in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>a volume of the Talmud dealing with law and the messianic age</note> in the chapter *Helek*: where it is read word-for-word: In the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>an ancient collection of interpretations on Genesis</note> of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, regarding that passage in Genesis 49, "He washes his garment in wine," it is said: **When the King Messiah comes, he will be clothed in purple, beautiful to behold.** And after a few words: **And he himself shall be the head of Israel.** 

This agrees quite appropriately with that sentiment of Paul, when writing to the Philippians in the first chapter he says: **He gave Him to be head over all the Church, which is His body, and His fullness.** <note>Though the author cites Philippians 1, this quote is actually from Ephesians 1:22–23.</note> And again to the Colossians in the first chapter he says: **And all things consist in him, and he is the head of the body of the Church.** <note>Colossians 1:17–18</note> 

This is enough for the third book, in which it has been abundantly proven that the Messiah was to be both God and man at the same time. Many other things besides those which have been said—both regarding the Divine Trinity in the second book and the divinity of the Messiah in this third book—could have occurred to be said at the appropriate time. However, I have chosen to omit them so that the present work does not become longer than is fitting. In these books, I have taken care to bring forward only those things (as I shall do in the others) which seemed necessary for unlocking the secrets of Catholic truth found in the Hebrew codices. For this reason, I have thought it best to bypass the subtleties of theological difficulties that are not necessary for uncovering secrets of this kind. 

This is especially so since Georgius Benignus de Salviatis <note>Juraj Dragišić (c. 1445–1520), a prominent Franciscan theologian and scholar</note>, the Archbishop of Nazareth—a man certainly endowed with outstanding talent and most learned in every kind of discipline—is now composing a work no less elegantly than subtly. That excellent work, titled *On the Banner of Christian Victory*, is to be dedicated to the Most Christian King of the French, Francis, the first of this name. Indeed, in that work, to prove that Christian victory is our faith—by which we believe there are three who bear witness in heaven, and that Jesus is the Son of God—sixty-three contemplations are set forth regarding the Divine Trinity and the incarnation of the Divine Word.

> Each of these begins: "Light of the deity, as I have seen with my own eyes."

### BOOK FOUR

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut headpiece featuring a central mask or grotesque face flanked by symmetrical scrolling foliage, floral motifs, and two seated figures at the far ends.</image-desc>

# ON THE FIRST ADVENT OF THE MESSIAH
### CHAPTER ONE

->*That there is a twofold advent of the Messiah: one with humility, to redeem the human race; the other with glory and majesty, to judge the whole world.*<-

<margin>CAPNIO</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, in a landscape setting.</image-desc>
**CAPNIO:** <note>Capnio was the humanistic name for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Hebraist.</note> Since our contemporary Jews deny two things above all else regarding the Messiah—namely, his divinity and that he has already come (for they assert he is a mere man and still look forward to his future arrival)—you must now show that he has already come, just as you have abundantly proved through their own scriptures that the Messiah was to be both God and man. Thus, when they recognize through their scriptures (which speak most clearly on this matter) that the very one they still await with the greatest longing has already come, they may be forced to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Messiah and Savior of the world. **GALATINUS:** I shall certainly show this. But first, one thing needs to be explained which none of you has asked about. **HOGSTRATEN:** What is that? **GALATINUS:** I will tell you immediately. Because it should be our intention not only to conquer their obstinacy <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> with the truth, but also to strive with all our might to lead them back to the recognition of the truth, we must certainly report where they find the occasion for such great error that they never cease waiting for one who has clearly already come. This way, by removing the cause of this error, the effect itself—that is, the very lack of belief arising from such error—may be removed, unless they wish to remain obstinate in the blindness of their faithlessness. It is therefore necessary to know that there is a twofold advent of the Messiah, of which the Prophets have spoken throughout. One is indeed with humility, for redeeming or saving; the other, truly, is with glory and majesty, for judging. However, the more recent Jews, as if entirely blinded and not knowing how to distinguish this twin advent of the Messiah, confound the prophecies of the Prophets, entangling themselves in various errors and composing almost infinite lies regarding the mysteries of the Messiah. For some expect the Messiah to appear in such virtue and power immediately upon his arrival that

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
they affirm he will subject all the kingdoms of the world to himself, and, having liberated the Jews and restored the kingdom of Israel, he will reign temporally. Even the disciples of Christ were once in this error, believing that he would take up the scepter of an earthly kingdom immediately after the resurrection. For this reason, some of them, desiring primacy over the others, asked to sit at his right and left. Others, indeed, after his death, as if they had been cheated of their hope, said: **We hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.** <note>Luke 24:21</note> Finally, some asked him if he would restore the kingdom of Israel at that time. But other Jews (to return to where I digressed), confounding the prophecies of the first and second advent and asserting they must be fulfilled at one and the same time, say the Messiah has not yet come. Still others, both because of what the Prophets predicted about the Messiah’s humility and the suffering he would undergo in his first advent, and because of what those same Prophets announced regarding the manifestation of his majesty and glory in his second advent, affirm that *two* Messiahs are to come. They call the first the "Son of Joseph," whom they say must be killed in the battle of Gog and Magog. The other they call the "Son of David," whom they say will both raise the first Messiah from the dead and redeem Israel, restoring the kingdom of Israel itself. But if they were willing to correctly understand the sayings of the Prophets and the expositions of the ancient Talmudists, they would not only avoid falling into so many errors but could also easily recognize the truth itself. For to speak first of the Prophets: if they would notice the various ways of coming that they assign to the Messiah, they would find that these cannot be verified in one and the same advent. Rather, they would themselves concede from these diverse ways of coming that there are two advents of the Messiah. If they did this, they could easily arrive at the recognition of the truth. **CAPNIO:** I would like you to bring forward some example of this twin advent. **GALATINUS:** Have you not read that Zechariah predicted the Messiah would come in the form of a poor man, riding upon a donkey and its foal? For in the ninth chapter he says: <term>Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King...</term> <note>original Hebrew: גִּילִי מְאֹד בַּת צִיּוֹן הָרִיעִי בַּת יְרוּשָׁלַם הִנֵּה מַלְכֵּךְ (Gili me’od bat Tziyon, hari’i bat Yerushalayim, hinneh malkech)</note>

<summary>This page introduces the argument that the Messiah has two advents—one humble and one glorious—and argues that Jewish rejection of Jesus stems from a failure to distinguish between these two roles in prophecy.</summary>

### BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> **“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King will come to you, the righteous one and the savior; he is poor, and riding upon a donkey, even upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.”** <note>original Hebrew: Zechariah 9:9</note> This means: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem, behold your King shall come to you, righteous and the savior himself, poor, and ascending upon a donkey, and upon a young colt of a donkey. Have you not also found in Daniel that the same Messiah is to come in the clouds of heaven, as if a son of man? For thus the Prophet himself says in the seventh chapter in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaicè"</note>, **“I was watching in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming.”** <note>original Aramaic: Daniel 7:13</note> Since I know you are no amateur in both the Hebrew and Aramaic languages, and I am aware you are a most diligent student of rare literature, I believe you have read these passages frequently. **CAPNIO:** I have certainly read these very often. **GALATINUS:** It is certain, therefore, that both Prophets spoke about one and the same Messiah in these places; yet they attribute to him vastly different ways of coming. For one says that he will come poor and sitting upon a donkey; but the other says he will descend from heaven with glory, as if with the clouds of heaven. The Talmudists <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> wonder at this no small amount. For as it is read in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, Rabbi Joshua son of Levi asked why it was that in Daniel the Messiah is described as coming with the clouds of heaven, but in Zechariah he is poor and sitting upon a donkey? Because, therefore, these two ways of coming which are assigned to the Messiah by these Prophets cannot occur at the same time, since they are incompatible, it must be said that there are two arrivals <note>term: adventus; the Latin word for "coming" or "arrival"</note> of the Messiah: one with humility, for redeeming; the other with majesty, for judging. Zechariah spoke of the first; Daniel of the second. This can also be easily seen from what they add in the same place. For Zechariah there not only calls the Messiah himself poor, humble, and a savior—because through humility and poverty he was to bring salvation to the human race—but he also expresses the work of redemption which was to be done through the Messiah himself, when he says there, **“As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, you have sent forth your prisoners from the pit.”** <note>original Hebrew: Zechariah 9:11</note> Moreover, a little before he says, **“And he shall speak peace to the nations.”** <note>original Hebrew: Zechariah 9:10</note> All of these things openly hint at the mystery of redemption. Daniel, however, says this among other things in the same chapter: **“The judgment sat, and the books were opened.”** <note>original Aramaic: Daniel 7:10</note> From these things it is clearly evident that he was speaking of the second coming of the Messiah. From the sayings of these prophets and others, it is therefore clearly gathered that the coming of the Messiah is twofold. If the Jews dare to deny this, we confront them with the sayings of the ancient Talmudists, who did not keep silent about this truth. For in *Midrash Koheleth*—that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes—regarding the verse "There is nothing new under the sun," it is read that Rabbi Berachiah said, **“The last redeemer was revealed, and he returns and is hidden.”** <note>original Hebrew: הגואל האחרון נגלה וחוזר ונתכסה</note> There, almost all the ancients say that the Messiah the redeemer will appear twice. However, as to how much space of time there will be between his first and second appearance, there is no determination among them. The same point is held even more clearly in the book *Tanhuma*, where it is said: **“We read in Psalm 126: ‘When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we were like those who dream; then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.’ What is ‘When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we were like those who dream’? The answer given was: this will be in the war of the Messiah son of Ephraim; for when he withdraws himself from helping the children of Israel, they will all be as those who dream—not sleeping, nor waking. But when the Messiah returns to show himself to them, then their mouth will be filled with laughter, and they will be rejoicing, and they will verify his first coming by reason of this second appearance, and they will say: ‘The Lord has done great things for us.’”** This is the tradition. Although the younger Jews twist this into a different meaning, and some of our own people piously apply it to the death and resurrection of Christ, the tradition itself speaks expressly of two arrivals of the Messiah. For the following words of the Psalm which he introduces openly suggest both the conversion of the Jews (which will happen around the end of the world) and the reward for good works which everyone will receive in the second coming of the Messiah. For in the same Psalm it follows: **“Then they will say among the nations: ‘The Lord has done great things for these’ (meaning kindly, as the Aramaic translation says); ‘The Lord has done great things for us’ (supply 'kindly' as the same says); ‘we were glad. Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like streams in the South. Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.’”** They also handed down this twin arrival of the Messiah allegorically—namely, through the "Messiah son of Joseph" and the "Messiah son of David." For through the Messiah son of Joseph—whom they said would suffer, be killed, and rise again—they hinted at the first arrival. But through the Messiah son of David, they signified the second, because the Messiah himself in the second arrival, as King of the entire world, will come with the glory of majesty. And although the ancient Talmudists designated not two Messiahs, but two very different arrivals of one and the same Messiah through the "son of Joseph" and the "son of David" (as is clearly evident from their words), nevertheless some of the more recent Jews, poorly understanding the sayings of the ancients—indeed, attempting to pervert them—take from this the occasion for saying that two Messiahs will come, whom they wait for in vain. Therefore, regarding the twofold arrival of the Messiah among the ancient Talmudists, there is no doubt. Though the younger Jews deny it, lest they be forced by Christians to confess that his first arrival has already passed.

### CHAPTER II.

->*On the two Messiahs, whom the more recent Jews vainly expect to come.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>B</margin>
From where did this delusion <note>original: "deliramentum"</note> regarding the two Messiahs, whom the Jews of our time wait for, take its origin? GALATINUS: From a poor understanding of the Scriptures. For in the *Genesis Rabbah* <note>a collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the book of Genesis</note> regarding that verse in Genesis chapter 49, which says: **“Issachar is a strong-boned donkey,”** <note>original Hebrew: יששכר חמור גרם</note> it is read as follows: It is written in Isaiah 32: **“Blessed are you who sow beside all waters.”** This “sowing” is nothing other than giving alms and performing works of mercy, as it is said in Isaiah 55: **“Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters.”** If anyone does this, he will be worthy of Elijah and the two Messiahs. This is what is written in Isaiah 32: **“Sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey.”** The one who “sends” is Elijah, about whom it is written in the last chapter of Malachi: **“Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet.”** The “foot of the ox” refers to the Messiah, the son of Joseph, as it is said in Deuteronomy 33: **“His glory is like the firstborn of his ox.”** And the “foot of the donkey” refers to the Messiah, the son of David, about whom it is written in Zechariah chapter 9: **“Poor, and riding upon a donkey.”** All of this is found there. Therefore, from these and other similar words of Holy Scripture, the more recent Jews argue that two Messiahs must be sent to them. Also, in the book *Sukkah* <note>a volume of the Talmud dealing with the Festival of Booths</note> in the chapter *He-chalil* <note>The Flute</note>, it is said word-for-word: The <term>Rabbanan</term> <note>the great Masters or Rabbis</note> handed down that the Messiah, the son of David, who is to redeem us, will redeem us quickly in our days; and the Holy and Blessed God will say to him: **“Ask of me anything, and I will give it to you,”** as it is said in Psalm 2: **“I will tell of the decree; the Lord said to me, ‘You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.’”** And when he sees the Messiah, the son of Joseph, has been killed, he will say before Him—that is, God: **“Lord of the world, I ask nothing from you but life.”** The Holy and Blessed God will say to him: **“You ask for life from me? Even before you spoke, your father David already prophesied this concerning you,”** as it is said in Psalm 21: **“He asked life of you, and you gave him length of days forever and ever.”** This is from the Talmud. Indeed, these things contain nothing that is contrary to our Lord Jesus Christ. Furthermore, regarding what follows—that the Messiah, the son of David, was not to die—it can be fittingly said that although the Lord Jesus suffered and died as a man according to his humanity, he nevertheless sought life, and length of days was given to him forever and ever, since God raised him on the third day after his death, never to die again. Moreover, from this tradition, many other points are held against the Jews. First, that the Messiah, the son of David, was to redeem them quickly; and consequently, that the Messiah, the son of David, would come in their days—that is, while they were still lords and powerful in their own land. For the “days” of any nation or king are said to be those in which they rule and flourish. Next, that Psalm 2

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
speaks about the Messiah. From this, it follows that the Messiah is the Son of God, because it is said in that same Psalm: **“God said to me, ‘You are my son.’”** And he is not an adopted son, because of what is immediately added: **“Today I have begotten you.”** To him, as a true Son, He gave the nations as an inheritance and the entire world as a possession—which is clearly fulfilled in the Christian people. Finally, Psalm 21—namely, **“The King shall rejoice in your strength, O Lord”**—is understood entirely to be about the Messiah. Furthermore, in the same book and chapter, it is read: **“And the land shall mourn, family by family apart.”** Why will this mourning happen? Rabbi <note>Rabbi</note> said: Rabbi Dossa and the Masters disagree on this. One said it is because of the Messiah, the son of Joseph, who shall be killed. But the other said it is because of the “evil inclination” <note>the impulse toward sin</note>, or because of sensuality, which shall be slain. Peace be to him who said the mourning will be for the Messiah, the son of Joseph, being killed. For this is what is written of him in Zechariah chapter 12: **“And they shall look upon me, whom they have pierced.”** <note>original Hebrew: והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו</note> Thus far the tradition. From this, a very strong argument is taken against the Jews. For he who says in the same Prophet immediately before the aforementioned words: **“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of devotions”** <note>original Hebrew: ושפכתי על בית דוד ועל יושב ירושלם רוח חן ותחנונים</note> must be God—for to do this belongs to God alone. And since that same person immediately adds what was just said—namely, **“And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced”**—which the Masters of the Jews have explained as being said about the killing of the Messiah, the son of Joseph (as is clearly seen in this tradition), it certainly follows that the Messiah, the son of Joseph, must be both God and man at the same time. This is so that, as God, he would have the power to pour out the spirit of grace and devotions upon those believing in him, and as man, he could be pierced by nails on the cross. Therefore, from these traditions being incorrectly understood, the foolishness of the Jews of our age expects two Messiahs to come: one the son of David, the other the son of Joseph. But it is twice evident that they are most foully deceived. First, through Holy Scripture. For although Saul, David, and certain others were called "messiahs" <note>anointed ones</note>, it can nowhere be shown in all twenty-four books of the Holy Page that Scripture mentions any but one single Messiah who is to come for the sake of salvation. Secondly, this is also most clearly demonstrated through their ancient traditions. For among the ancient Jews, both the Messiah, son of Joseph, and the Messiah, son of David, were held to be one and the same. CAPNIO: From where do you prove this? GALATINUS: Listen first to what is said in *Genesis Rabbah*. This “great mountain” is the Messiah, the son of David. And shortly after, it is added: “Grace to him,” which is said because he himself will be the one giving grace and devotions to Israel. As it is said in Zechariah 12: **“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of devotions.”** All this is from tradition. it is said that the Messiah, the son of David, was to give grace and devotions to Israel. As proof of this, the authority of Zechariah is brought forward: **“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of devotions.”** <note>Zechariah 12:10; original Latin: "spiritum gratiae & devotionum"</note> However, this same authority was cited in the preceding tradition regarding the Messiah, the son of Joseph. From this, it is manifest beyond doubt that the Messiah, the son of David, is exactly the same person. Therefore, just as it was necessarily shown there that the Messiah, the son of Joseph, is both God and man, it necessarily follows here as well that the Messiah, the son of David, would be God and man. For when it is said here in the person of the Messiah, the son of David, **“And I will pour out... the spirit of grace,”** this is something that belongs to God alone; and yet it is immediately followed by, **“And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced,”** <note>original: "Et aspicient ad me quem confixerunt"</note> which can in no way apply to God [in his divine nature]. It is surely clear and evident, then, that the Messiah, the son of David, was necessarily going to be both God and man: so that as God, he could pour out the spirit of grace and devotions through men, and as a true man, he could be pierced and die without any loss to his divinity.

In the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "Midras tehilim"; an ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, another tradition is placed from which it is clearly gathered that the Messiah, the son of Joseph, and the Messiah, the son of David, are undoubtedly the same. For there, upon that verse of Psalm 92, **“But you, O Lord, are on high forever,”** <note>Hebrew: ואתה מרום לעולם יהוה</note> it is held as follows: Rabbi Berachiah said, “Forever your hand, O Lord, shall be exalted from above, like the horn of a unicorn <note>original: "monocerotis"</note> is my horn.” For just as the horns of a unicorn are higher than the horns of all beasts, and it tosses <note>or winnows; original: "ventilans"</note> toward the four winds of heaven: so shall the Messiah, the son of David, be a winnower to every wind. And of him Moses said in Deuteronomy 33: **“His glory is like the firstborn of his ox. And his horns are the horns of a unicorn. With them he shall push the people together. And they are the ten thousands of Ephraim. And they are the thousands of Manasseh.”** <note>The text links the "ox" of Joseph/Ephraim to the "unicorn" of the Davidic Messiah.</note> The Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> indeed says: **“And these shall be the ten thousands of the house of Ephraim: and these shall be the thousands of the house of Manasseh.”** <note>Aramaic: ואינון ריבבתא דבית אפרים ואינון אלפיא דבית מנשה</note> And against him Kings shall rise up to kill him: just as it is said in the second Psalm: **“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Messiah.”** <note>Hebrew: יתיצבו מלכי ארץ ורוזנים נוסדו יחד על יהוה ועל משיחו</note> The Israelites, however, who are in the land at that time, shall be in great tribulation; nevertheless, in their tribulation, they shall be like a most fruitful olive tree: as it is said, **“And my old age in fruitful oil.”** And the Israelites shall be seeing their own ruin. As it is said in Psalm 92: **“My eye also shall see my spies,”** or my enemies, **“mine ears shall hear of the wicked that rise up against me.”** <note>Hebrew: ותבט עיני בשורי בקמים עלי מרעים תשמענה אזני</note> Then follows in the same place: **“The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.”** <note>Hebrew: צדיק כתמר יפרח כארז בלבנון ישגה</note> This "righteous one" is the Messiah, the son of David, who is likened to a palm. For just as the palm is beautiful to look upon, and all its fruits are sweet and good, so the Messiah, the son of David, shall be beautiful in his appearance, and all his acts shall be sweet and good before God, the Holy and Blessed.

<margin>A</margin> Rabbi Isaac said: Just as the shadow of a palm tree is far from the tree itself, so the granting of the reward of the righteous—which will be given through the Messiah—is far from them until the world to come: as it is said in Deuteronomy 7: **“And it shall come to pass, after you hear these judgments, and keep and do them, the Lord your God shall keep unto thee the covenant and the mercy which he swore unto thy fathers.”** It is also written in Deuteronomy chapter 5: **“Showing mercy unto thousands of them that love him and keep his commandments.”** "Unto thousands" means after a long time, and not immediately in this life. All of this is tradition. Although it contains many things against the Jews, it most especially shows, for our purpose, that the Messiah, the son of Joseph, and the Messiah, the son of David, are one and the same. This is because it teaches that the passage in Deuteronomy spoken in the blessing of Joseph—**“His glory is like the firstborn of his ox”**—is to be understood as referring to the Messiah, the son of David.

It was not without reason that those ancient fathers signified one and the same true Messiah through the "Messiah son of Joseph" and the "Messiah son of David." In this, they not only designated his two comings (as has been said), but they also suggested his humility and gentleness in the Messiah son of Joseph, and his nobility and kingdom in the Messiah son of David. Therefore, it is most clearly established that our Lord Jesus Christ was both Messiahs. For he was the legal <note>original: "putatiuus"; traditionally meaning "supposed" or "reputed," here referring to the legal foster-father relationship</note> son of Joseph, the spouse of his mother—not by the flesh, but by upbringing and nourishment. He was also the son of David according to the flesh, as will be abundantly proven elsewhere; therefore, the kingdom was justly his due. Even the Jews themselves admit this. For in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>a volume of the Talmud dealing with law and courts</note> in the chapter **“The trial is finished,”** <note>Hebrew: נגמר הדין; *Nigmar Hadin*</note> it is read as follows: Rabbi Ula said: **“That Jesus the Nazarene was near to the kingdom,”** <note>original: "propinquus erat regni"</note> namely the Davidic kingdom, **“and they hanged him on the eve of the Passover.”** For these reasons, the ancient Jews quite aptly designated the Lord Jesus himself through the two aforementioned Messiahs: that is, through the Messiah son of Joseph and the Messiah son of David.

# BOOK FOUR.

...it is established that the oracles of the prophets have met and been fulfilled. ### CHAPTER IV.

*The first reason by which it is proved that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has already passed, taken from the destruction of the Jewish scepter. For which it is first demonstrated that around the first coming of the Messiah, the scepter of the Jewish Kingdom ought to fail entirely.*

#### GALATINUS.

<margin>E</margin>
For the foundation of the first reason, the words of the patriarch Jacob must be recalled; who, desiring the salvation of his sons, decided to explain the mystery of the Messiah to them in his testament among other secrets of future things. Therefore, to make them more cautious, he assigned the determined time of his coming (as is read in Genesis, chapter 49) in these words: <term>לא־יסור שבט מיהודה ומחקק מבין רגליו, עד כי־יבא שילה ולו יקהת עמים</term> <note>Genesis 49:10; Original Hebrew: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be."</note>. That is, **The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe or lawgiver from the midst of his feet, until Shiloh (that is, the Messiah) comes. And to him shall be the gathering of the peoples (that is, the nations).** **CAPITO:** You have brought forward these words far differently than our edition <note>The "our edition" refers to the Latin Vulgate bible common in the 16th century.</note> has them. For it has it thus (as you know): *The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a Leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.* **GALATINUS:** It is exactly as you say. But the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraica veritas"; a term used by scholars like Jerome and Galatinus to refer to the original Hebrew text as more authoritative than translations.</note> is much better for our faith. For that exposition of ours is more according to the sense than the literal word. Whence the Jews of our time have a wide path for escaping and denying the truth. For they can easily object that this prophecy is not to be understood regarding the Messiah, but regarding someone else. And especially regarding Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who was to be sent to punish their and their fathers' innumerable sins, and to destroy the city of Jerusalem and the temple, and to take the people captive. Just as it had been predicted many times by the Prophets, and was fulfilled in the time of King Zedekiah. For then (as they say) the scepter was taken from Judah by Nebuchadnezzar, when their city was demolished, the temple burned, and those who had not fallen in the slaughter were led captive into Babylon: as is said in the last chapter of Jeremiah. From then on (they say) we never had a King or a Leader from the house of Judah. What also follows, *And he shall be the expectation of the nations*, they want to be understood regarding Nebuchadnezzar himself: since his dominion was over all nations, and he himself, as is said in Daniel chapter 2, was the "head of gold." Whence the excellence of his kingdom is denoted over all other kingdoms of the nations that were to follow. These and many other things the Jews are accustomed to oppose us with according to our translation, which they can by no means object to according to the truth of the Hebrew text. **CAPITO:** Nay, even so they frequently resist us. For since this Prophecy does not speak openly of Christ under the name of Messiah, but obscurely under the name <term>שילה</term> *Silo* <note>Shiloh</note>—where our edition has *until he comes who is to be sent*, the Hebrew text says *until Shiloh comes*, which word indeed is ambiguous among the Hebrews: for <term>שילה</term> *Silo* can be the proper name of a certain place so called, and can signify a "sending" or "one sent," drawn from the verb <term>שלח</term> *Salach* <note>Shalach</note>, which means "to send" among them—for that reason some of the more recent Jews, trying to evade the true sense of this Prophecy, and taking *Silo* for a place, say it should be understood not of the Messiah, but of Saul. Which Saul, having been elected King, came to be anointed in Shiloh, where the Ark of the Lord was, in which the anointment was kept. And then they say the scepter, which is taken for a certain primacy and had until then been in the tribe of Judah, was moved from that tribe and transferred to the tribe of Benjamin, from which Saul himself was. **GALATINUS:** This exposition of theirs is entirely false. Firstly, because before the election of Saul, the Ark of the Lord in which the anointing was kept had already been transported from Shiloh to Kiriath-Jearim: as is clear from the first book of Kings, chapter 7. And consequently, Saul was anointed not in Shiloh, but in Kiriath-Jearim. Secondly, because immediately after Saul—indeed while Saul himself was still reigning—David, who was the first of the tribe of Judah to reign, was appointed King and anointed by Samuel the Prophet. Therefore it seems least likely that the scepter was taken from the tribe of Judah then, when that same tribe was closest to the perfection of the kingdom. **CAPITO:** There are <margin>Another objection.</margin> also some others who, also taking *Silo* for a place, say this prophecy should be understood regarding Jeroboam, who was descended from the tribe of Ephraim...

### BOOK FOUR.

...to be. For when the ten tribes, because of the harsh response given to the people by King Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, had departed from the kingdom of Judah, they chose Jeroboam himself as their King. And then they say that the scepter was taken away from the tribe of Judah and transferred to the tribe of Ephraim: hence they thus explain that saying of the Prophet, *Until Shiloh comes*, that is, *Until Jeroboam comes to be crowned in <margin>Refutation.</margin> Shiloh*. GALATINUS: That explanation is also most false: first, because that assembly of the ten tribes, which appointed Jeroboam as its King, took place not in Shiloh, but in Shechem: as is clearly gathered from the twelfth chapter of the third book of Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 12.</note>: then also, because the kingdom was not then removed from the house of Judah: which is evident primarily from the fact that Kings from that tribe continued through hereditary succession until the Babylonian captivity for nearly 492 years without interruption: and they alone were considered the true Kings, since they reigned in the royal city of Jerusalem and were established through the anointing that took place in the <margin>Third objection.</margin> temple. CAPITO: Finally, there are some others who, taking this word *Shiloh* as signifying a certain "sending," explain this prophecy as referring to Nebuchadnezzar (as you said before): who, because of the sins of the people, was sent by God for the destruction of that entire land and for the removal of the kingdom. Hence they explain the Prophet's saying thus, *Until Shiloh comes*, that is, *Until he who is to be sent comes, namely Nebuchadnezzar*. For then (as they say), after King Zedekiah—who was of the tribe of Judah—and his sons were killed, the kingdom of Judah completely failed: since from 그 time onward, no one from that tribe ever reigned. Therefore, <margin>Refutation.</margin> show clearly that these people also have lied. GALATINUS: I shall show it in three ways.

And first indeed, because as Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> also says in this place, the scepter was not taken away from the house of Judah through the Babylonian captivity: which is also proven most strongly by the fact that not all the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews.</note>, who were the heads of the Jews, were killed by Nebuchadnezzar: since many of them went down into Babylon, and there, according to their law and customs and with the King's consent, they determined and judged the legal cases of the Jews. That they went down into Babylon is clearly testified by the <term>Midrash Shir HaShirim</term> <note>A traditional Jewish commentary on the Song of Solomon.</note>, that is, the exposition of the Song of Songs, upon that saying: *My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices*: where the <term>Targum</term> <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> also says: *The Lord of the world accepted their prayer with favor, and descended into Babylon to the wise men of the Sanhedrin, and gave a sweet fragrance to his people.* Since therefore the Sanhedrin, that is, the ordinary judges in whose hand the scepter was, did not fail at the time of the Babylonian captivity, it is plainly follow that the scepter did not fail at all then. Secondly, this is proven by the fact that after that Babylonian captivity, the Jewish people were governed by those who had come from the tribe of Judah until the time of Herod the Ascalonite. For Zerubbabel, who stood as the prince of the people at the return from that same captivity, was from the tribe of Judah, as is read in Zechariah chapter 4 and in Haggai chapter 1. Similarly, all others in whose hands the governance of the people remained until the Maccabees, were from 

<column-break/>

the tribe of Judah: as even the Talmudists themselves pass down. The Maccabees also, who afterwards held the principality of the Jews until Herod the Ascalonite, were reckoned as being of the tribe of Judah, because the royal tribe and the priestly tribe were intermingled: as is evident in the eleventh chapter of the fourth book of Kings <note>Commonly known as 2 Kings 11.</note>. Hence the Maccabees themselves had proceeded from the tribe of Judah according to their maternal lineage. All these things are excellently confirmed in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> in the chapter <term>Dine Mamonoth</term> <note>original: "דיני ממונות" — meaning "Laws of Money" or "Civil Jurisdictions."</note>, that is, concerning the judgments of wealth. For there it is said: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah; these are the heads of the exiles, who ruled Israel with rod and scepter. And the scribe from between his feet; these are the sons of the sons of Hillel.* Where the gloss <note>A scholarly commentary written in the margins or between lines.</note> says: *The heads of the Babylonian exiles were Zerubbabel and his kin, and the Prince who was in the land of Israel, who was Mattathias and his kin, namely the <term>Hasmonai</term>, that is, the Maccabees, and the others descending from them.* The sons of the sons of Hillel were the Sanhedrin, that is, the aforementioned judges taught by the disciples of Hillel: for which reason, by way of their teaching, they are called the sons of his sons. From these things it is manifest that, until the times of Herod the Ascalonite himself, the scepter had not departed from the tribe of Judah. Thirdly and finally, this is most clearly shown through the Targum, that is, through the Aramaic translation of Rabbi Onkelos, which says in this place: <note>original Aramaic: "לא יעדי עבד שולטן מדבית יהודה וספרא מבני בנוהי עד עלמא עד דייתי משיחא דדי ליה היא מלכותא וליה ישתמעון עממיא"</note> That is: *The ruler or doer of power, or of royal dominion, shall not pass away from the house of Judah, nor the scribe from the sons of his sons forever, until the Messiah comes, whose the kingdom is. And to him shall the peoples obey, or the nations of the gentiles shall gather themselves to him.* From this Aramaic translation and exposition, if it be diligently examined, many things are held for our purpose. The first of which is that through the Hebrew word <term>Shevet</term> <note>original: "שבט"</note>, which is interpreted as "rod" or "scepter," a certain royal act and dominion is understood: with which that of Psalm 45 agrees: *The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.* The second is that through the word <term>Mehokek</term> <note>original: "מחוקק"</note>, which is the same as "scribe," a great lawgiver must be understood. Hence in Deuteronomy chapter 33, in the blessing of Gad, where it says "Teacher" in Latin, the Hebrew has *Mehokek*: which Onkelos explained in Aramaic concerning Moses: *In his possession Moses the great scribe of Israel, that is, the great lawgiver, was buried.* Also in that which we have in Isaiah 33, *The Lord is our lawgiver*, in the Hebrew this word <term>Mehokeknu</term> <note>original: "יהוה מחקקנו"</note> is placed: for it is said there, that is, *God is our lawgiver*. The third point is that this word *Shiloh* signifies the Messiah: which is also excellently proven in the ancient <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term> <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the book of Genesis.</note>, when upon this place, *Until Shiloh comes*, it is said: *Until Shiloh comes; that is the Messiah: and to him the nations shall gather themselves: because he himself shall judge the whole world.* And this is what was said in Micah chapter 4: *And he shall judge between the nations, and shall rebuke many peoples.* And again in Isaiah chapter 11: *And he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and shall rebuke with equity for the meek of the earth. And he shall strike the earth...*

<summary>Galatinus refutes Jewish interpretations that the "scepter" left Judah during Jeroboam's reign or the Babylonian exile, arguing instead that authority remained with Judah through the Sanhedrin and the Maccabees until the Messiah's arrival. He uses Aramaic Targums and Midrash to prove that "Shiloh" refers specifically to the Messiah as a global lawgiver.</summary>

### BOOK FOUR.

...with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked <note>original: "virga oris sui, & in spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium," a quote from Isaiah 11:4</note>. All these things are found there: to which is quite fittingly connected what is read in the *Ekhah Rabbati* <note>The Great Midrash on Lamentations</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah: where, regarding that verse in the first chapter of Lamentations, *Because the comforter, who should restore my soul, is far from me*, it is said: "What is the name of the Messiah? Those of the house of Rabbi Sela said, <margin>Why the Messiah is called Shiloh.</margin> *Shiloh* is his name: just as it is said in the 49th chapter of Genesis: *Until Shiloh comes*, that is, the Messiah." <term>CAPITO</term>: If, therefore, in this prophecy "Shiloh" can be understood as nothing other than the Messiah, why did the Prophet not say, "Until the Messiah comes," but rather, "Until Shiloh comes"? <term>GALATINUS</term>: Truly, he did not speak this way without reason. For in this he wished to clearly hint that the Messiah was to be born of a mother without a father, or rather, to be conceived from maternal matter without the seed of a man. Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a famous medieval Jewish scholar</note> clearly testifies to this in the book *Serafim* <note>referring to Kimhi’s *Sefer Shorashim* or Book of Roots</note>, when he says of him: "The Messiah is called Prince and Ruler: for it is the custom of a Ruler to have a rod in his hand. And because the rod of discipline for the people will be in his hand, he is also called *Mehokek* <note>original: מחקק, meaning a lawgiver or scribe</note>, which signifies a scribe."

<margin>Shiloh: its etymology and interpretation.</margin>
Furthermore, *Until Shiloh comes* is interpreted as "his son of the feminine gender" <note>This refers to a grammatical reading of the Hebrew word as implying a birth from a woman</note>. And it is a prophecy concerning the Messiah. The word *Shiloh* is derived from the word *shilya* <note>original: שליה, meaning the afterbirth or placenta</note>, which is a certain pouch in which the infant remains in the mother's womb, which is sometimes used in scripture for the embryo in the womb. All these are the words of Rabbi Kimhi. From these things it is most clearly evident that "Shiloh" in the aforementioned prophecy is the same as "the son of a woman." From this it is plain that the Prophet spoke of "Shiloh" to show that the Messiah himself was to be born of a mother without a father. From all of which it is manifest, against the faithlessness of the Jews of our time, that according to the expositions of the ancient Talmudists, the aforementioned prophecy can be rightly understood of no one else but the Messiah. And consequently, according to the sayings of the ancients, it is concluded that at the arrival of the Messiah himself, the scepter of the Jewish Kingdom had to utterly fail.

### CHAPTER V.

->*That judicial power also was to be completely taken away from the Jews at the arrival of the Messiah. And concerning the judges of the Jews.*<-

->G A L A T I N V S.<-

Where, moreover, our edition <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> in the predicted prophecy has, *Nor a Leader from his thigh*, the Hebrew text has *Scribe* in that place, which is more consistent with the truth and provides a more express testimony concerning Christ. For not only was the power of Dominion to be taken away from the Jews at the Messiah’s arrival, but also the judicial authority of the wise men, who were called the *Sanhedrin*. Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>an 11th-century preacher from Narbonne</note> openly affirms this in his commentaries on the book of Genesis, regarding that word of the same prophecy, *And a scribe from his thigh*: "These are the *Sanhedrin*, sitting in the *Gazith* chamber <note>the 'Chamber of Hewn Stone' in the Temple where the high court met</note>, to judge capital cases <note>original: "iudicia animarum," literally "judgments of souls"</note>. These shall never be removed from the land of Judah until Shiloh comes, who is the Messiah." This is his statement. Also in the *Bereshit Rabbah Kesarta* <note>An abbreviated version of the Great Midrash on Genesis</note>, it is read in this manner: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet*. These are those sitting as "counselors of Jabez" <note>original: יועצי יעבץ - *iahbez*</note>, teaching the *halachot* <note>original: הלכות, meaning religious laws or legal rulings</note>, that is, sentences, in the Great *Sanhedrin*, which sits in the *Gazith* chamber, in the portion of Judah. Of whom it is said in the second chapter of the first book of Chronicles: *And the families of the scribes sitting at Jabez*. *Until Shiloh comes*, that is, the Messiah. Because it is destined that the nations of the world shall bring gifts to the Messiah, the son of David. Just as it is said in the 18th chapter of Isaiah: *At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts* <note>Galatinus provides the Hebrew: בעת ההיא יובל שי ליהוה צבאות</note>. All this is tradition. From which not only is the proposition clear, but an argument is also taken that the Messiah is the Lord of hosts, to whom the nations, through the Magi, were to bring gifts. <term>HOGOSTRUTUS</term>: What is signified by the name *Sanhedrin*? And what was their office, or what power did they have? <term>GALATINUS</term>: Just as is read in the 11th chapter of Numbers, in the time of Moses by God's command, seventy Elders advanced in age and proven in knowledge were chosen to be Moses' assistants in the government of the people. It pertained to them to declare and define all difficulties or doubts of the law and faith, and to judge in grave matters and difficult cases. Regarding them, that passage in the 17th chapter of Deuteronomy is understood to be written: *If you perceive a judgment to be difficult and ambiguous for you, between blood and blood, case and case...* and a few words later, *Rise*, he says, *and go up to the place which the Lord has chosen, and you shall follow their sentence, nor shall you decline to the right hand or to the left*. These were called the *Sanhedrin*, whom we can call "Ordinary Judges"; they were also called *Mehokekim*, that is, Scribes or Lawgivers, because whatever they handed down and wrote was held as law by others. Their college represented the scepter given by the Holy Spirit through Jacob to the house of Judah, and the scepter itself depended upon them. Therefore, not only while residing under kings and leaders did they exercise the power of judging, but even when no King or Leader existed among the Jews, their authority nonetheless still endured. Concerning their quality, it is read in the book *Sanhedrin* in the chapter *Dine Mamonoth* <note>original: דיני ממונות, "Monetary Laws" or "Civil Judgments"</note>, as follows: "Rabbi Johanan said, they did not appoint anyone to the Sanhedrin except masters of wisdom, stature, and appearance, and of old age, and masters of incantations, as well as those knowing seventy languages, so that it would not be necessary for them to hear other interpreters." On this point, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> says: "Stature and appearance were required in them so that they might be held in reverence. Moreover, that they should be masters of incantations was required so that they might convict and put to death sorcerers and evildoers who trusted in their evil deeds and incantations." Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Concerning their power and manner of judging, in the Babylonian book *Sanhedrin* in the chapter *Arba Mitot* <note>original: ארבע מיתות, "The Four Deaths"</note>, it is held: "Four deaths, that is, four modes of killing, were handed down to the house of judgment, that is, to the Sanhedrin themselves: namely, stoning, burning, slaying, and strangling" <note>original: סקילה שרפה הרג וחנק</note>. That is, to stone, to burn, to slay...

### BOOK FOUR.

...to strike down and to strangle. <note>original: "dere, & strangulare," continuing a list of judicial punishments</note> Rabbi Akiba said: "How do we know that when the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme council of seventy-one elders</note> had executed a soul—that is, when they had judged someone to be put to death—they would taste nothing at all for that entire day?" It is from where it is written: *You shall not eat anything with the blood.* <note>Leviticus 19:26</note> One also reads in the book of the *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Dine mamonoth* <gloss>Judgments of wealth</gloss>, that is, the "Judgments of Riches," that trials regarding wealth, money, or movable goods were conducted by three judges; but judgments of souls <note>capital cases</note> were conducted by twenty-three. This means that twenty-three of the seventy ordinary judges—and no fewer—could judge a man guilty of death or liable to be executed. 

However, they did not judge a tribe, nor a scepter <note>likely referring to a king or tribal leader</note>, nor a false prophet, nor a High Priest, except by the "House of Judgment" <note>the *Beit Din* or Sanhedrin</note> of seventy-one judges. Nor did they go out to a permitted war <note>an optional war, as opposed to a commanded one</note> except by the word of the House of Judgment of seventy-one judges. Nor did they add to the city <note>expand the boundaries of Jerusalem</note> or to the courts of the Temple, except by the word of the House of Judgment of seventy-one judges. Nor did they establish *sanhedrioth* <gloss>sanhedrins</gloss>, that is, the local assemblies of ordinary judges for the tribes, except through the House of Judgment of seventy-one judges; this was done through the laying on of hands <term>Semikhah</term> <note>the formal ordination of a judge</note> upon the tribe, as Rabbi Ishmael says. Rabbi Judah, however, said that five were necessary for the laying on of hands. Furthermore, a wolf, a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a serpent were to be killed <note>if they had killed a human</note> by twenty-three judges.

The Great College, which was called the *Sanhedre ghedola* <gloss>Great Sanhedrin</gloss>, consisted of seventy-one judges. The Lesser Sanhedrin consisted of twenty-three. How do we know that the Great Council of the Sanhedrin was seventy-one judges? From that which is said in Numbers, chapter 11: *Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel.* And Moses was over them. Thus, there were seventy-one. So far the *Talmud*. 

From this, an argument is made that the entire House of Judgment of seventy-one judges met together to judge Christ, because, as has been said, they did not judge a tribe, nor a scepter, nor a false prophet, nor a High Priest, except through the House of Judgment of seventy-one judges. <note>The author is arguing that because Jesus was accused of being a false prophet or king, he would have required the full High Court.</note> It should also be known that a lesser assembly of the Sanhedrin could not be ordained except by the assembly of the seventy elders, as is said in the same place. For those seventy judges ordained the assemblies of other judges who ruled the people in other cities and locations round about. This was under the condition, however, that every assembly of every region was subject to the Great Assembly of Elders located in Jerusalem, in the place called *Gazith* <gloss>the Chamber of Hewn Stone</gloss>. 

In the same book of the *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Veellu hen* <gloss>And these are they</gloss>, it is said word-for-word: "There is a tradition that Rabbi Yose said: In the beginning there was no controversy in Israel, but the House of Judgment of seventy-one judges sat in the consistory of *Gazith*—that is, the place of hewn stone. And other Houses of Judgment of twenty-three sat in various places. For one of them sat at the gate of the Temple Mount; another at the gate of the court. The remaining Houses of Judgment of twenty-three judges sat in the individual cities of Israel. When a question needed to be asked, it was asked of the House of Judgment in one’s own city. If they heard the answer, they gave it. If not, they went to the rank of judges in the nearest city. If they heard it, they told them. If not, they went to the rank of judges at the gate of the Temple Mount. They would say: 'Thus I have interpreted, and thus my colleagues have interpreted; thus I have taught, and thus my colleagues have taught.' If they heard the answer, they told them; if not, they came to the rank of judges at the gate of the Temple court. They would say: 'Thus I have interpreted, and thus my colleagues have interpreted; thus I have taught, and thus my colleagues have taught.' If they heard the answer, they told them. If not, both these and those went to the consistory of *Gazith*—that is, the 'hewn' or 'polished' chamber—where the Sanhedrin sat from morning until evening. On Sabbaths and festival days, they sat on the wall. But once the disciples of Shammai and Hillel <note>two famous competing schools of Jewish law</note> multiplied, who did not serve as was fitting, schisms grew in Israel, and the Law became like two Laws."

### CHAPTER VI.

->*When, how, and why the kingdom of the Jews and their judicial power failed.*<-

#### CAPNIO.

<note>Capnio is the scholar Johann Reuchlin, a famous 16th-century Hebraist.</note>

Now it remains for you to explain, for the conclusion of this reasoning, at what time, in what manner, and for what reason both the kingdom of the Jews and their judicial power came to an end. 

#### GALATINUS.

Both failed during the reign of Herod the Ascalonite <note>Herod the Great</note>, who was not only a foreigner but also once a servant of the Maccabees. For a clearer understanding of this matter, it must be known that there were three Herods: the first was called the Ascalonite, the son of Antipater, whom the Jews call *Horodos ben antipatar* <gloss>Herod son of Antipater</gloss>. He was the first foreigner to reign in Judea after Hyrcanus. Under him, Christ was born, specifically in the thirty-first year of his reign, for all the years of his reign were thirty-seven. It was he who killed the infants of Bethlehem aged two years and under when Christ was born. 

The second Herod was surnamed Antipater <note>Herod Antipas</note>, the son of the elder Herod; he succeeded his father in Galilee by the judgment of Caesar, while his brother Archelaus succeeded in Judea. It was this Herod who beheaded John the Baptist, and in his time Christ suffered His passion. 

The third Herod was called Agrippa, the son of this second Herod and grandson of the first. About him, it is written in the *Midrash* <gloss>exposition</gloss> regarding that saying in Deuteronomy 17: *From the midst of your brothers you shall set a king over you; you may not put a foreigner over you who is not your brother.* When Agrippa reached that *pasuc* <gloss>verse</gloss>, he wept until his eyes shed tears. But all Israel said to him: "Do not fear, Agrippa, for you are our brother." 

One also reads of him in the *Bava Batra* <note>a volume of the Talmud dealing with civil law</note>, in the chapter *Hassuttaphin* <gloss>The Partners</gloss>, that the Romans wrote to him among other things: "If you have torn down and rebuilt, you are a wicked servant; the successors of servants make themselves kings. For if you reread the book of your lineage, you will not find yourself noble, nor the son of a noble, but a servant owned by Herod the Ascalonite." All this is from the *Talmud*. Therefore, Herod the Ascalonite, the first foreigner, obtained the kingdom of the Jews by trickery. For as Josephus and others [write]...

### BOOK FOUR.

...and other historians relate, born of an Edomite father, Antipater of Ascalon, and an Arabian mother, Cypris, Herod was an Idumaean by his father’s line and an Arab by his mother’s. He received the kingdom of the Jews from the Romans so that he might oversee the tributes and obey the Roman Empire; he took as his wife the granddaughter of Hyrcanus, the High Priest and Prince of the Jews, who drew his origin from the Hasmoneans <note>original: "Achabæis," likely a corruption of "Asmonaeis," the Hasmonean or Maccabean dynasty</note>. And by circumcising himself, out of love for the kingdom and for her, he became a proselyte. Yet, eventually, he killed that same Hyrcanus through treachery, because it was said that the Kingdom was rightfully his. For while Hyrcanus himself, the High Priest, had been captured by the Parthians, Herod received Judea (to which he had no claim) from Augustus and the Senate; later, when Hyrcanus returned from Parthian captivity, Herod killed him along with Antigonus his son, who had succeeded his father in the High Priesthood and Kingdom. He also killed as many as had come from the royal line, on account of what is written in Deuteronomy 17: *From the midst of your brothers you shall set a King over you*; he even ordered all the books containing the genealogies of the kings to be burned, so that neither he nor his sons would be judged as foreigners to the kingdom. Among other cruel deeds he committed, he also killed the husband of his sister Salome. And when others had given her as a wife to another, he killed him as well. He also killed the Scribes and doctors of the divine law with similar wickedness, so that he might strip away from the Jews every means and hope of recovering the kingdom. Therefore, the scepter of the kingdom was then properly and truly taken away from the tribe of Judah, since it was believed that no one of the royal line remained. At that time also, judicial power was removed from them, when Herod himself ordered all the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>the supreme legal council</note> to be killed. The Talmudists record all these things. For it is held in the <term>Bava Batra</term> <note>a tractate of the Talmud concerning civil law</note>, in the chapter <term>Ha-Shuttafin</term> <gloss>Partners in Business</gloss>, that Herod himself destroyed both the leaders of the Babylonian exiles and the Sanhedrin members themselves. There it is said word-for-word: Herod was a servant of the house of <term>Hasmonai</term> <note>the Hasmoneans</note>, that is, the Maccabees; and he cast his eyes upon a certain girl from that same house and family, who was called <term>Mariamne</term>. One day, therefore, he heard a daughter of a voice <note>original: "filia vocis," a literal translation of the Hebrew *Bat Kol*, a divine heavenly echo or revelation</note> saying from heaven, "Every servant who rebels at this time shall prosper." He rebelled, therefore, and killed all his masters, and all the sons of his masters, with only the aforementioned girl being spared, so that through her he might contract a marriage alliance. But she climbed up into a tower, raised her voice, and said, "Everyone who says 'We proceed from the house of <term>Hasmonai</term>' (the Maccabees) is a servant. For no one remains from there except me." Having said these things, she threw herself down and died. He, however, preserved her in balsam for seven years. There were those who said that he had relations with her; and there were those who said he did not. Those who said he did so assigned this cause: that he might fulfill his lust and passion. But those who said he did not gave this reason: that by keeping her thus, he might be called an affine <note>a relative by marriage</note> of the Maccabees, because he possessed the daughter of a king. Therefore the <term>Rabbanan</term> <gloss>Masters</gloss> said, it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 17: *From the midst of your brothers you shall set a King over you.* He rose

<column-break/>

up, therefore, and killed all the <term>Rabbanan</term> <gloss>Masters</gloss>, sparing only <term>Baba ben Buta</term> for himself, so that he might consult him. One day, however, he ordered him to be summoned and plucked out his eyes. And a little while later, this man <note>Herod</note> extinguished the light of the world, that is, the <term>Rabbanan</term>; just as it is written in Proverbs chapter 6: *Because the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light.* All this is tradition. From which it is clear enough that in the time of this Herod, who killed both the heads of Babylon—that is, the Hasmoneans—and the ordinary judges, the scepter departed from Judah and utterly failed. 

<margin>CHAPTER: If a Jew should object that the scepter did not depart from Judah in the time of Herod, since the aforementioned Baba ben Buta, being spared from the Sanhedrin, could still have established other Sanhedrin members, what should be the response?</margin> 

GALATINUS: That is entirely false: Since it is nowhere found written that he did this, nor could he have done so by law. This can easily be seen from what is written in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> in the chapter <term>Dine Mamonoth</term> <gloss>Judgments of wealth</gloss>, that is, the "Judgments of Riches." There it is said among other things: <term>Rabbi son of Rav Ashi</term> said, that the confirmation or institution of the aforementioned judges was done either by the hand or by name only. For either they would place a hand upon his head and confirm him, or they would institute him by name, calling him <term>Rabbi</term>; but one man alone could not institute a judge. Thus he said. And the reason why one person could not institute a judge is (as it is said in the same place) because an institution of this kind through the laying on of hands could not be done except by three, as <term>Rabbi Ishmael</term> said, or by five, as <term>Rabbi Judah</term> said. For that many were necessary. However, even if other judges of this kind of college were later instituted with Herod’s permission, who were under the king himself (just as they had existed before under others), because they were not true judges, they had no power of judging in grave or criminal matters. Thus it was clearly shown that under Herod himself, this authority of judging, along with the scepter of ruling, had utterly failed among the Jews. For this reason, our Lord Jesus Christ, while speaking of these judges who were usually chosen from the Scribes and Pharisees in that time, said in Matthew 23: *The Scribes and the Pharisees have sat <note>original: "Sederunt," using the perfect tense to imply a completed action</note> on the chair of Moses.* He said "they have sat," and not "they are sitting," to demonstrate clearly that their power had then already ceased. This is something they themselves also confessed. For they said even to Pilate: *It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death*; since the judgment of blood had been taken from us. And then, on account of the false judgment brought against the blood of the righteous Christ himself, they were expelled from the <term>Gazith</term> <note>The Chamber of Hewn Stone, the official meeting place of the Sanhedrin</note> chamber forty years before the destruction of the last temple; and later, by the order of the Romans and the persuasion of a heavenly voice, they were all killed anew, as is contained more broadly in the Talmud. For in the Jerusalem <term>Sanhedrin</term> book it is said among other things: The Masters read that for forty years before the destruction of the temple, the judges were expelled from the <term>Gazith</term> chamber and lived in <term>Hamith</term> <note>likely *Hanot*, meaning "The Shops"</note>. Explaining this, <term>Rabbi Sichim</term> says that <term>Gazith</term> and <term>Hamith</term> were locations in Jerusalem. And immediately from that time (as <term>Rabbi Abdimi</term> says in the same place), they never again judged a criminal case, since a judgment of this kind was not permitted unless it was done in <term>Gazith</term>. In <term>Bereshit</term> <note>Genesis</note> indeed...
