### BOOK FOUR.

...the Rabbah, that is, in the Great Exposition of the book of Genesis <note>The *Bereshit Rabbah*, a collection of ancient Jewish explanations of the book of Genesis</note>, on that verse in Genesis chapter 49, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," along with the rest that follows, it is read as: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah"; this refers to the <term>Chamber of Hewn Stone</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Lishkat HaGazit*, the meeting place of the Great Sanhedrin in the Temple</note>, that is, the chamber of cut or polished stone, which was given as part of the territory of Judah. As it is said in Psalm 78: "He rejected the tent of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim; but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion which he loved." I say "the mount of contemplation" through the law. And so Psalm 87 says: "The Lord loves the gates of Zion," that is, the gates of contemplation in judgment. "And the scribe from between his feet"; these are the ones sitting and giving judgments in Israel in the **Great Sanhedrin**, which sits in the <term>Chamber of Hewn Stone</term> <note>original Hebrew: *belishkat haggazit*</note>, that is, in the consistory or chamber of cut or polished stone in the portion of Judah. As it is said in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 2: "And the families of the scribes sitting at Jabez, the gatekeepers or singers." And what does "The scepter shall not depart from Judah" mean? Have the **Sanhedrin** not already departed from the Chamber of **Gazith**? But it is said there that the power was not given to the Sanhedrin—that is, to the ordinary judges themselves—to judge capital cases <note>original: *animarum iudicia*, literally "judgments of souls," referring to crimes punishable by death</note>, except during the time when they were sitting in the Chamber of **Gazith**. When they migrated to another place, capital judgments were abolished, as it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 17: "And you shall do according to the word of the mouth which they shall tell you from that place." From this we are taught that the location was necessary. "Until Shiloh comes," that is, the Messiah. It is also read in the book <term>Foreign Worship</term> <note>The Talmudic tractate *Avodah Zarah*</note> in the chapter <term>Before their festivals</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Liphne edehen*</note>, and in the book **Sanhedrin**, in the chapter <term>They were examining</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Haiu bodkin*</note>, that for forty years before the House of the Lord was destroyed, the **Sanhedrin**—that is, the college of seventy judges—migrated from **Gazith** and sat in **Hamith** <note>likely referring to *Hanuth*, the "Shops" or "Trading Stalls" on the Temple Mount</note>. And why did it depart from there? Rabbi Isaac the son of Abudiia said: because they did not judge judgments of penalties. Does it then seem to you to be on account of judgments of penalties? No, rather because they did not judge judgments of souls <note>capital cases</note>. This is the tradition. Where the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> says: "And was the <term>Chamber of Hewn Stone</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Lishkat haggazit*</note> necessary for judgments of penalties? By no means; rather it was for judgments of souls, namely when someone was judged to death." For judgments of souls were not judged in every place, but only as long as the Sanhedrin—that is, the college of ordinary judges—existed in the Chamber of **Gazith**, as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 17: "And you shall arise and go up to the place." By this it is taught that the place was necessary for judgments of this kind. They migrated from there, and they no longer judged judgments of souls, since they were abolished forty years before the destruction of the House, that is, the Temple. All this is according to the literal meaning of Rabbi Solomon. Furthermore, it is read in the Jerusalem Sanhedrin that Rabbi Rahamon said that when the members of the Sanhedrin migrated from the Chamber of **Gazith**, and the judgments of souls were taken away from them, they sewed sackcloth upon their skin and tore out their hair to make themselves bald, weeping and saying: **"Woe to us, for the scepter has departed from Judah, and the son of David has not come."** This means: Woe to us, because the scepter has departed

### CHAPTER VII.

->*Conclusion of the reasoning, that the Messiah has already come.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> Now that all these things have been brought forth, the argument itself must be formed, and we must conclude that the Messiah has already come. GALATINUS: If, therefore, the Messiah was absolutely destined to come at that time when these two things—the power of ruling and the authority of judging—entirely failed among the Jews (and it has been proven through their own scriptures that these were taken away from the Jews at the time of Herod of Ascalon, under whom Christ was born), then it is certain that the time of the Messiah's coming has already passed, and the Messiah himself has already come. The primary premise of this reasoning is clearly evident through what has been said. For when Jacob, through the Holy Spirit in the blessing of Judah, said—and Moses, full of the same Spirit, wrote in the Law—that the scepter and the scribe would not depart from Judah until <term>Shiloh</term> <note>original: *Silo*</note> should come; and when the scepter and the scribe, according to the exposition of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, refer to the assembly of the **Sanhedrin** (that is, the seventy-one judges) and the consistory of **Gazith** (that is, "hewn," specifically constructed of polished stones); and when "Shiloh" is none other than the Messiah, as has already been proven through their own scriptures; and since the assembly of the **Sanhedrin** and the power of judging were lost nearly forty years before the destruction of the second Temple (as has been shown); it follows by necessity for all who are not entirely ignorant of logical consequences, that either the Messiah came around that time, or Jacob and Moses were completely lying. But since no one, neither among them nor among us, would concede the latter, they must concede the former. For when the prophecy says, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the scribe from between his feet, until Shiloh (that is, the Messiah) comes," it is certainly the same as if it said: "When the scepter and the scribe depart from Judah, then Shiloh (that is, the Messiah) shall come." For the letter *he* [ה] is placed in the position of *vav* [ו]. This is a frequent occurrence in Hebrew scripture, and *Shil* properly signifies "Son," and the meaning is: "Until his son comes," namely, the son of Judah. These are the words of <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note> Rabbi David Kimhi. Since this proposition has the force of a conditional statement, where the reality of the first part necessitates the reality of the second, the necessary consequence is that at the time the scepter and scribe departed from the Jews, Shiloh himself—the Messiah—arrived.

Afterward, he fell ill for seven days and died; and his brother priests ceased from that hour to bless in the name of the Lord. This is the tradition. From this, a great argument for the truth is taken: that Simeon the Just knew beforehand that he would die (as the Gospel relates) because he had seen the Christ of the Lord <note>The author is identifying the Talmudic "Simeon the Just" with the "Simeon" from Luke 2:25-35 who was promised he would not die until he saw the Messiah</note>. Nor is this surprising: for if our faith is nothing other than that of the Prophets, it was certainly necessary for the ancient Hebrew Doctors, wishing to correctly explain the prophecies speaking of the Messiah, to agree with us in their interpretations. # BOOK FOUR

...Rabbi Akiba’s <note>Akiva ben Joseph (c. 50–135 AD), a foundational figure in Rabbinic Judaism</note> gloss: "Yet a little while remains until the revelation of the Messiah." If, therefore, according to the error of the Jews of our age, the first coming of the Messiah were still to be expected, it would surely follow that the Prophet suggested a falsehood when he said that only a "little while" remained until the Messiah's coming. For from the time that this prophecy was brought forth, more than two thousand years have passed. Therefore, from the first part of this prophecy, it is necessarily inferred that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has already passed. This is then shown also by what he says: *And I will fill this house with glory.* For no one doubts that the Prophet was speaking of the second house of God, which was to be erected after the return from the Babylonian captivity. This glory was to be filled by the presence of the Messiah. Therefore, while that house was still standing, the Messiah was to come. But since that house was utterly destroyed by Titus, the Leader of the Roman army, in the forty-second year after the passion of Christ, it is certainly established that the time of the Messiah’s arrival has already passed. Finally, this same point is made even more clearly by what follows in the same prophecy. For when he says: *Great shall be the glory of this latter house, more than the first,* the Prophet was speaking (as has been said) of the second house of God, to the building of which he wished to lead the people.

For God, seeing that those who were applying themselves to the structure of the same temple were proceeding so slackly that they either did not dare to begin the work or wished to desist from what they had started, sent the prophet Haggai to them. In order to lead them to the beginning and completion of the work, he foretold to them the mystery that was to be accomplished in that same temple.

<margin>The glory of the second house.</margin>
And among other things he prophesied that this final house of God which was to be built would have a greater glory than that first one which had been erected by Solomon. Let the Jews say, therefore, in what the excellence of this glory—which this final house was to have—consisted?

<margin>Duration of the 1st and 2nd temple.</margin>
Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> responds that according to some, the excellence of this glory consisted in the size of the building, but according to others, in the duration of time. He himself, however, asserts that it consisted in both. For no building was ever seen to be like that of Herod, who restored that final temple, and the second temple itself lasted ten years longer than the first: since the first stood for four hundred and ten years, while the second (as he says) stood for four hundred and twenty. But truly, this latter point is of no importance, as is most apparent from these facts: first, because even if it had outlasted the first temple, it would seem very absurd for the Prophet to have mentioned such a small amount of time, especially since the words he used seem to imply a great excellence; and also because even if it had remained for more than ten years, since it was nevertheless violated many times, that longer duration of time

<margin>How many times the temple was profaned.</margin>
would have added not to its honor and glory, but rather to its disgrace. For first it was profaned by Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king whose actions led to the Maccabean Revolt</note>, who both plundered the vessels of God used in the ministry and placed an image of Olympian Jupiter in the same temple. Then indeed

<column-break/>

<page-num>210</page-num>
# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> by Pompey, who—when Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, the sons of Alexandra the Queen of the Jews, were fighting over the Empire—came to Jerusalem, and having captured the city and forced open the same temple, went even into the Holy of Holies. Furthermore, Cassius plundered the temple itself in the seventh year of Cleopatra after Judea was captured. Therefore, that duration of time by which the second temple is said to have exceeded the first is to be attributed not to its glory, but rather to its reproach. Nor can the statement of Rabbi Solomon regarding the size or beauty of the building be verified, since there could be no comparison between the first and second temple. For concerning the first, it is written in the second book of Chronicles <note>original: *Paralip.*, an older name for Chronicles</note>, chapter 3: <margin>B</margin> *The large house he wainscoted with cypress wood, and covered it with fine gold, and carved palms and chains upon it. And he adorned the house with precious stones for beauty; and the gold was gold from Parvaim. He also overlaid the house, the beams, the thresholds, and its walls and its doors with gold, and carved Cherubim on the walls.* <note>original Hebrew: הבית הגדול חפה עץ ברושים ויחפהו זהב טוב ויעל עליו תמרים ושרשרות: ויצק את הבית אבן יקרה לתפארת והזהב זהב פרוים ויחף את הבית הקורות הספים וקירותיו ודלתותיו זהב ופתח כרובים על הקירות</note> These words are interpreted thus: *And the great house was covered with fir wood. And he covered it with the best gold, and* <margin>C</margin> *raised or carved palms and little chains upon it. And he covered the house with precious stone for decoration. Furthermore, the gold itself was the purest gold. He also covered the house, the beams, the posts, and its walls and its doors with gold. And he carved Cherubim on the walls.* Likewise, concerning the same temple in 1 Kings 6 <note>original: *3. Reg. 6.*, following the Vulgate numbering</note>, it is said: *And the whole house he covered with gold, until the finishing of the whole house.* <note>original Hebrew: ואת כל הבית צפה זהב עד תם כל הבית</note> *And the whole altar of the oracle he covered with gold.* And a little later it is added: <margin>D</margin> *The floor of the house he covered with gold inside and out.* <note>original Hebrew: ואת קרקע הבית צפה זהב לפנימה ולחיצון</note> Furthermore, concerning the glory of the first temple itself in the book *Yoma* <note>original: *toma*</note>, that is, *of Days*, in the chapter *Seven Days*, it is said that Rabbi Hisda <note>original: *Hassidā*, a 3rd-century Babylonian scholar</note> spoke thus: "When Solomon built the house of the sanctuary, he planted in it all kinds of fruits made of gold, and the fruits were produced in their season. And when the wind blew upon them, they would fall off. As it is said <margin>E</margin> in the seventy-second Psalm: *Its fruit shall shake like Lebanon.* And from these was the livelihood for the priests. But when the Gentiles entered the temple, the trees became dry—namely, the golden ones. As it is said in the first chapter of Nahum: *And the flower or bud of Lebanon languished or withered.*" These things are found there. Even if these things are said metaphorically, they are highly relevant to the point. From these, therefore, it can be gathered how great the glory of the first temple was. Therefore, as is read in the first book of Ezra, chapter four <note>Actually Ezra 3</note>, when the work of the second temple was completed, many <margin>F</margin> of the priests and others who had seen the first temple wept while the others exulted, because that second temple, in respect to the first, was almost nothing. Also, almost all the vessels which had been gold in the first temple were made of bronze in the second, as the Talmudists report. Nor does the statement of Rabbi Solomon regarding Herod’s building—even if (as Josephus says) it was immense—hold truth, since Herod was able to be compared with Solomon neither in riches, nor in <margin>G</margin> power, nor in any other matter. Nor can it even be said that the excellence of glory by which the second house of God was to exceed the first was the holiness of the place itself; since, as the Talmudists say, among the other [marks] of holiness...

<summary>This page argues that the "greater glory" of the Second Temple predicted by Haggai cannot refer to physical size, beauty, or duration, as the First Temple was far more opulent and the Second Temple was repeatedly profaned. The author concludes that this glory must refer to the arrival of the Messiah during the Second Temple period.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> ...signs of the first temple, which were missing in the second: neither the fire which descended from heaven in the first temple to consume the burnt offerings was ever seen to descend in the second; nor did the glory of God, which used to appear in the first temple in the Holy of Holies between the Cherubim, ever appear in the second; nor was the Holy Spirit, who very frequently came to speak with the Prophets in the first temple, accustomed to come in the second. All these things are excellently proven through the Talmud. For in the book of the *Jerusalem Sanhedrin* <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with the high court and legal procedures</note> in the chapter *Ellu ben haggolim* <note>original: "אלו הן הגולין", meaning 'These are those who are exiled'</note>, it is said: <margin>B</margin> Rabbi Samuel says, Five things were missing in the last <margin>Five things were missing in the second temple.</margin> temple which were in the first. And from where is this proven? From what was said in the first chapter of Haggai: *Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be honored, says God.* <note>Haggai 1:8</note> The word *Veeccabda* <note>original: "ואכבד", meaning 'and I will be honored'</note> is written in a diminished way, without the letter *He* <note>ה</note>, which designates the number five. This signifies the five things in which the last sanctuary was diminished from the first: namely, the fire, the ark, the *Urim and Thummim* <note>original: "אורים ותומים", sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will; translated here as 'lights and perfections' or the 'breastplate of judgment'</note>, the anointing oil, and the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, the Gloss of Rabbi Salomon <note>The famous commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> on the word *Veeccabda*, that is, "and I will honor it," says: The letter *He* is missing here, which signifies five, on account of <margin>D</margin> the five things that were missing in the second temple but had been in the first: namely, the *Urim and Thummim*, the ark, the fire, the divinity <note>The Shekhinah or Divine Presence</note>, and the Spirit. Likewise, in the book *Yoma* <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Day of Atonement</note>, it reads: Rabbi Aha said, Why is it that in the word *Veeccabda* the letter *He* is missing? Because by it are designated the five things that were in the first temple and missing in the last. These are: the Ark with the mercy seat, the Cherub, the Fire, the *Shekhinah* <note>original: "שכינה", the dwelling or Divine Presence of God</note>, the Holy Spirit, and the *Urim and Thummim*. Also in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Song of Songs</note>, regarding the statement in the eighth chapter, *We have a little sister, and she has no breasts*, it is said: "A sister to us"—these were those ascending from captivity. "Little," because they were few in their armies. "And she has no breasts"—<margin>F</margin> these are the five things in which the last house stood diminished from the first. Moreover, in the book *Yoma* it is said: In the second sanctuary there was no ark. For there is a tradition that from the time the ark was hidden, there was hidden with it the jar of manna, the flask of anointing oil, the rod of Aaron with its almonds and flowers, and the chest which the Philistines sent as a gift to the God of Israel. As it is said in 1 Kings 6: *And all the vessels which you returned to Him for a guilt offering, put in a chest at its side.* Since, therefore, the Prophet Haggai said that the glory of the last house of God would be greater than that of the first, and yet the first house shone with such glory that the second house <margin>G</margin> could not be compared to it in even a single thing, it must necessarily be said that this "greater glory" was nothing other than the presence of the Messiah, by which the last house itself

<column-break/>

# BOOK FOUR

was to be honored more than the first. For if this excellence of glory cannot be understood as referring to the duration of time, nor the excellence of the building, nor wealth, nor sanctity (as has been proven), it must necessarily be understood as the presence of the Messiah, since no other cause can be assigned. Therefore, one of two things must be granted: either the Messiah came while the second temple was still standing, or the Prophet prophesied falsely. But since the latter is utterly absurd, the former must necessarily be granted. From the words of this prophecy, therefore, it is clear that the time of the Messiah's first coming has already passed. For he was to come while the second temple was still standing, which was nevertheless so overturned in the destruction of the city of Jerusalem by Titus, the son of Vespasian, that not even one stone remained upon another.

### CHAPTER X.

->*Refutation of the objection of the Jews, and a universal explanation of the prophecy of Haggai itself, according to their own glosses: and a confirmation of the aforementioned reasoning through Jeremiah.*<-

->CAPNIO <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), the famous Christian Hebraist, appearing here as a character in the dialogue</note><-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter I showing a scholar in a landscape.</image-desc>The Jews of our time, being of a very stiff neck and the most obstinate of all, oppose the things you have said, saying: Since the Prophet says, "Yet once more, in a little while, and I will shake all nations," and later adds the words by which you have tried to show that the Messiah's coming has already passed, it appears clearly enough from the words of the same Prophet that all these "shakings" were either to precede the Messiah's coming or were to happen around the time of his birth. But since it is known that shakings of this kind have not yet occurred, it is plainly a consequence <margin>E</margin> that this prophecy is not yet fulfilled, and the Messiah himself has not yet arrived. Therefore, show through their own scriptures that they are entirely speakers of falsehood in this matter. **Galatinus:** We shall prove that all these shakings of which the Prophet speaks did happen around the birth of Jesus the Nazarene, even according to them. For if we wish to explain this prophecy even according to their own expositions, we shall find that it was entirely fulfilled in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ. For this reason, it should be noted that when, a little before, Haggai himself had said to Zerubbabel, the prince of the Jews, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the High Priest, among other things: *And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says God; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the High Priest*; afterward, as if giving a reason, he added the words of this prophecy, saying: *My Spirit shall be standing in your midst*, that is, according to the gloss of Rabbi Salomon: "I will place, or I will cause my Spirit to descend upon your Prophets; do not fear." For thus says the Lord of hosts: *Yet once more, in a little while*, that is, according to the exposition of Rabbi Akiba, whom they call *Akiva*: "A short time yet remains until the coming of the Messiah; and I will shake..."

# BOOK FOUR

...I will shake the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land, and I will shake all nations. <note>Haggai 2:6-7</note> Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note> and Rabbi David <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, known as Radak (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi, biblical commentator, and grammarian.</note>, although they strive by every means possible to twist this prophecy from its true sense to show it should not be understood as referring to the Messiah, they nonetheless could not remain entirely silent about the truth. For Rabbi Solomon said that the heaven, the earth, and the rest were to be moved by miracles so that everyone would understand that God himself was in that second temple. Rabbi David, however, although he says those "shakings" are to be understood metaphorically (which is proven false primarily because the Prophet speaks in this whole prophecy not metaphorically or in parables, but in plain speech), nevertheless says he found written in the book of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> that a massive earthquake occurred in Judea during the time of Herod the Ascalonite. He says the fact that the nations were "shaken" should be understood to mean that God moved their hearts so that they would leave their own places and come to see the glory of this temple—and not with empty hands, but with their "desired things" <note>referring to gifts and treasures</note>. All of these points should not be considered entirely foreign to the truth, as will soon be seen in our exposition.

We say, therefore, that the heaven and the earth were shaken by miracles and wonders (as Rabbi Solomon explained) around the birth of Christ, since many and great miracles were seen both in heaven and on earth. For in heaven—to set aside the three suns <note>A parhelion or "sun dog" phenomenon, historically interpreted as an omen.</note> that arose simultaneously in Rome around the time of Augustus, under whom Christ was born, and which gradually merged into the same orb—soon after Christ was born, that new and wonderful star appeared, which provided leadership to the three Kings from distant regions to the place of his birth. Regarding this, Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his Latin translation and commentary on Plato's Timaeus.</note> in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* says: "That star did not announce diseases or death, but the arrival of a venerable God." When certain of the Chaldeans, truly excellent men and quite experienced in the science of celestial matters, had observed it, they are said to have sought the birth of the recent God. 

The earth also was then moved, not only by portents—which occurred at nearly the same time throughout the whole world, such as oxen speaking, serpents flying through the air, infants proclaiming certain words from their mothers' wombs, and women being changed into the masculine sex; and in Rome on the same day Christ himself was born, a spring of oil abundantly flowing from the earth; and in Judea, of whose land the Prophet specifically speaks, a massive earthquake occurring—but also because of the victory which the Romans obtained everywhere on earth. Then, therefore, the land, then the sea (that is, the islands of the sea), then also all the nations were moved, when at the birth of Christ, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled, and each person set out for their own city.

Next, the Prophet adds: *And the desired of all nations shall come*, which is to say, according to Rabbi David’s gloss, "And they shall come to worship with their desired things." This is never read to have happened in the second temple. Therefore, it ought to be understood rather as referring to those three kings who came from the East with gifts to worship Christ, just as Isaiah had foretold in the 60th chapter, saying: <note>original: "כלם משבא יבאו זהב ולבונה ישאו ותהלות יהוה יבשרו"</note>

<column-break/>

# 214

That is: All they from Sheba shall come: they shall bring gold and incense; and they shall show forth the praises of the Lord. <note>Isaiah 60:6</note> Concerning these matters we shall speak more extensively elsewhere. After this follows in the prophecy: *And I will fill this house with glory.* This, as Rabbi Akiba <note>A leading Jewish scholar and sage of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries.</note> explains, is understood to refer to the Messiah, by whose presence the second temple was to be made illustrious. Malachi also foretold this more clearly at the same time, when he says in the third chapter in Hebrew: <note>original: "הנני שולח מלאכי ופנה דרך לפני ופתאם יבא אל היכלו האדון אשר אתם מבקשים ומלאך הברית אשר אתם חפצים הנה בא אמר יהוה צבאות"</note>

That is: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts. <note>Malachi 3:1</note> Here Malachi also spoke of the second temple. Therefore, through the three things he posits, he signified that the arrival of the Messiah was then only a short time away. In saying "Behold," he shows the matter as if it were present. In saying "Suddenly," he hints at a time very close at hand. In repeating finally "Behold, he comes," he assigned the shortest possible time for his arrival. 

Furthermore, he said "to his temple" so that he might show two things at once which the Jews were going to deny. In this, he insinuated his divinity. For unless the Messiah was going to be God, he would have said in vain that he would come to *his* temple. And he fixed the time of his arrival, since he foretold that he would come while that temple was still standing. Here the error of the Jews of our time is refuted, who claim that the Messiah, when he comes, will find the temple desolate and them dispersed in captivity.

But let us return to Haggai: who, lest they believe he had spoken of the temporal glory which that second temple was to have, added this: *The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the Lord of hosts* <note>Haggai 2:8</note>; as if to say, "Do not think that I consider an abundance of silver and gold to be glory, since these are mine wherever they may be." Therefore, the Prophet was not speaking of temporal glory, but of spiritual glory, with which that temple was to be filled because of the presence of the Messiah himself. For which reason he also added: *The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former.* <note>Haggai 2:9</note> This is to be understood regarding the miracles which the Messiah, by his divine power, was going to perform in that second temple, not to mention his very presence. For in this, it is most established that the glory of the second temple stood far greater than that of the first: namely, that in the first temple God spoke to the people through the Prophets; but in the second he spoke through himself, taught the crowds through himself, and performed miracles through himself.

And notably he said "the last <note>Latin: *nouissima*</note> of this house," and not "the second," so that it might become openly known from there that a third temple was not to be built, and that the temple which was to be constructed through the Messiah was not to be a material one (according to the error of the younger Jews), but a spiritual one. Also, that which he added at the end, *And in this place I will give peace*, cannot be understood as temporal peace, since from the beginning of that temple until the end, the Jews were always afflicted by various hardships of war from other nations. Therefore, it must be understood as the spiritual peace which the Messiah was going to give. Rabbi Akiba also...

<margin>A</margin> ...perceives, as is clearly evident in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec* <note>A famous section of the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 90a–110b) discussing the world to come and the arrival of the Messiah</note>. Since these things are so, it is sufficiently clear and transparent that, notwithstanding the objections of the Jews, the Messiah was to come before the destruction of the second temple. This is also necessarily drawn from what is read in *Jeremiah, chapter 30*, if the Targum—that is, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translation found in that place—is diligently examined. *Jeremiah* thus says there:

"Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob..."</note> That is: "Behold, I turn back the captivity of the tents of Jacob (which was fulfilled under Zerubbabel) and I will have mercy on his dwellings. However, those words, "And his Leader shall be from himself, and his Ruler shall proceed from his midst," Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets</note> translates into Chaldean thus: <note>original Aramaic: ויתרבא מלכיהון פנהון... "Their king shall be raised up from among them..."</note> That is: "And their King shall be nourished, or anointed, from among them, and their Messiah shall reveal himself from their midst." Therefore, from the aforementioned words of Jeremiah, if one pays diligent attention, it is openly given to be understood that when the future state of the children of Judah—who had returned from the Babylonian captivity to build the temple and the city—would be as it was in ancient times (which occurred in the time of the Maccabees), then the Messiah was to be born and revealed. The Targum clearly shows this when it says, "And their Messiah shall reveal himself from their midst." The Prophet manifests that this was to happen after the union of the divine and human natures which was to occur in the Messiah, when he says in the person of God: "And I will cause him to approach, and he shall cling, or be joined to me." From these points, it is certain that the time of his coming has already passed.

### CHAPTER XI.

->*That the Messiah was born near the end of the second temple.*<-

->**CAPNIO.**<-
<note>Capnio is the Hellenized name of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

ALthough you have very well shown through the Jewish scriptures that the Messiah was to come while the second temple was still standing (which Titus utterly destroyed), yet because you have said nothing definite about *what time* during the endurance of that temple he was to come (since neither the Prophets whom you

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> introduced, nor the Jewish expositions you brought forward, assert this precisely), you would therefore do a very useful thing if, for a clearer expression of this truth, you would reveal at what time the Messiah himself was to come while the second temple was still persisting, both through the testimonies of the Prophets and the Talmudists. GALATINUS: It is certain, my dear Capnio, that even according to them, the Messiah was not only to come, but actually did come, near the end of the second temple. CAPNIO: Oh, a matter most opportune for crushing the hardness of the Jews of our time!
<margin>B</margin> Can what you say, then, be proved through their scriptures? GALATINUS: It certainly can; both through the Prophetic and the Talmudic writings. And first, through the prophetic ones. Let us hear Isaiah speaking thus in his last chapter <note>Isaiah 66:7</note>: <note>original Hebrew: כטרם תחיל ילדה... "Before she travailed, she gave birth..."</note> That is: "Before she was in labor, she gave birth: before the pains of childbirth came to her, she had already brought forth a male child. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen things like these?" Indeed, I contend that this prophecy should be explained exactly as the Jewish doctors explain it. For Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>A prominent 11th-century scholar and preacher from Narbonne</note> in the *Perush*—that is, in the Hebrew gloss—explains it thus: <note>original Hebrew: קודם שנולד מוליך... "Before he was born who led Israel into the last captivity, the redeemer was born."</note> That is: "Before the one who led Israel into the latest servitude was born, the redeemer was born." Therefore, through this gloss, it is manifest that before the birth of Titus <note>The Roman Emperor who, as a general, besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD</note>—who reduced the Jews into this final captivity and leveled the temple and the city of Jerusalem to the ground—the Messiah had been born. Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan the son of Uzziel, in the Targum (the Chaldean translation), explains the same prophecy in this way: <note>original Aramaic: עד לא ייתי לה עקא... "Before distress comes to her, she shall be saved..."</note> That is: "Before distress comes to her, she shall be saved; and before the pains and pangs of birth come to her, her King shall be revealed." From these things it is clear that Isaiah, in the aforementioned prophecy according to the exposition of this Chaldean Doctor, compares the Jews to a woman in labor because of the vehement distress they were to suffer from the Romans in the destruction of their city and temple. For as Rabbi Samuel says in *Beressith Rabba* <note>Genesis Rabbah, a midrashic text containing homilies on the Book of Genesis</note> regarding that which is said in the thirtieth chapter of Genesis, "In all the heat of the sheep": "In that hour when the house of the sanctuary was destroyed, the Jews cried out like a woman in labor." Just as it is said in the 4th chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original Hebrew: קול כחולה שמעתי... "I heard a voice as of one in labor..."</note> That is: "I heard a voice like that of a woman in labor, the distress of one giving birth for the first time." But before that distress (as Rabbi Jonathan explains), the Messiah was to be born, and through his death, the human race was to be saved. Thus, it has been shown by prophetic testimony that the Messiah was born around the end of the second temple. Now we shall prove this same point through the Talmudists. For it is read in *Beressith Rabba* (that is, in the Great Exposition of the book of Genesis), that while a certain Jew was following his plowing oxen to till the earth, an ox gave a great lowing. When a certain Arab, passing by that way, heard it, he said to the Jew: <note>original Hebrew: התר שוריך... "Unloose your oxen and all their gear..."</note> That is: "Unloose your oxen and their gear, and do not delay, because the end of your temple and your sanctuary has come." When this was said, and another ox lowed...

<margin>A</margin> "To the people," the Arab said again, <note>original Hebrew: אמר שוריך ואת כליו</note> "Tie up your oxen and their equipment, and prepare yourself: for King Messiah is born." Also in *Echa Rabboth* <note>The "Great Lamentations," a Midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, regarding the verse "Because the comforter is far from me" <note>Lamentations 1:16</note>: <note>original Hebrew: מה לנו ללמד מן אגון הער בים... "Why must we learn this from an Arab? Is it not a full scripture written: 'And Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one,' and what is written after? 'And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse...'"</note> That is: "Why is it necessary for us to learn this from Arabs? Since the text is already clear: for this is what is written in Isaiah 11: 'And Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one,' or 'through a mighty one.' What is written immediately afterward? 'And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots,' or 'shall bear fruit.'" So it says there. In those words of Isaiah, "Lebanon" is understood to mean the Temple, which was to fall by a "mighty one"—that is, by Nebuchadnezzar. Although these things recounted in the aforementioned traditions might seem like fables if understood literally, four conclusions against the Jews of our time are drawn from them. The first is that the Messiah was born shortly before the destruction of the second Temple. The second is that the Messiah’s name is <note>original Hebrew: מנחם</note> Menahem, that is, the Comforter, because he brought comfort to the human race. The third is that the Messiah is the Son of God, because it says his Father's name is Hezekiah, which is interpreted as "the strength of God." The fourth and last is that he was born in Bethlehem of Judah. From all these things it is concluded that the Messiah was born around the end of the second Temple; which was to be proven.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XII.

->A refutation of the Jewish opposition and a rebuke of their insanity, who admit that the Messiah was born long ago but say he has not yet come.<-

->CAPNIO.<-

The more recent Jews, convicted by these authorities, do indeed admit that the Messiah was born long ago, because the Talmudic testimonies you have just brought forward state that he was born on the very day the Temple was destroyed. But they say he has not yet "come" <note>meaning he has not yet revealed himself or begun his reign</note>. They attempt to show that this insanity of theirs is true <margin>G</margin> by using those very words of Isaiah by which you so excellently proved the Messiah was born before the destruction of the Temple and the city of Jerusalem.

<column-break/>

BOOK FOUR.

<margin>E</margin> This is primarily based on what is read in *Beresith Rabba* <note>The "Great Genesis," a Midrashic commentary</note>, regarding what is said in the thirtieth chapter of Genesis: "In every heat of the sheep." It is recorded that Rabbi Samuel said: "How do you prove that the Messiah was born on the very day the house of the sanctuary was destroyed? From what was said in the sixty-sixth chapter of Isaiah: 'Before she travailed, she brought forth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a male child. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things?' For in the hour that the house of the sanctuary was destroyed, Israel cried out like a woman in labor." Therefore, by this authority of Isaiah and the Talmudic traditions you introduced in the previous chapter, the younger Jews strive to prove that the Messiah was born on the day the Temple was overturned by Titus, the son of Vespasian. From this they infer that we cannot possibly show through these same scriptures that our Lord Jesus Christ was the Messiah, since he was not born on the day the Temple fell, but long before. GALATINUS: Responding to this, we first concede that the Messiah is called a "male child" in the aforementioned words of Isaiah because of his absolute perfection; and that the Jewish people "brought him forth," since he was born of the tribe of Judah according to the flesh. But we entirely deny that he was born on the day the Temple fell, since he was born about seventy-five years before. For that word <note>original Hebrew: טרם</note> *terem*, placed in the words of Isaiah, does not mean "while/during," as the more recent Jews take it, but signifies "before."

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> From this it is clear that since the Messiah was born not "while" the Jewish people were in labor—that is, grieving over the Temple's destruction—but "before" they travailed. This is established by three reasons. The first is the Prophet’s own amazement, saying: "Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things?" For if she had brought forth while in labor, there would be nothing miraculous, since all women bring forth while in labor. Therefore, so that the Prophet’s wonder is not in vain, nor the comparison inappropriate, the Jews must concede that the Messiah was born *before* the destruction of the Temple itself. The second reason is that this Hebrew word <note>original Hebrew: טרם</note> *terem*, both in these words of Isaiah and in almost all other places, is always taken to mean <note>original Hebrew: קודם</note> *kodem*, which signifies "before." This is perfectly clear through Rabbi Kimhi, their most excellent expositor of words; for in the book *Sefer Hashorashim* <note>The "Book of Roots," a famous Hebrew dictionary</note> he says: "Before she travailed, she brought forth. The sense of this word *terem* is *kodem*, that is, before." As it is in 1 Samuel, chapter three: <note>original Hebrew: טרם ידע את יהוה וטרם יגלה אליו דבר יהוה</note> That is: "Before he knew God, and before the word of God was revealed to him." There, *terem* is used for *kodem*, which is the same as "before." Rabbi Kimhi brings forward many other authorities in which this word *terem* is placed, and at the end of each one he says that *terem* means nothing other than *kodem*, which is exactly the same as "before." Finally, the third reason, the strongest of all, is that both the Hebrew commentary of Rabbi Moses Haddarsan and the Targum—that is, the Chaldean translation—render this word *terem* as "before."

He specifically analyzes the word "terem" to show it means "before" rather than "during," identifying Jesus as the fulfillment of these prophecies.</summary>

...they take it not for "not yet," but for "before" (as was seen above). From these points it follows that the Messiah was born not on the day of the Temple's destruction, as the Jews wildly claim, but before (as the Christians assert). Furthermore, regarding the traditions of the Talmudists, who say the Messiah was born on the same day the Temple was destroyed, we say that the word "day" is usually understood in three ways: First, for the time when the sun is above the horizon, which astronomers call the artificial day. Second, for a space of 24 hours, which they call the natural day. Finally, for some indeterminate period of time. In this third sense, it is used only in the feminine gender. We find this very often in Holy Scripture, especially in Isaiah, who says in almost countless places <term>ביום ההוא</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ba-yom ha-hu*</note>, that is, "in 그날" or "in that time." It is certain that this can only be understood as a course of several years. This is how the Talmudists understand "day" when they say the Messiah was born on the day the Temple fell. For although that Temple remained as a physical structure for forty-two years after the passion of Christ, its holiness was destroyed at the very hour He suffered. For then (as we have said elsewhere) it lost all its sanctity. Therefore, at the moment Christ died, the veil of the Temple was immediately torn from top to bottom as a sign of this. The most powerful evidence of this fact was the cessation of miracles. For as we have shown elsewhere through their own writings, the miracles that used to occur in the Temple completely failed forty years before its actual ruin. From these statements, it is clear that the Messiah was not born on the same day the Temple was overturned (as the Jews of our time falsely claim), but before the Temple's overturning, as we have already proven.

**CAPNIO:** <note>Capnio is the pseudonym for the scholar Johann Reuchlin, who acts as the questioner in this dialogue.</note> If the Messiah (as they say) was born in Bethlehem on the same day the Temple was destroyed, and since he has not yet appeared anywhere, where do they say he has been hiding for so long?

When Elijah (of blessed memory) heard this, he thought the whole world was to be destroyed. He went out and found men plowing and sowing, and he said to them, "The Holy and Blessed God is angry with His world; He wishes to destroy His house and take His children captive among the nations of the age. And yet you care for and are anxious about this temporal life?" But the "daughter of a voice," that is, the heavenly voice, came forth and said to him: <term>הנח להם שכבר נולד לישראל מושיע</term> <note>original Hebrew: *hanach lahem she-kevar nolad l'Yisrael moshia*</note>. That is: "Leave them alone, for already a Savior has been born to Israel." Elijah said, "And where is he?" The voice said, <term>בבית לחם יהודה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *be-veit lechem yehudah*</note>. That is: "In Bethlehem of Judah." So he went and found a certain woman sitting at the door of her house, and her son was lying before her, covered in blood.

All this is found there. But he unties one wound and binds it back before moving to the next, for he does not wish to do otherwise, lest he be delayed. The gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "The Messiah unties one wound, wipes it, and immediately binds it. And thus he does with the others, and does not untie them all at once. For he fears lest he be delayed in binding all his wounds if he were told to go and liberate Israel." ## BOOK FOUR.

Elijah said, "Today," namely, if you will hear his voice. All these things are found there. Although they may not be true—unless perhaps understood metaphorically and spiritually—they are nonetheless excellent arguments to use against the Jews. For through these points they can be convinced both that the Messiah was born long ago, and that he was once in Rome <note>The author refers to a Talmudic legend that the Messiah waits at the gates of Rome among the poor and sick</note>. Also, those words of Isaiah, *Behold, my servant shall understand* (with the rest, up to the end of the fifty-third chapter), were understood by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> to refer to the Messiah, even though elsewhere he has struggled to twist these same words to refer to the Jewish people. And according to the word of Elijah, that passage from Psalm 95 is also to be understood regarding the Messiah: *For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.* <note>original Hebrew: כי הוא אלהינו ואנחנו עם מרעיתו וצאן ידו היום אם בקולו תשמעו אל תקשו לבבכם</note> This is, to render it word for word, "Since he himself is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." This is the clearest testimony that the Messiah is God; and that today the wretched Jews would have the Messiah—namely, our Lord Jesus Christ—if they were willing to hear his voice through obedience and belief, and did not harden their hearts.

### CHAPTER XIII.

*The third reason by which it is proved that the time of the Messiah's first coming has already passed, taken from the devastation of the assigned place.*

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>C</margin>
If the Talmudists <note>The scholars and compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> said that the Messiah was born or would be born in Bethlehem of Judah (as was clear in the preceding points), then it is not without reason that we ask whether it can be proved from the place assigned for the Messiah's birth that the time of his coming has already passed. GALATINUS. It certainly can. For Micah indeed—whom the ancient Talmudists followed (as was seen a little earlier)—predicted that he would be born in Bethlehem, when he says in the fifth chapter: *And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are a little one among the thousands of Judah. Out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler in Israel; and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.* <note>original Hebrew: ואתה בית-לחם אפרתה צעיר להיות באלפי יהודה ממך לי יצא להיות מושל בישראל ומוצאותיו מקדם מימי עולם</note> These words sound thus in Latin: "And you Bethlehem Ephrata, you are small among the thousands of Judah. From you shall go out for me he who is the ruler in Israel. And his going out is from before, from the days of the age," that is, according to the exposition of Rabbenu Hakkadosh <note>Judah the Prince (c. 135–217 AD), the chief redactor of the Mishnah</note>, "from eternity, and from the days of the age." This prophecy can only be understood as referring to the Messiah: both because of the <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> of Rabbi Jonathan, which explains those words, *Out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler*, in the Chaldean language thus: *From you shall come forth before me the Messiah* <note>original Aramaic: מנך קדמיי פוק משיחא</note>; and also because of Rabbi Solomon’s gloss, which explains this prophecy as follows: "And you Bethlehem Ephrata, from which David went out; as it is said in the seventeenth chapter of the first book of Kings, *The son of that servant of yours, Jesse the Bethlehemite.* Bethlehem is also called Ephrata; as it is said in the forty-eighth chapter of Genesis, *On the way to Ephrata, which is Bethlehem.* You are small among the thousands of Judah. This is because of the low status of Ruth the Moabitess, who was in you. Out of you shall come forth for me the Messiah, 

<column-break/>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<margin>A</margin>
the son of David: just as he himself says, *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* Now Jonathan translated this thus: 'From you to me,' that is, from my side shall come forth the Messiah. 'And his going forth was before the days of the age': just as it is said in Psalm 72, *Before the sun, Innon* <note>original Hebrew: ינון. A name interpreted by the Talmud as one of the names of the Messiah, meaning 'he shall flourish' or 'son'</note>, that is, born or begotten or 'son' is his name; which Rabbi Jonathan translated thus: *And his name was called King before the days of the age.*" <note>original Aramaic: ושמיה אמר מלדמין מוקמי עלמא</note> It follows in the prophecy: *Therefore he will give them up until the time that she who is in labor has given birth.* <note>original Hebrew: לכן יתנם עד עת יולדה ילדה</note> Our masters have said, "From this we have it that the son of David (that is, the Messiah) would not come until the wicked kingdom (that is, the Roman Empire) had ruled over the whole world for nine months." However, this Scripture is mystical. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. He has explained these words concerning the Messiah well enough and faithfully (to tell the truth), which he very rarely does—except for this one thing: where it was said of the Messiah, *And his going forth is from before, from the days of eternity*, he seems to want this understood only regarding the Messiah’s *name*, when he says, "And his name was called before the days of the age." We, however, departing in no way from the truth of the text, do not deny that the name of the Messiah, *Innon*, was before the sun and before the days of the age: which is nothing other than saying that the Messiah existed as God from eternity; since *Innon* (as we have said elsewhere) is exactly the same in Latin as "born" or "begotten" or "son." Since, therefore, this prophecy speaks of the Messiah, it is surely clear according to it that the Messiah himself was to be born in Bethlehem of Judah at a time when the Jews still ruled in that region. Therefore, since Bethlehem itself and all of Judea have been desolated, and the Jews remain captives throughout the world, they must concede one of two things: either that the Messiah was born before that desolation, or that they are first to return to their own land. But since the second cannot stand with their own expectation, they must necessarily grant the first. This is also proved by the ancient Talmudists. For so we read in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*: "Master Judah said: In the age in which the son of David comes, the house of the assembly shall be for harlots, and Galilee shall be laid waste." <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי יהודה דור שבן דוד בא בית מועד יהיה לזנות והגליל יחרב</note> Since, however, from the burning of the Temple and the city of Jerusalem until now there has been no assembly of judges—on the contrary, as we have shown elsewhere, their assembly of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme judicial council of the Jews in ancient Israel</note> or judges utterly failed forty years before the destruction of the Temple itself—and Galilee with the entire region of the Jews has long since been laid waste, it is perfectly clear that the son of David, or the Messiah, came long ago; since the time of his coming (as has now been proved) has long since passed. GALATINUS. Rabbi David <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note>, among others, strives to distort it thus; saying, "And you Beth-"

## BOOK FOUR.

"...Bethlehem, though you are small among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth for me one who is to be the Ruler in Israel." <note>original Latin: "lehem, etsi minima sis in millibus Iuda..." quoting Micah 5:2</note> And this is the King Messiah, who is to be born from the seed of David, of whom it was said: "And his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." <note>original: "Et egressus eius ab initio à diebus feculi."</note> For the goings forth of the Messiah began from the time of David. He said "from the beginning, from the days of eternity," however, because of the great length of time that was to exist between David and the Messiah.

To the Christians, however—who attribute this part of the prophecy to Jesus of Nazareth, affirming both that he was born in Bethlehem and that he was God from the beginning and from the days of eternity—a response is given from that same passage: that he himself was not a ruler in Israel, but rather the Israelites ruled over him. And when they prove that the Messiah is God because he is said to be "from the days of eternity," answer them that they argue falsely in this; since God existed before the beginning of the world, it would follow by their logic that he was created then, which is an absurd thing to say. But if they bring forward that authority, "From eternity and unto eternity, you are God," and that other, "From eternity I have anointed my King," you should say that those are to be understood not as "from the era" <note>the author is distinguishing between *seculum* as a finite age and *aeternitas* as timelessness</note> but "before the era." 

So says all these things that treacherous Rabbi David <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and commentator</note>. To confute these points, we shall first explain this prophecy according to the glosses of the ancient Talmudists. Then we shall refute his distorted and false exposition. We explain it thus: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, though you are the least among the thousands of Judah, because the first King of Judah, that is, David, arose from you, the Messiah—who shall be the last—shall also come forth from you for me." And he rightly says "shall come forth," to show that he ought not to be generated from human seed alone. In this, with wonderful brevity, he also suggested his twin nature, namely the divine and the human. For when he said, "out of you," he demonstrated his humanity. But when he said, "for me," he hinted at his divinity. For he said "for me" as if to say: "That man who shall come forth from you shall be worthy to be united to me, that is, to my divinity." 

He expressed this more clearly afterward, saying: "And his goings forth are from eternity, and from the days of the era." Indeed, the word for "goings forth" <note>original: "egressus"</note> in this place is plural in the Hebrew language, just as it is in Latin. Therefore the meaning is: the goings forth—that is, the proceedures—of this ruler or Messiah are two. One is from eternity, by which he proceeded from the Father according to his divinity. The other is from the days of the era, by which he came forth from a mother according to his humanity. This certainly agrees perfectly with that saying of Athanasius: "He is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, and he is man, born from the substance of his mother in the age." <note>A reference to the Athanasian Creed, a foundational Christian statement of faith</note> However, Athanasius says "In the age," because he accepted the birth itself; but the Prophet says "From the days of the age," because when the matter of Adam was formed, the matter of the glorious Virgin was immediately present in that same matter, and the humanity of the blessed Christ was present in the most precious blood of the Virgin herself. 

Indeed, our contemporary Jews cannot deny any of this, since nearly these same things are said by the Holy Rabbi <note>referring to *Rabbeno Haccados* or Judah ha-Nasi</note> in the book <margin>The Revealer of Secrets <note>Hebrew: גלי רוזיא Gale Razaya</note></margin> when explaining the same prophecy: "And his goings forth are from eternity, and from the days of the era." The Prophet says "goings forth" in the plural number because there are two goings forth of the Messiah. One of divinity, which is eternal, and therefore he says "from eternity." The other of humanity, which exists in the substance of his mother, which was created from the hour of the world's creation. And for that reason he says,

<column-break/>

"From the days of the era." For as the same author says a little earlier in the same place, the mother of the King Messiah was created by God so that the Messiah himself might sit within her, to show the glory of his majesty to all mortals; therefore she herself is shown to be the first creature of God in the human race. These are the words of that Holy Rabbi, whom they themselves call "our holy master." 

From these things that have been said, the perversity of Rabbi David is easily disproved. For the Prophet asserts that the goings forth of the Messiah were from eternity and from the days of the era; to say they were merely from the days of King David (as R. David wishes) is both depraved and impious. For even if the Prophet meant "from the beginning" (as R. David falsely explains) and not "from eternity," that time which he says passed between David and the Messiah was by no means "from the beginning" or "from the days of the era." Indeed, the very authorities he brings forward in the name of the Christians (see how great his blindness is!) show this more clearly. For one affirms that the Messiah is God; the other shows that his going forth according to his humanity was simultaneous with the creation of the world, just as was explained from the opinion of the Holy Rabbi. Furthermore, when he says that Christ our Lord did not have dominion over Israel, but rather those of Israel ruled over him, he certainly wanders very far from the truth. For as the sacred scriptures frequently foretell, the Messiah was to rule over Israel—that is, over his good and faithful ones who received him—in his first coming. Although near the end of the world, he is also destined to have dominion over the remnants of the Jews who shall be converted to him.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*The fourth reason effectively demonstrating that the time of the Messiah's first coming has already passed, taken from the expiration of the determined time through the prophecy of Daniel according to the expositions of the Talmudists. ...Holy of Holies. Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times. And after sixty-two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined. And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate.

This is, to render it word for word: And while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice, and he instructed me, and spoke to me, and said: "Daniel, I have now come forth to teach you understanding. At the beginning of your prayers the word went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are a man of desires <note>original Latin: "vir desideriorum"; a traditional rendering of the Hebrew "ish hamudot," meaning a man greatly beloved or precious</note>. Therefore consider the matter, and understand the vision. Seventy weeks are shortened <note>or "decreed"; original: "præcisum est"</note>—that is, the time—upon your people and upon your holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to wipe out iniquity, and to bring in everlasting justice, and to fulfill the vision and the prophecy, and to anoint the holy of holies. Know therefore and take heed: from the going forth of the word to return and to build Jerusalem—or from the exit of the word so that Jerusalem might be built again—until the Messiah the Leader—or the Prince, or the Principal—there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks. She herself shall return, and the street and the trench shall be built, but in a narrowness of times. And after sixty-two weeks, the Messiah shall be slain, and he shall have nothing <note>original: "non ei," meaning "not for him" or "he shall have nothing"</note>. And the people of a coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be in a rush or a snatching away. And until the end of the determined war, there shall be desolations. Moreover, he shall confirm the covenant for many in one week; and in the middle of that week he shall cause the slaughter of sacrifices and the offering to cease; and upon the abominations shall be desolation. And even until the end and the pre-defined limit it shall persevere, or be forged, or it shall melt itself upon the desolation."

**CHAPTER.** Since, as I see it, this prophecy contains many and great mysteries, and since the more recent Jews strive to pervert it with many kinds of distortions so that they may prepare a refuge for themselves against the truth, it is therefore necessary to discuss it more diligently than others. And first, indeed, in what way these "weeks" are to be understood. **GALATINUS.**

<margin>Porphyry the Jew against Daniel.</margin>
I shall indeed do so, as soon as I have first refuted the treacherous impudence of a certain Jew of the Sadducee sect named Porphyry <note>Galatinus mistakenly identifies the famous Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) as a Jewish Sadducee; Porphyry was actually a pagan critic of Christianity who argued that Daniel was written in the 2nd century BC</note>. In order that he might not be forced to confess the truth through this prophecy of Daniel, he dared to speak against the opinion of everyone else, saying that one should not care about such words of Daniel, since he was not a prophet, nor should he be numbered among the prophets. Against him we say that Daniel was not only a prophet, but is held to be greater than many of the prophets by almost all the Hebrews. For it is clearly shown that he stood as a prophet in the book *Meghila* <note>The Talmudic tractate Megillah</note>, in the chapter *Meghila nikreth* <note>original: "Meghila nikreth," Hebrew for "The Megillah is read"</note>, that is, the History is read, where it is said word for word: "Baruch son of Neriah, and Seraiah son of Mahseiah, and Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, and Daniel the man of desires, and Mordecai, and Haggai, and Zecha-

<column-break/>

riah, and Malachi all prophesied in the second year of Darius." So it is said there. Since, therefore, Daniel is called a prophet here and is numbered among the prophets, it cannot possibly be denied that he was a prophet. His book also holds its own rank among the twenty-four books of Holy Scripture for the Hebrews, and has always been held among them as the truest among the truthful—excepting only the histories of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon <note>These are the "deuterocanonical" or "apocryphal" additions to Daniel found in Greek versions but not in the standard Hebrew Bible</note>, which, according to the Hebrews, the volume of Daniel rejects. Nor has anyone ever been found among them so violently foolish that he presumed to detract from the holiness and truth of Daniel, except for this most wicked Porphyry the Sadducee. With a resisting conscience, he preferred to blacken Daniel’s authority rather than confess the Lord Jesus Christ when convicted by such clear testimony from the same Daniel. Yet it is not man, but God Himself who refutes his rashness, when He says in Ezekiel chapter 14: "Son of man, when a land sins..." and below, "Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in the midst of it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, says the Lord God." And again in chapter 28, He says: "Son of man, say to the Prince of Tyre <note>ironically, of course</note>: Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that they can hide from you." From these and many other passages, it is clear enough—to disprove the impudence of this most impious Sadducee—how great the authority of Daniel ought to be among men, seeing that it is so great with God.

Now, however, we must see how the "weeks" are to be understood in this prophecy of Daniel. To settle this in a few words, I say that here all the commentators, both Christians and Hebrews, agree on the method of counting the weeks. For they take a "week" here for a space of seven years, just as we do. Although some of the Jews of our age—if they happen to be shaken and cornered by these words of Daniel into confessing the truth—assert that a "week" in this place should be understood not as seven years, but as a space of seven jubilees <note>A jubilee is 50 years</note>, or centuries, or decades. Yet none of them, however perverse, has been found to have written this until now, whether in the Talmud or elsewhere. The Angel Gabriel himself beats down their impudence when he says in the preceding words: "And in the middle of the week," namely, of the sacrifices and the offering—that is, of all the others. For since this failing or cessation of sacrifices is found to have occurred before the destruction of the temple, both through the Lord Jesus Christ and through the Romans, and since that slaughter of sacrifices has never and nowhere been performed by the Jews since that time (as they themselves admit), it clearly stands that these seventy weeks were entirely completed before the overturning of the temple. For this week, in the middle of which the bloody heap of sacrifices was to cease, occupies the last place, showing it is the final one of all. From which it necessarily follows that these weeks are not indeed of jubilees, nor centuries, nor decades, nor any other kind.

### BOOK FOUR.

...not just numbers, but rather intervals of years; otherwise, they would by no means have been completed at that time. For from the burning of the first Temple until the destruction of the most recent one, there were not, according to them, more than the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity and the four hundred and twenty years during which they say the last Temple remained in its perfection. From all of these, the Jews constitute these seventy weeks of Daniel, as will be more broadly revealed in what follows. Furthermore, that the aforementioned weeks of Daniel are of years is shown first from the ways in which Holy Scripture understands "weeks." For it is not accustomed to take them in any but two ways. In one way, it takes a "week" for a span of seven days, as is clear in Leviticus chapter 23, where it is said that seven weeks are to be counted from the feast of Passover, which makes 49 days, and on the fiftieth day is the feast of Pentecost. In the other way, it takes a "week" for a cycle of seven years: as is said in Leviticus 25, "You shall number seven weeks of years," which make 49 years. And the fiftieth year immediately following is commanded to be the Jubilee, which among the Jews was the year of remission. Since, therefore, no other way is found in the Holy Scriptures by which a "week" is understood, and since in the aforementioned words of Daniel a "week" cannot be taken for a span of seven days—because thus the whole prophecy of Daniel would have been completed within a year and a half—it is necessarily consequent that it be taken for a cycle of seven years. This is then proven by Rabbi Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish-Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note>, a great glossator and Doctor among them, in this manner, when he says: "Our venerable Master <term>סעדיא</term> Seadias <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), an influential Jewish philosopher and exegete</note> said that these seventy weeks are of years." A witness of this matter is that which is said in Daniel 10: "After this, I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks of days; I ate no pleasant bread," and so forth until the completion of three weeks of days. He did not, however, count "days" with the seventy weeks. For the aforementioned "middle of the week" is one thousand two hundred and twenty days <note>The text here says 1220, though Daniel 12:11 traditionally cites 1290 days; the author addresses this later</note>, as I shall prove by sufficient proof. Furthermore, it is possible that "the middle" is not a perfect middle, having neither less nor more, like that in Numbers 32: "And the half <insert>tribe</insert> of Manasseh." And many things of this sort. Know, however, that "days" are always days, and not years, specifically in Holy Scripture. Nevertheless, it is possible that when "days" is said, it may be a perfect year, the year returning again <term>ימים</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yamim*</note>, that is, "from days to days," which is to say, from year to year, which are a perfect year. But when "days" is said with a number, such as "two days" or "three," they cannot be years, but it is necessary that they be days, just as they are called. And because of this, it is said in Leviticus 24 <note>Likely referring to Leviticus 25:8</note>: "And you shall number for yourself seven weeks of years." And for that reason I said that one thousand two hundred and ninety days are the midpoint or "middle" of the aforementioned week. And this is that from Daniel 12: <term>אשרי המחכה ויגיע לימים אלף שלש מאות שלשים וחמשה</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ashrei ha-m'khakeh v'yagia l'yamim elef sh'losh me'ot sh'loshim v'hamishah"</note>—this is, "Blessed is he who waits and reaches the one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days." For if "days" were said here to be years, how could it be true that a man might wait a thousand years and

<column-break/>

attain them? Especially since it is written in Psalm 90: "The days of our years in them are seventy years." These are the words of Rabbi Abraham regarding Daniel. From these, three arguments are taken. The first indeed is that the aforementioned weeks of Daniel are of years. The second is against the Jews of our time who more frequently say that the 1,335 days mentioned in Daniel 12 are years, by which they ought to be visited and have the Messiah, which years they calculate from the destruction of the last Temple. That this is false is clearly evident from the preceding exposition of Rabbi Abraham. The third finally is that these aforementioned days are the half of the last of Daniel's weeks. At which time, specifically, Christ came to his baptism, and preached, and called the disciples to himself. From all these things it is clear that in this prophecy of Daniel, a "week" is not understood except for a span of seven years. Wherefore those seventy weeks contain four hundred and ninety years.

<margin>Whether the years of these weeks are solar or lunar.</margin>
This <insert>leads to the question</insert>: How are the years of these weeks to be understood? For Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and scholar who wrote extensively on chronology</note> and certain others of our people say they are lunar, moved chiefly by a twofold reason: first, because in the text these weeks are said to be "shortened"; therefore, since lunar years are eleven days shorter than solar years (for a solar year contains 365 days and one quarter, and 5 minutes, while the lunar consists of 354 days), it follows plainly that the years of these weeks ought to be lunar, not solar. Also, because when the Angel spoke to Daniel, who was a Hebrew, and since the Hebrews calculated by lunar years, it is reasonable to believe he was speaking not of solar but of lunar years.

**Galatinus:** Those who say this err not a little. For the text itself (to respond to their reasons) does not say these weeks are "shortened." For where our edition has "they are shortened," the Hebrew letter says <term>נחתך</term> *Nehtach*, which is the same as "cut off" or "decreed," since it comes from the Hebrew verb <term>חתך</term> *hatach*, which properly signifies to cut, or to cut off, and to determine and establish. For which reason these weeks, according to the Hebrew truth, ought not to be called "shortened," but rather "cut off," "pre-finished," or "pre-defined": because they were predestined through the 70 years before they were announced to Daniel by Gabriel. This is excellently shown in the book called <term>סדר עולם</term> *Seder Olam* (that is, *The Order of the World*), since at the end of that same book it is written that Rabbi Jose said: "What is 'seventy weeks are cut off'?" By this it is taught that they were cut off by a decree through seventy years. Furthermore, if the Jews had a year eleven days shorter than the solar year, since according to their law they are bound to celebrate Passover on the 14th day of the first month of any year, it would surely follow that by celebrating Passover, they would always anticipate the celebration of the Passover of another year by eleven days in every single year. If this were so, within a short time they would celebrate their Passover in every month, nor would they agree with us in the time of celebration. That this is false is clearly evident from their practice, since they always celebrate the Passover at almost the same time. Wherefore it is manifest that they <insert>calculate</insert> by years...

Galatinus uses Rabbinic authority and chronological logic to refute the idea that these are shorter lunar years, insisting they are solar-aligned years decreed by God.</summary>

...solar years, just as we also compute the seasons. For although they have lunar months, every third year among them has thirteen months or lunations, while each of the others contains only twelve months. Thus, by performing adjustments of the seasons through intercalations <note>Intercalation is the insertion of a leap day, week, or month into some calendar years to make the calendar follow the seasons.</note>, they measure the seasons by solar years, just as we do. For they also have twelve months which they assign to both the first and second year, and they begin the year from the month of March, which they call *Nisan* <note>original Hebrew: ניסן</note>. But to the last month of the third year—that is, February, which they call *Adar* <note>original Hebrew: אדר</note>—they add another month which they call *Veadar* <note>original Hebrew: ואדר</note>, that is, "And-February" <note>This is the intercalary month Adar II in the Hebrew calendar.</note>.
