The Messiah answered Moses, "Moses, Jacob your father saw the house which will be built on earth. He also saw the house which the Holy and Blessed God builds with His own hands in the heavens. And he understood with his whole mind that the house which the Holy and Blessed God builds with His hands in the heavens out of precious stones and pearls, with the ornament or splendor of the Divinity, is the house which will remain for Israel forever and for ages of ages. And so he spoke on the night when he slept upon the <margin>A double Jerusalem: the heavenly and the earthly.</margin> stone, and saw the Jerusalem to be built on earth and the Jerusalem to be built in the heavens. When therefore your father Jacob saw both Jerusalems, one on earth and one in heaven, he said: *This one which is on earth is nothing.* As it is said in Genesis 28: *And he was afraid and said, How terrible is this place.* This is not it, but the house which remains from generation to generation. For that is the house of God which He himself builds with His hands in the heavens, and so He builds it on earth: according to that saying in Exodus 15: <note>original Hebrew: "מקדש אדני כוננו ידיך"</note> This is: *The sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established.* And when Moses heard these words from the mouth of the Messiah son of David, he rejoiced with great joy. <margin>A</margin>From your gates, Jerusalem. *Jerusalem which is built as a city, which is joined together as one.* <note>A reference to Psalm 122:2-3.</note> All of this is tradition, which primarily contains six points. The first is that when Moses was about to die, he ascended into heaven, and there he saw God building the house of the heavenly sanctuary. The second is that he saw the Messiah sitting in the middle of that heavenly house or temple. The third is that he requested from God the ability to speak with the Messiah. The fourth is that God was intended to build the house of the sanctuary <margin>B</margin> on earth, yet with His other hand He was building it in the heavens, and it was made of precious stones and pearls. The fifth is that Jacob saw both Jerusalems—namely, the heavenly and the earthly—and compared to the upper one, the lower is as nothing. Finally, the sixth is that the saying of the psalmist, *Jerusalem which is built as a city*, must be understood as referring to the heavenly Jerusalem. The Targum <term>Targum: an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</term>, that is, the Chaldaic translation, also clearly shows this. For it says: <note>original Aramaic: "ירושלם דמתבניא ברקיעא היך קרתא דמתחברא לה כחדא בארעא"</note> This means: *Jerusalem which is built in the firmament like a city, which is joined to her as one on the earth.* This is also clearly evident in the book *Taanith* <term>Taanith: a volume of the Talmud focusing on fast days and communal prayers</term>, that is, the Book of Fasting, where it is read that Rabbi Yohanan said: "I will not enter the Jerusalem above until the Jerusalem below has been built." They asked him: "What is the Jerusalem above like?" He answered them: "Just as it is written in Psalm 122: *Jerusalem is built as a city that has participation together*." From all these premises, it must be concluded that the Jerusalem and the temple of which Ezekiel speaks are to be understood mystically. Similarly, the temple which Zechariah said would be built by the Messiah must be understood spiritually. For He was to build a spiritual temple—that is, the Church <term>Ecclesia: the gathering of the faithful</term>—made of living and chosen stones, which are His faithful. Therefore, for those who received the Lord Jesus Christ and heard His word (that is, the Gospel), the temple has been built in the heavens; but for those who do not receive Him, it is not built.

## CHAPTER XI ##

*Regarding the tenth objection of the Jews: That the Messiah has not yet come because they themselves have not yet been saved.*

### CAPNIO ###

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure in a landscape, used for the word 'Etiam'.</image-desc>
They also bring against us what is said concerning the Messiah in Jeremiah, chapter 23, in this manner: <note>original Hebrew: "הנה ימים באים נאם יהוה והקימותי לדוד צמח צדיק ומלך מלך והשכיל ועשה משפט וצדקה בארץ בימיו תשע יהודה וישראל ישכון לבטח וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקינו"</note> That is: *Behold the days come, says God, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch: and a king shall reign, and he shall understand, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence. And this is his name by which they shall call <margin>F</margin> him: Our Righteous God.* They say these things were spoken of the Messiah, as is clear through the Targum (the Chaldaic edition), which says: <note>original Aramaic: "הא יומין אתין אמר יהוה ואקים לדוד משיח דצדקא"</note> that is, *Behold the days come, says God, and I will establish for David the Messiah <margin>G</margin> of righteousness.*

<column-break/>

<page-num>314</page-num>
<margin>C</margin>Therefore, from the fact that it says, *In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence*, it is openly shown that we Jews ought all to be saved at the coming of the Messiah. Since, therefore, at the coming of Jesus the Nazarene we were not saved at all, but rather lost (for we never suffered so many and such grave evils as happened to us in his days, when we were utterly destroyed, scattered, and dispersed throughout the world), it is entirely manifest and certain that neither was he the Messiah, nor has the true Messiah yet come.

GALATINUS: We give them no other response than that which is given by their own ancients, who say that in this passage "Judah" is nothing other than "confession," and that all who confess the Savior or the Messiah were to be saved through Him. For so it is read in the Commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan on the book of Genesis, upon that saying in Genesis 41: <note>original Hebrew: "ויאמר פרעה אל יוסף אני פרעה ובלעדיך לא ירים איש את ידו"</note> that is, *Pharaoh said to Joseph: I am Pharaoh, and without you no man shall lift up his hand.* Rabbi Aha said: "From 'I', spoken by flesh and blood, you learn of 'I', spoken by the Holy and Blessed God. For if from that which Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I am Pharaoh,' Joseph merited all this <margin>D</margin> blessing; when the 'I' of the Holy and Blessed God comes—of whom it is said in Isaiah 46: <note>original Hebrew: "אני עשיתי ואני אשא ואני אסבול ואמלט"</note> *I have made, and I will lift up, I will carry and will deliver*—how much more should I wonder? Can it be said that the Redeemer will be a respecter of persons? Far from it. For all who confess Him with their mouth, and their works, and their heart, He will save and deliver, just as it is written in Jeremiah chapter 23: *In his days Judah shall be saved*—as if he were to say, 'those who confess Him.'" And again He says in Isaiah 45: <note>original Hebrew: "פנו אלי ותושעו כל אפסי ארץ"</note> That is: *Turn to me, and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth.* Thus far Rabbi Moses Hadarsan. From this tradition, therefore, it clearly appears that in the aforementioned words of Jeremiah, when he says, *in his days Judah shall be saved*, "Judah" is not taken for the faithless Jews who deny the true Messiah, but for <margin>E</margin> all people whatsoever who confess the Savior himself. And all who confess Him in heart, word, and <margin>Who the true Jews are. How "Judah" is interpreted.</margin> deed shall be saved. For "Judah" is interpreted as "the confession of God." For the name *Yahweh* <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> is the same as God, and *huda* <note>original Hebrew: יהודה</note> means confession; from which is composed *Yehuda*, that is, Judah, which is the same as "the confession of God." It is also read in Hosea, chapter 1: <note>original Hebrew: "לא אוסיף עוד ארחם את בית ישראל כי נשא אשא להם ואת בית יהודה ארחם והושעתים ביהוה אלהיהם ולא אושיעם בקשת ובחרב ובמלחמה ובסוסים ובפרשים"</note> *I will no longer add to have mercy on the house of Israel, for I will utterly forget them. But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God. And I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by war, nor by horses and horsemen.* Which Rabbi Jonathan translated and explained in Chaldaic thus: <note>original Aramaic: "לא אוסיף עוד לרחמא על בית ישראל ברם אם יתובון משבק אשבק להון ועל דבית יהודה ארחם ואפרקינון במימרא דיהוה אלההון ולא יתפרקון בקשתא ובהרבא ובעבדי קרבא ובסוסון ובפרשין"</note> That is: *Behold I will no longer add to have mercy upon the house of Israel. Nevertheless, if they repent, I will surely forgive them. But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them <margin>H</margin> in the Word of the Lord their God. And I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by those who make war with horses and horsemen.*

and horsemen. Moreover, that the Messiah was to come from God was seen most extensively in the third book. ### CHAPTER XII ###

->To the eleventh objection of the Jews: That the Messiah has not yet come because Gog has not yet been destroyed, nor Magog conquered.<-

### CAPNIO ###

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'O' showing a floral or foliate design.</image-desc> THE Jews, moreover, hurl another argument against us and against our Lord, the true Messiah, because of those things which are read in the Sacred Scriptures concerning Gog and Magog, especially in Ezekiel chapter 38, which says: <note>original Hebrew: "בן אדם שים פניך אל גוג ארץ המגוג"</note> This means: *Son of man, set your face against Gog, the land of Magog.* Where the commentary of Rabbi Solomon says: "Gog is the name of the king, Magog the name of the nation." Just as it is said in Genesis chapter 10: <note>original Hebrew: "גומר ומגוג"</note> that is, *Gomer and Magog.* Then, in the same prophet, it follows a little later: <note>original Hebrew: "האתה הוא אשר דברתי בימים קדמונים ביד עבדי נביאי ישראל הנביאים בימים ההם שנים"</note> which means: *Are you he of whom I have spoken in old time by the hand of my servants the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days for years?* Here the commentary of Rabbi Solomon says: "The Holy and Blessed God said: Are you the one of whom I announced in ancient days through the hand of my servants the prophets of Israel? Such as Ezekiel and Zechariah: for Zechariah himself also prophesied concerning the battle of Gog and Magog." In chapter 14, he says: <note>original Hebrew: "ואספתי את כל הגוים אל ירושלם למלחמה ונלכדה העיר ונשסו הבתים והנשים תשגלנה ויצא חצי העיר בגולה ויתר העם לא יכרת מן העיר: ויצא יהוה ונלחם בגוים ההם"</note> This means: *And I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle. And the city shall be taken, and the houses plundered, or torn apart, and the women shall be ravished. And half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the rest of the people shall not be cut off from the city. Then God shall go forth, and fight against those nations.* Indeed, our masters <note>Referring to the Jewish Sages or Rabbis.</note> have said that Eldad and Medad <note>Figures mentioned in Numbers 11:26-27 who prophesied in the camp of Israel.</note> also prophesied concerning the war of Gog and Magog. This is indicated by the word *shanim* <note>original: "שנים"</note> mentioned here. However, you should not read it as *shanim*, meaning "years," but as *shenaim*, meaning "two."

<column-break/>

<page-num>318</page-num>
<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

that is, "two." For two prophets announced one prophecy at the same time. Thus far Rabbi Solomon. Therefore, from these things and from others which Ezekiel himself mentions in chapter 39 concerning Gog and Magog, the younger Jews <note>Likely referring to contemporary or post-biblical Jewish polemicists.</note> take up an argument for their wickedness, saying: "That through the Messiah, God will conquer Gog and Magog, and that the Messiah will kill Gog himself, according to that saying of Isaiah, *And with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked*; and we shall be led back into our land, to reign together with him in Jerusalem forever." Since this has not yet happened in the slightest, they claim it is clear and certain that the Messiah has not yet come, and that your Jesus was not the Messiah. 

**GALATINUS.** Since neither a third temple is to be built (as was shown more extensively in the preceding parts), nor are the Jews ever to possess their own land again, nor are the ten tribes ever to return (as will be shown most extensively in what follows), we therefore say that the aforementioned words of Ezekiel, and any others read anywhere concerning Gog and Magog, are to be understood not according to the letter, but spiritually. That the ten tribes are never to return is shown now by what is read in the book *Sanhedrin* <term>Sanhedrin: A major tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and the courts</term>, in the chapter *Helec*, in this manner: "The ten tribes were not destined to return," that is, they are never to return to the land of Israel. The *Rabbanan* <term>Rabbanan: The Rabbis/Teachers of the Talmud</term>, that is, the Masters, handed down that the ten tribes shall have no part in the world to come, just as it is said in Deuteronomy 29: <note>original Hebrew: "ונתשם יהוה מעל אדמתם באף ובחמה ובקצף גדול"</note> that is, *And the Lord rooted them out of their land in anger, and in wrath, and in great indignation.* This is the tradition. Therefore, since a third temple is not to be built, and the Jews are never again to return to their land nor possess it further, and they have been rejected by God forever, and the ten tribes are not to return further to the land of their fathers (as shown by the previous tradition), for that reason, whatever is read in Ezekiel or elsewhere concerning Gog and Magog must be understood not literally, but spiritually. Indeed, this can be shown from the fact that in the aforementioned chapter *Helec*, it is read thus: "Rabbi Abba said: The house which is before the Holy and Blessed God is eighteen thousand leagues, just as it is said at the end of Ezekiel: <note>original Hebrew: "סביב שמנה עשר אלף"</note> that is, *Round about eighteen thousand.*" Where the commentary of Rabbi Solomon says: "The scriptures at the end of Ezekiel spoke of the heavenly Jerusalem." Likewise, in the *Midrash Coheleth* <term>Midrash Coheleth: A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes</term>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes upon that saying in chapter 10, "Who is like the wise man?", it is said: "This is the first Adam, of whom it was said in Ezekiel 28: <note>original Hebrew: "בן אדם שא קינה על מלך צור ואמרת לו כה אמר אדני יהוה אתה חותם תכנית מלא חכמה וכליל יופי:"</note> that is, *Son of man, take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyre, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord God: You are the seal, or ring of resemblance, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.*" Also in the book *Baba Bathra* <term>Baba Bathra: A tractate of the Talmud concerning property and civil law</term>, in the chapter *Hammocher eth hassefina*, that is, "One who sells a ship," it is read thus: "Rabbi Hanina said: The Holy and Blessed God made ten coverings for the first Adam in the garden of pleasure, just as it is said (in Ezekiel, namely in the same place, immediately): <note>original Hebrew: "בעדן גן אלהים היית כל אבן יקרה מסכתך אדם פטדה ויהלום תרשיש שהם וישפה ספיר נפך וברקת וזהב מלאכת תפיך ונקביך בך ביום הבראך כוננו"</note> that is, *You have been in the delights of the garden of God. Every precious stone was your covering: the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold; the workmanship of your timbrels and of your pipes was prepared in you in the day that you were created.*"

Sardius, topaz, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, beryl, carbuncle, emerald, and gold—the workmanship of your timbrels. And your pipes were prepared in you on the day of your creation. <note>original: "Sardius, topacius... opus tympani tui." This is a list of gemstones from Ezekiel 28:13, describing the King of Tyre, often interpreted by medieval theologians as referring to the fall of Lucifer or the state of Adam in Paradise.</note> Having laid this groundwork, let us say to the Jews: since those things which were so expressly said concerning the King of Tyre in Ezekiel were understood not of himself, but of Adam (as is clear from what was said before); and since those things written at the end of the same Ezekiel concerning Jerusalem and the Temple are to be taken not of the earthly, but of the heavenly Jerusalem: Since these two things, I say, which we have now mentioned, were understood by the wise men of the Jews not as the letter sounds outwardly, but far otherwise, it is undoubtedly necessary that what is said between these two concerning Gog and Magog be understood differently than the letter outwardly shows. Especially since (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), also known as Rambam.</note> says near the beginning of the book *More* <note>The *Guide for the Perplexed* (Moreh Nevukhim).</note>) the key to understanding everything the prophets said is to understand parables, metaphors, similes, and enigmas. This is even more clearly held from what is read in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, regarding that saying in Isaiah chapter 9: <note>original Hebrew: "למרבה המשרה ולשלום אין קץ"</note> which is: *Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end.* For so it is said there: Rabbi Tanhuma said, "Why is every *mem* <note>The Hebrew letter Mem (מ) has two forms: open (מ) for the beginning/middle of words and closed (ם) for the end. In Isaiah 9:7, the word "le-marbe" (לםרבה) unusually uses a closed 'final' Mem in the middle of the word.</note> which is in the middle of a word open, yet this one is closed? Because the Holy and Blessed God sought to make Hezekiah the Messiah, and Sennacherib Gog and Magog. Then the <term>Attribute of Judgment</term> <note>original: "מדת הדין" (Middat ha-Din), a personification of God's strict justice in rabbinic literature.</note> spoke before God: 'Lord of the world, what shall this be? David, who spoke so many songs and so many praises in Your sight, You did not make the Messiah; yet Hezekiah, for whom You performed all these signs but who did not sing a song before You, will You make him the Messiah?' Then a <term>Daughter of a Voice</term> <note>original: "בת קול" (Bat Kol), a heavenly or divine voice or revelation.</note> went forth and said: <note>original Hebrew: "רזי לי רזי לי"</note> that is, 'My secret is mine, my secret is mine.'" This is the tradition. In which, even if this—namely, that God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog—is legendary unless understood spiritually, we nevertheless have the intended meaning concerning Gog and Magog: that they must be understood mystically.

<margin>Who are understood by Gog and Magog.</margin>
From these things, therefore, it is clearly evident that Gog is not some future king, nor Magog some specific nation, as the more recent Jews dream and rave; rather, any impious persons who persecute and trouble the people of God, they themselves are Gog and Magog. For it is not as the Jews and even some of our own who follow Jewish interpretations think, that Gog and Magog are innumerable and fierce Scythian tribes who they say extend beyond the Caucasus mountains and the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> and near the Caspian Sea even unto India, and whom they assert will be stirred up by the devil after a thousand-year reign to come into the land of Israel and fight against the saints with many other nations joined to them. And first indeed <note>original Hebrew: "משך"</note> Meshech, whom Josephus says are the Cappadocians. Then <note>original Hebrew: "תובל"</note> Tubal, whom the same man thinks are the Iberians or Spaniards, and the Hebrews suspect are Italians, having with them Persians, Ethiopians, Africans, and the rest. They try to prove this chiefly from what Saint John says in Revelation chapter 20: *And when the thousand years are finished, Satan shall be loosed, to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog.* However, they fall into this error because they do not notice that the whole

<column-break/>

book of John, which is prefaced with the title of Revelation, is mystical. Therefore, those who want Gog and Magog to be understood according to the letter err with the Jews. For just as the prophet foresaw and foretold the reward of the holy and the just in the vision of the Temple and the distribution of the land, so here he foresaw and foretold under the figure of Gog and Magog the persecution of the Church of God and the just, which has happened and happens daily as much through heretics as through other persecutors of the holy faith and Catholic truth, who are the covering and habitation of demons.

For Gog is named from the Hebrew name *Gag* <note>original: "גג"</note>, which is the same as "roof." As is that saying in Proverbs chapter 25: <note>original Hebrew: "טוב שבת על פנת גג מאשת מדינים ובית חבר"</note> That is: *It is better to sit in a corner of the gag (the roof), than with a quarrelsome woman in a shared house.*

<margin>How Gog and Magog are interpreted.</margin>
And from this comes *Magog* <note>original: "מגג"</note>, which is the same as "from the roof." <note>In Hebrew, the prefix 'Ma' or 'Mi' can signify "from."</note> Wherefore the devil is rightly called Magog, who proceeds from the house.

Gog, however, will especially be the Antichrist in the final times, who will be the roof and house of the devil, from whom Magog—that is, the devil—will go out through open persecution. And therefore, in Ezekiel it was said to Gog himself: <note>original Hebrew: "באחרית הימים"</note> That is: *In the end of days you shall be.*

### CHAPTER XIII ###

-> Regarding the twelfth objection of the Jews: That Jesus the Nazarene was not the true Messiah, because he did not leave behind seed, nor did he have sons. <-

### CAPNIO ###

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'H' showing a person in robes holding a book.</image-desc>Notwithstanding these things, Jewish perfidy, wishing to show that our Lord Jesus Christ was not the true Messiah, finally opposes us with that which is said of the Messiah in Isaiah chapter 53: <note>original Hebrew: "יראה זרע יאריך ימים וחפץ יהוה בידו יצלח"</note> That is: *He shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of God shall prosper in his hand.* And also that which is written in Psalm 88 concerning the same: <note>original Hebrew: "ושמתי לעד זרעו וכסאו כימי שמים"</note> That is: *And I will establish his seed forever, and his throne as the days of heaven.* Since therefore (they say) your Jesus had no sons, nor did he leave the seed of sons after him, he could by no means have been the Messiah.

**Galatinus.** Their madness in this can easily be refuted if even one of the things I say is committed to memory. For it is read thus in the *Lesser Beresith* <note>Bereshit Rabbati, a midrashic commentary on Genesis.</note> regarding that saying in Genesis chapter 25: <note>original Hebrew: "ויוסף אברהם ויקח אשה ושמה קטורה"</note> That is: *And Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.* It is written in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: <note>original Hebrew: "בבקר זרע את זרעך ולערב אל תנח ידך"</note> that is: *In the morning sow your seed and in the evening let not your hand cease.* For you do not know which will be more suitable or right.

Whether this or that, or if both are good together. Rabbi Akiba says: "If you have had disciples in your youth, instruct disciples also in your old age. For you do not know which of them God will credit to you, or whether

...or whether all will be good together. These are the words there. Since the disciples here, having been taught by someone, are called his seed, then the Apostles and his other disciples were the seed of Christ. In the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>original: "Berefith rabba"; a classic collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note>, concerning that passage in **Genesis 28**: *To you I will give it and to your seed,* it is said: "Your seed shall be like you," just as it is said in **Deuteronomy 33** <note>The text cites Deut 23, but the verse "Israel shall dwell in safety, the fountain of Jacob alone" is Deut 33:28.</note>: *and Israel shall dwell in confidence, the eye of Jacob alone.* And regarding this, the prophet **Amos** asked for mercy, saying in chapter 7: *Lord God, forgive, I pray, or forgive now. Who shall raise up Jacob, for he is small?* <note>original: "Quis furget Iacob, id eft, vt Iacob?"</note> That is, who shall stand like Jacob? Although he himself is small, or is he not small? He had mercy upon this. And so forth. This is the tradition. Here it should be noted that those who are like Jacob are called his seed. We also read this in **Massekhet Bikkurim** <note>original: "מסכת בכורים"; The Tractate of First Fruits in the Mishnah.</note>, that is, in the book of first fruits, they handed down in the name of Rabbi Judah that a **Ger** <note>original: "גבר gher"; a resident alien or a convert to Judaism.</note>, that is, a converted stranger who comes from the gentiles to the faith, brings the first fruits himself, and learns or reads that passage from **Deuteronomy 26**: *I declare today to the Lord your God, that I have entered the land which God swore to your fathers.* What is the proof of this? That which was said in **Genesis chapter 17**:

<margin>Why Abram was called Abraham.</margin>

**Neither shall your name be called any more Abram, but your name shall be Abraham: for a father of a multitude of nations have I made you.** <note>original: "ולא יקרא עוד את שמך אברם והיה שמך אברהם כי אב המון גוים נתתיך"</note> For in the beginning he was the father of Aram <note>A region in the ancient Near East; "Abram" is often interpreted as "Exalted Father" or "Father of Aram."</note>, and therefore he was called Abram. But finally, he became the father of the whole world, and for that reason, he was called Abraham. This is the tradition. Also, in the book **Sanhedrin** <note>A major volume of the Talmud dealing with law and courts.</note> in the chapter **Dinei Mamonot** <note>original: "דיני ממונות"; Laws of Monetary Cases.</note>, that is, Judgments of Wealth, it is said: It is written in **Genesis chapter 49**: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah.* These are those who were the heads of the Babylonian captivities, who ruled Israel with a scepter. *And a scribe from the midst of his feet.* These are the sons of the sons of Hillel <note>A famous Jewish sage from the 1st century BCE.</note>, teaching the law to Israel. These are the words there. Therefore, the masters taught by Hillel were called his sons. For among the Hebrews, everyone is called the son of him by whom he was taught or nurtured. Hence, in the same book, in the chapter **Cohen Gadol** <note>original: "כהן גדול"; High Priest.</note>, that is, the High Priest, we read: It is written in the **Second Book of Kings** <note>Now commonly known as 2 Samuel 21:8.</note> chapter twenty-one: *And the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul.* Rabbi Yehoshua said: Merab gave birth to them, but Michal nurtured them, though she never had children herself. For as it is written in the **Second Book of Kings** chapter six, no son was born to Michal the daughter of Saul until the day of her death. Therefore, because she nurtured them, they were called her sons: so that the scripture might teach you that whoever nurtures an orphan or a

<column-break/>

**A** ward in the midst of his house is regarded as their father, just as if he had begotten them. Rabbi Yohanan said: Whoever teaches the son of his neighbor, the scripture regards him no differently than if he had begotten him: as it is said in **Numbers chapter 3**: **And these are the generations of Aaron and Moses.** <note>original: "ואלה שמות בני אהרן ומשה"</note> Then it follows: **And these are the names of the sons of Aaron.** <note>original: "ואלה שמות בני אהרן"</note> But Aaron indeed begot them, while Moses taught them; and therefore they are called his sons, just as they are Aaron's. All this is from the Talmud. From
**B** all these things it is clear that even if our Lord Jesus did not have biological children, he nevertheless had infinite spiritual ones. For not only were the Apostles and his other disciples, who were immediately taught by him, called his sons, but also all other Christians who follow and observe his teaching. Therefore, the "seed" he left behind, which lasts into the distant future, is not physical but spiritual. This was not done without a mystery. For just as he himself descends from a
**C** spiritual seed rather than a physical one, so too he ought to have a spiritual rather than a physical seed. Moreover, that the Messiah was to come forth from a spiritual seed is evident from the promise made to Abraham concerning the Messiah himself, when God said to him in **Genesis 22**: **And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.** <note>original: "והתברכו בזרעך כל גויי הארץ"</note> And in the preceding chapter it is said that the Lord told him: **In Isaac shall your seed be called.** <note>original: "כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע"</note> And yet it is established that Isaac was conceived according to the spirit 
**D** and not according to the flesh, as Ishmael was: as the Apostle says writing to the **Galatians**. <note>Referring to Paul's argument in Galatians 4:22–31.</note> Therefore, by a stronger reason and far more so, the Messiah—who was to be conceived not from male seed, but from a mystical breath (as will be most extensively proven in what follows)—is said to be conceived according to the spirit. Because, therefore, Jesus the Nazarene, the true Messiah, was born entirely according to the spirit of a virgin without a man, he ought to have not physical but spiritual sons. This is also clearly shown from the Hebrew gloss which, upon that verse *In
<margin>Two ages.</margin>
Isaac shall your seed be called,* says that two ages <note>original: "Secula duo"; or two worlds.</note> are
**E** noted there: one of the Law, the other of the Messiah; and that in the age of the Messiah, the seed and sons were to be spiritual, just as Isaac was born according to the spirit. And David spoke of sons of this kind in **Psalm 45**, which according to the ancient Hebrews is explained as referring to the Messiah, saying: **Instead of your fathers, you shall have sons.** <note>original: "תחת אבותיך יהיו בניך"</note>

# ON THE REDEMPTION
## AND SALVATION OF THE HUMAN RACE, FOR
### WHICH THE MESSIAH WAS TO COME, AND
#### which could only be accomplished by God and man.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

---

->That no one was to be the savior and redeemer except God, who would give himself as the price for human redemption.<-

---

->C A P N I O.<-
<note>Capnio is the humanist name of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous scholar of Hebrew and a character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'O' showing a person in a rural setting with trees and a building in the distance.</image-desc>

O MY Galatinus, you have indeed excellently and quite abundantly proven in the preceding sections, through the authentic scriptures of the ancient Jews, not only that the appointed time for the first coming of the Messiah has already passed, but also that the Messiah himself has already come, and that this same Messiah was none other than our Lord Jesus. Therefore, so that the impiety of the Jews of our age may be further refuted, we must now speak of the redemption and salvation of the human race, for which the Messiah himself was to come, and which could only be accomplished by a God-man. For this reason, in order to proceed in an orderly fashion, it must first be shown that there was to be no savior and redeemer except God, who was to give himself as the price for human redemption. <margin>A</margin> To suggest this, the prophets first proclaimed everywhere that God alone is the savior, and then the ancient <term>Talmudists</term><note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> clearly handed down this same teaching. Hear Isaiah first, then, speaking in the person of God in chapter 43: <term>I, even I, am the Lord, and besides me there is no savior.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אנכי אנכי יהוה ואין מבלעדי מושיע"</note> Hear next also Hosea, likewise speaking with the voice of God in the thirteenth chapter: <term>And I am the Lord your God from the land of the Egyptians, and you shall know no gods or God but me, and there is no savior except me.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ואנכי יהוה אלהיך מארץ מצרים ואלהים זולתי לא תדע ומושיע אין בלתי"</note> Furthermore, so that the opinions of the Talmudists may be understood, those things written in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A "Midrash" is a form of rabbinic commentary; "Tehillim" refers to the Book of Psalms.</note> on this matter are to be noted. First, concerning that passage in Psalm 13: <term>But I have trusted in your mercy; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ואני בחסדך בטחתי"</note> For there it is held: <term>The Holy One, blessed be He, said to David: "David, by what [authority] do you say these things?" He said to Him: "Because I trust in Your mercy," as it is said, "But I have trusted in Your mercy," in that mercy of which it is said:</term>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <term>The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.</term> <note>Psalm 33:5</note> <term>Of which it is also said: "If I said, my foot has slipped, Your mercy, O Lord, sustained me." Another interpretation: "But I have trusted in Your mercy," that is, in the Law; as it is said, "And the law of kindness is on her tongue." "My heart shall rejoice in your salvation." This is one of the most difficult scriptures—that the salvation of the Holy One, blessed be He, is the salvation of Israel. It is not written "our salvation" here, but "Your salvation." David said: "Our salvation is Your salvation."</term> <note>original Hebrew: "בך חסד יהוה מלאה הארץ... אמר דוד ישועתנו היא ישועתך"</note> These are the words there. <margin>A</margin> From the scriptures, it is shown that the salvation of Israel is the salvation of the Holy and Blessed God. And why is this so? Because He promised him this in the ninetieth Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 91:15–16.</note>, saying: "I will be with him in trouble, I will deliver him, and honor him; with long life I will satisfy him, and show him my salvation." And likewise He says in Psalm 80: <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "עוררה את גבורתך ולכה לישועתה לנו אלהים השיבנו והאר פניך ונושעה"</note> that is, "Stir up your strength, and your salvation shall be ours: O God, restore us, and enlighten, or make your face to shine upon us, and we shall be saved." Rabbi Berachiah the priest, son of a Rabbi, said: "Look at what is written in Zechariah chapter 9: 'Behold, your King will come to you, righteous and saved himself.' It is not written 'Behold your savior,' but 'Behold your saved one.'" <margin>C</margin> From what is written in the Law, this can be stated. For Israel shall be saved and redeemed. And it will be as if the Holy and Blessed God Himself were redeemed and saved. And this is one of the harder and more serious scriptural points: that the salvation of Israel is the salvation of the Holy and Blessed God. Rabbi Enia said: "Moses said in Deuteronomy chapter 33: 'Blessed are you, O Israel. Who is like you, a people saved?' It is not written simply thus, but 'a people saved in the Lord.'" This is similar to a man who has a small amount of the <term>second tithe</term> <note>A portion of agricultural produce set aside to be eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed for money to be spent there.</note>. What does he do? He gives the price and redeems it. So by what shall Israel be redeemed? Since it is written in the Law, it can be said: "A people saved <gloss>badonai</gloss>," that is, in God. This means, namely, that God is the price of his redemption. It is also written in <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A traditional rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>, concerning that verse in Psalm 90: "He shall call upon me and I will answer him," which Rabbi Isaac, explaining this, said: "If they seek me in the hour when trouble comes upon them, I will answer them immediately: just as it is written (as above), 'He shall call upon me and I will answer him.'" And further on, "And I will show him my salvation"; because after that salvation, there will be no more trouble: as it is said in Isaiah chapter 45, "Israel shall be saved in God with an everlasting salvation." Moreover, He says, "And I will show him my salvation": because the salvation of Moses, and Deborah, and David, and Ezra was such that trouble came after the salvation. And this is one of the harder scriptural points: that the salvation of Israel is the salvation of the Holy and Blessed God. <margin>E</margin> Here it is not out of place to add what is read in the book <term>Siphre</term> <note>An ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, concerning that verse of the forty-ninth Psalm, <margin>F</margin> <note>original: "אח לא פדה יפדה איש לא יתן לאלהים כפרו"</note> that is, "A brother does not redeem; can a man redeem? This was indeed after they were given manna for the reviving of the dead. "I will kill and I will make alive. Let my soul die the death of the righteous. Let Reuben live and not die. He will revive us in a day of days." Another discourse: <margin>B</margin> "I will kill and I will make alive." Can I understand from this that death is in one person and life in another? Not at all. For it is said: "I will inflict the wound, and I will heal." Thus death and life are in one and the same person. And there is no one who can rescue from my hand. Fathers shall not save their sons; Abraham shall not save Ishmael, nor Isaac save Esau. From this it is held that fathers shall not save sons. But as for brothers not saving brothers, how is it proved? <margin>C</margin> From that which is said: "A brother does not redeem; can a man redeem?" For Isaac will not save Ishmael, nor Jacob save Esau. And even if they gave for their redemption all the wealth in the world, it would not suffice to save them, nor is it a worthy price for their souls. And this is what is written: "A brother does not redeem; can a man redeem? And he will not give to God his ransom." From the aforesaid, therefore, it is most clearly evident that God alone was to be the Savior and Redeemer of Israel, and that He Himself would give Himself as the price of human redemption. <margin>D</margin>

In many places this is manifest. First, therefore, I will bring forward those things written to our purpose in the <term>Bereshith Rabba</term> of Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century rabbinic commentary on Genesis.</note> regarding that passage in Genesis chapter 23: "And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother." Furthermore, as it was proven in the third book that the Messiah is the Word of God, it follows that this salvation of the ages—or eternal salvation—was to be accomplished through the Messiah. <margin>A</margin> This is also confirmed by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>, who, in explaining that phrase in Daniel—"And the sanctuary shall be justified" <note>original: "וצדק קדש", from Daniel 8:14.</note>—says: "Sin shall be pardoned for Israel, and they shall be redeemed with an eternal salvation through the King Messiah, just as it was said in the 45th chapter of Isaiah: 'Israel shall be saved in God (or through God) with the salvation of the ages.'" These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, since the traditions we brought forward in the previous chapter from many authentic books prove (through those same often-cited words of Isaiah) that this Savior is none other than God, and now in this present tradition, through those same words, this eternal salvation is attributed to the Messiah—as the commentator Rabbi Solomon does—and through the Chaldaic translation <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> this same salvation is attributed to the Word of God; it necessarily follows that this Savior-God, who was to save the human race with eternal salvation, is none other than the Messiah, the Word of God and the Son of God. <margin>C</margin> For if God alone was to be the Savior with the salvation of the ages (or eternal), as was proven in the preceding chapter through the testimony of the prophets and ancient traditions, and yet now, with those same testimonies and traditions, the Messiah is called the Savior with the salvation of the ages, it is a necessary consequence—to all who understand logic and whose minds have not been blinded by the devil due to their sins—that the Messiah is undoubtedly not only man, but also God. <margin>D</margin> However, if you wish to see something even greater than what has been concluded here against the faithlessness of the Jews of our time, listen to what is written in the first chapter of Hosea: "I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, for I will utterly forget them (or taking them away, I will take them away); but on the house of Judah (that is, the house of confession) I will have mercy, and I will save them in the Lord their God (or through the Lord their God)." <margin>E</margin> Rabbi Jonathan, translating this into Chaldaic, explained it thus: "I will no longer add to have mercy on the house of Israel. However, if they repent, I will surely forgive them. But on the house of Judah I will have mercy, and I will save them by the Word of the Lord their God." Since the Targum <margin>F</margin> (the Chaldaic translation) put "the Word of God" where the prophet, in place of "God," used the Tetragrammaton name of God—which is YHWH <note>original: "יהוה", the four-letter holy name of God.</note> and is the same as "Lord God"—it is openly suggested that the Word of God is God. Consequently, it is clearly shown that the Messiah is the Word of God and the Lord God, in whom and through whom this eternal salvation was meant to occur. <margin>G</margin> Hence, it was not without reason that He was called "Jesus" <note>original: "ישע", Yeshua/Jesus.</note>, as we have proven elsewhere, which is interpreted as "Savior" or "Salvation."

# CHAPTER III.

->*That the Redeemer, in order to be a perfect redeemer, had to be both God and man.*<-

## CAPNIO.

From what you have said, it is clearly evident that the redeemer of the human race was to be both God and man. GALATINUS: Exactly so; otherwise he could not have sufficiently satisfied for the sin of the human race. CAPNIO <note>The dialogue persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note>: I would like you to prove this more clearly by the testimonies of the ancient Talmudists, in order to further confound the faithlessness of the younger Jews who deny this entirely. GALATINUS: I shall certainly do so. But first I will relate what is read on this subject in the commentaries of Rabbi Abraham Picus, which are entitled *On the Significance of the Tips* <note>The "Taghin" or decorative crowns found on certain letters in a Torah scroll.</note> which are written above the letters of the book of the Law, which the Hebrews call <margin>תגין</margin> <term>Taghin</term>. There, among other things, we find this: "Solomon (peace be upon him) handed down this hint: 'I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second child who shall stand in his place' (Ecclesiastes 4). It is certain that it is characteristic of man to be born a boy and a youth, and to progress daily and receive increase until he reaches perfection. And this is what he says: 'All the living proceeding (that is, progressing) under the sun with the second child.' And the meaning of this word according to my teaching—by which I command you to perceive this with your intellect—is that the 'second child' is the First Intelligence, which is God. And it is not permitted to reveal or disclose these things except only to him who understands them by himself. And this is what is found in Job chapter 33: 'Twice' (namely, forgiveness was made by God), but 'the third' time man did it. And soon he adds: 'That he might redeem souls from hell and give them another luminous body, that it might shine in life.' And by 'life' is understood eternal life." Thus it is written there. From these words, it is crystal clear that the redeemer was to be both God and man. Then, to prove this even more clearly, I will bring forward what is said in *Echa Rabbathi* <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah. For there, upon that saying in the first chapter of Lamentations, "And they went without strength before the pursuer," it is read that Rabbi <margin>רודף מלא</margin> Aha said: "Just as Israel was not led into captivity except by a 'full pursuer' <note>original: "Rodeph male", meaning a complete or powerful persecutor.</note>, so they shall not be redeemed except by a 'full redeemer' <margin>גואל מלא</margin> <note>original: "Goel male", meaning a perfect or complete redeemer.</note>, or a perfect one; as it is written in the fifty-ninth chapter of Isaiah: 'And there came to Zion a full or perfect redeemer.'" <margin>גואel מלא</margin> "Full redeemer" or "perfect redeemer" is what is written there.

<meta>The previous page established that the eternal salvation mentioned in Isaiah and Daniel is specifically linked to the Messiah, who is identified as both God and the "Word of God" (Memra). This page continues that argument by using the Midrash on the Song of Songs to show that the Messiah possesses the divine power to forgive all sins and act as a shield for Israel.</meta>

<header>BOOK SIX.</header>

<columns>2</columns>

This is the tradition. From this manifestation of divinity comes the full and perfect power of the Messiah to redeem and save, which the <term>Midrash Shir HaShirim</term> <note>original: "Midras Sir hasirim"; a rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs</note>, that is, the exposition of the Song of Songs, shows more clearly. For regarding that verse which our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has in the first chapter as: "A cluster of cypress is my beloved to me in the vineyards of En Gedi," the Hebrew truth <note>The original Hebrew text</note> has: <term>אשכול הכופר דודי לי בכרמי עין גדי</term> <note>original: "Eshkol ha-kofer dodi li be-karmi En Gedi"</note>. <margin>A</margin> This means: "A man who spares all, or satisfies all, is my beloved to me in the vineyards of <term>En Gedi</term>," that is, of the fountain or the eye of the kid. Rabbi Berachiah said that the Assembly of Israel spoke before the Holy and Blessed God: "Lord of the world, in the hour when You afflict me, You are my beloved. For You are my beloved to me, and my provider. O, what a man that shall be who is in me! He will be able to say to the Attribute of Judgment <note>A Jewish concept where God's justice is personified as a quality that demands punishment for sins</note>: 'It is enough.' And You will be the one receiving, or pledging, or handing him over for me." <margin>B</margin> And this is what is meant by <term>איש כל הכפר</term> <term>Ish kol ha-kofer</term>, that is, "the man who spares all" or "satisfies all." And what is "the man of all"? The man in whom all things are. And what is "sparing" or "satisfying," except that he will spare or satisfy for the sins of Israel? It follows: "in the vineyards of <term>En Gedi</term>," that is, the fountain or eye of the kid. These are the fathers of the age <note>The Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</note>, who were drawn after You like kids, and received the blessing, which is the fountain and eye of the age, or the eternal fountain. However, Rabbi Levi said in the name of Rabbi Hanina: "There was a murmur of words there." And who murmured? Abraham murmured, saying: "Lord of the world, You struck a covenant with Noah; I stood and stored up good works before You more than he did—shall his covenant exclude mine?" The Holy and Blessed God said to him, <margin>D</margin> Genesis chapter 15: <term>אל תירא אברם אנכי מגן לך שכרך הרבה מאד</term> <note>original: "Al tira Avram, anochi magen lach, secharacha hirbe me’od"</note>, that is, "Fear not, Abraham. I am your shield, and your reward is very great." For regarding Noah, I did not establish shields, or protectors, or Princes, or righteous men. But regarding you, I shall establish righteous men and Princes as protectors. And not only this, but even your children will come to my hand with transgressions and evil works, and I will be providing. O, what a man that shall be who is among them, and will be strong enough to say to the Attribute of Judgment: "It is enough." And I will receive him, and pledge him, or hand him over for them—just as it is said in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: "A man who spares all, or satisfies all, is my beloved to me." And why a man who spares all? Because he will spare the sins of Israel. Another exposition: "A man who spares all or satisfies all." <term>Ben Sira</term> <note>An ancient Jewish scribe and author of the Wisdom of Sirach</note> said that this man is the Holy and Blessed God, in whom all things are. Thus far the tradition. Now, that this aforementioned beloved is the Messiah is held in the previously mentioned <term>Midrash Shir HaShirim</term>, where, regarding that verse in the second chapter of the Song of Songs: "The voice of my beloved, behold he comes leaping over the mountains," Rabbi Elazar the son of Jacob says: "The voice of my beloved, behold he comes—this is the King Messiah; and the mountains are nothing but idolatry." And this is what is said in Hosea chapter 4: "They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains." This is the tradition. Regarding this beloved—that is, the bridegroom of the Church—it is also held in the same <term>Midrash</term>, concerning that verse in the fifth chapter of the Song of Songs: <term>חכו ממתקים וכלו מחמדים</term> <note>original: "Hikko mamtakim ve-kullo machamadim"</note>. <margin>G</margin> This means: "His palate is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable." For so it is said there: "This is my beloved, and this is my friend (or my kinsman), O daughters of Jerusalem." It is written

<column-break/>

<page-num>332</page-num>
indeed in Amos, chapter 5: <term>כה אמר יהוה לבית ישראל דרשוני וחיו</term> <note>original: "Ko amar Adonai le-veit Yisrael dirshuni ve-chiyu"</note>, <margin>A</margin> that is, "Thus says God to the house of Israel: Seek me and you shall live." Is there any palate more sweet than this, of which it is said in Ezekiel 33: <term>חי אני נאם אדני יהוה אם אחפוץ במות הרשע כי אם בשוב רשע מדרכו וחיה</term> <note>original: "Chai ani ne’um Adonai Elohim, im echpotz be-mot ha-rasha, ki im be-shuv rasha mi-darko ve-chaya"</note>, that is, "As I live, says the Lord God, if I desire the death of the impious—that is, I do not desire the death of the impious—but rather that the impious man be converted from his way and live"? And it is added: "Is there a palate more sweet to you than this, of which it is said in Ezekiel chapter 18: <term>לא אחפוץ במות המת נאם יהוה</term> <note>original: "Lo echpotz be-mot ha-met ne’um Adonai"</note>, <margin>B</margin> that is, 'For I do not desire the death of the one who dies,' says God?" And again in the same place a little earlier: <term>ובשוב רשע מרשעתו אשר עשה ויעש משפט וצדקה הוא את נפשו יחיה</term> <note>original: "U-ve-shuv rasha me-rish’ato asher asa, ve-ya’as mishpat u-tzedaka, hu et nafsho yechayeh"</note>, that is, "In the conversion of the impious man from his impiety, or if the impious man has turned from the impiety he committed and does judgment and justice, he himself shall make his soul live." Have you a palate sweeter than this? This is the tradition. In this attribution to the divine "Beloved," who in the preceding tradition is said to be the Messiah. Therefore, <margin>C</margin> so that the Messiah could be a perfect redeemer, or the man who would spare all sins or satisfy for all (as the other preceding tradition says), he was necessarily going to be God and man. Furthermore, because of the merit of this coming redeemer, God has always protected the Hebrew people through every single generation and from enemies, and redeemed them from temporal slaveries, as a figure of that greatest protection and redemption which <margin>D</margin> was to be accomplished through this perfect coming redeemer. This is best seen in the same <term>Midrash Shir HaShirim</term>, where, regarding that verse in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs: <term>אלף המגן תלוי עליו</term> <note>original: "Elef ha-magen talui alav"</note>, which means "A thousand shields hung upon it," it is said: "All those thousands and ten thousands of those who stood before Mount Sinai, I protected them. I did not protect them except because of the merit of that one who is to come for a thousand generations. And not only are you suspended in him, but also all powers or authorities, or <margin>E</margin> all the shields of the strong." Likewise, another discourse (that is, another exposition) on "A thousand shields hung upon it": Rabbi Berachiah said: "The Holy and Blessed God said: I have caused a thousand generations to follow so that I may bring that shield, who has become the desire of your children." Rabbi Barachiah said in the name of Rabbi Isaac: "Abraham said before God: 'Lord of the world, You became a shield to me. Will You not also become a shield to my children?' The Holy and Blessed God said to him: 'To you I was one shield,' as it is said <margin>F</margin> in Genesis 15: <term>אל תירא אברם אנכי מגן לך</term>, that is, 'I am your shield.' But for your children, I shall become many shields." And this is what is written in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs: "A thousand shields hung upon it." And it immediately follows: <term>כל שלטי הגברים</term> <note>original: "Kol shilte ha-gibborim"</note>. This means: "All the shields of the strong," that is, of the Priests and Kings. This is the tradition. From which we not only have the intended point, but also that the Messiah is the aforementioned shield. For he himself has always been the desire of all the righteous.

### CHAPTER IV.
->That the salvation and redemption to be accomplished through the Messiah was to be spiritual.<-
->CAPNIO.<- <note>Johannes Reuchlin’s pseudonym, under which he speaks in this dialogue.</note>

<summary>This page uses rabbinic interpretations of the Song of Songs to argue that the Messiah is the "man who spares all" (Ish Kol Ha-Kofer), possessing both human and divine natures to satisfy the requirements of divine justice. It portrays the Messiah as the "shield" of Israel, whose merit has protected the people throughout history.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.

**C A P N I O.**

<margin>Arguments of the Talmudists.</margin>
Although from what you have said, it is openly suggested that eternal salvation—or the most essential redemption which was to be achieved through the Messiah—was not to be temporal or physical (as the Jews of our age fabulate), but rather spiritual. However, to further convict them of their stubbornness, you must prove this to me more clearly through their own scriptures. **GALATINUS.** First, I bring against them that which is read in Psalm 72, which is entirely explained by the ancient Hebrews as referring to the Messiah: <note>original: יחוס על דל ואביון ונפשות אביונים יושיע מתוך ומהמס יגאל נפשם ויקר דמם בעיניו</note> "He shall spare the poor and needy: or, He shall have mercy upon the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the needy. He shall redeem their soul from fraud and iniquity, and their blood shall be precious, or honored, in his eyes." This same point is proved through the Talmudists as well: and first, indeed, from the fact that they say belief in this redemption is necessary for salvation; which would certainly not be the case if the primary redemption were merely temporal. Furthermore, it is the opinion of many ancients that the reward for good works is not to be expected in this world, as is held in <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term> <note>A classic collection of ancient rabbinic interpretations of the Book of Genesis</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis regarding that saying in Deuteronomy: <note>original: אשר אנכי מצוך היום לעשותם</note> "Which I command you today to do them." For it is said there: <note>original: היום לעשותם ולא להן שכרם היום</note> "Today to do them, but not for their reward to be given today." Here, almost all Talmudists understand "Today" to mean the present age; whence they also say elsewhere: <note>original: שכר מצוה בהאי עלמא ליכא</note> "The reward for a commandment is not in this world." Therefore, since by the consensus of all, the redemption of the Messiah is not to be expected except through repentance and the works of virtues (by whose merit the salvation of redemption is hoped for), and since no salvation of this world is to be hoped for as a reward for good works, it follows naturally that the redemption or salvation which the Messiah was to perform—which is numbered by them among the articles of faith they call "roots of faith"—must not be believed to be temporal or of this world. For since the Messiah's redemption is the reward for good works, and the reward for good works is not temporal, it necessarily follows that the Messiah’s redemption was to be not temporal, but spiritual. This is also confirmed by Rabbi Jonathan, who almost everywhere, and especially in the Psalter, when there is talk of salvation or redemption, always explicitly explains it as spiritual. That saying of Isaiah 12 also: <note>original: ושאבתם מים בששון ממעיני הישועה</note> "You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of salvation," which in the opinion of all Hebrews is understood to refer to the Messiah, is interpreted by him in Aramaic as: <note>original: וילפון אולפן חרש מבחירי צדיקיא</note> "And they shall learn a new doctrine from the chosen of the righteous." The ancient Talmudists also understand spiritual salvation by the "promised land" and by "Jerusalem" or "Sion." Also, in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term>, at the beginning of the chapter <term>Helek</term>, it is said: <note>original: כל ישראל יש להם חלק לעולם הבא שנאמר ועמך כלם צדיקים לעולם ירשו ארץ</note> "All Israel has a portion in the world to come. As it is said in Isaiah: And your people, all of them righteous, shall forever

<column-break/>

inherit the land." Thus it is written there: where by "the land" they understand the spiritual world, which they call "the world to come." Furthermore, Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>The famous philosopher Maimonides</note> in the <term>Hilchoth Teshuvah</term> <note>The Laws of Repentance</note>, chapter 8, says this: <note>original: החיים הנצחי׳ מן הנביאי׳ ברמזי׳ נבדלי׳ הם רמזו כמו אלו: הר יהוה מקום קדשו ודרך הקדש: חצרות יהוה נעם יהוה אהל יהוה היכל יהוה שער יהוה</note> "Eternal life is designated by the prophets with different metaphors, such as the Mountain of the Lord, the Place of His Holiness, the Way of Holiness, the Courts of the Lord, the Sweetness of the Lord, the Tabernacle of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Gates of the Lord." Seeing these things, who will doubt that Israel (that is, the congregation of the righteous) and the rebuilding of the temple also require a spiritual sense? Rabbi Solomon <note>The commentator Rashi</note> explicitly affirms this regarding the temple that Ezekiel describes, in the chapter <term>Helek</term>. <margin>Conclusion.</margin> From all these things it is clearly evident that the salvation of the ages, or eternal and perfect redemption which was to be achieved through the Messiah, was to be neither temporal nor physical (as the delirious Jews of our time claim), but spiritual and of the soul. For the Messiah himself was to redeem and save the human race from original sin, from other sins, and from the devilish servitude which humans had incurred because of the sin of our first parents; and he was to lead them back to the heavenly and eternal bliss which they had lost because of that same sin. Rabbi Nehuniah ben Ha-Kana, a most esteemed man whose authority is great among the Hebrews, clearly expresses and confesses this at the beginning of the <term>Iggereth Ha-Sodoth</term> <note>The Letter of Secrets</note>, which he wrote to his son Ha-Kana, saying: "When I considered the end and perfection of the human race, for which our souls are greedy, I saw that bliss and happiness consist in the soul being bound in the bundle of life with the Lord our God. This, however, consists in the advent of our Messiah, without whom we can by no means arrive at that immense and inestimable perfection, which cannot be compared to colors dyed in the day, nor to the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire."

### CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning original sin, by which the entire human race was corrupted because of the sin of our first parents. And what original sin is according to the Hebrews, and by what name they call it.*<-

**C A P N I O.**

Therefore, in order to further crush the very hard necks of the Jews, so that it may appear more clearly that eternal salvation and the perfect redemption which was to be achieved through the Messiah was to be spiritual and of the soul, we must now discuss original sin itself, on account of which the whole human race was corrupted. Tell me then, I pray, what is original sin according to the Hebrews, and by what name do they call it? **GALATINUS.** Although the <margin>What original sin is.</margin>

# BOOK SIX.

Initial sin, properly speaking, is the lack of initial or original justice that was due to us but lost in our first parents. It flows from the actual fault of those first parents to all their descendants through natural propagation (excepting those prevented by a special privilege of grace). This sin binds humanity to a twofold death—both spiritual and physical—and to the other punishments that follow such a lack. Sometimes, however, we call this original sin "the kindling of sin" <note>original: "fomes peccati"</note>, namely, concupiscence, because of its effects.
<margin>The kindling of sin or concupiscence.</margin>
This concupiscence of sin is sometimes called the law of the members, sometimes the law of the flesh, sometimes the weakness of nature, and sometimes the tyrant who is in our members. For there is in us (as Augustine says) a concupiscence that must not be allowed to reign. There are also its desires, which are actual concupiscences; these are the weapons of the devil that come from the weakness of nature. This weakness, moreover, is the tyrant that stirs up evil desires. If, therefore, you wish to be the victor over the tyrant and find the devil to be a defeated enemy, do not obey evil concupiscence. This is from Augustine’s opinion in the book *On the Baptism of Infants*. 

Similarly, among the Hebrews, this initial sin is called by many names. Indeed, they call it original sin, and there they call the kindling <note>original: "fomitem"</note> the *yetzer hara* <note>original: יצר הרע; a Hebrew term literally meaning "evil inclination" or "evil formation"</note>, 
<margin>How original sin is named by the Hebrews.</margin>
which is the same as an evil "plasma" or "imagination." Whence Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century Jewish scholar and compiler of Midrashic commentaries</note>, commenting on that passage in the eighth chapter of Genesis, says: "The imagination <note>original: "Figmentum"</note> of man’s heart is evil from his youth," or from his childhood, or from his shaking off—that is, from the moment he is shaken out from his mother’s womb. Thus he says: This is what is written in Psalm 103: "For he knows our frame <note>original: יצרנו, "ietzerenu"</note>; he remembers that we are dust." Rabbi Joses said: Sad or dark is the imagination against which its Creator bears witness that it is evil. The Masters have said: Sad is the plant against which its Planter bears witness that it is evil, according to what is said in Jeremiah chapter 11: "And the Lord of hosts who planted you has spoken evil against you," or concerning you. Furthermore, the Consul Antoninus <note>Often identified in Jewish tradition as a Roman emperor, possibly Marcus Aurelius, who debated with the rabbis</note> asked our Holy Master <note>original: "Rabbenu Haccados," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the primary redactor of the Mishnah</note>, saying: "When is the *yetzer hara* (the evil imagination)—that is, the kindling or original sin—given to a man?" He answered him: "From the hour in which he is formed." All this is from Rabbi Moses Hadarsan. 

In the *Midrash Coheleth* <note>A homiletic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, those words from the fourth chapter of that book are explained: "Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take heed." The "poor and wise youth" is the good imagination, or the good affection, or good reason, or good intellect. And why is it called a youth? Because it is not joined to a man until after his thirteenth year. And why is it called poor? Because not all obey it. Why indeed wise? Because it teaches the creatures and instructs them in the right way. It follows: "Than an old and foolish king." This is the *yetzer hara* (the evil imagination), that is, the evil 

<column-break/>

imagination, or original sin, or the kindling. And why does it call him a king? Because almost everyone obeys him. And for what reason does it call him old? Because he is coupled and joined to a man from his infancy until his old age. But why does it call him foolish? Because he shows a man a way that he does not know. 

The same is also found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrashic commentary on the Psalms</note>, in the exposition of Psalm 9: "I will confess the Lord with my whole heart." This is explained there as: "with both the good and evil imagination," so that there is no division <note>original: "schisma"</note> in my heart. This is also what is written in Ecclesiastes 4: "Better is a poor and wise youth," and so forth. The poor and wise youth is the good imagination, that is, good reason or good intellect. And why does it call it a youth? Because it is joined to a man from the thirteenth year and upward. But why poor? Because not all people obey it. And why wise? Because it directs the creature to the good way. It follows: "Than an old and foolish king." This is the evil imagination, or the kindling. For what reason does it call him a king? Because all the members obey him. And why old? Because he is joined to a man from infancy even unto his old age. 

Also in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan on Genesis, regarding that statement in the 21st chapter: "And it was at that time, and Abimelech said," it is said: This is what is written in Proverbs 16: "When a man's ways please the Lord, he will make even his enemies to be at peace with him." Rabbi Jehoshua said: This refers to the plasma, or evil imagination. For according to the ways of the world, a man is nourished with a companion for two or three years, and from this he is bound to him by love. But the *yetzer hara* (the evil imagination or kindling) grows and is nourished with a man until old age; and nevertheless, if it finds an opportunity in the middle of seventy years, or in the middle of eighty, it will cast him down. 

In the *Midrash Tehillim* on Psalm 34: "The Lord redeems the souls of his servants," it is read thus: You find in the first chapter of Genesis: "And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." But behold, far better than that is: "The Lord redeems the souls of his servants." Rabbi Samuel, son of Nachmani, said: It is written in Proverbs chapter 25: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread." The Scripture is speaking of the *yetzer hara* (the evil imagination or kindling). For a man walks with his companion for one hour and he becomes his friend. But the *yetzer hara* is born with a man and grows with him all his days; as it is written in Genesis chapter 8: "The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." And yet, if it finds a place to cast him down when he is 20, or 30, or 40, or 70, or 80 years old, it will cast him 

<summary>This page defines original sin as a lack of original justice and explores its equivalent in Jewish thought, the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination). Through various Midrashic sources, it portrays this "evil imagination" as a lifelong, tyrannical companion that only the Messiah's spiritual redemption can fully address.</summary>

...will cast him down. Who, then, is a greater enemy to you than that one? This is also very well confirmed in the *Midrash Kohelet* <note>original: "Midras coheleth"; a Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, in the exposition of the 9th chapter of that same book, upon those words: *A small city with few men in it; and a great king came against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks around it. And there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city.* This is interpreted there as follows: "The small city" is the body, or the human being, as is said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "Midras tehilim"; a commentary on the Book of Psalms</note>. "The few men in it" are the 
<margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin> members of the human body. "The great king who came against it and besieged it" is the evil inclination <note>original: "figmentum malum," referring to the Hebrew *yetzer hara*</note> or the kindling of sin. And why does he call him "great"? Because he is thirteen years older than the good inclination <note>According to Jewish tradition, the evil inclination is present from birth, while the good inclination only arrives at age thirteen, the age of religious responsibility</note>. "And he built great bulwarks against it": these are the snares and deceptions of sin. "And there was found in it a poor man": this is the good inclination. And why does he call him "poor"? Because he is not found in all creatures, and most creatures do not obey him. "And he delivered the city by his wisdom": because whoever obeys the good inclination—or the intellect and reason—shall be delivered. For David said that it will be well for him who is obedient to it. And this is what is written in *Psalm 41*: *Blessed is he who considers the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the day of trouble.* It follows in the same 9th chapter of *Ecclesiastes*: *But no man remembered that same poor man.* Therefore, the Holy and Blessed God said: "I will remember him," just as it is said in *Ezekiel 36*: *And I will cause the heart of stone to be removed from your flesh.* In the *Midrash on the Psalms*, regarding that verse in *Psalm 78*: *A spirit that passes away and does not return; and He remembered that they were but flesh, a spirit that passes and does not return*, it is written: "Some were of the opinion that the dead would not live again because it is written: 'A spirit that passes and does not return.' But this 'spirit' is the *yetzer hara* <note>original: יצר הרע; the evil inclination</note>, which goes away at the hour of death and does not return with the person at the hour when the dead shall rise." Likewise, in the same *Midrash* regarding *Psalm 103*: "For He knows our frame <note>original: "figmentum"; in Hebrew 'yitzrenu,' related to 'yetzer'</note>," it is read: "Rabbi Hiyya said, 'Woe to the dough when its own baker testifies that it is bad,' because the inclination of Adam was evil." It follows in the same Psalm: *For a spirit passes over it, and it is gone.* Here it was said by some that the dead would not live again. But this spirit is the *yetzer hara*, that is, the kindling of sin that goes away with him, as it was said: "It is a spirit passing away, and not returning." For this *yetzer hara* shall not return with him any further. Then it follows: *And its place shall know it no more.* From all these things, it has been abundantly made clear what original sin is among the Hebrews, and by what name they call it.

# CHAPTER VI.

### That all the fathers of the Old Testament, no
### matter how holy, were guilty and
### subject to God on account of original

<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist</note>

NOW, therefore, to prove the necessity of the human redemption to be performed by the Messiah, it must be shown that all the fathers of the Old Testament, no matter how holy, remained guilty and subject to God until the coming of the Messiah. GALATINUS: That is clearly shown from almost innumerable places in both the Holy Scriptures and the Talmud itself. Therefore, listen first to what is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* (the exposition of the Psalms) regarding the saying in *Psalm 16*: *I have said to the Lord, You are my Lord; my goodness is not above You.* David said before the Holy and Blessed God: "Lord of the world, although You made me king, I have set You as King over me." The Holy and Blessed God said to him: "I do not confirm this good for you; My goodness is not above you. And for whom do I confirm this good? For the saints who are in the earth." For the Holy and Blessed God does not call the righteous "holy" until they are committed to the earth, that is, until the day of their death. And why? Because the 
<margin>No one is called holy except after death.</margin> 
*yetzer hara*, that is, the evil inclination, which is the kindling of sin or evil concupiscence, is formed or fashioned or renewed in a person in this world, and one is not secure from it until the day of one's death. For this reason, Solomon said in the eighth chapter of *Ecclesiastes*: *There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.* For even the Patriarchs were not called "holy" as long as they were not committed to the earth. Therefore it was said in the twenty-fifth chapter of *Job*: *Behold, He does not trust His holy ones.* <note>The text argues that because the inclination to sin exists until death, true holiness is only attributed by God to the deceased who finished their lives in righteousness.</note>

...he trusts. When, therefore, does he trust in them? In that hour when he spoke to Moses in the thirty-second chapter of Exodus, "Go, go down to the elders of Israel." Rabbi Pinhas said: If the fathers of the world <note>The patriarchs of Israel</note> had sought for their dwelling to be on high, they would have obtained it. Yet they were not called "holy" for this reason, so long as their faces were not veiled with a shroud <note>meaning they were not called truly holy until after death</note>. Rabbi Abba, the son of Papa, said: What is it that is written in Job, chapter 24: *He also draws the mighty by his power*? This is the *yetzer hara* <note>original: "ietser hara"</note>, that is, the evil inclination, which is original sin. For it drew the mighty by its power—that is, the generation of Enos, the generation of the division of languages at the Tower of Babel, and the people of Sodom. As it is written of him in Genesis, chapter 3: *In sorrow* <note>original: "be-itzavon"</note> *shalt thou eat of it*, that is, in affliction, or in pain, or in labor you shall eat it. And again in the same place: *Multiplying, I will multiply your labors*. You, O Eve, have multiplied labors for the fathers of the world. As it is said in the sixteenth Psalm: *Their labors*—or their grievances—*shall be multiplied; they have endowed another*, that is, because Adam and Eve "endowed" another besides God—namely the devil—by surrendering themselves to him through their consent. And did they perhaps lose anything because of this? The text teaches what should be said in what follows: *I will not offer their drink offerings of blood*. All of this is tradition. Rabbi Abraham <term>Ibn Ezra|A famous 12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar and philosopher</term> <note>original: "Auen Ezra"</note>, explaining that saying in Psalm 51, *Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me*, said this: It is as if he said, "Behold, because of the concupiscence <note>intense desire or lust</note> planted in the heart of Adam, it is as if I were born in sin." And the meaning is that at the hour of birth, the evil inclination itself is planted in the heart. As for what he says, *And in sin did my mother conceive me*, it is a strange way of speaking, as if he were saying, "she was heated by me." And there are those who say that by this it is hinted that Eve did not give birth until after she had sinned. It follows in the same Psalm: *Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right*—or stable, or fit—*spirit within me*. And he says this for this reason: because he had remembered that he was born with sin. And the meaning is that the planted concupiscence led him to guilt, and therefore he prays to God to help him against the evil inclination—that is, his inner "tinder" <note>original: "fomitem"; a spark or fuel for sin</note>—lest he commit such a sin again. Moreover, when he says, *A clean heart and a right spirit*, along with the rest, it is a repetition of the same idea. These are the words of that Rabbi Abraham. Also, in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan on the book of Genesis, that saying in the 4th chapter of the same book is explained thus: *If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? And if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door*. This means: If you act well, will you not receive a blessing? And if you do not do well, will you not receive a curse? Alternatively: If you act well, will you not receive pardon from me? But if you do not act well, it will lie heaped up at the

<margin>A</margin> door. The word *rovetset* <note>original: "rouetset"</note>, that is, "crouching" or "lying," is not written in the feminine gender, but *rovets* <note>original: "rouets"</note>, in the masculine. This is because in the beginning, the "tinder" of sin is weak, like a woman; but later it becomes strong, like a man. Rabbi Akiba said: the *yetzer hara* <note>original: "ietser hara"</note>, that is, the evil inclination or "tinder," is in the beginning like a silken thread, but in the end it becomes like a ship’s rope, which is commonly called a *poggia* <note>An Italian nautical term for a halyard or rope used in sailing</note>.
