<margin>B</margin> "tinder," at first becomes a stranger, or a guest; then a traveler; and finally the Master: as it is written in the 2nd Book of Kings <note>modern 2 Samuel</note>, chapter 12: *And there came a traveler unto the rich man*. Rabbi Abba said: And of him the scripture says in Job, chapter 21: *The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him, and every man shall draw after him, and there are innumerable before him*. This is like a certain solitary robber who, 
<margin>C</margin> sitting at a crossroads, said to everyone passing by, "Give me what you have on you." When a certain wise man passed by and saw that the robber had neither a sword nor anything in which there was hope for him, he began to crush him. The gloss of Rabbi Solomon <term>Rashi|Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</term> says here: *And unto thee shall be his desire*—namely, of sin—because the evil inclination is constantly desiring and striving to make you fall. *And thou shalt rule over him*—that is, if you wish, you shall prevail against him. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Four things are to be noted in this tradition: the 
<margin>F</margin> first is that the "tinder" is weak in the beginning, like a silken thread, but afterward strong, like a ship's rope. The second is that the Messiah, of whom he speaks parabolically—saying that like a wise man he began to crush the robber at the crossroads—was the first who had crushed the evil inclination. The third is that the evil inclination or "tinder" destroyed many strong men. Finally, the fourth is that it is subject to free will. So also we read 
<margin>G</margin> in Isaiah, chapter 43: *Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers*—or the loquacious ones, or your interpreters—*have transgressed against me*. *Therefore I have profaned*—or excluded, or repelled—*the princes of the sanctuary* or of holiness.

"And our sins," namely original and actual, "take us away like the wind": both in this world, through various passions, and after death, to the lower regions through different conditions of outcomes. For the wicked <margin>F</margin> were taken away on account of their crimes, as they are even now taken away, to eternal punishments; but the righteous, on account of original sin, to the *Limbo* of the Fathers <term>Limbo of the Fathers: a temporary place for the souls of the righteous who died before Christ’s redemption</term>, which was called "Abraham’s Bosom," and was dark because of the lack of the divine vision. From this, therefore, it is clearly evident that on account of Adam's sin, not only was he himself deprived of much goodness, but so also was the entire human race. For by the loss of the goodness of original justice, which he had received for himself and his posterity, he earned death and hell for himself and his children. Since original sin (as we have said) is nothing else than the lack of that original justice. However, that all men have been sinners not only because of original sin, <margin>D</margin> but also because of actual sin, appears clearly not only from what was said before, but also from the opinion of Solomon, saying in Ecclesiastes chapter seven: <note>original Hebrew: "כי אדם אין צדיק בארץ אשר יעשה טוב ולא יחטא"</note> "For there is no just man upon earth, that does good and sins not." And yet from this, as will be proved elsewhere, the Mother of the Messiah is excluded, who, by the preventing grace of the Holy Spirit with which she was filled, was preserved from all sin. From the foregoing, therefore, it has been widely shown that all the fathers of the Old Testament, however holy they were, were guilty and culpable before God on account of original sin until the coming of the Messiah.

...of character upon that verse of the Psalm, <note>Psalm 104:33</note> *I will sing to the Lord as long as I live*, I shall bring forward. **CAP.** Since I see you have said that one escapes under this name *שאול* <note>Sheol</note>, that is, hell, and it does not escape me that the Jews of our time are carried away by such malice in contradicting us and the truth that they do not fear to deny the true meanings of almost every single word: therefore, since this word *שאול* <note>Sheol</note> is equivocal—for it signifies both hell and a pit, or a grave—so that no opportunity for denying the truth is given to them, show me first, I beseech you, through their own scriptures, that hell is signified by the name *שאול* <note>Sheol</note>.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Names of hell.</margin>
**GAL.** Hell among them (as you well know) is called by many names. Of these, one is *שאול* <note>Sheol</note>, as is clear in the book *ערובין* <term>Erubin: A volume of the Talmud dealing with Sabbath laws, here referencing a section on the geography of the afterlife</term>, in the chapter *אוסין פסין* <note>original Hebrew: "Ofin Pasim"</note>: where it is read word for word: Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said, there are seven names for Gehenna <note>the place of punishment or purification in the afterlife</note>: and these are, *שאול* <note>Sheol</note>, that is, hell; *אבדון* <note>Avaddon</note>, that is, destruction; *בור שחת* <note>Bor Shachath</note>, that is, the pit or lake of corruption; *בור שאון* <note>Bor Seon</note>, that is, the pit of tumult or roaring; *טיט היון* <note>Tit Hayaven</note>, that is, the miry clay; *צלמות* <note>Tsalmaveth</note>, that is, the shadow of death; and *ארץ תחתית* <note>Eretz Tachtith</note>, that is, the land of crushing, or of dread, or the lower earth. All these things are found there. Furthermore, among them, hell is called by its proper name *גיהנם* <note>Gehenna</note>, that is, a deep valley. Likewise, that *שאול* <note>Sheol</note> is hell, and that all men have descended into hell, and that none of them could satisfy the price of redemption, is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <term>Midrash Tehillim: An ancient Jewish commentary or homiletic interpretation of the Book of Psalms</term>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms upon that verse of Psalm 49: <note>original Hebrew: "גם בני אדם גם בני איש יחד עשיר ואביון"</note> That is, *Both the sons of Adam and the sons of man, the rich and the poor together*. Where it is said: *Sons of Adam*: This Adam is the first Adam. Although others say this is Abraham, who is called in Joshua chapter 14 the "Great Adam among the giants." It follows, *Both the sons of man*: These are the sons of Noah, who was called a just

man. There are, however, some who say these are the 70 nations, all of whom descend into Gehenna. It follows, *Together the rich and the poor*. <margin>B</margin> For Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor, worshipped alien gods. Nevertheless, since Abraham was a most faithful worshipper of God and a just man, he was neither to be tormented by the fire of hell nor infested by demons. Therefore, he was said to be about to go to his fathers "in peace."

# BOOK SIX #

...interpreters, clearly shows, who translated these Hebrew words *el beni* <note>Hebrew: אל בני</note>, that is, "to my son," into Chaldaic <term>Chaldaic: The Aramaic language used in the Targums, the ancient Jewish translations of the Bible</term> as *Leuath beri* <note>Aramaic: לוות ברי</note>, that is, "with my son" or "to my son." From this it is openly clear that *el* <note>Hebrew: אל</note> in this place does not mean "because of," but "to," or "again," or "near." And so, wherever this Hebrew word *el* is placed in the Pentateuch <term>Pentateuch: The first five books of the Bible</term>, the interpreter himself translated it into Chaldaic as *Leuath* <note>Aramaic: לוות</note>, which is the same as "near," "to," or "towards." For that which is written in the book of Genesis in Hebrew, "And Esau went *el Ismael*" <note>Genesis 28:9; Hebrew: אל ישמעאל</note>, that is, "to Ishmael," he himself translated into Chaldaic as *Leuat Ismael* <note>Aramaic: לוות ישמעאל</note>, that is, "near," "towards," or "to Ishmael." Also that which is said in Genesis 18 in Hebrew, "And Abraham ran *el habakar*" <note>Genesis 18:7; Hebrew: ואל הבקר</note>, that is, "and to the cattle," he translated into Chaldaic as *Vluath tore* <note>Aramaic: ולוות תוריא</note>, that is, "towards," "near," or "to the cattle." If, therefore, in the aforementioned words of Jacob, this word *el* meant "because of," the interpreter would not have put *Leuath*, which means "near," "to," or "towards," but would have used *Bedil* <note>Aramaic: בדיל</note>. For properly, *Bedil* in Chaldaic is the same as "because of" <note>Latin: "propter"</note> in Latin. For that word of the Lord concerning the Sodomites spoken to Abraham in Genesis 18, "I will not destroy it *propter decem* (because of ten)," he thus turned into Chaldaic, "I will not destroy it *Bedil hasra*" <note>Aramaic: בדיל עשרה</note>, that is, "because of ten." And so it is in many other places. Since these things are so, it is truly manifest that Jacob knew his soul was going into hell <note>Latin: "infernus"; in this context, it refers to the Limbo of the Fathers</note>: and consequently he did not doubt concerning the souls of all others, since he himself was holy and a Prophet. Wherefore he believed that the soul of his son—since he was most righteous—had nonetheless traveled there because of the contagion of original guilt <note>Latin: "originalis noxæ"; original sin</note>. That the rest of the Patriarchs and all the Prophets down to the passion of the Messiah descended to hell is clearly evident not only from the preceding, but also from the Talmud. For in the book called *Hagiga* <note>Hebrew: חגיגה</note>, that is, "History," in the chapter beginning *Haccol hauuin* <note>Hebrew: הכל חייבין</note>, that is, "all are bound," it is chosen thus: When Rabbi Elazar approached this scripture written in 1 Kings 28, "And Samuel said to Saul, why have you disturbed me by making me ascend?" <note>1 Samuel 28:15</note> he said: "Since Samuel the righteous feared the judgment, how much more should we?" And what is it that is written there? "And the woman said to Saul, I saw *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: אלהים</note>, that is, gods or judges, ascending from the earth." Because there were two, one of whom was Samuel, and the other Moses. For Samuel went and brought Moses with him, and said, "Perhaps (which God forbid, and let there be peace) I am sought for judgment. Arise therefore with me. For there is not a single word written by you in the Law that I have not fulfilled."

**CAP.** I would like to hear this history of Samuel—whom, when he was dead, the pythoness <term>pythoness: A woman possessed by a spirit of divination; the Witch of Endor</term> made to ascend from hell at the request of King Saul (as is read in the 28th chapter of the first book of Kings)—explained according to the glosses of the Hebrew Doctors.

And was it really night? But that hour was dark to them as night. And he said, namely Saul to the woman, "Divine for me, I pray, by *ob* <note>Hebrew: אוב</note>, that is, by a pythonic spirit, and make ascend for me from hell the one I shall tell you." And Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying, "As the Lord lives, no sin shall happen to you in this deed or word."

<margin>B</margin> Moreover, the woman said, "Whom shall I make ascend for you?" Saul said to her, "Make Samuel ascend for me," the Master of all the Prophets of his time. Therefore the woman did what she did, and made him ascend. As it is said in the first book of Kings, chapter 28: "And the woman saw Samuel, and cried out, 'Why have you deceived me? And he said to her, "What is his form?"—meaning Samuel's. She said, "An old man ascending, and clothed in a mantle." And Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you terrified me or made me tremble, to make me ascend?" Behold the words in which there is a reasoning from the greater to the lesser. For if the most excellent of all Prophets, namely Samuel, feared judgment, how much more should all others? And what is it that he added to him? "And tomorrow you and your sons will be with me." "With me," that is, in my peace. And when Saul heard this, he hurried and fell to the ground according to the fullness of his stature. Abner and Amasa said to him, "What did he say to you?" Yet behold, this man descends into battle, knowing he is to be killed, and nevertheless takes his sons with him, rejoicing and applauding divine justice, which he was not ignorant was hanging over him."

For if Moses and Samuel, the princes of the Prophets and the holiest of all (about whom God himself bore witness in Jeremiah 15, saying: *Im yaamod Mosheh ve-Shmuel lefanai en nafshi el ha-am ha-zeh* <note>original Hebrew: אם יעמד משה ושמואל לפני אין נפשי לעם הזה</note>, that is: "Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my heart would not be toward this people"), were detained in the underworld
<margin>B</margin>
because of original sin, as was clear from this tradition: how much more must it be judged that all others—who were neither like them, nor endowed with such great holiness or dignity—descended there and were detained there until the redemption of the Messiah?

<margin>*Objection.*</margin>
CAPNIO: Some say, and quite piously indeed, that it was not Samuel whom the medium <term>medium: literally "pythonissa," referring to the Witch of Endor</term> caused to rise, but the very enemy of the human race, who, in order to deceive Saul, lied and said he was Samuel.
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>*First reason.*</margin>
For how, as it is said in the Decrees (26, question 5, chapter "Nor is it a wonder"), could Samuel—who was holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life—be pulled down by magic arts? But if he was not "pulled," yet he consented, believing either of these things about a righteous man is contrary to truth. For righteousness has no support there. Whether pulled or voluntary, he would have lost the spiritual merit he sought while placed in the flesh.

<margin>*Second reason.*</margin>
Furthermore, if Samuel had truly appeared to Saul, he would by no means have permitted himself to be worshipped by him with honors, since he had preached that God alone is to be worshipped.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>*Third reason.*</margin>
Moreover, how could a man of God, who was with Abraham in a place of refreshment <note>A reference to "Abraham's Bosom," a place of rest for the righteous</note>, say to a man of pestilence, worthy of the fire of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, "Tomorrow you shall be with me"? Therefore, that malignant spirit betrayed the subtlety of his deception by these two titles: because under the habit and name of Samuel, he permitted himself to be worshipped against the law; and he lied that a man weighed down by a burden of sins would be with the most righteous Samuel (since there is a great distance between sinners and the righteous).

<margin>*Response.*</margin>
GALATINUS: These people wonder in what way a malignant spirit could rouse the soul of a righteous man so that he might be seen and speak with Saul. Is it not more
<margin>E</margin>
wonderful that Satan took up the Lord himself, and placed him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and transported him to a high mountain? For it is not absurd, my dear Capnio, to believe that some things were permitted by divine dispensation. So that, not through the dominance of magic art, but by the hidden disposition of God (which was hidden from both the medium and Saul), the spirit of the righteous man might show himself to the sight of the king, about to strike him with a divine sentence.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>*Another objection.*</margin>
CAPNIO: Why then did Samuel permit himself to be worshipped by Saul, when the cult of worship should be exhibited to God alone, according to that saying in Deuteronomy chapter 6: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve"?

<margin>*Response.*</margin>
GALATINUS: First, it must be noted in this place what the scripture says in the first book of Kings, chapter 28 <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Samuel 28</note>. For it says thus: *Vayikod apayim artzah vayishtachu* <note>original Hebrew: ויקד אפים ארצה וישתחו</note>, that is: "And he bowed his face to the ground, and worshipped." It does not say, therefore, that Saul worshipped Samuel, but only that "he worshipped." For which 
<margin>G</margin>
reason it can not incongruously be said that he worshipped God 
<meta>catchword: better</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>BOOK SIX</header>

<margin>A</margin>
then, and not Samuel. For whatever is doubtful, kindness ought always to interpret in the better sense. Then, even granted that he worshipped Samuel, Samuel himself should not be said to have acted against the law by permitting himself to be worshipped. For this word *vayishtachu* <note>original Hebrew: וישתחו</note>, which signifies "to worship," is taken in two ways (as you yourself know) among the Hebrews, just as "to adore," "to cult," "to venerate," and "to revere" are used among the Latins: namely, for the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: the supreme worship offered to God alone</term>, which is owed to God alone, and for the adoration of *dulia* <term>dulia: the honor or veneration given to saints or created beings</term>, which is exhibited to creatures: as can be seen from many places of holy scripture. If, therefore, 
<margin>B</margin>
Saul were wicked because he worshipped Samuel, and Samuel were therefore to be judged a devil because he permitted himself to be worshipped (since the same judgment ought to apply to similar cases), then by the same reasoning Nathan the Prophet should be called wicked, and David himself judged a devil: since one of them worshipped the other, and the other permitted himself to be worshipped by the first. For it is read of them in 3 Kings chapter 1 <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Kings 1</note>: *Vayagidu lamelekh lemor hineh Natan ha-navi vayavo lifnei ha-melekh*
<margin>C</margin>
*vayishtachu lamelekh al apav artzah* <note>original Hebrew: ויגידו למלך לאמר הנה נתן הנביא ויבא לפני המלך וישתחו למלך על אפיו ארצה</note>. This is: "And they told the king, saying: 'Behold Nathan the prophet.' And he entered, or came before the face of the king, and worshipped the king upon his face on the ground." CAPNIO: Why did Samuel say to Saul, "Tomorrow you shall be with me"? For if Samuel was righteous, and Saul was liable to the punishments of sinners, they could not be together in the next world.

<margin>*Response of our people.*</margin>
GALATINUS: Some of our people <note>Meaning Christian theologians</note> say, and rightly so, that since the dead man was then foretelling death to the living man, that phrase, "Tomorrow you shall be with me," refers to an equal 
<margin>D</margin>
condition not of place, but of death.
<margin>*Of the Hebrews.*</margin>
<margin>*Response of the Hebrews.*</margin>
However, the Hebrews assert that Saul was saved, and after death was received into the place of the righteous. For even though he had been a sinner, yet having been rebuked by Samuel because he had left the Lord and consulted a medium, he performed sufficient penance. Which indeed is hinted at (as they say) because, as if rejoicing in divine justice, he himself with his three sons ran prudently and studiously toward his own death and theirs (of which he had foreknowledge) for the defense of the people of God. Nor does it stand in the way (as they say) that 
<margin>E</margin>
he killed himself after being lethally wounded by archers: since he was not ignorant that he would no longer be able to fight, nor live further except for a little while, and that in contempt of God and in mockery of himself. For they say it is no sin, but rather a merit, for a man to destroy himself when he sees he will live to the contempt of the Creator. Hence they say Samson killed himself. Hence they affirm that venerable man laid hands on himself, of whom it is read in 2 Maccabees chapter 14: "When he was now being seized, he sought himself with a sword, choosing
<margin>F</margin>
rather to die nobly than to be made subject to sinners and to be led with unworthy injuries above his noble birth." Since therefore Saul, both because of the penance he was about to do, and because of the martyrdom which he had to undergo by waging the war of the Lord, was to be justified, therefore they say Samuel could rightly say to him: "Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me."

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>*Author's response.*</margin>
Therefore, the aforementioned objections notwithstanding, I say—saving the definition of the Holy Roman Church, to which I always submit myself in all things—that then truly Samuel himself, and not a devil, appeared to Saul. For although some things said in the preceding history pertain both to the sight of the medium, who said she saw "gods," and to the understanding of Saul, who [judged] the one ascending to be Samuel...

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the appearance of the prophet Samuel to King Saul. Galatinus is explaining that the biblical text must be taken literally—that it was indeed Samuel's soul, not a demonic illusion—to preserve the integrity of the Holy Scriptures and to demonstrate the state of the righteous in the underworld (Limbo) prior to the coming of Christ.</meta>

...he had understood himself, and they cannot be pulled away from the reasoning of truth. Nevertheless, because of three things reported there, if the soul of Samuel had not truly been present, the writer of the sacred history would not seem to be excused from lying, nor could he be considered truthful: which is surely an absurd thing to say. The first of these is: *And Samuel said to Saul, Why have you terrified me, or made me tremble, or disturbed me, so as to make me come up?* The second is when it is added: *And Samuel said, Why do you ask me, since the Lord has departed from you?* Finally, the third is when it is further mentioned: *And tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.* And the rest follows until that place: *Saul feared greatly because of the words of Samuel,* as is read in the twenty-eighth chapter of the first book of Kings <note>1 Samuel 28</note>. From these points, therefore, it is clear enough (as I judge) that if he who is named "Samuel" so many times had been the devil, the author of this sacred history would by no means have called him "Samuel" so diligently and so often, to the great injury of that holy man, to the danger of error for the faithful, and to the detriment of the authority of Holy Scripture. Lastly, although the evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmon"</note> brought or dragged Samuel to Saul by God's permission, his justice or holiness did not for this reason lose its merit. Just as it was not lost in holy Job when he was so vehemently afflicted by the devil, nor in Paul when he was struck with blows by the same, nor in Anthony when he was driven by dire lashings from him, nor even in the Lord Jesus Christ himself when he was fixed to the wood of the cross by the members of the devil himself. Especially since, through the truth of this event, the magnitude of the loss from original sin is shown to us, and the necessity of the coming, mercy, and grace of the Redeemer is demonstrated, and finally, the impudence of the more recent Jews—who deny the descent of the righteous and holy fathers of old to the Limbo—is more effectively refuted.

# CHAPTER IX.

->That the holy fathers were detained in the underworld by the devil,<-
->God permitting, on account of Adam's sin.<-
->And concerning the Limbo, to which<-
->they descended.<-

<margin>See folio 491.</margin>

## CAPNIO.

<note>Capnio is the pseudonym of the famous Hebrew scholar Johann Reuchlin.</note>

Were the holy Fathers, the Prophets, and the other righteous people who descended to the underworld <note>original: "infernum"</note> until the death of the Messiah, detained there by the devil? Tell me, I pray, what the ancient Jews thought about this. GALATINUS: The demons indeed had the power of detaining the holy and the righteous in the underworld until the passion of the Messiah; however, they had no power at all to harm them or to inflict any evil upon them. For unless they had been detained by the devil, by God's permission, until the arrival of the Messiah, it could in no way be true or even likely that the devil himself would have dragged Samuel, the holiest of all Prophets, and Moses with him, at the command of the medium <term>medium: "pythonissa," the Witch of Endor</term>. For it is well established that whatever she did, she did through demons. Moreover, it gives me confidence in speaking that, before the arrival of Christ, the saints were detained in the lower regions by the devil through divine permission because of Adam’s sin—

<column-break/>

<page-num>354</page-num>
<margin>A</margin>
not only because of what has been said, but even more so by the opinion of the Apostle Paul, speaking of our Lord Jesus Christ in the second chapter to the Colossians: *That he was despoiling principalities and powers*, namely the infernal ones (as the gloss says there), by taking away from them Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the other righteous ones; *he translated them*, that is, he led them far from the place of darkness to heaven. HOGOSTRATUS: <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a contemporary theologian and inquisitor.</note> You speak correctly indeed, Galatinus. For as a confirmation of this opinion of yours, upon that verse of the Psalm which is twenty-third in order <note>Psalm 24 in modern numbering</note>, *Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter*; the gloss says: "It is the voice of the Angels, who preceded Christ as he descended to the underworld, saying: O princes of hell, take away your power, by which you have until now detained all the righteous in the underworld." GALATINUS: You speak well and piously, Hogostratus. But be careful of the Jews, who have the text in this place as follows: <term>שאו שערים ראשיכם והנשאו פתחי עולם ויבא מלך הכבוד</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Se'u she'arim rasheichem ve-hinnase'u pitchei olam ve-yavo melech ha-kavod"</note> That is: *Lift up your heads, O gates, and be lifted up, O eternal doors, and the King of glory shall come*, or enter. <margin>C</margin> However, the Hebrew letter allows it to be said: *Lift up, O gates, your heads*. But not *Lift up your gates, O princes*, as our edition <note>the Vulgate</note> has it. But (to return to the question of our friend Capnio), that the evil spirits had no power of harming the holy fathers detained there is gathered from what is written in the <term>Midrash Koheleth</term>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes: where, upon that saying of the third chapter, <term>מי יודע רוח בני האדם העלה היא למעלה</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Mi yodea ruach benei ha-adam ha-olah hi le-malah"</note> <margin>D</margin> that is, *Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of Adam ascends upward?* it is said: "The souls of the righteous are stored in a storehouse or cellar." And this is what Abigail said to David through the Holy Spirit, speaking in the twenty-fifth chapter of the first book of Kings: <term>והיתה נפש אדני צרורה בצרור החיים את יהוה אלהיך</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-hayetah nefesh adoni tzerurah bi-tzror ha-chayim et Adonai Eloheicha"</note> That is: *And the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living (or of life) with the Lord your God.* Was it possible for the souls of the wicked to be thus? The following teaches us this: <margin>E</margin> <term>ואת נפש אויביך יקלענה בתוך כף הקלע</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-et nefesh oyveicha yekall'ennah be-toch kaf ha-kalla"</note> that is, *And the soul of your enemies shall be whirled around in the middle of the palm of a sling.* Where the gloss of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Rashi</note> says: "The palm of the sling is a wide piece of leather, made like a palm, in the middle of the sling, where the stone is placed." Likewise, the gloss of <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term> says: "When it says *Eth Adonai*, the word *eth* is placed here in the place of *el*, that is, 'to' or 'with'." Just as in the nineteenth chapter of the book of Judges: <margin>F</margin> <term>ואת בית יהוה אני הולך</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ve-et beit Adonai ani holech"</note> *eth beth*, that is, *To the house of the Lord I am going.* Likewise in the twenty-sixth chapter of Job: <term>את מי הגדת</term> *Eth mi*, that is, *to whom have you announced words.* From these things it is clear that what Abigail, through the Holy Spirit (as was said by them a little earlier), called "the bundle of the living"—like a conservatory of gems or money which are bound and kept in a bag or cloth—this the Doctors of the Jews called the "storehouse" or "cellar" of the souls of the righteous. And what in the preceding parts is called Gehenna, and by many other names, this they themselves called the "palm of the sling." From which it clearly appears that there were formerly <margin>G</margin> two receptacles of souls among the Hebrews: one, clearly, for the good, and the other for the bad: yet both were called the underworld <note>original: "infernus"</note>. But the place of the wicked was indeed called <term>שאול תחתית</term> <term>seol tahtith</term>, that is, the lower underworld: but the place of the righteous was called the upper underworld—

<margin>Two receptacles of souls, according to the ancient Hebrews.</margin>

BOOK SIX.
<meta>catchword: Narcissus, three</meta>

...is gathered. This can be gathered from what is written in the 32nd chapter of Deuteronomy, when it says: <note>original: "כִּי אֵשׁ קָדְחָה בְאַפִּי וַתִּיקַד עַד־שְׁאוֹל תַּחְתִּית"</note> *For a fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn even to the lowest hell.* A gloss in the book *Tanhuma* <note>A collection of Jewish homilies (midrash) on the Pentateuch.</note> says: *In my anger*, that is, in the midst of Gehenna. Just as it says afterward: *And it shall burn even to the lowest hell.* Likewise, in the fifteenth chapter of Proverbs: <note>original: "אֹרַח חַיִּים לְמַעְלָה לַמַּשְׂכִּיל לְמַעַן סוּר מִשְּׁאוֹל מַטָּה"</note> *The path of life leads upward for the wise, so that he may turn away from the lower hell.* This is the tradition. In the *Midrash Tehillim* as well—that is, in the commentary on the Psalms—regarding that passage in the eighty-fifth Psalm: <note>original: "כִּי־חַסְדְּךָ גָּדוֹל עָלָי וְהִצַּלְתָּ נַפְשִׁי מִשְּׁאוֹל תַּחְתִּיָּה"</note> *For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lower hell;* we read that Rabbi Yoden said: "The way of adulterers is given over to the depths of hell." And this is why it says: *For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lower hell.* On this point, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: "The way of adulterers is such that they are in the depths of hell, and from there you have delivered me, when Nathan said to me, 'The Lord also has put away your sin.'" Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Therefore, since a "lower" place is only spoken of in relation to an "upper" place (for "upper" and "lower" are relative terms, which, when established, define each other, and when destroyed, negate each other, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, specifically in his work the *Categories* (Predicamenta).</note> says in his *Categories*), it is surely clear that when David mentions a "lower hell," he necessarily implies that there is an "upper hell." This is also clearly shown through their own commentaries. This upper hell Hezekiah called the "gates of hell" when he spoke in the thirty-eighth chapter of Isaiah: <note>original: "אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי בִּדְמִי יָמַי אֵלֵכָה בְּשַׁעֲרֵי שְׁאוֹל"</note> *I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of hell.* That is: "I shall go to Limbo," which, since it is at the very beginning of hell, is not inappropriately called the "gate of hell." And this hell Christ despoiled when he led out the souls of the holy fathers from there.

<margin>How the Hebrews called the Limbo of the Fathers.</margin>
For what we call Limbo—that is, a place of rest, or the Bosom of Abraham—the ancient Hebrews called <note>original: "צרור"</note> *tseror*, meaning a "bundle" or "repository," or <note>original: "אוצר"</note> *otsar*, meaning a "storehouse" or "cellar," or the "gates of hell," or the "upper hell." From this it is clear that their faith and ours were entirely one and the same.

### CHAPTER X.

### That the souls of the elect could not, and ought not, be liberated from hell except by the Messiah, who is God and man.

### CAPNIO.
<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived nickname of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

It is now fitting for you to show that the souls of the just, who were kept thrust down in hell as if in a prison on account of Adam's sin, were to be liberated from there by God alone. GALATINUS. To prove this, I first bring forward what is read in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim*, that is, in the commentary on the Song of Songs. For there, regarding what is said in the second chapter: <note>original: "אֲנִי חֲבַצֶּלֶת הַשָּׁרוֹן שוֹשַׁנַּת הָעֲמָקִים"</note> *I am the nar-

<column-break/>

cissus (or the rose) of the fertile plain, the lily of the depths (or valleys).* It is said: This is what is written in Psalm 130: <note>original: "מִמַּעֲמַקִּים קְרָאתִיךָ יְהוָה"</note> *Out of the depths I have called to you, O God.* For the Masters have said that the Assembly of Israel said this: "I am beloved by God. Indeed, I shall be given over to the depths of Gehenna until the Holy and Blessed God redeems me from there." This is also what is said in Psalm 40: *And he made me come up out of the pit of tumult, and out of the miry clay,* that is, out of hell.

Unless the scripture had said it in the 66th chapter of Isaiah, one would not be allowed to say it; but since it is written: <note>original: "כִּי בָאֵשׁ יְהוָה נִשְׁפָּט"</note> *For in fire (or through fire) God was judged.* For it is not written <note>original: "שׁוֹפֵט"</note> *shophet*, that is "judging," but <note>original: "נִשְׁפָּט"</note> *nishpat*, that is "judged." <note>This is a mystical interpretation where God is seen as entering into judgment or suffering alongside His people to redeem them.</note> And this is the very thing David said through the Holy Spirit in the 23rd Psalm: <note>original: "גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא־אִירָא רָע כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְּׁעַנְתֶּךָ הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי"</note> *Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death (that is, of hell), I will fear no evil, because you will be with me.* *Your rod* (that is, your torments) *and your staff* (that is, your law), *they shall comfort me.* But will this be possible without torments? He teaches what should be said regarding this when he says in the same place: <note>original: "אַךְ טוֹב וָחֶסֶד יִרְדְּפוּנִי"</note> *Truly, or at least, goodness and mercy shall follow me.* And is this possible in this world? He teaches what should be said in what follows: <note>original: "כָּל יְמֵי חַיָּי"</note> *All the days of my life.* And why? <note>original: "וְשַׁבְתִּי בְּבֵית־יְהוָה לֹאֹרֶךְ יָמִים"</note> *Because I will dwell in the house of God for length of days.*

All this is the tradition. Furthermore, that Adam, and also his children on account of his sin, were thrust into the prison of hell until the coming of the Redeemer, and that they could be restored by no other than by God himself, is excellently hinted at in the *Midrash Koheleth* (that is, the commentary on Ecclesiastes). There, regarding what is said in the 7th chapter of that same book: <note>original: "רְאֵה אֶת מַעֲשֵׂה הָאֱלֹהִים כִּי מִי יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן אֵת אֲשֶׁר עִוְּתוֹ"</note> *Behold the work of God. For who can adapt (or repair) that which he has twisted (or made crooked)?* One reads there literally: Rabbi Azdrias said: In the hour when the Holy and Blessed God created the first Adam, he took him and led him and showed him all the trees of paradise, and said to him: "See my works, how beautiful and how praiseworthy they are; and whatever I created, I created for your sake. Give your mind to this, so that you do not corrupt or destroy my world. For if you destroy it, there will be no one after you to repair it." And not only this, but you will even cause death for the righteous person himself; just as it is written in the 57th chapter of Isaiah: <note>original: "הַצַּדִּיק אָבָד וְאֵין אִישׁ שָׂם עַל לֵב"</note> *The righteous one has perished, and there is no man (or anyone) who takes it to heart.* Just as it is also said in Ecclesiastes chapter 7: <note>original: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ"</note> *There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness.* To whom was Moses our Master similar? He was like the son of a pregnant woman who was held captive in a house of prisoners. She gave birth there, she nursed him there, and she died there. But after some days, the King passed by the door of the prison. And when the son of that woman saw him passing by, he began to cry out and say: "My Lord King, here I was born, here I was raised. And I do not know for whose sin I am detained here." The King answered him: "Because of the sin of your mother." Thus far the tradition. In which brief and fitting similarity, by the ancient Masters of the Jews...

It emphasizes that Adam's original sin created a spiritual 'crookedness' or imprisonment that only the divine King could rectify.</summary>

# BOOK
### C

...it has been clearly shown that the entire human race was once, because of the sin of Eve and Adam, detained not unjustly in the prison of the king of the whole world. For if Moses—the greatest of all the Prophets among them (according to that final chapter of Deuteronomy: <term>ולא קם נביא עוד בישראל כמשה אשר ידעו יהוה פנים אל פנים</term> <note>original Hebrew: "And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face."</note>, that is, "And there did not arise further in Israel a Prophet like Moses, whom God knew face to face." <term>דאתגלי ליה אפין באפין</term> <note>original Aramaic: "To whom the face was revealed face to face."</note>, that is, as <term>Ankelos</term> <note>Onkelos, the 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> says in the <term>Targum</term> <note>The Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note>)—could not be exempted, as the preceding parable clearly shows, how much less could anyone else be exempted from there? 

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Man could not repair the human race.</margin>

Furthermore, in that aforementioned tradition, it is recorded that God said to Adam that if he were to somehow corrupt or destroy his world by sinning, there would be no one after him who could repair it. This openly suggests that the universe, having been corrupted in a certain way due to Adam's sin, could not be restored except by God. For when Adam sinned, he infected and corrupted the whole human race with his sin, binding himself and his descendants to a double death and to the infernal prison. Therefore, the entire universe, which had been created for the sake of man (as the aforementioned tradition attests), was frustrated in its purpose and was, in a sense, corrupted and destroyed.

<margin>D</margin>

Because of this, for the restoration of the universe itself, someone was necessary who would surpass Adam—not just in power, time, dignity, virtue, or holiness, but in all these ways at once, and even in eternity. Since Adam preceded all men, no pure human being could have restored the human race itself, and consequently, the universe. And although the Angels preceded Adam himself in both time and dignity according to their nature, man nonetheless ought not to have had an Angel as his restorer and redeemer. This is partly because for such a great task no power except the divine was sufficient, and also because if an Angel had delivered man from eternal damnation, man would appear to be bound to that Angel's service and servitude.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>An Angel ought not to have restored human nature.</margin>

<margin>F</margin>

Thus, man would by no means be restored to that dignity which he would have possessed had he not sinned; for man himself, who was intended to be a servant of God alone and equal to the Angels through grace, would instead be the servant of one who was not God, nor would his fellow servants be Angels. Wherefore it is concluded that man, lost in the manner described above, had to be restored and liberated from eternal damnation not by a pure creature, but by God Himself. Indeed, God alone was sufficient for this through His omnipotence, wise through His infinite wisdom, and willing through His immense mercy.

<margin>G</margin>

However, He ought not to have restored the human race without the satisfaction of His justice, since mercy can by no means prejudice justice. Hence it is that in the sacred writings, just as He is very often proclaimed as merciful, so too is He frequently called just. For although clemency or mercy exists in God, which overcomes every offense, there is also justice in Him, which permits no sin to remain unpunished. For if sin were not punished through justice, but were always forgiven through mercy alone, God would certainly behave in the same way toward the sinner

I would like you to prove that logical consequence through their own scriptures. **Galatinus**. I shall certainly prove it. That this entire world, which had been corrupted in a way because of Adam's sin, was to be restored by the Messiah, is excellently shown in *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>original: "Beresith rabba," the Great Genesis, a collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the first book of the Bible.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding that statement in the second chapter of the same book: **Hae sunt generationes coeli & terrae in creatione eorum** <note>original Hebrew: אלה תולדות השמים והארץ בהבראם; "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created."</note>. For there it is read word for word: Rabbi Berachias said: "Although they were created according to their fullness and perfection, nevertheless, when the first Adam sinned, they were diminished, corrupted, and shaken; they shall not return to their proper composition until the son of Perez <note>Perez was the son of Judah and an ancestor of King David; "Son of Perez" is a traditional title for the Messiah.</note> comes," according to that passage in the last chapter of Ruth: **Hae sunt generationes Peres** <note>original Hebrew: ואלה תולדות פרץ; "These are the generations of Perez."</note>. This is written in a "full" manner <note>In Hebrew, the word for "generations" (Toldot) is usually spelled "deficiently" (missing the letter Vav), but in this specific verse and the verse about creation, it is spelled "fully." Kabbalists saw this as a sign of perfection.</note>, as a sign, namely, that all things which had been diminished because of sin ought to be perfected and completed through the son of Perez, who is called *Phares* in our scriptures. There follows the word **hibbaram** <note>original: בהבראם</note>, that is, "in their creation," or "when He created them." Rabbi **Abhu** <note>original: אבו</note> said: "He created them with the letter **he** <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note>." Therefore, this world was created with the letter *He*. Now the letter *He*, which is closed on every side but open at the bottom (for thus is **ה** made), is an indicator that all descend to the underworld. However, the part of it that tends upward is a sign that they shall ascend from there. The "window" in its side <note>The small gap in the upper-left of the letter ה.</note> indicates the men of repentance. But the world to come was created with the letter **yod** <note>The Hebrew letter י</note>. For just as the *Yod* has a bent-over stature, so shall the stature of the ungodly be bent, and their faces shall be troubled in the future, as it is said in Isaiah 2: "And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." And what is it that follows? "The idols [or images] he shall utterly abolish." That which is written in Isaiah 26: **Quia cum ioth he, formavit Deus secula** <note>original Hebrew: כי ביה יהוה צור עולמים; "For in Yah (the Lord) is the rock of ages" or "the former of worlds."</note>, that is, "Because with **YH** (*Yod* and *He*), God formed the worlds." For with these two letters, the Holy and Blessed God created the worlds. This is the tradition. These things are found in almost the same way in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note> regarding Psalm 113, which begins "When Israel went out [of Egypt]," where it is said: "Rabbi Judas the Prince <note>Rabbi Judah HaNasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> said:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>Hebrew quote from Midrash Tehillim: "This world was created with He; why is its shape open below and closed from all sides? So this world, all who are created in it descend to Sheol..."</note> **"This world was created with the letter He; and why is its shape such that it is open below and closed on all its other sides? So is this world: all who are created in it descend to the underworld. And that shape contains a hint of the descent of death. But the world to come was created with Yod..."**

<margin>B</margin> "Woe unto those who search and do not find! <note>A common rabbinic expression of lament for lost knowledge or difficult truths.</note> I asked Rabbi Elazar what this meant, and he did not tell me the truth. As it is said in Isaiah 26: *For in **YH** (*Yod* and *He*), God formed the worlds.* And we do not know whether this world was created with *He* and the future world with *Yod*. And what made us not know this?"

<margin>C</margin> "Because it is said in Genesis chapter 2: *These are the generations of the heaven and the earth.* Where, according to the property of Hebrew scripture, it seems that both worlds were created with **YH** (*Yod* and *He*). Truly, this present world was created with **He**. For just as the arrangement of this letter **He** is open at the bottom and closed on every side, so is this age arranged. For whoever is created in it descends into the underworld. But that which is upright in it signifies the reviving of the dead. But the world

<margin>D</margin> to come was created with **Yod**. Why? Because just as the arrangement of the letter **Yod** has a bent stature, so the faces of the ungodly will be pale; they will be contracted and saddened in the future. <margin>E</margin> that is, 'Praise God.' The two last letters of this word are **YH** (*Yod* and *He*)." Thus far the Midrash. Now, that the "Son of Perez" through whom all things ought to be perfected and completed (as the preceding tradition says) is the Messiah himself, is held in **Ve-elle Shemot Rabbah** <note>original: ואלה שמות רבה; the Great Exodus, a midrashic commentary on the book of Exodus.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Exodus, regarding that statement in chapter 21: *And these are the judgments.* Where it is said: "You find all the 'generations' recorded in Scripture are 'diminished' <note>Spelled without the letter Vav.</note>, except for these two, namely: *These are the generations of the heaven and the earth* (Genesis 2), and *These are the

<margin>F</margin> generations of Perez* (Ruth, last chapter). This indeed carries great meaning. For why, when it is said *These are the generations of heaven and earth*, are 'generations' written 'fully' <note>Spelled with the letter Vav.</note>, that is, they do not lack the letter **Vav** like the others? Because God created His world, and the Angel of Death was not in it. For this reason, the aforementioned word **toldot** <note>original: תולדות</note>, that is, 'generations,' is written **male** <note>original: מלא</note>, that is, 'fully.' But when Adam and Eve had sinned, God 'diminished' the 'generations' <note>original: תולדת, spelled without the Vav.</note> which are in Scripture. But

<margin>G</margin> when Perez stood [forth], the **toldot**, that is, 'generations,' were made **male**, that is, they were written 'fully.' For the letter **Vav** is not missing there. # CHAPTER XII.
## That the ruin of the Angels also was to be repaired through the Messiah.
### CAPNIO.

<note>The following section features Johannes Reuchlin, using his Greek-style pen name 'Capnio', in dialogue with Galatinus.</note>

Since, according to the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note>, that is perfect which lacks nothing, and since the repair of the angelic ruin <note>The "angelic ruin" refers to the vacant places in heaven left by the fall of Lucifer and his followers.</note> seems to pertain to the perfect restoration of the universe, it is therefore necessary to prove that the Messiah himself was to be the perfect restorer of the whole universe, and that the ruin of the Angels was also to be restored through him. **GALATINUS**. That is found most especially and clearly in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note>, in the place where it comments on the beginning of Psalm 89: **A song of instruction for Ethan the Ezrahite. I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever.** <note>original Hebrew: משכיל לאיתן האזרחי. חסדי יהוה עולם אשירה (*Maskil le-Eitan ha-Ezrachi. Chasdei Adonai olam ashira*)</note> This means: "Understanding for the strong one, or the one to come, the native, or the illustration, or the oriental: I will sing the mercies of God forever." It is read in this way: this is what is written in Jeremiah, chapter 9: **But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who exercises mercy, judgment, and justice on the earth.** <note>original Hebrew: כי אם בזאת יתהלל המתהלל השכל וידע אותי כי אני יהוה עשה חסד משפט וצדקה בארץ</note> For these are the things I have desired, said God. Because of this, it is said in Psalm 101: **I will sing of mercy and judgment.** Then, in the same *Midrash*, it follows immediately: **He said to them: I said, the world shall be built in mercy; you shall also prepare the heavens. And not only in the heavens, but even the throne itself does not stand except through mercy, as it is said: And it shall be prepared in mercy. And if one [leg] should totter, he took a stone and propped it up. So was the throne on high, as it were, which tottered until the Holy One, blessed be He, propped it up. And with what did He prop it? With mercy. Behold, the world shall be built in mercy, even the heavens. And so David said: To Him who made the heavens with understanding. And by what means do they stand? Upon mercy, as it is said: For His mercy endures forever. To Him who stretched out the earth. And by whose hand? For His mercy endures forever.** <note>This Hebrew passage uses a parable of a four-legged throne to describe the stability of the cosmos being dependent on Divine Mercy (the Messiah).</note> That is, he said to them (namely, David to Israel, at the start of the eighty-ninth Psalm): "Since I said, the world shall be built in mercy, you, O God, shall repair, or rectify, or fit the heavens." He said "Mercy," because not only the heavens, but even the throne itself is not persistent except through mercy. Just as it was said through Isaiah in the sixteenth chapter: *And the throne shall be prepared, or fitted, or rectified*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *in mercy, or through mercy.* This is parabolically similar to a throne, or a seat having four feet, one of which had moved itself; someone therefore took a clod, or a fragment of stone, and propped it up. So the supernal throne (from what is written in the Law, it can be said) had been moved, or shaken, or diminished, until the Holy and Blessed God propped it up. And with what did He prop it? With Mercy. And this is what was said: *The world shall be built in mercy,* <margin>B</margin> *you shall repair or restore the heavens.* And so David says in the one hundred and thirty-sixth Psalm: *To Him who made the heavens with prudence.* And upon whose hands are they standing? Upon mercy, as was said consequently: *For His mercy is for an age, or for eternity. He stretches out the earth.* And by whose hand? *For His mercy is for an age.* Because of this, Psalm 63 says: *Because your mercy is better than life.* All these things are from the aforementioned *Midrash*. Here it is very fitting to notice <margin>C</margin> that saying of Isaiah 16, which was introduced in the preceding tradition: **And the throne or seat shall be prepared in mercy, and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and expediting or hastening justice.** <note>original Hebrew: והוכן בחסד כסא וישב עליו באמת באהל דוד שפט ודרש משפט ומהר צדק</note> Rabbi Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> translates these things into Aramaic thus: **Because of this, the Messiah of Israel shall establish his throne in goodness, and shall sit upon it in truth in the city of David, and shall seek judgment and do truth.** <note>original Aramaic: בכין משיחא דישראל יתקן בטוב כרסוהי ויתיב עלוהי בקשוט דוד בקרתא דדוד ויתבע דין ועביד קשוט</note> That is, in this <margin>D</margin> or because of this, the Messiah of Israel shall set up, or fit his throne in goodness. And he shall sit upon it within the city of David, and shall judge judgment, and shall perform truth. Since, therefore, in the preceding tradition it was proved through these words of Isaiah that God was to confirm and restore the supernal throne with mercy, by applying a clod or fragment of stone to its diminution and shaking or movement; and since here, through the Aramaic translation, it is openly shown that <margin>E</margin> these very same words speak of the Messiah: it is surely a necessary and manifest consequence that the Messiah himself is the restorer of the supernal throne. For no one can be understood to have more rightly placed the fragment of the aforementioned stone than the Messiah, the restorer of celestial and terrestrial things: who, by his immense mercy and passion <note>suffering</note>, by healing sinful men through the bruise of his passion (according to the testimony of Isaiah), and by leading them into the supernal Jerusalem, restored the angelic ruin by joining us to the Angels, and propped up the <margin>F</margin> supernal throne—that is, the choir of Angels, which had been diminished because of the ruin of the demons. And it is called the supernal throne for this reason: because God sits upon it in a certain way, according to that saying of the Psalmist in Psalm 80: **You who sit upon the Cherubim.** <note>original Hebrew: ישב אל הכרובים (*Yoshev el ha-Keruvim*)</note> And again in Psalm 99: **He sits upon the Cherubim, let the earth be moved.** <note>original Hebrew: ישב הכרובים תנוט הארץ (*Yoshev ha-Keruvim tanut ha-aretz*)</note> From these things, it is clear that through the Messiah, not only the universe—which had been corrupted in a certain way because of the sin of our first parents—was to be repaired, and death <margin>G</margin> itself destroyed (as was shown in the preceding sections), but the angelic ruin also (as has now been proved) was to be restored.

# BOOK SIX

### CHAPTER XIII.

### *That the holy fathers desired the coming of the Messiah with the greatest longing.*

### CAPNIO.

Therefore, the holy fathers yearned for the arrival of the Messiah with the greatest desire. GALATINUS. Precisely so. For this reason, the holy Job said in his ninth chapter: **"Would that there were an arbiter between us, who might lay his hand upon us both"** <note>original Hebrew: לו יש בינינו מוכיח ישת ידו על שנינו (*Lu yesh beinenu mokhiach yashet yado al shneinu*); Job 9:33</note>. Isaiah shows that this "arbiter" of divine justice—under whose severity the house of all men lay—is the Messiah. Speaking of him in his ninth chapter <note>The text cites chapter 9, but the quote is from Isaiah 11:4</note>, he says: **"And he shall judge the poor in justice, and shall reprove with equity for the humble"** <note>original Hebrew: ושפט בצדק דלים והוכיח במישור לענוי ארץ (*Ve-shafat be-zedek dalim ve-hokhiach be-mishor le-anvei aretz*)</note>, or the poor, or the meek of the earth. 

It should be noted that in these same words of Job, some Hebrew manuscripts have the word **Lu** <note>original Hebrew: לו (*lu*)</note> written with the letter *vav*, which means "would that" or "if only." In that case, his words are interpreted as we said: "Would that there were an arbiter between us who would lay his hand upon us both." Other manuscripts, however, have the word **Lo** <note>original Hebrew: לא (*lo*)</note> written with the letter *aleph*, which signifies the negative "not." In that instance, the words are translated: **"There is no arbiter between us."** Thus, our Latin edition <note>The Vulgate</note> has: "There is no one who is able to reprove both, and to lay his hand upon both." 

Both readings are good and lead to the same meaning. According to the first reading, which the Talmud uses, the holy Job—considering how perversely and ruinously the first man had sinned, and how inexorably the Creator of men had been angered—was searching for the Messiah as a mediator between God and man. This mediator would "lay his hand on both," which is to say, he would simultaneously embrace and bear both natures, namely the Divine and our own. He alone among men would appear as an innocent man, yet he would proceed voluntarily to bear the penalty of guilt without having any guilt himself. Thus, by example and word, he would reprove man so that he might not sin; and by suffering an ignominious penalty for man’s sake despite being innocent, he would stand against the severity of divine justice so that it might not strike. 

According to the other reading, the same holy Job, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit that no one before or after the Messiah would come who, unburdened by his own sins, could take on the guilt of others' sins or satisfy divine justice, lamented the loss of time caused by the long delay of the Messiah’s coming. He said, "There is no arbiter between us"—that is, between God and man—who might lay his hand upon us with equity (as was said) and alone reprove the humble of the earth for the sake of their salvation. Isaiah also sought this arbiter with burning desire in his sixty-fourth chapter, saying: **"O that you would rend the heavens and descend!"** <note>original Hebrew: לוא קרעת שמים וירדת (*Lu karata shamayim ve-yaradta*); Isaiah 64:1</note>.

<margin>An objection of the more recent Jews.</margin> CAPNIO. The younger generations of Jews, misinterpreting the aforementioned scripture of holy Job as they do others, say that he desired some judge other than God, under whom he might show God to be unjust and himself to be innocent—as it is 

<column-break/>

<margin>Refutation.</margin> A found in the book **Bava Batra** <note>The "Last Gate," a tractate of the Talmud dealing with civil law and tradition</note>, in the chapter beginning **Hassuttafin** <note>The Partners</note>. There, Rabba says regarding those same words of Job: "Let there be dust in the mouth of Job." For a servant who reproves his Lord God is nothing. GALATINUS. Without a doubt, Jewish blindness unjustly and impiously condemns the holy man Job by misinterpreting his words. Against them, we first bring the testimony of Him <note>God</note> who says in the first chapter: **"In all this Job did not sin, nor did he attribute folly to God."** B And again, in the last chapter of the same book: **"And the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken what is right or fitting to me, as my servant Job has."** It also grants no small authority to the book of Job among the Hebrews that the same book is said to have been written by Moses, as is held in **Bava Batra**, in the chapter **Hassuttafin**, where it is read: C "The Masters have handed down that Moses wrote his own volume, and the section of Balaam, and Job." Therefore, that Job spoke rightly and fittingly is proven not only by the testimony of Moses, but even by that of God. 

Nothing, then, is more right or fitting to be said here, according to the literal sound of his words, than that according to the first reading he desired the presence of God and man in the Messiah, or according to the second reading, he lamented the delay of the Messiah, who is both God and man. By laying D his hand on both, the Messiah would restore the ruins of each—justifying men and gathering them into the companies of Angels. From this, his supreme desire for the Messiah’s coming is clear. 

The same is affirmed by **Rabbenu Haccados** <note>Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> in the book **Gale Razeya** <note>The Revealer of Secrets</note>, regarding the rest of the holy fathers and all the righteous, in response to the fifth petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome. For when the same Antoninus asked him what sacrifice Israel would make after the cessation of the sacrifice that was then being performed, he replied to him among other things: E "Because you ask to be given knowledge of the sacrifice that Israel will perform after the coming of the Messiah, I will tell you what I found written by **Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai** in the book titled **Machkar Hassodoth** <note>The Investigation of Secrets</note>." 

"Once, while I was sacrificing from Mount Ebal toward Mount Gerizim <note>Two mountains in Samaria; Gerizim is the mountain of blessing</note> to seek grace from God and worship Him, I found Elijah standing upon Mount Gerizim, praying and weeping. I offered him a greeting of peace, F but he was unwilling to look at me. When I saw this, I began to weep. Soon he turned his face toward me and said: 'Son of Yochai, it is not a convenient hour.' And he departed. Later, I returned to Mount Gerizim and found him praying and praising the Lord of the world. Then I saw eighty thousand legions of Angels coming upon Mount Gerizim, and in each legion were eighty thousand ranks, and in each rank were eighty thousand Angels. They were carrying before them Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Mo- G ses, and Aaron, David and Solomon, and all the kings of the house of David, and the prophets and the righteous who have been in the world. The Angels themselves were petitioning God, saying: 'Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel your servants, to whom you swore by your own self...'"

### CHAPTER No. 1.

<margin>D</margin> **A**LTHOUGH from all these things which have been said so abundantly and truthfully from the fourth chapter until now, it may be clearly gathered that the eternal salvation and perfect redemption which was to be accomplished through the Messiah was not to be a physical one (as the more recent, raving Jews assert), but was to be spiritual. By this redemption, the Redeemer—himself God and man—was to redeem and save the human race <gloss>genus</gloss> from hell and from eternal death, which all men had incurred because of the sin of our first parents. 
<margin>E</margin> However, because many of the Jews say that this redemption or salvation was to be for Israel alone and not for the Gentiles, we must therefore prove through their ancient scriptures—so that their treachery may be even further convicted—that not only the Jews who were to receive the Messiah, but the Gentiles also were to believe in the Messiah himself, and were to be redeemed and saved by him. GALATINUS. This is clearly held in many places. # CHAPTER XV.

### That the Messiah himself willed to come forth from both Jews and Gentiles to designate that the future salvation of both would be through him.

---

->CAPNIO.<-

I believe that for this reason the Messiah proceeded from both Jews and Gentiles: so that the future salvation of both through him might be pre-figured by this fact. GAL. You speak rightly, my Capnio. For this is most clearly evident from what is written in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moses ha-Darshan (11th century) was a famous Jewish scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) commentaries.</note> concerning that which is said in Genesis, <margin>Chapter 19</margin> **"And the elder said to the younger: Behold, I lay yesterday with my father; let us make him drink wine tonight also, and go in, and lie with him, and let us preserve seed from our father."** <note>original Hebrew: ותאמר הבכירה אל הצעירה הן שככתי אמש את אבי נשקנו יין גם הלילה ובאי שכבי עמו ונחיה (*Vatomer ha-bechirah el ha-tzeirah hen shachavti emesh et avi nashkenu yayin gam ha-laylah u-vai shichvi immo ve-nichayeh*)</note> Rabbi Tanhuma said: "It is not written 'And let us preserve a son from our father,' but 'seed.' And this is the King Messiah, who comes from both. For David indeed proceeded from Ruth the Moabitess, and Rehoboam from Naamah the Ammonitess. But the King Messiah is from the sons of their sons." And this is what Zophar said to Job in the eleventh chapter: **"Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the <term>Almighty</term> <note>original Hebrew: שדי (*Shaddai*), a divine name often translated as Almighty or 'The All-Sufficient One.'</note> to perfection?"** <note>original Hebrew: החקר אלוה תמצא אם עד תכלית שדי תמצא (*Ha-cheker Eloah timtza im ad tachlit Shaddai timtza*)</note> That is, can you stand above the depth of God, you who seek it? If the judgment of a man who lay with his daughter-in-law had come before you, what kind of sentence would you have given against him? He answered: Stoning. And if the judgment of a man who <margin>q</margin> lay with his daughter had come before you, what would you have judged against him? He said to him: Burning. Zophar said to him: "But these judgments came before the Holy and Blessed God. For Lot lay with his daughters, and Judah with his daughter-in-law. Yet the Holy and Blessed God took from both of them, and established from them kings in this age, and a Redeemer in the future. And this is the King Messiah." This is the tradition. Likewise, in the same book it is read that Rabbi Hanina said: "What does the text of Genesis 19 mean where the daughters of Lot said, 'That we may preserve seed from our father'?" Because they said "seed" and not "sons," it seems a secret was revealed to them concerning the coming of the Messiah, and that the Messiah was to come forth from the seed of Adam and from them. They were hinting at that "seed" of the Messiah of which Adam said, "The Lord has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel," which was to proceed from them. And therefore they wished to lie with their father to preserve such a seed—not led by any malice or indecency, but because they thought no other man existed in the world besides their father. Lest the coming of the Messiah be omitted, each of them lay with their father for one night, and having become pregnant, they bore two sons: one Ammon, the other Moab. From these, two great nations emerged who are called Ammon and Moab. From Moab indeed proceeded Ruth the Moabitess, who took Boaz as her husband. From his lineage came King David, as appears from his genealogy—

<column-break/>

<page-num>370</page-num>
<header>BOOK SIX. 370</header>

<margin>A</margin> King Solomon, among other wives, had Naamah the Ammonitess, and from her was born Rehoboam, King of Judah. David, among other sons, had Solomon and Nathan. From Nathan proceeded the most blessed Virgin according to the genealogy of Luke. From Solomon and his son Rehoboam proceeded Joseph, the spouse of the same Virgin, as we shall say more extensively in the following book. Since, therefore, the daughters of Lot did not know from which of them the Messiah was to come forth, and each <margin>B</margin> thought he would proceed from her, they said, "That we may preserve seed from our father," which must be judged as having been done for no small mystery. For since God foreknew that the Jews would for the most part deny the Messiah and not believe in him, but the Gentiles would receive him, and accordingly he would make them a new people, as stated by the Psalmist in Psalm 102: <note>The text cites Psalm 100, but the quote is from Psalm 102:18.</note> **"A people who shall be created will praise the Lord."** <note>original Hebrew: ועם נברא יהלל יה (*Ve-am nivra yehalel Yah*)</note> Likewise in Isaiah chapter 43: <margin>C</margin> **"This people I have formed for myself; they shall declare my praise."** <note>original Hebrew: עם זו יצרתי לי תהלתי יספרו (*Am zu yatzarti li tehillati yesaperu*)</note> Therefore, by divine providence, it was brought about that the Redeemer and true Messiah would proceed from Gentiles and from Jews, so that it might be known to all from that source that he was to come for the salvation of both. Therefore the Lord himself also called the Gentiles his sheep, saying, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; those also I must lead, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd." For that reason King David said, "Praise the Lord, all you nations; praise him together, all you <margin>D</margin> peoples." But what will you say to him? "Because his mercy is confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever." And for this reason, because the Messiah was to save both, namely Jews and Gentiles, he is rightly called the Redeemer of the whole human race and the Savior of the entire world.

# CHAPTER XVI.

### That the world was to be saved through the remission of sins; and concerning the general remission of sins which was to be performed through the Messiah.

---

->CAPNIO.<-

<margin>E</margin> In what way, then, was the world or the human race to be saved through the Messiah? For you must show that also through their scriptures. GAL. The ancient scriptures show that the world itself, or the human race, was to be saved <margin>F</margin> at the time of the Messiah specifically through a general remission of sins. For that there would be a future remission of sins through the Messiah is best proven in the book <term>Yoma</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement.</note>, that is "of Days," in the chapter <term>Yom HaKippurim</term>, that is "The Day of Atonements," where it is read as follows: "There is a tradition that Rabbi Meir said: Repentance is great; for on account of one who has performed repentance, they shall be <margin>G</margin> absolving the entire world." (He says "they shall be absolving" in the plural on account of the trinity of divine persons in one essence, who must concur together for the remission of sins.) Then it is added in the same tradition: as it is said in the fourteenth chapter of Hosea,
