He says again in the same place, **"For to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear."** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki li tichra kol berech tishava kol lashon* (Isaiah 45:23)</note> And concerning him it is also written in the forty-ninth chapter of Isaiah, **"And I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation even to the ends of the earth."** <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-netaticha le-or goyim lihyot yeshuati ad ketzeh ha-aretz*</note> A "I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation even to the ends of the earth." And because of this David also says in the sixty-seventh Psalm: **"Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you. Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity, and guide the nations on earth. Selah. Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you."** <note>original Hebrew: *Yoducha amim Elohim yoducha amim kullam...*</note> B That is: Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you. Let the nations be glad and rejoice, because you judge the peoples in equity, and you direct the nations on the earth. Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you, the earth has yielded its fruit. Where he commemorates "they shall praise" four times, it is as if he had said: They shall praise you with their heart, they shall praise you with their mouth, they shall praise you with their works, they shall praise you equally with all things; just as it is said in the third chapter of Zephaniah, **"For then I will restore to the peoples a pure lip, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve him with one shoulder."** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki az ehpoch el amim safah berurah likro kullam be-shem YHVH le-ovdo shechem echad*</note> "Because then I will convert the peoples to a chosen lip: so that all may call upon the name of God, and that they may serve him with one shoulder." <note>The phrase "one shoulder" implies acting in unison or with a single purpose.</note> However, the name of God is not mentioned in this place except for the King Messiah, of whom it is said in Isaiah chapter 30: **"Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar"** <note>original Hebrew: *Hineh shem YHVH ba mi-merchak*</note> that is, "Behold, the name of God comes from a distance." The same is taught concerning God, the Holy and Blessed: as it is said in Jeremiah chapter 23: **"Am I a God at hand, says the Lord, and not a God afar off?"** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-Elohim mi-karov ani neum YHVH ve-lo Elohei me-rachok*</note> D that is, "Am I a God from nearby, says God, and not a God from afar?" And why shall they serve him with one shoulder? For this reason, because the government was placed upon his shoulder: as it is said in Isaiah chapter 9: **"And the government shall be upon his shoulder"** <note>original Hebrew: *Va-tehi ha-misrah al shikmo*</note> that is, "And the government was upon his shoulder." Thus far the tradition. In which many things are to be noted as most worthy of remark. First, indeed, is that the redeemer ought not to be a respecter of persons, but the savior of all those confessing him. Therefore it is necessary that this redeemer be the Messiah, on account of those words of Jeremiah introduced there, "In his days Judah shall be saved": which in the Hebrew scriptures, and in the Chaldean translation <note>The <term>Targum</term>, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, are explained as being about the Messiah, as was proved in the previous sections. Second, truly, is that in the aforesaid words of Jeremiah, by "Judah," the Jews themselves are not understood—as they often argue against us—but all those, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews, who were to confess the Messiah in heart, mouth, and work. Third, moreover, is that the Messiah was to be given as a light to the nations, and salvation even to the ends of the earth. Fourth is that the Messiah is the Name of God, whom the peoples—that is, the Gentiles—ought to serve with a chosen lip. Fifth is that he himself was to come from afar, that is, from God the Holy and Blessed. Which is proved there by that passage of Jeremiah, "Am I a God from nearby, and not a God from afar." Wherefore it follows that the Messiah is God. Sixth is that those words of Isaiah written in chapter 9, "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government shall be upon his shoulder," are understood to be about the Messiah. This is against the ravings of the younger Jews <note>A common polemical phrase used by Christian authors of this period to distinguish between ancient Jewish traditions they respected and contemporary Jewish interpretations they rejected.</note>. It is to be noted further, that just as through the preceding tra-

<column-break/>

dition in those words of Jeremiah, "In his days Judah shall be saved," by Judah the Jews themselves are not understood, but all those confessing the Messiah: so in the same words when it immediately follows, **"And Israel shall dwell safely"** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-Yisrael yishkon le-vetach*</note> That is, "And Israel shall dwell in trust": by "Israel," for the same reason, one should not understand men of the Israelite people, but all those "seeing God"—that is, all those from the Israelite nation as well as from the other nations who were to see the Messiah himself, true God and man, by faith and work. Such were the Apostles and the rest, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, converted to Christ, who, seeing Christ, saw the true God. And this is the literal exposition. For "Israel" was not the proper name of Jacob himself, but was imposed upon him in the vision of the Angels. Since therefore the Messiah, as has been shown most extensively in the preceding parts, is greater than the Angels; since he is true God, those are the true Israelites who have seen and do see the Messiah himself. <margin>Who are the true Israel.</margin> To this tradition it must also be added what is said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> is an ancient rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note> on that part of Psalm 67: **"That your way may be known upon earth, your salvation among all nations"** <note>original Hebrew: *La-daat ba-aretz darchecha be-chol goyim yeshuatecha*</note> that is, "To know your way on the earth, your salvation in all nations." It is said thus: "Let the Holy and Blessed God be known saving Israel on account of their works, but so that he may make known his power, and that he may make his name known to the nations." For Asaph says in Psalm 76: **"In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel."** <note>original Hebrew: *Noda be-Yehudah Elohim be-Yisrael gadol shemo*</note> That is, "Known in Judea is God, in Israel his name is great." And again he says in Psalm 77: **"You are the God who does wonders; you have made known your power among the peoples."** <note>original Hebrew: *Atah ha-El oseh fele hodata va-amim uzzecha*</note> That is, "You are the God doing a wondrous thing, you have made known your power among the peoples." Could they say to them—the Jews to the Gentiles, namely—that the redeemer is a respecter of faces, that is, of persons? By no means, but of those confessing him. Just as it is said in Psalm 67: "Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you," with the rest. And thus it is what Isaiah says in chapter 61: **"For as the earth brings forth its sprout, and as a garden causes its seeds to spring up, so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations."** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki cha-aretz totzi tzimchah ve-che-gannah zeroeha tatzmiach ken Adonai YHVH yatzmiach tzedakah u-tehillah neged kol ha-goyim*</note> E That is, "For as the earth produces its germ, and as a garden germinates its seeds, so the Lord God will germinate justice and praise before all nations." Thus far the Talmud. Likewise in the same Midrash Tehillim on that part of Psalm 100: **"A Psalm for thanksgiving. Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth! Serve the Lord with gladness! Come before him with singing!"** <note>original Hebrew: *Mizmor le-todah hariu le-YHVH kol ha-aretz ivdu et YHVH be-simchah bou le-fanav bi-renanah*</note> That is, "A Psalm for confession. Shout to God, all the earth, serve God in joy, come before him with a song." It is written thus: **"Rabbi Jacob said, it was said by Rabbi Abhu in the name of Rabbi Aha: A Psalm for confession; all the nations shall confess me, and I will receive them, as it is said, 'For to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.'"** <note>original Hebrew: *Amar Rabbi Yaakov amar Rabbi Abhu be-shem Rabbi Aha mizmor le-todah yodu li kol ha-umot ve-ani mekabbelan she-neemar ki li tichra kol berech tishava kol lashon*</note> F That is, "Rabbi Jacob said, it was said by Rabbi Abhu in the name of Rabbi Aha: A Psalm for confession: All nations shall praise me, and I will receive them. As it is said in Isaiah 45: Because to me every knee shall bow and every tongue shall swear, and I will receive them." From these things which have been said, it has been openly demonstrated that not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles, were to be redeemed and saved through the Messiah. G Yet not all Jews, nor all Gentiles, were to be saved at the time of the Messiah, but only those from both who would receive the Messiah himself, and confess him with heart, mouth, and work.

# BOOK SIX.

### CHAPTER XV.

*That to designate the salvation of both Jews and Gentiles through the future Messiah, the Messiah himself willed to arise from both.*

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' featuring a figure standing amidst classical or biblical architectural ruins.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin> For this reason (as I believe), the Messiah proceeded from both Jews and Gentiles, so that from this, the future salvation of both through him might be foreshadowed. GALATINUS: You speak rightly, my Capnio. For this is most evident from what is written in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>original: "Rabbi Mosis Hadarsan," a 11th-century commentator known for using midrashic legends</note> on that passage in the <margin>spoken in Chapter 19</margin> 19th chapter of Genesis: "And the firstborn said to the younger, 'Behold, I lay last night with my father; let us make him drink wine tonight also, and you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father.'" <note>original Hebrew: *Vatomer ha-bechirah el ha-tzairah hen shachavti emesh et avi nashkenu yayin gam ha-laylah u-voi shichvi immo ve-nechayyeh me-avinu zarah*</note> <margin>This is, etc.</margin> This means: "And the elder said to the younger, 'Behold, I slept or lay yesterday with my father. Let us give him wine to drink this night also, and come, and lie, and sleep with him. And let us bring life to a seed from our father.'" Rabbi Tanhuma <note>A famous 4th-century Rabbi known for his collections of homiletic teachings</note> said: It is not written "let us bring life to a *son* from our father," but "a *seed*." And this is the King Messiah, who comes from both. For David indeed proceeded from Ruth the Moabite, and Rehoboam from Naamah the Ammonite. <note>Moab and Ammon were the sons born to Lot's daughters; thus the Messiah has "Gentile" blood through these women</note> But the King Messiah comes from the children of their children. And this is what Zophar said to Job in the eleventh chapter, saying: "Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the Almighty to perfection?" <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-cheker Eloah timtza im ad tachlit Shaddai timtza*</note> That is: Can you find the depth or the investigation of God? Can you discover even to the completion of the Almighty—that is, of him who is sufficient? Do you who seek to stand above the depth of God? If the judgment of a man who lay with his daughter-in-law had come before you, what kind of sentence would you have given against him? He answered him: Stoning. And if the judgment of a man who lay with his daughter had come before you, what would you have judged against him? He said to him: Burning. Zophar said to him: Yet these judgments came before the Holy and Blessed God. For Lot lay with his daughters, and Judah with his daughter-in-law. <note>Referring to Tamar in Genesis 38</note> And yet the Holy and Blessed God took from both of them, and established from them kings in this age, and the Redeemer in the future. And this is the King Messiah. This is the tradition. Likewise, in the same book it is read that Rabbi Hanina said thus: What does the text of the nineteenth chapter of Genesis mean where the daughters of Lot said, "That we may preserve seed from our father"? Because they said "seed" and not "sons," it seems a secret was revealed to them concerning the coming of the Messiah, and that from the seed of Adam and from them the Messiah was to proceed: hinting that the seed of the Messiah, about whom Adam said, "The Lord has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel," <note>Genesis 4:25</note> was to proceed from them. Therefore, they wished to lie with their father to preserve this kind of seed, led not by any malice or dishonor, but because they thought no other man besides their father existed in the world; lest the coming of the Messiah be prevented, each of them lay with their father one night, and having become pregnant, they gave birth to two sons: one Ammon, the other Moab. From whom two very great nations emerged, which are called Ammon and Moab. From Moab, moreover, proceeded Ruth the Moabite, who took Boaz as her husband. From whose lineage came King David, as appears from his genealogy.

Now King Solomon, among other wives, had Naamah the Ammonite, and from her was born Rehoboam, King of Judah. David, among other sons, had Solomon and Nathan. "For his mercy is confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever." <note>Psalm 117:1-2</note> And for this reason, because the Messiah was to save both—namely, Jews and Gentiles—he is rightly called the Redeemer of the whole human race and the Savior of the entire world.

# BOOK SIX.

<margin>A</margin> "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him." <note>original Hebrew: *Arpa meshuvatam ahevam nedavah ki shav api mimennu*. Hosea 14:4</note> This is to say: I will heal their perversity, or their turning away; I will love them freely or spontaneously. Because my fury shall be turned away from him—that is, on account of him <note>The author interprets "from him" as referring to a specific individual, the Messiah, whose actions turn away God's wrath from the people.</note>. This is the tradition. Regarding the words of Hosea introduced in this tradition, Rabbi Jonathan translates them into Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaice," referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> as follows: "I will receive their repentance, I will forgive their debts, I will have mercy on them when they perform penance." <note>original Aramaic: *Akabbeltehon bityuvatehon eshvok lehovaihon kad yatuvan bidehilta*</note> 

Now, that the aforementioned "one," through whose repentance the world was to be absolved from sins, is shown to be the Messiah by the Targum (the Aramaic translation), is clear from what Hosea immediately added: "I will be as the dew unto Israel." <note>original Hebrew: *Ehyeh katzal le-Yisrael*. Hosea 14:5</note> Jonathan himself translated this into Aramaic as: "My Word shall be as the dew to Israel." <note>original Aramaic: *Ehei memri kitala le-Yisrael*</note> Having accepted this Aramaic translation, which asserts that the Word of God was to be as dew to Israel, let us see what the prophet adds in the text concerning this Word. For he says: "He shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon." <note>original Hebrew: *Yifrachu kashoshanah ve-yach*</note> The gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> explains it thus: "And the dew itself shall produce its roots, and make them prosper like Lebanon—that is, like the roots of the trees of Lebanon, which are very great." 

The Prophet continues: "His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon." <note>original Latin: *Ibunt propagines eius, & erit sicut oliuæ splendor, vel gloria, vel confessio eius, & odor erit eius, vt Libani*. Hosea 14:6</note> Jonathan turns this into Aramaic as: "Sons and daughters shall multiply, whose splendor shall be like the splendor of the sanctuary's lampstand, and their scent like the scent of the smoke of incense." <note>original Aramaic: *Yisgin benin u-venan ve-yehei keziv matara kudsha zivhon ve-reihon ke-reiach ketoret bosmaya*</note> 

The prophecy further follows: "They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the memorial thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon." <note>Hosea 14:7</note> Jonathan also explains this in Aramaic: "The children of their captivities shall be gathered; they shall dwell or sit in the shadow of their Messiah; the dead shall be revived, and good shall be multiplied in the land. And their memorial shall ascend, or be fruitful, like the memorial or remembrance of the trumpet-house over the old wine that was mixed in the house of the Lord's sanctuary." 

With these things established, the Jews must be asked: Since it is said here by the Prophet, "They that dwell under *his* shadow shall return," to which of the preceding things does this pronoun "*his*"—which they call a *suffix* <note>term: <term>Chinnoi</term> (Hebrew: *Kinuy*), a grammatical term for a pronominal suffix attached to a word</note>—refer? Indeed, the nature of such suffixes <note>term: <term>Chinnuim</term> (plural of Kinuy)</note> is to refer to the closer and previously mentioned things, as can be gathered from many places in Holy Scripture. For when it is said in Exodus chapter 15, "The Lord is a man of war: the Lord is his name," this pronoun "*his*" refers to the other preceding terms—that is, to God, or to the man, or to both. So also here, when it is said, "Those dwelling or sitting in his shadow," this pronoun "*His*," having carefully inspected the circumstances of the preceding words, must refer either to that "one" of whom it was said just before—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> that on account of his repentance God was to absolve the entire world—or to the "dew," which the Aramaic translation (as we have seen) explains to be the Word of God. Because, therefore, where the prophet placed "In his shadow," Rabbi Jonathan interpreted in Aramaic as "In the shadow of the Messiah," it is certainly shown openly that one of these, or even both, must be the Messiah.

Of this repentance, which the Messiah, as God and man, was to perform for the salvation of the world or for the saving of men, <margin>B</margin> the Psalmist openly makes mention in the eighty-fifth Psalm, saying: "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease. Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all generations? Wilt thou not turn again and revive us, that thy people may rejoice in thee?" <note>Psalm 85:4-6</note> From these things we have said, it is clearly evident that because of the repentance which <margin>C</margin> the Messiah was to perform, the human race was to be saved. For he was not to perform this penance for himself, since he was to have no sin for which it would be necessary for him to perform penance; as Isaiah testifies when he says of him in chapter 53: "Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." 

Therefore, he had to perform this penance for the human race, insofar as he was to undergo the punishment for the sins <margin>D</margin> of the whole human race; according to what was said by the same prophet in the same chapter: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows." <note>Isaiah 53:4</note> As we shall see more extensively in the eighth book.

<margin><unclear>The world already</unclear> <unclear>before</unclear> <unclear>the conception</unclear> <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>future mother</unclear> <unclear>of the Messiah</unclear></margin>

Therefore, before He brought forth the world, He foresaw the glorious Virgin who would conceive His Son and become the mother of the Messiah. And so, she was already created in His mind, according to that saying of the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon in the Book of Proverbs.</note> speaking in the person of the mother of the Messiah herself in the eighth chapter of Proverbs, saying in Hebrew: <note>original: "יהוה קנני ראשית דרכו קדם מפעליו מאז: מעולם נסכתי מראש מקדמי ארץ: באין תהומות חוללתי"</note> *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His way, before His works of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth was made; when there were no depths, I was brought forth.* <note>Proverbs 8:22–24. While traditionally associated with "Wisdom," the author applies this to the Virgin Mary.</note> Likewise, in the 24th chapter of Ecclesiasticus, Jeshua son of Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus.</note> says: *From the beginning, and before the ages, I was created.*

<margin>False opinion of the Jews, claiming the Law was established before the production of the world.</margin>
Nevertheless, the younger Jews oppose us, asserting that the Wise Man did not speak the aforementioned words regarding the mother of the Messiah, but regarding the Law of God <note>The Torah.</note>, which they say was created before the condition of the world. They claim it was written with letters of black fire on a background of white fire, and that it preceded the world by two thousand years. To them, we reply that they tell the emptiest of dreams. First, because they can gather no number of years before the constitution of the world. This is proved by a twofold reason.

<margin>Refutation. First reason.</margin>
The first of these is that God is not subject to time. The second is that time follows the motion of the celestial spheres and is joined to it. For a planet makes the hour, governing one hour at a time. And the motion of the sun makes the day, which lasts 24 hours from the moment it rises until it begins to rise again in the east. Moreover, the seven planets make the week, each of which governs one day. For the Sun governs the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday.</note>. Hence some have wished the Lord’s Day to be named from the dominion of the Sun, which is the king of the planets. The Moon itself governs Monday; Mars governs Tuesday; and so on for the rest. The course of the Moon completes the lunar month. The solar month is completed by the course of a [zodiac] sign, because each sign of the zodiac dominates its own month. The Sun completes the year, traversing the 12 signs of the zodiac in a full year. Therefore, if the heavens were not created, there was no time. Thus, since time did not exist, "two thousand years" before the creation of the world is falsely cited by the Jews.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
It is also clear that their opinion is heretical from this: that fire is one of the four elements. However, the elements were not created except at the creation of the world. If their opinion were true, two inconsistencies against their own Law would follow. First, that the world would have been eternal, since fire already existed. Second, that God did not create the world from nothing, but made it from something. Both of these are the greatest heresies even according to them, since it is against what is said in Genesis chapter 1: <note>original: "בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ"</note> *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* Therefore, the aforementioned words of the Wise Man can by no means be understood as referring to the Law. Thus, they must be understood as referring to the Virgin Mother of the Messiah. Nor do I think their opinion should be 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
approved who affirm that those same words are spoken not of the most blessed Virgin, but only of Divine Wisdom. This (if I may say so with their permission) is entirely false. For although the preceding words of Proverbs, *The Lord possessed me*, along with the rest, are rightly said of Divine Wisdom which was begotten from eternity—just as we also explained those words regarding that same Wisdom in the third book—

<margin>B</margin>
nevertheless, those words of Ecclesiasticus, *From the beginning and before the ages I was created*, can by no means be suited to that same Divine Wisdom. The reason for this is: because, according to the opinion of sacred theologians, there is nothing in God which is not God Himself. The ancient Talmudists also felt this, as is clear through Our Holy Master <note>Rabbenu Hakkados, or Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah.</note> in the first petition of the book *Gale Razeya* <note>The "Revealer of Secrets," a mystical/cabalistic text used by Galatinus to find Christian truths in Jewish sources.</note>, speaking thus: <note>original: "לא נמצא שום דבר באל אשר לא יהיה אל"</note> *Nothing is found in God which is not God.* Therefore, it follows necessarily that the Wisdom which is in God is God. Wherefore it must also be uncreated.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, since those words, *From the beginning and before the ages I was created*, cannot be understood as referring to Divine Wisdom <note>Because "created" contradicts God's eternal/uncreated nature.</note>, they must be understood as referring to the most holy mother of the Messiah.

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>A Kabbalistic Method.</margin>
Finally, it must be noted that these Hebrew names <note>original: "יהושוע ומרים"</note>—that is, Jesus and Mary—ascend by arithmetic calculation to the number of the word <term>Covenant <note>original: "ברית" (Berith). In the system of Gematria, where letters represent numbers, words with the same numerical value are seen as having a spiritual connection.</note></term>, which is the same as a "pact." For the names "Jesus and Mary" among the Hebrews contain the number 612 by arithmetic calculation. For the letter *yod* contains 10, *shin* 300, *vav* 6, and thus the name <note>original: "יהושוע"</note>—that is, Jesus—contains 316. Again, *vav* contains 6, *mem* 40, *resh* 200, *yod* 10, *vav* 6, and *mem* 40. Thus, the phrase <note>original: "ומרים"</note>—that is, "And Mary"—contains 296. Therefore, the names "Jesus and Mary" together among the Hebrews contain 612. Now, consider what number is contained in the word <note>original: "ברית"</note> *Berith*, meaning "covenant" or "pact." For *beth* contains 2, *resh* 200, *yod* 10, and *tav* 400. From this it is clear that "Jesus and Mary" among the Hebrews ascend by arithmetic calculation to the number of *Berith*, the Covenant—that is, the number 612. This number is mentioned in a significant way in the <term>Kabbalah <note>A school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note></term>, which, whenever it can find such numbers, values them highly and places no small faith in them. For this reason, the words of the prophet Jeremiah are interpreted thus: *Unless my covenant were...* <note>Jeremiah 33:25.</note>—that is, "Unless for the love of my Jesus and Mary, I would not have set the laws for heaven and earth day and night"; meaning, I would not have created the world. The reason for this is found in Adam’s sin. Since the end for which God created the world is man, and the end of man is salvation and happiness, and since Adam’s sin corrupted the whole world in a certain way, God said He did not want to create the world. But His Word—that is, the Son of God—argued that the world should indeed be created, because by taking on human flesh, He Himself would satisfy the debt for Adam’s sin. And therefore, for the love of Jesus and Mary, God created the world. This is also confirmed by <term>Rabbi Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism and author of an influential Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note></term> in his Chaldaic gloss on the first chapter of Genesis, where it says, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* He says: <note>original: "בחוכמא ברא יהוה ית שמיא וית ארעא"</note>—that is, *Because of Wisdom, God created the heaven and the earth.* This means: "For the love of the immaculate Virgin, who is the world’s wisdom, God created heaven and earth"; or "for the love of the Messiah His Son, to whom Wisdom is attributed in divine matters." Moreover, the whole world was not only established for the love of the most blessed Virgin, but it is also sustained by it. For because of our wicked actions, the world itself could by no means stand, unless the glorious Virgin herself sustained it with her mercy and kindness, by praying for us. From these things it also follows that she and her Son were entirely immune from the sin of Adam.

To explain these things, it must be noted that D the opinion of certain ancient Jews was that the mother of the Messiah was not only created in the mind of God from the beginning and before the ages (as was said a little earlier), but also that her matter was produced within the matter of Adam, and the glorious mother of the Messiah herself stood out as the principal part—since for her love (as has been said) the world was created. For when God molded Adam, He made a kind of mass, from the more noble part of which He took the matter of the immaculate mother of the Messiah, and from the remainder and surplus of it He formed Adam. From the matter of the immaculate E mother of the Messiah, a power was made which was preserved in the more noble place and member of Adam’s body. This power later flowed down to Seth, then to Enos, then in successive order to the rest, until it reached Saint Joachim <note>Traditionally identified as the father of the Virgin Mary.</note>. From this power, finally, the most blessed mother of the Messiah was formed. And for this reason, Zechariah in the 4th chapter of his prophecy correctly called her <note>original: "את האבן הראשה"</note>—that is, *the primary stone.* <note>Zechariah 4:7.</note> From her, as F the ancient Jews explained, the Messiah was to be cut out. This is not without reason, since she was to be primary in time, rank, and excellence. From this opinion it is clearly concluded that the flesh of the glorious mother of the Messiah was not infected by original sin, but was preserved as most pure by divine providence. Therefore, her soul was not going to contract such a sin at her conception.

# BOOK SEVEN.
## HOOGSTRATEN <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527) was a Dutch Dominican theologian and inquisitor known for his controversies with humanists like Reuchlin.</note>

Given the truth of this opinion, it would follow that the glorious mother of the Messiah did not truly descend from the Davidic line, nor was she truly the daughter of Saint Joachim (whom you, contrary to the common way of writing, have called Jehoiakim). For Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> says the following in Book 3, Distinction 3, in the question that begins: *Whether the flesh of Christ was not infected:* There was another error of those who said that the flesh of Christ, as it came from his parents, was not infected. For they say that when Adam sinned, the Lord preserved something incorrupt and uninfected in Adam, through which human nature could be saved; and that this same part was passed down without any infection to the Blessed Virgin, and from that, the body of Christ was formed. 

However, this is considered an error for two reasons. First, because according to this position, Christ would not truly be the son of the Virgin, nor truly born from the line of any ancestor except Adam alone. For that part, because it remained incorrupt in human nature, would have been like something foreign to everyone else after Adam, and only natural to Adam himself in his original state. Second, because the proper order of atonement is removed. For just as it was not fitting for someone to make atonement for Adam and his corrupted descendants who was not of that same race, so also it would not have been fitting for the Son of God to heal the infected nature by making atonement unless he assumed the very thing that was previously infected. And therefore, it must be said that the flesh of Christ, as it existed in his parents and even in the Blessed Virgin herself, was infected by sin before it was assumed. But in the very moment of assumption, it was purged of all infection of sin, so that as it became the actual flesh of Christ, no stain could be found in it. These are the words of Saint Thomas. From these, it is clearly evident that the most blessed flesh of the Virgin was infected by the sin of Adam. 

**Galatinus:** <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), a Franciscan friar who wrote "De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis," a work attempting to prove Christian truths through Jewish texts.</note> Since by these same arguments which Saint Thomas brings forward, it could be proven that the unstained Virgin was not the daughter of Jehoiakim, nor that she came from the tribe of Judah and the royal line—if we wished to follow the opinion of those ancient Jews who say that a certain tiny portion of flesh in Adam was preserved most pure from every stain, and that it descended from generation to generation even to the immaculate Virgin herself. For that reason, we shall prove this opinion to be true using the testimonies of both the Old and New Testaments of Holy Scripture, as well as those of the ancient Hebrew Doctors. 

For from the Old Testament, we bring forward that saying from Genesis, chapter 4: <note>original Hebrew: "וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת כִּי שָׁת לִי אֱלֹהִים זֶרַע אַחֵר"</note> *That is,* "And she called his name Seth, saying: Because God has appointed for me another seed." For Adam, seeing that all souls were going to be lost because of his sin (and therefore, according to the edition of the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, he abstained from intimacy with his wife for 130 years after he fathered Abel, so that he would not father children who would be condemned), nevertheless, after he prophesied the coming of the Messiah through whom the world was to be saved, he knew his wife and fathered Seth. And because he knew that power was in him from which the mother of the Messiah was to be born, in whose most precious blood

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> the Messiah himself was present, he therefore called the name of his son Seth, which is derived from the word <note>original Hebrew: "שֵׁת"</note> (*sath*), which means "to place" or "to appoint," saying: "Because the Lord has appointed for me another seed." The meaning is: "In me has been found a foreign seed, and a certain power from which the Messiah is to be born." 

From the New Testament, we have among other things the testimony of John the Baptist, speaking thus in John, chapter 1: "But in the midst of you stood one whom you do not know. He it is." And again in the same place: "Behold," he says, "the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world. This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who was made before me."

<margin>B</margin> From these things, therefore, it is clear that the aforementioned opinion is true. For if we were to say that what he said—"Who was made before me"—is to be understood regarding his divinity, it would be entirely false, since the Son in the divine nature was not created nor made, but begotten by the Father. If, however, we wished to say that he was speaking of his arrival into this world, that would also be completely false, since John the Baptist was born six months before the birth of Christ.

<margin>C</margin> From these things, it necessarily follows that the aforementioned opinion of the ancient Hebrews is true, which says that the Mother of the Messiah was made from the more noble part of Adam’s mass, and therefore conceived without original sin. And although her matter was created at the same time as the matter of Adam, she was nevertheless first in excellence of cause and dignity. Because of this, certain ancient Jews called the mother of the Messiah the "primary rock," and the "first of creatures in the human race," and the "first human."

<margin>E</margin> *That is,* The just man is first in his own cause; his friend comes and searches him out?" The meaning is: When the Holy and Blessed God comes to judge the world on the Day of Judgment, the whole world will tremble and fear 그 terrible day, and they will say: "O King David, pray to God for us, since from you the Messiah proceeded." <margin>Catholic exposition.</margin>
Therefore, the authority of Proverbs which he brings forward—namely, *The first to plead his case seems right, and his friend comes and searches him out*—must be explained thus: This "first man," who is the mother of the Messiah (on account of whom the Messiah himself, or Christ, is called the "Son of Man"), is "just in her case," in which she was accused by adversaries of having been conceived in original sin. *And his friend comes*—that is, God—*and investigated this case*, and brought forth the sentence, saying: *You are altogether beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you.* Indeed, it seems that the ancient teachers of the Hebrews brought forward this authority to confirm the immaculate conception of the mother of the Messiah.

<margin>Why the mother of the Messiah is called "first man."</margin>
She is called the "first man" or the "first creature" in the human race because she was produced first of all in terms of her matter. From this, a corollary follows: that all humans are her children. For if the mother of the Messiah existed first as the "cause" of Adam, and Adam himself proceeded from her, even though they were at the same time (just as the sun, although it is prior in cause to its brightness, yet both exist at the same instant, though the brightness follows the sun), so the mother of the Messiah, even if she was produced in matter at the same time as Adam: because

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Adam nevertheless proceeded from her (for which reason she is called the "first man") and the whole human race from Adam, all people can in a certain way, not inaptly, be called the children of the mother of the Messiah herself. Nevertheless, her true and natural and firstborn son is the Messiah himself, formed from her purest blood and born of her: according to what is said in Luke chapter 1: *She brought forth her firstborn son.* <note>Luke 2:7 (the text cites chapter 1, but the verse is traditionally in chapter 2).</note> One also reads in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>A 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> on the Book of Genesis, regarding the saying in chapter 5 of that book:

<margin>B</margin> <term>זה ספר תולדות אדם</term> <note>Hebrew: *Zeh sefer toldot Adam*.</note> That is: *This is the book of the generations of Adam.* So Rabbi Joshua ben Levi <note>A 3rd-century Jewish scholar often cited in mystical and legal traditions.</note> said word-for-word: When God saw Adam formed, He called all the angels and said to them, "Humble yourselves and be obedient to this man." A large part of them accepted the command and bowed themselves to him, according to the will of God.

<margin>C</margin> But Satan—that is, Lucifer, the most excellent of all—said with his sect to the Holy and Blessed God: "O Lord of the world, You created us from the brightness of Your glory, and now You command us to bow to a man whom You formed from the earth?"

<margin>D</margin> The Holy and Blessed God answered him: "In this man who was created from the dust of the earth, there is more wisdom and understanding than in you." And for that reason, Isaiah said in chapter 14: *How you have fallen, Lucifer, from heaven, you who rose in the morning!* <note>Isaiah 14:12.</note> This is the tradition. It speaks only of the glorious mother of the Messiah, whose matter was produced at the same time as the matter of Adam, even if she stood prior in cause and excellence, on account of which Christ himself is called the "Son of Man." For it cannot speak of Adam for a double reason: First, because God would not have commanded the angels to bow to Adam, whom He knew would soon fall into sin. Second, because even if Adam were intelligent and wise, there was still more knowledge in the angels than in him.

<margin>E</margin> But the tradition says that there was more knowledge in that "first man" than in the angels. Therefore, it is necessary that it speaks of the mother of the Messiah, who had to be full of all wisdom and knowledge, and superior to all things after God. From this tradition, therefore, not only is the proposition held, but also that the mother of the Messiah herself was to be superior to the angels.

And there is also in him the virtue of man, and then the virtue of an animal."

<margin>G</margin> "Therefore, when the virtue of Socrates is strong, a male is generated; but when it is weak, a female is generated. If, however, the proper virtue of Socrates prevails, the son is made like Socrates, whether it be a male or a female. But if the virtue of Socrates' father prevails, a son is generated similar not to Socrates' father, but to the grandfather." Thus then—

### CHAPTER V.
#### To the second objection of Hoogstraten. And that the opinion concerning the immaculate conception of the glorious Virgin is most ancient.

This is most clearly evident from the fact that Moses, and Samuel, and all the greatest of the Prophets, with everyone else, descended to the underworld (as was shown in the preceding book). If, therefore, circumcision had unlocked the gate of the heavenly kingdom to them, they certainly would have migrated to heaven rather than to the 
<margin>Objection of Hoogstraten.</margin> <margin>C</margin> underworld. HOOGSTRATEN: I say this, however, that according to the exposition of some, this text speaks not of the immaculate Virgin, but of God's Church. GALATINUS: This also (if I may say so) is entirely false. <margin>Refutation.</margin> Both because all things which Mother Church sings were instituted by the Holy Spirit, whom it is impossible to lie. And Holy Church attributes this saying of the Wise Man <note>Solomon</note> to the Mother of God. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that it speaks of her. Also, because the praises of the glorious 
<margin>D</margin> Virgin herself are immense and incomprehensible. If we, therefore, wishing to praise her, attributed the praises of another to her, we would undoubtedly show that those praises were not in her but were borrowed from another. But this is utterly false, since she herself lends her praises to others and does not receive them from others, being most worthy of every praise. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that this text can be appropriately understood of no other than the Mother of the Messiah. This is also clearly shown in many other places. 
<margin>E</margin> For in the same book, the Wise Man himself says in the first chapter: <note>original Hebrew: "נָאווּ לְחָיַיִךְ בַּתּוֹרִים"</note> "Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove." Where he compares the Mother of the Messiah to a turtledove for this reason: to show that just as the turtledove lacks gall <note>symbolic of bitterness or sin</note> and was created so from its beginning, so neither original, nor actual, nor even mental sin was to be attributed to the Mother of the Messiah. Therefore, in the 2nd chapter of the same book, he likened her to a dove, which also 
<margin>F</margin> lacks gall, saying: <note>original Hebrew: "קוּמִי לְכִי רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי לָךְ יוֹנָתִי בְּחַגְוֵי הַסֶּלַע בְּסֵתֶר הַמַּדְרֵגָה הַרְאִינִי אֶת מַרְאֵיִךְ"</note> "Arise, hasten, my love, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, show me your face." From which it is gathered that the Mother of the Messiah's very foundation and beginning was to be without original sin. And because a rock is the beginning and foundation upon which a building is sustained: therefore he says "in the clefts of the rock," that is, in the embryo where she was conceived, in which there is a cleft where she was 
<margin>G</margin> built; there she was a dove, most pure without the gall of original sin. Moreover, that the beginning is likened to a rock is clear from Isaiah chapter 51 <note>text says 55, likely 51:1</note> saying: "Look to the rock from which you were hewn." Hence Christ says: "And upon this rock I will build my church."

...to sacrifice your son <note>referring to Abraham and Isaac</note> for the love of God, pray to God for us. He likewise will answer that he is not sufficient, because he fathered Ishmael. Then the first man will come and ask God for them. God, moreover, will judge the good and the righteous for their good and moderate works, and because of the prayers of the first man, He will adjudge them to eternal life. This is what was said in *Proverbs 18: And his friend comes and will search him out.* According to what was said in the *Song of Songs, chapter 4: You are all beautiful, my love, and there is no spot in you.* All these things are from the aforementioned tradition, word for word. From which it is gathered that the aforementioned tradition speaks of the mother of the Messiah, when it says that all the holy fathers will approach to ask the first man, and will testify that he is free of all sin. This can least of all apply to Adam, who infected the whole world with his sin. Therefore, the authority of *Proverbs* which he introduces, namely, *The first to state his case seems right, and his friend comes and will search him out,* <margin>Catholic explanation.</margin> is to be explained thus: This first man, who is the mother of the Messiah (on account of whom the Messiah himself, or Christ, is called the "Son of Man"), is righteous in her case, in which she was accused by adversaries of having been conceived in original sin. And her friend comes, that is, God, and investigated this case, and brought forth the sentence, saying: *You are all beautiful, my love, and there is no spot in you.* Which authority indeed the ancient teachers of the Hebrews <margin>Why the mother of the Messiah is called the "first man."</margin> seem to have brought forward for the confirmation of the immaculate conception of the mother of the Messiah. She is therefore called the "first man," or the "first creature" in the human race, because she was produced first of all in terms of matter. From which a corollary follows: that all humans are her children. For if the mother of the Messiah existed first in the cause of Adam, and Adam himself proceeded from her, even though they were in the same time (just as the sun, which although it is prior in cause to its brightness, yet they are together in the same instant, nevertheless the brightness follows the sun), so the mother of the Messiah, even if she was produced in matter at the same time as Adam: because

<margin>A</margin> nevertheless Adam proceeded from her (for which reason she is called the "first man"), and from Adam the whole human race, then not ineptly can all humans be called the children of the mother of the Messiah in a certain way. Nevertheless, her true and natural and firstborn son is the Messiah himself, formed from her purest blood, and born of her: according to what was said in *Luke, chapter 1: She brought forth her firstborn son.* One reads also in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses Hadarsan, an 11th-century Jewish scholar often cited by Christian authors for Christological interpretations of the Midrash.</note> on the book of Genesis, upon that which is said in the 5th chapter of the same book: <margin>B</margin> *And all the days of Adam's life were...* <note>original Hebrew: ויהיו כל ימי אדם אשר חי</note> that Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said word for word: "When God saw Adam formed, He called all the Angels and said to them: 'Humble yourselves, and be obedient to this man.' A great part of them accepted the command and bowed themselves to him, according to the will of God. But Satan, that is, Lucifer, the most excellent of all, said with his sect to the holy and blessed God: 'O Lord of the world, you created us from the brightness of your glory, and now you command us that we should bow to a man whom you formed from the earth?' <margin>C</margin> The holy and blessed God answered him: 'In this man who is created from the dust of the earth, there is more wisdom and intelligence than in you.' But the holy and blessed God, seeing that Satan with his sect did not want to bow, nor obey this man, expelled him from heaven, and he became the devil. And for that reason *Isaiah* said in *chapter 14: How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning!*" <margin>D</margin> This is the tradition. It speaks of nothing else but the glorious mother of the Messiah. Her matter was produced at the same time as the matter of Adam, even if she stood prior in cause and excellence, on account of which Christ himself is called the "Son of Man." For it cannot speak of Adam, for a twofold reason. First, because God would not have commanded the Angels to bow to Adam, whom He knew would quickly fall into sin. Second, because even if Adam were intelligent and wise, there was nevertheless more knowledge in the Angels than in him. But the tradition says that <margin>E</margin> there was more knowledge in that "first man" than in the Angels. Therefore, it must be that it speaks of the mother of the Messiah, who ought to be full of all wisdom and knowledge, and superior to all after God. From this tradition, therefore, not only is the proposition held, but even that the mother of the Messiah herself was to be superior to the Angels. Now let us respond to the arguments of the blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>. To the first, then, when he says: *That if it were so, it would follow <margin>F</margin> <margin>Response to the arguments of the blessed Thomas.</margin> that Christ was not the son of the blessed Virgin, nor did he proceed from the true stock of the fathers:* we say we shall satisfy this with the authority of Aristotle and Pliny. For Aristotle indeed, in the eighteenth book *On Animals*, says thus: *In Socrates is the power proper to Socrates, and also of his parents, and grandfathers, and the rest of his predecessors, both paternal and maternal, and this all the way to the last. And there is also in him the power of "man," and then the power of "animal."* When therefore the power of Socrates is strong, <margin>G</margin> a male is generated; when it is weak, a female is generated. If, however, the proper power of Socrates wins, the son is made like Socrates, whether it be male or female. But if the power of the father of Socrates wins, the son is generated similar not to Socrates' father, but to the grandfather. So...

# BOOK SEVEN.

...ascending in sequence. And if the power of kinship fails, a human is born who resembles none of their kindred. If, however, the power of the human form fails—where the movement of all things fails—there remains only a monstrous power of generation. And the process is the same on the mother’s side. Likewise, the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in the seventh book of the *History of Animals* says: Some are born resembling their parents, or their grandfathers, or their ancestors. Some carry no resemblance at all; as happened in Sicily, where a woman committed adultery with an Ethiopian. Her daughter did not reflect the color of the Ethiopian father, but the son born from that daughter did. He brought back the likeness of his Ethiopian grandfather. For the most part, females resemble the mother and males the father. But it also happens the other way around: females are procreated resembling the father, and males the mother. Thus says the Philosopher. From these examples, it is clearly evident: whether a son is like his parents or not, and whether the birth is perfect or monstrous, the offspring is always the child of those who generated it—since, as has been said, Ethiopians have generated white children. Therefore, the untainted Virgin, although she was not like her progenitors in their guilt <note>Original: "in culpa," referring to the stain of Original Sin.</note>, is not for that reason to be called anything other than their daughter. And thus the first argument of Saint Thomas is answered. To the second, we say: just as (witnessed by the ancient Talmudists) the human race emanated more strongly because the matter of the untainted mother of the Messiah was present together with the matter of Adam, and she existed as the first cause in that same Adam—in that same way, we say the order of satisfaction was most fitting. For since the body of Christ was contained within the most precious blood of the most blessed Virgin, it was fitting that he should come to purge sin. Just as when a boy happens to soil a house, we call his mother to wipe away the child's filth and clean the house; so too it was fitting that Christ’s humanity should come to wash away the impurities that Adam had made. Therefore, notwithstanding the arguments of the Holy Doctor <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>, the truth of the conclusion of the ancient Talmudists remains in its full strength regarding the immaculate conception of the most blessed mother of the Messiah.

### CHAPTER V.

#### To the second objection of Hogostratus. And that the opinion of the immaculate conception of the glorious virgin is most ancient.

->HOGOSTRATUS<-

<note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527) was a prominent Dominican inquisitor and a fierce opponent of the scholar Johannes Reuchlin. Here, he serves as a literary foil for the author's arguments.</note>

**O**pinion on the conception of the Virgin Mother of God, which now seems to prevail, is quite recent. For although it may be supported by the testimonies of the ancient Jews whom you have introduced, it possesses no firmness because it is strengthened neither by the authority of Sacred Scripture nor by the ancient saints whom the Church has approved. GALATINUS: On the contrary, this opinion is most ancient. For first of all, the writers of the sacred pages, inspired by the Holy Spirit, held it themselves. Thus among others, Solomon in the fourth chapter of the *Song of Songs* says: 
<margin>Authors of the sacred pages of the Old Testament.</margin>
"You are all beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you." <note>original Hebrew: כֻּלָּךְ יָפָה רַעְיָתִי וּמוּם אֵין בָּךְ (Kullach yafah ra'yati umum ein bach).</note> CAPITO <note>Likely Wolfgang Fabricius Capito, another contemporary scholar.</note>: More recent Jews say this text is understood to be about the children of Israel who were circumcised a second time in the desert, and they were all pure. 
<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin>

<column-break/>

**A** For once all the sinners had died who had gone out of Egypt and whom they had sent to scout the land, only those remained who had been born in the desert, all of whom were righteous. And because of them (as they say) this text says: "You are all beautiful, my friend," and so on. GALATINUS: It is clear that this reasoning of theirs is false because the text says, "And there is no blemish in you," which hardly fits them, since they were not immune to original sin. CAPITO: Regarding this, 
<margin>Objection of the same.</margin>
**B** they themselves respond that circumcision cleansed them from original sin and sufficiently opened the gate of paradise for them. GALATINUS: That too is false. This is most clearly evident from the fact that Moses, and Samuel, and all the greatest Prophets, with all the others, descended to the lower regions (as was shown in the preceding book). If, therefore, circumcision had unlocked the gate of the Kingdom of Heaven for them, they certainly would not have departed to the lower regions, but to heaven. But I say this: according to the exposition of some, this text speaks not of the untainted Virgin, but of the Church of God. 
<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Objection of Hogostratus.</margin>

Firstly, because everything that Mother Church sings was instituted by the Holy Spirit, whom it is impossible to lie. And the Holy Church attributes this saying of the wise man to the Mother of God. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that it speaks of her. Furthermore, because the praises of the most glorious Virgin herself are immense and incomprehensible. 
<margin>Confutation.</margin>
**D** If we, therefore, wishing to praise her, attributed the praises of another to her, we would undoubtedly show that those praises were not in her, but were borrowed from someone else. This, however, is deeply false, since she herself lends of her praises to others, and does not receive from others, and she is most worthy of all praise. From these points, therefore, it is manifest that this text can be fitly understood of no one else but the mother of the Messiah. This is also clearly shown in many other places. For in the same book, the Wise Man himself in the first chapter 
**E** says likewise: "Your cheeks are beautiful like the turtledove." <note>original Hebrew: נָאווּ לְחָיַיִךְ בַּתֹּרִים (Na'vu lechayayich batorim).</note> Here he compares the mother of the Messiah to a turtledove for this reason: to show that just as the turtledove lacks gall <note>A common medieval belief that doves lacked gall, representing a lack of bitterness or sin.</note> and was created so from her beginning, so neither original, nor actual, nor even mental sin was to be attributed to the mother of the Messiah. For that reason, in the second chapter of the same book, he likened her to a dove, which also lacks gall, saying: 
**F** "Arise, make haste, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, show me your face." <note>original Hebrew: קוּמִי לָךְ רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי לָךְ יוֹנָתִי בְּחַגְוֵי הַסֶּלַע בְּסֵתֶר הַמַּדְרֵגָה הַרְאִינִי אֶת מַרְאַיִךְ (Kumi lach ra'yati yafati ulechi lach yonati bechagvei hasela beseter hamadregah har'ini et mar'ayich).</note> From this it is gathered that not only the foundation and beginning of the mother of the Messiah would be without original sin. **G** sin. That the "beginning" <note>term: "principium" - source or origin</note> is likened to a rock is clear through Isaiah chapter 51, saying: "Look to the rock from which you were cut." Hence Christ says: "And upon this rock I will build my church."

<meta>This page continues the author's argument for the Immaculate Conception of Mary. # BOOK SEVEN.

In the fourth chapter of the **Song of Songs**, it is written: <note>original Hebrew: הנך יפה רעיתי הנך יפה עיניך יונים מבעד לצמתך</note> "Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves, besides that which lies hidden within." This is where this truth is best expressed. For a distinction is made between the perfections of her soul that are visible and those that are hidden within her. From this, it is shown that she was to be conceived without original sin. And again in the same book: <note>original Hebrew: פתחי לי אחותי רעיתי יונתי תמתי</note> "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one," or "my immaculate one." <note>The Hebrew term *temati* can be translated as "my perfect one" or "my undefiled."</note> He calls her "my immaculate one" so that this truth may be more and more confirmed. Likewise in the same place: <note>original Hebrew: אחת היא יונתי תמתי אחת היא לאמה ברה היא ליולדתה</note> "One is my dove, one is my perfect one, she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." It is as if he were saying: she alone among all women was conceived without original sin, just as Christ alone was among all men. Therefore, as is said in the first chapter of the same book, he says: <note>original Hebrew: הנך יפה רעיתי הנך יפה</note> "Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful." He repeated the phrase to show that she was beautiful—that is, pure—both in her conception and in her future life. To which she responded: <note>original Hebrew: הנך יפה דודי אף נעים אף ערשנו רעננה : קרות בתינו ארזים רחיטנו ברותים</note> "Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and handsome; our bed is flowery, the beams of our houses are cedar, our rafters are cypress." The meaning is: "Certainly, just as I was conceived without the stain of original sin, so also were you, my beloved." And for that reason, you are beautiful and fair, and our "bed"—that is, our conception—is flowery and fragrant, without the corruption of sin. For the beams of our house are of cedar and the rafters of cypress, which do not suffer any decay.

Likewise, in the second chapter, he speaks thus: <note>original Hebrew: כשושנה בין החוחים כן רעיתי בין הבנות</note> "As a rose among thorns, so is my love among the daughters." The meaning is: just as a rose, beautiful and fragrant, from which many aromatic things are made, is born among thorns yet lacks thorns itself, so my love was born among women who were conceived in original sin; like a rose among thorns, she was entirely free from that same sin. He used the word "daughters" because of the dignity of the <term>Messiah’s</term> mother, though the text is understood to refer to all people, both male and female. She truly responded: <note>original Hebrew: כתפוח בעצי היער כן דודי בין הבנים</note> "As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons." The conclusion regarding the nature of all things concerning the Messiah and his mother is touched upon in the sixth chapter of the same book, when it is said: <note>original Hebrew: אני לדודי ודודי לי</note> "I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine." The sense is: "As I was conceived without original sin, so also was my beloved." Likewise in the first chapter: <note>original Hebrew: עד שהמלך במסבו נרדי נתן ריחו</note> "While the King was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance." While the King was at his table—that is, in his <term>Incarnation</term>—my nard—that is, my conception—being brought about without original sin, gave forth its fragrance, namely of purity and innocence. Likewise in the second chapter: <note>original Hebrew: שמאלו תחת לראשי וימינו תחבקני</note> "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me." If Christ, therefore, held his left hand under the head of the Virgin and his right hand embraced her, it is impossible that he would have permitted her to

<column-break/>

<page-num>388</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN.</header>

<margin>A</margin> fall into original sin. Likewise in the third chapter: <note>original Hebrew: עד שמצאתי את שאהבה נפשי אחזתיו ולא ארפנו עד שהבאתיו אל בית אמי ואל חדר הולתי</note> "I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go, until I have brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me." The meaning is: "When I found my beloved in his incarnation, I took hold of him and did not let go until I led him into the house and the room of my mother." It is as if she were saying openly:
<margin>B</margin> "Just as I was conceived in the womb of my mother without original sin, so also I gave birth to him." Likewise
<margin>C</margin> in chapter 6: <note>original Hebrew: מי זאת הנשקפה כמו שחר יפה כל בנה ברה כחמה</note> "Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, bright as the sun?" The meaning is: "Who is she who shows herself coming like the dawn?" For just as the dawn begins the brightness of the day, so certainly the glorious mother of the Messiah, coming soon, began to illuminate the whole world. And as the moon receives its brightness from the sun, so the mother of the Messiah received all her privileges and graces from her son. And she is as bright as the sun, which at the instant of its creation obtained all its brilliance. For the very matter of the immaculate Virgin, at the instant of her conception, attained all material perfections, and she was conceived without original sin. This is indeed evident through Isaiah, speaking in the person of the mother of the Messiah in the 61st chapter: <note>original Hebrew: שוש אשיש ביהוה תגל נפשי באלהי כי הלבישני בגדי ישע מעיל צדקה יעטני כחתן יפאר וככלה תעדה כליה</note>
<margin>D</margin> "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God. For he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, and with a robe of righteousness he has covered me, as a bridegroom decks himself with glory [or a crown], and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels." For the Prophet, seeing in spirit that the mother of the Messiah would say, *My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,* uttered the aforementioned words in her person, saying: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord (*ba-Adonai*)," that is, in God (the <term>Tetragrammaton</term>), who, as
<margin>E</margin> **Rabbi Hibba** says, signifies God the Father. "And my soul has exulted in my God (*be-Elohai*)," which, as the same man says, designates God the Son. He says therefore: "I will greatly rejoice in God, who is the Father. And my soul shall exult in my God, who is the Son. Because he has granted me a double grace. One indeed, because he clothed me in the garments of salvation, which is that I was conceived without original sin. The other truly, because he surrounded me with a robe of righteousness—namely, original justice."
<margin>F</margin> He says "surrounded," because all the members of the Virgin, from the top of her head to the tips of her toes, and all her senses and thoughts, obeyed the command of her soul without any resistance. Indeed, to such an extent that her eyes never looked upon anything dishonest or illicit. In fact, she never even raised her eyes as other people are accustomed to do, but always kept them fixed on the ground, except while praying to God. By whom, among other perfections, she was gifted with the spirit of prophecy: so that if by chance she were about to hear or see anything forbidden or unlawful, her ears and eyes would immediately be closed; so that

...crown, or glory, and as a bridegroom he has adorned her with his jewelry. With these words, she embraces two things because of two graces granted to her. For two things are necessary for a bride. One, that the bridegroom give her jewelry freely. The other, that the bride use them well and adorn herself. The first pertains to the bridegroom, while the second pertains to the bride. Regarding the first, he says: *As a bridegroom he has adorned [me]*, namely with glory or a crown; that is, just as a bridegroom gives jewelry to his bride, so God conferred this grace upon me, that I might be conceived without original sin. Regarding the second, she says: *And as a bride he has adorned [me] with his jewelry.* It is as if she were saying: just as it is the bride’s responsibility to adorn herself well, so also the fact that I am surrounded by original justice—stemming from good governance and my senses obeying the free will of my soul—has come to me, even though God confirmed me in grace. It follows: <note>original Hebrew: כִּי כָאָרֶץ תּוֹצִיא צִמְחָהּ וּכְגַנָּה זֵרוּעֶיהָ תַצְמִיחַ כֵּן אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה יַצְמִיחַ צְדָקָה וּתְהִלָּה נֶגֶד כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם</note> "For as the earth brings forth its sprout, and as a garden causes its seeds to spring forth; so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all nations." <note>Isaiah 61:11</note> By these words, she says: The reason why God has accepted me as a bride and granted these graces is because the Messiah is to be incarnated in me. He is to be like a sprout that lacks a father and has only the earth as its mother. For in this way, God will make the Messiah germinate within me, who will be the righteousness and praise among all nations; and as far as his humanity is concerned, he shall have no other father besides me, his mother. Moreover, he speaks of "righteousness" because it was for the sake of this that God was to suffer. He says "praise" because this is done by grace and not by any merit of her own. Therefore, since the most blessed Virgin was allotted these graces, she is rightly said to be clothed in the garments of Jesus and the cloak of righteousness, with which no one else born of man and woman was ever endowed—especially the garments of Jesus, who is the salvation of the whole world. For this reason, it is necessary to say that she was conceived without original sin. 

HOGELMUS. Our edition <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> does not say, "Because he has clothed me in the garments of Jesus," but rather, "Because he has clothed me in the garments of salvation." 

GALATINUS. Where our edition has "garments of salvation" in this place, the Hebrew truth <note>a common term for the original Hebrew text</note> says "garments of *yesha*" <note>original Hebrew: יֶשַׁע</note>. This word *yesha* has a double meaning: for it signifies both "Jesus" and "salvation." Here, however, it is taken according to the first meaning when he says, "Because he has clothed me in the garments of Jesus." This is just as if he were saying: Just as Jesus, according to his humanity, shall be conceived without original sin, so also I shall be conceived without it. Therefore, I shall be clothed in his garments, which are purity and innocence. Nevertheless, the translator of our edition <note>St. Jerome</note>, yielding to the Jews so that they could not find fault with him, translated it as "salvation" and not "Jesus." He does this in almost infinite other places. For wherever the sense has a duality, he almost always accepts the one that favors them. For he could have said here—and rightly so—"Because he has clothed me in the garments of Jesus." Just as in Habakkuk, chapter 3, it says: "I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus," where the Hebrew text has the same name, that is, *yesha*. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that the ancient authors of Holy Scripture firmly 

<column-break/>

held that the immaculate mother of the Messiah was to be conceived without original sin. The writers of the New Testament also held this same view. <margin>Authors of the Holy Scripture of the New Testament.</margin> Indeed, one reads in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter eleven, that our Savior said of John the Baptist: "Among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist." Since, therefore, Saint John the Baptist was not greater than Christ himself (who was born of a woman), and since the text says, "There has risen"—which can only be said of one who first fell and afterwards rises—we are necessarily compelled to interpret this saying of the Savior thus: "Among those born of women (that is, among those conceived in original sin), there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist." Christ, however, did not fall into sin; therefore, John is not greater than him. Since, then, the most blessed Virgin is also greater than the same John the Baptist, it necessarily follows that she did not fall into original sin. If this were not granted, it would plainly follow that John the Baptist stood out as greater than her, which is entirely false. Therefore, from the Gospel and the opinion of our Savior, it is necessarily concluded that she was conceived without original sin. 

<margin>Objection.</margin> HOGELMUS. That would indeed be true if the Gospel said "among those born [masculine] and born [feminine]"; but since it only says "among those born" <note>the Latin *natos* is masculine</note>, it clearly shows that our Savior’s saying is to be understood not of women, but only of men. Therefore, it cannot be inferred from this that the most blessed Virgin did not fall into original sin. 

<margin>Response.</margin> GALATINUS. Your objection is worth nothing, since according to the grammarians, the masculine gender includes the feminine. Therefore, when he said "among those born," he meant both men and women. The Apostles also held this opinion regarding the immaculate conception of the Virgin. This is clearly evident from the sayings of the blessed Apostle Andrew; when he was explaining the mystery of the cross to the Proconsul Aegeas, he said among other things: "And since the first man had been made from immaculate earth, who through the tree of transgression brought death into the world, it was necessary that the Perfect Man be born of an immaculate Virgin, in whom the Son of God, who had made the first man, might restore the eternal life which men had lost through Adam." The blessed Dominic, the founder and leader of the Order of Preachers, later followed this same sentiment, saying in his treatise on the Body of Christ: "Just as the first Adam was formed from virgin earth that was never cursed, so it was fitting to happen in the second Adam." Furthermore, the ancient Doctors of the Church, both Greek and Latin, firmly held this opinion as most true and certain. <margin>Ancient Doctors of the Church.</margin> Among the Greeks, men such as Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, John Chrysostom, and all the others, as is clearly evident to those reading their books. As a sign of this, they celebrated the feast of the immaculate conception of the Virgin herself for nearly a thousand years. And in the martyrology that is read on the day after that feast, which was edited by Saint John of Damascus, among other things pronounced about the most blessed Virgin, she is called <note>original Greek: πρὸ συλλήψεως ἁγνή</note> "pure before conception." From this, the holy and ancient Greek fathers, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, seem to have held the opinion of the ancient Hebrews, which, as was seen in the preceding pages, [they maintained].

From these things which have been said, it is clearly established that the opinion concerning the immaculate conception of the Virgin is not recent, but most ancient. Rather, we say that the opposite opinion, which our adversaries stubbornly hold, is the more recent one. God permitted it to sprout for a time so that it might be seen how great a grace He had conferred upon His mother: by preserving her immune and immaculate from original sin, which she would have naturally contracted had she not been preserved.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### To the third objection of Hogostratus: where it is proved by natural reasons that the mother of the Messiah was to be conceived without original sin.

->HOGOSTRATUS.<-

<image-desc>Intricate woodcut decorative initial 'H' featuring floral motifs and a figure nestled within the scrollwork.</image-desc>If this were true, the word of Paul the Apostle would be utterly false, who, writing to the Romans in the 3rd chapter, says: "All have sinned in Adam, and lack the glory of God." <note>A paraphrase of Romans 3:23 combined with the traditional interpretation of Romans 5:12.</note> Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the glorious Virgin sinned in Adam; and consequently, both her material was infected by the sin of Adam, and she herself was conceived in original sin.
