First, I will prove by seven natural reasons both that the material of the unde-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>filed mother of the Messiah ought to have been preserved clean and immaculate in Adam, and consequently that the mother of the Messiah herself was conceived without initial sin. Then, I will respond to the authority of Paul the Apostle. <margin>First reason.</margin> For the foundation of the first reason, I will put forward two premises. The first is that in every subject, four <term>causes</term> <note>The "four causes" is an Aristotelian framework: material (what it's made of), efficient (who made it), formal (its shape/essence), and final (its purpose).</note> ought to be found: namely, the material, efficient, formal, and final; of which the final cause is more sublime than the others and more excellent. <margin>B</margin> The second is that the final cause and the <term>design of nature</term> <note>original: "opinio naturae," referring to the inherent teleological direction of the natural world.</note> always remain, nor do they ever cease to hand over a more perfect form to their subject and individual, if they find material suitable for receiving a form of this kind. Therefore, it is necessary for every efficient cause—whether natural, voluntary, or artificial—to arrange the most suitable material possible for any subject, so that its peculiar end may come to it, according to the thought and purpose devised by the agent. For example, pepper, whose end is heat and dryness, naturally performs <margin>C</margin> the operation of fire. On the contrary, the violet, which nature disposes toward the quality of water, is a thing suited to coldness, which is its peculiar end. By the same reasoning, the sapphire, the diamond, and other precious stones—which nature and the final cause dispose from the four elements into a certain sublime, bright, and transparent material—receive their own peculiar form, despite the fact that they are from the <term>earthly element</term>, <margin>D</margin> which is dark and gloomy. Since this is so in natural things, it is certainly follows that the glorious Virgin—since she was the subject in whom the Son of God was to be incarnated—would have been disposed more perfectly and sublimely than every human creature, indeed, every created being. Just as the peculiar end for which she was created was more perfect and sublime than all others, since she alone was created so that the Son of God might be born from her. <margin>E</margin> But if her material had been unclean, and she herself conceived in original sin, she would by no means have been disposed more perfectly and sublimely than every created being. Therefore, it was necessary both that her material be preserved pure and immaculate, and that she herself be conceived without original sin. <margin>Second reason.</margin> Likewise, in every being which lacks some perfection, there is implanted a natural appetite for assimilating itself to a more perfect being, and it hates <margin>F</margin> things lower than itself. Nature, moreover, if the disposition of the subject is fit for receiving, gives it all the greater perfection the more capable it is. Therefore, the sapphire, whose material is from the earth, naturally desires to ascend to the degree of clarity which is in the element of air, and receiving clarity from it, becomes bright and transparent. The mineral desires to become vegetative, even if it does not have a vegetative soul. For nature gives it the perfection of growing, when it has material suitable for growth. The vegetative desires to become animal. Thus, to the <term>mandrake</term>, <note>A plant whose roots were historically thought to resemble the human form.</note> because of the disposition of the material which it has, nature gave the figure of a man, even if <margin>G</margin> it lacks a sensitive soul. Furthermore, the animal desires to become man, because of which the ape has the likeness of a man and imitates those things which man himself does, although it lacks a rational soul. Since, therefore, the appetite of the material of the Messiah's mother was to be conceived without original sin, and the disposition of its material for receiving this—

He performed the works of a glorified Christ. For in his birth, he came forth from the virginal womb without any corruption of his mother. For glorified bodies <note>In scholastic theology, a "glorified body" is the perfected state of the human body after resurrection, possessing qualities like "subtlety" (the ability to pass through matter).</note> have this special quality: that by their subtlety, they pass through a wall without breaking it. Therefore, it follows that the glorious Virgin, at the very instant of her conception, was without the stain of original sin; rather, in her conception, her matter possessed all the perfections she was to have. Indeed, as soon as her soul was infused into that same matter, it actually attained all the perfections that can be found in a soul, such as knowledge, wisdom, intelligence, prophecy, grace, and whatever else can be attributed to a soul. When the Son of God came to her to be incarnated, she ascended to the highest rank; for he left to her, as to his own mother, the rule and governance of the entire world, and he made her the queen of the heavens and of the angels.

<margin>Regarding the authority of the Apostle Paul.</margin>
Now let us respond to the words of the blessed Paul. When he says, "All have sinned in Adam" <note>original: "Omnes in Adam peccauerunt"; a reference to Romans 5:12, a primary text used to argue that Mary must have shared in original sin.</note>, let us explain the saying thus: "All," namely, those who are subject only to the rule of Adam and do not obtain a higher rank. For these are truly sinners in Adam and conceived in original sin. But the glorious Virgin, since she ascended to a higher rank than Adam, cannot be said to have fallen into Adam’s sin. For she alone among all other creatures was granted this privilege: that the Son of God should be conceived in her. That this was her ultimate purpose, and the purpose of her conception, is most clear from the fact that no other creature besides her was ever conceived for this—that the Son of God should be incarnated in her—because in no other but her was the Son of God incarnated. Therefore, she was conceived so that the Son of God might be conceived in her. It is concluded, then, that the incarnation of the Son of God existed as the final cause <note>The "final cause" is the purpose for which something is created.</note> of the Virgin's own conception. Therefore, as gathered from the preceding reasons, it was necessary that the matter and form of the immaculate Virgin herself be a perfection more sublime than any other matter and form in the human race, and produced without the infection of original sin.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*To the fourth objection of Hogostratus, where the conclusion concerning the immaculate conception of the Virgin is confirmed by seven theological as well as natural reasons.*<-

->HOGOSTRATUS.<- <note>Jacob Hoogstraeten (c. 1460–1527) was a prominent Dominican theologian and inquisitor who famously opposed the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.</note>

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'C' featuring scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
IT IS CERTAIN that God does not wish to remove the order of nature which he himself established. But if God had preserved the most blessed Virgin immune from original sin, he would have surely removed, or rather perverted, the order of nature he established, since because of Adam’s sin, he decreed that all men

<column-break/>

<page-num>396</page-num>

descending from him by natural propagation are to be conceived with original sin. Therefore, it should by no means be said that the untainted Virgin was preserved from the stain of original sin. GALATINUS: <note>The speaker "Gal." refers to Petrus Galatinus, the author, defending the Immaculate Conception against Hogostratus.</note> You are certainly quite deceived, Hogostratus (forgive me). I shall prove this by seven theological and natural reasons, so that at last an answer may be given to your objection, which is of no weight.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
The first reason is this. It is certain that greed and stinginess cannot be attributed to God, since he gives to each creature as much perfection as it is capable of receiving. For example, when God created the world, he gave as much perfection to each thing as its subject <note>In this context, "subject" refers to the underlying material or nature of a thing.</note> could hold. For if the subject of an ass could have received the perfection of a horse, or a lion, or even a man, he certainly would have given it. But since it was not fit to receive it, he did not give it. Since this is so, it clearly follows that God made the glorious Virgin without original sin, because her subject was so fit for it. Otherwise, he would have been greedy and stingy himself. This is entirely false. Therefore, she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
The second reason is this. It is certain that the beginning of knowledge is the end of the work. It follows that since the beginning of divine knowledge was to cleanse and purify the most blessed Virgin from original sin, it was far more fitting to have made her clean and without sin than to have cleansed her afterward. For if it were not so, divine operations would be likened to the various and inconstant works of humans. But this is false. Therefore, he made her entirely clean and pure from original sin.

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
The third reason is this: a certain appetite is implanted by nature in every man, that his mother should be more perfect in all the perfections of the world. And this is because he is brought forth from her blood. For if the mother consists of clean and excellent matter, the son will also be made of that same matter. Therefore, a son always desires the perfection of his mother and hates imperfection. If, therefore, the Son of God—who loves virtues and perfections above all things, but greatly detests vices, sins, and imperfections—had not desired that his mother be more noble and perfect in goodness, justice, holiness, and other perfections, he would surely have been disordered in his will and appetite. Indeed, he would have inclined his desire toward vile and imperfect things rather than toward more noble and perfect ones. Furthermore, it would follow that he had a viler appetite than any pure human creature, since he would have willed his own matter and humanity to be imperfect. But this is manifestly false and entirely against reason. Since, therefore, God is perfect with the highest perfection, and it is the mark of the perfect to love perfect things rather than imperfect ones, he surely ought to have both desired and made his mother perfect with every possible perfection. Therefore, he caused her to be conceived without original sin.

<margin>The fourth reason.</margin>
The fourth reason is this: it is certain that before the creation of the world, God foreknew both that Adam would sin and that he himself would be incarnated for the redemption of that sin. From which it follows that if God had decreed to be incarnated in a woman conceived in original sin, then God himself would have emerged as the cause of sin, and Adam would have been forced to sin, with his free will taken away. If this were so, Adam...

If she had sinned, Adam would have deserved the punishment far less. From this, however, many inconveniences would follow. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the woman from whom God was to be incarnated was preserved from the stain of original sin from all eternity. 

<margin>Fifth reason</margin>
The fifth reason is this: Adam was the beginning of the human race, and its end was Christ, for whose love the human race was created. Therefore, so that the beginning, the middle, and the end may agree with one another, it was necessary that—just as Adam, who is the beginning, and Christ, who is the end, were made without original sin—likewise the middle, which is the most blessed Virgin, should be conceived without that same sin. Furthermore, it follows that just as Eve was one flesh with Adam and was the first medium <note>In this context, "medium" refers to a middle point or a means through which something is accomplished.</note> for the preservation of the human race, made without original sin: so also it was necessary that the undefiled Virgin, who is the final medium for the salvation of souls and one flesh with Christ (who is the end), be conceived without original sin. Otherwise, the beginning and the first medium would not agree with the final medium and the end, which is highly inconsistent.

<margin>Sixth reason.</margin>
The sixth reason is this: It is well known that every most powerful king, wishing to build a palace for himself or to erect a basilica to the honor of God the Best and Greatest, first seeks and prepares whatever materials are necessary for the building, finding the most perfect and excellent ones possible. 

<margin>A beautiful figure of the Virgin’s conception.</margin>
As we read that King Solomon did: who, because of the excellence of the Temple which he built in service to God, willed that in the craftsmanship and the cutting of stones, no hammer or any kind of iron instrument should be used, nor should even the sound of them be heard. Instead, he found a worm named *Zamir* <note>original: "Zamir"; This refers to the "Shamir" of Jewish legend, a miraculous substance or creature capable of cutting stone without metal tools.</note>, which, when placed upon a stone and walking across it, immediately broke it. It is clear that this happened as a prefiguration. For in the building of the Temple in which the Son of God was to be incarnated, and in the tabernacle in which God was to show his brightness and holiness, there could be no lack of material of such perfection for its construction; nor was it necessary that in the cutting of the stones—that is, in the conception of the undefiled Virgin—any "iron" (which signifies original sin) should be applied. 

The reason for this is that one sin cannot be healed with another, except with a simple and, in a way, tiny thing: that is, with a worm. Therefore he found *Zamir*, which is Christ, who is compared to a worm and is called such by the Psalmist in Psalm 22, when he says:

<note>original Hebrew: "ואנכי תולעת ולא איש"</note> *But I am a worm and no man.* And he fashioned the most blessed Virgin without iron, that is, without any sin. And just as in the building of the Temple, not even the sound of iron was heard: so in the building and conception of the immaculate Virgin, not even the "voice" of original sin was found. For if the most holy material had been lacking for her conception, God would have been in a state of greater defect and of a lower degree than King Solomon. But this is false; therefore, she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>Seventh reason for the response to the objection of Hogostratus.</margin>
The seventh reason is this, as a response to the objection of Hogostratus <note>Jacob van Hoogstraaten (c. 1460–1527) was a prominent Dominican theologian and inquisitor who often debated humanist scholars and defended traditionalist views, including opposing the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.</note>, who says that God does not wish to remove the rule and order of nature which He himself instituted. We indeed admit that this is true, yet it ought not to be understood in every respect exactly as Hogostratus himself understands it. For God, when necessity demands,

<column-break/>

has many times acted against the rule and order of nature. For it is not the rule and order of nature that a cut and dry tree should produce flowers, leaves, and fruit. Yet the rod of Aaron produced buds, flowers, foliage, and almonds. Nor is it a work of nature for a tree to bring forth all these things in a single night. Yet Aaron’s rod brought them all forth in one night. Nor is it according to the course of nature for a tree, whether green or dry, to have a sensitive soul. Yet the rod of Moses was turned into a serpent. Nor is it possible by the order of nature for any brute animal to speak and reason. Yet Balaam’s donkey disputed with him. 

Also, by the course of nature, prophecy can only be found in the human race. For no brute animal can prophesy. Yet we read that God spoke with Jonah’s whale. Also, according to the order of nature, it is impossible for the wheels of the heavens to cease from their circular motion. Yet in the time of Joshua, during the battle at Gibeon, the sun positioned itself in the middle of the sky and stood still for an entire day—that is, for 24 hours—immobile. 

It is also impossible according to the order of nature for the wheels of heaven, which move from East to West, to move backward. Yet in the time of Hezekiah, the sun retreated ten degrees from the path it had made. It is also impossible according to the course of nature for a lion to cease its ferocity and refrain from killing, especially when it is famished. Yet when Daniel was thrown into the lions' den, the lions brought him no harm. Fire also, according to the order of nature, always burns and devours; but to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah <note>Better known by their Babylonian names: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note>, placed in the most burning furnace, it brought no distress, nor did it harm even a hair of their clothing. 

Furthermore, after God created Adam and Eve, He gave this rule and order to nature: that no human could be generated without the seed of a man and a woman. Yet we find Christ was generated without human seed. From all these examples, it is clearly evident that sometimes God, when necessity demands, acts outside the order of nature. Therefore, it is plainly evident that although God does not wish to take away the order of nature in general and in every part, He nevertheless does so occasionally in particular cases. And because of this particularity, He is not said to "break" the rule of nature. Or, if we wish to speak according to the opinion of the Hebrews, God does this sometimes due to a "special condition," and what He does is even less likely to be called "against nature." For the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>, seeing all these things that seem to happen against nature and wishing to give a reason why they happen, say that when God created the world, He granted nature the faculty to operate according to the order instituted by Him, and promised He would not contradict it—except upon this standing condition: that if necessity required it to be otherwise, He Himself could do whatever seemed best to Him, even if it were against nature itself. 

<margin>The response of the Talmudists.</margin>

Since, therefore, the glorious Virgin alone among all those born of man and woman was conceived without original sin, it can by no means be said to have been against nature, but rather one of the cases mentioned above. Now let us respond to the words of the blessed Paul. When he says, *All have sinned in Adam* <note>original: "Omnes in Adam peccauerunt"</note>, let us explain the saying thus: "All," meaning those who are subject only to the rule of Adam and do not obtain a higher rank. These people are truly sinners in Adam and are conceived in original sin. However, since the glorious Virgin ascended to a higher rank than Adam, she cannot be said to have fallen into Adam’s sin. She alone among all other creatures was granted this privilege: that the Son of God should be conceived within her. That this was her ultimate purpose and the reason for her conception is most evident from the fact that no other creature was ever conceived for this purpose—that the Son of God should be incarnated in her—because in no one else but her was the Son of God incarnated. Therefore, she was conceived so that the Son of God might be conceived within her. It is concluded, then, that the Incarnation of the Son of God was the final cause <note>In medieval philosophy, the "final cause" is the ultimate purpose for which something exists</note> of the Virgin’s own conception. Therefore, as gathered from the preceding reasons, it was necessary that the matter and form of the immaculate Virgin herself be more perfect and sublime than any other matter and form in the human race, produced without the infection of original sin.

You are certainly quite deceived, Hogostratus (forgive me for saying so). <margin>First reason.</margin>
Let the first reason be this. It is certain that greed and stinginess cannot be attributed to God, since He gives to every creature as much perfection as that creature is fit to receive. For example, when God created the world, He gave as much perfection to every kind of thing as its subject could hold. For if the nature of a donkey could have received the perfection of a horse, or a lion, or even a man, He certainly would have given it. But since it was not fit to receive it, He did not. This being the case, it clearly follows that God made the glorious Virgin without original sin, because her subject was so fit for it. Otherwise, He would have been greedy and stingy—which is entirely false. Therefore, she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Let the second reason be this. It is certain that the "principle of knowledge" is the end goal of a work. It follows that since the principle of divine knowledge was to wash and purify the most blessed Virgin from original sin, it was far more fitting to have made her clean and without sin from the start than to have cleansed her afterward. If this were not so, divine operations would be likened to the various and inconsistent works of humans. This, however, is false. Therefore, He made her entirely clean and pure from original sin.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>

He would have been someone who inclined His desire toward base and imperfect things rather than noble and perfect ones. Furthermore, it would follow that He had a baser desire than any pure human creature, since He would have willed His own matter and humanity to be imperfect.

This is clearly false and entirely against reason. Since God is perfect with the highest perfection, it is the mark of a perfect being to love His own possession with every possible perfection, and to desire it and bring it about. Therefore, He caused her to be conceived without original sin.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
Let the fourth reason be this: It is certain that before the creation of the world, God foreknew both that Adam would sin and that He Himself would be incarnated for the redemption of that sin. From this it follows that if God had decreed to be incarnated in a woman conceived in original sin, then God Himself would have been the cause of the sin, and Adam would have been forced to sin, his free will having been taken away. # CHAPTER VIII.

## To the fifth objection of Hogostratus. And that the untainted 
## mother of the Messiah was generated without lust and 
## concupiscence.

### HOGOSTRATUS.

<margin>A</margin> If the most blessed Virgin had been conceived without original sin, she would have been generated without <term>libido</term> <note>Latin: libido; refers here to the "disordered desire" or lust that theologians believed transmitted original sin.</note> and concupiscence. This is proven because original sin is mixed with lust, concupiscence, and pleasure. <margin>B</margin> Saint Augustine affirms this in the first part of his book *On Faith, to Peter*, in the twenty-fourth question. His saying is placed in the *Decretals* <note>The collection of Canon Law used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> regarding consecration, in the fourth distinction, the chapter beginning *Firmissime* ("Most Firmly"). There it is said: "Hold most firmly, and doubt not in any way, that every human being who is conceived through the sexual union of a man and a woman is born with original sin, subject to impiety and subject to death." Therefore, all those generated from the lust and pleasure of coitus are conceived with original sin. But the glorious Virgin was generated with the lust and pleasure of coitus: since she was generated from the very real union of Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, just like other human beings. It follows, therefore, that she was conceived in original sin. GALATINUS. It is certain that † the greater deprives the lesser. For we know by experience that the sun deprives the moon and a candle of their brightness. We also see that a greater sense deprives a lesser one. For a person who places all his thought and imagination intensely upon one thing, whether by studying or by contemplating, loses his lesser senses for that time. For if someone were to pass in front of him then, he would not see the one passing; and if someone spoke to him, he would not hear. I admit, therefore, that Saint Joachim and Saint Anne joined together maritally; however, because of the ardent devotion and vehement contemplation by which both were held, being of one mind and intent upon the generation of the most blessed Virgin, the <term>fomes</term> <note>original: "fomes," literally "tinder." In theology, this refers to the "spark" or "inclination" toward sin remaining in human nature.</note> was entirely extinguished in that act. Therefore, original sin had no place in the conception of the immaculate Virgin. Moreover, we trust that we can show what we say to be true. For when her parents had been expelled from the temple with reproach by the priests as if they were profane—because they were sterile and, though already worn out by old age, had not yet fathered children—they, mournful and suppliant, asked God to grant them offspring to be procreated for His service. When they were heard, an Angel appeared to each of them separately, announcing that they would generate offspring for the service of God, saying (as Jerome witnesses): "I am the Angel of the Lord sent to you, to announce to you that your prayers have been heard, and your alms have ascended into the sight of the Lord. For I have seen your shame, and I have heard of the sterility and the reproach unjustly cast against you. For God is the avenger of sin, not of nature. And therefore, when He closes someone's womb, He does this so that He may open it again more miraculously: so that what is born may be known to be not of lust, but of a divine gift."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, according to the Angelic command, both of them meeting each other, rejoiced at the mutual vision; and being secure and certain of the promised offspring, they returned home after worshipping the Lord, joyfully awaiting the divine promise. And they joined together with such devotion that they generated the glorious Virgin, the future Mother of God, without lust or bodily pleasure. For the most vehement devotion and delight of the soul extinguished all bodily pleasure, concupiscence, and lust. Hence, not without merit, the <margin>B</margin> <margin>How Joachim and Anne are interpreted.</margin> names Joachim and Anne were given to them. For "Joachim" is interpreted in Latin as "God will lift up," or "will erect," or "will raise," and also "will confirm." The name "Anne," truly, is derived from the name <note>original: חן (chen)</note> *grace*. As will be openly known from the names themselves, through the offspring they were to generate, God, out of the grace of His mercy, was to lift up the human race from the sin of our first parents, and raise it from eternal death, and erect and confirm it for heavenly glory. <margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, the most blessed Virgin was generated without concupiscence and lust, it is a necessary consequence that she was also conceived without initial sin, since lust and concupiscence were the cause of Adam's sin. For Adam himself, clinging to worldly vices and carnal concupiscence (as is clear through that passage of Genesis chapter 3: <note>original: "ותרא האשה כי טוב העץ למאכל וכי תאוה הוא לעינים"</note> "And the woman saw that the tree was good for eating, and that it was a delight to the eyes") <margin>D</margin> filled himself with pride and disobedience, and transgressed the command of God; and in that way he infected his flesh, so that all those descending from him are conceived with the same pride and disobedience which is the origin of all sins. And for that reason, it is called original or "initial" sin. For that reason, they are also procreated with lust and unbridled pleasure, and they are inclined to fulfill their own will, and are liable to sinning and transgressing the command of God. <margin>E</margin> This is most obvious to the senses. For when a man is in the appetite of unbridled lust, the genital member raises itself with pleasure and proceeds to fulfill the desired act, so that he is not even deterred from that act by the threat of death: which is found to be the case in none of the other members. For when someone approaches a theft, and before he completes it, he repents of the theft, immediately at his will his feet stop from walking and his hands refrain from the robbery, and they are obedient to the will. <margin>F</margin> Nevertheless, as the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose book of "Sentences" was the standard textbook for theology students.</note> says in the 19th distinction of the second book, if the first humans had not sinned, they would have come together in carnal union in paradise without any sin or stain; and there would have been an immaculate touch, and a mixing without concupiscence, and they would have commanded the genital members just like the others, so that they would have felt no illicit movement there. And just as we move other members of the body to others without the heat of lust—as the hand to the head—so they would have used the genital members without the itch of the flesh. For this lethal sickness clung to human members because of sin. <margin>G</margin> They would have generated children in paradise through immaculate coitus without corruption. Hence Augustine says regarding Genesis: "Why should we not believe that the first humans, before sin, could have commanded the genital members for procreation, just as one uses the others in any work without the itch of pleasure?"

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate between Galatinus and Hogostratus regarding the Immaculate Conception of Mary. ->**BOOK SEVEN.**<-

For it is not unbelievable that God made those bodies in such a way that, if they did not sin, they would command those members just as easily as they command their feet. They would neither sow with the heat of lust, nor give birth with pain. But after the Fall, they earned that involuntary movement which marriage now brings into order and continence restrains. The human weakness that is prone to the ruin of shame is instead taken up by the honor of marriage, so that what would have been a duty for the healthy becomes a remedy for the sick. From this reasoning, it is gathered that the untainted Virgin was conceived without original sin. For although it is not naturally possible for anyone to be propagated without sin—since the "matter" <note>Referring to the physical biological substance or "seed" provided by parents.</note> is prone to sin due to the infection inherited from Adam—the glorious Virgin achieved her propagation without sin not by nature, but by grace. It was more reasonable and fitting for God to have cleansed the matter from which his mother was to be made, while it was still the physical substance provided by the parents and before it became the substance of the one suffering the human condition. Therefore, from Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, God removed all bodily lust and unbridled pleasure, so that in this way they might generate the immaculate Virgin herself in the same manner that the first parents would have generated their children in paradise if they had not sinned. From these points <margin>Response to the argument of Hogostratus.</margin> the solution to Hogostratus's objection is clear. As for the saying of Saint Augustine which he brings forward, we say it is indeed true insofar as all humans generated through the sexual union of man and woman with bodily lust and pleasure are not free from original sin. But our saying is truer still, insofar as the glorious Virgin herself was propagated without unbridled lust and bodily pleasure. We say this proceeded from divine grace and will, since she was to be the "tabernacle" for God, from whose most precious blood the body of Christ (both God and man) was to be formed. And therefore, it was necessary that she be the most perfect and purest of all creatures. Augustine himself supports this opinion with his own words, saying in his book *On Heresies* against the Manichaeans in the person of Christ: "If my mother could have been defiled when I made her, I could have been defiled when I was born of her." And in the book *On Nature and Grace*, he says: "Excepting the Virgin Mary, about whom, for the honor of my Lord, I wish to make no question at all when discussing sins." In many other places, he also proclaims her immaculate, purest, and immune from all sin.

### CHAPTER IX.

->To the sixth objection of Hogostratus. And that by the merit of Christ’s passion, the glorious Virgin ought to have been redeemed from original sin in the most noble manner.<-

### HOGOSTRATUS.

THE glorious Virgin was redeemed through the passion of Christ. Otherwise, she would have been deprived of such a great good, and Christ would not have stood as the universal redeemer of all, which is highly unfitting. Therefore, he was the redeemer and savior of the Virgin herself as well. This she herself confesses in her
<meta>catchword: song</meta>

<column-break/>

song <note>Referring to the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55).</note>, saying: "And my spirit has rejoiced in God my savior." <note>original: "Et exultauit spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo."</note> But redemption or salvation presupposes a fault. For one cannot be understood as redeemed and saved except from some fault. Since she never had an actual fault, it clearly follows that she was redeemed from original sin. Wherefore, it follows that she was conceived in original sin. GALATINUS. Your reasoning is invalid: since he who guards a person so that they do not become a captive is just as much a redeemer and savior as he who frees them from captivity. In the same way, one is called a physician <margin>What medicine is.</margin> who gives a person a rule and order of life so that they may preserve health and not fall into sickness, just as much as the one who heals someone already sick. For this reason, <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> defined medicine as the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known—both how it is healed (removing infirmity) and how health already possessed is preserved or recovered if lost. By the same reasoning, we say that he who prevents someone from falling into sin should be called a "redeemer" and "savior" just like the one who lifts a person up from sin. From this, we can say there is a twofold redemption: <term>uplifting</term> <note>Latin: "sublevativa"; the act of helping someone who has already fallen into sin.</note> and <term>preservative</term> <note>Latin: "praeseruatua"; the act of preventing someone from falling into sin in the first place.</note>. <margin>Twofold redemption.</margin> And the preservative type is far more noble and perfect than the uplifting type. For just as it is much better to preserve someone from receiving a wound than to apply a remedy to them after they have been wounded, so it is far more noble and perfect to preserve someone from sin so they do not fall into it, than to free them from sin after they have fallen. Therefore, he is redeemed in a more noble and perfect way, and receives a greater benefit, who is preserved immune from a future sin than the one who is snatched from a sin already committed. Thus, preservative redemption is much more excellent than uplifting redemption. All other humans were redeemed from sin by "uplifting" redemption. But the glorious Virgin alone, of all those born of a man and a woman, was redeemed by "preservative" redemption. This is also how the good Angels were redeemed from sin so that they would not fall with Lucifer, as <term>John Chrysostom</term> <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and Church Father.</note> excellently perceives. Regarding the immaculate Virgin herself, <term>Anselm</term> <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> says in the second book of *Why God Became Man*, chapter 10: "The blessed Virgin needed redemption and the passion of Christ, not because of sin that was in her, but because of sin that *would have been* in her, unless he himself had preserved her by a special privilege." Furthermore, the perfection of human redemption itself necessarily required this. For there are six modes of redemption. <margin>Six modes of redemption.</margin> The first is when someone is redeemed from actual mortal sin after they have fallen into it. In this way, sinners are redeemed through the sacrament of penance. The second mode is when someone is preserved from mortal sin itself. In this way the Apostles were redeemed: who, after they received the Holy Spirit, never committed a mortal sin. The third mode is when someone is redeemed from a venial sin <note>A "lesser" sin that does not result in a complete break with God, unlike mortal sin.</note> already committed: in which way the "just" are usually redeemed, who by common law cannot entirely avoid venial sin; for as the Wise Man says, "The just man falls seven times a day, and rises again." <note>Proverbs 24:16.</note> This can only be understood as referring to venial sin. The fourth mode is...

<summary>This page argues that Mary was conceived without sin through a "preservative redemption," a special grace from God that prevented her from ever falling into sin, rather than saving her after the fact. Galatinus uses medical analogies and citations from Avicenna, Augustine, and Anselm to show that preventing an illness or a fall is a higher form of "salvation" than curing it.</summary>

### CHAPTER VIII.

->To the fifth objection of Hogostratus. And that the untainted<-
->mother of the Messiah was generated without<-
->lust and concupiscence.<-

->HOGOSTRATUS.<-

If the most blessed Virgin were conceived without original sin, she would have been generated without lust and concupiscence. This is proven because original sin is mixed with lust, concupiscence, and pleasure. Divine Augustine affirms this in his book *On the Faith, to Peter*, in the first part, twenty-fourth question. His saying is placed in the *Decretals* <note>The *Decretals* are a collection of rulings in Canon Law.</note> regarding consecration, in the fourth distinction, the chapter beginning *Firmissime*; where it is said: "Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that every human being who is conceived through the intercourse of a man and a woman is born with original sin, subject to impiety, and liable to death." <note>original: "Firmissime tene, & nullatenus dubites, omnem hominem qui per concubitum viri & mulieris concipitur, cum peccato originali nasci, impietati subditum, mortique subiectum."</note> Therefore, all those generated from the lust and pleasure of coitus are conceived with original sin. But the glorious Virgin was generated with the lust and pleasure of coitus: since she was generated from the very real union of Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, like other human beings. It follows, therefore, that she was conceived in original sin. 

GALATINUS. It is certain that the greater deprives the lesser. <note>The OCR reads "thuius," which appears to be a printer's error for "maius" (greater).</note> For we know by experience that the sun deprives the moon and the candle of their brightness. We also see that a greater sense deprives a lesser one. For a man who places all his thought and imagination intensely upon one thing, either by studying or speculating, loses his lesser senses for that time. For if someone were to pass before him then, he would not see the one passing, and if someone spoke to him, he would not hear. I confess, therefore, that Saint Joachim and Saint Anne coupled as a married pair; however, because of the burning devotion and vehement contemplation in which both were held, being of one mind regarding the generation of the most blessed Virgin, the "tinder" <term>fomes: a theological term for the "kindling" or inclination toward sin</term> was entirely extinguished in that act. Therefore, original sin had no place in the conception of the immaculate Virgin. Moreover, we trust that what we say can be shown to be true. For when her parents had been expelled from the temple by the priests with reproach as if they were profane, because they were sterile and, though now worn out by age, had not yet fathered children: they sadly and suppliantly prayed to God that He would grant them offspring to be procreated for His service. When they were heard, an Angel appeared to each of them separately, announcing that they would generate offspring in God's service, saying (as Jerome witnesses): "I am the Angel of the Lord sent to you to announce that your prayers have been heard, and your alms have ascended into the sight of the Lord. For I have seen your shame, and heard of the sterility and the reproach unjustly cast against you. For God is the avenger of sin, not of nature. And therefore when He closes someone's womb, He does this so that He may open it again more miraculously: so that what is born may be known to be not of lust, but of a divine gift."

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, following the Angelic command, they both met each other and rejoiced in the mutual vision. Being secure and certain of the promised offspring, they adored the Lord and returned home, joyfully awaiting the divine promise. And they joined together with such devotion that, without lust or bodily pleasure, they generated the glorious Virgin who was to be the Mother of God. For the most intense devotion and delight of the soul extinguished all bodily pleasure, concupiscence, and lust. Hence, it was not without merit that <margin>B</margin> the names Joachim and Anne were given to them. <margin>How Joachim and Anne are interpreted.</margin> For "Joachim" is interpreted in Latin as "God will lift up," or "will erect," or "will raise," and also "will confirm." The name "Anne," truly, is derived from the name <note>Hebrew: חן</note> *Hen*, which means "Grace." Thus, from the names themselves, it would be openly known that through the offspring they were to generate, God, out of the grace of His mercy, was going to lift up the human race from the sin of the first parents, raise them from eternal death, and erect and confirm them in heavenly glory. <margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, the most blessed Virgin was generated without concupiscence and lust, it necessarily follows that she was also conceived without initial sin, since lust and concupiscence were the cause of Adam's sin. Indeed, Adam himself, clinging to worldly vices and carnal concupiscences (as is clear through that passage in Genesis chapter 3: <note>original Hebrew: ותרא האשה כי טוב העץ למאכל וכי תאוה הוא לעינים</note> "And the woman saw that the tree was good for eating, and it was a delight to the eyes"), filled himself with pride and disobedience, <margin>D</margin> and transgressed the command of God. In that way, he infected his flesh so that all descending from him are conceived with that same pride and disobedience which is the origin of all sins. For that reason, it is called original, or initial, sin. Because of this, they are also procreated with lust and unbridled pleasure, and they are inclined to fulfill their own will, and are liable to sinning and transgressing God's command. This is most obvious to the senses. For when a man is in the appetite of <margin>E</margin> unbridled lust, the genital member is so aroused by pleasure and proceeds to fulfill its desire that he would not cease from that act even if death were set before him. This is found to be true of no other limb. For when someone approaches a theft, and before he completes it, he repents of the theft, his feet immediately stop walking and his hands abstain from the robbery according to his will; they are obedient to the will. However, as the Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, the standard medieval theology textbook author.</note> says in the 19th distinction of the second book, <margin>F</margin> if the first humans had not sinned, they would have come together in carnal union in paradise without any sin or stain. There would have been an immaculate touch there, and a mixing without concupiscence; and they would have commanded their genital members just like the others, so that they would feel no illicit movement there. And just as we move other members of the body to others without the heat of lust—as one moves the hand to the head—so they would have used the genital members without the "itch" of the flesh. For this lethal sickness clung to human members because of sin. They would have, therefore, generated children in paradise through <margin>G</margin> immaculate coitus without corruption. Hence Augustine says on Genesis: "Why should we not believe that the first humans, before sin, could have commanded their genital members for procreation just as the rest of the members are used in any work without the itch of pleasure?"

<summary>Galatinus argues that Mary was conceived without the "stain" of lust because her parents, Joachim and Anne, were so focused on God that their spiritual devotion extinguished all carnal desire. He contrasts this pure generation with the "unbridled" nature of lust in fallen humanity, citing Peter Lombard and Augustine to suggest this mirrors how humans would have procreated in Paradise.</summary>

Galatinus is explaining that God granted her parents a special state of grace to conceive her without the "stain" of lust.</meta>

<page-num>401, 402</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN.</header>

For it is not unbelievable that God created those bodies in such a way that, had they not sinned, they would have commanded those members just as they command their feet. They would have neither sown with the heat of lust nor given birth with pain. But after sin, they earned that "movement" <note>This refers to *concupiscence* or involuntary sexual desire, which medieval theologians believed was the "fuel" or carrier of Original Sin.</note> which marriage regulates and continence restrains. This weakness, prone to the ruin of shame, is caught by the honor of marriage, so that what would have been a duty for the healthy becomes a remedy for the sick. From this reasoning, therefore, it is gathered that the untainted Virgin was conceived without original sin. For although it is not naturally possible for anyone to be propagated without sin—since the material itself is prone to sin due to the infection of Adam—the glorious Virgin nevertheless achieved propagation without sin not by nature, but by grace. It was more reasonable and fitting that God should have cleansed the matter from which his mother was to be made while it was still the material of the "agent" <note>The parents</note> and before it became the material of the "patient" <note>The child/Mary</note>. Wherefore, God took away all bodily lust and unbridled pleasure from Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, so that in this way they might generate the immaculate Virgin herself in the same manner that the first parents would have generated their children in paradise, had they not sinned.

<margin>Response to the argument of Hogostratus.</margin>
From these points, the solution to Hogostratus's objection is clear. As for the saying of the divine Augustine which he introduces, we say it is indeed true insofar as all humans generated through the intercourse of man and woman with bodily lust and pleasure are not free from original sin. But our statement is even more true, insofar as the glorious Virgin herself was propagated without unbridled lust and bodily pleasure. We say this proceeded from divine grace and will, since she was to be the tabernacle of Him from whose most precious blood the body of Christ, God and man, was to be formed. Therefore, it was necessary that she be the most perfect and purest of all creatures. Augustine himself supports this opinion with his own words; for instance, in the book *On Heresies against the Manichaeans*, speaking in the person of Christ, he says: "If my mother could have been defiled when I made her, I could have been defiled when I was born from her." <note>Original Latin: "Si potuit inquinari mater mea, cum eam facerem, potui inquinari ego, cum ex ea nascerer."</note> And in the book *On Nature and Grace*, he says: "Except for the Virgin Mary, concerning whom, for the honor of my Lord, I wish to raise no question at all when discussing sins." <note>Original Latin: "Excepta virgine Maria, de qua propter honorem Domini mei, cum de peccatis agitur, nullam prorsus volo facere quæstionem."</note> In many other places as well, he proclaims her to be immaculate, most pure, and immune from all sin.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Regarding the sixth objection of Hogostratus. And that by the merit of Christ’s passion, the glorious Virgin ought to have been exhibited as redeemed from original sin in the most noble manner.<-

->HOGOSTRATUS.<-

VIRGO—the glorious Virgin was redeemed through Christ’s passion. Otherwise, she would have been deprived of such a great good, and Christ would not have existed as the universal redeemer, which is highly unfitting. Therefore, he was also the redeemer and savior of the Virgin herself. She herself confesses this in her song <note>The *Magnificat* (Luke 1:46-55).</note>, saying: "And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savi-

<column-break/>

-or." <note>Original Latin: "Et exultauit spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo."</note> But redemption or salvation presupposes a fault. For she cannot be understood as redeemed and saved unless from some fault. Since, therefore, she never had actual fault <note>Personal sins committed during one's life.</note>, it follows plainly that she was redeemed from original sin. Wherefore, it follows that she was conceived in original sin. GALATINUS: Your reasoning is nil; since one is equally a redeemer and savior who guards a person so they do not become a captive, as one who frees them from captivity.

Just as a physician is so named who <margin>What medicine is.</margin> gives a person a rule and order so that they may preserve their health and not fall into sickness, as much as one who heals the sick. For this reason, Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) whose medical and philosophical texts were central to medieval university education.</note> defined medicine as the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known, from the part by which it is healed, or by which infirmity is removed from it, and health already possessed is preserved, and lost health is recovered. By the same reasoning, we say that he should be called a redeemer and savior who prevents someone from falling into sin, just as he who lifts a person up from sin. From these things, we can say that there is a double redemption: "sublevative" <note>Lifting up or curative; saving someone *after* they have fallen.</note> and "preservative." <margin>Double redemption.</margin> And preservative redemption is far more noble and perfect than sublevative. For just as it is much better to preserve someone from a wound than to apply a remedy after the wound is received, so it is far more noble and perfect to preserve someone from sin so they do not fall into it, than to free them from sin after they have fallen. Therefore, he is redeemed in a nobler and more perfect way, and receives a greater benefit, who is preserved immune from future sin, than he who is snatched from sin already committed. Preservative redemption is therefore much more excellent and perfect than sublevative redemption. All other humans were redeemed from sin by sublevative redemption. But the glorious Virgin alone, of those propagated from man and woman, was redeemed by preservative redemption. In the same way, the good Angels were redeemed from sin so that they would not fall with Lucifer, as John Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> most excellently believes. Concerning the immaculate Virgin herself, Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> says in the second book of *Why God Became Man*, chapter 10: "The blessed Virgin needed redemption and the passion of Christ, not because of sin that was in her, but because of the sin that *would have been* in her, had He himself not preserved her by a special privilege." Furthermore, the very perfection of human redemption necessarily required this. For there are six <margin>Six modes of redemption.</margin> modes of redemption. The first is when someone is redeemed from actual mortal sin after they have fallen into it. And in this way, sinners who have fallen into mortal sin are redeemed through the sacrament of penance. The second mode is when someone is preserved from mortal sin itself. And in this way the Apostles were redeemed; after they received the Holy Spirit, they never committed a mortal sin. The third mode is when someone is redeemed from a committed venial sin; in this way the just are usually redeemed, who by common law cannot entirely avoid venial sin itself—since according to the saying of the wise man, "the just man falls seven times a day, and rises again." This can only be understood as venial sin. The fourth mode is...

<summary>This page argues that Mary was conceived without the "stain" of lust through a special divine grace granted to her parents, and introduces the concept of "preservative redemption"—the idea that Christ saved Mary by preventing her from ever falling into sin, rather than by cleaning it away after the fact.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument of Galatinus regarding the unique nature of the Virgin Mary's conception and redemption. Having established that she was conceived without the "stain" of lust, Galatinus now categorizes the different ways God redeems or preserves individuals from sin to show Mary’s unique status.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

...when someone is preserved from venial sin <note>Venial sins are considered "lesser" sins in Catholic theology, which do not destroy the relationship with God but weaken it.</note> itself. In this way, John the Baptist was redeemed. As some believe, he was entirely free from venial sin, which is why the Church sings of him: *That you might not be able to stain your life with even a light word.* <note>original Latin: "Ne leui saltem maculare vitam famine posses." This is a line from the hymn "Ut queant laxis," traditionally sung for the Feast of St. John the Baptist.</note> Furthermore, the fifth mode of redemption is when someone is redeemed from original sin after having contracted it; this is how baptized infants are redeemed through the sacrament of baptism. Finally, the sixth mode is when someone is preserved unharmed from original sin itself. In this way, among all those born through natural procreation, only the most blessed Virgin was redeemed. Therefore, unless she had been preserved entirely immune from original sin by the foreseen merit of her son's death, then neither would the human race have been perfectly redeemed, nor would Christ himself have stood as the perfect redeemer of the human race—since he would not have redeemed it in every way that it was capable of being redeemed.

### CHAPTER X.

*Regarding the seventh objection of Hogostratus. <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527) was a prominent Dominican inquisitor who often debated the author, Galatinus.</note> And that the glorious Virgin never fell ill, nor did she ever suffer menstruation. And the reason why she died. And that, having died, she immediately rose again.*

->HOGOSTRATUS.<-

Original sin was the cause of death, according to that divine saying in the second chapter of Genesis: *On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.* But the most blessed Virgin was physically dead, as the Catholic Church holds. Therefore, she was a participant in the sin of Adam. Consequently, it follows that she was conceived in original sin. Otherwise, she would have had punishment without fault, whereas punishment alone should hold its authors responsible. GALATINUS: I grant, indeed, that death was the effect of sin after Adam sinned, for those who sinned in him and are born in sins. Yet Adam himself, before he had sinned, was occupied in the contemplation and enjoyment of eternal things.

<margin>What the tree of life is.</margin>
And this was the "tree of life" situated in paradise, according to the Talmudists. But because he abandoned the contemplation of divine things and clung to worldly vices and carnal desires, he fell into sickness and death. And that is why we die. This is the "tree of the knowledge of good and evil" which is the cause of death, according to their opinion.

<margin>What the tree of knowledge of good and evil is.</margin>
Hence is that saying in the second chapter of Genesis: <term>For on the day you eat from it, you shall surely die <note>original Hebrew: "כי ביום אכלך ממנו מות תמות"</note></term>. This is clearly apparent in man, who is composed of four elements, from which four humors <note>In medieval medicine, the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—were believed to control health and temperament. An imbalance caused disease.</note> proceed.

<margin>Four types of vices.</margin>
For although human vices multiply, they are divided into four kinds. The first consists in food and drink. The second in sexual intercourse. The third in the governance of things. The fourth, finally, in the increase of wealth. For from food and drink, it is certain that four humors are generated, peculiar to each type: such as phlegm for the phlegmatic, yellow bile for the choleric, black bile for the melancholic, and blood for the sanguine. By the same reasoning, for one who pursues lust...

<column-break/>

# BOOK SEVEN.

...and wishes to satisfy the appetite of lust, heat is increased. And if he is cheated of the desired thing, melancholy is multiplied. The same must be said of the remaining humors; thus it happens that a person departs from their natural balance and increases one humor over another, which through excess causes sickness. From this follows the division of the elements and the separation of soul and body, which is called death. From this it follows that Adam, having pursued vices, fell into infirmities and death.

<insert>B</insert> <margin>Why Adam was made mortal.</margin>
But the glorious Virgin and her son, since they were by no means participants in Adam's sin and remained entirely foreign to original sin, deserved by right to be impassible <note>Incapable of suffering.</note> and immortal. However, because the death and passion of Christ were necessary for our redemption—since divine justice would not spare the human race without it—Christ necessarily had to have a body capable of suffering and death. Likewise, since the untainted Virgin was to give birth to a son capable of suffering and death, who was to be one flesh with her, and since a mortal and suffering being cannot naturally proceed from an immortal and impassible one...

<insert>C</insert> <margin>Why the Mother of the Messiah died.</margin>
...she was necessarily mortal as well. Therefore, both the mother and the son died. Nevertheless, the blessed Virgin herself was delivered from the evils and punishments that occur because of Adam's sin and which were not necessary for Christ's passion. Such things include giving birth with pain (which was given to Eve as a curse), being stained by menstruation, and being affected by infirmities arising from sin; of all these things...

<insert>D</insert> the glorious Virgin was entirely free. And because the death and passion of Christ and the untouched Virgin were for the redemption of the human race, as has been said, so too the resurrection of Christ—regardless of the fact that it was necessary for the confirmation of the Catholic faith—had to occur by necessity, because he was entirely free from original sin.

<margin>The Mother of the Messiah, having died, soon rose in glory.</margin>
By the same reasoning, the immaculate Virgin herself rose as soon as she was dead. Taken up into the highest heaven together with her son, and raised high upon the throne of the heavenly kingdom, sitting at the right hand of her son, she reigns most gloriously in both soul and body together. And for this reason the Psalmist, speaking in Psalm 132 of the resurrection of the son and the mother, says: <term>Arise, O Lord, into your resting place, you and the ark of your strength <note>original Hebrew: "קומה יהוה למנוחתך אתה וארון עוזך"</note></term>. Regarding her sitting at the right hand of her son and the glory of her body, the same author says in the forty-fifth Psalm: <term>The Queen stands at your right hand in a diadem, or golden clothing <note>original Hebrew: "נצבה שגל לימינך בכתם אופיר"</note></term>. Where, by "golden clothing," the heavenly glory and the most excellent state of the body (which is the garment of the soul) is expressed. CAPITO: <note>Wolfgang Fabricius Capito (1478–1541), a reformer and contemporary of the author.</note> You have spoken correctly that the glorious Virgin never suffered menstruation, since she had to be most pure, so that from a most pure mother (as Augustine says) a most pure son might be born. Hence Anselm also says: "It was fitting that the Virgin should shine with that purity, greater than which cannot be understood under God."

<insert>G</insert> For this reason, she not only had to be most pure from every stain of sin, but no other impurity could be attributed to her. Therefore, since reason itself demands that she be outside the common rule of women regarding menstruation, I have no doubt that she was never stained by it. I would like you, however, to prove it with arguments. GALATINUS: To...

<summary>This page argues that the Virgin Mary was exempt from the physical "penalties" of original sin, such as illness and menstruation, but died only so her nature would match her Son's mortal body for the sake of human redemption. It concludes that because she was free from sin, she was resurrected and assumed into heaven immediately after death.</summary>

<meta>The previous page established the Virgin Mary's unique status as the only human preserved from original sin from the moment of her conception. This argument continues by addressing specific physical and theological consequences of her sinless nature.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>The Mother of the Messiah never suffered menstruation.</margin>
Therefore, to satisfy your devotion and the request you make, I will prove this to you by a three-fold reason. First, because she was so perfectly proportioned and possessed such a balanced physical constitution <note>In medieval medicine, health was viewed as a balance of "humors" and "complexions." A "perfect complexion" implied a body in such harmony that it produced no waste.</note> that she lacked menstruation entirely. For Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> and other natural philosophers write that the cause of menstruation in women is a surplus of matter. Therefore, nature found the way of menstruation so that it might expel this kind of superfluity. However, since the glorious Virgin, on account of the excellent constitution she possessed, had no surplus of matter in herself, menstruation had no place in her.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Secondly, because when a woman suffers menstruation, she becomes ill and is in pain throughout. Since all illnesses proceed from the sin of our first parents, and since that untainted Virgin was in no way a sharer in their sin, it follows clearly that she never suffered menstruation. Hence, we do not read that she was ever ill or labored under any pain.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Finally, because a menstruating woman is called "polluted," according to what is said in the eighteenth chapter of Leviticus: <margin>C</margin> <note>original Hebrew: ואל אשה בנדת טמאתה לא תקרב</note> *And you shall not approach a woman in the uncleanness of her menstruation.* If, therefore, we were to say the most blessed Virgin suffered menstruation, it would surely follow that she was polluted. If that were the case, that saying of the Wise Man in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs, spoken of her in the person of God, would be entirely false: *You are all beautiful,* <margin>Objection.</margin> *my love, and there is no spot in you.* <note>original Latin: "Tota pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te." This verse is a cornerstone of the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
**HOOGSTRATEN:** <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a Dominican inquisitor and traditionalist opponent in these dialogues.</note> If the most blessed Virgin had died before the Passion of her son, tell me, where would her soul have gone? To the lower regions <note>Hell or the Underworld.</note>, or into the celestial paradise? For if you say into the celestial paradise, that could in no way have happened, since the gates of heaven were not yet open. Therefore, you must say that she would have descended to the lower regions—specifically to the higher hell, which we call *Limbo*, where the holy fathers descended before the death of Christ. But the holy fathers traveled there for no other reason than because of original sin. Therefore, she too would have traveled there because of original sin. Consequently, she would have been conceived <margin>E</margin> in original sin.

<margin>Answer to the first point.</margin>
**GALATINUS:** I give you two answers. First, I say that she would have entered neither place, but rather another most holy place in the heavens.

<margin>Second answer. It was impossible for the Mother of the Messiah to have died before the Passion of her son.</margin>
Next, I say that your proposition regarding her death before her son's Passion is completely false, as it was impossible for her to die before the Passion of her son. This is proved by a three-fold reason. The first is because it had been so preordained by God that she should see the Passion of her son. Therefore, <margin>F</margin> it could not happen otherwise. The second is because it was necessary that she also intervene in the remission of sin, since all things that had participated in the perpetration of Adam's sin had to participate in its release. Therefore, just as that sin was committed by means of a woman, so also by means of a woman it had to be remitted; so that just as a sinful woman brought death into the world, so a most holy and immaculate woman might bring life. This is according to Saint Augustine: *Eve was the author of sin, Mary the author of merit. Eve hindered by killing, Mary helped by giving life. The former struck the blow, the latter healed it.*

<margin>Answer to the third point.</margin>
Finally, the third reason is that God makes no one die before their appointed time

<column-break/>

<page-num>406</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN.</header>

unless for two reasons: either on account of their crimes, by which they deserve death, or on account of their goodness and virtues, lest they lose them by sinning. For when God knows that someone will fall back into sin and be damned for it, in His mercy, not wishing their soul to be lost, He makes them die in the time of His justice. Since, therefore, the most blessed Virgin was immune from every stain of sin and could not fall into sin, she could not have died before her time; since nothing <margin>B</margin> unjust can proceed from divine justice. From these things said in the preceding chapters, it is clearer than the sun that, despite Hoogstraten's objections, the opinion of the ancient Hebrews regarding the most immaculate conception of the Mother of the Messiah is most true and Catholic.

### CHAPTER XI.

->That for the sake of the Mother of the Messiah, Israel was called the peculiar people of God.<-

### REUCHLIN. <note>Johann Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, appearing here under his Greek-derived pen name "Capnio."</note>

<margin>D</margin> From the blessed things you have said, I judge that the Israelite people were called the "peculiar people of God" because of the love God had from eternity for the Mother of the Messiah. **GALATINUS:** You judge very well indeed. For so great and so immense was God’s love from eternity for the Mother of the Messiah, that for her sake He made the Israelite people His own peculiar people, because she was to come forth from them. This was most clearly suggested by that Rabbi who holds such authority among the Hebrews that they call him <note>original Hebrew: רבנו הקדוש</note> *Rabbenu Hakkados*, that is, "Our Holy Teacher." <note>This refers to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah.</note> For in the book called <note>original Hebrew: גלי רזיא</note> *Gale Razeya*, that is, "The Revealer of Secrets," in response to the sixth petition of the Consul Antoninus, he said among other things: "Regarding what you asked, <margin>E</margin> why Israel was called the peculiar people of God, I will tell you what I found written by Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai <note>Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar.</note> in the book entitled <note>original Hebrew: מחקר הסודות</note> *Mechkar Hassodoth*, that is, 'The Inquirer of Secrets,' saying thus: Rabbi Isaiah began his sermon and said, 'Woe to you, Moab; you are lost, people of Chemosh; he has given his sons into flight and his daughters into captivity.' Woe to them, woe to them, who are called the fathers of the whole world and of the human race, and moreover, the peculiar people of God." And after a few words: "Seeing," <margin>F</margin> he said, "that from Israel was to be cut out the 'stone without hands,' which is the primary stone from which the Messiah is to come, who will extend his mercies over the whole world, for that reason He willed Israel to be called the father of the whole world and His peculiar people." Thus he spoke. Moreover, Rabbi Nehuniah son of HaKanah, in the <note>original Hebrew: באגירת הסודות</note> *Beigereth Hassodoth*, that is, "The Epistle of Secrets," explaining the aforementioned words, says: "This primary stone is the mother of the King Messiah." For the clarification of these things, I say that this ancient doctor felt that Israel was called <margin>G</margin> the peculiar people of God for no other reason than because of a certain property hidden from us. This is because every agent acts for one of three reasons...

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of the Virgin Mary's physical and spiritual purity, arguing that her unique nature exempted her from the common ailments of humanity. This page shifts the focus toward the theological reason for the election of the Jewish people: the "hidden property" of producing the Messiah’s mother.</meta>

<page-num>407</page-num>
<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>BOOK</header>

...acts upon another in various ways: namely, by quantity, quality, or by a certain property inherent in itself. That which acts by quantity is, for example, food; if someone takes more than the proper measure, they fall into stomach pain, but if they take less than what is due, they fall into a wasting sickness. That which acts by quality is like fire, which heats, or snow, which cools. One of these is hot by its heat, the other cold by its coldness. Both heat and cold are qualities. Finally, that which acts by a hidden property <note>In medieval philosophy, an "occult" or "hidden property" (proprietas occulta) was a natural power that could be observed—like magnetism—but whose cause was not immediately apparent through the four elements.</note> is like a magnet, which draws iron to itself; or a small stone commonly called *turphina* <note>Likely referring to a legendary stone mentioned in medieval lapidaries, sometimes called the "orphan stone," said to protect the wearer from injury during a fall.</note>, which if someone wears it and falls from a high place, the stone itself breaks if the person's limbs were meant to be broken, while the wearer remains unharmed. Or like the amethyst, which prevents drunkenness when worn. Or like other small stones and gems having various properties. If anyone asks why they perform such operations, jewelers respond that these effects proceed from their hidden properties. They say the reason for this matter is unknown to them. I, however, say that although such properties are hidden from us, they are known to God, who created the world out of nothing and instilled a specific power into every single thing. Therefore, He knows best why the magnet draws iron. And so it is with each individual thing.

Having established these premises, let us ask the Jews: By which of these operations did God choose the Israelite people, so that they might be an elect and peculiar people for Him above all nations? Was it by quantity, quality, or property? If they say by quantity—meaning because of their great number—this is entirely false, since it is written in the 7th chapter of Deuteronomy: *The Lord your God chose you to be a peculiar people to Himself out of all the peoples who are upon the earth. Not because you surpassed all nations in number was the Lord joined to you and chose you, for you are the fewest of all.* But if they answer by quality—that is, on account of their holy works—this is likewise false; as it is also written in the 9th chapter of Deuteronomy: *Not because of your righteousness and the uprightness of your heart do you enter to possess their lands.* Therefore, they must concede that for no other reason did God choose the Israelite people except for a hidden property that was inherent in them, which was the immaculate mother of the Messiah who was to proceed from them. Just as that ancient teacher of theirs asserted, whom we have said they call <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: רבּינו הקדוש (Rabbeinu HaKadosh), meaning "Our Holy Master," a title for Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, our holy Master.

### CHAPTER XII.

->That the mother of the Messiah was to come from the royal lineage of David and the tribe of Judah. Wherein Matthew and Luke, describing the genealogy of Christ, are in excellent agreement.<-

->CAPNIO.<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived nickname of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
If God chose the entire Israelite people for Himself and made them peculiar on account of the Messiah's mother, how much more so that tribe and family from which she herself was to proceed...
