<margin>A</margin> ...must He be thought to have chosen for Himself. From which tribe, therefore, and from which family did the ancient Jews assert she would come? GALATINUS: From the tribe of Judah, and from the house or family of David. For if it is abundantly clear both through Holy Scripture and through the volumes of the Talmud that the Messiah was to be born from the tribe of Judah and the house of David—and the ancient Jews themselves handed down that the Messiah would be generated from a woman without a man (as will be proved abundantly in what follows)—it surely follows that they were by no means ignorant that his mother <margin>B</margin> would also be from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic lineage. And to omit others who lived before her time, that ancient teacher of theirs whom they call <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term>, that is, our holy Master, in that book which he named <term>Gale Razia</term> <note>Hebrew: גלי רזיא (Galei Razaya), meaning "The Revealer of Secrets," a mystical and polemical work often cited by Galatinus.</note> (meaning "The Revealer of Secrets"), responding to the third petition of the Roman Consul Antoninus <note>A reference to the famous dialogues in the Talmud between "Antoninus" (a Roman Emperor) and Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note> and reporting those things which he had received from Elijah appearing to him while he was praying in a cave, <margin>C</margin> says thus: *As for what you asked—whose daughter she would be (namely the mother of the Messiah of whom they were speaking) or from what tribe—you ought to notice that her parent will have a double name, one Eli, the other Jehoiakim. And Eli indeed, which is a derivative name, shows that he will ascend to a sublime rank. But Jehoiakim, which is a compound name, signifies that God will raise up in his hand the greatest salvation of Israel. Moreover, the tribe of Judah descends from the house of Zerubbabel <margin>D</margin> son of Shealtiel. Just as it is written in the fourth chapter of Zechariah: "Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel? He shall bring forth the primary rock into the plain." This primary rock is the mother of the King Messiah.* Thus spoke that <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term>. 

CAPNIO: Even if certain ancient Jews who lived before the mother of the Messiah predicted that she would be from the tribe of Judah and the house of David, as is clearly shown from these things you have just brought forward: nevertheless, their younger descendants <margin>E</margin> <margin>The argument of the younger Jews.</margin> certainly admit that the Messiah would be born from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic lineage (which consequently they could not deny regarding his mother, if they were willing to concede according to their scriptures that the Messiah himself was to be conceived of a virgin without male seed). But they deny that the glorious Virgin Mary herself, the mother of our Messiah, was sprung from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic progeny, since that is not established from the Gospel. For if (they say) Mary the mother of your Christ was born of the tribe of Judah and the royal line of David, why did the Evangelists, when writing the genealogy of your Christ, <margin>F</margin> fail to mention this? For neither does Luke report it—who traces the genealogy of your Christ from Joseph all the way back to Adam—nor does Matthew attest to this, who tracing it from Abraham to Joseph, says at last: *And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.* Therefore, you must concede one of two things: either your Christ had Joseph as a father, or he was not <margin>G</margin> descended from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic lineage. Wherefore, so that their deceitful lips may be made silent, I would wish you to prove through their own scriptures that the Virgin Mary descended from the Davidic progeny by a direct line...

...had said. **GALATINUS.** The wicked cleverness of the Jews finds slanders on both sides to attack the truth. But they certainly labor in vain, since the light of truth itself cannot remain hidden in the darkness. <margin>The response of some of our own writers.</margin> Therefore, some of our own people, wishing to remove this difficulty, say that Mary and Joseph were from the same tribe: which is why Joseph was compelled by law to marry her. They say the order of Christ's generation is traced down to Joseph because it is not the custom of the Scriptures for a lineage to be woven through the female line. But while these writers speak the truth, they do not at all remove the difficulty that the Jews pose to us. For they do not prove that the most blessed Mary herself descended from the tribe of Judah and the house of David, nor consequently that she and Joseph were from the same tribe. <margin>Another response from certain writers.</margin> For this reason, some others, wishing to prove this, say that Levi—who (as Luke reports) descends in a straight line from the chain of Nathan, son of David—fathered Melchi and Panther. Panther then fathered Barpanther (so called). Barpanther then fathered Joachim, and Joachim fathered the Mother of God herself. <margin>Confutation of the previous response.</margin> But these writers certainly depart far from the truth and in no way solve the objection made to us by the Jews: since it is not at all true (if I may say so with their permission) that Levi fathered Melchi and Panther. On the contrary, Melchi fathered that Levi: as appears clearly enough from Luke, who, following the generation of Christ from sons to fathers, says: *And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, who was the son of Eli, who was the son of Matthan, who was the son of Levi, who was the son of Melchi.* From this it is clearly evident that Melchi was not the son of Levi, as those writers assert, but the father. Even if it were as they say, they still do not prove it to be so through the Gospel or through the scriptures held as authentic among the Jews. Thus, they by no means satisfy the Jews' argument. What then shall we say? I will say whatever I feel on this matter, yet saving a better judgment and the determination of the Holy Church, to which I always submit myself in all things. <margin>Galatinus's true response.</margin> We read that David had two sons among others: namely Solomon and Nathan. Through Solomon's line descended Joseph, the spouse of the glorious Virgin. But through Nathan's line descended the most blessed Virgin herself, the mother of the true Messiah. Matthew, therefore, describes Joseph's genealogy by descending through Solomon's line. Luke, however, expresses the lineage of the Mother of God by ascending through the line of Nathan. This is especially suggested by the prophecy of Zechariah, who, having seen in the spirit that the most blessed Virgin would come forth from Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel (from whom the Messiah was to be born), said in the fourth chapter: <note>original: "מִי אַתָּה הַר הַגָּדוֹל לִפְנֵי זְרֻבָּבֶל לְמִישׁוֹר, וְהוֹצִיא אֶת הָאֶבֶן הָרֹאשָׁה תְּשׁוּאוֹת חֵן חֵן לָהּ"</note> "Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain. And he shall bring forth the primary stone, and shall set grace of grace upon it." <note>Zechariah 4:7. The author interprets the "primary stone" as the Virgin Mary.</note> Here, by "primary stone," he understood the undefiled Virgin, from whom the Messiah was to proceed, as Rabbenu Haccados <note>A title for Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> explained a little earlier. Therefore, Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, explains these words of Zechariah, "And he shall bring forth the primary stone," in Aramaic as follows: <note>original: "וּמִינָהּ אַנְפֵּיק יָת מְשִׁיחָא וּשְׁמֵיהּ יְהֵי לְעָלְמָא"</note> That is, "And from that stone shall come forth the Messiah, whose name is eternal." This agrees with that Evangelist who said: *In the beginning was the Word.* Now, why the glorious Virgin is called the "primary stone" 

<column-break/>

<page-num>410</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> has been discussed in the preceding parts. However, it must be noted that this Zerubbabel is the one about whom Luke writes when weaving the genealogy of the Virgin through Nathan's line; he is not the one mentioned by Matthew, who describes Joseph's genealogy through Solomon's line. For there were two Zerubbabels and two Shealtiels, the fathers of those same Zerubbabels. This is most clear from the fact that the Zerubbabel of whom Matthew writes was born two generations after the <margin>B</margin> Babylonian Exile. For he says: *Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian Exile. Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel. Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.* But the Zerubbabel mentioned by Zechariah and Luke lived before the Babylonian Exile. This can be clearly seen from the words of the prophet Haggai, who says in the second chapter: *The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and <margin>C</margin> to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying: Who is left among you who saw this house in its first glory?* From these words, it appears that this Zerubbabel had seen the House of God in its first building, and consequently was born before the Babylonian Exile itself. Furthermore, the prophecy of Zerubbabel was during the Exile itself, as is held in the second chapter of Ezra. From these things, therefore, <margin>D</margin> it is openly shown that the Zerubbabel of whom Zechariah and Luke wrote was one man, and the one mentioned by Matthew was another. Therefore, in the genealogy described by Matthew, only eleven generations are placed from Zerubbabel to Joseph. But in the one Luke treats, many more are found from Joseph to Zerubbabel, because of the greater span of time that <margin>E</margin> intervened. From all this, it is plainly gathered that the glorious Virgin Mary, the mother of our Savior, existed from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage of David, and came forth through the straight line of Nathan, son of David, which Luke describes so well. If anyone should object to what we have said—on the grounds that in the series of the same genealogy no mention is made of Saint Joachim, the Virgin's father—I say that Eli was Joachim, who is placed first in the ascending order. For among the Syrians, Joachim, Eli, and Eliakim are the same, as Philo the Jew writes. Hence the father of the Messiah’s mother was <margin>F</margin> called Eli and Joachim, just as Rabbenu Haccados had previously predicted through the revelation of Elijah, as was clear in the preceding sections. And afterward, Rabbi Nehumia's son testified most excellently in the letter he wrote for the recognition of the Messiah’s generation, saying: "There was a certain girl in Bethlehem of Judah named Mary, daughter of Joachim Eli, of the lineage of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, from the tribe of Judah." The Evangelist, therefore, took his proper name, which was Eli. But the Holy Church took his common name, which was <margin>G</margin> Joachim. Nor was this without reason: since Joachim (as has been said previously) is interpreted as "God raises up," or "stirs up," or "confirms," and God himself, incarnate from his daughter, [raised up] the human race, which had fallen through sin and was condemned to eternal death...

<summary>Galatinus argues that Matthew and Luke provide two different genealogies because they trace two different lines: Matthew follows Joseph through Solomon, while Luke follows Mary through Nathan. He also resolves discrepancies regarding the name of Mary's father (Joachim/Eli) and the identity of Zerubbabel.</summary>

He now prepares to offer his own resolution based on legal and marital tradition.</meta>

<margin>Question.</margin>
...he had been, he would raise and lift him up to grace and glory. Eli, moreover, is derived from the word *'alah* <note>original: עלה; ala</note>, which means "to ascend," because the human race was to ascend to the highest level through his daughter. <margin>Response of some of our writers.</margin> **CHAPTER.** If, therefore, Joseph was not his son, but rather the son of Jacob, as Matthew records in his genealogy, why does Luke call Joseph himself the son of Eli, saying, "Who was of Eli," meaning his son? **GALATINUS.** Some of our writers say that Jacob and Eli were brothers, and when Eli died without children, his brother Jacob—in order to raise up seed and a name for him (as the law commanded)—took his wife, from whom he fathered Joseph. For this reason, they say he had one father according to nature and the other according to the law. But to speak the truth, they are greatly mistaken. <margin>Confutation of the aforementioned response.</margin> First, because even if Jacob and Eli were from the same tribe and produced from the Davidic line, they still could not have been brothers: since one descended through the line of Solomon and the other through the line of Nathan; therefore they were very distantly related. Second, because when someone took the wife of a deceased brother, he would give the son he had by her the name of the deceased brother, according to the ancient institution: so that he might raise up both seed and a name for his brother, since the law commanded both to be raised. Therefore, if Jacob (as they say) took the wife of his deceased brother Eli, he would have given Joseph the name not of Joseph, but of Eli, just as the deceased had been called. <margin>Galatinus’s response.</margin> I say therefore, saving better judgment, that because spouses became "one flesh" through true marriage—according to that passage in Genesis: *They shall be two in one flesh*—the father of one spouse was rightly called the father of the other. This is also confirmed in the *Bereshit Rabba* <note>A classic collection of ancient Jewish explanations of the Book of Genesis.</note>, commenting on the passage in Genesis chapter 37: *And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him*, namely Jacob. For it is said there: "Why is it said 'all his daughters' when Jacob had only one daughter, namely Dinah? Because it is not forbidden for a man to call his son-in-law his 'son' and his daughter-in-law his 'daughter.'" and although a carnal union did not occur between the most blessed Virgin and Joseph, there was nonetheless a true marriage between them, and therefore they were true spouses. The Angel testified to this when he said in the first chapter of Matthew: *Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.* For that reason, Joseph could not inaptly be called the son of Eli (or Jehoiakim), who was the father of his untouched wife. Therefore, since it was not the custom of the Scriptures to weave genealogies through women, Luke, in the genealogy of the glorious Virgin, placed Joseph in the place of the Virgin herself and called him the son of Eli—that is, of Jehoiakim.

### CHAPTER XIII.
->That the mother of the Messiah was destined to be called Mary.<-
### CAPNIO <note>The Latinized name of the scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated drop cap 'D' at the beginning of the text, depicting a figure seated at a writing desk.</image-desc>

Tell me, I pray, did the ancient Jews who preceded the mother of the Messiah know by what name she was to be

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> called? For if the name of her father (as you showed in the preceding sections) was not hidden from some of them, one must think that her own name was not hidden from them either. **GALATINUS.** Exactly so. For some of their ancients (wonderful to say) were not ignorant of even the name by which the mother of the Messiah was to be called. For they predicted that she must be called Mary. Among them stood out one who is of such authority among them that they call him *Rabbenu Haccados* <note>original: רבנו הקדוש; Rabbenu Haccados</note>, that is, "Our Holy Teacher." <margin>B</margin> For in the third portion of that book which is called *Gale Razeya* <note>original: גלי רזיא; Galera zeia</note>, that is, "The Revealer of Secrets," wishing to satisfy the inquiry of Antoninus <note>Often identified in Jewish tradition as a Roman emperor who befriended Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note>, a consul of the city of Rome—who among other things had asked him about the name of the Messiah’s mother—he answered him thus, as Elijah had revealed to him while he was praying in the Cave of Machpelah: "As for what you asked, by what name the prophetess is called, Mary [Miriam] is her name." 

And for this reason Isaiah sang in the 9th chapter, saying: *For a child is born to us, a son is given to us.* And further on: *To the multiplication of the empire* <note>Latin: *Ad multiplicandum imperium*. The Hebrew text is "lemarbe hamisra."</note>, or "the principality," or "That the empire or principality may be multiplied." <margin>C</margin> These words signify that the Messiah is to be generated by God, who will multiply the empire, because he is the Lord of the whole world. And he shall be born from Mary the Lady. And this is what it says: *lemarbe hamisra* <note>original: לםרבה המשרה</note>, that is, "To the multiplication of the empire." For from these words arises *Miriam sara* <note>original: מרים שרה</note>, that is, "Mary the Lady," <margin>D</margin> in this manner: If you take the *Lamed* [ל], *Mem* [ם], and *Resh* [ר], they constitute the first part of *lemarbe*, which is *lumar* [לםר]. If, however, you take the *He* [ה] from *lemarbe*, and the *He* [ה] of this word *hamisra*—the numerical value of each of which is five, and both together make ten—they signify the *Yod* [י] of this word *Miriam*. Then, adding the *Mem* [ם] of the word *hamisra*, behold, you have *Miriam* [מרים], that is, Mary. From the word *hamisra*, moreover, there remains *sara* [שרה], that is, "Lady," which is written with three letters. <margin>E</margin> Behold, from *lemarbe hamisra*, which is the same as "To the multiplication of the empire" or "principality," you have *Lemiriam Sara* [למרים שרה], that is, "To Mary the Lady." This is to make known to us that this Mary is the Lady and superior of the universe, and the Queen of the heavens. 

Antoninus said to him, "Why then is the *Yod* divided into two *He*s? And why is the *Beth* <note>Likely a typo in the original Latin text for another letter or part of the phonetic analysis.</note> placed in the middle of the name *Miriam*, that is, Mary? And what does the closed *Mem* [ם] of this word *lemarbe* <margin>F</margin> signify, which by right ought to have been open, since it is placed in the middle of the word?" <note>In Hebrew, the letter Mem has a special "closed" form used only at the end of words; however, in Isaiah 9:6, it appears closed in the middle of a word, which ancient commentators viewed as a great mystery.</note> He replied: The *Yod* was divided into two *He*s to open wonderful secrets to us. For just as a *He* is composed of a *Daleth* and a *Vav* in this figure [ה], so the King Messiah is composed of divinity and humanity. And just as these two *He*s are two *Daleth*s, from which proceed two *Vav*s, like two sons arising from them in this way [דוד]: so in the substance of the King Messiah are found two filiations: one <margin>G</margin> is of divinity, by which he is the Son of God; the other is of humanity, by which he will be the son of this prophetess. And just as these letters *Daleth* and *Vav* which constitute the *He* are each distinct from the other, although...

...although it is one letter, for it is written ה <note>The Hebrew letter 'He'</note>: so in the Messiah, the substance of divinity and the substance of humanity, which are united together, are one Messiah. Furthermore, the fact that the *beth* <note>original: 'beth'; ב</note> of this word לםרבה *le-marbe* <note>original: 'le-marbe'; 'to the increase' (Isaiah 9:7)</note> is placed in the middle of the name מרים <note>original: 'Miriam'; Mary</note> shows that the mind and entire thought of this prophetess was to preserve her virginity. ->### CHAPTER XIV.<-

->*That the mother of the Messiah was to be a virgin. And concerning her complete virginity: namely before birth, during birth, and after birth.*<-

->### CAPNIO.<-

<margin>Concerning the <term>closed mem</term> <note>The letter 'mem' (ם) usually only appears at the end of a word, but in Isaiah 9:6 it appears in the middle of 'le-marbe', which mystical traditions interpret as a secret sign.</note>.</margin>
Through the *closed mem*, written in the middle of the word *lemarbe*, not only is a determined number of six hundred years suggested (as Rabbenu Haccados <note>Our Holy Master, Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi</note> handed down in the preceding chapter), which were to flow from the time that prophecy was brought forth until the birth of the Messiah, but also the complete virginity of the mother of the Messiah is signified. For in this word לםרבה *lemarbe*, in which the mother of the Messiah’s name is shown (as proven), the *closed mem* is placed contrary to custom; it openly hints that the Messiah was to be born of the Virgin Mary contrary to the custom of nature. Therefore, to further convict the perfidy of the Jews, you would do a useful thing if you showed through their own scriptures that the mother of the Messiah was to be a virgin. **GALATINUS.** Jewish impiety can by no means deny that the mother of the Messiah was to be a virgin. For this is demonstrated everywhere and most clearly through the Law, through the oracles of the prophets, and through the testimonies of the ancient Talmudists. And first, in Leviticus chapter 12, it is plainly held when it is said: אשה כי תזריע וילדה זכר וטמאה <note>original: 'Ishah ki tazria ve-yaldah zakhar ve-tameah'</note> That is: "A woman who has received seed, and has given birth to a male, shall be unclean." Since, therefore, naturally no woman can give birth without seed, yet the text says, "A woman who has received seed and born a male," it follows certainly that at some time a woman would bear a male without receiving male seed, and would be clean from every stain. This was to be none other than the mother of the Messiah, about whom the prophets later spoke more openly. For Isaiah says this of her in chapter 7: "And God added to speak to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign, or a miracle, from the Lord your God, make the petition deep, or exalt it on high." And Ahaz said: "I will not ask, and I will not tempt God." And he (Isaiah) said: "Hear then, O

<column-break/>

house of David, is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary also my God? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign, or a miracle. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel." Although these words are so clear that they do not need explanation, the Jews of this current time try to distort them from their true sense in many ways. We shall refute their false claims in the following chapter when we respond to their objections. Now let us hear Jeremiah, saying in chapter 31: ברא יהוה חדשה בארץ נקבה תסובב גבר <note>original: 'Bara Yehovah chadashah ba-aretz nekevah tesovev gaver'</note> That is: "God has created a new thing on the earth, a woman shall encompass a man," or "a strong one," or "a powerful one," that is, God—according to the glosses of the ancient Jews, and especially of him whom they call Rabbenu Haccados, that is, Our Holy Master, in the book which he called גלי רזיא *Gale Razia*, that is, *The Revealer of Secrets*, at the second petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome. That this was the Messiah, and that he was to be encompassed by a virgin woman in the womb through conception (for otherwise no "new thing" would have occurred in the world), is clear from what is read in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>A famous 11th-century preacher from Narbonne</note>, upon that saying in Genesis chapter 41: "And Pharaoh was dreaming." For there it is said that Rabbi Joshua the son of Levi said these exact words: "Come and see, for the way of the Holy and Blessed God is not like the way of flesh and blood. For flesh and blood wounds with a scalpel or a razor, and heals with a plaster. But the Holy and Blessed God does not have this kind of art; rather, he heals and cures with the very same things by which he wounds. And this is what is written in Jeremiah chapter 30: 'For I will bring a scar over you, and I will heal you from your wounds.' And so also you will find in Israel. For with the same thing by which he wounded them, he healed them. For they indeed sinned in a virgin. As it is said in Ezekiel chapter 23: 'And there the breasts of their virginity were pressed.' They were also punished in a virgin. As it is said in Lamentations chapter five: 'They humbled the women in Zion, the virgins in the cities of Judah.' And he also comforted them in a virgin, according to that saying of Jeremiah chapter 31: 'Return, O virgin of Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you wander, O apostate daughter? ...and that he might preserve the unconsumed substance of humanity within the very flame of divinity. We also read in the sixth chapter of the Book of Judges that Gideon said:

The virginity and integrity of the Mother of God was also signified by the rod of Aaron. Without any external moisture, by the power of God alone, it flowered, grew leaves, and bore fruit that was equally sweet and useful to both the healthy and the sick. For thus we read of it in the seventeenth chapter of Numbers:

It does not hinder our argument that the text says Aaron’s rod flowered "for the house of Levi." For the Messiah was destined to be born not only from the tribe of Judah, but also from the tribe of Levi, and even for the sake of the Gentiles. Therefore, against all laws of nature, Aaron’s rod produced what could be supplied neither by seed nor by root. If a rod was able to produce nuts against the course of nature, could the Virgin Mother of God not generate a Son beyond the laws of nature by the command of God? Let the unbelieving Jews tell us: by what means did a dry rod flower, leaf, and bring forth almonds? Then we shall tell them how a Virgin conceived and gave birth to the Son of God. But the Jews will not be able to explain the "conception" of the rod to us, nor can we explain the birth from a Virgin to them. Since they furthermore believe that Eve was formed from the body of Adam—claiming this happened by a miracle of the divine will—then they must be answered in the same way regarding the conception and birth of the Messiah from a Virgin. For the divine will has no need for the usual course or order of nature.

### CHAPTER XV.

->Refutation of the objections of modern Jews who<-
->attack the virginity of the Messiah's mother.<-

## CAPNIO.
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pen name of Johann Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a man's face and leafy vines.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH these things are so, the Jews of our time, desiring to attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother, do not cease to contradict in various ways that wonderful sign given by Isaiah concerning the virginal conception and birth, which you have introduced. They deem it impossible for a virgin to conceive and bear a son. Therefore, they assert that these words of Isaiah, when he said, "A virgin <term>Alma</term> <note>Isaiah 7:14 uses the Hebrew word 'Almah,' which Christians translate as 'virgin' and Jewish commentators often translate as 'young woman.'</note> shall conceive and bear a son," should not be understood as referring to the mother of the Messiah, as their ancient predecessors explained, and as the Catholic faith affirms those words were spoken concerning the glorious Virgin Mary. On this point, they are accustomed to make many arguments against us.

<column-break/>

<page-num>418</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

<margin>The first argument of the Jews.</margin>
To ensure that their "barking" against the mother of the Messiah may be silenced, I desire you to answer them using their own scriptures. First, they argue as follows: This sign (they say) which the prophet gave, was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. However, your Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz. Therefore, this could not be a sign of his conception from a virgin.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
GALATINUS: It will be easy for us to answer this argument if we first briefly note the history for the sake of understanding the prophetic truth. In the time when Ahaz reigned in Judah, two powerful kings—namely, those of Syria and Israel—besieged Jerusalem with a massive army, as written in Isaiah chapter 7 and 2 Kings 16. Then the Lord God sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But he, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), refused to believe the prophet’s words. For this reason, the prophet urged him,

since he did not believe, to ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: *Ask a sign for yourself, or a miracle from the Lord your God. Ask it in the depths or in the heights above.* That is: Ask for a sign of your liberation to be made, whether from the depths of hell through the resurrection of some dead man, or from heaven by the stopping of the sun, as was done in the time of Joshua. But he, being impious and unwilling to ask for a sign from God, offered an excuse, saying that this would be tempting God. Whence he said: *I will not ask, and I will not tempt.*

Since Isaiah knew that Ahaz had not said this in good faith, but rather because he had no fear of God, he judged him unworthy of such a sign. He refused to give the sign to him personally, but gave it to the House of David, saying: *Hear then, O House of David; is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.*

From this it is clear that the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was not given to Ahaz himself, but to the House of David, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born according to the flesh. Therefore, we must deny what is said in the argument—namely, that this sign was given to Ahaz. Furthermore, to the point that Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, and thus his virginal conception could not be a sign of liberation from those two kings, we say that two types of signs are found in Holy Scripture: one is <term>prognostic</term> and the other is <term>rememorative</term>.

<margin>The two types of signs: prognostic and rememorative.</margin>
A **prognostic** sign is one regarding a future event. An example is the one given to Gideon (as said in Judges chapter 6) regarding the fleece, which indicated a future victory. A **rememorative** sign, however, is one regarding the past [or confirming a promise]. Such was the sign that the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus chapter 3, saying:
**"And this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall worship God upon this mountain."** <note>original: וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים על ההר הזה; Exodus 3:12</note>
That is: you shall give thanks to me for this mission which is imposed upon you. Therefore, the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was rememorative, not prognostic. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way...

**"For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her vindication shines out like the dawn, and her salvation like a blazing torch."** <note>original: למען ציון לא אחשה ולמען ירושלם לא אשקוט וגו׳; Isaiah 62:1</note> That is to say: *For Zion’s sake I will not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not be still, until her righteous one goes forth as brightness, and her salvation burns like a lamp.* And this is what the Scripture says in the fifth chapter of Judges: **"God chooses new things; then he shall fight at the gates."** <note>original: יבחר אלהים חדשים אז לחם שערים; Judges 5:8. <margin>A</margin> **"Countenance by countenance, or face by face, he leads us into the knowledge of the faces. ->Refutation of the objections of modern Jews who impugn the virginity of the Messiah's mother.<-

### CAPNIO

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a figure (putto) surrounded by grapevine and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
Although these things are so, the Jews of our time, desiring to attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother, do not cease to contradict in many ways that wonderful sign of the virginal conception and birth given by Isaiah and introduced by you. They consider it impossible for a virgin to conceive and bear a son. Therefore they assert that these words of Isaiah, when he said, "The *Alma* <term>Hebrew: almah; usually translated as young woman or virgin</term> shall conceive and bear a son," ought not to be understood as referring to the mother of the Messiah, as their ancient predecessors interpreted it, and as the Catholic faith affirms those same aforementioned words were spoken concerning the glorious Virgin Mary. On this account, they are accustomed to make many arguments against us.

<sig>S iij</sig>

Against these arguments—so that their barking against the Mother of the Messiah may fall silent—I desire you to respond through their own scriptures. 
<margin>*The first argument of the Jews.*</margin>
This sign (they say) which the prophet gave, was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. But your Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz. Therefore, this sign could not have been for his conception from a virgin. 
<margin>*The Solution:*</margin>
GALATINUS: It will be easy for us to answer this argument if we first briefly note the history for the understanding of prophetic truth. At the time when Ahaz reigned in Judea, when two powerful kings—namely of Syria and Israel—had besieged Jerusalem with a massive army, as is written in Isaiah chapter 7 and 2 Kings chapter 16, the Lord God then sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But he, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), would not believe the words of the prophet. For this reason, the prophet warned him that, since he did not believe, he should ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: *Ask a sign for yourself, or a miracle from the Lord your God. Ask it in the depths, or in the heights above.* That is: Ask for a sign of your liberation to be made, whether from the depth of hell through the resurrection of some dead man, or from heaven through the standing still of the sun, as was done in the time of Joshua. But he, since he was impious and unwilling to ask a sign from God, offered an excuse: that this would be tempting God. Whence he said: *I will not ask, and I will not tempt.*
<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, when Isaiah realized that Ahaz had said this not in good faith, but rather because he had no fear of God at all, he judged him unworthy of such a sign and refused to give the sign to him. Instead, he gave it to the House of David, saying: *Hear then, O house of David; is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.*
<margin>E</margin>
From these things it is clear that the sign concerning the virgin's conception and birth was not given to Ahaz himself, but to the house of David, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born according to the flesh. Therefore, what is said in the argument—namely, that this sign was given to Ahaz himself—must be denied. As for the claim that since Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, his conception from a virgin could not be a sign of the aforementioned liberation from those two kings, we say that a two-fold sign is found in Holy Scripture: one is prognostic, the other rememorative. 
<margin>*The two-fold sign: prognostic and rememorative.*</margin>
A prognostic sign is one in respect to a future event. Of such a kind was that which (as is said in Judges chapter 6) was given to Gideon in the fleece as an indicator of future victory. A rememorative sign, however, is in respect to the past. Of such a kind was that which the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus chapter 3, saying:
<margin>F</margin> 
**"And this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."** <note>original: וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים אל ההר הזה; Exodus 3:12</note> 
This is: *And this will be a sign for you, that I have sent you. When you have led my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice upon this mountain,* namely, giving thanks to me for this mission which is imposed upon you. Therefore, the sign of the virgin's conception and birth was rememorative, not prognostic. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way...
<margin>G</margin>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological debate regarding the prophecy of the Virgin Birth in Isaiah 7:14. Galatinus is responding to Jewish objections concerning the specific Hebrew vocabulary used to describe the "virgin."</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...just as a sign of remembrance looks back to a past event from a great distance, so a prophetic sign looks forward to the future. It was certainly fitting for this sign to be given from a great distance so that Ahaz, who was unbelieving toward the prophet’s word, would have a sign as far removed from himself as his own mind was from belief. Nevertheless, those who were to descend from him were destined to see it eventually. Therefore, this sign was given not to him alone, but to the house of David. <term>Capnio</term> <note>Representing the scholar Johann Reuchlin.</note> Then they object:

<margin>*The second Jewish argument.*</margin> 
<margin>B</margin>
That where our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> says, *Behold, a virgin*, the Hebrew letter places **העלמה** (*haalma*). They say that among them, *Alma* does not signify a "virgin," but rather a "young woman," a term used for both a virgin and one who has been "corrupted" <note>A period term for a woman who has had sexual intercourse.</note>. Therefore, they say the prophet was not speaking of a virgin’s conception and birth, but that of a young woman. For if he had spoken of a virgin’s conception, he would not have said "Behold, the *alma*" (that is, the young woman), 

<margin>*The Solution.*</margin>
but "Behold, the **בתולה** (*bethula*)," which is the specific word for "virgin." <term>Galatinus</term> As you know, there are three words among the Hebrews that mean nearly the same thing: namely **נערה** (*Naara*), **בתולה** (*bethula*), and **עלמה** (*alma*). 

<margin>C</margin>
*Naara* refers only to age, signifying a girl or a young woman, whether she is a virgin or corrupted. *Bethula*, however, refers strictly to virginity, signifying a virgin whether she be a young girl or an old woman. But *Alma* refers to both: namely, to youth and to virginity; it designates both a young woman and a virgin. Therefore, a woman—whether she be a girl or advanced in years—can be called a *bethula* as long as she is a virgin. 

<margin>D</margin>
As long as she is a young girl, whether virgin or corrupted, she is called a *naara*. But she cannot be called an *alma* unless she is both a young woman and an untouched virgin. The very interpretation of the word clearly indicates this. For **עלמה** (*alma*) is derived from the verb **עלם** (*alam*), which means "to hide" or "to conceal," as Rabbi Kimhi says in his *Book of Roots* <note>original: "Serafsim," referring to Sefer HaShorashim by David Kimhi, a famous 12th-13th century grammarian.</note>. It is like what is said in <term>Psalm 90</term>: 

<margin>E</margin>
**שת עונותינו לנגדך עלמנו למאור פניך** 
That is: *You have set our iniquities before you, our hidden sins in the light of your countenance.* And again in <term>Psalm 44</term>: 
**הוא יודע תעלמות לב** 
This is: *He himself knows the secrets of the heart.* And in <term>Job chapter 28</term>: 
**ותעלמה יוציא אור** 
That is: *And the hidden things he brings forth into the light.* Likewise in <term>Genesis chapter 24</term>: 
**העלמה לשאב** 
This is: *The Alma [young woman] coming out to draw water.* All these (says Rabbi Kimhi) signify "hiding" and "concealing." 

<margin>F</margin>
For this reason, *alma* among them signifies a young woman hidden, concealed, and kept away from the sights of men, and entirely untouched—one whose modesty and integrity is beyond doubt. This is especially true when the "article" is prefixed to it, which in Hebrew is the letter **ה** (*he*). This makes the word refer to a specific person and is often added to those who are either well-known or of whom prior mention has been made. Nor in all of Holy Scripture is this word **העלמה** (*haalma*) found written with the letter *he* (the article) except in three places. 

<margin>G</margin>
The first is indeed in <term>Genesis chapter 24</term>, when it is said of Rebecca: 
**הנה אנכי נצב על עין המים והיה העלמה היצאת לשאב ואמרתי אליה השקיני נא מעט מים מכדך** 
That is: *Behold, I stand by the spring of water, and it shall be that the haalma [the young woman], who comes out to draw water, and I say to her: Give me, I pray, a little water from your jar.* While she was called *alma*, she was a virgin and untouched, as is clear from

---

<page-num>420</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

<margin>A</margin>
the text, which says of her in the same place: 
**בתולה ואיש לא ידעה** 
This is: *A virgin, and no man had known her.* <note>Genesis 24:16</note> Next, it is found in <term>Exodus chapter 2</term>, when it is written of Miriam, the sister of Moses: 
**ותלך העלמה ותקרא את אם הילד** 
That is: *And the haalma [the young woman] went and called the mother of the child.* And she also was a young virgin at that time. 

<margin>B</margin>
Thirdly and finally, it is found here in this passage of Isaiah, as was shown a little earlier. Excepting these three places, nowhere else in the entire Holy Scripture of the Hebrews is this word *haalma* found written with the article. If, therefore, the first two women so named were untouched virgins when they were thus described, the same must be held for the one of whom Isaiah speaks. For according to the opinion of the wise, entirely similar cases must be subject to an entirely identical judgment. 

<margin>C</margin>
For that reason, when the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> reached this place, they translated *haalma* as "the virgin" with the article prefixed, saying **ἡ νεᾶνις** <note>original Greek: "the young woman"; though usually the debate focuses on "parthenos," Galatinus here cites "neanis" while arguing for its virginal meaning.</note>. And so on. Furthermore, that it must be understood this way is clear from the fact that the sign given by Isaiah for the liberation of the city was intended to be truly miraculous, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says. 

<margin>D</margin>
But for a young woman to conceive and bear a son without remaining a virgin is no miracle, since this happens naturally every day. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the sign the prophet gave them—namely, that a virgin would conceive and bear a son—would occur contrary to the way of nature and by the miracle of God alone. 

Because, then (to respond to the Jewish objection), the woman who was to conceive and bear the Son of God had to be both a girl (a young woman) and an entirely untouched virgin, Isaiah said "Behold, the *haalma*" to imply both. He did not say "Behold, the *bethula*," which designates only one of those things. 

<margin>E</margin>
Moreover, if he had said "Behold, the *bethula*," he would not have prefigured the absolute virginity of the Messiah's mother. For although *bethula* signifies a virgin, it does not always mean one who is entirely untouched. Rabbi Solomon shows this clearly when commenting on that passage in <term>Genesis chapter 24</term>: *She was a bethula [virgin], and no man had known her.* 

Wanting to give the reason why the text, after saying she was a *bethula*, added "and no man had known her," he says: 
**בתולה ואיש לא ידעה לא ידעה שלא כדרכה לפי שבנות הגוים משמרות עצמן ממקום בתוליהן ומפקירות עצמן ממקום אחר על כן העיד על זו הפכו שהייתה נקייה מכל** 

<margin>F</margin>
This means: *She was a virgin, and no man had known her—that is, even in an "unnatural" way. For the daughters of the nations used to guard themselves in the place of their virginity, but prostituted themselves in another place; therefore, the text testifies that this one was the opposite, for she was clean in everything,* that is, entirely unknown and untouched. From this it is manifest that a *bethula* is not necessarily someone entirely untouched and unknown, since she could be corrupted in an "unnatural" manner and known by men. But *Alma* signifies one entirely untouched and completely unknown in every way.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>*The third Jewish argument.*</margin> 
<term>Capnio</term> To this the Jews say: If **העלמה** (*haalma*) with the article requires some prior mention of the person to have been made, and of this virgin—whom you Christians claim was to conceive and bear a child while preserving her virginity—no mention preceded in Isaiah himself, nor in any other prophet: it plainly follows...

<meta>This page continues the debate between Galatinus and his interlocutors regarding the Hebrew word "almah." Having established that "almah" refers to a hidden virgin, the text now moves to a specific scriptural defense using the Book of Proverbs and the interpretations of ancient rabbinic authorities to prove the Messiah’s miraculous birth.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...that the virgin of whom you speak is not the one mentioned by Isaiah when he says, *Behold, a virgin (haalma) shall conceive and bear a son.* <note>Isaiah 7:14</note>. Therefore, by these words, you cannot prove the virginity of the Messiah’s mother. **GALATINUS.**

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
On the contrary, Solomon made mention of that same virgin under the name *almah* long before Isaiah. In the thirtieth chapter of Proverbs, he says: <note>Proverbs 30:18-19</note> *Three things are wonderful to me, and a fourth I have not known: the way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the heart (or middle) of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman (haalma),* that is, with a virgin. With these words, Solomon most excellently described the "ways" of the Messiah. Beginning with his final way—that is, his ascension into heaven—he eventually arrives at the first—that is, his incarnation, which was to come from a virgin. We need not seek any other commentator for these "ways" than the one whom the Jews themselves call **Rabbenü haccados** <note>Hebrew: "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>. In the book titled **Gale razia** <note>Hebrew: "Revealer of Secrets."</note>, in response to a petition from Antoninus, a Consul of the city of Rome, who asked for an explanation of these same words, he says: "You have asked a great thing. But because it is said in the 11th chapter of Proverbs: *He who hides grain (meaning doctrine or the explanation of the law) shall be cursed among the people,* I will tell you a most sublime thing. The *way of the eagle in the heavens* is the King Messiah, who after his passion shall ascend into heaven. Just as it is said in the ninth chapter of Amos: *He who builds his ascension in heaven.* The *way of a ship in the middle of the sea*: This is also the King Messiah, whose way shall be tossed like a ship in the middle of the sea, as it is said in the thirtieth chapter of Jeremiah: *Why have I seen every man with his hands on his loins?* <note>Jeremiah 30:6</note>. 'Man' here refers to God, who in Hebrew is called **gheber**, meaning strong or powerful, since God himself is the strength and power of all. And the *way of the serpent upon a rock*: This is also the King Messiah, who shall make himself like the serpent that Moses placed upon a rock to lead the children of Israel into the holy land." Furthermore, Rabbi Judah said: "And the *way of the serpent upon a rock*: This is the King Messiah, who shall pass through the rock after he has been buried and shall emerge from it, and the path by which he passed shall not be seen; as it is said in the thirty-third chapter of Exodus: *Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand upon the rock. and when my glory passes by, I will set you in a hole in the rock.* <note>Exodus 33:21-22</note>. And the way of the **gheber** (the man, or the strong and powerful one) in the **alma** (the young woman/virgin): This too is God, who loves the daughters of Jerusalem so that the King Messiah may be generated from one of them. She shall conceive and bear a son, yet remain a virgin; as it is said in the thirty-first chapter of Jeremiah: *Because God has created a new thing upon the earth, a woman shall encompass a man (**gheber**),* that is, the strong and powerful one, which is God." All of this is according to the word of **Rabbenü haccados**. Therefore, the *way of the gheber*—the strong man or God—in the *alma*—the virgin—was the incarnation of the Son of God from a virgin.

<column-break/>

And this "way" Solomon could not fully and perfectly know: for how a virgin could conceive without human seed, and enclose the perfect God and man in her womb, and give birth to a son while remaining a virgin, Solomon's intellect could not fully grasp, nor could any tongue ever explain. For this reason, he rightly said: *And a fourth I have not known.* Justly, therefore, does Isaiah say of the mother of the Messiah: **Hinne haalmah hara**, that is, *Behold, the virgin shall conceive,* using the letter *he* (the definite article "the"), as if speaking of someone already known among the prophets, whom Solomon had already mentioned.

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
**B** The perversity of the Jews of our age, in opposition to what has been said regarding the *alma*, still cries out with mockery and blasphemy, saying: "Follow the text you have introduced! Read further what follows in Proverbs 30." For there you will find written immediately after: *Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who eats and wipes her mouth and says, I have done no wickedness.* <note>Proverbs 30:20</note>. "Behold," they say, "the word *alma* in this place can only mean a 'corrupted' woman, because it is compared to an adulteress."

<margin>Confutation.</margin>
**C GALATINUS.** To repress their audacity, it is answered that Solomon's words in this book are called **Misle** <note>Hebrew: *Mishlei*, meaning Proverbs or Parables.</note> because they almost always present one thing on the surface but intend another. Otherwise, a **Massal** (a Parable, similitude, or example) would not be a *Massal* if it were understood exactly as it sounds.

**D** Therefore, we should not take "the way of the adulterous woman" here literally, but rather as the life and wicked behavior of someone else who imitates the actions of an adulteress. For this reason, some of the ancient Jews understood "the way of the adulterous woman" in this passage to mean the transgression of our first parent <note>Adam</note>.

**E** Hence, that same teacher whom we said is called **Rabbenu Haccados** (Our Holy Teacher), explaining this passage in the same place, says: "*Such is the way of an adulterous woman,* etc. Adam did all of this, for he excused himself for his sin and refused to confess it, but said: *The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave to me from the tree, and I ate.* He acted like a harlot who eats and wipes her mouth, contending she has done nothing wrong. For this reason, it is consistent with reason that the whole world should be punished. And when the time of salvation comes, it is just that God should descend to the depths and save them. And this is what was said in the second chapter of Jeremiah: *Behold, I will judge with you because you said, I have not sinned.* Also in the sixty-sixth chapter of Isaiah: *For in fire the Lord shall be judged.*" Thus far the Rabbi.

<margin>The Jews are compared to an adulterous woman.</margin>
**F** We, however, can say that the "way of this adulterous woman" also aptly designates the faithlessness of the Jews, to whom the Lord says through Isaiah in the fifty-seventh chapter: *But draw near hither, you sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the harlot.* <note>Isaiah 57:3</note>.

**G** Concerning them, it is also written in the sixteenth chapter of Ezekiel: *Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem... and you were not like a harlot in scorning hire, but like an adulterous woman who takes strangers instead of her husband.* <note>Ezekiel 16:30-32</note>.

<margin>A</margin>...not a price to be despised, but like an adulterous woman who, while under her husband or in place of her husband, receives strangers. And later in the same place, <note>original: "ושפטתיך משפטי נואפות ושפכת דם ונתתיך דם חמה וקנאה"</note> *And I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and those who shed blood, and I will give you the blood of fury and jealousy.* <note>Ezekiel 16:38</note> From these things, therefore, it is clear that the adulterous woman in the aforementioned parable of Solomon is the Jewish synagogue, which eats, and does not cease to eat, that bread most savory to her, about which it is written in the 20th chapter of Proverbs: 

<margin>B</margin><note>original: "ערב לאיש לחם שקר ואחר ימלא פיהו חצץ"</note> *The bread of deceit is savory to a man, and afterwards (or finally) his mouth shall be filled with gravel.* <note>Proverbs 20:17</note> In this place, "gravel" is nothing other than the eternal punishment of hell. For since gravel is hard, it cannot be chewed, nor consumed, nor swallowed, nor spat out when the whole mouth is full; thus the punishment of hell is indeed most harsh and durable, and it can in no way be escaped, nor ended, nor diminished, nor softened by any moisture of tears. Moreover, that the bread of deceit is sweet and savory to the Jews is 

<margin>C</margin>most clearly shown by what is said of them in the ninth chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: "ואמת לא ידברו למדו לשונם דבר שקר"</note> *And they do not speak the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies.* <note>Jeremiah 9:5</note> Likewise, in the fifth chapter of the same: <note>original: "ואם חי יהוה יאמרו לכן לשקר ישבעו"</note> *And though they say, "As the Lord lives," yet they will swear to a lie, or to falsehood, or to fraud.* <note>Jeremiah 5:2</note> Just as, therefore, the way of an eagle in the sky, and the way of a serpent upon a rock, and the way of a ship in the heart or middle of the sea, and the way of a man or a powerful one—that is, God—in an *almah*, that is, in a virgin, were made wonderful and difficult to Solomon, and far distant from his understanding: so the way of this most wicked adulteress was to him extremely wonderful and far distant from his reason. For how could or should Solomon's reason have grasped the immensity of malice, the depth of impiety, and the magnitude of perfidy by which this adulteress was to condemn the just and 

<margin>E</margin>entirely innocent Messiah to death, and to ask for the release of Barabbas, the seditious murderer? Or how could the intellect of the same wise man have sufficed to comprehend by what folly, what madness, what poverty of mind, stimulated by what diabolical envy, or driven by what blind demon, she could reject the true Messiah—who by his word alone gave light to the blind, direction to the lame, healing to the weak, cleansing to the lepers, speech to the mute, and hearing to the deaf, who freed the demon-possessed, and satisfied many thousands of men with a few loaves—and to accept two false Messiahs, 

<margin>F</margin>who had never done any such thing, one after another as the true Messiah? Namely, Bencozba <note>The text refers to Simon bar Kokhba, the leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 CE). His name was often punned as "Bar Koziba," meaning "Son of a Lie."</note> before the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and Barcozba at Bittir <note>The final fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> not long after the burning of the same city; whom she should have held in horror and suspicion by their name alone, since both are interpreted as "son of a lie" or "falsehood." Most excellently, therefore, did Solomon himself, marveling at the height of the mysteries of the four aforementioned ways—that is, of the Messiah—and the ingratitude, impiety, and perfidy of this adulterous woman, add these words: *Such is the way of an adulterous woman;* so wonderful, namely, and difficult to understand, and more astounding than can be

<margin>A</margin>expressed: she who eats the bread of so many lies, and still does not cease to eat it so greedily. <margin>Exposition of the preceding words of Isaiah.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>the holy and hidden virgin herself, whom Solomon remembered long before, *shall conceive* by divine power *and bear a son.* And the virgin herself, forewarned and instructed by the Angel Gabriel, and filled with the Holy Spirit, shall call his name Emmanuel, which is the same as "God with us," by which the union of divine and human natures in the one person of the Messiah is clearly demonstrated. As for the other arguments of the Jews, which they are accustomed to make against us so that they might pervert the true sense of this prophecy, we have already responded more fully in the 

<margin>C</margin>third book, where we showed that the Messiah was to be called Emmanuel.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->That the mother of the Messiah, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, was to<-
->conceive the Son of God.<-

### CAPNIO <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

<margin>D</margin>I would like to know, not without reason, whether the ancient Jews, just as they predicted that the mother of the Messiah would conceive and give birth as a virgin, also foretold that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit. **GALATINUS.** That was indeed foretold by the prophets long ago, and expressly explained by the ancient Doctors of the Jews. For among the prophets, Isaiah, speaking in the person of the

<margin>A</margin>...[swift] to the robbing of spoils, and hastening to the plundering of prey. These things in no way fit the son of Isaiah, since he was never called by such a name, nor is there any mention in Holy Scripture of his name, his life, his deeds, or his death. Therefore, these descriptions most aptly fit the Messiah, who was to be swift in plundering Hell <note>This refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," a traditional Christian belief that Christ descended into the underworld to liberate souls after his death.</note> and hastening to take the prey—that is, to take away from the devil the prey he possessed because of the sin of the first man. Our Messiah testified that this was already being fulfilled in himself when he said in the 11th chapter of Luke: "When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are undisturbed. But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted and distributes his spoils." <margin>B</margin> Concerning the preceding points, however, let us ask two things of the Jews. First, for what purpose did the prophet bring in those witnesses? Did he truly need witnesses when approaching his wife for intercourse? It is shameful even to think of such a thing, let alone say it. Furthermore, who were these witnesses—namely Uriah the priest <margin>C</margin> and Zechariah the son of Berechiah? It is certain that this Uriah was not that worshiper of idols (as some of our people think) to whom Ahaz wrote letters from Damascus (as read in 2 Kings, chapter 16). Rather, he is the one mentioned by Jeremiah in chapter 26, saying: "There was a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah the son of Shemaiah, whom King Jehoiakim killed." It is also certain that this Zechariah, son of Berechiah, was the one who is the eleventh among the twelve minor prophets. <margin>D</margin> According to the expositions of the Hebrews, Isaiah speaks of these men here. However, it happened that these men were born long after Isaiah. From this, it is clear that Isaiah did not speak those words in his own person, but in the person of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, before the Holy Spirit approached the "prophetess"—that is, that Virgin who was to conceive and bear the Savior—so that by his power and cooperation she might conceive and bear the Son of God without a man’s seed, he ought to have employed these prophets as witnesses of the future truth. <margin>E</margin> For one of them, namely Uriah the son of Shemaiah, predicted many evils that would come upon the Jews and their city, which later befell them in the Babylonian captivity. The other, however—that is, Zechariah the son of Berechiah—prophesied many and very great good things that would come to them at the arrival of the Messiah. This is especially true when he said in the 2nd chapter: <note>original: "רני ושמחי בת ציון כי הנני בא ושיכנתי בתוכך נאם יהוה"</note> That is, "Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion. For behold, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord." <note>Zechariah 2:10</note> And again in the ninth chapter: <note>original: "גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע הוא"</note> <margin>F</margin> that is, "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, the Just One and the Savior himself." <note>Zechariah 9:9</note> That this is as we have explained is most clearly seen through the *Targum* <term>Targum: An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</term> of Rabbi Jonathan, which reads in that place: <note>original: "ואסהיר קדמי סהדין מהימנין ית לוטי דאמרית לאיתאה בנבואת אוריה כהנא והא אתו ואף כל נחמתא דאמרית לאיתאה בנבואת זכריה בן ברכיה אנא עתיד לאיתאה"</note> <margin>G</margin> which is: "And I have called to witness on my part the bad testimonies which I said would come in the prophecy of Uriah the Priest: Behold, it shall also be so, that every consolation which I said would come in the prophecy—"

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section, where the author uses Jewish sources and chronological calculations to prove that the "witnesses" mentioned by Isaiah were prophetic figures who lived long after Isaiah’s time, thereby identifying the "prophetess" not as Isaiah’s wife, but as the Virgin Mary.</meta>

### BOOK SEVEN

...[the prophecy of] Zechariah will be fulfilled. Having heard this, they spoke words of this kind to Rabbi Akiba: "You have comforted us, you have comforted us." All these things are found in the Talmud. From this it clearly follows that these are the same prophets of whom Isaiah spoke in the person of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, it can easily be seen that these prophets were born long after Isaiah. For Uriah was indeed slain by King Jehoiakim, but Isaiah uttered the aforementioned words in the fourth year of King Ahaz (as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> says). Now, from the fourth year of Ahaz until Jehoiakim, 140 years passed. For all the years in which Ahaz reigned were 16. Subtracting four from these, 12 remain, at the beginning of which the aforementioned prophecy of Isaiah occurred. Then his son Hezekiah reigned for 29 years. After him, Manasseh for 55. Then Amon for two years. Afterward, Josiah for 31 years. Then Jehoahaz for three months. After him, Jehoiakim—who killed the aforementioned prophet Uriah—reigned for 11 years. All these years, taken together, total 160 years and three months. <note>The author's arithmetic here (12+29+55+2+31+11) actually equals 140; the total of 160 may reflect a different chronological tradition or include the full reign of Ahaz and other factors.</note> From this it is quite clearly evident that the first witness, namely Uriah, whom Isaiah (or the Holy Spirit) called to himself, was not yet born when he was called. Regarding the second witness, Zechariah, no one should doubt this: since from the fifth year of Ahaz until the second year of Darius, when Zechariah himself prophesied, 250 years passed. Therefore, since these prophets—great as they were—whom the Holy Spirit called through Isaiah as witnesses regarding the virgin prophetess and her son Emmanuel, were not yet born in the time of Isaiah, it is revealed to all who have a sound use of reason that the prophetess of whom the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah (saying: "I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son") was not yet born either. Consequently, she could not have been Isaiah’s wife, as the younger, delusional Jews falsely affirm. Rather, she was that Virgin who, by the intervention of the Holy Spirit, was to conceive and bear the Son of God, of whom he had also made mention a little earlier, saying: "Behold, a Virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel." From this it is also clear that this "approaching" the prophetess was to be a spiritual event. Since things are so, it is clear that this prophetess was none other than the Virgin Mary, who was to conceive and bear the Messiah, the Son of God. The Holy Spirit "approached" her when—as Luke says in Chapter 1—in the sixth month after the conception of John the Baptist, the Angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin's name was Mary. And the Angel, having entered to her, said: G <note>original Hebrew: "Shalom hen mele'ah Yahweh immakh berukhah at ba-nashim"</note> "Greetings, full of grace, the Lord is with you, blessed are you among women." When she heard this, she was troubled by his speech and pondered what kind of greeting this might be. And the Angel said to her: <note>original Hebrew: "Al tira'i Miryam ki matzat hen..."</note> "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace

<column-break/>

before God. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. A He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God shall give to him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." But Mary said to the Angel: B <note>original Hebrew: "Eikh yihyeh ofan ve-asiyah ve-zeh ki ish eineni yoda'at"</note> "How shall this be done, since I do not know a man?" And the Angel answering said to her: <note>original Hebrew: "Ruakh ha-Kodesh yavo alayikh ve-yekholet elyon yasokh lakhi..."</note> "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. And therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God. And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman, she also has conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren. Because no word shall be impossible with God." Then Mary said: C <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-hinneh shiphkat Yahweh ye'aseh li ki-devarekha"</note> "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word." Having said this, she immediately conceived the Son of God. Nor is it a wonder that the more recent Jews by no means understand these things, so evident as being handed down by their own fathers, since the same prophet D showed this in the same chapter, saying: <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-hikkiti l'Yahweh ha-mastir panav mi-beit Ya'akov"</note> "And I will wait for God, who hides His face from the house of Jacob."

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
CHAPTER [V]. There is one thing that the younger Jews object against us here. They say that when the prophet, in the person of the Holy Spirit, said, "And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived, and bore," he spoke not of the future, but of the past.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
GALATINUS. This objection certainly does not strike at us, nor does it satisfy their hunger. For it is the custom of Divine Scripture (as is well known to you) very often to put the past tense in place of the future.

<margin>The past is put for the future.</margin>
E This is because the word of God is considered no differently than a completed deed. As is beautifully said in the *Midrash Tillim*—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—regarding that statement in Psalm 107: <note>original Hebrew: "Yomru ge'ulei Yahweh asher ge'alam mi-yad tzar"</note> "Let the redeemed of the Lord say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the oppressor." There, among other things, these words are found written in Hebrew: F <note>original: "Amar Rabbi Yehudah bar Shalom..."</note> "Rabbi Judah bar Shalom said: It is beautifully said, 'He redeemed,' although it was yet to be in the future. Because the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is as a deed. Rabbi Hunna said in the name of Rabbi Dustai, in the name of Rabbi Samuel bar Nahman: We are taught from another place also that the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is a deed. From whom do you learn this? From Abraham. What is written in the book of Genesis, the fifteenth chapter? 'On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your descendants I have given [this land].' It does not say 'I will give,' but 'I have given,' and yet up to that time he had not yet fathered children. But the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is a deed. The Holy One said: I have spoken the word, and the deed is done."

<meta>This spread, comprising pages 429 and 430, continues the dialogue between Capnio (Johann Reuchlin) and Galatinus. <margin>A</margin> <term>On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your seed I have given this land.</term> <note>original: "ביום ההוא כרת יהוה את אברהם ברית לאמר לזרעך נתתי את הארץ הזאת" (Genesis 15:18)</note> That is, on that day God established a pact with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I have given this land." He did not say: "I will give," but "I have given." And how could this be, since Abraham had not yet fathered children? Because God’s word is as good as an action already performed; that is why He spoke this way. From this we are also taught that God’s word is an accomplished deed when it is said, "I the Lord have spoken, and I have done it." And when did He do it? Is it not because God’s word is considered a finished act? Therefore, it was rightly said, "He has redeemed," even though it was yet to happen. This is the tradition. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, in the commentaries of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note> on that passage of Isaiah, "I have done these things for them," he says: "I have done," that is, "I will do." For the entire language of the prophets speaks of the future as if it were already done. From these points, it is clear that the Jewish objection carries no weight at all. Since, according to the aforementioned tradition, those words of Isaiah must be understood as: "And I went," meaning "I shall go to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore," meaning "she shall conceive and shall bear a son."

<margin>D</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial E depicting a bearded scholar or saint seated at a desk with a book on a lectern.</image-desc> From these points, it has also been excellently shown that the glorious Virgin, the mother of the Messiah, was to be a prophetess. <margin>A</margin> all things, from the beginning even to the end—something that none of the prophets was ever able to know. For she is the mistress and teacher of all the prophets. <margin>C</margin> ## CHAPTER XVIII.

->That the mother of the Messiah was to be the throne of God, upon which the Divine Majesty was to sit.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>D</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial E depicting a figure walking through a classical doorway or archway towards a landscape.</image-desc> When Jeremiah uttered those words in chapter 17: <term>A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary, the hope of Israel, the Lord;</term> <note>original: "כסא כבוד מרום מראשון מקום מקדשינו מקוה ישראל יהוה" (Jeremiah 17:12)</note> what is understood there by the "throne of glory"? GALATINUS: You speak rightly, my Capnio. Explaining in what way a "throne" is attributed to God, he says among other things: "It is known what a throne signifies. When anyone sees one decorated and prepared in the manner of a high priest, he will suppose that some King or Emperor is to sit in it. For the throne itself shows the excellence and majesty of the one sitting. By this reasoning, the house of God is called the throne of God, since it shows His dominion and power, He who reveals His glory and <margin>F</margin> brightness within it. This is why Jeremiah said, 'A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary.' By the same reasoning, the heavens are called the throne of God, insofar as they show the strength of the Creator, the mover and governor of this lower world, and reveal the influence of His grace. Therefore it was said in Isaiah, chapter 66: <term>The heavens are my throne.</term> <note>original: "השמים כסאי"</note> It is as if He says: 'The heavens continually show my essence, strength, and power.' Just as a throne suggests the dominion and majesty of him who is worthy to sit in it. This, however, is necessary for one who believes in God: not that this throne is a physical body in which God sits. Far be it, that anyone should fall into this error..."

<meta>This page continues the theological debate regarding the nature of the Messiah and his mother, drawing heavily on the works of "Rabbi Moses the Egyptian" (Maimonides) and mystical interpretations of the Hebrew Bible to argue that the Virgin Mary was the "throne" of God foretold in prophecy.</meta>
