...we fall into error. For since we have already proved that God is not corporeal, how shall we say that He requires a physical place or tabernacle? It is certain, however (as we have said), that any place magnified by God with His glory, such as the Holy House <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note> or the heavens, is called His seat. Nevertheless, when God spoke more broadly in Exodus 17, saying: *Because the hand is on the throne of the Lord, and the war of the Lord is against Amalek from generation to generation*: <note>original: "כִּי יָד עַל כֵּס יָהּ מִלְחָמָה לַיהוָה בַּעֲמָלֵק מִדֹּר דֹּר"</note> this refers to the proper substance and essence of God. Nor should it be imagined that this seat is a thing distinct from Him, or created by God like His other creatures. For it would follow that God exists in time, and was without a seat before He had created it. To say or believe this is the greatest heresy, since it is written in Psalm 102: **ואתה יהוה לעולם תשב כסאך לדור ודור** <note>original Hebrew: "And you, O LORD, shall sit forever; your throne from generation to generation."</note> that is, *And You, O God, remain forever; Your throne from generation to generation.* This means: Just as You, O God, are eternal, so also Your throne is eternal. And for this reason, it is shown that this seat is not a thing distinct from God. Therefore, this seat, and whatever else signifies God’s own essence, are not things distinct from Him. Thus far speaks that <term>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>. From his words, three conclusions are drawn, as he himself introduces three kinds of seats, two of which are created, while the third is uncreated.

<margin>A triple kind of seats.</margin>
The first conclusion is: That the first created seat—which the Teacher himself <note>Maimonides</note> accepts as the Holy House, saying that in it the majesty of the seat is known because of its excellence—is more correctly understood as the pure mother of the Messiah. Because of her perfection and excellence, she was to be the seat of God, in whom He was to show His glory and brightness, which is the Messiah, the glory, light, and brightness of the whole world. Because of this, it was said in Isaiah chapter 9: **העם ההולכים בחשך ראו אור גדול יושבי בארץ צלמות אור נגה עליהם** <note>original Hebrew: "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; those dwelling in the land of the shadow of death, light has shone upon them."</note> that is, *The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; to those who sat in the land of the shadow of death, light has arisen.* Therefore, the words of Jeremiah, when he says, *A throne of glory, high from the beginning*; are not understood to mean the Holy House that was in Jerusalem. For although God showed His glory in it, that glory was nothing in comparison to the glory and brightness He was to show in the mother of the Messiah. Nor do we find that the Holy House existed from the beginning of the world, as it was proved in preceding sections that the mother of the Messiah existed. Furthermore, that Holy House cannot be called a "throne of glory," since the glorious seat of God must be perennial or perpetual, and not vanish away. For whatever God once accepts, He never dismisses. And although the two other seats of God which he mentions—namely the heavens and God’s own essence—one is perpetual and the other eternal, the Holy House in Jerusalem passed away and vanished in destruction. Finally, it follows in the text of Jeremiah: *The expectation of Israel, O God.* The true expectation and hope of Israel was none other than the Messiah, who was to come forth from his most holy mother. By these reasons, therefore, it is openly shown that the aforementioned words of Jeremiah must be understood not of the Holy House (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian felt), which fell along with Jerusalem, but of the mother of the Messiah, as you yourself most excellently perceive they should be understood. For she

<column-break/>

herself (as <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, though the work cited, "Gale Razia" (Revealer of Secrets), is a later mystical text attributed to him.</note> says in the book *Gale Razia*, in response to the third petition of Antoninus, the consul of the city of Rome) was to be the seat which God constructed, so that the King Messiah might sit in her, to show the glory of His majesty to all mortals. The second and third conclusions are: that the second seat is created, while the third is uncreated. These two seats of God are the Messiah himself.

<margin>The second conclusion is the humanity.</margin>
For his humanity is indeed created, which was made a seat for the Word of God; but the divinity itself is uncreated.

<margin>The humanity of the Messiah.</margin>
That the humanity of the Messiah is called the seat of God is clear through that saying of Psalm 45: **כסאך אלהים עולם ועד שבט מישר שבט מלכותך** <note>original Hebrew: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom."</note> *Your seat, O God, is perpetual and eternal; the scepter of direction, the scepter of Your kingdom.* For just as from the operation of the heavens, the glory of their designer is shown by this argument—whatever is moved necessarily has a mover and a governor; the heavens are moved, therefore they have a mover and a governor—so from the humanity of the Messiah, because of his divine works, it is shown that his underlying person is God, the founder and governor of the entire world. For just as the heavens show the glory of their mover and the moderation of this lower world by means of the influence of His grace, so the humanity of the Messiah shows the magnificence and dominion of the designer and mover of this world, by means of the influence of salvation, which God pours into that humanity.

<margin>The third seat is the divinity.</margin>
But the third seat he said was the divinity, which is uncreated. For the Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated, and the Holy Spirit is uncreated. The sense of those words which he cites—*But You, O God, remain forever; Your seat from generation to generation*—is this: Just as You, O God, are eternal, so Your seat, which is Your Son, is eternal; for the Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, the Holy Spirit is eternal. Therefore, from the words of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian himself, it is plainly shown (as we have proved) that the aforementioned words of Jeremiah—*A throne of glory, high from the beginning, the place of our sanctification*—must be understood regarding the most blessed mother of the Messiah, who is the seat of the most high God. He said, *From the beginning*, to show that she was conceived without original sin. This same point is also excellently suggested by that saying in the first chapter of Ezekiel: **וממעל לרקיע אשר על ראשם כמראה אבן ספיר דמות כסא ועל דמות הכסא דמות כמראה אדם עליו מלמעלה** <note>original Hebrew: "And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it."</note> that is, *And above the firmament, which was overhanging their head, like the appearance of a sapphire stone, was the likeness of a throne; and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above.* Here Ezekiel prophesied concerning the immaculate mother of the Messiah. For after he had seen the four living creatures and their movement, he said that he saw standing above the heads of the creatures in heaven the likeness of a throne or a seat, which is the glorious mother of the Messiah.

<margin>The Messiah is likened to a sapphire.</margin>
And immediately above this, the likeness of a man, who is the incarnate Son of God, or the Messiah. He says, moreover, that the appearance of this seat is like a sapphire, so that he might hint not only at the glory of this pure virgin, but also her complete purity. For just as the sapphire, though it has its origin from a terrestrial element, opaque and dark, is nevertheless from its beginning transparent and...

# BOOK EIGHT.
# CONCERNING THE MYSTERIES OF THE MESSIAH,
## WHICH WERE FULFILLED IN OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

### CHAPTER ONE.

->*That the Messiah according to the flesh was to descend from Jacob and the other patriarchs through a direct line.*<-

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>CAPNIO</margin> <note>"Capnio" is the Greek-derived name for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>
As I am now about to speak of the mysteries of the Messiah, by which the <term>perfidy</term> <note>A common, though harsh, period term used by Christian polemicists to describe Jewish refusal to accept Jesus as the Messiah.</note> of the younger Jews is best refuted (for through these mysteries it is openly shown that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Messiah, since in him all those mysteries of the Messiah foretold by the Prophets were fulfilled to the letter), you must first reveal that the Messiah himself was to descend from Jacob and the other patriarchs through a direct line. GALATINUS: I shall therefore bring forward what is written on this matter in the 24th chapter of Numbers, in this manner: <margin>B</margin> <margin>C</margin> *A star shall come forth out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel, and shall strike the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Seth. And Edom shall be his possession. Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies, and Israel shall act valiantly. And out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion, and shall destroy the remnant of the city.* <note>original Hebrew: "דָּרַךְ כּוֹכָב מִיַּעֲקֹב וְקָם שֵׁבֶט מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל וּמָחַץ פַּאֲתֵי מוֹאָב וְקַרְקַר כָּל בְּנֵי שֵׁת..."</note> Where the commentary of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> <margin>D</margin> says: *Of the city*—meaning the famous city of Edom, which is Rome. But of the King Messiah it is said, *And out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion*, along with the rest. For of him it is said in Psalm 72: *And he shall rule from sea to sea.* Likewise in Obadiah: *And there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau.* Thus far Rabbi Solomon. Furthermore, these words, *A star shall come forth out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel*, <margin>E</margin> were translated into <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic.</note> by Rabbi Onkelos <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, the official Aramaic paraphrase of the Torah.</note> as: *A king shall rise out of the house of Jacob, and the Messiah shall be anointed and magnified out of*

*Israel.* From this Chaldean translation, two points are held. First, indeed, that this scripture speaks of the Messiah. ### CHAPTER II.

->That the Messiah was to be born in a new way, that is, without the seed of a man, or from a mother without a father.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Ornamental drop cap letter Q, containing a depiction of a scholar or prophet seated at a desk with an open book.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH you have said much in previous sections concerning the virginity of the Messiah's mother: yet because the more recent Jews assert that the Messiah is to be fathered by a man and a woman in the manner of all other men—inflicting no small blasphemy upon both the mother and the son—therefore, to restrain their false-speaking and impious boldness, prove, I pray, through their own scriptures, that the Messiah himself was to be born in a new way, that is, from a mother without a father. 

GALATINUS: That the Messiah was to be generated in a new way, and would have no earthly father, has been said in many ways by the ancient fathers. Wherefore, it must first be noted what is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The "Midrash on the Psalms," an ancient homiletic commentary.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that which is said in Psalm 2: <note>original: "אספרה אל חק יהוה אמר אלי בני אתה אני היום ילדתיך"</note> "I will tell the decree: God said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you." 

<margin>B</margin>Where it is said: <note>original: "מספרים הם תנאי מלך המשיח , בתורה של נביאים וכתובים..."</note> "The matters, or mysteries, of the King Messiah are narrated in the scripture of the prophets and the hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings" or Ketuvim, the third section of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. As it is said in Psalm 110: 'From the womb of the dawn,' or 'from the matrix of the dawn, to you is the dew of your birth.' Rabbi Hunna said, or (as it is read elsewhere) Rabbi Idi: The tribulations were divided into three divisions. One was borne by the fathers of the world (namely Abraham and the others) and all generations. The second was borne by the generation of destruction (namely those who were destroyed by the Romans). But the third belongs to the generation of the Messiah. And when his hour comes, the holy and blessed God will say: 'It is upon me,' that is, it belongs to me, 'to create him as a new creature.' And this is what he says: 'Today I have begotten you.'" 

Thus far the tradition. In which there are two things that show clearly enough that the Messiah was not to be conceived and generated like other men, but in a new way. One is that which he says at the end, namely that God was to create him as a new creature. The other is what he said shortly before according to the Hebrew truth, in that place where we have: "From the womb before the morning star I begot you." In Hebrew it is: "From the matrix of the dawn, or the womb of the dawn, to

<column-break/>

436

you is the dew of your birth." For the Hebrew text has it so, which is more in harmony with the truth of our faith. For once it is proved by this tradition that these things were said of the Messiah, nothing else can be reasonably or appropriately understood by "the matrix of the dawn" than the literal matrix or womb of his most holy mother. She was to conceive and bear him by divine power, without the seed of a man, and with her virginity intact: just as the dawn receives the sun and brings it forth without corruption. All of this is understood through the "dew of the birth" of the Messiah from the matrix of the dawn.

<margin>What the Dawn is.</margin>For the "Dawn" is that part of the sky and earth which appears illuminated in the morning before the sun rises, at the place where the sun breaks forth. As soon as it begins to grow light, it is called the dawn; but as soon as the sun rises and is seen, it is no longer called the dawn. 

<margin>What the Matrix of the Dawn is.</margin>Now, the "Matrix" or "Womb" of the dawn is said to be that space between the earth or the sea of our horizon, <margin>C</margin>through which the sun brings itself forth and raises itself, and is seen to rise and ascend. 

<margin>What the Dew of Birth is.</margin>The "Dew of Birth" is the first conception of a man in the womb, which is not without reason called "dew." For just as dew is quickly dissolved by the sun, so also the first conceptions of both humans and other animals most easily become abortions, whereas those of longer duration are aborted with difficulty. Therefore, the sense is: 

<margin>The Catholic explanation.</margin>That just as the pre-existing sun brings itself forth from the center of the dawn by itself without any other drawer-out: so the Word of God, by himself, without a generating man, <margin>D</margin>was to receive the first conception of the birth of his humanity from the center of the dawn, that is, from the womb of a virgin, with no man cooperating: while remaining the same Son of God who existed before. 

This is also confirmed by what is read in the annotations of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher and commentator from Narbonne, known for including many midrashic traditions in his work.</note> regarding that verse of Psalm 85: <note>original: "אמת מארץ תצמח וצדק משמים נשקף"</note> "Truth shall spring out of the earth, and righteousness shall look down from heaven." For it is said there: <note>original: "אמר רבי יודן זאת היא הישועה שנצמחה מארץ..."</note> 

<margin>E</margin>"Rabbi Yoden said: This is our salvation, which shall arise from the earth by the mediation of God, and both shall be joined together (namely, truth and righteousness). And why did he say, 'It shall spring forth' or 'it shall sprout,' and did not say, <margin>F</margin>'it shall be born'? Because, surely, his generation or birth will not be like the generation or birth of the creatures that are in the world; rather, it will be different and distant, without a partner or union. And this will be our Savior and our Righteous one, whom God shall send." And this is what he says in the same Psalm: <note>original: "גם יהוה יתן הטוב וארצנו תתן יבולה"</note> "The LORD shall also give that which is good, or goodness, and our land shall yield her fruit." 

Furthermore, it is established that there is no one found, and no one who can declare <margin>G</margin>the name of his Father, nor any who knows it; but this is hidden from the eyes of the common people until he himself comes and makes it manifest. These are the words of that Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, who also says in his commentaries on the book of Genesis, regarding chapter 25 of that book: "And Reuben said to them, Do not shed blood..."

will this be? This will be the King Messiah. Thus it is written there. Therefore, it is necessary to understand that seed of which it is said in Psalm 101 <note>Likely referring to Psalm 105:6 in modern numbering</note>: <term>זרע אברהם עבדי בני יעקב בחיריו הוא, יהוה אלהינו</term>—This is: "The seed of Abraham his servant, the children of Jacob his chosen: he is the Lord our God." A seed [who is] God." <note>Malachi 2:15</note> Upon which Abraham Ibn Ezra and Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> said: "Our teachers have explained this: That the spouses of foreigners gathered to the Prophet, and said to him, 'Did not Abraham do thus, who took Hagar in addition to his wife?' The Prophet said to them, 'Another spirit was in him. For his intention was not as your intention is. Because he did not set his eyes upon her.' They said to him, 'And what was that one seeking? What was his intention?' He answered them, 'That he might have for himself <term>זרע אלהים</term> <gloss>Zera elohim</gloss>, that is, the seed of God, or the Seed [who is] God.'" Thus they say. Where it should be noted that just as <term>יהוה אלהים</term> <gloss>Adonai elohim</gloss> is the "Lord God," so not incongruously <term>Zera elohim</term> can be the "Seed [who is] God." Furthermore, that the Messiah was to be generated from a woman without a man, or from a mother without a father, is still proven by the testimony of Jacob himself, saying thus in Genesis chapter 49: <term>לא יסור שבט מיהודה ומחקק מבין רגליו, עד כי יבא שילה</term>—This is: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from between his feet, until <term>שילה</term> <gloss>Shiloh</gloss> comes" <note>Genesis 49:10</note>—that is, "his son," namely, of the woman. For Rabbi Kimhi explains this word *Shiloh* in his concordances, under the entry *Shiloh*, as was more widely apparent in the 4th chapter of the fourth book. For the declaration of which it must be observed that the Hebrews make a great distinction in their grammar (as you yourself well know) in the masculine and feminine demonstrative suffixes. For if they are to say "his son" or "of him" with a masculine demonstration, they say <term>בנו</term> <gloss>Beno</gloss>, with the letter *vau* <note>original: ו</note> at the end of the word. But if they are to say "her son" or "of her" with a feminine demonstration, they say <term>בנה</term> <gloss>Bena</gloss>, with the letter *he* <note>original: ה</note> at the end of the word. Now this word <term>שילה</term> <gloss>Shiloh</gloss>, although in pronunciation it is spoken with a masculine demonstration—though by right it should have been said <term>שילה</term> <gloss>Shila</gloss>, which the scribes adapted—it is nevertheless written with the letter *he* <note>original: ה</note>, a feminine demonstration. For it is said <term>שילה</term> <gloss>Shiloh</gloss>, which is "the son of her," namely, of the woman. Thus therefore the text says: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from between his feet, until the son of the woman herself comes." Moreover, so that it may be known what "the son of the woman" signifies, the words written in Genesis chapter 15 must be noted: <term>ודור רביעי ישובו הנה</term>—that is, "And in the fourth generation they shall return hither." <note>Genesis 15:16</note> Which things were said by God when he announced the Egyptian captivity to Abraham, which <margin>The false exposition of the younger Jews.</margin>prefigured the captivity of souls in hell. But indeed, some of the younger Jews explain these four generations as having been four hundred years, asserting that each <margin>Refutation.</margin>of them was a hundred years. Their exposition is indeed null. Since they calculate these years either from the time the prophecy was uttered, or from when the Egyptian captivity itself began. Both of which are false. For if they calculate from that time when the prophecy was uttered, they will find much time beyond four hundred years has run its course. If indeed from the beginning of the captivity itself...

Since, therefore, according to the doctrine of Aristotle <note>A reference to the *Categories* or *Topics*</note>, the study of contraries is the same, and once one side of a contradiction is placed, it is necessary to place the other. (For if black is found, white must also be found; if sweet is discovered, then bitter must also be granted as a possibility.) Therefore it is necessary, given the two previous generations, to assign two opposites. Thus, the generation opposite <note>D</note> to that of Adam (who was brought forth without man or woman) is the third generation, in which all are commonly generated from a man and a woman. It was because of this generation, therefore, that Jacob said: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from the midst of his feet, until the son of that woman comes"—that is, the Messiah, who was called the "son of the woman" because he was to be born of a woman without a man.

# BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin> ...from what was said in the sixtieth chapter of Isaiah: <term>A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come; they shall bring gold and frankincense; and they shall proclaim the praises of the Lord.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שפעת גמלים תכסך בכרי מדין ועיפה כלם משבא יבאו זהב ולבונה ישאו ותהלות יהוה יבשרו"</note> that is: A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba shall come, they shall bring gold and frankincense, and they shall announce the praises of God (the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH, often translated as "the Lord."</note>). For this refers to the King Messiah, just as it was said in the 23rd and 33rd chapters of Jeremiah: <term>And this is his name by which they shall call him: The Lord Our Righteousness.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקינו"</note> This is: "And this is the name by which they shall call him, God (the Tetragrammaton) our just one." <margin>B</margin> And so Isaiah says in the sixtieth chapter, "And over you the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) shall arise, or shall dawn, and his glory shall appear over you. And the nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising." Thus far the tradition. In which five things are especially to be noted. The first of these is what it says: That the Queen of Sheba, having heard of the fame of Solomon, came in the name of God to test him with riddles. And assigning a cause, it says: Because when Solomon had been magnified in his kingdom, <margin>C</margin> she had said, "Perhaps this is the Messiah." Furthermore, from the fact that it says we should not read "Queen of Sheba" but "Kingdom of Sheba," he responds to an objection that the younger Jews are accustomed to make against us. They falsely try to prove that our Christ was not the Messiah because the Prophet said, "All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense," yet according to the Gospel, not all those from Sheba, but only a few, came to worship Christ. Here, therefore, they are best refuted by their own Talmud when it says: Do not read "Queen of Sheba," but "Kingdom of Sheba." Because since a King represents everyone existing in his kingdom, the Queen of Sheba herself, who came to Solomon, <margin>D</margin> represented that entire kingdom. Therefore, since among the Kings who came to worship the newborn Christ, there was one King of Sheba who represented all from that same kingdom, it was rightly predicted by Isaiah that "All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense." It was also proven in the preceding pages that in the Sacred Scriptures "all" is rarely used for <margin>E</margin> every single individual, but rather is frequently used for even a very small part. Second, in the same tradition, it should be noted that it says those of Sheba would come in the days of the Messiah and would serve him; which he shows was to happen through the aforementioned words of Isaiah. Third, that it says those of Sheba were children of Abraham, which he proves by the authority of the Sacred Scripture which he introduces there. And that there was a prophet among them who prophesied words to them in the name of his God, which had been handed down to them and which had come to their <margin>F</margin> hands successively from Abraham. Fourth, because in explaining that passage of Isaiah—"All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense, and shall announce the praises of God (the Tetragrammaton)"—he says this "God" written with the name Tetragrammaton, to whom those of Sheba were to offer those gifts and announce his praises, is the King Messiah. This he proves by the testimony of Jeremiah, who says, "And this is the name by which they shall call him, God (the Tetragrammaton) our just one." Which (as was said in the preceding sections) is a name unique to God and appropriated to Him alone, indicating the essence of the Creator Himself. Therefore, no pure creature can be called by that name. From which it clearly follows that the Messiah is God. Fifth, that the Gentiles would go to the light of this

<column-break/>

442

Messiah who is called by the name of God, the Tetragrammaton. This agrees perfectly with what John the Evangelist says: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world." And also with what the Church sings in the Creed: "Light of Light, true God of true God." Furthermore, that the Messiah was to be adored as God is found in Psalm 72, where it reads: <term>The kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שבא וסבא אשכר יקריבו"</note> That is: The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall render a gift, the kings of Sheba and Seba shall bring a present. And a little after it is added: <term>And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold of Sheba, and they shall pray for him continually; all day long they shall bless him.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "יחי ויתן לו מזהב שבא ויתפלל בעדו תמיד כל היום יברכנהו"</note> That all these things ought to be understood regarding the Messiah is clear from the fact that in the *Beresith Rabba* <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient Jewish commentary on the book of Genesis.</note>—that is, in the great exposition of the book of Genesis—regarding what is said in chapter 33, "And he urged him, and he took it," it reads as follows: "Rabbenu (that is, our Master) said: All those gifts which our father Jacob gave to Esau, the Kings of the world are destined to restore to the King Messiah." Whence is this proven? From that which is written in Psalm 72: "The kings of Tarshish and the isles shall bring a gift." It is not written "shall bring," but "shall restore." That all the aforementioned things were fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ is shown from those things which are written in the second chapter of Matthew in this manner: "When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of Herod the king, behold, Magi from the East came to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to adore him," and so forth. Then it is added: "And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. And falling down, they adored him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh."

### CHAPTER IV.

->That the Messiah was to be recalled from Egypt; where, fleeing Herod after his birth, he was destined to go.<-

->CAPNIO.<- <note>Capnio is the scholarly nickname for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and student of Hebrew who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>G</margin> THERE is yet another mystery which was to happen after the Messiah was born: namely, his journey into Egypt, and his subsequent return from there into the land of Israel. And afterward, when Herod was dead, he returned to the land of Israel. I would therefore like to hear from you if the ancient Jews, who preceded the coming of Christ, predicted anything regarding this mystery.
GALATINUS. That the Messiah, fleeing the persecution of Herod after his birth, would go away into Egypt and would afterward return by God's command, those ancient fathers certainly did not remain silent. For it is written in the exposition of the book of Genesis by the Rabbis...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the theological argument regarding the Messiah's identity, moving from the gifts of the Magi to the symbolic image of the "Vine." It explains how Jewish tradition interprets the Messiah's predicted journey to Egypt and addresses the miraculous nature of his work.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...of Moses Hadarshan <note>A 11th-century Jewish scholar and exegete from Narbonne.</note>, concerning that which is said in the fortieth chapter of Genesis: <term>Behold, a vine was before me.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "והנה גפן לפני"</note> This is: This is Israel, just as it is written in the eightieth Psalm: <term>You shall transfer (or move) a vine out of Egypt.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "תסיע גפן ממצרים"</note> Another explanation: "And behold, a vine was before me": This is the King Messiah, of whom it was said in the eightieth Psalm: <term>And prepare (or perfect) that which your right hand has planted.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "וכנה אשר נטעה ימינך"</note> or, "And the prepared and arranged vine." Or, "And the base (or pedestal), which your right hand has planted." Where it must be <margin>B</margin> noted that *chana* <note>original Hebrew: "כנה"</note>, which is placed there and is a name for a well-ordered and properly arranged vine, also signifies a "base" or "pedestal." *Chana* is also an imperative verb from the Hebrew word *can* <note>original Hebrew: "כון"</note>, which signifies to prepare, to arrange, or to perfect. This *chana* therefore—that is, the well-arranged and ordered vine—is the King Messiah, who was to be transferred out of Egypt. To the aforementioned also contributes much of what is written in the book <term>Berakhot</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ברכות" - "Blessings," a volume of the Talmud.</note>, that is, of "blessings," in the chapter beginning <term>Haroe makom</term> <note>original Hebrew: "הרואה מקום" - "He who sees a place."</note>, that is, "he who sees a place." For it is said: He who sees in a dream <term>Soreka</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שורקה"</note>, that is, a vine-branch, <term>shall see (or contemplate) the Messiah</term> <note>original Hebrew: "יראה צפיה למשיח"</note>, of whom it is written in Psalm 80: "You shall transfer a vine from Egypt." Where it should be noted that the text says "you shall transfer" [future/present] and not "he transferred" [past], as our version <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> has it. By this, therefore, it is clearly evident that the Prophet was speaking not of Israel, but of the Messiah, who was to be recalled from Egypt. Which <margin>D</margin> is shown more clearly through the explanation of <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>A title meaning "Our Holy Rabbi," usually referring to Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah.</note>, in the book which he called <term>Gale Razia</term> <note>original Hebrew: "גלי רזיא" - "The Revealer of Secrets."</note>, that is, the "revealer of mysteries." For in the seventh petition of that same book, it is read that among other things, Antoninus, a Consul of the city of Rome, asked him what was meant by that saying in Psalm 80: "You shall transfer (or remove) a vine out of Egypt?" He answered him: "This is the Messiah." Antoninus said to him: "Therefore is the King Messiah to be born in <margin>E</margin> Egypt? Is it not in Bethlehem? As it is said in Micah, chapter 5: And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, you are small among the thousands of Judah; out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be the Ruler in Israel." Rabbenu answered him: "I confess that the King Messiah is to be born in Bethlehem. But it says: 'You shall transfer a vine from Egypt.' For when the Messiah is born, Herod, who shall reign in Jerusalem, will seek him for death. By divine revelation, however, he will be compelled to flee into Egypt, where he will <margin>F</margin> stay for some time, and afterward he will return to Jerusalem by the command of God. Therefore the text says, 'You shall transfer a vine from Egypt.' Indeed, concerning his mother it says: 'And the base (or pedestal) which your right hand has planted.'" These are the words of that truly holy Rabbenu Haccados. Moreover, why the Mother of God is compared to a "base" or "pedestal" was said sufficiently and abundantly in the third chapter of the seventh book, according to the opinion of the same Rabbenu Haccados. Furthermore, according to the traditions set forth above, which assert that the Messiah was to be recalled from Egypt, that word of the Lord in Hosea, chapter 11, <margin>G</margin> fits the same Messiah perfectly: <term>And out of Egypt I called my son.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "וממצרים קראתי לבני"</note> Nor does it stand in the way of our proposition that it says "I called" [past] and not "I will call" [future]. Because, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Commonly known as Rashi, a preeminent medieval French rabbi.</note> says regarding that saying in Isaiah, chapter 42:

<column-break/>

"I have done these words for them": All prophetic language speaks of the future as if it were the past. And this is because the word of God is held as a deed, according to the opinion of the ancient Talmudists, as has been declared more broadly in the preceding pages. From the premises, therefore, it is clearly evident not only that the Messiah was to be recalled from Egypt, but also that he would be the vine planted by God. This agrees well with the saying of the same Lord in John, chapter 15, saying: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener."

### CHAPTER V.

->*That the Messiah was to perform miracles by his own power. And concerning the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and his disciples from the Talmud.*<-

### CAPNIO. <note>The pen name of the Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

OUR LORD Jesus Christ,
since he performed many miracles by
his own power, therefore, to prove
that he was the true Messiah,
you ought to show that the Messiah
himself was going to perform miracles. GALATINUS <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, responding to Reuchlin.</note>: Isaiah, among others, openly predicted this when in chapter 35 he says: <term>The reward of God (or God the reward) himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. Then the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall sing.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "גמול אלהים הוא יבא ויושעכם : אז תפקחנה עיני עורים ואזני חרשים תפתחנה אז ידלג כאיל פסח ותרון לשון אלם וגו׳"</note> From which it is manifest that the Messiah was not only going to perform miracles by his own power as God, but that he was going to be God. Since the ancient Jews handed down that the aforementioned words of Isaiah must be understood regarding the Messiah himself: who also openly predicted that the Pharisees—whom he calls <term>paretzim</term> <note>original Hebrew: "פריצים" - meaning the wicked, or those who break through/are reckless.</note>, that is, wicked or corrupt in morals, or rash—would not believe in the miracles of the Messiah. As Rabbi Moses Hadarshan beautifully testifies in his commentaries on that passage of Psalm 74: <term>Our signs we have not seen; there is no longer a prophet, nor is there anyone among us who knows any more, or for how long.</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אותותינו לא ראינו אין עוד נביא ולא אתנו יודע עד מה"</note> Speaking thus: <term>Rabbi Natronai asked: What is this that is written, "Our signs we have not seen, there is no longer a prophet, nor is there anyone among us who knows any more, or for how long?" Rabbi Aha answered him: This was said concerning the generation of the wicked, who will not believe the signs that our righteous Messiah shall perform. But they will say of him that he works them by magical art and by the names of impurity. ->*That the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and his disciples can in no way be denied.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>F</margin> **SINCE** we have begun a discourse concerning the miracles of our Redeemer and his disciples: therefore, so that the impious rashness of the more recent Jews—who so obstinately either deny or attack them—may be further refuted, it must be proved that the miracles themselves are so firmly established that they cannot be denied by any wickedness of the adversaries. **GALATINUS.** This is certainly shown in three ways: namely, through diverse scripture, through widespread fame, and through necessary reason. ...which (as the first interpretation suggests) the prophet said the Lord would recount the truth. <term>Gal.</term> <note>Pietro Galatino, the author, refers here to himself or his earlier arguments.</note> Namely, the scriptures of the Gentiles, who were to receive the Messiah. <margin>What Muhammad thought of the miracles of Christ.</margin>
In the law of the Saracens, therefore, which is called the <term>Alchoranus</term> <note>The Quran</note>, it is contained among other things that the Angel Gabriel was sent by God to the Virgin Mary, to announce to her the conception of the Lord Jesus by the power of God alone, without the seed of man. In the same book it is also read that the Lord Jesus himself, once grown, raised the dead, cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, and healed the sick of every kind by his word alone. And that from clay he formed little birds, to which he gave life and flight at the same time. And moreover, he caused a table to descend from heaven, upon which he dined with his disciples. The miracle of the seven sleepers—who, because of their confession of Christ, were enclosed by Emperor Decius in a certain cave behind a very strong wall, and having been awakened from a sleep lasting two hundred years in the time of the Emperor Theodosius, bore witness to the Christian faith and the future resurrection—is also beautifully found in that same Quran.

<margin>What is "Common Report"?</margin>
Furthermore, the miracles of Christ are established through "Common Report" <note>Latin: *crebra fama*, a term for widely accepted historical testimony</note>: which is, according to the opinion of the wise, the account of many people concerning something perceptible by the senses, occurring either in the present time or in a continuous, uninterrupted succession from the past. It is impossible, according to common experience, for such a multitude of people to secretly conspire to invent such a thing. Of things (as they say) which are held by common report, there are two kinds: the first is when those who create the report narrate something they themselves perceived either by sight or some other sense. Such a narration provides true knowledge when two things coincide. One of these is that the multitude of narrators reaches such a number that it is impossible, according to

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
common experience, for that multitude to have secretly conspired to invent a lie. For example, if we see men from different and distant regions, with different customs and languages, agreeing and affirming that there is a city in the world called Rome: it will be established as certain to us that this city exists in the world.

<margin>B</margin>
The other requirement is that the thing narrated must be capable of being subjected to the senses. For if all the people of the East and West were to narrate that the world had a beginning, or that it was eternal, and said that there was one creator of the world or many, their narration would certainly not provide certain knowledge, but rather faith: since such narrations cannot be subjected to the senses. If, however, they narrated for example that in some region—say, in Flanders—they use clods of earth <note>referring to peat</note> instead of wood to make a fire, their narration would produce certain knowledge, since what they narrate can be apprehended by the senses.

<margin>C</margin>
Whenever, therefore, these two things coincide—namely, that the narrators are so many and of such a kind that they could not have secretly conspired to invent a lie, and the thing narrated was sensible—then without a doubt, according to the opinion of <term>Avicenna</term>, <term>Al-Ghazali</term>, and <term>Ibnazatib</term> <note>referring to major Islamic philosophers and scholars often cited in medieval Latin scholasticism</note>, it provides certain knowledge. In this way, Jacob knew that his son Joseph, whom he believed to be dead, was alive.

<margin>D</margin>
The second kind of things held by common report is when the narrators are as described, but they say they did not see the thing they are narrating themselves; they assert, however, that they saw and heard a multitude of the kind we described, which said that it had seen and heard what they themselves are narrating. This kind provides certain knowledge when those two things we mentioned in the first kind coincide.

<margin>E</margin>
And there is this third point: if the chain of narrators extends quite far, it must never be interrupted, nor entirely weakened, but the end and the middle must always correspond to the beginning in both quantity and quality. Just as if some people said regarding the law of <term>Moses</term> that it came down to Ezra and a few others. In this way, people today know that Alexander, Caesar, Plato, Aristotle, and other most excellent men whom ancient antiquity has handed down, actually existed.

<margin>F</margin>
In this way also, if you pay attention, the Jews of our time ought to know that Moses existed, performed wonders, gave the law, and also that the ancient Jews worshipped the calf, killed many prophets, and rejected the Lord Jesus who asserted he was the Messiah, and in his place received two false Messiahs. For this reason, Moses directed the Jewish people to this mode of knowing when he said in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: <note>original Hebrew: זכר ימות עולם בינו שנות דר ודור שאל אביך ויגדך זקניך ויאמרו לך</note> *Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask your father, and he will show you; your elders, and they will tell you.* <note>Deut 32:7</note> David also sets down this mode of knowing when he says in Psalm 78:

<margin>G</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: למען ידעו דור אחרון בנים יולדו יקומו ויספרו לבניהם וישימו באלהים כסלם ולא ישכחו מעללי אל ומצותיו ינצרו</note> That is: *That the last generation might know, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children: That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments.* <note>Psalm 78:6-7</note> CHAPTER. reputation, according to the doctrine of Aristotle, seems very weak. First, because regarding individual sensible things far removed from the senses, there is no direct sensation, and consequently no scientific knowledge. Second, because we are not simply devoid of faith and belief for this reason; for there are "probable propositions," which are set down by Aristotle in his book on the *Greater Rhetoric*. Finally, because what is "famous" <note>meaning widely reported or of common repute</note> according to Aristotle is the same as what is "probable," as is clear in the five modes of probability placed by him in the first book of the *Topics*. <term>Gal.</term> <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, responding to these philosophical doubts.</note> To this 

<margin>Response of Ibnazatib.</margin>

objection, Ibnazatib <note>Likely a Latinization of an Arabic philosopher, possibly Ibn al-Khatib or Al-Farabi/Abu Nasr</note>, one of the Arabic philosophers enumerated above, responds, saying among other things: "Know that there has been a controversy among the wise, whether the knowledge which is held through frequent report <note>Common Fame</note> is necessary or merely probable. Regarding this, after many things were said for both sides, the choice of all at last is that it is necessary. For that is 'necessary' which we do not wish to doubt, nor are we able to, even when testing ourselves. Furthermore, when having heard all that is objected against frequent report, we test ourselves: we find our souls judging precisely that Moses, for example, existed; and that he said he was the messenger of God sent to the faithful of Israel. Nor do we find anything among the objections that pierces through this certainty. Such things are like those that are necessary truths. Therefore, nothing that is against frequent report deserves a response. For a response ought to be 'probable' <note>meaning open to debate</note>. However, to hold a necessary truth in a circular argument with a probable one is impossible." These are his words, translated word-for-word from the Arabic. From these things, it is clear that what has been said against frequent report does not deserve a response. 

Finally, the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ are proved to be established through "necessary reason," that is, through their effects. For the art of reasoning and demonstrating teaches us to best conclude causes from their effects. Indeed, no one participating in reason doubts that a "lot" <note>an outcome or fate</note> exists when he sees the act of the lot occurring. And to whomever speed belongs, it is manifest that he is fast. For the nature of each thing acts according to what is proper to itself, nor is it mixed with the effects of contrary things. 

Therefore, it is clear that our Lord, Jesus Christ, and his followers visibly performed works in his name that surpass the power of all nature: in the miraculous healing of the sick, in the raising of the dead, in the stupendous changing of celestial bodies and elements, and what is even more wonderful, in the sudden inspiration of human minds—when uneducated and ignorant men were instantly filled with the Holy Spirit and attained the highest wisdom, understanding of the scriptures, and skill in various languages. 

All these things, I say, were done by our Lord Jesus Christ, and after him by his followers in his name, as the subsequent effect clearly shows: namely, that not by the violence of arms, nor by the permission or license of pleasures, but through the unrefined and simple disciples of Christ—very few and poor men—against the unheard-of rage and tyranny of the persecutors of the entire world (both Jews and Gentiles), innumerable crowds, not only of the unrefined and common folk but also of the wisest men, turned most affectionately to the faith of the Lord, despising the worship of demons which had so enticed their minds that never before, either through Mo-

<column-break/>

# EIGHTH

<margin>A</margin> -ses or through anyone else, had even the Jews themselves been so thoroughly turned away, despite seeing many stupendous miracles. In this faith, things are taught that transcend all human intellect and reason; the pleasures of the body, most desired by mortals, are restrained; and men are commanded to laboriously seek invisible things and to despise all worldly things. That the minds of mortals should assent to these things is both the greatest miracle and a manifest work of divine inspiration. 

Furthermore, that this was not done by fortune or chance is clear most especially from this: that God foretold many centuries before through the oracles of the prophets that He would do it, designating both the time and the manner of its being done. Therefore, this so wonderful conversion of the world to the faith of Christ is the most certain evidence of the past miracles which are narrated and read in the written books. Thus, it is not necessary that they be repeated further, since they appear most evidently in their effect. Although even in our own times, for the preservation of the Christian faith, God does not cease to perform miracles through His saints.

<margin>C</margin> Wherefore, if the Jews with whom we are at war <note>meaning a theological conflict</note> wish to deny the miracles of Christ to us, one great and greatest miracle of all remains for us: That the world was led away from its errors and vices, by which it was enticed and absorbed, by so few men—ignorant according to the world and its physicians—to believe such arduous things, to do such difficult things contrary to flesh and blood, and to hope for such high and hidden things, and believed them even without miracles <note>The argument is: if there were no miracles, then the conversion of the world without them is the greatest miracle of all.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> Moreover, that the Jews should reject the miracles of Christ, while the Gentiles would look upon them, was announced long ago by the prophets. Hence the Psalmist in Psalm 86 says: <note>original: "אין כמוך באלהים אדני ואין כמעשיך : כל גוים אשר עשית יבואו וישתחוו לפניך אדני ויכבדו לשמך כי גדול אתה ועושה נפלאות אתה אלהים לבדך"</note> i.e., "There is none like You among the gods, O God, nor is there anything like Your works. That the Messiah is the "face of God," the "name of God," and "God," has been made very clear in the preceding sections. From these things that have been said, it is openly clear that the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and those of his followers done in his name were of such a kind, and so firmly established, that they cannot be denied by any slander of adversaries.

### CHAPTER VII.
#### That the Messiah ought to be a prophet.
#### CAPNIO. <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

BECAUSE the malice of certain Jews of our time is so great that they utterly deny that the Messiah would be a prophet, we must prove that the Messiah himself was to be a prophet, so that from this mystery also we may conclude that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Messiah. <term>Gal.</term> This is shown manifestly from what Moses said concerning him in Deuteronomy, chapter 18: <note>original: "נביא מקי בך מאחיך כמני יקים לך יהוה אלהיך אליו תשמעון"</note> That is, "A prophet from the midst of you, from your brothers, like me, the Lord your God will establish or raise up for you; to him you shall listen."

<meta>Continuity: This page transitions from a philosophical defense of historical testimony to a specific scriptural debate between the characters Capnio (representing the scholar Johannes Reuchlin) and Galatino (the author, Pietro Galatino). <margin>An objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
**CAPNIO.** The Jews themselves assert that this prophet, who was to be like Moses, is not the Messiah, but rather each of the individual prophets who were to come after Moses. Therefore, they say that the authority you have now brought forward should be understood not as the Messiah, but as the individual prophets who happened to follow Moses. For that reason, to restrain their boldness, you must prove through their own scriptures that this prophet who was to be like Moses had to be the Messiah. **GALATINO.** In the *Midrash Kohelet* <note>original: "Midras coheleth"</note>, which is the exposition on the book of Ecclesiastes, regarding that passage in the first chapter of the same book which says: *What is that which was? The very thing that shall be* <note>Hebrew: מה שהיה הוא שיהיה — Ma she-hayah hu she-yihyeh</note>, we read that Rabbi Berachiah said in the name of Rabbi Isaac: "As the first redeemer was—that is, Moses—so shall the last redeemer be—that is, the Messiah." Now, what was the first redeemer like? Such as is described in Exodus chapter 4: *And Moses took his wife and his sons and made them ride upon a donkey.* So too shall the last redeemer do, as it is said in Zechariah chapter 9: *Lowly, and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.* And just as the first redeemer caused manna to descend—as it is said in Exodus chapter 16: *Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you*—so will the last redeemer do, as it is said in Psalm 72: *There shall be a portion of grain in the earth.* And just as the first redeemer caused a spring to rise up, so the last redeemer, who is the Messiah, shall cause waters to rise up, as it is said in the last chapter of Joel: *And a fountain shall come forth from the house of the Lord, and shall water the torrent—or the valley, or the plain—of Shittim.* This is the tradition by which the Jews who deny that the Messiah was to be a prophet like Moses are easily refuted. However, this resemblance by which the Messiah was to be like Moses ought to consist chiefly in the giving of the Divine Law. For although there were to be many future lawmakers—since Mercury Trismegistus was to give laws to the Egyptians, Phoroneus to the Greeks, Lycurgus to the Spartans, and Numa Pompilius to the Romans—nevertheless, no one was going to give a Divine Law as Moses had given, except the Messiah. For all the others were to establish not divine laws, but only human ones. Therefore, the Messiah was to be raised up as most similar to Moses specifically in the giving of Divine Law, as will be more fully revealed in the tenth book when we come to speak of the institution of the new Law of God through the Messiah. For now, it is enough to have proved through the Hebrew scriptures that this prophet, like Moses, to be raised up from among the Jews, was to be the Messiah.

<margin>Another objection of the Jews.</margin>
**CAPNIO.** The Jews still object to us, saying: "We have never heard that your Christ stood forth as a prophet. Nor do you even call him a prophet yourself. If, therefore, the Messiah had to be a prophet, and your Christ was not a prophet, it follows necessarily that he was not the Messiah." **GALATINO.**

<margin>The Response.</margin>
Let it be answered to them that our Christ was indeed a prophet, and that we hold him as a prophet. For of him, Luke says in chapter 24: *Who was a man, a prophet, mighty in work and word.* Furthermore, that Samaritan woman (as John reports in the fourth chapter) said: *Lord, I see that you are a prophet.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Moreover, if they ask us what he prophesied, we shall answer them: many things indeed, and especially regarding himself, his disciples, and the Jews. For regarding himself, he prophesied that passage in Luke chapter 18: *Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things shall be accomplished that were written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man. For he shall be delivered to the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and scourged, and spit upon. And after they have scourged him, they will put him to death, and on the third day he shall rise again.*

<margin>B</margin>
Likewise in Matthew chapter 16: *The Son of Man,* he says, *is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. And then he will render to every man according to his works.* Concerning his disciples, he spoke in Matthew chapter 10: *Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Be therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves. But beware of men, for they will deliver you up in councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues, and you shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles,* and so forth.

<margin>C</margin>
Finally, he prophesied concerning the Jews when, as Luke says in chapter 19, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: *If you had known, even you, and indeed in this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For the days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall cast a trench about you, and compass you round, and straiten you on every side, and beat you to the ground, and your children who are in you; and they shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you knew not the time of your visitation.*

<margin>D</margin>
He spoke similarly in other places as well. Therefore, there is no doubt that he was a true prophet, and none other than that same one of whom Moses spoke, as we have already shown.

# CHAPTER VIII.

### That the Messiah was to preach repentance.

<margin>E</margin>
## CAPNIO.

We read in the Gospels that our Lord Jesus Christ taught repentance <term>Poenitentia</term> <note>While usually translated as "penance" in a Catholic context, here it refers to the act of repenting or turning back to God.</note>; indeed, when he first began to preach, he put forward these words: *Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.* It is also certain that by preaching repentance, both by himself and through his disciples, he brought the whole world to the worship of the one and true God.

<margin>F</margin>
For this reason, so that you may be able to show by this mystery also that he truly existed as the Messiah, you must show through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was to preach repentance, and through repentance would lead the entire world to the goal of salvation. **GALATINO.** Concerning the repentance which the Messiah was to preach both by himself and through his disciples, it is written in the Jerusalem book *Maccoth* <note>The Talmudic tractate Makkot, meaning "Lashets" or "Stripes."</note>, in the chapter beginning *Ellu hen haggolin* <note>Hebrew: אלו הן הגולין — "These are those who go into exile."</note>, where it is said word for word:

<margin>G</margin>
Rabbi Phineas said: It is written in Psalm 25: *Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will teach sinners the way* <note>Hebrew: טוב וישר יהוה על כן יורה חטאים בדרך — Tov ve-yashar Adonai al ken yoreh chata'im ba-derech</note>. Why is he good? Because he is upright.

<summary>This page refutes Jewish objections by using Midrashic and Talmudic sources to prove that the "prophet like Moses" refers specifically to the Messiah, highlighting parallels in their miracles and law-giving. It further argues that Jesus fulfilled the prophetic role by accurately predicting his Passion, the fall of Jerusalem, and the necessity of repentance.</summary>

...upright. And why is he upright? Because he is good. For this reason, he will teach the way to those who err. Indeed, he will teach the way through which they may perform penance. For it was asked of Wisdom: "What is the condemnation of the sinner?" And it said to those who asked, that which is written in Proverbs 13: *Evil shall pursue sinners* <note>Hebrew: חטאים תרדף רעה — Chata'im tirdaf ra'ah</note>. They also asked the Prophet: "What is the condemnation of the sinner?" And he said to them in Ezekiel 18: *The soul that sins, it shall die* <note>Hebrew: הנפש החוטאת היא תמות — Ha-nefesh ha-chote't hi tamut</note>. They likewise questioned the Law, saying: "What is the condemnation of the sinner?" And it answered them: "Let him offer a sacrifice, and it shall be forgiven him," as it is written in Leviticus 1: *And it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him* <note>Hebrew: ונרצה לו לכפר עליו — Ve-nirtzah lo le-kapper alav</note>, that is, he will be appeased toward him, so that he spares him. Finally, they asked the Holy and Blessed God: "What is the condemnation of the sinner?" And He said to them: "Let him perform penance and he shall be forgiven." And this is what is written in Psalm 25: *God is good and upright, for this reason he will teach those who err (or sinners) the way (or in the way).* Because he himself will show sinners the way of performing penance. This is the tradition. In the book also called *Yoma* <note>Hebrew: יומא — Yoma</note>, that is, *of Days* <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding the Day of Atonement</note>, in the chapter that begins *Yom Ha-Kippurim* <note>Hebrew: יום הכפורים — Yom ha-Kippurim</note>, that is, *The Day of Atonements*, it is read thus: Rabbi Isaac said, "Come and see that the custom of the Holy and Blessed God is not like the custom of flesh and blood. For the custom of flesh and blood is that if a man offends his neighbor, sometimes he may appease him with words, and sometimes he cannot appease him with words alone. But the custom of the Holy and Blessed God is not so. For a man commits a transgression, and yet he appeases Him with words." As it is said in Hosea 14: *Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord* <note>Hebrew: שובה ישראל עד יהוה אלהיך כי כשלת בעוניך קחו עמכם דברים ושובו אל יהוה — Shuvah Yisrael ad Adonai Elohecha ki chashalta ba-avonecha; kechu immachem devarim ve-shuvu el Adonai</note>. That is, convert, or perform penance, O Israel, as far as the Lord your God. For you have stumbled, or fallen, in your iniquity. Take words with you, and return to God. And not only this, but he even bestows goodness upon him. As was said consequently: *Say to him, take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously* <note>Hebrew: יאמרו אליו כל תשא עון וקח טוב — Yomeru elav kol tisa avon ve-kach tov</note>. Say to him, take away all sin, and accept the good. Nor only this, but the scripture regards it just as if he were offering calves in sacrifice. As was said thereafter: *And we will render the calves of our lips* <note>Hebrew: ונשלמה פרים שפתינו — Ve-neshallemah farim sefatenu</note>. This means: And we shall pay back the calves of our lips. Perhaps you will say: "The calves of guilt?" He teaches what should be said to this in that which follows: *I will heal their backsliding (or their conversion), I will love them freely* <note>Hebrew: ארפא משובתם אוהבם נדבה — Erpa meshuvatam ohavam nedavah</note>. That is, I will heal their perversity, or their conversion; I will love them of my own accord. This is the tradition.

<margin>The efficacy of penance.</margin>
How great the efficacy and power of penance still is, appears most clearly from what is written in the *Midrash Shir Ha-Shirim* <note>Hebrew: שיר השירים — Shir ha-Shirim</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs, regarding that saying in the 5th chapter of the same book: *Open to me, my sister.* For there it is said: Rabbi Joses said, "The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: My children, open for me one opening of penance, even as the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings of mercy, through which wagons and chariots shall enter." Rabbi Levi said, "If the children of Israel had performed penance for even a single day, they would have been redeemed immediately, and the son of David—that is, the Messiah—would have come to them immediately." Whence is this proved? From that which is written in Psalm 95: *Today, if you will hear his voice* <note>Hebrew: היום אם בקולו תשמעו — Ha-yom im be-kolo tishm'au</note>. This is the tradition. From these words of the Psalm finally brought forward concerning the Messiah, by the reasoning of the preceding parts of the same Psalm, it necessarily follows that the Messiah is God. For in the same Psalm, it is thus prefaced: *Let us worship*

<column-break/>

*and bow down, let us kneel before the face of the Lord our maker. For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand* <note>Hebrew: נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה לפני יהוה עושנו כי הוא אלהינו ואנחנו עם מרעיתו וצאן ידו — Nishtachaveh ve-nichra'ah nivrechah lifne Adonai osenu; ki hu Elohenu va-anachnu am mar'ito ve-tzon yado</note>. And immediately afterward is added that which was explained concerning the Messiah: *Today, if you will hear his voice.* From which it is certainly a consequence that God, who was to teach the way of penance, so that the confirmation of Jerusalem might be noted, is still further to be noted from that which is said in the *Midrash Shir Ha-Shirim* also, regarding that saying in the 7th chapter of the Song of Songs: *Looking toward Damascus* <note>Hebrew: צופה פני דמשק — Tzofeh fene Damasek</note>, or *with the face of Damascus*. Where it is read thus: Rabbi Johanan said, "It is to come to pass that Jerusalem shall reach as far as the gates of Damascus." What is the proof of this matter? That which is written in Zechariah 9: *The burden or prophecy of the word of God in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be its rest* <note>Hebrew: משא דבר יהוה בארץ הדרך ודמשק מנוחתו — Massa devar Adonai be-eretz Hadrach ve-Damasek menuchato</note>. What is Hadrach? Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Nahmias are in disagreement on this. For Rabbi Judah indeed says that it is a place near Damascus which is called Hadrach. But Rabbi Nahmias says that this is the King Messiah, who is *Had* <note>Hebrew: חד — Chad</note>, that is, sharp to the nations of the world, and *Rach* <note>Hebrew: רך — Rach</note>, that is, tender to Israel. Another exposition says that *Hadrach* <note>Hebrew: הדרך — Hadrach</note> is the King Messiah who is to come *to lead* <note>Hebrew: להדריך — Lehadrich</note>, that is, for directing or for leading the whole world through penance to the face of the Holy and Blessed God. It follows: *And Damascus shall be his rest.* And when Damascus shall be his rest, it shall be his rest only as the house of the sanctuary; as it is written in Psalm 132: *This is my rest forever, here will I dwell, for I have desired it* <note>Hebrew: זאת מנוחתי עדי עד פה אשב כי אותיה — Zot menuchati ade ad, poh eshev ki ivitiha</note>. All these things are tradition. For the understanding of these things, it must be observed that this word *Hidrach* is spoken and pronounced by the Hebrews in two ways. For sometimes it is written with the letter *He* <note>original: "ה he"</note>, which is the fifth in the alphabet, and then it is one word, which signifies to lead by the way. But sometimes it is written with the letter *Cheth* <note>original: "ח heth"</note>, which holds the eighth place in the alphabet, and then there are two words, namely *Had*, that is, sharp, and *Rach*, that is, tender. These two things indeed apply best to Christ, who will be sharp toward the penitent through justice <note>Though the Latin says "penitents," the context of justice implies he is strict in his requirements for those seeking to turn, or perhaps "sharp" toward the impenitent</note>, and tender through mercy. He was also sharp to Paul when he was a persecutor, near the gates of Damascus, and afterward tender to the same man when he was penitent. And then Damascus was the rest of His divinity in the mind of Paul. And also Zion in the other Apostles and the rest of the faithful. Not only then, but even forever. For Christ as God will never cease to dwell in the minds of the faithful. Moreover, the other word written with a *He*, namely *Hadrach*, which sounds like directing or leading by the way, also fits our Savior most appropriately. For he himself, both through himself and through his disciples by preaching penance, directed and led almost the entire world to the recognition of the one true God and the goal of salvation.

...they hear that the poverty and humility of our Lord Jesus Christ was so great and wonderful that he had nowhere to lay his head (as Matthew witnesses), nor wherewith to pay the tax <note>original: "didrachma" – a silver coin worth two days' wages, used for the Temple tax</note>, nor wherewith (as Luke relates) to satisfy the hunger of his poor disciples; lest they be compelled to confess him to have been the true Messiah, they deny that the Messiah himself was to be poor and humble. To convict them of their treachery, it is necessary to show this through their own scriptures. <term>GAL.</term> <note>Galatinus</note> Although Jewish blindness and pride have erred so greatly in this—to the point that they decided the Lord Jesus was not the Messiah because he was so very poor and humble—they nevertheless used to read that the King Messiah would be poor. Yet, because of their pride, they did not understand that he was to come in such a manner. <term>CAP.</term> <note>Capnio/Reuchlin</note> This is, I say, what you must especially prove. <term>GAL.</term> Therefore, let them first hear Zechariah saying these things among others:

<note>original Hebrew: גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע הוא עני ורוכב על חמור ועל עיר בן אתונות</note>
Which is: *Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, the just one and the savior, he is poor and riding upon a donkey, even upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.* And a little later:
<note>original Hebrew: ודבר שלום לגוים ומשלו מים עד ים ומנהר עד אפסי ארץ</note>
That is: *And he shall speak peace to the nations, and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.* Now, that these things must be understood as referring to the Messiah is clear through the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, which says: "Behold, your King will come to you. This cannot be explained except as concerning the King Messiah. Because it is said here, 'And his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.' And we do not find that there was such a ruler in the time of the second house <note>The Second Temple period, 516 BCE – 70 CE</note>." From this it is clearly evident that the Kingdom of the Messiah must be understood spiritually, since a temporal kingdom and such poverty cannot exist together. To this also points what Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses ha-Darshan, an 11th-century scholar</note> says in his exposition of Genesis, regarding that which is said in the forty-ninth chapter: *Binding his foal to the vine*. He says: "When the Messiah comes to Jerusalem, he will be the one girding his donkey, and he will ride, and upon it he will come into Jerusalem, to conduct himself in poverty or humility, just as it is written in Zechariah chapter nine: 'Poor and humble, riding upon a donkey, or an ass.'" It follows in the book of Genesis in the same place: *And his donkey’s colt to the choice vine*. For when he comes to gather Israel (as is said in Zechariah chapter 10: <note>original Hebrew: אשרקה להם ואקבצם כי פדיתים</note> *I will whistle for them and gather them, for I have redeemed them*), then he will ride upon the foal of his donkey. And so Zechariah says in chapter 9: *And upon a colt, the foal of a donkey*. This is the tradition. Likewise in the <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term> <note>A classic collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (Midrash) on the book of Genesis</note> regarding that which is written in Genesis chapter 49, *The scepter shall not depart from Judah*, among other things, it is read: "The scepter shall not depart: this is the King Messiah, the son of David, who is to come to shatter the kingdoms with a rod, as is said in the second Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: תרועם בשבט ברזל ככלי יוצר תנפצם</note> *You shall break them with a rod of iron, and like a potter's vessel you shall dash them in pieces*." It follows: *And a scribe (or crusher) from between his feet*. This is also the King Messiah, who is to come to crush the nations with his feet. Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 26: <note>original Hebrew: תרמסנה רגלי עני</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> That is, *The foot of the poor man shall trample it.*
For that poor man is the Messiah, of whom it was said in Zechariah chapter 9: *Poor and riding upon a donkey.* Thus far the tradition. From these things which have been said, it is quite clearly evident that the Messiah was to be poor and humble, and would come riding upon a donkey to bring salvation. Therefore, the Jews can by no means deny that our Savior was the true Messiah simply because he was poor and humble.

<margin>B</margin> ## CHAPTER X.

->That the Messiah was to undergo many sufferings, and God<-
->also was to suffer much.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>A large decorative square initial 'Q' containing intricate leafy scrollwork and patterns.</image-desc> SINCE the Jews of our time—when they hear that our Redeemer was hungry after a fast of 40 days and nights, and was tempted in many ways by the devil, or was weary from his journey when he went about the cities and towns preaching the kingdom of God and leading sinners to repentance, or that he fled like a fearful man from the Jews who wanted to stone him, or that at the hour of his passion he began to fear and be sorrowful so that he might demonstrate himself to be a true man—say that he was neither the true Messiah nor God: for that reason, you would do well if <margin>D</margin> you showed through their scriptures that both the Messiah and God himself (for both were to be the same) would suffer such things, and far more grevious ones. <term>GAL.</term> I will therefore first bring forward Jeremiah, who says in chapter 14 among other things: <note>original Hebrew: מקוה ישראל מושיעו בעת צרה למה תהיה כגר בארץ וכאורח נטה ללון למה תהיה כאיש נדהם כגבור לא יוכל להושיע ואתה בקרבנו יהוה ושמך עלינו נקרא אל תניחנו</note> That is: *O Hope of Israel, its Savior in time of trouble, why should you be as a stranger in the land, and as a <margin>E</margin> traveler turning aside to stay or to lodge? Why should you be as a man astonished or terrified, like a mighty man who cannot save? Yet you, O God, are in our midst, and your name is called upon us. Do not leave us.* Also supporting what was said above is what is read in the book <term>Torat Kohanim</term> <note>A Hebrew title meaning 'The Law of the Priests,' another name for the Sifra, a commentary on Leviticus</note>, that is, the exposition of the book of Leviticus, regarding that which is said in chapter 25 of the same book: <note>original Hebrew: כי גרים ותושבים אתם עמדי</note> That is: *For you are strangers and sojourners, or <margin>F</margin> tenants with me.* For there it is said: "The Holy and Blessed God said, 'Do not make yourselves a permanent possession. For you are strangers and temporary sojourners with me.'" And thus David says in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 29: <note>original Hebrew: כי גרים אנחנו לפניך ותושבים ככל אבתינו</note> That is: *For we are strangers or pilgrims before you, and dwellers or tenants, as were all our fathers. Our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no staying.* And he also says in Psalm 39: <note>original Hebrew: כי גר אנכי עמך תושב ככל אבותי</note> That is: <margin>G</margin> *For I am a stranger or pilgrim with you, a dweller or tenant, as all my fathers were.* Therefore, you are with me <term>gherim vetossabim</term> <note>Hebrew: גרים ותושבים — gerim ve-toshavim</note>, that is, strangers, or pilgrims, and dwellers, or tenants. It is enough for the servant to be as his Master:
