# BOOK EIGHT

... "when that which is to happen to me comes, behold, it will be the same to me as it was to you." This is the tradition. Moreover, the previously mentioned words of both Jeremiah and this tradition do not properly fit God alone, nor man alone. Therefore, they fit best only the Messiah, who is both God and man. For he himself, by reason of his divinity, is the "hope of Israel," and by reason of his humanity—as a stranger and a pilgrim, and as one terrified and trembling, as well as a strong man who cannot save—he was so in his passion. Also relevant to this purpose is that which is written in the fifth chapter of Isaiah according to the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> translation: <term>לכן גלה עמי מבלי דעת</term> <note>original Hebrew: Laken galah ammi mibbelit da'at</note> This is: *Therefore my people are led into captivity without knowledge.* Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>R. Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "Because of this, namely, because they are without science and knowledge." And the rest follows until: <term>לכן הרחיבה שאול נפשה ופערה פיה לבלי חק</term> <note>original Hebrew: Laken hirchivah Sheol nafshah u-fa'arah fiha livli chok</note>, That is: *Therefore hell has enlarged its soul, and opened its mouth without limit.* Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Hell enlarged its soul, that is, itself. And it opened its mouth without limit. Because there was no <term>חק</term> (*hok*), that is, a divine precept, in their hand." And after a few words: <term>וישח אדם וישפל איש</term> <note>original Hebrew: Va-yishach adam va-yishpal ish</note> This is: *And man shall be bowed down or bent, and the great man shall be humbled.* Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> translated this into Chaldean thus: *And man shall be bent or bowed, and the high or strong among men shall be humbled.*" It is clear through this kind of exposition that those who were spoken of there were such in the presence of God, the Holy and Blessed, that He showed Himself as a man <term>נדהם</term> (*Nidham*), that is, terrified or trembling. And this is what He Himself says in the thirty-second chapter of Deuteronomy: <term>צור ילדך תשי ותשכח אל מחוללך</term> <note>original Hebrew: Tzur yelad'ka tashi va-tishkach El mecholaleka</note> This is: *The God who caused you to be born, who begat you, you shall weaken or afflict; and you shall forget the God who wounds you, or your slain, or afflicted, or sorrowing one.* Thus far Rabbi Solomon. Similar to this is <margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin> what is held in the book <term>ספרי</term> (*Siphre*) <note>An ancient legal commentary (Midrash) on Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, where in that place the previously mentioned words, "The God who begat you, you shall weaken or afflict," along with the rest, are explained; thus it is said word for word: "The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: You have made me as if I were a male wishing to give birth. For if a woman were in labor, sitting upon her birth-stool, would she not be troubled? Just as it is said in the thirty-seventh chapter of Isaiah: <term>כי באו בנים עד משבר וכח אין ללדת</term> <note>original Hebrew: Ki ba'u banim ad mashber ve-koach ein laledet</note>, *For the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth.* And if there were one in pain, and giving birth for the first time, would she not be even more troubled? As in Jeremiah chapter 4: <term>קול כחולה שמעתי צרה כמבכירה</term> <note>original Hebrew: Kol ke-cholah shamati tzarah ke-mavkirah</note> This is: *I heard a voice as of one in labor, anguish as of one giving birth for the first time.* And if there were two in her womb, would she not be in even greater distress? As it is said in Genesis chapter 25: <term>ויתרצצו הבנים בקרבה</term> <note>original Hebrew: Va-yitrotzetzu ha-banim be-kirbah</note> that is: *And the children struggled together within her.* And if it were a male, for whom there is no way of giving birth, who sought to give birth, would not his anguish be doubled? Certainly, several things are to be noted in this tradition. First, that the coming of the Messiah was desired with great affection by everyone, even by those who, because of the torments he was to suffer, did not wish to see him. Second, regarding that authority of Jeremiah which they bring in to explain why they did not wish to see him, namely: *Ask, I pray you, and see if a male gives birth.* For what reason? *Because I saw every man with his hands on his loins, like a woman in labor.* The Talmudic sages explain that "every man" there refers to the Holy and Blessed God. Thus, God himself, in the time of the Messiah, was to suffer extreme torments. This is the tradition. 

The same thing is also placed in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrash on the Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that which is said in Psalm 20: *May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.* Concerning this, moreover, Jeremiah says in the last chapter of Lamentations: <margin>The breath of our nostrils, the Messiah of the LORD, was caught in their corruptions.</margin> This is: *The breath of our nostrils, the Messiah of God <note>original: "tetragrammaton," the four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>, was caught in the nets (or corruptions) of those of whom we said: Under his shadow we shall live among the nations.* From all these things it is perfectly clear that the Messiah, being God and man, was to suffer the greatest passions and unheard-of torments.

## CHAPTER XI.

->That the Messiah was to voluntarily undertake the most bitter torments for the sake of the human race.<-

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'C' with intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

SINCE we read that Christ suffered voluntarily for the salvation of the human race, I would like to know whether the ancient Jews predicted that the Messiah would voluntarily suffer torments. 

GALATINUS: Exactly so. For, to leave aside the prophets for now, it is most clearly shown in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moses ha-Darshan, an 11th-century scholar of Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> that the Messiah himself would suffer torments willingly and voluntarily out of love for the human race. There, upon that which is said in the first chapter of the same book: <margin>And God said, Let there be light, and there was light.</margin> 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This is: *God said, Let there be light, and there was light.* Thus it is read: This is what is written in Psalm 97: <margin>Light is sown for the righteous.</margin> that is, *Light has risen for the righteous.* Rabbi Abba said: It is also written in Daniel chapter 2: <margin>And light dwells with him.</margin> This is: *And the light is with him.* For this is the light of the King Messiah. For so it was said of him in Psalm 36: <margin>For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light.</margin> that is, *Since with you is the fountain of life, in your light we shall see light.* For that is the light of the King Messiah. 

He teaches, however, that God hid the Messiah and his generation under the <margin>B</margin> throne of His glory. Satan then said before God: "Lord of the world, this light hidden under the throne of your glory—to whom does it belong?" He answered him: "To the Messiah and his generation." Satan said before Him: "Lord of the world, permit me, and I will oppose the Messiah and his generation." God said to him: "You will not be able to prevail against him." Satan said again before Him: "Permit me, and I will be able." The Holy and Blessed God said to him: "If you, Satan, are so eager for this, I will destroy him from the world. Nevertheless, not even one <margin>C</margin> soul of that generation will I destroy." 

And soon the Holy and Blessed God began to speak with the Messiah, and said to him: "Messiah, my righteous one, those who are hidden with you will be of such a kind that their sins will bring you into a heavy yoke. For your eyes shall not see light, and your ears shall hear great reproach. Your nose shall smell stench, and your mouth shall taste bitterness; your tongue shall cleave to your palate, and your skin shall stick to your bones, and your strength shall be thinned by <margin>D</margin> grief and groaning. Is it, therefore, your will to accept these things?" For if you take these upon yourself, it will be well. But if not, behold, I will drive them away from now on. 

The Messiah answered before Him: "Lord of the world, I indeed joyfully take these tribulations and torments upon myself, on this condition: that in my days you will give life to the dead, even those who have died from the first Adam until that time. And not only should you save them, but also those who were <margin>E</margin> devoured by wolves and lions, and those who happened to be submerged in the seas and rivers. And not only them, but even the stillborn. And not only the stillborn, but also those who have ascended in your foreknowledge to be created—save them in my days." 

The Holy and Blessed God said to him: "I grant it." Immediately, therefore, the Messiah out of love took upon himself all the torments and tribulations, just as it is written in Isaiah chapter 53: <margin>He was offered and he was afflicted.</margin> This is: *He was offered, and he himself was afflicted.* This is the whole tradition. 

Wherein five things especially worthy of note against the Jews of our age <margin>F</margin> are contained. The first of these is that the Messiah, before he existed according to his humanity, was light and illumination with God, and in God, even at the beginning when God created the world. To this, that word of the Lord Jesus himself is very much in agreement, saying in John chapter 8: *Before Abraham was, I am.* Likewise in chapter 7 <note>The author likely means John 8:12 or 12:46.</note>: *And I, the light, have come into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.* 

The second thing is that by divine permission, Satan was to oppose the Messiah and those believing in him, and <margin>G</margin> was to disturb him with every effort. To this, that saying of the same Lord in Luke chapter 22 is most harmonious: *Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat.* From this it is clear that it detracts nothing from Christ that he was tempted by the devil. <margin>A</margin>The Messiah was destined to suffer in manifold and most grievous ways because of the sins of the human race. This is noted where it is said that God entered into a pact with the Messiah, saying to him: "Messiah, my righteous one, those who are stored up with you—namely, through predestination—shall be of such a kind that their future sins will lead you into a most heavy yoke." From this it is clear that nothing our Savior suffered prevents him from having been the Messiah; for it was necessary for the Messiah to suffer for the salvation of men and so that the scriptures might be fulfilled. <margin>B</margin>The fourth point is that, just as through Adam all died, so through the Messiah all were to be brought to life. This is noted where the Messiah is introduced speaking with God, saying: "Lord of the world, I indeed joyfully take these tribulations or torments upon myself on the condition that in my days you will bring the dead to life," along with the rest of the promise. Finally, the fifth point is that the Messiah was to be tortured and suffer torments not unwillingly, but freely and voluntarily out of love for the sake of the salvation of the human race. From these points, not only is the proposition clear, but it is also evident that the Messiah himself, who was to be afflicted with torments, is the true God.

### CHAPTER XII.

->That God was to suffer strikes, reproaches, insults, and even death.<-

->C A P N I O.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter "E" depicting a scholar or religious figure seated at a desk in a classical vaulted room, surrounded by various observers.</image-desc>
<margin>C</margin>Even though in the preceding pages you have shown abundantly enough that the Messiah is God and man, and that God himself would undergo many torments: nevertheless, so that Jewish stubbornness <note>original: "perfidia," a common early modern term for the refusal to accept Christian doctrine.</note> may be more and more convinced, you ought to prove even more expressly from their own scriptures that God himself was to be afflicted by strikes, reproaches, and even death for the salvation of the human race. GALATINUS: This is first clear from what is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: <note>original: "Thren. 3."</note> *He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has borne it upon himself. He shall put his mouth in the dust, if so be there may be hope. He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproach,* or insult. <note>original Hebrew quoted: Lamentations 3:28-30.</note> That these things ought to be understood as referring to God is clear in the *Midrash Echa* <note>A Rabbinic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Where, upon those same words, it is said word-for-word: Rabbi Samuel son of Nahman said, that the Holy and Blessed God called the ministering angels and said to them: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He hangs a sack over his door." He said to them: "I also shall do so." Just as it is said in the fiftieth chapter of Isaiah: *I will clothe the heavens with blackness, and I will make sackcloth their covering.* Again he said to them: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He extinguishes the lights." He said to them: "I also shall do so." And this is what is written in the third chapter of Joel: *The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their shining.* He asked them further, saying:

<column-break/>

462 BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin>"When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They answered him: "He goes barefoot." He said to them: "I also shall act thus." And this is what is written in the first chapter of Nahum: *The Lord’s way is in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.* Again he asked them, saying: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He sits and is silent." <margin>B</margin>But he said to them: "I also will do so." And this is what is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: *He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has borne it upon himself; he shall put his mouth in the dust; perhaps there will be hope. He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he shall be filled with reproach.* Therefore, the Rabbi, explaining this scripture and coming to these *pasukim* <term>verses</term>, always wept. All this is from the tradition. Micah also spoke of the striking of God's cheek in this way in the fifth chapter: *With a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.* <margin>C</margin>Who that judge of Israel is, Isaiah shows when he says in the thirty-third chapter: *The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our King; he will save us.* <note>original: "יהוה שפטנו..." (YHWH is our judge...)</note> Furthermore, that God was to suffer the most grievous insults from the Jews was foretold through the prophet Hosea, speaking thus with the words of God in the seventh chapter: *Woe to them, for they have departed from me. Destruction to them, for they have trespassed against me. And I redeemed them.* <margin>D</margin> *But they have spoken lies against me.* In these words, God threatened the Jews with two greatest evils: namely, eternal damnation in the world to come, because by denying him before Pilate, they would depart from him. And therefore he says, *Woe to them because they have departed,* that is, they will depart from me. And their final destruction and dispersion throughout the world, when he says, *Destruction to them, because they have sinned,* that is, they will sin against me. <margin>E</margin>And wishing to express the cause, he adds: *And I redeemed,* that is, I will redeem them. *But they have spoken,* that is, they will speak lies against me. It is as if he had said: "Behold how great their ingratitude will be; for while I redeem them, they themselves will speak lies against me," namely, by accusing me falsely before Pilate and afflicting me with the heaviest insults. That these things ought to be explained exactly as they have been set forth is clearly evident through their ancient Teachers, and especially through those things said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note> regarding that which is said in the thirty-ninth Psalm: *I said: I will guard my ways from sinning with my tongue.* <margin>F</margin>For it is said there: This is what is written in Proverbs, chapter 15: *A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up fury.* For an evil tongue—namely, one that speaks against God—is more grievous than idolatry. For when the children of Israel finally sinned in the desert, the sentence of judgment was not brought against them until they sinned against God with their mouths. For thus the scripture says: <margin>G</margin> *And God heard the sound of their words, and was angry.* And again it says in Numbers, chapter 14: *As I live, says God, if I do not do to you exactly as you have spoken in my ears.* And so also Malachi says in the second chapter.

BOOK EIGHT.

"You have wearied the Lord with your words," <note>original: "הוגעתם יהוה בדבריכם" (Malachi 2:17)</note> that is, you have vexed God with your speech. He does not say you vexed him in your deeds, but in your words. And so Isaiah himself says in his third chapter: "Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because their tongue and their deeds are against the Lord, to rebel in the eyes of his glory." <note>original: "כשלת ירושלם ויהודה נפל..." (Isaiah 3:8)</note> Likewise, he says through Jeremiah in the twelfth chapter: "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned or cast away my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul—or, I have given my soul out of love—into the hand of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me, therefore I have hated her." <note>original: "ידידות נפשי בכף איביה" (Jeremiah 12:7-8)</note> Thus far the tradition. 

From this, the proposition is clear. For when God says that he has given his soul—or himself—out of love, there is surely no doubt that he gave himself over to passion and death for their redemption. This is noted when it is said, "Into the hand of her enemies." Moreover, that God would give his soul (that is, himself) because of his love for his people is clear through the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <term>Midrash: an ancient Jewish commentary on the Hebrew Scriptures</term> on the Song of Songs. Regarding that saying in the first chapter of the same book, "Tell me, [you] whom my soul loved," <note>original: "הגידה לי את שאהבה נפשי" (Song of Songs 1:7)</note> it explains it thus: "Tell me of the people whom my soul loved; the people, namely, for whom I gave my soul <note>original: "נפשי" (*naphsi*)</note>, that is, my life, or myself, or my very person." 

That God was to undergo death is also clear from what is written in the first chapter of Malachi: "And you said, 'Behold, what a weariness!' and you have made me expire, says the Lord of hosts." <note>original: "והפחתם אתי" (Malachi 1:13). The author interprets the Hebrew word for 'sniffed at' or 'scorned' as 'made to expire' or 'killed'.</note> For there it was written "you made *me* expire," but the scribes changed it to "you made *it* expire," as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note> testifies there in his gloss. Likewise, in the first chapter of Habakkuk: "Are you not from of old, O Lord my God, my Holy One? You shall not die." <note>original: "לא תמות" (Habakkuk 1:12)</note> For so it was written there; but the scribes placed "we shall not die" <note>This refers to the *Tiqqune Sopherim*, or "Corrections of the Scribes," where ancient editors altered the text to avoid appearing to speak of God's death.</note> instead, as is said in the book *Siphre* regarding that saying in Numbers chapter 10: "Rise up, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee." From these things which have been said, it is manifest that God was to suffer strikes, insults, and death. Since God cannot suffer these things [in his divine nature], it is plainly evident that they were to be understood concerning the Messiah, who was to be both God and man, since the prophets also predicted that he would suffer all these same things.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->That the Messiah in his passion was to be sold, reproached,<-
->beaten with whips and fists, afflicted with countless<-
->shames and insults, clothed in purple,<-
->and crowned with thorns.<-

### CAPNIO.

<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pen name of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist of the Renaissance.</note>

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut decorative initial 'C' featuring intertwined leafy vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>
SINCE our Lord Jesus Christ in his passion was sold, reproached, despised, beaten with whips and fists, afflicted with the gravest shames and injuries, and clothed in pur-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>ple and crowned with a crown of thorns, I would like to know whether all these same things—that the Messiah was to undergo them in his passion—can be proved through the writings of the ancient Jews. 

**GALATINUS:** It certainly can. For that the Messiah, God and man, was to be sold for a low price—that is, thirty pieces of silver—Zechariah predicted in his eleventh chapter, speaking thus in his [the Messiah's] person: "And they weighed out my wages at thirty pieces of silver. And God said to me, 'Throw it to the potter'—or the statue-maker—'the handsome price at which I was valued by them.'" <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "וישקלו את שכרי..." (Zechariah 11:12-13)</note> Concerning this, Amos also says in his second chapter: "For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back—or lead him back, or transfer him—because they have sold, or traded, the Just One for silver." <note>Amos 2:6</note> The explanation of these words is set forth very extensively in the 24th chapter of the fourth book. 

That the Messiah himself was to be reproached in his <margin>C</margin> passion is found in Psalm 89, where it is said: "Wherewith your enemies have reproached, O Lord; wherewith they have reproached the heels of your Messiah." <note>original: "עקבות משיחך" (*ikvot mashiach*), often translated as 'footsteps'.</note> Here the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "The heels of your Messiah, that is, the final times of the King Messiah." For then the final things of the Messiah were reproached, when he was despised by everyone in his passion and death. 

That this interpretation <margin>D</margin> is correct is clear from the explanation of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan regarding what is said in chapter 39 about Joseph: "And he fled outside." For there it is read that Rabbi Judas said: "David said, 'Just as I did not sing a Song until I was reproached or despised, so the children of Israel are not going to sing a Song when the King Messiah comes until he himself has been reproached, or despised, or reviled,' just as it is written: 'For your enemies have reproached, O God, they have reproached the heels'—that is, the extremities or the end—'of your Messiah.'" 

Regarding the Messiah's <margin>E</margin> reproach, it is also held in the *Midrash Tehillim* (that is, the explanation of the Psalms) regarding the title of Psalm 18, "The words of this Song." For it is said there: "When the Messiah comes in haste, they will not sing a Song until the Messiah himself has been reproached. Just as it was said: 'For your enemies have reproached, O God, they have reproached the heels'—that is, the final things—'of your Messiah.'" 

In the *Mishnah* also (that is, in the *Talmud*), it is written that against the "heels"—that is, the final things—of the Messiah, impudence will be multi-<margin>F</margin>plied. 

That he was indeed to be struck with whips and blows to the head, and afflicted with the most serious insults, is especially clear through what Isaiah said, speaking in his person in chapter 50: "I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pluck—or tear—the hair. I did not hide my face from confusion and spitting." <note>Isaiah 50:6</note> The Psalm-<margin>G</margin>ist also indicated that this was to happen in Psalm 129, saying: "The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows." Which the Chaldean interpreter <term>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Bible</term> who is at hand translates thus: "Upon my body the plowers plowed..."

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the physical suffering of the Messiah. It moves from the general concept of the "dying God" to specific prophetic symbols of the Passion, such as the scourging (plowing), the purple robe (wine-stained garments), and the crown of thorns (the vineyard's "wild grapes"). ...the plowers plowed, they lengthened their plowing. <note>original: "arauerunt arantes, prolongauerũt arationes suas" (Psalm 129:3)</note>

<margin>A</margin> Here the prophet, speaking in the person of the Messiah, uses the past tense to represent the future—a common prophetic style used to show that the coming truth is absolutely certain. Therefore, the "plowers plowed upon the body of the Messiah" because the Jews were to strike him most cruelly with whips. Furthermore, the "furrows or plow-lines were lengthened" upon him because they were to cover his entire body with strikes and wounds, according to what is said in the first chapter of Isaiah: "From the sole of the foot even to the top of the head, there is no soundness in him." <note>original: "A planta pedis vsque ad verticem, non est in eo sanitas" (Isaiah 1:6)</note> That he was also to be clothed in purple as a mockery is found in the commentary on the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, <term>Hadarsan: "The Preacher," an 11th-century scholar known for his Midrashic compilations</term> regarding what is said in the 49th chapter of that same book: "He shall wash his garment in wine, and his covering or clothing in the blood of grapes." <note>original: "כבס ביין לבשו וברם ענבים סותה" (Genesis 49:11)</note> There it is read as follows: "He shall wash (it says) his garment in wine." For when the Messiah comes, he will be clothed in purple, beautiful to look upon, which will be similar in color to wine. It follows: "And his clothing in the blood of grapes." For the clothing of the King Messiah will be silk, red as blood, and it will be embroidered on top with other colors. And he himself will be the head of Israel. This is also what was said in the sixty-third chapter of Isaiah: "Why is [your garment] red?" <note>original: "מדוע אדום"</note> "And his clothing in the blood of grapes." Just as was said by the same prophet in that same place: "Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one who treads in the wine-press?" <note>original: "מדוע ללבושך ובבגדיך כדורך בגת"</note> Thus far the tradition. While this refers literally to the purple garment with which the Messiah was mocked, and his seamless tunic woven from the top throughout, the words of Isaiah and the Patriarch Jacob must be understood mystically. For when he says, "He shall wash his garment in wine, and his covering in the blood of grapes," he intended to explain the great mystery of the Messiah's passion by repeating the same idea with different words. For this Hebrew word *anauim* <note>original: "ענבים"</note>—that is, "of grapes"—which is contained in the second clause, can be read as "of the humble" by the Hebrew grammatical rule where the letters *bumaph* <term>Bumaph: A mnemonic for the labial letters (B, V, M, P) which often substitute for one another in Hebrew grammar</term> are swapped (changing the letter *beth* to *vau*). Then the sense of the text would be: "and in the blood of the humble [he shall wash] his covering." This shows that the Messiah, in his humility, would wash his covering or garment—that is, his body—in his own blood. The words of Isaiah express this even more clearly. Furthermore, that he was to be crowned with thorns is clearly gathered from the words of the same prophet, when he says in the 5th chapter: "My beloved had a vineyard." <note>original: "כרם היה לידידי"</note> and shortly after: "And he hoped that it would bring forth grapes, but it brought forth thorns." <note>original: "ויקו לעשות ענבים ויעש באשים"</note> In this passage, although the Hebrew word *beushim* <note>original: "באשים"</note> is ambiguous, meaning either "wild grapes" or "thorns," here it signifies thorns, not wild grapes, as the commentaries of the ancients clearly indicate. Rabbi Jonah explains it this way in this place, saying: "And it made *beushim*, that is, thorns." Just as it is said in Job, chapter 31: "Let thorns grow instead of wheat." <note>original: "באשה" (Job 31:40)</note> This is suggested by the preceding clause, which says: "Instead of wheat, let the briar come forth." Rabbi Kimhi <term>Kimhi: David Kimhi (Radak), a medieval rabbi and grammarian</term> also affirms this, saying that *beushim* in this text of Isaiah is a type of thorn. It is certain, therefore, that all of this was fulfilled when, as

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> John reports in the 19th chapter, "The soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, and surrounded him with a purple robe." From all these things it is clear that the Messiah, in his passion, was to be sold, reproached, and despised; he was to be beaten with whips and fists, afflicted with the gravest insults and outrages, clothed in purple, and crowned with thorns. These things, and all the others we have mentioned regarding the Messiah's passion, were pronounced more expressly and distinctly by Isaiah himself.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*That the mystery of the Messiah's passion was expressly and distinctly foretold by Isaiah.*<-

## CAPNIO.

Thus far the prophet <note>This entire passage is a translation of Isaiah 52:13–53:12, a foundational text in Christian-Jewish polemics regarding the identity of the Messiah.</note>. In these words, many mysteries of the Messiah himself are revealed.

<margin>Sixteen mysteries.</margin>
The first mystery is that the Messiah himself, the servant of God, according to his humanity, was to be more excellent than the other saints, whether existing in heaven or on earth. Concerning this he says, *He shall be exalted, and raised up, and be very high.* For this is explained in the book of the Sanhedrin, in the chapter *Helec*, as follows:
<note>original Hebrew: ירום מאברהם ונשא ממשה וגבה מאד יותר ממלאכי השרת</note>
"He shall be exalted more than Abraham, raised up more than Moses, and be very high, more than the ministering Angels"—that is, those who serve God.
<margin>Talmudic explanation.</margin>
From this, it follows that the Messiah was to be God. For since God alone exceeds the nature of Angels, and the Messiah was to be higher than the Angels who serve God—who, according to the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, are more worthy and more sublime than all others—the Jews must necessarily concede from their own scriptures that he is God. The second mystery concerns his exaltation on the cross, through which he was to be exalted, raised up, and very highly elevated: for through his passion and resurrection he was to draw all things to himself. Therefore it follows: *As many were astonished at you, and as his appearance—or face—was despised or marred by men, and his form by the sons of men, so shall he sprinkle many nations:* namely, with the water of baptism. Through this, he was to lead those who were to receive his law to eternal salvation. It is no obstacle that the prophet sometimes speaks in the second person and sometimes in the third, since he does so according to the prophetic style. Wherefore the kings of the nations...

<column-break/>

...were to wonder at him, and were to shut their mouths, placing their hands over their mouths: because they were to see what had not been told to them, and contemplate what they had not heard. For it is certain that the mysteries of the Messiah were not told by the prophets except to the Israelite people. Therefore he adds, *Who has believed our report? And over whom—or to whom—is the arm of the Lord revealed?* This is to say: Who ever believed our announcement, so that those to whom a mystery of this kind was never told, nor ever revealed by what means God would fulfill it, should believe it most firmly?

The third mystery is that the Messiah was to be a little child in the beginning, and have a humble birth, when he says, *And he shall grow up like a tender plant before him, and like a root out of dry ground:* where both the poverty of the nascent Messiah is expressed, and the virginity of his suffering mother. For on account of poverty, he was rightly to be compared at his birth to a slender and thin branch; and his mother, on account of her virginity, is not inaptly likened to dry ground, because she was to conceive and give birth to him having been moistened by no human seed at all.

The fourth mystery is that in his progress he was despised and regarded as almost nothing. Concerning this he says, *He has no form nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we did not desire him.* For even if the text says affirmatively, *And we desired*, it is nevertheless to be understood negatively. For the preceding negative word <term>lo</term> <note>Hebrew: לֹא</note>, that is "not," as <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator often cited in Christian works.</note> Rabbi David says, serves both clauses: as if he were saying, "And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, nor did we desire him." And wishing to give the reason why they did not desire him, he immediately added: *He was despised, and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and known by infirmity, and as with a hiding of faces from him.* As if he were saying: We hid our faces so that we would not look at him. And this was because he was vile. Whence we did not even esteem him.

The fifth mystery is that he was to suffer because of our sins. Therefore he says, *Truly he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows. And we esteemed him as one stricken, a smitten God, and afflicted.* Here it should be especially noted that the Hebrew text has "a smitten God" and not "smitten by God," as our <note>The Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible translation of the Catholic Church.</note> edition says. For the Hebrew text itself says: <note>original: מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים — Mucche Elohim</note> *Mucche Elohim*, that is, a struck or wounded God. For if it were "smitten by God," it would say <note>original: מַכֵּה מֵאֱלֹהִים — Mucche Meelohim</note> *Mucche Meelohim*, with the preposition <term>min</term> <note>The Hebrew letter Mem acts as a prefix meaning 'from' or 'by'.</note>, which signifies "by," "from," "of," or "out of" among the Hebrews. It follows: *But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our sins. The discipline*—that is, the correction—*of our peace was upon him, and in his bruise or wound*—that is, through his bruise and wound—*we are healed.*

The sixth mystery is that all the righteous except himself and his mother have strayed from the way of salvation by common law, and he bore the sins of all, specifically as far as the punishments are concerned. Therefore he says, *All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside to his own way. And God made the sin of us all to meet in him,* so that he might satisfy for us all.

The seventh mystery is that he voluntarily and patiently sustained these punishments or sorrows for us even unto death. Therefore...

<margin>A</margin> Therefore he says: *He himself was offered as an afflicted one, or as one who is voluntary and willing, and he shall not open his mouth. Like a lamb he shall be led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers he shall be silent, and he shall not open his mouth.* The eighth point is that although he was to suffer as a man, yet as God he was to be entirely impassible <term>impassible: a theological term meaning incapable of suffering or changing</term>. Therefore he adds: *From anguish and from judgment he was taken away, and who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "generationem eius quis enarrabit?"</note> For here God the Father speaks concerning the Messiah as a man, saying: "After he has been taken away from those things which could happen to the Messiah regarding his humanity," <margin>B</margin> that is, when he is considered with that human part having been removed, "who shall declare his generation?" This means: who will be able to declare the manner and cause of his incarnation? For to no one will such great capacity be given that he might be able to declare it fully and perfectly. And giving the reason, he adds: *Because he was cut off,* that is, he shall be cut off *from the land of the living, for the wickedness of my people, and their wound,* or *the wound that was theirs.* This is understood as the wound of original sin. For a "wound" (as is pleasing to physicians) is an ancient injury. <margin>C</margin> The ninth point is that just as the Prophet described him as the redeemer of the faithful through the merit of his passion, so he suggested him to be the judge of the damned unfaithful through the power of his divinity, where he says: *He shall give the wicked in his grave, or in his pit.* This is, according to the exposition of Rabbi Jonathan <note>original: "Rabbi Ionathae." Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note>: "He shall deliver the wicked into Gehenna <term>Gehenna: a place of spiritual punishment or hell</term>, and the rich in their riches, who have acted iniquitously, into the death of perdition." The tenth point is that he ought to be entirely righteous and free from all sin, when he says: *Because he did no iniquity, nor was deceit found* <margin>D</margin> *in his mouth. And God willed to crush him with infirmity.* It is as if he were saying: "Even if he shall be entirely righteous and devoid of all sin, he is nevertheless going to suffer for the sins of others." The eleventh point is that on account of the merit of his death, he was to have many spiritual sons—that is, disciples—even until the end of the world. And this is what he says: *If he shall lay down,* that is, because he will lay down *his soul for sin, he shall see a seed of length of days.* This is understood <margin>E</margin> regarding his faithful ones and his faith, which shall stand forever. It follows: *And the will of God shall prosper in his hand.* And the reason is because, as it is said: *From the labor,* that is, for the labor *of his soul, which he himself shall see, he shall be satisfied.* The twelfth point is that through the wisdom of his doctrine he was to justify many. Wherefore he adds: *In his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their sins.* The thirteenth point is that he ought to have victory against the Devil and divide the spoils of the strong, because he was to hand himself over to death. <margin>F</margin> Therefore he says: *Therefore I will divide for him among many, or I will cause him to share with many, and with the strong he shall divide the spoil,* that is, the spoils. *Because he exposed or handed over his soul to death,* that is, himself. The fourteenth point is that he was to be numbered with the wicked like a guilty man and an evildoer. Therefore he says: *And he was counted with the iniquitous.* The fifteenth point is that although his passion ought to be sufficient <margin>G</margin> to blot out the sins of all, it was not, however, going to blot out the sins of everyone, but only of those who would believe in him and perform penance. For that reason he adds: *And he himself bore the sins of many.* The six-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> -teenth point is that the charity of the Messiah was to be so great that he was going to pray to his eternal Father even for his adversaries, and those afflicting and killing him. Wherefore he finally adds: *And he shall intercede for the sinners.* No one who has diligently scrutinized his deeds both in life and in death would think it should be denied that all and each of these things were fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER XV.

<margin>B</margin> ->*A refutation of the objection of modern Jews who falsely explain the words of Isaiah, through the expositions of the ancient Talmudists.*<-

<meta>This page continues the theological debate regarding Isaiah 53. Having previously analyzed the physical and spiritual suffering of the "Servant of God," the author now refutes the contemporary Jewish interpretation that this "Servant" represents the collective people of Israel in their exile, arguing instead that the text can only refer to a sinless Messiah.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin> With no one disagreeing, they say that the nations who now suppress and afflict the Jewish people in this captivity <note>The "captivity" refers to the Jewish Diaspora and their status in medieval Europe.</note> are likewise to be punished by God for this. To prove this, they bring forward the saying from the last chapter of Joel: *I will gather all nations, and will lead them into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will contend with them there over my people.* Since, therefore, the Prophet says that by the bruise or wound of this servant of God, of whom he speaks here, healing was given to others; and that God made the sin of all other men to fall upon him: it follows surely that <margin>B</margin> he does not speak here of the Jewish people, for whose punishments others are not saved, but rather punished.

<margin>Second.</margin> The second point is truly when the Prophet, speaking of the same servant of God, says: *Because he had done no iniquity, neither was guile found in his mouth.* This is clearly false regarding the Jews, as is plainly evident by the reality of the matter: since for the most part they are immersed in usury, iniquities, deceits, sorceries, evil deeds, and other outrages. Furthermore, it is clearly held from the testimony of Holy Scripture that in this most recent captivity (as we have <margin>C</margin> proved elsewhere) they are only there because of their own crimes. Indeed, if they wished to perform penance for their sins, they would be redeemed immediately (as will be clear in the following pages). This, moreover, is against their own interpretation: for they, presupposing that they are not in this captivity except because of a great sin, or great sins, and seeking among themselves what that sin might be, or what those sins are, different people hold different views. Yet in this they all agree: that the Jewish <margin>D</margin> people are not in this captivity without sin or iniquity, nor because of the sins of other nations, but only because of their own. From which it is openly clear that this servant of God, of whom Isaiah speaks, cannot be understood as the Jewish people, but the Messiah himself, who was to be entirely immune from sin. Finally, the third point is when <margin>Third.</margin> the Prophet last says of the same servant of God: *And he shall pray for the sinners.* This can by no means be understood <margin>E</margin> of the Jewish people living in this captivity. For they not only do not pray for the salvation of the sinners of other nations, but rather for their destruction, and especially for the ruin and perdition of the Roman Empire and the Christian Church: thinking that after the downfall of the Roman Empire and the destruction of the Church of Christ, they are soon to be liberated from this servitude and captivity, as we have shown elsewhere. From which it is manifest that this saying of the Prophet, *And he shall pray for the sinners,* can in no way be verified of them. From these <margin>F</margin> things, therefore, and many others contained in this prophecy, which can in no way fit the Jewish people living in this captivity, it is clear and transparent that the servant of God himself, of whom the Prophet speaks, cannot possibly be the Jewish people themselves. Moreover, that the aforementioned words of Isaiah can rightly fit no one else than the Messiah himself is clearly evident not only from the things said before and the text itself, but also appears more clearly and evidently from the sayings of the ancient interpreters. <margin>G</margin> Indeed, all the ancient interpreters, both those who preceded Christ’s

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> advent and those who were after Christ suffered, interpreted these same words of Isaiah only as referring to the Messiah: just as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator.</note> himself openly testifies, while explaining that passage: *Behold, my servant shall understand,* along with the rest: he says thus, "Our masters affirm that all this is to be understood regarding the Messiah." This can also be seen through many others, who in various places assert that the words themselves were spoken concerning the Messiah. For in the exposition of the book of Genesis, Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Rabbi Moses ha-Darshan (11th century), a famous preacher and scholar of Narbonne.</note>, on that saying in chapter 24, <term>ויביאה יצחק האהלה שרה אמו</term> <note>original Hebrew: "And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother."</note>, that is, <margin>B</margin> *And Isaac introduced her into the tabernacle of Sarah his mother*: it is said thus word for word, "This is the King Messiah, who was in the generation of the impious, and he rejected them, and chose the holy and blessed God, and His holy name, so that he might worship Him with all his heart. And he gave his heart to seeking mercies for Israel, and to fasting, and to humbling himself for them. Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 53: *And he was wounded for our faults, bruised* <margin>C</margin> *for our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him.* And since the children of Israel were sinning, he himself shall pray for them. Just as it is said in the same chapter of Isaiah: *And in his bruise we were healed.* And therefore God preserves him, so that he may save Israel, and that he may exult with them in the resurrection of the dead. Just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 33: *Blessed are you, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by God, the shield of your helper?* Just as Isaiah also says in chapter 45: *Israel* <margin>D</margin> *shall be saved in God with an everlasting salvation,* or *eternal. You shall not be ashamed, nor confounded, world without end.*" This tradition is furthermore written in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with legal proceedings and the Messiah.</note>, in the chapter <term>Helec</term> <note>The 11th chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin.</note>, that it was said from the house of Rab, that is, by the disciples of Rab, that "The Languid One" <note>original Latin: "languidus." In the Talmudic source, the name is given as *Cholaia* (the Sickly One).</note> is the name of the Messiah: according to that saying of Isaiah chapter 53: *Truly he himself has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows.* In the same place it is also read that Rab said, "If the Messiah is among the living, he is like our holy Teacher. <margin>E</margin> If truly among the dead, he is like Daniel, the man of desires." Where the little gloss of Rabbi Solomon says, "If the Messiah is (he says) among those who are still living, in truth he is like our holy Teacher. For he both bore infirmities and was holy. If truly he is among those who are already dead: behold, he was like Daniel, the man of desires, who was sentenced to sufferings in the den of lions, and was holy and perfect, and a prince." However, <term>כחגון</term> <term>chegon</term>, that is, *as* or *like*, is not taken strictly here. Thus says Rabbi Solomon. From which things it <margin>F</margin> clearly appears that there was a doubt among the ancient Jews whether the Messiah then lived or was dead: for it was established to them that he had already come. Furthermore, in the same book and chapter, those words, *Behold my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and extolled, and shall be very high* (as we said in the preceding chapter) are interpreted thus: "Behold, my servant Messiah shall prosper; he shall be exalted more than Abraham, extolled more than Moses, and shall be higher than the ministering Angels who namely minister to God." From all of which it is quite clearly evident that all <margin>G</margin> the words of Isaiah from that place, *Behold my servant shall understand,* until the end of the 53rd chapter, were understood by the ancient wise men of the Jews to be concerning the Messiah.

# BOOK EIGHT.

## CHAPTER XVI.

->Confirmation of the previous refutation through the Aramaic paraphrase of Rabbi Jonathan on these same words of Isaiah.<-

### CAPNIO

<image-desc>A decorative circular woodcut containing the capital letter V within a laurel wreath.</image-desc>Since the Aramaic translation <note>Aramaic was the common language of Judea; the "Targum" refers to the traditional paraphrases used in synagogues to explain the Hebrew scriptures.</note> of Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel—which they call the *Targum*—carries such great authority among them that none of them dare to contradict it, I would like you to show, for the confirmation of this refutation, how through that same Rabbi’s *Targum* all the previously mentioned words of Isaiah cannot be understood as referring to the Israelite people, nor to any other man, but only to the Messiah himself. GALATINUS: It is not without reason, my dear Capnio, that you urge me to do this; for that same Rabbi, in his Aramaic paraphrase, explains all these same words (as you know) concerning the Messiah, according to our purpose. <margin>Isaiah 52:13.</margin> For where the Hebrew text says, *Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, and extolled, and be very high*, the Rabbi says in Aramaic: <note>original: הא יצלח, עבדי משיחא ירום ויסני ויחקיף לחדא</note> **"Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper, he shall be exalted, and increased, and shall be very strong."** <margin>Verse 15.</margin> Where the Hebrew text has, *So shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him*, he says in Aramaic: <note>original: כן יבדר עממין סגיאין עלוהי, ישתקון מלכין ישוון ידיהון על פומיהון</note> **"So shall he scatter (or cleanse) many peoples; before him kings shall be silent, and they shall place their hands upon their mouths."** From this it is clear that the Hebrew word *yazah* <note>original: יזה</note> which is placed there is ambiguous (for it can mean both "to sprinkle/scatter" and "to shut" or "to constrain"). Here it is not taken for "to sprinkle" (as the author of our [Latin Vulgate] edition understood it), but for "to constrain" or "to shut." Where the Hebrew letter says, *For that which had not been told them they shall see, and that which they had not heard they shall consider*, Jonathan himself says: <note>original: ארי דלא ישתעיו להון חזון ודלא שמעו יסתכלו</note> **"For those to whom it was not told concerning him have seen, and those who did not hear have considered."** <margin>Isaiah 53:1.</margin> And where it is said in Hebrew, *Who hath believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?*, he says in Aramaic: <note>original: מאן הימין לבסורתנא ודרע גבורתא דיהוה ברין על מאן אתגלי</note> **"Who has believed this, our announcement? And the strength of the mighty arm of the Lord, upon whom has it been revealed in this way?"** <margin>Verse 2.</margin> And what is held in Hebrew, *He hath no form nor comeliness*, and so on, he explains in Aramaic: <note>original: לא חזו חלוא חזויה ולא אימתיה אימת הדיוט ויהי זיו קודשא זיחיה דכל דיחזיניה אסתכל ביה</note> **"His appearance shall not be a common appearance, nor his respect like that of a commoner; his glory shall be a holy splendor, and whoever sees him shall gaze upon him."** Because of this, it shall be for a good announcement. <margin>Verse 3.</margin> And where the Hebrew text has, *And as it were a hiding of faces from him*, and so on, he translated into Aramaic: <note>original: וכמא דהות מסלקא אפי שכינתא מננא בסריין ולא חשיבין</note> **"And as if the face of his Divine Presence had been taken away or removed from us, we seeing him yet not regarding him."** As for what is said in Hebrew, *Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows*, he turns it into Aramaic

<column-break/>

<margin>A Verse 5.</margin> as: <note>original: בכין על חובנא הוא יבעי ועויתנא בדיליה ישתבקון לנא</note> **"Thus, or then, he shall pray for our guilts, and our sins shall be forgiven to us because of him."** And what is held in Hebrew, *The chastisement of our peace was upon him*, and so on, he translated into Aramaic: <note>original: ובלביתניה לפחמנוהי חובנא ישתבקון לנא</note> **"And in his teaching, peace shall be multiplied upon us; and by his word, our guilts shall be forgiven to us."** <margin>B Verse 6.</margin> Truly, what is said in Hebrew, *All we like sheep have gone astray*, and so on, he explained in Aramaic: <note>original: כלנא כענא אתבדרנא גבר לקבל אורחיה גלינא ומן קדם יהוה הות רעוא למשבק חובני כולנא בדיליה</note> **"All of us were scattered like sheep, each one was exiled toward his own way; and from the part of God, it was a pleasure to spare, or to remit, the guilt of us all because of him."** <margin>C Verse 7.</margin> And where the Hebrew text has, *He was offered, and he was afflicted (or voluntary, or willing), and he opened not his mouth*, he translated into Aramaic: <note>original: בעי והוא מתהב ועד לא פתח פומיה אתקבל עממיא תקיפי עממיא ימסור</note> **"He prayed, and he was heard, even before he opened his mouth; he shall deliver the strong ones of the nations."** And where it is held in Hebrew, *He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter*, and so on, he says in Aramaic: <note>original: כאמרא לנכסתא ימסר וכדחל דקדם גוזזהא שתקא ולית לקבליה דפתח פומיה</note> **"Like a ram he shall be delivered to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers he shall be silent. And there shall be no one before him who opens his mouth or speaks a word."** <margin>D Verse 8.</margin> And what the Hebrew text has, *And who shall declare his generation?*, he translated into Aramaic: <note>original: ופרישן דיתעבדן לנא ביומוהי מאן יכיל לממני</note> **"And the wonders that shall be done for us in his days, who shall be able to recount them?"** <margin>Verse 9.</margin> What is read in Hebrew, *And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death*, he explained in Aramaic: <note>original: וימסר ית רשיעיא לניהנם וית עתירי נכסיא דאנסו במותא דאבדנא</note> **"And he shall deliver the wicked into Gehenna <note>The place of punishment or hell.</note>, and the rich in possessions who acted iniquitously into the death of perdition."** <margin>E Verse 10.</margin> And what is said in Hebrew, *Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him in infirmity; when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin*, and so on, he also explained in Aramaic: <note>original: ומן קדם יהוה הות רעוא למצרף ולדכאה ית שארא דעמיה כדיל לנקא מחובן נפשיהון יחזון במלכות משיחיהון יסנון בנין ובנן וירכון יומין ועבדי אוריתא דיהוה ברעותיה יצלחון</note> **"And from the part of God it was a pleasure to refine and purify the remnant of his people, so that their souls might be cleansed of guilt. They shall see the Kingdom of their Messiah; they shall multiply sons and daughters who shall prolong their days. And those who perform the law of God shall prosper in his good pleasure."** <margin>F</margin> <margin>Verse 11.</margin> What is also said in Hebrew, *By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities*, he translated: <note>original: בחכמתיה יזכאן בדיל לשעבדא סגיאין לאוריתא ועל חוביהון הוא יבעי</note> **"In his wisdom he shall justify the righteous, so that he may bind many to the law; and for their guilts he himself shall pray."** <margin>Verse 12.</margin> Finally, what the Hebrew text has, *Because he hath poured out (or delivered) his soul unto death*, with the rest until the end, he translated and explained: <note>original: חלף דמסר למותא נפשיה וית מרודיא שעביד לאוריתא והוא על חובין סגיאין יבעי ולמרודיא</note> **"Because he delivered his soul to death, and subjected the rebellious to the law; and he shall pray for many sins, and for the rebellious..."** <margin>G</margin>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin>
<note>original: "ישתבק בדיליה"</note> **“It shall be forgiven because of him”**: That is, because he delivered his soul unto death, or offered himself, and bound the transgressors to the law: And he himself shall pray for many guilty ones, and the transgressors shall be spared on his account. From this Aramaic translation, therefore, it is clearly shown that all the aforementioned words of Isaiah, from the beginning to the end, can rightly apply to no one else but the Messiah himself.

### CHAPTER XVII.

### That God was to be hung on a cross and affixed to a cross, and that he is the Messiah, who was to die the death of the cross.

### CAPNIO.

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' inside a square frame with floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH through those things which you have said so far concerning the passion of the Messiah, the bad faith of the Jews of our time is so thoroughly refuted that they ought to fall completely silent: yet, to expose their impiety even more clearly, it is necessary to show through their own scriptures that the Messiah, as both God and man, was destined to be hung on a cross and to undergo the death of the cross. This is necessary because many of them deny that our Lord Jesus was the true Messiah precisely because he was affixed to a cross, and some of them even lie by claiming he was merely "hanged" <note>This refers to historical polemics where the death of Jesus was described using the Hebrew term 'talui' (hanged/suspended) to strip it of its sacrificial or Roman 'cross' context.</note>. GALATINUS: I must do two things here. First, I must prove that God himself was to be suspended and affixed to a cross. And finally, I must show that the Messiah himself was destined to die the death of the cross. That God was to be suspended is found clearly enough in Deuteronomy, chapter 28, where it is said: <note>original: "והיו חייך תלאים לך מנגד ופחדת לילה ויומם ולא תאמין בחייך"</note> <margin>C</margin> <margin>D</margin> **“And your lives shall be hanging before you, and you shall fear night and day, and you shall not believe in your lives.”** Here, perhaps, he used the plural word, "lives," because just as the nature of the Messiah is twofold, so is his life—namely, God and the soul. Furthermore, these "lives" of the Messiah, which were to be hung on the cross for us, are truly ours. For regarding the life that is God, we read in Deuteronomy, chapter 30: <note>original: "הוא חייך ואורך ימיך"</note> **“For he is your life, and the length of your days.”** It has already been proven above that the Messiah is also "Life." For even the Lord Jesus himself testified to this, saying: *I am the way, the truth, and the life.* In the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>The "Lesser Genesis," an ancient midrashic commentary.</note>, that is, in the shorter exposition of the book of Genesis, this truly wonderful thing which I am about to say is written regarding that verse in the 22nd chapter of the same book: <note>original: "ויקח אברהם את עצי העולה וישם על יצחק בנו"</note> **“And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son.”** For it is said there: **“Like this one <note>original: "Ze" (זה)</note>, that is, God, who carries his cross upon his shoulder.”** Something similar to this is also found in the Jerusalem *Berachoth* <note>A volume of the Jerusalem Talmud focusing on blessings.</note>, in the chapter beginning <note>original: "מאימתי קורין"</note> *Me'emathai korin*, that is, “From what time do they read?” For it is said there: **“And it was, when Solomon had finished praying to the Lord this entire prayer and supplication, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, where he was kneeling on his knees, and his hands were spread out toward the heavens.”**

<column-break/>

<page-num>476</page-num>
Rabbi Abhu said: **“And his hands were spread out toward the heavens.”** For he was just like *this one* <note>original: "ze" (זה)</note>, that is, this crucified one, or one stretched out on the cross standing up. In this context, the word *ze*, which is interpreted in Latin as "this one," refers to nothing other than God. This is most strongly proven by what is written in the book *Menahoth* <note>A Talmudic tractate regarding grain offerings.</note>, in the chapter beginning *Hammenahoth*: <margin>E</margin> **“The Holy and Blessed God is called *Ze* (This/He); as it is written in Exodus chapter 15: <note>original: "זה אלי ואנואו"</note> *This is my God, and I will glorify him.*”** This is the tradition. Therefore, according to these two traditions, God was to carry the cross on his shoulders and be affixed to the cross with his hands stretched out. Since God, by his own nature, cannot suffer these things, they must necessarily be understood as referring to the Messiah, who was to be both God and man, and who was to die the death of the cross. Moreover, the Psalmist announced in Psalm 22 that the hands and feet of the Messiah himself were to be pierced on the cross, saying: <margin>F</margin> <note>original: "כי סבבוני כלבים עדת מרעים הקפוני כארי ידי ורגלי"</note> **“For dogs have surrounded me. The council of the wicked has besieged me; they pierced my hands and my feet.”** However, the *Sophrim* <note>The Scribes/Jewish scholars of the early Masoretic period.</note>, changing that word *caari* (they pierced) into *caari* (meaning "like a lion"), perverted both the scripture and its meaning. We showed most extensively in the first book that they have done this in many other places as well. Nevertheless, some of our own people (though with piety and good zeal) say that when the Hebrew text says here, “Like a lion my hands and my feet,” the construction is defective, and it should be understood as: “The wicked, like a lion, have dug into, pierced, fixed, or ill-treated my hands and my feet.” To prove this, they bring forward the Aramaic translation, which in this place says: <margin>G</margin> <note>original: "מטול דאחזרו עליי רשיעיא דמתילין לכלביא סגיאי כנישת מבאשין אקפוני נכתין ידי ורגלי כאריא"</note> **“Because the wicked have surrounded me, who are like many dogs; a congregation of evildoers has encircled me, biting my hands and my feet like lions.”** From this, they infer that the Hebrews did not corrupt this passage. But to speak the truth, this opinion of theirs does not please me at all. First, because although in nearly infinite manuscripts which the Jews now commonly have at hand, it has been corrupted to *caari* (like a lion), yet in some very ancient ones *caru* (which means "they pierced") is still found written. Although the Jews do not read it as *caru* even when it is written that way, they read it as *caari*. For they say there is a *ketiv* <note>What is written.</note>, that it should be written as *caru*, but a *keri* <note>What is read.</note>, that it must be read as *caari*. This is the third method of corrupting the scripture, as was shown more fully in the first book. Furthermore, the Aramaic translation they bring forward is not by Jonathan son of Uzziel (who lived many years before the birth of Christ), but by Rabbi Joseph the Blind (as they themselves seem to affirm), who flourished nearly three hundred and forty years after the passion of Christ; so it should not seem strange if, following this corruption, he wrote it this way in this place. Nevertheless, even this translation works greatly against the Jews of our time and supports our purpose in many other places (which is most noteworthy). Finally, because that—

that not <term>caari</term> <note>original: "כארי"</note>, that is, "like a lion," but <term>caru</term> <note>original: "כרו"</note>, that is "they dug" or "pierced," was written here, is clearly evident. This is seen not only in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan (as was seen in the eighth chapter of the first book) regarding the verse "And Abraham still stood before the Lord," but also through the edition of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, who translated these words as: "For many dogs surrounded me, the assembly of the wicked enclosed me, they pierced my hands and my feet." <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἐκύκλωσάν με κύ- νες πολλοί, συναγωγὴ πονηρευομένων περιέσχον με, ὤρυξάν χεῖράς με καὶ πόδας με."</note> From this it clearly appears that <term>caru</term>, meaning "they pierced," and not <term>caari</term>, meaning "like a lion," was written in this place. <margin>B</margin> This can also be seen most strongly from that Aramaic translation used by the Indians and Ethiopians <note>This likely refers to the Syriac Peshitta, as Syriac was often called "Chaldaic" or "Aethiopic" in this period due to its use in Eastern churches.</note>. For it contains <term>Cauanuni oiuotia vaogaria</term>: that is, "They wounded," or "they pierced my hands and my feet." Therefore, David did not utter these words in his own person, as the more recent Jews deliriously claim, but in the person of the Messiah, whom he foresaw would suffer such things. This is also clearly hinted at from the words immediately following, when it is said: <margin>C</margin> "I will count all my bones; they look and stare at me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." <note>original: "אספר כל עצמותי המה יביטו יראו בי יחלקו בגדי להם ועל לבושי יפילו גורל"</note> Since David never suffered these things, nor were they ever fulfilled in him, they must be understood as referring to the Messiah. This is especially true since it is written in the book <term>Sabbath</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud.</note>, in the chapter beginning <term>Bamme haissa iotsea</term> <note>original: "במה האישה יוצאה"</note>, that is, "with what a wife may go out," that Rabbi <term>Hiia</term> <note>original: "חייא"</note> said that all the prophets only prophesied concerning the days of the <margin>D</margin> Messiah. The ancient Talmudists also attribute that saying of Zechariah, chapter 12, "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced" <note>original: "והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו"</note> to the "Messiah son of Joseph," as Rabbi David Kimhi reports in that same place. This is also easily proven by what is contained in the book <term>Sukkah</term>, in the chapter <term>Hahalil hammisia</term> <note>original: "החליל המשיח"</note>. For there it is read: It is written in Zechariah chapter 12, "The land shall mourn, every family apart." <note>original: "וספדה הארץ משפחות משפחות לבד"</note> For what purpose shall this mourning be? There is a controversy there between <margin>E</margin> Rabbi <term>Dossa</term> <note>original: "דוסא"</note> and the masters. For one says that the mourning will be over the Messiah son of Joseph, who will be killed. And the other says it will be over the "evil inclination" which will be slain. <term>Bislama</term> <note>original: "בשלמא"</note>, that is, "peace be to him" who said that the aforementioned mourning will be over the Messiah son of Joseph. For this is what is written in Zechariah 12: "And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and shall be in bitterness over him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn." <note>original: "והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו וספדו עליו כמספד וגו'"</note> This is the tradition. Although the commentators there leave it debated whether that Messiah is called the "son of Joseph" because he was to come from the tribe of Joseph, or from a father named Joseph: nevertheless, the saying of the Talmudists is understood to refer to Christ our Lord. The Talmudists called him the "son of Joseph" because he was to have no other father on earth except a putative one, namely Joseph, the spouse of his virgin mother, who, as the Evangelists report, was thought to be his father. For this reason, the glorious Virgin herself said to him in Luke chapter 2: "Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing." From this tradition, it necessarily

<column-break/>

follows that God himself was to be wounded and pierced. For since those words, "And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced"—which the ancient Talmudists wanted to be understood as referring to the Messiah—were uttered by the prophet in the person of God, as if God himself were to be crucified: this could not even have been imagined unless the divinity were to be hypostatically <note>A theological term meaning the union of two natures (divine and human) in one individual person.</note> united with humanity in the Messiah himself. It follows, therefore, that the Messiah who was to be crucified was to be both God and man. Moreover, since pouring out the spirit <margin>F</margin> of grace upon men belongs to no one but God alone, it is certainly clear that he in whose person the prophet speaks is entirely God, saying: "And I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of devotion, or of prayers. And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced." <note>original: "ושפכתי על בית דויד ועל יושב ירושלם רוח חן ותחנונים והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו"</note> <margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin> CHAPTER: The younger Jews, unable to corrupt such evident testimony of the passion of God and man, say in this place that "They shall look upon him," and not "upon me," is written among them. <margin>G</margin> <margin>Refutation.</margin> GALATINUS: First, their falsehood is evident from the fact that all their ancient books (as you yourself well know) have it exactly as I have written and translated. Furthermore, it is shown through the Aramaic translation of Rabbi Jonathan, which provides the same words in Aramaic: "And I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of piety and mercies, and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced." Wherefore the same prophet says in chapter 13: "And one shall say to him: What are these wounds in the midst of your hands? And he shall say: With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me," that is, who ought to have loved me. "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my fellow," or "like me," or "joined to me," says the Lord of hosts. "Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered." <note>original: "ואמר אליו מה המכות האלה בין ידיך ואמר אשר הכיתי בית מאהבי : חרב עורי על רעי ועל גבר עמיתי נאם יהוה צבאות הך את הרעה ותפוצין הצאן"</note> From all of which it is clearer than light that the Messiah, as God and man, was to be hung on the gallows of the cross and die the death of the cross.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->*Response to the objection of the Jews, who claim that Christ was not God because he cried out on the cross that he was forsaken by God.*<-

### CAPNIO.

Here the impious perfidy of the more recent Jews opposes us, saying: "If your Christ was God, why, when he was about to die on the cross, did he cry out that he was forsaken by God, saying: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'" <note>original: "אלי אלי למה עזבתני"</note> For if he had been God and man, that man could never have been deserted by the God to whom (as you say) he was hypostatically united. For as you yourselves assert, what he once assumed, he never let go. Therefore, since he cried out that he was forsaken by God, he openly protested himself that he was not God. <margin>H</margin> To this, Jerome says that Christ sang Psalm 22 on the cross, and the others following, up to that verse of Psalm 31: "Into your hands, Lord..."

<summary>This page argues that the Messiah must be both God and man because Hebrew prophecies (Psalm 22 and Zechariah 12) depict God Himself being "pierced" and "forsaken." It refutes Jewish claims that these verses refer to David or a different Messiah, using the concept of the hypostatic union to explain how Jesus is the "Son of Joseph."</summary>
<keywords>Messiah son of Joseph, Zechariah 12:10, Psalm 22, crucifixion prophecy, hypostatic union, Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, Talmud, Aramaic Targum, Septuagint, St. Jerome</keywords>
