<meta>This page continues the discussion on the messianic interpretations of the Psalms, specifically moving from the "piercing" of hands and feet to the words spoken by Jesus on the cross. Galatinus is using Hebrew and Aramaic sources to defend the Christian interpretation of the Messiah against contemporary Jewish objections.</meta>

478 BOOK EIGHT. 479

<margin>A</margin>
into your hands I commend my spirit." <note>original: "in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum"</note> From which it follows that he did not say those words, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" <note>original: "Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me?"</note> in order to show himself abandoned by God, but because those words occurred in the same Psalms he was reciting. **GALATINUS:** I certainly do not contradict Jerome, but I add this one thing: that just as he said to the Jews in the 33rd chapter of Isaiah, "And why will you die, O house of Israel?" <note>original: "Et quare moriemini domus Israel?"</note>—not so that he might learn this from them, but rather to healthfully rouse them to consider their own perdition—so too Christ, when as a man he cried out and asked God why He had left him in the hands of the Jews to be mocked, spat upon, scourged, crucified, and killed, did so not as one ignorant, nor as one complaining about God or accusing Him. Rather, he did it so that the Jews who heard him might be led to a most healthful consideration of and faith in his passion. The words immediately following in that same place clearly suggest this. For when the Prophet, speaking in the person of the Messiah (as has been said), had said, *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>original Hebrew: "אלי אלי למה עזבתני"</note> he immediately added, *far from my salvation are the words of my roaring.* <note>original Hebrew: "רחוק מישועתי דברי שאגתי"</note> Truly, the "words of the roaring" of Christ, by which as a man he cried out that he was forsaken by his God, were "far from the salvation" of the hearts of those Jews desiring to kill him—the salvation by which God raised him up and elevated him into heaven in the sight of his disciples.

<margin>B</margin>
Or alternatively: since it was said in the sixth book, according to the opinion of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, that our salvation is the salvation of God (because God is said to save Himself by saving Israel), for this reason the Messiah himself, who was to save the human race, is often called "the saved one" in his capacity as Savior. For that reason, it can also be said quite fittingly that the "words of roaring"—that is, the lamentation of Christ—were to be "far from his salvation," which is to say, far from the future redemption of the human race, at least regarding those who, because of their impenitent and obstinate hearts, were not going to receive the fruit of human redemption. Wherefore, shortly after, he says "I thirst," <note>original: "Sitio"</note> meaning "I desire the salvation of all," because he suffers for all, even if not all are to be saved by the merit of his passion.

<margin>F</margin>
And the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> interpreter seems to have translated the aforementioned words in this sense; for he says in Aramaic: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Far from my redemption are the words of my lamentation.* <note>original Aramaic: "אלהי אלהי מטול מה שבקתני, רחוק מן פורקני מילי אבליתני"</note> **CAPNIO:** Our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has this much differently than how you yourself have translated it. For it says: "My God, look upon me, why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins." <note>original Latin: "Deus meus, respice in me, quare me dereliquisti? longe a salute mea verba delictorum meorum."</note> **GALATINUS:** As is evidently clear to anyone looking, the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>A term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> holds much better for the Christian faith here than our own Greek or Latin edition. I do not know what spirit moved their authors to remove the pronoun "my" from the beginning of the verse, and to add "look upon me" in the middle, and to change "the words of my roaring" at the end into "the words of my sins." These three things—that is, subtracting, adding, and changing—are found to have been done very often

<column-break/>

in many other places in the face of the Scriptures, among the Greeks as well as the Latins. Therefore, from the fact that our Savior cried out that he was forsaken by God, the excessive and false cleverness of the Jews of our time can by no means conclude that he was not God. Nor will they be able to argue against us because we confess and believe that God—who is entirely incapable of suffering, immortal, and unchangeable—was crucified, pierced with nails and a spear, and died.

<margin>B</margin>
For we assert that the Messiah, being himself both God and man, suffered all these things not according to his divinity, but according to the nature of our mortality which he assumed. The Prophets and the other holy fathers and the ancient Talmudists all confessed and believed these things with us long before, as is clearly evident in the preceding sections. For these reasons, they themselves (as seen above) not ineptly called him *the broken, crushed, or terrified God.* <note>original: "אל נערץ" / "El naarats"</note>

<margin>C</margin>
For he is *El*, that is, God, according to the form of God; and he is *naarats*, that is, broken, crushed, or terrified, according to the form of a servant. According to this form, in his passion (as Mark reports in chapter 14), he began to be afraid and weary, and he was crushed by scourges, beaten with buffets and slaps, and crucified, and pierced and broken by nails and a spear.

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore the <term>Psalmographer</term> <note>The writer of the Psalms, King David.</note>, addressing God and arguing as if God were acting against the promises He had made regarding the Messiah—judging by the opinion of the wicked—says in Psalm 89: *But you have cast off and abhorred, you have been very angry with your Messiah. You have neglected the covenant of your servant, you have profaned his crown on the earth.* <note>original Hebrew: "ואתה זנחת ותמאס התעברת עם משיחך: נארת ברית עבדך חללת לארץ נזרו"</note> And a little later: *How long, O God, will you hide yourself? Shall your wrath burn like fire forever?* <note>original Hebrew: "עד מה יהוה, תסתר לנצח תבער כמו אש חמתך"</note> On this, the <term>gloss</term> <note>An explanatory note or commentary.</note> of Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra says: "How long (he says) O God, will you hide yourself?—from one side, that is, or from one corner or summit, as if you were hidden so that you do not see the evils of your Messiah, but your wrath burns like fire against him?"

<margin>E</margin>
And below: *Where are your former mercies, Lord, which you swore to David by your faith?* <note>original Hebrew: "איה חסדיך הראשונים אדני נשבעת לדוד באמונתך"</note> Where the gloss of the same Rabbi Abraham says: "Establish, O Lord, your oath, which you made concerning the coming of the Redeemer."

<margin>F</margin>
And finally: *Blessed be God forever, Amen and amen.* <note>original Hebrew: "ברוך יהוה לעולם אמן ואמן"</note> Where the gloss of the Rabbi himself says: "The meaning is that the Psalmist saw through the Holy Spirit the coming of the Messiah, and therefore he gave praise to the name of God, that is, to God." There was, however, in Spain a certain great wise and upright man to whom this Psalm was so very heavy that he could neither read it nor listen to it patiently, because the Psalmist here speaks such heavy things against God. Thus he spoke.

> That the Messiah was to be given gall and vinegar to drink at his death, and as he died, darkness was to fall over all the earth.

### CAPNIO.

Since we read that Christ our Redeemer was given gall and vinegar to drink in his passion, and that darkness occurred over the whole earth as he died...

<margin>A</margin>
...to have happened: for that reason, in order to further refute the impious and obstinate incredulity of the Jews of our time, it must also be proven through their own writings that all these things were destined to happen at the death of the Messiah. **GALATINUS:** First, therefore, it should be noted what is read in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal procedures and the high court.</note>, in the chapter that begins, <margin>B</margin> *Nigmar baddin* <note>original Hebrew: "חסדא Nigmar baddin"</note>, that is, "The judgment is finished": where it is said word for word: Rav Hisda <note>A prominent Jewish scholar of the 3rd century.</note> said, "One who was going out to be killed was given a drink of frankincense powder in a cup of wine, so that his senses might be separated from him" <note>This was intended as a narcotic to dull the pain of execution.</note>: just as it is said in *Proverbs*, chapter 31: *Give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those who are of a bitter heart.* <note>original Hebrew: "תנו שכר לאובד ויין למרי נפש"</note> There were, moreover, honorable women in Jerusalem who sent these things voluntarily. Thus says the *Talmud*. Therefore, the Jews drank the good wine sent for this purpose to the Lord Jesus Christ and the others to be crucified with him. Because of this, that which had been said long ago through *Amos*, chapter 2, was then fulfilled: <margin>C</margin> *And the house of their God shall drink the wine of the condemned* <note>original Hebrew: "ויין ענושים ישתו בית אלהיהם"</note>: as if he were saying, "The house of Israel shall drink the wine of the condemned," and what will be a greater crime, "even the wine of their God." Nor should it seem unfitting to anyone that the prophet attributes the deed of a very few Jews to the whole house of Israel: since not only was a huge multitude of people present there, consenting to what was done as described, but also those of whom it is said in *Matthew*, chapter 27, that likewise the <margin>D</margin> chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: "He saved others, himself he cannot save. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let Him deliver him now, if He wants him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" It is also the custom of Divine Scripture to sometimes ascribe to a multitude what was done by only one. For it is read in *Joshua*, chapter 7, that the Lord said to Joshua himself: "Israel has sinned, and they have transgressed my covenant which I commanded them, and they have even taken of the forbidden things, and they have also stolen," and so on. See how the Lord attributed to Israel what Achan alone had perpetrated. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, instead of the frankincense and good wine that was drunk, Jewish impiety offered the Lord Jesus myrrh and vinegar mixed with gall. And then that saying of *Psalm* 69 was fulfilled: *And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.* <note>original Hebrew: "ויתנו בברותי ראש ולצמאי ישקوني חמץ"</note> That these things were to be understood concerning the Messiah appears more evidently in *Midrash Ruth* <note>A traditional Jewish commentary on the Book of Ruth.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ruth, upon that which Boaz said in the second chapter: "Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar." For it is said there: "He speaks of the King Messiah. 'Come here,' that is, draw near to the Kingdom. 'And eat of the bread': this is the bread of the Kingdom. 'And dip your morsel in the vinegar': these are the sufferings or torments of the Messiah," of whom it is said in *Isaiah* 53: *And he was wounded (or killed) for our <margin>G</margin> crimes, bruised for our sins.* This is the tradition. From which it is clearly shown that the vinegar of Ruth signified and prefigured the sufferings and torments of the Messiah. How much more, therefore, ought it to be said in the person of the Messiah, as was already sent before: *And they shall give gall for my food, and in my thirst*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
*they shall give me vinegar to drink?* This is especially hinted at in the just retribution of the Jews, when it is immediately added in the same *Psalm*: *Let their table become a snare before them, and their peace offerings a trap. Let their eyes be darkened from seeing, and make their loins continually shake. Pour out your indignation upon them, and let the wrath of your fury overtake them. Let their habitation be desolate, let there be no inhabitant in their tents.* <note>original Hebrew: "יהי שלחנם לפניהם לפח ולשלומים למוקש תחשכנה עיניהם מראות ומתניהם תמיד המעד: שפך עליהם זעמך וחרון אפך ישיגם: תהי טירתם נשמה באהליהם אל יהי ישב"</note> <margin>B</margin> And immediately after this it is added: *For they have persecuted him whom you have smitten, and they will tell of the pain (or affliction) of your wounded (or killed) ones. Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not come into (or with) your righteousness. Let them be blotted out of the book of life (or of the living), and let them not be written with the righteous.* <note>original Hebrew: "כי אתה אשר הכית רדפו ואל מכאוב חלליך יספרו: תנה עון על עונם ואל יבאו בצדקתך: ימחו מספר חיים ועם צדיקים אל יכתבו"</note> Now, the Chaldean <margin>C</margin> interpreter <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated and explained all these things in Chaldean thus: *Let their table which they prepared before me so that I might eat, be for a snare, and their sacrifices for a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and affect their loins with a continual trembling. Pour out your fury upon them, and let the strength of your fury seize them. Let their habitation be desolate, and in their tents let there be no inhabitant. For they have persecuted him whom you wounded, and they will speak against the one afflicted <margin>D</margin> on account of those killed by you. Add sin upon their sin, and let them not deserve to enter into the Assembly of your righteous. Let them be blotted out from the book of the memory of the living, and with the righteous let them not be written.* <note>original Aramaic: "יהי פתורהון דסדרו קדמוי באכלי קרבנהון לקלא ונסבתהון לתקלא... ועם צדיקיא לא יתכתבו"</note> For the declaration of these words of the Psalmist, it should be noted that "table" in Holy Scripture sometimes signifies "kingdom." Hence in *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrash on the Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that saying of *Psalm* 23: <margin>F</margin> *You shall prepare a table before me* <note>original Hebrew: "תערוך לפני שלחן"</note>: it is said, "This table is the Kingdom." But sometimes all of Divine Scripture itself, which is distinguished into twenty-four books, is called a "table": according to that saying of *Deuteronomy*, chapter 8: *Man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds out of the mouth of the LORD does man live.* <note>original Hebrew: "לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם כי על כל מוצא פי יהוה יחיה האדם"</note> Both of these "tables" became a snare to the Jews. For because they gave the Messiah myrrh-flavored wine and vinegar mixed with gall to drink, they therefore lost both the Kingdom and the true understanding of Scripture. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, concerning their blindness, it is added: *Let their eyes be darkened from seeing*, that is, so that they may not see. Hence also the true Messiah, who ought to have been for their peace, and is called "Peace," was made a stumbling block to them by the just judgment of God: because they embittered his mouth with gall and vinegar. And this is what Jeremiah says in his lamentation, chapter 1...

Galatinus uses the Talmud and Midrash to claim that the Jews' rejection of the Messiah resulted in a spiritual "blindness" where their own scriptures (the "table") became a snare to them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the physical sufferings of Jesus—specifically the bitter drink offered on the cross—were not random acts of cruelty but fulfillments of prophetic and rabbinic tradition. Galatinus is currently interpreting Lamentations and Ezekiel to show how the "bitterness" of the passion was foretold.</meta>

### BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin> *The Lord is righteous, for I have rebelled against his mouth* <note>original Hebrew: "צדיק הוא יהוה כי פיהו מריתי"; Lamentations 1:18</note>, which is to say: God himself is just, because I have made his mouth bitter. For at that time, the wickedness of the Jews made the mouth of God bitter when they placed a sponge full of vinegar and gall upon a reed and held it to the mouth and nose of our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah. Because of this, that saying from Ezekiel chapter 8 was also fulfilled: *And behold, they put the branch to their nose.* <note>original Hebrew: "והנם שולחים את הזמורה אל אפם"</note> Explaining this, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a famous 12th-century Hebrew grammarian known as Radak.</note> says: "It means to say, a foul odor." **CAPNIO:** In these places, our Scripture <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> reads far differently than how you have translated it. For that passage in the Lamentations of Jeremiah says: *The Lord is just, because I have provoked his mouth to anger.* And this one from Ezekiel says: *And behold, they apply the branch to my nostrils.* **GALATINUS:** In both places, the author of our edition—by his leave—<margin>B</margin> was too indulgent toward the Jews. For the word *marithi* <note>original Hebrew: "מריתי"</note> which is placed in the words of Jeremiah, is derived from the verb *marah*, which properly signifies "to make bitter." Therefore, *marithi* is the same as "I have made bitter." 

Furthermore, the saying of Ezekiel has been thoroughly corrupted among us as well as among the Hebrews, but much more among us than among them. For they have what they call the *Sophrim* <note>original: "סופרים"; refers to the 'Tikkun Soferim' or Emendations of the Scribes.</note>, that is, the Scribes; these scribes, observing that the prophet brought forth these words in the person of God, and judging it both unseemly and impossible for a "foul odor" to be placed at His nose—lest such a locution cause scandal to the simple—changed this scripture as they did many others of that kind, as we showed more extensively in the first book. In this place, "to my nose" was originally written, but they, changing it, wrote "to their nose," as we also proved there through their own writings. 

As for the fact that the sun was to be darkened at the death of the Messiah, and darkness was to fall over the whole earth, this was announced long before by the prophet Amos, saying in chapter 8: *And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord God, that I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day. And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head.* <note>original Hebrew: "והיה ביום ההוא נאם אדני יהוה..."</note> No one denies that darkness occurred on that day and hour when Christ died, since even the Gentiles themselves testify to it. This "baldness" and inconsolable mourning happened then, or shortly after: specifically in the fortieth year before the destruction of the Temple, when the Judges of the Jews were expelled from the Gazith chamber <note>The "Lishkat HaGazit" or Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Sanhedrin met.</note> and all judicial power was taken away from them, as was made very clear in the fourth book.

### CHAPTER XX.

->On the merit of the Messiah’s passion, and death, and the shedding of his blood.<-

<column-break/>

<page-num>484</page-num>
<header>CAPNIO.</header>

<margin>C</margin> Since the human race has been saved through the merit of Christ's passion, lest anything concerning the Messiah’s passion be overlooked, please reveal something from the Jewish writings regarding the merit of his passion, death, and the shedding of his blood. **GALATINUS:** I shall certainly do so. Concerning the merit of the Messiah's passion, one should listen to what is written in the book they call *Siphre* <note>An ancient Jewish legal commentary (Midrash) on Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, in the words of Rabbi Yosi: "Go out and learn the merit of the King Messiah and the reward of the righteous from the first man, Adam; to whom only one negative commandment was given, and he transgressed it. See how many deaths were decreed for him, and for his generations, and the generations of his generations, until the end of all generations. Furthermore, which measure is greater: the measure of good or the measure of vengeance? Say that the measure of good is multiplied, and the measure of vengeance is diminished." <note>A rabbinic principle that God’s reward for good is far more abundant than His punishment for evil.</note> It is as if he says: God always punishes less than is deserved and rewards more than is deserved. Therefore, the King Messiah, afflicted and humbled by fasting and affected by penalties, will restore merit and reward to all, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 53: *And the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.* This is from the Talmud. 

In this same way, that greatest Talmudist, Paul, argued when writing to the Romans in chapter 5: *If by the offense of one many died, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of one <margin>D</margin> man, Jesus Christ, has abounded unto many.* 

The merit of the Messiah's death is shown most clearly because in the same book <note>referring back to Siphre or a related Midrashic source</note> it is read as follows: "Judah, who shed innocent blood in their land at that hour... And <margin>E</margin> Judah shall remain forever, and I will pardon, but their blood I will not pardon. Yet his land—that is, his corpse—will pardon his people." <note>original Hebrew: "ויהודה לעולם תשב ונקיתי דמם לא ניקיתי..."</note> And from where do you have it that his death, which is at the hand of the nations of the world, will pardon them in the world to come? Because it is said in the Psalm of Asaph: *O God, the nations have come into your inheritance.* This is the tradition. From which it clearly appears that through the death of the Messiah, there was to be the remission of sins: both from the fact that it says his land—that is, his body—will pardon his people; and also <margin>F</margin> because it says that his death (namely, the Messiah's) ought to pardon the nations in the world to come, that is, in the time of the Messiah. And rightly so. For the Messiah himself was to die for the salvation of the human race, and especially for the sake of saving the fathers. This is openly shown from the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses ha-Darshan of Narbonne, an 11th-century scholar.</note> upon that verse of Psalm 49: *He shall live forever and not see the pit, when he sees the wise men dying,* or, *so that he may see the <margin>G</margin> wise men dying,* as some have interpreted it. For it is said there: "Rabbi Moses the Preacher said: This verse is spoken concerning the King Messiah, who will die in order to redeem the fathers, and afterward will live forever and not see the pit like the wise men who die." This is what Rabbi Moses Ha...

<summary>This page argues that Jewish tradition and scripture foretold the darkening of the sun at the Messiah's death and the redemptive power of his suffering. Galatinus uses sources like the Sifre and Moses ha-Darshan to claim that the Messiah dies specifically to redeem humanity and the patriarchs, drawing a parallel to the Apostle Paul's arguments in Romans.</summary>

### BOOK EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin> ...of Moses Hadarsan <note>Rabbi Moses Hadarsan was an 11th-century scholar known for his midrashic (interpretive) commentaries.</note>: This text is spoken concerning the King Messiah, who shall die to redeem the fathers, and afterward shall live forever. Nor shall he see the underworld <note>original Latin: "infernum"</note> as do the wise men who die. Furthermore, it is clear that the faithful could only be cleansed from sins and liberated from the underworld through the shedding of the Messiah’s blood, according to what is said in the ninth chapter of Zechariah: *As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water.* <note>original Hebrew: "גם את בדם בריתך שלחתי אסיריך מבור אין מים בו"; Zechariah 9:11</note> To understand this saying, it must be noted that these words "you" and "your" used here are in the feminine gender. Therefore, they must refer to some feminine subject mentioned previously. <margin>B</margin> What that feminine subject is, is shown in the same place a little before these words, where it says: *Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you, he is just and having salvation.* <note>original Hebrew: "גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע הוא"; Zechariah 9:9</note> Here, the Aramaic translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says: <margin>C</margin> *Rejoice with joy, O Church of Zion; shout, O Church of Jerusalem.* <note>original Aramaic: "חדי לחדא כנשתא דציון נילי קהלא דירושלם"</note> Therefore, these pronouns used there—*even you, in the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit where there is no water*—must refer to the daughter, that is, the Church <note>The author uses "Ecclesia" (Church) to translate the Hebrew "congregation" of Israel, viewing the faithful of Israel as the precursor to the Christian Church.</note> of Zion and Jerusalem. <margin>Interpretation of Rabbi Selomo.</margin> Indeed, Rabbi Selomo <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains these words thus: "Even you, O Church of Zion and Jerusalem, shall be saved with the Messiah, just as he himself is just and saved. By the blood of your covenant, that is, by the merit of the blood of the covenant which was poured out over you at Sinai, concerning which it is said in Exodus chapter 24: *Behold the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made with you.* I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit, that is, from captivity." Thus says he. However, when he says "from the pit, that is, from captivity," this cannot be understood as the "pit" of the Egyptian or Babylonian captivity, since both places abound in water, and the prophet says the pit of which he speaks lacks water. Therefore, his saying must be understood as referring to the pit of Gehenna <note>The place of punishment or the underworld.</note> in which there is no water, but fire and sulfur, as is clear in the prologue of *Echa Rabbethi* <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a collection of midrashic interpretations of the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah, where it is said: "The holy and blessed God promised us that he would snatch us from Gehenna through the merit of circumcision. And where did he say this? In Zechariah, who says: *Even you, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.*" This is the tradition.

Now, when it says that salvation was to come through the merit of circumcision, it intended to be understood as through the merit of the shedding of Christ’s blood, of which circumcision was a type <note>In Christian theology, a "type" is an Old Testament event or person that foreshadows a New Testament reality.</note>. For since all the patriarchs and prophets and all the holy fathers, however holy they were and though they received circumcision, descended into the underworld until the passion of Christ—as is clear in many places in the Talmud, and especially in the book called *Hagigah*, in the chapter beginning *All are bound* <note>original Hebrew: "הכל חייבין"; Hagigah 2a</note>, as we have shown more extensively in the preceding pages—it clearly follows that we were to be liberated from the underworld not by the merit of circumcision, but by the merit of Christ’s passion, which circumcision prefigured. Furthermore, since neither the pardon of sins, nor satisfaction, nor consequently the salvation of the soul ought to occur except through the shedding of blood, as is clear in the book *Yoma* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement.</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> that is, the "Book of Days," in the chapter that begins, *Seven days before the day of atonement*: where it reads thus word for word, "There is no pardon or remission of sin except through blood," just as it is written in Leviticus chapter 17: *For it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul.* <note>original Hebrew: "כי הדם הוא בנפש יכפר"</note> Since salvation would not occur except through the Messiah, as proved in the previous sections, <margin>B</margin> it follows by necessity that God did not remit sins by the merit of circumcision, nor by the merit of the blood poured over the children of Israel on Mount Sinai, but solely by the merit of the blood of the Messiah to be shed—which the aforementioned bloods prefigured—without which there never was, is, nor will be a perfect remission of sins.

## CHAPTER XXI.
->That the Messiah was to descend into the underworld and lead out all the elect from there.<-

## CAPNIO. <note>Johann Reuchlin, the famous German humanist and Hebraist, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>E</margin> Since we both believe and confess that Christ our Lord descended into the underworld after his death and led out the souls of his elect from there: for that reason, so that the stubbornness of the younger Jews may be more and more convinced, it is necessary to prove through their own scriptures that the Messiah was to do that very thing. <margin>D</margin> **GALATINUS:** That the Messiah would descend into the underworld and lead out all the elect from there is evident primarily from what is read in *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient midrashic commentary on the book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan, where, upon that saying in chapter 24 of the same book, *And he brought me into the tabernacle*, it is said word for word: "Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: I went with the Angel of Death, named *Kippod*, until he reached the gates of Gehenna. And immediately I sent the Angel Kippod, who is in charge of Gehenna, so that he might measure Gehenna from the beginning to the end, and he had no free hour for measuring. Because then they killed Rabbi Simeon, the son of Gamliel. And I wanted to go, and I could not. But after this, I went with the Angel Kippod, and the Messiah son of David went with me, until I reached the gates of Gehenna. And when the captives who were in Gehenna saw the light of the Messiah, they rejoiced to receive him, saying: 'This one shall lead us out from these darknesses,' as it is said in Hosea chapter 13: <margin>F</margin> *I will ransom them from the hand of the underworld; I will redeem them from death.* <note>original Hebrew: "מיד שאול אפדם ממות אגאלם"; Hosea 13:14</note> And so Isaiah also says in chapter 35: *And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come*—or enter—*into Zion*, <note>original Hebrew: "ופדויי יהוה ישבון ובאו"</note> and the rest until: *Sorrow and sighing shall flee away.*" <note>original Hebrew: "ינוסו יגון ואנחה"</note> Now, "Zion" in this place is not called anything other than *Gan Eden*, that is, the garden of pleasure, which is Paradise. Thus far the tradition. And though this might seem to posit some foolish fable, because the Talmudists were accustomed to hand down the secrets of the Messiah only in parables, they fashioned that story so they might suggest the Messiah's descent to the underworld and the joy of the holy fathers existing in Limbo <note>Limbo of the Fathers: the place where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ's redemption.</note>, which they were to have on account of his advent and their own liberation. <margin>G</margin> This they prove excellently by the testimonies of Hosea and Isaiah. This same thing is also said by that Doctor of theirs, whom they call *Rabbenu Haccados*, that is, our Holy Master...

### BOOK EIGHT.

...whom they call our holy teacher <note>original Latin: "magistrum nostrum sanctũ"; referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishna</note>, showed quite clearly long before the birth of Christ in the book which he called *The Revealer of Secrets* <note>original Hebrew: גלי רזיא *Gali Razayya*</note>. He did this especially in response to the second petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome. Among other things, this same Antoninus asked him: "Since the word *man* <note>original Hebrew: גבר *ghever*</note> signifies God, what does that text from Lamentations chapter 3 mean: *I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath; he hath led me, and brought me into darkness, but not into light*?" <note>original Hebrew: אני הגבר ראה עני בשבט עברתו : אותי נהג וילך חשך ולא אור; Lamentations 3:1-2</note>. Our Teacher responded to him: "This is the holy and blessed God, who says, 'I am the man who saw poverty.' He has led me and brought me into darkness, and not into light. This is likewise the holy and blessed God who said: 'I have decreed to descend to the underworld to redeem the souls of the righteous, which my Father who is in heaven thrust there with the rod of his indignation because of the sin of Adam.'" Likewise, in the same book, in response to the sixth petition of the same Antoninus, the same Holy Teacher says that he found these words among others in the book of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai, which is called *The Investigation of Secrets* <note>original Hebrew: מחקר הסודות *Mechkar ha-Sodot*</note>: "Upon hearing these things, Rabbi Hoseas began to weep and said: 'Woe to them, woe to those impious ones, the murderers of Israel! Out of love for them, so that he might forgive their sin, the holy and blessed God will send his holy Son, and he will clothe himself in human flesh. Woe to them, because on account of their wicked deeds they will be rebellious against this Messiah, and they will reject the words by which he will command them to be cleansed with the water of purification to purge their sins. But they will not walk in the ways pleasing to God, nor will they do his will; rather, moved by great wrath, they will kill him. Then his soul shall descend to the underworld, where he will remain for three days, so that from there he may lead out all the souls of the fathers and the righteous.'" Just as it was said in Genesis chapter 47: *I will go down with thee into Egypt, and I will also surely bring thee up again.* <note>original Hebrew: אנכי ארד עמך מצרימה ואנכי אעלך; Genesis 46:4 (cited here as 47)</note> And the holy and blessed God will cause him to lead them into paradise, and they shall be joyful in the glory of God, according to that saying of Hosea chapter 6: *After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.* All these things were said by him whom they call our holy teacher. From all of this, it is quite clearly evident that the Messiah, as God and man, was to descend to hell immediately after his death and lead out the souls of his elect.

## CHAPTER XXII.

->That the Messiah was to rise from the dead on the third day.<-

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'I' depicting classical architectural columns and floral motifs.</image-desc>
The Evangelists have written that Jesus Christ our Lord also rose from the dead on the third day. Therefore, you ought to show from the Hebrew scriptures that this same thing was to happen to the Messiah. GALATINUS: I will first say, then, what the ancient Talmudists understood concerning that saying of Psalm 17: *As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness...*

---

<page-num>488</page-num>
<header>BOOK EIGHT.</header>

<margin>A</margin> *...thy likeness* <note>original Hebrew: בהקיץ תמונתך; Psalm 17:15</note>, that is, I shall see your face in justice, or through justice; I shall be satisfied when your form—or figure, or image, or likeness—shall have risen. It was proven above through the <margin>Talmudic explanation.</margin> writings of the Talmudists that the Messiah is the "Face of God." Furthermore, this form, or figure, or image, or likeness of God of which the prophet speaks here, is none other than the Son of God, or the Messiah himself according to his divinity, according to which the Son of God himself is like the Father. As was also shown above, that is, in the third book. And this <margin>B</margin> was that figure, or image of God, which Moses saw, when it is said in Numbers chapter 12: *And the similitude of the Lord shall he behold.* <note>original Hebrew: ותמונת יהוה יביט; Numbers 12:8</note> Which Rabbi Onkelos <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> translated into Aramaic in this way: *And he understands the likeness or image of the charity of God.* Therefore, according to this sense, the aforementioned words of the prophet can be explained: "I shall see your face," that is, your Messiah. "I shall be satisfied when your form—or figure, or likeness, or image—shall have risen," that is, your Son. <margin>C</margin> Although they also explain this in another way, as will be said below when we come to speak of the general resurrection, the explanation we have placed here is best confirmed in the *Bereshit Rabba Ketanna* <note>The "Smaller Great Midrash on Genesis," a collection of interpretive stories.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding what is written in the third chapter of the same book about Adam: *And the Lord sent him forth from the garden, or from the paradise of pleasure.* For there it is read literally: "Rabbi Hamia said: Adam was sent out of paradise in this age, but in the age to come he shall not be sent out." <margin>D</margin> This saying of Rabbi Hamia is supported by what is written in Psalm 17: *As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness, or through righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when your form—or figure, or image, or likeness—shall have risen.* The holy and blessed God said: "In that hour I will justify him," namely, Adam, from that sentence. David said to the holy and blessed God: "And in that hour when he who is your likeness shall rise, I shall be satisfied, and in justice I shall contemplate, or see, your face." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: <margin>E</margin> "I shall contemplate your face," just as it is said in Isaiah 52: *For they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall dwell or inhabit.* <note>original Hebrew: כי עין בעין יראו בשוב יהוה ציון; Isaiah 52:8</note> Which Rabbi Jonathan translated into Aramaic thus: *For with their eyes they shall see his power, or the strength which God shall perform, when his divinity shall sit or dwell in Zion.* All this is tradition. In these things, three very great mysteries are contained. <margin>F</margin> The first of which is that God was going to justify Adam, who had once been expelled from paradise, by taking away the sentence passed against him. The second is that this was to happen when, according to David’s prophecy, the *temuna* <note>Likeness or form</note>, that is, the form, or figure, or image, or likeness of God, should rise. The third is that through him who was the likeness of God—that is, like God the Father according to his divinity—and who was to rise according to his humanity, David then knew that he himself would be healed, and through justice would see and contemplate the face of God. <margin>G</margin> Yet he did not say through whose justice he was to obtain these things; perhaps because he preferred this to be said through Isaiah, who, speaking after him about the Messiah the Son of God (as we showed in the preceding part), says in chapter 53: *My righteous servant shall justify many; and their sins he himself...*
<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "rum ipse" (their sins he himself [shall bear]).</meta>

...he himself will carry. Here it can also be said, not inappropriately, what is written in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, in this manner: Rabbi Nahman said to Rabbi Isaac, "Have you heard when *Bar Niphli* <note>original Hebrew: בר נפלי; literally 'the son of the fallen' or 'the fallen one'</note> is to come?" He said to him, "Who is *Bar Niphli*?" He replied, "The Messiah." He asked him, "Do you call the Messiah *Bar Niphli*, that is, the fallen son?" He answered him, "Yes, just as it is written of him in Amos chapter 9: 
<margin>A</margin> *In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen* <note>original Hebrew: ביום ההוא אקים את סכת דוד הנופלת; Amos 9:11</note>, that is, in that day I will rouse or set upright the small, cast-down, or prostrate house of David." This is the tradition. In this passage, this ancient Talmudist not without reason called the Messiah *Bar Niphli*, the fallen son. For, as he proves his statement by the testimony of the prophet, the Messiah himself, as far as his body is concerned, was destined to be the cast-down or prostrate "booth" of David in his passion and death, but was to be raised and set upright by God in his resurrection. Here I also think it should not be passed over in silence what is read in *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the title of Psalm 22, *Upon the hind of the morning* <note>original Hebrew: על אילת השחר; Ayelet HaShachar</note>: where it is said: "This is what is written, *Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp; I myself will awake the dawn.*" <note>Psalm 57:8</note> And further: "Awake in Edom, that is, among the Romans. For it is destined that you shall make the King Messiah stand before us. And what is this, *I will awake the dawn*? For the dawn does not awake me; from the beginning of time the dawn never came upon me and found me sleeping. And this is: *I will awake the dawn*." And so he himself says in Psalm 119: 
<margin>C</margin> *At midnight I rise to give thanks to thee* <note>original Hebrew: חצות לילה אקום להודות לך</note>. Thus far the tradition. Here it must be noted that the glory of David was in the Messiah, as is held in *Midrash Tehillim* on that verse of Psalm 16: *My heart is glad*, namely in the words of the law, *and my glory rejoiceth*. To the preceding points it must also be added what is written in Psalm 16 in this way: *Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoiceth: my flesh also shall rest in hope. <margin>E</margin> speaks openly of the incorruption of Christ's body and of his resurrection. <margin>A</margin> "On the third day Abraham shall lift up his eyes." As it is said in Psalm 80: *Restore us, O Lord God of hosts; cause thy face to shine*—that is, your Messiah—*and we shall be saved.*" This is the tradition. Furthermore, in the book *Mechilta* <note>A collection of legal and homiletical interpretations of Exodus</note> regarding that verse of Psalm 30: *For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life* <note>Psalm 30:5</note>, we read it written thus: "Rabbi Moses Hadarsan said: *For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life.* This was said concerning our righteous Messiah. For his death and life shall be in a moment, by his own will, to give life to others and to receive it back for himself. And to this

### BOOK EIGHT.

...whom they call our holy Master <note>original: "magistrum nostrum sanctum"; referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah</note>, clearly showed long before the birth of Christ in the book which he called *Galezazeia* <note>original: גלי רזיא; "The Revealer of Secrets"</note>. This is found especially in his response to the second petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome. Among other things, this same Antoninus asked him: "Since *gheuer* <note>original: גבר; a Hebrew term for a strong man or hero</note> signifies 'man,' what is the meaning of that text written in Lamentations chapter 3: *I am the man [gheuer] who has seen affliction by the rod of his wrath; he has led me and brought me into darkness and not into light*?" <note>Lamentations 3:1–2</note> Our Master replied to him: "This refers to the Holy and Blessed God, who says: 'I am the man who has seen poverty. He has led me and brought me into darkness and not into light.' This is likewise the Holy and Blessed God who said: 'I have decreed to descend to the lower regions to redeem the souls of the righteous, whom my Father who is in heaven cast down there with the rod of his wrath because of the sin of Adam.'" Likewise, in the same book, regarding the sixth petition of the same Antoninus, this same "Holy Master" says that he found the following in the book of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai, which is called *Mechkar hassodoth* <note>original: מחקר הסודות; "The Investigation of Secrets"</note>: Upon hearing these things, Rabbi Hoseas began to weep and said: "Woe to them, woe to those impious ones, the murderers of Israel! Out of love for them—so that he might forgive their sin—the Holy and Blessed God will send his holy Son, and he shall clothe himself in human flesh. Woe to them, because on account of their wicked deeds they will be rebellious against this Messiah, and they will reject the words with which he shall command them to be cleansed with the water of purification to purge their sins. Indeed, they will not walk in the ways pleasing to God, nor will they do his will; but, moved by great wrath, they will kill him. Then his soul will descend to the lower regions, where he will remain for three days, so that he may lead out from there all the souls of the righteous fathers." Just as it was said in Genesis chapter 47: *I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will surely bring you up again.* <note>Genesis 46:4 is the likely reference, here cited as 47</note> And the Holy and Blessed God will cause him to lead them into paradise, and they shall be joyful in the glory of God, according to that which was said in Hosea chapter 6: *He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.* <note>Hosea 6:2</note> All these things were said by the one whom they call "our holy Master." From all of this, it is quite clearly evident that the Messiah, as God and man, was to descend to hell immediately after his death and lead out the souls of his elect from there.

### CHAPTER XXII.

->That the Messiah ought to rise from the dead on the<-
->third day.<-

->CAPNIO.<-

The Evangelists also wrote that our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day. You ought, therefore, to show from the Hebrew scriptures that this same thing was destined to happen to the Messiah. GALATINUS: First, then, I will tell you what the ancient Talmudists felt regarding that saying in Psalm 17: *As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied...*

<column-break/>

### PAGE 488

<margin>A</margin> *...when your form awakes.* <note>Psalm 17:15. The author uses the word "forma" to translate the Hebrew "temuna," which can mean image, likeness, or form.</note> It has already been proven through the writings of the Talmudists that the Messiah is the "Face of God." This "form," or figure, or image, or likeness of God of which the prophet speaks here, is none other than the Son of God, insofar as the Son of God himself is like the Father—as was also shown above in the third book. And this was that figure or image of God which Moses saw, as it is said in Numbers chapter 12: *And he beholds the form of the Lord.* <note>Numbers 12:8</note> Rabbi Onkelos <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic (the Targum Onkelos)</note> translated this into Aramaic as: *And he understands the likeness of the glory of the Lord.* Thus, according to this sense, the aforementioned words of the prophet can be explained: "I will see your face," that is, your Messiah. "I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or likeness, or image awakes," <margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin> that is, your Son. Although they also explain this differently elsewhere, as will be mentioned when we come to speak of the general resurrection, the explanation we have placed here is best confirmed in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>original: "Bereſith קטנה ketanna"; likely referring to a "Lesser" Midrash on Genesis</note>—that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis—regarding what is written in chapter 3 of that same book about Adam: *And the Lord sent him out of the garden [or paradise] of pleasure.* <note>Genesis 3:23</note> For there it is read literally: "Rabbi Hamia said: Adam was sent out of paradise in this age, but in the age to come he shall not be sent out." This saying of Rabbi Hamia is supported by what is written in Psalm 17: *I will behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or image, or likeness awakes.* The Holy and Blessed God said: "In 그 hour, I will justify him"—namely Adam—"from that sentence." David said to the Holy and Blessed God: "And in that hour when he who is your likeness shall rise, I shall be satisfied, and in righteousness I will contemplate [or see] your face." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: "I will contemplate your face," just as it is said: <margin>E</margin> <margin>Isaiah 52</margin> *For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord returns to Zion.* <note>Isaiah 52:8</note> Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally the author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets</note> translated this into Aramaic thus: *For with their eyes they shall see the power [or strength] which God shall perform when his divinity dwells [or remains] in Zion.* All this is tradition. In these things, three very great mysteries are contained. The first is that God was going to justify Adam, who was once expelled from paradise, by taking away the sentence passed against him. The second is that this was to happen when, according to David's prophecy, the *temuna* <note>original: תמונה; form, image, or likeness</note> of God should rise. The third is that he who was the likeness of God—that is, like God the Father according to his divinity—was to rise according to his humanity; then David knew he was to be healed, and through righteousness he would see and contemplate the face of God. Yet he did not say by whose righteousness he was to attain these things; perhaps because he preferred this to be said through Isaiah, who, speaking after him about the Messiah the Son of God (as we showed in preceding sections, chapter 53), says: *By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their sins.*

<margin>A</margin> the same Rabbi says word for word: "This is what is written in Hosea chapter 6: <note>original: יחיינו מיומים ביום השלישי יקימנו ונחיה לפניו ונדעה נרדפה לדעת את יהוה</note> *He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up. And we shall live before his face. And we shall know, so that we may follow on to know the Lord.* On the third day, that is, in a period of three days: just as it is written in Genesis chapter 42: *And Joseph said to them, 'On the third day.'* But on the third day of the giving of the law, according to that in Exodus 19: *And it happened on the third day when it became morning, there were voices and lightning.* <margin>B</margin> Also on the third day of the spies, as was said in Joshua 2: *And hide yourselves there for three days.* Also on the third day of Jonah, according to that: *Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights.* Also on the third day of those coming up from captivity, as was said in Ezra chapter 8: *And we camped there for three days.* Finally, on the third day of the <margin>C</margin> quickening of the dead, according to that stated in Hosea chapter 6: *He will give us life after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up. And we shall live before his face*—which is the King Messiah. As was said in Psalm 80: <note>original: יהוה אלהים צבאות השיבנו האר פניך ונושעה</note> *Lord God of hosts, convert us; show your face*—that is, your Messiah—*and we shall be saved.*" This is the tradition.

<margin>D</margin> In the book <term>Mechilta</term> <note>A legal commentary on Exodus, though here used in a broader sense of midrashic collection</note>, regarding that verse of Psalm 30: *For a moment in his anger, life in his favor*, we read it written thus: <note>original Hebrew text provided in OCR</note> "Rabbi Moses Hadarsan said: *For a moment in his anger, life in his favor.* This was said <margin>E</margin> concerning our righteous Messiah. For his death and life shall be in a moment, by his own will, to give to others and to receive it in himself." And immediately joined to this in the same Psalm is the following: *Weeping shall linger for the evening, and singing for the morning.* For when he brings death upon someone, they will weep over him, but when he restores him to life, they will sing a song. Moreover, when he himself dies, all the followers of his name will be sorrowful because of his death, and when he returns to life, or when he rises again, they will rejoice and sing. And to this is added that: *He will give us life after two days, and on the third day he will cause yours to rise again, and we shall live before his face.*

<margin>Universal exposition.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> Therefore the words of the prophet Hosea are to be understood, according to their expositions, in this way: *He will give us life*, namely the Messiah will from the death of sin, *after two days*, during which he will lie in the tomb. *On the third day he will raise us up*, namely through the hope of the resurrection. For Christ's resurrection was the example and cause of our general future resurrection. For just as <margin>G</margin> Christ rose, so we also shall rise. For that reason, Peter, as if wishing to explain this prophecy of Hosea, says in the first chapter of his first epistle: *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us into a living hope, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.* This very thing, however, through Rabbi...

...our Holy Teacher <note>referring to Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, known as 'Rabbenu HaKadosh'</note> was stated more explicitly in that book titled *Gale Razia* <note>original: גלי רזיא; 'The Revealer of Secrets'</note>, where he said: "Truly, after three days the soul of the Messiah shall return to his body, and he shall go out from that stone in which he was buried; just as it is said in Exodus 33: *Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand upon the rock; and it shall come to pass, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of the rock.*" These are the words of him whom the Hebrews call our Holy Master.

### CHAPTER XXIII.
#### That the Messiah was to ascend into heaven, leading with him those whom he was meant to free from hell.
->CAPNIO<-
<note>'Capnio' is the Greek-derived pen name of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>See above, folio 353. Cornelius à Lapide on Micah 11:13, folio 415.</margin>
<margin>The first testimony.</margin>
The Catholic faith also firmly holds that Christ ascended into heaven. Therefore, it must be proved through the testimonies of the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah was to do this very thing after his resurrection. **Galatinus:** We can prove this especially through seven testimonies. Of these, the first is that which is placed in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: *For I will lift up my hand to heaven.* <note>original: כי אשא אל שמים ידי</note> Rabbi Onkelos <note>R. Ankelos; the famous translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note>, turning this into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language, explained it thus: *Because I will ordain, or prepare, in heaven the house of my Divine Presence* <note>original: בית שכינתי; referring to the Shekhinah</note>, *and I, remaining, shall speak for eternity.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi; the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> also explained it this way: *I will lift up my hand to heaven*, that is, to the place of my divinity. Now, the "place" and "house of divinity" is the Messiah according to his humanity. This is sufficiently shown through Isaiah, speaking in chapter 57: *Thus says the high and lofty One, who inhabits eternity, and whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.* <note>original: כה אמר רם ונשא...</note> In the gloss of Rabbi Solomon, it says: *I dwell in the high and holy place, and from there I am with the contrite and humble spirit. For I extend my divinity over him.* Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Now, no one is more aptly called "contrite and humble in spirit" than the Messiah. Concerning him, Isaiah says in chapter 53: *Struck by God, and humiliated. And he was wounded, or killed, for our crimes, and contrite for our sins.* It seems, therefore, that Rabbi Solomon follows the prophet in the aforementioned explanations, even if he did not fully realize what he was prophesying.

<margin>The second testimony.</margin>
The second testimony is from Micah, speaking thus of the Messiah in chapter 2: *The breaker-up has gone up before them; they have broken through and passed the gate, and gone out by it; and their King shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.* <note>original: עלה הפרץ לפניהם...</note> That these words are to be understood as referring to the Messiah is clearly evident through their own writings. For in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>R. Mofis Hadarsan; an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note>, regarding the statement in chapter 40 of the same book: *In my dream, behold, a vine was before me*; it is said: This is what is written in Psalm 80: *And the plant which your right hand has planted.* <note>original: וכנה אשר נטעה ימינך</note>

<column-break/>

<page-num>492</page-num>
<header>BOOK EIGHT.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...that is, *And perfect, or prepare, what your right hand has planted.* Specifically, the plant from below: this is Abraham; and the plant from above: this is the Messiah. Concerning whom it was said in Micah, chapter 2: *The breaker-up ascended before them.* Thus far the tradition. Furthermore, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon explains those same words of Micah in this way: *The Savior of them shall ascend as a breaker-up; specifically, breaking through the hedges of thorns and briers, to direct the way for them.*

<margin>B</margin>
Rabbi Moses the Preacher also, regarding that statement in Genesis chapter 44: *And Judah approached him*, says: This is what is written in the Song of Songs, chapter 1: *We will exult and rejoice in you.* And when will this be? *When the captivity ascends from Gehenna* <note>hell</note>, *and the Divine Presence is at their head.* Just as it was said in Micah, chapter 2: *And their King shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.* The same Rabbi, in his exposition of the book of Genesis regarding the statement in chapter 41: *After the end of two years, Pharaoh dreamed*, says: But what else is it that is written in Psalm 146: *The Lord releases the bound* <note>original: יהוה מתיר אסורים; 'Asurim' meaning those bound or imprisoned</note>, that is, the captives of hell, the captives of death. Thus far Rabbi Moses the Preacher.

<margin>C</margin>
Likewise, in the *Midrash Rabbathi* <note>Lamentations Rabbah; an ancient commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, in the exposition of the lament of Jeremiah regarding the statement in chapter 1: *For my sighs are many, and my heart is faint*; it is said: You find that in the very same things in which Israel sinned, they were punished, and afterward comforted. They sinned in the "head": As it is written in Numbers 14: *Let us appoint a head, and return to Egypt.* And they were punished in the "head": As it is written in Isaiah 1: *The whole head is sick.*

<margin>D</margin>
And they were to be comforted in the "head." Just as it is written in Micah, chapter 2: *And their King shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.* That the Messiah is the head of Israel has been sufficiently proved through their scriptures in the preceding pages: which is also best shown through the statement in Hosea, chapter 1: *Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint for themselves one head.* <note>original: ונקבצו בני יהודה...</note>

<margin>E</margin>
Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: *One head*, that is, David their King. Because great is the day of the gathering of the seed of God. However, since Hosea prophesied in the time of King Ahaz, his words cannot be understood as referring to David the son of Jesse, since he lived long before. Therefore, they must be understood as referring to the Messiah, who (as we showed above) is also frequently called "David" in the Holy Scripture.

<margin>The third testimony.</margin>
The third testimony is found in Psalm 68, where it is said: *You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive; you have received gifts among men, and even for the rebellious, that the Lord God might dwell among them.* <note>original: עלית למרום שבית שבי...</note>

<margin>The fourth testimony.</margin>
The fourth testimony is in Amos, who says in chapter 9: *It is he who builds his ascents in heaven, and has founded his troop on the earth; who calls for the waters of the sea, and pours them out on the face of the earth: the Lord* <note>the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note> *is his name.*

<margin>F</margin>
Which Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel <note>R. Ionathas Vzielis; the author of the Aramaic Targum on the Prophets</note>, thus translated into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>: *He who placed the Divine Presence of His glory in the highest strength, and his Church upon the earth he con-firm...* <note>the text cuts off at the catchword</note>

It emphasizes the Messiah's role as the "head" of Israel and the "house of divinity."</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...confirmed. He who said that the troops, or multitudes, should be gathered like the water of the sea, and He shall scatter them over the face of the earth: the Lord <note>original: 'tetragrammaton' refers to the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH</note> is His name. In the preceding sections, we have proved that the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, belongs to God alone, and therefore the Messiah was to be called by that name. The fifth testimony is found in Deuteronomy, chapter 33, where it is said:
<margin>The fifth testimony.</margin> <margin>B</margin> *There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides the heavens for your help, and in His majesty through the clouds.* <note>original Hebrew: אין כאל ישרון רכב שמים בעזרך ובגאותו שחקים</note> This means: "There is no one like the God of Jeshurun, the rider or equestrian of heaven as your helper, and in His magnificence ascending the clouds or the heavens." Rabbi Onkelos <note>a famous convert and author of the Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> translated this into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language as follows: *There is no God like the God of Israel, whose Divine Presence is in the heavens for your help, and His power or strength is in the highest heavens.* <note>original Aramaic: לית אלה כאלהא דישראל די שכינתיה בשמיא בסערך ותוקפיה בשמיא שמיא</note> Also, in Rabbi Solomon's <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> gloss on the word "Rider of heaven," he says: "He is that God who is your helper, and in His magnificence He Himself is ascending the *sehakim*"—that is, the heavens or the clouds. It was stated above that the Messiah is called "the helper." <margin>C</margin> The sixth testimony <margin>The sixth testimony.</margin> is found in Psalm 104, where it reads: *Who makes the clouds His chariot, walking upon the wings of the wind; who makes His messengers spirits, and His ministers a flaming fire: He founded the earth upon its base, it shall not be moved forever and ever.* <note>original Hebrew: השם עבים רכובו המהלך על כנפי רוח : עושֶה מלאכיו רוחות משרתיו אש להט : יסד ארץ על מכוניה בל תמוט עולם ועד</note> Mystically, in this place, the "earth of Israel" refers to the apostles and other <margin>D</margin> disciples of our Messiah, who, as proved elsewhere, were the true Israelites. The "basis" of the earth is the foundation of the Church. Toward the goal of this explanation, one may look to what is read in the *Midrash Koheleth* <note>a homiletic commentary on Ecclesiastes</note>, regarding the statement in the first chapter of that book: *A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.* <note>original Hebrew: דור הולך ודור בא והארץ לעולם עומדת</note> There it says word-for-word: "Rabbi Isaac said: 'This kingdom <margin>E</margin> enters, and this kingdom departs. But Israel remains. And this is why it says: the earth remains forever.'" This is supported by the scripture in Judges chapter 18: *And Jonathan the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land.* Now, does the land itself go into captivity or move? No, but these are the people of Israel, who are called "the earth," just as it is said in Malachi chapter three: *And all nations shall call <margin>F</margin> you blessed, for you shall be a desirable land.* <note>original Hebrew: ואשרו אתכם כל הגוים כי תהיו אתם ארץ חפץ</note> All this is from tradition. The seventh testimony <margin>The seventh testimony.</margin> is from our Holy Teacher <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, in the book he called *Gale Razia* <note>The Revealer of Secrets</note>, speaking thus: "The Messiah, after his resurrection, shall dwell with the righteous, who will hear his precepts for 40 days, in the image of those 40 days in which he will be in the desert to afflict his soul before they kill him. And when these things are finished, he shall ascend into heaven, and sit at the right hand of God. Just as it is said in Psalm 110: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.*"

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->That the Messiah would sit at the right hand of God the Father.<-

<margin>A</margin> **T**his also is something you ought especially to prove through their own scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was to sit at the right hand of God the Father. **GALATINUS:** This too we can prove through many sayings of the ancients. Especially, however, through that same statement of the Psalmist which has now been cited by him whom they call *Rabbenu Haccados* <note>Our Holy Teacher</note>. <margin>B</margin> For the Psalmist himself says in Hebrew in Psalm 110: *The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.* <note>original Hebrew: נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני</note> <margin>C</margin> **CAPNIO:** Although the point is excellently proved by this very clear testimony of the Psalmist, the more recent Jews, attempting to extinguish the light of truth, assert that David spoke these words not about the Messiah, but about someone else. Indeed, some claim he spoke these same words about Abraham. They affirm that David called him "my Lord" out of a display of paternal reverence. Others, however, say that David uttered these words about the Angel appointed for his protection. They say he called the Angel "his Lord" for this reason: because since every man has one of the Angels destined for his guardianship, the Angel is rightly said to preside over the one whose care he manages. Therefore, he can also be rightly called "Lord" in a certain sense. They also <margin>D</margin> object to us with many other things of this kind besides this, so that they might escape the truth. **GALATINUS:** They can say such things to those who are ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are skilled in them. For such people (as you well know) easily convict them through their own scriptures. Therefore, through the authentic and approved <margin>E</margin> writings of their ancients, it is most clearly shown that David spoke those words neither of Abraham, nor of the Angel appointed as his guardian, nor of any other, but of the Messiah, God and man, since it is not fitting for any pure creature to sit at the right hand of God. First, then, this is evident through the *Targum* of Rabbi Jonathan <note>an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets</note>, that is, through his Chaldean edition, which explains these same words in Aramaic: *The Lord said to His Word: Sit at my right hand.* <note>original Aramaic: אמר יהוה למימריה תיב לימיני</note> Some, however, say that it is not so in the Chaldean translation <margin>F</margin> as I have reported it, but rather: *The Lord said in His word, or through His word, that He would give me dominion, because I sat to learn the law; wait at my right hand.* <note>original Aramaic: אמר יהוה למימריה לימינו למיתן לי רבנותא חלף דיתיבית לאולפן אורייתא</note> To these I say it is true that in the Chaldean translation of the Psalms which the Jews now more frequently have in hand, it is as they say. However, that translation is not by Jonathan, but by Rabbi Akilas, or Rabbi Joseph the Blind, who flourished nearly three hundred years after the destruction of the second temple. But the translation of Jonathan, which they themselves have not yet seen, is exactly as I have reported it. They ought not to deny it just because <margin>G</margin> they have not seen it. For Jonathan himself (as we have proved elsewhere) translated the entire Bible into Aramaic, although not all of his books are now held in hand. Next, it is proved that those words of David, "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at the right..."

...my right hand, was meant to be understood as referring to the Messiah, according to the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "Midras tehilim"; a rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note> regarding that verse of the second Psalm:
<margin>A</margin>
*The decree: I will tell of the decree* <note>original Hebrew: אל חק (el chok)</note>. In that place it is said: *They are recounted in the decree of the Law, in the decree of the Prophets, and in the Writings. In the decree of the Law: "Israel is my firstborn son" [Exod. 4]. In the decree of the Prophets: "Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled" [Isa. 52]. In the Writings: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand" [Psalm 110].* This means that his mysteries—namely, those of the King Messiah—are narrated in the scripture of the law, such as in Exodus 4, "Israel is my firstborn son"; in the scripture of the prophets, such as in Isaiah 52, "Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up"; and in the hagiographa <note>the "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>, as in Psalm 110, "God said to my lord, sit at my right hand." Then this very thing is proven through the *Midrash Tehillim*, that is, through the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the statement in Psalm 17:
<margin>B</margin>
*You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand has supported me* <note>original Hebrew: ותתן לי מגן ישעך וימינך תסעדני</note>. This means: "And you shall give to me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall comfort, support, or receive me." For it is said there:
<margin>C</margin>
*Rabbi Yoden said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya: In the time to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will cause the King Messiah to sit at His right hand, as it is said in Psalm 110: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand."* This same point is also very well suggested in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>an 11th-century preacher from Narbonne</note>, when commenting on the passage from the eighteenth chapter of that same book, "And the Lord appeared to him in the oak grove of Mamre." It is said there: Rabbi Barachias, in the name of Rabbi Levi, revealed (that is, explained) this by what is written in Psalm 17, "And you have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall comfort or receive me." For in the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will cause the Messiah to sit at His right hand, just as it was said, "God said to my Lord, sit at my right hand." This is the tradition. From all these things, it is clearly shown that the aforementioned words of David are to be understood entirely as referring to the Messiah, and consequently, that the Messiah himself was to sit at the right hand of God the Father, which was the point to be proven.

# CHAPTER XXV.

->That the Messiah was to send the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and others believing in him.<-

### CAPNIO.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting floral motifs and scrollwork within a rectangular border.</image-desc>
Since we read that Christ sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and his other disciples on the day of Pentecost, it is necessary to prove through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was destined to do this very thing, so that all the mysteries of the Messiah may be made apparent. GALATINUS: That the Holy Spirit was to be sent upon the Apostles and other disciples of the Messiah, as well as upon the converts and those baptized from among the Gentiles, is primarily held from those things said in the forty-fourth chapter of Isaiah. For there it is read: *Fear not, O Jacob my servant, and Jeshurun whom I have chosen. For I will pour water upon the thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows by the watercourses. One shall say, "I am the Lord’s"; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord,*

<column-break/>

*and surname himself by the name of Israel.* This means: "Fear not, my servant Jacob, and most upright one whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and flowing streams upon the dry land. I will pour my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your lineages. And they shall sprout in the midst of the hay, or the grass, like willows upon the channels of water. This one shall say, 'I am of God.' And that one shall call upon the name of Jacob. And this one shall write with his hand (or his strength) to God, and shall be named by the name of Israel." Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation</note> translated these words, "I will pour my Spirit," along with the rest, into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language thus: *I will give my Holy Spirit upon your children, and my blessing upon your children’s children, and the righteous—tender and delicate—shall be nourished or multiplied like the sproutings of grass, and like a tree sending its roots over the channels or flows of water.* Furthermore, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> on those words of the prophet, "For I will pour water upon the thirsty," says: "Just as I pour waters upon the thirsty, so I will pour my spirit upon your seed." Concerning the aforementioned pouring of waters upon those to be baptized, as well as the mission of the Holy Spirit, Ezekiel also makes mention in the 36th chapter, saying:
<margin>D</margin>
*I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your filthiness* <note>original Hebrew: וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים וטהרתם מכל טמאותיכם</note>. And a little later: *And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my judgments, and do them.* Where Rabbi Jonathan interpreted this, "And I will put my Spirit within you," in the Chaldean language as: *And I will give my Holy Spirit in your bowels* <note>original Aramaic: ורוח קדשי אתן במעיכם; "bowels" or "inward parts" signifies the seat of emotion and thought</note>. Regarding the outpouring or sending of the Holy Spirit upon the
<margin>E</margin>
Apostles and other disciples of the Messiah on the day of Pentecost, it is also found in Isaiah 32, which says: *Until the spirit be poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness be a Carmel (or the vineyard of the Lord), and Carmel (or the vineyard of the Lord) be counted for a forest.* Here, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Until he pours out the spirit upon us." Just as it was said in Genesis chapter 24, *vattear* <note>original: ותער</note>, meaning, "And she poured out her pitcher." 
<margin>F</margin>
For the word *sephicha* <note>original: שפיכה</note>, meaning "outpouring," is frequently used in relation to the spirit, according to that which was said in Zechariah chapter 12: *And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications.* And it was also said in Joel chapter 3: *And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit. And I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire,*
<margin>G</margin>
*and pillars of smoke.* That is: "And it shall be after these things, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams. Your young men shall see visions. And even upon the servants and the handmaids in those days I will pour out..."

**GALATINUS.** In this matter, the more recent Jews err greatly, firmly asserting that a promise of God regarding good things is never revoked by God—even if it was made to one who falls from justice into injustice—but <margin>E</margin> is always necessarily fulfilled.
