<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio (the scholar Johannes Reuchlin) and Galatinus (Pietro Colonna Galatino). In the previous section, they established that the Messiah would bring a New Law intended for both Jews and Gentiles. Here, they transition to the specific ritual of the New Law—baptism—arguing that it was prophesied in the Hebrew Scriptures to replace circumcision.</meta>

BOOK TEN.

# CHAPTER II.

->*That the Messiah was to institute the sacrament of baptism, through which circumcision was to be abolished.*<-

# CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> Since Christ—when the Apostles were about to proclaim the Gospel Law to the Gentiles throughout the world—commanded them to baptize the nations and delivered to them the form of baptizing, saying in the last chapter of Matthew: *Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you;* and since the sacrament of baptism is the gate to the sacraments of this new and evangelical law; therefore, both for a clearer expression of Catholic truth and for the greater confusion of Jewish obstinacy, it is necessary to prove through the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah himself was to institute baptism for the remission of sins. 

**GAL.** This is first understood from what Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Messiah, brought forth in the 44th chapter: <note>Isaiah 44:2-5</note> *Fear not, my servant Jacob, and the Most Upright whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. One shall say, "I am the Lord's." And another shall call on the name of Jacob. And another shall write with his hand to the Lord, and be named by the name of Israel.* 

These words, *For I will pour waters upon the thirsty,* along with the rest, Rabbi Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> thus translated and explained in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>: *For just as waters are given upon a thirsty land and flow upon the dry ground, so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your children, and my blessing upon your children's children. And the righteous shall grow, leaning and delicate, like shoots of grass as if their beginning was delayed over the courses of water. This one shall say, "I am of those who fear the Lord," and this one shall pray in the name of Jacob, and this one shall offer his sacrifice before the Lord, and shall be called by the name of Israel.* 

(To render it word for word): *Because just as waters are given upon a thirsty land, and floods upon the dry: so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your son, and my blessing upon the sons of your son. And the righteous, tender, and delicate shall be anointed, or multiplied, like a tree that sends its roots over the stretches of water. This one shall say, "I am of the fearers of God." And this one shall pray in the name of Jacob. And this one shall offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel.* From these words of the prophet, where he speaks openly of baptism, it is most evidently clear that by the power of baptism, those converted from the Gentiles and all Christians were to be made children of Israel. 

In confirmation of this matter, it should be noted that in the book *Yoma* of the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter beginning *Yom Ha-Kippurim* (that is, the Day of Atonement), it is read in this manner: It is written in Jeremiah, chapter 17: <note>Jeremiah 17:13</note> *The Mikveh <note>The Hebrew word "Mikveh" means "hope" but also refers to a "collection of water" used for ritual purification.</note> of Israel is God.* For just as a gathering—or a sea of waters—cleanses the polluted, so the Holy and Blessed God will be the one cleansing Israel in the future. For He Himself says so in Ezekiel, chapter 36: 

<column-break/>

<page-num>534</page-num>
<header>LIBER DECIMVS.</header>

*And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed; from all your filthiness and from all your idols I will cleanse you.* This is the tradition. 

To understand these things, <margin>B</margin> it must be noted what is written in the *Bereshit Ketanna* (that is, in the Lesser Exposition of the book of Genesis), regarding the saying in the 49th chapter of the same book: <note>Genesis 49:11</note> *Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt to the choice vine.* For it is said there: *This is he of whom it is written in Zechariah, chapter 9: "And riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass." And he is the one who will plant all Israel like a "Sorekah," <note>Hebrew: שורק (Soreq), a high-quality red grape vine.</note> that is, a choice branch.* As it is written in the second chapter of Jeremiah: <margin>C</margin> *And I planted you a choice vine, wholly a seed of truth.* And how will he act? As it was said in the thirty-sixth chapter of Ezekiel: *And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness,* and so forth. This is the tradition. 

You see how clearly it is said here that the Messiah was the one who would sprinkle these waters of Ezekiel, and by so doing, would plant all Israel—both literal and spiritual—of which we spoke shortly before. For <margin>D</margin> the aforementioned words of Zechariah can be understood of no one else but the Messiah. For upon that saying in the ninth chapter of the same prophet, *Behold your King comes to you, just and having salvation,* the glosses of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105).</note> say: *It is not possible to explain this except concerning the King Messiah.* 

To the things already said, it is also quite fittingly added what is written in the book *Kiddushin* (that is, of Sanctifications), in the chapter that begins *Asarah Yohasin* (that is, Ten Noble Families): The *Rabbanan* (that is, the masters) have handed down <margin>E</margin> that the illegitimate <note>original: *spurii*, referring to mamzerim</note> and the children of menstruating women shall be clean in the future (these are the words of Rabbi Yose), as it is said in Ezekiel, chapter 36: *And I will sprinkle clean water upon you,* with the rest. 

The water of baptism and its power was also prophesied in that place where it was said through Zechariah in the 13th chapter: <note>Zechariah 13:1-2</note> *In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for cleansing and for sprinkling <note>original: *aspergendum*</note> or for removal. And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered.* 

These words are most precisely explained as: *In that day* (that is, in the time of the Messiah, just as we have proved the prophet speaks of the Messiah there) *there shall be a fountain* (namely, of baptism): *opened* (that is, common to all men): *to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem* <margin>G</margin> (that is, to the Church of Christ gathered from Jews and Gentiles): *for cleansing* (namely, souls from original sin and from other sins): *and for sprinkling* (that is, for washing sinners from every stain of sin): *or for removal* (that is, for taking it away).

<summary>This page presents a collection of Old Testament prophecies and Rabbinic commentaries to argue that the Messiah would institute baptism as a universal ritual for spiritual purification. It specifically links the "clean water" of Ezekiel and the "fountain" of Zechariah to the Christian sacrament of baptism, intended to replace circumcision.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

->That the Messiah was to institute the sacrament of baptism, through which circumcision was to be abolished.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin> Since Christ commanded the Apostles, who were about to proclaim the Gospel law to the nations throughout the world, to baptize the Gentiles and gave them the form of baptizing, saying in the last chapter of Matthew: *Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you* <note>Matthew 28:19–20</note>; and since the sacrament of baptism is the gateway to the sacraments of this new and Gospel law: therefore, both for a clearer expression of the Catholic truth and for the greater confusion of Jewish obstinacy, it is necessary to prove through the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah himself was to institute baptism for the remission of sins. <margin>C</margin> GALATINUS: This is first understood from what Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Messiah himself, brought forth in the 44th chapter: <margin>Fear not</margin>
> Fear not, my servant Jacob, and most upright one whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and floods upon the dry land. I will pour my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. This one shall say, "I am the Lord's." And that one shall call on the name of Jacob. And another shall write with his hand to the Lord, and shall be surnamed by the name of Israel. <note>Isaiah 44:2–5</note>

Moreover, these words, *For I will pour waters upon the thirsty*, along with the rest, Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum (translation/paraphrase) of the Prophets.</note> translated and explained in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaice"</note> as follows:
<margin>E</margin>
> For just as waters are given upon the thirsty land and flow upon the dry ground, so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your children, and my blessing upon your children's children. And the righteous shall increase, tender and delicate, like a tree that sends its roots over the stretches of water. This one shall say, "I am of those who fear the Lord." And this one shall pray in the name of Jacob. And this one shall offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel. <note>An English rendering of the Aramaic Targum text provided in the source.</note>

(To render it word for word): *For as waters are given upon the thirsty land, and floods upon the dry: so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your son, and my blessing upon the sons of your son. And the righteous shall be anointed, or multiplied, tender and delicate, like a tree which sends its roots over the tracts of waters. This one will say, "I am of those who fear God." And this one will pray in the name of Jacob. And this one will offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel.* <margin>G</margin> From these words of the prophet, therefore, where he speaks openly of baptism, it is most clearly evident that by the power of baptism, all those converted from the Gentiles were to be made children of Israel and Christians. For the confirmation of this matter, it should be noted that in the Jerusalem <term>Yoma</term> <gloss>The "Day" (referring to the Talmudic tractate on the Day of Atonement)</gloss>, in the chapter beginning <term>Yom HaKippurim</term> <gloss>The Day of Atonements</gloss>, it is read in this way: It is written in the 17th chapter of Jeremiah, <term>The hope (Mikveh) of Israel is God</term> <note>original: "Mikveh Yisrael Adonai". The word "Mikveh" means both "hope" and "a collection of water/ritual bath."</note>. This means: The gathering—

This is the tradition. For the understanding of these things, <margin>B</margin> it should be noted that in the <term>Bereshit Ketanna</term> <gloss>The Lesser Genesis (a Midrashic commentary)</gloss>, regarding that saying in the 49th chapter of the same book: <term>Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt to the choice vine</term> <note>Genesis 49:11</note>, it is written thus: "This is the one of whom it is written in the 9th chapter of Zechariah: *And riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass.* And he is the one who will plant all Israel like a <term>Soreka</term> <gloss>a choice vine</gloss>." Just as it is written in the second chapter of Jeremiah: <margin>And I planted you a choice vine, wholly a seed of truth.</margin> <margin>C</margin> *And I planted you a choice vine, entirely a seed of truth.* <note>Jeremiah 2:21</note> And how will he act? As it was said in the thirty-sixth chapter of Ezekiel: *And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness*, and so forth. This is the tradition. You see how evidently it is said here that the Messiah was to sprinkle these waters of Ezekiel, and by so acting, he would plant all Israel, both literal and spiritual, of which we spoke a little earlier. For <margin>D</margin> the aforementioned words of Zechariah can be understood of no one else but the Messiah. For upon that saying in the ninth chapter of the same prophet—*Behold, your King comes to you, just and having salvation*—the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "It is not possible to explain this except concerning the King Messiah." Also, the water of baptism and its power was prophesied in that place where it was spoken through Zechariah in chapter 13: <margin>In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness. > In that day there shall be a fountain open to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for cleansing and for sprinkling <note>original: "ad mundificandum, & ad aspergendum"</note> or for removing. And it shall be in that day, says the God of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the earth, and they shall be remembered no more. <note>Zechariah 13:1–2</note>

These words are indeed most aptly explained: *In that day*, that is, in the time of the Messiah (since we have proved the prophet is speaking of the Messiah there), *there shall be a fountain*, namely of baptism: *open*, that is, common to all men: *to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem*, <margin>G</margin> that is, to the Church of Christ gathered from Jews and Gentiles: *for cleansing*, namely of souls from original sin and from other sins: *and for sprinkling*, that is, for washing sinners from every stain of sin: *or for removing*, that is, for taking away...

<margin>A</margin> it is necessary for the impurity of every sin to be washed away from the soul. The time when all of this was to be accomplished is shown when it is immediately added: *And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered.* <note>Zechariah 13:2</note> Since, therefore, this was not done through Abraham, nor through any of the prophets, nor in their days, but was done only in the days of Jesus our Messiah, through himself and his disciples and others believing in him, it is truly <margin>B</margin> clear that our Savior himself is "David"—that is, the Messiah—and was so in the previously mentioned words of Zechariah. His baptism is also the fountain open to all, of which it was spoken in the same place. The prophet gave another most evident sign of this truth when he immediately added these words: <term>ונם את הנביאים ואת רוח הטומא אעביר מן הארץ</term> <note>original: "And also the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness I will cause to pass from the land"</note> That is, *And I will also remove the prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.* Rabbi Jonathan explained this in Aramaic as: <term>ואף ית נביאא שקרא וית רוח מסאבא אבטיל מן ארעא</term> <note>original: "And also the prophets of the lying spirit and the unclean spirit I will abolish from the earth"</note> That is, *And I will also destroy the prophets of the lying spirit and the unclean spirit from the land.* If modern Jews deny that this was fulfilled in the days of our Messiah, let them be reminded of how great a multitude of false prophets there were in the world before our Savior’s coming—not only among the Gentiles, but even among themselves. This was such that Elijah, the prophet of the Lord, said to Ahab, the King of Israel: *Gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the <margin>C</margin> four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and the four hundred prophets of the groves (or of the forest) who eat at Jezebel's table.* <note>1 Kings 18:19</note> Besides these, there were many other false prophets among the Jews, whom Ahab later consulted as to whether he should go to Ramoth-Gilead. Let them also recall that before the times of our Messiah, in the days of their fathers, unclean spirits were accustomed to give responses in idols. For as we read in the first chapter of 2 Kings <note>traditionally 3 Kings in some older Latin Bibles</note>, Ahaziah of Israel said this to his messengers: *Go, inquire of <term>בעל זבוב</term> Baal-Zebub <note>meaning "Lord of the Flies"</note>, the god of <term>עקרון</term> Ekron, whether I shall recover from this illness.* In the tenth chapter of Zechariah, idols are also said to have spoken deceit. Since, therefore, in the days of the Jews and before the coming of Christ our Lord, idolatry flourished so greatly not only among the Gentiles but also among the Jews—as well as false prophets and unclean spirits, as has been shown by these few examples out of many—and since it is established that in the days of our Messiah all these things were so deleted that there is no need of proof: it follows without a doubt that whatever we concluded a little earlier is entirely true. To what has been said, I think it is appropriate to add <margin>D</margin> what is found written in the Babylonian book <term>יומא</term> *Yoma* <note>meaning "The Day," referring to the tractate on Yom Kippur</note>, in the chapter <term>יום הכפורים</term> *Yom Ha-Kippurim* <note>the Day of Atonement</note>: *Rabbi Akiba said: Blessed are you, O Israel! Before whom are you purified, and who cleanses you? Your Father who is in heaven.* Of whom it is said in the 36th chapter of Ezekiel: *And I will sprinkle clean waters upon you, and you shall be cleansed.* And so forth as above. And again <margin>E</margin> in Jeremiah 17: <term>מקוה ישראל יהוה</term> <note>original: "The hope (or gathering of waters) of Israel is the Lord"</note> This means: *The Lord is the gathering or collection of the waters of Israel.* For just as a gathering or collection of waters cleanses the unclean, so

<margin>A</margin> the Holy and Blessed God will cleanse Israel. This is the tradition. Since, therefore, this act—through the authority of Ezekiel—was attributed to the Messiah by the ancient teachers of the Jews shortly before, it follows necessarily according to their words that the Messiah is God, who was to cleanse all Israel through the waters of baptism by the power of his Holy Spirit, as was explained above. Furthermore, that baptism was to be instituted against all sins, and especially against original sin, was <margin>B</margin> principally foretold through Ezekiel in chapter 36, saying: <term>וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים וטהרתם מכל טמאתניכם ומכל גלוליכם אטהר אתכם: ונתתי לכם לב חדש ורוח חדשה אתן בקרבכם והסרתי את לב האבן מבשרכם ונתתי לכם לב בשר: ואת רוחי אתן בקרבכם ועשיתי את אשר בחקי תלכו ומשפטי תשמרו ועשיתם</term> <note>Ezekiel 36:25–27</note>
This means: *And I will pour clean waters upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness, and from all your filthiness I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give in <margin>C</margin> your midst. And I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit in your midst. And I will cause you to walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments, and do them.* Now, this "stony heart" which he says must be removed—to be succeeded by a "heart of flesh" and the Holy Spirit through grace—is understood to be original sin, which was to be entirely taken away by God through the mediation of baptism. To know, however, that baptism was meant to <margin>D</margin> empty the requirement of circumcision, the saying of Rabbi Joshua must be highly noted, when in the book <term>יבמות</term> *Yebamoth* <note>meaning "Sisters-in-law," regarding Levirate marriage</note>, in the chapter <term>החולץ</term> *Ha-Cholets* <note>meaning "The one who removes the shoe"</note>, he says: <term>מי שהוא טבול ואינו נימול הנה הוא גד כמו שהוא נמצא באמות שנטבלו ולא נימולו:</term>
This means: *He who is baptized but not circumcised, behold, he is a "gher"* <note>term for a convert from the Gentiles to the true faith</note>. *For so we find in the mothers, namely Sarah and Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, who were baptized but not circumcised.* At <margin>E</margin> this point it should also be known that circumcision was a figure of the shedding of Christ’s blood; he began to shed it at his circumcision and finally poured it all out in his passion for the salvation of the human race. Nor was circumcision to be performed ever again after Christ commanded baptism to take place in its stead, which deletes sins more perfectly, and which both women and men can use. That the sacrament of baptism was also to be proclaimed throughout the whole world <margin>F</margin> can be gathered from what is read in *Midrash* <term>קהלת</term> *Koheleth* <note>an exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes</note>, when commenting on that saying from the first chapter of the same book: <term>מה שהיה הוא שיהיה</term>—*What is it that has been? The same as that which shall be.* Rabbi Berachiah said in the name of Rabbi Isaac: *As was the first redeemer (that is, Moses), so shall be the last redeemer.* And after a few words, he says: *Just as the first redeemer caused a well to rise up, so the last redeemer, who is the Messiah, will cause waters to rise up.* As it is said in <margin>G</margin> the last chapter of Joel: <term>ומעין מבית יהוה יצא והשקה את נחל השטים</term> <note>Joel 3:18</note> That is: *And a fountain shall come out of the house of God and shall water the torrent (or valley, or plain) of Shittim.* This last part Rabbi Jonathan translated into Aramaic as: <term>ויהי משקי ית מישר שיטין</term> that is, [it shall water the plain of Shittim].

The author argues that because baptism can only be received once, a second remedy was necessary for those who fall back into sin.</meta>

And it shall water the valley of Shittim. <note>Joel 3:18. The author refers to the "plain of Setim."</note> Now, Shittim is the name of a certain region of Greece. It is from this place, as stated in the beginning of the first book of Maccabees, that Alexander the Macedonian went forth. <note>The author appears to connect the "Shittim" of the prophets with the "Kittim" of 1 Maccabees 1:1 to link the prophecy to the Greek world.</note> This, therefore, was fulfilled when the Apostles preached baptism throughout the whole world and the Greeks were baptized.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the sacrament of penance which the Messiah was to institute through vocal confession for the remission of sins.*<-

### CAPNIO <note>This is the persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'Q' with central flower and symmetrical scrollwork.</image-desc>
SINCE the Lord instituted not only baptism but also the sacrament of penance for the remission of sins (and rightly so: for since baptism can be received only once, it was necessary for penance to be instituted so that the sacrament of penance might come to the aid of those who happen to sin after receiving baptism. For this reason, some have aptly said that penance is the "second plank after a shipwreck"), <note>A classic theological metaphor comparing baptism to the ship of salvation and penance to a plank one grabs after falling overboard into sin.</note> therefore, since enough has been said regarding baptism, something must now be said from the Hebrew scriptures regarding the sacrament of penance, which the Messiah was meant to institute through vocal confession for the remission of sins. <margin>GALATINUS</margin> Because we have already said enough (as I judge) in the eighth book regarding the penance which the Messiah was to preach through himself and his disciples, and regarding its efficacy and power, it should now suffice to reveal those things from the writings of the Hebrews which pertain to vocal confession. Therefore, let what is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—be heard first: where, regarding Psalm 100, it is said exactly thus: <term>מזמור לתודה הריעו ליהוה כל הארץ</term> <note>original: "Mizmor l'todah hari'u l'Adonai kol ha'aretz"</note> This means: *A Psalm for confession. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.* <note>The Hebrew word "Todah" can mean both thanksgiving and confession.</note> The holy and blessed God said: "All nations shall confess to me, and I will receive them." Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 45: <term>כי לי תכרע כל ברך</term> <note>original: "Ki li tikhra kol berekh"</note> This means: *For every knee shall bow to me.* Another discourse—that is, another exposition: *A Psalm for confession.* This is what is written in Proverbs chapter 28: <term>מכסה פשעיו לא יצליח ומודה ועוזב ירוחם</term> <note>original: "Mikhaseh pasha'av lo yatzliach u-modeh v'ozev yerucham"</note> This means: *He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses and leaves them behind shall obtain mercy.* *He who conceals his crimes:* Such a one was Saul, to whom it was said in 1 Samuel 15: "What is this sound of sheep?" But he himself replied: "They brought them from Amalek." *But he who confesses and leaves them behind shall obtain mercy:* Such a one was David, of whom it was said in 2 Samuel chapter 12: *And David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the Lord." And Nathan said to David, "The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die."* This concludes the tradition, from which an argument is drawn regarding the efficacy of confession. For this, it should also be noted what is said in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>Likely referring to Bereshit Rabbah, a major midrashic collection on Genesis.</note>—that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis—regarding what is said in the forty-ninth chapter of that same book: <term>יהודה אתה יודוך אחיך</term> <note>original: "Yehudah attah yodukha akhekha"</note> that is: *Judah, your brothers shall confess [or praise] you.* For there it is said: This is the confession of which it was spoken by the Holy Spirit 

<column-break/>

<page-num>538</page-num>
<header>BOOK TEN.</header>

<margin>A</margin> through the hands of Job, chapter 15: <term>אשר חכמים יגידו ולא כחדו מאבותם</term> <note>original: "Asher chakhamim yaggidu v'lo kichedu me-avotam"</note> This means: *Because they are wise, they confess (or indicate) and do not hide from their fathers*—namely, their sins. Regarding whom this was said: regarding the just, who conquer or subdue their <term>fomes</term> <note>Literally "tinder"—a theological term for the internal inclination toward sin.</note> or sensuality, and confess their acts to their fathers. For everyone who confesses his acts is worthy of the world to come. Just as it is said in Psalm 50: <term>זובח תודה יכבדנני ושם דרך אראנו בישע אלהים</term> <note>original: "Zoveach todah yekhabdan'ni v'sam derekh ar'ennu b'yesha Elohim"</note> that is: *He who sacrifices confession shall honor me, and to him who sets a way, I will show the salvation of God.* 
<margin>B</margin> And thus you find it in Judah. For in the hour when the matter of Tamar reached him, he confessed, just as it is said in Genesis chapter 38: <term>הכר נא את בוראך ואל תכחד ממני</term> <note>The text provides a midrashic variation of Genesis 38:25</note> This means: *Acknowledge, I pray, your Creator, and do not be ashamed before flesh and blood*—that is, before man. Immediately, therefore, he conquered his sensuality or his affection, and he confessed. 
<margin>C</margin> Moreover, the holy and blessed God curses everyone who does not confess his works. For so we find in Cain, who denied it and said in Genesis chapter 4: *Am I my brother's keeper?* Therefore he was cursed. As it is said in the same place: *And now you are cursed.* And so forth. But when he recognized that he had sinned, he sought pardon from the holy and blessed God, and said: "Lord of the whole world, my sin is great, even so much that it 
<margin>D</margin> cannot be borne or tolerated. Great, I say, is my sin, more than that of the six hundred thousand who will sin before you." <note>A reference to the number of Israelites at the Exodus; Cain argues his singular sin is heavier than all theirs combined.</note> Exodus chapter 34. "And when they shall say to you, 'Take away sin,' immediately you will be the one who absolves." Directly following this, He whose name be blessed forever said: "If I do not absolve Cain, I shall close the door to all who repent." and because he did not perform perfect penance, He spared him by half. And from where is this held? From that which is said in Genesis chapter four: *You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.* But after he performed penance, it says: *And he dwelt in the land of Nod*—that is, of commotion. And 
<margin>E</margin> regarding him, Solomon says in Proverbs chapter 28: *He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper. But he who confesses and leaves them behind shall obtain mercy.* Thus far the tradition. In addition to this, that confession must be made to another man, and not to God alone who knows all things, that which is read in the Jerusalem *Sanhedrin* <note>The Jerusalem Talmud's volume on the high court.</note> in the chapter beginning <term>נגמר הדין</term> (*Nigmar haddin*), that is, *The Verdict is Finished*, is most relevant to our purpose: "Everyone who confesses has a portion in the world to come." 
<margin>F</margin> For so we find in the case of Achan, that Joshua said to him: *My son, give, I beseech you, honor to the Lord God of Israel, and give confession, and tell me, I pray, what you have done; do not hide it from me.* And Achan replied to Joshua and said: *Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and thus and so have I done.* And from where is it held that his sin was forgiven? From that which is said in the same place—namely, Joshua chapter 7: *And Joshua said: As you have troubled us, so the Lord troubles you this day.* "In this day" (he says) "you are troubled, 
<margin>G</margin> but you shall not be troubled in the future [world]." All this is tradition. Furthermore, that all sins and all circumstances aggravating a sin ought to be told in confession is not only held from the aforementioned confession of Achan, but also from that which...

BOOK TEN.

<margin>A</margin> This is written in the book *Yoma*, that is, *Days*, at the beginning of the chapter *Yom Ha-Kippurim*, that is, *The Day of Atonement*: Rabbi Huna said, "Whoever has committed a transgression is required to express the sin specifically." This is just as it was said in the 32nd chapter of Exodus: *And they made for themselves gods of gold*, along with the rest of the passage. <note>original: "Et fecerunt sibi deos ex auro"</note> Furthermore, that this penance may be done at any time and is always accepted by God is found in *Midrash Tehillim*, that is, in the *Exposition of the Psalms*, regarding that verse of the 65th Psalm: <margin>B</margin> *To you silence is praise, O God in Zion; and to you shall the vow be performed.* <note>original: "לדומיה תהלה אלהים בציון ולך ישלם נדר"</note> For there we read: Rabbi Hanina the son of Papa asked Rabbi Samuel the son of Nachmani, "What is the meaning of <margin>C</margin> what is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: *You have covered yourself with a cloud, so that prayer should not pass through*?" He replied to him, "Because the gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes closed. But the gates of repentance are never closed in this world." As it is said in the 65th Psalm: *The hope of all the ends of the earth, and of the sea afar off*; this refers specifically to repentance. For just as this sea is never closed, but whoever wishes to wash himself there may do so at any hour he desires, so too with repentance: at whatever hour a person wishes to perform it, he may do so, and God, holy and blessed is He, receives it. <margin>D</margin> Prayer, however, has set times. As it is said in Psalm 69: *But as for me, my prayer is to You, O God, in an acceptable time.* This is the tradition, from all of which our proposition is clear.

### CHAPTER IV.

->That the Messiah was to institute a new sacrifice, in which <margin>E</margin> he himself was to be the bread and the food.<-

### CAPNIO <note>The scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial D featuring floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

HAVING spoken of baptism and of penance regarding vocal confession, we must now speak of the sacrament of the Eucharist. This is the sacrament which the Messiah was to institute in bread and wine, <margin>F</margin> transubstantiating the bread into his body and the wine into his blood by divine power. Therefore, it must first be proven through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was to institute a new sacrifice, of which he himself should be the bread and food. GALATINUS: First, then, it should not be overlooked that Psalm 72, which begins *Give the King Your judgment, O God*, is understood by the ancient Jewish doctors to speak entirely of the Messiah. This is shown most clearly in what is read in *Midrash Tehillim*, that is, in the *Exposition of the Psalms*, regarding the title of that same Psalm, which is *To Solomon* (L’Shlomo), that is, to the Peaceful One. For it is said there: "This is <margin>G</margin> the King Messiah, of whom it was said in Isaiah, namely in the 11th chapter: *There shall come forth*

<column-break/>

*a shoot from the stump of Jesse.*" <note>original: "Egre-dietur virgultum de stipite Issai"</note> Although Rabbi Solomon <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> attempts to interpret this Psalm as referring to King Solomon—whence he explains those words of the same Psalm, *In his days shall the righteous flourish, and abundance of peace until the moon be no more*, by saying "In his days, that is, in the days of Solomon, the righteous shall be multiplied, and there shall be abundance of peace until the end of the world"—nevertheless, when he reached that passage where our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> has *There shall be a firmament on the earth on the tops of the mountains*, while the Hebrew truth has *Yehi pissath bar*, that is, *There shall be a cake of corn* or *a piece of grain in the earth on the top of the mountains*, he was unable to remain entirely silent about the truth. Against his own position, he brought forth these words: "Our masters have explained this to be a type of fine cake in the days of the Messiah, and they have explained the whole Psalm as referring to the King Messiah." Thus says he. Moreover, how and in what manner the Messiah was to be *pissath bar*, that is, a cake of grain, according to the exposition of the wise Jewish Masters, is found in the book which is called *Siphre* among them. There, regarding that which is said in the 32nd chapter of Deuteronomy, *The Lord alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him*, it is said as follows: "Another interpretation: The holy and blessed God said, 'It is to come to pass that I will seat you in the tranquility of the spirit in this world.' And there shall be no strange god with him. For there will be no sons of Adam among you engaged in any commerce, just as it was said in Psalm 72: *There shall be a cake of grain in the earth, on the top of the mountains.* For in the days of the Messiah, the grain shall produce *gheluscaoth*, that is, fine cakes, as large as the fullness of the palm of the hand." It follows: *His fruit shall shake like Lebanon*, which means that the grains shall rub against each other and drop their fine flour onto the earth. And you, coming there, shall take from it a handful, the size of a *pissath*, that is, a small round cake the size of the palm of the hand, according to your refreshment or provision. So it is written there. This same thing is found in the book *Ketuboth*, that is, *Marriage Contracts*, in the chapter beginning *Sene daliane*, that is, *Two Judges*, where it is read word for word: "Rabbi Ira said, 'It is to come to pass that the land of Israel shall produce cakes and ornaments of purple.' As it is said: *There shall be a cake of grain in the earth.*" And note that in the language of the Romans, a thin and spread-out cake is called *pissa*. <note>The author is making a linguistic connection between the Hebrew 'pissath' and the word for a flat bread or 'pizza/placenta'.</note> The Masters read regarding that verse of the Psalm, *There shall be pissath bar*, that is, a cake or piece of grain in the earth. And they said: "It is to come to pass that the wheat shall grow as tall as a palm tree and shall ascend like a palm," according to that verse: *There shall be a cake of grain in the earth.* But perhaps you will say, "What labor will there be in gathering it?" He teaches what should be said to this in what follows: *The fruit thereof shall tremble, or be moved, like Lebanon.* For God, holy—

But this is not Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel, but rather Rabbi Aquila, or <margin>E</margin> Rabbi Joseph the Blind. For Rabbi Jonathan himself (as you know) interpreted this place exactly as I cited it. Although his interpretation of the Psalter is very rare, it must not be denied, since it is cited everywhere not only by our people but by the Hebrews themselves. For in the *Sefer Hibbukim* <note>original: "besepber bibukim," likely a "Book of Collections" or anthologies</note>, mention of it is frequently made. <margin>F</margin> Whence in that same book, regarding this place, it is said: "The Aramaic translation says, namely that of Rabbi Jonathan, *And there shall be a sacrifice of bread in the earth at the head of the mountains of the Church.* Let him who has eyes see that, as it has been said, this is the Messiah of whom the whole Psalm speaks. When he says, therefore, *There shall be a cake of wheat in the earth at the head of the mountains*, he means to say that <margin>G</margin> a cake of bread shall become a sacrifice in the hands of the priests <note>original: "capitibus sacerdotum," literally "heads of the priests"</note> who are in the Church." Thus it is written there. I believe these things are sufficient against the stubbornness of the Jews and those who support them. What then is more rightly designated by the "mountains of the Church" in the aforementioned Targum of Rabbi Jonathan...

...than the prelates and priests of the Church itself? <margin>A</margin> In whom this scripture is certainly fulfilled and verified when they elevate the body of Christ above their heads. Nor should we wonder at the ancient wise men of the Jews who, explaining the aforementioned authority in the way described, said that the Messiah would be a cake of wheat or a piece of bread. For what better thing could they have said, to whom the truth of the matter had not yet been fully revealed? That the sacrifice of the Messiah's body was meant to be our food is found in the <margin>B</margin> exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne</note>. As it is said in the first chapter of Malachi: *I have loved you, says God.* And, *I will be to them as those who lift the yoke.* Because I have lifted their tribulations above them. Why all this? On account of their jaws, that is, on account of the word which they sent out from <margin>D</margin> their throats or their jaws, saying in the twentieth chapter of the second book of Kings: *We have no part in David.* And *I will incline food to him*, that is, I will submit to him food that is good, sweet, and great, to which no other is similar. Regarding which it is said in the seventy-second Psalm: *And there shall be a cake of wheat, or a piece of bread, in the earth.*" All this is tradition. Since, therefore, it has been proved according to the exposition of the ancients and the edition of Rabbi Jonathan that the Messiah was to be this cake of wheat <margin>E</margin> on the earth, and a sacrifice of bread at the head of the mountains of the Church, it clearly follows that the Messiah himself was destined to be this sweetest food, inclined and submitted by God, to which no other can be similar. And note his secrets of this kind, and do not depart from them. And he himself will receive the beauty unto himself when it shall be pleasing to him. Just as you will understand from the blessing of the priests: *The Lord will lift up his countenance to you.* And if you understand this well, you will also understand what was said above." Thus far the Rabbi. Where "beauty descending from the heavens to the earth" <margin>G</margin> signified the Messiah, the true Son of God, who was to be the heavenly bread, of which the heavenly manna was a figure. All these things agree perfectly with that saying of our Lord Jesus Christ: *I am the living bread, who came down from heaven. If anyone...*

## CHAPTER VI.

### *That this sacrifice was to be instituted not by bread alone, but also by wine, through which all sacrifices of the old law ought to cease.*

->CAPNIO.<-

<margin>B</margin>The sacrifice which Christ instituted, he did not establish with bread alone, but with bread and wine, and commanded it to be done so. For a greater expression of this universal <note>original: "catholicæ"</note> truth, it must also be proved through the sayings of the ancient Jews that this new sacrifice, which the Messiah was to institute, was to be established by him with bread and wine together. GALATINUS. This is clearly shown in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his Midrashic compilations</note>, when commenting on the statement in the 14th chapter of the same book, <margin>C</margin> *And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine* <note>original Hebrew: "ומלכי צדק מלך שלם הוציא לחם ויין"</note>. It is said there: "This Melchizedek was Shem, the son of Noah." And what does it teach us to say when it says, "He brought out, or produced, bread and wine"? Rabbi Samuel son of Nahman said: "He handed over the decrees of the priesthood." For he himself was sacrificing bread and wine to the holy and blessed God. As it is said in the same place: *And he was the priest of the Most High God.* For a place sometimes justifies its inhabitants. Another discourse, that is, another <margin>D</margin> exposition: "He produced bread"—this is the Bread of the Presence <note>original: "panis facierum," also known as the Shewbread</note>, that is, of the proposition. "And wine"—namely, of the libations. For the Masters said: "That he revealed the law to him," which says in the ninth chapter of Proverbs <note>The text says "nineteenth," likely a scribal error for Proverbs 9:5</note>, *Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mixed for you* <note>original Hebrew: "לכו לחמו בלחמי ושתו ביין מסכתי"</note>. These are the words of that Rabbi Moses Hadarsan. Who also immediately adds in the same place, <margin>E</margin> "Another matter: Melchizedek... I have blessed you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the word of Melchizedek, King of Salem." <note>original Hebrew provided: "דבר אחר מלכי צדק ברכתיך נשבע יהוה ולא ינחם אתה כהן לעולם על דברתי מלכי צדק מלך שלם..."</note> And who is this King of Righteousness <note>original: "mely chzedek"</note>? This is the righteous and savior, the King Messiah: as was said in the 9th chapter of Zechariah, *Behold your King comes to you, righteous and a savior.* And what does it teach us to say when it says, "he offered bread and wine"? This is as if it said what is written in Psalm 72: *And there shall be a cake of wheat in the earth.* And this is what was said: *And he was the priest of the Most High God.* Furthermore, that by this sacrifice all sacrifices of the ancient law were to cease, while this one itself would never fail, is held from what is read <margin>G</margin> upon that which is said in the 28th chapter of Numbers: *Command the children of Israel and say to them: My offering, my bread for my fires of the odor of my sweetness you shall observe to offer to me in its time* <note>original Hebrew: "צו את בני ישראל ואמרת אליהם את קרבני לחמי לאשי ריח ניחוחי תשמרו להקריב לי במועדו"</note>. That is, "Behold the oblation of my pa-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>-n-is [bread] <note>the word "panis" is broken across the column</note> for my fires, of the odor of my sweetness, you shall look to, that you may offer it to me in its time." And below: "And you shall say to them: The sacrifices which you ought to offer, the Lamb and the rest." For there it is said: Rabbi Pinhas son of Yair said: "In the time of the Messiah all sacrifices will cease, and the sacrifice of bread and wine will never cease." As it was said in Genesis 14: *And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine.* Melchizedek, that is, the King Messiah. Moreover, he is called <margin>C</margin> *Malki* [My King], because he is King of the whole world; and *Tzedek* [Righteousness], because he will send his righteousness and grace over the entire world. As it is said in Psalm 85: *Truth shall spring out of the earth, and righteousness shall look down from heaven*, or be looked upon, or appear. "King of Salem," this is the Jerusalem from above, he brought out bread and wine: that is, He will separate from the cessation of sacrifices the sacrifice of bread and wine, as it was said in the one hundred and tenth Psalm: *You are a priest forever according to the word of Melchizedek.* Our edition says, "Melchizedek bringing forth bread and wine." Therefore he brought it out (which <margin>D</margin> is the same as carrying it out) Melchizedek bread and wine, and did not "except" it, as that Rabbi says. GALATINUS. Our edition would indeed be correct if it said "he brought out" or "produced." But this Rabbi, in order to declare the sacrifice of bread and wine as excepted from the other kinds of sacrifices which were to cease, therefore said "excepted." Wherefore it is established that he also spoke correctly. Likewise upon the same text of Numbers <margin>E</margin> chapter 28, *Command the children of Israel*, etc.: Rabbi Yohai <note>likely referring to Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note> says thus: "In the time of the Messiah all sacrifices will fail, but the sacrifice of bread and wine will never fail." Regarding the sacrifice of wine: as it is written in the forty-ninth chapter of Genesis, <margin>F</margin> *Binding his foal to the vine* <note>original Hebrew: "אסרי לגפן עירה"</note>. This is: "Binding to the vine his city," that is, his body. For the body is the city of the soul. Likewise it is written elsewhere, namely in the 9th chapter of Judges: *Can I leave my wine, which cheers God and men?* <note>original Hebrew: "החלתי את תירשי המשמח אלהים ואנשים"</note> And if it indeed cheers men, in what way does it bring joy to God? <margin>G</margin> In the sacrifice which shall be made of it. That the sacrifice of bread indeed will never fail appears from what was said in Psalm 72: *And there shall be a cake of wheat in the earth, on the tops of the mountains.* All these things were said by that Rabbi Yohai, who preceded Christ by many years.

## CHAPTER VII.

### *That the Messiah in this sacrifice was going to transubstantiate bread into his body, and wine into his blood.*

->CAPNIO.<-

The universal <note>original: "catholica"</note> faith firmly confesses and holds that in this sacrifice, the bread is really transubstantiated into the true body of Christ, and the wine into his true blood, by divine power. Therefore, I would like to know whether it can be proved through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the bread was truly and really to be transubstantiated into the Body of the Messiah, and the wine into his blood, in this very same sacrifice. GALATINUS. It certainly can. For concerning the conversion of bread into the flesh of the Messiah himself...

<margin>A</margin>
...of the true God is found in the Commentaries of Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne, famous for his Midrashic compilations.</note> on that verse of Psalm 136: *Who gives bread or food to all flesh.* <note>original Hebrew: "הנותן לחם לכל בשר"</note> Where it is said: "It is further said, etc. It is known that He gave to all flesh. This is what they say: 'Taste and see that the Lord is good.' He gave to everyone, and that is His flesh; and He tasted the bread that returns to the guardian; and this is what it said: 'And see that the Lord is good,' and this will be a great wonder." <note>original Hebrew: "עוד נאמר וכו' יודע נתן לכל בשר היה הוא דאמרי טעמו וראו כי ח טוב נתנו לכל והוא בשרו וטעמו לחם שב לשמר וזהו שאמר וראו כי טוב יהוה והיה עלא גדול"</note>
Furthermore, a well-known word was spoken: *Who gives bread to all flesh.* This is what was said in Psalm 34: *Taste and see, because God is good.* Because the bread that He gives to all is His very flesh.
<margin>B</margin>
And while the bread is tasted, it is converted into flesh. And this is what was said: *And see, because God is good.* And this will be a great wonder. These few words, if well examined, are understood as the conversion of bread into the body of the Messiah. But concerning His blood, which is sacrificed daily on the altar—invisible to us, that is, hidden under the appearance of wine, but visible to God alone—it is written in the book *Mechilta* <note>A legal and homiletic commentary on the Book of Exodus.</note> as follows: *And in the blood of the innocent you acted impiously.* <note>original Hebrew: "ודם נקי תרשיעו"</note> 
<margin>C</margin>
This is what was said: *And I will see the blood* <note>Exodus 12:13</note>, which will be seen by me and not by others—the words of Rabbi Ishmael. And next to this is: *And the blood shall be a sign for you.* A sign, I say, for you, but it shall not be a sign for others. <note>original Hebrew: "זה הוא שאמר וראיתי את הדם וקראה לי ולא לאחרים דברי רבי ישמעאל וסמיך ליה והיה הדם לכם לאות לאות לכם ולא לאחרים לאות"</note> CAPNIO. I would like you to show more clearly from their writings this conversion from both species into the body and blood of the Messiah. GALATINUS. Rabbi Cahana clearly declares this regarding both species in his commentary on Genesis 49: *Binding his foal to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes.* <note>original Hebrew: "אסרי לגפן עירה ולשרקה בני אתנו כבס ביין לבשו ובדם ענבים סותה"</note> This means: Binding his city to the vine, and his donkey to the branch, O my son. He will wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are redder than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk. 
Where Rabbi Cahana says: These words, *Binding his city to the vine,* show that the sacrifice made from wine will not only be transmuted into the substance of the blood of the Messiah, but will also be converted into the substance of His body. Those words, *And to the branch, O my son, his donkey,* signify that the divinity and the Son of God will be united to the "donkey," that is, to his matter. For <term>hamor</term> <note>Hebrew for donkey.</note> is interpreted as material matter. Just as the donkey carries burdens and the clothes of travelers, so the King Messiah will carry the sins of the whole world upon Himself, according to Isaiah 53: *And God made the sin of us all to meet in him.* When it is said, *He will wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape,* the same meaning is expressed in different words; for "garment" refers to matter. Just as it is said in Job 10: *You have clothed me with skin and flesh.* <note>original Hebrew: "עור ובשר תלבישני"</note> And *in the blood of the grape his cloak,* that is, His divinity. Because just as a cloak surrounds the whole man, so God fills the whole world. *His eyes are redder than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk:* This means: In the sacrifice made from bread, notwithstanding that it is white like milk, the substance will be converted into the substance of the body of the Messiah, and there will be in that same sacrifice the red substance of the blood of the Messiah, like

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
wine. Likewise, in the sacrifice of wine, there will be the blood and the flesh of the Messiah, and the same will be in the bread: because the body of the Messiah cannot be divided. And reason demands this. For if the flesh and blood were divided, they would be distinguished from one another. But the body of the Messiah cannot be divided: as it is written in Exodus 12: *And you shall not break a bone in it.* <note>original Hebrew: "ועצם לא תשברו בו"</note> Furthermore, flesh without blood, and vice versa, are dead things; but the body of the Messiah, because it will be glorified after the resurrection, 
<margin>B</margin>
will live forever. As for what he says—that the body of the Messiah will be always living after the resurrection—this is because (as was proved more extensively above) the ancient Hebrews say that one of the names of the Messiah is David; and he proves this especially by the testimony of Jeremiah, in the thirtieth chapter, who speaks thus: 
<margin>C</margin>
*And they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will raise up for them.* <note>original Hebrew: "ועבדו את יהוה אלהיהם ואת דוד מלכם אשר אקים להם"</note> Therefore, because he says "I will raise up," which is in the future tense, they say these words of Jeremiah must be understood not as the David who preceded him by a long time, but as the Messiah. Wherefore Rabbi Jonathan also translated them thus into the Chaldean language <note>The Targum, or Aramaic translation.</note>: *And they shall serve before the Lord their God, and they shall obey the Messiah the son of David their King.* <note>original Aramaic: "ויפלחון קדם יהוה אלההון וישתמעון למשיחא בר דוד מלכהון"</note>
<margin>D</margin>
For that reason they asserted that one of the names of the Messiah would be David. Wherefore Rabbi Cahana rightly said: From this comes that secret, *David the King of Israel lives forever.* 
CAPNIO. Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note> renders the aforementioned words from Genesis 49 quite differently. For it says: *Binding his foal to the vineyard, and his ass, O my son, to the vine. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape.*
<margin>E</margin>
*His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.* From which it is clear that where Rabbi Cahana says "his city," our text has "his foal." And where he says "His eyes are redder than wine," we have "His eyes are more beautiful than wine." Where you translated "his donkey" <note>masculine *asinum*</note>, our text has "his she-ass" <note>feminine *asinam*</note>. From where does this discordance arise? 
GALATINUS. Certainly from the ambiguity of the words. For that which the author of our edition translated as "his foal," is written as <term>iro</term> <note>עירה</note> in Hebrew. 
<margin>F</margin>
This word among the Hebrews signifies both "city" and "foal," depending on the variety of the points <note>The Hebrew vowel system.</note>. For if it is pointed with a single point called <term>hirik</term>, thus <term>iro</term> <note>עִירָה</note>, it sounds the same as "his city" among us; but if it is pointed with two points, namely <term>patha</term> and <term>sheva</term>, in this manner <term>yairo</term> <note>עַיְרֹה</note>, it signifies among them what "his foal" signifies among us. Although before the scripture was pointed, this word could have been read in both ways, 
<margin>G</margin>
namely *iro* and *airo*, nevertheless now it ought to be read not as *airo* but as *iro*, for so it has been pointed. Therefore the author of our edition should have translated it as "his city" and not "his foal." That also...

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the fact that our letters say "more beautiful," he says: in Hebrew it is written <term>חכלילי</term> (*hachlili*), which is ambiguous, meaning both "red" and "beautiful." <note>This refers to Genesis 49:12, describing the eyes of the tribe of Judah.</note> Here, however, it more closely matches the literal text and the truth to say "redder" rather than "more beautiful." Finally, that our text has "his she-ass," while I have translated it as "his donkey," is because <term>חמור</term> (*hamor*), meaning "donkey" among the Hebrews, is of common gender. Therefore, among them, it signifies both a male and a female donkey. <margin>H o G.</margin> Also, that text which the same Rabbi Cahana cited to prove that the body of the Messiah cannot be divided, taken from Exodus, saying, "And you shall not break the substance in it": in our version, it says "bone" and not "substance." For it says, "Nor shall you break a bone of it." <note>Exodus 12:46, regarding the Passover Lamb.</note> GAL. There the Hebrew truth uses the word <term>עצם</term> (*etsem*), which signifies both "substance" and "bone." <note>In Hebrew, *etsem* literally means bone, but idiomatically refers to the "self-same" or "essence" of a thing.</note> The author of our edition, referring it to the paschal lamb (none of whose bones were to be broken), translated it as "bone" and not "substance." But Rabbi Cahana referred that same thing to the body of the Messiah, for which that lamb was a figure. For that reason, he translated it as "substance" and not "bone." <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it is manifest that both spoke the truth: since one spoke of the figure, and the other spoke of the reality represented by the figure. I think it also worth adding a most noteworthy point: what Rabbi Iohai says regarding the text written in the 28th chapter of Numbers, "My offering, my bread," and so forth. He says: "My offering, my bread, you shall look to the fires of my sweet savor to offer to me in its time," that is, in the time of the Messiah. And you shall say to them: "The sacrifices which you ought to offer." <margin>D</margin> "A lamb," with the rest. This is the sacrifice which you perform in the present. But this will be the "Bread of Two Faces," about which it is written in the 25th chapter of Exodus: <term>לחם פנים לפני תמיד</term> (*lechem panim liphnai tamid*), which means "The Bread of the Presence [or Faces] before me always." <note>Commonly known as the Showbread in the Tabernacle.</note> As for why it is called "Bread of Faces," the reason is that, as Rabbi Judas says, it will be transformed from the substance of bread, when it is sacrificed, into the substance of the body of the Messiah, who will descend from the heavens. And he himself will be the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "You shall look to offering to me," that is, to my being offered. And it will be invisible and impalpable. The "Seat of Elijah" provides proof of this matter. And the masters say it is called "Bread of Faces" because in the sacrifice itself there will be two substances: divinity and humanity. Thus says that Rabbi, who lived many years before Christ. <margin>H o G.</margin> How is the saying of Rabbi Judas understood, when he said that the Seat of Elijah bears witness to this matter—to prove that the body of the Messiah in the sacrifice itself would be invisible and impalpable? GAL. The Hebrew doctors report that God gave this prerogative to Elijah: that no circumcision should ever occur without his presence. For this reason, the Masters themselves established that whenever a circumcision was to be performed, two very ornate seats should always be prepared. One in which he who was to circumcise the infant would sit. The other, in which no one could sit, but would remain empty, because they said Elijah would come to sit in it. Therefore, for that reason, Rabbi Judas said that the Seat of Elijah provides proof for the body of the Messiah being invisible and impalpable in the future sacrifice of bread and wine. He said this so that the more recent Jews—whose treachery he foresaw—would not claim the body of the Messiah is not in this sacrifice because it is neither seen nor felt there: since they believe and confess that Elijah

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is invisible and impalpable in that seat, and also that he can exist in many places at the same hour. <margin>H o G.</margin> That which Rabbi Iohai above called "Bread of Faces," we call "Bread of Proposition." For so our edition names it. How, then, should it be said: "Bread of Faces" or "Bread of Proposition"? GAL. Without a doubt, it should be called "Bread of Faces" and not "Proposition," as the text of the Hebrew truth makes manifest. For in this way it better serves the purpose of our faith, as is clearly evident from the words of the aforementioned ancient Jews. It can also be said that our people did not call it "Bread of Proposition" without reason: because the Lord commanded it to be "proposed" [set forth] upon the table of the tabernacle before the Holy of Holies.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*How great the future efficacy of this sacrifice would be, how great the dignity of the priests handling it, and what kind of life they should lead.*<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>C</margin> You have indeed brought forth many and wonderful things from the scriptures of the Hebrews concerning the mysteries of this ineffable sacrifice. It remains for you to now reveal what their ancient ones thought regarding its efficacy. <margin>D</margin> GAL. They thought truly marvelous things. For among the other signs and figures of this unspeakable sacrament handed down to the Hebrew fathers, that which is read in the Chaldean interpreter <note>The Targum, or Aramaic translation/paraphrase.</note> of the most holy book of Job—whoever he may have been—is not to be counted among the least of signs and figures, concerning its wonderful conversion and efficacy. For it is said there: <margin>E</margin> <term>The three companions of Job perceived all the evil that had come upon him. When they saw the trees in their gardens had withered, and saw the bread by which they were sustained turned into living flesh, and the wine which they were about to drink turned into blood.</term> <note>original Aramaic: "ושמעו תלתא חברי איוב..."</note> And they each departed from their place. And by the merit of this thing they were delivered from descending into the place that was appointed for them in hell. Eliphaz of the region of Teman (which, as many agree, is an island in the Arabian Gulf), Bildad from the province of Shuah (which they believe to be part of Upper Egypt), Zophar from the region of Naamah (that is the land of Judea, which they call the land of promise). And they gathered together as one to come to him, namely Job, to comfort him. Thus it is said there. <margin>F</margin> When it is said, "And by the merit of this thing they were liberated from the place of hell," the efficacy of this sacred mystery is openly suggested, by which those using it were to be liberated from eternal death. One must also not overlook in this place what that <margin>G</margin> ancient doctor of theirs, whom they call <term>Our Holy Rabbi</term> <note>original Hebrew: "רבינו הקדוש" (*Rabbeinu HaKadosh*), usually referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into the Hebrew roots of Christian sacraments, specifically the Eucharist. It transitions from discussing the indivisibility of the Messiah's body to an account of a vision regarding the future sacrifice of bread and wine that will replace all ancient rituals.</meta>

# BOOK TEN

<margin>A</margin> They call him *Rabbenu Haccados*, that is, "Our Holy Master" <note>This refers to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah</note>; he relates in the book which they call <term>Gale razeia</term> <note>original: *Gale razeia*, meaning "Revealer of Secrets"</note>, that in responding to the fifth petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome, he said among other things that he found it written by Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai <note>Traditional author of the Zohar</note> in the book called <term>Mechkar hassodoth</term> <note>original: *Mechkar hassodoth*, meaning "Investigation of Secrets"</note>: That once, while the same Rabbi Simeon was praying in a double cave, he <margin>B</margin> saw Elijah appearing to him, dressed as a High Priest and performing a sacred rite, at which all were rejoicing. Finally, after many questions, Simeon asked: "That sacred rite which you were performing before God, the Holy and Blessed One—what was it?" Elijah answered him: "This is the sacrifice which the priests will perform before God, the Holy and Blessed One, after the Messiah has come. For then all the sacred rites that were done previously shall cease. Moreover, he shall perform that sacrifice from bread and wine." When <margin>C</margin> the priests first practice this, all the Angels of heaven, hearing those sacred and holy words coming forth from the mouths of the priests and understanding them, will wonder at them and tremble with extraordinary envy. All of them, being angry, will come to God, saying: "O Lord of the world, how great is this praise which You have given to Israel, who are full of sins, yet You have not given it to us, who are immune from sins before You?" God will answer them, saying: "There is no place for envy among you regarding Israel, since you yourselves have approached to pray for them. <margin>D</margin> Because they are sinners and prone to sinning, I have sent the Messiah to forgive them, and I have taught them this excellent praise. You, however, who cannot sin, do not need this kind of praise." Then the Angels, departing from their anger, shall say: "O Lord our God, how admirable is Your name in all the earth! For Your magnificence is elevated above the heavens." Then God will be filled with mercy, and by the immense power of the holy words that flowed from the mouth <margin>E</margin> of the priests, that sacrifice which shall be celebrated on every altar shall be converted into the **body of the Messiah**. Then, moreover, the Angels shall give forth the greatest praises with various instruments before God, the Holy and Blessed One, saying: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts. Heaven and earth are full of Your glory." CAP. Therefore, happy and blessed are the priests who perform this sacrifice for their God, and for that reason, they must be chaste and holy. CAL. They certainly must be: Just as it is written <margin>F</margin> in Leviticus, chapter 21: <note>original: *v’hai lehem eloheihem hem makrivim v’kodesh*</note> That is, "They shall offer the flesh of their God, and therefore they shall be holy." <note>The author is interpreting the Hebrew word *lehem* (bread/food) as "flesh" to support the doctrine of the Real Presence.</note> All these things are found there word for word.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What kind of angelic praise this was meant to be, which the Angels were to perform at the hour of the offering of this sacrifice, can be easily understood from the words of Rabbi Nehunia son of Hakana: when, in the epistle of secrets which he called <term>Ighereth hassodoth</term> <note>original: *Ighereth hassodoth*, meaning "Epistle of Secrets"</note>, he says: "I say that if any mortal could hear and perceive that song—so sweet and honey-flowing—which the Angels sing together, his soul would be separated from the powers of the <margin>B</margin> body, and being joined with that sweetness of song, it would depart." The Lord Himself suggests what the life of a priest handling this sacrifice ought to be, when He speaks both of the sacrifice of our time and of the quality of the one consecrating it in Leviticus, chapter 21: <note>original: *v’kiddashto ki et lehem eloheikha hu makriv kadosh yihyeh lakh ki kadosh ani Adonai mekaddishkhem*</note> that is, "And you shall sanctify him, because he himself is or shall be sacrificing the flesh of your God. He shall be holy to you, because I, the Lord who sanctifies you, am holy." <margin>C</margin> GAL. Here our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> has two significant corruptions. The first is that the first clause of this text is entirely missing, namely, "and you shall sanctify him"; this could be due to a scribe's error. The other is that in the second clause, the Hebrew truth holds it far differently. For where we have, "And he offers the bread of proposition"; in the Hebrew it is held: "Because he himself is or shall be sacrificing the flesh <margin>D</margin> of your God." This agrees more with the truth of our faith. I cannot ascribe this corruption to the author of our edition, since the cause of this error was nothing but the ambiguity of a word. For this Hebrew word <term>lehem</term> <note>original: *lehem*</note> has many meanings. For sometimes it signifies food, sometimes bread, and sometimes flesh. As Rabbi David Kimhi says in the book <term>Shorashim</term> <note>original: *Shorashim*, meaning "Roots," a famous Hebrew dictionary</note>, the meaning of this word *lehem* encompasses everything <margin>E</margin> edible. Sometimes, however, it is said of bread alone: as in that saying in Deuteronomy, chapter 8: "Man does not live by bread alone." <note>original: *lo al ha-lehem levado yihyeh ha-adam*</note> Sometimes, indeed, it refers to flesh alone, as in Numbers, chapter 28: "My sacrifice, my flesh for a fire-offering," or "for my fire." <note>original: *korbani lahmi l’ishai*</note> And so it is in Leviticus, chapter 21: "He is sacrificing the flesh of your God." <note>original: *lehem eloheikha hu makriv*</note> Thus also it is in Job, chapter 6: "They are like the sorrows of my flesh." <note>original: *hemmah k’davai lahmi*</note> <margin>F</margin> These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi. Therefore, where it should have been translated "the flesh of your God," the author of our edition translated it as "the bread of proposition."

<header>BOOK ELEVEN.</header>

# ON THE CESSATION OF THE ANCIENT LAW.

### CHAPTER ONE.

->*That upon the arrival of the law of the Messiah, the Mosaic law was to cease in all its ceremonial requirements.*<-

---

<margin>CAPNIO</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Historiated initial 'C' containing a figure of a man sitting at a desk with an open book, surrounded by a circular border and decorative foliage.</image-desc>
Since you have said much in the preceding pages—not only concerning baptism, through which circumcision was to be rendered void, and the sacrifice of bread and wine, through which all sacrifices of the old law were to fail, but also concerning the institution of the new divine law itself, which was to be established by the Messiah, and through which the entire ancient law was to fail in regards to its ceremonies—it is now necessary for you to prove from their own scriptures that the ancient law was to have an end in all its ceremonies upon the arrival of the Messiah’s law. This is required so that the stubborn persistence of the modern Jews may be more effectively refuted, as they assert that the old law is immutable and destined to last until the end of the world. Thus, it must be shown how it can be kept along with the law of the Messiah, not according to the letter, but according to the spiritual and mystical sense.

<margin>B</margin> Galatinus: That this was indeed to be so is shown most clearly in the *Midrash* <term>Koheleth</term> <note>original: *Midras Cobeleth*; a Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, in the exposition of the second chapter of the same book, on the verse: "I said in my heart, 'Come now, I will test you with joy and see the good.' And behold, this also is vanity" <note>Ecclesiastes 2:1; original Hebrew: אמרתי אני בלבי לכה נא אנסכה בשמחה וראה בטוב והנה גם הוא הבל</note>. For it is said there: "And see the good"—namely, the good of the law. "And behold, this also is vanity." Was it not necessary for the scripture to say, "And behold, this also is joy"? <margin>C</margin> Why, then, did it say, "Behold, this is vanity"? Rabbi <term>Hizkiya</term> said: "Because all the law which you learn in this world is <term>habelim</term> <note>original: הבלים; vanities or breaths</note>, that is, vanities in the presence of the law of the world to come." That this "law of the world to come" is the law of the Messiah, and the "days of the world to come" are his days, is clear from what is read in the same *Midrash* regarding that verse in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: "If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. And let him remember the days of darkness" <margin>D</margin> <note>Ecclesiastes 11:8; original Hebrew: אם שנים הרבה יחיה האדם בכלם ישמח ויזכר את ימי החשך</note>. For there these things are explained thus: "If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in all these; namely, in the joy of the law. And let him remember the days of darkness: These are the days of malice; and how many will they be? For whatever preceded will be *habel*, that is, vanity: for all the <term>Torah</term> <note>original: תורה; Law or Instruction</note> which a man learns in this age is vanity in the sight of the law of the Messiah." Thus far the tradition.

To this is very much in agreement what is written in the same *Midrash Koheleth* regarding that verse in the first chapter of the same book: "There is no remembrance of the former things, nor of the later things that are to come. That is, there will be no remembrance of them along with those things that will be at the end" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:11</note>. How many signs or miracles were performed for the children of Israel from the time they went out of Egypt, and even before they had gone out of Egypt? Of these it says: "There will be no remembrance of the former and the later things," and those which will be after the exit, namely from Egypt. For there will be no remembrance of them in comparison with those things which will be in the end, and with the signs or miracles of the world to come. Just as it is written in Jeremiah 23: "And they shall no longer say, 'As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of Egypt.' Rather, 'As the Lord lives, who brought up and who led the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the North, and from all the lands to which I drove them'" <note>Jeremiah 23:7-8; original Hebrew: ולא יאמרו עוד חי יהוה אשר העלה את בני ישראל מארץ מצרים : כי אם חי יהוה אשר העלה ואשר הביא את זרע בית ישראל מארץ צפונה ומכל הארצות אשר הדחתים</note>. Thus far the tradition. Moreover, the signs and miracles mentioned in this tradition are the miracles which were to take place in the time of the Messiah. For "the future age" or "the world to come" (as has been said many times) is understood in Hebrew literature to be the time of the Messiah. This is easily shown through the <term>Targum Jerusalem</term> <note>An Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible produced in Jerusalem</note>, which translated and explained the aforementioned words—"There will be no remembrance of the former things, nor of the later things that are to come"—in this way: "There will be no record of them <margin>E</margin> in the generations that will be in the days of the Messiah."

Hoogstraten: What is this *Targum Jerusalem*?

Galatinus: It is perhaps (as I myself think) that which is called by our people...
