A it is called the common edition: its author is unknown, though it is recognized that he held the manner of an expounder rather than a translator. To this same point (to return to our purpose), much is contributed by what is read in the book *Berachoth* <note>original: ברכות; "Blessings," a tractate of the Talmud</note>, that is, "Of Blessings," in the Jerusalem version, in the chapter beginning *Mai* <note>original: מאמתי; "From when," the opening word of the tractate</note>, where it is read:
Ben Zoma said, "In the future, Israel will not make mention of the departure from Egypt in the future age, nor B in the days of the Messiah." And what is the proof of this matter? Because it is written in Jeremiah, chapter 23: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says God. And they shall no longer say, 'As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'" with the rest. For the sages said, "Not that the name of Egypt should be uprooted from its place, but that the wonders which will happen in the days of the Kingdoms of the nations will be the *substance* <note>original: עיקר; *iccar*</note>, and Egypt will be *secondary* <note>original: טפלה; *taphla*, meaning an accompaniment or accidental detail</note>, because the wonders that were done in Egypt and in the departure from Egypt will behave as an accidental feature." And in this way it is said in Genesis 35: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be C your name." Explaining this, the Masters said, "Not that Jacob is uprooted from his place, but that Israel will be the substance, and Jacob an addition to it or an accident." And so Isaiah also says in the forty-third chapter: <note>original Hebrew: אל תזכרו ראשונות וקדמוניות אל תתבוננו:הנני עשה חדשה עתה תצמח הלא תדעוה</note>
That is: "Do not remember the former things, and do not look at the ancient things. Behold, I make a new thing. Now it shall spring forth. Shall you not know it?" "Do not remember (he says) the former things": these are the *Egyptian signs* <note>original: מצות; *mits-uon*, likely interpreted here by the author as 'signs' or 'commandments' related to Egypt</note>. "And do not care for the ancient things": these are the things D which were done after the departure from Egypt. "Behold, I make a new thing," and the rest. These things will concern Gog in the days of the Messiah. Thus far the tradition. Moreover, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explains it thus: "Do not remember the former things," that is, the signs and miracles which I remind you of and which I did in Egypt, do not remember them hereafter. But for that redemption you shall be diligent to confess and praise. It follows: "And do not care for the ancient things," that is, do not pay attention E nor set your heart to them. Thus far Rabbi Solomon. Almost the same thing that was said in the preceding tradition is also placed in the Babylonian book *Berachoth*, that is, "Of Blessings," at the end of the chapter *Meemathai korin* <note>original: מאמתי קורין; "From when do we read [the Shema]"</note>, where it is said: It is a tradition that Ben Zoma said to the sages, "And how will they remember the departure from Egypt in the days of the Messiah? Is it not already written in Jeremiah in the twenty-third chapter, 'Behold, the days are coming, says God, and they shall no longer say, As the Lord lives, who brought up F the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' along with the rest?" They answered him, "Not that the departure from Egypt is uprooted from its place, but because the event of the Kingdoms—that is, the signs that will happen in the times of the Kingdoms—will be the substance. And the departure from Egypt—that is, the signs of the departure from Egypt—will be an addition to it; that is, they will behave like an accident, which is present or absent without the destruction of the substance." And thus says Isaiah in the forty-third chapter, "Do not remember the former things," with the rest, as above. This is the tradition. G 
To this also very much pertains what the Lord commanded the Jews through Moses in Leviticus, chapter 26, saying: <note>original Hebrew: וישן מפני חדש תוציאו</note> that is, "And you shall exclude the old from the face of the new." Moreover, that this must be accepted in this sense

<column-break/>

is held from what is read in the book called *Siphre* <note>original: ספרי; *Sifre*, a halakhic midrash on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> upon that which was said in Leviticus, chapter 26: "And I will look toward you and make you fruitful, and I will multiply you, and I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall eat the old store, and you shall exclude or expel the old from the face of the new." For these things are explained there thus: "And I will look upon you for good, and I will make you fruitful through fleshly generation, and I will multiply you or make you grow through an upright stature. And I will establish my covenant with you: Not like the first covenant which you transgressed, as it is said in Jeremiah 31, 'That they themselves transgressed my covenant.' But a new covenant, which they shall not transgress thereafter. Of which it is said in Jeremiah, chapter 31: <note>original Hebrew: זכרתי את בית ישראל ואת בית יהודה ברית חדשה לא כברית אשר כרתי את אבתם ביום החזיקי בידם להוציאם מארץ מצרים</note> That is: 'And I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah: Not like the covenant which I struck with their fathers on the day in which I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.'" And therefore he says, "and you shall eat the old store, and you shall exclude the old from the face of the new." This is the tradition. 
Furthermore, that "covenant" in the aforementioned words is the same as the "Law" is clearly shown in the book *Mechilta* <note>original: מכילתא; an early Rabbinic commentary on Exodus</note>, where upon that which was said in Exodus, chapter 12, "In the tenth of this month," it is said: "There is no covenant except the Law." As it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 29: "These are the words of the covenant which God commanded Moses to strike with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he struck with them in Horeb." Likewise elsewhere, namely in Exodus, chapter 34: "And he wrote upon the tablets the ten words of the covenant." These things are in the same book, *Mechilta*. 
From the preceding tradition, therefore, it is clearly held that upon the arrival of the new law of the Messiah, the old law ought to cease. Moreover, in the book called *Irubin* <note>original: ערובין; *Eruvin*, a Talmudic tractate on Sabbath boundaries</note>, in the chapter that begins *Osin Pasin* <note>original: עושין פסין; "Making strips"</note>, it is read that Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: <note>original Hebrew: דכתיב ושמרת את המצות ואת החקים ואת המשפטים אשר אנכי מצוך היום לעשותם היום לעשותם ליתן שכרם היום</note> This is what is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 7: "And keep the commandment and the decrees and the judgments which I command you today to do them." "Today" (he says) "to do them," and not tomorrow to do them. This is the tradition. Therefore "today," that is, before the Messiah should come; and "not tomorrow," that is, not after he had already come, were the ceremonial precepts to be observed. 
From all these things it is quite clearly evident that upon the coming of the Messiah, who was to institute a new law, the old law was going to cease in all its ceremonies. Since, therefore, it has been most broadly proved in the preceding sections that the Messiah has already come, and that he was our Lord Jesus Christ—who did not cease to write the new law of the Gospel for nearly three and a half years by deeds and words in the hearts of believers, and especially of the Apostles and his disciples—and finally, having sent the Holy Spirit, he rendered whatever he had written in their hearts by teaching so firm that it could be deleted thence by no persecution and no forgetfulness: it is certain that what was prophesied long before through Jeremiah in the thirty-first chapter was then fulfilled...

# CHAPTER II.
### How and why Christ fulfilled the old law.
## CAPNIO.

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
The Jews oppose us in this matter in many ways, wishing to prove that the ancient law was by no means intended to cease upon the arrival of the Messiah. They argue that because we Christians say Christ our Lord was the Messiah, and yet he himself observed that entire law and led others to observe it by both word and deed. For he says in the fifth chapter of Matthew: "I have not come to abolish the law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them." And again, a little later: "Whoever," he says, "breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them, this person shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." Therefore, from the words and deeds (they say) of your Christ, whom you claim to be the Messiah, it is clearly evident that the Mosaic law has not ceased at all. Therefore, you ought not to say that it should have ceased upon his arrival. <margin>Response.</margin> **GALATINUS:** It is indeed true that Christ fulfilled the entire old law. However, they can by no means infer from this that it has not ceased in those parts where it was destined to cease.

<margin>What the old law contained.</margin>
So that it may become known to everyone how he fulfilled the law itself and the Prophets, it must be noted that five principal things were contained in that same law and the Prophets: namely, **Moral**, **Judicial**, **Ceremonial**, **Promises** (including warnings), and **Sacramental** matters. <margin>Moral laws.</margin> The **Moral** laws are indeed the Ten Commandments, without which salvation is impossible for adults. These are specifically contained in the twentieth chapter of Exodus, where it is said: <note>original: לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים...; Exodus 20:3-17</note> "You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy. Honor your father and your mother. You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor." These,

<column-break/>

however, were not meant to cease upon the arrival of the Messiah, but to be perfected. Therefore, our Savior, the true Messiah, in order to perfect them, forbade not only the act of murder and other evil deeds, but also the intent of the mind. "You have heard," he says in the 5th chapter of Matthew, "that it was said to the ancients: You shall not murder; and whoever murders shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment," along with the rest that follows. For that reason, he both observed them himself and led others to observe them; whence in the nineteenth chapter of Matthew, he says: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." <margin>Judicial laws.</margin> The **Judicial** laws are those such as are mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter of Deuteronomy: "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," and the rest. Since these were incomplete, being carried out with too much severity and without mercy, they were to be mitigated by the sweetness of mercy in the time of the Messiah. Therefore, they are now perfectly fulfilled when they are balanced and tempered with mercy, especially in the court of the Church. <margin>Ceremonial laws.</margin> The **Ceremonial** laws, however, were all those outward acts and things done concerning them, such as circumcision, new moons, <term>fringes</term> <note>original: fimbriæ; ritual tassels (tzitzit) worn on garments</note>, and <term>phylacteries</term> <note>original: phylacteria; small leather boxes containing scripture (tefillin) worn during prayer</note>, and many other things of that kind. Since these were "figures" <note>symbolic previews or types</note> of the things that were to be done in and by the Messiah, they were therefore destined to have an end when the Messiah arrived. Yet the Messiah himself, Jesus our Lord, perfectly fulfilled them: first by observing them according to the letter until the determined time of their cessation; then, through himself and his followers, by bringing them back to their spiritual and mystical meaning. <margin>Promises.</margin> The **Promises** were the coming of the Messiah, the promised land, the conversion of the Nations, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation. These our Savior also perfectly fulfilled by taking on flesh from a Virgin, being born, performing miracles possible only for God by his own power, suffering, dying, rising again, ascending to heaven in the sight of many, and by promising far better things than the old law promised. For that law promised its practitioners only temporal and earthly goods, which nevertheless designated spiritual and eternal things. But our Savior and Messiah promised his worshippers spiritual and eternal things, which that law prefigured. For he said in Matthew chapter 19: "Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold, and shall possess eternal life." And again in Luke 6: "Blessed are the poor," he says, "for yours is the kingdom of God." Therefore, as it is said in the fourth chapter of Matthew: "Jesus began to preach and to say, 'Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.'" <margin>Sacraments.</margin> Finally, the **Sacraments** <note>here used in the sense of holy signs/rituals</note> were the paschal lamb, the red heifer, and others of this kind: which were figures and shadows of the passion of Christ. Therefore, upon the arrival of him whose type they bore, they had to cease entirely. Christ himself fulfilled these by suffering and dying. To this the Evangelist testified when he said: "These things were done that the scripture might be fulfilled which says, 'You shall not break a bone of him.'" From these points, therefore, it is clear how and why Christ fulfilled the law and the Prophets. And as for the Prophets (as Chrysostom says), all the things they had foretold...

It categorizes the law into five parts—Moral, Judicial, Ceremonial, Promises, and Sacraments—detailing how each was completed through Jesus's life and teachings.</summary>

...as they had said, by completing it. Moreover, he fulfilled the Law by first transgressing nothing of the legal requirements, and finally by justifying through faith—something the Law itself was not able to do through the literal word. For this reason, he said, *I have not come to abolish the law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them.* From these points it is also clearly shown that even if Christ fulfilled the old law in the manner we have described, it does not follow that the Law did not cease in those matters which were destined to end upon his arrival.

### CHAPTER III.

#### Refutation of Jewish arguments. And that the Mosaic Law was changeable.

#### CAPNIO.

<margin>Arguments of the more recent Jews.</margin>
The more recent Jewish scholars, attempting to prove the permanence of their law, bring forward several arguments against us which you must resolve: so that their stubbornness may be more forcefully overcome, and the truth of the Catholic faith may shine more clearly. Thus, they argue first as follows: <margin>The first argument.</margin> As long as the cause of an effect remains, that effect continues; however, the cause of the Law always remains, therefore the entire Law will always endure. They prove that the cause of the Law remains in this way: the "final cause" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" is the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing.</note> of the whole Law is the intention of leading humans back to their proper perfection. This intention always remains. Therefore, the entire Law will always remain. <margin>Second argument.</margin> Next, they argue: The perfection of every power is its own proper action. Of human powers, some are bodily and others are intellectual. Therefore, human perfection consists in both bodily and intellectual action. The Law, being ordered toward human perfection, necessarily leads humans back to these two things. From this it follows that whatever the Law intends is directed toward the adornment of either the body or the soul. But the body is adorned by morals, while the soul is adorned by intelligence. The literal and "tropological" <note>Interpretive methods: tropological refers to moral meaning; allegorical to symbolic meaning; anagogical to spiritual or future meaning.</note> interpretations of the Law demonstrate the former, while the allegorical and "anagogical" understandings suggest the latter. Since a human being in this life always needs both the refinement of morals and the understanding of the intellect, the Law, which administers all these things, must necessarily remain forever. Finally, they argue: While the thing represented stands, the representation stands. This is proved because since the object of faith is uncreated truth (for nothing corruptible can be the perfection of an incorruptible power, such as the intellectual soul), if anything among the foundations of faith was created in symbols, it is believable precisely because it is led back to uncreated truth, <margin>Third argument.</margin> just as matter is led to form. Therefore, while the thing represented stands, the representation stands. But the thing represented is eternal, because it is eternal truth. Therefore, the representation is also eternal. Consequently, it follows that the Mosaic Law itself, which is full of such symbols, is eternal. From these points, they conclude that the old law remains stable forever regarding its ceremonial requirements. <margin>Refutation of the Jewish conclusion.</margin> GALATINUS: These arguments are certainly quite frivolous, and like the chaff of falsehood, they are to be burned by the fire of truth. First, I will show that their conclusion is entirely false. Then, I will respond to the arguments themselves. Thus, the conclusion—by which they assert the ancient law is binding forever in the same ritual manner—is defeated by this reason: Whatever is received by some-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> thing changeable can itself be changed. This is proven because everything that can be received is received according to the manner of the recipient. This can be judged in individual cases as well as in the powers of our own souls. The old law is of this kind, because it is received by man, whose nature is agitated by constant change; therefore, the Law itself can be changed. Just as a father raises his son with different rules when he is an infant, a boy, an adolescent, and a young man, so too is the human community led by one law <margin>B</margin> when it is wise and just, and by another when it is foolish. Now, the Jewish race was foolish and wicked when it was redeemed from Egyptian slavery by Moses. Mosaic scripture itself testifies to this many times. Whence many of the ceremonial precepts of the Law (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> testifies in the third treatise of his book called *The Guide* <note>The *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>) were required more by the dullness of that people and their wicked habit of idolatry than by their perfection. This is according to the saying of the Psalmist: *With bit and bridle bind their jaws, those who do not draw near to you.* <margin>C</margin> Therefore, because the dullness and wicked habits of the recipient have changed—as if moving past the age of infancy—the thing received, that is, the Law, has also happened to change. The Law, therefore, does not always bind in the same ritual manner. This is confirmed by the testimony of both the Law itself and the ancient Talmudists. For the Law itself did not bind anyone to its observation (except for the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>) except in the Promised Land, specifically while the Temple and the Jewish scepter held sway. <margin>D</margin> Outside the Promised Land, it was not binding at all. And the scripture itself clearly shows this, saying in Deuteronomy chapter 4:
> <note>original: ראה, למדתי אתכם חקים ומשפטים כאשר צוהני יהוה אלהי, לעשות כן בקרב הארץ אשר אתם באים שמה לרשתה: </note> See, I have taught you statutes and judgments as the Lord my God commanded me, to do so in the midst of the land which you are entering to possess.

And a little later it says:
> <note>original: ויגד לכם את בריתו אשר צוה אתכם לעשות עשרת הדברים ויכתבם על שני לוחות אבנים : ואתי צוה יהוה בעת ההוא ללמד אתכם חקים ומשפטים לעשותכם אתם בארץ אשר אתם עברים שמה לרשתה: </note> And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, the Ten Words <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, which he wrote on two tablets of stone. And the Lord commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and judgments, which you should perform in the land which you are crossing over to possess.

<margin>E</margin> Here, two things are very much to be noticed: First, that he called the Ten Precepts specifically "His covenant," the way the entire Law is also frequently called, <margin>F</margin> so that it might be known that the intention of the whole Law consists in and depends upon these ten precepts. The Jewish doctors suggest this more clearly, especially Rabbi Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), an influential Jewish philosopher.</note> in the book *Ha-Emunoth* <note>The *Sefer Ha-Emunot ve-ha-De'ot* (The Book of Beliefs and Opinions).</note>, that is, *Of Beliefs*. There he teaches that all the mandates of the Law are reduced into the ten precepts of the Decalogue. Second, it must be noticed that he commanded these "Ten Words" to be done simply, without adding any condition of place. And this was done <margin>G</margin> to show that they would never cease: since those ten precepts belong to natural law, and are the innate participation of the eternal law within us, which varies by neither place nor time. But speaking of the rest of the Law's mandates, he immediately added, saying: *Which you should perform in the land which you are entering to possess.* From this it is clearly evident that the Jews, outside of that land...

Galatinus refutes these by arguing that the Law's ceremonial aspects were temporary measures for a spiritually "infant" people and were geographically tied to the Land of Israel, whereas the Ten Commandments represent universal, eternal natural law.</summary>

# BOOK ELEVEN

<margin>The opinion of the Talmudists regarding the changeability of the law.</margin>

<margin>Response to the arguments.</margin>
**D** things, therefore, the conclusion of the Jews' falsehood concerning the perpetual obligation of legal observance is clearly evident. Now I come to their arguments. Although the solution to the reasons by which they strive to prove their conclusion can be easily established from what has already been said, let us nevertheless respond to them so that the falsity of those same reasons may appear more clearly. 

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**E** Therefore, when they argue first: "As long as the cause remains, the effect remains," this is granted regarding a cause which necessarily and by itself follows the effect. But then the "minor premise" must be denied: namely, that the cause of the <unclear>entire</unclear> law always remains, if one takes the whole for its individual parts. For although the most powerful intention of the law always remains, the intention of every single particle of the law does not. For there are many things in the law which are not necessitated by the end goal by themselves or by primary intention, but are either removing a prohibition or are for "well-being" <note>A philosophical term meaning something beneficial but not strictly essential for existence.</note>: such as sacrifices and very many ceremonial matters, as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian also shows in the third tractate of the book *More* <note>The *Moreh Nevukhim* or "Guide for the Perplexed".</note>. And according to the opinion of the Talmudists, such things are those which do not bind one to observance outside the promised land; which could not happen if they pertained to human 

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
**F** salvation by themselves and necessarily. But the second reason, which seems more uniquely theirs, proves nothing else than that those things which pertain to knowledge and morals remain: which Catholic truth does not reject. Indeed, it commands all the moral parts of the law to be kept—not because they are of the Mosaic law, but because they are of the eternal law, the inscription of which on our minds can be called the "law of nature." 

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
**G** Finally, when they argue thus: "As long as the thing symbolized stands, the symbol stands; but the thing symbolized stands forever because it is eternal truth; therefore the symbol also stands forever," we certainly approve of all that.

<column-break/>

But it does not follow from this that the external observance of the law remains obligatory. For the symbols of the law consist chiefly in the literal understanding itself, which leads and stimulates us toward an intellectual allegory. An external physical act, although it may assist in stimulating us, has little power in this regard; rather, the literal interpretation once conceived chiefly leads and stimulates us to this, even if we perform nothing externally. Truly, how much the secrets of the law exceed the literal sense was made very clear in the first book of this work. Therefore, notwithstanding the aforementioned Jewish reasons, it is clear from what has been said that the law of the Jews was changeable. And indeed, it was frequently changed.

GAL. <note>Likely the character Galatinus.</note> Regarding these, it is written in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy: <note>original: "וקשרתם לאות על ידך והיו לטטפת בין עיניך"</note> "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets—that is, as phylacteries—between your eyes." You should know, then, that "phylactery" is a Greek name, and it is derived (as some prefer) from the Greek word *phylassein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φυλάσσειν"</note>, which means "to keep" or "to guard," and from the Hebrew *tora* <note>original: "תורה"</note>, which signifies "law." Therefore, I say this word is entirely Greek, and in Greek it is called *phylaktērion*. For they used to make four such "guardians" in which the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> was placed; they would bind one on the head, where the skull of young children pulses. In the Talmud these are called *tephillin*, but in Deuteronomy they are <margin>Conclusion of the preceding points.</margin> *totaphoth*. From all this, it clearly appears that the Mosaic Law was not only changeable but has actually been changed in many places. Therefore, arranging all the previous points into a rational order, let us finally conclude: Since all the commandments of the Law which a prophet—or even another sage lesser than a prophet—might say should be transgressed (except for idolatry), must indeed be transgressed (as was proven through the Talmud in the preceding chapter; for which reason David reduced the 613 commandments of the Law to eleven, and after him Isaiah to six, then Micah to three, again Isaiah to two, and finally Habakkuk to one: namely, to faith working through love of God and neighbor, as was shown earlier in this chapter); and since the Messiah, as was clear in the preceding sections, is greater than Abraham and the other patriarchs, and greater than Moses and all the Prophets, and also greater than the ministering Angels who assist God more closely than others: nothing prevents the Messiah from being able to revoke all the ceremonial precepts of the Law and bring them back to a spiritual meaning. Especially since it is established that this was going to happen, as has been proven above.

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the duration and nature of the Mosaic Law. The previous page established that the core moral principles of the Law are unchanging, while its ceremonial aspects were subject to the interpretation of the Sages. This page specifically investigates the Hebrew word "olam" to determine if "everlasting" laws were truly intended to last for all eternity or merely for a specific age.</meta>

# BOOK ELEVEN

...pertain to morals, they remain forever and must always be observed. In this way, Catholic truth (as has been said above) commands that the moral aspects of the Law be observed, not because they are precepts of the Mosaic Law, but because they belong to the eternal law. If, however, their argument refers to the ceremonial laws: I say that in those cases, "eternal" or "everlasting" is understood to mean "perpetual" or for the duration of an "age." For wherever we have "eternal" or "everlasting" in these places in our <margin>The meaning of the Hebrew word *Olam*.</margin> edition, the Hebrew text has *olam* <note>original: "עולם", a word often translated as "forever," but which has a more nuanced meaning regarding time.</note>, which is taken there to mean "perpetually" or for "an age." If, therefore, *olam* is taken in those same places for "perpetually," then *olam* is the same as "continuous," and that which lasts for the "age" or lifetime of some thing without interruption. For "perpetual" is properly the same as "continuous." According to that line from Ovid:

->*Lead down a perpetual song to my own times.*<-

Hence we speak of a "perpetual" speech, which is continuous and without interruption. Hence a "perpetual" Consul, a "perpetual" Censor, or a "perpetual" Emperor is one who remained a Censor, Consul, or Emperor always and continuously while he lived; yet when he died, another was substituted. In this way, circumcision and other ceremonies were given to the Jews to be observed as a "covenant of *olam*," that is, a "perpetual" covenant: meaning always and continuously for as long as they were meant to be observed, and no further. If, however, *olam* is taken for "an age," then *olam* does not imply eternity, but a determined time. To prove this, I will first bring forward what was said of Samuel by his mother Hannah in the first chapter of the first book of Kings: *And I will bring him, and he shall appear in the sight of God, and dwell there "le olam"* <note>1 Samuel 1:22; original Hebrew: "והביאתיו ונראה את פני יהוה וישב שם עד עולם"</note>, that is, "for an age." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: that is, until the "age of the Levites," just as it is said in the eighth chapter of Numbers: *And from the age of fifty years he shall cease the business of serving, and shall serve no more* <note>Numbers 8:25; original Hebrew: "ומבן חמשים שנה ישוב מצבא העבודה ולא יעבד עוד"</note>. And thus all the days of Samuel were 52 years. Furthermore, it is particularly noteworthy that in the *Midrash* <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary.</note> on *Elle hadebarim* <note>The Hebrew title for the book of Deuteronomy.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Deuteronomy, we read regarding what is said in the 15th chapter of that same book: *And you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear and into the door, and he shall be to you a servant "olam"* <note>Deuteronomy 15:17; original Hebrew: "ולקחת את המרצע ונתת באזנו ובדלת והיה לך עבד עולם"</note>, that is, "of an age." For there *olam* is said to mean all the days of the master’s "age" until the Jubilee <note>A special year of release every 50 years in the Jewish calendar when slaves were freed and debts forgiven.</note>, even if he had been bought in the thirtieth or fortieth year before the Jubilee. Thus says the Midrash, that is, the exposition. From which it is clear that in this place *olam* (for which our translator put "eternal") can be one year or even less, depending on how much sooner or later the master of that servant might die. Moreover, Rabbi Solomon proves this in his gloss on those same words: *And he shall be to you a servant "olam"*. He says: "This can be as his hearing shows," as is written in the 25th chapter of Leviticus: *And you shall return, every man to his possession, and everyone shall return to his family* <note>Leviticus 25:10; original Hebrew: "ושבתם איש אל אחזתו ואיש אל משפחתו תשבו"</note>. Behold, from this you are taught that this *olam* is nothing other than the age of the Jubilee. These are the words of Rabbi

<column-break/>

<page-num>566</page-num>
<margin>A</margin> Solomon. This is also confirmed in the book *Kiddushin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning betrothals.</note>: when it is said there among other things, "What is that which is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus: *And his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him "le olam"* <note>Exodus 21:6; original Hebrew: "ורצע אדניו את אזנו במרצע ועבדו לעולם"</note>, that is, "for an age"? Until what age? Until the age of the Jubilee, or until the death of his master; just as it is written above: *And he shall serve him*—therefore he shall not serve his son." This is the tradition. The same is also clear <margin>B</margin> through Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian (1160–1235).</note>, saying thus in the book *Serafim* <note>Likely referring to his *Sefer HaShorashim* (Book of Roots), a Hebrew dictionary.</note>: It is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus, *And he shall serve him "le olam"*, that is, "for an age"; he means to say all the days until the Jubilee. The same is written in the twenty-second chapter of Proverbs: *Do not repel or set aside the boundary of "olam"* <note>Proverbs 22:28; original Hebrew: "אל תסג גבול עולם אשר עשו אבותיך"</note>, that is, the word of the many which your fathers made. Likewise in the second chapter of Jeremiah: <margin>C</margin> *For from "olam" I have broken your yoke* <note>Jeremiah 2:20; original Hebrew: "כי מעולם שברתי עלך"</note>, that is, from a long time ago. And in Psalm 119: *In "seculum" [olam] I will not forget your mandates* <note>Psalm 119:93; original Hebrew: "לעולם לא אשכח פקודיך"</note>: he means to say *le olam*, or for an age—that is, "for all the days of my life I will not forget your mandates." Thus says Rabbi Kimhi. From all these things, therefore, it is manifest that this word *olam* signifies neither eternity nor everlastingness, but an age and a determined time, and sometimes a very small one, as has already been shown. From which it is clear that the author <margin>D</margin> of our edition, both Greek and Latin, and whatever other translators translated *olam* as "eternal" or "everlasting" where the divine Scripture speaks of circumcision, the Sabbath, tabernacles, or other ceremonies, interpreted it far differently than the truth holds. Because of this, some have fallen into the Jewish error and been irrevocably led away from the Christian faith, since it happened that they heard or read that circumcision and other ceremonies were an "eternal covenant" or an "everlasting law." <margin>E</margin> However, what truly counts as "eternal" or "everlasting" among the Hebrews, Rabbi Kimhi declares excellently in the book *Serafim*, when he says: It is written in Psalm 84, *They will praise you "sela"* <note>Psalm 84:4; original Hebrew: "יהללוך סלה"</note>, that is, forever. For they explained this word *sela* as *had* <note>original: "עד", meaning "until" or "forever."</note>, that is, in perpetuity. So also in the words of our Masters, the tradition from the House of Rabbi Elazar is: That every place in which *Netzah* <note>original: "נצח", meaning "victory" or "perpetuity."</note>, *Sela*, or *Vahed* <note>original: "ועד", meaning "and ever."</note> is placed, it has no <margin>F</margin> intermission, but signifies "for an age and for ages of ages." *Netzah* is as it is written in the 57th chapter of Isaiah: *And I will not be angry "le-netzah"* <note>Isaiah 57:16; original Hebrew: "ולא לנצח אקציף"</note>, that is, forever or everlastingly. *Sela* indeed is as it is written in Psalm 48: *He will rectify, or compose, or ordain it until "olam sela"* <note>Psalm 48:8; original Hebrew: "יכוננה עד עולם סלה"</note>, that is, for an everlasting age, or always. *Vaed*, however, is as it is written in Exodus 15: *God shall reign for "olam vaed"* <note>Exodus 15:18; original Hebrew: "יהוה ימלוך לעולם ועד"</note>, that is, for eternity or everlastingly. <margin>G</margin> Thus says Rabbi Kimhi. Since, therefore, none of these words are used in the Law where mention is made of circumcision, the Sabbath, sacrifices, and other ceremonies, but only *olam* (as has been seen), it is openly and without doubt manifest...

Here, the speakers transition into explaining why the ceremonial laws are described in scripture as "not good" and how they were intended to be replaced by spiritual observances upon the arrival of the Messiah.</meta>

it is manifest that those ceremonial things were not to be observed forever according to the letter, but for a determined time, namely until the coming of the Messiah. Especially because, since they were not good according to the letter, they were to be observed only spiritually in the days of the Messiah.

### CHAPTER VI.

->That the ceremonial precepts of the old law were not<-
->good, yet they were not evil.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>A</margin>Since the ceremonial mandates of the Mosaic law were given by God, I wonder that you have said they were not good. GAL. I called the Jewish ceremonies "precepts that were not good" for this reason: because God himself called them so, when in Ezekiel chapter 20 he said: <margin>B</margin> <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "אני נתתי להם חקים לא טובים ומשפטים לא יחיו בהם : ואטמא אותם במתנותם בהעביר כל פטר רחם למען אשימם למען אשר ידעו אשר אני יהוה"</note> *I gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live. And I defiled them through their own gifts—in the sacrificing of every firstborn of the womb—in order that I might make them desolate, so that they might know that I am the Lord.* Here, the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains that word *Lemaan ashimem* <note>original: "למען אשימם"</note>—that is, "so that I might make them desolate" and destroy them. *Ashimem* is a word of desolation, meaning "causing devastation." Therefore, whoever explained this using a word for "sin" (saying "on account of their sins") is in error. For the letter *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the author is engaging in a technical grammatical debate about the root of the word.</note> which is there does not belong to the root of the word. "So that they might know that I am God"—namely, when I shall have brought evils upon them. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. If, therefore, God himself called the ceremonial precepts which he gave to the Jews "not good," it ought not to seem strange to you, nor to anyone else, if I have also called them such. CAP. Why, then, were they called "not good"? GAL. Because through them men were not justified. For they were shadows, prefiguring the grace by which we are now justified. Yet they are not to be called "evil," since they were divinely commanded, being appropriate for the time and the persons. And for that reason, perhaps, God did not call them evil, but only "not good"—that is, not such that men might become good and righteous through them. Wherefore Abraham and all the other fathers were held liable and guilty before God, to such an extent <margin>F</margin> that, notwithstanding the sacrifices and other ceremonies, they descended into the underworld <note>original: "infernum," referring here to Limbo or the "Bosom of Abraham" where the righteous awaited the Messiah.</note>, as we have sufficiently proved in the preceding sections. Hence, not without reason, Isaiah said in chapter 40: <note>original: "ולבנון אין די בער וחיתו אין די עולה"</note> *And Lebanon is not sufficient to provide fuel, nor are its animals sufficient for a burnt offering.* This, the commentary of Rabbi Solomon explains, is "to satisfy for the sins of the Nations." Moreover, "Lebanon" is understood as nothing other than the Temple, as is clearly evident in the *Midrash* <note>A form of rabbinic interpretation or commentary.</note> on the *Shir HaShirim* <note>original: "שיר השירים", the Song of Songs.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs; where it is said concerning that statement in chapter 7 of the same book: <note>original: "אפך כמגדל הלבנון"</note> *Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon*, meaning the house of the sanctuary. For just as this nose is placed at the height of a man, so

<column-break/>

# BOOK ELEVEN

<margin>A</margin>the house of the Lord, that is the Temple, was placed at the height of the world. Therefore, when it is said, "Like the tower of Lebanon," Lebanon is nothing but the house of the sanctuary; just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 3: <note>original: "ההר הטוב הזה והל בנון"</note> *This good mountain and Lebanon.* This is the tradition. Therefore Lebanon—that is, the Temple—just as it was not sufficient with all its burnt offerings and sacrifices to satisfy for the sins of the nations (according to Rabbi Solomon’s exposition), so also it was not enough to satisfy for the sins of the Jews: since all men, both good and bad, though in different ways, descended to the underworld. This is also <margin>B</margin> excellently proven by what is written in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarshan <note>An 11th-century preacher and commentator from Narbonne.</note>, when he comments on the statement in the twenty-seventh chapter of that same book: <note>original: "ויהי כי זקן יצחק"</note> *And it came to pass when Isaac was old.* It is read thus: Rabbi Nahmia said, "Tribulations are more beloved by God than sacrifices." For sacrifices were from a man's riches, but tribulations are from his very body; as <margin>C</margin> is said in Job chapter 2: <note>original: "עור בעד עור וכל אשר לאיש יתן בעד נפשו"</note> *Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul.* Here, "soul" is taken for the animated body. From all these things the proposition is clear: namely, that although the ceremonies of the Mosaic law were not evil because they were commanded by God, they were nevertheless "not good" because they were not able to justify men. Therefore, upon the arrival of the Messiah, they were to come to an end in such a way that they should be observed only spiritually.

### CHAPTER VII.

->That circumcision in the time of the Messiah was to be<-
->kept not carnally, but spiritually.<-

### CAPNIO.

<margin>E</margin>So that the stubbornness of the Jews may be more and more refuted, it must now be proved through their own scriptures that in the days of the Messiah, their ceremonies were to be observed spiritually. I pray you, show this first regarding circumcision. GAL. First, then, let them hear the voice of Almighty God speaking to the men of Judah and Jerusalem in Jeremiah <margin>F</margin> chapter 4: <note>original: "נירו לכם ניר ואל תזרעו אל קוצים : המלו ליהוה והסירו ערלת לבבכם איש יהודה וישבי ירושלם פן תצא כאש חמתי ובערה ואין מכבה מפני רוע מעלליכם"</note> *Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my indignation go forth like fire, and be kindled, and there be none to quench it, because of the wickedness of your doings.* Deuteronomy chapter 10 also says: <note>original: "ומלתם את ערלת לבבכם וערפכם לא תקשו עוד"</note> *And you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and you shall no longer be stiff-necked.* CAP. I would like you to prove through their own doctors that circumcision was to be kept spiritually in the time of the Messiah. GAL. I shall certainly do so. In the <margin>G</margin> *Midrash* on *Shir HaShirim* (the Song of Songs), on that saying in the second chapter of the same book: <note>original: "ענה דודי ואמר לי"</note> *My beloved answered and said to me...*

It highlights that even Jewish tradition, through figures like Rashi and Moses Hadarshan, acknowledges the insufficiency of physical sacrifices and the shift toward spiritual devotion, such as the "circumcision of the heart."</summary>

...said to me: thus it is read, "The Church of Israel said: He answered me by the hand of Elijah; he gave the exposition by the hand of Daniel; and he told me of the dwelling-place of the King Messiah." And what did he say to me? <note>original: "קומי לך רעייתי יפתי ולכי לך"</note> *Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away; for lo, the winter is past,* and so forth, until the phrase *the time of pruning has come.* This means: The time of pruning has arrived; for the time has come for Israel to be redeemed. The time has come for the foreskin to be cut away, of which it is said in the thirtieth chapter of Deuteronomy: <note>original: "ומל יהוה אלהיך את לבבך ואת לבב זרעך לאהבה את יהוה אלהיך"</note> *And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring, to love the Lord your God.* And the law shall be converted to a newness, and Israel shall be renewed; just as it is said in the thirty-first chapter of Jeremiah: *And I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,* that is, a new law. Thus far the tradition. 

In this tradition, two points to be noted are clearly evident. The first is that in the time of the Messiah, circumcision was to be performed spiritually. This is proven by that passage from Deuteronomy, *And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring.* This can only be understood spiritually, since according to the literal letter, nothing can be removed from the heart without causing death. The second point is that the law was to be converted to a newness, specifically because of the new law which the Messiah was to give. To prove this, he brings forward the passage from Jeremiah, *And I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.* In this context, the ancient Talmudists understand "covenant" to mean "the law," as was shown in previous sections. This is also proven most strongly by what is read in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>The "Lesser Genesis," likely referring to a Midrashic commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding what is said in the seventeenth chapter of that book: <note>original: "ואתנה בריתי ביני ובינך"</note> *And I will give my covenant between me and you.* There, Rabbi Akiba <note>A foundational 1st-century Jewish sage.</note> is said to have spoken thus: "There are four kinds of foreskins. A foreskin is mentioned regarding the ear, of which it is written in the sixth chapter of Jeremiah: *To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot listen. Behold, the word of the Lord is a reproach to them; they have no delight in it.* A foreskin of the mouth is also mentioned, as it is written in the sixth chapter of Exodus: *And I am of uncircumcised lips.* And again in the same place: *Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips.* A foreskin is also mentioned in the heart, according to that passage in the ninth chapter of Jeremiah: *And all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.* And again in the twenty-first chapter of Leviticus: *And I will bring them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart be humbled, and they then accept the punishment for their iniquity.* And again it says in Deuteronomy chapter 10: *Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart.* And once more in the 30th chapter of the same book: *And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring.* Finally, a foreskin in the body is mentioned, according to that passage in Genesis chapter 17: *And the uncircumcised male child who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people.* Rabbi Tanhuma said: A doubt 

<column-break/>

<margin>Four types of circumcision.</margin>
exists regarding this scripture, which says, *And the uncircumcised male*: For is there such a thing as an uncircumcised female? But the meaning is that from whatever place a person is estranged from God, whether they be male or female, from there they must be circumcised." These are the words of Rabbi Akiba. From which it clearly follows that just as there are four types of foreskins, so also there are four types of circumcision. Three of these—namely of the ear, the mouth, and the heart—which are spiritual, are always and necessarily required for everyone. 

The fourth kind, however, because it is physical and a shadow or figure of the others, since our Messiah has come—the Teacher of spiritual precepts—it is not only useless, but even quite ruinous to all who practice it. Hence Paul, in whom Christ spoke, writing to the Galatians in the 5th chapter, says in these words: *I, Paul, say to you, that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.* And again to the Romans in the 4th chapter: *For we say,* he says, *that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? While he was circumcised, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.* And further down: *For the promise to Abraham or his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not made through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.* Likewise to the Galatians in chapter 1: *Knowing,* he says, *that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ. And we believe in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law.* These are the words of that most excellent of Talmudists, in whom Christ spoke, as he himself testified in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 13. In that which he says, then—that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness in uncircumcision and not in circumcision—he openly suggests that Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised. This can be proven as follows: For it is written in Genesis chapter 17: <note>original: "ואברהם בן תשעים ותשע שנה בהמלו בשר ערלתו"</note> *And Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin.* But earlier, in the 15th chapter of the same book, it is read of him: <note>original: "והאמין ביהוה ויחשבה לו צדקה"</note> *And he believed in God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.* Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> says: "The Holy and Blessed God reckoned it—namely the faith with which Abraham believed God—as righteousness and justification." 

From these things it is clear that Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised. This is also confirmed by what is read in the *Bereshit Ketanna*, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, when commenting on the statement in the 1st chapter of the same book, *Noah was a righteous man,* and so forth. It is said there: Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Hanina both said, "At forty-eight years of age Abraham knew his Creator and believed in Him." And what did he establish in Him—that is, what did he propose to do for Him? To lead the whole world to repentance. From this it follows that just as Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised, so also Noah (as the sacred scripture attests) was righteous, upright, and perfect, yet not circumcised. So also was Melchizedek. So also Job. So also many others. Therefore, that saying of Rabbi Joshua is very much to be noted, when in the book *Yevamot* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with levirate marriage and conversion.</note>, in the chapter *Ha-Choletz* (that is, "The One Who Removes the Shoe"), he says word for word: "One who is baptized but not circumcised, behold, he is a *gher* <note>original: "גר"</note> (that is, a convert to the faith)." For so we find it among the mothers, namely in Sarah and Rebecca and the others...

than the others, who were being baptized and not circumcised. For this reason, the Apostle Paul must be judged to have spoken excellently when, writing to the Galatians in the 5th chapter, he says: *In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith which works through love.* And again in the same place he says: *For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creature,* that is, the regeneration which happens through baptism, and a new life. For when the Gentiles worshipped demons in the form of idols, they were nothing before God, according to what was <margin>A</margin> said in the 40th chapter of Isaiah: <term>הן גוים כאין נגדו מאפס ותהו נחשבו לו</term> <note>original: "Hen goyim ke-ayin negdo, me-ephes va-tohu nekhshavu lo"</note> which is to say: *Behold, the nations are as if they were not before Him; they are accounted by Him as nothing and vanity.* Therefore, when these same Gentiles cast aside their idols and were converted to God and baptized, they were, as it were, created by God out of nothing. Furthermore, it must not be ignored that circumcision was given to the Jews as a sign. Regarding this circumcision, since I have said much in the oration I delivered concerning the circumcision of the Lord to Pope Leo X, I will say nothing more about it now. By the same reasoning, the Sabbath is also to be kept by Christians only spiritually, since it too was given as a sign to the Jews; for God spoke to them thus in the 31st chapter of Exodus: <margin>C</margin> <term>את שבתתי תשמרו כי אות היא ביני וביניכם לדרותיכם</term> <note>original: "Et shabtotai tishmoru, ki ot hi beini u-veinekhem le-dorotekhem"</note> This is: *You shall keep my Sabbaths, because they are a sign between me and you throughout your generations.*

# CHAPTER VIII.

### *That the Sabbath also, in the days of the Messiah, was to be kept only spiritually.*

# CAPNIO.

<margin>D</margin> It must now be explained in what way the Sabbath was to be kept spiritually in the time of the Messiah. The spiritual Sabbath is nothing other than being without sin; for it was commanded that no servile work be done on it, as is clear from the twentieth chapter of Exodus. But what else is servile

<column-break/>

<page-num>582</page-num>
work but sin, since according to the Lord’s word in the eighth chapter of John: *Everyone who commits sin becomes a slave of sin?* The Sabbath, therefore, was to be kept spiritually in the days of the Messiah because, with the help of the law of the Gospel, one was then to abstain most especially from every servile work—that is, from every vice and sin, which makes men slaves of the devil. This spiritual worship of the Sabbath finally leads its worshippers to the everlasting Sabbath. For Sabbath is interpreted as "rest." Wherefore, it <margin>E</margin> signified not only the rest of the Messiah in the tomb <margin>How the Sabbath is interpreted and what it figured.</margin> that was to be on the seventh day, but also that seventh rest which those who have kept the Sabbath spiritually—abstaining from every vice and sin—shall have in the seventh age of the world after the general resurrection. Concerning this everlasting Sabbath, it is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The "Midrash on the Psalms," an ancient rabbinic homiletic commentary.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that passage of Psalm 90: <term>שמחנו כימות עניתנו</term> <note>original: "Samkhenu ke-yomot initanu"</note> That is: *Make us glad according to the days, or in proportion to the days, in which you have afflicted us.* For it is said there: *According to the days in which you have afflicted us:* namely, through Babylon, through Greece, and through the Romans, and in the days of the Messiah. And how many are the days of the Messiah? Rabbi Joshua said: That they are two thousand years. Just as it is said here, *According to the days in which you have humbled us,* that is, according to two days. For one day of the Holy and Blessed God is a thousand years, according to that saying of the same Psalm: <term>כי אלף שנים בעיניך כיום אתמול</term> <note>original: "Ki elef shanim be-einekha ke-yom etmol"</note> That is: *For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday.* <margin>F</margin> The Masters also said: That according to the future, the "day" of the Messiah shall be one. For the Holy and Blessed God in the future will make for him one day, of which it is said in the 14th chapter of Zechariah: <term>והיה יום אחד הוא יודע ליהוה לא יום ולא לילה והיה לעת ערב יהיה אור</term> <note>original: "Ve-hayah yom ekhad, hu yodea l'Adonai, lo yom ve-lo laylah; ve-hayah le-et erev yihyeh or"</note> This is: *And it shall be one day, and it is known to God. Neither day nor night. And it shall be, that at evening time there shall be light.* This "day" is the world to come, and the making alive of the dead. And this is the light which the Holy and Blessed God reserved for the righteous at the beginning of the world—namely, that of which it is said in Genesis 1: *And He saw the light itself, that it was good.* And again of the same it is said in Psalm 36: *For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light.* Furthermore, Isaiah says in the last chapter: <term>והיה מדי חדש בחדשו ומדי שבת בשבתו</term> <note>original: "Ve-hayah mi-dei khodesh be-khodsho u-mi-dei shabbat be-shabbato"</note> that is: *And it shall be,* (namely their seed), *from the sufficiency of the month in its month, and from the sufficiency of the Sabbath in its Sabbath.* That Sabbath is the world to come, which is entirely Sabbath, that is, rest. Thus far the tradition. From which the proposal is clear. But for the understanding of the words of Isaiah, which <margin>G</margin> this tradition brings forward very fittingly at the end, it should be noted: that "month" in Hebrew is called <term>חדש</term> (*hodes*), and it is used among them for the perfection of all the days in which the moon completes its course. For the Jews calculate their times by the moon, and not by the sun. "Month," therefore, is used for "perfection," while "Sabbath" is used for "rest." Thus, according to the aforementioned tradition, the words of Isaiah themselves are to be explained: *And it shall be,* namely their seed—that is, the spiritual children of the Apostles and holy teachers—*from the sufficiency of the month,* that is, from the sufficiency of the perfection of the present life, *in its month,* that is, in the perfection of their glory in the future. So also the aforementioned seed from the sufficiency of the Sabbath...

### CHAPTER IX.

->The solution to the objections of the Jews, by which they attempt to show that the Sabbath ought to be literally observed by Christians and all others, let alone by the Jews themselves.<-

### C A P N I O.

<margin>Jewish objections regarding the observance of the Sabbath.</margin>
<margin>The first objection.</margin>
The impious perfidy <note>The author uses "perfidy" here in the medieval sense of "unbelief" or "lack of faith" regarding the Christian gospel.</note> of the Jews of our age opposes us in this matter in many ways, wishing to prove with every argument that the Sabbath must be literally observed, not only by the Jews themselves, but also by us Christians and all others of whatever sect they may be. And first, indeed, because its observance is numbered among the ten moral precepts. For it is the third in order among the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>: since the Lord himself said in Exodus chapter 20, <term>זכור את יום השבת לקדשו</term> <note>original: "Zakhor et yom ha-shabbat le-kadsho"</note> This is: *Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.* Therefore, since the precepts of the Decalogue are to be observed by all because they are of natural law, it follows clearly that the Sabbath ought to be observed by everyone.
<margin>The second objection.</margin>
Secondly, because the Sabbath regards the benefit of creation, which is common to all. For on the Sabbath, God rested from every work that He had made; therefore He sanctified and blessed it. For this reason, when He commanded it to be sanctified, as if assigning a reason, He immediately added: *Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it, you, and your son, and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, your cattle, and the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it.* Since, therefore, by reason of creation all are bound to God, it follows that all are held to the observance of the Sabbath.
<margin>The third objection.</margin>
Finally, thirdly, because a natural example leads everyone to this: the Sabbatic River <note>The Sambation, a legendary river in Jewish mythology that was said to flow with stones all week but stop on the Sabbath.</note>, which (as they say) flows rapidly throughout the whole week, dragging stones along, but rests on the Sabbath. Whence we read in the <term>Berešith ketanna</term> <note>Also known as Genesis Rabbah, a collection of ancient rabbinic interpretations of the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the Lesser Exposition of the Book of Genesis, on that statement in the 2nd chapter of the same book, <term>ויברך את יום השביעי</term> <note>original: "Va-yevarekhet yom ha-shevi'i"</note> that is, *And He blessed the seventh day*: That the Roman Lord Rufus <note>Tineius Rufus, a Roman governor of Judea who appears in many stories debating Rabbi Akiba.</note> questioned Rabbi Akiba, saying to him, "What is the difference between this day and other days?" Rabbi Akiba answered him, saying, "And what is the difference between this man and other men?" Rufus said to him, "What have I said to you? And what have you said to me?" He answered him, "You indeed said to me: In what does the Sabbath differ from all other days? And I said to you: In what does Rufus excel all other men?" Just as, therefore, the King exceeds all others because of his glory, so God also willed this day to be honored above the rest. Rufus said to him, "How will you make me know this?" The Rabbi answered, "The Sabbatic River shows this,

which throughout the whole week drags stones along, and on the Sabbath it rests." By these reasons, therefore, the more recent Jews attempt to prove that the Sabbath not only should never have ceased, but also must always be kept by everyone. Although these reasons are of little weight, nevertheless, to further confound the obstinacy of those who lean upon such a fragile and ruinous foundation, you should first refute them. Then, it is necessary that you show through their own scriptures that even among
<margin>B</margin>

<margin>Response to the first objection.</margin>
To their first reason, therefore, I say briefly: That the precept concerning the observance of the Sabbath was partly moral and partly ceremonial. It was moral insofar as through it, men were commanded to be free at some time for divine matters. According to that in Psalm 46: *Be still, and know that I am God.* And according to this, it was counted among
<margin>C</margin>
the moral precepts of the Decalogue. But it was ceremonial as far as the institution of the time of the seventh day is concerned. And according to this, it was not numbered among the precepts of the Decalogue, but among the other ceremonials. Hence it is that we find many times in the Old Testament that the Sabbath was dissolved. This would by no means have been done if, as far as the observance of the seventh day is concerned, it were numbered among the precepts of the Decalogue, since it is never permitted to dissolve those, because they are of natural law. Hence also our Lord Jesus, the
<margin>D</margin>
true Messiah, after He reached thirty years of age, is read to have dissolved the Sabbath itself several times in regard to that part. For on it, He both cured the sick, giving them the power to carry their beds, and He permitted His hungry disciples to pluck and rub ears of grain.
<margin>Response to the second objection.</margin>
To the second, I say: That just as the Sabbath regards the benefit of creation, so the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday.</note> displays the benefit of redemption. For just as God completed the work of creation on the Sabbath, so on the
<margin>E</margin>
Lord’s Day He perfected the work of redemption through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ himself (as the Apostle says) died for our justification and rose for our glory. Since, therefore, in the opinion of all, the work of redemption is greater than the work of creation (For in creation indeed, God spoke, and the world was made, as the Talmudists say. But in
<margin>F</margin>
redemption, as they themselves also say, it was necessary for God not only to speak, but also to do many things, and to suffer: as we have proved most extensively from their words in the 8th book), for that reason the Sabbath, in regards to its ceremonial aspect, had to be changed by the same One who instituted it into the Lord’s Day: which regards the benefit of both creation and redemption. For on that day, the world took its beginning, and through the resurrection of the Lord, death received its destruction, and life received its beginning.
<margin>Response to the third objection concerning the Sabbatic River.</margin>
Finally, to the third I answer,
<margin>G</margin>
by turning that Jewish fiction about the Sabbatic River against them. For just as that fictitious river was a sign of observing the Sabbath, when in the whole week it would flow by rolling stones and on the Sabbaths it would rest, as they tell in their fables: so also now it is an effective argument against them for not observing the Sabbath; since nowhere

<meta>This page continues the debate between Capnio (Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding the Sabbath. Capnio has just presented the Jewish argument that the Sabbath is a natural and eternal law, even evidenced by a miraculous river that rests on the Sabbath. Galatinus now begins his rebuttal by addressing this "Sabbatic River" and then arguing that the Sabbath was never intended for all nations and has been frequently "broken" even in sacred history.</meta>

than there is now any river under heaven that rests more on the Sabbath than on other days. For merchants travel across the entire world, and just as they bring medicines and various pigments from the farthest lands, they would surely tell one another if such a thing were true; nor would they remain silent about the name of the province where such a river was located if the Jews questioned them. **CAPNIO.** On the contrary, Josephus, in the book titled *The Jewish War*, reports where that river was. Rather than say more myself, I will quote his own words; for he says in Book 7, Chapter 35: *Prince Titus stayed for some time at Beirut, as we have said. Then departing from there...* And below: *On his journey, he beheld a river most worthy of note. It flows midway between Arca and Raphanea, cities in the kingdom of Agrippa. It possesses a certain peculiar miracle. For when it flows, it is very full and its current is not sluggish, yet when six days have passed, it fails from its sources and shows a dry place to the sight. Then, as if no change had occurred, it rises again on the seventh day. It is certain that it always observes this order. Whence it is also called the Sabbatic River, so named from the sacred seventh day of the Jews.* So says Josephus <note>Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian. The river he describes is often identified with the legendary Sambation.</note>. Pliny also, in Book 31 of his *Natural History*, Chapter 2, mentions this river, saying: *In Judea, a river dries up every Sabbath.* Therefore, the Jews would say it is not a fiction but the truth that there was a river of this kind, since both Josephus and Pliny mention it and assign the place where it was. **GALATINUS.** I admit that such a river existed at that time. Now, however, there is no one who says they have seen it themselves, or reports it was seen by anyone else. Therefore, to say such a river exists now must rightly be judged as both a fiction and a lie. Furthermore, neither Josephus nor Pliny says that it *rested* on the Sabbath, as these people claim; rather, one records that it *failed* and the other that it *dried up* on the Sabbath. From this, it portended the future failure and dryness of the Sabbath—namely, that on that day, it was no longer to be venerated. From these points, therefore, the solution to the Jewish arguments is clear, by which they strive to prove that the Sabbath must be observed literally by everyone. Their opinion is best refuted even by their own ancient writers. For so it is read among them in the <term>perush</term> <gloss>explanation</gloss>, that is, in the gloss upon that passage of Exodus: <term>See, for the Lord has given you the Sabbath</term> <gloss>original: "Re’u ki Hashem natan lakhem et ha-shabbat"</gloss>. And what does "He gave you the Sabbath" mean? That He gave it to *you*, namely the Jews, and not to the nations of the world. Also in the book <term>Bitza</term> <gloss>Egg, a tractate of the Talmud</gloss>, in the chapter <term>Yom Tob</term> <gloss>Good Day, or Festival</gloss>, it is said: *Rabbi Johanan said: Every commandment that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel, He gave to them publicly, except for the Sabbath, which He gave to them in secret.* Just as it is said in Exodus 31: <term>between me and between the sons of Israel</term> <gloss>original: "beini u-vein b'nei Yisrael"</gloss>. If this is so, the <term>goyim</term> <gloss>nations or Gentiles</gloss> are not obligated to the Sabbath. This is the tradition. From these things, the falsehood of the Jews' aforementioned conclusion is clearly evident.

->That the Sabbath among the Jews was dissolved many times.<-

IT REMAINS now for me to satisfy your second request by showing through their own scriptures that the Sabbath itself was frequently dissolved among them. First, therefore, I say that the Sabbath was dissolved at the very beginning of the world. For where our edition has Genesis chapter 2, *And God finished his work on the sixth day which he had made*; the Hebrew truth has it thus: <term>And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made</term> <gloss>original: "Va-yekhal Elohim ba-yom ha-shvi'i melakhto asher asah"</gloss>. Where we, both Greeks and Latins (except Saint Jerome), say in our edition that

<margin>D</margin>

<margin>E</margin>

For since natural law is inscribed on the mind of every person, it has obligated all people capable of reason to its observance ever since the beginning of the world. This notwithstanding, I will show through their 
<margin>F</margin>

<margin>A</margin> <term>House of Israel <note>Hebrew: *Beth Israel*</note></term> This refers to the passage: "Did you offer sacrifices and offerings to me in the desert for forty years, O house of Israel?" <note>Amos 5:25</note>. For what reason? Because he is a messenger of a commandment. And a messenger of a commandment sets aside the Sabbath laws. From all these examples, it is clearly established that the Sabbath was frequently set aside among the Jews.

### CHAPTER IX.

->*That even the sacrifices of the Jews were to be kept only*<-
->*spiritually in the time of the Messiah.*<-

->CAPNIO. <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and scholar of Hebrew who often appears as a character in these dialogues.</note><-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' showing a figure among foliage.</image-desc>
Now we must speak concerning the sacrifices of the Old Law, and whether in the days of the Messiah they were to be observed only spiritually. They were indeed, as is clearly shown through their own scriptures. For in the <term>Midrash on the Psalms <note>Hebrew: *Midrash Tehillim*</note></term>, regarding Psalm 56, <term>Upon me, O God, are your vows; I will render praises <note>Hebrew: *Alai Elohim nedarekha ashalem todot*</note></term>. <margin>F</margin> It reads that Rabbi Pinhas said in the name of Rabbi Levi, and Rabbi Johanan in the name of Rabbi Menahem: All prayers shall be abolished in the future, but [the sacrifice of] confession or praise shall never be abolished. For thus it is written in Nehemiah chapter 12: "And two companies of those who gave thanks stood in the house of the Lord." One stood in the place of prayer, and the other in the place of sacrifice. This is the tradition; and that saying of David in Psalm 51 is very much in agreement with it: <margin>G</margin> <term>O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise. For you do not desire sacrifice, or I would give it; you take no delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise <note>Hebrew: *Adonai sephtai tiphtach u-phi yagid tehillatekha: ki lo tachpotz zevach ve-ettenah olah lo tirtzeh: zivchei Elohim ruach nishberah lev nishbar ve-nidkeh Elohim lo tivzeh*</note></term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Should I give a burnt offering? You would not desire it. The sacrifices of God are a shattered spirit; a shattered and contrite heart, O God, you will not look down upon. Hence we read in the book <term>The Booth <note>Hebrew: *Sukkah*</note></term>, in the chapter <term>The fool despises his wife <note>Hebrew: *Sotah hamegalesito*</note></term>: That Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said, "Come and see how great the humble are." For in the time when the Holy House <note>the Temple</note> stood, a man would offer a burnt offering, and the reward for that burnt offering was in his hand. If he offered a grain offering, the reward for that offering was <margin>B</margin> in his hand. But for the one whose conscience is humble, the Scripture regards him as if he had offered all the sacrifices combined. According to that saying: "The sacrifices of God are a shattered spirit." Not only this, but his prayer is not rejected either, according to what follows: "A shattered and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise." In the book <term>Sanhedrin <note>the Jewish high court</note></term>, in the chapter <term>The judgment is finished <note>Hebrew: *Nigmar ha-Din*</note></term>, it is said: That Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said, for everyone who slaughters his fuel—that is, his lust—<margin>C</margin> and confesses it, the Scripture considers it as if he honored God in two worlds: the present world and the world to come. This is according to the Psalm: "He who offers a sacrifice of confession honors me." To explain these things, it must be noted that if one considers the animals that were sacrificed rationally, some would be found to signify the killing off of vices, while others signify virtues and good character, or the suffering of Christ. For the firstborn of the sheep—the lambs, which <margin>D</margin> Abel began to offer to the Lord—and the Passover lamb prefigured the suffering of the Messiah and his being sacrificed for the sins of humanity. But goats and she-goats and certain others designated nothing but vices and sins, and the killing of the flesh through repentance. For in the he-goat and she-goat, the foul-smelling, lewd, and petulant nature of every sinner, full of impudent words, was signified. Similarly, pride was signified in the bull, lasciviousness in the calf, noise and inconstancy in the kid and the sparrow. When these vices <margin>E</margin> are slaughtered and destroyed through confession and repentance, they are sacrifices acceptable and most pleasing to God himself, which were prefigured in those ancient sacrifices. However, the sacrifices that pre-signified virtues and good character were the sheep, the lamb, the ox, the ram, the turtledove, the young pigeon, and others of that kind. For simplicity and gentleness were signified in the sheep, innocence in the lamb, fruitful preaching in the ox, and a useful and mild leadership in the ram. <margin>F</margin> In the turtledove, which never joins with another once its mate is lost, chastity was prefigured; while in pigeons, which lack gall <note>historically believed to be the source of bitterness/anger</note> and fly in flocks, charity was prefigured. From the foregoing, it is clear why God says in Hosea chapter 6: <term>For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings <note>Hebrew: *Ki chesed chaphatzti ve-lo zavach ve-da’at Elohim me-olot*</note></term>. Finally, that he wished these spiritual sacrifices to be offered to him by the Gentiles who were to receive the Messiah, and not by the Jews—the unfaithful Jews having been rejected—is shown openly in Malachi chapter 1, where it is said: <margin>G</margin> <term>I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hands. <summary>This page argues that the Sabbath and physical sacrifices were never meant to be eternal physical obligations, citing Rabbinic texts where the Sabbath was broken for holy work. ### CHAPTER XII

->*That all things which according to the old law were unclean, in the time of the Messiah ought to be clean, and pork could be lawfully eaten.*<-

# CHAPTER XIII.

### That the literal observation of the old law was prohibited to the Jews by the Romans, and was afterwards restored by the devil.

->*That the second coming of the Messiah will be around the end of the world.*<-

**CAPNIO.** <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note>

With so many and such great secrets regarding the first coming of the Messiah—which until now lay hidden in the preceding sections—having been reported by you from the Talmud and other books of the Hebrews, it is now certainly fitting, indeed necessary, that those things which lie hidden in the Talmud and their other volumes concerning his second coming should also be revealed. From these things, therefore, it is clear that according to the opinions of the ancient Jews, the second coming of the Messiah will be at the end of the world.

-> That there will be a general resurrection of the dead. <-
