SINCE the Catholic faith firmly believes that the dead will rise again at the second coming of Christ, therefore, for the confirmation of this Catholic truth and for the refutation of Jewish disbelief <note>original: "perfidiae," often used in medieval polemics to mean "lack of faith" or "stubbornness."</note>, it must be proved through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists both that there will be a general resurrection of the dead (which the Sadducees deny) and that the dead themselves will be raised through the Messiah (which the younger Jews dare to say is false). GALATINUS: You urge me here, my Capnio, to show two things through the ancient scriptures of the Jews: namely, that there will be a general resurrection of the dead, and that it will be accomplished through the Messiah. The first, therefore, is clear not only through the testimonies of Holy Scripture, but also through the sayings of the Talmudists. For that saying in Psalm 17: <margin>G</margin> **"As for me, I will behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with your likeness"** <note>original: "אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך"</note>. ### CHAPTER III.

->That the general resurrection of the dead at the end of the world<-
->will occur through the Messiah.<-

### CAPNIO <note>The speaker Capnio is the pseudonym for Johann Reuchlin, the author and a famous Renaissance scholar of Hebrew and Cabala.</note>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, you must now prove the second point: that this general resurrection must occur through the Messiah. Galatinus <note>Pietro Galatino, the other participant in this dialogue.</note>, that too can be proven in many ways. First, through a gloss in the book of Genesis upon that verse in the second chapter: *And the Lord God made every tree to spring up from the earth.* For it is said there word-for-word: this is what is written in Psalm 31: <note>original: "מה רב טובך אשר צפנת ליראך"</note> *How great is Your goodness, which You have laid up for those who fear You!* And further down in the same Hebrew gloss it is said: all the fathers, and the just, the tribes, and Moses, and Aaron, and David, and Solomon, and all the Kings of the house of David, and all the Prophets will say to the Messiah: "The end is near; it belongs to you to bring us back to life." Just as it is said in Hosea, chapter 6: <note>original: "יחיינו מיומים ביום השלישי יקימנו ונחיה לפניו"</note> *He will revive us after two days; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live in His sight.* Korah also, and his company, as well as Absalom, will come to him and say: "How long until the end of these wonders? And when will you return and bring us to life?" Just as it is said in Psalm 85: <note>original: "הלעולם תאנף בנו תמשוך אפך לדור ודור : הלא אתה תשוב ותחיינו ועמך ישמחו בך :"</note> *Will You be angry with us forever, or will You extend Your wrath from generation to generation? Will You not turn and revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?* This is the tradition. From this, it is clearly evident that the reviving and resurrection of the dead belongs to the Messiah, and that he himself will come at the end of the world to judge all men. Also in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A traditional Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse in Psalm 93: *Your throne is prepared from of old,* it is said: The Messiah ascended the mountain of the holy and blessed God before the creation of the world. Just as it is said in Psalm 72: <note>original: "לפני שמש ינון שמו"</note> *Before the sun, his name was Yinnon,* <note>Yinnon is considered one of the names of the Messiah in Jewish tradition, derived from the Hebrew word for "increase" or "offspring."</note> which is to say, "begotten," or "he shall bring forth sons," or "he shall cause to be born." For it is destined that he himself, <note>original: "ינון"</note> *Iannin*—that is, he shall bring forth as sons or cause to be born—all those sleeping in the dust. Rabbi Rhamon said: "Those sleeping in the dust" are the dead. This is according to what is said in Daniel, chapter 12: <note>original: "ורבים מישיני אדמת עפר יקיצו אלה לחיי עולם ואלה לחרפות לדרעון עולם :"</note> *And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and others to reproach and everlasting shame.* Also, regarding what is said in Psalm 3: <note>original: "אני שכבתי ואישנה הקיצותי כי יהוה יסמכני"</note> *I lay down (meaning, I shall lie down) and I slept, and I have risen (or I awoke, meaning, I shall rise and awake), for God will uphold me,* namely through the hands of the Messiah, as the *Midrash* (that is, the gloss) says in that place.

<column-break/>

<page-num>598</page-num>

The Cabalists <note>Followers of Cabala, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> also frequently admit this. For, to pass over their other sayings on this matter, I will relate only those which are found in the Cabalistic fragments in this manner: <note>original Hebrew text omitted here for brevity; it is translated below.</note> *It is well known that the reviving of the dead is placed in the hand of Matatron.* <note>Matatron, or Metatron, is an archangel in mystical Judaism often identified as the "Prince of the Presence" or a mediator between God and man.</note> *As it is written in Isaiah, chapter 11: "And he shall judge the poor with righteousness, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth; and <margin>C</margin> he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked."* The Prophet shows in this place that he is not going to wage war with his own hands, but by divine power. And that all things which he shall bless will be blessed, and all things which he shall curse will be cursed. For God will not change, either by increasing or diminishing, the salvation which He Himself will work. From this we are also taught that it will not be necessary for him to move to war, because God provides salvation not by sword <margin>D</margin> or spear. As it is said in Psalm 147: *His pleasure is not in the strength of the horse, nor is His delight in the legs of a man. The will of God is toward those who fear Him, and those who hope in His mercy. Blessed are all who hope in Him.* And it is found in that which he says, "The rod of his mouth," that "mouth" is a sign of divine power. Truly, in that which he says, <note>original: "ורוח שפתיו"</note> *and the breath of his lips* (that is, of his mouth), there is contained half of the name of God. And it encompasses wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. And, as the wise <margin>E</margin> men say, these three things shall be given to the King Messiah. May he come quickly in our days! These things are written there. Among other noteworthy things placed there concerning the Messiah, it is said that the resurrection of the dead is placed in his power. From all these things which have been said, it is openly shown that the general resurrection of the dead, which will occur at the end of the world, will be performed through the Messiah. This is the saying of a true Talmudist <note>The author here is likely referring to the Apostle Paul as a "Talmudist" or student of Jewish law.</note>, who says in 1 Corinthians, chapter 15: *By man came death, and by man the resurrection of the dead. And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.*

->That after the general resurrection all men<-

### CAPNIO

<margin>S</margin> The Prophet Zephaniah, speaking of the coming of the Messiah for judgment, which will occur after the general resurrection, says that a "chosen lip" <note>Referring to a pure or refined language.</note> is to be turned toward all men and they are to be brought back to it. For he says thus in the third chapter: *Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, until the day that I rise up for the witness; for my determination...*

BOOK TWELVE.

<note>original Hebrew: "לכן חכו לי נאם יהוה ליום קומי לעד כי משפטי לאסף גוים לקבצי ממלכות לשפך עליהם זעמי כל חרון אפי כי באש קנאתי תאכל כל הארץ׃ כי אז אהפך אל עמים שפה ברורה לקרא כלם בשם יהוה לעבדו שכם אחד׃"</note>
Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, until the day that I rise up for the prey; for my determination is to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them my indignation, even all my fierce anger; for all the earth shall be devoured with the fire of my jealousy. For then I will restore to the peoples a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve Him with one accord <note>literally: "with one shoulder"</note>.

<margin>A</margin> This means: "Wait for me," says God, "in the day of my resurrection in the future. For my judgment is to gather the nations, to collect the kingdoms, to pour out my indignation upon them, all the anger of my nose <note>A common Hebrew idiom for fierce wrath</note>. For in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be devoured. For then I will turn to the peoples a chosen language <note>original Latin: "labium electum"</note>, so that all may call upon the name of God and worship Him with one shoulder." These are the words of the Prophet Zephaniah. The Midrash—that is, the commentary—says: "With one shoulder," that is, with one part. Just as it is said: <note>original Hebrew: "ואני נתתי לך שכם אחד"</note> *And I have given to you one portion <note>shchem</note>*, which means one part. Therefore, since the Prophet speaks with the voice of God, saying "I will turn to the peoples a chosen language," what is understood by this "chosen language"? Or what is this language that the Lord has chosen, so that His name may be invoked in it and He may be worshipped by all nations with one shoulder—that is, as one part?

<margin>The Opinion of the Greeks.</margin> <margin>B</margin> GALATINUS: On this matter, various people say different things. For some say that this chosen language is the Greek tongue, which the Lord chose so that His name might be invoked in it and He Himself might be worshipped through it. For the New Testament (except for the Gospel of Matthew) was written entirely in the Greek language, and the entire primitive Church was founded in the Greek tongue. The very name of "Christians" is the greatest evidence of this; for <term>Christos</term> <note>the Greek word for "Anointed One"</note>, from which Christians are named, is a Greek name. Not only this, but also the names of the dignities and offices pertaining to the Christian religion and the worship of God are almost all Greek, such as: Church, Pope, Patriarch, Archbishop, Bishop, Presbyter, Deacon, Subdeacon, Acolyte, Cleric, Laic, and others of that kind. Therefore, they say the Greek language was chosen by God so that His name might be invoked everywhere throughout the world and He might be worshipped by all. From this, even the Messiah Himself, the Son of God, is called "Christ" by all nations in the Greek tongue to this day.

<margin>The Opinion of the Latins.</margin> Others, however, assert that this chosen language is the Latin tongue, in which many regions—such as Italy, Germany, Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary and surrounding areas</note>, Gaul, Spain, and many other nations—both invoke the name of the Lord and worship God Himself. For this reason, the Lord significantly said in the aforementioned words of the Prophet that He would turn this chosen language not universally to everyone, but "to the peoples" <note>in the plural</note>. For not all peoples who confess Christ invoke the name of the Lord or worship Him in the Latin tongue chosen by God, but only some. This is expressed more clearly by what follows, when it says: "With one shoulder." Has this not also been plainly fulfilled? For whoever invokes the name of the Lord in the Latin or Roman tongue, they all invoke Him under the "shoulder" and authority of the one Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>. For from him they receive canonical penalties, and from him they obtain the benefit of absolution from those same penalties as well as from sins. And they worship God according to his laws and statutes, following the rite of the Roman Church—which is the mistress and teacher of all churches—and according to the functions of the Roman

<column-break/>

Pontiff, who is the Vicar of Christ and acts in God's stead, they perform divine service and fulfill the sacred offices. The Talmudists, however, assert that this chosen language is the Hebrew tongue, because God chose it above all others to speak to the fathers and to give His Law. For this reason, He willed that the Law itself and nearly all the secrets revealed to the Prophets be written in that language. Hence, they call it by the specific name "the Holy Language." Because of these things, they say that then, according to the prophetic prediction, the Lord Himself will turn the chosen language toward the peoples for calling upon His name and worshipping Him with "one shoulder," when all the nations to be saved through the Messiah will praise God in the Hebrew language under one shoulder—that is, under the one Kingdom of the Messiah himself. This will be fulfilled among the elect after the general resurrection. For just as the whole earth was of one language before the general division made at the Tower of Babel, so in the general resurrection all men will speak one language, <margin>C</margin> namely Hebrew, which the first parents spoke in Paradise, and which all the elect would have spoken in the state of innocence if the first parents had remained in the grace of God. And this opinion is indeed more consistent with the literal text. For the Prophet speaks in these words not of the first coming of the Messiah, but of the second, when he shall come to judge. This is more clearly evident through the Targum of Rabbi Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets</note>, who translated and explained these very words of the Prophet into Aramaic:

<margin>D</margin> <note>original Aramaic: "בכן סברו לממר אמר יהוה ליום אתגליותי"</note>
That is: "Therefore expect my word," says God, "in the day of my appearance for judgment." And below: <note>original Aramaic: "ארי באשת פורענותי וסופני יכלא רשיעי ארעא"</note> that is, "Because in the fire of my vengeance all the impious of the earth shall be consumed." Since the Messiah is the Word of God (as we have shown above), it is manifest that the Messiah himself will come at the end of the world to judge. From which it <margin>E</margin> clearly appears that the Prophet Zephaniah was speaking of the second coming of the Messiah in the aforesaid words. This was the point to be proven.

->*That the general judgment will be conducted by the Messiah, who will judge in a glorious human form.*<-

<margin>F</margin> The entire Church of Christians confesses and believes without doubt that Christ our Lord will be the judge of the living and the dead, and that He will come in a glorious human form to judge. Therefore, so that the stubbornness <note>literally: "perfidy"</note> of the younger Jews may be further convinced, you ought to prove through their own scriptures that the Messiah will conduct the universal judgment at the end of the world and will come in a glorious human form to judge. <margin>G</margin> GALATINUS: That the universal judgment at the end of the world must be conducted by the Messiah is most evident through what is read in the ancient *Bereshit Rabbah*—that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis. For there, regarding that verse in the 49th chapter of the same book, "Until Shiloh comes," it is said: "This is the Messiah. And to him the peoples shall gather themselves. Because he shall be judging the entire world." And this is what is written...

It is written in the fourth chapter of Micah: <note>original Hebrew: "וְשָׁפַט בֵּין עַמִּים רַבִּים"</note> *And He shall judge between many peoples, and rebuke strong nations.* It is also said in the ninth chapter of Isaiah <note>The author cites chapter 9, but the quoted text is actually from Isaiah 11:4</note>: <note>original Hebrew: "וְשָׁפַט בְּצֶדֶק דַּלִּים וְהוֹכִיחַ בְּמִישׁוֹר לְעַנְוֵי אֶרֶץ וְהִכָּה אֶרֶץ בְּשֵׁבֶט פִּיו וּבְרוּחַ שְׂפָתָיו יָמִית רָשָׁע"</note> *And He shall judge the poor with righteousness, and rebuke with equity for the meek of the earth. And He shall strike the earth with the rod of His mouth, and with the breath of His lips He shall slay the wicked.* All of this is according to tradition.

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, that He is to judge in a glorious human form is found in the seventh chapter of Daniel, where he says: <note>original Aramaic: "חָזֵה הֲוֵית בְּחֶזְוֵי לֵילְיָא וַאֲלוּ עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ אָתֵה הֲוָא וְעַד עַתִּיק יוֹמַיָּא מְטָה וּקְדָמוֹהִי הַקְרְבוּהִי וְלֵהּ יְהִיב שָׁלְטָן וִיקָר וּמַלְכוּ וְכֹל עַמְמַיָּא אֻמַיָּא וְלִשָּׁנַיָּא לֵהּ יִפְלְחוּן שָׁלְטָנֵהּ שָׁלְטָן עָלַם דִּי לָא יֶעְדֵּה וּמַלְכוּתֵהּ דִּי לָא תִתְחַבַּל"</note> *I was watching in the visions of the night. And behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days, and they brought him before Him. And He gave him power, and honor, and a Kingdom. And all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, and his Kingdom shall not be destroyed.*

<margin>B</margin> Now, Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish rabbi, philosopher, and biblical commentator</note> says concerning this passage in Daniel that Rabbi Joshua stated this "one like a son of man" is the Messiah, and that he spoke most excellently. Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> also confirms this, saying in his gloss upon the words "one like a son of man" that he is the King Messiah.

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, it is primarily evident that Daniel speaks of the second coming of the Messiah in the aforementioned words because in his first coming he was to come in humility and poverty, as was shown most extensively in the preceding pages. In the second coming, however, he is to come with majesty and glory, as the words of Daniel themselves clearly suggest. Both the preceding and following verses in the same chapter openly demonstrate this.

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, before the quoted words, he placed these: <note>original Aramaic: "חָזֵה הֲוֵית עַד דִּי כָרְסָוָן רְמִיו וְעַתִּיק יוֹמִין יְתִב"</note> *I was watching until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat.* And a little later he says: <note>original Aramaic: "דִּינָא יְתִב וְסִפְרִין פְתִיחוּ"</note> *The judgment sat, and the books were opened.* The "books" refer to the consciences of every individual, which will be laid open to all. Then, after a few intervening words, he adds the aforementioned: *And behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven*, and so forth.

<margin>E</margin> Also in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms</note>, in the exposition of the 118th Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: "יְהוָה לִי בְּעוֹזְרָי וַאֲנִי אֶרְאֶה בְשֹׂנְאָי"</note> *The Lord is for me among my helpers, and I shall look upon those who hate me.* Or: *and I shall see my enemies.* It is said word-for-word as follows: "This is similar to the sons of men who, when coming to judgment before a tribunal, were terrified of the judgment. It was said to them: 'Do not fear, nor let your hearts be heavy.' For so it shall be when Israel stands in judgment before the Holy and Blessed God; they will indeed be terrified, but the ministering angels will say to them: 'Do not fear, nor be afraid, nor be terrified. For He is a son of your own city <note>meaning a fellow citizen or one of your own kind</note>.'" <margin>G</margin> Since in the universal judgment each person will receive their own reward according to their merits, it is therefore not irrelevant—in order to refute the error and impiety of the younger Jews <note>The author uses "younger Jews" to refer to contemporary Jewish thinkers who he believes have departed from "ancient" traditional interpretations</note> who hope for and assert that they will receive the reward for good works only in this present life—to say something here concerning the eternal reward that the righteous will have after the universal judgment, according to the opinions of the ancients themselves. ->That the Messiah Himself after the universal judgment will be<-

WHEN Isaiah, speaking of the coming of the Messiah to judgment, says in the 40th chapter: *Behold, the Lord God will come with strength, and His arm shall rule for Him; behold, His reward is with Him, and His work is before Him. <margin>D</margin>
GAL. <note>Short for Galatinus, the author of the work, Pietro Galatino.</note> The Messiah Himself: who will be the eternal wages and reward of the righteous, as much according to His divinity as according to His humanity. Wherefore Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Aramaic Targum (translation/commentary) of the Prophets.</note> translated these words into Chaldean [Aramaic] thus: *Behold, the Lord God shall be revealed in power, and the power of the arm of His strength shall rule before Him; behold, the treasure of the works of those who perform His word is with Him, for all their works are manifest before Him. # CHAPTER VII.
# CONCLUSION OF THE WHOLE WORK.
# GALATINUS.

<margin>B</margin> **T**hese, Capnio <note>The humanist name for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German scholar of Hebrew.</note> and Hogostratus, <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and opponent of Reuchlin.</note> are the secrets of Catholic truth which I have gathered in this work—to the honor and praise of God the Best and Greatest, for the confirmation of the orthodox faith, for the glory of the universal Church, for the benefit of the Christian Commonwealth, and for the salvation of all souls. I have plucked them from the Talmudists, the Kabbalists, and other Hebrew books, like roses from thorns, as a foundation for your debate (with the help of divine aid). I have collected them into these twelve books like small bundles, so that from them one might easily perceive what should be thought of the Talmud, which has been the subject of such long dispute between you. Indeed, in another work, which I hope to publish soon (God willing) in six distinct books according to the distinctions of Hogostratus’s articles, a very wide space for debating will be given to you. Thus, once the articles themselves are skillfully discussed and the arguments of both of you are diligently heard, the truth itself, which you seek with such zeal, may appear more clearly determined. But now, I would ask this of you: if anything in this work seems to you to have been stated incorrectly by me, please reveal it to me in a friendly manner. For since only a year and a half was given to me to complete such a great task—a task for which, to tell the truth, a man's entire lifetime would scarcely have sufficed—I fear greatly that due to excessive haste, I may have happened to say many things otherwise than was fitting. Therefore, I am prepared to correct everything I have poorly stated according to the judgment of wise friends and, where necessary, to retract it. **HOG.** The things you have said in this work, Galatinus, seem to me to be all well-stated, except for one. **GAL.** Tell me, I pray, what is that one thing? **HOG.** That in many places you have not preserved the common manner of writing and speaking. For you have produced some words written with an "aspiration" <note>An "aspiration" refers to the breathy 'h' sound.</note> that usually reject it, and you have pronounced others far differently than common usage has maintained. **GAL.** Tell me, I pray, what those might be. **HOG.** The ones you have recorded with an aspiration contrary to the usual way of writing are indeed many, but especially these: Heua, Habel, Hanna, Iohannes, Halleluia. <note>In standard Latin: Eva, Abel, Anna, Ioannes, Alleluia.</note> As for those you have pronounced contrary to the law of our orthography—though they too are many—these seem the most prominent among the rest: Hanoch, Methuselas, Noas, Peres, Moses, Iehofuas, Pinhas, Semuel, Selomo, Sealthiel, Iehoiakim, Hoseas, Bathseba, Elisheba, Amora. Yet these are commonly written and pronounced by our people as: Enoch, Mathusale, Noe, Phares, Moyses, Iosue, Phinees, Samuel, Salomon, Salathiel, Ioakim, Osee, Bethsabea, Elizabeth, Gomorra. Therefore, I have no doubt that you will be criticized by many. **GAL.** To those whom I think will

<column-break/>

criticize me for that, I ask and beseech that they do not wish to accuse me before they hear the reason why I have done it. For that reason, I want both you and them to know that the author of our Latin edition <note>Referring to the Vulgate Bible translation.</note> imitated the Greek edition. Just as in many places he rendered a meaning entirely different from the Hebrew truth, so too he translated almost infinite words in a corrupt and distorted way. Since these are not Greek but Hebrew, we ought to follow not the Greeks, but the Hebrews in them—especially in those words where a variation in meaning follows from a variation in the letters. These are the ones I have taken care to correct in this work above others. Therefore, whatever is written among the Hebrews with the letter <term>he</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ה (H).</note> or <term>heth</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ח (Ch/H).</note> must be written with an aspiration among us. I do not agree with the opinion of those who, comparing <term>heth</term> to the Greek "rough breathing" and <term>he</term> to the "smooth breathing," say that only those occurring with <term>heth</term> among the Hebrews should be written with an aspiration by us. This is partly because in Hebrew words (as I said), the orthography of the Hebrews—as far as our letters allow—must be preserved, rather than that of the Greeks. It is also because, although <term>heth</term> is a strong aspiration and <term>he</term> is a light one, both letters are aspirations for them. For that reason, wherever either <term>heth</term> or <term>he</term> is placed among them, an aspiration must be placed among us, except at the end of words; for our aspiration can never be final, except in certain interjections. Therefore, those who write Heua, Habel, Hanna, Ioannes, and Halleluia without an aspiration err significantly, since these are usually written among the Hebrews with either <term>heth</term> or <term>he</term>. For Heua is written by them with a <term>heth</term>, like this: חוה <gloss>hauah</gloss>, since it is derived from the verb חיה <gloss>haia</gloss>, which means "to live," with the letter <term>iod</term> changed into a <term>vau</term>. Hence Heua (as Holy Scripture testifies) is interpreted as "the mother of the living." Hanna is also written with a <term>heth</term>, like this: חנה <gloss>Hannah</gloss>, since it is derived from the noun חן <gloss>hen</gloss>, which is the same as "grace." Ioannes <note>The name John.</note> is also written by them with a <term>heth</term>, like this: יוחנן <gloss>iohanan</gloss>. For it is composed from the "four-letter name" <note>The Tetragrammaton, the holy four-letter name of God.</note> of God, which is יהוה, and from the noun חן, which is grace. Therefore, Ioannes is interpreted as "the grace of God." Habel, however, is written among them with a <term>he</term>; for it descends from the verb הבל <gloss>habal</gloss>, which is the same as "he vanished." Similarly, Hallelu-ia is written with a <term>he</term>, in this way: הללויה <gloss>hallelu-iah</gloss>. For they are two words. The first is הללו <gloss>hallelu</gloss>, which is in the imperative mood, second person plural of the verb הלל <gloss>hillel</gloss>, which is "praise." The second is יה <gloss>iah</gloss>, which is one of the divine names and signifies God or Lord; hence "hallelu-ia," which is translated into our language as "praise God" or "praise the Lord." From the aforementioned, then, it clearly appears that not only these, but all other words that are written with either <term>heth</term> or <term>he</term> among the Hebrews, must be written with an aspiration among us. For in these and in all other Hebrew words, the Hebrew manner of both writing and pronouncing must always be preserved by us (as far as can be done with our letters). Otherwise, the same word would not retain entirely the same meaning among us as it has among them. This is why (to bring forward a few examples out of many) I have corrected...

<margin>A</margin> ...you mentioned) it is not Enoch but Hanoch; not Methuselah but Methuselas, with the second-to-last syllable lengthened; not Noah but Noas; not Phares but Peres; not Moses <note>original: "Moyses"</note> but Moses <note>original: "Moses"</note>; not Joshua but Jehosuas, with the second-to-last syllable lengthened; not Phinehas but Pinhas; not Samuel but Semuel; not Solomon but Selomo; not Salathiel but Sealthiel; not Joachim but Jehoiakim; not Hosea but Hoseas, with the second-to-last syllable lengthened; not Bathsheba but Bathfeba, also with the second-to-last syllable lengthened; not Elizabeth but Elisiba, likewise with the second-to-last syllable lengthened; not Gomorrah but Amora. We ought both to write and <margin>B</margin> pronounce them this way, since that is how the Hebrews both write and pronounce them. It is permitted, however, that these letters, <term>he</term> <note>ה</note>, <term>het</term> <note>ח</note>, and <term>ayin</term> <note>ע</note>—which are the final letters in these as well as other masculine names—are very frequently changed by us into the letter "s" for the sake of euphony <note>for a more pleasing sound in Latin</note>. Yet this change brings about no change in meaning. For to provide just two examples of each of these letters: among the Hebrews, <term>משה</term> <note>Moshe</note> and <term>ישעיה</term> <note>Isaiah</note> end in <term>he</term>; <term>נח</term> <note>Noah</note> and <term>משיח</term> <note>Messiah</note> end in <term>het</term>; <margin>C</margin> <term>יהושוע</term> <note>Joshua</note> and <term>מושיע</term> <note>Saviour/Moshia</note> end in <term>ayin</term>. Nevertheless, these and others of this kind are very often ended by us with the letter "s" without any change in meaning, such as: Moses, Isaias or Esaias (for it can be said either way), Noas, Messias, Jehosuas, and Mossias, which is interpreted as "Saviour." This same thing often happens in proper masculine names ending in <term>aleph</term> <note>א</note>, such as <term>עזרא</term> <note>Ezra</note>, which becomes Ezras; <term>שלמה</term> <note>Salma</note> (though it is sometimes found written with <term>he</term>) becomes Salmas, who was the son of Nahshon and was also called Salmon, just as we read <margin>D</margin> him named in the genealogy of our Saviour in Matthew. Furthermore, for those names ending in <term>yod</term> preceded by the vowels <term>pathah</term> or <term>qamets</term> <note>Hebrew vowel markings</note>, we add the syllable "us," changing the <term>yod</term> and the preceding <term>pathah</term> or <term>qamets</term> into a long "e" or the diphthong "ae." For example: <term>חגי</term> <note>Haggai</note> becomes Haggaeus; <term>מרדכי</term> <note>Mordecai</note> becomes Mardocheus; <term>זכאי</term> <note>Zaccai</note> becomes Zacchaeus. In most other cases, "us" is joined to the final letter by us in such a way that they form a single syllable, with the acute accent—which among them was on the last syllable—remaining on the second-to-last syllable for us. For example: <term>יעקב</term> <note>Yaakov</note> becomes Jacobus; <term>יוסף</term> <note>Yosef</note> becomes Josephus. And this indeed is done when we wish to bring them into the declensions of our own names. Since these things are so, no one, Hogostratus <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, the inquisitor</note> (as you might think), ought to carp at me, nor should anyone accuse or argue with me for not having followed the customary way of writing

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and pronouncing them in the preceding pages and many other places. For I have not done this out of ignorance or rash presumption, but so that I might correct them and render them better. Nevertheless, I by no means deny that many things said in this work could have been said more elegantly and ornately, had it not been necessary to use a humbler style and more well-known, common words. This was done partly so that the mysteries of the Christian faith found in Hebrew books might become better known to all, and also <margin>B</margin> so that the translation of the Hebrew words might be more faithful. Since I wished to translate these word-for-word, I could scarcely maintain the proper flow of the Latin language in some places. 

<term>CAPRIO.</term> <note>Johannes Reuchlin</note> I certainly, Galatinus (to speak from my heart’s conviction), judge that you have spoken whatever you have said so well and so elegantly that I think no one could have spoken better or more elegantly, especially in such a short time. This you certainly would have been unable to do unless you had been inspired by the Holy Spirit; so that He who once pronounced the mysteries of the Messiah through the prophets <margin>C</margin> might now through you explain those same mysteries more clearly. From this it is openly shown how useful, how profitable, and how beneficial it is for the Christian Commonwealth that a Christian theologian not be ignorant of Hebrew letters, from which you have so exactly drawn out so many secrets of Catholic truth. By these, not only is the obstinate perfidy of the Jews of our time so thoroughly convinced that they dare not even open their mouths further; but also the truth of the orthodox faith is greatly confirmed, and many—nearly infinite—passages of <margin>D</margin> Holy Scripture in the Old Instrument <note>The Old Testament</note>, which are considered corrupted among the Greeks and Latins either by the fault of scribes or the length of time, are corrected with precision for the sake of our faith. For all these things, the entire Christian religion owes you very much. 

<term>GALATINUS.</term> Although you, my Caprio, say these things sincerely out of your immense goodwill toward me, nevertheless, since I am not entirely unaware or unmindful of my own limitations, I leave and submit everything I have said in this work to the judgment of the Apostolic <margin>E</margin> and Sacrosanct Church for correction and determination. And I do so in such a way that bad or poorly said things may be ascribed to my own ignorance; but whatever is good may be attributed to Almighty God, from whom all the best things proceed. To Him be praise, honor, and glory through infinite ages of ages.

### THE WORK on the secrets of Catholic Truth, extracted from Hebrew books and dedicated to the Most Invincible Maximilian, Emperor and ever August, is COMPLETED by the help of divine grace. At Bari, in the year of the Virgin Birth 1516, on the day before the Nones of September. <note>September 4, 1516</note>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN
# OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR
# OF LAWS, ON THE CABA-
## LISTIC ART, IN THREE BOOKS.

<note>original: "Ioannis Reuchlini Phorcensis Legum Doctoris De Arte Cabalistica Libri Tres"</note>

<note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a preeminent German humanist and the first major Christian scholar to master the Hebrew language. Although he was a professional <term>Doctor of Laws</term> <note>a high-ranking legal expert</note>, his passion for "Sacred Philology" led him to study Jewish texts. This work, *On the Cabalistic Art*, published in 1517, sought to harmonize the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>the Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition</note> with Christian philosophy.</note>

<note>The term <term>Pforzheim</term> <note>original: "Phorcensis"</note> identifies Reuchlin by his place of birth in the Black Forest region of Germany, a common naming convention for scholars of this era.</note>

The page introduces Reuchlin’s credentials as a legal doctor and marks the transition into his three-book dialogue on mystical knowledge.</summary>

# TO POPE LEO X, JOHANNES REUCHLIN

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting an interior scene with several figures, possibly scholars or clerics in discussion.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>
ITALIAN PHILOSOPHY, Leo the Tenth, brought over in ages past by Pythagoras <note>the famous Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BC) who founded a school in southern Italy</note>, the first father of that name, to the highest men endowed with excellent genius, had for many years perished under the immense barking of the Sophists <note>original: "latratu Sophistarum"—a disparaging term for the rigid Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages</note>. It lay buried in shadows and thick night until, by the favor of the Gods, that most illustrious Sun of every kind of excellent study, Lorenzo de' Medici <note>original: "Laurentius Medices"; the father of Pope Leo X and the de facto ruler of Florence</note>, your father, the offspring of Cosimo the Elder <note>original: "Magni Cosmi"</note> and prince of the Florentine state, arose. <margin>B</margin> Although we know him to have been so masterly in his spirit and knowledge of governing the Republic, and in conducting all affairs at home and in war with counsel and prudence, that no one in his age seemed more deserving of praise in civic practice; yet, we must admit that he was born—or rather sent down from heaven—for this purpose: <margin>C</margin> that after the disciplines of eloquence and the arts of fine speaking had been handed down to the Florentine youth by the rhetoricians Petrarch, Philelphus, and Aretino <note>Francesco Petrarch, Francesco Filelfo, and Leonardo Bruni (of Arezzo)—pioneers of the Renaissance movement to restore classical Latin</note>—so that the citizens might, without controversy, be more distinguished than all foreign nations by a more polished pen and purity of language—he himself might finally bring into his fatherland that wisdom which expels vice and the method of investigating secrets, which had remained hidden in the books and monuments of the ancients until his own time. <margin>D</margin> To this end, he diligently summoned from everywhere the most learned men and those most skilled in the ancient authors, who possessed both knowledge of things and sufficient eloquence: Demetrios Chalcondyles, Marsilio Ficino, Giorgio Vespucci, Cristoforo Landino, Angelo Poliziano, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>a "who’s who" of Renaissance scholars; they translated Plato, Plotinus, and other Greek works into Latin</note>, and other most erudite men of the world, through whom the skill of the ancients and the secrets of antiquity, obliterated by the malice of chance, might return to the light. These great men worked in competition. For this one taught, another commented, that one read, this one interpreted, and they translated languages into languages. Marsilio <note>Ficino</note> led Greece into Latium <note>meaning he translated Greek philosophy into Latin</note>. Poliziano led the Romans back to Greece. <margin>E</margin> All pressed on with the work, everyone offering the highest praise to the Medici. Upon these heroes, most blessed Leo, your "divine birth-wand" (as they say) happily fell, by the grace of the Gods; certainly so that there remained no kind of elegant learning in which you did not turn out to be most skilled—so much so that even as a boy you em-

<column-break/>

braced the sweetness of the most polished Poliziano. What more can be said? In that age, nothing was more flourishing than Florence. In her, all the best arts that had previously perished were being reborn; nothing regarding languages and letters remained untouched that the noble Florentines did not practice. At that time, I was vehemently moved by that fame, touched by a desire for that place—not only for the magnificent and (to us <term>Hercynians</term> <note>meaning Germans; the Hercynian Forest was a common classical name for the German wilderness</note>) unusual architecture of your ancestral home, which they named after Cosimo the Elder, but also by the longing to see your father, from whom such great benefits had come forth in our century. Therefore, having set out for Italy with the illustrious Eberhard the Bearded <note>original: "Eberhardo Probo," the first Duke of Württemberg and a patron of Reuchlin</note>, the first Duke of the Swabians in our time, to whom I was Secretary, I entered Flor- <margin>1487.</margin> ence around the twelfth of the Calends of April, in the year of salvation one thousand four hundred and eighty-seven. And when I had commended the remarkable nobility of the Medici family to the Duke, as indeed I was duty-bound by the truth of the matter, he desired to have a conversation with that man <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>. When Lorenzo noticed this, with some revealing it to him, I know not who, he took the stranger's right hand most humanely and led us all into his home, showing us every single thing worthy of sight. First, the most skillfully made stables for horses; then the armory filled with every military apparatus; after that, the individual bedchambers adorned with the most precious wall hangings and beautiful carpets; and high upon the roof of the building, a planted grove of trees—the Gardens of the Hesperides <note>a reference to the mythical golden apple gardens</note> and their golden apples. When I extolled his library to the heavens with words, that most pleasant man responded most humanely, as was his custom: that he had a "greater treasure in his *liberis* than in his *libris*." <note>This is a famous Latin pun: "liberis" means "children" and "libris" means "books." Lorenzo was saying his children (including the future Pope Leo X) were more valuable than his vast library.</note> I beg you, Most Holy Father, allow me to speak with you somewhat more freely, a man from the lowest of the common people. How great an admiration do you think seized me then? With what singular joy—when I heard, amidst universal applause, that you had ascended to the highest peak of affairs—did I suddenly remember, like some <term>hierophant</term> <note>a priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries</note>, that paternal omen, equal to a true prophecy? What could sprout from this "Laurentian Laurel" <note>a pun on Lorenzo's name (Laurentius) and the laurel tree (Laurus)</note> more precious, not only for the people of the <term>Laurentum</term> <note>an ancient city in Latium, here used poetically for the papacy or Rome</note>, but for the whole world? What greater treasure could be imagined than that ineffable reign of yours, from which all riches flow to us as if from the abyss of the <term>Pactolus</term> <note>a river in modern-day Turkey famous in antiquity for its gold-bearing sands</note>—all graces, all ornaments of the best literature, and everything that is good in human affairs? ### BOOK ONE

...of all ancient philosophy, which now, with you as the son, rise up into stalks, so that while you reign we may be permitted to reap its ears of grain in all languages: Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic, Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>, and "Chaldiaca" <note>likely a variant spelling or a specific dialect of Aramaic</note>, in which books are offered to Your Majesty at this time. All things begun so prudently by your father are being brought to a richer completion under your dominion. Therefore, reflecting that only the Pythagorean teachings were missing for scholars—though they lie hidden here and there in the Laurentian Academy <note>The Platonic Academy in Florence, sponsored by the Medici</note>—I believed it would not be ungrateful to you <margin>B</margin> if I were to bring into the light <note>original: "foro afferrem," literally "to the marketplace"</note> those things which Pythagoras and the noble Pythagoreans are said to have felt, so that they might be read under your happy divine influence, having been unknown to the Latins until now. Marsilio [Ficino] published Plato for the Italians; Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples restored Aristotle for the French. I, Capnion <note>Reuchlin's Greek nickname, meaning "Little Smoke," a play on his German name "Rauch" (smoke)</note>, will complete the number, and through me, I will present Pythagoras, reborn for the German lands and dedicated to your name. However, this could not be done without the Cabala of the Hebrews, because the philosophy of Pythagoras took its beginnings from the precepts of the Cabalists. Having departed from Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note> within the memory of our fathers, it settled again into the volumes of the Cabalists. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, almost everything had to be dug out from there. For this reason, I have written about the Cabalistic art, which is a symbolic philosophy, so that the dogmas of the Pythagoreans might become better known to scholars. In all these things I affirm nothing; I only recite them as the "infidels" <note>original: "infideles"—here referring to the non-Christian characters in his dialogue</note> think of them. These men, coming together to hear Simon the Jew, an expert in Cabala, meet from different journeys at an inn in Frankfurt: Philolaus Junior, a Pythagorean, <margin>D</margin> and Marranus, a follower of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahometista"</note>. Now, having set aside their small bundles in the lodging and desiring to drive away their hunger, they dread the noisy crowd of fellow diners; but after those others left the tavern following their banquet, Marranus began thus:

I restrained myself from many words amidst such a murmur of local feasters, who, having drunk too much after lunch, are now leaving. I feared I would be ill-regarded if I, a stranger, had interrupted the din of those <margin>E</margin> whom I knew to be burdened by a ruinous drunkenness. But after they departed from here, and we alone meet in this long-standing inn—both of us, as can be seen, travelers and not a little tired from the journey—I pray you, if you agree with me, order the innkeeper to bring the second tables <note>the dessert course</note> and some sweets—not at all "Sybaritic" <note>excessively luxurious</note>—since we may now dine and converse with more freedom. But look, the servers approach, bringing I know not what treats, with nuts and cheese—would that it were from Bithynia <note>a region in modern Turkey famous for cheese in antiquity</note>—and a jug, uncertain whether of malt-liquor <note>original: "zythico," a type of beer</note> or wine, <margin>F</margin> though we suggested nothing of the sort to them. Then Philolaus, with no small skill, says: The shopkeeper here plays the part of an innkeeper; as one who sets traps for money everywhere, he even adds "eared ministries" <note>listening servants/spies</note> to his guests, so that he may sell more wine to those eager to guzzle it. For as soon as the talk of sweets fell away, the dishes were ready. Now, truly, amidst these honorable cups, I hope for a more relaxed fellowship for us. For indeed, by my counsel, my fellow guest, a new face <margin>G</margin> must be adopted, and rest must be provided for tired limbs. This is especially so for me after a path too long and rough, and the hard trails I have traveled until now. What your situation is, I do not know, since I have not yet been informed of your pilgrimage—how far it was, or who you are, or from where you came. "From Byzantium," he said,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "the city of Constantine, which many call the New Rome. For I am a Byzantine by birth, varied in my studies, whether you wish for Greek or Hebrew, or rather Latin; yet I am more skilled in the doctrine of the Arabs. And unless it is a burden, do not refuse in turn to indicate who you are." "They call me Philolaus," said the other, "an Alan by nation <note>the Alans were an Iranian nomadic people; here perhaps suggesting a northern/Germanic origin</note>, a Pythagorean by discipline, and perhaps a talker not unlike yourself; but what shall be your name, I ask?" "Those in Constantinople call me Marranus," he said, "a name known to scholars from Cerinthus and Ebion <note>early Christian heretics who merged Jewish and Christian practices</note>; because I am both dipped in water <note>baptized</note> and a 'circumcised Apella' <note>a Roman slur for a Jew</note>, I am initiated into both the laws of Moses and the doctrine of the Christians to some extent."

Philolaus replied to this: "I hear you mention 'scholars.' But I ask this: are there schools of humanity <note>liberal arts/humanities</note> in Constantinople now, among those most cruel and savage Turks?" "Very many," he said, "to which men of the most excellent talents have devoted themselves. For there are more than ten thousand students there from Persia, Greece, Latium <note>Italy/the West</note>, and Judaism within a single set of walls. Since I have been a listener to many arts there for eighteen years, I finally chose to wander elsewhere, to see if perhaps even across the Alps I might find those endowed with a river of wisdom, who are able to discourse copiously and probably on the greatest questions." "Then of what school of philosophy are you?" asked Philolaus. And Marranus replied: "Of any you like, since I am not bound by the laws of any one discipline, so that I am not even prohibited by a sect of faith from defending freely whatever I feel." "Certainly you have a desire for exploration equal to mine," said Philolaus, "as I see. For I joined myself as a companion to merchants migrating from Thrace to this noble German marketplace of Frankfurt, because I heard there was a Jew here of great fame in Cabalistic works and of enormous reputation. This one faculty (as I have often heard the most learned men, overflowing with sweet leisure and the richest counsels, judge in my presence) can be more closely related to the Pythagorean philosophy than any other, as if nothing were more similar. For they say that Pythagoras fished out almost all his dogmas from that source. They say that Jew’s name is Simon, son of Eleazar, of the ancient lineage of the Jochaici <note>referring to the circle of Simeon bar Yochai, traditional author of the Zohar</note>, whom I have decided to approach now that the tables are cleared." "Truly," said Marranus, "if you permit, I will go with you to the man myself; although I am little instructed in Pythagorean matters, the Arabs have always been more in my veneration: Algazel, Al-Farabi, Abucaten, Hali, Abumaron, and Ibn Sina, whom the Latins call Avicenna, and Ibn Rushd, whom they call Averrhoes, and other similar Peripatetics <note>Aristotelians</note>. Although it was never denied to anyone in my age at Constantinople to pursue whatever philosophy of nearly every language and sect, especially with teachers of different nations teaching publicly every day." Then Philolaus said: "Have confidence, for you may easily be a Pythagorean, as you both willingly believe the word and can keep silent for a time, and you understand all precepts intellectually. "And he replied: "I will at least stand by, where you allow, like some Pythagorean, and I will hear what the talk between you is about. Thus you will make me drenched in inexpressible joy, when..."

### BOOK ONE

...I would have highly valued in the conversation of the wise.
<margin>A</margin> And Alanus said: "Let us go, for he is said to be walking alone now in the orchard of his home where he lives, and indeed he is in this place, and the door is open. Do you see him coming toward us from the garden? Come, let us enter more quickly. Greetings, Master."
To this, Simon replied according to the custom of his people: "The Lord be with you." <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum"</note>
"Are you that Simon the Jew?" the newcomers ask.
Then he replied: "Both; for
<margin>B</margin> I am a Jew, and I am Simon. But what names shall I take for you both, so that I may address you more correctly?"
Each answered to this: "I am Philolaus," and "I am Marranus." They responded: "Having traveled different paths without knowing one another, after a long pilgrimage we have finally met here. It was not this widely famous marketplace <note>Frankfurt am Main, known for its international book and trade fairs</note>, celebrated throughout almost all of Europe for its vast trade and its markets renowned for so many precious goods, nor the beautiful gathering of diverse nations that drew us to look upon it, but the fame of you alone led us here. We have a great desire that you might briefly and conveniently
<margin>C</margin> reveal your noble thoughts on all Cabalistic reasoning—which, as the learned have seen, is to be greatly cherished and sought after—thoughts that are praised even in Scythia and Thrace."
Simon replied: "Is there a memory of us even among the Scythians and Thracians, so distant a people?"
"There is indeed," said both, "and a very great one. For about twenty years ago <note>original: "four lustra," a lustrum being five years</note>—at that time your people calculated it as the year 5,238 from the beginning of the world <note>The Jewish calendar year 5238 corresponds to 1478 CE; the text refers to the era of the mass expulsions from Spain in 1492</note>—
<margin>D</margin> when 124,000 Jews were driven out of Spain, and from there the greatest part of them went as exiles to our lands in various directions. They proclaim that in you, a man very well known to them, there is a great mastery of the arts and disciplines, much learning, an incredible sharpness of wit, and a clear integrity of philosophical speech. Above all, they speak of your divine skill in Cabalistic speculation, which is admirable to all who hear you, so that
<margin>E</margin> in the eyes of all those eager for learning, your light shines even beyond the Sarmatians and the icy Ocean."
He answered: "Such a great estimation of me by you, men of the Pythagorean school, brings no small blush to my face. I fear lest, if this judgment of yours—conceived from popular rumor—proves vain or false through my own fragility, I myself might seem to have committed a painful injury against the divine study of the Cabala
<margin>F</margin> through my own laziness. For clearly, whatever you find in me that is weak, broken, or imperfect might turn into a certain disgrace for this wisdom which you desire, as if the defects of the craftsman must lead to the unworthiness of the art—something I would least of all desire. For I myself, however small I may be (and I know how tiny I am), or all other Cabalists together, whatever they may be thought to be—whether you wish to call them praised or despised, I will not say—yet there is nothing more desirable to be granted by God to the human race, for those who
<margin>G</margin> are worthy of it and excel in high talent and flourish in mind, nothing more beneficial for the salvation of souls, nothing more fit for attaining immortality, by which the human mind, in harmony with nature...

<column-break/>

...might more closely ascend toward Deification—that is, to the height of blessedness, which the Greeks call the *telos* <note>original: "τέλος," meaning the end, goal, or ultimate purpose of a thing</note>, whether you please to call it the extreme, the ultimate, or the end. From this, it happens that we may live fortunately, tranquilly, and happily, lacking nothing and always without impediment, when we have skillfully plucked form from form through certain symbols—rejecting all earthly things and setting aside the matter of things—until we have ascended to the first "all-form" and "formless form." Concerning this, the Cabalists understand this divine command of Genesis: *Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind* <note>Genesis 1:24</note>, namely toward the divine idea, which is itself the "land of the living" in the power of the Living God, who flows that life through the name Adonai. Thus you may know, on the authority of Joshua, that "the living God is within you, and he will destroy the opposing forces in your sight" <note>Joshua 3:10</note>. These things are read in the second chapter of the book inscribed *Sha'ar Orah* <note>original: "שער אורה," meaning "The Gate of Light," a foundational work of Spanish Cabala by Joseph Gikatilla</note>. Thus it happens that all things having life tend upward by their own instinct, and all things flowing with life incline downward. For in this sensible world, whatever consists of the four elements is "silent" <note>original: "דומם," *domem*, a term for inanimate matter</note>—that is, it either lacks a soul to effect diverse and wandering movement, lying motionless and at rest like stone and iron; or it vegetates and grows like a plant and herb; or it moves in many ways, progresses, and merely lives, like brute animals and shellfish; or it even speaks rationally, like man. Our youths are accustomed to learn these things from the book *Ruach Chayim* <note>original: "רוח חיים," meaning "The Spirit of Life" or "Grace"</note>, being named in Hebrew as follows: *the silent, the budding, the living, and the speaking* <note>original: "הדומם הצומח, החי והמדבר"</note>. Truly, there is none of these that does not touch the heaven in a certain way, as if longing for a certain use of its own power and shaping its character: as we see the highest mountains of the earth rising toward heaven from the lowest valleys, according to the song of the Psalmist: *The mountains ascend, the plains descend* <note>Psalm 104:8</note>; as we experience the storms of the sea being raised on high, as "the surging sea ascends" in Ezekiel; as we feel the blasts of air rising from caverns (for the Lord of nature in that same Prophet "makes the spirit of tempests break forth"); and finally, as we see all fiery things lifted up. For *fire ascended from the rock* in the Book of Judges <note>Judges 6:21</note>. So, excellent men, such is the force of your intellect that you understand we are forced by a certain necessity to confess that the more noble a nature each thing possesses, the more it rejoices in a higher attainment: just as a grain of wheat cast into the earth does not rest until it breaks the bowels of the soil, looks out beyond the paths of the earth, and enjoys the celestial breeze. The same logic applies to metals as well; since that which is more noble bubbles up into higher spirits when sublimated by alchemy, so that those things which are higher always seem purer. Thus, those things said to be among the lower regions we judge as ghastly, filthy, and weighed down by dregs; while those things among the higher regions we admire as white and illustrious, adorned with incredible beauty, and we follow them with heralds of praise. Therefore, since skillful nature grants such dispositions to things lying low, vegetating, and breathing, so that they seek higher things, surely it does not seem that she has neglected man by a much stronger reason—man, the ruler of all living things, a beautiful and venerable animal, the most noble animal...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Simon, Philolaus, and Marranus begin their deep investigation into the Cabala. Having established their meeting in Frankfurt, Simon now begins a formal discourse on the nature of humanity as a "microcosm" and the soul's journey toward the divine.</meta>

### BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> ...the most capable, set over the rest, being not only prudent and wise, but also contemplative and capable of religion. Indeed, God has adorned him with better and holier gifts, and especially granted him a condition of this kind so that, from an innate desire of nature, he may strive toward the highest and best things with whatever strength he can. For God, a nature better than our own, composed Man—as it stands in the most sacred history—from two things: the mud of the earth and the breath of life. <note>A reference to the creation of Adam in Genesis 2:7.</note> Thus, clothed in mud, he might prudently care for corporeal things, and endowed with the breath of life, he might wisely love divine things. He brings forth the "living soul" of the earth into his own proper form—namely, that peculiar <term>Idea</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, an eternal, perfect pattern.</note> which belongs not to beasts, plants, stones, or wood, but was born from the mouth of God and breathed into his face by the divine spirit: the very illumination of his own mind. 

This is what we called <term>Deification</term> <note>The process of the human soul becoming god-like or united with God through contemplation.</note> a moment ago: when, in the presence of an object, the external sense passes through its medium into internal perception, and that into the imagination, and the imagination into estimation, and estimation into reason, and reason into the intellect, and the intellect into the mind, and the mind into the light which illuminates the man and catches the illuminated one up into itself. 

From this, it appears correctly understood that the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of the Jewish mystical tradition known as Kabbalah.</note> decided that in the tree of the ten numerations, <term>Tiferet</term> <note>original: "Thiphereth," the Sephirah representing Beauty, Balance, and the Heart.</note> or the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικρόκοσμον," meaning "little world," the idea that man mirrors the entire universe.</note>, should be placed in the middle of the <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite is revealed.</note>. This is that "Great Adam," like the Tree of Life in the middle of the ideal paradise, or like a middle straight line (as they say). For "God made man upright," as says the <term>Book of Ecclesiastes</term>, flexible toward both the higher and lower things. Thus, through the "strife and friendship" of Empedocles <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who believed the universe was governed by the opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note>, noted below in those numerations designated by <term>Netzach and Hod</term> <note>original: "נצח וחוד," meaning Victory and Splendor; these are the 7th and 8th Sephiroth.</note>, man recognizes by his own thought that he is a participant in the elements and this worldly kingdom. 

But by the fear of God and sanctification, through <term>Pachad and Chesed</term> <note>original: "פחד וחסד," meaning Fear (Justice) and Loving-kindness; the 5th and 4th Sephiroth.</note> which expand above, he may apprehend—according to his capacity—the notions of the three simplest Deities: <term>Keter, Chokmah, and Binah</term> <note>original: "כתר חכמה בינה," meaning Crown, Wisdom, and Understanding; the highest triad of the Sephiroth.</note>. Therefore, man was born here on earth for this purpose, and nature shaped and formed him for this: that he might walk on the earth with the beasts on his feet, yet alone among all living things, with his head held high, he might converse with the Angels in heaven. His two hands, located between his feet and his head, he may either fix in the earth by working for necessary food, or lift to heaven by contemplating eternal life. For their protection, the globes of the eyes—alone among the instruments of all the senses—were given to man to be movable, so that they might look toward the earth for the safety of the body, and toward heaven for the salvation of the soul. 

Such is the aptitude and power of man, this faculty, this potency, which neither God (the highest good) nor nature would have implanted unless the faculty were to be put to use and the potency eventually reduced to action—especially in a man who is industrious and prepares himself for it. For if that grasp of divinity were not possible for man, nature would have implanted the desire for it in vain. For an agile and fit man is never satisfied by corporeal sense or the rough touch of building materials, but is carried forward by every thought toward the purity of separated things and the knowledge of the highest matters. Clearly, that is the restlessness of all

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> scholars. To them, a vehement application of the soul through moral, natural, and mathematical truths is born for the arrangement of supernatural things, and finally, a faithful ascent to the First Entity is granted. 

For example: you see a most brilliant fire burning at a distance. Its form is extended through a clear medium—which the Greeks call the <term>diaphanes</term> <note>The "transparent," a term from Aristotelian physics for the medium (like air or water) through which light travels.</note>—all the way to the bodily eye. The spiritual vision waits within and perceives that the form of the object presented is its own; therefore, it willingly receives it as a relative and neighbor into its hospitality. Through the medium of appearance—which you call <term>phantasia</term> <note>Imagination or the faculty of forming mental images.</note> in Greek—it offers it spiritually to the sensitive and animal judgment. It then leads this image upward again to human judgment, and a little higher promotes that whole thing to reason itself. Finally, after an agile discourse, reason transfers that sublimated and sifted abstraction of the corporeal fire to the intellect. 

In this ascent, therefore, three regions are found, and in each, one state of abstraction. In the first region are the object, the <term>transparent medium</term>, and the external sense; there it stops. In the second are the internal sense, the <term>imagination</term>, and the animal judgment; there it stops a second time. In the third are human judgment, reason, and the intellect; and there it stops a third time. The Mind, mistress of all these, having received a higher light, illuminates and perfects the human intellect. Should we believe the Cabalists taught anything else regarding <term>Sechel, Sandalphon, and Metatron</term>? <note>Reuchlin is equating the psychological faculties with Cabalistic angelic/intellectual principles. Sechel means "Intellect"; Sandalphon and Metatron are powerful archangels in Jewish mysticism.</note> 

Each state, moreover, has a double difference. In the first, the body ends and the soul begins, whence it is called "animal." In the second, the soul ends and reason begins, whence it is called "man." In the third, the intellectual power ends and the Mind begins—which alone, without controversy, comes from without—whence it is called "God," according to the oracle: "I said, you are gods." <note>A quote from Psalm 82:6, often used in mystical literature to describe the divinization of the soul.</note> Thus, the names of the states are sense, judgment, and intellect. The middle intervals carrying the forms themselves are the <term>transparent medium</term>, <term>imagination</term>, and reason. Regarding this, the Cabalists of the <term>Merkavah</term> <note>The "Chariot" tradition of Jewish mysticism, focusing on the divine throne.</note> put forward something not dissimilar: the three fathers, who are Abraham the higher, Isaac the lower, and Jacob the middle. 

When, therefore, the two intervals of the three regions—sense and judgment—are doubled according to lower and higher, and each is led to two terms, there remain ten steps of a ladder. Through these, we can ascend from the bottom to the top toward the knowledge of all things that truly are, whether by sense, science, or faith. About which Abraham the Cabalist, in the wonderful book <term>Yetzirah</term> <note>The "Sefer Yetzirah" or Book of Formation, one of the earliest works of Jewish mysticism.</note>, says this:
> **Ten numerations out of nothing: and not nine, and not eleven.** 
> **Understand with wisdom, and be wise with understanding; examine them and inquire from them,** 
> **and establish the matter upon its clarity, and restore the Creator to His throne.**
<note>original Hebrew: "עשר ספירות בלימה • ולא ט׳ ולא יא׳ • הבן בחכמה וחכם בבינה בחון בהם וחקור מהם • והעמד דבר על בוריו והשב יוצר מכונו׃"</note>

Thus far it is so. For the human intellect understands what is above in wisdom, and perceives what is below in intelligence. And the external sense establishes the matter offered by the object through its forms, and the internal sense establishes the matter upon its "clarities"—that is, the abstractions of the forms—which previously belonged to the transparent medium and finally to the imagination...

# THE CABALA

...peculiar to them. Then, judgment mediates between the imagination and reason, investigating those same appearances; and reason, through various discourse and conclusion, proves the truth within them.

<margin>A</margin> Then I return to the beginning and say that the intellect places the Creator, as the first cause of all causes, upon His throne, which is the very mind of speculations. Thus, you have here, most skillful men, the **Active Intellect** <note>original: "שכל הפועל" (Sekhel Ha-Poel), a concept in medieval philosophy describing the intellect that moves human potential into actual thought.</note> and the ten numerations by which it happens that a man apprehends things. These are: the object, the **transparency** <note>original: "διαφανές" (diaphanes), the medium through which light or sight passes.</note>, the external sense, the lower sense, the imagination, the lower judgment, the higher judgment, reason, and the intellect. And all these are not so much the "what" of a thing as they are the "means by" which we know.

<margin>B</margin> Truly, the supreme mind in man is something else entirely. Wherefore, just as God is in the world, so the mind is in man; among the ten *Sephiroth* <note>The ten creative powers or emanations in Cabalistic thought.</note> of the kingdom, it wears the diadem. It is rightly named **Keter** <note>original: "כתר", meaning "Crown," the highest Sephirah representing the Divine Will.</note>, which is to say, the Crown. As Aristotle asserts in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, this alone is divine, and it alone enters man from the outside; from its received light, the lower powers are directed and governed.

<margin>C</margin> This continues **until the intellect, the one who understands, and the thing understood are one and the same** <note>original: "עד שכל השכל והמשכיל והמושכל אחד". This is a core Aristotelian and Maimonidean concept: in the act of pure contemplation, the thinker and the thought become unified.</note>. So writes the Commentator on the tree of the ten *Sephiroth*, which the Masters, regarding the words of the Prophet, "In your light we shall see light," have judged thus: **For in the influence of the mind which flows from You, we understand and are made straight.** <note>original: "כי בשפע השכל אשר שפע ממך : נשכיל ונתישר".</note> I think it is now made clear to all who have diligently searched the condition of human nature: first, that we are led by a natural desire—or if it pleases you to say more correctly, we are drawn—to apprehend the highest and divine things; second, that we can apprehend them (insofar as is sufficient for our happiness) by applying ourselves according to our measure and capacity. Nature inclines us to one, divinity to the other; both are demonstrated by the Cabalists through the figure of fire tending upward, which in a certain way comprehends and skillfully licks all things.

<margin>D</margin> Regarding this, Rabbi Joseph Castiliensis <note>Joseph Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a major Spanish Cabalist.</note> in the *Orchard of the Nut*, book two, says among other things in these words: **Know that the intellectual soul, emanated into man and formed after its supreme Creator, is itself called fire.** <note>original: "תדע לך כי נפש השכלית, הנאצלת באדם ומצוירת ביוצרה עליונה היא דקראת אש".</note> To this they apply that saying of Solomon: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord." Yet, to speak plainly, as both reason proves and the experience of practice confirms, a man must first be instructed in no few arts, in no small sciences of human study, and in no light doctrine. His industry, readiness, and talent must be so tamed for the contemplation of the separate forms and the simple substances of the superior and intelligible world that he may almost creep into the very secrets of God. For before all things, it is fitting that we be learned in the ethics and good morals of prudent men, so that we may shun the base and follow the honorable. This is what Ecclesiastes warned: "Guard your foot when you go to the house of God"; because Ethan the Ezrahite sings thus in his instruction: "Justice and judgment are the preparation of His throne." By this song, he encompasses not only the works of men, which ought to be perfected by justice itself, but also the thoughts of the heart and the words of the

<column-break/>

mouth, which must consist of right judgment. For this reason, with one voice and a similar sentiment, the Cabalists teach: **By following after desires alone, as if they were a deficiency, contemplative longings are cancelled.** <note>original: "כי בהמשך אחר התאוות לבד כמו, חסרונה יבטלו התשוקות העיוניות".</note> Therefore, after morals are settled and the soul is purged (I remain silent now regarding the almost infinite rules of speaking rightly, truly, or well, which are merely the vestibules and doors of the sciences, not the sciences themselves), there will then be a need for Mathematics and Physics. These encompass innumerable things contained everywhere in the volumes of the Arabs, Greeks, and Latins: whether concerning universal number, weight, and measure; or concerning every motion and rest essentially inherent in things, which they call nature. For nature is, as Rabbi Judah Ben Levi <note>Judah Halevi (c. 1075–1141), author of the *Kuzari* (*Al Khazari*).</note> writes in the book *Al Khazari*: **A principle and cause by which a thing in which it exists rests and moves by itself, and not by accident.** <note>original: "התחלה, וסיבה אשר בה יהיה וינוע הדבר אשר הוא בו בעצם ולא במקרה".</note> In this definition, you see how great and of what kind, how many and how boundless are the things gathered together, so that almost everything must be undertaken by us as we investigate nature—from the highest heaven to the lowest center of the earth. We must study whether things stand and subsist by their own strength, or how they rest upon and belong to a substance, so that in a man's whole lifetime, even the names of each individual thing cannot be found (to say nothing of their properties, conditions, powers, ways, and operations). This is due to the near infinity of those things we desire to know, the capacity of our rational power, the difficulty of investigating things, the fragility of human power, and the manifold distraction of our desire. For why? Was it not said to Abraham, "Look up at the heaven and count the stars, if you can"? And he could not; although in his own time, according to Rambam <note>Maimonides (1138–1204).</note>, he was a distinguished astrologer. Whence the Cabalists teach: **Man knows nothing of all that is in the heavens, except in this small measure of the mathematical disciplines.** <note>original: "כל מה שבשמים לא ידע האדם דבר ממנו אלא בזה השעור הלמודי".</note> By this saying, I am reminded that the ancients erred in many things in Mathematics, even those upon which they spent almost their entire lives, as is the custom of scholars. This is recorded in the writings of Abubacher <note>Ibn Bajja, also known as Avempace (c. 1085–1138).</note>, witnessing to us, his descendants, that the ancients even up to the time after Aristotle did not fully know Mathematics. For he says: **The mathematical sciences were not perfected in the time of Aristotle.** <note>original: "כי הלמודים לא נשלמו".</note> Since, therefore, as Solomon says, all things are difficult, and in natural things themselves (of which at least the principles are known to us, or can be)—**Matter, form, and privation** <note>original: "החומר הצורה, המעדר". These are the three principles of Aristotelian physics.</note>—there sits in men such a slowness of apprehension, what shall we think will become of us when we seek to gaze upon those supreme species of spiritual causes? For this, there will be need of abstractions from all lower things, and of discourse, reason, and logical speculations, which could easily occupy a man's whole life. For there is no small weight in discerning **the Categories** <note>original: "המאמרות", referring to Aristotle’s *Categories*, the basic classes of things that can be predicated.</note> as we call them, and so as to...

He emphasizes that reaching divine knowledge requires rigorous preparation in ethics, mathematics, and physics to move beyond physical desires and intellectual limitations.</summary>
