<meta>This page continues the speaker Simon’s explanation of the intellectual ladder. He moves from the basic faculties of the mind to the formal structures of logic and the categories of existence, eventually arguing that divine wisdom (theology) transcends these human tools and requires a purified soul.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> And to speak according to their custom, there are the "most general kinds"—namely: **substance**, **quantity**, **quality**, **relation**, **time**, **place**, **position**, **state**, **action**, and **passion** <note>original: "עצם כמה איכות מתי אנה מצב לו יפעל יתפעל" (Etzem, Kamah, Eichut, Matti, Anah, Matzav, Lo, Yif'al, Yitpa'al). These are the ten Aristotelian categories used in medieval logic to classify everything that exists.</note>. For by these categories, they believe all things contained within the Creator's orb are both constituted and understood. Nevertheless, they find that certain things are published and spoken concerning these very categories and what they encompass; for this reason, they are called the "predicables": **genus**, **species**, **difference**, **property**, and **accident** <note>original: "סוג מין הבדל סגולה מקרה" (Sug, Min, Hevdel, Segulah, Mikreh). These five terms define how a characteristic relates to a subject.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> For all these things, they set up traps, nets, and enclosures day and night, investigating through the individual causes of any given thing, which are: **matter**, **form**, the **efficient cause**, and the **end** or purpose <note>original: "החומר הצורה הפועל והתכלית" (Ha-Chomer, Ha-Tzurah, Ha-Poel, ve-ha-Tachlit). These are Aristotle's Four Causes.</note>. From these, as we softly flatter ourselves, we might be able to hunt down the truth of every matter by a certain "evident demonstration" (as they call it). They name this a **proof** <note>original: "מופת" (Mofet).</note>—namely, running from one extreme to the other, as if from the starting gates to the finish line, in the manner of a certain artifice to which they have given the name **syllogism** <note>original: "הקש" (Heikesh), a logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two linked premises.</note>. But indeed, our teachers have shown with what cleverness and through what twists and turns the "sophisms" of those men are constructed—men who are usually better at showing off these things than actually performing them.

<margin>C</margin> Every syllogism and proof is joined together from two propositions—the **major** and the **minor**—and consists of three parts which are called **terms**. One of them is the **subject** of the inquiry, and it is called the "minor extremity." The second part is the **sharing** part, and it is called the "middle term." And the third is the **predicate** of the inquiry, which is named the "major extremity," and from these comes the **conclusion** <note>original Hebrew: "יתחבר כל הקש ומופת משתי הקדמות...". This section describes the standard structure of a logical argument (Syllogism).</note>.

<margin>D</margin> This is that net, this is that hook, the birdlime and the trap—this is the bond by which, in their opinion, the free truth is captured. They use this indiscriminately, and sometimes in vain, regarding things subject to nature (such as **physics**), or things accompanying nature (such as **mathematics**), or things that in some way strip away nature (such as **metaphysics**).

<margin>E</margin> However, those things which are essentially absolute and separated from nature entirely, and from all matter and motion, we call **theological**. Indeed, these are not subject to those talkative methods and syllogistic whispers; for regarding such "immediate" things, there is not—properly speaking—"science," but rather a firmer and more powerful **knowledge**.

<margin>F</margin> Aristotle suggests this to us more absolutely in the first volume of those *Illustrious Books* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, so named because they were placed "after the Physics."</note> which he wrote after his works on Nature. He implies that the possession of such knowledge is not human. This is because, as we see, it rarely happens to even one in a thousand; it seems to glide into us rather than being acquired by human effort. It is also because it is established in the greatest difficulty due to the thin and meager instinct of our intellect from the beginning.

<margin>G</margin> Zophar produced a certain figure of this in the Book of Job: *Man is born like a wild donkey’s colt.* Then, there is the lack and defect of natural aptitude, even when aided by education. This occurs because, having been deceived for a long time by bad teachers,

<column-break/>

boys who are not yet prudent are forced toward filthy sophisms while still at a tender age, having abandoned the study of the best literature. They are driven by those whose ears admit nothing except "whether it is this" or "whether it is that," along with their propositions and corollaries. Another cause is the rapid promotion of students to higher degrees; they should not yet have been entrusted with such high matters when they have consumed so little "oil" <note>A metaphor for late-night study and effort.</note> in the study of the humanities. Therefore, having exhausted themselves in vain with painful labor among so many thorns and thickets, they shrink back before they have reached the years of venerable old age—indeed, while still flowering in the prime of life. 

Listen, I pray you, to the words of Job: *Wisdom is found in the elderly, and prudence in a long life.* This is why Rabbi Eleazar was once moved to respond to his teacher, Johanan, who kindly said to him: "Come, I will teach you the **Work of the Chariot**" <note>original: "מעשה מרכבה" (Ma'aseh Merkavah), the most profound and secret part of Jewish mysticism, dealing with the vision of God's throne.</note>—that is, the most sublime contemplations. Eleazar replied: "I have not yet grown gray" <note>original: "לא קשתי" (lo kashiti).</note>, as if to say, "I am not yet an old man." For that wise disciple and youth of precocious genius knew that those who are not yet fit or suitable for such sublime and high wisdom are those whose fires of desire have not yet settled and whose youthful heat has not yet cooled. They must be advanced in years, yet grow old with a certain natural integrity. For what benefit would old age bring, unless it added integrity and a constant uprightness of life? 

Therefore, I would wish that no one believe those men to be true theologians—no matter how old they are or how much "contentious talkativeness" they possess—who are defiled by any kind of vice: pride, hypocrisy, greed, hatred, envy, and (often hidden under a cloak of religion) lust. Such men follow animalistic affections while neglecting the light of the mind. Solomon agrees with my opinion, saying: *A perverse man is an abomination to God.* This is he who, having turned away from the heights, inclines toward the downward slopes, no matter how much nature has raised him toward the high things. 

Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazel," the 11th-century Persian philosopher and theologian.</note>—your fellow countryman, Marrano <note>Simon is addressing a companion here.</note>—did not ignore this. He showed that these contrary motions in the soul, pulling upward and downward, are most unhappy for a learned man. In his book *On Divine Science*, he demonstrates that the strongest and most fearful torment in the soul arises from the conflict of these attracting impressions. Thus, besides vices, secular affairs also pervert and turn us away: perhaps parents, a wife, children, household matters, friends, enemies, accidents, events, and any number of requirements of kin do not allow human strength to ascend to the highest steps of understanding. 

But suppose that for any of you, there is nothing within us to hinder us; imagine our natural talent is happy and fortunate, and there is no shadow of madness or foolishness. Suppose everything is ready and helps us to take up the highest matters, so that no one can rightly complain of our fragility. Even so, will not the very obscurity of divine things deter many? It is higher than heaven, deeper than hell, and cannot be tracked by sense or reason. Unlike other sciences, it does not receive light from our studies, but brings light with it. From its own storehouse, it radiates and shines upon men who are not unworthy. Yet, it does not prostitute itself everywhere of its own accord as something "useful," nor does it offer itself in a common way; rather, it requires our will and prior human knowledge...

<summary>Simon discusses the limitations of Aristotelian logic and the ten categories, arguing that while they help classify the physical world, true theology requires a purified, mature soul and divine illumination. He emphasizes that mystical knowledge (the Work of the Chariot) should only be studied by those who have outgrown youthful passions and worldly distractions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speaker Simon’s discourse on the limits of human reason. He has previously argued that while human logic and the Aristotelian categories can classify the physical world, they fall short of grasping divine truths, which require a different mode of reception.</meta>

# CABALA

...instituted very elegantly, not strongly resistant, it is drawn in, just as if blunt iron, as Solomon says, and if it has not been polished beforehand, it will be sharpened with much labor, and after industry, wisdom will follow. For those things which are carried forward from the senses to the intellect are gathered by a certain diligence of studies and artificial reason; but beyond that, those things which reach from the intellect to the mind and to its light, put on a quasi-divine person, and lack a human idol <note>In this context, "idol" refers to a mental image or representation (from the Greek *eidolon*). Divine truth is seen directly, not through a conceptual "image."</note>, so that nothing can be thought by us more profoundly than them. 

Therefore, the same Solomon seemed to have groaned over this matter when he said: "A high deep" or "deep deep" (for so it is read in Hebrew <note>original: "עמֹק עמֹק" (Amok Amok) from Ecclesiastes 7:24.</note>), "who shall find it?" He did not say, "who shall have it?" for some have had it. But "who shall find it?" as if it were difficult, but not in every way impossible, because the Lord gives wisdom, and "blessed are those who find her," as it says in the sacred oracles. It is the lot of few, therefore, to find her, and indeed of those blessed ones upon whom, not by their own merits but by the gift of God, the splendor of such venerable light shines. 

Truly, I think there is no one who does not know that it is not for the multitude to hear the words of God; wherefore they cried out to Moses, "Speak you to us and we will hear, let not God speak to us." "You," they say, "you we will hear": which Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert and author of the Targum Onkelos, the authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> translates as *Nekabel* <note>original: "נקבל" (Nekabel), meaning "we will receive" or "we will accept."</note>. Wherefore in the Chapters of the Fathers <note>The *Pirkei Avot*, a compilation of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period.</note> it is read thus: *Mose kibel*, that is, "Moses heard and received the law from Sinai." 

From this *Kabala* is named, a "reception from hearing." This I think should be noted and stored in a mindful soul: that out of such a great multitude of men, and so many saints, Moses himself was the one destined to receive the recognition of truth and equity from the mouth of God, and besides him, no other. For so that Cabalist, Azariel Bar Solomon of Gerona <note>Azriel of Gerona (c. 1160–1238), a central figure in the early development of Kabbalah in Spain.</note>, writes: <margin>A</margin> 

*לא כל הנביאים היו יכולים לשמוע הדיבור השכינה כי אם משה* 
<note>original Hebrew: "Not all the prophets were able to hear the speech of the Divine Presence except Moses."</note>

Which is: "Indeed, not all prophets were powerful enough to hear the speech from the mouth of God, except *Moses*."

You, therefore, most excellent men, whose minds are wonderfully bound to my love for you by our common studies, easily perceive from these things which have escaped me in passing, that the Cabala is a thing most necessary for the human race, granted from heaven, without which no one can attain so rare, so difficult an apprehension of Divine things. These certainly are not subject to the proofs of mortal reasons, nor to the thorny contentions of empty words, nor to human syllogisms because of their Divinity. On the contrary, they are so great, so grand, so infinite, that in one human age, or (if you like) in several, they cannot be overcome by any labor, however tireless, even if the years of our life should extend for many centuries, while we are clearly breathing in this mud, in this clay and cement of a thick body, and presuming everything by corporeal sense. For the wise Masters of the Hebrews say:

*כי להגיד כח מעשה בראשית לבשר ודם אי אפשר*
<note>original Hebrew: "For to tell the power of the Work of Creation to flesh and blood is impossible."</note>

Which is, to explain the power of the work of *Bresith* <note>original: *Bereshit* (Genesis), referring to the "Work of Creation," the study of the physical world's origins.</note> to flesh and blood is impossible. How much more so concerning the *Mercaua* <note>original: *Merkavah* (Chariot), referring to the "Work of the Chariot," the study of the divine realm and God's throne.</note>. Therefore, we must do as singular technicians and craftsmen are accustomed to doing when teaching. Let us believe each person skilled in his own art. For the logician believes concerning the part of speech received from the 

<column-break/>

Grammarian, the Rhetorician takes the places of arguments from the logician, the Poet and orator from the musician, the Geometer borrows proportions from the Arithmetician, and Astronomy trusts in mathematical numbers, figures, and dimensions. Supernatural things <note>referring to Metaphysics.</note> use the conjecture of natural things. And every higher science rightly presumes from the statutes of the lower ones, attempting to prove none of those things which it has heard to be established by any prior art, but freely believes what is said, lest the whole life of men fail <margin>B</margin> before even the smallest reason of a single discipline can be perfectly investigated. 

If this is done in human affairs, and in quasi-cheaper and sedentary crafts, so that they receive by hearing and believe those men whom they judge to be endowed with singular learning above others, shall we think that in the science of the highest and divine things—which not even one or two of us can hardly reach by our own strength—the tradition and reception of holy men is to be despised? This is what is called *Cabala* in Hebrew. 

For <margin>C</margin> Cabala is a symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the salvific contemplation of God and of separate forms <note>Philosophical term for angels or purely spiritual beings that exist without physical matter.</note>; those who obtain this by a heavenly inspiration are rightly called "Cabalici": their disciples we shall call by the name "Cabalæi," and those who otherwise attempt to imitate them are to be named "Cabalists": just like those sweating with daily labor over their published discourses. 

Indeed, Philolaus, *Marranus* says: if it is permitted by you, I think this Jew has embraced in one bundle whatever could be said of Cabala with Nestorian eloquence <note>A classical reference to King Nestor of Pylos, known in Homer's epics for his persuasive, honey-sweet speech.</note>, <margin>D</margin> so that we may thoroughly learn what the name itself designates, and from where it arises; whether there is anything of this sort in nature or in human use which they call Cabala; finally, for what cause or for what purpose it is so, to what extent and for what it is useful, and how necessary it seems to be for divine contemplation, and how much is possible for a suitable man preparing himself for it. Who ought to be called a Cabalicus, who a Cabalæus, and who a Cabalista? What need is there for <margin>E</margin> words? From head to heel he is to be praised in this: that he pours no darkness over the eyes. 

Then Philolaus said: You have untied the rope, *Marrane*, having entered a great and hardly navigable sea; you are not yet sailing in port, and those things which this Simon has depicted as if on a small tablet, you seem to see through a mist, and to look at through the middle of a cloud: for we have not yet been brought even to the doors of that art. Therefore, my Simon, most contemplative of the Hebrews, we shall love you if you proceed further; for so far you have <margin>F</margin> profited us no more than to provide an occasion for thinking more broadly about the Cabalistic art: what that thing is which was revealed, who revealed it, who received it, what benefit that reception brings, what is the mode of this art, through which (as the rumor is) miracles are performed: for that last point brought me here from afar. 

I shall take issue, Simon said, first of all with that "Nestorian eloquence" of which I am accused by Marranus. For in my judgment, that would be a reproach to me as both a Philosopher and a Jew, as if I were a lover of <margin>G</margin> flattery; since eloquence cannot be contained in such brevity of speech—for it requires an abundance of both words and things—and it is not the custom among us Jews to pursue the deceptive colors of speaking. For we have learned to speak properly, not "eloquently" under the rod, and the truth of the cause...

<summary>Simon defines Cabala as a "symbolic reception" of divine truth that transcends human logic, tracing its origin to Moses receiving the Law at Sinai. The dialogue explores the necessity of trusting in sacred tradition for divine matters, just as one trusts experts in human sciences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Simon, a practitioner of the Cabala, and his companions Philolaus and Marranus. ### BOOK ONE

...we seek truth more than the ornament of speech. But I will finish in a few words what you so greatly desire, lest I leave you—exhausted by so many and such dangerous travels—dangling in mind as if yawning at the twists and turns of trifles. For after you have heard without any apparent boredom by what tracks and signs, and with what "dogs," as it were, I have hunted down and caught the definition of Cabala, I would not have you err regarding the name itself. 

Certain Sophists <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to academic theologians who rely on rigid logic and wordplay rather than spiritual insight.</note>, worthy of mockery, have falsely asserted through their own rashness—or, if you prefer, their negligence in learning—that "Cabala" was a diabolical and heretical man. From this, they claim all Cabalists are heretics. (I pray you, restrain your laughter if you can, though it is a great absurdity; I wish these monsters and portents of men would stop making us laugh!) 

Therefore, I shall conveniently bring forth those things about whose certainty you asked me, having first warned you that Cabala is not to be sought by the crude touch of the senses, nor by the overbearing arguments of logical artifice. Its foundation is established in the third region of knowledge, where neither urgent judgment, nor evident proof, nor demonstrating syllogism holds sway; indeed, where human reason itself does not dominate. Rather, it is a nobler form of knowledge, where the light of the mind falling upon the intellect moves a free will to believe. For those things perceived by the sense are below knowledge and more certain than reason; but those things which the mind pours in, we place above knowledge, just as they are more solid than rational discourse. 

I have paused and lingered a little while, lest you think such divine matters are subject to the inventions of human fragility and the so-called "logical rules." Forgive me, friends, I am not asserting premeditated thoughts, but as other causes intervene, I draw one thing from another. For now I hasten to that which you want: what is that thing? What has been revealed? No one will get me to think that you have proposed this concerning every revelation of all things believed (which seem almost infinite), but rather: what is that primary, universal, and principal revelation of divinity, into which every single revelation of divine things is directed and reduced? 

"Certainly that is the very thing," said Philolaus. Then Simon replied: "Rightly so; and it is indeed nothing other than the universal restoration of the human race after the primordial ruin, which is called by us *Yeshua* <note>original: "ישוע"</note>, and by the Latins 'Salvation'. The first revelation of this very thing was made to our species—if I weigh the universal beginning of the world exactly—and there was none prior to it. For Adam, not seized by a dream as if prophesying, spoke about his wife after his deep sleep: 'This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.' But sensing himself to have fewer ribs on the other side upon waking, and after he had made a circuit to all the living creatures of the earth, sea, and air one by one, he suddenly beheld Eve. A robust young man, he began to burn with mutual desire and be filled with a generative longing for the young girl with a full face, lovely appearance, charming countenance, and endowed with human energy—feelings he had not felt toward any other animal. For so says Eleazar, our Master, and Solomon, the ordinary commentator on the Sacred Scriptures:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <gloss>Adam came to every beast and animal, and his mind was not satisfied with them until he came to the woman.</gloss> <note>This is a reference to a passage in the Talmud (Yebamot 63a) discussing Adam's search for a companion.</note> That is to say: "That Adam came to every beast and animal, and his sense was not moved by them until he had come to his wife." 

From these words—alas for the faith of men!—a twisted crime has occurred through the malice of perverse men (if they even be men, and not rather incarnate devils and furies to be feared), who are prepared to stir up sedition in Christianity against us. Though we live innocently and peacefully according to the laws of the emperors, they are ready to incite any kind of injury. Often elsewhere, and recently in this very city, they have falsely interpreted the words of our Masters, explaining them thus: "That Adam then foully copulated with all the beasts and animals." 

Good God! What audacity from such most foul scoundrels, aided by the assent and favor of infantile Sophists! For the word *ba* <note>original: "בא"</note> never signifies the intercourse of lust according to the property of the Hebrew language, even if <margin>C</margin> sometimes, by a certain metaphor, it is understood to mean female copulation out of modest shame when the subject matter requires it—as in Genesis chapter 16: "Go in <note>original: "בא"</note> to my maid, if perhaps at least from her I may receive children." In that place, *ba* means "Go in to the maid"; it did not say "Copulate with the maid." Which is not the same here, to such an extent that it cannot be accepted similarly even by the most wicked men, because of the impossibility of the matter being discussed. <margin>D</margin> For surely, how could it be understood that so great and significant a man as Adam sexually copulated with a gnat, a flea, a fly, or a cricket? 

I have recounted these things for this reason: so that no credit be given to these and suchlike forgers—slanderous, cursed, and most fickle defectors—either in this or any other part, concerning the Sacred Scripture which they do not know. 

I return to where I digressed. By the instigation of nature, therefore, when both were alone in the world, the man felt that the woman <margin>E</margin> belonged to him; yet this was not yet "Cabala." Furthermore, it was a mark of a singular and most sharp genius that the first-formed man, already Lord of the world, added a name to each thing by a spontaneous designation, by which we may know it was an act of will, not of nature. Nor was it without reason that, after the transgression of the law, he feared the penalty of death threatened in the warning—which he judged by the guidance of reason would not be bodily, <margin>F</margin> because he did not feel himself die as soon as he had eaten from the tree. Therefore, according to Ramban <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman (Nachmanides), a 13th-century philosopher and Cabalist.</note>, he understood it as "dying in sin," just as we Cabalists understand it. 

Now, in all these things, I ask, what is to be thought of as having been divine revelation? Certainly we have found nothing so far that everyone has not passively doubted, either by the counsel of reason or the movement of sense. But that most destructive transgression of the law, that great insult against God the Best and Greatest, that hostile rashness, that contagious lust, that earthy and poisonous plague, <margin>G</margin> that toxic and foul corruption of the human race—sitting in the tunnels of the veins and creeping into posterity with the very flow of the seed in a continuous passage—by what way or in what manner could it be expiated and averted? No thought of human fragility was strong enough to find the answer.

### THE CABALA

<margin>A</margin> ...to conceive through presumed action. Here, I say, here at the brink of imminent despair—a disease than which nothing is more destructive—there was need of an effective remedy through divine revelation. For God, the Creator, had not entirely deserted His own handiwork, but instilled a certain hope that it would not be impossible for this very crime, however immense and committed against infinite majesty, to be abolished, removed, and extinguished in the fullness of time. God therefore said to the Angels in the hearing of Adam: *And now, lest he put forth his hand and take also*
<margin>B</margin> *of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever*; and the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of pleasure <note>original: "paradiso voluptatis," referring to the Garden of Eden</note>. This was the last voice the wretched man heard from the mouth of God as he was being driven from the garden. Yet, amidst such great sorrows and griefs, he received from his Creator that firm hope: that so horrible a sentence would, by God’s mercy, become revocable in the course of time. The words of the oracle indicated this to him, for He said: *Now*, or *Already, lest he put forth his hand and take from the tree of life*. Truly, it was not in vain that God added the word
<margin>C</margin> *now* (or *already*), by which the present time is designated, suggesting that the sentence would not be perpetual. Instead, an abolition of it could be obtained in a future time, if ever a man destined to eat from the tree of life should come. This was so even though Adam suspected that as long as his spirit ruled his limbs, he would pay the penalty irrevocably, because God was no longer with him on the day after next <note>original: "perendie," meaning the third day or a future time</note> to speak face to face as He was accustomed. This was now a sign of indignation, and of a mind alienated from Adam; for He, the Creator of all things, who previously spoke with every living thing and beast,
<margin>D</margin> now deigned not to speak mouth-to-mouth with a sinful man. Yet, lest the most merciful Father leave him utterly destitute of all consolation, He immediately sent an Angel from whom Adam might more fully learn the future restoration of such a great ruin. For thus the Cabalists write in their commentaries on the book *Yetzirah* <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," a foundational text of Jewish mysticism</note>: *That the fathers' teachers were known angels* <note>original Hebrew: שהאבות רבותיהם היו מלאכים ידועים</note>,
<margin>E</margin> that is, *Adam's teacher was Raziel* <note>original Hebrew: רבותיו של אדם רזיאל</note>. This angel, by the nod of the Most High God, showed him the way of expiation and explained the divine speech as something to be received through allegory, according to the Cabalistic manner. In this tradition, not only is no word placed in vain, but not even a letter—however minute and thin—nor even a single stroke <note>original: "apex," referring to the small decorative crowns or points on Hebrew letters</note> is without purpose. But I call upon you, *Philolaus*, and you, *Marranus*—men most learned among the learned—grant me this pardon: that perhaps my religion would have prohibited me from
<margin>F</margin> betraying such recondite and secret things to those outside our sect and those not initiated into the Jewish rite. For the knowledge of these things—as God loves me—is often and greatly denied even to our own disciples, so that it is scarcely permitted to find them in rare books, even then wrapped in coverings and enigmas. For thus it is read in the Talmud: *The secrets of the Law are not handed over except to a counselor, a wise master of arts, and one who understands a whisper* <note>original Hebrew: אין מוסריב סתרי תורה אלא ליועץ וחכם חרשים ונבון לחש. This refers to the restricted transmission of mystical knowledge</note>.
<margin>G</margin> Therefore, shall I say more, or keep silent? The prohibitions of the masters, as well as the immense ardor of both of you (inflamed, as I believe, by a divine fire) to examine the highest things, make me hesitate not a little. Yet, I will boldly proceed...

<column-break/>

### THE CABALA

<margin>A</margin> ...being more indulgent to myself, I will temper the harshness of the precepts. For I see that the light of the sun is dispersed without discrimination upon all who remove the barrier. I shall speak—albeit quite inelegantly according to the custom of our people—yet as best I can, those things which I have received as being spoken by most learned and wise men and left behind in divinely inspired writings. I shall nonetheless explain that most secret discourse held by the Creator of the world with the blessed Angels in the inner chambers of His divinity. For God said:
<margin>B</margin> *Behold, Adam is become as one of us* <note>Genesis 3:22</note>. He did not say "one of you," but *one of us*. For in you Angels, there is number and "otherness" <note>original: "alteritas," the state of being diverse or separate</note>. In *Us*—that is, in God—there is infinite, eternal, most simple, and most absolute unity. Nor can that "one" which might exist in Angels be like the Unity in God. Therefore, God did not count the Angels with Himself when He spoke of unity, since it is contradictory for anything to be "one" in nature with both God and Angels; such is the distance between the Creator and the creature.
<margin>C</margin> What, then, is this that He says: *Behold, Adam is like one of us*? From this we certainly infer that there is another, a certain *Heavenly Adam*, shown to the Angels in heaven, who is "one" from God, whom He had made by His Word; and that there is another *Earthly Adam*, rejected by God, whom He had formed from mud with His hands and driven from the garden. The former is one with God; the latter is not only "other," but indeed different and a separate thing from God. Thus, after the miserable fall of the human race, God taught His Angels about the restoration of
<margin>D</margin> salvation that would eventually come, and through whom it would come. Indeed, He taught not as much as He Himself could teach, but as much as the Angelic condition could grasp, demonstrating in their presence who it was that would redeem the human race. For then the salvation of men had been clearly predestined. Wherefore He said: *Behold, this is that Adam who not only exists essentially after the birth of the world and of yourselves, but who also was "one of us" in eternity before all creation, before time began.* This is what *Onkelos* <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note>
<margin>E</margin> interprets in Chaldaic thus: *Behold, Adam was my only-begotten (or unique one) in eternity from myself* <note>original Aramaic: הא אדם יהיה יחידי בעלמא מניה</note>. This is the same term God uses to Abraham, saying: *Take your only-begotten son*. And when He had already indicated the person of the future Redeemer to the Angels, lest they think that He would soon, in a perfunctory way, avert the hatred of such a wicked crime by some sudden intercession, He immediately removed all doubt and deferred the business into the future, adding: *And now, in this present time, lest this my
<margin>F</margin> unique one who subsists from myself in eternity put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life.* By this He suggested that what He prohibited from happening *now*, He would one day grant. By this they prudently understood that although not now, yet later, in the course of time, this ruin caused by the fruit of the tree would be repaired by that *Heavenly Adam* who is co-eternal with God. Therefore, all the hosts of heaven standing by the Lord of the universe as He sat upon His throne—at His right hand and at His left, as *Micah* says—
<margin>G</margin> gave thanks for such great clemency toward the weakness of mortals. The Angel *Raziel* was therefore sent to the fallen and grief-stricken Adam to console him, to whom he spoke thus: "Do not be consumed beyond measure by groaning and distress because you..."

<meta>This page continues the discourse by Simon the Cabalist, following the account of the Fall of Man. He is explaining how the first promise of a redeemer—the "first Cabala"—was given to Adam and passed down through the early generations of Genesis, from Abel and Seth to Enos.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...the human race fell into the deepest perdition. Because this original sin will be expiated. For from your lineage a just and peaceful man will be born, a heroic man, whose name will contain, amidst his mercies, even these four letters **I. H. V. H.** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew</note> and he, through right faith and a peaceful offering, will stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and the fruit of that tree will be the salvation of all who hope. When this speech was finished, that condemned and wretched Adam, amidst all the miseries into which he had fallen—amidst the pain and the mourning with which he had been afflicted in such great calamity—conceived a hope of changing his transgression by trusting in God. Therefore, moved by an incredible love toward his Maker, he gave thanks for the grace of divine mercy. This was the very first **Cabala** <note>original: "Cabala," meaning "reception" or "tradition"</note>, the primordial messenger of salvation. O pleasing thing! O desirable cause! What could be more beneficial? What more acceptable? What could be brought from the heavens more opportune for the lost condition of mortals? What help could be more suitably provided than to announce public salvation to the captives? This is that most holy and supreme revelation into which all divine revelations are led back; this is the most longed-for tradition, this the most healthful reception, in which all Cabalistic receptions are recapitulated, all traditions of divine things, all teachings of heavenly things, and the visions of prophets and meditations of the blessed are united and communicated. For this reason, when Adam had openly reported these individual things to his wife, he began to sacrifice to God at an altar he had erected, in the presence of his wife, for the commemoration of posterity and the giving of thanks. For so our Masters have handed down: **There Adam the first man offered a young bull** <note>original Hebrew: "שם אדם הראשון הקריב שור פר"</note>. But Eve, now the future mother of the living, her despair removed, finally having been known by her husband, conceived and bore her firstborn. Whereupon, infused with immense and incredible joy because she thought a savior had soon been born to her, she exclaimed: **I have acquired a man from the Lord** <note>original Hebrew: "קניתי איש את יהוה" (Genesis 4:1). In Cabalistic thought, she believes she has birthed the bearer of the Divine Name</note>. That is, "I have acquired that man of the four letters," which letters they had already received from the Angel; and she named the one acquired Cain. When the parents recognized that he was, contrary to hope, perverse in his wicked character, they began a second birth and begot Abel. When both sons were adolescents, they passed on this Cabala to them—that is, the reception by hearing concerning the restoration of salvation—which was then ardently loved by Abel, but vilely despised by Cain. Indeed, Abel was led by the opinion that he himself might be that same one for whom they expected the revealed restoration. Since he felt himself pleasing to God through right faith and an accepted offering—because the Lord had looked upon him and his gifts, but did not look upon Cain and his gifts—he began with his whole heart and the affection of his mind to desire the fruit of the tree, which he judged to be established in the offering of life. For that reason, it was called the tree of life, and so named because it was the wood of life to be offered to the Creator who gave it. Therefore, he attempted to stretch out his hand to it, so that he might take from the wood, consume it, and abolish it; for this is what **Abel** <note>original Hebrew: "אבל" (Hevel), which the text here links to the concept of mourning or vanishing/abolishing</note> designates. Hence he patiently bore his brother's hatred against him, and to the one seeking an occasion for a quarrel, even when he was vehemently angry, he did not expostulate with smooth words

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> to mitigate him, but remained entirely silent. And when he saw death threatening him from Cain, who had snatched a branch from the tree or a wooden club, he rejoiced greatly, hoping to be killed by the wood. For the use of iron did not yet exist before the birth of Tubalcain, who was the first hammerer and smith in all works of bronze and iron. Armed therefore with a very large wooden club, Cain said to Abel his brother... And it happened when they were in the field that Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. The Romans <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate or Western traditions</note> add by reading: Cain said, 

<margin>B</margin> "Let us go outside," which is not in the context of the Holy Scripture <note>a reference to the Masoretic Hebrew text vs. the Samaritan/Septuagint/Vulgate versions</note>. Abel, however, being unarmed, did not resist the armed man, but willingly and gladly offered himself to death. He was prepared not only to satisfy God the creditor on our behalf, but even to pay the original debt entirely, if it were possible, and to be presented as an acceptable, devoted, and appointed victim in payment. After he had died without children, Adam waited for a long time, hoping perhaps that what he had not found in his sons might happen in his grandsons. But what could he now hope for in the reprobate generation of Cain, 

<margin>C</margin> from which all confidence had long ago vanished? He saw that they were all intent on sedentary arts and crafts, performing work with servile zeal, pursuing meager comforts and duties necessary for the body, thinking nothing divine, nothing noble, nothing worthy of a heroic man. Therefore, he sought and obtained another offspring and another seed from God, by which the most pious father was gladdened beyond what can be said, saying: "God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." And therefore he called his name Seth, whom 

<margin>D</margin> he begot in his own image and likeness—not because his other children did not have human form and image, for they were also men, but because the generation of the rest until now, except for Abel, ought rather to have been called a generation of demons than of men, on account of their execrable malice and detestable vices. It is not, therefore, that he had begotten substantive demons and devils (as certain impious and profane people lie), but that he was evil by will. 

<margin>E</margin> Nothing is evil except vice and the demonic. I will proceed, then, if you wish, further along the door through which I entered. And they said: "Proceed diligently, we beseech you." Again Simon said: Our father Adam again received a grandson from Seth. Mindful of that Cabala which Raziel <note>In Jewish lore, Raziel is the angel who gave Adam a book of secrets</note> had delivered to him—that from his propagation a man would be born as a future savior—therefore he was called Enos, which means "man." At that time it was thought, and indeed 

<margin>F</margin> greatly hoped, that he would be called according to the angelic Cabala by the name of four letters **I. H. V. H.**, or at least, more Cabalistically, "in mercies" through the letter **S** <note>the Hebrew letter Shin: ש</note> in the middle of the four letters **I. H. V. H.** <note>This refers to the Christian Cabalistic name of Jesus, *Yeheshuah* (I-H-Sh-V-H), formed by inserting Shin into the Tetragrammaton</note>. For so it is written in the sacred history: **Then it was begun to call upon the name of the Lord** <note>original Hebrew: "אז הוחל לקרא בשם יהוה" (Genesis 4:26)</note>, which the Latins read not very learnedly as "He began to invoke the name of the Lord." But certain rare and most contemplative Cabalists interpret it more correctly regarding the property of the language, thus according to **ghematria** <note>a system of assigning numerical value to words</note>: "Then he was 

<margin>G</margin> expected to be called through the letter **S** <note>Shin</note>," which in the Cabalistic art is the same as **in miseries** <note>original Hebrew: "ביסורים"</note> (or mercies); and the letter **S** through **notariacon** <note>a system of shorthand or using letters of a word as an acronym</note> designates **in the midst** <note>original Hebrew: "בתוך"</note>, namely, in the middle of those four letters **I. H. V. H.** It should be understood in this way: **Then...** <note>The text cuts off at the catchword "Then" (אז)</note>

# CABALÆ

**"Then it was begun to call upon the name of the LORD"** <note>Hebrew: *Huchal likro be-shem Yehovah* (Genesis 4:26). The author interprets this as the beginning of a specific mystical invocation.</note>: that is, then it was expected that he would be called through the letter **Shin** <note>original: "Sin," referring to the Hebrew letter ש (Shin)</note> placed in the middle of the name **I. H. V. H.**, as if for the sake of the Angel's announcement, Enos might take from the **tree of life** and redeem the world. He himself was named a hero: **I. H.** in mercies **V. H.** Mark well this secret and attend to the mystery. But when he was not yet called in this way by the appointment of any Angel, they left that path and placed their hope in another. For by the warning of the Angels—that is, the messengers of God—names were bestowed upon the fathers for various events: whether past, as **Cain** was named "because I have possessed"; or present, as **Enos** was named "because he is a man"; or future, as **Abel** was named "because he would bring mourning to his parents."

This expectation was drawn down into the fourth generation of Enos, and from Jared was born **Enoch**, who walked with God but disappeared, because God took him. Three generations from there came **Noah**, for the public consolation of all—that salvation received by hearing and hoped for by right faith, of whom out of the entire multitude only eight were found who pleased God. For Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God; he received the command to make an **ark of wood**, in which he might save the world. **Cabalistically**, therefore, he hoped in the wood, for so Job says: **"For there is hope for a tree"** <note>Hebrew: *Ki yesh la-etz tikvah* (Job 14:7). The author punningly links "tree/wood" (*etz*) to the wood of the Ark and the Tree of Life.</note>; having been made certain of this fate, that life had been promised to man in the wood.

But after his drunkenness, confusion followed. From this, **Babel** received its name, which is now **Babylon**, from *Balbel*, which in Chaldean <note>A term often used for Aramaic in this period</note> means "confusion." This arose under the family and children of Noah. His sons were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. To the future servant of God, **Shem**, in whom he hoped for salvation above the others, Noah gave this blessing: **"Blessed be the Lord God of Shem"** <note>Hebrew: *Baruch Yehovah Elohei Shem* (Genesis 9:26)</note>. This is translated **Cabalistically** as: *Blessed be the four-letter Name of the God of Shem.* Through this, the Cabalists say: **"The LORD made known that Shem was a servant of God"** <note>Hebrew: *Hodia Yehovah Shem oved ha-Elohim*</note>, as Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nahmanides</note> writes. By this we understand that the desire of the pious father was that Shem should be blessed with the invocation of the four letters **I. H. V. H.**, so that he might become the redeemer of original sin.

But even then, the time appointed by God had not yet come in which the restoration of so great a fall should occur; the Angel **Jophiel** announced this to Shem himself. For the Cabalists write: **"The teacher of Shem himself was Jophiel"** <note>Hebrew: *Rabbo shel Shem Yofiel*</note>. Those ages, therefore, suspended their thoughts upon such reflections until the years of **Abraham**, son of Terah, who was first named Abram. That man had a certain familiar Angel, **Zadkiel**; for so the Cabalists write: **"The teacher of Abraham was Zadkiel"** <note>Hebrew: *Rabbo shel Avraham Tzadkiel*</note>. He delivered the same **Cabala** to the recipient as the Angel Raziel had delivered to Adam, the first-formed. 

Finally (as I judge), the rest is not unknown: that for as long a time as he had been called **Abram**, and his wife **Sarai**, they had never begotten an heir for themselves. But after the man’s name was changed to **Abraham**, and the wife’s name to **Sarah**, they soon received their son **Isaac**. When God commanded him concerning Isaac—that he should take his only son whom he loved and sacrifice him upon a certain high mountain upon **wood**—it seems incredible with what joy and great gladness he exulted, mindful of the divine

<margin>A</margin> promise, by which God pledged to him in these words: "I will establish," He said, "my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations as an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you, and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." Therefore, the salvation of the human collective, which we have spoken of, he trusted he would bring about through his son. He took him up suddenly at the voice of God, and he himself cut all the **wood** for the offering with his own <margin>B</margin> hands. 

Indeed, the oracle taught that the original fall could be repaired through **wood**. Whence the Scripture says that Abraham took the wood of the offering and laid it upon Isaac his son, and placed him upon the altar on the pile of wood, and stretched out his hand and snatched up the sword to sacrifice his son. For unless Isaac had received from his father the handed-down **Cabala** of human salvation through the **tree of life** and the future offering of a certain just man, then—since it is naturally horrific for all living things to die—he certainly would not have embraced the death seen before his eyes with such benevolence, <margin>C</margin> such a ready countenance, and such cheerfulness of soul. Rather, as is the condition of mortals, he would have either dodged the drawn blade or at least mitigated his father’s severity with some gentler words, or fled. Yet, suspecting that he himself might be the one through whom the restoration of the primordial ruin would occur, he considered nothing more pleasant than that sacrifice, and nothing sweeter than that death, for the sake of which he believed he might redeem the whole human race.

<margin>D</margin> This very hope was made even firmer for him because God had destined that same place for sacrifices since the founding of the world. For the land of **Moriah** was pointed out to Abraham by the finger of God; it was there that the first **Adam** built an altar and offered gifts to God, and where **Cain** and **Abel**, and where **Noah** and his sons sacrificed. So our Masters dispute in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*, with the agreement of **Ramban** <note>Nahmanides</note> and **Rabbi Joseph son of Carnitol** <note>Joseph Gikatilla, author of *Sha'are Orah*</note> in the book *The Gates of Justice*; and in that same place the holy city of **Jerusalem** was built, as **Solomon the Gaul** <note>Rashi (Rabbi Solomon Isaac)</note> testifies. 

<margin>E</margin> However, when the task was left unfinished and the father and son departed from Moriah, the voice of **Zadkiel** was heard speaking to Abraham: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." By this, it was known that universal salvation was deferred to a future generation. And the very voice of God through the Angel **Raphael** fell from heaven upon Isaac also: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed"—lest perhaps he should believe that he himself was that savior. For this also belongs to the Cabalists, who write: <margin>F</margin> **"The teacher of Isaac himself was Raphael"** <note>Hebrew: *Rabbo shel Yitzchak Rafael*</note>. 

That man [Isaac] had no hope for one of his sons, who had already lost his father's blessing through his preoccupation with hunting; his name was **Esau**. Regarding the other son, the father, having promised great things to himself, predicted with these words a prophecy of the coming reality: "Peoples shall serve you and nations shall bow down to you." It was not without cause, therefore, that such a vast expectation of universal salvation was held by our ancestors regarding **Jacob** (for so that son was named). It was because <margin>G</margin> he was the first of all mortals to see the **gate of heaven** opened, and a **ladder** stretched from earth to heaven, and the four letters **I. H. V. H.** standing upon it, which he desired in his prayers to take hold of. He also saw the consonant **Shin** through the **Notariacon** <note>A Cabalistic method of using letters as acronyms</note> for the word **Oil** <note>Hebrew: *Shemen* (Oil/Anointing), which begins with the letter Shin. The author likely links this to the concept of the "Anointed One" or Messiah.</note>...

The suspicion grew because the Angel Peliel was an intimate of Jacob, who forewarned him of many things through constant inspiration and speech: both because God chose Jacob for Himself, and because "blessed shall he be whose help is the God of Jacob." Moreover, the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystical scholars who study the hidden meanings of the Torah.</note> write thus: <term>The teacher of Jacob was Peliel</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבו של יעקב פליאל</note>. But having been taught by his Angel, Jacob realized that he himself would not be that savior whom the heavenly Cabala had thus far preferred; by divine revelation, he deferred the matter to another age, saying: "Gather yourselves together, and I will tell you what shall happen in the last of days: The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a lawgiver from his thigh, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the gathering of the nations." By this prophecy, it became known that someone would eventually be the savior of the human race, who would be born from Judah in the last of days, and would be *Shiloh*, and would carry the scepter of the kingdom, and the nations would flow to him. Therefore, after these Patriarchs, the great Moses did not offer himself voluntarily to death—as Abel once did, or as Isaac long ago—but he refused and wished to withdraw himself from the care of the people, even though he spoke with God as a friend with a friend, face to face, and used a staff for a scepter, and the entire nation of the Jews flowed to him. Yet he knew he was not from the family of Judah, but born of the house of Levi, nor was he born in the last of days; nor was he *Shiloh*, which according to the Syriac translation of *Onkelos* the Chaldean <note>An influential 2nd-century translation/paraphrase of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> signifies "the anointed one," whom we call the *Messiah*. Nevertheless, concerning the whole reason and manner of restoring the state from the original fall, he was more than sufficiently instructed by his Angel, *Metattron*. This tradition was received from the fathers and passed down through succession to the college of the prophets, who all individually conferred among themselves in daily study concerning the golden age of the *Messiah*, exulting with the greatest joy in that blessed school of the Holy Spirit. They brought forth their joys from the bottom of their hearts, connected by a single bond of fellowship in the *Messiah* the savior himself. Although they spoke of that same coming king at different times and in many different ways, each one nevertheless arrived at a similar and clearly consistent conclusion. One indeed said in these words: "I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send." Another, in the person of the *Messiah*, said: "Send me," which is <term>Sent</term> <note>original Hebrew: שלוח (Shiloach)</note>. In the arithmetic progression <note>Referring to Gematria, where letters have numerical values.</note> through the art of the Cabala, according to the tradition of Raziel mentioned above, this word also signifies the proper name of that *Messiah* through the equality of the number three hundred and ninety-eight. And another thus: "Unto you that fear my name, the sun of justice shall arise." Why do I linger over many examples? All rejoiced with one heart; all with one mouth spoke and praised all the good things of that day of the savior, and desired that time of which David cried out before God: <margin>C</margin> "Send out thy light and thy truth; they have led me and brought me unto thy holy mountain, and into thy tabernacles." Regarding that word "light," Rabbi Salomon Gallus <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famed French commentator.</note> said: "Thy light, that is the King *Messiah*," according to what is written: "I have prepared a lamp for my *Messiah*." It was therefore to be understood as another seed of his than the son of Bathsheba. For that Solomon loved women, by whom his heart was corrupted, so that he followed strange gods, nor was his heart perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father. Wherefore God raised up an adversary against Solomon, so that he who had only the name of peace should not have complete peace. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, as many Cabalists as there are who have turned the entirety of salvation toward Solomon, they intend a certain *other* Solomon than that Solomon who subjected the temple he built to the law of destruction, to whom God foretold: "The temple which I have sanctified to my name will I cast out of my sight." For this reason, they were not able to abolish original sin—neither this Solomon, nor this temple—however much it stands written by a Cabalist in the *Gate of Light* <note>The *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Cabalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>: <term>At the beginning of the creation of the world, the Shekhinah [Divine Presence] dwelt among the lower beings; and while the Shekhinah was below, heaven and earth were found to be one, and the sources and channels were acting in perfection and were drawn from above to below, and the Name, blessed be He, was found filling the heights...</term> <note>original Hebrew: בתחלת בריאתו של עולם שכינה הית' שרויה בתחתונים ובהיות השכינה למטה נמצאו שמים וארץ אחדים והיו המקורות והצינורות פועלים בשלימות ונמשכים מלמעלה למטה ונמצא השם ית' ממלא מעלה</note>

<meta>This page continues the historical and mystical lineage of the secret tradition. ### THE KABBALAH OF KABBALAHS

<margin>A</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "What happened when the first Adam came and sinned, the ranks were corrupted, the channels were broken, the pool ceased, the Divine Presence departed, and the bundle was separated; afterward Solomon came and built the House, and then the channels and the flows returned."</note> At the beginning of the world's creation, the <term>Divine Presence</term> <note>Shekhinah: the localized, indwelling presence of God on earth.</note> descended into the lower realms. While this Divine Presence was below, the heavens and the earth were found to be united; the springs and active channels were in perfection, drawing energy from the higher to the lower, and God was found filling both the heights and the depths. Then <margin>B</margin> Adam, the first man, came and sinned. The pathways of descent were torn down, the channels shattered, the aqueduct failed, the Divine Presence departed, and the holy fellowship was divided. Later, Solomon came and built the Temple; at that time, the channels, the flows, and the conduits were restored. 

When the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Mystics who study the hidden traditions of the Torah.</note> speak of Solomon here, they seem to be alluding to a reality rather than just a name. They understand this to refer to a certain "Peaceful King" to come, in accordance with the words of Isaiah, whom the Worker of Miracles himself shall name: Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the Future Age, <term>Prince of Peace</term> <note>original Hebrew: Sar Shalom</note>. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, some have thought King Hezekiah was meant here; but others, reading the following words—"His empire shall be multiplied, and of peace there shall be no end upon the throne of David"—understand it to refer to the King Messiah. He is the one who will take away the sins of all, which stir up daily wars and battles in the souls of men—those sins which our parents committed, as Jeremiah wrote in the Book of Lamentations: "Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities." 

<margin>D</margin> This was certainly the view of <term>Jonathan the Chaldean</term> <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of an ancient Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note>, who instead of "Prince of Peace," translated the passage as the <term>Messiah of Peace</term> <note>original Aramaic: Messiha di-Shelama</note>. Of him, Isaiah says again: "The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises and welts we are healed." This will be that true Solomon, who will erect a much more sublime Temple that is entirely eternal and indestructible. For thus the Cabalists write: <note>original Hebrew: "Because the house of the sanctuary below is set over against the house of the sanctuary above."</note> This means the earthly sanctuary is arranged to mirror the heavenly sanctuary.

From Solomon, the builder of that earthly temple, until King Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah—for both names share the same letters, though rearranged), the expectation of universal salvation was placed in the coming Messiah by the entire company of prophets: from Isaiah down to Malachi. Malachi said, "The Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple." Regarding this, <term>Rabbi David Kimhi</term> <note>A famous medieval French rabbi and grammarian, also known as Radak.</note> writes that this "Lord" is the Messiah, who will himself be the messenger of the covenant, whom Jonathan the Chaldean interprets as <term>Our Master</term> <note>original Aramaic: Rabona</note>.

After the prophets, the expectation of the Messiah's saving arrival—and the entire practice of the Cabalists, which they rightly gather and direct toward the eternal liberation brought by that same Messiah—descended to the scribes of the Law and the elders. These were called the "Heads of the Fathers," who are too many to count, and the men of the Great Council. This tradition was received successively in the manner of the schools, starting from Ezra, who handed the Cabala to Simeon the Just, the High Priest and leader of the Synagogue. From him, it was received by his student Antigonus and his associates, among whom were Za-

<column-break/>

dok and Boethus, the root of the heretics. From them came the <term>Sadducees and Boethusians</term> <note>Jewish sects that rejected the oral tradition and the resurrection of the dead.</note>, as Judah Halevi writes in the third discourse of the book *Al-Khazari*. 

Then the tradition passed to Joseph son of Joezer and Joseph son of Johanan of Jerusalem; from them to Joshua son of Perahiah—who had a certain disciple named Jesus of Nazareth during the time of the Maccabees, though not the one known to Christians—and Nittai of Arbela. From them it went to Judah son of Tabbai and Simeon son of Shetah, and then to Shammai and Abtalion. From these it went to Hillel and Shammai, who had many thousands of disciples. From them it reached <term>Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai</term>, who fostered five disciples: Eliezer (written as Eliezer son of Hyrcanus), Joshua son of Hananiah, Joseph the Priest, Simeon son of Nathanael, and Eleazar son of Arach. 

From Rabban Johanan, who lived one hundred and twenty years, Rabban Gamaliel received his Cabala; then his son Simeon; then from his children, <term>Judah the Prince</term> <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, who is called "Our Holy Master." His son Gamaliel followed him in receiving it. Thus far the Cabalists, whose sayings and allegorical expositions of Holy Scripture were followed by the assembly of Cabalists: Hananiah son of Akashia, Abba Saul, Rabbi Tarphon, Akavia son of Mahalalel, Hananiah the Prince of Priests, Hananiah son of Teradion, Hananiah son of Hachinai, Nehunia son of HaKanah, Halafta, Duschai son of Jannai, Hanina son of Dosa, Dosa son of Archinas, Rabbi Akiba, Eleazar son of Azariah, Eleazar of Modi'im, Rabbi Levitas, and Rabbi Johanan son of Beroka, followed by Simeon from his children. Then Zadok, then Jose; he was followed by Ishmael, and from another lineage Rabbi Meir, from whom Eleazar son of Jacob, Johanan the Sandal-maker, and Eleazar son of Samma received it. Then Nehorai, after whom came Jannai, Mattathiah, Samuel the Less, Elisha son of Abuyah, Eleazar of Kappadokia, Judah son of Thema, Joshua son of Levi, and many others besides. 

Because of their legal disputes in the Talmud, these men are sometimes called <term>Thanaim</term> <note>Teachers/Repeaters; the sages of the Mishnah period.</note>, as if they were "dictators" of the law. But because of their meditations on the highest matters—tracing everything from the lowest individual things back to the most exalted heights, received from their ancestors and handed to posterity with total devotion—they are called <term>Mekabulim</term> in Hebrew. In our own age, thanks to <term>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</term> <note>An Italian Renaissance philosopher who was the first to synthesize Kabbalah with Christian theology.</note>, before whom their name was unknown to the Latin tongue, they are called Cabalists or Cabalic scholars.

Then Marranus asked: "Do you know that man, most learned Simon—the one who first brought the word 'Cabala' to the Latins?" 

And Simon replied: "I believe you know him well. He once <margin>F</margin> lived among the Gauls and the Savoyards, driven from his homeland and fiercely hunted by envious men in a detestable persecution because of his extraordinary philosophical studies and noble intellect. There is indeed a race of men (as Terence says) who wish themselves to be the foremost in all things, yet they are not. They are hatched from that egg of the bird—as the fables go—which until the years of Coroneus was clothed in white feathers, but later in black. It provides them with a garment of white and black, which is why they are called the 'clothed-in-black' brothers <margin>G</margin> <note>A biting reference to the Dominican friars (who wore black and white) who led the Inquisition against Pico.</note>. That bird is always hated by Phoebus Apollo because of its wicked betrayals. But you both know this poetry: these men were the gadflies, the scourges, the dogs of such a noble and learned Christian, who in our century brought many secrets of the Hebrews [to light]."

### BOOK ONE

...having most learnedly shared these secret dogmas with Roman ears. To this Philolaus said: "Leaving these historical deeds aside, I propose that we must return (if you agree with me) to the **Cabalistic Art**, since it will be evening shortly, and it can hardly be said how much our desires tend elsewhere." Simon replied, "I have indeed run through the individual points; you should expect nothing further from me." 

And Marranus said, "If that is so, I have certainly interrupted your discourse quite inconveniently. For you were weaving the thread of a speech that was most suited to the matter we desire, and nothing was more pleasing than, after a correct definition of <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, literally meaning 'reception' or 'tradition.'</note>, to know what it is that was so excellently revealed to the human race above all others—then who revealed what, and who received it. At that point, I led you away with my interruption, which I somewhat regret. Therefore, my friend, we pray that you return to it." 

"I will indeed comply cheerfully," Simon said, "and I will hasten at last to the method of the Art which I noticed you desired, unless evening is already imminent, since you perhaps are weary of listening and I myself am exhausted from speaking. For quite enough has fallen from us in these brief hours, and such was my boldness (if you will) or—what is more true—my singular affection toward you, that I spoke everything unprepared and off-the-cuff, which ought not to be done in so great a matter." 

Then Philolaus said, "But we both beseech you: complete the list with an account of the authors who both held and handed down the Kabbalah, so that this part of the discourse is not left unfinished when we depart for our lodging to dine, as is necessary."

After this was said, Simon spoke again: "Truly," he said, "in my judgment, there are innumerable <term>Cabalists</term> (for it does not matter to include them all by number). Some of them only heard the tradition, while others were both listeners and writers. Nevertheless, since you urge me so, I will cursorily review some whose books on Cabalistic contemplations are in daily use, as far as my memory serves. However, not all are complete in every part; for of some, only fragments have floated down to us. The rest, alas, are so extinguished that they are scarcely known by the record of their names in the monuments of the most learned men. For just as the fathers lost the ancient volumes through the iniquity of the times and the long passage of years—with no small loss to posterity, though our people still remember them—so we, living now in the sixth millennium of the world, have lost the books of our ancestors. This happened either through age, which consumes all things, or through the malice of wars, or floods and devastation, or the unforeseen accident of fire, or sometimes through shameful and detestable hatred and envy, which has stirred up foolish and idle book-burners even in our own age. 

Books of **Enoch** and of our father **Abraham** are cited by trustworthy men; indeed, even Moses alleges the **Books of the Wars of the Lord**. Joshua cites the **Book of the Just**, and the whole collection of books from **Kiriath-sepher** <note>original Hebrew: "City of Books"</note>, which Othniel captured under the leadership of Caleb. Ahasuerus mentions the **Books of Records**. Jonathan in the Book of Maccabees mentions the **Holy Books concerning the Spartans**. The Chronicles commemorate the **Books of Lamentations**, the **Books of Samuel the Seer**, and of **Nathan the Prophet**, and of **Gad** <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> **the Seer**, and of **Shemaiah the Prophet**, and of **Iddo the Seer**, and of **Ahijah the Shilonite**, and the books of **Jehu son of Hanani**—all of which are nowhere to be found. We also lament the library of **Darius**, as found in Ezra; those precious things in Ecbatana. 

By the same example, innumerable authors of our own century have perished, although we do not doubt that many things survive which we ourselves have not yet seen. I cannot boast that same glory as <term>Pico della Mirandola</term> <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who sought to synthesize Kabbalah with Christianity.</note> <margin>B</margin>—that when Ezra once ordered seventy volumes of Cabalistic secrets to be written, he [Pico] sought them out at the greatest expense. I do not have nearly as much gold and silver as would be needed to bid for those books if they survived and were offered. 

We, however, not being so well-supplied with books, use according to our strength the book of our father **Abraham**, which is titled *Yetzirah* <note>original: יצירה</note>, meaning **On Creation**. The learned assign no small part of this to **Master Akiba**; it is certainly adorned with noble commentaries, as it would otherwise be hidden and obscure. And we use the book *Ha-Zohar* <note>original: הזוהר</note>, meaning **Of Splendor**, which **Simeon son of Yohai** composed <margin>C</margin> when he hid in a certain vast and dark cave for twenty-four years. And the book *Ha-Bahir* <note>original: הנהיר</note>, meaning **Of Brightness**, which is called the *Lucidarius* <note>The Enlightener</note> by your people. 

There are also those which that **Abraham Abulafia** published on Kabbalah, and the distinguished commentaries of **Ramban** (for so **Rabbi Moses son of Nahman** is collectively named) on the secrets of the Law, whom you call the **Gerundese** [Nahmanides]. And there are the commentaries of the most learned of all recipients, **Rabbi Menahem Recanati**, on the secrets of Ramban. And the <margin>D</margin> *Book of the Perplexed* of **Rambam**—ending with an 'm,' that is, **Rabbi Moses son of Maimon**, whom they call **Moses the Egyptian** [Maimonides]. 

And the book *Sha'are Tzedek* <note>original: שערי צדק</note>, that is, **Gates of Justice**, which **Rabbi Joseph son of Karnitol** wrote. And the book *Sha'are Orah* <note>original: שערי אורה</note>, that is, **Gate of Light**, by **Master Joseph Castiliensis** (as they say) in Spain [Joseph Gikatilla]. And the book *Ha-Emunot* <note>original: האמונות</note>, that is, **Concerning Beliefs**, whose author in Asia was **Rabbi Saadia**. And the book *Sod ha-Torah* <note>original: סוד התורה</note> on the **Mystery of the Law**, which that wise man **Abraham ibn Ezra** completed. 

And the <margin>E</margin> book of **Rabbi Hamai son of Hanina**, who is called the head of the most eloquent in Kabbalah, and the same author's book *Ha-Iyun* <note>original: העיון</note>, that is, **Of Speculation**. Then another book, *Perush Kedushah* <note>original: פירוש קדושה</note>, that is, **Commentary on Holiness**, which **Rabbi Azariel** wrote. And the book *Shemot* <note>original: שמות</note>, that is, **On Names**. And the **Book of Explanations of the Alphabet**, whose title is *Seder Perush Alphabeta* <note>original: סדר פירוש אלפאביתא</note> from **Rabbi Akiba**. And the book of **Rabbi Ama**, *Sha'ar ha-Razim* <note>original: שער הרזים</note>, on the **Hidden Things of the Nineteenth Psalm**. 

And <margin>F</margin> the book *Ha-Yichud* <note>original: היחוד</note>, that is, **The Unique**, on union or collection, which **Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra** mentions in the first chapter of the *Mystery of the Law*. And the book *Sodot* <note>original: סודות</note>, that is, **Of Secrets**. And the **Book of Abstruse Questions**. And the little book of Kabbalah published by **Azariel**, also known as Oriel of Gerona. And the book titled *The Way of Faith and the Way of Denial* <note>original: דרך האמונה ודרך הכפירה</note>. And the **Book of Roots** by **Rabbi Joseph Albo**, to which they likewise prefixed the title of Kabbalah, although he comments more on ethics than on mystical meanings. Finally, there exists a most elegant book <margin>G</margin> in Kabbalah against the pseudo-philosophers named *Al-Khazari* <note>original: Alkozer</note>, in the Arabic manner, which **Rabbi Judah Halevi** composed, whose words are these: "For there is no good Kabbalah except with a good heart" <note>original Hebrew: כי אין קבלה טובה אלא עם הלב הטוב</note>.
