### BOOK FIVE OF THE KABBALAH

->639<-
<header>V KABBALAH</header>
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

...it seemed to me wise to have repelled malignant sophists from such holy contemplation; for they, like dying flies, destroy the sweetness of every ointment, however precious. Finally, we use the commentaries on the *Book of Yetzirah* <note>original: יצירה; 'The Book of Creation,' one of the earliest and most influential Jewish mystical texts</note> by Master Jacob Cohen, and on the same book, the composition of Rabbi Isaac, which he titled the *Explanation of the Holy Name*. There is also the book published by Rabbi Todros <note>Text reads 'Tedacus'</note> Levi concerning the ten Kabbalistic numerations <note>The Sefirot, or the ten attributes/emanations through which God interacts with the universe</note>. I do not wish to include the book of Solomon inscribed under the name of Raziel, for it is a magical fiction.

Thus far, I have clearly revealed to you strangers the poverty of my own paper library—something I am not usually wont to do for others. But in my opinion, no one has ever written about this art more skillfully, more distinctly, or more clearly than Rabbi Joseph Bar Abraham of Castile <note>Joseph Gikatilla (1248–1305), a major figure in Spanish Kabbalah</note>, a citizen of Salerno, who labored over three volumes of this discipline for the student, through which he made the whole instruction of the Kabbalists clearer: the first volume on words, the second on letters, and the third on the [vowel] points. The title of his book is *Ginnat Egoz* <note>original: גנת אגוז</note>, that is, the *Garden of the Nut*, following the Song of Solomon: *I went down into the garden of the nut to see the pleasant fruits.* 

It appears that this "nut" is like a golden apple enclosed in a silver network, as we read in Proverbs: *Golden apples in silver carvings is a word spoken in its proper place.* So the Kabbalah is that golden and divine apple bound with silver threads—namely, ingenious instructions and human arts—just as is customary in the work of goldsmiths. In their subtle engravings, they do not entirely cover or hide the golden apple of good scent with silver so that none of it can be seen; rather, through certain hollowed openings and silver lattices, they allow the color of the apple to shine through and the scent of amber to waft out. To those looking from afar, the whole mesh appears to be solid silver; but looking closer, if they examine it studiously, they will also find the gold. And just as gold differs from silver, so too is the Kabbalistic art proven to differ from the Kabbalah itself, although one single genre of spiritual instinct embraces both species. 

But one precedes the other, as the oracle precedes the priests <note>original: Hierophantas</note>. Just as in one category of gold, one type is "good" but another is "best"—in the same way that it is told in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> regarding Havilah: *the gold of that land is good.* For it is not written there as "the best," as some read it, but "good." And in Isaiah concerning Ophir: *I will make a man more precious than fine gold, even the gold of Ophir.* Thus, whatever lovers of the finest arts learn from Sacred Scripture through natural science is equal to "good gold," and it is called the *Work of Bereshit* <note>original: בראשית; 'In the beginning,' referring to the study of the physical creation</note>. But that which we receive through spiritual knowledge is called the *Work of the Merkavah* <note>original: מרכבה; 'The Chariot,' referring to the mystical study of the divine realm and Ezekiel's vision</note> and is equated to the best and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write thus:

*She-maaseh Bereshit chokmat ha-teva u-maaseh merkavah hu chokmat ha-elohut* <note>original: שמעשה בראשית חכמת הטבע ומעשה מרכבה הוא חכמת האלהות</note>

That is: *The Work of the Beginning is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity.* And since both forms of wisdom are concerned in some way with the world and those things that exist in the world, it is the unanimous judgment of the Talmudists and Kabbalists on this matter that

<column-break/>

->640<-
<page-num>640</page-num>
<meta>catchword: but only</meta>

<margin>A</margin> there are two worlds: the first is intellectual, which is called *Olam Ha-Ba* <note>original: עולם הבא</note>, that is, "the world to come" (at least for us); and the second is sensible, which is called *Olam Ha-Zeh* <note>original: עולם הזה</note>, that is, "this present world." As we have received from the words of our sages concerning the devoted practitioner of the Divine Name of forty-two letters, such a person undoubtedly exists as:

*Ahuuv le-ma’alah ve-nechmad le-mata ve-nochel shene olamim ha-olam ha-zeh ve-ha-olam ha-ba* <note>original: אהוב למעלה ונחמד למטה ונוחל שני עולמים העולם הזה והעולם הבא</note>

<margin>B</margin> That is: *Beloved above and desired below, and inheriting two worlds, the present world and the future world.* 

Therefore, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists are divided into two separate disciplines, although both similarly arise and emanate from the accepted traditions <note>The word 'reception' is a literal translation of 'Kabbalah'</note>. For both have faith in the traditions of their ancestors, even when no reason is given. But they are distinguished by this assigned order: that the happy and blessed Kabbalist finally transfers and translates all study, all effort, all counsel, labor, and diligence—indeed the entire intention of <margin>C</margin> his mind—from the sensible world to the intellectual world. 

The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universe. Even if he occasionally proceeds toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Creator and cause of things, occupied with His creations. He assigns the angels to daily ministries and the execution of the effects of the divine will, always relating the contemplations of the highest things back to this lower world. 

Yet, one of these disciplines often borrows the meanings of the other and <margin>D</margin> draws them toward its own desire. Indeed, the Talmudists and Kabbalists sometimes share their studies back and forth, like the active life and the contemplative life, although one and the same context of Sacred Scripture often incites one toward "slavish fear" and the other toward "filial love" in their own charming ways of <margin>E</margin> persuasion. 

For the Talmudist will appear to reside with sharp study around the precepts and mandates of the Law, explaining them, directing them, venerating them, and kissing them. Thus, we may correctly define the Talmud as nothing other than the explanation of the Law according to the intention of the author. Hence, the Talmudists are called *Meforshim* <note>original: מפורשים; 'Expositors'</note> and *Darshanim* <note>original: דרשנים; 'Preachers' or those who 'search' the text</note>, who are always at their work from the pulpit and the chair of Moses. They preach and exhort the people with the royal prophet [David], saying: *Serve the Lord in fear*; and with <margin>F</margin> Joshua: *Fear the Lord and serve Him.* They say: "Indeed, do this in such a way, and omit that in such a way, with this and that regulation." From this, they have reduced the six hundred and thirteen commandments—comprehended in the single word *Taryag* <note>original: תריג; the numerical value of the word is 613</note>—into two headings: *Aseh* and *Lo Taaseh* <note>original: עשה לא תעשה</note>, that is, "Do" and "Do not do," which you are accustomed to calling "affirmative" and "negative" precepts, which are very advantageous to know and extremely necessary in practice. 

The Kabbalists, however—although they are men who piously observe the Law in truth—nevertheless dwell more upon contemplation. Therefore, they are called <margin>G</margin> *Anshei ha-Iyyun mi-Ba'alei ha-Torah* <note>original: אנשי העיון מבעלי התורה</note>, that is, "Men of Speculation from among the Masters of the Law." They leave the care of the republic and private affairs, the rituals and customs of home and war, and judicial and moral matters—along with their history—to the Talmudists, and as if...

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>
...they have reserved only those things which pertain to the peace and tranquility of the soul and to the love of God. For thus they say: <note>original: כונת כלל התורה שני דברים והם תקון הנפש ותקון הגוף</note> "The intention of the entire Law consists of two things: the proper disposition of the soul and the proper disposition of the body." Indeed, the whole Law tends primarily toward the perfection of man, and according to it, we attain two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. That which aids the soul and perpetuates life is by far worthier and of a higher preeminence, although a suitable condition and proper composition of the body is prior in time and nature. Therefore, the Kabbalists must be held in a higher place and a worthier rank, following that exposition of the Law which, through certain symbols, most powerfully impels the elevation of the mind toward the heavens and toward divine matters. This, your Greeks call the <term>anagogic</term> <note>From the Greek 'anagoge,' meaning 'leading upward'; a method of spiritual interpretation that seeks deeper, mystical meanings</note> institution, which is not only philosophy but is <term>sophia</term> <note>original: σοφία</note> itself—that is, wisdom. Hence they are deservedly called "the wise," <note>original: להלוך נגד החיים</note> "to walk before the living," as Solomon the Preacher says, since they proceed to where life is; and according to the capacity of mortals still dwelling in small bodies, they ascend from time to eternity, and from the lowest things to the highest.

Make a trial if you wish, honored guests. "In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth." Truly, by the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> "heaven" is the name for everything in the visible world that is above the moon, and they call that which is below it "earth." Furthermore, they interpret heaven to be "form" and they wish the earth to be "matter." Therefore, they say that in the beginning, God created form and matter, the composition of which He later fashioned in each individual thing by His creative decree; and He did not so much turn everything by hand as He shaped it nine times by His word. For it is read: <note>original: ויאמר אלהים</note> "And God said, Let there be light; and God said, Let there be a firmament; and God said, Let the waters be gathered; and God said, Let the earth sprout; and God said, Let there be lights; and God said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things; and God said, Let the earth bring forth; and God said, Let us make man; and God said, Behold, I have given you every herb." Therefore, the heavens and the earth were finished with all their belongings and their entire furniture, such as the four elements which are called the "darkness" first named, the "spirit of the Lord," the "waters under the firmament," and the "dry land." Likewise follow the other mixed things, which are commonly called "elementated," such as birds and winged creatures, beasts and creeping things, fish and great whales, and the ruler of them all, man, to whom alone among all corporeal beings free will was granted. Lest he use it poorly, laws are established for him, constitutions are promulgated, and punishments for transgression are threatened. Just as inflowing fire is called "heaven"—that is, <note>original: שמים (Shamayim)</note> as if it were <note>original: אש ומים (Esh u-Mayim)</note> "fire and water"—and produces nothing from itself, but rather nourishes produced things only with celestial (that is, moist) heat, so in the proper order are recited the most strongly influential things established within it: the sun and the moon, by whose leadership all the remaining "armies" are marked—the lights and stars, night and day, splendor and darkness, signs and seasons, days and years. These things, therefore, concern the corporeal globe and the mixed things enclosed within it.

However, two worlds are accepted by the Kabbalists: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mental, the mate-

<column-break/>

rial and the ideal. The lower world and the upper world, when they read, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth"; and thus they think that symbolically "heaven" designates the highest things and "earth" the lowest, interpreting it in this way: <note>original: בהתחלה ברא השם העליונים והתחתונים</note> "In the beginning, God created the upper things and the lower things." By this, they surely judge that the simple and immaterial world contains the highest things, while this compact and "cemented" world contains the lowest. Whence also the divine law concerning creation began with the word <term>Bereshit</term> <note>original: בראשית; The first word of Genesis, 'In the beginning'</note> starting 
<margin>B</margin>
with the letter *beth*, which in the art of Arithmetic signifies the number "two" among the numerals. This was done as if to notoriously insinuate that God principally created two things: the whole supreme world with all those dwelling in it, and the whole lowest world and everything pertaining to it. For otherwise, it would have been sufficient for Moses to have written <note>original: ראשית ברא אלהים שמים וארץ (Reshit bara Elohim...)</note> which would be read by the Latins in the same manner as "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." For that summary 
<margin>C</margin>
of creation could have begun without the letter *beth*. Just as Solomon says in Proverbs, "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways," where the word for "beginning" is placed without *beth* and without any other preposition. 

Furthermore, beyond custom, He joined two double markers, *et* (את) and *ha* (ה), to these two created things. One is the marker of excellent demonstration, which is called *ha*, and the other is of all-encompassing comprehension, which is composed of *aleph* (א), the first element of the alphabet, and the last, *tau* (ת). This is what the Greeks say is "Alpha and Omega," and the Romans 
<margin>D</margin>
call "the prow and the stern" <note>An idiom meaning from beginning to end</note>. Through "heaven," all excellently simple and spiritual things were seen from *aleph* to *tau* (from first to last); and through "earth," similarly from head to heel, all excellently corporeal things and those contained within them were seen. Nevertheless, each single thing exists in that one "beginning" as a single creation. Just as Ezekiel’s "wheel within a wheel," with all its involved parts, was seen to be one likeness of the glory of the Lord; and to use the very words of Rabbi Saadia in his book *Amunoth* (that is, *The Book of Beliefs*): 
<margin>E</margin>
<note>original: כחלמון בתוך ביצה</note> "Like the yolk in the middle of an egg," or (as I myself am wont to say) like the white of a single egg, contained by the shell-like firmament and encircling the yolk itself. Thus, that first intelligible world enfolds the second, so that its entire power is governed from there. By this, both are bound by the chains of concord, so much so that they often exchange their own natures and the names of their comprehensions with mutual freedom. For in the second world—that is, the sensible world—the nine 
<margin>F</margin>
spheres are moved by the immobile Empyrean, over which <term>Metattron</term> <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Jewish angelology, often described as the celestial scribe or the prince of the Divine Presence</note> presides continually. But in the first world, the nine choirs of Angels are moved by the immobile God. Just as in the immobile silence, the Creator of all things created all things simultaneously at first, then afterward moved each to its own proper distinction by speaking with a ninefold discourse. 

In turn, fire is named "seraph," air "cherub," water "tharsis," and earth "ariel." Those things which are in the lower world are known by a much better mark in the upper ones. Wherefore these 
<margin>G</margin>
lower things may be appropriately called "models" of the true things, and shadowed images, signs, marks, and symbols of the heavenly ones, by which we are moved to think about the super-celestial and Angelic substances, powers, and operations through a certain...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Law’s dual purpose, specifically focusing on the Kabbalistic interpretation of spiritual rewards and punishments. # CABALA

...by way of abstraction, or through a path of assimilation, or by some other reason and manner possible for us who are clothed in flesh. For this reason, they establish two paradises: one celestial and the other terrestrial. In these, both the earthly man and the heavenly man may attain the rewards of their virtues. The earthly man, having dwelled longer in the body in this world as if in some corruptible garden of pleasure, may gain glory, honor, joy, gladness, and every desire of his delight on account of some heroic or preeminent virtue praised by the children of this world—yet these are but shadows and fleeting things, much like smoke. 

But in the celestial land, and more truly in the super-celestial land of the living, where the unfading paradise of eternal loveliness exists, the most merciful, Greatest, and Best God reveals "all good" to the human soul. This soul, once having acted rightly according to virtue during its mortal life, is now stripped of its heavy and dense corpse of a dark body, which previously prevented it from seeing. In both the Kabbalah and the Talmud, this vision is called **Illuminating Speculation** <note>original: איספקלריא המאירה - *Ispaklaria ha-Me'irah*; literally "The Illuminating Mirror" or lens, referring to the clear prophetic vision of Moses</note>, which means "life-giving." You call this the intuitive knowledge of God, as it befalls the separated soul through the light of glory, and is proven by the most mature penitents to be the only thing that is truly beatific. 

For there is another kind of vision through connatural species <note>Knowledge gained through natural means or images rather than direct divine light</note> which is not beatific; this is called **Non-Illuminating Contemplation** <note>original: איספקלריא שאינה המאירה - *Ispaklaria she-einah ha-Me'irah*; the "mirror that does not shine," referring to the lesser vision of other prophets</note>. Now, since the clear vision of God and the perpetual enjoyment of the highest divinity are granted to the highest part of man—the intellect and the will—it follows by the best right that these things happen to no one except in the highest world. Thus the Kabbalists say: "Before he attains this intuition, his soul is separated from him" <note>original: כי טרם שישיג לראות הפרד נפשו מעליו</note>. Therefore, if God is ever said to be seen by a mortal man, it is thought to happen through an Angel, <margin>in the visions of the angels <note>original: במראות המלאכים</note></margin> as Ramban of Girona <note>The scholar Nachmanides (1194–1270)</note> writes regarding Exodus. 

Consequently, for the twofold condition of man, spiritual and corporal, and for the twofold retribution of reward, they assert a double paradise, as you have heard, saying: "Because paradise and its rivers, along with the individual things you see in the Work of Creation <note>original: מעשה בראשית - *Ma'aseh Bereshit*; refers to the opening chapters of Genesis</note>, are all arranged according to intellectual and supernal forms." This I also believe regarding the gold of Havilah, the bdellium and the onyx stone, and other gems of infinite price. 

In the same way and form, these same Kabbalists affirm that a double Gehenna <note>Hell</note>—namely two Tartaruses—has been designated: one of the upper and one of the lower world. These exist to torment harmful bodies in time and wicked souls in eternity. A common name given to them is **Arka** <note>original: ארקא - One of the seven earths in Kabbalistic cosmology, often associated with a place of punishment</note>. This is the place of Tartarean punishment which, among other things, contains seven monstrous receptacles of the harshest punishments, destined for those guilty of crimes by the just judgment of God. Just as that Kabbalist in the *Garden of Nuts* <note>original: *Ginat Egoz* by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, in the second volume, treats the seven dwellings of the lower regions in these words: "There are two kinds of Gehenna, upper and lower: one for the body in this world, and one for the soul in the world to come after this; and the place containing all of these is called Arka, because in it..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "...are Gehenna, and the gates of death, and the shadow of death, and the pit of corruption, and the miry clay, and perdition, and the grave." <note>original: הם גיהנם ושערי מות וצלמות ובאר שחת וטיט היון ואבדון ושאול</note> These are the two species of Gehenna, upper and lower: one for the body in this world, and one for the soul in the world to come after this. And the place encompassing all these is called Arka, for in it are Gehenna, and the gates of death, and the pit of destruction, and the miry clay, and perdition, and the pit. Thus far Joseph of Castile <note>Joseph Gikatilla</note>. 

Now these chains, this prison, these fetters, this servitude, and this captivity await the sins of the harmful, <margin>B</margin> both of bodies in the present world and of souls in the future world, so that just rewards for virtues may accompany the righteous, and deserved torments for vices may follow the wicked. For what else is owed to the upright but life and honor? What else to the depraved but death and horror? 

Nor is this to be understood only temporally; as the Kabbalists wish, it is also understood intellectually. For they write thus: "The righteous, even in their death, are called living; and the wicked, even in their life, are called dead." <note>original: צדיקים אפילו במיתתן קרואים חיים ורשעים אפילו בחייהם קרואים מתים</note> <margin>C</margin> To those skilled in Kabbalah, God's sentence will not be obscure: *In the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death.* This refers not to a corporal death but a spiritual one. For Adam lived more than nine hundred years after eating the forbidden fruit; yet in the very moment he transgressed the law, he died the death. I mean he died in his sin, which was so poisonous and contagious to the whole human race and the propagation of future offspring, who were destined for the eternal dwellings of the lower regions. 

This remained so until, by God's <margin>D</margin> pleasure, that Messiah the Redeemer should come, who would lead man back into paradise—not the terrestrial one, but the celestial—and restore to the children the eternal life which the parent had lost. This life is not temporal, nor of the body, but of the soul: that very familiarity with God and the most pleasant sight of divinity, filled with every delight. In this Messiah, all true, non-sophistic Kabbalists fix and place all their trust. To him, they turn all the saving prophecies of the Holy Scriptures: concerning the land of promise, <margin>E</margin> the city of Jerusalem (which is built as a city that is compact together), the mountain of God, his holy place, the holy way, the sanctuary, the temple of the Lord, the house of the Lord, the gate of the Lord, and many other similar things. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note>, in his *Mishneh* <note>original: *Mi ne*; referring to the *Mishneh Torah* or his commentary on Deuteronomy</note>, also wished these to be understood as celestial beatitude. 

For this reason, we often and greatly contend with the Talmudists, and we frequently go our separate ways into two opinions. They attempt to refer every liberation of the King Messiah <margin>F</margin> from our corporal captivity (or more truly, our dispersion) to tumult, the noise of arms, military expeditions, the conquest of regions, the devastation of lands, and the victory of the Israelite army—just as we read happened to our ancestors under the savior Moses against the Canaanites and Palestinians. Or at least they refer it to a clever ingenuity of escape, which they have used in other liberations. Many have used this craftily, though I think some used it piously, during the many centuries they have been dispersed and exiled under so many kingdoms: <margin>G</margin> such as seventy years under the Babylonian, fifty-four under the Persian, one hundred and thirty under the Greek, and now one hundred and four hundred <note>1,400 years</note> under the Roman, and the end is not yet. We, on the contrary, in my judgment, more rightly and according to Kabbalah, believe the Messiah to be...

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> We believe that he will come of his own accord to deliver the wretched mortals of the human race from the chains of original injustice. He comes to forgive sins and to save the souls of those who piously serve God—souls which, in our father Adam, were excluded from eternal life until the satisfaction of the Messiah. To fulfill the justice of a merciful and clement God, the Messiah shall "stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat of it," so that through him we may live forever. This satisfaction was not meant to occur in royal pomp, nor in the boasting of honor and glory, because the original sin to be expiated by <margin>B</margin> the Messiah sprouted from pride and self-exaltation. Instead, it was to be achieved in humility and endurance: not with chariots and horses, but in the name of the Lord our God. It was not to be found in victory or human triumph, but in labor, fasting, vigils, strength of soul, contempt for the world, compassionate mercy, a supreme love for God, a right love for men, and finally in that heroic, liberal, and spontaneous death itself. This is because vice can only be fought with virtue. No wise man has ever highly valued the empires, princedoms, genealogies, or crowns of this world. Rather, true wisdom consists in despising the glory of this world; for when the glorious rich man dies, he shall not take everything with him (as the Psalmist says), nor shall his glory descend with him. Therefore, whatever is written in the sacred letters regarding trophies and the subjection of peoples is understood by the Kabbalists—even after accepting the historical truth of the events narrated—to refer to the intellectual world and the supernal powers. Thus, the future King Messiah, by his supreme right, will not only neglect but even despise these light and abject delusions of this age—the magistracies, honors, and kingdoms—as things vain and foolish. He comes to abolish the guilt of the human species and to open the path to virtue. Hence, if we are guided by right reason, the true Messiah will be recognized most clearly from that noble chapter of Isaiah which begins thus: *Hineh yaskil avdi* <note>original: הנה ישכיל עבדי</note>—that is, "Behold, my servant shall understand"—and ends thus: *v'lifoshim yapgia* <note>original: ולפשעים יפגיע</note>—"and he prayed for the transgressors." I marvel beyond what can be said—and not without a unique sense of shame on behalf of other foreign nations (I speak confidently to you alone)—that Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105)</note> and David Kimhi <note>A famous grammarian and commentator (1160–1235)</note>, along with other learned men of our sect, have through some faint-heartedness (or perhaps out of shame before the Gentiles) interpreted that entire context of Isaiah as referring only to the people of Israel who are now scattered everywhere. Yet it is most plainly prophesied concerning the Messiah himself, as the Aramaic translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets</note> expressly states: *Ha yitzlach avdi Meshicha* <note>original: הא יצלח עבדי משיחא</note>—that is, "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper." This is the one truly seen by Isaiah in a prophetic spirit: a man experienced in sorrows and infirmity, with a hidden face, a man of no honorable reputation, struck by a divine blow, despised and avoided, shorn like a lamb, slain like a sheep, cut off from the land of the living, and counted among the wicked, inglorious among the sons of men. But what of him among the sons of God? Clearly, he is greatly exalted, elevated, and exceedingly sublime. For who shall tell of his generation? The will of the Lord God is directed by his hand, and the Lord <margin>G</margin> has laid upon him the iniquity of us all, because

<column-break/>

on account of the crime of the people, he struck him. For he was wounded for our crimes and bruised for our iniquities—he who certainly never committed iniquity, and in whose mouth there was no deceit. But the Lord willed the crushing of this wounded one. Therefore, since he is the righteous servant of God, he shall justify many through the knowledge of himself; he shall bear their iniquity, take away the sins of many, and intercede for sinners. Isaiah saw all these things concerning the true <margin>B</margin> Messiah, and he certainly did not lie. This is firmly that "assembly of Israel" according to the opinion of the Kabbalists, and that salvation of our God so often promised: that we might be justified *be-da'ato* <note>original: בדעתו</note>—that is, "in the knowledge of him." We are not saved in a tumult, nor in flight, but standing under one King and in one army of faith, we are liberated in the death and knowledge of the Messiah. Through this, sin is ended, and the obstacle to the clear vision of God—namely, the original and contagious guilt of the human race—is removed. Concerning this, we read in the Book of Kabbalah on Faith and Expiation: <margin>C</margin>

> The path demonstrating the grace-given or infused power, which is a created power, is described by seven variations. These are the thirteen orders of expiation by which the world is directed until sin is finished and the Messiah comes, who is the power of God. <margin>D</margin> And in the power of grace—which is the angelic power—and in the grace-given power infused from it—which is the power of prophecy—the spirit of the Lord Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH</note> shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Behold the seven variations <margin>E</margin> which the Messiah uses to do good for the righteous and to destroy the wicked, according to what is written: "And with the breath of his lips he shall slay the impious."

These are the words of the aforementioned Kabbalistic volume, by which we are reminded that the King Messiah conquers the adversaries of God's people not by hand but by mouth, not by arms but by spirit. He grants the sevenfold grace of God to the pious and slays the impious, and all this by the "spirit of his mouth"—that is, by his spiritual doctrine, which he shall scatter and sow among all nations through just men and the chosen disciples of the Just One. This refers to that oracle of Isaiah regarding the time of the Messiah: "You shall draw waters from the fountains of the Savior." Jonathan son of Uzziel translated this into Aramaic with these words: *V'tikablun ulpan chadat <margin>F</margin> be-chedvah mi-bechiri tzidka* <note>original: ותקבלון אולפן חדת בחדוה מבחירי צדקא</note>—that is, "And you shall receive a new doctrine with joy from the chosen ones of the righteous." This is indeed that new doctrine by which the true light shines; he who hates it is in darkness, and he who loves it dwells in light. The end of the commandments <margin>G</margin> is therefore this: that we love one another in the doctrine of the Messiah, "who shall teach the peoples to walk in the ways of the Tetragrammaton," as Rabbi David Kimhi writes regarding that verse in the fifty-first chapter of the same Prophet.

# OF THE KABBALAH

<margin>A</margin> "For the law shall go forth from me;" <note>referencing Isaiah 51:4</note> which law, if a man follows it, he shall be saved, but if he despises it, he shall perish. For the old things belong to fear, but the new things belong to charity, **of upright love from the heart** <note>original Hebrew: "shel ahavat yesharah mi-lev"</note>, and **completeness** <note>original Hebrew: "shalem"</note>, which is of right love from an integrated heart, according to our masters. The Messiah shall therefore be the example of life for all who are to be set free; upon him depends the universal salvation of the world, which is called "eternal salvation." This is explained by our scholars as lasting "through all the days of the ages," where it is read: "Israel is saved in the Lord <note>original Latin uses IHVH</note> with an eternal salvation." Something regarding this is written in the book <margin>B</margin> *Ancient Kabbalah* <note>Original: "Cabalae Hacadma"</note>: **And this is the secret of the King Messiah, who will come quickly in our days, whose entire work will be based on grace and mercy, which is the secret of the eighth, and this is the name that rules and will give every request through his hands.** <note>Original Hebrew: "Ve-hu sod Melekh ha-Mashiach she-yavo bimherah ve-yameinu she-kol pe’ulato tihyeh al chen ve-chesed she-hu sod ha-shemini ve-hu ha-shem she-moshel ve-yitten le-kol ha-mish’alah al yadav"</note> That is to say: this is the mystery of the King Messiah. His every operation will begin in the letters V and H, and also I and H <note>The components of the Tetragrammaton, IHVH</note>, which is the mystery of the seventh day. This name is his integrated name, and every work shall be perfected in his hand. Behold, it is defined by the wise Kabbalists that all things are to be perfected through the Messiah, <margin>C</margin> and his entire operation is carried out through the most sacred four letters I.H.V.H. in the mystery of the seventh day—not called so by the number of days, but by the transition from the active life to the contemplative life. That is, in the very quietude of the soul and peaceful tranquility, withdrawing from the excessive anxieties of this world and from the physical works performed. For it is written: "And he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had done."

Although the Talmudists attribute many names to this King, <margin>D</margin> as can be understood from the citations of many Doctors in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A legal tractate of the Talmud</note> in the volume <term>Helek</term> <note>The eleventh chapter of Sanhedrin, dealing with the afterlife and the Messiah</note>, cited from the beginning where it is written: "And Rabbi Yochanan said, what is the name of the Messiah?" up to the place where Rabbi Eliezer takes up the discussion, saying, "The days of the Messiah." And later in many of their writings, such as the commentaries on the *Song of the Synagogue*: **He is called the head and the first.** The names of the Messiah are explained as <term>Shiloh</term>, <term>Innon</term>, <term>David</term>, <term>Hanina</term>, <term>the Sprout</term>, <term>the Just One</term>, and <term>the Comforter</term>. Yet each of these <margin>E</margin> is considered a symbolic title, much like the seven examples listed there, which are: the <term>Ark</term>, the <term>Mercy Seat</term>, the <term>Tablets</term>, <term>Aaron’s Rod</term>, the <term>Jar of Manna</term>, and the <term>Spirit of God</term>.

But according to the Kabbalists, you have heard how this one ineffable name **IHVH** <note>The Tetragrammaton</note> is proper to the Messiah, which will integrate and perfect his substantial name. For they teach that it must be believed that this is his integrated name, which is piously and holily integrated in mercies. No Talmudist can secretly deny this, since that great Master said in the mentioned place in the Talmud that the name of the Messiah will come to be called <margin>F</margin> similarly <term>Hanina</term>, that is, "mercy," citing <term>Jeremiah</term> chapter 16, verse 13. However, the Romans <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate translation</note> read this loosely and improperly as: "Who will not give you rest." But that is not an etymological interpretation. For in my judgment, it is more correctly read: "Because I will not give you mercy." Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The author of the Targum, the Aramaic translation of the Prophets</note> translated <margin>G</margin> this as **mercies** <note>original Aramaic: "rachamin"</note>. It is as if he wished to say, according to the Talmudists, that for you who walk in the depravity of your heart so that you do not hear God, there will be no Messiah, who is named "mercies." By this, it clearly becomes known that **in him are mercies** <note>original Hebrew: "bo rachamim"</note>; that is, through the mercies in the midst of I.H.V.H., the name shall be the proper name

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> of the Savior Messiah. His dignity and office, even if they consist of rigor and severity according to the prophecy of King David expressed without controversy regarding the Messiah—"He shall judge your people," he says, "in justice, and your poor in judgment"—nevertheless, because "judgment" (**mishpat** in Hebrew) according to all Kabbalists admits clemency along with justice. For so it is read in the fourth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>The *Sha'are Orah*, a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>: **For judgment is half rigor and half clemency.** <note>Original Hebrew: "ki ha-mishpat chetsyo din ve-chetsyo chesed"</note> By these means, the reconciliation of the first fall shall occur through a repeated union and a certain new betrothal of the people with God, as <margin>B</margin> Hosea predicted: "I will betroth you to me in justice and judgment; in mercy and in compassions," where it is placed as **in compassions** <note>original Hebrew: "be-rachamim"</note>. This is so no one might think that the coming of the Messiah is destined from some legal necessity, and not rather from pure grace and the most liberal gift of God. The illustrious name of clemency is rightly imposed on this Savior, which will be composed of all the letters—both vowels and the consonant—signifying only mercy and nothing else besides.

<margin>C</margin> And this perhaps we infer through the four holy letters by which, as if by signs and symbols, the Ineffable is depicted, and through the consonant <term>Shin</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ש</note>, by which the Ineffable Name is pronounced. For it is a common saying in the Kabbalah that this mark **שׁ** is explained as **The name of the Lord is called** <note>original Hebrew: "Shem IHVH Nikra"</note> through <term>notariacon</term> <note>A shorthand system where each letter of a word stands for another word</note>; that is, the Name of the Four Letters [Tetragrammaton] spoken or brought forth. There are no other letters by which bare mercy alone is designated, except these five: <margin>D</margin> I, H, V, H, and the consonant <term>Shin</term> <note>This identifies the name as IHShVH, or Yeshua/Jesus</note>. Regarding the four vowels <note>the letters of the Tetragrammaton were often treated as vowels by Christian Kabbalists</note>, it is read in the book *Gates of Justice*: **And this is the secret of what they said, that behold, the Lord [IHVH] goes out from his place, and he goes out from the attribute of mercy.** <note>Original Hebrew: "ve-hu sod she-ameru ki hinneh IHVH yotze mi-mekomo ve-yotze mi-middat ha-rachamim"</note> This is the mystery that our Masters (may their memory be in peace) spoke of: that behold, the four-lettered name (Micah says) I.H.V.H. shall go out from his place; he shall go out through the property of mercies.

Regarding the consonant <margin>E</margin> <term>Shin</term>, all Kabbalists who are not ignorant in Kabbalistic <term>Gematria</term> <note>The practice of calculating the numerical value of Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings</note> will not deny that the letter <term>Shin</term> contains within itself the ratio of the entire four-lettered name according to arithmetic proportion, and that the same property of clemency and mercy is possessed by it. Therefore, the salvation of all men is to be expected from the mercy of God alone, which Habakkuk openly expressed when addressing God: "When you are angry, you will remember mercy." There, David Camhi, whom our people <margin>F</margin> call Kimhi (just as others pronounce "Rabbi" and Germany says <term>Ribi</term>, through the easy conversion of the vowel *a* into *i*, as a similar judgment exists among the Greeks and Latins—they say *grammatikē* and *logikē*, we say Grammatica and Logica; they say *mētēr*, we say *mater*; so also Samson becomes Simson, and Camhi becomes Kimhi, and many others)—that David, I say, a Spanish Jew, teaches that through the name **mercy** <note>original Hebrew: "rechem"</note> placed there, it is to be understood symbollically according to Kabbalistic arithmetic as referring to Abraham. <margin>G</margin> It is as if Habakkuk were saying: "O God, when you are touched by the anger of our sin, remember the seed of Abraham, to whom you promised that in him all the families of the earth shall be blessed." And again, "O God, you spoke to him: in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." Moreover, Habakkuk himself indicated this...

# BOOK ONE

He himself, concerning what that "seed" <note>Referring to the "seed of the woman" in Genesis or the Davidic line</note> would be, added: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Messiah." <note>Habakkuk 3:13</note> Regarding this, David Kimchi <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish commentator and grammarian, also known as the Radak</note> writes: <margin>A</margin> **He is the Messiah, the son of David.** <note>original Hebrew: "Hu Mashiach ben David"</note> I say, therefore, along with the wise Kabbalists, that the true salvation of us all depends upon the Messiah, as many of us as can reach him. Thus it happens that, freeing ourselves as much as possible from all created things, we should strive to ascend through all the degrees and migrate into him, so that if we do not fully attain him, we may at least follow him <margin>B</margin> according to the strength of each individual. For he is our very purpose, to whose coming the whole Law is referred by us (even intellectually); and not only the writings of Moses, but also the Prophets and whatever is contained in the Hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms and Daniel</note>. For that entire context, which we call the **Twenty-four** <note>original: "Esrim ve-arba," referring to the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible</note> and you call the Bible, we designate as a whole by the name **The Torah** <note>original Hebrew: "Ha-Torah"</note>, that is, the Law. As it says in Daniel chapter 9: "By walking in the law of the Lord our God, which he set before us by the hand of his servants the Prophets." <margin>C</margin> We have determined that this scripture alone is so stable and so firm that we can safely ground all our thoughts upon it, and place the sublime contemplations of speculative men there without confusion—both because it was proclaimed by the voice of the Most High God, and because it is accustomed to work with such great energetic power in the minds of the most contemplative men. Through it, one can ascend from any mixed things to the simple, from the simple to the most simple, from effects <margin>D</margin> to causes, and finally from the lower world to the superior; from the superior to the Messiah, who is the supreme object of our mind and conceivable at the final degree, as if to the King of Ages. Through him, we may at last pass plainly into the incomprehensible God. Furthermore, through these sacred letters—as if through Jacob's ladder, whose top touches the heavens and upon which God himself leans—our angels ascend and descend: carriers of prayers from here, and of gifts from there, <margin>E</margin> who carry aid back and forth, as one of your own authors says. And truly, nothing else in our senses, or even that could be imagined, binds our soul more closely to God (just as several threads are woven together) than that very sacred scripture mentioned, which first leads us into the admiration of divine things, then into an acknowledgment of them according to human capacity, and finally into that most ardent love of the divinity however it is known, which brings with it the most certain <margin>F</margin> effect of hope. Through this, with Ezekiel's living creatures and wheels, we are lifted from the earth, so that with those who go, we go, and with those who stand, we stand. This is the only field of true contemplation, whose individual words are each sacraments, and its individual speeches, syllables, peaks, and points are full of secrets—as even the Christians attest. This is the Kabbalah, which does not allow us to dwell on the ground, but extols our mind to the highest goal of comprehension, which nevertheless cannot rationally transcend the Soul of the Messiah, <margin>G</margin> except by a certain incomprehensible intuition, by way of a momentary rapture, which we think is not impossible for us Kabbalists <column-break/> to be caught up in spirit near the third world, <margin>A</margin> where the Messiah flows into all lower things. For the most general worlds are three in number. The first is material, the second formal, and the third formless. Or if you prefer: the first is the lowest, which is also sensible; the second is the highest and mental, which is also intelligible; and the third is **super-supreme** <note>original Greek: "hyperotatos"</note>, or if I may say, the "most supreme," incomparable and divine. I intended this corporeal world to be considered the first world in relation to us, though it is the foundation for the others; <margin>B</margin> perhaps in a reversed order, since by just reason in the category of causes it ought to have been last, acting as a receptacle for all superior things. This world is constituted first from the heavens and celestial things; second from the elements and things made of elements; and third from human nature and individual men, who are called in Hebrew **the little world** <note>original Hebrew: "Olam ha-katan"</note>, in Greek **microcosm** <note>original Greek: "microcosmos"</note>, and in Latin **parvus mundus**. This entire body, as your Aristotle pleases in his book *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo"</note>, is a globe constituted of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them, namely with seven celestial dwellings and seven terrestrial dwellings. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, Rabbi Menahem Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist</note> enumerates these in chapter 25 of Leviticus. Those pertaining to heaven are: **Heavens, Firmament, Skies, Abode, Residence, Foundation, and the Highest Heavens** <note>original Hebrew: "Shamayim, Raquia, Shachakim, Zevul, Maon, Machon, Arabot"</note>. Second, those pertaining to the earth are: **Earth, Void, Valley, Dry Land, World, Age, and Earth** <note>original Hebrew: "Eretz, Arka, Geya, Yabashah, Tevel, Cheled, Eretz"</note>. Joseph of Salerno <note>Referring to Joseph Gikatilla, a 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist; "of Salerno" may refer to the origin of a specific manuscript or tradition</note> in his *Garden of the Nut* <note>original Latin: "Horto nucis"; Hebrew: "Ginnat Egoz"</note> also recited by name (as you heard a little earlier) the seven dwellings of the underworld. Regarding the Microcosm, it is not hidden from any of us that seven things pertain to the condition of man, in whichever part you look: <margin>D</margin> these are the body, the soul, and that which is composed of them, which we call **the person** <note>original Hebrew: "Nephesh"</note>, as in that saying of the King of Sodom: "Give me the person" <note>Genesis 14:21</note>, that is, give me the man; composed, of course, of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the greater world. This world, since it is animated, is illuminated by its own mind, which is called **Metattron** <note>A supreme angel in Kabbalah, often described as the "Prince of the Countenance" or the mediator between the divine and the physical realms</note>. The second is the supreme world of separate intelligences, which <margin>E</margin> the Kabbalists call **separate intellects** <note>original Hebrew: "Sekhalim nifradim"</note> and the Hebrew philosophers call **separate minds** <note>original Hebrew: "De'ot nifradot"</note>. This world—full of species, forms, and unbound minds and angels—is encompassed, surrounded, and ruled by the **Soul of the Messiah** itself. Among Kabbalists, this is the prototype of all lives, and into which all individual, specific, and generic vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery, all life is drawn; it is named by the Kabbalists the **Land of the Living** <note>original Latin: "terra viuentium"</note>. Therefore they comment on the verse: "Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind" <note>Genesis 1:24</note>: <margin>F</margin> **This is the Soul of the Messiah.** These words are read thus in the second chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Porta lucis"; Hebrew: "Sha'are Orah"</note>: Just as in the human world, which is called the Microcosm, the mind rules the man, so Metattron rules the celestial world, the Soul of the Messiah rules the angelic world, and Adonai <note>The Lord</note> rules the incomparable world. Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the active intellect, so the light of <margin>G</margin> Metattron is **Shaddai** <note>Almighty</note>, and the light of the Soul of the Messiah is **El-Chai** <note>The Living God</note>, and the light of Adonai is **Ein Soph** <note>The Infinite, the boundless divine essence</note>. And as it easily appears to the most skilled investigators of natural things, the lowest part of a higher nature communicates with the highest part of a lower nature...

From this arises the intimate friendship of the Kabbalist with the Angels, through which, sometimes by rightly knowing the divine names, he performs wonderful things which the common people call miracles. <margin>A</margin> In the memory of our fathers, the Kabbalists' performance of miracles was of such a kind that they were often disgracefully labeled "cunning magicians" by the envious and the profane, as if those works were not perfected through Michael <note>The archangel Michael, often seen in Kabbalah as the protector of Israel and a force of mercy</note>, but much more through Samael <note>original: "Samael"; in Kabbalistic tradition, the primary archangel of the "other side" or the forces of severity and death</note>—namely, through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets. Yet the staff of the Kabbalists always devours the staffs of the jugglers, and anything divine acts more healthfully than anything demonic. For the artifice of the Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas, on the contrary, the poison of magical vanity always inclines toward destruction. The latter works through the names of darkness and evil spirits; the former through the names of light and the blessed angels. Concerning these—were it not for the fact that, according to our custom, the restful day of the Sabbath was already approaching this very hour of the evening—I would certainly treat more amply whatever I might feel, especially since it pertains to this point as the fruit of this art which you so greatly desire. But the night is nearly rushing upon us, excellent men, and we must withdraw—not only so that I do not receive many lashes for neglecting the commandment, but also so that I do not fail my Kabbalistic profession if, on this Sabbath, I were to dig out supreme and hidden secrets with laborious effort beyond *Sabbathai* <note>original: "Sabbathai"; the Hebrew name for the planet Saturn, which corresponds to the seventh day, the Sabbath</note>, which is Saturn, rather than tarrying in silence and enjoying leisure until the following day has passed. The remaining matters we shall explain here on the day after tomorrow, or at whatever time you choose, concerning the Kabbalistic art.

Then Philolaus said, "You have sustained the most difficult parts of speaking quite strongly for our sake; after midday, when we approached you, you brought forth so many things, so wonderful and in such number, in a continuous discourse, yet you seemed moved by no trouble at all."

And he replied then, "My love toward you, which I hope is mutual, has taken away all trouble. Were it not for the holidays, I would not think it right to send away such great men as yourselves, who have traveled here for the sake of learning, so <margin>B</margin> hungry and unsatisfied by the doctrine of the Kabbalah; but the law must be obeyed."

To this, Martanus said, "I truly confess, Simon, that I have never departed from anyone’s presence more learned. To me—or if you prefer, to both of us, as I speak for him too—it is certain that you have done enough, as much as it is believed the time allowed to be endured."

Soon Philolaus said, "I wish you would plead only your own cause, Marranus; as for me, I shall not think I have been satisfied yet by these things—though they are very great and approach the Pythagorean doctrine <note>Philolaus is a character representing the Pythagorean philosophical tradition, which Reuchlin believed was derived from ancient Hebrew wisdom</note> most closely—unless the postponed day brings an end to the art for me as a listener more copiously. For this reason, after this Sabbath of yours, Simon, since you bear with us with such singular kindness, we shall return."

And he said, "Return then, fearlessly, and meanwhile, fare you well in good health."

As both departed from there—the younger Philolaus and Martanus—toward home, there was various conversation between them as they went, and not foolish conversation, as they were philosophers learned beyond measure. They spoke of this very Hebrew man, whose singular humanity toward strangers they commended alongside his supreme learning, and his dignity of character in all things and above all things. All things about the man pleased them, except for this one Sabbath, which they judged would be full of boredom, by which they were torn away from the most grateful conversation of such a great master and cast aside until the third day, not without a troublesome loss of time, since they did not know what they would do on the morrow. Then, as they walked, they ruminated on the juice of the doctrine they had received, recounting to one another brief summaries of what had been said.

But while they were burning with the fervor of learning, there came to mind and suddenly returned to memory the speech of that admirable Jewish man: the sharpness of his debating, his grave and erudite instruction which delights without satiety, not faked, not colored, <margin>F</margin> but which, where it most lacks flowers, there it produces the most fruit. # KABBALAH

<margin>A</margin> This art was once held to be barbaric, superstitious, worthless, cast aside, and far removed from the brilliance of all good arts. Believe me, I would have willingly remained in this perpetual night to look upon this man’s face and hear his spoken words, if this wretched Sabbath evening had not intervened. Then Philolaus said: Not even all the Greeks, to whom by universal consent the mastery of many arts, sharpness of wit, and abundance of speech are attributed, could have ascended into the high summits of secret things, <margin>B</margin> unless perhaps that famous Pythagoras of mine, the father of philosophy, had received that excellence of doctrine—not from the Greeks, but rather from those very Jews. Therefore, he too should be named a "receiver" <note>A play on the word "Kabbalist," derived from the Hebrew root *QBL*, meaning "to receive."</note> by the best right—that is, a Kabbalist—although, so that he might bring back something worthy of admiration to his homeland after a long pilgrimage from afar (which would be more easily believed by the common people), he changed that name of "Kabbalah," which was unknown to his peers, into the Greek name "Philosophy." <margin>C</margin> We correctly infer this by the argument that he left his disciples no faculty for inquiring by any reason, but rather willed that the first principle of his dogma be this: that to those seeking a reason, they should answer, *He himself said it* <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (*autos epha*); a famous phrase used by Pythagoreans to cite their master's authority without further proof</note>. This is the custom of the Kabbalists, who cite the reasons for knowing things in almost no other way than saying, *The Sages have said* <note>original Hebrew: "אמרו חכמים" (*Amru Chakhamim*); the standard formula for citing Rabbinic tradition</note>. So did our man say, *He himself said it*. This same man is Pythagoras, who is said to have bestowed the name of philosophy in this manner, <margin>D</margin> since the highest authors of the Hebrews were called *Hachamim* <note>Hebrew: "Wise Men"</note> and the Greeks before him were once called *Sophi* <note>Greek: "Sages"</note>; thus he attempted to clothe an ancient discipline with the ornament of a new name. However, the things Simon the Jew brought forth ought not to seem less worthy of praise to you because they were taken from an ignoble Teacher of the Hebrew nation, as if from barbaric authors, or brought by a barbarian man; for that same Pythagoras, the greatest of all, <margin>E</margin> entered into his first studies of the sciences together with a certain barbarian named Zora <note>Likely referring to Zoroaster</note>. Indeed, he did this outside of Greece, at the time when he philosophized among the Egyptians (who were then called Prophets), the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls, the Samanaeans <note>An ancient term for Eastern monks or ascetics</note> from the Bactrians, many of the Celts, the Magi among the Persians, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked wise men"; a term used by Greeks for Indian philosophers</note> among the Indians, that Anacharsis among the Scythians, and Zamolxis in Thrace (formerly Pythagoras's own slave). All of this was left in writing by the famous Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor, in his book <margin>F</margin> *On Pythagorean Symbols* <note>original Greek: "περὶ Πυθαγορικῶν συμβόλων"</note>. Finally, among the Indians, he encountered the Jews, whom they called Brahmans, as Aristobulus the Peripatetic mentions. Truly, if the truth be told, Pythagoras is certainly not found to have learned anything of things divine or human from the Greeks or the Romans. But as Antiphon published in his book <margin>G</margin> *On the Lives of Those Who Precelled in Virtue* <note>original Greek: "περὶ βίου τῶν ἐν ἀρετῇ πρωτευσάντων"</note>: Pythagoras went to the Egyptians, the Arabs, and the Chaldeans for the sake of learning, after he had obtained Pherecydes as his master and teacher from Syria, which is and is called Judea. Whence he himself was also commonly called a Syrian, though others called him a Tyrian,

<column-break/>

others a Tyrrhenian, *so as to proclaim that this first of all philosophers was a barbarian and not a Greek* <note>original Greek: "ὥστε βάρβαρον ἀλλ' οὐχ' ἑλληνὰ γεγονέναι τοῦτον ὁμολογεῖν τὸν πρῶτον φιλόσοφον"</note>. These things, Marranus, my most learned table-companion, I know for certain you have read in the writings of Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian</note>—in the volume, if I recall rightly, *On the Gospel Preparation*, book eleven—who also added this: *Only that he had nothing from the wise Greeks, who lived in a poverty of wisdom and a lack of resources* <note>original Greek: "μένον ότι οὐδὲ τὴν Ἑλλήνων ἔσχεν οὐδὲν, πενίᾳ σοφίας καὶ ἀπορίᾳ συνοικούντων"</note>. Concerning these people, as it is in Plato's *Timaeus*, a certain Egyptian barbarian, and a very old one at that, truly seemed to have said to Solon: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; you have no ancient opinion, no discipline gray with time." Nor should that be anything but highly praised in Pythagoras, a man of outstanding wisdom and nobility: that on foreign and distant soil, he gathered through immense labor, cold, and sweat, through much study and meditation over many years, things from barbaric men. These things he brought back to his homeland—I will not say better, but certainly more splendid—and even into Italy, which was then called Great Greece, as if on his own shoulders. He did this with the incredible admiration of everyone for himself and his followers, so that anyone who excelled in wisdom and learning was believed to have been a listener of Pythagoras. Whence Italic Philosophy took its name chiefly from him. Numenius the Pythagorean supports this praise in his first volume *On the Good*, when he says that whatever the Brahmans, Magi, Egyptians, and Jews established, Plato and Pythagoras themselves set forth in Greek. Because of this, we strongly suspect that what the most learned men and those skilled in various languages assert is true: that the accepted discoveries of the Jews are set forth through the thefts of others, here by the Greeks, there by the Latins. Nothing in Philosophy is ours that was not first the Jews', however much in this century their deserved glory is taken from them, and now all their things are despised, because the present age desires a more illustrious and polished explanation of all studies. Then Marranus said: You speak the truth, excellent Philolaus, and thus I more strongly agree with Hecuba in Euripides: *For a speech coming from the ignoble and from the famous does not have the same power* <note>original Greek: "λόγος γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ἀδοξούντων ἰὼν κ’ ἐκ τῶν δοκούντων αὐτὸς οὐ ταυτὸν σθένει"</note>. For if some Aristotle or some Theophrastus had brought forth those things which Simon taught us today, in everyone’s opinion nothing would be more worthy of hearing, nothing weightier, nothing more memorably balanced, or possessing some veneer of eloquence. Now, because it is a Jew who has treated the whole matter a little more rustically and concisely in his own fashion, there is no doubt that these things will be filthy in the ears of those Sophists of our age (as they seem to themselves, clearly very subtle). If any should hear or are about to hear, or rather to all those now philosophizing either perversely or foolishly, these things may appear tangled, clamorous, gaping, meager, horrid, sounding of rustic bitterness and foreign strangeness—even though (as is their custom) they have not first examined them as much as is necessary.

<summary>Philolaus and Marranus argue that Greek philosophy, including the work of Pythagoras and Plato, was largely adapted from Jewish and "barbaric" wisdom. They conclude that Jewish learning is unfairly dismissed in their own time simply because it lacks the polished rhetorical style favored by modern scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Kabbalah, Jewish wisdom, Greek philosophy, Plato, cultural transmission, cultural bias, Hachamim, Sophi, translation of knowledge</keywords>

# SECOND BOOK #

...examined indeed, as if gold were not gold <margin>A</margin> simply because we seek it in the mud. But after we have now returned by a straight path from this man to our inn, with no one to guide us, and since dinner is perhaps not yet ready for us, I suggest that we each recite to one another what we have heard—especially the more worthy things—and fix them in our memory so they do not slip away while everything is still fresh. 

And Philolaus said, "How prudently you have pre-planned those things, Marranus! For in this way we shall approach the day after tomorrow <note>The day after the Sabbath.</note> better prepared for listening, after this Sabbath marvel <margin>B</margin>—the sacred rites performed by the Jew on the seventh day, as Ovid says <note>original Latin: "Cultaet Judaeo septimo sacra viro"</note>. Meanwhile, you take this chair, I will take the other, and sitting together let us speak quickly of all things until what is suitable for dinner is prepared. Moreover, lest a place be given to useless contention while we are alone—for that would be nothing other than a waste of time—you speak first whatever comes to your mouth, whether for the sake of remembering the past or present, or for the sake of commenting in whatever way it happens."

<margin>C</margin> Thus Marranus began his discourse: "And although," he said, "this whole business around which we have been occupied this afternoon seems to me, as I weigh each part exactly, to be higher than we who are stretched out on the ground can look up to, nevertheless, things which at first glance appear arduous and impossible to men often become both plain and easy through continuous and indefatigable exercise and hard labor, according to that saying of Maro <note>The poet Virgil.</note>:

<margin>Labor conquers all.</margin>

<margin>D</margin> Therefore I will gladly bring into the open what I remember hearing from that man, and I will add to them what I myself feel. Our Hebrew teacher, being about to treat the Kabbalah at our request, conveniently showed what is to be understood by that name. For *Kabbalah* designates 'reception'; at the same time, he brought this point: that it is always implanted in our souls, which by their natural condition tend toward the highest things. On account of this, a desire for it is known to be engendered in us, and that the highest and more sublime divine matters are held to be more worthy than what can be comprehended and discerned by human reason.

<margin>E</margin> Moreover, this is a commonplace dogma among the worthy Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>. For to allow me to cite my Arabs, with whom I have a usual familiarity: Al-Farabi <note>Alpharabius, a famous medieval Islamic philosopher.</note>, in the book he wrote *On the Sciences*, uses this sentiment: that divine things and those believable through pious faith are of a higher order, since they are taken from divine inspiration, because in them human reasons are weakened and do not reach them. These are the words of that Arab, which our Simon also affirmed; he calls those orders 'regions,' and in the third region of our soul he places incorporeal things and substances free and immune from all weight of matter—not those fantastic and logical universals that Antisthenes <note>A Greek philosopher often associated with a rejection of abstract Platonic ideas.</note> thought of. But I mean the real forms themselves, the species, the ideas, the essences, which are the highest things around which the Kabbalists occupy themselves (as I hear) with their nearly inexpressible contemplations. Every single thing that we think we perceive or know, they bring to this point, and finally they lead all things back into the One—which is the Good itself and the First—through intermediate steps, as if to the most healthy end of our mind. This is what Aristotle, in the 14th book of those things he wrote *After the Natural* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note>, 

<column-break/>

called that which is <term>αυταρκες και η σωτηρια</term> <note>original Greek: *autarkes kai hē sōtēria*</note>, that is, 'Self-sufficient and Salvation,' and what Simon named in Hebrew as <term>ישועה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yeshu'ah*</note> (Salvation). Just as the Royal Psalmist says, 'Salvation is of the Lord'; and upon this salvation of the human race, Simon laid the foundations of all Kabbalists. These things are neither to be investigated by reason, nor are they investigated through reason, as they are things for which neither the senses provided a foundation <note>original: *hypostasim*</note> nor the intellect a discipline. For they are the highest things, for which an adequate cause cannot be found, and from the knowledge of which the most eloquent Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> took away the faculty of science. For he wrote thus in his *Supernaturals*: <term>Μεχρι μεν ουν τινος δυναμεθα δι' αιτιου θεωρειν, αρχας απο της αισθησεως λαμβανοντες, οταν δε επ' αυτα τα ακρα και πρωτα μεταβαινωμεν, ετι δυνάμεθα ειπειν το μη εχειν αιτιαν, ειτε δια την ημετεραν ασθενειαν.</term> <note>original Greek: "Up to a certain point we are able to contemplate through cause, taking principles from the senses; but when we pass over to the extremes and first things themselves, we are no longer able [to speak], either because they have no cause, or because of our own weakness."</note> For concerning the celestial and divine things, before which there is nothing, from where, I ask, could any middle ground for demonstration be taken?

Wherefore Plato says in the *Timaeus* that to explain those things is more than our strengths are sufficient for; but he commands that they be believed by those who spoke before, even though they speak with no necessity of demonstration. These words of Plato and the mandates of a truly wise man I value so much that I think they should be held by me in the place of an oracle. And if there are any fixed and established foundations of the Kabbalah, these are they. 

On account of which, I judge the logical syllogism to be the sharpest enemy and waylayer of divine knowledge—which consists in naked faith. By the daring and use of the "God-talkers" <note>original: *Theophosophistarum*</note>, the syllogism subjects God, the Angels, the blessed and simplest minds beyond the powers of the mundane world, the entire army of eternity, and whatever exists anywhere in the histories of supernatural things, to human mortality to be found, proved, and directed by the discourse of reason—just as if one were trying to shut those illustrious substances into some Roman dungeon <note>original: *Tullianum*</note>. This is surely to want to conquer Jove, or to bind him with a willow twig or a nautical rope. Which not even Thetis (according to Homer) would permit, nor that hundred-handed Briareus, Aegeon. By which I judge the contentious theologians and the bellowing sophists to be no less stormers of heaven and the super-celestial things than the twin Aloidae <note>Giants in Greek myth who tried to pile mountains to reach heaven.</note> with their immense bodies, as Virgil says, who attempted to tear down the great sky with their hands. They are no different than the Shinarites and Babylonians of old, the sons of Adam—that is, those born from human weakness, which they did not recognize in themselves—building a very high tower whose top would reach all the way to heaven, the leaders of <term>בלבל</term> (Balbel) <note>original Hebrew: *balbel*, meaning "to confuse" or "confound."</note>, that is, the authors of Confusion. From this comes Babel, which you call Babylon, where no one understood the language of another. For through these talkative syllogizers, in matters of belief, all piety toward the university of divine things is lost, and brotherly hatred is stirred up by the zeal for winning; they are like hunting dogs most ready for sedition, a poison of the highest contemplation that must be expelled from the whole world. Let these things triumph: if it is right."

<sig>Ee</sig>

Citing ancient philosophers and the story of Babel, Marranus warns that trying to subject the divine to human reason leads only to spiritual confusion and social discord.</summary>
