<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. They are discussing the limitations of human logic—specifically the "syllogism"—when applied to divine matters, arguing that true sacred knowledge (Kabbalah) comes from a higher "Mind" or faith rather than human reasoning.</meta>

# CABALA #

...the artifices of syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> have their place in nature and in human inventions and fictions. But let them not hope for any place for themselves in the sacred oracles. For this is the dogma that Parmenides, in the works of Plato, handed down to Socrates concerning separate substances, saying: "But in the same way, we do not rule those divine beings by our authority, nor do we know anything of the divine by our own knowledge." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ ὁμοίως ἡμεῖς ἐκείνων ἂν ἀρχομεθα τῇ παρ' ἡμῖν ἀρχῇ, οὐδὲ γιγνώσκομεν τὰ θεῖα οὐδέν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ ἐπιστήμῃ."</note> The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> agree with this speech, and even Aristotle himself—who was both the craftsman and the "organon" (instrument) of knowing—affirms in the first volume of his *Posterior Analytics* that the knowledge of *Immediate Principles* is indemonstrable. 

A little later he says: "And we say that there is not only knowledge, but also some principle of knowledge by which we recognize terms." Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and rhetorician.</note> calls our own mind the "principle of knowledge" there; while "terms" refers to the subject and predicate from which the greatest propositions are composed. But Philoponus (who is commonly called John the Grammarian) explained these things much more sublimely and truly, writing thus: "The philosopher here sought out the explanation of the preceding statement and rendered it so: taking the 'Mind' as the principle of knowledge—not our human mind, but the divine mind that is above us. For the 'terms' are the intelligible and divine forms. Indeed, they are called 'terms' because they are the ends (limits) of all things." <note>original Greek: "ὁ μὲν φιλόσοφος πὼς ἐζήτησεν... ὅρος δὲ αὐτὰ καλεῖσθαι διὰ τὸ πέρατα εἶναι πάντων."</note> 

Therefore, the cognition of supernatural beliefs depends on the Mind, not on Reason, which can err by its own reckoning. For Aristotle writes: "Falsehood is possible in opinion and in reasoning." <note>original Greek: "ἐνδέχεται τὸ ψεῦδος καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ λογισμὸς."</note> This is why it is called a "syllogism" <note>literally "reckoning together".</note>. Finally, he concludes the *Posterior Analytics* thus: "All knowledge," he says, "is with reason. Of the first principles, there will certainly not be 'knowledge' (in the sense of logical demonstration). Since, however, nothing happens to be more true than the Mind, the Mind must belong to the principles." Now, the "first principles" are the primary things: and Hesiod and all the ancient theologians made the gods to be the principles; therefore this cognition is properly named "Divine." And as that same Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was from the city of Stagira.</note> wrote in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, the possession of it is "not human." That is, it is justly a possession that is not human: because either God alone, or God most of all, possesses it, and it is unworthy for a man to seek any such "science" concerning Him. For God alone has this honor, according to Simonides. 

But since nothing is more conducive to our happiness than the knowledge of the highest and divine things, by what other way (I ask you, Philolaus) must a man proceed to them, if not by science? Or by what modes can such great heights be grasped? 

Then Philolaus said: "By Pollux! You yourself have shown a plain and open path. For since there are five workers of cognition, according to the testimony of Ammonius—following Aristotle, who mentions only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*—they are: Mind, Discourse, Opinion, Imagination, and Sensation." <note>original Greek: "νοῦς, διάνοια, δόξα, φαντασία, αἴσθησις."</note> That is:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Sensation. The Mind and Sensation do not use syllogisms: the one is far above reason, the other far below it. But neither does Imagination, since it is a resting place for sensation and a reservation for the appearances migrating from there. Since the senses do not reason at all, one must not even think that the appearances of the senses are able to reason. There remain, therefore, Opinion and Discourse; but Opinion is the conclusion of Discourse itself, wherefore it does not reason on its own. Only to Discourse, therefore, which is called *dianoia*, is the faculty of syllogizing left: this is the opinion of Ammonius in the commentaries he published on Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*.

<margin>B</margin> And since I have briefly touched upon the types of comprehension and the things comprehended, lest my speech wander too far, I believe that divine things are above the syllogism, and cannot be understood by human reason. These things do not take their origin of knowing from the senses, but depend on pure faith; they are received only out of a reverent love and believed for the happiness of men. There are, however, very many things that are often mixed into divine speculation—just as the freedmen and tenants of a single family sometimes use a common name—and these things frequently (I confess it) allow themselves to be treated by the sacred theological faculty because they have obtained some order toward God, either through themselves or through reduction, or perhaps by some other relation such as creation, preservation, perfection, justification, happiness, salvation, and the like.

<margin>C</margin> I am not thinking of those things at present, because I know they are made known to us naturally; their existence is asserted in the *Metaphysics*, and their purpose in the theological works. I certainly grant "reason" to those things, since they once arose from the senses and are given over to human discourse; but those things whose truth depends solely on the authority of the one revealing them—of those I do not think there is a "science," nor would I wish the syllogism to dominate them.

<margin>D</margin> But only that which will be more excellent than all things: Faith. He who possesses it is called by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* "one who is better disposed by fortune and respect" <note>original Greek: "βέλτιον διάκειμενοί εἰσι τύχῃ καὶ αἰδῷ."</note>—that is, better disposed than if he were "knowing." Philoponus explained this as: "to know better than through demonstration."

<margin>E</margin> To this Marranus replied: "I agree with you, Philolaus, and with you I also forbid those very things which are of pure faith and purely believable from being subjected to 'logical snares,' which are clearly more of a detriment than a gain to contemplation; and our people, both Greeks and Latins, have asserted the same.

<margin>F</margin> Jerome the Dalmatian <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin.</note>, writing on the 104th Psalm, compares the art of the syllogism applied to theology to the plagues of Egypt, saying: 'The gnat is understood as the sting of the dialectical art, which, though it may seem to have a small needle of deception in the thing itself, nevertheless wounds human minds most severely.' Therefore, that most learned man removed and rejected this trickery—which he also calls 'vanity of the senses' and 'obscurity of the mind'—entirely from Hebrew studies, as he did elsewhere many times, but most clearly to Damasus concerning the questions proposed to him, where in the second one he uses these words: 'It is not fitting for one disputing about Hebrew matters to go looking for the arguments of Aristotle.'

<margin>G</margin> And in Psalm 143, he writes thus about the theosophists: 'When they begin to dispute with you, their words are so brief, so concluded with artificial speech, that it is difficult for you to escape; for when they have bound you with syllogisms...'

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence as Marranus quotes Jerome's warning about being trapped by logical arguments in spiritual matters.</meta>

<summary>This passage argues that divine knowledge and the Hebrew tradition (Kabbalah) transcend human logic and Aristotelian syllogisms, relying instead on a higher "Mind" and faith. It cites classical philosophers and Church fathers like Jerome to warn that applying rigid dialectics to sacred truths is like a "sting" that obscures spiritual understanding.</summary>
<keywords>syllogism, logic, faith, Aristotle, Jerome, Philoponus, mind, nous, discourse, dianoia, Hebrew studies, divine knowledge, Kabbalah</keywords>

--- Page 377 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. It deepens the argument that human logic—specifically the "syllogism"—is a trap when applied to divine mysteries, contrasting the "simplicity of faith" with the "curiosity of reason."</meta>

## BOOK TWO ##

...with their syllogisms, and have enclosed you, as if they had stripped you and built a stone wall of logic around you, it cannot collapse, and you cannot pass through; you are held prisoner. There is no breaking the wall, nor any way across. And when they hold you there, as if enclosed in a certain circle, then you will not be on the narrow way that leads to life, but on the broad way that leads to death. For, <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡ τῆς ἁπλότητος πίστις, βελτίων ἐστὶ τῆς ἐκ περιεργασίας πιθανολογίας"</note> **the faith of simplicity is better than the persuasive logic of meddlesome curiosity.** That is to say, since the faith of simplicity is better than the reasoned persuasion of curiosity, as Athanasius <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian famous for defending orthodoxy.</note> said in his third book *Against the Arians*.
<margin>A</margin>
He confirms this same point in his work *Against the Greeks*, which begins thus: <note>original Greek: "ἡ μὲν περὶ τῆς Θεοσεβείας καὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων ἀληθείας γνῶσις, οὐ δεῖται τῆς παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων διδασκαλίας δεῖται, ὅσον ἀφ’ ἑαυτῆς ἔχει τὸ γνώριμον"</note> **"Indeed, the very knowledge of divine worship and of the truth of all things does not so much require instruction established by men, as it possesses its own clarity from within itself."**
<margin>B</margin>
So says Athanasius. Let everyone decide for themselves that nothing is truer than this. For what zeal for speaking, or what effort at persuasion, will be needed for that which I am prepared to believe of my own accord? I have already gladly received it through my love and singular veneration for the one revealing it, compelled or led by not even the slightest force of reason—at least not the kind of reason that the dullness of a soul, submerged and bound in this dark body, can devise.
<margin>C</margin>
Justin, that Christian philosopher and martyr, treats these matters much more abundantly in his book *On the Right Confession*, citing an ancient iambic verse: <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀνθρώποισι περὶ θείων σαφές"</note> **"For nothing regarding divine matters is clear to men."**
<margin>D</margin>
This sentiment even flowed from the mouth of Socrates. There is a letter from Xenophon (the student of Socrates) to Aeschines, where he says it is obvious to everyone that divine matters cannot be grasped by human knowledge. Therefore, it is enough to worship the gods themselves piously from the heart; but as to what they are like, it is neither possible for us to find out, nor is it right to ask. For it is not beneficial for servants, nor would I call it praiseworthy, if they wished to scrutinize the plans of their masters beyond what pertains to their own service.
<margin>E</margin>
And as for Socrates and the followers of other philosophers, the same author wrote in the *Memorabilia*: <note>original Greek: "ἐθαύμαζε δὲ εἰ μὴ φανερὸν αὐτοῖς ἔστιν, ὅτι ταῦτα οὐ δυνατὸν ἔστιν ἀνθρώποις εὑρεῖν"</note> **"He wondered, however—meaning Socrates—if it was not manifest to them that it is not possible for men to find these things."** Such has always been the opinion of all ages and almost all religions: that those things which were not previously in human sensation cannot be captured by the human intellect. And what the intellect does not capture, reason does not discuss; and what reason does not discuss, the discourse of reasoning—which they call <term>dianoia</term> <note>Discursive reasoning; the step-by-step process of the mind moving from one idea to another.</note>—will not judge.
<margin>F</margin>
This is especially true of divinely revealed truth, even if we form some conceptual images of them in our minds. Whatever we have received religiously and piously, we should not subject it to the violence of argumentation, nor to any phantom of the imagination. Therefore, Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop known as "The Theologian" for his eloquence.</note> followed the ancestors; he stands out among all our people in every branch of theology, with a beauty of words and weight of thought. He supports this doctrine similarly in his second book of *Theology*, affirming: <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὴ ληπτὸν τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ διανοίᾳ τὸ θεῖον, μηδ’ ὅλον ὅν ἐστὶ φαντάζεται"</note> **"The divine is not comprehensible to human discourse, nor can the mind imagine it in its entirety."**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
"Lest you suspect me, Marranus, of being entirely ignorant or negligent of Christian authors," Philolaus responded, "I remember that Athenagoras, the Athenian philosopher, acting as an envoy to the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, spoke thus on behalf of the Christians: <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ καὶ δι’ αὐτῆς τῆς δογματικῆς προσεχόμεθα ἐν ἀνθρωπικοῖς οὖσιν, ἀλλὰ θεοδιδάκτοις πείσαι ὑμᾶς μὴ ὡς περὶ θεῶν ἔχειν δυνάμεθα"</note> **'Since we also hold fast to these very dogmas, not as human things but as God-taught ones, we are able to persuade you (treating them not as profane things).’** Here he suggests that persuasion works one way for profane things, and another for divine ones."
<margin>B</margin>
"And yet, I know quite a few among you who throw everything into confusion with logical attachments. They treat natural things as if they were mathematical principles, and then turn around and establish theological truths based on natural ones. But divine causes are by no means equal to natural ones. Natural things have no power to direct the divine, and much less can things that stand by faith alone be demonstrated by any humanly knowable reason. Just as things that are purely believed do not necessarily imply things that are naturally known."
<margin>C</margin>
"For your most excellent Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A mystical theologian who was believed to be a convert of St. Paul.</note>—whom I would not foolishly consider to be either a remnant or an image of the Pythagoreans—speaks thus regarding these theological insights in his book *On the Divine Names*: <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲ γὰρ, ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια τοῖς αἰτιατοῖς καὶ τοῖς αἰτίοις, ἀλλ’ ἔχει μὲν τὰ αἰτιατὰ τὰς τῶν αἰτίων δεχομένας εἰκόνας, αὐτὰ δὲ αἰτία τῶν αἰτιατῶν ἐξῄρηται, καὶ ὑπερίδρυται κατὰ τὸν τῆς οἰκείας ἀρχῆς λόγον"</note> **'For there is no exact resemblance between effects and causes; rather, the effects possess the received images of the causes, but the causes themselves are set apart from the effects and reside above them, according to the principle of their own origin.'**"
<margin>D</margin>
"Because of this, the 'little net' of some of your people is even more deceptive and fallacious when they claim that in matters consisting of things revealed by faith alone, one must not only use the properties of syllogisms, but also believe with equal weight whatever follows from the sacred oracles through the artifice of logic—as if it were inferred by a good, formal, and necessary logical consequence. Nothing is so distant as that which is divinely revealed and that which is humanly discovered."
<margin>E</margin>
"Hence, in the realm of pure faith and things purely believable, 'believing' and 'knowing' are entirely distinct; a conclusion never follows the weaker part. We are right, therefore, to affirm that in the same subject and regarding the same truth, the habit of acquired faith and the habit of science generated by demonstration cannot exist at the same time."
<margin>F</margin>
"Whoever contradicts the sacred oracles, therefore, execrably contradicts faith. But he who contradicts some conclusion gathered and inferred from the sacred oracles by human wit, subtle inventions, Aristotelian tricks, and the Eleatic discipline—of which Zeno was the leader, as Galen <note>A famous ancient Greek physician and philosopher.</note> says—or by the traps of Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher famous for his complex logic.</note> or the syllogisms of sophists, does not contradict faith. Rather, he resists human science. He is not rejecting divine illumination, but merely human industry."
<margin>G</margin>

<summary>Philolaus argues that divine truths cannot be grasped by human logic or syllogisms, citing various Church Fathers and Greek philosophers to prove that faith is superior to meddlesome reasoning. He concludes that while contradicting scripture is a sin against faith, contradicting logical conclusions derived from scripture is merely a disagreement with human intellect.</summary>
<keywords>syllogism, faith vs reason, Athanasius, Socrates, Justin Martyr, Dionysius the Areopagite, dianoia, divine revelation, human science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus regarding the superiority of faith over human logic. The previous page established that the "simplicity of faith" is a sturdier wall than the "stone wall of logic."</meta>

# CABALÆ #

...nodding not in a detestable way, but perhaps wanderingly, or sometimes with insight, yet never shamefully. In what way, then, can anyone dare to affirm that what is divinely revealed and what is humanly discovered should be believed with equal dignity, unless he is fed entirely on <term>syllogisms</term><note>A formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note>, just as an ox is fed on hay? Truly, I ask you, what equality of dignity exists between the former and the latter? The former is "credible" (to be believed), while the latter is "scible" (to be known). The mind is the seat of the former, while reason is the seat of the latter. One flows down from the heavenly light; the other takes its origin from the senses. In the region of the mind, some things are necessary which are impossible in reason. In the mind, it is granted that contraries and contradictories may coincide, whereas in reason they are separated by the greatest distance. It is not, therefore, entirely true that if the premises are matters of faith, the conclusion will therefore be a matter of faith. For this proposition is execrable: *No creator is to be adored.* Even more execrable is this: *Every carved image is to be adored.* In both of these, faith is blasphemed. Yet, the following conclusion is both sacred and faithful: *No carved image is a creator.* Because we can demonstrate this by natural reason, its truth does not depend on the authority of the one revealing it; rather, its evidence is far less than the faith we have believed. We are easily deceived by persuasion into thinking that because a conclusion is a matter of faith, one of the premises must also be a matter of faith. For who does not know that it is believed with the highest faith by Hebrews, Christians, and <term>Agarenes</term><note>A historical term for Muslims, referring to descendants of Hagar.</note> that a carved image is not to be adored? Yet, to infer this assertion, I shall use natural premises: *No stone is to be adored; and we see that a carved image is a stone.* Then Marranus said: "Philolaus, you aptly bring to my memory the <term>sophistic</term><note>Clever but fallacious or misleading reasoning.</note> refutations of certain of our people when they say: 'The conclusion is heretical, therefore one of the premises must be.' In this matter, I wonder more than can be said that they ever find any men who believe such things from them. But why do I try to wash an Ethiopian? <note>A Latin idiom meaning to attempt the impossible or to try to change someone's inherent nature.</note> He does not become white by any effort. Furthermore, there are things which, although they are revealed, also follow from what is revealed; if these are accepted by the believer, they will be faith because they were revealed, rather than science because they were inferred. Just as the things my Church commands to be believed, even if composed by any human wit, are presumed to be revealed by the Holy Spirit rather than discovered by human reason, however much they may be introduced with a certain syllogistic subtlety. Thus the Emperor Constantine wrote to the Church of Alexandria concerning the Council of Nicaea, saying: <note>original Greek: "ὁ γὰρ τοῖς τριακοσίοις..."</note> **'For what was pleasing to the three hundred bishops together is nothing other than the judgment of God, especially since the Holy Spirit, residing in the minds of such and so many men, has revealed the divine will.'** He speaks here of the Bishops representing the Universal Church moved by the divine Spirit, not of the irregular, brainless heads of any <term>Polyphemuses</term><note>A reference to the brainless Cyclops of mythology; here meaning crude or unintellectual giants.</note> whatsoever. Let the mixtures of syllogisms regarding being, necessity, and contingency—or whatever other possibilities or impossibilities of logical curiosity there may be—go away to their own workshop. For there is no comparison of a speech faithfully believed to...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...necessaries could be doubtful, while nothing is more evident than revealed truth. Therefore, let such mixtures not occupy the inner sanctuaries of deeds, nor trouble the <term>hierophants</term><note>Priests or officials who explain sacred mysteries.</note>; rather, let them withdraw (if they wish to have any power) to the mechanical arts, or the nature of masonry, or mathematical calculations. Let them not cross the boundaries; let them not touch the <note>original Greek: "πρὸ ἀδιδακτον καὶ κρυφίαν τῶν μυστηρίων καὶ συμβόλων ἐξέδυσαν"</note> **unlearned and hidden nature of the mysteries and symbols.**
<margin>B</margin> "You are walking a straight path, my friend," said Philolaus, "to the obscure hiding places of Pythagoras—a man truly imbued with divine doctrine—which are not to be investigated by any cleverness of human wit. Such cleverness instills in us the fear of doubting more than it generates the firmness of adhering. For such great splendor of divine things cannot be seen so narrowly by our nocturnal eyes through such thin and old-womanish cracks of sophisms. Instead, there will be a need for the greatest powers of thinking and believing, especially (as Terence says) **faith and silence.**"
<margin>C</margin> Moved by this, Pythagoras—the first 'believer' in philosophy, having drunk from all the disciplines in the whole world—taught his disciples nothing before he taught them to be silent (as Apuleius wrote). For this was the first rudiment of contemplative wisdom: to learn how to meditate and to unlearn how to chatter. It was as if the sublimity of such august Pythagorean majesty were much more worthy than what could be comprehended by speaking and babbling with childishly boastful gestures.
<margin>D</margin> It is clear enough to us from what we received from Simon that Pythagoras also brought this kind of doctrine to Greece, just like the other things of the Cabalists: namely, that a disciple who is about to ask about a most high question should remain silent. When questioned, however, he should only respond: <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ἔφα"</note> **'He himself said it.'** In the same way, the Cabalists respond: <note>original Hebrew: "אמרו חכמים"</note> **'The Sages have said.'** And Christians also say to their own: <note>original Greek: "πιστεύειν"</note> **'Believe.'**
<margin>E</margin> Then Marranus said: "Perhaps you are rebuking us, Philolaus, whom the Emperor Julian the Apostate also insulted, saying: <note>original Greek: "εἰ μὴ ἡ ἀλογία..."</note> **'If it were not for irrationality and rusticity, and nothing beyond it, "Believe" is your only wisdom.'** Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> prudently met this insult in his first invective, stating that this was likewise the first and greatest foundation of discipline for the Pythagoreans: to be silent. Then, to offer no reason for their sayings except 'He himself said it.' Therefore, Julian unjustly blamed us, since <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ ἔκοντος τοῦ..."</note> **'his "He himself said it" and our "Believe" come to the same thing, though in different syllables and words.'** So says Nazianzenus.
<margin>F</margin> We now hold in our memory the unanimous way of learning used by those who handled sacred things more diligently than any others: namely, the <note>Hebrew</note> **'They said'** of the Cabalists, the <note>Greek</note> **'He said'** of the Pythagoreans, and the **'Believe'** of the Christians. Furthermore, whatever belongs to others is not divine.
<margin>G</margin> "Indeed," Philolaus said, "long ago I only thought that all those things flowed from the Kabbalah of the Hebrews; now I know it for a certainty. For I see clearly that whatever Simon has shown us of the 'Italic philosophy' matches the Pythagoreans exactly, so that I would not be wrong to judge that the affairs of the Cabalists and the Pythagoreans are all of the same flour <note>A metaphor meaning "of the same kind" or "from the same source."</note>. For all our studies will certainly lead back to the salvation of the human race, and they refer all beings that exist or subsist continually to the <term>Ideas</term><note>In a Platonic/Pythagorean sense, the eternal, perfect forms or patterns of which all earthly things are shadows.</note>."

<summary>This page explores the limits of human logic (syllogism) when applied to divine mysteries, arguing that faith and silence are the true paths to wisdom. It links the Pythagorean tradition of silence and the "He said it" authority to the Jewish Kabbalistic tradition and Christian faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metaphysical hierarchies, moving from the defense of faith to a systematic explanation of the three worlds: the Sensible, the Intellectual, and the Divine. It explores how ancient philosophers like Pythagoras and Plato understood the "Ideas" that bridge these realms.</meta>

### BOOK TWO ###

...things that truly are, and the "Idea of Ideas." Whence both asserted that the worlds are eternal; and that there is a third which is infinite, or rather not finite, and that all things consist of three, <note>original: καθάπερ γὰρ φασὶν οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι τὸ πᾶν καὶ τὰ πάντα τοῖς τρισὶν ὥρισαι</note> that is: *For just as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are determined by the three,* as Aristotle wrote in his books *On the Heavens*.

<margin>A</margin> For some things, he says, are bodies and magnitudes; others, however, inhabit and observe those bodies and magnitudes; and finally, others are the sovereignties and origins of those inhabitants and guardians.

<margin>B</margin> This I understand thus: Since the lower world encompasses bodies and magnitudes, each with its own powers and intelligences assigned as movers of the spheres, and as curators and guardians of things that are born and perish—those who are said to observe bodies providently, as a province is assigned to each. Antiquity sometimes called them "powers," sometimes "Angels," then sometimes "gods," and also "daemons." Or, because of the anxiety and care for the things to which they are bound, it frequently called them

<margin>C</margin> "demons." <note>The author makes a subtle distinction between the neutral Greek 'daemon' and the more burdened 'demonium'.</note> About these Homer sings: <note>original: Θεοὶ ὀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντες</note> *The gods inhabiting Olympian dwellings.* Specifically, those who are set over natural things are often disturbed by a complaining affection, and being relegated from the highest to the lowest, they plead the causes of their labors: <note>original: πολλοὶ γὰρ πλήθει ὀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντες, ἐξ ἀνθρώπων χαλεπ' ἄλγε' ἐπ' ἀλλήλοισι τιθέντες</note> *For many of us who inhabit Olympian dwellings suffer at the hands of men, inflicting heavy pains on one another,* as found in the fifth book of the *Iliad*.

<margin>D</margin> For the ancients understood "Olympus" to be the <term>fifth essence</term><note>Also known as the "ether" or "quintessence," this was believed to be the celestial material that makes up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> or nature, that is, the heavens. Therefore, the "Olympian dwellings" are the celestial spheres or heavens, named from *celando* (concealing), just as dwellings (*tecta*) are named from *tegendo* (covering). Finally, Hesiod, in his *Theogony*, says that the celestial powers, elemental forces, and properties of natural things are "gods" born of heaven and earth; and Orpheus, the first theologian of the Greeks, writing to Musaeus, calls these same beings "daemons"

<margin>E</margin> in these verses: <note>original: δαίμονας οὐρανίους καὶ ἠερίους καὶ ἐνύδρους καὶ χθονίους καὶ ὑποχθονίους ἢ δὴ πυρειφοίτους</note> *Celestial, aerial, watery, terrestrial, subterranean, and fire-walking or fire-assisting daemons.* In his book *Works and Days*, Hesiod also says: *Good daemons are the earthly guardians of mortal men.* Apollo himself once replied to the questioning Theophilus that they were similar daemons—that they are "Angels" according to the office of administration incumbent upon them, as is found in the oracles.

<margin>F</margin> For thus he sang, as he usually does all things in a heroic manner: <note>original: οὔνομα μηδὲ λόγῳ χωριζόμενον ἐν πυριναίων, τοῦτο Θεός, μικρὰ δὲ Θεοῦ μερὶς ἄγγελοι ἡμεῖς</note> *The Name not even captured by reason, dwelling in fire—this is God; we angels are but a small portion, a part of God.* Let us, if you please, raise our intellect to higher things, namely to the vital influences of this entire globe. For the superior world encompasses the celestial beings, incorporeal essences, divine patterns, and the "seals" of this orb, in whose likeness the faces of all lower things are made. These, Pythagoras

<margin>G</margin> called <note>original: ἀθανάτους πρῶτα θεούς</note> *the first immortal gods,* like the principles of things—Ideas produced from the divine mind—so that they are the essential <term>archai</term><note>Greek for "origins" or "first principles."</note>, the sovereignties and origins of those inhabiting bodies (that is, of the species), which give form to the composite things of this world.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> By this it is clearly understood that there are also other "second immortal gods" there (for the "first" imply the "second"): individual and indivisible incorporeal beings, differing among themselves not by material number but by formal form. These spirits are free from all matter, simple and unmixed, dwelling by their own nature outside the sensible heavens; and as Aristotle says, they are bound neither by time nor place. Whence they neither grow old nor are transformed—much less are they affected by any variation, alteration, or

<margin>B</margin> passion. They lead a most self-sufficient and excellent life and inhabit eternity, which is called *aeon*, <note>original: αἰών quasi ἀεὶ ὤν</note> as if it were "always being," because that same age always was, is, and will be, outside of time, in the divine mind. However, it was created outward by the energy of God and established outside the curves of our heaven as a most splendid home for blessed spirits. The Pythagoreans consider these to be the true gods, located at the sublime peak of the

<margin>C</margin> ether; eternal both in their foresight and their origin—that is, endowed with an immortal and divine age. From this same eternity, the power "to be" and "to live" is dispensed and granted to others—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely, as Aristotle likewise said. But as to what that thing is through which existence is dispensed and granted from this divine and immortal eternity to other things (that is, lower things), and that it does not fall into them by chance or perfunctorily, but exists consistently in every species—certainly the

<margin>D</margin> first of all, the Pythagoreans, followed by Socrates and Plato, taught the disciples of that school. When they heard Pythagoras (who always spoke obscurely of divine matters) habitually say that the <term>Tetractys</term><note>A triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows, a mystical symbol for the Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe.</note> provided our soul with the "fountain of perennial nature," they then clearly understood that the *Tetractys* is the "Idea" in the divine mind that provides, the "fountain" is the "exemplary Idea" provided, and the "perennial nature" is the "essential Idea" of things received.

<margin>The nature of Ideas.</margin> <margin>E</margin> Therefore, as Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> testifies, they spoke in this way: <note>original: ἔστιν ἡ ἰδέα ὡς μὲν πρὸς Θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς πρὸς τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον, παράδειγμα, ὡς δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν ἐξεταζομένη, οὐσία</note> *An Idea is, in relation to God, His thought; in relation to the sensible world, an exemplar; and considered in itself, an essence.* Just as the voice of a speaker (as it is in the writings of the <term>Areopagite</term><note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian.</note>), although it is one and the same, is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the speaker, second in the vocal quality, and third in each listener.

<margin>F</margin> Just as in the sensible world a prior sphere always flows into all those following it, so in the intellectual world we believe not only that each superior choir flows into all the inferior choirs, but also that the whole superior world flows into the whole inferior world. Thus all things, according to their capacity, are brought back—as much as possible—from the momentary to the eternal, and from the lowest to the highest. Yet nothing among mere creatures is capable of such sublimity by its own nature, except God. But I say that third world, the super-supreme,

<margin>G</margin> which contains all other worlds, belongs to the Deity alone. It consists of a single divine essence, so that it seems to me quite rightly named <note>original: παντοκράτειραν ἕδραν</note> *the Almighty Seat,* located—nay, existing—above every age and every century.

Ee iii

<summary>This page outlines a Neoplatonic cosmology consisting of three worlds: the sensible world of matter, the intellectual world of Ideas and spirits (angels/daemons), and the divine world of God's essence. It synthesizes Pythagorean, Platonic, and Aristotelian thought to explain how divine influence flows from the eternal "Idea" down into the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Pythagorean and Platonic origins of the "Ideas," specifically how these ancient thinkers used numbers not as mundane tools, but as symbols for the divine architecture of the universe and the nature of God as the "One."</meta>

### CABALÆ ###

(for it is the age of ages) a pre-existing entity and unity of existence, substance, essence, and nature. <note>original: ὑπάρξεως ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, φύσεως, ὀντότης καὶ ἑνότης προῦλα</note> This is what our Pythagoras called "Being," and the Pythagorean Parmenides likewise called "the One" <note>original: ὃν</note>; both did so for a similar reason, because it is the "supersubstantial One and Being." <note>original: ὅτι ὑπερούσιον, ἓν, καὶ τὸ ὄν</note> But no one in antiquity could have been so hateful or such a contemnor of the ancestors as to think that the great and wise Pythagoras was seized by such an old woman's madness as to believe that the numbers on a counting board, or children’s dice—with which they might throw a "four vultures" score—or the tokens of merchants and other things of that sort, were the principles of all things. Such things do not preside over reality; rather, they are merely accidental to it.

Instead, he wanted it to be understood that this "One" is essentially and simply the Source—from which, by which, through which, in which, and toward which all things are, and are ordered, remain, are contained, fulfilled, and transformed. This same "One" is the "First One" and "First Being," as Aristotle testifies in the second book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: Postnaturalium</note> in these words:

<margin>Why Pythagoras used numbers</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
*For Plato and the Pythagoreans held that Being and the One are not something else, but that this is their very nature—that their essence is the same as being the One and a certain Being.* <note>original: Πλάτων μὲν γὰρ καὶ Πυθαγόρειοι οὐχ ἕτερόν τι τὸ ὄν...</note> Indeed, Xenophanes, the teacher of Parmenides and a contemporary of Pythagoras, although it was their custom to hide everything in mystery, nevertheless seemed to explain most clearly to us what they understood "the One" to be when they spoke of the principles of things. He said that this "One" is God. This makes the secrets of Pythagoras more evident to us when he establishes that the "Infinite," the "One," and "Number" are the first principles of things. By "the Infinite," he signifies nothing other than *Ability* itself <note>term: Posse — The divine power or potentiality from which all creation flows</note>; for no one could ever conceive of anything prior to Ability itself. This is what is most infinite in God—or rather, God is himself the Infinite, in whom *being* and *ability* are not separated. In Him are contained the essences, virtues, and operations of all things that can be produced, along with all the connected differences and unions of their properties and accidents. 

Furthermore, Anaxagoras agrees with Pythagoras in this matter. Eusebius Pamphili is our witness that before these men, no Greeks had any knowledge of God. For Anaxagoras said: *All things were together.* And Democritus said: *All things were together in potentiality* <note>original: δυνάμει</note>, that is, in Ability itself.

<margin>F</margin>
This is also that "mixture" or "commingling of things" spoken of by Empedocles and Anaximander. However, it is by no means confused in some Chaos, Night, or Erebus <note>term: Erebus — A mythological personification of darkness or a region of the underworld</note> as described by Hesiod or Aristophanes. Rather, it is distinct in the full light of the Deity and ordered in the innermost sanctuary of the Infinite Light. Though if Hesiod is understood fairly, he certainly established that Chaos, Night, and Darkness are not the very first principles of things, but rather arose from those principles. For he stated this in his *Theogony*: *From the beginning, I say, what first was made of them: certainly first of all Chaos was made.* <note>original: ἐκ δ’ ἀρχῆς καὶ εἶπόν ὅτι πρῶτον γένετ’ αὐτῶν...</note> Then follows: *And from Chaos, Erebus and black Night were born.* That is, from the beginning, if ever anything was first made of them, certainly Chaos was made first. But from Chaos...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...Erebus and black Night were born. Aristophanes, however, wrote differently in *The Birds*: *First there was Chaos and Night and black Erebus.* <note>original: χάος μὲν καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον</note> But he fashions it thus in the manner of the poetic Muses, alluding to his birds, so that Love could hatch from an egg; at the same time, he follows Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, who held a similar view. Therefore, by repeating this same point again and again, let me remember: all things and each individual thing exist in that "Ability" itself—not confusedly, not in Chaos, not in Erebus, nor in dark Night, but—

<margin>B</margin>
—distinctly and orderly in full light. That is, they exist in that luminous and most splendid clarity of all shining rays, within the intuition, notice, and knowledge of the illustrious and illuminating Divine Essence. This is rightfully called the "Idea" by the most ancient philosophers—*existing in form, I know* <note>original: ἐν εἴδῳ, τὸ γινώσκω</note>. Since this "Ability to Be" embraces all things—mental, rational, intelligible, sensible, vital, substantial, and both the things that can be attached and those that attach—and not only those things that *are*, but also those that *are not*, then Pythagoras could truly call it "the Infinite." It was also called by the wisest of men "Infinite Power" <note>original: ἀπειροδυνάμει</note>. This is because it is itself infinite, and it embraces infinite things in one and the same infinite and essential Idea. For there was, is, or will be nothing in the super-celestial, celestial, earthly, corporeal, or incorporeal realms—in Angels, humans, beasts, plants, minerals, or in the whole nature of the universe—that is not "possible," or

<margin>D</margin>
(to speak grammatically) that He is not "able" <note>original: potis sit</note> to do. From this, all things proceed, and this is the *Infinite and Omnipotent Potency that makes all things possible* <note>original: ἀπειροδύναμος καὶ παντοδύναμος ὁ δυναστικὸς δυνάμεις</note>. This is nothing other than the Divine Essence, within which, before all things, the "One" produces "Two."

<margin>E</margin>
Here, Marranus <note>note: Marranus is the name of one of the characters in this dialogue, representing a converted Jew</note>, grasp the core of my Pythagoras. "Two" is the first number, but "One" is the principle of number. Because if you believe Xenophanes, as you heard before, that "One" is God, and since the production of "Two" remains within the divine essence (for number is constituted by itself, according to the Peripatetic Boethius, and naturally only the dyad follows the One), then necessarily those "Two" are also God, because nothing is within God except God. Therefore, the Three are the principle and are the first, and they do not leave the one essence of God; thus, they are plainly one God. For the essence is not split by the fact that Two are numbered as produced from the One. Just as in corporeal things it often happens that a unity, through motion, progresses into a duality (if the comparison be pardoned) and even to a trinity, while the substance of the things remains—as with a trunk and its shoots, or more aptly, as a human body, an arm, and a finger. Thus, from the One producing in divine things, and the Two produced, the Trinity arises. If to these things the Essence is added—which is formally distinct from them—there will be a "Formal Quaternity" <note>term: Tetractys — The Pythagorean sacred number four (1+2+3+4=10) symbolizing the perfection of the universe</note> which is the Infinite, the One, and the "Number of the Two," the substance, perfection, and end of all number. For one, two, three, and four, in a collective progression,

<margin>G</margin>
make ten, and beyond ten there is nothing. Wherefore, by this very thing, Pythagoras understood that there is a certain principle of all things, which he named the *Tetractys*. For *Tetractys* in Greek is "Quaternity," and "Perfect," the formal aspect of the sun, or a ray from such...

<summary>This passage explains the Pythagorean philosophy of the "One" as God and "Ability" (Posse) as the infinite potentiality within the Divine Essence. It reconciles ancient Greek cosmology with theological concepts, describing how the Trinity and the sacred Tetractys (number four) represent the unfolding of the universe from a single divine source.</summary>

### BOOK TWO ###

Even in its supersubstantial formality, God himself constitutes a single illustrious name of the fourfold, as if composed of four elements formally distinct among themselves. And so that the sacred might be separated from the profane, there is an excellent reason why the holy name was written with an *Ypsilon* <note>The Greek letter 'Y'</note>, whereas "ray" <note>original: ἀκτὶς</note> is commonly written with an *Iota*. Furthermore, he himself refers to the *Tetractys* <note>The Pythagorean "four," often represented as a triangular arrangement of ten dots</note> as a specific God here, pronouncing it in the masculine gender, like a Cupid or Venus, whereas elsewhere they speak of the instrumental number of "fourness" itself as the *Tetractys* in the feminine gender. He wished to show that he is that God by whom he swore the oath, "By the Tetractys" <note>original: μὰ τὸν τετρακτὺν</note>, than which nothing ought to be held more worthy of veneration. For as Aristotle says, "An oath is the most honorable thing" <note>original: ὅρκος τὸ τιμιώτατόν ἐστιν</note>. 

I certainly will not agree with Hierocles <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Pythagoras</note> in this place, as I believe Pythagoras himself wrote the verses previously. Yet, out of reverence for its wondrous sanctity, I would likewise wish that in the Roman <note>Latin</note> tongue, the *Tetractys* were called not "the four" or "fourness," but by a changed word, "quaternio" or "quaternitudo." This mirrors what you Christians observe, separating the sacred from the use of the profane commoners: for while "threeness" <note>original: ternitas</note> should popularly be read from the word "three," you call the most holy hypostasis <note>The underlying reality or "person" of the Trinity</note> by the altered name "Trinity" <note>original: trinitatem</note>, as if it were a "tri-une unity," borrowing a letter from the "One" itself because of the nature of the unity of each. 

But to sound the retreat: I say that the one great sum of all things is the *Tetractys*, the Pythagorean principle. Then Marranus said: I recall a most beautiful example of this from Philolaus—that character of four letters in which the entire salvation of the human race is present. Simon confirmed this for us with such an abundance of scripture, where it truly seemed to me that Pythagoras did not do badly to change the Jewish *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHVH</note>, or rather the four letters themselves from which the name of the Savior is composed, into the Greek symbol of the *Tetractys*.

Immediately then, Philolaus said: Truly, I departed not yet fully satisfied by that *Tetragrammaton* and that "salvation" to which Simon has reduced almost the entire human race. Therefore, when I return to him, I will ask more about these matters if he is willing—especially about that man who is to bring salvation to each and every one of us, as the anointed King of the universe, and is therefore called the Messiah. But see now, I wonder if it is Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing</note> who is to come into this world again, perhaps through "trans-animation" <note>metempsychosis or reincarnation</note> as they say. Regarding him, the Emperor Julian wrote in his second book *Against the Galilaeans* as follows: 

"For Zeus, among the intelligible beings, generated Aesculapius from himself, and revealed him to the earth through the generative life of the Sun. This god, making his progress from heaven to earth, appeared in a uniform way in human form around Epidaurus; having grown there in his

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> successes, he stretched out his saving right hand over the whole earth, so that he might restore souls that were poorly disposed and bodies that were in a weak state." <note>original: ὁ γὰρ Ζεὺς ἐν μὲν τοῖς νοητοῖς... Translation of Julian the Apostate's Greek text provided in the main Latin prose.</note>

If he had possessed a name composed of those four letters, even with any other character added for reading, he would certainly have to be thought of as the Savior himself. Or certainly, as great as he was, Hercules, the son of Alcmene born of the divine seed of Jove, whom the people of Thasos named "Savior" and inscribed on their public coinage thus: "Of Hercules, Savior of the Thasians" <note>original: Ἡρακλέος σωτῆρος Θασίων</note>. <margin>B</margin> I recently turned and re-turned such a silver coin, struck in the ancient style, with my own fingers and with incredible pleasure, as is my habit with very ancient things. From this I conjectured, not without reason, that by the voice and consensus of all, Hercules was numbered among the gods and proclaimed a savior. 

Aside from these, there were many others who brought help to mortals as saviors, which is <margin>C</margin> beyond doubt. Among their number we remember King Ptolemy of Egypt, whose name was *Soter*, which is to say, "Savior." For the Romans, Curtius himself by his own death gave back the land safe, and the Decii bravely devoted their own heads <note>sacrificed their lives</note> to preserve the fatherland; they were the wondrous authors of the common safety. 

Then Marranus said: By interrupting you, I would gladly advise you to notice more perceptively and understand a little more justly those things handed down to us by Simon. For after that man, who is skilled in every part of his sect, had discussed many things regarding the Kabbalah—what it <margin>D</margin> is and for what it is useful—he showed that it was a received revelation, and that it easily opened a path for us to the summit of blessedness and the highest happiness. Then, when we asked what that principal thing was which he thought had been revealed concerning the divinity, to which all revelations of divine things might generally be reduced, he said it was what is called, after the primordial ruin of the human race, the "universal restoration," which is named "salvation." 

He said this would be given by a just and peaceful man, a heroic man, whose name would contain four letters in its mercies. To him we ought to strive to ascend, freeing ourselves from all secular business, and migrate into him through all suitable steps, each according to his own strength. He said that all our acts must be shaped toward this, all contemplation directed here; toward this tends all the sacred scripture of the Jews, which can be for us like the "Ladder of Jacob" <margin>F</margin> placed upon the earth with its top touching the heavens. Through it, we transcend this corporeal world even into the other angelic world, reaching the very soul of that Messiah Savior, which is the rest and satisfaction of all souls to be saved. This is the final end of all things, beyond which we cannot proceed, because it bounds the highest habitation of the supreme world and communicates with the "super-supreme" world—or if I may speak through the Grammarians, the "most supreme"—nay, rather the incomparable world. In short, <margin>G</margin> this is the perpetual salvation of all men, completed by the gathering together of all good things. 

If you remember that these things were proposed by Simon, although through riddles, in my opinion you will not doubt that neither those saviors of yours, nor even those of the Jews...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. In the previous section, they discussed the sacred nature of the number four (the Tetractys) and its link to the divine name of God. Here, the conversation shifts to whether pagan figures like Asclepius or Hercules can be considered "saviors" or moral guides in the same way as the figures in the Bible or the Christian Messiah.</meta>

# CABALA #

...certain individuals, of whom the twenty-four books of the Bible have often made honorable mention, were ever established in such great dignity that they could have brought universal salvation to the human race. Through such salvation, all men across the entire span of the earth, however many there might be, could joyfully enjoy eternal life and, after the Fall, be able to return to God’s grace. 

As for your Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing</note>, you must see what many others have felt: they assert he was born of meretricious incest from a beautiful young woman named Coronis, of whom it is sung: *More beautiful in all of Larissa than Coronis.* <note>original: "Pulchrior in tota quam Larissa Coronis." This is a quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses.</note> She was not from Haemonia, and the priests often overpowered and compressed her in the temple of Apollo; these priests, having fathered Asclepius through adulterous embraces, then pretended he was the son of the God worshipped in that place. 

Furthermore, Apis of Egypt, who first brought the art of medicine to Greece, was so distinguished a temple-official in that age that even after death he was worshipped in temples as a God. Led by a singular favor toward the priests of Apollo, he took up the infant to be nourished and instructed. He later commended him to his former disciple, Chiron the Centaur <note>A mythological creature known for his wisdom and medical skill</note>, a most expert physician, so that he might transfer the art of curing and protecting the body into Asclepius. 

When this was done, Asclepius turned out to be a man of great fame and wealth. However, driven by greed and a desire for honor, he traveled through diverse regions of the world to scrape together money through his medical art. Already abounding in great riches and endowed with immense fame, he foolishly named himself a God, promising not only health to the sick but even life anew to the dead. For this pride, he paid the penalty to Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, for he perished, struck by a thunderbolt. 

Thus the Pythagorean Pindar sang of Asclepius in the third of his *Pythian Odes*: <note>original Greek: χερσὶ δὲ ἄρα κρονίων ῥίψας δι’ ἀμφοῖν, ἀμπνοὰν στέρνων καθεῖλεν ὠκέως, αἴθων δὲ κεραυνὸς ἐνέσκιψε μόρον</note> "The son of Cronos, casting with both his hands, swiftly took the breath from his chest; the blazing thunderbolt inflicted his fate." In this same vein, Apollo is depicted by Euripides complaining over the death of his son Asclepius: <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς γὰρ κατακτὰς παῖδα τὸν ἐμὸν αἴτιος ἀσκληπιὸν στέρνοισιν ἐμβαλλὼν φλόγα</note> "For Zeus is the cause, having killed my son Asclepius by casting a flame into his chest." 

Therefore, unless we are completely dull in divine matters, we will not think a man so far removed from dignity to be the savior of the human race—nor even a healer of the whole world, since he brought help nowhere else but to Pergamum, Ionia, Taranto, Rome, Cos, and Aegae, and the regions surrounding them.

"Overcome by a too-great love for your own people, Marranus," Philolaus said, "more than by the truth, you value all men less—indeed, you think them of the least possible value—who are not 'Galileans' <note>A common term used by critics in antiquity to refer to Christians</note>. This is a perverse habit, in my opinion (if I may say so), not only to refuse praise to others but even to revile them. Nor is it enough for you and those like you to contend that the best men, famous for virtue in their own age, whom antiquity counted among the Gods for their egregious deeds, are not Gods—unless you also make them out to be infernal devils. Thus you imitate your Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who argued against paganism</note> here, who wrote in the tenth chapter of his first book to the Emperor Constantine: 'Asclepius himself, born not without the disgrace of Apollo, what else did he do worthy of riches and honors, except that he healed Hippolytus? He certainly had a more famous death, because he deserved to be struck by a lightning-bolt from God.'

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> So he says. But every tongue that is infected with gall lacks a true taste. Yet he admits that it is a thing worthy of divine honors to bestow health, which all sick people admit along with him. But if Lactantius does not know what else Asclepius did, let him ask Socrates, the wisest of men, who vowed a cock should be offered to him, as is written in Plato's *Phaedo*. This was not so that he might heal his body—for Socrates, already condemned to death, had drunk the poison—but so that he might return the soul of one dying peacefully, with a shout of joy and a *Paean* <note>A song of triumph or thanksgiving</note>, to the radiant Apollo—that is, to the primary and incorporeal Sun, the dispenser of eternal life. 

For the cock is sacred to Phoebus Apollo, who is called the Sun, as the joyful herald of the hours and the day. Moreover, Asclepius was called by the ancients the 'Jubilation of Apollo,' the victory and triumph called a *Paean*, because they signify a 'pause,' a cessation, and rest after liberation. For in that age, it was the custom for those about to enter battle to offer a song to Mars first, and after the battle, the victors would return a *Paean* to Apollo. 

How aptly, therefore, Socrates worshipped the Sun as the giver of life in the form of Asclepius (who is the *Paean*). Now that he was about to die, let the right judgments of the most learned men see that he rightly judged it a dutiful service for every best man—once the great serpent 'Python' of this world <note>A metaphor for worldly vices or the material body</note> had been conquered and trampled underfoot—to offer a cock to Asclepius as one begins the journey through death toward true life; that is, to celebrate the *Paean*. 

So Orpheus, the most ancient of poets and a contemporary of those Gods (for he is said to have sailed with the Dioscuri and Hercules), sang in his hymns: <note>original Greek: ἰητὴρ πάντων ἀσκληπιὲ δέσποτα παιὰν, ἐλθὲ μάκαρ σωτὴρ βιοτῆς τέλος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάζων</note> "Healer of all, Lord Asclepius, the Paean, come, blessed savior, granting a good end to life." 

The Emperor Julian asserts that he knew many helped by Asclepius in the greatest dangers, and he himself confesses that, when laboring in sickness, he often escaped safe through his medicines, citing Jupiter as a witness to this.

"But what does this have to do with the whole world?" Marranus replied, "whose Messiah is preached as the Savior, not only of bodies, but of souls."

And Philolaus replied to that: "But you, Marranus, what of Hercules? Was he not a shaper of morals and a teacher of every noble discipline in all places of the world? From this comes that very ancient and lifelike image of Hercules among the Celts, where he himself, as an old man, draws innumerable men, each with their necks bound by little golden chains hanging from his tongue, wherever he wishes. The Celts call him 'Ogmion' <note>The Celtic god of eloquence, often equated with Hercules</note> in their native tongue. Lucian makes mention of him in his discourse on the Celtic Hercules, about whom they say: <note>original Greek: ἡμεῖς τὸν ἡρακλέα λόγῳ τὰ πάντα ἡγούμεθα ἐξεργάζεσθαι, σοφὸν γενόμενον</note> 'We consider that Hercules accomplished everything by speech and reason, since he was wise.' 

For to tame vices by virtue and to remove ignorance by doctrine is nothing other than to trample monsters, to kill snakes, to strike the Nemean lion with a club, to slay the Lernean Hydra, to kill the Erymanthian boar, to capture the hind with golden horns in the Maenalian grove, to pierce the Stymphalian birds in the clouds with arrows, to strangle Antaeus in one's arms, to fix columns in the Ocean, to conquer the three-bodied Geryon, to drive away the cattle, to kill the bull, and to overcome Achelous in single combat—I omit...

<summary>Philolaus defends pagan figures like Asclepius and Hercules against Marranus's skepticism, interpreting their myths as allegories for spiritual healing, eloquence, and the triumph of virtue over vice. He specifically explains Socrates's deathbed sacrifice and the Celtic concept of Hercules as a master of persuasive reason.</summary>

<keywords>Asclepius, Hercules, Apollo, Socrates, Pindar, Euripides, Lactantius, Ogmion, Celtic Hercules, universal salvation, allegory, virtue, Paean, healing, Greek mythology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Marranus and Philolaus regarding the nature of a true Savior. Following the discussion of the birth of Asclepius on the previous page, Marranus now critiques the heroic status of Hercules and provides a philosophical and linguistic definition of "salvation" based on Greek and Roman authorities.</meta>

### SECOND BOOK ###

...and Diomedes’ horses, and Cerberus, and the golden apples of the Hesperides, and many other deeds of that kind; his entire virtue consisted in this, the whole duty of right instruction, and an example of living well. 

Then Marranus said: I would speak of the opinion others have of him, were it not that you previously took such things poorly; I could briefly show that he was a man just as we are, or perhaps a little more unworthy, even if he was noble by the lineage of Proetus and Agenor. For Proetus was descended from Agenor, and Belus was the brother of Agenor, from whom was born Aegyptus, then Lynceus, then Abas, then Danae, who bore Perseus, who bore Alcaeus, who bore Amphitryon, who (as was believed) was the father of Hercules. Yet they say he was in truth the son of Jupiter—that is, the child of a certain adultery. For from Alcmena, Iphiclus was born to Amphitryon and Hercules to Jupiter in a single birth, if the story is believed. 

Indeed, Hercules perished consumed by a sacred fire, because he avenged the attempted assault on his wife Deianira’s modesty by the Centaur Nessus with an arrow—a modesty he himself did not display toward the captive girl Iole. Through this, he wrongly drew the suspicion of adultery upon himself; he who was conceived through adultery committed adultery himself. I do not know how just he was toward others, but he was certainly most just toward himself. Philolaus, do you believe such a man would be the savior of the world, such as Hercules was, or as Asclepius? If for no other reason, then at least because both died with a shameful mark. For as Momus says of both in Lucian's *Assembly of the Gods*, <term>they still bear the marks of the fire</term> <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὰ σημεῖα ἔχουσι τοῦ πυρός" (epi ta sēmeia echousi tou pyros)</note>, meaning both were burned up. 

Others praise Curtius and the Decii <note>Roman heroes famous for self-sacrifice in battle</note> for their magnanimity; I accuse them of imprudence. What of the fact that some, led by flattery and adulation or forced by the power of tyrants, honored with the name of "savior" those who not only did not heal or save them, but utterly devastated and destroyed them? For example, the Sicilians inscribed "Savior" on a public statue for Verres <note>A notoriously corrupt Roman governor</note> in Syracuse—that is, <term>one who gave safety</term> <note>original: "σωτῆρα" (sōtēra)</note>—according to Cicero’s testimony in his fourth speech against Verres. But these examples are irrelevant to this place, where we treat the true salvation of men, which those figures did not provide. 

For true salvation is eternal permanence, which exists in God and is granted by God, as Aristotle wrote in the book *On the Universe* <note>The pseudo-Aristotelian "De Mundo"</note> dedicated to Alexander: "From God," he says, "and through God all things consist for us, and no nature is sufficient unto itself if it lacks that salvation which comes from Him." Then he adds, <term>by His very essence, He is already truly the savior of all things</term> <note>original: "τῇ γε οὐσίᾳ σωτὴρ μὲν ἤδη ὄντως ἁπάντων ἐστίν" (tēi ge ousia sōtēr men ēdē ontōs hapantōn estin)</note>, which is to say, God is essentially the savior of the universe. 

Whence in the fourteenth book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle says again: <term>It would be a wonder if the first, eternal, and most self-sufficient being did not possess self-sufficiency and salvation as its primary good</term> <note>original: "Θαυμαστὸν δ', εἰ τῷ πρώτῳ καὶ αἰδίῳ καὶ αὐταρκέστατῳ τῷ αὐτῷ τὸ πρῶτον οὐκ' ὡς ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχει τὸ αὔταρκες καὶ ἡ σωτηρία" (Thaumaston d', ei tō prōtō kai aidiō...)</note>. By this we are warned that true salvation for us consists in the first, eternal, and most sufficient good, which is God, the Best and Greatest, and is not to be sought elsewhere. For He alone is the maker and ruler of the world, who, out of the most merciful will of His super-eminent liberality, can give incorruption to corruptible things, eternity to those subject to time, and to those who must pass away, an insoluble 
<meta>catchword: permanence</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> permanence, though it is their own nature to perish after being born and to grow old after increasing. For so God speaks in Plato’s *Timaeus*: "The things made by me are indissoluble, provided I will it; otherwise, everything that is bound together is indeed dissoluble." Behold, we receive testimony not only from the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> but also from Plato himself and the Platonists, that permanence is granted to any things whatsoever only by the will of God, according to their capacity, and this is true salvation. For we say something is "saved" when it is preserved from harm so that things may remain in peace.

<margin>B</margin> This was explained with the unanimous consent of the Greeks by the once magnificent and most distinguished legates in the year 1438 from the birth of Jesus, at the universal Council of Basel <note>An important ecumenical council of the Catholic Church</note>, in a certain illustrious and most eloquent speech, using these words: <term>For to be saved, to be preserved, and salvation itself, simply mean nothing else to the Greeks and in our language than to remain and to be</term> <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ σωθῆναι καὶ σώζεσθαι καὶ ἡ σωτηρία ἁπλῶς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἔχει τοῖς Ἕλλησι καὶ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ βούλεται γλώττῃ ἢ τὸ διαμένειν" (To gar sōthēnai kai sōzesthai...)</note>. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore men, who by their nature are subject to death so that they cease to be, are rightly said to achieve "salvation" when they conform themselves to God's will so as to become immortal and enjoy a blessed age. And He who bestows that blessedness of immortality upon them is rightly called "Savior." This term, previously unheard of, was adopted into use by the successors of Cicero so that "Savior" (*Saluator*) can now be said in Latin. Indeed, every other thing is named "salvation" improperly and only in the imagination.

<margin>D</margin> For what of it? If a doctor brings health to a brute animal today, and the day after tomorrow it falls back into a plague and dies, never to return—shall that be called salvation? What of the gardener who aids a wilting flower that is bound to fall the next day and be ground into dust—is this three-day preservation of a completely inconstant thing to be named salvation? Thus Hercules helped the Thasians once, by which he is said to have given them salvation, yet they frequently perished afterward, and today nothing remains of them but the name. Thus Ptolemy saved Egypt, which was afterward devastated by so many wars and enemy incursions. Thus the Decii liberated Rome, yet it was later destroyed in a subsequent overthrow and fire.

<margin>E</margin> Believe me, every salvation that is broken by time is imperfect; perfect salvation is that which makes the fleeting eternal. As Apollo taught concerning Helen when she was removed from death in Euripides’ *Orestes*, when he said: <term>She is the one whom you see in the folds of the ether, saved and not dead; I have saved her for you</term> <note>original: "ἣ δ' ἔστιν, ἣν ὁρᾶτ' ἐν αἰθέρος πτυχαῖς σεσωσμένη, κ' οὐ θανεῖσα· πρὸς σὲ δ' ἐξέσωσα" (hē d' estin, hēn horat' en aitheros...)</note>. 

<margin>F</margin> And so that we might not be ignorant that this salvation did not proceed from Apollo, nor from other gods except as mediators, but more truly from the highest God to whom she dedicated herself by remarkable virtue, he then adds: <term>Since she belongs to Zeus, it was fitting for her to live incorruptibly</term> <note>original: "Ζηνὸς γὰρ οὖσαν, ζῆν νιν ἄφθιτον χρεών" (Zēnos gar ousan...)</note>.

<margin>G</margin> "By Castor, Helen's brother," said Philolaus, "Marranus, you speak the truth, and you seem to have spoken wisely concerning true salvation. I agree that the Savior—of whom the sacred oracles prophesy so magnificently and so perpetually—must be one who is the savior not so much of this great world, nor of regions and cities, nor of the weak elements and stars, nor of wood and stones, nor..."

<summary>This page defines true "salvation" as eternal permanence granted by God, contrasting it with the temporary help offered by mythological heroes like Hercules or historical figures like the Decii. Marranus uses Aristotelian, Platonic, and linguistic evidence from the Council of Basel to argue that only a divine Savior can grant true immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and his companions (likely Philolaus and Simon). The previous page concluded a critique of Hercules as a "savior" figure, contrasting his mythological flaws with the philosophical requirements for a true healer of the soul.</meta>

# CABALAE #

<margin>A</margin>
...of plants and trees, not of fish, nor of birds, nor of cattle—all of which follow nature as their guide and the instinct of their condition correctly and without error, and remain fixed toward their appointed end, however many they may be—than he is the preserver and restorer of that "lesser world," <note>The "lesser world" or *microcosm* is a common philosophical term for a human being, viewed as a miniature version of the universe (*macrocosm*).</note> that is, of man. For man often falls away from the standard of equity handed down to him and from the judgment of right reason; through a heap of vices, he voluntarily plunges his nobility into the deep marshes of evil and the eternal abyss of corruption, from which he cannot retrace his steps by his own strength or help. Here, Marranus, 
<margin>B</margin>
here, I say, we have need of health, and here we have need of a savior. Pythagoras calls this class of creatures <note>original Greek: αὑθαιρέτους αὑτῶν πήματ’ ἔχοντας</note> "those having miseries of their own choosing," <margin>p. 54.</margin> that is, men having detriments by their own spontaneous choice. Concerning whom he wrote thus in his *Golden Verses*: <margin>p. 54. 55. 56. 57. 58. 59.</margin> <note>original Greek: τλήμονες οἵτ’ ἀγαθῶν πέλας ὄντων οὐκ ἐσορῶσιν, οὔτε κλύουσι, λύσιν δὲ κακῶν παῦροι συνíεσι, τοίη μοῖρα βροτῶν βλάπτει φρένας, οἱ δὲ κυλίνδροις ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλα φερόμενοι ἀπείρονα πήματ’ ἔχοντες.</note> "Wretched indeed are these who do not look upon nor hear the good things existing near them, and few understand the release from evils; such a fate of mortals harms their minds, for they are carried on rollers from some things to others, having infinite losses." Certainly, our own prince of philosophers <note>Referring to Pythagoras.</note> felt that man is a rational being more noble than other things, as if of a more divine nature—not content with only one operation nor a uniform effect like other creatures, which are led by nature alone acting always in the same way. Rather, man is endowed with various gifts like a *Pandora*, <note>In Greek myth, Pandora was "all-gifted"; here used to describe the multifaceted nature of human potential.</note> by which he is moved spontaneously toward every outcome according to his free 
<margin>D</margin>
will. Because of this freedom, he says: <margin>v. 63.</margin> <note>original Greek: θεῖον γένος ἐστὶ βροτοῖσιν, οἷς ἱερὰ προφέρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν ἕκαστα.</note> "The race of mortals is divine, to whom sacred nature, bringing forth, reveals each thing." This "sacred nature" is the intellectual soul. Therefore, according to the intellect, man approaches God as the pure to the pure; but according to the lower senses, he 
<margin>E</margin>
recedes from God as the impure from the pure. Thus it happens that reason—which (as he says) shows us each thing—makes us blessed when it turns itself toward the enjoyment of the mind. On the other hand, when it runs down into the lust of the senses, it makes us miserable. Thus man appears placed in the middle between virtue and vice, like the substituted apex in the "letter of Pythagoras" <note>The Greek letter Upsilon (Y) was used by Pythagoras as a symbol of the path of life: a single trunk that splits into two paths—one of easy vice and one of difficult virtue.</note> split by a two-horned distinction, at which that famous Hercules of Prodicus <note>Referring to the "Choice of Hercules," a famous parable by the sophist Prodicus where a young Hercules chooses between personifications of Virtue and Vice.</note> sat thoughtfully in his tender youth. Truly, just as Solon affirmed to Croesus in Herodotus, "no one ought to be called blessed before his death and final funeral," so certainly no one should be thought truly miserable while he lives this life. But the final day must always be awaited for a man; if, having cast off the body, he then remains burdened with vices, he begins to be truly miserable. As you heard in the previous discourse, Pythagoras divided that misery into two kinds. For after death, the miserable either have "good things near them"—which are the goods of blessedness—even though they do not yet see or hear them because they do not yet enjoy the vision of God. These are among the number of those to be saved, not weighed down by extreme misery, so that they may eventually escape the appointed punishments. Or finally, the good things are most distant from them, so that their evils will never have any
<meta>catchword: end</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
end, and these are called "those having infinite losses." Two dwellings of those below are thus described here: the **Elysian Field**, which is transitory, for those to whom good things are near so that they may return to the higher realms as if connected; and **Tartarus**, named from a horrible sound, as if called "foul twisting terror" <note>A creative etymology linking Tartarus to *tortor* (torturer), *teter* (foul), and *terror*.</note>, for those whose losses are infinite. These hang distracted by the rollers and spokes of wheels, where the unhappy Theseus sits and will sit forever, along with those like him, <note>original Greek: ὅθεν οὔποτε ἐκβαίνουσι</note> "from whence they never depart," as was written by 
<margin>B</margin>
Plato, imitating Pythagoras. At this point, let the detractors approach me, who do not cease to babble against this same Pythagoras—so great and distinguished a man, whose teaching was trusted like an oracle of the gods. For this reason, he was named the "Dictator of Truth" for that age, like another Apollo; indeed, the very name *Pythagoras* signifies this. <note>The author likely associates "Pyth-" with the Pythian Apollo.</note> However, they spread a rumor about him everywhere that his opinion was this: that the human soul, after death, informs the bodies of certain 
<margin>C</margin>
beasts. This ought to seem incredible to men using reason, concerning such an excellent author of philosophy and most abundant fountain of the sciences, from whom the knowledge of divine and human things flowed to us. Rather, that suspicion of "trans-animation" <note>Metempsychosis or the transmigration of souls.</note> arose from those who were partly ignorant of the Pythagorean mysteries and partly hated them out of envy. Indeed, the most outstanding virtue of that man did not lack the malice of rivals: 
<margin>D</margin>
his most innocent life, remarkable teaching, and celebrated fame. As often happens, envious critics—Timon, Xenophanes, Cratinus, Aristophon, Hermippus, and others, of whom there is no small multitude—left nothing unpolluted. They wrote many lies about Pythagoras in their books and handed down things that were never said or written by him. Or, if he had said anything of that sort, they twisted it into a worse sense, so it might easily be believed that such a great man had wandered into error by teaching thoughtlessly about the principles of things, about numbers, 
<margin>E</margin>
about not tasting beans, about abstaining from eating living things, about the underworld, and about *metempsychosis* and the passage of souls, which we are now discussing. For he who distinguished the patterns and species of things so clearly that they cannot be mutually changed or confused—how could he communicate the human essence, which is its own form, to a beast? For he himself is the author of the idea that not even the substance of unity in a certain number is, according to nature, the unity of another number. Wherefore he says, <note>original Greek: αἱ μὲν μονάδες ἐν τῇ δυάδι αὐτῇ, πρὸς τὰς ἐν τριάδι αὐτῇ ἀσύμβλητοι</note> 
<margin>F</margin>
"The units in the 'two' itself are incomparable to those in the 'three' itself." Thus it is established in physics, although it is dealt with far differently in mathematics, with which we have no business at present. The "One" of each thing is its participated essence, which will not occupy the essence of another thing; <note>original Greek: ἑκάστη μὲν οὐσία ἑνὸς εἴδους μετέχει</note> "for any substance participates in one form." Therefore, it cannot pass into the life of a different animal, or any 
<margin>G</margin>
beast whatsoever; rather, it remains in the law of its own nature, holding its own duty, <note>original Greek: ὥστε τὸ εἶδος εἰς εἶδος οὐ συνέρχεται</note> "so that one form does not merge into another." For although one seal impressed upon many pieces of wax shapes multiple forms, nevertheless [it does not make them] of many...
