<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagorean philosophy, transitioning from the concept of human misery and the need for a savior to a specific defense of Pythagoras's views on the soul. The author argues that Pythagoras did not believe in the literal migration of souls into animals (metempsychosis) but used it as a metaphor for the soul's moral condition and its "descent" into the physical world.</meta>

## BOOK SECOND ##

<margin>A</margin>
...the same wax can bear the different forms of many seals. Therefore, a seal of human form, which is the image of God, is not permitted to seal a lower nature. Pythagoras proposed this enigmatically, as he did all his teachings; thus, he designated the certain meaning of this opinion with his own specific mark, celebrating this among his other symbols as his most favorite: <note>original Greek: ἐν δ’ αὐτῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ περιφέρειν</note> "Do not carry the image of God in a seal." In my judgment, this is rightly understood in roughly this way: the image of God, which is the soul of man, is not able to seal or form other natures around it.

<margin>B</margin>
For so says Hermes Trismegistus, the Teacher of the Egyptians, in his book to Asclepius: "One part of man," he says, "is simple, which we call the form of divine likeness." And a little lower: "There are two images of God: namely, the world and man." Therefore, they have explained it unfairly—whether out of envy or ignorance—concerning the passage of souls after death, as well as their descent before the generation of man. Surely there is now no one endowed with any mind who does not feel as I do. For when many thought the soul of man was drawn out from the potentiality of matter, our teacher himself determined it was more to be believed that it is infused into the body by God himself. On account of this, he asserted that the soul exists before the body—which is to be understood not in terms of time, but in terms of purity and the dignity of its nature.

<margin>C</margin>
*And so he called this infusion the "descent of the soul,"* which followers of various sects later treated with many circuitous arguments, each in his own way, and not always according to the will of the author. He commanded that the descent of the human soul into the body should not be understood according to physical location, nor according to a movement from the intellectual world through individual spheres to the elemental world (as Proclus and other supporters suggest), but as part of the series of natural forms, in which the rational soul is the ultimate perfection of the human body. It so perfects the whole that man is most justly called a "divine animal." Pythagoras therefore intended that only living beings whose nature is sacred—that is, those whom reason distinguishes individually—are of a divine genus, namely, propagated by God, as the *Golden Verses* state. The species of this genus is neither changed nor converted; thus the forms of individual genera are permanent, even if they are dissimilar within that same form.

<margin>p. 69</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
After the death of a man, if he dies a just man, his soul transcends the pure ether and spends its age with the blessed, as a God among Gods. For he says: <note>original Greek: ἰσόθεοι γνώμῳ ζῆσας καθ’ ὕπερθεν ἀείστως, ὡς ἂν ἄτομός φας σῶμα, ἔς’ αἰθέρ’ ἐλεύθερον ἐλθῇς, ἔσεαι ἀθάνατος θεὸς ἄμβροτος οὐκ ἔτι θνητός.</note> "Living with a godlike mind... when you leave the body and come into the free ether, you shall be an immortal God, incorruptible, and no longer mortal." Establishing the "Charioteer" <note>A Platonic and Pythagorean metaphor for the Intellect or Reason that guides the soul.</note> as the best judgment from above. But if a man dies unjust and wicked in incurable and mortal sins, then Pythagoras taught that his soul must wash away all its guilt through various punishments. He taught that these punishments would be more or less harsh and durable according to the magnitude and multitude of the crimes. To these souls are assigned these lower places of nature and bodies that are either imaginary or figural, or sometimes real—not that the soul forms them as an essential part, but that it inhabits them like a tenant for the sake of enduring punishments.

<column-break/>

Or, the soul may assist these bodies through local presence, like an internal mover to the thing being moved, or it may be twisted while subjected to tortures nearby—like Tityus around the vultures, Ixion on the wheels of serpents, Tantalus in the river, Sisyphus at the stone, and Prometheus with the eagles. <note>These are famous figures from Greek mythology punished eternally in the underworld: Tityus's liver is eaten by vultures; Ixion is bound to a fiery wheel; Tantalus is forever hungry and thirsty; Sisyphus rolls a boulder uphill; and Prometheus has his liver pecked out by an eagle.</note> Since a Tartarean demon <note>A demon from Tartarus, the deepest abyss of the underworld.</note> can seize and possess a body, why could not a foul soul, damned to the punishments of the lower world, enter a real body of any species by God’s dispensation? Or, having "clothed itself in air," it might show any form to our sight, just as Dido, about to die, addresses Aeneas: "I shall follow you, glowing with black fires." <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> And Pliny the Younger writes of a believed event concerning a house that the philosopher Athenodorus of Tarsus had bought; it was infamous for an unseasonable noise because the phantom of a horrific old man was seen there. Daily in our own age, similar terrors occur, though in coarser forms. Then various shapes and faces of wild beasts mock the sight: "for suddenly he will become a bristling boar, a black tiger, a scaly dragon, and a lioness with a golden neck, or he will give out the sharp sound of flame; all things transform themselves into the wonders of the world: fire, and a horrible beast, and a flowing river." <note>A poetic description of shapeshifting, likely referencing Proteus.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
We call these "phantastic bodies," which is to say, "apparitional," which the released souls of men can assume just as demons do. We know this regarding the Lamia of the philosopher Menippus of Lycia, a bold harlot converted into a beautiful woman at Corinth, whom Apollonius of Tyana publicly exposed as being a *lemur* <note>A restless ghost or spirit.</note>. Finally, that old man in rags and a beggar at Ephesus, who was once the cause of a pestilence, is noted for this kind of metamorphosis; they say that when he was overwhelmed with stones, he was seen to be a dog, like a Molossian hound. Philostratus II wrote about both of these in the fourth book of the *Life of Apollonius*.

<margin>E</margin>
Furthermore, regarding what Pythagoras is reported to have said—that he was once Euphorbus—there is another explanation. He was not the first to institute such a manner of speaking; rather, it had been used long before in popular custom among the most ancient people. It meant that someone endowed with a certain virtue or vice was likened to another who had formerly been eminent in that same condition. For they called any man they pleased who was most outstanding in strength "Hercules." Thus Marcus Varro says: "Rusticellus, called Hercules, used to lift a great weight." And Numenius the Pythagorean writes openly that Plato is nothing other than "Moses speaking in the Attic tongue." Often too, Cicero was said to be the "Latin Demosthenes." All of these titles come from a parity of virtues and works and a similarity of character, not from the sharing of a single substance. In the same way, Litanus, the slave of Plautus, said that Argyrippus was "Solon," who likewise writes laws; he says of him in the *Asinaria*: "For now he is busy during the day; clearly he is Solon, so that he may write laws." These words of Plautus indicate an ingrained custom of speaking among the ancients, so that they would say this man *is* a certain person who was more similar in nature, talent, character, love, affection, and work.

<margin>G</margin>
Whence the Romans were accustomed to add the little word "Another" to this adage, as in "You are another me," and "I am another you"—even though they knew and saw that in truth I am not you, nor are you me. But in both...

It argues that ancient accounts of reincarnation or shapeshifting were often metaphorical ways of describing character similarity or the soul's temporary "phantastic" forms during divine punishment.</summary>

The author argues that Pythagoras used this concept as an allegory for the persistence of character and virtue across generations, rather than a literal rebirth into animals.</meta>

### CABALA ###

<page-num>679</page-num>

...for us, feeling that there is the same talent, equal study, the same will, the same effort, spirit, and mind, <note>original Greek: τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν μεταβαλλομένης</note> "even as their essence is changed." For the ancients called the movements and wills of men "souls"; therefore, men of a single character, care, and diligence, of a similar purpose, equal movement, and equal drive and feeling, are commonly called "unanimous" (of one soul). Moreover, it is by no means foreign to the ancient philosophers to say that the soul is the source of movements and sensations in man: <note>original Greek: τὸ ἔμψυχον τοῦ ἀψύχου... δυοῖν μάλιστα διαφέρειν δοκεῖ, κινήσει τε καὶ τῷ αἰσθάνεσθαι</note> "The animate," says Aristotle, "seems to differ from the inanimate chiefly in two things: motion and sensation." Whoever, therefore, is affected and moved toward the same thing, and seems to think and feel the same way, is commonly said to be of "one soul" <note>original Greek: ψυχῆς</note>. Whence that famous <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>the transmigration of souls</note>, or "trans-animation," is in truth nothing else to rightly learned men than the equal care, similar motion, and equal study of some deceased man found after some time in another, or the same, living man. 

By such emulation of common and familiar speech, Pythagoras, once returning from the Magi of the Persians (for so those wise men name their own), perhaps for the sake of cheering a banquet among friends, was able to use the manner of the Magi and say that he contained within himself the soul of the Trojan soldier Euphorbus, of Callicles, Hermotimus, Pyrrhus, Pyrandrus, Calidona, Alce, and finally his own soul as Pythagoras. He said this because he bore an affection, study, and will inclined toward certain noble things situated chiefly in each of those individuals, toward which those very men were more readily moved in their own lives. Most of all, since warlike virtue had shone in the Trojan Euphorbus, he himself had obtained the soul of Euphorbus, as if he now possessed the heart of Euphorbus. 

He could certainly boast of this when <term>pugilists</term> <note>boxers or fighters</note> of warlike study praised him, seeing the strength of his sides and arms and his whole body, and weighing his incredible love toward the strongest athletes. He showed this love to them both with precious equipment and magnificent expense; for previously athletes were nourished on dry figs, soft cheese, and wheat, but our Pythagoras is found to be the first to have nourished them with meat. Therefore, when they marveled that such a great love of fighting could exist in a philosopher devoted to the study of letters, what wonder if he replied that the soul of Euphorbus flourished in him? That is to say, the talent, study, movement, and will of Euphorbus resided within him, so that although he was a teacher of peace and an author of quiet contemplation, he nevertheless felt within himself a desire for war, as if he were a Trojan. 

Upon hearing this, a rumor soon arose among those who believe rashly, and the report spread far—either through ignorance of the Pythagorean mysteries or the malice of the envious, who always pervert the best things and repeat what they have heard much differently than it was said—that the soul of Euphorbus, slain in the Trojan war, had migrated into Pythagoras. This opinion was later assisted by writers and poets. Thus Ovid, in the 15th book of his *Transfigurations* <note>The *Metamorphoses*</note>, having borrowed these things among other trifles from the Greeks (who are accustomed to <note>original Greek: κρετίζειν</note> "play the trickster" or "invent fables" in their own way), sang thus of Pythagoras:

> Souls lack death, and always having left their prior 
> Seat, they live in new homes and dwell there when received.

<insert>B</insert>

<insert>C</insert>

<insert>D</insert>

<insert>E</insert>

<insert>F</insert>

<insert>G</insert>

<page-num>680</page-num>

> I myself (for I remember) in the time of the Trojan war
> Was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose breast once
> Stuck the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus.
> I recognized the shield, the burden of our left hand,
> Recently in the temple of Juno in Abantean Argos.

But do not be amazed, excellent Marrano <note>a character in the dialogue</note>, for you will find none of these things written in the books of Pythagoras. <margin>The Writings of Pythagoras</margin> For he himself published only three volumes: the first <note>original Greek: παιδευτικόν</note> *Educational*, the second <note>original Greek: πολιτικόν</note> *Political*, and the third <note>original Greek: φυσικόν</note> *Physical*. <note>The OCR text here contains a fragmented sentence "sit igitur tertium nobis au- Lysirea carmina," possibly a mangled reference to Lysis or other attributed poems.</note> Run through each one, and nowhere in that man will you find anything about trans-animation; by which you may more easily believe that whatever is feigned regarding that <term>metempsychosis</term> was sown by a false rumor through the envious. 

The matter is clearly indicated when some say this shield was brought back to the temple of Juno at Argos, while others affirm it was dedicated to Pallas at Athens, and that this very inscription was on the shield: <note>original Greek: παλλαδὶ ἀθηνᾷ, μενέλεως ἀπὸ εὐφόρβω</note> that is, "To Pallas Athena, Menelaus [took this] from Euphorbus." Tyrius Maximus is the author of this in his 16th Disputation. Now, the legal experts may see how much faith ought to be placed in testimony of this kind. For my part, I cannot be led to believe that a man so excellent in all science and weightiness taught Ovid's fable about the passage of souls; and I should think it less to be believed the more that outstanding authors have handed it down otherwise. 

For what many assert—that among the Greeks, Pythagoras first discovered that souls are immortal—they speak a manifest falsehood. For Homer, nearly the most ancient of the Greeks and far prior, produced this dogma; in his works, the souls of the dead among the inhabitants of the underworld discuss many things and prophesy many things. I ask you, what else does that admirable poem of his, <note>original Greek: δι’ ὅλης νέκυας</note> "throughout the Book of the Dead," suggest than that our souls remain after death? Furthermore, in the companions of Ulysses, he openly shows that the souls of imprudent men, separated from the body, do not indeed take on the natures of beasts, but only put on the *habits* of brutes, and with such horror pay the penalties which Circe commanded. Moreover, whoever holds the root and flower of the herb Moly, their souls, by the authority of Mercury, shall be secure, as it is in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*. 

But let us return to that irony concerning Euphorbus, of which suitable authors, whenever they write, confess that all the divine dogmas of Pythagoras <note>original Greek: αἰνίττεσθαι</note> are "expressed in riddles," that is, handed down by a more obscure allegory. Apollonius of Tyana, that famous Pythagorean, confirms this in the sixth volume of Philostratus, in a treatise held with Thespesion, the Chief Philosopher of the Gymnosophists, speaking thus: <note>original Greek: εἰ δὴ αἰνιγμάτων ἅπτωμαι, σοφια πυθαγορα ξυγχωρει ταυτα, παρεδωκε γαρ δη το αινιττειν</note> that is, "If I touch upon enigmas, the wisdom of Pythagoras permits these things, for he himself handed down the use of riddles." 

Furthermore, when he was disputing with the Brahmins of the Indians in the third book of the same work, asking how they felt about the soul, Iarchas said: "Just as Pythagoras handed it down to you, we handed it down to the Egyptians." Apollonius took this up: "Will you then say that you were one of the Trojans? Just as Pythagoras said he was Euphorbus." Listen now, Marrano, how cleverly Thespesion replied, first asking: whom among the leaders of the Greeks who led the army to Troy did he consider more worthy of admiration?

It refutes the literal interpretation found in poets like Ovid by citing the lack of such doctrines in Pythagoras's own writings and comparing them to Homeric allegories.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into Pythagoras's claim of having lived previous lives, specifically addressing the transition from a literal interpretation of reincarnation to a symbolic understanding of the transmutation of matter and the divine power of resurrection.</meta>

### SECOND BOOK. ###

To him Apollonius replied, that Achilles had first been found by Homer. Then Iarchas said, <gloss>towards my body, or rather, the progenitor body; for Pythagoras himself considered himself to be Euphorbus.</gloss> <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν ἐμὸν μᾶλλον ἢ, τὸ πρόγονον σῶμα· ταυτὸ γὰρ καὶ Πυθαγόρας, εὔφορβον ἡγεῖτο.</note> That is, he said, "Apollonius, consider me to be that very progenitor, or rather the body that generated me; for this is what Pythagoras thought regarding Euphorbus." Then he recounted how Ganges, once King of the Indians and son of the river Ganges, had surpassed Achilles in many virtues, and that he himself was that very "progenitor body" which he now inhabited. These words do not indicate the migration of a soul, but rather the transmutation of bodies, like any piece of matter that is fit to receive this or that form. It is just as if a comedy were to say, "I was previously a tragedy," because tragedy and comedy are born from the same letters and elements, as Aristotle says in the first book of *On Generation*. Or if a certain dog were to say, "I was long ago a horse," because the dog fed upon the body of a certain horse; once that nourishment was converted into the substance of the creature fed, that horse might be called in common speech the dog’s <gloss>progenitor body</gloss> <note>original Greek: πρόγονον σῶμα</note>, which is to say, the body from which it was generated. Yet no one would think from this speech that the soul of the horse had passed into the dog. Why then should I believe that Pythagoras taught that souls pass into other bodies, solely because he said he was previously Euphorbus? For here it is clearly evident and agreed upon that it was not the soul, but the body itself that was judged to be Euphorbus. Nevertheless, this saying of his was not plain, but a pure enigma, by which he wished to hint at a certain secret unknown to that age: namely, that the "Prime Matter" <note>the fundamental substance underlying all physical reality</note> is not only capable of all forms, but is even greedy for them, and, moved by constant desire, is satisfied by no single form. This seemed equally true to the philosopher-emperor Marcus Antoninus, when he wrote in the third book of his *Meditations*: <gloss>that the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change all things and make new things like them. For in a certain way, everything that exists is a seed for that which will come from it.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐδὲν οὕτως φιλεῖ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, ὡς τὸ τὰ πάντα μεταβάλλειν καὶ ποιεῖν νέα ὅμοια. σπέρμα γὰρ τρόπον τινα πᾶν τὸ ὂν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐξελθόν.</note> And the same author in the seventh book says: <gloss>The nature of the universe, out of the universal essence as if from wax, has now fashioned a horse; then, dissolving this into the nature of a tree, it makes use of its matter; then into a little man, then into something else.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ νῦν μὲν ἵππον ἔπλασε. συγχέας δὲ τοῦτο εἰς δένδρου φύσιν, συνεχρήσατο τῇ ὕλῃ αὐτοῦ. εἶτα εἰς ἀνθρώπειον, εἶτα εἰς ἄλλο τι.</note> Hence nature is named by Orpheus with these epithets: <term>multi-skilled mother</term> <note>original Greek: πολυμήχανος μήτηρ</note> and <term>decreer of foreign forms</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλλοτριομορφοδίαιτος</note>. Whatever the case may be, I for my part would far rather believe that if Pythagoras said he was Euphorbus or someone else, he introduced it as an enigma for the sake of an example. But if it is believed that he was weaving a history, he must be thought to have done so for no other reason than to show that a soul separated from the body can, by God's authority, return again into the very same body which it has already completely left and deserted, and not into any other

<column-break/>

<page-num>682</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> one: for we have long been able to learn from Iarchas, the wisest of the Indians, that it was one and the same body, however many different names it was called by, in which Pythagoras lived again so many times—not in size and quantity, but in substance and entity. Just as the sea, although it is <gloss>of the same nature</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὁμοφυές</note> and one, we nevertheless call this part the Aegean, that the Ionian, this the Myrtoan, and another the Cretan. So also one man, born again several times, was first named Aethalides, then Euphorbus, after that Hermotimus, then Pyrrhus, and finally our famous Pythagoras. He, as a most speculative and divine philosopher, did not attribute so many regenerations to the forces of nature, but to God alone, whom—as Heraclides Ponticus reports regarding this "Palingenesia" <note>rebirth or restoration of life</note>—he called Mercury, to show that no one lives again except by divine power. For as that philosopher and Christian martyr Justin relates in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, God was especially honored by Pythagoras with this title: <term>Animation of the universe</term> <note>original Greek: ψυχώσει τῷ ὅλων</note>, because He infuses the soul into all men, takes it away once infused, and restores it when taken away, as often and whenever He wills. Such a thing has often been seen in other men and confirmed by certain experience, as recorded by the most noble writers. For Aristeas once died at Proconnesus in a fuller's shop. Then, seven years later, he appeared alive to the citizens of that city, and he then composed poems about the Hyperborean Arimaspians, which Herodotus mentions excellently in the fourth book of his *Histories*. Furthermore, Er the Pamphylian lived in Armenia; when he had fallen in battle and the other corpses were taken up ten days later already decayed, he was found whole with an uncorrupted body. Carried home for the funeral office, on the twelfth day after his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he revived and recounted what he had seen in the meantime. Plato wrote these things in the tenth book of the *Republic*. Here also occurs what we read of a girl who died at Rome, who was restored to life by Apollonius of Tyana as she was being carried to the tomb, in the fourth book of Philostratus; and Alcestis is also told to have lived a long time again after being raised by Hercules.

<margin>F</margin> Then Marranus said, "How closely you approach our own traditions, Philolaus! For if Simon were standing here, he would recount to us from the Hebrew books how God once took of the spirit that was in Moses and gave it to the seventy men. After some time, when Elijah was taken from among men, his spirit settled upon Elisha; and likewise, Elisha himself made the dead son of the Shunammite woman live again. I add now the dead Samuel, whom a certain woman in Endor raised, and who after his resurrection spoke with King Saul. Listen truly to what that Prophet Ezekiel saw: namely, a field full of the dry bones of the dead, and bone drew near to bone, each to its joint, and behold, sinews and flesh grew upon them, and skin was stretched over them from above, and the spirit entered into them, and they lived again, and stood upon their feet. These things are contained in the sacred writings of the Hebrews; and many more are read described in the histories of the Christians. Indeed, for my part, I tell you this—"

# CABALA #

<margin>A</margin>
I would dare to affirm, without parable, without enigma, and with all irony removed, that Jesus of Nazareth truly and plainly raised the brother of Martha, named *Lazarus*, who had been dead for four days. Furthermore, he restored to life the deceased son of a certain widow. And he raised the daughter of *Jairus*, a leader of the synagogue, along with others commemorated in Holy Scripture. God also raised this same *Jesus*, and at his death, many bodies of those who had passed from life arose; leaving their tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. Finally, Paul of Tarsus restored *Eutychus* to the light alive, after he had accidentally departed from life. *Martin* <note>St. Martin of Tours (c. 316–397 AD), a famous bishop and miracle-worker.</note>, though not yet a bishop—indeed, not yet even baptized—raised <insert>three dead men</insert>.

<margin>B</margin>
I could produce a catalog of men recalled from death to their former life, were you not already aware that for us Christians it is easy to believe that the souls of men return to their bodies; for we plainly confess that a general resurrection of all human bodies will occur again for living. Concerning this, the most eloquent *Athenagoras*, an Athenian philosopher, composed an entire book for the Christians entitled *On the Resurrection* <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀναστάσεως</note>, which is certainly worthy of learned ears. Even to the Turks, Moors, and Hagarenes <note>A term used for Muslims, referring to Hagar.</note>, Muhammad speaks thus in the Quran <note>The text refers to the "Alcoran," using the Latinized spelling.</note> when they ask: "When we are bones, or reduced to nothing, how shall we be made into new men?" He responds: "Even if you were stone or iron, or whatever is harder, He who created you the first time will recall you to be raised to life again." Thus it is said in *Surah* 26. And again in 45, he says: "He who first formed you shall give you life a second time."

For this reason, I would wish that we follow Pythagoras with all the greater veneration, since he, more closely than almost all other Greek philosophers in nearly every matter, and not only in this cause, has approached our faith. For we see how Aristotle believed nothing of these things which he could not touch with his hand, perceive with his eyes, or grasp through a syllogism. Therefore, at the end of his treatise *On Generation and Corruption*, he in no way admits the return of a dead man, using a very weak argument and agreeing more with *Alcmaeon* than with his own teachers, contrary to the proverb common in his time: *that human affairs are a circle* <note>original Greek: κύκλον εἶναι τὰ ἀνθρώπινα; referring to the idea that things repeat in kind but not as individual instances.</note>. Others followed him—indeed, a whole cohort of philosophizers—who are to be blamed for this: presuming that they know everything and others know nothing, they mock Pythagoras after all the rest, exclaiming that line of Lucian: *Who will buy? Who has a shaft of wit above man? Who wants to know the harmony of the universe and to live again?* <note>original Greek: τίς ὠνήσει; τίς ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον ἔχει βέλος; τίς εἰδέναι τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ἁρμονίαν, καὶ ἀναβιῶναι πάλιν. This mocks an auction where Pythagoras’s soul is supposedly for sale.</note> Thus they ridiculously bid for him under the spear <note>A Roman custom of placing a spear in the ground to signify a public auction.</note>, as if he were a piece of livestock to be despised or a cheap slave. I will gladly allow them to know many things, provided they also allow that others have learned something. I have flared up now against them with more heat than was perhaps necessary, because I am moved to indignation against those who are accustomed to easily disparage the most ancient teachers and the princes of philosophy. I do this so that you may know that I love your Pythagoras no less than is right, and that I vehemently hate his detractors—who are not men, but monsters of men.

Then *Philo-laus* said: "There are some who must be forgiven because they are ignorant of such deep

<margin>B</margin>

These and similar crimes of sycophancy are the defamations and slanders of the most frivolous sophists, who defile everything with their unclean touch, polluting the feast with their mouths and leaving foul traces behind.

<margin>D</margin>

For that distinguished writer *Aristoxenus* says that Pythagoras did not abstain from living things, but ate meat. *Porphyry* proves this in the first book of *On Abstinence from Living Things* <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων</note>, noting that while other athletes were nourished by some with cheese and previously by others with figs, Pythagoras was the first of all to nourish them with the food of meat. He said that meat has an incredible power for acquiring strength; so says *Porphyry*. And *Apollodorus* the arithmetician testifies that Pythagoras sacrificed a hundred oxen when he had discovered: *that in a right-angled triangle, the side subtending the right angle is equal in power to the sides containing it.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι τριγώνῳ ὀρθογωνίῳ ἡ πλευρὰ ἡ πρὸς τὴν ὀρθὴν γωνίαν ὑποτείνουσα ἴσον δύναται ταῖς περιεχούσαις. This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
That is, the side lying beneath the right angle of a triangle is worth as much as the sides that contain it. Nevertheless, he was of a most modest life, of moderate nourishment, and drank very little, as *Lycon of Iasus* wrote concerning Pythagoras. Hence, his use of meat was perhaps rare, for he was often fed on thin honey alone. All these things are found in *Athenaeus*, in the tenth book of *The Banquet of the Learned*. And for this reason, if he warned students of letters to diligently avoid those things which would be heavy food,

For he had learned among the Hebrews that certain hard foods were prohibited in their law; he likewise knew things to be avoided among the Indians, such as sea fish (which are neither useful for the stomach nor accepted as offerings to the gods—for no one has ever heard of a fish being immolated in sacrifices). Finally, he had accepted from the Egyptians that the bean is not a clean legume, as *Herodotus* noted in his *Euterpe*.

<margin>G</margin>
They simply did not take those things for food, seeking tranquility of mind through the perpetual study of letters; though he did not wish such pious warnings to be observed as exactly and to the letter as the Law of the Twelve Tables. For *Xenophilus* and *Aristoxenus* record that he himself lived on small pigs and tender goats.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pythagoras, moving from the physical reality of his life and diet to a profound exploration of why he used numerical symbolism and enigmas to hide deep philosophical truths from the uninitiated. The author argues that Pythagoras used "numbers" as a mystical language to explain the origins of the universe, rather than referring to literal counting stones.</meta>

### SECOND BOOK ###

...by Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum, a Greek philosopher and music theorist who was a pupil of Aristotle</note> and certain others of greater age, his near-contemporaries. In the fourth book of Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights* <note>A 2nd-century collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history</note>, you will find it recorded that Pythagoras used no vegetable more frequently than the bean, specifically to gently soothe his bowels. However, the matter of beans will be explained later among the other symbols. 

For now, call to mind the things I have already said about numbers, as well as those I am about to say. This will help you recognize how impiously certain base buffoons of philosophy mock Pythagoras, the prince of philosophers, behind his back. They ridicule him because he taught that "number" is the principle of all things. These critics argue that since number is a "discrete quantity," it must follow after things rather than precede them—as if Pythagoras himself understood "numbers" to be merely literal pebbles <note>original: "calculos"</note> thrown out, from which all things originated. 

I wonder at these critics, not without a laugh; for although they have heard from the testimony of many wise men that nearly all Pythagorean philosophy—and especially that which concerns divine matters—is mystical and presented through enigmas, they nevertheless insist that this most divine part of wisdom concerning numbers should be taken plainly and without any metaphor. In doing so, they imitate the stupidity of the Tyrrhenians <note>A term often used by ancient writers for Etruscans, sometimes associated here with a literal-minded or superstitious nature</note>. 

However, it was the custom of the ancients and the sages of the most remote ages to hand down the profound inquiry of wisdom through the allegories of secret letters and the mysteries of the senses. Thus, the works of the most ancient philosophers and poets alike are completely full of enigmas. This was done both because of the inherent obscurity of the subject matter and out of a slight contempt for the common crowd. As Maximus Tyrius <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician</note> says in his tenth dissertation: *the myth elegantly interprets the outpouring of errors resulting from human weakness when things are not clearly seen* <note>original Greek: σφαλμάτων χύσιν ἀνθρωπίνης ἀσθενείας οὐ καθορωμένης σαφῶς, εὐσχημόνως ἑρμηνεύει ὁ μῦθος</note>. According to Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial who wrote on philosophy and grammar</note>, it is truly fitting for philosophers to express noble and upright truths under a pious veil of fictions, clothed in symbolic names. I believe this method is most effective for exciting and introducing the minds of scholars to the understanding of wonderful things. For we seek with less diligence that which is ready at our door than that which is situated far off, hidden in the depths of an abyss. Thus, ease of apprehension (believe one who has experienced it) breeds negligence in the studies of disciples, and that which is obtained very easily is sought after coldly. 

It also happens that sometimes we cannot express abstruse matters with any proper choice of words. We would be forced to express them with long, winding explanations and varied, complex speech if the convenient invention of the brief enigma had not been found. This is also useful for practical reasons: just as military commanders in opposing camps are accustomed to issue certain signals, which they call *tesserae* <note>In the Roman military, a *tessera* was a small tablet with a watchword or passcode written on it</note>, so that each leader can recognize his own soldiers and the soldiers can recognize one another. For example, Caesar used "Venus the Mother," Sulla used "Delphic Apollo," Marius used "The God Lar," and Jephthah used "*Shibboleth*" <note>A Hebrew word used as a password in the Book of Judges to identify enemies who could not pronounce the "sh" sound</note>. 

In the same way, it was not at all unseemly to hand down peculiar and secret symbols of doctrine to his close associates. In this way, whichever of the disciples used them most frequently would become more beloved by the master and would love one another more than the rest. From this, the Pythagoreans forged for themselves a kind of chain of indissoluble love and friendship through certain secret symbols. For Pythagoras was, above all, most zealous for the fostering of friendship; and if he learned that someone had shared in his symbols,

<meta>Catchword: shared (com-)</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> he would immediately adopt him as a companion and friend, as Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> confirms. And so it happened that everyone desired more ardently to use the Pythagorean symbols—that is, the marks of the mysteries—both because they would be more pleasing to their teacher and so that they would appear noble as Pythagoreans to all. Moved by this, in Plutarch's eighth book of *Table Talk*, Philinus was the only guest of Sulla the Carthaginian who abstained from animal meat during the banquet, specifically so that he might be recognized as a Pythagorean. 

<margin>B</margin> For this, he was rebuked by Lucius, a Tyrrhenian by birth and a disciple of the Pythagorean Moderatus. Lucius argued that Philinus followed the "letter" of the doctrine more than its "meaning." This was a fault worthy of rebuke in other "Pythagorists" as well, who, affected by immodesty and having peculiar or separate customs, either would not break bread like others at the dinners of companions and friends, or would not eat brains, or would roll up their blankets upon rising from a feast, or would sacrifice with bare feet, or would turn away from the sun when about to speak, or would leave the public road to travel <margin>C</margin> by side-paths. Or, when others were laughing, they would never laugh or laugh very little; or they would abstain entirely from eating beans. They practiced such things remarkably, led more by superstition than by right reason. They clutched only at the "husk" <note>The external, literal shell of the teaching</note> of the symbols, neglecting the underlying intent, merely so that they might be known by such marks and appear to the common people as Pythagoreans of that same order.

Therefore, symbols of this kind are signs of a single college. But let us also add that these enigmatic symbols—that is, marks fixed in the mind—contribute greatly to memory when we are measuring the vast distances of divine and human affairs <margin>D</margin> and dealing with innumerable subjects. Whenever we wish to remember, these symbols are quickly presented to our sight. 

Therefore, the most convenient symbol concerning the principles of things will be "one" and "two." For what occurs more quickly to those looking at individual things than "one" and "two," when we wish to scrutinize the causes and origin of the universe? For at first glance, the eye perceives that which is "the same" and that which is "the other." <margin>E</margin> From this, we conceive in the mind before all else that "Same" and "Other" are One and Two. 

Alcmaeon of Croton <note>An early 5th-century BC philosopher and medical theorist, often associated with Pythagoras</note>, who lived in the time of Pythagoras, called "two" those "many" things which he said were "contrarieties"—perhaps like the "Strife" of Empedocles. However, he posited those diverse things vaguely and without end, such as white and black, sweet and bitter, good and evil, small and large, as Aristotle testifies in the first book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Postnaturalium", a Latin term for the Metaphysics</note>. 

The Pythagoreans, however, because of their love for the art of arithmetic, compressed those diverse things (which are naturally contrary to one another and which the followers of Alcmaeon called "contrarieties") <margin>F</margin> into the number "ten"—that celebrated "denary" <note>The number ten, or Decad, which the Pythagoreans considered the most perfect number</note> which contains all things. These pairs include: finite and infinite, odd and even, one and many, right and left, male and female, resting and moving, straight and curved, light and darkness, good and evil, square and oblong. 

But these things are "either/or" because they are two; they are diverse precisely because they are two. For if they were one, they would not be contraries. They reduced all things <margin>G</margin> into "ten" because this number is the most perfect of all. It is the number by which all nations and all peoples (except the Thracians), both Greeks and Barbarians, count individual things, neither stopping short of it nor progressing beyond it, as if by natural calculation...

<summary>This page defends Pythagoras's use of numerical symbolism and enigmas as a "secret language" to protect deep truths and foster brotherhood, while mocking those who follow the literal "husk" of his rituals without understanding the philosophy. It introduces the fundamental Pythagorean dualism of the "One and Two" and the "Table of Ten Opposites" (the Decad) as the building blocks of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of Pythagorean number theory, moving from a general defense of the system to a specific technical and mystical breakdown of the "Decad" (the number ten) and the "Tetractys" (the number four). It connects these mathematical concepts to the ten Categories of Aristotle and the divine Mind.</meta>

<header>KABBALAH</header>

...ten fingers. Surely the perfection of that number is demonstrated by this most adorned world, which we see—according to the Pythagoreans—is moved by only ten spheres. It is also more perfect than the others because it contains more types of counting: even, odd, square, cube, oblong, plane, the first incomposite <note>A prime number</note>, and the first composite. Nothing is more absolute than this, because within ten proportions, four cubic numbers are completed, from which the Pythagoreans say the universe consists. 

**Archytas** <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician of the Pythagorean school, active in the 4th century BCE</note>, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, also encompassed everything that exists within the number ten. **Aristotle**, the "leader of the Peripatetic school," imitated him and named the ten genera of being the "ten categories." He chose to title his volume with this name, showing philosophically (as **Eustrathius** <note>A 12th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> maintained) the ten *real things* <note>original: "πράγματα" (pragmata)</note>, that is, real entities. **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle, circa 200 CE</note> called them the ten *voices* <note>original: "φωνάς" (phonas)</note>; **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> called them the ten *understandings* or *concepts* <note>original: "νοήματα" (noemata)</note>. Or, as **Iamblichus** perhaps more correctly argued, they are ten simple voices—not merely as sounds, but as they signify simple things themselves by means of ten simple concepts. 

**Alexander of Aegae**, **Ammonius son of Hermias**, and **Simplicius**—all distinguished lovers of wisdom—agree with this. They also diligently judged that within these ten most general entities, two primary divisions can be found into which they are divided, even though they arise from a single essence: such as substance and accident, or corporeal and incorporeal, or material and immaterial, or simple and composite. 

For the number ten loves the number two in such a way that, having proceeded from the one, it is born through the two, and through the two it returns to the one. For the first incomposite triad <note>the number 3</note> consists of one and two; it is not truly "composed," but rather "consisting," because the One does not have a "position" according to **Iamblichus**. Therefore, it does not create a "composition" if we wish to follow the proper use of words: *For neither does unity, while remaining unity, assume position; nor does a point, while remaining a point, lose position,* as **Simplicius** says in his commentaries on the category of quantity. From this, we can recognize the difference between a unit and a geometrical point. 

And since nothing exists before the one, we rightly say that one is the first. The binary <note>the number 2</note>, however, is not composed of numbers, because it is coordinated from the single unit twice (one and one). Therefore, it is the first number because it is the first "multitude," and it can be measured by no number except by the single unit—the common measure of all numbers. For "once two" is nothing other than two. For this reason, that multitude called the triad <note>the number 3</note> is most truly called the "first incomposite number" by arithmeticians. The binary preceding it is not an "incomposite" number, but more properly a "not-composed" number. 

Thus, the triad, desiring not to be idle, but rather to multiply its goodness among all creatures without envy, proceeds from power into operation. It gazes upon and reflects with a perpetual mind on that fruitfulness which is within it (the abundance of multitude, productive as number from number) and that essential quality which is the One (the source and origin of all production, as well as the

<column-break/>

<page-num>688</page-num>
<header>KABBALAH</header>

<margin>A</margin>
beginning of every procession and the permanence of every immutable substance). Thus, it turns back into itself, multiplying itself by way of unity and duality, saying: *once twice two are four.* 

Behold that **Tetractys**—that fourfoldness—about which I spoke with you before. This is the "idea" of all things that have been created because, as the arithmeticians say, every progression is perfected in the number four. From this arises that decad <note>the number 10</note> which we call the ten most general categories of all things. 

<margin>B</margin>
For one, two, three, and four, emerging from omnipotent power into the act of energy, produce ten. The half of ten is five. Therefore, place five in the middle, like a standard-bearer in the middle of an army. On its right side, place the next higher number, which is six; on its left side, the next lower number, which is four. These two joined together also constitute ten. 

<margin>C</margin>
Again, place on the right side the next higher number, which is seven, and on the left, the next lower, which is three; these two joined together similarly constitute ten. Again, place on the right side the next higher, which is eight, and on the left, the next lower, which is two; these two joined together also constitute ten. Finally, place on the right the remaining nine, and on the left the one; and now reduce those nine to one, and ten rises again. These, being referred back to twenty, begin anew to be a unity, and so on through all the cardinal numbers up to a hundred. 

<margin>D</margin>
For just as "twice one" makes two, and "thrice one" makes three, and "four times one" makes four, and so on, so "twice ten" makes twenty, and "thrice ten" makes thirty, and "four times ten" makes forty, and so on. It is the same for a hundred, the same for a thousand, and beyond. 

This, indeed, is the reason why we write "ten" in Greek using the letter *Iota* (which is an upright stroke), or note it in Hebrew with a single point <note>the letter Yod</note>. These signs, both for the barbarians and the Latins, otherwise represent a simple unit, precisely because the number ten arises from it and ends in it. 

There exists a Pythagorean symbol for this: namely, "one, two," which **Zaratas** <note>A name often associated with Zoroaster, whom some traditions claimed was a teacher of Pythagoras</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, used to pronounce using names of propagation: calling the one "Father" and the two "Mother," as witnessed by **Plutarch of Chaeronea** in his *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus*. 

<margin>E</margin>
For as you heard before, the one and the two, along with the divine essence, produce that fourfoldness—the **Tetractys**—which is the "idea" of all things completed in the number ten. **Pythagoras** affirms that it is the *fountain of perpetual nature* <note>original: "πηγὴν ἀενάου φύσεως" (pēgēn aenaou physeōs)</note>, which is nothing other than the knowledge of things in the divine mind working rationally. 

<margin>F</margin>
Indeed, **Pythagoras** called the Mind of God itself "Number" allegorically when he said that "Number is the principle of the universe." For **Plutarch**, in the fourth book of *Opinions of the Philosophers*, writes: *Pythagoras takes number in place of mind* <note>original: "τὸν δὲ ἀριθμὸν Πυθαγόρας ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῦ προσλαμβάνει" (ton de arithmon Pythagoras anti tou nou proslambanei)</note>. 

This is clearly a fitting sign, because among incorporeal things, nothing is more divine than the mind; among separate things, nothing is simpler than number. Furthermore, nothing can be thought of that is more similar to the mind. 

<margin>G</margin>
And from this fountain of perpetual nature, the Pythagorean number "one and two" flows down through streams and channels—that which from eternity was, will be, and indeed always is, gushing abundantly in the very fountain of the immense Ocean, which men in the ancient age named **Zena** <note>A variation of Zeus, often linked to 'Zēn', the Greek word for 'to live'</note>: that very thing...

<summary>This page explores the mathematical and mystical properties of the number ten (the Decad) and the number four (the Tetractys), arguing that Pythagoras used numbers as allegories for the Divine Mind. It reconciles Pythagorean numerology with Aristotle’s categories and the philosophical commentaries of Simplicius and Plutarch.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> They speak of that **One** (as *Aristotle* wished, citing this from *Homer*: "let there be one ruler" <note>original: "εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω" (heis koiranos estō)</note>) calling him *Zen* instead of *Zeus*, namely from "living" <note>original: "à viuendo"</note>. The Romans called him *Jove*, as if naming him after *Zeus*. *Cornutus* <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century CE</note>, in his book on Greek Theology, asserts that he is the soul of the whole world. The **Two**, however, is named *Hera*, who is both sister and wife to that *Zenos*—that is, Jupiter. Regarding this, *Homer* writes in the fourteenth book of the *Iliad*: "Hera of the golden throne saw with her eyes her own brother and brother-in-law Zeus <note>original: "Zena"</note> sitting on the highest peak of many-fountained Ida." <note>original: "ἥρη δ' εἰσεῖδε χρυσόθρονος ὀφθαλμοῖσιν αὐτοκασί-γητον καὶ δ' αέρα ζῶνα δ' ἐπ' ἀκροτά-της κορυφῆς πολυπίδακος ἴδης ἥμενον"</note> 

<margin>B</margin> By this sense, we can more easily understand the thoughts of the wisest poets regarding the origin of things: that on "many-fountained Ida"—a mountain named for "vision" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰδεῖν" (apo tou idein)</note> or from "foreknowledge" <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ τὸ γιγνώσκειν" (ek tou to gignōskein)</note>—Jupiter and Juno reside. They are like the **One** and the **Two** within the illustrious idea of the **Quaternio** <note>The number four, or Tetractys</note>. From here flow the principles of all things, which philosophers of a <margin>C</margin> later age named **Form** and **Matter**. Likewise, what we call primary Form and Matter, the most ancient philosophers called "One" and "Two." The suitable and illustrious poets called them *Jupiter* and *Juno*, who unite on Mount Gargarus <note>A peak of Mount Ida</note> and converge in the "Idea" of the Divine Mind. Both are pulled by two chariots and both by four horses; yet in descending, Jupiter remains on Olympus while Juno tends toward the lower regions. *Homer* bears witness to this, saying: "I go to see the ends of the fertile earth... but now I come here through this part of Olympus for your sake." <note>original: "ἀμὰ γὰρ λυρὸν πολὺ- / φόρβου σείρατα γαίης. νυνὶ γδ' ὃ λυμπόν πολύ- λύμπατον ἴκανω"</note> <margin>D</margin> Neither, however, completely abandons the other. 

In this manner, the beginning of the universe proceeds from the Divine Mind. For the **Tetractys**, looking back at its own essence—which is the first Unity, the producer of all things—and at the same time remembering its origin from the first product (since it is a duality), if "one" falls once, and "two" twice, the **Quaternary** <note>The number four</note> is soon established. It holds at the peak of its summit the unity of the sums, and suddenly becomes a **pyramid**, whose base is a flat quaternary, representing a "surface" to mathematicians. Upon this, the already mentioned light of divine unity radiates, creating the form and appearance of **incorporeal fire**. Because of Juno's departure (that is, Matter) to the lower regions, there immediately arises the nature of essential light—not the kind that burns, but the kind that illuminates. This is the creation of the "Middle World," which *Simon the Jew* <note>Likely referring to a mystical or Kabbalistic source</note> called "Supreme," because the world of the Deity does not allow for comparison; therefore, in his judgment, that other is named "Super-supreme" and "Incomparable." 

Truly, this middle world is rightly called **Olympus**, because it is entirely luminous, and being separated [from matter], it is most full of forms. As it says in the eighth book of the *Iliad*: "where the seat of the immortals is" <note>original: "ἵν' ἀθάνατων ἕδος ἐστί" (hin' athanatōn hedos esti)</note>—that is, where the floor, surface, or pavement of the immortals exists. For it is named the "dwelling of the Gods," or, as *Virgil* <note>original: "Maro"</note> more correctly says in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*: "the high house of the Gods." Its summit is **Unity**, its walls are **Trinity**, and its surface is **Quaternity**. This is seen more clearly when the number, by emanating from its divinity, declines a little and turns toward the shape of creatures. For let us then place a square for the Tetractys, and in each of its corners a 

<column-break/>

point representing the units. And for the unity of the summit, which now begins to have a position, let us raise the highest peak as much as possible. Once this is done, the four sides raised upward will be four triangles constructed over their quadrangular width, all drawn to a single high point. Behold the pyramid itself, which is the "form of fire," according to the testimony of *Timaeus Locrus* the Pythagorean in his book *On the Soul of the World*, writing in the Doric dialect: "From which the pyramid, having four bases and equal angles, is composed, a form of fire that is most mobile and fine-particled." <note>original: "ἐξ οὗ ἁ πυραμὶς τέσσαaras βάσιας καὶ τὰς ἴσας γωνίας ἔχευσα συντίθεται, εἶδος πυρὸς εὐκινατότατον καὶ λεπτομερές αἴτι"</note> 

This is surely without matter—a separated essential light, closest to God, and eternal life. As is read in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Postnaturalia"</note> and the second book of *On the Heavens*: "The work of the Mind is life; the operation of God is immortality; and that is eternal life." *Aristotle* borrowed these things from the Pythagoreans. Yet God himself is not "created light," but the "Light-bringing Author" of all light. Wherefore, God the Best and Greatest contains within His divine Trinity the most absolute and "tetractic" pyramid, which raises itself from a triangular base into the heights and similarly signifies fiery vigor. 

Hence both the **Chaldeans** and the **Hebrews** proclaim that God is a fire. The pyramid produced by the quaternary is the fiery light of the world of separated intelligences, incorporeal and immaterial, outside the visible heavens. This is called *Aion* <note>original: "αἰών"</note> by the Greeks, and by us the "Age," "Eternity," and "Aether." From this, "Aethra" is said to be the splendor of eternity, where there is no body, no place, no vacuum, no time, no old age, and no change. Instead, there are unchangeable and impassive beings possessing the best life, which they enjoy for the whole *Aeon*—that is, eternity or the age. 

These are almost the very words of *Aristotle the Stagirite*, which both he and the Platonists and Socratics derived from *Pythagoras*, who wrote thus in his *Golden Verses*: "If, having left the body, you reach the free aether, you will be an immortal God." And here, having overcome things in this life, you will know the cohabitation of immortal gods and mortal men, which he elegantly calls the *Heavens* <note>original: "οὐρανὸν" (ouranon)</note>, from "standing together." Through this, he shows us three properties of the **Middle World**, which he names the "Free Aether": because it is segregated from the power of matter and preserved in freedom, it glows with the heat of God and warms the lower things with an imperceptible motion. For *Aether* is named from "always warming" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀεὶ θέρειν" (apo tou aei thereein)</note>. <margin>F</margin> Its properties are these: **condition**, **chorus**, and **order**. 

The condition of that world is that whatever it is, it is the purest form. They assert its nature is "Jovial" <note>Of Jupiter</note>, which gives form to immortals and mortals alike, and by a specific nourishment, preserves all things of both worlds in their being. About this, *Virgil* writes: "O Father, O eternal power of men and gods!" Because of this nourishing heat, the spiritual sun was called *Jupiter* by the ancients. Hence the *Salii* (priests of Mars Gradivus) called him *Lucetius* <note>Light-bringer</note>, and the Cretans called him *Phosphorus*. From him, *Olympus* is named, because it shines entirely; in it, Jove shines completely and presides—indeed, he is everything that it is. Hence that line in the 9th book of the *Aeneid*: "He nodded, and made all Olympus tremble with his nod."

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical relationship between the numbers One, Two, and Four, identifying them with Jupiter (Form), Juno (Matter), and the creation of a luminous "Middle World" or Aether. It uses the geometry of the pyramid to explain how divine light becomes the "incorporeal fire" that sustains the universe.</summary>

# CABALA

<margin>A</margin> Its condition, I say, is to receive simple, immaterial, separate, and self-existing forms, which are both universal and individual. For it contains all the conceptual ideas of genera and species, acting as the very models to be imitated by more limited copies; the original "sealing" model of these consists in the divine mind. For we wish to name them thus: in the physical world, there is the absolute model of the Deity. In the intelligible world, there is the abstract model, and in the sensible world, there is not the model itself, but that limited copy—much like a seal, the shape it leaves, and the wax that is stamped. To this is added a second property of this "choir" <note>A group of celestial beings</note>, named <term>from joy</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς" (apo tēs charas)</note>, that is, from the infinite joy of the blessed spirits and the unchanging pleasure of the Gods. These inhabitants of that spring-like dwelling and citizens of Olympus, rejoicing with myrtle crowns, perpetually enjoy the nectar and ambrosia of the divine banquet, laughing with inextinguishable laughter. Regarding this, the wisest of poets, Homer, said: <term>Indeed, inextinguishable laughter was stirred up among the blessed gods</term> <note>original: "ἄσβεστος δ' ἄρ' ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν"</note>. This clearly shows their everlasting joy, which the famous Melesigenes <note>Another name for Homer</note> elegantly expressed in the first book of the *Iliad* through their constant harmony with harps and other instruments of the Muses, dances, processions, banquets, peaceful resting places, and occasionally sweet sleep. 

Why not, Marranus? What greater pleasure can be imagined than to behold God's will, and after Him, to see the ideas and forms of all things more purely and transparently than through any other creature? Furthermore, to reveal these visions to those below, which is the unique privilege of the Gods. And so they are sometimes called "Gods" in Latin, who in Greek are <term>gods from vision</term> <note>original: "θεοὶ ἀπὸ τῆς θέας" (theoi apo tēs theas)</note>, that is, from speculation and sight; hence the word <term>to behold</term> <note>original: "θεάσασθαι" (theasasthai)</note> means to look upon and see. They are also sometimes called angels when they announce what they have seen to others, as Orpheus says when invoking Mercury: <term>Hear me, Hermes, messenger of Jove, son of Maia, interpreter of all things</term> <note>original: "κλῦθί με ἑρμεία διὸς ἄγγελε μαιάδος υἱέ ἑρμηνεῦ πάντων"</note>. For we say <term>to announce</term> <note>original: "ἀγγέλλειν" (angellein)</note> means to report and explain. Frequently, however, we use one term for the other without considering their specific offices, so that in common speech we use "Gods" and "Angels" interchangeably. For when Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> wrote in his *Introduction* that "both we and the angels are rational," Boethius, translating into Latin, said: "both we and the gods are rational." This is found in the books of many others in this manner. 

Therefore, let no one think that when we name "Gods," we are equating them to the supreme and ineffable God, who has no name. For we call that supreme majesty "God" because He infinitely penetrates all beings and runs through each one, <term>from running</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θέειν" (apo tou theein)</note>, that is, to run. Indeed, God is much more interior and intimate to every single thing than that thing is to itself; though He is nowhere, He is everywhere. But we do not call those "gods" in the same way who only carry out a limited province assigned to them and are sent for a destined work. As for demons, however good they may be, they are not admitted into this choir of the middle world by Pythagoras and his followers. For Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism</note>—who, according to Porphyry and Longinus, seemed to follow the mysteries of the Pythagoreans most perfectly—says in his book *On the Love of the Gods*: "We say and believe the 

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> genus of the gods is free from passion. But we attach passions to demons, saying also that they are eternal, in the rank following after the gods." It is certainly better to call no one in the intelligible world a "demon"; rather, if a demon were placed there, one should consider him a God. Thus far Plotinus, who is certainly brief in all his teaching and must be weighed with an attentive mind, especially in this difficult passage where the secrets of the Poets speaking about the Gods can be read without trouble and without provoking the bitterness of many.

The third property of the intelligible world was demonstrated by Pythagoras himself when he said: "If you live by right reason, grieving over evil deeds and rejoicing in good ones, and pray to the Gods to perfect your work, then, having cast off the body and departed into the ether, you shall be an immortal God." <margin>C</margin> We must consider here the order Pythagoras observes in pursuing human blessedness. For that incorporeal heaven of the middle world, and that invisible Olympus of the blessed, admits nothing impure. Therefore, vices must be fled and virtues embraced. Furthermore, the salvation of men lies in the mercy of God: wherefore the divinity must be worshipped, and those above must be entreated to perfect our work. Only then is nothing of matter, nothing of body, and nothing of the mixed received; therefore, one must die and holily cast off the body before being counted among the gods. <margin>D</margin> This is the order of the ages: that for holy, pure, and chosen men, the super-celestial hall of the native gods is granted. There, human nature may share a common life of eternal duration with the sacrosanct angelic spirits in the invisible, yet all-formed super-celestial heaven and restful orb outside the sensible world. This is where the true Olympus is—not imaginary, nor poetic; not something that rolls or rotates or never rests. 

Then Marranus said: "How closely," he said, "Pythagoras, more than all others, approaches the beliefs of our own times! <margin>E</margin> For in the Christian Law, we similarly read that dead men from the number of those rising again are like the angels of God in heaven, where the tabernacle of God is with men. Nothing defiled, or anyone practicing abomination or lying, shall enter there. There will be the voice of harpers playing their harps, and a new song; and the dead who are written in the book of life see a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away from them. <margin>F</margin> There also is the city of the blessed having the glory of God, and its walls are built of Jasper, and its foundations are adorned with every precious stone. And the Lord Almighty is the temple of that city, and from His throne proceeds a river of the water of life, as bright as crystal. The foundation and surface of His city is a square; for the words of the Apocalypse, from which these are taken, are these: <term>and the city lies foursquare</term> <note>original: "καὶ ἡ πόλις τετράγωνος κεῖται"</note>. <margin>G</margin> This was explained by Pope Hippolytus as being so <term>on account of its solidity and firmness</term> <note>original: "διὰ τὸ ἕδραιον καὶ πάγιον"</note>. You seem to me to lead this back to the number of your Pythagoras and the figure of the pyramid, erected from a square base, which mathematicians are accustomed to count among the solids."

<summary>This page explores the "intelligible world" or Olympus, defining it as a realm of eternal joy and pure forms where Gods and Angels reside. It draws direct parallels between Pythagorean philosophy regarding the soul's ascent and the Christian vision of the New Jerusalem described in the Book of Revelation.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

...not only yours, but I would call him our true Pythagoras. Indeed, I shall call him ours as long as I live, because he alone, out of the entire crowd of ancient philosophers, understood our wisdom more aptly, more harmoniously, and more appropriately. Nor does he differ greatly in the foundation of his doctrine from the Persians, the Palestinians, and the Arabs of our own age—this same author of the Italian philosophy <note>The "Italian philosophy" refers to the school founded by Pythagoras in Southern Italy (Magna Graecia).</note>. For thus we read in the first Sura <note>original: "Azoara," a Latinization of the Arabic 'Sura'</note> of the law of Muhammad: God will lead the good into paradise, where they will possess the sweetest waters, many kinds of orchard fruits, various produce, and the most delightful and pure women, and every good thing for eternity. And in the fifty-first Sura, he says: "But those who believe and do good works shall possess the most beautiful places of paradise and fulfill all their desires; this is the greatest gain." Such a promise announces the highest joy to them. Then, in the *Doctrine of Muhammad* <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Islamic teachings</note>, it is written: "If any kind of delight were missing there, blessedness would be far from full." Therefore, pleasures would be present in vain if delight were absent. And a little earlier, he says: "Whatever can be desired will immediately be present for its inhabitants, who will all be perfect in the stature of Adam and the form of Jesus Christ, never suffering any increase or decrease." And in the Quran <note>original: "Alkoran"</note>, chapter 64: "There the believers will recline upon silk carpets and purple coverings, and they will perpetually enjoy all things dear to them, and they will marry most beautiful girls, like hyacinth and pearls, who have never been deflowered by men or devils, nor are subject to menstruation. There will also be trees there shining with a color between green and saffron, and strongly flowing fountains, and palms, and pomegranates."

Do you not perceive here, Philolaus, that the greatest part of these things is symbolic? Almost everything you have heard is narrated allegorically, in the manner of the Pythagoreans. Muhammad openly confesses this in the *Book of Doctrine* when he says: "There is another age after this world, of which no likeness can be explained; for its inhabitants are not mortal, nor are its days numbered." By this, he declares that what he wrote concerning divine matters was written allegorically, and not plainly or openly, even when he counted the days of blessedness as days of a thousand years, and years as forty thousand years. He also taught that paradise has a golden pavement distinguished by frequently interspersed emeralds and hyacinths, planted with every fruit-bearing tree, with streams running through pleasant fields—some of which pour forth milk, others white honey, and others the purest wine. These things are in the *Book of Doctrine of Muhammad*, where by a "sensible paradise" <note>A paradise perceived by the physical senses</note> he designates that garden of the intelligible world which reason cannot grasp. For Muhammad proposed two paradises to us in the Quran, when he says in the sixty-fourth Sura <note>The text likely refers to Sura 55, "The Merciful," which mentions two gardens</note>: "He who fears while standing before God shall receive as an inheritance two paradises, fertile with manifold things and every kind of good." Thus he also shows two cities of Jerusalem; for in the *Book of Doctrine*, Abdias asks: "Why is Jerusalem called the blessed house?" Muhammad replied: "Because it is situated directly beneath the celestial Jerusalem." These things allude not a little to the Cabalistic things of our friend Simon which we have heard: namely, concerning two paradises, one celestial and the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> other terrestrial, signifying twin worlds, the visible and the invisible; the former present to us, the latter future. You have explained quite a lot about the former in a few words; therefore, I pray you, Philolaus, proceed with the rest concerning our Pythagoras, whom we revere.

"I shall do so diligently," said Philolaus, "if I first warn you not to err with those crude pseudo-philosophers who only understand what they see with their eyes. As Ammonius, son of Hermias, wrote concerning Antisthenes, <margin>B</margin> who said: 'I see the man, but I do not see humanity.' From this, he thought that humanity was nothing but a fiction of thought." <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐκεῖνος ἔλεγε, τῇ αἰσθήσει μόνη ζῶν, καὶ μὴ δυνάμενος τῷ λόγῳ εἰς μείζονα εὑρεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἀνάγειν."</note> This is translated as follows: *He said these things, living by sensation alone, and being unable by reason to raise himself to a greater discovery.* So says Hermiades in the *Isagoge* <note>An introductory text, likely referring to the commentary on Porphyry</note>. In no different way, there are some of such blunt wit that they cannot contemplate sharply except for what the pupil of the eye encompasses or the hands touch. Whatever they hear concerning <margin>C</margin> the celestial life, the higher gods, souls in heaven, or the heavenly beings, they immediately refer to the visible sky, the spheres of the stars, the moving firmament, and those orbits we perceive by sense—as if a blessed life could consist in such a whirlwind of motions and unquiet tumult of changes! But those who follow the spiritual sense and the subtle illumination of the mind understand that there is greater truth in those things which are not seen than in those which are seen. To this, the will of the Pythagoreans is inclined: <margin>D</margin> to believe that this world and whatever is placed within it is a shadowed image of that true world which exists outside the heavens, containing only intelligences, forms, and souls separated from bodies in substance, power, and operation. Hence, they firmly hold that the souls of men, purified from all foul filth and having cast off the bodily mass, dwell without doubt outside and beyond this entire visible heaven, beyond any risk of hardship, in the Olympus of eternity—gifted with all liberty <margin>E</margin> and bound by no necessity. For thus the famous Plotinus, that distinguished Pythagorean, says in his book *On One's Own Daemon*: "It must be thought that souls having departed outside the sensible world have transcended the daemonic nature, every fate of generation, and every necessity of this world, as long as they dwell in the intelligible world." Thus far Plotinus.

Whenever, therefore, mention is made of true gods, separate intelligences, purer forms, divine spirits, <margin>F</margin> those above, angels, and the souls of the blessed, always remember and turn over in your mind that supreme world: intelligible, immaterial, simple, abstract, the incorporeal heaven, the invisible Olympus, the mental paradise, the supernatural ether, perceptible neither by sense nor by reason. Having dismissed that for now, let us descend to our corporeal and sensible world, the model of which is in the incomparable world of the Deity, the example of which is in the intelligible world of <margin>G</margin> formality, and the "self-signifier" <note>original: "τὸ αὐτόσημον" (to autosēmon)</note> of the models within itself. And as "One" is the origin of the mental world, so "Two" will be the beginning for us of the corporeal world, which would not be corporeal unless it consisted of these four: point, line, surface, and thickness <note>depth/solidity</note>, according to the model...

<summary>This page compares the sensory descriptions of Paradise in Islamic tradition with Pythagorean and Cabalistic allegories, arguing that such descriptions represent an "intelligible world" beyond physical sight. Philolaus warns against literalism, citing Plotinus and Ammonius to argue that true reality exists in immaterial forms rather than the visible, moving heavens.</summary>
