<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue exploring the mathematical and geometric foundations of the universe, moving from the description of paradise into the Pythagorean construction of reality using shapes like the cube, pyramid, and dodecahedron.</meta>

# THE KABBALAH

<margin>A</margin> ...of the cubic figure, which is established by one, two, three, and four. For "One," fixed in its position, creates a point. A line, stretched from one point to another, is made of "Two." A surface arises from "Three" lines. Thickness <note>That is, three-dimensional depth.</note> is born from "Four": forward, backward, upward, and downward. Therefore, just as the number two multiplied by itself produces four (two times two), so too the number two, folding and turning back upon itself (saying "two times two, twice"), creates the first cube <note>In this mathematical system, 2 cubed ($2^3$) equals 8.</note>. Therefore, after the five-sided figure <note>The pyramid.</note>, which is the tetragonic pyramid and indeed the principle of the intelligible world, there follows the eight-cornered cube of six sides, which we appoint as the architect of the sensible <note>The physical or "perceptible" world.</note> world. For among the principles of things, there is no memory of the number seven, since it is a virgin that gives birth to nothing; for this reason, it is named Pallas <note>Referring to Pallas Athena, the virgin goddess who was not "born" but sprang from the head of Zeus.</note>. We turn, then, to the first cube, a truly fertile number and the prince of multitude and variety, as it is made through two and constituted by four. Hence, just as the master Pythagoras—whom Zaratas <note>Likely referring to Zoroaster, whom Renaissance thinkers often linked to Pythagoras.</note> called "Two"—named it "Mother," so we call the cube proceeding from it "Matter," the bottom and foundation of all natural things, and the seat of substantial forms. Concerning this, Timaeus of Locri, that famous Pythagorean, writes in his book *On the Soul of the World*: <margin>B</margin> <term>From the square is produced the cube, the most robust and stable body in every way, having six sides and eight angles.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐκ δὲ τοῦ τετραγώνου γνώμαται τὸν κύβον εὐρωστότατον καὶ σταδαῖον πάντη σῶμα. ἓξ μὲν πλευράς, ὀκτὼ δὲ γωνίας ἔχον."</note> If any form, having been plunged in, rests upon this foundation—if it has slipped into this solid receptacle and been placed in this material seat—it is not received in a wandering or general way, but becomes stable, singular, individual, and incommunicable. It is as if it were bound to the soil, subjected to time and place, and proscribed from freedom into the slavery of matter. Therefore, we see twin principles of temporal things flowing from a single source: the pyramid and the cube, which is to say, Form and Matter. These are discovered to have come forth from the same tetragon <note>The square or the power of four.</note>, the idea of which, as we showed before, is the Tetractys, the divine exemplar of Pythagoras. I have explained these primordial symbols as briefly as I could, for they truly designate nothing other than matter and form. And since it is necessary to propose a third thing by which they are united (for they do not flow together of their own accord, nor does a chance meeting of any forms into matter occur, nor does the matter of one thing receive the form of another by accident—for brass or iron is not generated from a human body as soon as the soul has departed, nor is wool made from stone)—since, I say, it is necessary to propose a third thing by which they are united, it will, in my opinion, be necessary to bring in a principle other than the Aristotelian "privation" <note>Aristotle's "privation" refers to the absence of a form that a thing could potentially have.</note> to move matter toward the desire for form, so that as this or that form ceases, this or that one may be introduced in turn. For privation and potentiality do nothing substantive, since they possess no real activity and are therefore of the least entity; how much less can they join or unite a certain form to any matter? Hence, there are those who have said that "Motion" is the third principle instead of privation; but since motion is an accident, how can it be a principle of substance? Or who shall be the mover of that motion?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For this reason, those two wiser Athenians, Socrates (son of Sophroniscus) and Plato (son of Ariston), placed God as the most agile of actors in the place of "promotion" or "privation." They said there are three principles of things: God, Idea, and Matter. Pythagoras had previously symbolized this secretly through these arcane notes, asserting that the principles of all things are the Infinite, the One, and the Two. He designated God as the Author of Infinitude, Form as Unity, and Matter as Alterity <note>The state of being "other" or "different."</note>. He placed the Infinite in the super-supreme and incomparable world, the One (or Identity) in the intellectual world, and the Two (or Alterity) in the sensible world; for matter is indeed the mother of alteration. God, however, joins matter and form through a law imposed upon nature itself. Therefore, long before the time of Pythagoras, that most ancient Orpheus, in his *Book of Hymns*, placed after Jove—that is, Form, whom he calls <margin>B</margin> <term>the beginning of all things</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὴ πάντων"</note>—and after Juno—that is, Matter, whom he calls <term>the bedfellow of Jove and the mother of all</term> <note>original Greek: "διὸς σύλλεκτρον παγγενέθλιον"</note> (for he addresses matter with the surname of Juno in these words: <margin>C</margin> <term>Without you, nothing at all has known the nature of life; you communicate with all things, mixed in more than modestly</term> <note>original Greek: "χωρὶς δὲ σέθεν οὐδὲν ὅλως ζώης φύσιν ἔγνω κοινὸς ὃς ἅπασιν κεκραμένην πείσεισθε"</note>). So, after Jove (Form) and Juno (Matter), I say, the same Orpheus added "Law"—that is, distribution—as the third principle of nature, and he nicknamed it <term>the confirmation of nature</term>. <margin>D</margin> <note>original Greek: "φύσεως τὸ βέβαιον"</note> For "Law" is called *nomos* in Greek, as you know, from the words meaning to distribute and to divide, just as it distributes to all what is their own or what pertains to them. This, he says, is <term>the celestial law, the just seal</term> (as he sang in his hymns); for the law of nature seals many matters with one form, just as a notary seals many waxes with one image from a ring. Now, any forms sealed into matter are no longer called "ideas" (which means "species"), but <margin>E</margin> <term>eidos</term>, which is to say "shape" or "appearance," namely: <term>like the impressions in wax, inseparable from the matter</term>, <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὰ ἐν τοῖς κηροῖς ἐκτυπώματα ἀχώριστα τῆς ὕλης"</note> as Ammonius wrote. Accordingly, the origin of this sensible world now stands open to us, which the marriage of the pyramid and the cube, celebrated by the law of nature, has brought forth. The square bases of those figures, when united, immediately create a dodecahedron <note>A twelve-sided solid.</note>—a Pythagorean symbol, indeed, by which the universe itself, composed of matter and form, is designated. Alcinous rightly remembers this concerning the dogma of Plato, saying: <margin>F</margin> <term>God used the dodecahedron for the whole universe</term> <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ παντὶ ὁ Θεὸς κατεχρήσατο"</note>—that is, when he was fabricating this world. For if you place a pyramid raised from four equal triangles upon an eight-cornered cube, you will have skillfully constructed the building of a dodecahedron, where the cube (or die) settles below like a mother, and the pyramid rests upon it like a father. For thus that noble Pythagorean, Timaeus of Locri, says in his <margin>G</margin> book *On the Soul of the World*: <term>Form has the character of the male and the father, while matter has that of the female and the mother; and the third things are their offspring.</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν εἶδός λόος ἔχει ἄρρενός τε καὶ πατρός, ἁ δ' ὕλα, θήλεός τε καὶ ματέρος, τρῖτα δὲ τὰ τούτων ἔκγονα"</note> That is...

<summary>This page explains the Pythagorean creation of the physical world using geometry, identifying the Cube as Matter (Mother) and the Pyramid as Form (Father). It argues that a third principle, "Law" or "God," is necessary to unite these two into the Dodecahedron, which represents the complete Universe.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> ...that these things are twin-like. From these, therefore, we correctly affirm that all things which exist in this world are created by certain seeds and a secret faculty, appearing indeed with a marvelous variety because of the different proportions of their forms to their materials, and the admixture of almost infinite accidents which Epicurus calls <term>symptomata <note>original: "συμπτώματα"; referring to properties or occurrences that are not essential to a substance's nature.</note></term>, through abundance and deficiency, strife and friendship, motion and rest, impulse and tranquility, the rare and the dense.
<margin>B</margin> From these arise the spheres and stars, and likewise the four elements, from which evaporate the hot and the moist, the cold and the dry, and then any objects of the senses. From there, one thing happens to some and another to others. It causes all things to turn their forms and change their colors, by the testimony of Lucretius. Do you perceive how much we are now walking with the common crowd of philosophers, and treading the well-worn path when we have slipped into these physical matters? Therefore, since many have written many things about nature, we must apply less of our own strength to show what Pythagoras felt about natural things, taking our beginning from the nobler and more divine things. There are natural gods, but also supernatural "gods of gods": the lower world nourishes the former, while the superior world fosters the latter, whence they are called the "higher ones," concerning whom we have previously discussed quite a lot. These "gods of gods" are most simple and pure, and because they are nowhere <note>Meaning they are not confined to a specific physical location.</note>, they are therefore super-celestial; because they are everywhere, they are therefore with us—inhabitants there, guests here. For they are never in our world unless they are sent, which is why they rejoice in the name of **Angels** when they descend to these lowest parts, since they are the messengers of the King of Kings. Yet they appear to us in whatever habit and face they wish according to the freedom of their will, always most loving in their benefits toward us. But other, lower spirits never migrate to the super-celestial realms, yet they sometimes take up an embassy to us and our affairs, from which it is the same when they are called Angels. God, however, the Best and Greatest, dwells most deeply within the lowest, the highest, and the middle things individually, so that there is nothing among beings without God. Furthermore, the gods of our world are more excellent. Lower, however, are the souls in the human body, although the former are *near* bodies, while the latter are *within* bodies. In the middle of these, the <term>daemons <note>original: "dæmones"; in the Greek sense of intermediate spirits or guiding geniuses, rather than "demons" as purely evil entities.</note></term> and heroes hold their places—the daemons near the gods, the heroes near the souls. Pythagoras mentions these in his *Golden Verses*, and attributed to each their own worship. Yet he did not permit their altars to be defiled with blood, nor animals to be sacrificed, except for the sake of public utility; rather, he wished daily and private sacrifices to be made with incense and hymns. From this comes the saying:

> Appease God with incense, and let the calf grow for the plow.

And since man is a certain image of this world, whence he is called the <term>microcosm <note>original: "μικρόκοσμος"; meaning "little world."</note></term>, he has received many worldly names in equal measure, <term>metaphorically <note>original: "μεταφορικῶς"</note></term> and in the manner of a translation. For the **Mind** in man is called God, after the likeness of the highest and first Mind, either by sharing a name or by participation. And the rational soul, which through the mind inclines the will toward virtues and all the best things, is called a "good daemon" or "genius"; but that which through phantasy and depraved affections drags the will toward vices and all the worst things, is named an "evil daemon." For this reason, Pythagoras prays to God that he might deliver men from evil, and show to all

<column-break/>

what daemon they might use. Finally, once the body is cast off, if the soul remains defiled by vices, it will become an evil daemon, and its life is called <term>dysdaimonia <note>original: "δυςδαιμονία"; meaning misery or ill-fortune.</note></term>, that is, unhappiness. But if it has cast off vices, and nevertheless the character of its worldly care remains impressed upon it, and it has not completely left behind all affection toward human and even mortal customs (however much of virtue they have), it will be for some time a good daemon, and will dwell happily and fortunately in the pleasantness of this world with singular joy. It revolves in its mindful soul the things it has done well, and retains a not-yet-extinguished will to perform those same things rightly; the Greeks call its life <term>eudaimonia <note>original: "εὐδαιμονia"; meaning flourishing or true happiness.</note></term>. From this arose that saying of Virgil:

> The same joy in chariots and arms
> which they had while living, the same care to feed
> sleek horses, follows them now buried in the earth.

<margin>C</margin> I have heard that the ancients called that soul a *lemur* <note>A restless spirit of the dead.</note>; if there is one of this kind who is led by such benevolence toward us that, having obtained the care of us and our people, he possesses the house as a peaceful and quiet divinity, he is called a *Lar familiaris* <note>A Roman household protector spirit.</note>. But if, because of the adverse merits of its life, it is punished by being unsettled—an exile from any good dwelling—it is called a *larva* <note>An owl-like or ghostly spirit that terrifies the living.</note>, an empty terror to good men but harmful to the wicked. When it is uncertain which lot it enjoys, whether it be a *Lar* or a *larva*, they call it by the name of a "God-Manes"; to which they added the title of "God" for the sake of honor, since they also pronounce
<margin>D</margin> those to be gods who, having governed the course of life justly and prudently, have met a holy death. Furthermore, we indiscriminately call "Gods," "Angels," and even "Daemons" those noble spirits who, assigned as guardians to each individual human, are always present (though least visible), not only as witnesses of our deeds but even of our thoughts; they also follow us after death all the way to the power, judgment, and tribunal of the highest daemon. All these things flowed to us from Pythagoras, which he himself learned partly
<margin>E</margin> from the Egyptians, partly from the Hebrews and Chaldeans, and among the wisest Magi of the Persians, and handed down to posterity. The most excellent authors remember these: Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Termaximus"</note>, the illustrious legislator of the Egyptians and most contemplative writer in his *Perfect Discourse* to Asclepius; Timaeus of Locri in his book *On the Soul of the World*; Hesiod in *Works and Days*; Plato through Diotima in the *Symposium*, through Socrates in the *Phaedrus*, and likewise in the *Philebus*, the *Epinomis*, and other places
<margin>F</margin> in his books; Porphyry in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*; Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries*; Proclus in *On the Alcibiades*; Plotinus in his book *On Love*, and in the book *On One's Own Daemon*; Maximus of Tyre in two disputations on the daemon of Socrates; and many others of the Greeks, whom among the Latins Cicero imitated in his volumes *On the Nature of the Gods*, *On Divination*, and in the sixth book of the *Republic*; and also that man of Madaura, Apuleius, in the book *On the God of Socrates*, and others
<margin>G</margin> followed after them. Nor are there lacking those among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> who treated the movers of the spheres, the constellations and stars, and the presiding spirits of the elements, whether they assist those bodies or are within each of them as their soul...

<summary>This page outlines the Pythagorean and Neoplatonic hierarchy of the universe, describing how the soul's virtue determines its status as a guiding spirit (daemon) or a haunting ghost after death. It traces these spiritual concepts from ancient Egyptian and Hebrew sources through Greek philosophers like Plato to Roman thinkers like Cicero.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speaker's exposition of Pythagorean philosophy, transitioning from the structural physics of the elements to the broader cosmology, the nature of the soul, and the pedagogical purpose of the mathematical arts as a bridge to the divine.</meta>

### CABALA

...to do. Now we shall enumerate for a few the remaining things concerning the sensible world. Therefore, *Pythagoras* said that this world, which is an imitator of eternity, is the containment of all wholes according to the order established within it; and although it is corporeal, it possesses incorporeal primary principles. The Stoics did not agree with him in this, for they thought those principles were corporeal because they were spiritual. He asserted that the world was both generated and corruptible, yet by the providence and indulgence of God, it would never actually be destroyed. He also said that the bodies of the elements are round, except for fire, which takes the shape of a cone. He stated that color is the appearance of a body. Time he called a circle, the outer limit of the world, a motion, or a certain difference or "otherness" in matter; he believed that matter is subject to the passivity of generation and corruption. Necessity weighs upon the world: some things happen by necessity, some by fate, some by choice, some by fortune, and some by chance. The cause of these things is hidden from human reason, a view in which *Anaxagoras* also concurs. Our philosopher thought the world began from fire. Its right side is in the east, and its left is in the west. Then, following *Thales*, he divided the heavens into five zones, then into equinoxes and solstices (two of each), and the <term>infinite <note>original: "ἄπειρον" (apeiron); the boundless or indefinite source of all things in Pre-Socratic philosophy.</note></term>. He divided the orb of the earth in no different a manner. Furthermore, he was the first of all to discover the obliquity of the zodiac along the sun's path. He said the moon appears only as an ignited terrestrial body, containing within itself fields, mountains, and valleys. Concerning the soul, he pronounced in this way: that it is a self-moving number. He distributed it by its powers as follows: the Vital power is around the heart; the rational and mental power is around the head. The whole soul cannot perish, for the rational part is the work of the eternal God, while the irrational part is indeed corruptible. To the same author we should attribute the truer form of divination through sacrifices. He maintained that human seed is the foam of the most useful blood of corporeal matter, but endowed with incorporeal virtue. Moreover, he held that the female likewise emits seed. Furthermore, he believed that not only man but also other living creatures possess reason, though they lack a mind. As for why a great part of these animals do not seem to act rationally, the blame is surely placed on a <term>bodily imbalance <note>original: "δυσκρασία" (dyscrasia); a "bad mixture" of the bodily humors or qualities.</note></term>, because they are not endowed with the proper instruments. Therefore, they do not have words, whether they are tame or wild, but they hold certain symbols and marks in place of words, by which signs they express their thoughts to one another. Thus, beasts "talk" but do not "speak," which the Greeks express more significantly: <term>they chatter, but do not declare <note>original: "λαλοῦσι μὲν, οὐ φράζουסי δὲ"; a distinction between making sounds (lalein) and structured, meaningful speech (phrazein).</note></term>. I cite the volumes of *Plutarch* on the "Opinions of the Philosophers" as very good witnesses of all these things. Regarding the rest of this world, whether substances or accidents, there exist almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers: some have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as *Aristoteles*, *Theophrastus*, and almost all of your *Arabs* and *Moors*; others have written particularly about individual things, such as *Julius Pollux*, *Dioscorides*, *C. Pliny*, and those like them. Yet, every single one of the later scholars has taken up the heads of all these disciplines from the treasury of *Pythagoras's* philosophy like an heir, and has cultivated that inheritance with literary study, each adorning and extending it as much as he was able according to the particular excellence of his own talent. But why does it help to either...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...know or have opinions on all these things, if in this life they do not take away all our sorrow and torment, and in the next life, after the vacancy of evils, they do not add the most cumulative embrace of all the good things we have so studiously learned? What use is it, finally, that by knowing well we act poorly, and by acting poorly we can never be free from fear, and thus can enjoy no tranquil state of mind? What use is it, again, that by properly obeying warnings like beasts of burden we always execute orders, while otherwise in all
<margin>B</margin> things we are fools, dullards, simpletons, "mushrooms," slow-witted, and "bleary-eyed," differing in no way from a brute? Therefore, it seemed appropriate to *Pythagoras* to destine all philosophy toward the summit of longed-for beatitude and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the contemplation of the highest and divine things. He thought that such fruit, as if from a happy tree, would undoubtedly follow our untiring studies of philosophizing, if we—having first purged our soul—vehemently turn away from vices and
<margin>C</margin> diligently cultivate virtues. Thus, being conscious of no evil within ourselves, we may apply ourselves with a joyful mind and cheerful study to mathematical speculations. These stand for us as a middle ground between natural and divine things: for they are partly inseparable from matter, like natural things, and partly separated, like divine things. For a circle or a harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is nevertheless understood without matter; indeed, no concern is given to any matter when we treat any mathematical subject. Since, therefore, it would be difficult, if not 
<margin>D</margin> impossible, for our intellect to leap suddenly from natural to supernatural things, and from the entirely material to the inwardly immaterial, *Pythagoras* wished to place before his disciples certain things in the middle which they could comprehend both by sense in some way and by intellect. For this reason, he named the demonstrations of these things <term>lessons <note>original: "μαθήματα" (mathemata)</note></term> or <term>learning <note>original: "μάθησις" (mathesis)</note></term>, that is, "disciplines." The book he composed about them he titled *On Erudition* or *On Instructions*, as if suited for youths and
<margin>E</margin> boys, for whose sake he also chose the name <term>educational <note>original: "παιδευτικόν" (paideutikon)</note></term>. In this, he explained everything that could be said about numbers, figures, and harmonies. From there, as if from one illustrious spring, four very clear streams flowed forth, which we call the four liberal faculties of the arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy. Indeed, counting Astronomy among natural things for the most part, he gathered it into the book he called *The Physical*, because it consists in the motion of bodies. But since,
<margin>F</margin> among so many most learned men of our age, there is such a broad expedition concerning those arts—so much so that each of those things creates a singular faculty, and each faculty leads its own class—I shall commit each one to its own teachers. And because it is now late in the night, and our dinner preparations are present, I shall make an end of speaking, I who have dared so immodestly to beat upon your most tolerant ears with so many words. Then *Marranus* said: "I swear by the gods above, you have filled me with such pleasure by speaking that
<margin>G</margin> no Muse is more pleasing to me; and now, having forgotten dinner, I have redirected almost all my hunger toward a craving for your teaching. Although I see the innkeeper is concerned about the magnificence and expense of the feast, I would nevertheless like you to explain the rest of *Pythagoras's* philosophy more intently..."

<summary>This page concludes the physical descriptions of the Pythagorean universe—touching on elements, animal intelligence, and the soul—before arguing that the ultimate goal of philosophy is spiritual beatitude, achieved through the "bridge" of the four mathematical liberal arts.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, cosmology, soul, animal reason, mathematics, Quadrivium, beatitude, Marranus, liberal arts</keywords>

It bridges the gap between how the universe is structured and how a person should live within it.</meta>

## BOOK TWO.

->**THE SECOND BOOK**<-

<margin>A</margin>...explain that part which pertains to virtues, morals, and the industry of the state, doing so as briefly as you can, while the builders set the table in the dining room for our dinner and prepare the rest. Therefore listen, Marianus: Philolaus said that Pythagoras wished for this entire section to be contained under the name of "urbanity" <note>original: "vrbanitatis"; here meaning civility or the refined conduct of a citizen.</note>. For this reason, he composed one volume among the others which he titled *Politikon*, that is, *Civil Matters*, or as the Latins translated it—perhaps not quite properly—*On the Republic*. He did this as if to explain not only what concerns the masses,
<margin>B</margin>but also the individual concerns of each person regarding their character and virtue. For a man who is set over a city, unless he be worthy to rule his own house and himself as well, is clearly chosen under a bad omen. *Ethics is therefore, it seems, both a portion and a principle of politics itself,* as Aristotle—the <term>Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note></term>—says in his book the *Magna Moralia*. Indeed, this civility consists of the whole number of virtues, whose parts are men endowed with virtue who have been admitted into a single shared way of life. For the company of the wicked is not to be considered a city, but rather a "conventicle" <note>A secret or unauthorized meeting, often used here to describe a gang or a lawless gathering.</note> where vices prevail, just as virtue does among the good. As the famous Theognis of Megara says in his book to Cyrnus: *You will learn right things from the righteous; but if you consort with the wicked, you will lose both yourself and your soul.*
<margin>C</margin>Setting aside, then, that contemplative wisdom which Pythagoras applied to nature and enclosed in his book on physics—concerning principles and the modes of causes—he taught how from the <term>Indefinite Monad <note>original: "Monade indefinita"; the 'One' or the primary unity in Pythagorean thought.</note></term>
<margin>D</margin>comes duality; from these come numbers; from numbers, points; from points, lines; from lines, plane figures; and from planes, solid figures. From these arise solid bodies and the sensible globe of the world with its orbits and the elements of mixed things—fire, air, water, and earth. Nearly all these things he wrapped in allegory (as is his custom). Then, finally, leaving aside the mathematical matters which he demonstrated in his book *Paideutikon* (that is, *On Instruction*), I think we should briefly review what he taught concerning morals. He wrote
<margin>E</margin>more diffusely on these matters in his *Politikon*, and more concisely, like a summary, in his *Golden Verses*. Since these are read publicly in our age, I shall now pursue only those "symbols" <note>Pythagorean "symbols" were short, cryptic proverbs or maxims meant to be decoded by students.</note> which were handed down without writing. He did this so that his disciples, relying on the strength of their memory, might grow accustomed to living by these spoken signs of good character, and daily affirm their professing of the philosophical order among themselves through these secret tokens. Not a few of these were brilliantly expressed by the illustrious Erasmus—a native of Rotterdam, a theologian by profession, easily the prince of the eloquent in our
<margin>F</margin>century, and a "sweet siren" of letters. He rightfully deserves the highest praise from all students of refined literature for his book of *Adages*, which will be admired by posterity. In the pursuit of virtues, Pythagoras attributed a great deal to habit, for it matters much to be accustomed to things from a tender age. From this, morals were called *ēthē* as if they were *ethē*—that is, "habits"—as the Stagirite often
<margin>G</margin>approves in his ethics. Our master himself commanded us to "choose the best way of life; for habit will render it pleasant." He organized the whole of moral philosophy into three goals: First, the worship of God and divine things. Second,

<column-break/>

the respect of each individual for themselves. Finally, duty toward others. Regarding the excellence of divine things, he taught first that nothing is pleasing to the powers above which does not come from a heart that is empty of vanity and entirely purified. Therefore, he gave this
<margin>Adages of Pythagoras.</margin>adage to be frequently on one's lips: *Do not pour libations to the gods from unpruned vines* <note>original: "μὴ πὰν ἀποσπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλων ἀτμήτων"</note>. He also established that sacrifices should be made of the purest scent; hence the saying: *Do not sacrifice without flour.* This Pythagorean sacrifice is very ancient, being made of wine and bread. Furthermore, things dedicated to God should not be transferred to human use; he therefore often warned, saying: *Abstain from the white cock.* He commanded true worshippers to persevere in humility with this symbol: *Sit down to worship* <note>original: "καθῆσθαι προσκυνήσοντας"</note>. As for the fact that one ought to look all around during worship (from which arose the saying, *Worship turning around*), this indicates prudence regarding divine prayers, lest it be rightfully thrown back at us: *You know not what you ask.* Furthermore, for ourselves, the rule of right living consists in human "decorum," which is the middle point between extremes—between abundance and deficiency. For in either extreme, a person is vicious, crippled, or "hundred-handed" <note>An allusion to the Hecatoncheires, monstrous giants; here meaning someone who is chaotic or over-reaching.</note>. Hence this symbol: *Do not step over the balance* <note>original: "Stateram ne transilias"</note>. It commands that moderation be applied to all studies and actions. Even more clearly, he said: *Set salt on the table*; this pertains directly to our affections, which are called passions. For salt is a mark of modesty, since it is admitted into human food in neither too much nor too little quantity; both the unsalted and the oversalted are rejected. Therefore, *Do not overstep the salt* was also a proverb. Furthermore, all the affections and passions within us are moved by some appearance of good or evil; we rejoice in good things and are saddened by present evils; likewise, we desire future goods and fear future evils. Therefore, joy and sorrow are the elements of the passions from which all motions of our souls arise. Their rectitude is called virtue; their crookedness, vice. Yet, things often appear to us as good which are actually evil, and conversely, good things seem not to be good. For as Seneca says, the truth and the "verisimilar" (the truth-like) differ greatly from one another. Thus, error easily occurs in the rule of the common people, of whom there is a great multitude. Pythagoras sought to turn his disciples away from this by symbolically warning: *Do not walk the public road*, that is, do not follow the errors of the masses. Yet, because he also wished this to be practiced: *Do not go outside the public road*, he had already hinted that one should speak as the many do; rather than fighting against what is established among all people. Hence the saying: *Do not speak against the sun*—that is, do not fall into danger—which is also advised by: *Decline the sharp sword.* This is achieved if you use honest shame in public, the sign of which is: *Do not urinate against the sun.* Now, having removed error concerning good and evil, he established that one must temper pleasure and sorrow, desire and fear. For this reason he said: *One must not give one's hand to laughter as much as to sadness.* For he commanded us to enjoy joys and pleasure according to "harmony"—that is, with a certain honest temperance, which he called the *lyre*. Hence this...

### THE CABALA

// The symbol **do not sing songs without a lyre** <note>original Greek: "ὠιδὰς μὴ ᾄδειν πρὸς λύραν"</note>: that is, one must use songs accompanied by the lyre; this was not a completely empty mystery. They always used this before the onset of sleep so that they would not be troubled by disturbed dreams. // If such dreams rushed in, he ordered those rising to shake out and roll up the bed coverings—that is, to gather the dreams into one and cast them away, lest the memory of them should cause distress. Concerning sorrow, he spoke thus: **Do not wear a tight ring**, by which he excluded all pain of the soul except for that regarding a committed sin; // for which reason he sang thus in his poems: *If you have done evil things, indeed, grieve.* Regarding other matters, Pythagoras commanded that **the heart must not be eaten**, which means: do not torment yourself. Furthermore, **when you have boiled over in anger, stir the mark of the pot in the ashes**, // which signifies that one must cool down from anger and that the memory of past evils must be removed. Concerning greed, he spoke in this way: **Do not nourish those things which have hooked claws**, and this is established against rapacious hands; indeed, do not be overly anxious even about daily food, // wherefore he says: **Do not sit upon a *choenix*** <note>A *choenix* was an ancient Greek dry measure, roughly a day's ration of grain.</note>: for the *choenix* is the daily food, which some call a "prebend" and others call "doles." Likewise, so that you might show no sign of avarice hidden in your soul, he gave this warning: // **Do not pick up what has fallen**, by which he forbade that anyone should be an overly passionate lover even of his own things. Concerning fear, he said: **Do not turn back when you have reached the boundaries**, by which symbol he not only prohibits trembling at death, but also whatever is in the fates, however much it may terrify. // For these are defined and determined boundaries which you will not be able to cross. Therefore, you fear in vain that which you cannot turn back from or avoid; indeed, to never shrink back from such a lot is a mark of praised fortitude and extraordinary magnanimity. We have enumerated the Pythagorean signs in a cursory manner—first those pertaining to divine matters, then those pertaining to individual men. // Now listen briefly to what manners one should use toward another. Since nothing is more desirable than friendship, the greatest care after the gods is incumbent upon us to acquire friends through virtue, as is found in the *Golden Verses*; yet one should not take just anyone in passing. For this reason, he himself said: **Do not extend your right hand to everyone.** // And when you have found a friend worthy of your inner chambers, you should make him a partner in all your affairs. For that reason, Pythagoras himself used this proverb before all others: **Friends have all things in common**, as Timaeus and Cicero attest. For a friend is another self, which makes friendship an **equality** <note>original Greek: "ἰσότης"</note>; that is, equality and the same soul. // However, men who are otherwise white on the inside but wear a black tail on the outside are by no means to be admitted into friendship (believe one who has experienced it), than whom the earth brings forth nothing more pestilential: like the begging, blue-and-white magpie with a tail blackening between its shoulder blades, they are hypocrites feigning and dissembling everything. // Therefore Pythagoras said **not to taste of those with black tails** <note>original Greek: "μὴ γεύεσθαι τῶν μελανουρῶν"</note>. That is, do not taste of those who have a black tail: these are the false brothers whom they call "the blackened ones," for **falsehood turns black in its extremities** <note>original Greek: "τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις μέρεσι μελαίνεται"</note>, as the grammarian Tryphon wrote; that is, "for the false turns black at the ends." As for others of lighter friendship who are of little use, whether relatives or friends, you should neither despise nor accept them beyond measure. This is what this allegory establishes: **The clippings of nails and hair**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**neither urinate upon nor stand upon.** Nor is it far-fetched that we are commanded to shrewdly avoid every ungrateful companion, and every whisperer and talkative person among us; hence that saying: **Let us not have swallows living with us.** Furthermore, a friend is to be received with deliberation, but once received, he is not easily cast away. Indeed, to break a friendship is inhuman, wherefore he said: **Do not break bread.**
<margin>B</margin>
Truly, you should wish to be a friend in such a way that you care for all the friend's affairs just as your own, whom you should please not with flattering words and the dye of speeches, but with the zeal for truth. For the seat of friendship is truth, not adulation, because of which he himself said: **Do not wipe the seat with oil.** And just as the love of the good must be won, so the wrath of the wicked must not be stirred up; he warns of this very thing: **Do not poke the fire with a sword.** Moreover, it is the duty of a good man to benefit all and harm no one. For if you approach either as the author of trouble or as a companion in imposing a burden, you are said not to have benefited, but rather to have weighed them down, so that you seem to have given place to vice.
<margin>C</margin>
But then you will deserve thanks for your virtue when you help one who is putting down a burden, so that he may be relieved of the weight more swiftly; this is what he meant by **helping to take down a burden, not helping to lay it on** <note>original Greek: "φορτίον συνκαθαιρεῖν μὴ δὲ συνιπιτιθέναι"</note>: that is, "to lay down a load together, but not to impose it together." It is no different than if he were to say: help toward this, that men may be relieved of trouble, not burdened. Indeed, a man unworthy and of perverse character, just as he should not be killed suddenly, so should he by no means be nurtured by you. Wherefore he forbade: **Do not put food into a chamber pot.**
<margin>D</margin>
Finally, we must lay aside that ferocity so that absolutely no one acts cruelly toward any innocent person. For Pythagoras also commanded this: **A gentle tree must not be violated or harmed.** From this comes that saying in the symbols: **Do not eat fish.** A fish is indeed an animal of such a kind that by its very nature it harms a human in no way. Now, as far as pertains to the State, this remains to be cited, which he himself said: **Do not pluck the crown**, signifying that the law must not be violated. And this likewise:
<margin>E</margin>
**Do not chop wood on the road.** By this we are warned that public matters, and those which belong to the community, are not to be disturbed. Truly, how much pride and the inflation of majesty, or the swelling of public honor, does not become a wise man; this secret symbol exhorts us: **Abstain from beans.** For magistrates were chosen by beans according to the custom of the ancients. Moreover, whoever is anxiously occupied in taking up the State desires an uncountably large evil. So that he might not offend the people by discouraging them, he preferred,
<margin>F</margin>
as a faithful teacher, to turn his disciples away from all ambition by a hidden mystery, so that they might always keep in memory, namely, **that one must not engage in politics** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι οὐ δεῖ πολιτεύεσθαι"</note>. There is no doubt that Hipparchus and Lysis, listeners of Pythagoras, held more of these precepts of the teacher in memory, which they, along with other schoolmates, preserved in their minds instead of books, and brought forth in the auditorium of Thebes. However, I have not seen all of them, and hurrying toward the end, I did not wish to touch upon everything. This one thing I wished, lest you be
<margin>G</margin>
ignorant and fail to commit to memory, that almost all Pythagorean philosophy is full of signs in words and coverings for things; and that method of teaching, as I said before, is believed to have been transferred by him from the Hebrews and Egyptians to the Greeks first.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philolaus and Marranus. # BOOK TWO
# 705

...carried. For the Egyptians were accustomed to communicate sacred matters among their priests through certain artificial characters, so that they might be kept secret from the common people; in this way, they would be admired for a longer time and grasped more attentively. For this reason, those Colossi, statues, altars, arches, and publicly engraved bronzes, prominent with the sacred letters of the Egyptians, stood out for all to see, but their hieroglyphs were understood only by the mystics and the initiated—just as Chaeremon, Horus, and many of the Egyptians have written. Thus, my Pythagoras did not think it was the part of a wise man to explain the lyre to an ass, or mysteries to those who would receive them as a sow hears a trumpet, a jackdaw hears a lute, or a beetle perceives perfumes. For this reason, he commanded silence upon his disciples, lest the secrets of divine things be laid open to the common crowd, as they are more easily apprehended by meditation than by speaking.

<margin>A</margin> Then Marranus said: "I beg you, my Philolaus, do not possess Pythagoras all for yourself, but allow him to be ours, not yours alone. Indeed, I seem to myself to be not at all deaf to your discourse, nor to have turned out unmindful of the Pythagorean way. So that I might commit to memory all the mysteries, metaphors, enigmas, maxims, apophthegms, allegories, symbols, marks, signs, and sacraments of so great a man—the first of all philosophers—which you have reviewed in passing and superficially in the manner of a catalog, I used the 'Tullian places' <note>A mnemonic system, often called the 'Method of Loci,' associated with Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> and the Art of the Rhetoricians while listening to you.

<margin>B</margin> Why don't you let me put it to the test? For you asserted, if I remember correctly, that Pythagoras encompassed all parts of philosophy in three volumes: the physical, the educational, and the political—that is, the natural, the disciplinary, and the moral. As he was dying (so I have heard elsewhere), he is said to have entrusted these to his daughter in his will, that she should not publish them even outside the family, or rather, not publish them at all.

<margin>C</margin> But while he lived, he demonstrated all that was contained therein plainly by living voice, using no covering, but only to those who were worthy and few in number—and especially the mathematical matters. To the rest, he spoke in parables. Therefore, speaking one way but thinking another (though always the same wise man), he imparted his doctrine to his followers through certain symbols as reminders, so that, in imitation of the ancients, one thing was said but another understanding was conveyed.

<margin>D</margin> From him, to start from the very beginning, the **Infinite** and the **One** are used for God; **numbers** for incorporeal things; **figures** for corporeal things; **harmony** for mixed things; **unpruned vines** for filth and sins; and **flour** for that which is purest in life. A **white rooster** is the mark of one dedicated to God. To **sit** designates humility. **Turning around** signifies prudence; and these pertain to divine things.

<margin>E</margin> The following look toward private matters and virtues: **The scale** is a symbol of justice. **Salt** denotes moderation. **The public road** represents the errors of the common people. **The sun** is placed in the position of the manifest and open. **A sharp sword** signifies dangers. **Urine** <note>original: lotium; used here to represent public indecency or shamelessness.</note> denotes shamelessness. **Song** denotes pleasure. **The lyre**, harmony. **Bed coverings**, insomnia. **A tight ring**, pain. **Eating the heart**, torment. **A pot**, the boiling over of anger. **Hooked claws**, robbery. **A *choenix*** <note>A dry measure for a day's grain ration.</note>, nourishment. **Falling things**, fortune. **Boundaries**, fate. These are the things of a man regarding himself.

<margin>F</margin> That which follows concerns the other person. The **right hand** <margin>G</margin> denotes friendship. A **black tail**, false brothers. **Nails and hair** are symbols of relatives. **Swallows** represent talkative people and those who leave ungratefully. **Bread** is the mystery of true friendship. **Oil** is a sign of flattery. **Fire**, of wrath. **A sword**,

<column-break/>

# 706

<margin>A</margin> of exacerbation. A **burden** suggests trouble. A **chamber pot** <note>original: matella</note> figures the unworthy man. A **mild tree**, a useful man. A **fish**, an innocent man. So much for private matters. Now for the republic. A **crown** is a sign of law and government. **Wood by the road**, the things of the community. A **bean** demonstrates ambition: everything is symbolic, everything is figured and allegorical. Unless you thought more could be found in the disciples of Pythagoras, I would certainly reduce all these things to the mathematical proportions of that man. For since one and two in the first progression become three, behold: the republic; <margin>B</margin> three times three become nine, behold: divine matters; and three times four are twelve, behold: private matters regarding another; and four times four are sixteen, behold: private matters regarding oneself. Therefore, the republic is a **triangle** <note>original: trigonus</note>, and the private matter is a **square** <note>original: tetragonus</note>; and just as sixteen is to twelve, so is twelve to nine, each in a **hemiolic** proportion—that is, **sesquialterate** <note>A 3:2 ratio, essential in both Pythagorean music theory and mathematics.</note>. See how teachable I am under your instruction, and how excellently I 'Pythagorize.' But what will you make of me?"

<margin>C</margin> Then Philolaus said: "Clearly a Pythagorean! For I now permit you to break the silence; you have had enough of discipleship if you understand all formal things intellectually."

To this Marranus replied: "I certainly do not know what this means."

"I will tell you," he said. "It is if you transfer everything that appears to you from the sense to the mind; that is, if you reject all corporeal passions and enjoy the contemplation of the mind. Now, for example, I would have you see a man standing far away from you in a very wide space of a field. You, being ignorant of what it is, will think it is either a field boundary stone or a tree trunk, for it has a straight figure and, in your opinion, unmoving matter.

<margin>D</margin> When you look closer, it will be thought to have grown into a small tree; having therefore rejected the idea of a masonry mass, you think it has the vegetative life of a plant. Then, if both of you approach each other with progressive motion, the form of the tree immediately vanishing, there occurs to you the image of some animal, while you are uncertain and doubting whether it be a griffin or a stork, or any other large bird, for it is two-legged.

<margin>E</margin> And now, having become closer, you see that it has no tail or wings, and it walks with its head erect; soon you leave behind all previous forms and think of a human form. Therefore, when you are once together, you are the first to say 'hello,' and he responds, speaking rationally; then no suspicion of Fauns or Satyrs or any other phantom arises in you, but you clearly recognize it to be a man, either a neighbor or a friend. When you ask him about his parents and relatives, as is usually done, he departs after satisfying your every question.

<margin>F</margin> And as he departs, you meditate alone with yourself that this man was born of parents, and the parents again from parents, and those themselves likewise from human seed, and that seed from a certain man; and finally, since nature rejects an infinite series, it will perhaps seem not at all impossible to assign one certain man who arose without human seed. So Aristotle wrote in the 12th book of the *Post-Naturalia* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note>, and he calls him **the perfect** <note>original Greek: τὸ τέλειον</note>. And since you accept that such a 'perfect man' is granted by <margin>G</margin> philosophers—whose body was not born as other men's—then you will discourse by reason to the soul of the man, always moving from the perfect to the more perfect and more noble. And by that same possibility, you will think it granted..."

# CABALAE
# 707, 708

...also a certain soul, not created in the same way as other souls, but perhaps one that co-created itself. This soul is not only perfect or more perfect than others, but is indeed the most perfect of all that have been, are, will be, or could ever be. You shall separate this soul—situated within the body of a mortal man—from that body, and you shall place it above all other separated souls (since it is the most noble) not in a physical "place," but in the most noble **dwelling**. Truly, the most noble mansion is that which is closest to God, a point which the **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> pursues at length in his book *To Alexander on the World*. We judge that this soul dwells on the "horizon" of the supreme world, which is called incomparable, where the union of God and creature exists. Just as on the horizon of eternity we place the **immovable mover** <note>A term for God as the first cause of motion in the universe</note> of the first movable sphere, in whom the corporeal and incorporeal worlds meet. By this path, you have intellectually transformed the human form into a "separated form," and have mentally led it to the supreme mansion of eternity. From there, it instills the highest **blessedness** into all angels and gracious souls, and all souls that bring salvation are regulated by this same soul as if by a standard. Indeed, regarding that most perfect body we mentioned before, I would not deny it in the **Pythagorean** <note>The followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed in the transmigration of souls and the harmony of the universe</note> manner. For he himself said that a man could become an **immortal God**, through which he clearly showed his opinion: that a single glory can glorify both parts of a man and make the whole man blessed. This happens when the greatest God either absorbs both parts and soaks them in his Divinity, or commits it to the soul to flow its brightness and glorification into the sublimated body, *as a yoke-mate and wing-mate, enrolled together and having struggled together* <note>original Greek: ὡς ὁμοζύγῳ καὶ ὁμοπτερύγῳ, σωμαπογραφέντι τε καὶ συναθλήσαντι</note>. This means: just as to a spouse and a companion of the road, counted together, and one who has fought the battle alongside. This dogma of Pythagoras sprouted again from **Orpheus** <note>A legendary Greek hero and musician, credited with mystical hymns</note>, as is found at the end of his *Hymn to Mercury*. Now you see hanging before your eyes the **Golden Chain of Homer** <note>A famous metaphor from the Iliad representing the connection between Heaven and Earth</note> in *Iliad* book 8, let down from heaven to our fragility on earth by Jove. By this chain, you may lift yourself into the sublime by divine help, both through action and through contemplation. For it is necessary first to live according to the mind, and finally to contemplate with the mind, and while contemplating, to ascend ardently. Since life comes before contemplation, and since it is fitting for both to be pure to attain that which nothing is purer than, life must certainly be purged first, and then contemplation must be illuminated. Therefore, what you have seen in the abstraction of things from things that we have brought forth, experience it in yourself. Return through reason to the mind, and unfold yourself from all external things, as the Emperor **Marcus Aurelius** <note>referred to here as M. Antoninus Imperator</note> commands: *simplify yourself* <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶσον σεαυτὸν</note>; that is, unfold yourself. For it is necessary for one migrating from this life into the other to have stripped off every garment and to depart naked—not only from all matter and bodily appendages, but also as a fugitive and free man from the whole mass of disturbances, affections, and passions. This was quite skillfully taught by **Lucian of Samosata** <note>A Syrian satirist and rhetorician</note> in his dialogue of *Charon and Mercury*, the most philosophical of all; if you have not read it, read it and imitate it. What else, I ask, is it that Pythagoras divided into three things which place us in the tracks of divine virtue, if not **purgation, illumination, and perfection**? For he says: *Work at these things, meditate on these things; these you must love; these...*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *...will set you in the tracks of divine virtue* <note>original Greek: τῶν ᾱ πόνες, ταῦτ’ ἐκμελέτα, τούτων χρὴ ἐρᾶν σέ, ταῦτα σὲ τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς εἰς ἰχνία θῆσει</note>. This means: Labor at these, meditate on these, it is necessary for you to love these, and these will place you in the tracks of divine virtue. **Hierocles** <note>A Neoplatonist commentator on the Pythagorean Golden Verses</note> wanted this to be understood equally regarding the powers of our rational soul applied to the love of divine things, and "these things," he says, "will make us like God." Let us consider the words of Pythagoras, for he set down three things which, joined together, allow us to arrive "anagogically" <note>Anagogical: Interpreting something in a way that leads the soul upward to spiritual matters</note> at the highest beatitude: the **Labor** of virtue which consists in action; the **Meditation** which is <margin>B</margin> nourished by many studies of the disciplines; and the **Love** which connects us to God as a necessary bond. The first (Labor) is provided abundantly by moral philosophy; the second (Meditation) by natural and mathematical philosophy; and the third (Love) by theology for those who are studious. Not one of these is sufficient by itself without the others, but it is necessary that these three come together. This is treated learnedly—as he does all things—by **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, the greatest investigator of the Pythagoreans, in his first book *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. He discusses it in these words, which I have chosen to include because of the heavy authority of his testimony: *Contemplation that makes us happy,* he says, <margin>C</margin> *is not an accumulation of words and a multitude of disciplines, as someone might think; nor does it consist in their number, nor does it receive its increase from the quantity of reasons and speeches. For if that were so, nothing would prevent those who gather every discipline from being happy* <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἔστιν... ἡ εὐδαιμονικὴ ἡμῖν θεωρία, λόγων καὶ μαθημάτων πλῆθος...</note>. And a little later, to omit the rest for the sake of brevity, he says: <margin>D</margin> *And we must depart from here (if indeed we intend to return to our truly own things) and cast away everything we have taken on from mortal nature, along with that very affection toward those things through which our descent happened. We must remember the blessed and eternal essence, and hasten to return to the incorporeal and impassive state, making two meditations: <margin>E</margin> one by which we may put aside everything material and mortal, and the other so that we may return or be sent back, ascending to them in a way opposite to how we descended here* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡμᾶς δ’ ἐπὶ ἐντεῦθεν... ἃ μὲν ὂν τὰ θνητῶς προσειλήφαμεν φύσεως, ἀποθέσθαι πάντα...</note>. And again, after a discourse that is not very long, <margin>F</margin> Porphyry orders us there to thoroughly segregate the soul from sense and imagination, and from every irrational condition that follows from them, and from passions of that kind—as far as the necessity of nature permits. We must rightly dispose and arrange part by part those things which pertain to the mind, preparing tranquility and peace from the war we have waged against irrationality. In this way, we may not only hear about <margin>G</margin> **intellect** and **intelligible things**, but also, according to our strength, be those who enjoy their contemplation—transformed into the incorporeal nature and living with the truth through the mind, no longer deceived by the relatives of bodies. It is necessary, therefore, to loosen many of our garments...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Marranus, Philolaus, and Simon. # BOOK THREE.

...we owe these garments, both this visible fleshy covering and those inner garments with which we are clothed, which are closest to our skins <note>Porphyry, a Neoplatonist philosopher, often wrote about the "garments" of the soul—the layers of materiality it acquires as it descends into the physical world.</note>. Thus far speaks **Porphyry**, who proceeds at much greater length in his discussion of this matter; all his points tend toward the idea that we might come to the enjoyment of intelligible and mental goodness through sensible things—by living honorably, contemplating purely, and loving divinely. He drew all these things from our **Pythagoras**, as if from some great river of all disciplines. 

"Indeed," Marranus said, "from the things you have recounted to me in order, I am clearly moved to the opinion that Pythagoras channeled his river from the infinite sea of the **Kabbalists** <note>The Jewish mystical tradition</note>—the successful navigation of which Simon promises us—into the fields of the Greeks, so that we might finally irrigate our own studies from it. Thus, both the discourses and the opinions of Simon regarding the Kabbalists and yours regarding the Pythagoreans seem to me to be equal. For what else does either a Kabbalist or Pythagoras intend, except to return the souls

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> of men to the Divine—that is, to promote them to perfect happiness? And what other path is there than their similar method of teaching? Both use an equal exercise through symbols and signs, adages and proverbs, through numbers and figures, and through letters, syllables, and words. 

Thus, the **Upsilon** <note>The Greek letter Y</note> of Pythagoras stands as a symbol of youth <note>Pythagoras used the letter Y to represent the fork in the road of life: the narrow path of virtue and the broad path of vice.</note>. Thus the first syllable of the *Iliad* <note>The syllable "Men" from *Menin* (wrath)</note> is the sign and mark for all the books of **Homer**, indicating how many there are in each work. Thus the word "white" signifies good, and "black" signifies evil. 

<margin>B</margin> In no different a way, our Simon has applied the first letter of the **Pentateuch** <note>The letter *Bet* (B), the first letter of Genesis</note> and the middle letter of the **Pentagrammaton** <note>In Reuchlin's Christian Kabbalah, this refers to the name of Jesus (YHSVH), where the letter *Shin* (S) is placed in the middle of the four-letter name of God (YHWH)</note> to other things; and he borrowed **Raham** <note>Hebrew for "mercy" or "womb"</note>, following the authority of **David Kimhi** <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator</note>, as an allegory for Abraham, and other things from the discourse held with us which we remember well enough. 

But hear with what a great shout the innkeeper himself calls us to the dining room: "Hey! To the feast!" 

And Philolaus said: "Indeed, I shall eat most willingly; let us go."

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN
## OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS,
### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH,
### BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial P within a square frame, filled with intertwining floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

AFTERWARDS, when they had departed, and the dim moon in turn suppressed the light, and the falling stars invited sleep, they both surrendered to slumber. They had first exchanged an exhortation to one another that they should not sleep past early morning, and so they arranged to be awakened. 

The next day, while they were dressing as was their custom, they meanwhile remembered the long and varied words of the innkeeper of that lodging. He had recounted to his guests at yesterday's feast that certain propositions and conclusions had been sent from the Roman Court to **Frankfurt** the previous day. These had been devised and fashioned by a certain **Astaroth** <note>Astaroth is the name of a high-ranking demon; Reuchlin uses it here as a biting pseudonym for one of his real-life inquisitorial opponents, likely Jacob Hoogstraeten or Ortuin Gratius</note> against the Apostolic prohibition and against **Johannes Reuchlin**. 

For more than five years now, Reuchlin has innocently suffered cruel persecutions with a brave and unbroken spirit because he argued that [Jewish] books should not be burned. These propositions had been posted at the doors of wisdom and the vestibules of temples in Rome, and soon thereafter were thrown into the mud, dung, and filth, and trampled there—and for just reasons. First, because such a crime had been attempted against the will of the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note> and without the knowledge of the most reverend judges, before whom that lawsuit (following the appeal of "Astaroth") has been pending in the Court for three years.

<column-break/>

Secondly, it was known to everyone that this writing teemed with the most obvious lies. For in the beginning, Astaroth promised that those conclusions would be disputed in the presence of the Pope; yet the Pope refused and certainly prohibited it. This was because, in many public sessions held in Rome this past summer, that case had already been fully disputed and discussed before the most learned lights of the world: prelates of the Catholic Church, archbishops, bishops, generals of the [religious] orders and their procurators, penitentiaries, and doctors—a great number of men most skilled in Theology and Law—who had decreed that **Capnion** <note>original: "Capnionem". Reuchlin's humanist nickname, a Greek translation of his German name Reuchlin (Rauch = smoke = Kapnos)</note> should be acquitted. 

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, he [Astaroth] insultingly called the ***Eye-Mirror*** <note>original: "Oculare speculum". This refers to Reuchlin's book *Augenspiegel*, a defense against the destruction of Hebrew literature</note> a source of scandals and errors, even though that book has been definitively admitted by an Apostolic sentence. 

Then also, he wrote concerning that same book that it had long ago been condemned to the fire by five Universities. These are certainly mere trifles—clear and transparent lies—because there is not, nor has there ever been, any University in the whole world that has condemned the *Eye-Mirror*. Rather, only certain individual "chapters" <note>Referring to specific groups or factions within the universities</note>, people of dizzying brains and irregular character, deceived by a previous error, acted in a conventicle and conspiratorial manner against the form of Law and justice against the *Eye-Mirror*.

<margin>A</margin> ...they have wasted away in their own malice, and, as they say, have concocted their own sentiments. Finally, they say that those who have rolled and re-rolled those trivial arguments in mud and filth are accustomed to asserting that in these same writings, nothing is contained from <term>alpha</term> to <term>omega</term> <note>From beginning to end</note> that was not previously justified, settled, and resolved in the public defense of **Johannes Reuchlin** <note>Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a pioneering German humanist and Hebraist who famously defended Jewish books against destruction by the Inquisition.</note> against his detractors from Cologne—a fact which would shine more brightly than the stars to any reader. Thus, the demon Astaroth always sings the same tune with his foul tongue. **Philolaus the Younger** and **Marranus** said that these were the sorts of tavern-talk <margin>B</margin> held with guests and fellow-diners, thinking it quite regrettable that in such a small and childish matter, men should fight so fiercely for so many years. And as soon as they were dressed, they hurried quickly to Simon's house as they had planned. And when they were conversing most amiably among themselves, as was their custom, Marranus began thus: "It is quite incredible, venerable Simon, and can scarcely be told, how much yesterday’s disputation delighted us. We were so impatient of delay while you were away that, without any <margin>C</margin> embarrassment, we have arrived before dawn, just as your Sabbath has passed." And he replied, "May your coming be prosperous, my best friends. Does the holiday not also hold you today, on the day you call the Day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note>?" Then Philolaus said, "We are a Pythagorean crowd; we treat every day as a festival when we contemplate with a cheerful mind. We do not consider the Sabbath to be anything other than leaving behind worldly business to ensure we are joined to the Divine. For so Pythagoras commanded us, according to **Laertius**: <term>you must be in harmony with the gods</term> <margin>D</margin> <note>original Greek: ξυνωδὸς δ᾽ εἴ τοῖς θεוῖς</note>. Except that you venerate the number seven, which is most suited to leisure; among us Pythagoreans, this number produces nothing and is named for **Minerva** <note>The virgin goddess; because 7 is not "born" from any number in the first decade by multiplication, nor does it "produce" any.</note>." Then Simon said, "One must listen to the Law, which distributes to each person their own portion and is like a soul to nature itself. For the Law wished to serve the strengths of our bodies, without which neither sound reason nor the light of the mind can be strongly preserved. Therefore, it established that a mediation of the lunar month—that is, a seventh part of life—should be at rest, in which nothing may be done except that which, if omitted, would cause irreparable harm. These are called, if I remember correctly, by the Romans 'stationary holidays,' common to the whole people and consecrated for performing divine rites. And just as that Neoptolemus in the works of **Ennius** does not allow one to philosophize always, so too there are those among your people who teach that one should not meditate on everything regarding God at all times or with everyone; rather, there is a 'when,' a 'for whom,' and a 'how much,' according to **Nazianzen** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father</note> in his work against the Eunomians, a man most learned and eloquent whom I once read in Greek when I lived in Achaia. In this way, that which is best will not become cheapened, and the infinite will be conceived finitely according to our measure. For six days, then, we work, but on every seventh day we rest corporally as much as the necessity of living permits, and mentally, after the purging of the will, we are intent upon divine things. Festively and with all tranquility, we praise sacred things, and then we serve God alone. This is what our Kabbalists mean when they say <margin>G</margin> **the Sabbath is the mystery of the living God** <note>original Hebrew: שבת הוא סוד אל חי</note>, as it appears in the second chapter of the **Gates of Light** <note>Porta Lucis, or Sha'are Orah, a central Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>. For it is a symbol of the higher world, that is, of the Jubilee of eternity, where all labor ceases; for which reason, by a dual way of speaking, it is ordained in the laws:

<column-break/>

# KABBALAH

<margin>A</margin> Deuteronomy 5: **Observe the Sabbath day**—which is to be understood regarding external actions according to the lower world. And Exodus 20: **Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy**—namely, by joining the powers of the soul to the mind for the advancement of contemplation according to the higher world. Do you recognize it now? That the Sabbath is the mark of divine service, by which the senses and reason are released from material occupations as much as human weakness allows, and the energy of the mind is bound to formal <margin>B</margin> occupations, to consider the things that are above. The Law wished to hint at this through these two words, **Observe and Remember** <note>original Hebrew: שמור וזכור (Shamor ve-Zakhor)</note>. Certain of our masters understand by these that the precept of the Sabbath is both affirmative and negative, saying 'Observe'—that is, 'beware' (which always signifies avoidance to them)—insofar as it restrains us from everything contrary to holiness. Others explain 'Observe' as 'guard,' so that they attribute guarding to the night and remembrance to the day. And this fits quite directly the <margin>C</margin> foundation of the Kabbalists, who think that this world is night, and the world to come—that is, the higher and intellectual world—is day. In this world we dwell as servants; in that world, we live as free men. To the former must be said: beware, guard, observe; to the latter: recall, record, remember. For this word **Remember** <note>original Hebrew: זכור (Zakhor)</note>, containing the affirmative precept, proceeds from love, while the word 'beware,' the negative precept, is fulfilled out of fear. Love belongs to children, and fear to servants; thus we consider one of all the commandments to be more noble than the other. **Moses of Gerona** <margin>D</margin> <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban, a 13th-century philosopher.</note> wrote at length in this vein in his commentary on Exodus. From these things, we accept that there are two Sabbaths, led by the testimony of scripture in Ezekiel 20: *I gave them my Sabbaths*. For the plural phrasing is satisfied by the number two—not only because God wished to reproach us generally using one word for every kind of holiday enumerated in the law, as **David Kimhi** <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> and the Talmudists think, but also so that we might always embrace with a mindful spirit this <margin>E</margin> 'best gift' and 'perfect gift' granted to us by God, which we previously called the Higher Jubilee. Concerning which, the *Gates of Light* says: **This is the supernal seventh which is called Jubilee** <note>original Hebrew: זו היא שביעית עליונה שנקראת יובל</note>. From here all remission, propitiation, and infusion of grace descends—which no one can sufficiently describe, since no eye has ever seen it, O God, besides You. For there is a **Sabbath of rest** <margin>F</margin> <note>original Hebrew: שבתון (Shabbaton)</note>, and a Sabbath of Sabbaths, to which all pure human souls, their stains cast aside, will at last return free to the inheritance of the fathers. They shall be sent into a possession truly our own and proper, which we acquired and retain through the soul of the **Messiah** from the tribe of Judah, the seventh from the patriarch Abraham, acting as an advocate on the horizon of the highest world according to the scripture: *And above the Jubilee he shall send out his roots* (Jeremiah 17). This is interpreted by that most excellent Kabbalist **Sopher Ama** in the book *Ha-Chayyim* <margin>G</margin> <note>The Book of Life, or The Hidden Things.</note>, on the nineteenth Psalm at the verse 'Day unto day': **Each man shall return to his family and to the inheritance of his fathers** <note>original Hebrew: אל איש אל משפחתו ואל יחלת אבותיו ישוב</note>. That is to say, they shall be exalted by his power to the place of his emanation, which is the river of God full of water.
