# BOOK THREE

...that they would ascend through the Angels to the place of their destination, which is the river of God filled with waters. These are the words of Rabbi Ama, and they refer to the waters which are above the heavens, in the intelligible world, <note>original Hebrew: *she-hu yemot ha-Mashiach ha-Kadosh*</note> **which is the days of the Holy Messiah**, where those who observe the Sabbath enjoy and are fed by the heritage of Jacob their father, as Isaiah said. Truly, that very thing is the Sabbath of the Kabbalists, to be sanctified at all times, in which we follow the will not of the flesh, but of the soul, and we meditate on divine things, intending nothing against God; this stands as a law for all nations, since it has blossomed from nature itself. For you, to whom the Law of Moses was not given, are not bound by the ceremonies of the Jews to keep holiday by a specific number, a point which Iarchas <note>A legendary Indian sage mentioned in the life of Apollonius of Tyana.</note> once rightly denied to Apollonius. Nor will I extort a specific number from you, but I ask for a quiet and tranquil mind, dedicated to God alone and to divine things, which consists mostly in <term>anagogical speculation</term> <note>Interpretation that leads the mind from literal or sensory things to higher, spiritual realities.</note>, such as this discussion between us which you have so greatly desired.

Then Marranus said: "It must certainly be carried out, for you have begun to treat Kabbalah so gracefully that you have now shown us more than clearly that we not only *can* discuss the highest matters today, but indeed we *ought* to. Do you not ask the same as I, Philolaus?" And he replied, "Certainly. Indeed, we have now entered the ship of this discipline, and soon, at the very prow, we feel that Kabbalah is nothing other than (to speak in the Pythagorean way) <term>symbolic theology</term>, in which not only letters and names are signs of things, but things themselves are signs of other things. By this we observe that almost all the philosophy of Pythagoras originated from the Kabbalists, and he likewise transferred this symbolic way of teaching to the Greeks; indeed, I myself, along with this companion of mine, vehemently beg you to proceed in speaking, or rather, in teaching."

Then Simon replied: "I would not claim so much arrogance for myself as to dare to teach you; nor would it be entirely safe in a matter so complex, not yet known to outsiders—especially to learned Romans—except for the very few things which in recent years **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** and our friend **Paulus Ricius** <note>Ricius (d. 1541) was a Jewish convert to Christianity and a physician to Emperor Maximilian I who translated Kabbalistic works into Latin.</note> published, which even to this day are not sufficiently understood by the Latins. For I fear that if I were to teach such foreign doctrines, the crowd of the envious might ignominiously shout me down—just as has happened to many good men before—who disapprove of everything they do not know, and in their zeal for malice easily twist words into a foreign sense against the speaker's will. These people Cicero calls 'calumniators'; I, if I may speak grammatically, shall call them 'the Calumniating,' since you yourselves are equally accustomed to calling my fellow theologians 'Pharisees.' But I openly testify to both of you that I wish to teach nothing, but rather to speak and recount if I have read anything among the Kabbalists that I think might not displease you. I shall therefore execute first what they intend as the ultimate goal: for they take care to spend all their study and their entire labor on this one purpose: that in this life they may obtain happiness, and in the future age, according to each one's capacity, perpetual beatitude. They trust that this can be done most of all by this means: if finally they might diligently and industriously grasp that which they feel to be best for the state of both worlds, the possession of which...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is a pleasant and perfect rest to those who have attained it. Indeed, even animals, however mute, are seen to yearn for their own happiness when they enjoy those things they think best for themselves, and reach those things which bring satiety to their desires. You see an ox grazing in some flowery and green meadow; he does not eat the whole thing, but by deliberate choice seeks now this herb, now that. Suddenly he easily leaves one behind, and another he passes over entirely, until he arrives at the nourishment suitable for his use, <margin>B</margin> in which he settles and rests. In this way, after traveling through the widest fields of the sciences and the meadows of contemplation adorned with every pleasantness, the Kabbalists taste many and various herbs, smelling of this or that, so that finally, having surveyed the entire grassy expanse, they may find that divine **Moly** <note>In Homer's Odyssey, Moly is a magical herb given by Hermes to Odysseus to protect him from Circe's magic.</note>. <margin>Moly.</margin> Although its root is black, yet in Homer's opinion the flower shines white, like milk; once it is found, they seem to have repelled all miseries, having attained the happy end of their appetite in this world. <margin>C</margin> The power of Moly is "difficult works," the root is "tranquillity of minds," and the flower is "the end of miseries"—unless all this is the true happiness of the present age, nothing else could even be believed to exist. Beatitude of the future, however, is the apprehension of the Supreme Good, above which there is no good, and from which all goodness comes, which is comprehended by no mere creature. But it is said to be apprehended when, according to each one's capacity, it is most nearly approached—just as if someone were to grasp the hem of a garment, he would be said to have <margin>D</margin> grasped the man wearing it.

Toward that good which is called God, we cannot plainly ascend due to the fragility of our condition, except by steps and ladders. These are indeed, as you are accustomed to say, like the **Homeric Chain** <note>The 'Aurea Catena' or Golden Chain in the Iliad, which connects heaven and earth, often interpreted by Neoplatonists as the hierarchy of being.</note>; but as we Jews say according to the divine oracles, they are certainly stretched out to the earth from the super-celestial regions in the likeness of the **ladder of Jacob** our father, like a certain rope or golden cord directed to us from heaven, like a visual line penetrating various <margin>E</margin> natures. For you see the sun, whose ray proceeds to our sight through the sphere of Venus, through the sphere of Mercury, through the sphere of the Moon, through the sphere of fire, through the sphere of air, and touches the opaque body of a concave mirror, and reflects from there to tinder or dry wool, which it vehemently ignites by its splendor even into ashes. The likeness of that same flame reaches our eyes and is received by the interior sensation; once received, it is judged by the <term>estimative faculty</term>, and finally it is processed by reason <margin>F</margin> by returning through the path by which the entire present operation progressed. Then this reason prudently shows us in what way the interior forms are carried through the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In medieval physiology, these were subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> to the imagination and the judgment of the estimation; also in what way external things are received by internal ones; and likewise how the species from the flame are directed in the transparent medium all the way to the pupil; by what path the flame arose from the burning of the concave mirror; and how the ray was able to ignite it; and finally, in what way the splendor is <margin>G</margin> continued through many media not natural to it; and again, by what proportion the air is to be compared to the fire, the fire to the sphere of the moon, and the remaining spheres to the rest. Our reason disputes each of these things through the journey of composition and resolution, walking back and forth, up and down...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Simon explains the intellectual and spiritual ascent of the soul. # KABBALAH

716

Thinking now of these things, now of those, reason does not cease its reasoning until—through phantasms <note>Mental images or impressions stored in the imagination.</note>, the image, intentions, splendor, illumination, and light—it returns to the luminaries, specifically to that sun of which we speak. First, it recognizes the bright image; then it judges it to belong to that specific flame and flax which the eyes had seen before. It realizes that its intention, led from the thing seen through the *transparent* <note>original Greek: διαφανὲς (*diaphanes*)</note> to the eye outside, has also been received within. It concludes that the flax is earthy, the splendor is airy, the flame is fiery, and the whiteness is an accidental quality clinging to the transparent medium, passing through what is bright and clear—whether that be air, fire, or something celestial—according to the energy and peculiar operation of its substantial form. Then, always adapting its meditations to ever nobler things and leaving matter behind, reason begins to debate with itself concerning *form*. It does not focus on "artificial" form (which hither does not belong and is more rightly called "figure" or "shape"), but only on natural or superior form.

Reason proceeds and finds that some forms are "particular" (existing here and now), while others are "universal" (existing always and everywhere). Of the particular forms, it sees that some exist within bodies to give them being, while other "co-assisting" forms provide the way in which they exist. Other forms are entirely separated from bodily things in their essence, power, and operation; because of this, they sometimes lose the name "form" and are instead called gods, angels, intelligences, blessed souls, or minds. As for the universal forms, these are no longer called forms, but are called *Ideas* or *Species* by those who have learned to speak with proper precision.

Indeed, reason ascends in this way for as long as it can. However, when it has been so exhausted by this discourse that it can no longer comprehend forms that are neither in nor present to bodies (since they are not subject to nature), it quickly calls upon the *Intellect* as a helper. Just as the intellect abstracts *this* matter from *this* form—such as the form of a donkey buried in a field, which nature then clothes with the form of grass flourishing from that carcass—so it attempts to abstract form simply from matter. This, however, it finds to be an arduous task full of labor. For it is easy to abstract matter from form, but to abstract form from matter is difficult. Therefore, that purified intellect raises itself to allow the *Mind* <note>Latin: *mens*, the highest faculty of the soul in this hierarchy.</note> an opportunity to influence it. Relying on the Mind's clarity, the intellect recognizes that some forms are entirely absolute from bodily things in essence, power, and operation. Because of this, they are enclosed by neither place nor time; one must truly judge them to be "above the heavens," where motion and time cease. 

From here, the intellect instructs our will to believe that there are certain beings beyond the heavens leading the "best life," which they enjoy for all eternity. There, a world begins that knows no second, a world most abundant in living lights and purest minds. The human soul can enter this world through powerful contemplation, surely much more effectively than the bodily eye can transcend the orb of the sun by sharp looking. And just as we do not behold the sun unless the sun looks back at us, so we cannot see the higher world unless it also sees us: for that world is entirely an "eye" itself, and brighter than the sun. Moreover, just as we comprehend the sun through solar light, so we comprehend divine things through di-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> -vine light. Since we, with our bodily sight, can grasp not only the orb of the sun but even the higher stars and the very summit of heaven, why should our mind—which in a certain way infinitely excels bodily power—not be able to look up and see the contents of the *archetypal world* <term>archetypal world</term> <note>The original "blueprint" or divine model of the universe in the mind of God.</note>, especially since the concave and convex of the highest heaven are joined with such proximity that the horizon of eternity seems not to differ at all from that convex surface? Believe me: the soul gazes upon the divine things of the other world mutually, and they <margin>B</margin> in turn gaze upon us, like two eyes directly opposite one another, moving reciprocally along a single line of sight.

Then Philolaus said: "Everything you teach, Simon, is Pythagorean and proper to the 'Italian philosophy' <note>The school of Pythagoras, who lived in southern Italy.</note> which Marranus and I discussed briefly yesterday."

To this, Simon replied: "I do not know what you might choose to call Pythagorean, but I know that what I have proposed so far is *Cabalistic*, handed down by the ancient Kabbalists and all <margin>C</margin> contained within the divine Law of the Hebrews. From this is born that enumeration of the **Fifty Gates of Intelligence**, about which the studies of the Kabbalists toil so greatly. These gates were received divinely by Moses, the servant of God, and he handed down the knowledge of them to us, his descendants, as they explain the condition of the universe. <margin>D</margin> **And our Masters have already said: Fifty gates of intelligence were created in the world, and all of them were delivered to Moses, except for one; as it is said: 'You have made him a little lower than the gods [or God].'** <note>original Hebrew: וכבר אמרו רבותינו חמשים שערי בינה נבראו בעולם וכלן נמסרו למשה חוץ מאחד שנא' ותחסרהו מעט מאלהים quoting Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 21b and Psalm 8:5.</note> 

Regarding this discourse of the Kabbalists, Ramban <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, or Nachmanides, a major 13th-century commentator.</note> said in his introduction to Genesis that everything of this kind delivered to Moses through the gates of intelligence is contained in the divine Law of the Jews—either in the literal sense or the allegorical, through words, or arithmetic calculations <note>Gematria</note>, or geometric figures of letters (whether written or transposed), or the consonances of harmony resulting from the <margin>E</margin> forms of the characters: their junctions, separations, twists, directions, defects, superabundance, smallness, greatness, crowning, closure, opening, and order. 

And through that Law, the most wise King Solomon also obtained from the Divine Spirit everything he knew. Of him it is written in the Book of Kings that God gave him wisdom and very much prudence, like the sand on the seashore; and the wisdom of Solomon grew beyond the wisdom of all <margin>F</margin> the Easterners and the Egyptians, and he was wiser than all men. He disputed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that comes out of the wall; and he discoursed on beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. 

Beyond this, the Gerundite <note>Another name for Nachmanides (Ramban), referring to his birthplace, Girona.</note> confirms our opinion and concludes thus: <margin>G</margin> **And he knew all this through the Law, and he found everything in it through its expositions, through its grammatical subtleties, through its letters, and through the strokes of its pen.** <note>original Hebrew: וכל זה ידע בתורה והכל מצא בה , ובפירושיה בדקדוקיה באותיותיה ובקוציה</note> This happened to him after he had grasped by reason the full extent of the forty-eight <note>Note: Though 50 gates are mentioned, Reuchlin here uses the Latin *duodequinquaginta* (48). Traditionally, 49 are accessible to man.</note> gates of intelligence, which open the knowledge of all creatures. For they are all...

<summary>Simon explains the soul's ascent from sensory perception to the "archetypal world" and identifies these teachings as Kabbalistic rather than merely Pythagorean. He introduces the "Fifty Gates of Intelligence" given to Moses and explains how King Solomon derived his legendary wisdom from the hidden structures of the Torah.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

...created things are universally distributed into five conditions. For they are either elements, elementated <note>Things composed of the elements, such as minerals or plants.</note>, souls, celestial bodies, or super-celestial incorporeal beings. Each of these perhaps receives ten considerations, the headings of which follow: the most general genera, special genera, general species, most special species, and individual things which further consist of matter and form (or things proportional to both), and are uniquely narrowed down by differences, properties, and accidents.
<margin>A</margin> These ten modes—of essences as well as intelligences—multiplied by five, open the **fifty gates** through which we enter into the secrets of the creatures, designated by those eminent marks in the works of the Six Days of Creation, and studiously discovered and received by the Kabbalists. Now, by this artifice, the enigmatic writing of the Count of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note>, proposed among his nine hundred conclusions, will be easily explained in that same writing.
For he said: *He who knows what the decad <note>The number ten.</note> is in*
<margin>B</margin> *formal arithmetic, and has known the nature of the first spherical number, shall know the secret of the fifty gates of intelligence, and of the great jubilee, and of the thousandth generation, and the kingdom of all ages.* Thus says Mirandola. Therefore, I would wish that a flat sphere or circle of ten numerical figures be drawn around a center, which should be five—for five is the middle of the decad—and in its circumference let the individual numbers of the denary calculation be described in detail. Let a diameter pass from the minimum to the maximum, that is, from one to nine; its division will create two semicircles. On the right side of the sphere,
<margin>C</margin> after the one and before the nine mentioned above, are placed two, three, four, and five. On the left side, after the one and before the nine, are placed five, six, seven, and eight. Let lines be drawn through the center from two to eight, from three to seven, from four to six, and from five to five. Then, if you subtract from each maximum only as much as it exceeds five (which is the center of the denary sphere), and add that same amount to its minimum (which falls short of five), there will always arise from both opposite numbers an equalized five and five. Therefore, when the points of the lines are compared to each other, every numerical line described contains five and five.
<margin>D</margin> Thus, the number five in the circle of the denary revolution is called **spherical** because, as you have seen, all numbers of the sphere are reduced to five. This is achieved through the five lines drawn in the sphere, each of which contains ten. Therefore, that spherical number multiplied by ten will produce the fifty—the gates of intelligence, or the years of the Jubilee—whose double proportion (which is the formality of arithmetic), multiplied into itself, will procreate the thousandth generation. If you do this perpetually, there will appear the infinity which is the kingdom of all ages, named by the Kabbalists **אין סוף** <note>original: *Ensoph*</note> *Infinite*, and it is the Deity itself without a garment. For God produced the rest "clothed in light as with a garment," so that there would be light from light; and then, with the light of His garment, He created the intelligible world of separate and invisible spirits,

<column-break/>

which the Kabbalists call "heaven," as you have often heard from me. In this manner, I understand the words of the most wise and great Rabbi Eliezer, who, when he proposed the question of where heaven was created from, answered: **מאור לבושו לקח**, that is, "He took from the light of His garment." These things are recounted by Moses Maimonides, the shower of the *Perplexed* <note>Maimonides' famous work, *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the second book, and by the younger Rabbi Joseph of Castile (or of Shalom) in the second volume of the *Nut Garden* <note>original: *Horti nucis*; referring to Joseph Gikatilla's *Ginnat Egoz*.</note>. Moses, the servant of God, ascended this far,
<margin>A</margin> so that he might know the light of His garment, and the Sabbath of Sabbaths, and the higher Jubilee, and the thousandth generation—all of which is nothing other than the superior world of Ideas, Angels, and blessed souls. Therefore, since he was unable to transcend the clothing of God and see His face, it is rightly said that he lacked one of the fifty gates of intelligence. Some of us think this was **תחיית** <note>original: *techiyat*</note>, that is, "vivification" <note>Resurrection or the quickening of life.</note>;
<margin>B</margin> however, I do not agree with them. I think it is rather the essence of God, which the symbol of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter holy name of God, YHWH.</note> indicates; it is the incomparable world, comprehensible by no proportion. For God said to Moses, "You cannot see my face." Or more truly: "And my faces shall not be seen, but I will call the name Tetragrammaton
<margin>C</margin> before you," (Exodus 33). The Kabbalists explain this as: **שאקרא לפניך השם הגדול שלא תוכל לראותו**, that is, "I will call before you that great name which you cannot see." For so Ramban Nahmani <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note> writes, by which it clearly appears that God is His own Tetragrammaton, and was not seen by Moses. This is indeed the principle of all the gates, above every creature before the beginning of creation, of which it is read: "God created heaven and earth." And the Chaldean translation of Onkelos sounds thus: "The Tetragrammaton created heaven and earth." God, the Tetragrammaton, therefore created all things—He whom I have heard you call the *Tetractys*. Moreover, Rabbi Eliezer said, as it stands in his chapters:
<margin>E</margin> **עד שלא נברא העולם היה הקב״ה ושמו בלבד**, that is, "Until the world was created, there was God and His name alone." Other Kabbalists also bring the testimony of Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides.</note> in chapter 29 of the second book of the *Perplexed* thus: **חכמה שלא היה שום דבר נמצא כלל אלא השם וחכמתו**, that is, "From the beginning, when there was no thing existing at all, there was nothing but the name of God and His wisdom." Therefore, before
<margin>F</margin> there was anything of the creatures, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalah, there was nothing but God, and His name Tetragrammaton, and His wisdom. Certainly our tradition contains only these three, which made up the first gate of creation that was by no means open to our master Moses. Therefore, it is said that he investigated the divine law only through forty-nine gates. Joshua, however, had one less again—namely, forty-eight. For so we have received in the book of the *Explanations of the Alphabet* by Rabbi Akiba: **ואחר מותו של משה נתעלם מיהושע שער אחד ונשארו מח שערים ושלמה נתקשה על אותו שער להחזירו ולא היה יכול**, that is, "And after the death of Moses, one gate was hidden from Joshua, and forty-eight gates remained, and Solomon
<margin>G</margin> labored over that gate to restore it, but he was not able." This is how the Kabbalists received it...

It discusses the limits of human knowledge, noting that even Moses and Solomon could not access the final gate—the hidden essence of the Tetragrammaton that existed before creation.</summary>

## KABBALAH

...of the catapults <note>Likely a metaphorical reference to spiritual power or "balistae" of the mind.</note>, since it is written of Moses in Deuteronomy 34: "There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses." Therefore, Joshua was not able to ascend as high as Moses had ascended; for this reason, it is asserted not without cause that he was one degree lower. Regarding Solomon, however, we read in Ecclesiastes 12 that he sought to find "words of delight," but the Kabbalists add that God commanded him: "Write correctly the words of truth." We say these truths were delivered and received by way of the Kabbalah, insofar as he would not dare to write anything except what he had received; and this was two degrees lower than the reception of Moses. 

After God, the second gate is the archetypal world, called the Heaven created by God—the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH.</note>—in wisdom, according to the Jerusalem Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note>. In place of <term>בראשית</term> <note>original: "Berashit," usually translated as "In the beginning."</note>, it places <term>בחכמא</term> <note>original: "be-Chokhmah," meaning "In wisdom."</note>, thereby confirming what we have said: that the God of the Tetragrammaton created the heaven in wisdom. This is the chamber of the Angels, about which Moses clearly explained nothing, lest it become cheapened to a crude and rustic people who might not understand it, or lest it provide an occasion for idolatry. 

But by "earth" is understood this visible world, which we assert is the third among the gates. By "the void," we shall think that matter is symbolically noted—the fourth gate of intelligence. By "the vacuum," that is, privation, we find the fifth. The sixth is the appetite for these things, the natural abyss. Next follow the remaining gates for the works of the six days. For already the signs of the four elements indicate four gates: for the pure element of fire (according to Moses the Egyptian <note>The philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204), author of the "Guide for the Perplexed."</note> in the twenty-sixth chapter of the second book of his *Guide for the Perplexed*) is called "darkness"; "spirit" is air; "water" is elementary moisture; "light" is substantial form; and "day" represents the accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as color or size.</note> which most help us to know what a thing is. "Night" represents occult properties; "Evening," the way of corruption; "Morning," the way of generation. "Day One"—which for a specific reason is not called the "first day" but "one day"—signifies the composite thing brought into the light. 

On the second day, the waters above the firmament are the universal species of things. The firmament is the horizon of eternity and time. The waters under the firmament are the natural influences of the celestial bodies. On the third day follows another heaven, visible and material—namely, the nineteenth gate. Then the earth, which is the boundary; then the seas which we sail; and so herbs, seeds, wood, and fruit. On the fourth day come the luminaries, signs, seasons, days, years, splendor, the sun, and the moon; within these planets, the others are included by the communication of heat and cold, dryness and moisture. Saturn, Mars, and Jupiter (with their Sun) heat and dry; Mercury and Venus (with their Moon) moisten and cool, even if these seven spheres are specifically distinguished. Furthermore, the remaining stars designate the thirty-ninth gate. Then on the fifth day come forth living souls, which is the life of mortals: in the waters, creeping things, whales, and fish; and generally winged things, and particularly birds. On the sixth day, the progressive animal on the earth, the terrestrial reptile, cattle, and beasts. Finally, the fiftieth gate, which is Man. These are the forty-nine modes of knowing the creatures, and the <term>שערי בינה</term> <note>original: "Sha'arei Binah," the Gates of Understanding.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The supreme gate is the one Creator of all, fully known by no man except the Messiah, because he himself is the light of God and the light of the nations; and therefore he both knows God, and God is known through him. For the Royal Prophet David exclaims to God: "Send out your light." Rabbi Solomon the Gaul <note>The famous commentator Rashi (1040–1105).</note> interprets this as: <term>המשיח שנדמה לאור שנ' ערכתי נר למשיחי</term> <note>original Hebrew: "The Messiah who is compared to light, as it is written: 'I have prepared a lamp for my Messiah.'"</note>. <margin>B</margin> And Isaiah says: "I have given you for a covenant of the people, for a light of the nations." And again: "The nations shall walk in your light." 

Aristotle wrote that which I judge to be true: that the vision of a thing is impossible without light, as we read in his book *On the Soul*: <term>οὐχ᾿ ὁρατὸν ἄνευ φωτός</term> <note>original Greek: "nothing is visible without light."</note>. Therefore, as we walk toward the inspection of all things, it is very helpful to bring light to our journey, so that we may choose a path on which we can proceed with mature providence without injury to our feet. 

<margin>C</margin> For this purpose, the Kabbalists received certain luminous paths and illustrious experiences, which they named <term>לב נתיבות החכמה</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Lamed-Bet Netivot ha-Chokhmah," the Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom.</note>, which Abraham mentions in the *Book of Creation* <note>The Sefer Yetzirah.</note>, which begins thus: <term>בשלשים ושתים נתיבות פלאות חכמה חקק יה יהוה צבאות שמו</term> <note>original Hebrew: "With thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom, Yah, the Lord of Hosts, engraved His name."</note>. <margin>D</margin> Upon which Rabbi Jacob Cohen wrote that by saying "wondrous," he signifies that these paths are secret, hidden, and occult, confirming his interpretation through the Targum. And the commentator Rabbi Isaac, in the same book *Yetzirah* <note>Creation</note>, testifies that the ancient wise men—men of heart, mild and upright, heavily practiced in the Kabbalah through the foundations of the Law—taught us that our ancestors and fathers walked through many ways to finally stand in these paths, which are called the "admirable paths of wisdom," delivered by the angel Zadkiel to our father Abraham in the tradition of the covenant. Thus he says. 

<margin>E</margin> I shall therefore recount them to you, my excellent listeners, if only you judge them worthy of your esteem. 
And Philolaus <note>A character in the dialogue.</note> said: "I beg you, continue." 
And Marranus said: "Indeed, I beseech you, weave the beginning of the discourse immediately." 
Then he said: "There are thirty-two paths," he said, "tending from the highest peak to the lowest base, to be noted in this way: the first is the <term>שכל מופלא</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Sekhel Mufla," Miraculous Intelligence.</note>, so called by some, but more correctly named the 'Occult Intelligence.' 

<margin>F</margin> For Rabbi Solomon the Gaul, in the book of Deuteronomy chapter 30, proves that this word <term>מופלא</term> <note>mufla</note> signifies <term>מכוסה</term> <note>hidden/covered</note> in the verse: 'For this commandment, which I command you today, is not above you [too difficult].' There he teaches it should be read as 'it is not hidden from you,' and this through the Chaldean translations cited there. It is the light giving the understanding of the preceding things without beginning, and is named the 'First Glory,' because no mere creature is able to approach its essence and truth."

<margin>G</margin> The second is the <term>שכל מקודש</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Sekhel Mekuddash," the Sanctifying Intelligence</note>; it is the foundation of eternal wisdom, which is called faith, and it is named the 'parent of faith,' because from its virtue, faith is infused.

The third is the <term>שכל שלם</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Sekhel Shalem," the Absolute (or Complete) Intelligence</note>; it is the intention of the principles, which did not root to lead back—

<meta>catchword: ad redu- [to lead back]</meta>

### THIRD BOOK.

<margin>A</margin> ...to lead back some things into the inner chambers of His majesty, which overflow from the front.

The Fourth <note>original: "שכל טהור" - Sechel Tahor</note>, that is, the **Pure Intelligence**, purifies the Kabbalistic numerations <note>The Sefirot, or the ten divine attributes/emanations.</note> and corrects their formation; it arranges their boundaries and extremities so that they exist without being cut off or scattered.

The Fifth <note>original: "שכל מזהיר" - Sechel Mazhir</note>, that is, the **Radiant Intelligence**, is called the "second glory" by the Kabbalists.

The Sixth <note>original: "שכל מנהיג" - Sechel Manhig</note>, that is, the **Resplendent Intelligence**, sits upon the throne of splendor; it illuminates the brightness of the luminaries and pours its influence into the one who presides over surface and eminence.

The Seventh <note>original: "שכל מנהיג" - Sechel Manhig</note>, that is, the **Guiding Intelligence**, is the throne of glory itself; it perfects the truth of spiritual communications.

The Eighth <note>original: "שכל נשרש" - Sechel Nishrash</note>, that is, the **Rooted Intelligence**, is called the "fitting union"; it is the property of Prudence <note>The Sefirah of Binah.</note> itself, which flows from the higher Wisdom <note>The Sefirah of Chokhmah.</note>.

The Ninth <note>original: "שכל נצחי" - Sechel Nitzchi</note>, that is, the **Triumphant or Eternal Intelligence**, is called the paradise of delight prepared for the holy ones.

The Tenth <note>original: "שכל ההרגש" - Sechel ha-Hergash</note>, that is, the **Dispositive Intelligence**, prepares the holy ones in faith so that they may be clothed in the Holy Spirit; this is what is called <term>Thiphereth</term> <note>original: "תפארת" - meaning Beauty or Harmony.</note> in the state of the heavenly beings.

The Eleventh <note>original: "שכל בהיר" - Sechel Bahir</note>, that is, the **Intelligence of Brightness**, is the very form of magnificence called <term>Chazit</term> <note>original: "חזית" - meaning Vision or Outlook.</note>, because from it arises the vision for the prophets who see visions.

The Twelfth <note>original: "שכל קבוע" - Sechel Kavu'a</note>, that is, the **Fixed Intelligence**, is a mark of extraordinary rapture, from which spiritual virtues flow like an outpouring from one to another, according to the energy of the first influencer.

The Thirteenth <note>original: "שכל נסתר" - Sechel Nistar</note>, that is, the **Hidden Intelligence**, illuminates only the powers of those intellects who, through the meditation of faith, see by believing.

The Fourteenth <note>original: "שכל מאיר" - Sechel Me'ir</note>, that is, the **Illuminating Intelligence**, which is the Angel <term>Hasmal</term> <note>original: "חשמל" - The 'glowing metal' or 'amber' seen in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 1:4).</note> of Ezekiel; it is like the appearance of amber, the teacher of secrets, of the living creatures of the sanctuary, and of their intentions.

The Fifteenth <note>original: "שכל מצוחצח" - Sechel Metzuchtzach</note>, that is, the **Refined Intelligence**, arranges the order by which access is granted through the steps of ascension.

The Sixteenth <note>original: "שכל נאמן" - Sechel Ne'eman</note>, that is, the **Faithful Intelligence**, through which the graced virtues are increased according to the lives of those in whom they dwell.

The Seventeenth <note>original: "שכל נסיון" - Sechel Nisayon</note>, that is, the **Probatory Intelligence**, is the trial and testing that comes before, in which the gift of the Blessed God toward all His holy ones resides.

The Eighteenth <note>original: "שכל קיום" - Sechel Kiyum</note>, that is, the **Confirming Intelligence**, is the power that restores the Kabbalistic numerations if anything is lacking in them, by clothing them in the Spirit of His holiness.

The Nineteenth <note>original: "שכל הרצון" - Sechel ha-Ratzon</note>, that is, the **Intelligence of the Will**, provides for all created things; through it, the Kabbalists know the truth of the higher wisdom.

<margin>B</margin> The Twentieth <note>original: "שכל מעמיד" - Sechel Ma'amid</note>, that is, the **Establishing Intelligence**, makes creation itself stand in the "pure darkness." And the Masters of the Kabbalah say that it is darkness according to the verse: "Darkness is round about Him."

The Twenty-first <note>original: "שכל מחודש" - Sechel Mechudash</note>, that is, the **Renewing**

<column-break/>

**Intelligence**, through which all created things in this world are repaired and made new.

The Twenty-second <note>original: "שכל בית השפע" - Sechel Beit ha-Shefa</note>, that is, the **Intelligence of the House of Abundance**; from the midst of its outpouring are drawn the secret and the hidden thing, which dwell in its shadow and cling to the study of bringing things forth and the diligence that promotes one to the heights.

The Twenty-third <note>original: "שכל הפעולות" - Sechel ha-Pe'ulot</note>, that is, the **Intelligence of Activities**, is the collection and universality of spiritual operations, so called because of the influence that is gathered in it from the source of the higher sea and the sublime glory.

The Twenty-fourth <note>original: "שכל נבדל" - Sechel Nivdal</note>, that is, the **Mediating Intelligence**, by which the influence of graces is gathered; it pours abundance into all the pools or basins of blessings that it has claimed for itself.

<margin>C</margin> The Twenty-fifth <note>original: "שכל כללי" - Sechel Klali</note>, that is, the **Collective Intelligence**, by which astrologers, through the judgment of the stars, gather fated events and perfect their knowledge of them through their spheres and orbits.

The Twenty-sixth <note>original: "שכל נעבד" - Sechel Ne'evad</note>, that is, the **Assisting Intelligence**, runs to help all the operations of the planets and other heavenly influences.

The Twenty-seventh <note>original: "שכל תמידי" - Sechel Temidi</note>, that is, the **Perpetual Intelligence**, is continued daily through the path of the sun and the moon according to their conditions.

<margin>D</margin> The Twenty-eighth <note>original: "שכל מוגשם" - Sechel Mugsham</note>, that is, the **Corporeal Intelligence**, gives form to every body that is embodied beneath the orbits, and likewise to their magnitude.

The Twenty-ninth <note>original: "שכל החפץ המבוקש" - Sechel ha-Chefetz ha-Mevukash</note>, that is, the **Intelligence of the Desired Delight**, receives the divine outpouring so that it may participate in the watering of all created things.

The Thirtieth <note>original: "שכל מורגש" - Sechel Murgash</note>, that is, the **Sensing Intelligence**, which brings into being things under the supreme orbit, and all kinds of mixed things.

<margin>E</margin> The Thirty-first <note>original: "שכל דמיוני" - Sechel Dimyoni</note>, that is, the **Imaginary Intelligence**, by which all created figures and images are varied and altered according to the surfaces of things and their natures.

The Thirty-second <note>original: "שכל מוטבע" - Sechel Mutba</note>, that is, the **Natural Intelligence**, by which the nature of material things beneath the sphere of the moon is brought to its perfection.

<margin>F</margin> I have enclosed in this brief catalog, O men most desirous of foreign teachings, those things which our ancestors treated with much difficult study in many books regarding both the **Fifty Gates of Prudence** and the **Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom**. This is truly a matter worthy of a better teacher and certainly of much sweat; it has the greatest power to urge us to live almost always with the Angels in the contemplation of the highest and divine things. If we begin to be familiar with these, nothing will be difficult for us to say or do. The letters, which are their gift, bring about that familiarity.

<margin>G</margin> If we apply these letters to the **Ten Kabbalistic Numerations** <note>The Sefirot</note>, the number **Thirty-Two** immediately arises. This is written in the book <term>Iezira</term> <note>original: "Sefer Yetzirah" or Book of Formation.</note>: <term>Ten numerations of Belima, and twenty-two letters</term> <note>original: "עשר ספירות בלימה ועשרים ושתים אותיות"</note>. For this reason, not a few writers speak of both these ten properties worthy of silence...

# OF KABBALAH

...twenty-two letters make up this sum of paths, which I have arranged in this order according to my own custom, though others may not observe it in the same way. But truly, if we diligently apply that assembly of letters to the fifty gates, we shall discover from it the blessed series of seventy-two angels, by which the <term>Sem hamephoras</term> <note>original: "שם המפורש" — Shem HaMephorash, meaning 'The Explicit Name' or 'The Divided Name'. It refers to a 72-syllable name of God.</note>, that is, that great explanatory name of the supreme God, is said to consist. For when twenty-two is added to fifty, they produce 72. These are the mighty angels of the whole earth, through whom that Moses, the worker of miracles, is thought to have divided the sea with his hand until it was dry, because they themselves are the angels of division. As it is said: "And God divided the earth according to the number of his angels." For thus we read, among other things, in the *Book of the Gates of Justice* <note>The *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>, which Rabbi Joseph Ben Carnitol <note>Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a Spanish Kabbalist.</note>, a celebrated master in Kabbalah, wrote: "And all the nations remained delivered into the power of the seventy princes" <note>original Hebrew: "ו נשארו כל אומות מסורות ביד ע שרים" — referring to the seventy nations of the world, each ruled by a guardian angel.</note>. To these, Recanati <note>Menahem ben Benjamin Recanati, an early 14th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note>, a most skilled Kabbalist, in his commentary on Genesis 48, applies those seventy palm trees around the twelve springs which you know from scripture. Furthermore, it is certain that there were two columns there, of cloud and of fire, over which two angels were set in charge. Therefore, we shall not think it vain to believe that in such a cutting of the sea and the liberation of the children of Israel, there came to Moses' aid the seventy angels of the world and those two columnar ones for the ministry of salvation. This salvation comes to us clearly from the ineffable <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH, which was not spoken aloud.</note>, explained through the seventy-two names gathered from Holy Scripture in Exodus fourteen, from the verse "And the angel... taking himself up" <note>Exodus 14:19</note> until the end, where it is read, "And the waters were divided." These are surely for us sacred seals, stored in a mindful soul in this present age; by these symbols, the Angels, when called upon, bring help to men for the praise and glory of the ineffable God, about whom Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), the famous medieval commentator.</note> wrote in his exposition of the Talmud, by the testimony of the Gerundian <note>Nachmanides (Ramban), who was from Girona.</note>, at the beginning of Genesis. These, then, are the characters of the symbols, which I draw for you with my finger:

->VHV YLY SIT OLM MHS LLH AKA KHTh HZY ALD LAV<-
->HHE YZL MBH HRY HQM LAV KLY LVV PHL NLK YYN<-
->MLH HhV NThA HAA YRTh ShAH RYY AVM LKB VShR YhV<-
->LHh KVQ MND ANY HhAM RHhE YYZ HHH MYK VVL YLH<-
->SAL ARY ASshL MYH VHV DNY HhSh AMM NNA NYTh MBH<-
->PVY NMM YYL HRh MTzR VMB YHH ANV MhY DMB MNQ<-
->AYE HhBV RAH YBM HYY MVM<-
<note>These are the 72 three-letter names of God derived from Exodus 14:19-21. Each triplet is formed by taking one letter from each of the three verses in a specific order (forward, backward, forward).</note>

All these names flow from the property of Mercy, as the Kabbalists assert. Indeed, that one exists out of the ten numerations <note>The Sefirot.</note>, the tree of which I will show you, if the powers above are present and if you are ready to listen to me. "Indeed, we are most ready," they both say, "for this reason we have undertaken such great dangers of travel and spent so much at such great cost. But proceed," they say, "so that we may learn something of those angels, whose names have never been heard by me, Marrano, and I believe the same for you, Philolaus." "Certainly," he says, "just as those Angels have never even been seen by me, so their names are unknown to me; but we shall love you, best of men, if you proceed without ceasing." Then Simon says: "There were many Angels who converged for such a great and admirable work of Moses, when he divided the waters of the sea so that the Israelites passed through with dry feet—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> —that we can perceive from Holy Scripture itself, lest anyone think me a deceiver. For the divine words in that place are: "And the Angel of the Angels moved" <note>original Hebrew: "ויסע מלאך האלהים" — Vayissa Malach Ha-Elohim. Standard Bibles translate this as 'the angel of God'.</note>. Not as you pronounce it in Latin: "And the Angel of the Lord took himself up." For <term>Adonai</term> <note>The Hebrew word for 'Lord'.</note> is not placed here, which we interpret as Lord; but <term>Elohim</term> <note>A name for God often associated with judgment or power, but also used for 'angels' or 'judges'.</note>, which you likewise read translated daily as "Angels" in: "You have made him a little lower than the Angels," etc., and "In the sight of the Angels I will sing praise to you."

<margin>B</margin> Yet it is not written here simply as "Angel of *Elohim*," as it is frequently elsewhere; but memorably thus: "The Angel of *Ha-Elohim*," with the demonstrative article <note>The Hebrew prefix 'Ha-' meaning 'The'.</note> intervening. It is as if the sacred history wished to say: "By this Angel of the cloud preceding the camp, recognize that very many other Angels, the princes of the world, are also present here." The Talmud supports us in the *Mechilta* <note>A collection of midrashic interpretations on Exodus.</note>, where Rabbi Nathan sought the solution to this question from our Master Simeon Ben Jochai <note>The traditional author of the Zohar.</note>, my kinsman.

<margin>C</margin> "I ask," he said, "why is it written everywhere 'Angel of *Adonai*', but here 'Angel of *Ha-Elohim*'?" To which he responded: "The word *Elohim* is not used in every place except to signify a presiding officer or a prefect" <note>original Hebrew: "אין אלהים בכל מקום אלא דיין" — 'Elohim' always implies a judge or ruler.</note>. Therefore, that Angel is understood to have been present together with the seventy presiding officers of the provinces, and for that reason he is called <term>Mallach haelohim</term>, the Angel of those presidents or prefects. And there was another Angel of fire, the companion of those same presidents, so that by best right

<margin>D</margin> seventy-two are numbered, whose signs you have already seen described by me. If you wish—or rather because you wish (for I know you do)—I will teach you by what path they are drawn out from the sacred letters. Now take these three verses: *Vayissa*, *Vayavo*, *Vayet* <note>Exodus 14:19, 20, and 21.</note>. And in the manner of an upright column, write them down individually in the Kabbalistic fashion from right to left, so that the letters of each verse follow one another continuously from top to bottom. Then, place the first character of the first verse, which is named *Vau*.

<margin>E</margin> Next, take the last character of the second verse in a backward order, which is *He*. Then finally, return to the beginning of the third verse, which you will find is again *Vau*. And when you have joined the three characters in that order, the memorial of the first Angel will be born: *Vau*, *He*, *Vau* <note>VHV</note>. And of the second: *Yod*, *Lamed*, *Yod* <note>YLY</note>. And of the third: *Samech*, *Yod*, *Teth* <note>SIT</note>. So also for the remaining names, always by threes and threes. In the present way, with the three columns rightly erected as should be done, any explanatory sign of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> will be forged.

<margin>F</margin> Behold! Look, consider, contemplate well: is this not the height of joy, excelling every gladness of this age? To remember the holy gestures of God and the divine faces, which the Hebrews call <term>Malachim</term> <note>Angels (literally 'messengers').</note>, the Greeks *angeloi*, and the Latins *Deos* <note>Gods/Divine beings.</note>. To handle with mind and hands things so pure, so pious, so consecrated; to converse studiously with those brightest forms, whose splendor shines only upon the sharp-sighted eyes of noble minds. To participate in the banquets and conversations of the blessed spirits, who love us fraternally beyond

<margin>G</margin> what is common to all mortals—nay, they do not just care for us, they love us. The very walls seem to me to leap for joy and to congratulate us men that it has been brought about by God's goodness, that through certain seals and skillful characters of human weakness...

### BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin> May we be admitted into the joyful assemblies of the Angels according to the capacity of our own strength, so that we may rejoice and be glad with them with a peaceful heart. Let us cherish and venerate them, offering the honor due to such a sublime nature, and in turn, let us be loved, instructed, and guarded by them. Then Marranus spoke: "I see the characters indeed," he said, "but I do not hear the sounds of the names. Therefore, I do not know with what pronunciation the Angels should be invoked." To this, Simon replied: "Just as they are seen by the eyes, so they are heard by the ears; and just as they see us, so they hear those who call upon them."

<margin>B</margin> How this can be, I will say in two words: "In spirit and truth." <note>original Latin: "In spiritu & veritate"</note> Just as our minds have "tongues," so the Angels have "ears." And just as divine spirits speak with the tongues of Angels, so human spirits listen with the ears of their minds. Therefore, they do not impose names upon themselves out of a necessity to be publicly named or shouted for, but rather they provide memorial signs <note>original: "signacula memoriatiua" — symbols or marks used to trigger memory.</note> because they desire to be remembered by us. Do not think that all divine power lies hidden merely in the vocal sound.

<margin>C</margin> These symbols, therefore, demand a frequent memory of the Angels; the diligent remembrance of them leads us into a mutual love of God, and in turn, love leads back to remembrance. For we frequently remember those whom we love strongly, as it is said in the Proverb:

-> Lovers remember everything. <-
<note>original: "Meminerunt omnia amantes." A Latin proverb emphasizing that affection sharpens the memory.</note>

For this reason, God granted us the name <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce in Jewish tradition.</note>—not so that we might call Him by it, for it is ineffable and is rightly called by us *unutterable* <note>original Greek: "ἀνεκφῶνητον" (anekphoneton) — meaning that which cannot be spoken aloud.</note>, that is, not vocable. For what did the Creator answer 
<margin>D</margin> Moses when he asked, "What is your name?" He certainly said this: "I, H, V, H; this is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation." Therefore, the Tetragrammaton is a name for Eternity; but for the generations of man, it is only a memorial, because no human voice can compose a name that can equal the nature of divinity.

<margin>E</margin> We know the Angels by their works, which is why we pronounce names for them based on those same works of virtue. For example, from "medicine" we get **Raphael**; from "manliness" or "strength," **Gabriel**; and from "wonder and admiration," **Michael**, which is interpreted as "Who is so strong?" <note>Simon provides traditional etymologies: Raphael (God heals), Gabriel (Strength of God), Michael (Who is like God?).</note> As for their true names, since we are ignorant of their essence, the infirmity of our mortality is not able to find them, nor to impose them once found, except insofar as it is granted to us by divine revelation. Thus, from numbers and figures handed down by God, the most contemplative men are taught to form names for themselves according to the wills of the Angels, just as children are taught to compose words from letters—whether Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, or Egyptian. This is not because the voice to be uttered needs such letters, but for the sake of the memory of our weakness. These names are like "notations" <note>original: "notamina"</note> that stir our senses by figure or voice; in turn, the sense moves the imagination, the imagination moves the memory, memory moves reason, reason moves the intellect, intellect moves the mind, and the mind moves the Angel. Someone among your people, a famous philosopher named **Maximus of Tyre**, wrote something on this subject very elegantly in his eighth dissertation of the *Dissertations in Rome during his first stay*. <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἐν ῥώμῃ διαλέξεων τῆς πρώτης ἐπιδημίας"</note> From this, it becomes known to you by conjecture that it is enough if you read the three verses—previously resolved by me—in reverence

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and veneration of the seventy-two angels, in that order which the Holy Spirit dictated. Through your affection for them, you shall dwell in the most burning love and ecstatic adoration of the name of the most high God, commemorating bit by bit how the number seventy-two proceeds from the number of the Tetragrammaton by arithmetic proportion. In this way, seventy-two Angels are produced from the seal of the Creator by a certain divine outflow. Since every Hebrew letter 
<margin>B</margin> designates a specific number, seventy-two arises from *Iod*, *He*, *Vau*, *He* <note>The letters of the Tetragrammaton: י (Yod), ה (He), ו (Vav), ה (He).</note> in this manner: *Iod* denotes ten, *He* five, *Vau* six, and *He* again five. All of this is gathered together by the art of Arithmetic as follows: 

*   **Iod** is ten.
*   **Iod, He** is fifteen.
*   **Iod, He, Vau** is twenty-one.
*   **Iod, He, Vau, He** is twenty-six.

Now combine these individual sums: ten, fifteen, twenty-one, and twenty-six, and they result in seventy-two. Reflecting on these things, you will clearly understand that to invoke spirits, a spiritual voice is needed, not 
<margin>C</margin> shouting, like that of the priests of **Baal**, to whom the Prophet **Elijah** said in the Third Book of Kings, chapter 18: "Cry with a louder voice; perhaps your God is in an inn, or on a journey, or surely he sleeps and must be awakened." But if we use any prayer in our supplications, it is not done so that we may move God or the Angels by syllables or words—as if dealing with mortals—but so that we may stir our own powers into their fervor, and fix our confidence in them like an anchor. It is like sailors who, after casting a rope 
<margin>D</margin> or extending a cable to the shore, pull themselves toward the land, even though the land is immovable; by this effort, they draw themselves to the earth. By a similar logic, through sensible signs composed by any method, we seem to "pull" the invisible divinity to us, when in reality we, who are movable, pull ourselves toward the immovable divinity. Upon this secret foundation all the sacraments and rites of ceremonies stand. This is why we use signs, characters, and the voice; why we use hymns and songs; why we use the drum and the choir, strings, 
<margin>E</margin> cymbals, the organ, and other musical instruments of that kind. It is not to soften God as if He were a woman, nor so that the Angels might be captured by our flatteries and adulations; rather, it is so that by exulting in God and divine things, we may acknowledge the smallness of our condition, most humbly profess our subjection and obedience, and turn every human pleasure toward divine matters. Ultimately, by this means, we conceive an intense and burning love for the divinity, which—more than anything else—makes us 
<margin>F</margin> capable of all graces. For this reason, we stretch out our palms, expand our arms, bend our knees, and pray standing. We were also commanded to divide a three-year-old cow, a three-year-old goat, a turtle-dove, and a pigeon in the middle; we kill the ram caught by its horns in the thicket with a sword and burn it with fire; we mark the letter **Tau** <note>The mark mentioned in Ezekiel 9:4, often associated with the sign of the cross or salvation.</note> upon the doorposts of houses with blood; we look upon the **Brazen Serpent**; we fashion **Cherubim** and other images; we speak and vow composed words; we build a Sanctuary; 
<margin>G</margin> and we look with astonishment upon the **High Priest** clothed in such varied and wonderful adornment. All these things and the like are done for our own sakes: to move us, to incite us, to turn us away from what is base and toward what is invisible, and to increase our faith.

He provides the specific Gematria (mathematical derivation) showing how the 72 angels are rooted in the four-letter name of God (Tetragrammaton).</summary>

# KABBALAH

...that they might confirm our hope and transfer a true charity between us—which is most pleasing to God—into a love of divine things through a diligent <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν — a summing up or restoration of all things in a central point.</note>. All these are the teachings of the Kabbalists, who, as the third book of the *Guide for the Perplexed* by Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note> attests, say this:

> שכוונת העבודות ההם זכרון השם תמיד ויראותו
> ואהבתו ושמירת המצות כולן ושיאמין בשם ית׳
> רמה שהוא הכרחי לכל.
> <note>Translation of the Hebrew: "The intention of those rituals is the constant remembrance of the Name, the fear of Him, the love of Him, the keeping of all the commandments, and that one should believe in the Name, may He be blessed, which is necessary for everyone."</note>

<margin>A</margin> This means the intention of such ceremonies is the frequent memory of God, the fear of Him, the love of Him, and the observance of all the commandments, and that one should believe in the Most High God, which is a necessity for every person. To be sure, since we are oppressed by the heavy mass of the body, we greatly need things that stir us to awaken a slumbering soul—much like a noble horse, though weary from a long journey, stands tall with strength and pricks up its ears when the trumpet sounds; or like an elephant, sluggish with laziness, rises into boldness when shown fire. In the same way, our virtue, weakened by worldly matters, requires external and physical "incitements"—whether of voices or figures—so that the vigor of our soul may insist more robustly upon spiritual work, and our contemplation may be driven upward all the more sharply, the more we were previously struck with awe. 

<margin>B</margin> For this benefit, merciful Angels have often discovered and proposed to us mortals figures, characters, forms, and voices that are both unknown and wondrous. These do not signify anything according to the common use of language; rather, through the sheer wonder they provoke in our reason, they lead us into a constant investigation of intelligible things, and then into the veneration and love of those same things. 

<margin>D</margin> For they do not signify according to the institution or whim of man, but according to the pleasure of God. Hence, the Count of Mirandola <note>Pico della Mirandola</note>—the most learned man of your age and school—transmitted this to you when he said in his *900 Conclusions*: "Non-significant voices have more power in magic than significant ones." For any voice has power in magic insofar as it is formed by the voice of God, because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God. This is what Pico says. 

<margin>E</margin> Then Philolaus said: "Such names would move us men—who are sleepy and snoring—with a greater awakening if they moved more than one sense. I wish they would not only appear to our sight through figures and characters, but also strike our ears at the same time with an articulate voice. Therefore, I greatly desire, if possible, not only to see these things painted, but also to hear them spoken."

<margin>F</margin> Then Simon said: "In my opinion, those who need an external movement are to be thought quite sluggish and—if I may say so with your permission—quite dull. However, we are born such that one thing always affects one person more than another, and the same thing does not affect everyone equally." 

"I agree with you, most learned Simon, for you speak the truth," said Marranus. "Our people also affirm this: that Angels appear to men in different ways according to the condition and nature of the viewer. About this, Chrysostom writes extensively on Matthew, eventually writing these words concerning Joseph:

> κατ’ ὄναρ φαίνεται ὁ ἄγγελος, ἐκ διὰ τί μὴ φανερῶς, καθώς τοῖς ποιμέσιν καὶ τῷ Ζαχαρίᾳ καὶ τῇ παρθένῳ; σφόδρα πισὸς ἦν ὁ ἀνὴρ, καὶ οὐκ ἐδεῖτο τῆς ὄψεως ταύτης.
> <note>Translation of the Greek: "The angel appears in a dream; and why not clearly, as to the shepherds and to Zechariah and to the Virgin? The man was exceedingly faithful, and he did not need that vision."</note>

<margin>G</margin> That is to say: the Angel appears through a dream; and why not manifest, as he did to the shepherds, to Zechariah, and to the Virgin? That man was intensely faithful and did not need that [outward] vision."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> To which Simon replied: "And you are correct; the Kabbalists feel no differently. They say that the power of vision in Abraham was stronger than in Lot; therefore, men appeared to Abraham, but Angels appeared to Lot. But perhaps we shall speak of these things in another place. Now, as it pertains to our case, there is a great diversity among men, as you know. Some are grateful enough and perhaps content to have seen Angels in human form; others in the form of fire; others in the form of wind and air; <margin>B</margin> others in the form of a river and water; others in the form of birds; others in the form of gems, or minerals, or precious stones; others in the energy of prophecy; others in a certain spirit dwelling within them; others in the figure of letters and characters; others in the sound of a voice; and so on through the many types of visions found in Holy Scripture. 

But since these characters of the 70 names <note>A reference to the 72 names derived from Exodus 14:19-21, often rounded to 70 in some discussions.</note> will by no means seem to satisfy you, I will demonstrate the right path—not only in the characters already mentioned, but also in those to be mentioned hereafter—whereby an articulate word can be made from the shape of the letters so that it can be pronounced. 

<margin>C</margin> We have God Himself as the author of this art. For we read in Exodus 23: 'Behold, I send my Angel before you to guard you on the way, and to lead you into the place I have prepared. Be cautious in his presence, and hear his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not forgive your crimes, because my Name is in him.' By this we know that the name of an Angel, according to the best rite, <margin>D</margin> must sometimes encompass the name of God. 

Therefore the Kabbalah, when they could not pronounce the name of any Angel meaningfully, were accustomed to utter the whole thing at once with the help of some name of God which they joined to it. For just as they see these three characters—**רפא** (RPA) or **גברי** (GBRI) or **מיכ** (MIK)—usurped improperly to signify the name of an Angel unless the name of God, *El*, is added (as in Michael, Gabriel, Raphael), so they too, attempting to imitate Holy Scripture in other angelic names, <margin>E</margin> say Raziel, Jophiel, Zadkiel, Peliel, Malthiel, Uriel, and others in a similar manner. 

Indeed, just as the Romans called their Capitoline God 'Best and Greatest'—'Best' because of his benefits and 'Greatest' because of his power, according to Cicero’s testimony in his speech to the Priests for his house—so the nation of the Jews calls its God *Iah* because of His benefits, and *El* because of His power and virtue. For the Kabbalists, commenting on the word of King David when he says: 'If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, *Iah*, who could stand?' say: 

<margin>F</margin> **יה שהוא עולם הרחמים אדני שהוא עולם הדין** 
which means: *Iah* is the world of mercy; *Adonai* is the world of severity, as found in the eighth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>Sha'are Orah by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>. Regarding *El*, however, you read in Numbers 16: 'O *El*, the most strong God of the spirits of all flesh, will your anger rage against everyone because of one man’s sin?' 

Therefore, God is 'Best' to us because He is most merciful, and 'Greatest' because He is most strong; these two divine names, *Iah* and *El*, represent this. If you join either of these to each of the seventy-two names, <margin>G</margin> you will certainly make the word <term>oxytone</term> <note>accented on the last syllable</note> at the end. In this way, by always pronouncing them so that they become three-syllable words, and with the breathings written with this unique mark 'h' as a strong aspiration, just as...

they say: *There is no herb or plant below that does not have a star in the firmament that strikes it and says to it, "Grow."* They arrived at this opinion fortified by the Sacred Scriptures, as we read in Job, chapter 38: *Do you know the laws of the heavens, or can you set up their dominion or governor or executor upon the earth?* Therefore, do not let the great anxieties of the world or the cares of lower things—to which the above-named Angels are assigned by the Creator’s dispensation—hold you back from counting them also among the new choirs of the super-celestial hierarchies. Since an Angel represents "otherness," just as God represents "identity," and the first "otherness" is the number two <note>The binary</note>, we correctly believe that the number of Angels arises from the multiplication of the number two. Now, the cubic multiplication of the number two is done like this: two

### 730

<margin>A</margin> times two times two, and they will be eight, the first cube. If you distribute eight angels into nine choirs, there will be seventy-two, for nine times eight is seventy-two. Return now, if you wish, through the choirs to the cube, through the cube to your <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A Pythagorean symbol of ten points; here Reuchlin links it to the four letters of the Tetragrammaton.</note>, which we call the Tetragrammaton and the Romans call the "fourfoldness"; from that, return to the "two" representing the angelic nature, and from there to the "one," God the Best and Greatest. You will surely find that if we apply our study to the Angels, we are also joined to God through the Angels by the ineffable Tetragrammaton: *iod, he, vau, he* <note>YHWH</note>,
<margin>B</margin> in which the most noble nature of these Angels first shines forth. For if from those four letters יהוה you place *iod* four times, and descending, you place *he* three times, *vau* twice, and *he* once, the sum of seventy-two will soon arise for you—the explanation of the unutterable and incomprehensible name of God, to which all sacred names are referred. Of these names there is a vast abundance, yet each is a descriptive title; this name alone is God's own and appropriated, which is why it is called *Meyuchad* <note>original Hebrew: מְיֻחָד — the Unique or Singular Name.</note>. These
<margin>C</margin> seventy-two are called one symbolic name because their intention is to signify the one God, the Best and Greatest, though through many and various aspects of the Angels—just as we recognize a prince through his courtiers, or an emperor through his army. And indeed, the masters of the Cabala greatly venerate and cherish these, through which devoted men perform wonders—more wonderful than is lawful for me to speak. However, I will cite a most learned man as a witness in this matter: Recanati <note>Menahem Recanati, a 13th-14th century Kabbalist</note> in his commentary on Exodus 14. He affirms that these characters and letters are
<margin>D</margin> *flying letters above at the foundation of the spiritual Chariot <note>original Hebrew: הַמֶּרְכָּבָה — the Merkavah or Divine Chariot.</note>, and they are appointed as administrators of the spirit or prefects to perform every thing through them, and their operations are known to the Cabalists.* Thus far Rabbi Menahem Recanati. And according to Rabbi Akiba, they proceed from the throne of God's glory. But let no one, led by vain superstition, think that all things are granted to human mortality from heaven by the Angels,
<margin>E</margin> rather than all things being done by the majesty of God himself even *within* the Angels—as Nebuchadnezzar testifies in Aramaic in the book of Daniel: *And according to His will He acts in the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth.* For this reason, the Cabalists have received from the Book of Psalms pious prayers to be offered to God in seventy-two verses, each of which contains the name Tetragrammaton along with the name of an Angel
<margin>F</margin> from the seventy-two—with one exception, and not without reason, which points to the beginning of Genesis. They lift up their minds to God with these verses as much as possible, strongly ascending from Angel to Angel. And always, amid the praises of God, they stretch upward from one to another. The Angels help them in this, so that, having left behind worldly anxiety, they are carried toward God according to their capacity, just as a light feather is lifted to the high and heavenly places by the help of a thin breeze. Look and hear the prayer
<margin>G</margin> of the verses with the Tetragrammaton and the Angels; I will show you both with my finger and my voice as follows:
